title: The Israel Architecture
tagline: A library of the documented record, in reading order. Every volume ties each claim to its source.
note: The documented record, told in order, with every claim tied to its source. Tap a note number to see it, a name in a figure for its detail, or the + button for contents, bookmarks and notes.

books.title: The Baseline
books.subtitle: The Ground Before the Flag
books.intro:
This volume comes before the history, and its purpose is to clear the ground. Most readers arrive at the story of Israel and the Palestinians already carrying a map, a vocabulary and a set of claims, picked up in classrooms and places of worship, from news coverage, and in the comment threads where much of the argument now takes place. Some of those claims are accurate. Many attach a true fact to a conclusion it does not support. Some are false. The Baseline sorts them before the narrative begins, so that the volumes that follow can tell the history without stopping on every page to define a word or correct a premise.

It does three things. First, it sets out the facts that every later chapter assumes: where the lines run and who governs on each side of them, who the Palestinians are in law, who may become a citizen of Israel, and who lived on the land before either national movement existed. The map of the West Bank drawn by the Oslo II agreement of 1995 belongs here, and so does the Ottoman district of Jerusalem that answered directly to Constantinople from 1872.[cite:wiki_oslo_areas] [cite:wiki_mutasarrifate_jerusalem]

Second, it fixes the definitions. "Occupation," "apartheid" and "genocide" each have a meaning in international law, and different bodies, of very different standing, have applied them. "Semitic" is a linguist's term of 1781 for a family of languages; "antisemitism" names a hatred of Jews far older than the word.[cite:wiki_semitic_etymology] [cite:rs_ch01_ushmm_bloodlibel] Zionism is a political movement founded at Basel in 1897; Judaism is a religion and a set of lineages thousands of years old.[cite:basel_program] The volume keeps these apart because so much public argument depends on running them together.

Third, it examines the ways the story is told: in American textbooks, in historians' arguments over 1948, through state-funded messaging, and on the platforms that decide what stays posted. These channels are part of the record too, and they are held to the same standard as everything else, in both directions.

The volume has six chapters. Getting Your Bearings states the method and sets out the map, the population, the citizenship laws and the three legal words. The Land Before the State covers three thousand years in brief, Ottoman Palestine, the Jewish community before Zionism and the two peoples' histories on the land. Words and Names examines the name "Israel," the words "Semitic" and "antisemitism," the hatred itself, the flag, and the definitions now in contest. Peoples and Traditions describes the Jewish lineages, a thousand years of Jewish life in the Muslim world, the land's other communities, the line between Judaism and Zionism, Jewish dissent and the Christian argument over one verse of Genesis. Two Displacements tells the exodus of the Jews of the Arab world and tests its comparison with the Palestinian displacement of 1948. How the Story Is Told closes the volume.

The method is stated at the start and applied throughout. Each claim is presented as documented, reported, contested or unresolved; both sides' official records are used; advocacy is named as advocacy; and interpretive readings are labeled as readings. What the Baseline does not do is narrate. The sequence of events that led to the founding of the state, and the war of 1948, belong to the next volume. One question runs through every section here, and it is simple to ask and harder to answer: what does the record actually show, as distinct from the version most readers were handed?

chapters.label: Chapter 1
chapters.title: Getting Your Bearings
chapters.intro:
Every argument about Israel and the Palestinians uses a handful of terms before it uses any history: a map, a population, a passport and three legal words. This chapter fixes them first. The chapters that follow lean on them on nearly every page, and a great deal of public confusion begins with them rather than with the past. The chapter also states how this book weighs evidence, so that a reader can hold each later claim against a rule set out in advance.

It opens with [scene:sk_s00|the method]: four levels of evidence (documented, reported, contested and unresolved), both sides' official records, advocacy labeled as advocacy, and three questions for testing a viral claim. The map follows: Israel within the 1949 armistice lines, the West Bank as divided by the Oslo II agreement of 1995 into Areas A, B and C, Gaza, and East Jerusalem, annexed by Israel and declared part of its capital in a Basic Law of 1980, measures the Security Council declared null and void.[cite:wiki_oslo_areas] [cite:unsc478_text] Next comes the population: about 14.8 million Palestinians worldwide in 2024, living in four legal situations that run from Israeli citizenship to refugee registration, with the military government of 1949–1966 and the Nation-State Law of 2018 as two tests of what citizenship has meant.[cite:alquds_pcbs_refugees] [cite:jta_nsl_upheld] A section on citizenship reads the Law of Return of 5 July 1950, the Nationality Law of 1952 and the family-unification ban of 2003 from their own texts.[cite:rs_ch01_lor_text] [cite:rs_ch01_idi_citizenship] The chapter ends with occupation, apartheid and genocide: what each means in law, which bodies have applied each to Israel, among them the International Court of Justice in its advisory opinion of 19 July 2024, and Israel's rejection of every finding.[cite:icj_press_19jul24]

Nothing here settles a political question. The chapter's task is narrower: to make sure that when later chapters say "Area C," "a citizen" or "the court found," the reader knows exactly what is meant, and what is not.

sections.h: How This Book Weighs Evidence
sections.html:
A reader meeting this history for the first time has good reason to suspect that any account of it is someone's opinion dressed up as history. The suspicion is fair, and it deserves an answer before the history begins rather than after. The answer is not a promise of neutrality, which any author can make. It is a method, stated in advance, so that every claim in the chapters that follow can be held against it: what counts as evidence here, whose records are used, how advocacy is marked, who produced the work, and what happens when it is wrong.

Every factual claim in this book rests on one of four levels of evidence, and the prose says which one is in play. A documented claim rests on a primary record: a law, a court ruling, an official filing, a census, a signed document. A reported claim rests on a named news outlet or a named investigator, and the book names them, so that the reader knows whose account is being relied on. A contested claim is one on which credible sources disagree. There, both positions are set out with their evidence, and the dispute is left open rather than quietly settled in one side's favor. Finally, some questions are stated as unresolved, because the record does not settle them. How many of Gaza's dead were combatants is one such question, and later volumes treat it as open rather than pretending to an answer the evidence does not give. A fifth kind of passage is not evidence at all: where the book offers a symbolic or interpretive reading, it labels it as interpretation, and never presents it as a finding.

The levels matter because the same sentence can be true at one level and false at another. "A court found" and "a newspaper reported" and "critics argue" are three different claims, even when they concern the same event. Confusion in public argument about Israel and Palestine can come from sliding between them: a report repeated often enough comes to sound like a finding, and a finding that one side dislikes comes to sound like an accusation. Keeping the levels visible is the first defense against both slides.

The second principle concerns whose records are used. Where both sides keep official counts, both are used, and each for its own people. Israeli deaths are drawn from Israel's National Insurance Institute and Defense Ministry. Palestinian deaths are drawn from the Gaza Health Ministry, United Nations agencies and peer-reviewed studies. Court records and archives come from Israeli, Palestinian, American and international institutions alike. This is not a claim that every official source is equally reliable on every point; it is a rule that no side's records are excluded in advance, and that where they diverge the divergence is shown.

The third principle concerns advocacy. Organizations that argue a position are useful sources. They often gather material no one else does. But they are not neutral, and the reader should know when one is speaking. Groups on every side, among them UN Watch, IMPACT-se, Track AIPAC and the Washington Report (WRMEA), are identified as advocacy groups whenever they are cited. The label is not a verdict on their accuracy. It is information the reader needs to weigh what they say.

Who made this book is also part of the evidence. It is the work of Observe The System, an independent research project. No government, party, lobby or donor funds it or reviews it. When a source proves wrong, or has been misread, the claim is corrected and the change is noted. Every claim carries a citation that opens the source itself, so a reader who disagrees with a reading of a document can go to the document and judge.

Why should the record differ at all from what readers already learned? Not, for the most part, because they were told lies. Most people meet this history through textbooks, speeches and news headlines, and these are summaries. Summaries leave things out, and what they leave out shapes what remains. This book puts the underlying documents beside the summaries so that the two can be compared, section by section, in the boxes that open each one: what readers are commonly told, and what the record shows.

The same method applies to the claims that circulate outside textbooks, in the comment threads and viral posts where many readers now first meet this subject. Most of those claims are not pure invention. They take a true fact and attach to it a conclusion the fact does not support. Egypt built a wall. Rome renamed a province. Arafat was born in Cairo, which the record shows to be largely accurate, though some sources dispute it.[cite:w_arafat] Each detail can be checked, and each checks out, more or less. The trouble lies in what comes next. The birthplace of one leader, true or not, says nothing about the history of a people. The Roman renaming is real, but the name it imposed was centuries older than Rome's use of it, a point taken up in [scene:ah_s01|the section on the land's ancient names]. The pattern works because a verifiable detail creates trust, and the reader accepts the conclusion along with it. Anyone, on any side, can be fooled this way.

The remedy is to separate the fact from the conclusion and test each on its own. The method used throughout this book reduces to three questions.

The first question is whether the fact is true. The way to answer it is to find the primary source or a credible record, and often the answer is yes. The second is whether the fact proves the conclusion attached to it, and often it does not: a true fact can carry a false claim. The third is what has been left out, because the missing context usually decides the matter. A wall may exist and still have been built for reasons other than the one the post supplies. A province may have been renamed and still have carried a name older than the empire that renamed it. In each case the first answer is yes, the second is no, and the third explains why.

Claims tested this way receive one of four verdicts: true, partly true, false, or opinion. The last matters as much as the others. A statement of value, or of what someone ought to think, is not a fact that a record can confirm or refute, and calling it false would be as much an error as calling it true. Insults receive no verdict at all. Name-calling is not a claim; it is skipped, and the claims around it are checked. And the checking runs in every direction. The myths examined in this book are not one side's myths only. A claim that flatters Israel and a claim that flatters the Palestinians are held to the same test, and a false claim aimed at either people is treated the same way.

That last rule binds this book as well. The four levels of evidence, the use of both sides' records, the labeling of advocacy and the three questions apply to every claim, favorable or unfavorable to any side, and to the book's own conclusions as much as to anyone else's. What the method cannot do should be said plainly too. It cannot make a contested question uncontested, or supply a record that was never kept, or guarantee that every reading of every source is right. It can only show the reader where each claim stands and where its evidence lies. Where the evidence is strong, the prose says so. Where it is thin, disputed or absent, the prose says that, and the citation is there for the reader to check.

sections.h: The Map: Israel, the West Bank, Gaza and East Jerusalem
sections.html:
Most confusion about this conflict starts with geography. Four names recur through every volume of this book: Israel, the West Bank, Gaza and East Jerusalem. In everyday speech, and in a good deal of public argument, they are used as though they were one place under different names, or as though the differences among them were a technicality. They are not. Each is a specific territory with its own history since 1948, and each lives today under its own legal regime. When later chapters say "the West Bank," "Area C," "Gaza" or "East Jerusalem," they mean a particular piece of ground under a particular rule, and most of the conflict's arguments turn out to be arguments about where these lines run and who governs on either side of them.

The first line is the one from which the others are measured. Israel, in the sense used throughout this book, is the state within the 1949 armistice lines, the boundary commonly called the "Green Line." The West Bank is the territory east of that line. Jordan held it from 1948 to 1967, and Israel has occupied it since 1967. What "occupation" means in international law, and who has found what about it, is the subject of [scene:pr_s03|the section on the three contested legal words]; here the word describes the status the record assigns to the territory.

The internal map of the West Bank was drawn in 1995, by the interim agreement known as Oslo II. It divided the territory into three zones, as a temporary arrangement pending a final agreement.[cite:wiki_oslo_areas] Area A, about 18 percent of the West Bank, was placed under Palestinian Authority civil and security control. It contains the major cities: Ramallah, Bethlehem, Nablus, Jenin, Tulkarem, Qalqilya, Jericho and most of Hebron. Area B, about 22 percent, came under Palestinian civil control with joint security control. Area C, about 61 percent, remained under full Israeli control.[cite:anera_areas_abc] Areas A and B together hold some 2.8 million Palestinians.

The mechanism matters as much as the percentages. The accord divided authority by function, not only by territory: in Area A the Palestinian Authority held both civil and security powers; in Area B it held civil powers while security was shared; in Area C Israel held both. The zones were meant to be a stage, with the divisions transferred gradually to the Palestinians.[cite:wiki_oslo_areas] They never were. Since 2002 the Israeli army has entered Area A routinely, so that even the zone of fullest Palestinian control is not closed to Israeli forces. An arrangement written as transitional became, in practice, the lasting shape of the territory.

Area C is where the land is. Every Israeli settlement outside East Jerusalem lies within it. About 60 percent of Area C is designated as firing zones, military land, state land or nature reserves, and Palestinian building permits there are rarely granted.[cite:wiki_area_c] [cite:anera_areas_abc] The result is a territory in which the 2.8 million Palestinians of Areas A and B live in the two smaller zones, while all of the settlements outside East Jerusalem sit in the largest zone, under Israeli control. When later chapters discuss settlement growth or the prospects of a Palestinian state, the ground at stake is mostly Area C. In all, about 737,000 Israeli settlers live in East Jerusalem and the West Bank.

Gaza is a strip of land on the Mediterranean coast with a different history. Egypt held it from 1948 to 1967, and Israel occupied it from 1967. In 2005 Israel withdrew its settlers from Gaza but kept control of its borders, airspace and coast.[cite:jerusalemstory_area_a] [cite:minorityrights_palestine] The distinction between removing settlers and removing control runs through every later argument about Gaza's legal status, and the record supports both halves of it: the settlers left, and the borders, airspace and coast stayed under Israeli control.

East Jerusalem is the fourth place, and the one whose status is most directly disputed between Israeli and international law. Israel occupied it in 1967 and then annexed it, a step that has not been recognized internationally. Roughly 360,000 Palestinians live there.[cite:jerusalemstory_area_a] [cite:minorityrights_palestine]

How East Jerusalem's status came to be set in two contradictory ways is a story of three dates. A familiar claim holds that everyone recognizes Jerusalem as Israel's capital; its mirror image holds that no one should. Neither is what the record shows. In July 1980 the Knesset passed a Basic Law declaring "Jerusalem, complete and united," the capital of Israel. The law covered East Jerusalem, captured in 1967. In Israeli law, that is where the matter has stood since.

The international response came within weeks. On 20 August 1980 the United Nations Security Council adopted Resolution 478 by 14 votes to none, with the United States abstaining. The resolution censured the Israeli law "in the strongest terms," declared measures altering Jerusalem's status "null and void," and called on states that had diplomatic missions in the city to withdraw them.[cite:unsc478_text] [cite:un_photo_478] After Costa Rica and El Salvador moved their embassies out in 2006, no country kept one in Jerusalem.[cite:wiki_unsc478]

The change came from Washington. Following President Trump's announcement in December 2017, the United States opened its embassy in Jerusalem on 14 May 2018, the first embassy in the city since 2006.[cite:wiki_unsc478] Most countries still keep their embassies in Tel Aviv. Under the Oslo Accords, the city's final status was designated as a matter for negotiation between the parties.

The two positions, set side by side, are each accurately stated on their own terms. Israel holds that Jerusalem is its capital under its own law, and the talking point that Jerusalem is Israel's undivided capital describes that law correctly. The Security Council declared that law null and void, and most of the world does not recognize the annexation. Both facts are documented. What the record does not contain is a single legal answer accepted by both systems, and the Oslo framework, by leaving the city's final status to negotiation, put off that answer rather than giving it.

The same is true of the map as a whole. The divisions of 1995 were written as temporary, and the record shows that they have lasted three decades without the transfer they anticipated or the final agreement that was to replace them. What the permanent lines will be, if any are ever agreed, the record cannot say. What it can say is where the lines are now and who governs on each side of them. Who lives inside them, and under which of these regimes, is the subject of [scene:pr_s02|the next section].

sections.h: Who Are "the Palestinians"? One People, Several Legal Situations
sections.html:
When a sentence in this book, or in a newspaper, refers to "the Palestinians," it may mean any of several groups whose rights and daily lives differ sharply. A common picture has them all living in one place under one government. The record shows something else: one people spread across several territories and several legal systems, so that which laws apply to a given Palestinian depends on where that person was born and where he or she now lives. The map in the preceding section showed the lines; this section shows who lives on each side of them, and in what legal standing.

Begin with the total. The Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics estimated about 14.8 million Palestinians worldwide in 2024.[cite:alquds_pcbs_refugees] They fall into four legal situations, and beyond these lies a larger population of registered refugees.

The first situation is citizenship of Israel. Palestinian Arab citizens make up about a fifth of Israel's population. They vote, and they sit in the Knesset.[cite:jta_nsl_upheld] The Statistical Yearbook of Jerusalem, published by the Jerusalem Institute for Policy Research, gives the scale precisely. At the end of 2023 Israel's population was 9,699,200, of whom 7,631,800, or 78.7 percent, were counted as "Jews and others" and 2,067,300, or 21.3 percent, as Arabs.[cite:rs_ch01_jiis_pop] In 1967 the population was 2,776,300, of whom 392,700, or 14.1 percent, were Arabs.[cite:rs_ch01_jiis_pop] The table records population groups, not legal status, so it does not by itself say how many of those it counts as Arabs hold citizenship and how many hold residency only.

Citizenship has not meant one uniform standing over time, and two episodes, each told in full elsewhere in this library, show how its terms have been contested. The first came before Israel governed a single Palestinian in the West Bank or Gaza. From 1949 to 1966 most of Israel's Arab citizens lived under a military government: a separate administration that required permits to travel outside their localities, imposed curfews, and designated closed areas. It was a distinct legal regime for one category of citizens, and it was abolished in 1966.[cite:wiki_kafr_qasim_massacre] [cite:conversation_kafr_qasim_60] Its worst single event came on 29 October 1956, the eve of the Sinai War. Brigadier Issachar Shadmi moved up a dusk curfew on villages near the Jordanian border without adequate notice. When Major Shmuel Malinki asked how to treat villagers returning from work who did not know of it, Shadmi's answer, according to the court record, was that anyone who left his house would be shot. Two of the three units given the order disregarded it.[cite:wiki_kafr_qasim_massacre] The Border Police unit at Kafr Qasim, about a kilometer from the Green Line, did not. It killed 49 people returning home after a curfew they had not been told of: 19 men, 6 women and 23 children, a count that includes an unborn child.[cite:wiki_kafr_qasim_massacre] [cite:conversation_kafr_qasim_60]

The accounting afterward was documented in two directions at once. Eight officers and men were convicted in 1958, and all were released within a few years. Shadmi, tried separately, was fined one-hundredth of an Israeli lira, a sum Palestinian citizens remember as "Shadmi's penny." The same trial established a doctrine that the Israeli army still teaches: a soldier must refuse a "manifestly illegal" order, one over which "a black flag flies."[cite:conversation_kafr_qasim_60] [cite:wiki_kafr_qasim_massacre] The claim that Arab citizens have enjoyed equal civil rights since 1948 does not survive these eighteen years. The record also shows the regime's limits: the military government was abolished, the soldiers were convicted, and the principle of refusing an illegal order came out of the case. One reading of the period, made in [scene:mg_s01|the full account of the military government], holds that it was a template, a separate administrative regime for one population, alongside the absentee laws that kept its people from their property, that preceded the occupation of 1967 by eighteen years and was inherited by it. That is an argument about continuity, and the record of 1949–1966 is its evidence; whether the later regime was modeled on the earlier one is a question of interpretation rather than of documents.

The second episode is constitutional. On 19 July 2018 the Knesset passed Basic Law: Israel, the Nation-State of the Jewish People, by 62 votes to 55, with two abstentions.[cite:asianews_nsl_passed] Its eleven articles state that "the exercise of the right to national self-determination in the State of Israel is unique to the Jewish people." They make Hebrew the state's language and give Arabic "a special status," adding that this does not harm the standing Arabic held before the law. They declare the state open to Jewish immigration, and they state that "the development of Jewish settlement" is "a national value" that the state will encourage. The law contains no equality clause; a draft clause that would have permitted Jewish-only communities was dropped.[cite:jta_nsl_upheld] [cite:asianews_nsl_passed] Because Israel has no written constitution, its Basic Laws carry constitutional weight, which makes this text the closest thing Israel has to a defining clause on nationhood.

On 8 July 2021 the Supreme Court rejected the petitions against the law by 10 to 1. The majority held that it does not negate Israel's democratic character and that individual rights are protected by other laws. The lone dissenter was Justice George Karra, the court's only Arab member.[cite:jta_nsl_upheld] [cite:gktoday_nsl_upheld] The two readings of the law are both on the record. Its defenders say it merely enshrines what Israel already is, codifying the state's Jewish character. Its critics, among them Arab citizens' rights groups and some Jewish organizations, say it relegates Arab citizens, about a fifth of the population, to a lesser standing.[cite:christiancentury_nsl] [cite:jta_nsl_upheld] A familiar claim holds that Israel's founding commitment to equality is written into its constitution. The law that comes closest to a constitutional statement of who the state is for names one people and contains no equality clause; the court that upheld it located the protection of individual rights in other laws. The fuller story is told in [scene:nsl_s01|the account of the Nation-State Law].

The second situation is East Jerusalem. Roughly 360,000 Palestinians live in the part of the city Israel annexed after 1967, most of them holding Israeli residency rather than Israeli citizenship.[cite:minorityrights_palestine] They live under Israeli rule, but most without Israeli citizenship. The same yearbook shows how the city's population has changed since 1967. At the end of that year the city had 266,300 residents: 197,700, or 74.2 percent, counted as Jews and others, and 68,600, or 25.8 percent, as Arabs. At the end of 2022 the figures were 968,700, with 585,700 (60.5 percent) and 383,000 (39.5 percent). At the end of 2023 Jerusalem had 980,700 residents: 589,300, or 60.1 percent, Jews and others, and 391,400, or 39.9 percent, Arabs.[cite:rs_ch01_jiis_pop] Between the end of 1967 and the end of 2023, the Arab share of the city's population rose from about a quarter to about two-fifths.

The third situation is the West Bank, where about 3.4 million Palestinians lived in mid-2025. The Palestinian Authority governs them in Areas A and B, and the territory as a whole is under Israeli military rule. Israeli settlers in the same territory live under Israeli civil law.[cite:minorityrights_palestine] [cite:alquds_pcbs_refugees] Two populations thus live in the same territory under two legal systems.

The fourth situation is Gaza, home to about 2.1 million people in mid-2025. About two-thirds of them are refugees or their descendants.[cite:alquds_pcbs_refugees] [cite:minorityrights_palestine]

Beyond these four lies the largest single category. About 5.9 million Palestinians are registered with UNRWA, the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees. About 40 percent of them are in Jordan, and the others are in Lebanon, Syria, the West Bank and Gaza.[cite:alquds_pcbs_refugees] [cite:minorityrights_palestine] About 6.6 million Palestinians live in Arab countries overall. Registration as a refugee is a status in its own right, and it overlaps with the others: a registered refugee may live in Gaza or the West Bank, under one of the regimes above, or in Jordan, Lebanon or Syria.

These differences are not only descriptive. Say that Palestinians vote and sit in the Knesset, and the record shows it of citizens of Israel, not of residents of East Jerusalem, who mostly hold residency rather than citizenship. Say that they live under Israeli military rule, and the record shows it of the West Bank, not of Israel's Arab citizens since 1966. A refugee in Jordan, a resident of Gaza, a villager in the West Bank, a resident of East Jerusalem and an Arab citizen of Israel share a national identity; they do not share a legal status. That is why so much of the legal argument over Israel's conduct, including the argument over whether its policies amount to apartheid, turns on these distinctions. What courts, United Nations bodies, human rights organizations and governments have actually found on that question, and Israel's rejection of those findings, is the subject of [scene:pr_s03|the section on the contested legal words]. This section leaves the finding there.

Some of what a reader would want to know next is not in these figures. The population tables count groups, not citizenship, so they do not say exactly how many Arabs in Israel are citizens and how many are residents. Whether a Palestinian refugee, or the Palestinian spouse of an Arab citizen, can become a citizen of Israel is a question of Israel's citizenship laws, taken up in the next section. And the numbers themselves are estimates from different bodies at different dates, from 2023 to mid-2025; they describe the shape of the population, and they should not be added together as though they were a single count.

sections.h: Who May Become a Citizen: Return, Residence and the Marriage Ban
sections.html:
Arguments about Israel's character often come down to a question that can be answered from statute: who may become a citizen, and on what terms? Two laws passed in the state's first four years set the answer. One opened the door to every Jew in the world. The other decided which of the Arabs who had remained inside the new state in 1948 would be counted as its citizens. Half a century later a third measure, presented as temporary, closed a route by which Palestinians from the occupied territories could join spouses who held Israeli citizenship. Each of the three is read in two ways. Defenders call the first a law of refuge and the third a security measure; critics call the first discriminatory and the third demographic. The texts themselves, and the numbers that came with them, show what each law did and where the dispute begins.

The Law of Return, 1950. The Knesset passed the Law of Return on 5 July 1950. Its first section reads: "Every Jew has the right to come to this country as an oleh." The second section obliges the state to grant the immigrant's visa, with only three exceptions: the minister may refuse an applicant found to be acting against the Jewish people, or likely to endanger public health, or likely to endanger the security of the state.[cite:rs_ch01_lor_text] The structure matters. The law does not create a scheme of selection under which the state chooses whom to admit. It states a right held by the applicant, and it lists the narrow grounds on which an official may refuse.

Two amendments widened and then defined that right. On 23 August 1954 the Knesset added a fourth ground for refusal, a criminal past likely to endanger the public welfare, and moved the power to decide from the Minister of Immigration to the Minister of the Interior.[cite:rs_ch01_lor_text] The larger change came on 10 March 1970. Amendment No. 2 extended the law's rights to the child and the grandchild of a Jew, to the spouse of a Jew, and to the spouses of that child and grandchild. It excluded a person who had been a Jew and had voluntarily changed religion (Section 4A). For the first time the law also said who counted as a Jew: a person born of a Jewish mother, or converted to Judaism, and not a member of another religion (Section 4B).[cite:rs_ch01_lor_text] The two clauses pulled in different directions. The definition in 4B followed the religious line of descent through the mother. The grandchild clause in 4A reached well beyond it, to people with a single Jewish grandparent who were not Jews under that definition at all.

The effect of the grandchild clause showed up decades later. According to Christian Joppke and Zeev Rosenhek, people who were not Jews under the religious definition made up nearly 20% of immigrants in 1990–94, 45% in 1997 and 53% in 1998.[cite:rs_ch01_joppke_rosenhek] On these figures, by 1998 a majority of the law's immigrants were not Jews under the religious definition. The same study reports that 64% of Jewish Israelis surveyed at the time supported the Law of Return.[cite:rs_ch01_joppke_rosenhek]

The Nationality Law, 1952. A right to immigrate is not yet citizenship. That was settled by the Nationality Law, which came into force on 14 July 1952. It created two main routes. Citizenship by return went automatically to every oleh under the Law of Return. Citizenship by residence went to a former citizen of Mandate Palestine only if three conditions were all met: he had been registered as an inhabitant on 1 March 1952; he was an inhabitant on the day the law took effect; and he had been in Israel continuously from the establishment of the state, or had entered legally.[cite:rs_ch01_nationality_1952] A third route, naturalization, was open to others on conditions that included three years' residence out of the previous five, a right to permanent residence, some knowledge of Hebrew and renunciation of any prior nationality.[cite:rs_ch01_nationality_1952]

The residence route was the one that decided the citizenship of Arabs who remained. Its conditions were written around dates and registers. A person who had stayed put throughout, and whose name was on the register by March 1952, qualified. A person who was off the register, or who had left during the fighting and come back without legal entry, did not qualify by that route, whatever his family's history in the place. The scale of what was at stake appears in Joppke and Rosenhek's figures: of the 700,000–900,000 Palestinians they count, about 170,000 remained after 1948–49.[cite:rs_ch01_joppke_rosenhek] Those who were outside the state when the law took effect had no path through the residence clause. The property they left behind was governed by a separate statute, told in the next volume: [scene:ap_s01|the Absentees' Property Law].

The contrast between the two routes can be stated plainly from the texts.

The demographic setting explains why the state's founders gave immigration such weight. At the 1948 census, 65% of Israel's Jewish population had been born abroad, and from 1948 to 1995 net migration supplied nearly half of Jewish population growth.[cite:rs_ch01_joppke_rosenhek] Immigration was not a side policy of the new state. It was one of the means by which the state's population was built.

Refuge law or discriminatory law? The dispute over the Law of Return turns on whom it admits and whom it does not. The strongest form of the defense was put by Alex Stein in 2013: the law restores Jewish access to a homeland lost since 70 CE, and it provides a refuge, because states with non-Jewish majorities did not reliably protect their Jews.[cite:rs_ch01_dailybeast_lor] On that reading the law is a response to a documented history of persecution, and its preference for Jews is its purpose, not a flaw.

The strongest form of the criticism starts from the same text and asks who is left out. Palestinian refugees and their descendants cannot return, while any Jew, anywhere, may immigrate. Critics, including Palestinian advocates, make that point, as Stein's article itself records.[cite:rs_ch01_dailybeast_lor] Adalah, the Arab-Israeli legal center, lists the Law of Return in its database of discriminatory laws; the English text used in this section comes from that database.[cite:rs_ch01_lor_text]

A third reading treats the law as neither unique nor simply explained by Jewish nationhood. Joppke and Rosenhek, writing in 2001, set Israel beside West Germany, which admitted ethnic Germans as "resettlers." About 1.4 million resettlers arrived in 1950–87 and 2.2 million in 1988–97. Germany then changed course: a 1993 law ended the status for anyone born after 1 January 1993 and capped arrivals.[cite:rs_ch01_joppke_rosenhek] Israel's equivalent law survived. The authors explain that survival not by ethnic nationhood alone but by two particular pressures: the demographic rivalry with the Palestinians, and the memory of the Holocaust.[cite:rs_ch01_joppke_rosenhek] Their comparison answers one common claim and complicates another. Ethnic-priority immigration was not unique to Israel. But the one comparable democracy they study wound its scheme down, and Israel did not.

The family-unification ban, 2003–2022. The third measure concerned marriage. The Citizenship and Entry into Israel Law was passed in 2003, during the Second Intifada, as a one-year temporary measure. It generally barred residence permits for Palestinians from the occupied territories who were married to Israelis, and was later extended to citizens of Iran, Lebanon, Syria and Iraq. The temporary law was extended at least 17 times.[cite:rs_ch01_idi_citizenship] Its critics argue that it discriminates against Arab citizens of Israel, who are more likely than other Israelis to marry Palestinians from the territories.[cite:rs_ch01_idi_citizenship]

The courts came close to striking it down. In 2006 Israel's Supreme Court upheld the law by six votes to five in HCJ 7052/03, even though a majority of the justices found that it harmed family life and equality disproportionately. A second challenge, HCJ 466/07, failed by a single vote in 2012.[cite:rs_ch01_idi_citizenship] The law then ran on for nearly another decade. In July 2021 the Knesset failed to extend it and it lapsed. On 10 March 2022, the Times of Israel reported, it was re-enacted by 45 votes to 15, passing with votes from the right-wing opposition. The new version states that its aim includes protecting Israel's Jewish majority.[cite:rs_ch01_toi_citizenship2022] [cite:rs_ch01_idi_citizenship] After the vote, according to the Times of Israel, Interior Minister Ayelet Shaked called the result a victory for a "Jewish and democratic state" over "a state of all its citizens." Meretz and Ra'am voted against.[cite:rs_ch01_toi_citizenship2022]

Security or demography? The government's case was security. Its explanatory notes, and the State Attorney in court, argued that status gained through marriage could be exploited for terror.[cite:rs_ch01_idi_citizenship] Shin Bet testimony cited about 48 such cases in 2001–2021.[cite:rs_ch01_idi_citizenship] [cite:rs_ch01_toi_citizenship2022] Interior Ministry data for 2020, as summarized by the Israel Democracy Institute, give the scale around those cases: about 800–1,000 family-unification applications a year, and about 13,000 Palestinians living in Israel on permits or temporary status. Of those who had received status through family unification, 45 were linked to terror offenses between 2001 and 2020, and none in 2018–2020.[cite:rs_ch01_idi_citizenship]

The case for reading the law as demographic rests on what its supporters and its text said. Some supporters told the Knesset that the aim was to prevent large-scale Palestinian settlement in Israel; the 2022 text names the Jewish majority as part of its purpose; and, as noted above, critics argue that it discriminates against Arab citizens. Some of the justices themselves doubted the security case, given how small the numbers were.[cite:rs_ch01_idi_citizenship] [cite:rs_ch01_toi_citizenship2022] The two readings are not exclusive. A law can answer a real, documented security risk and also serve a demographic aim, and the 2022 version says in its own words that it does the second. What the record shows is the size of the risk the government cited, a few dozen cases over two decades against some thousands of applications, and the scale of the applications and permits around them.

What the record leaves open. Several questions a reader will ask are not settled by the material behind this section. The two counts of terror cases, 45 for 2001–2020 from Interior Ministry data and about 48 for 2001–2021 from Shin Bet testimony, cover different periods and come from different bodies; this book has not reconciled them case by case. The terms of the 2022 law beyond its vote and its stated aim, including any quota and how long it runs, have not been verified here, so this section does not say whether an Arab citizen's spouse from the West Bank can obtain residence today, or on what terms. Nor does the record here document any route by which a Palestinian refugee from 1948 who was outside the state in 1952 could become a citizen; the residence route was closed by its own dates, and naturalization required a right to permanent residence, which the record here does not show such a refugee could obtain. Whether the Law of Return is best understood as refuge or as preference is a judgment the texts cannot make for the reader. They show only that it extends a right to every Jew, that the critics' objection rests on the refugees of 1948 having no equivalent right, and that the people who defend it and the people who oppose it are describing the same law.

sections.h: Occupation, Apartheid, Genocide: What the Words Mean in Law, and Who Has Found What
sections.html:
The differences in legal standing traced in the last two sections are the ground on which three words are fought over. Occupation, apartheid and genocide run through almost every public argument about Israel and the Palestinians. Two opposite habits surround them. One holds that they are slurs with no legal meaning, used to wound rather than to describe. The other holds that all three have already been proven in court. Neither is accurate. Each word has a definition in international law, set down in a treaty or a statute. Each has been applied to Israel by bodies of very different standing: a court, a United Nations commission, human-rights organizations, an association of scholars. And each finding has been rejected by Israel. The first task in weighing them is to keep those bodies apart. A court's opinion, a UN commission's conclusion, a non-governmental report and a government's denial are different kinds of statement, and this book labels each one for what it is.

Occupation. In international law, occupation is the control of foreign territory by a state's armed forces. The question that matters is whether a particular occupation is lawful. On 19 July 2024 the International Court of Justice, the UN's highest court, gave its answer for the territory Israel holds.[cite:icj_press_19jul24]

The court was responding to a request from the UN General Assembly. It found that Israel's continued presence in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, meaning the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza, is unlawful. It said that Israel must bring that presence to an end as rapidly as possible, cease all new settlement activity immediately, evacuate all settlers, and make reparation. It added obligations for everyone else: all states and international organizations must not recognize the situation as legal, and must not assist in maintaining it.[cite:icj_press_19jul24] [cite:un_icj_ao_record] Several of these findings passed by 14 votes to 1.[cite:un_icj_ao_record] [cite:diakonia_icj_summary]

The reasoning is as important as the result, because it answers a common defense. The court noted that occupation law itself sets no time limit. Duration alone did not make the presence unlawful. What did were Israel's policies and its assertion of sovereignty: the court reaffirmed its 2004 opinion that the settlements and the regime attached to them violate international law, held that the prolonged occupation breaches the Palestinian people's right to self-determination, and found that the policies amount to annexation.[cite:transcend_icj_ao] [cite:adalah_icj_ao] It also found that they violate the prohibition on racial segregation and apartheid, a finding that bears on the second word.[cite:11kbw_icj_ao]

The opinion's limits are part of the record too. An advisory opinion is not a binding judgment. The court left it to the General Assembly and the Security Council to decide how to act on it.[cite:adalah_icj_ao] It therefore binds no one by itself, yet it is the world court's answer to whether the occupation is legal, and no body has enforced it. The day before the opinion was delivered, the Knesset passed a resolution calling Palestinian statehood an "existential danger."[cite:adalah_icj_ao] The familiar description of the occupation as a temporary security arrangement whose legality is a matter of opinion is contradicted by the court's advisory opinion. The court's opinion is told in full in a later volume: [scene:icj_s01|the ICJ's 2024 opinion].

Apartheid. Apartheid is a crime under international law, defined in the 1973 Apartheid Convention and in the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court. In both, it means an institutionalized regime of systematic domination by one racial group over another.[cite:fara_amnesty_explainer] Because the definition describes a structure of domination, the argument over the word turns on the different legal situations of the people Israel governs: citizens, residents of East Jerusalem, and Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza, set out in [scene:pr_s02|the previous section].

Three human-rights organizations have concluded that Israel commits apartheid: Human Rights Watch in 2021, the Israeli group B'Tselem in 2021, and Amnesty International in February 2022.[cite:fara_amnesty_explainer] These are reports by non-governmental organizations, not judgments. The nearest a court has come is the ICJ's 2024 finding that Israeli policies breach the prohibition on racial segregation and apartheid.[cite:11kbw_icj_ao] That finding is a breach of a prohibition stated in an advisory opinion; it is not a criminal conviction of any person for the crime of apartheid. Israel rejects the apartheid label.[cite:fara_amnesty_explainer] [cite:11kbw_icj_ao]

Genocide. Under the 1948 Genocide Convention, genocide means specified acts committed with intent to destroy a group, in whole or in part. Since late 2024 a series of bodies has concluded that genocide, or acts of genocide, have been committed in Gaza. Amnesty International did so in December 2024. Human Rights Watch, also in December 2024, concluded that Israel had committed acts of genocide through the deprivation of water. In July 2025 two Israeli organizations, B'Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights–Israel, reached the same conclusion. In August 2025 the International Association of Genocide Scholars passed a resolution to that effect, and in September 2025 a UN Commission of Inquiry concluded that acts of genocide had been committed.[cite:ips_amnesty_hrw_genocide] [cite:jta_un_coi_genocide] [cite:news9_un_coi]

These findings were challenged. More than 500 scholars called on the genocide scholars' association to retract its resolution, citing the process by which it was adopted.[cite:jta_un_coi_genocide] Israel rejects all of the findings.[cite:jta_un_coi_genocide] [cite:news9_un_coi]

No court has decided the question. The case brought by South Africa at the ICJ remains pending. In 2024 the court ordered provisional measures, which found that some rights were plausibly at risk; that order did not decide whether genocide had occurred, and it is not a verdict.[cite:jta_un_coi_genocide] It must be said plainly: as of the research behind this edition, completed in 2026, the genocide case is undecided. The claim that genocide "has been proven in court" is false, and so is the claim that the word has no legal footing in this case. Both a court proceeding and a set of formal findings by UN and non-governmental bodies exist, and the court has not ruled.

The sequence of legal steps is easiest to follow in order. The panel below traces it from South Africa's filing at the ICJ in December 2023, through the provisional-measures order of January 2024 and the July 2024 opinion on the occupation, to the UN Commission of Inquiry's finding in September 2025. It also records a separate track at a different court, the International Criminal Court, whose November 2024 arrest warrants for Netanyahu and Gallant concern war crimes and crimes against humanity, not genocide; that track is told in later volumes. The panel's last line is about enforcement, and the point it makes matches what the ICJ's own design implies: findings have been made, and no mechanism has carried them out.

Israel's stated position belongs beside those findings, as part of the same record. Israel rejects all of the genocide findings.[cite:jta_un_coi_genocide] [cite:news9_un_coi] As the next panel summarizes it, Israel also contests the ICJ's orders and the ICC's jurisdiction, and says its operations target Hamas, which it accuses of embedding in civilian areas. It rejects the apartheid label, and its parliament declared Palestinian statehood an existential danger on the eve of the occupation opinion.[cite:fara_amnesty_explainer] [cite:adalah_icj_ao]

"The only democracy in the Middle East." The legal findings sit uneasily beside one of the most repeated claims about Israel: that it is the only democracy in its region. For citizens, the indices largely bear the claim out. In the V-Dem Institute's 2024 report Israel remained the only electoral democracy in the Middle East and North Africa, a region where 98% of people live under autocracies.[cite:globes_vdem] Israel holds competitive elections and has a free press, and Arab citizens vote and sit in the Knesset.

The same report, however, demoted Israel from "liberal democracy" to "electoral democracy" for the first time in about 50 years. It cited government attacks on the judiciary and a "substantive decline" in freedom from torture.[cite:toi_vdem] Freedom House's score for Israel fell from 80 in 2017 to 73. The Israel Democracy Institute, an Israeli think tank, called the downgrade "troubling, but not catastrophic," noting that countries such as Austria and Portugal sit in the same category.[cite:idi_vdem]

The larger gap is structural, and it is the point at which the democracy indices meet the apartheid argument. Both V-Dem and Freedom House assess Israel without the occupied territories. Palestinians in the West Bank live under Israeli military control but cannot vote in Israel's elections. By one count, from PRIO, of roughly 15.5 million people under Israel's control, about 5.5 million lack citizenship.[cite:prio_democracy] Both facts stand together. Israel is a democracy for its citizens, and it governs millions of people who cannot vote for the government that governs them. The talking point states the first fact and leaves out the second, and the apartheid argument, as the previous section showed, turns on differences of this kind.

What the record does not settle. The most important open question is the one before the ICJ: whether genocide has been committed in Gaza. No court has answered it, and the formal findings by UN and non-governmental bodies, however detailed, are not a judgment. On apartheid, no court has convicted any person of the crime; the ICJ's finding concerns a breach of a prohibition in an advisory opinion, and the non-governmental reports are disputed by Israel. On occupation, the law is the clearest of the three, since the world court has spoken, but its opinion is advisory, and whether and how any state or UN organ will act on it remains open. These are live matters, and their status here is as of the research behind this edition in 2026. What a reader can take away is a way of reading the next headline: ask which word is being used, which body used it, and whether that body was a court, a UN commission, a human-rights organization or a government.

chapters.label: Chapter 2
chapters.title: The Land Before the State
chapters.intro:
The modern conflict did not begin on an empty map. This chapter sets out what the record shows about the land before either national movement took shape. It comes here because two of the most repeated claims about this history, that one people was absent for two thousand years and that the other appeared only in the twentieth century, are claims about this period, and the documents answer them directly.

It begins with three thousand years in brief: the Merneptah stele of about 1207 BCE, which names Israel as a people; the Tel Dan and Mesha stelae of about 840 BCE; Rome's conquest, the two failed revolts and the renaming of the province as Syria Palaestina; and the history of the name "Palestine" from Herodotus to Jund Filastin.[cite:rs_ch01_cojs_merneptah] [cite:rs_ch01_nyrb_bowersock] The next section shows Ottoman Palestine as an administered place. No province bore its name, but from 1872 the district of Jerusalem answered directly to Constantinople, and the land's three districts held roughly 600,000 people by the late nineteenth century.[cite:wiki_mutasarrifate_jerusalem] [cite:ips_ottoman_palestine] A section on the Old Yishuv follows the Jewish community that lived in the four holy cities before Zionism, about 7,000 people in 1800, and the long argument over whether Jews formed the majority of Jerusalem.[cite:rs_ch01_nli_oldyishuv] [cite:rs_ch01_un_s10138] The chapter closes by separating three questions that are often run together: who lived on the land (the Ottoman census of 1871–72 counted 381,954 people, excluding the Bedouin), whose connection to it runs back unbroken, and when each modern national identity took shape.[cite:cjpme_historical_demography]

The disputes are real and are given in full: over Hadrian's motive in renaming Judaea, over how far Palestinian continuity runs, over which count of Jerusalem should decide a claim. What the chapter establishes beneath them is that both histories are documented, and that neither erases the other.

sections.h: Three Thousand Years in Brief: Israel, Judah, Rome and the Name "Palestine"
sections.html:
Two short claims circulate whenever the deep history of this land is argued. One says that Jews were absent from it for two thousand years. The other says that Palestinians appeared only in the twentieth century. Both treat the past as though only one people could have one. The documented record does not support either. It shows Jewish kingdoms in the first millennium BCE and a Jewish presence that survived Rome's suppression of two revolts. It also shows centuries in which the majority of the land's people became Arabic-speaking Muslims and Christians, the ancestors of today's Palestinians.[cite:wiki_palestine_region] [cite:encyclo_israel_history] This section traces that record from the first inscriptions to the end of Ottoman rule, follows the history of the two names, "Israel" and "Palestine," and sets out where scholars disagree.

Israel in the stones. The earliest known mention of Israel outside the Bible is on a victory stele of the Egyptian pharaoh Merneptah, dated about 1207 BCE. Flinders Petrie found it in 1896 in the first courtyard of Merneptah's mortuary temple at Thebes; it is now in the Cairo Museum.[cite:rs_ch01_cojs_merneptah] The line that names Israel uses a stock phrase for a conquered place, rendered "Israel is wasted, its grain (or seed) is not." A detail of the writing gives it special weight. Egyptian scribes added to names an unpronounced sign, called a determinative, that told the reader what kind of thing was named. Names such as Ashkelon and Gezer carry the sign for a place. "Israel" carries the sign for a people or ethnic group.[cite:rs_ch01_cojs_merneptah] At the end of the thirteenth century BCE, then, an Egyptian royal scribe knew of a people called Israel.

Kingdoms appear in the outside record nearly four centuries later, and from the testimony of their enemies. The Tel Dan stele, an inscription in Old Aramaic dated about 840 BCE from its script, was found in 1993 at Tel Dan in northern Israel during excavations led by Avraham Biran; two smaller fragments followed the next year. It is held at the Skirball Museum in Jerusalem. On it an Aramaean king, most likely Hazael of Damascus, boasts of victories over the king of Israel and over the "House of David." Line 9 is the earliest known mention of David's dynasty outside the Bible.[cite:rs_ch01_cojs_teldan] From the other side of the Jordan comes the Mesha Stele, also called the Moabite Stone, of about the same date and written in Moabite. The missionary F. A. Klein saw it in 1868 near Dibon in Transjordan. It states that "Omri was the king of Israel, and he oppressed Moab for many days." It is now in the Louvre.[cite:rs_ch01_cojs_mesha] Two inscriptions from neighboring peoples, written in their own languages to celebrate their own victories, named the kingdom of Israel and the dynasty of David. These are the outside witnesses to the Jewish kingdoms of Israel and Judah that existed in the first millennium BCE.[cite:encyclo_israel_history]

Where the name "Palestine" comes from. The earliest surviving text to use the name Palestine is the Histories of the Greek writer Herodotus, from the second half of the fifth century BCE. He speaks of "Syria Palaistine" for the coast between Phoenicia and Egypt.[cite:rs_ch01_nyrb_bowersock] [cite:rs_ch01_totf_hadrian] According to one secondary account, Herodotus also mentions "Syrians who are in Palestine" who practice circumcision (Histories 2.104.3), and both Philo of Alexandria, who died about 50 CE, and Josephus, writing about 93–94 CE, used "Palestine" when writing about Jews.[cite:rs_ch01_totf_hadrian] The Greek name is generally linked to the Philistines, in Hebrew peleshet, an Aegean people who settled the southern coastal plain in the twelfth century BCE. The scholar G. W. Bowersock calls the older variant forms, such as Peleset and Phlishtu, etymologically obscure.[cite:rs_ch01_jvl_palname] [cite:rs_ch01_nyrb_bowersock] The name was in Greek use, then, more than five centuries before Rome attached it to a province.

Rome, the revolts and the renaming. Rome conquered the region in 63 BCE and in 6 CE created a province of Judaea whose population was predominantly Jewish.[cite:wiki_palestine_region] Two great revolts against Roman rule failed. The first ended with the destruction of the Second Temple in Jerusalem in 70 CE. The second, led by Bar Kokhba, is dated 132–135 in some accounts and 132–136 in others, the end date being uncertain. After it Rome killed, enslaved or expelled much of Judea's Jewish population. It rebuilt Jerusalem as a pagan colony, Aelia Capitolina, and barred Jews from the city.[cite:wiki_syria_palaestina] [cite:wiki_palestine_region] Roman inscriptions show that around the time of this revolt Judaea was merged with Galilee into a province called Syria Palaestina.[cite:rs_ch01_totf_hadrian] [cite:rs_ch01_bas_feldman]

Why Rome made that change is a real dispute, and the evidence is thinner than either side of the modern argument tends to admit. No ancient source states when or why the change was made.[cite:rs_ch01_totf_hadrian] [cite:rs_ch01_bas_feldman] The case that it was punitive is the more widely held. Reference summaries describe the renaming as one that most scholars see as aimed at severing the Jewish connection to the land, and many historians link it to the punishment of the Jewish rebels.[cite:wiki_palestine_region] [cite:w_syria_palaestina] Its strongest scholarly statement is Louis Feldman's, from 1990: the emperor Hadrian was the likely author, given his decrees against Jewish national and religious life. Feldman conceded that only circumstantial evidence links Hadrian to the change.[cite:rs_ch01_jvl_palname] [cite:rs_ch01_bas_feldman] The case against a punitive motive starts from the name's age. It had been in Greek and Latin use for centuries, including by Jewish writers. Ronald Syme suggested that the change may have come in 130 CE, before the revolt began, and David Jacobson, writing in 1999, and others have read it as an administrative or Hellenizing step rather than a punishment. These positions are known here through a secondary account that summarizes them.[cite:rs_ch01_totf_hadrian] Both cases agree on the facts that matter most: Rome did rename the province after, or around, a revolt it crushed, and the name it chose was not new.

The presence that remained. Rome's victory did not end Jewish life in the land. A continuous, smaller Jewish presence remained, and Galilee became its religious center. Much of classical Jewish literature was produced there.[cite:encyclo_israel_history] In the sixteenth century Jewish communities took root in the four holy cities of Jerusalem, Hebron, Tiberias and Safed, forming what came to be called the Old Yishuv, the pre-Zionist community. It was a minority whose size rose and fell.[cite:encyclo_israel_history] Its numbers, institutions and place in Ottoman Jerusalem are the subject of [scene:ch01_old_yishuv|the Jewish community before Zionism].

Byzantium, the caliphate and the empires that followed. The land passed next to Byzantine Christian rule.[cite:wiki_palestine_region] Under Byzantium the region was divided into First, Second and Third Palestine. After the Muslim conquest in the seventh century, First Palestine became Filastin and Second Palestine became al-Urdunn.[cite:rs_ch01_nyrb_bowersock] [cite:rs_ch01_jvl_palname] Under the Umayyad caliph 'Abd al-Malik, in the late seventh century, Palestine existed as a province of the caliphate, Jund Filastin.[cite:rs_ch01_nyrb_bowersock] The Arabic form of the name was used for the region from the early Islamic period onward.[cite:w_name_palestine] Crusader kingdoms followed, then the Mamluks in the thirteenth century, and from 1516 the Ottoman Empire, which ruled for four centuries until 1917.[cite:wiki_palestine_region] Over these centuries the majority of the population became Arabic-speaking Muslims and Christians.[cite:wiki_palestine_region]

Under the Ottomans, "Palestine" was an informal term rather than the name of a province; how the land was in fact administered is told in [scene:s00h|Ottoman Palestine]. The word "Palestinian" for Arabic speakers of the land is attested from 1898, in the writing of Khalil Baydas, and in 1913 Ruhi al-Khalidi wrote of "the Palestinian race" in the newspaper Filastin. Both dates come from Zachary Foster, as cited by the Jewish Virtual Library.[cite:rs_ch01_jvl_palname]

Four thousand years of Palestine? A second dispute concerns continuity. Nur Masalha, in Palestine: A Four Thousand Year History (2018), argues that Palestinian place-names and identity persisted through Roman, Byzantine and Islamic rule.[cite:rs_ch01_nyrb_bowersock] Reviewing the book, Bowersock called the four-thousand-year title indefensible. The documented name, he pointed out, begins with Herodotus, and its location and meaning kept changing from one empire to the next. He nonetheless praised the book's erudition.[cite:rs_ch01_nyrb_bowersock] The Jewish Virtual Library takes a further position: that the name was imposed by Rome, and that Palestinian nationalism dates from the 1910s and 1920s, as a reaction to Zionism.[cite:rs_ch01_jvl_palname] The record supports parts of each. Bowersock's point about the name is documented: it is about 2,500 years old in writing, not 4,000, and it described different territories at different times. The persistence of the name itself, through the Byzantine provinces and Jund Filastin, is also documented. And whatever the date of modern national feeling, which is taken up in [scene:s00i|a later section on presence and identity], the people who lived in the land through those centuries were real and are documented.

"Stolen from Rome." One form of the argument circulates widely in comment threads: that every Palestinian symbol was stolen from someone else, the keffiyeh, the flag and the name itself, the last taken from Rome to erase Judea. Checked against the record, the claim is mostly false, with one half-truth. The keffiyeh is a traditional headdress worn across the Arab world; its black-and-white pattern became associated with Palestinian nationalism during the revolt of 1936–39.[cite:w_keffiyeh] The Palestinian flag derives from the flag of the 1916 Arab Revolt, as do the flags of Jordan and other Arab states. That is a shared origin, not a theft.[cite:w_pal_flag] [cite:w_arab_revolt_flag] The half-truth is the name. Rome did rename the province after the Bar Kokhba revolt, as told above, but the name was already more than 500 years old, and the Arabic Filastin was in use for the region for centuries from the early Islamic period.[cite:w_syria_palaestina] [cite:w_name_palestine] A related line, that Arafat was born in Cairo, is largely accurate, as the opening section on method noted, and says nothing about a people's history.[cite:w_arafat]

What the record does not settle. Some questions remain open on the evidence. Why Rome renamed Judaea, and exactly when, is not stated in any ancient source; the punitive reading is the more widely held, and the administrative reading has serious scholarly support, but neither can be proven from the surviving texts. The end date of the Bar Kokhba revolt is given as 135 in some sources and 136 in others. How much continuity of identity, as opposed to continuity of residence and of place-names, ran from the Byzantine and early Islamic provinces to modern Palestinians is the substance of the Masalha–Bowersock exchange, and the record of names alone cannot decide it. The size of the Jewish population that remained at any given point between Rome and the Ottomans is described in the sources here only as smaller, and fluctuating.

What the record does settle is that two histories are both documented. A people called Israel is named in an Egyptian inscription of about 1207 BCE, and the kingdom of Israel and the House of David by its enemies about 840 BCE; Jews remained in the land after Rome. Arabic-speaking Muslims and Christians formed its majority across many centuries of residence, under a name that Greek writers used before Rome and Arab rulers used after it. Neither history erases the other. On this book's reading, the modern conflict is about how those two documented claims were handled after 1897.

sections.h: Ottoman Palestine: Named, Counted and Governed
sections.html:
From 1516 to 1917 the Ottoman Empire governed most of the Arab Middle East as provinces of a single state. Damascus, Baghdad, Jerusalem and Beirut were provincial cities of the same empire, and people and goods moved between them without passports. There were no international borders between what are now Syria, Iraq, Lebanon, Jordan and Israel and the Palestinian territories, because none of those states yet existed. Iran stood outside this order altogether: it was never Ottoman, and it kept its own dynasty, its own language and a Shia majority.

Inside the empire, law was organized by religion as much as by territory. Under what is called the millet system, recognized religious communities, Muslims, Christians of several churches and Jews, administered their own religious law, their own courts and their own schooling, and governed marriage and inheritance under their own leaders.[cite:w_ottoman_millet] It was not a golden age. Non-Muslims paid special taxes and held a lesser legal status; the empire taxed heavily, conscripted men, and put down revolts by force, and periodic violence was part of its record. The point of describing it is not that the order was just. The point is that it was not the map of rival states that the twentieth century produced. Almost every border that matters in today's conflicts was drawn in a six-year window, between 1916 and 1922, by two European powers, Britain and France.

Two claims about this period circulate widely, and they point in opposite directions. The first holds that before Zionism "Palestine" was an empty, undifferentiated stretch of Ottoman desert with no population or administrative identity of its own, and that the place became real only when the British Mandate invented it. The second holds that the Ottomans occupied Palestine much as settlers later would. The administrative record answers both, and it begins with a technical point that the first claim's defenders are right about.

The Ottomans generally named their provinces after their capital cities. No single Ottoman administrative unit was ever officially called "Palestine" on a map.[cite:wiki_ottoman_palestine] That is accurate, and it is not a concession invented to soften the argument. It is the strongest form of the claim that Palestine "never existed," and it deserves a precise answer rather than a denial. The answer is that a naming convention is a different thing from the absence of a place. The regional name was far older than the Ottomans. Rome designated its province Syria Palaestina in the second century CE, and the name persisted through Byzantine, Crusader and Mamluk rule. Throughout the Ottoman centuries it stayed in standing use in European maps, in travel writing, in religious texts and in Arabic geographic writing, including local Arabic-language sources.[cite:wiki_ottoman_palestine] (The longer history of the name, from the ancient writers onward, is told in the section before this one.) An American comparison helps. There was never a colonial charter for a place officially named "New England" in the way there was a Massachusetts Bay Colony. Massachusetts, Connecticut and Rhode Island were nonetheless real, governed and populated, and "New England" was the regional name in continuous use for the whole of them. Whether a province bore a name and whether the place existed are two different questions.

The technicality is effective as a talking point precisely because it is true. It lets a speaker correct a listener, "Palestine wasn't an official Ottoman province," while implying something much larger: that the place, its people and its government were not real. The record supports the narrow claim and contradicts the broad one. Both statements hold at once.

What the Ottomans did create was an administrative status for this region that was higher than that of most districts in the empire. Ordinarily an Ottoman district, a sanjak, sat inside a larger province, a vilayet, and reported upward through the provincial governor. Jerusalem was taken out of that chain. After an initial separation in 1864, the district of Jerusalem was raised in 1872 to the status of a mutasarrifate: it was governed by a mutasarrif who answered directly to Constantinople, bypassing the provincial governor altogether.[cite:wiki_mutasarrifate_jerusalem] That arrangement was reserved for a small number of especially significant districts across the empire, and Jerusalem held it because of the region's religious and strategic importance, both to the Ottomans themselves and to the Western powers. It ran without interruption until the British occupation in 1917, a span of 45 years.[cite:wiki_mutasarrifate_jerusalem] In plain terms, Jerusalem was one of the places important enough that the capital insisted on governing it directly, with no regional manager in between.

The status needs to be read for what it was. It reflected religious and strategic significance inside an Ottoman imperial framework. It does not show that the Ottomans thought of the territory in the national categories of the twentieth century, Arab, Palestinian or Zionist, and it anticipated none of the politics that came later.[cite:wiki_mutasarrifate_jerusalem]

By 1887–88 the territory that later became Mandate Palestine was organized in three units. In the south lay the independent Sanjak of Jerusalem, the mutasarrifate. In the north lay the Sanjaks of Nablus and Acre, both attached administratively to the larger Vilayet of Beirut. Taken together, these three districts map closely onto the later boundary of the British Mandate.[cite:ips_ottoman_palestine] Over four centuries the arrangement shifted. Across the whole Ottoman period, Palestine is described as having been governed chiefly as the district of Jerusalem together with parts of the provinces of Beirut and Damascus, and from 1831 to 1840 it passed out of Ottoman hands into Egyptian rule before returning. The boundaries were not identical in every detail from decade to decade; administrative lines moved at the margins, as they do in most territories. The continuity that matters is that a bounded, governed region existed, and that its outline was not an arbitrary line drawn later by the British.[cite:ips_ottoman_palestine]

The three districts were inhabited. Their combined population was approximately 600,000 by the late nineteenth century, roughly a decade before political Zionism existed as an organized movement.[cite:ips_ottoman_palestine] The figure is an approximation and is offered as one. Nineteenth-century imperial counting was real but imperfect, and "roughly 600,000" claims no precision to the individual. Other counts from the period give lower totals: a census of 1871–72, discussed in [scene:s00i|the section on peoples and identity], and the reconstructions from Ottoman registers set out in the next section, which left out foreign nationals. What all of them show is a counted population, not one that appeared from nothing. The counting continued across the transition from Ottoman to British administration between 1917 and 1922, which relabeled one continuous population rather than introducing a new one.[cite:ips_ottoman_palestine]

That population lived in named places. The administrative record itself names the towns governed under this system, among them Jerusalem, Gaza, Jaffa, Hebron, Nablus, Haifa, Acre, Safed and Nazareth. All nine are populated cities today. An 1885 British encyclopedia entry on the region gives a more granular count from the same period: 753 distinct named places, with more than 54,000 houses, meaning families, across the Ottoman districts.[cite:britannica_history_palestine] That entry is a contemporary, independent count, not a later reconstruction. It does not show that the settlement pattern was fixed. Populations and settlements shifted over four centuries of Ottoman rule, as they do everywhere. It does show a named and inhabited land.

Who were those people? Most were Arabic-speaking Muslims and Christians. Alongside them lived long-established Jewish communities in Jerusalem, Hebron, Safed and Tiberias, whose life is the subject of the next section. Most were Ottoman subjects, though many Jewish immigrants were foreign nationals.

This bears on the second claim, that the Ottomans occupied Palestine in the way later settlers did. The precise term for Ottoman rule is imperial administration. The empire ruled through governors, garrisons and taxation, over a population that stayed what it had been. It did not replace that population with its own. That is the distinction between an empire and a settler project, and the Ottoman record falls on the imperial side of it. The same record answers the "empty backwater" claim from the other direction: an empire does not post a governor answering directly to its capital over a district with no one in it.

The Ottoman Land Code of 1858 is told in the next volume, in [scene:ot_s01|the Ottoman Land Code].

Ottoman rule ended in war. British forces captured Jerusalem in December 1917, and the Mutasarrifate's long run ended with the occupation. The legal end came six years later. The Republic of Turkey, founded in 1923, renounced all rights over the former Arab provinces in the Treaty of Lausanne that year. Modern Turkey is therefore the empire's successor state, not a claimant to the land.[cite:w_lausanne]

The Arab majority that the Ottomans governed was still the majority when British rule ended. British Mandate figures for 1947 counted about 1.3 million Arabs and 630,000 Jews in Palestine. On 29 November 1947 the United Nations adopted Resolution 181, which proposed a Jewish state on 56% of the land and an Arab state on 44%, with Jerusalem under international administration, at a time when Jewish ownership amounted to approximately 7% of the land. The Jewish Agency accepted the plan and the Arab League rejected it. In the war of 1948 approximately 700,000 Palestinian Arabs fled or were expelled, the event Palestinians call the Nakba, "the catastrophe." From the 1980s, Israeli scholars working in newly declassified military archives, among them Benny Morris, Ilan Pappé, Avi Shlaim and Simha Flapan, documented both flight from war and systematic expulsions, against the earlier official account that the refugees left voluntarily. How each village was emptied is still argued village by village and historian by historian, as [scene:hd_s01|the section on how historians argue about 1948] sets out.

Several things remain open. The figure of about 600,000 is an approximation, and the period's counts do not agree with one another; how far apart they are, and why, depends on whom each count included. The administrative lines of the three districts moved over the decades, and how closely they matched the Mandate's border at any given date is a matter of degree. And the Mutasarrifate's elevated status tells us how Constantinople valued Jerusalem, not how the people who lived in the district understood themselves. That last question, of identity, is a separate one, and the record on it has to be read on its own terms.

sections.h: Before Zionism: The Old Yishuv and the Count of Jerusalem
sections.html:
Political Zionism did not bring the first Jews to the land. When the movement's first settlers arrived from 1881, they found a Jewish community already there, long settled and organized on entirely different lines. Historians call it the Old Yishuv, to distinguish it from the New Yishuv that began with the First Aliyah, the wave of immigration from 1881 onward.[cite:rs_ch01_nli_oldyishuv] It grew in the eighteenth century mainly through Orthodox groups, among them Hasidim and the disciples of the Vilna Gaon.[cite:rs_ch01_nli_oldyishuv]

Its life centered on four cities that Jewish tradition held holy: Jerusalem, Hebron, Safed and Tiberias. In the nineteenth century most of its members lived in Jerusalem.[cite:rs_ch01_nli_oldyishuv] [cite:rs_ch01_posen_ottoman] The previous section described the Ottoman province around them, a land most of whose people were Arabic-speaking Muslims and Christians; the Jewish communities of these four cities were long established within it, as Ottoman subjects or as foreign nationals living under Ottoman rule.

The community lived largely on halukka, a Hebrew word meaning "distribution." Jews abroad sent donations, and the money was handed out in the land by kollels, bodies organized by country of origin or by Hasidic affiliation.
