Over time the community became almost completely dependent on these funds.[cite:rs_ch01_nli_oldyishuv]

Politically, the community had a recognized place inside the Ottoman order. The Sephardi leadership, headed by a chief rabbi, the Hakham Bashi, a title later rendered Rishon LeZion, was officially recognized by the Ottoman authorities and represented the Jews before them. The arrangement resembled the millet order described in the previous section, under which recognized religious communities were led by their own heads. The Ashkenazi kollels, which had grown up separately, united at the end of the nineteenth century under a General Committee of Knesset Israel.[cite:rs_ch01_nli_oldyishuv]

How many people was this? The figures come with ranges, and the ranges matter. By the National Library of Israel's count, the Jewish population of the land was about 7,000 in 1800 and about 27,000 in 1880. Most researchers put the 1880 figure somewhat lower, at 23,000 to 26,000, and agree that about half of them lived in Jerusalem.[cite:rs_ch01_nli_oldyishuv] [cite:rs_ch01_posen_ottoman] The community roughly tripled or quadrupled between 1800 and 1880, before political Zionism existed.

The growth that followed was faster, and it changed the community's character. Roughly 60,000 Jews arrived between 1881 and 1914. The First World War then reversed much of it. By the summer of 1918, after wartime expulsions, hunger and disease, 56,000 Jews remained in the land, little more than half the number of 1914.[cite:rs_ch01_posen_ottoman]

A second set of numbers looks very different, and the reason is instructive. The historian Justin McCarthy reconstructed Palestine's population from the Ottoman registers. His counts of Ottoman-citizen Jews are about 13,000 of 369,000 people in 1860, 13,942 of 440,850 in 1878, 17,991 of 516,131 in 1890, and 38,754 of 722,143 in 1914.[cite:rs_ch01_mccarthy_pop] Set beside the figure of 23,000 to 27,000 for 1880, his count of 13,942 for 1878 is strikingly low. The explanation lies in what the registers counted. They recorded Ottoman citizens, and they did not include foreign nationals, among whom were many Jewish immigrants.[cite:rs_ch01_mccarthy_pop] Jews who lived in the land as foreign nationals do not appear in them. Neither set of figures is simply wrong. They answer different questions: how many Jews lived in the land, and how many Jews the empire counted as its own citizens.

The same caution applies to the total population. McCarthy's register totals, 516,131 in 1890 and 722,143 in 1914, are counts of Ottoman citizens; the approximate figure of 600,000 for the late nineteenth century given in the previous section comes from a different source. Comparing them requires knowing who each one left out.

In the second half of the nineteenth century Jerusalem's Jews began to build beyond the Old City. The first neighborhoods outside the city walls are associated with Moses Montefiore, Yoel Moshe Salomon and Yehoshua Yellin.[cite:rs_ch01_nli_oldyishuv]

The Old Yishuv did not last as the land's leading Jewish community. The decline of the Ottoman Empire and the successive Zionist immigration waves cost it that place.[cite:rs_ch01_nli_oldyishuv] The story of the newcomers begins with [scene:ideo_s01|the First Aliyah].

The most argued-over question about this community concerns Jerusalem itself. Did Jews form the majority of the city before Zionism? The question became a matter of state in 1971. On 22 February of that year, Jordan and the United Arab Republic wrote to the UN Secretary-General in a letter circulated as document S/10130. On 1 March 1971, Israel's ambassador to the United Nations, Yosef Tekoah, replied in a letter to the Secretary-General, document S/10138.[cite:rs_ch01_un_s10138] The Israeli letter set out a series of figures for the city of Jerusalem: 28,000 Jews among 43,000 people in 1887, citing Baedeker's guide of 1894; 40,000 of 60,000 in 1905, citing the thirteenth edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica; 33,971 of 62,578 at the British census of 1922; 51,222 of 90,503 in 1931; and 97,000 of 157,080 in 1944, citing the Survey of Palestine.[cite:rs_ch01_un_s10138] Its argument was that Jews had been the majority of the city itself in 1922, 1931 and 1944 and for decades before the Mandate, and that the Arab figures in S/10130 described the whole Jerusalem sub-district, a wider area in which Arabs were the majority, rather than the city.[cite:rs_ch01_un_s10138] The figures that Jordan and the United Arab Republic used are not reproduced in the sources available for this book, so their side of the exchange is known here only through Israel's description of it.

The same Israeli letter states that in 1948 Jordan destroyed the Jewish Quarter of the Old City, including 39 synagogues and places of learning, expelled its Jews, and barred Jewish access to the holy places from 1948 to 1967.[cite:rs_ch01_un_s10138] These are statements in an official Israeli document addressed to the United Nations, made in the course of a diplomatic dispute, and they are reported here as such.

A second compilation broadly supports the trend. Figures gathered by the Jewish Virtual Library, drawing on Oesterreicher and Sinai (1974), give Jerusalem 7,120 Jews of 15,510 people in 1844, 12,000 of 25,030 in 1876, and 28,112 of 45,420 in 1896, and 33,971 Jews at the British census of 1922.[cite:rs_ch01_jvl_jerpop] By these figures Jews were a little under half of the city's people in 1844 and 1876 and a majority by 1896.

The two compilations agree on the Jewish figure for 1922, 33,971, but not on the city's total. Israel's letter gives the 1922 census total as 62,578; the Jewish Virtual Library table gives 52,081.[cite:rs_ch01_un_s10138] [cite:rs_ch01_jvl_jerpop] The sources do not explain the difference, and it changes the Jewish share of the city in that year considerably. Which total is right cannot be settled from these documents alone.

Writers today draw opposite conclusions from these numbers. Making the case for a long Jewish claim to the city, the columnist Stephen Flatow, writing in the Jerusalem Post in 2023, cited visitors' calculations showing a Jewish plurality from the mid-1800s and the 1922 census showing Jews as the majority of the city.[cite:rs_ch01_jpost_flatow] The strongest form of this case rests on the series of figures Israel put before the United Nations, which a separate compilation broadly matches: by both, Jews were the city's largest group by the late nineteenth century.

The opposing caution rests on the quality of the evidence and on what it is taken to mean. The nineteenth-century figures come from visitors' estimates and secondary compilations, not from a systematic census, and many Jewish residents were foreign subjects outside the Ottoman registers, so the Ottoman state's own counts cannot confirm them.[cite:rs_ch01_mccarthy_pop] The analyst Seth Frantzman, writing in 2016, stressed who those Jews were: the Jews of nineteenth-century Jerusalem were largely Sephardi and religious, and the city was a Middle Eastern one.[cite:rs_ch01_frantzman_1888] His point bears less on the count than on what is read into it.

Both readings can be held against the same table. A Jewish plurality, and later a majority, in the city of Jerusalem is supported by several compilations, though the earliest of them rest on estimates. An Arab majority in the land as a whole is supported by every count here; an Arab majority in the wider sub-district is stated in Israel's own letter, though the figures behind it are not in these sources. Which unit, city or sub-district, should decide a political claim is not a question the numbers can answer.

Under British rule the Jewish share of the whole country rose quickly from a low base. Britain's census of 1922 counted 757,182 people in Palestine, of whom about 11% were Jews. The census of 1931 put the Jewish share at about 17%, and the estimate of the United Nations Special Committee on Palestine for late 1946, a population of about 1.85 million, put it at about 33%. The growth that the Old Yishuv's 7,000 of 1800 began, and the First Aliyah accelerated, continued at a far greater pace under the Mandate.

Several things the record here does not settle. The nineteenth-century figures are estimates, and their range, 23,000 to 27,000 for 1880, is the honest form of the answer. How many Jews lived in the land as foreign nationals, outside the Ottoman registers, at any given date is not established by these sources. The difference between the two 1922 totals for Jerusalem is unresolved. And the Arab side of the 1971 exchange at the United Nations is known here only from Israel's reply. What the record does establish is that a Jewish community lived in the land, chiefly in its four holy cities, before Zionism, that it was sustained from abroad and represented to the Ottomans through its Sephardi chief rabbi, and that by the figures available it was the largest group in the city of Jerusalem by the late nineteenth century while remaining a small minority in the land as a whole.

sections.h: Two Real Histories: Presence, Continuity and National Identity
sections.html:
Two claims about this land circulate constantly, and each comes in two mirror-image versions. The first holds that one people is indigenous and the other a recent colonizer: Jews native and Arabs latecomers, or the reverse. The second holds that there is no distinct Palestinian people at all, only Arabs in general, and that a Palestinian national identity was invented recently. Both claims rest on the same error. They fold three questions into one: who lived in the land, whose culture and connection to it run back unbroken, and when a modern national identity took shape. The documents treat these as separate questions, and they give separate answers. Kept apart, the answers do not produce a single winner.

The familiar version runs that only one population has a real and ancient claim to the land, and that the other's national identity was invented recently and has no deep roots. Taken one question at a time, the record supports neither half of that sentence as it is usually meant.

The first question: ancient Jewish presence. Ancient Jewish kingdoms existed in parts of the land, and Jewish religious, cultural and historical connections to the region are documented in archaeological, textual and religious sources over more than three thousand years.[cite:substack_historical_record_balfour] This is not in dispute among mainstream historians of any political orientation. It is one of the points in this history where the record is simply settled, and the section on the ancient record in this chapter sets it out in detail. What that continuity does not do, by itself, is settle a modern question of sovereignty or statehood. Ancient presence and modern political legitimacy are related, but they are not the same question.

The second question: a counted Arab population. The land was not empty. The Ottoman census of 1871–72 counted 381,954 residents of Palestine, excluding the Bedouin, of whom roughly 85 percent were Muslim, 11 percent Christian and 4 percent Jewish.[cite:cjpme_historical_demography] This Arabic-speaking population's presence under Ottoman rule is documented continuously for centuries, and modern genetic and archaeological studies find strong Levantine biogeographical continuity in it, consistent with long-term local ancestry.[cite:factually_archaeological_evidence] Two cautions belong beside those figures. The census left out the Bedouin, so the true population was larger than 381,954. And a counted population, however long its roots, is not the same thing as a formal national identity. That is the third question, and it has a later date.

The third question: when national identity formed. The most authoritative statement that Palestinian national identity is modern comes not from a hostile source but from the field's leading Palestinian historian. Rashid Khalidi, Edward Said Professor of Arab Studies at Columbia University and a past president of the Middle East Studies Association, set out the finding in his foundational study Palestinian Identity: The Construction of Modern National Consciousness. Formal Palestinian national identity, he documents, has its roots in the nationalist discourses that emerged among the Ottoman Empire's peoples in the late nineteenth century, and it sharpened through what he identifies as the critical years of 1917 to 1923.[cite:cup_khalidi_palestinian_identity] [cite:wiki_palestinian_nationalism] Khalidi is explicit that this modern political consciousness drew on a much older regional history and a real population presence. A late date for the political identity, in his account, does not mean the people or its culture was invented. He does not treat his own finding as delegitimizing, and it should not be quoted as if he did.

The same pattern describes the other side. Formal Zionist national identity was founded at the First Zionist Congress in Basel in 1897, as a modern political movement built on older religious and cultural material rather than as an ancient ethnogenesis; the movement's founding is told in [scene:s00c|the section on Zionism and Judaism]. The structural parallel is exact on this one point: in both cases a modern political consciousness took formal shape in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, drawing on a far older attachment. To treat "the national identity is recent, therefore illegitimate" as a test for one people and not the other is an inconsistent standard, not a historical finding. The parallel goes no further than that. It describes how formal national consciousness emerged in each case; it does not say that the two movements' histories run alike in every other respect.

"Invented in the 1960s." The sharpest popular form of the second claim says there was no Palestinian people before the Palestine Liberation Organization. The PLO was founded in 1964. The people it claimed to represent were already on the record decades earlier, and the markers are dated and public. A newspaper named Filastin, "Palestine," began publishing in Jaffa in 1911 and campaigned as a Palestinian voice; its story is told in [scene:fil_s01|the section on the newspaper Filastin]. Palestinian Arab congresses met from 1919 and petitioned the Paris Peace Conference. Britain's census of 1922 counted 757,182 people in Palestine. Historians date the emergence of Palestinian national identity to the late Ottoman and British Mandate periods, the same century in which the region's other national identities formed, Jordanian, Syrian and Israeli among them. Measured against that record, the claim is false. Its kernel of truth is the one Khalidi himself documents: the national identity is modern. Its error is to treat a modern identity as a fake one, a standard that would disqualify most of the region's nations, Israel included.

"A land without a people." The best-known slogan of the first claim has a documented origin, and it is not Zionist. Its earliest published version appeared in 1843 in a book by Alexander Keith, a Church of Scotland clergyman and an advocate of Jewish "restoration" who had traveled to Palestine in 1839 and had seen that it was inhabited. Lord Shaftesbury used similar wording in 1853. The first use by a Zionist came in 1901, when Israel Zangwill wrote that Palestine was "a country without a people."[cite:meq_land_without_people] [cite:aijac_slogan_origin] Historians debate what the phrase meant. One reading takes it literally, as a claim that the land was empty. The other holds that it meant a land "without a nation," a population that had not organized itself as a people in the national sense. The second reading is the stronger defense of the phrase, and it turns on the third of the questions above rather than the first. Whatever its users intended, every Ottoman and British census shows a populated country.

"A two-thousand-year war." A companion claim holds that Jews and Muslims have been fighting over this land for two millennia. Jews, Muslims and Christians lived together under Ottoman rule, as [scene:s00e|the section on coexistence] sets out. The national conflict is roughly a century old: it began with modern political Zionism in 1897 and with the British Mandate, and the first Palestinian national movement was organized jointly by Muslims and Christians: a national alignment, not a religious one. A third slogan of the same family, that the Arabs "rejected every offer," compresses a record that runs in both directions. Arab leaders rejected the Peel plan of 1937 and the partition plan of 1947; Israel's refugee offer at Lausanne in 1949 was made only within a full peace and later withdrawn; and the offer at Camp David in 2000 is disputed by participants on the American side, who say it was never written down. Those episodes belong to later chapters of this library. What the three slogans share is that each is short enough to travel, and the documented history behind each is longer and, in each case, less flattering to the side that repeats it.

The population, counted and growing. The panel below gathers the figures the British authorities and the United Nations recorded in the decades after the Ottoman census. Britain's 1922 census counted 757,182 people. Britain recorded 376,415 Jewish immigrants between 1920 and 1946. The United Nations Special Committee on Palestine (UNSCOP) estimated the population at about 1.85 million in late 1946. These figures bear on both of the claims this section examines. They show a substantial population on the land when the Mandate began, which disposes of "a land without a people" for the twentieth century as the 1871–72 census does for the nineteenth. They also show that immigration was a substantial part of the change that followed. The counts come from different authorities using different methods, and the Ottoman figure excluded the Bedouin, so the growth from 381,954 to about 1.85 million cannot be read off as a single like-for-like series.

The strongest case on each side. Put at its strongest, the Jewish claim to indigeneity rests on what is not in dispute: ancient kingdoms in the land, and a religious, cultural and historical connection to it documented across more than three thousand years in archaeology and text.[cite:substack_historical_record_balfour] Put at its strongest, the Palestinian claim rests on what is equally documented: a substantial Arabic-speaking population, counted by the Ottoman state itself, present continuously for centuries, with genetic evidence of long-term local ancestry, and forming the great majority of the land's people when the modern contest began.[cite:cjpme_historical_demography] [cite:factually_archaeological_evidence] Neither case requires the other to be false. Each popular version of the argument becomes false only at the point where it denies the other.

What the record does not settle. It settles the facts: an ancient Jewish connection, a counted and continuous Arab population, and a modern national identity on both sides that took shape through comparable nineteenth- and twentieth-century political processes. None of those three facts cancels either of the others. The record does not settle what follows from them politically: who should hold sovereignty, in what borders, under what arrangement. Those are questions of law and politics, and the historical record can inform them without deciding them. What it does rule out is the framing of "who is truly indigenous" as a contest with one legitimate winner. The documents do not support that framing for either side.

chapters.label: Chapter 3
chapters.title: Words and Names
chapters.intro:
Several words in this history carry arguments inside them. This chapter examines them before the story uses them: four words that are often swapped for one another (Hebrew, Jewish, Israeli and Zionist), the name "Israel," the term "Semitic," the word "antisemitism," and the symbols on the state's flag and seal. It comes after the land and before the peoples because later chapters cannot report what anyone said or did without these words, and because each has a documented history that is shorter, or longer, than people tend to assume.

It opens with those four words, because almost every later argument depends on keeping them apart. It then turns to Genesis 32, where the name first appears, given to one man, Jacob, at verse 28, and formed from El and a root meaning "to strive."[cite:genesis_32_biblegateway] [cite:wiki_israel_name] A second section offers a symbolic reading of the name, IS–RA–EL, labeled from its first line to its last as a reading and not a finding. Then comes the word "Semitic," coined by Schlözer in 1781 for a family of languages that includes Hebrew, Arabic and Amharic.[cite:wiki_semitic_etymology] Before the history of the word "antisemitism" comes the hatred it names, which is far older: the blood libel from Norwich in 1144, the badge decrees, the expulsion from England in 1290, Damascus in 1840, Kishinev in 1903 and the forged Protocols.[cite:rs_ch01_ushmm_bloodlibel] [cite:rs_ch01_ushmm_protocols] The word itself follows, from Renan's "Semitic race" to Wilhelm Marr's League of Antisemites in 1879.[cite:wiki_marr_1879] A section on symbols sets the menorah against the Star of David and traces the flag from Basel in 1897 to its confirmation on 28 October 1948.[cite:wiki_flag_of_israel] The chapter ends with the word as a shield: the IHRA definition and its rivals, its path from guideline toward law, and the record number of antisemitic incidents the ADL counted in 2024.[cite:peacenow_ihra_faq] [cite:algemeiner_adl_2024]

Two conclusions run through it. The root of "antisemitism" is a misnomer, and its meaning, hatred of Jews, is settled. Whether the word also reaches criticism of a state is the live dispute, and the chapter sets out who holds each position without deciding between them.

sections.h: Four Words: Hebrew, Jewish, Israeli, Zionist
sections.html:
Four words are often used as if they meant the same thing: Hebrew, Jewish, Israeli and Zionist. They do not. One is a language and an ancient name. One names a people and a religion. One is a citizenship. One is a political movement. Each has its own history, and the groups of people they describe overlap without matching. Much of the confusion in arguments about this region starts when one of the four is quietly swapped for another, so that a statement about a state is heard as a statement about a people, or a statement about a people is taken as a statement about a political program. This section takes the four words in turn, sets out what the record says about each, and ends with a diagram of who belongs to which.

Hebrew: a language and an ancient name. The word first appears in the Bible at Genesis 14:13, which calls Abram "Abram the Hebrew," ha-ʿIvri. [cite:fw_bg_gen1413] [cite:fw_thetorah_hebrews] Where the word comes from is not settled. The rabbis of the early commentary Genesis Rabbah already offered several explanations: that Abram stood on one side and the whole world on the other, that he descended from an ancestor named Eber, or that he came from across the river. Britannica notes that it may come from ʿever, "the other side." [cite:fw_thetorah_hebrews] [cite:fw_brit_hebrew_people] Many scholars have also linked the word to the Ḥabiru or ʿApiru, a marginal social class named in Near Eastern texts of the second millennium BCE, but there is no consensus on that link. [cite:fw_thetorah_hebrews] In the Hebrew Bible itself, "Hebrew" is mostly the name that other peoples use for the Israelites, or that Israelites use of themselves when speaking to foreigners; it is rarely their everyday name for themselves. Reference books follow a rough convention, "Hebrews" for the earliest period, then "Israelites," then "Jews" after the exile in Babylon, though the ancient texts do not follow it strictly. [cite:fw_brit_hebrew_people]

Today the word mostly names a language. Hebrew is a Semitic language of the Northwest branch, alongside Aramaic. [cite:fw_brit_hebrew_lang] A common line holds that for centuries it was used only in prayer and scripture. Half of that is right. Hebrew stopped being anyone's everyday spoken language over several centuries; scholars usually put the end somewhere between about 200 and 400 CE, with Aramaic taking its place in daily speech, and Britannica dates the start of the decline as early as the third century BCE. [cite:fw_wiki_mishnaic] [cite:fw_aha_medieval] [cite:fw_brit_hebrew_lang] But it never shrank to prayer alone. Through the Middle Ages it remained a working written language for poetry, both religious and secular, for some legal contracts, for philosophy and science, and for grammar and dictionaries. [cite:fw_aha_medieval] What came back in the late nineteenth century was Hebrew as a spoken mother tongue. Eliezer Ben-Yehuda moved to Jerusalem in 1881 and raised a son described as the first child to grow up speaking modern Hebrew; teachers who made Hebrew the language of their schools played a large part. [cite:fw_mjl_benyehuda] In 2018 the Knesset's Nation-State Law named Hebrew "the state's language" and gave Arabic a "special status"; NPR reported that this removed Arabic's earlier standing as an official language. [cite:fw_adalah_nsl] [cite:fw_npr_nsl]

Jewish: a people and a religion. To be Jewish is understood both as belonging to a people and as belonging to a religion, and Pew found that American Jews weigh the two differently: some see it mainly as religion, others as culture or ancestry. [cite:fw_pew2020_report] Under traditional Jewish law, a Jew is anyone born to a Jewish mother or converted according to that law. [cite:fw_mjl_whoisjew] In 1983 the American Reform rabbinate added that the child of a Jewish father may also be presumed Jewish, a presumption to be confirmed by public acts of Jewish identification such as a Hebrew name or a Bar or Bat Mitzvah. [cite:fw_ccar_1983] Israel's Chief Rabbinate, which controls Jewish marriage in Israel, does not accept every definition the movements use. [cite:fw_mjl_whoisjew] In Pew's 2020 survey of American Jews, 27 percent described themselves religiously as atheist, agnostic or "nothing in particular" while still considering themselves Jewish by ancestry or culture. [cite:fw_pew2020_report]

Nor is there one Jewish appearance. The Beta Israel of Ethiopia were recognized as Jews by Israel's Sephardi Chief Rabbi in 1973, and Operation Solomon in 1991 flew more than 14,000 of them to Israel. [cite:fw_ynet_betaisrael] Israel's statistics bureau counted 168,800 residents of Ethiopian origin at the end of 2022. [cite:fw_israelfact_immig] India had three historic Jewish communities, the Bene Israel near Mumbai, the Cochin Jews of Kerala and the Baghdadi Jews who came in the British era; most have since emigrated, chiefly to Israel. [cite:fw_jvl_india] In Kaifeng, China, a Jewish community is recorded from the Middle Ages, and several hundred people there still claim that descent, though Israel and Orthodox authorities require them to convert formally. [cite:fw_wiki_kaifeng] In the United States, Pew found that 8 percent of Jewish adults identify as Hispanic, Black, Asian, multiracial or another race, and 15 percent of those under thirty; the Jews of Color Initiative, counting differently, estimates at least 12 to 15 percent. [cite:fw_pew2020_key] [cite:fw_joci_counting] Israel's statistics bureau put the world's Jewish population at nearly 15.9 million on 1 January 2026, about 46 percent of them in Israel, as reported by i24NEWS; the Jewish Agency's estimate for the start of 2024 was 15.8 million. [cite:fw_i24fr_rh2026] [cite:fw_toi_wjp2024] Most of the world's Jews live outside Israel.

Israeli: a citizenship. An Israeli is a citizen of the State of Israel, whatever his or her religion or ancestry. [cite:fw_cbs_st02] In its release of 9 September 2026, Israel's Central Bureau of Statistics put the population at about 10.3 million: about 7.83 million "Jews and others," about 2.17 million Arabs, and about 304,000 foreign nationals. [cite:fw_uanews_rh2026] [cite:fw_i24fr_rh2026] Arabs are therefore about a fifth of the population. Most are Muslims, about 1.85 million at the end of 2025; Christians number about 184,000, most of them Arabs; and the Druze about 150,000 (at the end of 2022). [cite:fw_jns_muslims] [cite:fw_israelfact_christians] [cite:fw_cbs_druze2023] The bureau's "others" are mostly immigrants who came under the Law of Return, which since 1970 admits the children, grandchildren and spouses of Jews, but who are not registered as Jews themselves. [cite:fw_cbs_117_2026] [cite:fw_jvl_lor] Recent releases no longer report Jews as a separate headline figure; the last separate count found for this book was 7.2 million in 2023, about 73 percent. [cite:fw_wiki_israelijews]

Two details keep the count honest. First, the bureau counts residents, not only citizens. Its figures include East Jerusalem since 1967 and the Golan since 1982, and most Palestinians in East Jerusalem hold permanent residency rather than citizenship, as many Golan Druze long did. [cite:fw_cbs_st02] [cite:fw_toi_ej2020] [cite:fw_wiki_druze] Second, Israel's own records keep citizenship apart from a second entry called le'om, usually translated "nationality," which records a person as Jewish, Arab and so on. In 2013 Israel's Supreme Court refused to let a group of citizens register their nationality as "Israeli," holding that no distinct Israeli nationality had been shown to exist. [cite:fw_versa_ornan] In Israeli law, then, "Israeli" is a citizenship and not a nationality, which is one reason the words are so easily confused.

Zionist: a political movement. Zionism is the movement that sought a Jewish national home, and later a state, in the Land of Israel, and that has supported that state since 1948. [cite:fw_je_basel] [cite:fw_brit_basel] It is a political position, not a birthright: a person can be Jewish without being a Zionist, and a Zionist without being Jewish. It also did not begin with Theodor Herzl, though he gave it its organization. In 1843 Yehuda Alkalai, a Sephardi rabbi near Belgrade, called for organized settlement in the land, and later settled there himself. [cite:fw_jvl_alkalai] In 1862 Rabbi Zvi Hirsch Kalischer argued that redemption could begin by human effort, and the socialist Moses Hess argued that the Jews would remain a homeless people until they had a country of their own. [cite:fw_je_kalischer] [cite:fw_brit_hess] After the pogroms of 1881 Leon Pinsker published Auto-Emanzipation anonymously in 1882 and became a leader of the "Lovers of Zion" societies; the first Bilu pioneers landed at Jaffa in July 1882, and Baron Edmond de Rothschild began funding the new colonies in late 1882. [cite:fw_brit_pinsker] [cite:fw_jvl_firstaliyah] [cite:fw_ramathanadiv] Nathan Birnbaum coined the word "Zionism" in 1890. [cite:fw_jvl_birnbaum]

What Herzl added was the organization. His book Der Judenstaat appeared in February 1896, and it treated Argentina as well as Palestine as possible territories. [cite:fw_wiki_judenstaat] In August 1897 the First Zionist Congress in Basel founded the Zionist Organization, elected Herzl its president, and adopted a program seeking "a publicly and legally assured home in Palestine." [cite:fw_wiki_firstcongress] [cite:fw_je_basel] Even then the destination was argued over: in 1903 the movement voted to study a British offer of land in East Africa, in present-day Kenya, before rejecting it in 1905. [cite:fw_jvl_uganda] The movement had many schools: political, practical, labour, religious, revisionist and cultural, which disagreed about borders, methods and whether a state was the goal at all. [cite:fw_wiki_types] Who came first moves the start of the story back by half a century. It does not change how the state was built, which is the subject of the volumes that follow.

Jews who are not Zionists, and Zionists who are not Jews. Opposition to Zionism has come from Jews from the beginning. In 1885 American Reform rabbis declared that Jews were "no longer a nation, but a religious community" and rejected a return to Palestine, a position the movement revised in 1937. [cite:fw_aja_pittsburgh] The socialist Bund, founded in Vilna weeks after the Basel Congress, opposed Zionism and argued for Jewish life where Jews already lived. [cite:fw_wiki_bund] Within Orthodoxy, the Satmar rabbi Joel Teitelbaum argued in 1961 that Zionism is incompatible with Judaism, and Neturei Karta, founded in Jerusalem in 1938 (some accounts say 1937), rejects the State of Israel outright; it numbers in the low thousands, and other Haredi bodies have disavowed its activities. [cite:fw_wiki_vayoel] [cite:fw_wiki_nk] In January 2019 the American group Jewish Voice for Peace declared itself opposed to Zionism. [cite:fw_972_jvp] These positions are told more fully in [scene:s00b3|Dissent from Every Lineage].

Zionism has also had non-Jewish supporters. Christian Zionism grew out of English Puritan "restorationism" in the seventeenth century and later out of dispensationalist theology, which reads Jewish return to the land as part of a prophetic sequence. [cite:fw_wiki_christianzionism] In 1891 the American evangelist William Blackstone petitioned President Benjamin Harrison to "give Palestine back" to the Jews. [cite:fw_wiki_blackstone] Christians United for Israel, founded in 2006, announced in December 2020 that it had passed 10 million members, a figure it counts itself and has not defined. [cite:fw_heritagefl_cufi] How many Jews call themselves Zionists depends heavily on how the question is asked. Recent American surveys range from 37 percent, in a survey for the Jewish Federations, to about 80 percent "Zionist or slightly Zionist," in an opt-in panel run by the Jewish People Policy Institute, and federation leaders put part of the gap down to disagreement over what the word means. [cite:fw_inss_jfna] [cite:fw_jppi_2024] [cite:fw_jweekly_2026]

The diagram above puts the three groups of people side by side. The circles overlap, but none contains another. A person can be Jewish, Israeli and Zionist at once; or Jewish and Zionist but not Israeli; or Jewish, living in Israel, and opposed to Zionism, as Neturei Karta, founded in Jerusalem, is; or Jewish and neither, the position of the Satmar movement's founding text and of the organization Jewish Voice for Peace. About a fifth of Israel's residents are Arab, and some of the bureau's "others" are not registered as Jewish. And there are Zionists who are neither Jewish nor Israeli, the Christian Zionists among them. Hebrew has no circle, because it is a language and an ancient name, not a group anyone joins today.

What the record shows, and what it does not. The record settles the distinctions themselves. Hebrew is a language and an ancient name; Jewish is a people and a religion, entered by birth or conversion and held by believers and non-believers alike; Israeli is a citizenship shared by Jews, Arabs and others; and Zionism is a political movement whose ideas go back to the 1840s and whose organization dates from 1897. Not all Jews are Zionists, not all Israelis are Jews, and not all Zionists are Jews. Treating any of these words as a synonym for another produces errors in both directions: it turns criticism of a state or a movement into an accusation against a people, and it turns a people into the agent of a state's policy. The record also leaves some things open. The origin of the word "Hebrew" is debated; no single date marks the end of spoken Hebrew; the share of Jews who are Zionists depends on how the word is defined and how the question is asked; and Israel's headline statistics now combine Jews with "others," so the exact Jewish share of the population in 2026 is not published as a single figure. The section on [scene:s00c|Zionism and Judaism] takes the distinction between the religion and the movement further.

sections.h: Jacob Becomes Israel: What Genesis 32 Says
sections.html:
Before the word "Israel" named a people, a land or a state, it named one man. Its first appearance in the Hebrew Bible is a renaming, given at the end of a night of wrestling, in the thirty-second chapter of Genesis. Most of the ways the word is used today, as the name of a nation, of a promised land, of a modern country, are later layers built on that verse. Reading it on its own terms is the first step in seeing which layer is which.

The story runs through Genesis 32:22–32. Jacob is alone at the ford of the Jabbok river, on the night before he is to meet, and be reconciled with, the twin brother he had deceived years earlier. A figure wrestles with him through the night. The text calls that figure a man and an angel, and Jacob, afterward, in his own words, calls it God, seen face to face. He names the place Peniel, "face of God," because, in his words, "I saw God face to face, and yet my life was spared." Before the wrestling ends comes the verse on which everything else in this section turns. Genesis 32:28 reads, in the rendering consistent across the major translations: "Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel; for you have struggled with God and with men, and have prevailed."[cite:genesis_32_biblegateway] The Hebrew of the final clause, כִּי־שָׂרִיתָ עִם־אֱלֹהִים וְעִם־אֲנָשִׁים וַתּוּכָל, says "for you have striven with God and with men, and have prevailed."

The verse is documented as the word's first occurrence anywhere in the biblical text. The word Israel appears 2,362 times across the Hebrew and Christian scriptures, 2,284 times in the Hebrew Bible and 78 times in the New Testament, and every one of those uses comes after this one.[cite:genesis_32_biblegateway] The later biblical authors themselves treated Genesis 32 as the name's point of origin. The prophet Hosea, writing centuries afterward, recapitulates the same story in Hosea 12:3–4, which shows that the episode was understood within the tradition as the source of the name, not as one story among many that happened to use it.

What the name means. The Hebrew name Yisra'el (יִשְׂרָאֵל) joins two elements. One is El (אֵל), the ancient Semitic word for God, which was shared across Canaanite, Ugaritic and other Northwest Semitic languages and was not exclusive to Hebrew; it is the same shared root that appears in [scene:s00b|the section on the word "Semitic"]. The other is a root connected to sarah (שָׂרָה), "to strive, contend, or prevail." It is the root that also gives Sarah, Abraham's wife, her name, with connotations of "princess," or of one who contends with authority.[cite:wiki_israel_name] This derivation is not contested. It is the consistent reading of the standard Hebrew lexicons, Brown-Driver-Briggs among them, of rabbinic commentary and of Christian biblical scholarship alike.

The grammar allows two readings, and both are documented in the scholarly literature. With El as the object, the name means "he struggles with God," which matches the verse's own explanation of it. With El as the subject, it means "God strives," that is, God contending on Jacob's behalf or through him.[cite:wiki_israel_name] The text does not say which was intended, and this book does not choose between them.

The wordplay in the text. The renaming also sets the new name against the old one. Jacob's birth name, Ya'akov, is related to akev, "heel": he was born grasping the heel of his twin, Esau, and the root carries connotations of crookedness and of following from behind. The letters of Yisra'el can also evoke yashar, "straight" or "upright." Several Hebrew-language sources read this as a deliberate contrast built into the text: the grasping, deceptive Jacob against the upright, prevailing Israel, one person before and after a transformation.[cite:wiki_jacob] The two notes should be kept distinct. Sarah, "to strive," is the derivation the lexicons give; yashar, "upright," is an echo the letters allow, a play on sound and sense rather than a second etymology.

The layers added later. The common assumption is that "Israel" has always simply meant the Jewish nation, or the Promised Land. The text says something narrower. At the moment the name is given, it belongs to exactly one person: Jacob, who had deceived his brother and fled his own family, and who wrestles through a night and comes out of it renamed as one who has struggled and prevailed. Generations later the name passes to the descendants of his twelve sons. Centuries after that it becomes attached to a specific territory. Only in 1948 does it become the name of a modern nation-state. Each is a separate layer, added at a separate time, and each is worth tracking on its own rather than read backward into the verse as if the four had always been one thing.

Outside the Bible, the name's history runs on a different track, through inscriptions rather than scripture. Its earliest mention outside the biblical text, on the Merneptah stele, where Israel already appears as a people, is set out in [scene:ah_s01|the section on the ancient record].

What the verse settles, and what it does not. As a primary source, the verse establishes that the word's first appearance names one individual after one event, and the lexicons establish the derivation from El and sarah with high confidence. What the verse does not establish is how later biblical authors, ancient Israelite communities or modern political movements would extend the word. Those are separate and later developments, each documented in its own right. Reading the verse in its original context is not a claim about every later use of the word, in either direction: it neither empties the later meanings of force nor shows that they were present from the start. Nor does the documented etymology support any connection to Egyptian deities. A symbolic reading that breaks the name into IS, RA and EL works on the English transliteration rather than the Hebrew, and it is kept apart, and labeled as a reading, in [scene:s00g|the next section].

sections.h: IS–RA–EL: A Symbolic Reading of the Name, Labeled as One
sections.html:
This section is an interpretation, not a finding. Everything in it below the documented etymology of the previous section is a symbolic reading that this book offers and labels as such. It does not claim that ancient Hebrew scribes built the names of Egyptian gods into the word Israel, and it does not replace the Hebrew derivation from El and sarah, "to strive," which remains the scholarly record. It is included because readings of this kind are old, are named and practiced inside the religious traditions themselves, and are worth stating precisely, with their limits drawn in plain view.

The reading. Read through an esoteric lens rather than a historical-linguistic one, the name resolves into three syllables, which some inner traditions treat as a "consciousness architecture." IS evokes Isis, the Egyptian goddess associated in Hermetic and other inner-tradition frameworks with the receptive, magnetic, lunar principle, the polarity later traditions would call the divine feminine.[cite:wiki_isis_egyptian] RA evokes the Egyptian solar deity: radiant and generative, the polarity later traditions call the divine masculine. In this reading the middle syllable stands for the active, outward-moving principle, set in deliberate symbolic contrast to IS.[cite:wiki_ra_egyptian] EL, the third syllable, is different in kind. It is not a symbolic borrowing but the actual ancient Semitic word for God, the same root the documented etymology identifies. In the esoteric reading it stands for the unified field above both polarities, the divine that receives their integration.[cite:wiki_semitic_etymology] Read this way, "Israel" names neither a place nor a people but a state of being: the integration of feminine and masculine under the divine. One symbolic reading holds that this is what Genesis 32 describes happening to one man in a single night.

Where this reading rests should be stated exactly. The IS and RA readings are a modern esoteric reading of the English transliteration of the name. They do not work on the Hebrew original, Yisra'el, whose elements are El and the root sarah. The single piece of the reading that is real etymology is EL. What the reading proposes is a resonance rather than a derivation: that consciousness-transformation traditions across the ancient Near East and Egypt shared a common structural language of polarity, integration and ascent, and that the Jacob and Israel story reads coherently within that shared framework whether or not the etymology is literal.

Jacob as anyone. The heart of the reading is not the syllables but what it does with the story. Under this lens, Genesis 32 is less a genealogical account of where one group's name came from than a template. Jacob is any person who confronts honestly the crookedness the text itself names in him, the grasping, deceptive "heel" of his birth name, and who wrestles with both the human and the divine and comes through transformed into the state the name describes: upright, prevailing, in direct relation to God. Scripture, on this reading, works less as a history book than as a manual, describing a transformation open to whoever undertakes the struggle rather than a record reserved for one line of descent.[cite:sacks_jacob_israel]

That part of the reading is not new, and it is not confined to esoteric sources. Rabbi Jonathan Sacks, a mainstream and widely respected Orthodox authority, wrote of Jacob and Israel as two aspects of the same person, and asked his readers: "Are we Jacob, embarrassed by who we are? Or are we Israel, with the courage to stand upright?"[cite:sacks_jacob_israel] The reading of the story as an inner transformation has real roots in traditional Jewish commentary. The layer that is not part of mainstream Jewish or Christian commentary is the specifically esoteric one, IS–RA–EL as Isis, Ra and El, with its Hermetic vocabulary of polarity. That layer is this book's own interpretive addition, not a claim about anyone's historical intent. Nor does the transformation reading cancel the other: the personal reading and the national-genealogical one both stand in the text's own history of reception, and neither erases the other.

Reading below the surface is the traditions' own practice. A common objection holds that this is mere wordplay, with no basis and nothing to do with the religious traditions themselves. The IS and RA syllables, as shown above, have no basis in the Hebrew. But the broader practice of reading scripture on more than one level is not a modern imposition from outside. Both Judaism and Islam built it into their own formal scholarship and gave it names.

Rabbinic Judaism has PaRDeS, a structured four-level exegesis. Peshat is the plain, literal sense; Remez, the hint, is the allegorical or symbolic layer; Derash is the comparative and homiletical meaning drawn out through study; and Sod, the secret, is the mystical layer, the root from which the word "Kabbalah" itself grows. One documented framing of the method puts the idea of ascent at its center: the Torah descends from above, and the reader ascends through the four levels from below.[cite:wiki_pardes_exegesis] Islamic scholarship developed a parallel and equally formal distinction between tafsir, conventional exoteric exegesis, and ta'wil, esoteric or mystical interpretation, practiced across Shia, Sufi and Sunni traditions since at least the eighth century CE. The Quran itself points to an inner meaning, in the account of Khidr, whose actions require their own ta'wil, an inner explanation distinct from how they appear on the surface.[cite:wiki_esoteric_quran_interpretation] [cite:britannica_tawil] Neither tradition discards the literal level. PaRDeS and ta'wil both keep the plain sense as one real and valid layer among several, and neither implies that every practitioner reads every passage esoterically.

Christian scholarship held a similar standard. Origen, the third-century Church Father, was highly influential in establishing allegorical interpretation as a serious and legitimate mode of reading scripture within early Christianity, and the practice shaped the centuries of exegesis that followed.[cite:wiki_aggadah] It did not stay marginal. In the words of documented scholarship on medieval exegesis, "High Medieval Catholic scripture commentary was only thought perfect if it contained both elements, both literal and allegorical interpretation."[cite:hnet_tawil_medieval_catholic] By that standard, a purely literal reading with no allegorical layer would have counted as incomplete, not as more faithful. What many readers are taught today as simply "the" meaning of scripture is, by the tradition's own historical measure, half of what a complete reading was meant to include. That is a statement about a historical standard of interpretation, not about why any particular person's religious education stressed one layer over another.

Why the name carried weight anywhere. The reading also makes one argument about the modern political history. The founders of the Zionist movement weighed territories other than Palestine, Argentina and Uganda among them, before Palestine was chosen; that record is set out in [scene:s00c|the section on Zionism and Judaism]. The argument here is narrower. Whichever territory had been chosen, naming the resulting state "Israel," rather than "Zion" alone or a geographic name, would have carried the same layered scriptural weight, because that weight travels with the word and not with a particular stretch of land.[cite:genesis_15_18] On this reading, the founders were never only choosing a country; they were choosing which ancient vocabulary of transformation to attach to a modern political project. The question the argument raises is whether the name given to the state in 1948 was an incidental label or a deliberate invocation of religious and mystical weight. This book has no primary source establishing what the founders consciously intended on this point. What can be said is that the name carries this weight whatever the intent, and that a secular political movement chose it.

Where this reading stops. It does not establish, and cannot, that Herzl, the Basel Congress, Israel's founders in 1948 or any other historical actor intended an Egyptian or Hermetic meaning when the state was named; it rests on no documented evidence of any of them discussing such symbolism. It does not override the documented Hebrew etymology, which remains the linguistic record. It does not establish what ancient Israelite communities understood the word to mean as the name of a tribe or nation, and it does not displace the word's later, documented use as the name of a people and a place. What it offers is a symbolic key to the name's layered resonance, one a reader may apply to the documented facts or set aside. It is a reading, and it is offered only as one.

sections.h: "Semitic": A Family of Languages
sections.html:
A common claim folds two statements into one sentence: that "antisemitic" means anti-Jewish, and that criticism of Israel is therefore antisemitic. The first half is historically sound. The second is the subject of a live, documented dispute among scholars and governments. Neither can be weighed properly until the root word is clear, because almost every later argument over the term depends on remembering, or forgetting, where it came from.

The root is Shem, in Hebrew שֵׁם, one of the three sons of Noah in the genealogy of Genesis 10. In 1781 the German scholar August Ludwig von Schlözer coined the term "Semitic" (semitisch) for the family of related languages that the biblical genealogy traced to Shem. [cite:wiki_semitic_etymology] Schlözer was working as a linguist, sorting languages by their relationships. His term was a classification of languages. It was not a racial category and not a religious one. Schlözer's framework grouped together the languages now called Hebrew, Aramaic, Arabic, Ge'ez, Akkadian and Phoenician. [cite:wiki_semitic_etymology] He coined it more than a century before Zionism existed as a political movement, and long before the word became politically loaded in either direction.

The label works the way "Romance languages" does. That name, taken from Rome, covers French, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese and Romanian, and nobody takes it to mean that the French and the Romanians are one ethnicity or share one religion. "Semitic" names a language family after a figure in Genesis in the same way. Through most of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries it stayed a term of the comparative philology classroom, used as uncontroversially as "Indo-European" or "Sino-Tibetan" to group related tongues. [cite:wiki_semitic_etymology]

The family as linguists describe it today includes Hebrew, Aramaic, Arabic, Amharic (spoken in Ethiopia), Tigrinya, Maltese, Ge'ez, Syriac and Mehri, as well as Akkadian, which is extinct. Their speakers include Arabs, Jews, Ethiopians, Assyrians, Chaldeans and Maltese, and by the word's original meaning all of them are Semitic peoples. [cite:wiki_semitic_etymology] This is not a contested claim. It is the definition an introductory course in Semitic linguistics teaches in its first week. In that original sense the word applies equally to a Hebrew speaker, an Arabic speaker and an Amharic speaker.

Where the family was spoken. Seen on a map, the family was spoken mainly in Mesopotamia, the Levant, Arabia and the Horn of Africa, and later across North Africa and on Malta. Semitic is one branch of the larger Afroasiatic family, alongside Egyptian, Berber, Cushitic, Chadic and Omotic, and it is described as the only branch with members that originated outside Africa. [cite:sm_eb_afroasiatic] [cite:sm_wp_afroasiatic] Its oldest written members are Akkadian, the language of Babylon and Assyria, and Eblaite, from the archives of Ebla in Syria, both of the third millennium BCE. [cite:sm_eb_akkadian] [cite:sm_eb_eblaite] On the Levantine coast and inland, the Canaanite languages included Phoenician, Hebrew, Moabite, Ammonite and Edomite, the earliest of which, Phoenician, was written from at least the eleventh century BCE; Hebrew is the only one still spoken. [cite:sm_eb_canaanite] [cite:sm_eb_phoenician] [cite:sm_wilsonwright] Aramaic, first the language of the Aramaeans, became by the seventh and sixth centuries BCE the common language of the Middle East, largely replacing Akkadian, and parts of Daniel and Ezra and both Talmuds are written in it. [cite:sm_eb_aramaic] In the south, Old South Arabian was written in Yemen from the eighth century BCE, and Ge'ez, the classical language of Aksum, remains the liturgical language of the Ethiopian church; Amharic, written in an adapted Ge'ez script, and Tigrinya are spoken in Ethiopia and Eritrea today. [cite:sm_eb_southarabian] [cite:sm_eb_geez] [cite:sm_eb_amharic] [cite:sm_eb_tigrinya]

How the branches subdivide is debated: scholars place Eblaite, Arabic and Old South Arabian differently. [cite:sm_wp_semitic] [cite:sm_eb_eblaite] So is the family's starting point. Proposals include the Levant, northern Arabia and the Syro-Arabian desert; a 2009 statistical study by Kitchen and colleagues placed the common ancestor of the known Semitic languages in the Levant about 5,750 years ago, an estimate its own authors call uncertain, and most scholars put the older Afroasiatic homeland in Africa. [cite:sm_wp_protosemitic] [cite:sm_kitchen2009] [cite:sm_wp_afroasiatic] None of the proposals lies in Europe. The one Semitic language native to Europe, Maltese, descends from a medieval Arabic dialect of Sicily brought to Malta by Arabic-speaking settlers, and is the only Semitic language written in the Latin alphabet. [cite:sm_wp_protosemitic] [cite:sm_brincat_maltese] [cite:sm_wp_maltese]

The map above places each language at the approximate centre of where it was spoken, coloured by branch, with dotted arrows for documented spreads: Phoenician to Carthage, traditionally founded from Tyre in 814 or 813 BCE; Aramaic across the Middle East and into the Persian empire; and Arabic, after the conquests of the seventh century, through the Levant, Egypt and North Africa, where it took the place of Aramaic and Coptic over several generations. [cite:sm_livius_carthage] [cite:sm_eb_aramaic] [cite:sm_wp_levantine] [cite:sm_rubenson] One arrow, from southern Arabia to Ethiopia, shows a disputed proposal and is labelled so. [cite:sm_kitchen2009]

A language family, not a race. Careful modern usage keeps "Semitic" for languages. [cite:sm_ej_semites] By the mid-nineteenth century the word had been stretched into a supposed race; [cite:sm_ej_semites] [cite:sm_etym_semite] Ernest Renan's history of the Semitic languages, published in 1855, read differences between languages as differences between peoples and called a "Semitic race" inferior to the Indo-European. [cite:sm_bnf_renan] Modern scholarship rejects these theories: the historian Shmuel Almog calls the racial label a misnomer, and the US Holocaust Memorial Museum notes that there is no scientific evidence for distinct biological races. [cite:sm_ej_semites] [cite:sm_almog_hyphen] [cite:sm_ushmm_antisem] The speakers of Semitic languages, past and present, include Akkadians, Phoenicians, Arameans, Jews, Arabs, speakers of Amharic, Tigrinya and other Ethiopian Semitic languages, Maltese and Assyrians; they share a language family, not a single ethnicity. [cite:sm_ej_semites] Nor are all Jewish languages Semitic: Yiddish is a Germanic language written in Hebrew letters, and Judeo-Spanish is a Romance language. [cite:sm_eb_yiddish] [cite:sm_eb_ladino] The everyday language of Palestinians is Palestinian Arabic, a South Levantine dialect of Arabic. [cite:sm_jarrar2014]

Palestinian Arabs belong to this family on two separate grounds. The first is language: Palestinians speak Arabic, a Semitic language in the same family as Hebrew, Aramaic and Amharic. The second is descent. Peer-reviewed population genetics, including the Y-chromosome study of Nebel and colleagues (2000) and the genome-wide study of Behar and colleagues published in Nature in 2010, documents that Palestinian and Jewish populations in the Levant share substantial common ancestry, consistent with descent from populations that have lived in the region continuously since antiquity. [cite:nebel_pop_genetics_2000] [cite:behar_2010_shared] Haber and colleagues' 2013 work on ancient Canaanite DNA points in the same direction. [cite:haber_2013_bronze] On this evidence, Palestinians and Israeli Jews share more common ancestry with each other than either does with populations elsewhere. [cite:nebel_pop_genetics_2000] [cite:behar_2010_shared] [cite:haber_2013_bronze] The same body of genetic research is used in this book to trace the Ashkenazi, Sephardi and Mizrahi Jewish lineages [scene:s00b2|Jewish lineages and the genetic record]; here it is applied to the other population that draws on the same regional ancestral pool. Palestinian Muslims and Palestinian Christians alike are, in the word's own sense, a Semitic people.

This is a linguistic and genetic fact, not an argument built to win a political point, and it does not by itself resolve any policy dispute between Israelis and Palestinians. It does rule out one rhetorical move. Actions against Palestinians cannot coherently be described as "pro-Semitic," and a political conflict between two Semitic-speaking populations cannot be described as a contest between Semites and anti-Semites. The word was never built to do that work.

Nor does the linguistic origin make later uses of the word illegitimate. Words change their meaning over time, and that is normal. The compound "antisemitism" took on its own meaning in the 1870s and 1880s, and that meaning, set by use rather than by the parts of the word, is hatred of Jews. In 1879 the German agitator Wilhelm Marr made "antisemitism" the name of his movement against Jews, a euphemism for Judenhass, Jew-hatred. [cite:wiki_marr_1879] [cite:wiki_antisemitism_etym] That history is told in full in [scene:s00b0|the history of the word "antisemitism"]. What matters here is its result. In its original meaning, antisemitism meant hostility toward Jewish people. It did not describe hostility toward Arabic speakers, and it never did. [cite:wiki_marr_1879]

The live dispute concerns a different extension of the word: toward political criticism of a state and of a political movement. The International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance's working definition of antisemitism, adopted in 2016, carries 11 attached examples, 7 of which describe criticism of Israel or Zionism as antisemitic under certain conditions. [cite:ihra_definition] Its critics read this as redirecting the word toward a new target. On 25 March 2021 the Jerusalem Declaration on Antisemitism, signed by more than 200 scholars including Omer Bartov, Christopher Browning, Michael Rothberg and Noah Feldman, kept the core definition but named exceptions: boycott of Israel (BDS), criticism of settlements and criticism of Zionism as an ideology are not antisemitic. [cite:jerusalem_declaration] The three competing definitions, the legal uses made of the IHRA text, and the strongest case its supporters make for it are set out in [scene:s00b1|the word as a shield].

A widely repeated everyday version of this extension substitutes another phrase for the word itself. It holds that opposing or criticizing Israel denies Jews their right to national self-determination, and is therefore discriminatory, keeping a charge close to antisemitism without using the word. The formula appears in pro-Israel commentary, where a 2019 formulation by Bari Weiss is among the most widely cited, in the materials of hasbara (public-diplomacy) organizations, and in critiques of those materials alike. [cite:currentaffairs_snappy_hasbara] It is a current, documented instance of the argument, not a hypothetical one.

The Jerusalem Declaration has serious, named critics of its own, and a fair account has to hear them where the dispute is first raised. Dr. Dana Barnett, a researcher at Israel's Begin-Sadat Center for Strategic Studies, and analysts writing for NGO Monitor have argued in print that the Declaration's explicit exceptions do less to clarify than to shelter. In their reading, permitting comparisons of Israeli policy to settler colonialism or apartheid, and classifying BDS as ordinary non-violent protest, creates cover for anti-Zionist advocacy that can, in specific instances, cross into real antisemitism. [cite:besa_jda_barnett] [cite:ngomonitor_jda_bogus] So the argument runs in both directions. Some credentialed scholars hold that the IHRA definition reaches too far into legitimate criticism; other credentialed scholars hold that the Jerusalem Declaration reaches too far toward giving cover to the real thing. Both positions are in print under their authors' names.

Why this belongs at the start of the book is simple. If "Semitic" names a language family and all its speakers, and Palestinians are Semitic-language speakers descended from the region's continuous population, then the conflict cannot be framed as Semites against anti-Semites. It is a documented political dispute between a state, a political movement, and a displaced population native to the land, all of whom are Semitic in the word's original sense. Every later subject in this book, from funding and lobbying to the wars and the peace negotiations, reads differently once that conflation is cleared away: claims and counter-claims can be judged as a historical dispute between two real populations, rather than arriving with a framing that makes one side's grievance illegitimate before the facts are examined.

What this does not settle should be said as plainly. Clearing up the root word does not decide who is right in any of the specific disputes documented later. It does not show that a given criticism of Israeli policy is legitimate, or that it is not; that depends on what is said and at whom it is aimed. The genetic studies describe populations and shared ancestry; they settle no one's rights. And the argument between the IHRA definition and the Jerusalem Declaration remains open. This book does not resolve it; it records who holds each position, on what grounds, and leaves the reader to weigh them.

sections.h: An Old Hatred, Before and After Its Name
sections.html:
The word "antisemitism" dates from 1879. The hatred it names is far older. Arguments over the word, and over where legitimate criticism of a state ends, can make it easy to lose sight of the thing itself: a long, documented history of accusation, legal exclusion, expulsion and killing directed at Jews as Jews. This section sets out that record plainly, from the medieval ritual-murder charge to a forged text that kept circulating into this century, because no honest account of the words that follow can be written without it.

The oldest of these accusations is the blood libel: the charge that Jews kill Christians in order to use their blood. Earlier references to the idea occur in the writings of Apion. Its first medieval case came at Norwich, in England, in 1144, after the body of a boy named William was found in the woods. [cite:rs_ch01_ushmm_bloodlibel] [cite:rs_ch01_globe_heng] The charge then spread. Ritual-murder accusations followed at Gloucester in 1168, Blois in 1171, Saragossa in 1182, Bristol in 1183, Fulda in 1235, Lincoln in 1255 and Munich in 1286. In the fourteenth century the accusation was joined to another, that Jews had poisoned wells, during the Black Death. [cite:rs_ch01_ushmm_bloodlibel]

The case at Trent shows how the charge worked once it took hold. In 1475 a two-year-old named Simon disappeared. The town's Jews were tortured until they confessed, and they were burned. Simon was later counted among the saints. In 1965 the Catholic Church removed him from the list of saints and repudiated the charge. [cite:rs_ch01_ushmm_bloodlibel] The confession that had condemned the Jews of Trent was a product of torture, and the institution that had honored the supposed victim formally withdrew the accusation.

Alongside the accusations came law. In 1215 the Fourth Lateran Council decreed that Jews must wear distinguishing dress and barred them from public office. England, according to reporting on the Church of England's later reckoning with these decrees and to the historian Geraldine Heng, was the first country to require Jews to wear a badge, in 1218. In 1222 church leaders meeting at Osney Abbey, near Oxford, adopted a badge decree of their own; about 3,000 Jews are thought to have lived in England at the time. [cite:rs_ch01_algemeiner_oxford1222] [cite:rs_ch01_globe_heng] England's Statute of Jewry of 1275 barred Jews from living among Christians. In 1290 Edward I expelled the Jews of England, the first such expulsion in Christendom. Jews were permitted to return only in 1656, under Cromwell. [cite:rs_ch01_globe_heng] [cite:rs_ch01_algemeiner_oxford1222]

The mechanism visible in these decrees is worth naming. The badge made Jews legible as a separate category in public. The bar on office closed the instruments of power to them. The Statute of Jewry separated them physically from their neighbors, and the expulsion of 1290 removed the community altogether. Each step was taken by a named authority: a church council, a king, a statute.

The blood libel did not stay in medieval Europe. On 5 February 1840 a Capuchin friar named Thomas and his servant disappeared in Damascus. The Capuchins accused the city's Jews of ritual murder, and the French consul, Ratti-Menton, backed the investigation. Two of the accused died under torture. Sixty-three Jewish children were seized to put pressure on their mothers. [cite:rs_ch01_ej_damascus] On 25 April 1840 Muhammad Ali ordered the torture stopped. After a mission by Moses Montefiore and Adolphe Crémieux, the surviving prisoners were freed on 28 August 1840, without any declaration of their innocence, and the Ottoman Sultan issued a firman repudiating the ritual-murder charge. [cite:rs_ch01_ej_damascus] The Damascus affair is instructive for the way power ran through it: the charge came from a religious order, a European consul lent it official weight, the torture was halted by a ruler's order, and the release came only after Montefiore and Crémieux's mission. The record cited here does not give the date of the Sultan's firman.

In the Russian Empire the twentieth century brought a pogrom and a new ritual-murder trial. The Kishinev pogrom began on Easter Sunday, 19 April 1903, after articles in an antisemitic newspaper; over three days, almost 50 Jews were killed. Between 1911 and 1913 Menachem Mendel Beilis was tried in Kiev on a ritual-murder charge, and acquitted. [cite:rs_ch01_ushmm_bloodlibel] By then the word "antisemitism" had existed for a generation, coined in Germany to make this same hostility sound modern and scientific; its history, and the Jewish name for the hatred, "Judeophobia," are traced in [scene:s00b0|the history of the word].

The same year as Kishinev saw the first appearance of a forgery that would outlast every exposure. The Protocols of the Elders of Zion, a fabricated plan for Jewish world domination, was first serialized in the St Petersburg newspaper Znamya in the autumn of 1903. In 1905 Sergei Nilus appended it to a book of his own. [cite:rs_ch01_ushmm_protocols] It did not remain a Russian text. In 1920 Henry Ford's newspaper, the Dearborn Independent, ran a 91-part series based on it. In August 1921 The Times of London showed that the text was largely copied from Maurice Joly's satire of 1864 and called it a forgery. Ford apologized in 1927. [cite:rs_ch01_ushmm_protocols]

Exposure did not end its circulation. Hitler cited the Protocols in Mein Kampf in 1925, the same year the first Arabic translation appeared in Damascus. In 1935 a Swiss court in Bern ruled against its publishers. [cite:rs_ch01_ushmm_protocols] In 1943 Hajj Amin al-Husseini, the former Mufti of Jerusalem, echoed the Protocols' themes in Arabic broadcasts from Berlin. [cite:rs_ch01_ushmm_protocols] The text kept circulating after the war: an Iranian English edition appeared in 1985; Article 32 of the Hamas charter of 1988 drew on it; an Egyptian television series of 41 parts drew on it in 2002, and a series on Hezbollah's Al-Manar channel in 2003. A Russian court ruled it a forgery in 1993. [cite:rs_ch01_ushmm_protocols] Each of these uses is tied to a named publisher, author, movement or broadcaster. The record documents those specific actors, not the peoples or faiths in whose names they claimed to speak.

Taken together, the record shows a hatred with a recognizable structure that long predates any modern dispute over Zionism or Israel: accusations of ritual murder, confessions extracted under torture, legal markers of separation, expulsion, and, in the twentieth century, a forged document that kept circulating after a newspaper, a court in Bern and later a Russian court had all exposed or ruled against it. That history reached its documented extreme in the Holocaust, told in [scene:hol_s05|the scale of the Holocaust].

Several things the sources gathered here do not settle. They do not give casualty figures for most of the medieval cases, nor the numbers of Jews expelled in 1290. They do not name the newspaper whose articles preceded the Kishinev pogrom, or record the date of the Sultan's firman after Damascus. Nor do they set out the causes historians give for why these accusations arose and spread when and where they did. What they do establish, case by case and date by date, is that this was a real hatred, aimed at Jews, enacted through named institutions and documents, and that it existed long before its modern name.

sections.h: "Antisemitism": A Word Named by the Haters
sections.html:
It is often said that "anti-Semitism" is a precise term: that the Semites are a people, and that the word names hatred of them. The word's own paper trail tells a more complicated story. A linguist named a family of languages in 1781. Race science turned that family into a "race" in the 1850s. A Jewish scholar first wrote "antisemitic" in 1860, to attack that race theory. Then, in 1879, a German agitator who was not Jewish made "antisemitism" the name of his own movement against Jews. The name is a misnomer. Its meaning is not.

The first step, told in [scene:s00b|the section on the root word], was a classification of grammar: in 1781 the Göttingen historian August Ludwig von Schlözer coined "Semitic" (semitisch) for a family of languages that today includes Hebrew, Aramaic, Arabic, Amharic, Tigrinya and Maltese. [cite:wiki_semitic_etymology] The term said nothing about blood, race or religion.

The second step turned the language label into a ranking of human beings. The French scholar Ernest Renan's comparative history of the Semitic languages, published in 1855, treated their speakers, Hebrews and Arabs alike, as a "Semitic race" inferior to the "Aryans." [cite:wiki_renan] [cite:wiki_antisemitism_etym] This was the race science of the era: a term invented to group grammars was converted into a judgment about peoples. Historians now regard "Semitic race" as a discredited category, which is why the word still causes confusion. [cite:wiki_antisemitism_etym]

The adjective came next, and it came from a Jewish scholar. In 1860 the bibliographer Moritz Steinschneider wrote of "antisemitic prejudices" (antisemitische Vorurteile) to rebut Renan's claim that Semitic peoples were inferior. [cite:wiki_antisemitism_etym] In that first use the target of the prejudice was the whole invented "Semitic race," Hebrews and Arabs alike. Within twenty years, men who hated Jews in Germany would take the word over and narrow it to one people.

The man most associated with that narrowing was Wilhelm Marr (1819–1904), a German journalist and political agitator. He was a Lutheran, not a Jew as is sometimes claimed. [cite:jvl_marr] [cite:wiki_marr_1879] In the 1840s he had been involved in radical left politics; later in life he turned to German nationalist and anti-Jewish politics. In 1879 he published a pamphlet, Der Sieg des Judenthums über das Germanenthum ("The Victory of Judaism over Germandom"), which argued that Jews held a disproportionate and threatening influence over German cultural and economic life. [cite:wiki_marr_1879] The same year he founded the League of Antisemites (Antisemiten-Liga), the first German organization devoted to the alleged Jewish threat and one of the first to use the term as a self-description. It called for forcing Jews out of Germany. His "Antisemitic Pamphlets" of 1881 spread the word further. [cite:wiki_marr_1879] [cite:jvl_marr]

The choice of word was deliberate, and its purpose is documented. "Antisemitism" was a euphemism for Judenhass, Jew-hatred. [cite:wiki_marr_1879] Historians of the period, including Moshe Zimmermann in his biography Wilhelm Marr: The Patriarch of Anti-Semitism (1986), show that Marr borrowed the scientific-sounding "Semitic" from contemporary linguistics to give an old religious and cultural hatred a modern, secular, pseudo-scientific surface, at a time when openly religious Jew-hatred was becoming less acceptable in educated German circles. [cite:wiki_marr_1879] [cite:jvl_marr] The logic of the borrowed term did real work. If Jews were a foreign "Semitic race," then neither conversion nor centuries of life in Germany could make them German. [cite:jvl_marr] [cite:wiki_marr_1879] The word was coined by the people doing the hating, about the people being hated.

Nothing in Marr's own writing, or in the founding activity of his League, shows any concern with Arabic speakers, Ethiopian Christians, Assyrian communities or any other Semitic-language population. [cite:wiki_marr_1879] [cite:wiki_antisemitism_etym] From its first day as the name of a movement, the word referred to one specific people, dressed in the borrowed language of a much broader linguistic category, and it kept that narrow sense in actual use through the century that followed. Zimmermann also reports a turn at the end of Marr's life: Marr renounced antisemitism in a text he never published. [cite:jvl_marr]

Jews had their own name for the hatred, and it said plainly who the target was. In 1882, after pogroms in the Russian Empire, the Odessa physician Leon Pinsker published Auto-Emancipation. He called the hatred "Judeophobia": an irrational fear of Jews, which he described as an inherited disease. [cite:jvl_pinsker] [cite:wiki_antisemitism_etym] Pinsker concluded that Jews needed a homeland of their own, which makes the pamphlet one of the founding texts of Zionism. [cite:jvl_pinsker] The pogroms, the blood libel and the older history of the hatred that Marr renamed are set out in [scene:ch01_hatred|an old hatred, before and after its name].

The last step in the word's history came from the institutions most concerned with it. In April 2015 the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance recommended writing "antisemitism" without a hyphen. Its reason was that the hyphen "allows for the possibility of something called Semitism," lending weight to a discredited racial classification. [cite:ihra_spelling_2015] Style guides followed, and The New York Times dropped the hyphen in 2021. [cite:wjc_nyt_spelling] The spelling change is a small thing with a clear meaning: the bodies most invested in the word agree that its root is wrong.

What, then, does the word mean now? Two things are true together. The root is a misnomer: "Semitic" describes languages, Palestinians who speak Arabic are as Semitic as anyone, and many Jews have never spoken a Semitic language at home. And the meaning is settled by use: since the 1880s "antisemitism" has meant hostility to Jews, and nothing broader. [cite:wiki_antisemitism_etym] [cite:ihra_spelling_2015] That cuts in both directions. The claim "Arabs are Semites too, so I cannot be antisemitic" does not hold, because words mean what they are used to mean, not what their parts suggest. Stretching the word to cover political criticism of a state does not hold automatically either; that dispute, and the competing definitions behind it, are documented separately in this book. The test is the target and the content of what is said, not the label.

The etymology settles what the word originally meant and how its meaning was fixed. It does not settle how any particular modern claim should be judged. Knowing that Marr chose the word to dignify Jew-hatred does not make criticism of Israeli state policy automatically legitimate, and it does not make such criticism automatically illegitimate. Those are separate questions. The record of the word answers only the first.

sections.h: Two Symbols and a Flag
sections.html:
Most people who see the flag of Israel take its six-pointed star to be the ancient sign of the Jewish people, carried onto the flag as it has always been. The documents tell a more layered story. Two symbols have a claim to represent Jewish tradition, and they are of very different ages. The older one, the seven-branched lampstand called the menorah, reaches back to the Temple. The younger one, the six-pointed star called the Magen David, or Shield of David, became a distinctively Jewish emblem in the Middle Ages. The flag carries the younger. That choice was made by a political congress in 1897 and confirmed by the new state in 1948, and both decisions are on the record.

The menorah is the older of the two by a wide margin.
