But they produced the documents through which land in Palestine would later change hands, and they explain how a sale could be perfectly lawful between owner and buyer and still pass over the heads of the people who farmed the land.

The starting point is a prohibition. According to a reference summary drawing on work by Ruth Kark published in 1984, foreigners were officially barred from buying land in Palestine from 1856, and the ban held in practice until 1867. [cite:rs_rd0_landpurchase_wiki] For a decade, then, the question of who could own land was settled against outsiders, whatever the paper said about who owned it inside the country.

Inside the country the paper itself was about to change. In 1858, as part of the reforms known as the Tanzimat, the Ottoman state issued a Land Code, the Arazi Kanunnamesi. It classified land into categories and required titles to be registered individually. The purpose was fiscal and military: registration would secure tax revenue and the conscription rolls. [cite:wiki_ottoman_land_code_1858] The same year brought the Tabu law, the law of title deeds. [cite:rs_rd0_kark_2017] The two can be read as giving practical form to promises made in the Edict of Gülhane of 1839, which had pledged security of property, a regular tax system and regular conscription, as the [scene:rd0_tanzimat|previous section] describes. A state that wished to tax and conscript its subjects needed a register of what they held.

In Palestine the register opened a gap between who owned land on paper and who worked it. Many cultivators did not register the land they farmed. A reference summary, citing Nasser Abufarha, gives the reason: registration brought taxes and conscription, and cultivators resisted it for that reason. [cite:rs_rd0_landpurchase_wiki] Title was frequently recorded instead in other names: village heads, urban merchants or notables, and absentee families living in Beirut and Damascus. The fellahin, the peasant cultivators, went on working the same fields, in practice as tenants. [cite:wiki_ottoman_land_code_1858] Nothing on the ground had to change for this to happen. The village continued to plough and harvest. What changed was the document, and the document now named someone else.

Historians have described the result in strong terms. The same reference summary quotes Yehoshua Porath, writing in 1977, that the 1858 code "brought about the appropriation by the influential and rich families of Beirut, Damascus" and other cities of vast tracts. [cite:rs_rd0_landpurchase_wiki] Kark, in a study published in 2017, finds that land came to be concentrated in "families of urban effendis (absentee landlords)" who lived in cities in Lebanon, Syria, Egypt and Palestine. [cite:rs_rd0_kark_2017] The two readings agree on the shape of what happened: title flowed to urban families, often living outside the district, while cultivation stayed in the villages.

The third law opened the door to outside buyers. In 1867 the Ottoman state issued a law allowing foreigners to acquire real property. Its Article II, as quoted by the United States minister at Constantinople in a dispatch of 5 January 1898, placed foreign landowners "upon terms of equality with Ottoman subjects in all things that concern their landed property." The United States accepted the law by protocol in 1874. [cite:rs_rd0_frus1898_law1867] The barrier of 1856 was gone, and a foreign buyer stood, on paper, where an Ottoman subject stood.

Kark treats the three measures, the 1858 Land Code, the 1858 Tabu law and the 1867 law on foreigners, as one process of privatization, the process that began land survey, registration and mapping in nineteenth-century Palestine. [cite:rs_rd0_kark_2017] In her account, effendi ownership made it easier for Jewish immigrants to buy part of this land. [cite:rs_rd0_kark_2017] She also counts what the purchases built on. According to Kark, more than 52 estate buildings became the first core of Jewish agricultural settlements, and at least 15 became the core of German Christian settlements or religious institutions. [cite:rs_rd0_kark_2017] Those numbers matter for the claim at the head of this section. The estates were not empty ground. They were properties with buildings on them, held by owners who could sell, and they were bought by more than one kind of newcomer: German Christians as well as Jews.

That finding also adjusts the timing in the familiar account. The deeds did not wait for the British Mandate to become saleable. By Kark's count, estates bought under Ottoman rule were already the cores of the first Jewish agricultural settlements. [cite:rs_rd0_kark_2017] The settlements of the First Aliyah, described in [scene:rd0_aliyah|the section on the First Aliyah], were built on land that this legal sequence had made purchasable.

Historians characterize the 1867 law differently, and the difference is real. A thesis written at Marmara University in Turkey on land ownership by foreigners and Jews in late Ottoman Palestine calls the 1867 law, the "Safer Kanunu," an attempt to bring foreigners' purchases under legal control. On that reading the law was meant to regulate, and Jews used gaps in it to buy fertile, strategic land on which the first settlements were later built. [cite:rs_rd0_marmara_thesis] The strongest form of this case is that the Ottoman state did try to keep control of land sales to outsiders, and that the purchases succeeded where the law fell short. Kark's reading is structural. The 1858–1867 laws together concentrated land in effendi hands, and that concentration made both Jewish and German Christian purchases easier. [cite:rs_rd0_kark_2017] The strongest form of her case is that the sales followed from who held the deeds, a structure the laws themselves produced. The first reading places the weight on the buyers' use of the law; the second on the structure of ownership the law produced. The sources do not settle which is right, and the two are not entirely exclusive.

The consequence reached its largest scale after this chapter's period. Under the British Mandate the registered titles were the instruments that could be sold. The largest single transfer to Zionist purchasing companies was the sale of the Beirut-based Sursock family's holdings in the Jezreel Valley in the early 1920s. The land was populated and cultivated, and after the sale its tenant cultivators were evicted, with compensation on terms set by the purchaser. [cite:wiki_ottoman_land_code_1858] Who bought, from whom and at what cost is told in [scene:s04j|the account of the Mandate-era land purchases].

The finding should be stated at its proper size. The 1858 code did not cause the Zionist project. It created a documentary form: a registered deed held in the name of someone who did not farm the land. Through that form, populated land could be lawfully transferred over the heads of the people living on it. [cite:wiki_ottoman_land_code_1858] That is why the phrase "willing local owners" is both accurate and incomplete. The owner on the register might be willing. The family in the field was often not on the register at all, having stayed off it to avoid taxation and conscription.

The record leaves important questions open. The sources here give no figure for how much land in Palestine went unregistered or was recorded in absentee names, and none for how many cultivators stood in the gap between title and tillage. Kark's counts of more than 52 and at least 15 estate buildings are not broken down here by date or place. The Marmara thesis is known only through its abstract, and the 1856 ban and the Porath and Abufarha passages only through a reference summary. Nor do these sources say how often, before 1896, a sale under these laws displaced the people who worked the land; for that period the documented consequence is the settlements themselves, and the evictions on record belong to the 1920s.

sections.h: Does Scripture Forbid a Jewish State? Jeremiah, the Three Oaths, and a Debate Older Than Zionism
sections.html:
While Ottoman law was turning the land of Palestine into registered deeds, an older argument about the land ran inside Judaism. Two confident answers circulate about what Jewish tradition says on a Jewish state. One holds that Judaism commands it. The other holds that Judaism forbids it. Each speaks as if the tradition had one voice. The texts tell a different story: the question was argued inside Judaism long before anyone founded a political movement, and it is still argued now. This section sets out the argument as the sources give it. It does not rule between the sides, because the tradition itself holds both readings.

The oldest text in the debate comes from the book of Jeremiah. The prophet instructed the exiles carried off to Babylon to build lives where they had been taken, and to "seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it" (Jeremiah 29:7). [cite:sefaria_jer29] The verse does not speak of a state at all. Its weight in the later argument lies in what it asks of exiles: to build lives where they are, and to seek the welfare of the place that holds them.

The second text is legal and far more specific. The Babylonian Talmud, in tractate Ketubot (110b–111a), derives from the Song of Songs three oaths. Israel was not to go up to the land "as a wall", meaning en masse and by force. Israel was not to rebel against the nations. And the nations, in turn, were not to oppress Israel excessively. [cite:w_three_oaths] Two of the three oaths bind Israel; the third binds the nations. That structure matters, because each side of the later debate reads the three clauses together and draws a different conclusion from them.

For many Orthodox authorities, the oaths settle the matter. On this reading, a sovereign Jewish state established before the coming of the Messiah violates them: a return to the land could come only through divine redemption, not human political action, and to force it is a transgression. [cite:w_vayoel][cite:neturei_karta] The fullest statement of this view came well after the period of this chapter. Rabbi Joel Teitelbaum, the rebbe of Satmar, built his work Vayoel Moshe, published in 1959, on the three oaths, and Neturei Karta holds the same view today. [cite:w_vayoel] Earlier, in 1912, Orthodox opposition to secular Zionism took organized form with the founding of Agudat Israel, whose story belongs to a later part of this library, including [scene:dh_s01|the story of Jacob de Haan].

The opposite case rests on a different set of authorities. Religious Zionists cite Nachmanides, who counted settling the land among the commandments. On that view, settling the land is a religious duty in its own right. They cite as well Rabbi Abraham Isaac Kook, who would become the first Ashkenazi chief rabbi of Mandate Palestine and who saw even secular Zionism as part of the process of redemption. [cite:w_religious_zionism][cite:w_kook] Rav Kook's office, like Agudat Israel, lies beyond 1896; he enters this account as the clearest named voice of the reading that would answer the oaths. Against the oaths themselves, religious Zionists have made two further arguments. Some argue that the oaths lapsed after centuries of persecution. Others argue that the Balfour Declaration and the League of Nations supplied the nations' consent. Both arguments are recorded as positions some religious Zionists hold, not as the view of every authority on that side.

The strongest form of each case deserves to be stated plainly. The anti-Zionist reading can point to a Talmudic text that speaks directly to a mass return by force, and to the many Orthodox authorities who read it as barring a state before the Messiah. The religious-Zionist reading can point to Nachmanides, a classical authority who treated settlement of the land as a commandment, and to the argument that the conditions the oaths assumed no longer held. Neither side invented its texts. Both are arguing from inside the same tradition, over the same pages.

A third position stood outside both religious readings and falls squarely inside this chapter's period. In 1885 American Reform Judaism, in its Pittsburgh Platform, rejected a return to Palestine altogether, on the ground that its members were "no longer a nation, but a religious community". [cite:pittsburgh_platform_1885] Reform did not argue from the oaths; it set the whole expectation of national restoration aside. It later reversed that position. The platform and its place among the responses of the 1880s are told in full in [scene:s02|the idea appears, 1862–1885].

Why did the argument become so sharp at the end of the nineteenth century? Part of the answer lies in who led the new movement. Early Zionism was mostly secular, and the record gives that as one reason so many rabbis opposed it at first. One reading is that a movement of this kind raised the very objection the oaths name: a return pursued by human political action rather than awaited. The shift from a return awaited in prayer to a return pursued by human action, and the rabbis who first argued for that shift, are traced in [scene:ideo_s01|from prayer to program].

Where does the debate stand today? Most Orthodox Jews in Israel accept or support the state. Anti-Zionist Haredi groups, Neturei Karta among them, remain a minority. The minority's existence is the point. A religious tradition that still contains, in organized and named form, both a reading that commands settlement and a reading that forbids a state before the Messiah cannot be summed up as saying either thing alone. Zionism is a political movement; Judaism is a religion whose authorities have argued over that movement from its beginning.

Several things the record available here does not settle. It does not give the text of Nachmanides' ruling or its date, so the strength of his statement can be reported only as religious Zionists cite it. It does not measure how many rabbis or communities held each reading before 1896; "many Orthodox authorities" is as precise as the sources allow.

sections.h: From Prayer to Program: The Thinkers and Groups Before Herzl, 1840–1890
sections.html:
The debate over the Three Oaths turned on whether people might bring about the return themselves. A common account has Zionism springing fully formed from the mind of Theodor Herzl in 1896. The record shows something slower and more interesting. The idea passed through stages over half a century: a hope held in prayer, then an argument by two rabbis that people might begin the return themselves, then a political program written by a secular socialist and a doctor, then small societies, a conference and a handful of pioneers, and finally a name. Herzl came last. What he added was not the idea but the organization.

For centuries before any movement, the return to Zion lived in the liturgy. It was prayed for daily and awaited as a messianic event, an act of God rather than a matter for politics. It was a hope, not a plan. That distinction matters for everything that follows, because the religious argument over the Three Oaths, set out in the previous section, turns on exactly this question: whether the return is something people may bring about, or something they must wait for.

The first break came from inside that religious world. Yehuda Alkalai, a Sephardi rabbi in Semlin, urged practical settlement in the land as a step toward redemption. He did so after the Damascus affair of 1840, a blood-libel case. [cite:w_alkalai] Zvi Hirsch Kalischer, a rabbi in Thorn, made a parallel case in a book of 1862: redemption, he argued, could begin by natural means, through settling and farming the land. [cite:w_kalischer] These two were the first to argue that human settlement could begin redemption. [cite:w_alkalai][cite:w_kalischer] In the terms of the older debate, they stood on the side that treated action in the land as part of a religious process rather than a forcing of the end. The earliest step from prayer toward program was taken by rabbis and argued in religious terms.

The step into secular politics came from two very different men, whose work is told in full in the next section [scene:s02|the idea appears, 1862–1885]. In the same year as Kalischer's book, 1862, the secular socialist Moses Hess published Rome and Jerusalem. [cite:wiki_moses_hess] Twenty years later, after the pogroms of 1881, the Odessa physician Leon Pinsker published Auto-Emancipation (1882), which argued that Jews needed a territory of their own, not necessarily Palestine. [cite:wiki_auto_emancipation] Between them, a socialist and a doctor turned a religious hope into a national program.

Ideas became groups in the 1880s. Local societies calling themselves Hovevei Zion, "Lovers of Zion", spread across the Russian Empire. In 1884 they met in conference at Kattowitz, under Pinsker's leadership. [cite:w_hovevei] The record holds a small irony here. Pinsker's own pamphlet had not insisted on Palestine, and he and other early organizers discussed several territories before the movement settled on it. [cite:wiki_leon_pinsker] Yet the man whose argument was territorially open chaired the conference of societies named for Zion. Two years earlier, in 1882, a student group called BILU had sent its first pioneers to the land. [cite:w_bilu] The settlements they and others founded, and the numbers who stayed and left, are counted in [scene:rd0_aliyah|the Old Yishuv and the First Aliyah]. Finally, in 1890, Nathan Birnbaum coined the word "Zionism". [cite:w_birnbaum] By then there were societies, a conference and colonists. There was still no single organization.

Why did people move from prayer to program in these decades? The motives recorded across these writers are four: persecution and pogroms; the failure of emancipation to end antisemitism; the age of European nationalism; and religious longing. A fifth current pushed from outside the Jewish world altogether: Christian restorationism in Britain and America. That story is told in [scene:bc_s05|restoration before Zionism]. The motives did not all point the same way. Alkalai and Kalischer argued from redemption; Hess from nationalism and socialism; Pinsker from physical safety. What they shared was the conclusion that waiting was no longer enough.

The familiar account deserves its strongest form. Herzl's role was real and decisive in one respect: he did not invent the idea, but he gave a scattered movement an organization, a diplomacy and a bank, beginning in 1897. Before him there were groups without a single organization; after him there was a movement with its own organization, its own diplomacy and its own bank. That is a large contribution. It is a different claim from saying that the idea began with him, and the record of the half-century before 1896 does not support that second claim.

The record available here leaves several things unsettled. It names Kalischer's 1862 book but does not give its title or its argument beyond its central claim. It dates Alkalai's call after the Damascus affair of 1840, but does not establish how directly the one produced the other beyond that sequence in time. It gives no membership figures for the Hovevei Zion societies and no account of what the Kattowitz conference decided. And it does not show whether Hess, Pinsker or Herzl read the two rabbis; the four stages followed one another in time, but the record does not trace a single line of influence running through them.

sections.h: The Idea Appears, 1862–1885
sections.html:
The familiar account holds that Zionism is millennia old and that Jews always yearned for the land of Israel. Part of that is true: the hope of return lived for centuries in prayer, as the previous section showed. But a prayer is not a program. Zionism as a written political idea appears in the documents between the 1860s and the 1880s, in scattered proposals that answered a modern problem, modern European antisemitism. The record of those decades also shows two things the familiar account leaves out. When persecuted Jews in the Russian Empire could choose where to go, the great majority chose America. And the largest Jewish religious movement in the United States formally rejected a return to Palestine in 1885.

The first of the proposals came from an unlikely author. Moses Hess (1812–1875) was a German-Jewish philosopher and an early, influential figure in socialist thought. In the 1840s he collaborated and corresponded with Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, and some historians credit him with introducing Marx to communist ideas before Marx had fully formulated his own. [cite:wiki_moses_hess] In 1862 Hess published Rome and Jerusalem: The Last National Question. Its argument was that Jewish assimilation into European society had failed to end antisemitism, and that Jews therefore needed national self-determination. It proposed, explicitly, a socialist Jewish commonwealth in Palestine, joining Hess's two commitments, socialism and Jewish nationalism, in a single dated text. [cite:wiki_moses_hess]

Almost no one listened. The book sold poorly and drew little serious engagement from socialist or Jewish intellectual circles. Mainstream European Jewish thought in the 1860s and 1870s was moving toward emancipation and integration, not national separation, and Hess's socialist nationalism belonged to neither camp. He died in 1875 a minor and largely unread figure. [cite:wiki_moses_hess] Only after the Zionist Congress of 1897 was he rediscovered and placed in the movement's own origin story as a founding intellectual, a common pattern in political movements, which canonize an ignored forerunner once a later effort succeeds. His actual influence on the events of 1897 was close to nil. There is no strong documented evidence that Herzl, who reached his own position chiefly through the Dreyfus Affair, was significantly influenced by Hess's book before writing his own. [cite:wiki_moses_hess] Hess is best read as an early, isolated voice making a real proto-Zionist argument thirty-five years before the movement organized, not as the hidden origin of a plan that then unfolded on schedule.

The pressure that turned scattered ideas into a wider response came from Russia. The Romanov Empire was home to roughly five million Jews, the largest Jewish population in the world, confined by law to the Pale of Settlement. In March 1881 Tsar Alexander II was assassinated. Waves of pogroms followed across the Pale: organized mob violence against Jewish communities, in many cases with the complicity of local officials. [cite:wiki_pogroms_russian_empire] Under his son Alexander III, who reigned from 1881 to 1894, the state then wrote the hostility into law. The May Laws of 1882 formally restricted where Jews could live, what they could study and how they could earn a living. Further decrees imposed quotas on Jewish admission to universities and barred Jews from rural areas. [cite:wiki_may_laws] This was antisemitism as state policy: specific, named legal restrictions with a date, not a vague climate of prejudice. The pogroms and the May Laws were separate pressures, and the record keeps them apart. The law was the legislated escalation; the pogroms that came before it were often the more immediately violent cause of flight, and not every emigrant's decision can be traced to the law itself. [cite:wiki_may_laws][cite:wiki_pogroms_russian_empire]

The wave of 1881–1884 was only the first. A second, from 1903 to 1906, included the Kishinev pogrom of April 1903, which killed 49 people, wounded hundreds and became an international scandal. [cite:wiki_kishinev_pogrom] The third, during the Russian Civil War of 1917–1921, was by far the deadliest, with an estimated 100,000 to 250,000 Jews killed in Ukraine and the surrounding regions. [cite:wiki_pogroms_russian_empire] Those later waves belong to later parts of this library. They are named here because the three should not be flattened into one: the death tolls differ by orders of magnitude, and the founding texts of the 1880s answered the first wave, not the later ones.

The first territorial answer came from Odessa. Leon Pinsker (1821–1891) was a physician who had been decorated by the Tsarist state earlier in his life for public service and who had supported Jewish integration into Russian society: a model of the assimilated, patriotic Russian Jew. [cite:wiki_leon_pinsker] The pogroms of 1881 and the May Laws of 1882 convinced him that integration offered no safety. His pamphlet Auto-Emancipation, published in 1882, argued that antisemitism was a permanent, almost pathological feature of the nations among whom Jews lived as a perpetual minority. Jews would never be granted true equality as guests; they needed a territory of their own, where they would be the hosts, and they should stop relying on the goodwill of host nations. [cite:wiki_auto_emancipation] The argument was political, territorial and secular. It answered a safety problem; it did not invoke a scriptural promise.

Pinsker did not specify Palestine. He considered any suitable territory. One account documents him as open to alternatives including Argentina; another says he at points leaned toward a location in North America or Argentina rather than Palestine. [cite:wiki_leon_pinsker][cite:wiki_auto_emancipation] He and other early organizers of the Hovevei Zion societies discussed several possible territories before the movement's center of gravity settled on Palestine, a choice reinforced by the religious and historical resonance that a purely territorial safety argument did not by itself require. [cite:wiki_leon_pinsker] At its written origin, then, political Zionism was territorially agnostic. Herzl's Der Judenstaat would weigh Argentina and Palestine again in 1896, and the debates over a British offer of East African territory came later still. Exactly when Palestine became fixed is itself given differently in the sources: one account places it with Herzl and his Congress, another, the account of Herzl's later negotiations, with the movement's Russian base in 1905. Either way, the Palestine focus was a decision taken later, not the starting premise.

The strongest form of the case Pinsker made deserves to be stated as he made it. Its premise was empirical: an assimilated, decorated, loyal subject had watched the state that decorated him legislate against his community within a year of mob violence against it. Its conclusion, that Jews could be safe only where they were not a minority, was a judgment about the future. The record of 1881–1882 supports the premise. The conclusion is the political argument that the rest of this library follows, together with the costs it would carry for the people already living in the land Pinsker's successors chose.

The people fleeing the Empire made their own choice, and it is the clearest evidence the period offers. Roughly two million Jews left Imperial Russia in the pogrom era. The sources give the window differently: 1881 to 1914 in one account, 1881 to 1924 in another. Documented estimates put 90–95 percent of these emigrants in the United States and about 3 percent in Ottoman Palestine. [cite:wiki_pogroms_russian_empire] These shares are estimates, and they rest on a single reference source; they should be read as orders of magnitude, not as counts. Even so, the order of magnitude is unambiguous. On the source's own reckoning, those who could choose chose America over Palestine by a factor of about thirty to one. Jewish communities in New York, Chicago, Philadelphia and Boston grew from modest pre-1881 numbers into the multi-million American Jewish diaspora that exists today. The Lower East Side, not the colonies of the First Aliyah, was where most of the exodus went. [cite:wiki_pogroms_russian_empire]

What does that choice show? It shows that people fleeing for their lives went, overwhelmingly, to the country that offered civic equality and economic opportunity, rather than to the land the liturgy held sacred. It is the central evidentiary difficulty for any account that treats Palestine as the natural or inevitable destination of persecuted European Jews in this period. It also explains why Zionism had to be built as a political movement: the ancient longing, whatever its place in prayer, did not by itself move populations toward Palestine. What the choice does not show is that the 3 percent were unimportant. The settlements that smaller group founded, counted in the next section, shaped much of what followed. One further consequence is a matter of interpretation rather than record, and is offered as such: the demographic and financial center of world Jewry moved to the United States in exactly these decades, and when the political-Zionist project needed a great-power patron in the twentieth century, the community that had chosen America became central to securing one. The migration that bypassed Palestine helped, two generations later, to make the American relationship with Israel possible.

Opposition had a formal voice within three years of Pinsker's pamphlet. In 1885 American Reform Judaism adopted the Pittsburgh Platform, which stated:

"We consider ourselves no longer a nation, but a religious community, and therefore expect neither a return to Palestine..."

The sentence continues, in the platform's text, to reject "the restoration of any of the laws concerning the Jewish state." [cite:pittsburgh_platform_1885] This was the founding-generation position of what was then the largest Jewish religious denomination in the United States, adopted three years after Auto-Emancipation and twelve years before the Basel Congress. It was not this book's characterization of Reform Judaism but the movement's own words. Nor was it permanent: Reform Judaism embraced Zionism only in the mid-twentieth century, a documented later reversal. [cite:pittsburgh_platform_1885] It was one of several Jewish objections to the national idea present from its beginning, alongside the Orthodox reading of the Three Oaths set out earlier in this chapter, and the socialist and cultural objections told in the section on Dreyfus and Herzl.

Two more facts belong to these decades. The first concerns words. "Semitic" was coined in 1781 by the German scholar August Ludwig von Schlözer, from Shem, son of Noah in Genesis 10. It named a language family, including Hebrew, Aramaic, Arabic and Amharic, and its speakers, and it carried no political charge. [cite:wiki_semitic_etymology] That changed in 1879, when Wilhelm Marr coined "antisemitism", three years before Pinsker's pamphlet. The modern political vocabulary that later arguments would turn on was being assembled in the same narrow window in which the earliest Zionist texts were written. The overlap is one of timing; no causal link between the two is documented. The full history of both words is told in Volume I, in [scene:s00b|Semitic is not Jewish] and [scene:s00b0|the word 'antisemitism'].

The second fact concerns the land. Palestine was not empty. Its majority population in this period were Palestinian Arabs, speakers of a Semitic language. Two peer-reviewed population-genetics studies, Nebel and colleagues in 2000 and Behar and colleagues in 2010, describe them as descended from populations continuously present in the region since antiquity. [cite:nebel_pop_genetics_2000][cite:behar_2010_nature] The colonies of the First Aliyah were founded on land that was already inhabited.

It is often said that this population was named nowhere in the founding literature of political Zionism. That claim needs testing, and it does not survive in its strongest form. It holds for the earliest written texts as they are summarized here: neither Hess's argument nor Pinsker's, as the sources describe them, addresses the people already living on the land. That absence is a real fact about those texts, though it is not by itself proof of malice. But the absence was noticed from inside the movement, and early. Ahad Ha'am proposed a cultural rather than a political Zionism. [cite:wiki_ahad_haam] He raised exactly this concern in writing in 1891, less than a decade after Pinsker. And Herzl's own diary for 12 June 1895, published only after his death, contains a passage about spiriting "the penniless population" across the border, whose meaning and reference scholars dispute; it is examined, with both readings, in [scene:s03|Dreyfus and Herzl]. The defensible statement is narrower than the common one: the inhabitants were absent from the first proto-Zionist programs, and their presence was raised in writing within the movement within a decade.

Several questions the record available here leaves open. It does not give the exact years over which the two million left, since its two accounts end in 1914 and in 1924, and the 90–95 percent and 3 percent shares are estimates from one reference source, not counts. It does not quote Pinsker's pamphlet on the question of territory, so how far he leaned toward North America or Argentina, rather than simply leaving the question open, rests on two summaries that word it differently. It records Ahad Ha'am's 1891 concern but not the text in which he raised it. And it does not establish any line of influence from Hess to Pinsker or from either to Herzl: the ideas appeared one after another, in answer to the same pressures, but the documents do not show one man reading and building on the other.

sections.h: The Jews of Palestine before Herzl
sections.html:
The small share of Russia's emigrants who chose Palestine did not arrive in a country without Jews. When Theodor Herzl published his case for a Jewish state in 1896, Jews had been living in Palestine, and arriving there, for the whole of the century. They are easy to lose from view, because the story of political Zionism is usually told from Vienna, Odessa and Basel. The record allows a rough count of them, and it shows that two quite different Jewish communities stood in the country by the 1890s: an older one centered on the holy cities, and a newer one of agricultural colonies founded from 1878 onward. They did not always welcome each other.

The older community, known as the Old Yishuv, had grown steadily through immigration well before any political program existed. Büşra Barın, in a 2014 study of Ottoman policy toward Jewish immigration, estimates that about 5,000 Jews came to Palestine between 1800 and 1840 and roughly 25,000 between 1850 and 1880. She puts the Old Yishuv at about 24,000 people in 1880, of whom 13,900 lived in Jerusalem [cite:rs_rd0_barin_2014_pop]. A reference summary, citing Mordecai Elia (1971), gives a slightly lower figure for the same year, 23,000 [cite:rs_rd0_firstaliyah_wiki]. The two estimates are close; what they share is the point. On the eve of the first organized settlement movement, more than half of the country's Jews lived in one city, and Jerusalem's Jewish population was already counted in the thousands.

These figures matter for the argument that runs through this book. The strongest form of the Zionist case rested partly on continuity: Jews were not strangers to the country, and Jerusalem had a large Jewish population before any Zionist organization existed. The numbers above support that much. They do not, on their own, say anything about the political claims later built on them.

The Ottoman state that governed this community also permitted at least one Jewish institution from abroad to operate in it. On 5 April 1870 an Ottoman firman, an imperial decree, permitted the Alliance Israélite Universelle to establish an agricultural school in Jaffa. A copy of the firman is held by the Israel State Archives under the reference JM-ISA/AEB/83/32 [cite:rs_rd0_aiu_firman]. The document matters for what it does and does not say. It records an Ottoman grant of permission, through the regular instrument of imperial decree, to a foreign Jewish body to open an agricultural school in Palestine, eleven years before the pogroms in the Russian Empire set off the larger movement. The archival record of the firman does not name the school, and this book does not attach a later name to it.

The new community began before the pogroms and grew quickly after them. The First Aliyah, the first wave of Jewish immigration organized around settlement on the land, is conventionally dated 1881–1903. Its earliest colony had in fact been attempted before that. According to a reference summary, Petah Tikva was first settled in 1878 and then re-established in 1882 after that first attempt failed; Gei Oni was also founded in 1878, and was taken over in 1882 by the settlers of Rosh Pinna. Rishon LeZion and Zikhron Ya'akov also date from 1882, Ness Ziona from 1883, Gedera from 1884, Rehovot from 1890 and Hadera from 1891 [cite:rs_rd0_firstaliyah_wiki]. The settlers called these places colonies.

The violence of 1881–84 in the Russian Empire and the laws that followed it form the background to this wave, told in [scene:s02|the pogroms and the May Laws]. Within a year of the main foundings, at least one colony had turned to outside money. In 1883 the settlers' central committee transferred Zikhron Ya'akov's assets to Baron Edmond de Rothschild of the Paris banking house [cite:rs_rd0_firstaliyah_wiki], the first step in a patronage that is the subject of the section [scene:bc_s04|on Edmond de Rothschild's colonies].

The First Aliyah was not only European. Emigration from Yemen began in early 1881. A reference summary states that a few hundred Jews left Sanaa and nearby towns for Palestine in 1881–82, part of a movement that continued almost without break until 1914 [cite:rs_rd0_firstaliyah_wiki]. That summary gives no source of its own for the figure, and it should be treated as an estimate. The arrivals are nonetheless the point at which the Jews of the Arab world enter this story as participants rather than as background: their migration began in the same years as the Russian one, from a different country and under a different government, and the record does not show that the two movements were organized together.

How many Jews came in the First Aliyah as a whole, and how many stayed, is disputed, and the range is wide. Barın estimates about 20,000 to 30,000 arrivals [cite:rs_rd0_barin_2014_pop]. A reference summary reports estimates running from 25,000, a Jewish Agency figure, to 60,000 in total, the latter from the historian Anita Shapira (2012), who also estimates that between 50 and 70 percent of those who came later left [cite:rs_rd0_firstaliyah_wiki]. The sources available here do not explain how each figure was reached, so the gap between them cannot be resolved in this book. If Shapira's estimate of departures is right, a large share of the newcomers did not remain.

The same disagreement carries into the count at the end of the period. Barın puts the Jewish population of Palestine at about 50,000 by 1903; a reference summary gives about 55,000 at the period's close, without a source; and Elia, as cited in the same summary, gives 80,000 for 1907 [cite:rs_rd0_barin_2014_pop] [cite:rs_rd0_firstaliyah_wiki]. These dates fall after 1896, and they are given here only to show the direction of change. Read together with the 1880 figure, they suggest that the Jewish population roughly doubled, or more than tripled, in a generation, depending on whose estimate is used. That growth was what the Ottoman government was trying to limit in the same years, as [scene:rd0_limits|the next section] shows.

The newcomers also met opposition from Jews. According to a reference timeline citing an edited scholarly volume (Sobel and Beit-Hallahmi, eds., Tradition, Innovation, Conflict, 2012), in the 1880s the Orthodox community of Jerusalem regarded emerging Zionism as a threat and reported Zionist newcomers to the Ottoman authorities [cite:rs_rd0_antizionism_wiki_dissent]. That is a striking act: Jews in Jerusalem turning to the Ottoman state against other Jews over the new movement. In Europe the objection was made on other grounds. Adolf Jellinek, the preacher of Vienna's Jewish community, answered Leon Pinsker's Auto-Emancipation by denying that Jews had national characteristics as such. "We are at home in Europe," he answered, as the historian Robert Wistrich is cited quoting him [cite:rs_rd0_antizionism_wiki_dissent]. His objection went to the premise of Pinsker's pamphlet: that the Jews were a nation.

The record therefore shows a Jewish Palestine in 1896 that was older, more varied and more divided than the later national story usually allows. It held a long-established religious community concentrated in Jerusalem; a scattering of colonies, several of them already dependent on one Paris donor; a small migration from Yemen; and Jewish critics of the national idea both in Jerusalem and in Europe.

Much is left unsettled. The population figures are estimates from a thesis and a reference summary, and they disagree by tens of thousands at the end of the period. The material used here does not describe how the Old Yishuv supported itself, how it was divided internally, or how its institutions worked, and this section does not attempt it. The size of the Yemenite migration rests on an unsourced figure. Whether Jerusalem's reports to the Ottoman authorities in the 1880s were the act of the community's leadership or of particular individuals is not stated in the source available, and the matter needs the underlying study to settle it.

sections.h: The Porte Says No, and the Arabs of Palestine Object, 1882–1896
sections.html:
A familiar account holds that the Ottoman Empire welcomed Jewish settlement in Palestine, or even sold the country to the Zionist movement. The documents point the other way. From 1882, within months of the first colonies, the Ottoman government in Constantinople, known to diplomats as the Porte, issued a series of rules meant to keep foreign Jews from settling in Palestine and from buying land there. The rules were reissued, tightened and loosened over the next twelve years. They failed in large part, for reasons the diplomatic record makes plain. In the same years Arab notables in Jerusalem began to petition the government to enforce them. Both stories belong to this period, and both are told here from the documents that survive.

The policy began quickly. According to Büşra Barın's study of Ottoman policy (Middle East Technical University, 2014), in June 1882 the entry of foreign Jews into Ottoman territory, and their purchase of land, were forbidden. In July 1882 the rule was refined: Jews were allowed to settle anywhere in the empire except Palestine, provided they took Ottoman nationality [cite:rs_rd0_barin_2014]. A reference summary drawing on Neville Mandel's 1974 study dates the government's recognition of the new wave to November 1882, and records that restrictions were imposed despite a Sultan's permit issued in May of that year. It adds that in 1882 the American minister in Constantinople, Lew Wallace, was told that Jews would be welcome anywhere in the empire except Palestine [cite:rs_rd0_firstaliyah_wiki_bans] [cite:rs_rd0_antizionism_wiki_bans]. The two accounts differ on the month the government acted; they agree on the shape of the policy. Jews could become Ottoman subjects and live elsewhere in the empire. On this reading, what the Porte would not accept was a concentration of foreign Jews in one district.

The instrument was the pilgrimage. Barın writes that from 1882 only pilgrims were admitted to Palestine; from 1884 Jewish visitors needed visas from Ottoman consulates in their home countries; and pilgrim stays were limited to one month, later extended to three for Jews under foreign protection, whose passports were held against a red permit card [cite:rs_rd0_barin_2014]. The date of the red card is uncertain. Barın's own footnote says the card system was implemented from 1900, and the British and American diplomatic correspondence of 1887–88 documents the one-month and three-month limits without mentioning a card at all [cite:rs_rd0_barin_2014] [cite:rs_rd0_cojs_moore1887] [cite:rs_rd0_frus1888_may]. The safest reading is that the time limits are documented for the 1880s and the card belongs to a later stage.

The rules can be watched in operation through the consuls who had to deal with them. On 5 March 1887 the British consul in Jerusalem, Noel Temple Moore, reported to his ambassador that foreign Jews were "only allowed to come on a pilgrimage to Jerusalem for one month." The governor of Jerusalem gave three reasons: poverty, the overcrowding of the Jewish quarter, and public health. The ambassador, Sir William White, replied on 19 October 1887 that the rule was "ipso facto null and void" for persons under British protection, citing the Capitulations, the treaty privileges of foreigners in the Ottoman Empire [cite:rs_rd0_cojs_moore1887]. Britain had already protested to the Porte in September 1887 [cite:rs_rd0_frus1888_may].

The American record adds the Porte's own explanation. On 28 January 1888 the United States minister, Oscar Straus, reported that the Porte had limited the stay of foreign Jews at Jerusalem to one month and planned to extend it to three. The Grand Vizier gave him two reasons: tensions with Christians at Easter, and a rumor that Jews meant to re-establish a Jewish kingdom around Jerusalem. The American consul reported that a shipload of Russian Jews had been refused landing at Jaffa about two years earlier [cite:rs_rd0_frus1888_jan]. An Ottoman note of 2 March 1888 then set the rule in writing: foreign Jews would be admitted only on passports stating a pilgrimage, and for at most three months. On 19 May 1888 Straus told the State Department that the United States could not accept passport rules tied to religion, which he called "utterly repugnant" to the American Constitution [cite:rs_rd0_frus1888_may].

The exchange shows the structure of the dispute. The Porte framed its rule as public order and public health, and, to the Grand Vizier, as a guard against a political project. The Western governments did not argue for Jewish settlement in Palestine. They argued against a rule that treated their citizens differently because of their religion. Britain and the United States reached the same position from their own legal commitments; these papers show no sign of a shared plan, only a shared principle.

In the early 1890s the contest moved from entry to land. On 14 June 1893 the Foreign Office instructed its ambassador on petitions from British Jews in Jerusalem against regulations, in the Office's words, "Prohibiting Jews from buying & selling real Estate in Palestine." It held that rules aimed at Jews for their religion were inconsistent with Article 62 of the Treaty of Berlin [cite:rs_rd0_cojs_fo1893]. That article, agreed in 1878, declared that "in no part of the Ottoman Empire shall difference of religion be alleged against any person" [cite:rs_rd0_fo1893_berlin62]; its origins belong to [scene:rd0_tanzimat|the reform era]. On 29 July 1893 the American minister reported the Grand Vizier's assurance that earlier restrictions "had been modified" and that the government's aim was to prevent "the alienation of the land to nonresidents" and to speculators [cite:rs_rd0_frus1893_terrell].

The assurance did not last. An Ottoman note of 27 March 1894, quoted by the American minister in a dispatch of 1898, forbade Jewish immigrants to acquire real property in Palestine "for political reasons." Its stated object was "the prevention of the permanent establishment in Palestine of Jewish immigrants." The rule applied to native and foreign Jews alike, but a purchase could go ahead on a consular certificate stating that the buyer was not in a barred class [cite:rs_rd0_frus1898_angell]. The note is the clearest single statement of Ottoman purpose in this period. It named the concern as political, it named the group, and it built in an exception.

When the land ban began is disputed, and the sources give three answers. A reference summary, citing the historians Ocak (2002) and Porath (1977), dates it to 1892 and says it applied even to Ottoman Jewish subjects [cite:rs_rd0_landpurchase_wiki_bans]. Barın describes a decree of 1893 for Jewish immigrants in Jerusalem, extended the following April to all Jews [cite:rs_rd0_barin_2014]. The text that American diplomats treated as operative is the note of 27 March 1894, and in July 1893 the Grand Vizier had said that earlier restrictions were already modified [cite:rs_rd0_frus1898_angell] [cite:rs_rd0_frus1893_terrell]. These are not necessarily contradictory: a regional rule of 1892 or 1893, softened in mid-1893 and then generalized in 1894, would fit all three. The documents in hand do not settle it, and a firm's complaint of March 1893, discussed below, shows that even contemporaries disagreed about whether a ban was in force.

The reason the rules leaked lay in the empire's treaty obligations. Barın finds that enforcement was undermined by the Capitulations and the protégé system, which let foreign Jews live in Palestine under European consular protection; Britain had declared in 1847 that its consulates would protect Jews whose own states did not. Despite the bans, she concludes, more than 50,000 Jews settled [cite:rs_rd0_barin_2014]. Corruption is also named, in one account, alongside foreign consular protection as a reason the rules were enforced unevenly. The mechanism, then, ran like this. The Porte could issue notes. Local officials could refuse a landing at Jaffa or block a sale. But a Jew who held a British, American or other foreign passport could appeal to a consul, the consul could appeal to an ambassador, and the ambassador could invoke treaties the Porte had signed. On this record, a Jew without a foreign protector was the most exposed to the rules and a protected foreigner the least, and the settlements grew through the gaps.

The same years saw the first organized response from the Arab population of Palestine. Emanuel Beška, in a 2007 study of Arab responses to Zionism before 1908, dates modern Jewish immigration and colonization to the 1880s and finds that Arab opposition took time to form. The first reactions came from peasants, then from artisans and merchants whose livelihoods were affected [cite:rs_rd0_beska_2007].

The first political act on record came in 1891. According to a reference timeline citing Neville Mandel's The Arabs and Zionism before World War I, on 24 June 1891 Arab notables in Jerusalem petitioned the Grand Vizier to prohibit Russian Jews from entering Palestine and from buying land there [cite:rs_rd0_antizionism_wiki]. A 1978 review of Mandel's book in The Detroit Jewish News describes the same action differently, as a protest telegram from Arab leaders in Jerusalem and Jaffa calling for an end to Jewish immigration and land purchase, sent "barely a decade after the arrival of the Bilu'im," the BILU pioneers [cite:rs_rd0_djn_1978]. A Jewish Agency historical overview agrees that Jerusalem notables made the request in 1891 and says it was "repeated time and again" [cite:rs_rd0_jafi_opposition]. Whether it was a petition or a telegram, and whether Jaffa's leaders joined it, the sources leave open. Its text, its signatories and their number are not available in the material this book could reach.

The most persistent opponent in the record was the mufti of Jerusalem, Muhammad Tahir al-Husayni. Beška finds that he followed Jewish immigration "since the 1880s" and took an active stance against it [cite:rs_rd0_beska_2007]. He should not be confused with an earlier mufti of the city, Tahir Afandi al-Husayni, who acted as a mediator in the revolt of 1834 and was later exiled [cite:rs_rd0_rood_1834]; the sources name them separately. On 15 March 1893 the firm J. Frutiger & Co. complained to the German consul that the governor of Jerusalem and a "Commission for Sale" chaired by al-Husayni were blocking land sales to Jews. The firm said the ban had been "abolished some time ago"; the mufti held that it remained in force under new regulations. On 12 May 1893 the consul complained to his ambassador of a campaign to prompt Muslim petitions for a comprehensive ban [cite:rs_rd0_beska_2007]. Here the Ottoman rules and the Arab response meet in a single office: a local religious official sat on a commission that applied the state's land policy, read that policy strictly, while a European consul complained of a campaign to prompt petitions that would make it stricter still.

Opposition also began to appear in print. In 1895 Najib al-Hajj, editor of the Cairo paper Abu al-Hol, accused Jewish colonists of taking the means of livelihood of Arabs, according to a related paper excerpted with Beška's article [cite:rs_rd0_beska_2007]. Just after the period of this chapter, in 1897, a committee chaired by al-Husayni put land sales to Jews in the Jerusalem district on hold for several years [cite:rs_rd0_beska_2007].

Whether this opposition was political is a real dispute among the sources, and each side has evidence. The Jewish Agency overview describes the earlier local opposition as sporadic attacks and disputes over land and says it is "doubtful whether this opposition had any political connotations" [cite:rs_rd0_jafi_opposition]. The strongest form of that case is that peasants and merchants who clashed with the colonies were defending their own livelihoods, case by case, rather than pursuing a political program. The other side, drawing on Mandel as cited and on Beška, holds that the opposition was directed at the state from the start: the 1891 approach to the Grand Vizier and the mufti's campaign of 1893 over land sales were acts aimed at changing Ottoman policy, made by notables through the government's own channels [cite:rs_rd0_antizionism_wiki] [cite:rs_rd0_djn_1978] [cite:rs_rd0_beska_2007]. The two positions are closer than they look. The Jewish Agency overview itself records the 1891 request and its repetition; the dispute is over whether the earlier peasant clashes carried political meaning, not over whether the notables acted. On the evidence here, by 1891 at the latest Jerusalem notables were making a demand of their government about immigration and land; whether to call it political is the point in dispute.

Herzl entered this setting in 1896. He sought a charter from the Sultan from that year, offering to help consolidate the Ottoman public debt. His diary records a message relayed from Abdul Hamid II that the Sultan could not sell even a foot of the land, because it belonged not to him but to his people [cite:w_herzl]. Herzl met the Sultan only in May 1901, and came away without a charter [cite:w_abdulhamid]; that story belongs to [scene:tk_s02|the Sultan's refusal]. The legal form through which land was later bought in large tracts, the Ottoman Land Code of 1858, is the subject of [scene:ot_s01|the section on that law].

Several matters remain open. The exact start of the land-sale ban is not settled by the documents in hand. The red permit card may belong to 1900 rather than the 1880s. The text, signatories and authors of the 1891 protest have not been reached in this research, so its form and whether Jaffa joined remain uncertain. There is no count here of how many Jews were turned away under the rules, as against Barın's estimate of more than 50,000 who settled regardless. Her study covers 1882 to 1920, but the passage that gives the figure does not say which years it counts, so it cannot be read as a total for this chapter's period alone. And whether the peasant clashes of the 1880s carried political meaning is a question on which the sources disagree and the material here cannot decide.

sections.h: Edmond de Rothschild's Colonies, and His Refusal of Herzl
sections.html:
The colonies that grew through the gaps in the Ottoman rules had a patron in Paris. A durable story holds that the Rothschilds funded Zionism from the beginning, and that Herzl's movement was their project. The record separates two things that story fuses. One member of the family, Baron Edmond de Rothschild of the Paris house, paid for and ran Jewish agricultural colonies in Ottoman Palestine for some fifteen years before Herzl wrote a word about a Jewish state. When Herzl came to him in 1896 asking for backing for a political movement, Edmond refused. The First Zionist Congress met in Basel the following year without him [cite:wiki_edmond_james_de_rothschild]. Both facts are documented, and the history of the period cannot be told accurately without both.

Edmond's money came from the Paris branch of the family bank, de Rothschild Frères, which his father, James Mayer Rothschild (1792–1868), the youngest of Mayer Amschel Rothschild's five sons, had built into the largest private bank in France, as [scene:s01|an earlier section] describes. When James died in 1868 the bank passed principally to his sons Alphonse and Gustave. Edmond, the youngest, was 23. He inherited substantial capital but not the management of the bank [cite:schama_two_rothschilds]. That is the background to what he did with his inheritance fourteen years later.

Edmond was born in 1845 at Boulogne-Billancourt and trained in mining engineering and art collecting rather than banking [cite:schama_two_rothschilds]. His turn to Palestine came out of the crisis of 1881–82. After the assassination of Alexander II in 1881, pogroms in the Russian Empire sent thousands of Jewish refugees westward; some reached Palestine and met agricultural failure and disease. In 1882 Rishon LeZion, a new settlement south of Jaffa, was collapsing within months of its founding for want of water and of agricultural knowledge. Rabbi Samuel Mohilever appealed to Edmond, and Edmond accepted the appeal and began to fund the colony [cite:schama_two_rothschilds]. From there his commitment widened. In 1883, according to a reference summary, the settlers' central committee transferred Zikhron Ya'akov's assets to him [cite:rs_rd0_firstaliyah_wiki]. Over the following years he financed and administered roughly thirty Jewish agricultural colonies, including Rishon LeZion, Zikhron Ya'akov and Rosh Pinna, and earned the Hebrew title HaNadiv HaYadua, "the known benefactor" [cite:wiki_edmond_james_de_rothschild] [cite:betweenmyths_rothschild_israel]. The sources date this work differently: one gives 1882 to 1895, another 1883 to 1900 [cite:wiki_edmond_james_de_rothschild] [cite:schama_two_rothschilds].

The principal settlements are documented in Ran Aaronsohn's Rothschild and Early Jewish Colonization in Palestine (2000) and Simon Schama's Two Rothschilds and the Land of Israel (1978). Two of them carry the family in their names. Zikhron Ya'akov, "in memory of Jacob," was named for Edmond's father James, whose Hebrew name was Jacob; Mazkeret Batya was named for his mother, Betty, in Hebrew Batya [cite:schama_two_rothschilds]. The naming was not concealed; the same account says it appears on the settlements' founding charters. The patronage was public and celebrated in the 1880s and became part of the settlements' own identity, which is the plainest evidence that this was open philanthropy and not a hidden hand.

The colonies were run on Edmond's terms, through an administrative system of his own, and the colonists complained of his administrators [cite:wiki_edmond_james_de_rothschild]. That is the mechanism to hold on to. The money did not flow to a movement or a committee that set its own course. It flowed from a private fortune in Paris to officials employed by the donor, who managed the colonies on his behalf. The settlers depended on him, and the record of their complaints shows that the dependence chafed.

How much he spent is not settled. One detailed account gives approximately $5–6 million in period dollars, roughly $200 million in modern terms, and estimates it at about 40 percent of all early capital invested in the Jewish settlements, calling Edmond the single largest private funder of pre-state Jewish settlement. None of these figures carries a source, and they should be read as unsourced estimates, not as findings. The compiled record of pre-state funding in this library is more cautious. Its table of every documented money stream opens with Edmond's colonies, from 1882 to 1924, and records the amount as "Not totaled in the record," with what the money bought given as "~30 settlements, later handed to PICA (1924)." Every later stream in that table, from the Jewish Colonial Trust of 1899 to the Export-Import Bank loan of 1949, begins after Herzl's movement was founded; Edmond's is the only one that predates it.

In 1896 Edmond instructed the Jewish Colonization Association, the society founded by Baron Maurice de Hirsch in 1891 and described in the next section, to begin lending to colonists [cite:wiki_edmond_james_de_rothschild]. Another account dates the decisive step to 1899, when, frustrated by the cost of directly managing some thirty settlements, he transferred their formal administration to the Association, whose Palestine operations became a subsidiary [cite:schama_two_rothschilds]. Hirsch was a separate philanthropist and no relation. The two dates may describe two stages, first loans and then administration, but the sources do not say so, and the conflict is recorded here rather than resolved.

Into this world Herzl came in the summer of 1896, months after publishing Der Judenstaat. He was asking for something different in kind from what Edmond had been doing: a state secured by charter, not colonies secured by purchase. Edmond declined. Herzl's diary for 22–26 July 1896 records his "rude telegram to Edmond Rothschild" and his resolve that "from Rothschild's negative attitude I must salvage everything"; he turned instead to organizing the Basel Congress of 1897 [cite:herzl_diaries_vol2_archive]. A second account gives a different sequence. In it Edmond first refused to receive Herzl in Paris; then, in July 1896, the two met through an intermediary, and Edmond told Herzl to his face that he opposed political Zionism and would not fund it, an exchange this account also places in Herzl's diary [cite:schama_two_rothschilds]. The two versions agree on the outcome and on the month. They differ on whether there was a meeting, and the diary entry quoted in the first account, which speaks of a telegram, does not by itself settle the point.

Why did he refuse? The same detailed account gives two reasons and says both appear in his correspondence. Edmond preferred quiet philanthropic settlement to political statehood, believing that Jewish safety could be advanced by slow agricultural facts on the ground without a statehood project that would attract international opposition. And he thought that political and diplomatic Zionism, with its public meetings with the Sultan and its talk of territorial concessions, would alienate the Ottoman rulers whose consent his settlements needed, and so poison arrangements that were working [cite:schama_two_rothschilds]. The second reason fits what the Ottoman government was doing in the same years, when it was restricting Jewish immigration and land purchase in Palestine, as described in [scene:rd0_limits|the section on Ottoman limits]. The correspondence itself is not quoted in the material available here.

The refusal did not end with 1896. Edmond did not attend the Basel Congress in 1897 and continued to fund settlement through his own channels, not through the Zionist Organization Herzl founded there. Herzl died in 1904; Edmond went on funding settlement for another thirty years without changing his position on political Zionism [cite:schama_two_rothschilds]. Edmond's philanthropic colonization and Herzl's political Zionism, which produced the Congress, the Organization and eventually the state, were separate projects, and the second was launched after the first's patron had refused it [cite:wiki_edmond_james_de_rothschild].

The colonies outlasted the century and their founder. In 1924 Edmond transferred them to the Palestine Jewish Colonization Association, PICA, which after his death in 1934 was presided over by his son James, and which continued land purchase and settlement through the British Mandate [cite:betweenmyths_rothschild_israel]. The detailed account credits PICA with approximately 500,000 dunams (125,000 acres) by the 1930s and offices in Paris, London and Jerusalem, and says that in 1957 PICA transferred its remaining holdings and functions to the Jewish Agency for Israel [cite:schama_two_rothschilds]. Another source names Yad Hanadiv as PICA's successor, still acting in Israel for Rothschild family trusts, and records that James and Dorothy de Rothschild later funded the Knesset building [cite:betweenmyths_rothschild_israel]. The sources do not reconcile these two endings. Edmond was buried first in Paris; in 1954 his remains were moved to Ramat HaNadiv, "the Hill of the Benefactor," a memorial site in Israel he had funded in his lifetime [cite:schama_two_rothschilds]. David Ben-Gurion called him "the builder of the Jewish Yishuv" [cite:betweenmyths_rothschild_israel].

The family's two roles in this history are often merged into one. Walter Rothschild of the London branch was the addressee of the Balfour letter in 1917, a document drafted by others; Edmond of the Paris branch funded colonies and opposed Herzl [cite:schama_two_rothschilds]. Neither, on this record, set the course of political Zionism. The two branches did converge later, through Walter's receipt of the 1917 letter and through PICA's land work under the Mandate [cite:wiki_edmond_james_de_rothschild]. That later story belongs to the next volume.

The story that "the Rothschilds paid for it all" is examined elsewhere in this library against the whole record of pre-state funding, which shows money coming overwhelmingly from mass small-donor giving, with over a million American contributors in 1948 alone, and records that the Paris Rothschild who funded the early colonies opposed Herzl; see [scene:pn_s01|seven founding narratives, checked]. The correction cuts in both directions. Rothschild money did build much of the physical foundation of the early settlements, and that is documented and substantial. What it did not do was launch or own the political movement. The idea that "the Rothschilds" as a family engineered Zionism collapses one man's philanthropy, another man's ceremonial role and a political movement that one of them refused into a single hidden hand, which is the shape of an old antisemitic story, not of the record. The opposite move, saying the family had nothing to do with the settlements, is just as wrong.

One interpretive reading, offered here as a reading and not as a finding, goes further. It holds that without Edmond's money the First Aliyah would probably have collapsed at Rishon LeZion; that his combination of capital, agricultural assistance and management of relations with the Ottoman authorities produced the first lasting colonies and a template for later waves of immigration, the Second Aliyah of 1904–1914 and the Third of 1919–1923; and that the Ottoman restrictions of the period were a reaction to what his colonies made possible. It traces a line from those colonies, through the Jewish population and territorial position of 1917, to the state of 1948 and to the displacement of Palestinians in that year, while stating that Edmond, who died in 1934, took no part in the events of 1948 and was not their sole cause. This reading is a counterfactual, and parts of it rest on dates that the diplomatic documents of the period complicate: it places the first Ottoman land restrictions in 1892, a date that is itself disputed. The same account lists what survives of his work today, without sources: the settlements as Israeli towns and cities, Rishon LeZion among the country's largest, with more than 300,000 people; Ramat HaNadiv, where he and his wife Adelheid are buried; an Edmond de Rothschild Foundation in Israel working in education, the arts and science rather than political advocacy; his portrait on a 500-shekel note of the 1982–1985 series; and streets named for the family in several cities. It concludes that the family has no significant role in present-day political lobbying for Israel. These statements are recorded as that account gives them; they are not verified here.

What the record does not settle is substantial. The total Edmond spent is not documented in any cited source, and the much-repeated figures for it are estimates without citation. Whether he met Herzl in July 1896 or only exchanged messages depends on which account of the diary is followed. The dates of his handover to the Jewish Colonization Association (1896 or 1899) and the relation between that step and PICA's creation in 1924 are reported differently, as is PICA's end (a transfer to the Jewish Agency in 1957, or succession by Yad Hanadiv). His reasons for refusing Herzl are attributed to his correspondence, which is not quoted in the material available. What is not in doubt is the order of events: the colonies came first, the political movement came second, and the man who paid for the first said no to the second.

sections.h: Baron de Hirsch and the Argentine Alternative, 1889–1896
sections.html:
Edmond was not the only Jewish financier settling refugees on the land. In September 1891, six years before the First Zionist Congress met at Basel, a company was incorporated in London to move persecuted Jews out of the Russian Empire and Romania and settle them as farmers. Its founder was Baron Maurice de Hirsch, a German-Jewish financier and philanthropist. Its destination was Argentina. Its name was the Jewish Colonization Association, the JCA. [cite:hadassah_mag_hirsch] [cite:wiki_jewish_colonization_association]

A common account holds that Zionism was the first and only organized plan to resettle persecuted European Jews somewhere new. The record does not bear that out. The first large, organized and capitalized attempt to answer what the century called "the Jewish Question" through mass resettlement was the JCA, and it was not a plan for a state. It was a plan for refuge and for a change of livelihood, and the place it chose first lay on another continent. That precedent was in front of Theodor Herzl when he wrote his own pamphlet five years later.

The company and its capital. The JCA was incorporated under the English Companies Acts, a charitable body given the legal form of a company. Its authorized capital was £2,000,000, divided into 20,000 shares of £100 each that paid no dividend. Hirsch subscribed 19,993 of the 20,000 himself. [cite:hadassah_mag_hirsch] In practice, then, this was one man's fortune given the form of an institution. According to Hadassah Magazine's review of Matthias Lehmann's history of the association, the JCA's budget was described as "the greatest charitable trust in the world at that time." [cite:hadassah_mag_hirsch] One account in the research for this book adds that Hirsch put in a further £7,000,000 the following year. No separate source for that figure has been found, and it is given here only as that account's claim.

The association's purpose was written into its founding terms, and the Jewish Encyclopedia records it in these words: to "assist and promote the emigration of Jews...to any parts of the world, and to form and establish colonies in various parts of North and South America and other countries." [cite:wiki_jewish_colonization_association] The scope was deliberately open. "Any parts of the world" is not a Palestine project under another name. Argentina became the JCA's founding and primary field, but the charter did not confine it there.

The colonies. The Argentine work began before the company existed. Moisés Ville was founded in 1889 by Dr. Wilhelm Löwenthal with Hirsch's backing (one account calls the initiative Hirsch's, another Löwenthal's), and is described as the first large agricultural colony for Eastern European Jews in the JCA's network, although it predates the association's incorporation by two years. [cite:wiki_moises_ville] Further colonies followed: Mauricio, Clara (also called Villa Clara) and San Antonio. By 1896, the year Hirsch died, roughly 6,757 colonists lived across the Argentine settlements. By 1939 the JCA held about 1,519,000 acres in Argentina. [cite:wiki_moises_ville] [cite:wiki_hirsch_argentina_settlements]

The mechanism was simple to state. Money came from one fortune, held in a London company. The company bought land, brought families from the Russian Empire and Romania, and settled them on the land as farmers. The Argentine government was the sovereign; the JCA was a landowner and a sponsor inside it. Nothing in the arrangement gave the colonists, or the company, any political authority of their own.

The harder history. Popular memory has often treated Moisés Ville as a bright counterpoint to European persecution, a place free of prejudice. The documented record is more complicated. The settlers met real hardship, including a typhus epidemic and food shortages. There is also a documented history of violence within the community, examined directly in Javier Sinay's book The Murders of Moisés Ville. [cite:wiki_moises_ville] The numbers above are real and substantial. They do not show that the settlers' experience was a uniformly happy one, and an honest account keeps both.

The idea behind it: "productivization". What separated the JCA from the political movement that followed was not its scale but its theory. Its explicit goal was not sovereignty, and not autonomy. It was to "productivize" Jews: to move them out of urban trades, in which they were often persecuted, and into manual and agricultural labor, so that their social and economic position within existing nation-states would become normal. [cite:wiki_maurice_de_hirsch] It was assimilation through labor, not separation through statehood. Two answers were now on offer to the same nineteenth-century question of how persecuted European Jews could build a secure future. One said: a state of their own. The other, tried first and at real scale, said: a different livelihood inside the nations that already existed.

Whether productivization worked is a separate question, and the sources used here do not answer it. They establish that the theory was held and acted on in Argentina. They give no basis for saying that it was vindicated or refuted by what happened there, or that economic normalization reduced antisemitism.

Refuge, not a rival nation. Historians are explicit on the central point. The JCA aimed at agricultural resettlement and integration into Argentine society; there was no political program for Jewish national autonomy in Argentina. [cite:wiki_jewish_colonization_association] That is why Argentina could appear in Herzl's pamphlet of 1896 as a candidate territory rather than as a competing national project already under way. Had the JCA been building Jewish self-government on the Pampas, Argentina and Palestine would have been two national movements in competition. They were not. One offered refuge and integration; the other came to offer refuge and statehood. That difference let Herzl weigh Argentina as an option, a choice examined in [scene:s03|Dreyfus, Herzl and Der Judenstaat]. The distinction describes the institution's declared aim. It does not tell us how every colonist or organizer saw the two projects in private.

Nor were the two simply opponents. After Hirsch's death in 1896 the JCA also began to fund settlement in Palestine. [cite:wiki_jewish_colonization_association] In the same year, Baron Edmond de Rothschild instructed the JCA to begin lending to the colonists he supported there. [cite:wiki_edmond_james_de_rothschild] By one account he later transferred the formal administration of his colonies to the association, in 1899. [cite:schama_two_rothschilds] That story belongs to [scene:bc_s04|Edmond de Rothschild's colonies]. The overlap matters here because it rules out a tidy picture of Argentina against Palestine. The same philanthropic body, built for any country, came to work in both.

Hirsch's death and its date. Hirsch died in 1896, a year before the Basel Congress of 1897, and never saw it. [cite:hadassah_mag_hirsch] One passage in the research for this book says he died "five years before" the Congress; that is an error, and the dates above are the ones the sources support. Because he died before Basel, his record cannot show what he would have made of political Zionism. It shows only that he had chosen a different instrument, and that his foundation did not treat the two causes as exclusive.

What the precedent shows, and what it does not. Organized, heavily funded planning for Jewish resettlement existed years before Herzl and decades before the Holocaust. When the Zionist movement later fixed on Palestine, it was choosing among alternatives, one of which had already been tried on the ground at real scale. The record does not show that Hirsch opposed the later Zionist project or saw himself as its competitor. Nor do the sources here say how the colonists themselves weighed their choice, how many left the colonies, or how the Argentine settlements compared in cost per family with the colonies in Palestine. Those questions remain open in the material this book draws on.

sections.h: Dreyfus, Herzl and Der Judenstaat, 1894–1896
sections.html:
Three years after Hirsch's company was incorporated in London, in December 1894, a French court-martial convicted Captain Alfred Dreyfus of treason. Dreyfus was a Jewish officer of the French army, born in Alsace. He was convicted on forged evidence; at its center was the bordereau, a note supposed to prove that he had been spying for Germany. [cite:wiki_dreyfus] Among the journalists who covered the case was the Paris correspondent of the Neue Freie Presse of Vienna, Theodor Herzl. Fourteen months after the conviction Herzl published Der Judenstaat, the pamphlet that became the founding text of political Zionism. [cite:herzl_diaries] [cite:herzl_judenstaat]

A familiar account holds that Zionism arose from ancient scripture. As a hope, the return to Zion was much older than Herzl, and other sections of this book trace that hope and the rabbis who first argued for practical settlement. As an organized political movement, though, Zionism took shape in response to a specific, documented modern antisemitism, and it was contested inside Jewish life from the moment it appeared. The way to see this is to follow the sequence closely: the case, the man, the two years between them, and the text itself.

The case. The bordereau was later shown to have been written by another officer, Ferdinand Esterhazy. Once his guilt became clear, the army's General Staff protected him rather than admit that it had convicted an innocent man. Dreyfus was sent to Devil's Island. [cite:wiki_dreyfus] That protection, as much as the original false conviction, is what turned the case into the defining scandal of its era. The Affair divided France into Dreyfusards and anti-Dreyfusards, a rupture that shaped French politics into the twentieth century. Its resolution came after this chapter closes: Émile Zola's open letter "J'accuse!", published in L'Aurore in January 1898, forced the frame-up into public view, and Dreyfus was fully rehabilitated in 1906, twelve years after his conviction. [cite:wiki_dreyfus] The record shows a named culprit, a protecting institution and a documented effort to cover the error. It does not show that the whole French army or government was complicit. Zola and many others who exposed the frame-up were French and not Jewish, and the correction came from inside France as well as from outside it.
