Why France mattered. The setting gave the case its force. France had emancipated its Jews in 1791, the first European state to do so. A century later the same country produced the most publicized antisemitic trial of the nineteenth century, with crowds in the streets crying against the Jews while the case ran. [cite:wiki_dreyfus] French Jews had built substantial civic and professional lives in the intervening century, and emancipation had not been meaningless. That is exactly why the Affair felt like a rupture rather than a continuation. Herzl drew the conclusion that if antisemitism could survive in emancipated, republican Paris, no Jewish community in Europe was structurally safe. [cite:wiki_dreyfus]

The man. Herzl was born on 2 May 1860 in Pest, later part of Budapest, to an assimilated, German-speaking Jewish family; he was educated in German and was culturally German-Austrian. The family moved to Vienna in 1878, where he entered the university to study law. He took his doctorate in 1884 and turned almost at once to journalism and playwriting instead of legal practice. In 1891 the Neue Freie Presse, one of the most influential German-language papers in Europe, made him its Paris correspondent. [cite:herzl_diaries] He was secular in outlook and not religiously observant. He did not receive Zionism ready-made from Jewish tradition. His diaries, published after his death, record him constructing it step by step.

The ceremony and the crowd. The usual story says that Herzl saw Dreyfus publicly degraded, heard the crowd, and became a Zionist on the spot. The sources for this book differ on the details of that moment. The short account says Herzl watched "Death to the Jews" chanted in the streets of Paris. [cite:wiki_dreyfus] The fuller account in the research on his diaries says he heard the crowd shouting "À bas les Juifs!" ("Down with the Jews!"), which is a different phrase, and dates his attendance at the degradation ceremony to 22 December 1894. [cite:herzl_diaries] Neither the wording nor the date has yet been checked against a primary source for this book, so both versions are given here. What the accounts agree on is that Herzl was present and recorded the moment.

The fourteen months. The diaries show that Herzl's thinking did not settle overnight. Between the conviction in December 1894 and the pamphlet in February 1896 he worked through several answers. During 1895 he considered mass conversion of Jews to Catholicism as a way to end antisemitism structurally; he considered social integration through political engagement; and, increasingly, he came to see territorial concentration as the only stable solution. [cite:herzl_diaries] What the Affair did was fix a diagnosis. In Herzl's reading, European antisemitism was not a leftover religious prejudice that modern life would wear away. It survived assimilation and survived the successful entry of Jews into professional and cultural life. Dreyfus was the very picture of that success, an officer of the French army who had married into the elite, and he had still been convicted on forged evidence, with his public humiliation cheered. [cite:herzl_diaries] If safety could not be had inside European societies, Herzl concluded, it had to be had outside them, in a separate polity. That was the argument of Der Judenstaat.

This is the strongest form of the case Herzl made, and it should be stated in its own terms. It was an argument about physical and civic safety, made against a record that included the pogroms and May Laws in the Russian Empire and now a show trial in the first European state to emancipate its Jews. [cite:wiki_may_laws] [cite:wiki_dreyfus] It was also narrower than the later founding story, which presents the state as the fulfillment of an ancient religious commitment. Herzl's proposal answered a specific European failure of the 1890s and turned it into a permanent political program. The religious and historical language that later surrounded it came, in large part, from others.

The diary of June 1895. One passage from these months has become central to a lasting dispute. In an entry dated 12 June 1895, Herzl wrote:

"We shall try to spirit the penniless population across the border by procuring employment for it in the transit countries, while denying it any employment in our own country... Both the process of expropriation and the removal of the poor must be carried out discreetly and circumspectly."

The entry was not published in Herzl's lifetime. It appeared in the Complete Diaries edited by Raphael Patai in 1960. [cite:herzl_diaries] Its meaning is contested. Benny Morris, in Righteous Victims, and Nur Masalha, in Expulsion of the Palestinians, treat it as evidence that Herzl was aware early on that the Zionist project would involve moving the existing population. Other scholars have argued that the passage has been misread, or that it referred to a population other than the Arabs of Palestine. [cite:herzl_diaries] The research behind this book goes further than the evidence allows at one point: it states as undisputed that Herzl publicly assured Ottoman officials that Jewish settlement would benefit the local Arab population while privately entertaining plans for their displacement. That conclusion depends on reading the 1895 entry as Morris and Masalha read it. Scholars who read the entry differently would not accept it, so it belongs inside the dispute, not above it.

What the pamphlet says. Der Judenstaat (The Jewish State, or The Jews' State) was published in Vienna on 14 February 1896. [cite:herzl_judenstaat] It is not a religious text. It reads as a work of political engineering, close at times to a business prospectus. Herzl proposed a "Society of Jews" to act as the political leadership and a "Jewish Company", a chartered economic-development corporation, to carry out the practical work. He proposed an orderly transfer of population, a seven-hour working day, a flag and a bank: the administrative furniture of a nineteenth-century European nation-state, applied to the Jewish question. [cite:herzl_judenstaat] He used "Jew" as a national category rather than a religious one and said that irreligious Jews would be included on equal terms. He rejected rabbinic authority as a principle for organizing the state. The text makes no claim to fulfil prophecy, uses no messianic framing and asserts no divine right. [cite:herzl_judenstaat]

Above all, the pamphlet did not treat Palestine as the only or obvious answer. Herzl put the question directly: "Shall we choose Palestine or Argentine? We shall take what is given us, and what is selected by Jewish public opinion." [cite:herzl_judenstaat_1896] Of Argentina he wrote that it was "by natural resources one of the richest countries on earth, comprising a vast extent of territory, a sparse population, and a mild climate." [cite:herzl_judenstaat] The country was then recruiting European immigrants and offering wide, thinly settled land, and Baron de Hirsch's Jewish Colonization Association had already planted Jewish colonies there (see the preceding section). One summary of the text adds that Herzl expected Argentina's government to "gladly provide" land, and that he later wrote that Palestine would give "the Jewish problem" a solution "not only just, but brilliant." [cite:herzl_judenstaat_1896]

How much weight Herzl gave each country is itself read in two ways. One account in the research holds that he treated Argentina and Palestine with roughly equal weight. [cite:herzl_judenstaat] Another holds that he considered Argentina first and Palestine second, preferring Palestine for practical and political reasons, chiefly that it would move Jewish public opinion, rather than religious ones. [cite:herzl_judenstaat_1896] The Israeli writer and peace activist Uri Avnery went further: in his reading, Herzl "had obviously thought very little about Palestine as a concrete entity" and inserted Palestine into his blueprint as an afterthought. [cite:herzl_judenstaat_1896] Avnery's is an interpretation, not a fact about the text. What the text plainly shows is that at its founding moment political Zionism was open about territory.

One correction is needed. Part of the material behind this book says that Der Judenstaat weighed Uganda as a candidate. It did not. The British offer of land in East Africa, known as the "Uganda" scheme, came in 1903, seven years later, and is told in [scene:s04f|the Uganda offer of 1903]. [cite:sixth_zionist_congress_1903] The pamphlet's alternatives were Argentina and Palestine.

From pamphlet to movement. A program needs patrons, and in 1896 Herzl looked for two. From that year he sought a charter from the Ottoman Sultan, offering help with the empire's public debt; his diary records a message relayed from Abdul Hamid II that the Sultan could not sell even a foot of the land, because it belonged not to him but to his people. [cite:w_herzl] He did not meet the Sultan until May 1901, and then obtained no charter. [cite:w_abdulhamid] In July 1896 he asked Baron Edmond de Rothschild, the patron of the colonies in Palestine, to back a state secured by charter rather than colonies secured by purchase, and was refused. His diary records his "rude telegram to Edmond Rothschild" and his resolve that "from Rothschild's negative attitude I must salvage everything." [cite:herzl_diaries_vol2_archive] That refusal, and a different version of how it happened, are told in [scene:bc_s04|Edmond de Rothschild's colonies]. Herzl turned instead to convening a congress.

What followed, in brief. The First Zionist Congress met at Basel on 29–31 August 1897, with 200 delegates from 17 countries, and founded the World Zionist Organization. Herzl wrote in his diary afterwards: "At Basel I founded the Jewish State. Perhaps in five years, certainly in fifty, everyone will see it." (Another rendering of the same entry, dated 3 September 1897, reads "In five years perhaps, and certainly in fifty.") The State of Israel was declared fifty-one years later, in 1948. [cite:herzl_diaries] Between 1901 and 1903 Herzl negotiated with Abdul Hamid II, Kaiser Wilhelm II, Pope Pius X and the British Colonial Secretary Joseph Chamberlain, and weighed Argentina, Cyprus, El-Arish in Sinai and East Africa. By the account in the research, Cyprus was set aside in 1902 because of its existing Greek and Turkish population, El-Arish in 1903 for lack of water, and the Sultan refused any transfer of sovereignty over Palestine. [cite:herzl_diaries] (Another source in this book dates Herzl's meeting with Pius X to January 1904, not to 1901–1903.) In August 1903 Herzl provisionally accepted the British offer in East Africa as a refuge after the Kishinev pogrom; the Sixth Zionist Congress voted 295 to 177 to send an exploratory commission, and a minority, mainly delegates from the Russian Empire, walked out. [cite:sixth_zionist_congress_1903] [cite:herzl_diaries] (A tally elsewhere in this book gives 295 to 178.) Herzl died of heart failure at Edlach, Austria, on 3 July 1904, aged 44. His one visit to Palestine, in October 1898, had been made to lobby Kaiser Wilhelm II. [cite:herzl_diaries] The Seventh Zionist Congress rejected the East Africa scheme in 1905. [cite:sixth_zionist_congress_1903]

When Palestine became fixed, and why. The sources disagree on both questions. One account in the research says the Palestine focus was settled through the negotiations at the Basel Congress of 1897. [cite:herzl_judenstaat] Another says Palestine became the only acceptable territory in 1905, decided by the movement's Russian base rather than by Herzl or by the founding text. [cite:herzl_diaries] On the reason, the accounts also pull in different directions. One emphasizes that the choice was a political decision of the movement, not a theological inevitability. The other holds that the Uganda debate was resolved by the religious and historical attachment of most Zionist supporters to the specific land: those who walked out in 1903 were not looking for any refuge but for a return to Zion, and "Zion Zionism" defeated "Territorial Zionism", sometimes called Ugandism. [cite:sixth_zionist_congress_1903] These readings can be reconciled. The founding text was open about territory, and the decision that closed the question drew on attachments the text itself did not invoke. As the research itself cautions, the pamphlet's openness does not make Palestine arbitrary or interchangeable with any other place. Specific religious, historical and communal reasons, examined in later chapters, made it the destination.

A later chapter builds an argument on this point, and it should be identified as an argument. Because the movement chose Palestine, it inherited a body of biblical texts tied to that land: Genesis 15:18, which speaks of a land "from the river of Egypt to the great river, the Euphrates river"; Deuteronomy 11:24; and the borders of Numbers 34. [cite:genesis_1518_text] In Argentina or East Africa, that argument runs, no such texts would apply, and the idea of a "Complete Land of Israel" (Eretz Yisrael HaShlema) could not have arisen. The full case is made in [scene:gia_src_s01|the Argentina counterfactual]. For this chapter it is enough to note that the territorial openness of 1896 is the starting point of that argument.

Contested from the start. Herzl's answer was one Jewish answer among several, and for decades it was not the majority's. Four distinct objections were present at its creation. Reform Judaism had already rejected a return in its Pittsburgh Platform of 1885: "We consider ourselves no longer a nation, but a religious community, and therefore expect neither a return to Palestine... nor the restoration of any of the laws concerning the Jewish state." [cite:pittsburgh_platform_1885] The Jewish Labour Bund, founded in Vilna in October 1897, the same year as the Basel Congress, rejected Zionism in favor of doikayt ("hereness"): Jewish cultural and national autonomy within the multi-ethnic societies of Eastern Europe, pursued through socialist politics alongside non-Jewish workers. It became the leading Jewish political movement in Eastern Europe, larger through the interwar years than the Zionist parties, and it was destroyed by Nazi and Soviet violence, not by losing the argument. [cite:wiki_bund] Ahad Ha'am proposed a cultural and spiritual center rather than a state, an alternative within Zionism rather than outright rejection. [cite:wiki_ahad_haam] Orthodox rabbis who opposed political Zionism held that return could come only through divine redemption, and that forcing it by human politics was a transgression; their line runs to today's Neturei Karta. [cite:neturei_karta] These four positions shared a rejection of political Zionism and little else: a socialist workers' movement, an American religious reform movement, a cultural essayist and Orthodox theologians often disagreed with one another. The dissent has continuous successors. Satmar and much of Haredi Jewry reject Zionism today; Jewish Voice for Peace and IfNotNow criticize it; Peter Beinart's The Crisis of Zionism (2012) and Judith Butler's Parting Ways (2012) are critiques written from within Jewish tradition. To record that Herzl founded a modern political movement, distinct from Judaism as a religious tradition, is a matter of historical accuracy, and it is a distinction Herzl himself drew.

A reading, not a finding. The research behind this section also contains an interpretive argument that runs far beyond 1896, and it is set out here as an interpretation, not as documented history. It holds that the modern State of Israel still works on Herzl's 1896 template: secular nationalism as the state's main framing; the split between a "Society of Jews" and a "Jewish Company" surviving in the division of labor between the state and the Jewish Agency; Herzl's vision of citizenship for Jews carried into statute by the Law of Return of 1950; and the question of the non-Jewish inhabitants left unresolved, from the Palestinian Arabs who made up 20% of Israel's pre-1967 population to the more than 5.3 million Palestinians under military occupation since 1967. The same reading connects the 1895 diary's phrase about spiriting a population across the border with the displacement of 750,000 Palestinians in 1948, and lists later steps (the occupation from 1967, the annexation of East Jerusalem in 1980, the Nation-State Law of 2018 with its downgrading of Arabic and its declaration of Jewish settlement as a "national value", and the Gaza campaign from 2023) as the working-out of that framework. It concedes that Herzl did not commit these acts and argues that he set the framework within which others did. Those events belong to later volumes, where their figures and sources are examined. Against this reading stand the dispute over what the 1895 entry meant, the gap of half a century and more between Herzl and the events it lists, and the cautions already noted: the openness of the 1896 text does not make Palestine arbitrary, and a framework is not the same thing as a decision by the people who later acted.

What the record leaves open. Several things remain unsettled. The exact date of the degradation ceremony Herzl attended and the exact words the crowd used differ between the sources here and have not been checked against a primary document. How much weight Herzl gave Argentina against Palestine depends on how one reads a short text, and the accounts used here read it differently. The meaning of the June 1895 diary entry is a genuine scholarly dispute, and this book does not resolve it. The sources also disagree on when Palestine became the movement's fixed goal, at Basel in 1897 or with the rejection of East Africa in 1905.

sections.h: The Board in 1896: Who Could Act on Palestine Before Basel
sections.html:
When the First Zionist Congress met at Basel in August 1897, it did not build the structures that would later fund, permit, bless or block a Jewish state. It walked into them. A common assumption, reading backward from the twentieth century, holds that the Zionist movement created the international power structures that later supported Israel. The record documents the reverse. By 1896 a sovereign state in Istanbul governed Palestine and had already written rules against Jewish settlement there; European powers held rights inside that state that let those rules leak; a British Parliament seated a lobby for finance; banking houses had long lent to governments and to the Pope; Protestant restorationists had wanted a Jewish Palestine for sixty years; a Vatican would refuse one; a Rothschild had already said no to Herzl; and in Palestine itself Arab notables and Jewish communities had their own institutions and quarrels. This section sets out those pieces as they stood at the end of 1896.

The state piece: Britain and the City. The British state that would issue the Balfour Declaration in 1917 governed through a Parliament in which the Corporation of the City of London held a business franchise and kept its Remembrancer, a Corporation official seated in the Commons and reviewing legislation for the City's interests. [cite:greenparty_remembrancer_2013] [cite:wiki_city_of_london_corporation] Beneath that sat an older mechanism. Since 1694 the British Crown had borrowed from private subscribers through a chartered company in the City, the Bank of England, created to finance William III's war against France. [cite:rs_rd0_boe_museum] Finance had both a seat inside the legislature and a standing channel into the Treasury. Neither made the City a sovereign. Parliament legislated for it, and its own description of its role, "rather like a trade body", is the documented finding. [cite:ohuiginn_city_corporation]

The finance piece: lenders, not puppeteers. The Rothschild houses were documented creditors to Britain and Prussia, and from 1832 to the Holy See. [cite:wiki_nathan_mayer_rothschild] [cite:wiki_rothschild_loans_holy_see] The London house arranged a £5 million sterling loan for Prussia in 1818 and in November 1875 advanced the £4,000,000 with which Disraeli's government bought 44% of the Suez Canal shares, a purchase Disraeli defended as "a highway to our Indian Empire". [cite:jwatte_rothschild_myths_record] [cite:rs_rd0_hefler_2023] [cite:rs_rd0_disraeli_1876] The 1832 papal loan of £400,000 is documented, though the sources differ on whether the London or the Paris house was the counterparty. [cite:wiki_rothschild_loans_holy_see] From 1882 the Paris house, through Baron Edmond de Rothschild, financed agricultural colonies in Palestine, roughly thirty of them by one count, on his own philanthropic terms. [cite:wiki_edmond_james_de_rothschild] In July 1896 Edmond refused to back Herzl's political project. [cite:herzl_diaries_vol2_archive] Every connection in this piece is a contract or a loan. None supports the legend of a family directing governments from behind the scenes, a legend this chapter traces to an antisemitic pamphlet of 1846. [cite:wiki_dairnvaell_satan_pamphlet]

The money in the picture followed political alignment only in part. Edmond's money built settlements and refused the movement. Baron Maurice de Hirsch's money, £2,000,000 of authorized capital in the Jewish Colonization Association from 1891, chose Argentina and sought no state. [cite:hadassah_mag_hirsch] Herzl in 1896 had a program; the sources here record no fortune behind it. The two great philanthropic fortunes this chapter documents were therefore committed to resettlement on terms other than those of political Zionism, a year before its Congress met.

The church piece: a Protestant yes, a Catholic no. Protestant restorationists in Britain and the United States had pressed for a Jewish Palestine since 1839, when Lord Shaftesbury urged Palmerston to sponsor it. In March 1891 the Blackstone Memorial, signed by more than four hundred prominent Americans, asked President Benjamin Harrison to support a Jewish homeland in Palestine. [cite:wiki_christian_zionism] Their motives were prophecy and empire, and most Jewish communal bodies of the period opposed or ignored them. [cite:wiki_christian_zionism] The papacy had lost the Papal States in 1870 and held a different theology. [cite:wiki_lateran_treaty] When Herzl went to Rome, in January 1904 by one source's date (another places the meeting between 1901 and 1903), Pope Pius X refused him on the ground that the Church could not support a Jewish restoration to a land central to its own theology while the Jews denied Christ. The Holy See did not recognize Israel until 30 December 1993, forty-five years after its founding. [cite:jcpa_vatican_israel_recognition] [cite:wiki_fundamental_agreement] That story belongs to later volumes and is told in [scene:vat_s01|the Vatican's refusal and its 45 years of non-recognition]. Two confessions held two positions, and both were political.

The sovereign piece: the Ottoman state. None of the pieces above held power in Palestine. The Ottoman Empire did, and it had already acted. In June 1882 it forbade the entry of foreign Jews and their purchase of land; in July 1882 it allowed Jews to settle anywhere in the empire except Palestine, provided they took Ottoman nationality. [cite:rs_rd0_barin_2014] Through the late 1880s foreign Jews were admitted to Jerusalem only as pilgrims, for one month and later three. [cite:rs_rd0_cojs_moore1887] [cite:rs_rd0_frus1888_may] An Ottoman note of 27 March 1894 barred Jewish immigrants from acquiring property in Palestine "for political reasons", for "the prevention of the permanent establishment in Palestine of Jewish immigrants". [cite:rs_rd0_frus1898_angell] When Herzl sought a charter in 1896, his diary records the Sultan's message that he could not sell even a foot of the land, because it belonged to his people. [cite:w_herzl]

The rules leaked because the empire was not sovereign in full over foreigners on its soil. Under the Capitulations and the protégé system, foreign Jews could live under European consular protection, and Britain had declared in 1847 that its consulates would protect Jews whose own states did not. [cite:rs_rd0_barin_2014] Britain and the United States protested the restrictions on grounds of religious equality, Britain citing Article 62 of the Treaty of Berlin (1878), which declared that "in no part of the Ottoman Empire shall difference of religion be alleged against any person". [cite:rs_rd0_cojs_fo1893] [cite:rs_rd0_frus1888_may] By Barın's count, more than 50,000 Jews settled despite the bans; her study covers 1882 to 1920, but the passage that gives the figure does not say which years it counts. [cite:rs_rd0_barin_2014] How the rules were made and broken is told in [scene:rd0_limits|the Ottoman limits and the first Arab responses].

The Palestinian piece: deputies, notables and a petition. Palestinian Arab society was not a blank on this board. In 1877 Yusuf Diya al-Khalidi of Jerusalem sat in the first Ottoman parliament as the sole deputy for the Jerusalem district and an opponent of Abdul Hamid II, until the Sultan suspended the chamber in February 1878 and ordered him out of Istanbul. [cite:rs_rd0_khalidi_palquest] The first reactions to Jewish settlement came from peasants, then from artisans and merchants whose livelihoods were touched. [cite:rs_rd0_beska_2007] On 24 June 1891 Arab notables in Jerusalem asked the Grand Vizier to bar Russian Jews from entering Palestine and buying land; a 1978 review of Neville Mandel's work describes it instead as a telegram from leaders in Jerusalem and Jaffa. [cite:rs_rd0_antizionism_wiki] [cite:rs_rd0_djn_1978] In 1893 a "Commission for Sale" chaired by the mufti of Jerusalem, Muhammad Tahir al-Husayni, was blocking land sales to Jews. [cite:rs_rd0_beska_2007] Whether this early opposition was political is disputed: a Jewish Agency overview doubts that the local opposition before 1891 had "any political connotations", while Beška finds that the mufti followed Jewish immigration from the 1880s and took an active stance against it. [cite:rs_rd0_jafi_opposition] [cite:rs_rd0_beska_2007]

The Jewish pieces: an old community, new colonies, a movement and its critics. The Jews of Palestine were not newcomers in 1882. Barın puts the Old Yishuv at about 24,000 in 1880, 13,900 of them in Jerusalem; another estimate gives 23,000. [cite:rs_rd0_barin_2014_pop] [cite:rs_rd0_firstaliyah_wiki] Between 1882 and 1891 new settlements were founded from Rishon LeZion and Zikhron Ya'akov to Rehovot and Hadera. [cite:rs_rd0_firstaliyah_wiki] Behind them stood organized groups: the student pioneers of BILU from 1882, the Hovevei Zion societies that met at Kattowitz in 1884, and the word "Zionism", coined by Nathan Birnbaum in 1890. [cite:w_bilu] [cite:w_hovevei] [cite:w_birnbaum] Herzl's Der Judenstaat of February 1896 came last and gave these groups a program for a state. [cite:herzl_judenstaat] Jewish critics stood on the same board. Reform Judaism's Pittsburgh Platform of 1885 expected "neither a return to Palestine... nor the restoration of any of the laws concerning the Jewish state." [cite:pittsburgh_platform_1885] Vienna's preacher Adolf Jellinek answered Pinsker that "We are at home in Europe", and in the 1880s Jerusalem's Orthodox community reported Zionist newcomers to the Ottoman authorities. [cite:rs_rd0_antizionism_wiki_dissent]

Put together, the pieces show who could act on Palestine in 1896, and through what instrument. Only the Porte could decide who entered and who bought land. The foreign powers could blunt its decisions through consular protection and treaty. The Paris house and the Jewish Colonization Association had the money to settle people, the restorationists had a voice in London and Washington, and the Jerusalem notables could petition the Porte and, through the mufti's commission, slow sales on the ground. Herzl had a pamphlet.

The years in a ledger. Read year by year, the period from the pogroms to the Dreyfus conviction shows the same pieces moving. In 1881 pogroms broke out in the Russian Empire; of the roughly two million Jews who emigrated in the following decades, the great majority went to America, not Palestine. [cite:wiki_pogroms_russian_empire] In 1882 Edmond de Rothschild began funding colonies. [cite:wiki_edmond_james_de_rothschild] In 1885 Reform Judaism's Pittsburgh Platform rejected a return. [cite:pittsburgh_platform_1885] In 1891 Hirsch founded the Jewish Colonization Association with £2,000,000 of capital. [cite:hadassah_mag_hirsch] In 1894 Dreyfus was convicted, the event the ledger marks as Herzl's turn to political Zionism; his diaries show that turn developing over the following years. [cite:wiki_dreyfus]

The ledger's "Who objected" column records the emigrants who chose America and the Reform movement. It leaves blank two objections this chapter documents. In 1882, the year the ledger marks for Edmond's colonies, the Ottoman state forbade foreign Jews to enter and buy land. [cite:rs_rd0_barin_2014] In 1891, the year it marks for Hirsch, Jerusalem's notables petitioned against Jewish immigration and land purchase. [cite:rs_rd0_antizionism_wiki] Read with those two entries added, the ledger shows opposition from the sovereign in the first year of organized settlement, and from Jerusalem's notables within a decade.

What the board does and does not explain. To say the board existed is not to say it decided the outcome. Its pieces could move in different directions, and in 1896 several of the strongest were set against Herzl's project: the Sultan, Edmond de Rothschild, Reform Judaism and the Jerusalem notables, and the papacy would refuse Herzl after Basel. What the record supports is narrower and firmer: the structures that would fund, permit, bless or block a Jewish state were older than the movement that asked for one. Some questions remain open in the sources used here. They give no decade-by-decade count of the Arab population of Palestine for this period. They do not total Edmond's spending on the colonies. They do not preserve the text or the signatories of the 1891 petition. And they cannot say how any of these pieces would have moved had the movement chosen Argentina instead.

The next part of this book opens at Basel in 1897 and follows how a political program became a state in fifty-one years, through Basel, Sykes-Picot, the Balfour Declaration and the Mandate, beginning with the First Zionist Congress. Zionism did not build this board. It entered a game whose pieces were already set, and the chapters that follow trace what it did with them.

chapters.label: Stage One
chapters.title: Conceive
chapters.intro:
In 1896 Theodor Herzl (1860–1904), a Budapest-born journalist working in Vienna, published Der Judenstaat, a pamphlet that weighed Palestine against Argentina as the territory for a political answer to European antisemitism. [cite:herzl_judenstaat] The country he named first had no border and no government of its own. It was Ottoman land, administered since 1872 as the Mutasarrifate of Jerusalem, with the districts of Jaffa, Hebron, Beersheba and Gaza, and the sanjaks of Nablus and Acre to its north. [cite:rs_rd1_jerusalemstory] Most of its people were Arabic-speaking Muslims and Christians. Its Jews, about 7,000 in 1800 and about 27,000 in 1880 by the National Library of Israel's count, lived mostly in four holy cities, almost entirely on charity from abroad; since 1881 a new wave of immigrants had begun to change them. [cite:rs_rd1_nli_oldyishuv] From the 1880s the Ottoman government restricted Jewish immigration and land purchase, though the restrictions were enforced unevenly. In 1896 there was not yet a Zionist Organization, a movement bank, a national land fund or a Zionist office in Jaffa.

This stage asks how, in twenty-one years, a pamphlet became a working structure: who built it, with whose money, under which law, and against whom. It also tests a familiar claim, that the project of a Jewish state grew out of the catastrophe of the 1930s and 1940s. The dates in this stage stand against that claim. By 1905 the movement had weighed Argentina, a Sinai buffer at Suez and a British offer in East Africa, and it had chosen Palestine through its own contested votes. Herzl died in 1904 at 44 and never saw the state he predicted. [cite:herzl_diaries]

The cast is wide, and it argued with itself. On the Zionist side stood Herzl and his successors David Wolffsohn and Otto Warburg; Chaim Weizmann and Nahum Sokolow, who led the movement from London in wartime; Arthur Ruppin and Yehoshua Hankin, who organized the buying of land; the young workers of the Second Aliyah; and, in the United States, Henrietta Szold and Louis Brandeis. Against Herzl, or beside him on other terms, stood Jewish opponents: the German "protest rabbis", the Bund, Ahad Ha'am, Edmond de Rothschild, American Reform rabbis, Agudat Israel and, in 1917, the official bodies of British Jewry. The powers Herzl approached for a charter were Abdul Hamid II, Kaiser Wilhelm II, Joseph Chamberlain, Vyacheslav von Plehve and Pius X. In Palestine and its region, Yusuf Diya al-Khalidi wrote to Herzl in 1899, the Nazareth governor Shukri al-Asali tried to block a land sale in 1910, Najib Nassar and the El-Issa cousins built an Arabic press that argued against Zionism, and Jerusalem's deputies raised it in the Ottoman parliament. The sellers were landowners, many of them absentee, such as the Sursock family of Beirut; the tenants who worked their land held no title to it.

The sections follow that record roughly in time. They begin with the Ottoman country and the dispute over how many people lived in it, then the Basel Congress of 1897 and its opponents, the machinery of the Zionist Organization, and Herzl's search for a charter. Herzl's exchange with al-Khalidi sets out what the founders knew of the people already there and what they proposed. The money follows: the Jewish Colonial Trust, the Jewish National Fund, and the Anglo-Palestine Company, founded in the same months that the Kishinev pogrom drove the movement to vote on East Africa. The rejection of that offer in 1905, the split it caused and a labelled thought experiment about it come next, then the Jewish currents for and against, the Second Aliyah and the Yemenite immigration, the Palestine Office, and the Scofield Reference Bible. The land mechanism is examined from the Ottoman sale of the Jezreel Valley in 1872 onward, beside the Arab press that reported it. The American organizations, the founding of the Federal Reserve and the claim attached to it, and the war years in Palestine lead to the services Jews rendered Britain and to [scene:s07a|what stood by 1917]. The promise Britain made that November is told in [scene:s06|the next stage].
chapters.outro:
At the end of 1917 the project announced at Basel twenty years earlier had institutions but no sovereignty, land but no title to the country, and, in its last weeks, a British promise. Each layer of that architecture was laid by different hands, and each was contested.

The legal layer was still Ottoman. Until British forces occupied Palestine in December 1917 and the Mutasarrifate of Jerusalem was dissolved, the country's law was the empire's. [cite:rs_rd1_jerusalemstory] Under it the movement had won none of what it set out to win in 1897. The Basel Program asked for a home "secured under public law"; Herzl's search for a charter met the Sultan's refusal, the Kaiser's fading interest, Cromer's veto of El-Arish and Pius X's "we could never sanction it." [cite:rs_rd1_basel_wiki] [cite:w_herzl] [cite:wiki_kaiser_levant_1898] [cite:unu_water_elarish] [cite:jcpa_vatican_israel_recognition] What it had instead was private law. Land was registered under the Land Code of 1858 and could be bought from whoever held the title, often an absentee owner, while the tenants who worked miri land held no registered title and had no claim when it was sold. [cite:w_ottoman_land_code] [cite:badil_land_ownership_palestine] The Ottoman restrictions of 1881–83 and 1892 slowed purchase without stopping it: they were evaded through Ottoman Jewish buyers, consular protection and American naturalization, and Jewish-held land reached about 418,000 dunams, around 2 percent of the territory, in 1918. [cite:israelfactcheck_ottoman_land_laws] [cite:state_gov_1892_naturalization] The one commitment in public law came at the very end: a letter of November 1917 in which Britain backed "the establishment in Palestine of a national home for the Jewish people," issued before Ottoman rule in Palestine had ended. [cite:balfour_letter]

The administrative layer belonged to others. The Zionist Organization held no governing authority in Palestine. [cite:palquest_wzo] It built an administration for settlement alone: the Palestine Office in Jaffa from 1908, coordinating purchase with the Jewish National Fund, aiding immigration and placing settlers, and the Hashomer guards, who made the hiring of Jewish workers a condition of their service. [cite:wiki_palestine_office] [cite:rs_rd1_jvl_defense] Real administrative power lay with Ottoman officials, who could resist but not always prevail. Shukri al-Asali opposed the al-Fula sale of 1910 as governor of Nazareth, and permission came through Hankin's friends in Constantinople. [cite:rs_rd1_ruppin_emek] [cite:rs_rd1_asali_wiki] In wartime that power fell on Palestine's people directly: the expulsion of up to 6,000 Russian-citizen Jews from Jaffa in December 1914, the Ottomanization order of 1915, and the deportation of 6 April 1917, after which Jews were barred from returning until the summer of 1918. [cite:rs_rd1_jaffa_wiki] [cite:rs_rd1_yishuv_wwi]

The institutional and financial layer was the movement's own, and its shape lasted. A Congress elected under the 1899 constitution sat above a seven-member executive and a 37-member council. [cite:palquest_wzo] [cite:ismi_israel_yearbook] Its money came from many small holders and was controlled by a few. The Jewish Colonial Trust raised about £250,000 against a target of £2,000,000, while its first 100 founders' shares carried votes equal to all the rest combined. [cite:jct_wiki] [cite:jewishencyclopedia_colonial_trust] Its Anglo-Palestine Company lent in Jaffa from 1903 and financed Tel Aviv's first neighborhood; the Jewish National Fund held what it bought permanently, leased and never sold; and the Palestine Land Development Company had handled about 50,000 dunams by the war. [cite:apc_wiki] [cite:jnf_wiki] [cite:encyclopedia_otto_warburg] Shareholders and blue-box households paid; settlers on leased land gained; the cost fell on tenants without title, most of it, as later volumes show, after 1917. [cite:wiki_sursock_purchases] Jewish opinion did not stand behind this structure as one. The Bund, Reform rabbis, Agudat Israel and the Antizionistisches Komitee opposed it, and in May 1917 the Board of Deputies and the Anglo-Jewish Association declared against it in The Times. [cite:wiki_bund] [cite:rs_rd1_grill_currents] [cite:jpost_why_rothschild]

The Palestinian Arab layer was a public voice without an institution of its own. Yusuf Diya al-Khalidi set out its case in 1899: the land was Ottoman and inhabited, and should be left alone. [cite:rs_rd1_khalidi_wiki] From 1905 it had a voice in the press: Najib Nassar wrote against Zionism in Cairo and Beirut, then founded al-Karmil in Haifa in 1908, and Filastin appeared in Jaffa from 1911, sent to every village of the Jaffa district, and in 1911 the Jerusalem deputies raised Zionism in the Ottoman parliament, opposing immigration rather than Palestine's own Jews. [cite:rs_rd1_palquest_nassar] [cite:wiki_falastin] [cite:rs_rd1_ruhi_wiki] Nassar's call for a non-Zionist society in Nablus in 1913 suggests that no such body yet existed. [cite:rs_rd1_palquest_nassar] Its strongest case was consent: no documented negotiation sought the agreement of the Arab leadership before organized purchase began. The Zionist case at its strongest was legality and benefit: purchases lawful under Ottoman law, sellers who in Ruppin's account wanted cash, and Herzl's argument that settlement would increase the wealth of the people already there. [cite:rs_rd1_ruppin_emek] [cite:rs_rd1_khalidi_intercept]

The regional layer was an empire in which Arab reformers sought change before the war and Arab nationalists met repression during it. The Arab Congress in Paris in 1913 sought reform within the empire and said nothing about Zionism. [cite:rs_rd1_arabcongress_wiki] Then came famine in Greater Syria and the hanging of Arab nationalists in Damascus, al-Asali among them. [cite:rs_rd1_aub_famine] [cite:rs_rd1_asali_wiki] Britain's other wartime commitments in the region belong to [scene:s06|the next stage].

The American layer was built before the promise it later served. The Federation of American Zionists dated from 1898; Hadassah from 1912; Brandeis took up leadership in 1914 and worked the channel to President Wilson; and in 1918 the bodies merged into a Zionist Organization of America of 147,551 members. [cite:w_zf_gb] [cite:hadassah_wiki] [cite:brandeis_zionism_wiki] [cite:zoa_wiki] A separate Christian constituency had its text in the Scofield Reference Bible of 1909. [cite:wiki_scofield_bible] America was above all where Jewish emigrants went: about 2 million of the more than 2.5 million who left Eastern Europe between 1881 and 1914. [cite:rs_rd1_ettinger] The claim that the Federal Reserve of 1913 was tied to Zionist finance finds no support. [cite:federalreservehistory_fed_act]

What was settled by 1917 was the choice of territory, made by Congress vote in 1905, and the machinery to buy and hold land in it. What was contested was nearly everything else: whether lawful purchase from absentee owners could stand in for consent, whether Herzl's 1895 diary entry foreshadowed transfer, whether the Second Aliyah's institutions grew from ideals or from the contest over land and work, and whether services to Britain shaped the Declaration. The record leaves open even the baseline: the Jewish population of 1914 ranges from 38,754 to 94,000 depending on who was counted, and how far it fell in the war is disputed. [cite:rs_rd1_mccarthy_owen] [cite:rs_rd1_demog_wiki] The documents show that the structure existed before 1917. They do not show what it would become.

sections.h: The Country Before the Program: Ottoman Palestine, 1872–1914
sections.html:
When Theodor Herzl and his colleagues spoke of Palestine in the late 1890s, they were speaking of a place that had no border and no government of its own. From 1516 to 1917, apart from a period of Egyptian rule in 1831–40, the land was governed as part of the Ottoman Empire. It was administered chiefly as the district of Jerusalem and as parts of the provinces of Beirut and Damascus, and nothing separated it from the territories that are today Syria, Lebanon and Jordan. Damascus, Baghdad, Jerusalem and Beirut were provincial cities of the same state, and people and goods moved between them without passports. The national borders that frame every later chapter of this book did not yet exist. Syria, Iraq, Lebanon, Jordan and Israel were not states. Almost every line that matters in the region's conflicts was drawn between 1916 and 1922, in a window of six years, by Britain and France. Iran, a separate Persian state with its own dynasty, its own language and a Shia majority, was never Ottoman at all.

Two misreadings of this period are common, and they point in opposite directions. One holds that the Ottomans "occupied" Palestine in the way later settlers did. The other holds that Palestine was an empty backwater of the empire, waiting to be filled. The record supports neither. Ottoman rule was imperial administration: governors, garrisons and taxation imposed over a population that remained, for four centuries, largely Arabic-speaking Muslims and Christians, alongside long-established Jewish communities. The Ottomans ruled the country; they did not replace its people. A third misreading, that the Middle East has always been a set of hostile nations permanently at war, fails for a simpler reason. For four hundred years most of the region was one state.

The administrative shape that mattered in Herzl's lifetime dated from 1872. In that year the Ottoman government created the Mutasarrifate, or Sanjak, of Jerusalem as an independent administrative unit. It comprised the districts of Jerusalem, Jaffa, Hebron, Beersheba and Gaza. To its north lay two further sanjaks, Nablus and Acre. This arrangement lasted until Britain occupied Palestine in December 1917, when the Mutasarrifate was dissolved.[cite:rs_rd1_jerusalemstory] The country that Zionist delegates debated at Basel was therefore, in legal terms, one Ottoman unit centered on Jerusalem plus parts of two others. When later writers speak of "Palestine" in this period, they are describing a region that the Ottoman state itself divided among several administrations.

Inside this imperial frame, religion rather than nationality organized much of daily law. Under the millet system the empire recognized religious communities, Muslims, Christians of several churches, and Jews, and allowed each to govern marriage, inheritance and schooling through its own religious law, its own courts and its own leaders.[cite:w_ottoman_millet] The arrangement gave communities real autonomy over their internal lives. It was not, however, a golden age, and the record does not present it as one. The order carried heavy taxation and conscription, and it saw periodic violence. Non-Muslims paid special taxes and held a lesser legal status, and revolts were suppressed. The point is not that the Ottoman order was just. It is that it was a different order from the one the twentieth century built: an empire of religious communities, not a map of rival nation-states.

The Jews already living in this country when the Zionist movement was founded had their own long history, and their own institutions, quite separate from the movement that would arise in Europe. Historians call this community the Old Yishuv. According to the National Library of Israel, the Jewish population of the land grew from about 7,000 in 1800 to about 27,000 in 1880.[cite:rs_rd1_nli_oldyishuv] It was concentrated in the four cities that Jewish tradition held holy, Jerusalem, Hebron, Safed and Tiberias, and in the nineteenth century most of it lived in Jerusalem. The same four cities appear in the record of the wider Ottoman population as the places where Jewish communities lived among a mostly Arabic-speaking Muslim and Christian majority.

The Old Yishuv lived largely on money from abroad. It depended almost completely on the halukka, funds collected from diaspora donors and distributed through kollels, which were organized by the donors' and recipients' country of origin and by Hasidic affiliation. The money therefore moved through communal channels rather than through any political body. Before the Ottoman authorities, the Jews were represented by the Sephardi chief rabbi, the Hakham Bashi, a post later titled Rishon LeZion. At the end of the nineteenth century the Ashkenazi kollels united under a single body, the General Committee of Knesset Israel.[cite:rs_rd1_nli_oldyishuv] These were the Jews of Ottoman Palestine as the empire knew them: a recognized religious community within the millet order, Sephardi and Ashkenazi, supported by charity.

That began to change before Herzl. The National Library of Israel dates the beginning of a "New Yishuv" to the First Aliyah, the wave of immigration that began in 1881, and describes it as costing the Old Yishuv its leading position among the Jews of the country.[cite:rs_rd1_nli_oldyishuv] The Interactive Encyclopedia of the Palestine Question counts about 25,000 Jewish immigrants in 1882–1903, and more than 84,000 in 1850–1914, noting that not all of them stayed.[cite:rs_rd1_palquest_chron] The Ottoman Land Code of 1858, which governed how land in the country was held, is examined in the previous stage of this book: [scene:ot_s01|the Ottoman Land Code].

Palestine's Jews were also one community among several in the Ottoman Middle East with deep roots. Jewish life in Mesopotamia, modern Iraq, went back to the Babylonian conquest of Judah in 586 BCE, and the scholars of that community compiled the Babylonian Talmud, still the primary text of rabbinic study.[cite:huc_farhud][cite:ushmm_farhud] That continuous presence predated the Iraqi state of 1932 and the Israeli state of 1948 by millennia; its later history belongs to a different part of this library: [scene:irq_e01|the Jews of Iraq].

How many people lived in Palestine on the eve of the First World War, and how many of them were Jews, is a question on which the sources disagree, and the disagreement is not a technicality. The numbers below are the main ones in the record, with what each source actually counted.

The Ottoman census of 1914–15 recorded 722,000 people: 602,000 Muslims, 81,000 Christians and 39,000 Jews. Roberto Bachi's reconstruction for 1914 gives a smaller total, 689,000, made up of 525,000 Muslims, 70,000 Christians and 94,000 Jews.[cite:rs_rd1_demog_wiki] The gap between the two Jewish figures, 39,000 against 94,000, is larger than the whole Jewish population of 1880. The difference begins with who was counted. The Ottoman register recorded 38,754 Jews, and on the analysis of the historian Justin McCarthy it apparently counted only Ottoman subjects. Many Jews in Palestine were foreign nationals and did not appear in it. McCarthy, adjusting the Ottoman figures, gives a total of 722,143 for 1914–15 and puts the true Jewish figure, including foreign nationals, closer to 60,000. Against this stands the figure long accepted in the literature, 85,000, as summarized by Roger Owen in his review of McCarthy's work.[cite:rs_rd1_mccarthy_owen] The Interactive Encyclopedia of the Palestine Question agrees with McCarthy's order of magnitude: about 60,000 Jews at the start of the war in 1914, 39,000 of them Ottoman citizens, against more than 700,000 Muslim and Christian Ottoman subjects.[cite:rs_rd1_palquest_chron]

The same pattern appears a generation earlier. For about 1890, Bachi's reconstruction gives 532,000 people, 43,000 of them Jews; the Ottoman census of 1890–91 gives 516,000, with 18,000 Jews.[cite:rs_rd1_demog_wiki] Here the reconstruction is higher on both counts, and its Jewish figure is more than double the census's. The direction of McCarthy's corrections is also on record. He adjusts Ottoman registers chiefly for the undercounting of young children, especially girls, and for categories of people the registers missed, and on the same reasoning he re-estimates the population of 1922 at 823,684, above the official British census total, arguing that modern methods correct the census undercount.[cite:rs_rd1_mccarthy_owen]

Each side of this dispute has a serious case. The lowest figure, 38,754, is a contemporary official register, but on McCarthy's reading it counted Ottoman subjects only. McCarthy's estimate of about 60,000 adds back the foreign nationals the register left out, and his corrections are stated: young children, especially girls, and missing categories. Those who hold to the higher figures rest on the figure long accepted in the literature, 85,000, and on Bachi's reconstruction, 94,000. The sources available here do not set out Bachi's method in detail, so the case for his figure cannot be tested against the record in this book.

What none of the figures disputes is the order of magnitude that mattered politically. On every count, the Jewish population of Palestine in 1914 was a minority, living among a majority of Arabic-speaking Muslim and Christian Ottoman subjects. On every count, too, it had grown several times over since 1800, first through the Old Yishuv's slow increase and then through immigration after 1881. How far it fell during the war that began in 1914 is itself disputed, with one account holding that about a third left and McCarthy arguing the fall was much less than the commonly cited quarter, since many who fled to Alexandria returned; that story is told in [scene:rd1_wwi|Palestine at war].[cite:rs_rd1_palquest_chron][cite:rs_rd1_mccarthy_owen]

The empire that governed all of these people did not survive the war. British forces captured Jerusalem in December 1917, ending Ottoman rule in the city. The Republic of Turkey, founded in 1923, renounced all rights over the former Arab provinces in the Treaty of Lausanne that same year.[cite:w_lausanne] Modern Turkey is thus the empire's successor state, not a claimant to Palestine. The layers that followed, oil, the Anglo-French carve-up, installed rulers and revolts, were stacked on top of the Ottoman order, and later volumes take them up one at a time.

Some things stay open. The record gives no single agreed figure for the Jewish population in 1914, and none of its figures can be treated as settled: the range runs from 38,754 to 94,000 depending on who was counted and how. It does not say how many of the more than 84,000 Jewish immigrants of 1850–1914 stayed. Nor does it measure how the Old Yishuv's members themselves regarded the newcomers of 1881 and after, beyond the National Library's judgment that the New Yishuv displaced them from leadership.

sections.h: Basel, 1897: The Program and Its Opponents
sections.html:
The movement that set its sights on that Ottoman country has a precise birthplace and date. Political Zionism was founded at the First Zionist Congress, which met in Basel, Switzerland, from 29 to 31 August 1897. Its convener and chairman was Theodor Herzl, a journalist born in Budapest and a subject of Austria-Hungary, who had published Der Judenstaat the year before. The Congress adopted a platform, the Basel Program, and founded the Zionist Organization with Herzl as its first president. Its founding leadership was overwhelmingly European, and so were its funding and its location.[cite:zionism_founding_1897] The familiar claim that the State of Israel grew from an ancient national presence with no meaningful break therefore needs a qualification at the start. The movement that set out to build a state there was new, and it was organized in Europe in 1897.

A second familiar claim, that Jews embraced Zionism from the start, does not survive the record of that same summer. The Congress was opposed before it opened, it was opposed by rabbis in Germany and Britain, and in the same season a rival Jewish movement was founded on the opposite premise. The contest inside Jewish life over Herzl's project is one of the clearest pieces of evidence that Zionism and Judaism were not the same thing, and that Jewish opponents, religious and secular, were the first to insist on the difference.

Herzl had planned to hold the Congress in Munich. It never met there. On 5 June 1897 a notice in the Münchner Neueste Nachrichten rejected holding his congress in the city, and in mid-June, in letters dated 13 June, the board of the Munich Jewish congregation wrote to Herzl rejecting it as well.[cite:rs_rd1_grill_basel] The venue moved to neutral Switzerland. In one account, the protest of local Orthodox and Reform rabbis helped push the Congress to Basel, and the German Rabbinical Association refused to support holding it in Munich.[cite:wiki_first_zionist_congress] The documents of June 1897 name the congregation's board and the press notice as the first refusals.

The rabbis' formal protest followed. On 6 July 1897 the board of the Allgemeiner Rabbiner-Verband, the Union of Rabbis in Germany, published a resolution protesting Zionism, on the grounds of loyalty to the state and of religious messianism. Herzl gave its authors a name that stuck: the Protestrabbiner, the "protest rabbis".[cite:rs_rd1_grill_basel] The declaration appeared in English in the London Jewish Chronicle on 9 July 1897, on page 9. It was signed by the Union's executive committee: Maybaum of Berlin, Horovitz of Frankfurt, Guttmann of Breslau, Auerbach of Halberstadt and Werner of Munich. It called the Zionists' efforts toward a state "antagonistic to the messianic promises of Judaism", and it urged Jews to "hold aloof" from the movement and from its Congress.[cite:rs_rd1_posen_protest] The document is more precise than the label attached to it. The rabbis did not object to Jewish agricultural colonization of Palestine. What they rejected was a political state.[cite:rs_rd1_posen_protest] In Britain, the Orthodox Chief Rabbi Hermann Adler sided with the German rabbis and called Herzl's plan völlig unheilbringend, "completely disastrous".[cite:rs_rd1_grill_basel]

The Congress met in the Basel Municipal Casino. The figure most often given for its size is 208 delegates from 17 countries, among them 14 women who attended without a vote.[cite:wiki_first_zionist_congress] Herzl presided in top hat and morning coat, and a photograph of him leaning over the balcony of the Drei Könige hotel became one of the movement's most familiar images.[cite:wiki_first_zionist_congress] The size of the gathering is less certain than the famous number suggests. The Posen Library describes some two hundred delegates from seventeen countries.[cite:rs_rd1_posen_congress] The Jewish Virtual Library gives "some 200 participants" without naming the number of countries.[cite:rs_rd1_jvl_congresses_a] The historian Tobias Grill writes that the delegates came from fourteen states.[cite:rs_rd1_grill_basel] The sources agree on roughly two hundred people; they differ on the exact count and on whether the delegates came from fourteen states or seventeen countries.

The program that the Congress adopted unanimously on 30 August 1897 was short. Its aim, in a standard English translation, read:[cite:rs_rd1_basel_wiki][cite:rs_rd1_basel_palquest]

Zionism seeks to establish a home in Palestine for the Jewish people, secured under public law.

Another published translation renders the same sentence as "the establishment of a publicly and legally secured home in Palestine for the Jewish people". Both versions turn on one word. The German original uses Heimstätte, a home or homestead, and not Staat, a state.[cite:rs_rd1_basel_palquest] The wording was revised during the Congress itself. According to one reference account, the draft first read rechtlich, "legally" secured, and was changed to öffentlich-rechtlich, "secured under public law"; that account does not give the reason for the change.[cite:rs_rd1_basel_wiki]

The program then named four means to the aim. The first was the promotion of settlement in Palestine by Jewish agriculturists, artisans and tradesmen. The second was the organization of all Jews through local and general institutions "according to the laws of the various countries". The third was the strengthening of Jewish national feeling and consciousness. The fourth was preparatory steps toward obtaining the consent of governments, which was needed to reach the aim.[cite:rs_rd1_basel_wiki][cite:rs_rd1_basel_palquest] Read against the twenty years that followed, these four clauses can be read as a plan of construction: each can be matched to an institution or a line of action, set out below.

The founders said plainly what kind of project this was. Der Judenstaat had framed it as secular nationalism, modeled on the nation-building of nineteenth-century Europe, and Herzl himself was religiously non-observant.[cite:herzl_judenstaat] The First Congress's program, preserved in the Zionist Organization's own archives, deals with political organization, the mechanisms of land purchase and diplomatic outreach, not religious doctrine. Religious authority was contested at the Congress and largely absent from its decisions.[cite:wiki_first_zionist_congress] None of this shows that no delegate had religious motives, or that Zionism never took on religious meaning for its adherents later. It shows what the founding texts say about the founding project, and the texts are still there to be read.

The Congress's most durable product was an organization. The Zionist Organization was built as a standing, congressional-style body of elected delegates with a governing executive, and from 1899 it had its own bank, the Jewish Colonial Trust.[cite:wiki_wzo] Herzl was its first president; Chaim Weizmann would lead it in the period of the Balfour Declaration. It ran the Congresses, managed land purchase through the Jewish National Fund from 1901, and conducted the great-power diplomacy that produced the Declaration in 1917. In 1929 it created the expanded Jewish Agency for Palestine, which became the proto-government of the Jewish community under the British Mandate, running immigration, settlement, defense and diplomacy. When the state was declared in 1948, the Agency's executive effectively became Israel's provisional government. The organization continues today, and the Jewish Agency still administers immigration and diaspora relations with quasi-governmental status, formalized by an Israeli law of 1952.[cite:wiki_wzo] The line from Basel to the state is an institutional one: a durable, public bureaucracy that outlived everyone who built it, and whose working is traced in [scene:zorg_s01|the organization's machinery]. Herzl understood that the members would have to be won. At the Second Congress in 1898 his watchword was to "conquer the communities", meaning the established congregations.[cite:rs_rd1_grill_basel][cite:rs_rd1_jvl_congresses_a]

Herzl's own verdict on the Congress has become part of its legend. After Basel he wrote in his diary: "At Basel I founded the Jewish State. Perhaps in five years, certainly in fifty, everyone will see it."[cite:herzl_diaries] He was wrong about the five years and almost exactly right about the fifty: the state was declared in May 1948, fifty-one years later. He did not live to see any of it. He died in 1904 at the age of forty-four, exhausted by the diplomacy of offering his project to the Sultan, the Kaiser and the British. The prediction should not be read as more than it was. Herzl foresaw an outcome, not the path to it; nothing in the entry anticipates the Balfour Declaration, the Mandate or the war of 1948 through which statehood actually came.

Opposition to the project came from several directions at once, and the objections were different in kind. The most popular was secular and socialist. The General Jewish Labour Bund was founded in Vilna in October 1897, in the same season as the Basel Congress, and became Zionism's great rival for the loyalty of the Jews of Eastern Europe.[cite:wiki_bund] Against emigration to Palestine it set the idea of doikayt, "hereness": Jews should fight for their rights and build their culture where they already lived, as a national minority with autonomy inside democratic, multi-ethnic states, in solidarity with the non-Jewish working class. It was socialist, Yiddishist and committed to the diaspora. From the 1900s to the 1930s it was arguably the largest and most dynamic Jewish political movement in Poland and the Russian Empire, and in interwar Poland it regularly outpolled the Zionist parties in Jewish community elections. The Bund did not lose its argument with Zionism; it was destroyed. The Bolsheviks dissolved it in 1921, its leader Mark Liber was later executed in the Stalinist purges, its mass base in Polish and Soviet Jewry was murdered in the Holocaust or suppressed under Stalin, and the Polish Bund was suppressed a second time after the war.[cite:wiki_bund] For half a century the most popular Jewish political movement in the heartland of Zionist recruitment was explicitly anti-Zionist.

A second objection was theological. Orthodox anti-Zionist rabbis held that the return of the Jewish people to the land and the restoration of Zion were redemptive events reserved for divine action in the messianic age, not a political program to be forced by secular nationalists ahead of God's time. To many Orthodox authorities, a secular state built in the Holy Land by non-observant socialists was closer to sacrilege than to fulfillment.[cite:neturei_karta] This was a different argument from the Bund's: the Bund wanted Jewish autonomy without a state, while these rabbis rejected human political action as the means of return. The position has been held continuously since 1897, through Satmar Hasidism and, most visibly, the small Neturei Karta group, whose members still appear at Palestinian-solidarity demonstrations with signs distinguishing Judaism from Zionism. It is a minority position within Orthodox Judaism; most Haredi Jews today are not Neturei Karta and have made various accommodations with the state.[cite:neturei_karta] Reform Judaism's opposition and the wider range of Jewish positions in these years are traced in [scene:rd1_currents|Jewish currents for and against].

A third objection came from inside the movement. Ahad Ha'am, "one of the people", was the pen name of Asher Ginsberg (1856–1927), the founder of what came to be called cultural Zionism and political Zionism's sharpest internal critic.[cite:wiki_ahad_haam] He had visited Ottoman Palestine, and in his essay of 1891, "Truth from the Land of Israel", he reported what much of the movement preferred not to see: the land was not empty. It had a substantial Arab population, farming and living on it, who would not simply accept displacement, and he warned that treating them with contempt would poison the whole enterprise. This is Zionist testimony, from 1891, that Palestine was inhabited. Against Herzl he argued that a hurried political and diplomatic state would produce "a state of Jews" but not "a Jewish state": a polity Jewish in population but hollow in spirit, having skipped the slow cultural and ethical renewal he believed must come first. He wanted a spiritual center in the land that would radiate a renewed Hebrew culture to the diaspora, not a nation-state won through great-power maneuvering.[cite:wiki_ahad_haam] Israelis across the political spectrum still invoke him. What the record establishes is narrower and firmer: the warning was made at the founding moment, not in hindsight. It cannot show that his alternative would have produced a better outcome had it been adopted.

The fourth opponent was the movement's greatest existing patron. Baron Edmond de Rothschild (1845–1934), of the Paris branch of the family, had privately funded the struggling agricultural colonies of the First Aliyah in Ottoman Palestine since the 1880s, among them Rishon LeZion and Zichron Ya'akov, which was named for his father. His money, sums that would run to tens of millions in today's terms, effectively kept early Jewish settlement alive when it might otherwise have collapsed. Yet Edmond personally opposed Herzl and political Zionism. He distrusted Herzl's public, diplomatic, state-seeking approach and favored quiet, paternalistic philanthropic colonization that would not provoke the Ottoman authorities or make grand political claims, and for years he refused to place his settlements under the Zionist Organization. The two men held incompatible theories of the project, as Simon Schama documents in Two Rothschilds and the Land of Israel.[cite:schama_two_rothschilds] Edmond must be kept distinct from Walter Rothschild of the London branch, who twenty years later was the ceremonial addressee of the Balfour letter and who neither funded the settlements nor wrote the policy. The phrase "the Rothschilds created Israel" fuses two men with opposite roles and opposite views into one imaginary actor, the move by which a documented banking family is turned into an antisemitic hidden hand. The record shows members of one family reaching their own, divergent judgments, not a coordinated plan; his colonies and his first refusal of Herzl are told in [scene:bc_s04|the baron who built the colonies].[cite:schama_two_rothschilds]

Two questions about Herzl himself remain open. The first is what moved him. The usual account, repeated in many references, holds that his catalyst was the Dreyfus Affair: covering for a Vienna newspaper the 1894 degradation of a Jewish French officer, and watching a Paris crowd chant against Jews in the most emancipated society in Europe, he concluded that assimilation had failed as a strategy for Jewish safety and that a national home under public law was the only political answer.[cite:zionism_founding_1897] The historian Steven Beller, reviewing Derek Penslar's 2020 biography of Herzl, points to a difficulty: Dreyfus "is not mentioned by name in the Zionist diary of 1895", and Beller uses this to question whether the Affair was the catalyst at all.[cite:rs_rd1_beller_basel] The strongest form of the traditional case is that Herzl was in Paris as a correspondent during the Affair and that its lesson about European antisemitism fits his program exactly. The strongest form of the revision is that the diary in which he worked out his Zionism in 1895 is silent about the case. The record here does not settle which reading is right.

The second question concerns words Herzl never wrote. Fabricated quotations cluster around him, and the best known is a line claiming a Jewish state from the Nile to the Euphrates. It is not in his writings; the attribution has been traced to a misattribution of 1994 and debunked. The Herzl of the record was a secular nation-builder who weighed Argentina and entertained Britain's East Africa offer, not a maximalist with a scriptural map. Keeping the real Herzl distinct from the invented one is part of reading the founding of the movement accurately.

Three things about 1897 stay unsettled. The record gives no single agreed count of the delegates or their countries. It does not explain why rechtlich became öffentlich-rechtlich in the program's aim, only that it did. It does not measure how many Jews in 1897 supported Herzl, opposed him or were indifferent; it records the institutions and named individuals who took positions, and on that evidence the movement began as one current among several in Jewish life, contested from its first summer. It does show that the program asked for a "home", not a "state", in its text, while its convener wrote in private that he had founded a state.

sections.h: The Machinery: How the Zionist Organization Worked, 1897–1917
sections.html:
The organization founded at Basel is sometimes remembered as a loose collection of enthusiasts without formal structure, a mood more than a movement. The record shows the opposite. Within two years of Basel the Zionist Organization had a written constitution, an elected parliament, a standing executive, a council of national leaders, national branches in the United States and Britain, and a bank. By 1917 it had a land fund, an office in Palestine and a recognized channel to the British government.

Membership was open, and its dues were small. Any individual or group that accepted the Basel Program and paid an annual due, called the "shekel", could join.[cite:palquest_wzo] The sources consulted here do not give its amount or the number of shekel-payers in these years. The principle, however, is clear. The organization was built on mass membership by small annual dues.

Authority flowed from the Congress. Its constitution, adopted at the Third Congress in 1899, created two governing bodies. The Smaller Actions Committee, with seven members, was the executive, and its chairman was the president of the Congress. The Larger Actions Committee, with 37 members, was a council of national leaders.[cite:palquest_wzo][cite:ismi_israel_yearbook] The Congress itself met every year until 1901 and every two years after that; the Fifth Congress of 1901 made the change.[cite:palquest_wzo][cite:rs_rd1_jvl_congresses_b] Below the central bodies stood national federations, country-level organizations that recruited members and raised money. The Federation of American Zionists was founded in 1898 and later became the Zionist Organization of America. The English Zionist Federation followed in 1899.[cite:w_zf_gb]

The organization's tools followed one another quickly. The Jewish Colonial Trust, its bank, was established in 1899; the Jewish National Fund, to buy land, in 1901; and the Palestine Office in Jaffa in 1908.[cite:palquest_wzo] The mechanism was simple. The Congress, a body of delegates, decided policy. The small executive carried it out between sessions. The federations supplied members and money, and the financial and land instruments turned that money into assets in Palestine. What the machinery could not do is equally plain. It held no governing authority in Palestine, which remained Ottoman territory until 1917, and the consent of governments was still, as the Basel Program itself acknowledged, something to be obtained.

The Congresses between 1898 and 1913 show the organization working out what it was for, often by open argument and recorded vote. The Second Congress, at Basel in 1898, laid the groundwork for the Jewish Colonial Trust. The Third, at Basel in 1899, resolved that the Trust's funds could be spent only in Palestine or Syria, an early decision that bound the movement's money to one region before any territorial alternative had been offered.[cite:rs_rd1_jvl_congresses_b] The Fourth Congress met in London in 1900; there religious Zionists led by Isaac Jacob Reines urged that the organization keep a purely political focus. The Fifth, back at Basel in 1901, established the Jewish National Fund. At the same Congress a group called the Democratic Faction, among them Leo Motzkin, Martin Buber and Chaim Weizmann, pressed for Hebrew culture and for more democracy inside the organization. It was also this Congress that moved the meetings to every other year.[cite:rs_rd1_jvl_congresses_b]

The organization's sharpest crisis came over territory. The Sixth Congress, at Basel in 1903, voted "295 in favor, 178 against and 98 abstentions" to send a commission to examine settlement in East Africa, a British offer told in full in [scene:s04e|the East Africa offer].[cite:rs_rd1_jvl_congresses_b] Herzl died the next year. The Seventh Congress, at Basel in 1905, voted against a national home outside Palestine and its vicinity. Israel Zangwill's Territorialists walked out, and David Wolffsohn became president.[cite:rs_rd1_jvl_congresses_b] The decision settled that the organization's aim was Palestine, and it was taken by a vote of the Congress, not decreed by a leader.

The next argument was about method. At the Eighth Congress, held at The Hague in 1907, delegates debated "practical" against "political" Zionism. The Congress supported practical work, including a Palestine branch of the organization under Arthur Ruppin, and Weizmann's "synthetic Zionism" gained ground.[cite:rs_rd1_jvl_congresses_b] That branch became the Palestine Office, whose work is traced in [scene:s04g|the Palestine Office]. At the Ninth Congress, in Hamburg in 1909, the practical camp challenged Wolffsohn's leadership. At the Tenth, at Basel in 1911, the first session was held in Hebrew, and the botanist Otto Warburg succeeded Wolffsohn as president. The Eleventh Congress, in Vienna in 1913, backed the founding of a Hebrew University in Jerusalem, which opened twelve years later.[cite:rs_rd1_jvl_congresses_b]

Taken together, these meetings trace a shift in the organization's center of gravity. In its first years it sought a charter through diplomacy and built the financial means to use one. After Herzl's death and the East Africa split, it moved toward building in Palestine directly, while the Democratic Faction's push for Hebrew culture surfaced in the first Hebrew session of 1911 and the university resolution of 1913. The movement's leadership changed in the same direction, from Herzl the diplomat, to Wolffsohn, whose leadership the practical camp challenged in 1909, to Warburg.

The First World War cut across this structure. Before the war the organization's head offices were in Germany, and when war came it declared itself neutral. Its effective leadership passed to London, where Chaim Weizmann, a Manchester chemist and president of the English Zionist Federation, and Nahum Sokolow became its de facto leaders.[cite:ismi_israel_yearbook][cite:weizmann_papers_v9] The English Federation, founded in 1899 as one national branch among several, thus became in wartime the movement's channel to the British government.

That channel was contested within British Jewry itself. In May 1917 the community's official representative bodies, the Board of Deputies and the Anglo-Jewish Association, published an anti-Zionist statement in The Times. Days later the English Zionist Federation held a conference in London.[cite:jpost_why_rothschild] The episode explains a detail of the Balfour Declaration. Because British Jewry's official bodies opposed Zionism, the declaration was not addressed to them. It was instead addressed to Lord Rothschild, for transmission to the Zionist Federation.[cite:jpost_why_rothschild] The declaration itself, and the wider wartime context of competing promises, belong to the next stage of this book: [scene:s06|the Balfour Declaration].

The record here leaves real gaps. It does not give the size of the shekel, the number of members in any year, or the federations' budgets, so the scale of the money that flowed through this structure before 1917 cannot be stated from these sources. It does not show how the 37 seats of the Larger Actions Committee were apportioned among countries, or how far the seven-member executive in practice controlled the Congress rather than answering to it. It does not explain how the neutral organization's German headquarters and its London leaders divided authority during the war. None of these gaps touches the main point: by 1917 the movement was a constituted, voting, dues-paying organization, and its wartime leaders sat in the capital whose decision mattered most.

sections.h: Any Power That Would Sign: Herzl's Search for a Charter, 1898–1904
sections.html:
When the delegates left Basel in 1897, the program they had adopted named an aim but no patron. Theodor Herzl's answer to that gap was a charter. By a charter he meant legal backing for Jewish settlement, granted by a great power that could make it stick. The familiar telling of Zionist history has the movement looking to Britain from the start, as though 1917 had been the plan all along. The diplomatic record of Herzl's own years shows something looser and more opportunistic. Between 1898 and 1904 he approached the German Kaiser, the Ottoman Sultan, the British Colonial Secretary, the Russian Interior Minister and the Pope, and to each he brought whatever that power seemed most likely to want.[cite:wiki_kaiser_levant_1898] [cite:jewishencyclopedia_herzl]

The reason for this method lay in the structure of the problem. Herzl led an organization with a Congress and a program, but no territory, no army and no standing in international law. Palestine belonged to the Ottoman Empire. Only a sovereign, or a power that could lean on one, could turn a settlement scheme into a legal right. Herzl therefore needed someone else's signature, and he had no fixed view about whose it should be.

He tried Germany first. The introduction came through William Hechler, a Christian restorationist, a believer in the return of the Jews to their ancient land. Through him Herzl met Kaiser Wilhelm II three times in 1898: in Istanbul, at Mikveh Israel, an agricultural colony funded by the Rothschilds, and in Jerusalem itself.[cite:wiki_kaiser_levant_1898] [cite:jewishencyclopedia_herzl] The Kaiser did raise the matter with the Sultan. The request failed, and the Kaiser's interest faded after it.[cite:wiki_kaiser_levant_1898]

Herzl then went directly to the ruler of Palestine.
