That paper was advocacy, and its figures are examined in [scene:us_s06|the economy section]; this book uses the census figure of about 11 percent.

Land was counted too, and here the numbers have been bent in both directions. The Village Statistics of 1945 was compiled for the Anglo-American Committee of Inquiry and later used by UNSCOP. It classified land by ownership, by use and by tax category [cite:wiki_village_statistics]. In 1947, the United Nations partition plan allotted about 56 percent of the territory to the proposed Jewish state, at a time when Jews owned under 7 percent of the land; the proposed Jewish state would also have contained a large Arab minority [cite:historyskills_partition]. How the Jewish share of land was assembled in these years, through the purchases of the Jewish National Fund and others, is told in [scene:rd3_land|the land section]; the partition plan itself belongs to a later chapter.

With these figures, both slogans can be tested. "A land without a people" is refuted by every census the British took. The 1922 count found three-quarters of a million people, and the 1931 and 1946 figures found the Arab majority still growing [cite:jvl_census_1931] [cite:rebelion_unscop_figures]. The country was inhabited, and mostly by Arabs.

The counter-slogan fails in a different way. The claim that Palestinian Arabs privately owned 94 percent of the land counts large areas of state and public land as Arab-owned [cite:wiki_village_statistics]. The 1945 survey keeps those categories apart: land in private ownership is one column; land held by the state is another [cite:wiki_village_statistics]. Jewish ownership of under 7 percent does not mean Arab private ownership of the remainder. The honest comparison, for anyone making either case, uses the survey's own categories.

What do these numbers not settle? They do not tell us how the land not privately owned by Jews or Arabs was divided between state land and other public categories in any given year; the sources here give the distinction, not the totals. The 1946 population figure is an estimate, not a count, and the sources do not give its margin of error. And the gap between the census and the Jewish Agency's 1937 figures for 1922 is not explained in the material used here.

sections.h: How the Mandate Became Law, 1923–1925
sections.html:
The country the census counted in 1922 was governed under an instrument not yet complete in law. By the summer of 1922 Britain had governed Palestine for nearly five years. Its forces had taken Jerusalem in December 1917, and the text of the Mandate had been approved by the Council of the League of Nations. Yet two legal steps were still missing. The state that had ruled the country for four centuries had not yet given it up, and the Mandate had not yet formally entered into force. Between 1923 and 1925 both gaps were closed, or so the standard account holds, and the Mandate government then defined, for the first time, who was a citizen of Palestine. Each step has a date, a document and, in at least one case, a serious scholarly challenge.

The first step was taken at Lausanne. The peace treaty between the Allies and Turkey was signed there on 24 July 1923 [cite:rs_rd3_lausanne_fcdo]. In it the new Republic of Turkey, founded that year, renounced all rights over the former Arab provinces of the Ottoman Empire [cite:w_lausanne]. The treaty made modern Turkey the empire's successor state, not a claimant to Palestine [cite:w_lausanne]. Professor John Quigley stresses a further point about the wording: the renunciation was not made in favor of Britain or of the Allies [cite:rs_rd3_quigley_2026]. Turkey gave up its rights; it did not hand them to anyone. The treaty did not take effect at once. It entered into force on 6 August 1924 [cite:rs_rd3_abualia_khalil] [cite:rs_rd3_quigley_2026].

The second step was the Mandate's entry into force, and here the record holds two accounts. The League Council had approved the mandates for Palestine and Syria on 24 July 1922, on a condition: they would take effect once France and Italy reached a final agreement over Syria [cite:rs_rd3_unispal_mandate_force]. One scholarly source gives a different date for that approval, 12 August 1922 [cite:rs_rd3_abualia_khalil]; the UN's document gives 24 July [cite:rs_rd3_unispal_mandate_force]. At the Council's meeting of 29 September 1923, according to the minutes as reproduced by the United Nations, the mandates for Syria and Palestine "had thereby automatically and simultaneously entered into force," and the British representative, Sir Rennell Rodd, said the question was "finally settled" [cite:rs_rd3_unispal_mandate_force]. On this account, 29 September 1923 is the date the Mandate became law. Britain, the League Secretariat and, in 1947, the United Nations all treated it as such [cite:rs_rd3_unispal_mandate_force].

Quigley disputes it. He argues that the Council minutes used future-tense wording and that the Council took no resolution. In his reading, the past-tense formula, that the mandates had entered into force, was supplied afterwards by the League's Secretary-General, Eric Drummond, in his Circular Letter 101. If that is right, the 29 September 1923 date has no legal force, and since Lausanne did not take effect until 6 August 1924 and gave Britain no title in any case, Britain held Palestine without title [cite:rs_rd3_quigley_2026]. Quigley's argument was published in July 2026; it is a challenge to the standard date, not yet a settled finding.

Each side has a real case. The standard date rests on a primary document, the minutes, and on the conduct of the bodies involved: Britain administered the Mandate, the League supervised it, and the UN in 1947 started from that date. Quigley's case rests on the same kind of evidence read more closely: the tense of a verb, the absence of a resolution, and the question of who changed the wording. The practical history of the Mandate did not wait on the answer; the legal question remains open in the sense that the argument has been made and not, in the sources used here, answered.

The third step was to decide who belonged. The Palestinian Citizenship Order was issued on 24 July 1925 and took effect on 1 August 1925. It made Palestinian citizens of Ottoman subjects habitually resident in Palestine on that date [cite:rs_rd3_abualia_khalil]. Two groups stood outside that rule. The first were Arabs who had emigrated abroad: the Order, Lauren Banko notes, denied them citizenship [cite:rs_rd3_banko_podcast]. The second were immigrants, who could acquire citizenship by naturalization.

How naturalization worked in practice is known mainly through one study. According to Nadia Abu Alia and Asem Khalil, the Government of Palestine reportedly accepted about 100 of some 9,000 naturalization applications in one period, using an "absolute discretion" clause. By 1946, on their figures, about 130,000 foreigners had acquired Palestinian citizenship by naturalization, 99 percent of them Jews [cite:rs_rd3_abualia_khalil]. The two figures describe different things: the first a single period of tight refusal, the second the cumulative total over two decades. The sources do not say which period the first figure covers or whose applications were refused.

The historian Lauren Banko reads the Order as a first step and as a contrast at once. It was, she notes, the first Mandate legislation to treat the Arab population as citizens rather than as "ex-enemy Ottoman subjects" [cite:rs_rd3_banko_podcast]. But it treated Jewish citizenship and the naturalization of immigrants in sharp contrast to Arab citizenship, in Banko's account, and Palestinian Arabs answered it by invoking Ottoman-era principles of descent and birthplace [cite:rs_rd3_banko_podcast]. Descent and birthplace would have reached the emigrants abroad, whom the Order excluded. Read beside Banko's argument, the naturalization figures reported by Abu Alia and Khalil, in which 99 percent of those naturalized by 1946 were Jews, suggest which way the contrast ran in practice; that is a reading of the two sources together, not a finding stated in either [cite:rs_rd3_banko_podcast] [cite:rs_rd3_abualia_khalil].

The Mandate text's own provisions on nationality, passports and currency are set out in [scene:s07|the Mandate text] and are not retold here. Some things remain unsettled. Whether the Mandate ever validly entered into force is argued, not decided. The sources do not give the number of Arab emigrants who lost a claim to citizenship under the 1925 Order, nor the year-by-year breakdown of naturalizations, nor, for the reported period when about 100 of 9,000 applications were accepted, who the applicants were.

sections.h: The Revisionist Line, 1923–1935
sections.html:
While Britain's title was being settled at Lausanne and Geneva, the movement it had promised to help was dividing. Zionism is often described as a single political movement that divided into parties only after the state was founded. The institutional record shows otherwise. Its foundational split, between the movement led by Chaim Weizmann and the one led by Ze'ev (Vladimir) Jabotinsky, opened in the years of this chapter and was documented step by step: a youth movement in 1923, a secession in 1925, a second and final break in 1935. The organization Jabotinsky built is the direct ancestor of Herut and then Likud. It also produced the armed groups, the Irgun and later Lehi, that operated alongside and often against the Haganah and the Jewish Agency [cite:wiki_revisionist_zionism] [cite:wiki_new_zionist_organization].

Jabotinsky was a Russian-Jewish writer and Zionist leader [cite:wiki_jabotinsky]. He was not religious, and his claims to the land were territorial and historical rather than primarily religious [cite:jabotinsky_revisionist_1925]. In 1923 he founded Betar, a youth movement built on discipline and military training. Its watchwords were hadar, pride or dignity, and armed self-defense, and it spread through Poland, the Baltic states, Palestine and the Americas [cite:wiki_betar].

The same year he set out the argument on which his politics rested, in an essay called "The Iron Wall." Its claim was that the Arabs of Palestine would never voluntarily accept a Jewish majority, and that Zionism could therefore proceed only from a position of overwhelming military strength [cite:wiki_iron_wall_essay] [cite:theconversation_israels_iron_wall]. Its central sentence reads:

Zionist colonization, even the most restricted, must either be terminated or carried out in defiance of the will of the native population.

A follow-up essay, "The Ethics of the Iron Wall," argued that this approach was itself moral [cite:wiki_iron_wall_essay] [cite:theconversation_israels_iron_wall]. What the essay conceded matters as much as what it proposed. It did not pretend the land was empty or that its people would welcome the project; it said plainly that they would not, and drew the conclusion that consent could not be the basis of the plan.

Among the young men drawn to the movement was Benzion Netanyahu, born Mileikowsky in Warsaw in 1910, who had emigrated to Palestine in 1920. In the 1930s he edited the Revisionist newspaper Ha'Yarden [cite:jewishjournal_benzion_netanyahu] [cite:wiki_benzion_netanyahu] [cite:tabletmag_bibi_fathers_footsteps]. His later role belongs to a later chapter: in 1940 Jabotinsky sent him to the United States, where he served as Jabotinsky's personal secretary until Jabotinsky's death that year and then ran the movement's American operations for eight years [cite:jewishjournal_benzion_netanyahu] [cite:wiki_benzion_netanyahu] [cite:tabletmag_bibi_fathers_footsteps]. His son, Benjamin Netanyahu, told a Jabotinsky memorial audience in 2023 that one hundred years after the "iron wall" was set down in Jabotinsky's writings, Israel was "continuing to successfully implement these principles" [cite:counterfire_netanyahu_shadow]. He has also, separately, dismissed the idea that his father's formation under Jabotinsky shaped his own views as "psychobabble" [cite:jewishjournal_benzion_netanyahu]. Both statements are his own, and they sit in tension; this book records both and does not choose between them.

The organized break came two years after the essay. In April 1925, in Paris, Jabotinsky founded the World Union of Zionist-Revisionists, known by its Hebrew acronym Hatzohar [cite:wiki_revisionist_zionism] [cite:jabotinsky_revisionist_1925]. Its first president was Vladimir Tiomkin [cite:rs_rd3_ej_revisionists]. The founding is described as a secession from the World Zionist Organization that Weizmann led [cite:wiki_revisionist_zionism]; yet the Revisionists went on sending delegates to Zionist Congresses for the next decade, so in practice the break of 1925 created a rival faction rather than a separate body [cite:rs_rd3_ej_revisionists]. Its founding platform called for transforming Palestine and Transjordan into a Jewish commonwealth within the British Commonwealth, in direct opposition to the mainstream's gradualist strategy [cite:wiki_revisionist_zionism].

The heart of that platform was the claim to "both banks of the Jordan," a Jewish majority on both sides of the river, covering what is now Israel, the West Bank, Gaza and the whole of Jordan [cite:jabotinsky_revisionist_1925]. Jabotinsky argued that Britain's separation of Transjordan from the Palestine Mandate in 1922 was an arbitrary partition, which denied Jews the territory they would need to absorb millions of future immigrants [cite:jabotinsky_revisionist_1925]. He put the geography in one sentence, writing in 1929–1930:

What does the word Palestine mean? Palestine is a territory whose chief geographical feature is this: that the River Jordan does not delineate its frontier, but flows through its center.

The movement's anthem made the same point in a line: "Two Banks has the Jordan — This is ours and, that is as well" [cite:jabotinsky_revisionist_1925]. This is one of three documented versions of what is called "Greater Israel," and the narrowest in territory: a claim to the whole of the original Mandate area, territorial rather than primarily religious. How later religious-nationalist versions differ, and how the idea is used today, is traced in [scene:gia_src_s02|Greater Israel and its three versions]; the history of the "two banks" claim from 1922 to 1948 is told in [scene:ijr_src_s04|Two Banks of the Jordan].

In 1925 the Revisionists were a small faction. They had four delegates at the Fourteenth Zionist Congress that year [cite:rs_rd3_ej_revisionists]. Six years later they were a major force. In 1931 they won 17 percent of the vote for the Yishuv's elected assembly, the Asefat ha-Nivharim, and became its second-largest party. At the Seventeenth Zionist Congress in Basel the same year they had 52 delegates, and proposed a resolution for a Jewish state on both sides of the Jordan [cite:rs_rd3_ej_revisionists].

Growth brought internal conflict. In 1933, at Katowice, Jabotinsky suspended the party's executive. A plebiscite of the membership backed him, and his opponents, led by Meir Grossman, seceded to form the Jewish State Party. At the Eighteenth Congress the Jewish State Party had seven delegates to the Revisionists' 46 [cite:rs_rd3_ej_revisionists]. The Revisionists' quarrel with Labour Zionism grew sharper the same year, when Revisionists were accused of the murder of Chaim Arlosoroff (the accused were later cleared), and of the three agreements Ben-Gurion and Jabotinsky signed in London in 1934, the labor agreement was rejected in a Histadrut referendum; that story is told in [scene:rd3_arlosoroff|1933–1935].

How large was the movement by the mid-1930s? The figure most often quoted is 600,000, and it is used in two different ways. According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, more than 600,000 Jews in 24 countries signed a Revisionist petition addressed to the British king and Parliament in 1934 [cite:rs_rd3_ej_revisionists]. That is a count of signatures. Other accounts present the same figure as the membership the broader Revisionist movement claimed by 1934 [cite:wiki_betar]. A signature on a petition and a membership are not the same thing, and the first reading rests on the more specific source. Even as a membership figure, it was a claimed number, not a verified one. A smaller figure, for Betar alone, is given as over 70,000 by the mid-1930s in the account of the "two banks" claim cited above. The difference between 70,000 and 600,000 is the difference between a disciplined youth movement and a mass petition.

The final break came in 1935. That year the Zionist General Council adopted a "discipline clause" that barred independent political action by member parties [cite:rs_rd3_ej_revisionists]. The Zionist Executive formally rejected Jabotinsky's platform [cite:wiki_new_zionist_organization]. A Revisionist plebiscite chose secession, and the constituent assembly of the New Zionist Organization met in Vienna in September 1935, said to have been "elected by 713,000 voters," with Jabotinsky as its president [cite:rs_rd3_ej_revisionists]. He resigned from the World Zionist Organization altogether [cite:wiki_new_zionist_organization] [cite:wiki_hatzohar]. Where the 1925 secession had left room for a working relationship with the mainstream, the 1935 break did not. The New Zionist Organization ran its own political and fundraising work, parallel to and in competition with the Jewish Agency and, later, the American Zionist Emergency Council [cite:wiki_new_zionist_organization] [cite:wiki_hatzohar]. The "713,000" is reported with a hedge ("said to have been"); the sources do not say how those votes were counted.

The Revisionist case, in its own terms, was argued openly. Its premise was that the Arab population would never consent to a Jewish majority, so that any plan built on consent would fail; better to say so, and to build the strength on which the project could proceed without that consent. Its territorial claim held that Britain had cut the Mandate in two in 1922 arbitrarily, and that a state confined to the western bank could not take in the millions of Jews who would need it. Its method, a militarized youth movement and open political demands such as the 1931 resolution for a state on both banks, was set squarely against the mainstream's gradualist strategy.

The critics' case is in the same record. The Zionist leadership's answer is on record in what it did: the General Council's discipline clause barred exactly the independent political action the Revisionists practiced, and the Executive rejected their platform. Within the movement itself, Grossman's followers broke away in 1933 over Jabotinsky's suspension of the executive. And the Iron Wall essay is, on its face, a statement that the project would be carried out against the will of the people already living in the country. Read from the side of the population it named, it was not only an analysis of their opposition but a program for overriding it by strength. Both readings start from Jabotinsky's own words.

Jabotinsky held his position to the end of the period and beyond. In 1937 he testified before the Peel Commission against any partition of Palestine, insisting on Jewish rights to the entire Mandate territory, Transjordan included. He died of a heart attack in 1940 while visiting Betar in the United States [cite:wiki_jabotinsky]. The line he founded continued as an institution. Herut was founded on 15 June 1948 by Menachem Begin, a former Irgun commander, as a challenge to Hatzohar, which was then succeeded by and merged into Herut after the state was established. Herut joined the Liberal Party in 1965 to form Gahal, which in 1973 became the founding core of Likud, the party that has led or co-led Israeli governments for most of the past five decades, including under Netanyahu [cite:wiki_herut] [cite:wiki_hatzohar] [cite:wiki_gahal] [cite:wiki_likud]. That is a documented chain of foundings and mergers. It is not a claim that Likud's platform today is Jabotinsky's; parties change over a century.

Some questions the record here does not answer. The sources do not give a verified membership figure for the Revisionist movement or for Betar in any year; the 600,000 and the 713,000 are a petition count and a claimed electorate, and the 70,000 for Betar comes from a single account. They do not set out the specific policy disputes behind the Executive's rejection of the platform in 1935 beyond the discipline clause. And they do not show how much money the New Zionist Organization raised in its parallel campaigns. What they do show is that by September 1935 organized Zionism had two rival centers, each with its own leader, program and electorate, thirteen years before the state.

sections.h: Jacob de Haan and the Orthodox Opposition, 1919–1924
sections.html:
The Revisionists challenged the Zionist leadership from inside the movement. Jacob de Haan challenged it from outside, and paid with his life. On the evening of 30 June 1924, Jacob Israël de Haan left evening prayers at a synagogue on Jaffa Road in Jerusalem and was shot three times. He died soon after. No one was charged [cite:w_dehaan]. The killing is widely described by historians as the first political assassination inside the Jewish community of Palestine, and its victim was neither a British official nor an Arab leader. He was a Jew, a former Zionist sympathizer, and in the years before his death the most effective political voice, in English, of the Jewish community that rejected the Zionist movement's claim to speak for it [cite:w_dehaan].

A common account of these years holds that Jewish opposition to Zionism before 1948 was marginal, peaceful, and faded away on its own. De Haan's career does not fit that account. The opposition he represented was organized, it had a leadership, it took its case to the British authorities and to Arab rulers, and it was met, at least once, with a bullet.

De Haan was born in the Netherlands in 1881 and was a poet and a lawyer by training. He arrived in Palestine in 1919 as a newspaper correspondent, and he taught law in Jerusalem at the Mandate government's law classes [cite:w_dehaan]. He came with some sympathy for Zionism. He moved from that sympathy to the other side of the question entirely, into the Haredi camp, the strictly Orthodox community of the old Yishuv [cite:w_dehaan].

The "old Yishuv" was the name for the Orthodox Jewish communities of Jerusalem, Safed, Hebron and Tiberias, which had lived in the country for generations before political Zionism existed [cite:w_dehaan]. Its leadership, including Rabbi Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld, rejected a secular Jewish state on religious grounds, and objected to the Zionist Organization speaking in its name. That objection had an organizational form older than the Mandate. Agudath Israel was founded in 1912 as a worldwide movement to strengthen Torah-observant Judaism, and specifically to separate it from the emerging secular Jewish nationalist movement, which its founders regarded as a danger to Torah-observant Jewish life [cite:w_dehaan] [cite:unpacked_neturei_karta_history] [cite:wiki_neturei_karta]. Its opposition to political Zionism on religious grounds was thus organized thirty-six years before the State of Israel was founded. It was a theological position, not a reaction to any later political dispute [cite:unpacked_neturei_karta_history].

This was the community de Haan came to speak for. He wrote for British newspapers and lobbied Mandate officials directly [cite:w_dehaan].

De Haan's case was narrow and precise. The Zionist Organization, he argued, was one political movement among Jews. It was not the representative of all the Jews in Palestine [cite:w_dehaan]. For the old Orthodox community, whose presence in Jerusalem long predated the Zionist movement, that distinction was the whole point: a secular national movement should not speak in the name of religious Jews who rejected its aims. It was the argument he pressed on British officials [cite:w_dehaan].

It was, in method, a claim about representation, and de Haan carried it to two audiences: the Mandatory power, whose officials he lobbied, and Arab leaders, with whom he sought a separate understanding [cite:w_dehaan].

His most provocative act was diplomatic. He sought a separate understanding between Orthodox Jews and Arab leaders, on the premise that Jews who did not seek a state need not be in conflict with the Arab majority [cite:w_dehaan]. In 1924 this led him to meetings with the Hashemite leadership in Transjordan [cite:w_dehaan]. He was then preparing to travel to London with an anti-Zionist Orthodox delegation [cite:w_dehaan]. He was killed before he could go.

The sources in this book do not record what was said at the Transjordan meetings, what, if anything, was agreed, or what the London delegation intended to ask for. They establish the direction of his effort, not its content.

After the shooting on Jaffa Road, each side looked to the other. The Zionist leadership publicly condemned the killing. Orthodox leaders blamed Zionist circles [cite:w_dehaan]. No one was charged, and for sixty years the question of who had ordered the killing remained formally open [cite:w_dehaan].

The silence broke in 1985. Avraham Tehomi, by then elderly, said on Israeli television that he had shot de Haan, and that he had done so on the orders of the Haganah, the underground defense force of the Jewish community [cite:w_dehaan]. Tehomi was no peripheral figure. He was the Haganah's Jerusalem district commander from 1929 to 1931, and he then led a group that seceded from it and, together with Revisionist groups, formed the Irgun Zvai Leumi; he returned to the Haganah in 1937 [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah] [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_tehomi]. That later history is told in [scene:s07e2|the armed line].

Tehomi went further than naming the Haganah. He named Yitzhak Ben-Zvi, later Israel's second president, as the man from whom the order had come [cite:w_dehaan]. Here the record thins, and the two parts of the confession have to be weighed separately.

The first part, that the shooting was a Haganah operation, carried out by the man who was speaking, is the documented core of the case. It is a confession by the gunman himself, and it is what allows historians to treat the killing as an act of the Haganah rather than a private crime [cite:w_dehaan].

The second part rests on Tehomi alone. Ben-Zvi had died in 1963, twenty-two years before the interview, and could not answer. No second witness or document in the sources places the order with him, and some historians dispute his involvement [cite:w_dehaan]. Tehomi's account of his own act and of the organization behind it is a confession; his account of who stood above him is an accusation against a man who could no longer reply, given six decades after the event, with nothing else in the sources to support it. The honest conclusion is the narrower one: the record establishes the gunman and the organization he said he served, and it does not establish a single, settled chain of command above him [cite:w_dehaan].

Three things are established. Organized Jewish opposition to Zionism existed inside Palestine in the early Mandate years, with a leadership, an international organization behind it and a public spokesman. It was argued openly, to the British and to Arab leaders. And the Zionist movement's own armed wing, by its gunman's admission, killed its most effective spokesman [cite:w_dehaan]. The familiar picture of a dissent that was marginal and peaceful and simply faded is incomplete on each count.

This opposition was also distinct from the other Jewish dissent of these years. The binationalists of Brit Shalom, founded in 1925, argued from inside Zionism about the form a national home should take; the old Yishuv rejected the national project itself on religious grounds. Their story is told in [scene:rd3_brit_shalom|Brit Shalom and the Hebrew University].

Orthodox opposition did not end with de Haan's death. Its later history lies outside this chapter, but its next turn is documented: in 1938 Neturei Karta split from Agudath Israel to preserve a more uncompromising anti-Zionist position, after Agudath Israel began making practical accommodations with Zionist institutions [cite:britannica_neturei_karta]. The split itself shows that Agudath Israel, which had organized the old Yishuv's refusal, had by then begun to accommodate the institutions it once opposed. The 1912 founding marks where the organized religious objection began, not a full history of how each of its branches moved afterward [cite:unpacked_neturei_karta_history].

What remains unsettled is considerable. The sources do not say who, if anyone, above Tehomi gave the order, if Ben-Zvi did not. They do not record why no one was charged in 1924, what the British authorities established about the crime, or what the Hashemite leadership said to de Haan. They do not show whether his London delegation would have changed anything. The decision behind the shot stays where Tehomi left it, resting on his word alone.

sections.h: Immigration, 1923–1936: The Fourth and Fifth Aliyot
sections.html:
De Haan's community had lived in the country for generations. Most of the Yishuv of the 1930s had not. Between 1923 and 1936 the number of Jews entering Palestine each year rose and fell steeply. In 1925 more than 33,000 arrived; in 1928 barely 2,000. In 1935 more than 60,000 came, the highest figure of these years. The swings were not random. They followed pressures and decisions outside Palestine, in Poland and in Washington among them, and they passed through a British administration that counted the arrivals and set an allotment for those who came as workers. Two great waves came in these years, the Fourth Aliyah of the mid-1920s and the Fifth Aliyah of the 1930s, and the official figures for them do not always agree.

The Jewish Virtual Library puts the Fourth Aliyah at 82,000 Jews who came to Palestine between 1924 and 1929, of whom 23,000 left again [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_fourth_aliyah]. It attributes the wave to two pressures that operated together. One was in Poland: an economic crisis and anti-Jewish policies there pushed Jews to leave [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_fourth_aliyah]. The other was in the United States. The Jewish Virtual Library points to stiff American immigration quotas, and the Center for Israel Education ties the rise in immigration to Palestine directly to the US Immigration Act of 1924, which limited annual immigration from each country to 2 percent of its residents in the 1890 census [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_fourth_aliyah] [cite:rs_rd3_cie_1924_act].

Most of the Fourth Aliyah's immigrants were middle class, with modest capital [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_fourth_aliyah]. The town whose growth tracks the wave most visibly is Tel Aviv. It had about 15,000 inhabitants in 1922 and about 34,000 in 1925; by 1931 it had 45,564 [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_telaviv].

The wave broke quickly. The Yishuv, the Jewish community in Palestine, suffered an economic crisis in 1926–1928 [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_fourth_aliyah]. The annual figures show its scale. Recorded Jewish immigration, which stood at 33,801 in 1925, fell to 13,081 in 1926, 2,713 in 1927 and 2,178 in 1928 [cite:rs_rd3_frus1939_d828]. Many of those who had arrived left: the 23,000 departures are part of the Fourth Aliyah's own total [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_fourth_aliyah].

The British inquiry that followed the violence of August 1929 drew a lesson from those years. The Shaw Commission, reporting in March 1930, criticized what it called "excessive" immigration in 1925–26, and quoted Sir John Campbell's view that the crisis of 1927–28 had come from immigrants arriving "in excess of the economic absorbing power of the country" [cite:rs_rd3_shaw_palquest]. The phrase mattered. It tied the permitted level of immigration to an economic test, the country's capacity to absorb newcomers. The argument that followed Shaw, through Hope Simpson and the White Paper of 1930, is told in [scene:pf_s01|From inquiry to reversal].

Out of that low point came the Fifth Aliyah. Recorded immigration was 5,249 in 1929, 4,944 in 1930 and 4,075 in 1931, and then it climbed: 9,553 in 1932, 30,327 in 1933, 42,359 in 1934 and 61,854 in 1935, before falling back to 29,727 in 1936 [cite:rs_rd3_frus1939_d828]. The Jewish Virtual Library dates the Fifth Aliyah from 1929 to 1939. It states that nearly 250,000 Jews arrived in that wave by 1940, of whom 20,000 later left; that 174,000 settled in the four years 1933–1936 alone; and that the Yishuv reached 450,000 by 1940 [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_fifth_aliyah].

The steepest climb began in 1933. The emigration of Jews from Nazi Germany in these years, and the Transfer Agreement that let some of them bring capital, are told with their own numbers in [scene:hv_s01|the Haavara Agreement]. The sources used here do not break down the annual totals by country of origin, so they cannot say what share of the 1933–1936 arrivals came from Germany and what share from Poland and elsewhere.

Tel Aviv again shows the effect most plainly. A town of 45,564 in 1931 had about 120,000 people by 1935 [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_telaviv]. It received municipal status on 12 May 1934 [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_telaviv].

Not every immigrant entered on the same terms, and the 1935 peak shows how the categories fitted together. A State Department memorandum of 6 November 1936, written by Paul Alling for Assistant Secretary Moore, cites Palestine Government statistics for that year. Of the 61,854 Jews who entered in 1935, 14,653 came under the labor schedule and 13,076 were their dependants. Alling estimated that the remaining 44,000 entered in other categories, such as capital holders, professionals and skilled artisans [cite:rs_rd3_frus1936_d531]. The figures as reported do not reconcile exactly: 61,854 less the workers and their dependants leaves about 34,000, not 44,000, and the memorandum as summarized does not explain the difference. What the breakdown does show clearly is that in the peak year fewer than one immigrant in four entered as a worker on the schedule; the rest came as dependants or, on Alling's estimate, in categories defined by means or occupation.

The labor schedule was the part of immigration that came in fixed allotments. Alling lists them for half-year periods, and his figures show how they moved. The allotment was 5,500 for April–September 1933 and rose to 8,000 for April–September 1935. For October 1935–March 1936 it was cut to 3,250 [cite:rs_rd3_frus1936_d531].

Readers who look up the annual figures for these years will find more than one set. The memorandum by J. Rives Childs of the State Department's Division of Near Eastern Affairs, dated 3 June 1939, gives recorded Jewish immigration year by year, compiled from the British returns [cite:rs_rd3_frus1939_d828]. A second series, printed by the Jewish Virtual Library from the historian Yehoshua Porath, gives higher figures for most years [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_porath_table]. The two are set side by side below.

The pattern of the differences is itself informative. For 1928 to 1931 the two series agree exactly. For the mid-1920s the Porath figures are a few hundred to about a thousand higher each year. For 1932 to 1935 they are higher by roughly three to seven thousand a year, with the widest gap in 1933, 37,337 against 30,327. In 1936 the order reverses, and the Porath figure is slightly lower [cite:rs_rd3_frus1939_d828] [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_porath_table]. The sources do not explain the difference. It may reflect how arrivals who were not recorded at entry, or who registered later, were counted in one series and not the other, but that is a possibility, not a documented finding [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_porath_table]. This book uses the State Department figures as the recorded series and gives the Porath figures beside them where the difference matters.

A third figure does not fit cleanly with either. The Jewish Virtual Library's total of 82,000 for the Fourth Aliyah is higher than the sum of either annual series for 1924–1929, while its 174,000 settlers for 1933–1936 falls between the two series' totals for those years [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_fourth_aliyah] [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_fifth_aliyah] [cite:rs_rd3_frus1939_d828] [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_porath_table]. The wave totals and the annual returns may rest on different definitions; the sources do not say.

The same 1939 memorandum carries a finding that bears on one of the most argued questions of the Mandate. It cites a Consul General's report dated 10 January 1939, that the Jewish population had risen sixfold since 1920, almost entirely through immigration, while the Arab population had risen by about 57 percent, almost entirely through natural increase [cite:rs_rd3_frus1939_d828].

Read this way, the finding helps explain why the level of Jewish immigration, and the Shaw Commission's test of the country's "absorbing power," carried so much weight: on the consul's account, immigration was the means by which the Jewish share of the population changed. The consul's report is one official observer's assessment, made in 1939. The question of Arab immigration into Palestine in the 1930s, its scale and its sources, has not been researched for this book, and the prose here makes no claim about it beyond what the consul wrote.

The documents leave a good deal open. They do not settle the exact number who came in any given year, because the two published series differ and neither source explains why. They do not break down the 1930s arrivals by country, or say how many of the 1935 immigrants without a schedule place held capital and how many were professionals or artisans. And the 44,000 in Alling's memorandum does not square with the numbers it is drawn from.

sections.h: Bringing In the Non-Zionists: The Enlarged Jewish Agency, 1924–1929
sections.html:
American quotas, by one account, turned Jewish emigrants toward Palestine in the mid-1920s. American Jewish money was harder to steer. It is often assumed that American Jewish leadership was Zionist from the start, and that the money which built the Jewish national home flowed from a settled consensus. In the 1920s that was not so. Much of the wealthiest American Jewish leadership was non-Zionist, and a non-Zionist relief body ran its own appeals in competition with the Zionist fund [cite:einstein_papers_vol15_doc625]. Bringing those leaders and their money inside the movement's institutions took Chaim Weizmann the better part of five years. When it was done, in Zurich in August 1929, the Jewish Agency had become a body in which Zionists and non-Zionists sat in equal numbers, and the institution that would govern the Yishuv until 1948 rested on a funding base that reached well beyond committed Zionists.

The problem first showed itself as a fight over fundraising. The American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee, a non-Zionist relief body chaired by the banker Felix Warburg, ran its own campaigns. The Zionist Organization of America saw them as a rival to the Keren Hayesod, the movement's permanent fund, and the two clashed. To protect the Keren Hayesod, the ZOA created a United Palestine Appeal under Rabbi Stephen Wise [cite:einstein_papers_vol15_doc625]. Two appeals were now asking the same American Jewish public for money, one Zionist and one not.

The stakes were large, because the United States had already become the movement's main source of funds. From April 1921 to December 1929 the Keren Hayesod raised $20.1 million worldwide, about $370 million in today's dollars. More than half of it, $11.0 million, came from the United States [cite:jta_kh_decade] [cite:bls_cpi]. Over the fund's first twelve years, the United States gave about half of the £4.82 million raised [cite:jta_kh_12yr]. The money paid for the core of the movement's work in Palestine: before 1948 the fund's mandate covered immigration, settlement, defense, water and public works [cite:jvl_kh].

The country breakdown shows how lopsided the base was. After the United States came South Africa with $1.5 million, Germany with $0.98 million, Romania and Britain with $0.88 million each, Poland with $0.82 million and Canada with $0.74 million [cite:jta_kh_decade]. No other country gave even a seventh of the American total. And this was the Zionist fund alone; the non-Zionist Joint Distribution Committee under Warburg raised its money separately [cite:einstein_papers_vol15_doc625]. The longer-run story of who paid for the pre-state enterprise, through 1948, is told in [scene:gf_s01|the Global Funding Ledger].

Weizmann's answer was to stop competing with the non-Zionists and bring them in. From December 1924 to February 1925 he was in the United States, launching the annual Keren Hayesod campaign and negotiating an expanded Jewish Agency with Louis Marshall, president of the American Jewish Committee [cite:einstein_papers_vol15_doc625]. The offer was institutional: the non-Zionists were to be brought inside the Jewish Agency itself, as partners in its governance, rather than courted as donors to a rival appeal.

The negotiation took more than four years. It ended at Zurich in August 1929. There the Sixteenth Zionist Congress ratified the agreement, and the Council of the enlarged Jewish Agency met, with Albert Einstein, Léon Blum and Herbert Samuel present [cite:israeled_weizmann_vol14] [cite:israeled_weizmann_vol14_pdf].

The Council's membership was split equally between Zionists and non-Zionists. Louis Marshall became chairman of the Council and Lord Melchett its associate chairman. Felix Warburg, who had chaired the rival relief appeal, became chairman of the Administrative Committee. And the Keren Hayesod was recognized as the Agency's main financial instrument [cite:israeled_weizmann_vol14] [cite:israeled_weizmann_vol14_pdf]. The man who had chaired the rival relief body now held a chair inside the Agency, beside the Zionist fund.

Weizmann's papers record what he believed he had won. Marshall and Warburg assured him that his "financial troubles are over" [cite:israeled_weizmann_vol14] [cite:israeled_weizmann_vol14_pdf]. Whether they were is another matter, and the sources here do not show how much non-Zionist money actually flowed through the enlarged Agency in the years that followed.

The partnership lost its chairman almost at once. Marshall died weeks after Zurich, in September 1929. One summary of these events places his death in the same month that the riots in Palestine began; the violence in Jerusalem, Hebron and Safed in fact began in August 1929, weeks before he died, and is told in [scene:s07a4|Hebron, 1929].

The enlargement was not only an internal Jewish matter. The Shaw Commission, sent to investigate the August violence, listed the enlargement of the Jewish Agency among the immediate causes of the outbreak, beside the incidents at the Wall [cite:rs_rd3_shaw_palquest_d]. The two descriptions of Zurich sit uneasily together. For Weizmann, by his papers' account, it brought the assurance that his financial troubles were over. The Commission, by contrast, placed it beside the Wall incidents among the immediate causes of the violence. The record supports both: it was an act of Jewish communal organization, and a British inquiry judged it to have helped bring on the outbreak of 1929. The sources here do not record the Arab leadership's own statements about Zurich.

The importance of 1929 lies in what the Agency became afterward. By that year the body that would run the pre-state Yishuv had brought wealthy American non-Zionists inside its governance, widening its funding base well beyond committed Zionists, nineteen years before 1948. In the sequence of institutions shown below, from the Basel Congress to the State of Israel, the Jewish Agency stands between the British Mandate and the American political effort of the 1940s, enlarged in 1929.

The record leaves several things open. It does not say how much non-Zionist money the enlarged Agency actually received, or how Warburg's Administrative Committee used it. It does not show how far the non-Zionist half of the Council shaped the Agency's political decisions, as distinct from its finances. And the structure was tested at once: within weeks of Zurich, the Agency faced the crisis of August 1929 and lost the chairman around whom the partnership had been built.

sections.h: 1925: The Hebrew University and Brit Shalom
sections.html:
Four years before Zurich, the movement had marked a different kind of building. On 1 April 1925 Arthur Balfour stood on Mount Scopus above Jerusalem and opened the Hebrew University. Chaim Weizmann presided, as chairman of the university's board [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_hebrew_univ]. In the same year, and prompted by a lecture given at that same opening, a small group in Jerusalem founded an association around a question the rest of the movement answered differently: if Jews and Arabs were both to live in Palestine, on what terms would they share its government? The association was Brit Shalom, and its answer was a binational country in which neither people ruled the other [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_brit_shalom].

The university had been a long time in the making. Twelve foundation stones were laid on Mount Scopus on 24 July 1918, and Albert Einstein gave the first lecture there in 1923 [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_hebrew_univ]. At the opening in 1925, Balfour performed the ceremony and Weizmann presided. Judah Magnes became the university's chancellor, and later its president. The first degrees were awarded in 1931 [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_hebrew_univ].

Balfour's presence was itself an event in Jerusalem. A report in the Detroit Jewish Chronicle of 10 April 1925 described "excitement" among the city's Arabs at a rumor that he would visit the Omar Mosque, and stated that no incidents occurred [cite:rs_rd3_djc_1925_04_10]. That is the extent of what the sources used here record about the Arab response to his visit. Accounts of wider protests have not been verified for this book and are left out.

Brit Shalom was founded in Jerusalem in 1925 on the initiative of Arthur Ruppin. According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, the immediate prompt was a lecture by Professor Joseph Horowitz at the university's opening [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_brit_shalom]. Ruppin chaired the association until 1929 [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_brit_shalom]. Its early members included Ruppin, Jacob Thon, Joseph Lurie, Yitzhak Epstein, Haim Margolis-Kalvaryski and Rabbi Binyamin [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_brit_shalom].

Its program was simple to state and radical in its implications. Brit Shalom sought a binational arrangement in which Jews and Arabs would share the administration of the country equally, regardless of their numbers [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_brit_shalom]. The last three words were the heart of it. Brit Shalom proposed to separate political power from population: parity of government whichever people was the larger. For Jews, then a minority in the country, it meant giving up any claim to rule by majority should they become one. For Arabs, then the majority, it meant sharing power equally with a minority.

Its best-known figures, Buber and Magnes among them, are described as Zionists who rejected the model of sovereignty and partition specifically, not as anti-Zionists. In that they were a different current from the Orthodox opposition of the old Yishuv, which rejected the national project itself on religious grounds and whose spokesman was killed in Jerusalem the year before Brit Shalom was founded; that story is told in [scene:dh_s01|Jacob de Haan and the Orthodox opposition] [cite:myjewishlearning_brit_shalom] [cite:wiki_brit_shalom] [cite:fathom_mandate100_binationalism].

Brit Shalom never had more than 200 members [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_brit_shalom]. It functioned more as a small study circle of academics and intellectuals than as a political party, and it never grew into a mass constituency among either Jews or Arabs [cite:myjewishlearning_brit_shalom] [cite:wiki_brit_shalom]. Its character changed over time. According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, after 1929 Central European intellectuals influenced by Martin Buber predominated, among them Hugo Bergmann, Hans Kohn, Gershom Scholem, Ernst Simon and Robert Weltsch [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_brit_shalom]. It did have prominent public support. Albert Einstein, who had given the university's first lecture, publicly backed it, a fact rarely mentioned alongside his name [cite:wiki_brit_shalom] [cite:myjewishlearning_brit_shalom].

The sources disagree about who founded it, and the disagreement concerns its best-known associate. One account used elsewhere in this library calls Martin Buber and Judah Magnes "both founders of Brit Shalom (1925)," and names Gershom Scholem and Henrietta Szold among the colleagues who founded it with them [cite:myjewishlearning_brit_shalom] [cite:wiki_brit_shalom] [cite:fathom_mandate100_binationalism]. The Encyclopaedia Judaica gives a different picture. It credits the initiative to Ruppin and lists different early members; it places Scholem among those who predominated after 1929; it describes the later members as influenced by Buber rather than naming him as a founder; and it states that Magnes, though he advocated binationalism in this period and his name was often linked to the association, was never a member of it [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_brit_shalom].

The two accounts can be partly reconciled. Magnes advocated binationalism in these years, which may be why his name was so often linked to the association; that is an inference, not a documented finding. Buber's influence on its later members is common to both accounts. But on the narrow question of membership the sources conflict, and this book does not resolve it. The Encyclopaedia Judaica is the more specific of the two, naming founders and dates.

Brit Shalom drew open hostility from the rest of the movement. Most Zionist parties attacked it [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_brit_shalom]. The opposition came from both of the dominant currents, Labour and the Revisionists, and some of its opponents explicitly called its members traitors [cite:wiki_brit_shalom] [cite:myjewishlearning_brit_shalom].

Its decline is usually traced to events. The violence of August 1929, in Hebron above all, undermined the premise on which the association was founded: that Arab political leadership would accept binational equality [cite:wiki_brit_shalom] [cite:fathom_mandate100_binationalism]. The killings in Hebron and Safed, told in [scene:s07a4|the Western Wall and August 1929], came in the same year, and the sources here record no Arab political body that took up the offer. Ruppin left the chair in 1929 [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_brit_shalom]. The association carried on for a few more years, with the Buber circle now predominant. Its monthly, She'ifoteinu, appeared from 1930 to 1933. By 1933 Brit Shalom had virtually ceased to exist [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_brit_shalom], about eight years after its founding [cite:wiki_brit_shalom].

The sources record the hostility to Brit Shalom more fully than the reasoning behind it. Its own case is in its program: parity in government, fixed regardless of numbers, so that neither people would rule the other [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_brit_shalom]. The case against it, as historians reconstruct it, is that it depended on an Arab political partner willing to accept binational equality, and that 1929 showed none in view [cite:wiki_brit_shalom] [cite:fathom_mandate100_binationalism]. The record does not decide whether the binational idea could have worked. On the record here it was never put to the test, and the association never grew into a mass constituency, among Jews or among Arabs.

The binational idea outlived the association. Buber and Magnes went on to found Ihud in 1942, Hannah Arendt warned against an exclusively Jewish sovereign state in 1944, and Buber and Magnes testified against partition before the United Nations commission in 1947. [cite:wiki_ihud] [cite:researchgate_arendt_zionism_reconsidered] [cite:britainpalestine_buber_magnes] That later history lies outside this chapter and is told in [scene:s00b3|Opposition to Zionism across every lineage].

Several questions remain open. The sources do not settle who founded Brit Shalom or whether Magnes ever joined it. They do not record any formal Arab response to its proposals, or name an Arab group with which it negotiated. They give no membership figures beyond the ceiling of 200, and they do not say what Joseph Horowitz argued in the lecture that prompted its founding.

sections.h: Money, Currency and the Mandate Economy, 1922–1936
sections.html:
Brit Shalom argued about who would govern; the economy was being built regardless. New states, it is often said, need years to build a financial system: a currency, a central bank, the machinery of public credit. When Israel declared independence in 1948 it did not start from nothing. It inherited a currency managed by the Mandate, and a banking network that the Zionist movement had built and run for half a century before the state existed. The pieces that mattered were in place by the 1920s and 1930s.

In 1926 the British Colonial Secretary appointed a Palestine Currency Board, and from 1 November 1927 the board issued the Palestine pound [cite:wiki_palestine_pound] [cite:israelmint_pcb_notes]. The pound was fixed at par with sterling and divided into 1,000 mils [cite:wiki_palestine_pound]. The arrangement explains who could act. The board was appointed by the Colonial Secretary, and the currency it issued was tied one for one to the British pound. It was a currency managed from London. No body in Palestine, Jewish or Arab, issued the country's money or set its value. The Palestine Currency Board's notes stayed in circulation until 18 August 1948 [cite:wiki_palestine_pound] [cite:israelmint_pcb_notes].

Alongside the Mandate's currency ran a separate financial structure, owned by the Zionist movement. The Jewish Colonial Trust was chartered in London in 1899. Its operating subsidiary, the Anglo-Palestine Bank, was founded in 1902, was London-based, and was owned through the Jewish Agency [cite:wiki_israeli_pound] [cite:wiki_palestine_pound]. Together they carried the movement's finance for half a century. Their founding belongs to an earlier volume of this library; what matters here is that by the 1920s the Yishuv, the Jewish community in Palestine, had a bank of its own that operated in the Mandate's currency but answered to the movement's institutions.

The structure had a clear shape. The money that built the national home came from abroad, as donations to the movement's funds and as the capital that immigrants brought with them. The movement's own banking ran through institutions chartered in London, in a currency pegged to sterling. It was invested in building, citrus and industry. The figures for that investment come mainly from the Jewish Agency itself, and they have to be read as what they are.

In 1937 David Horowitz of the Jewish Agency's Economics Department prepared Economic and Social Transformation of Palestine for the Agency's case before the Peel Commission [cite:rs_rd3_horowitz_1937]. It is an advocacy document, written to persuade a British commission, and its figures are the Agency's own. They are reported here as Horowitz gave them.

According to Horowitz, "LP 80,000,000 have been invested by Jews in economic enterprise" over sixteen years. Annual Jewish investment in building, he wrote, rose from LP 900,000 in 1924 to LP 7,000,000 in 1935 [cite:rs_rd3_horowitz_1937]. He gave citrus exports rising from £200,000 in 1921 to £2,700,000 in 1934, and the area under citrus growing from 30,000 dunams in 1922 to 260,000 in 1935. Industrial output, in his figures, rose from under LP 1,000,000 in 1921 to over LP 8,000,000 in 1935 [cite:rs_rd3_horowitz_1937].

He gave the population too. In his account there were 84,000 Jews in 1922, 13 percent of the population, and 375,000 in 1935, 28 percent; the non-Jewish population was 565,000 in 1922 and 975,000 in 1935 [cite:rs_rd3_horowitz_1937]. His Jewish figure for 1922 is close to the census count of 83,794. His share is not. The 1922 census counted 757,182 people in all and put Jews at about 11 percent [cite:jvl_census_1931]. Horowitz's 13 percent rests on a smaller non-Jewish base of 565,000, and the source does not explain how that base was drawn. The country as the census counted it is described in [scene:cen_s01|the opening section of this chapter].

The Mandate government grew along with the economy. Horowitz gave government revenue as LP 2,371,000 in 1922–23 and LP 5,452,000 in 1934–35, and expenditure rising over the same years from LP 1,900,000 to LP 3,200,000 [cite:rs_rd3_horowitz_1937]. On his figures the administration took in more than it spent in both years, and its revenue more than doubled while its spending grew by about two-thirds. The cost of holding the country militarily was a separate account. The British garrison cost £1.5 million in 1923–24 [cite:league_report_garrison], more than three-quarters of the civil spending of 1922–23, and it was paid by Britain. The full ledger of what the Mandate cost Britain, to its end in 1948, is told in [scene:gf_s02|Charity for an Army].

The rows of that table for these years tell the story in brief: Mandate civil spending of £P1.9 million in 1922–23 and £P3.2 million in 1934–35 [cite:horowitz_1937]; the garrison's £1.5 million in 1923–24 [cite:league_report_garrison]; and, set beside them, the Agency's estimate of £P80 million of Jewish capital invested between 1921 and 1937 [cite:rs_rd3_horowitz_1937]. The figures come from different payers and different kinds of account, and they are shown side by side for scale, not added together.

Horowitz went further than investment totals. He argued that Arabs gained directly from Jewish economic activity: from Jewish contributions to government revenue, from land prices that had risen 400 to 500 percent, and from falling death rates in the districts of Jewish immigration. He set daily wages of 10–15 piastres in Palestine against 2–3 in Iraq and Egypt [cite:rs_rd3_horowitz_1937]. This is the strongest form of the Zionist economic case, and it was made in the movement's own words, to a British commission, for a political purpose.

A British official had reached a different conclusion seven years earlier. Sir John Hope Simpson, reporting in October 1930, found that Jewish National Fund leases required Jewish labor only, that a landless Arab class was forming, and that families displaced by land sales had not been resettled [cite:rs_rd3_hope_simpson_unispal_l]. On his account the benefits of Jewish investment did not flow freely across the population; the institutions that directed it were built to employ Jews, and some of the cost fell on Arab cultivators who lost their land. His figures, and the Agency's rebuttal of them, are set out in [scene:rd3_land|the section on land and labour].

The two positions are not strictly contradictory, since one speaks of average wages, prices and revenue and the other of the people displaced and excluded. But the sources used here do not measure how gains and losses were distributed among Arabs, and neither Horowitz's figures nor Hope Simpson's settle that question. Each was produced for a purpose, the first to argue for the national home before Peel, the second to advise the British government on land and immigration. The record supports neither the claim that Jewish investment benefited everyone nor the claim that it benefited no one.

One more flow of these years ran through Palestine without passing through either the Mandate's budget or the movement's banks. The Iraq Petroleum Company built a pipeline from Iraq to the Mediterranean between 1932 and 1934. At Haditha it split into two branches, one to Tripoli and one to Haifa [cite:rs_rd3_gulbenkian_pipeline]. The transit agreements with Palestine, Transjordan, Lebanon and Syria had been signed between 5 January and 25 March 1931 [cite:rs_rd3_gulbenkian_pipeline]. The first oil reached Haifa on 16 October 1934, and official opening ceremonies were held in January 1935. The line could carry four million tons a year [cite:rs_rd3_gulbenkian_pipeline]. Palestine had become a transit country for the oil of a neighbouring state, with a terminal on its coast. The arrangement lasted until 1948, when Iraq stopped sending oil to Haifa [cite:rs_rd3_gulbenkian_pipeline].

The banking structure built in these years carried the state through its birth. Before independence the Anglo-Palestine Bank's chairman, Eliezer Hoofien, persuaded the American Bank Note Company in New York to print new notes. Because neither the state's name nor its currency had been decided, they were denominated in "Palestine pounds." According to Israel's state mint, the notes were not marked "legal tender," and the printer's name was left off, to get around the need for the US Secretary of State's approval to print foreign currency [cite:israelmint_aplb_series] [cite:jhom_anglo_palestine_notes]. They reached the country secretly in July 1948 and became legal tender by law on 17 August 1948, the day before the Mandate's notes went out of circulation [cite:israelmint_aplb_series] [cite:jhom_anglo_palestine_notes] [cite:wiki_palestine_pound]. On 1 May 1951 the bank's assets passed to Bank Leumi le-Israel, and the currency became the Israeli pound [cite:wiki_israeli_pound].

The common assumption, then, has it backwards for this case. The state did not have to build a financial system after 1948. One already existed: a London-chartered bank that had operated for decades, inside a currency system the British had set up in 1926–27. On this reading, what 1948 required was a change of name and of sovereign, and the first notes for that change were printed in New York.

The record here is strong on structure and weaker on totals. The investment, output and export figures for 1922–1936 come from a single advocacy document, and no independent series in the sources checks them. The sources do not give the Anglo-Palestine Bank's own balance sheets, its lending, or how much of the £P80 million Horowitz reported passed through it. They do not say how the Currency Board's reserves were held, or what the peg to sterling cost or gained the country. And they do not measure how the gains of the Mandate economy were divided between Jews and Arabs, or among Arabs themselves, which is the question on which Horowitz and Hope Simpson most sharply disagree.

sections.h: The Wall and August 1929: Jerusalem, Hebron, Safed
sections.html:
The institutions of these years were built over a decade; the violence that tested them came in a single week. A common account of Mandate Palestine dates organized violence between Arabs and Jews to the Arab Revolt that began in 1936. The record puts a turning point seven years earlier. In the last week of August 1929, violence that began in Jerusalem over the Western Wall, which Muslims call al-Buraq, spread to Hebron and Safed. It left a precise death toll, ended one of the oldest continuous Jewish communities in the country for nearly four decades, led to a British commission of inquiry, and, in the judgment of historians, made the political reputation of the Mufti of Jerusalem, Hajj Amin al-Husseini [cite:wiki_hebron_massacre_1929] [cite:wiki_amin_al_husseini].

The dispute had a specific starting point. In September 1928, on Yom Kippur, Jewish worshippers set up a portable screen at the Wall to separate men from women, and its removal opened the conflict [cite:rs_rd3_ebsco_wwriots]. The ground mattered because of who owned it. The Wall belonged to Muslim religious authorities, and Jews prayed there. Through 1928 the tension built on both sides. A documented Arab campaign asserted Muslim rights over the site, and documented Jewish activity pressed for prayer arrangements there; each side treated the dispute as central to its larger claim [cite:wiki_hebron_massacre_1929]. Hajj Amin al-Husseini is documented as leading the 1928 campaign asserting Muslim rights over the Wall [cite:wiki_amin_al_husseini]. The record shows real escalation from both directions in the year before the riots. It does not settle which particular acts bear more of the blame.

The final days before the outbreak are dated precisely. On 15 August 1929 a few hundred Jewish youths, Betar members among them, marched to the Wall and raised a flag. On 16 August a Muslim demonstration went to the Wall, beat Jews who were there and burned prayer notes [cite:rs_rd3_ebsco_wwriots] [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_prayer_pogrom] [cite:rs_rd3_jerusalemstory_buraq]. In the days that followed, according to the historians cited here, rumor and organized propaganda inflamed the city, and the Mufti's activists distributed inflammatory material [cite:wiki_hebron_massacre_1929] [cite:wiki_amin_al_husseini].

The outbreak came on 23 August in Jerusalem. The Shaw Commission, which investigated it the following year, found that it began there as an attack by Arabs on Jews, that it "was not premeditated", and that it was not a revolt against British authority [cite:rs_rd3_shaw_palquest_d]. The police force was small. Only about 150 British police and 1,500 local police served the whole of Palestine [cite:rs_rd3_ebsco_wwriots] [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_prayer_pogrom]. The British command at the time is part of the story of the High Commissioners in [scene:s07a2|the High Commissioners].

The worst of the killing was in Hebron. There, on 24 August 1929, it began at about 9 a.m. Eight American students of the Slobodka Yeshiva were among the dead [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_prayer_pogrom]. Sixty-seven Jews were killed in the city [cite:wiki_hebron_massacre_1929]. The sources differ on how the count fell across the two days. Human Rights Watch gives 67 Jews killed and dates the massacre to 23 August; the EBSCO reference account records one yeshiva student killed on 23 August and 64 killed at the Heichal residence on 24 August [cite:rs_rd3_hrw_hebron] [cite:rs_rd3_ebsco_wwriots]. Those two EBSCO figures add to 65, not 67, and the sources used here do not reconcile the difference.

Hebron also produced a documented account of rescue. According to Human Rights Watch, the Zionist Archives list 435 Hebron Jews who found refuge in 28 Arab homes. Norman Bentwich wrote that many Jews were saved by their Arab neighbors [cite:rs_rd3_hrw_hebron] [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_prayer_pogrom]. The figure of 435 rests on that one archival list as reported by Human Rights Watch; it is not, in the sources here, independently counted. It belongs in the record beside the death toll.

After the killing the British authorities evacuated Hebron's surviving Jews. A community present in the city for centuries was removed within days, and organized Jewish life there did not resume until 1968, thirty-nine years later [cite:wiki_hebron_massacre_1929]. Unlike many episodes of violence in these years, this one produced an immediate, total and lasting change. The circumstances of the 1968 return, and what came after it, belong to a much later part of this book.

The violence reached Safed on 29 August 1929. Between 18 and 20 Jews were killed there and about 80 wounded, and some 200 Jewish homes were burned [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_prayer_pogrom] [cite:rs_rd3_jewishcurrents_safed].

By the end of the week the dead numbered 133 Jews and 116 Arabs, according to the EBSCO reference account and the Jewish Virtual Library. Most of the Arab deaths were caused by British police and military fire during the suppression [cite:rs_rd3_ebsco_wwriots] [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_prayer_pogrom]. The Jewish toll is itself disputed. The Jerusalem Story lexicon of the Institute for Palestine Studies gives 113 Jews and 116 Arabs, and adds that the Mandate probably under-reported Palestinian casualties [cite:rs_rd3_jerusalemstory_buraq]. The two accounts agree on the Arab figure and differ by twenty on the Jewish one; neither source, as used here, explains the gap.

The reckoning took several forms, and Britain's own report to the League of Nations for 1929 records the first of them. Collective punishments were imposed on towns and villages that took part in attacks on Jews at Hebron, Safed, Motza, Artuf and Beer Tuvia, with fines totalling £P17,840. The courts moved quickly. By the end of December 1929, 791 Arabs and 66 Jews had been tried summarily; 17 Arabs and 1 Jew had received capital sentences, and 7 death sentences had been confirmed on appeal [cite:rs_rd3_lon_report_1929]. These were measures of the Mandate administration, and Britain reported them to the League as the mandatory power answerable to it.

On 17 June 1930 three Arab men were hanged in Acre for their part in the riots. Twenty-five other death sentences, two of them on Jews, were commuted. This account rests on a single general reference, and the identities of the three men are not established in the research for this book, so they are not named here. Palestinians remember the day as "Red Tuesday" [cite:rs_rd3_wiki_1930].

The Shaw Commission reported in March 1930. On the question that has divided accounts ever since, the Mufti's role, it was precise. It found no evidence that Hajj Amin al-Husseini had incited the outbreak, but held that he "must accept a share in the responsibility". It found premeditation not proved against the Arab Executive [cite:rs_rd3_shaw_palquest_d]. On causes, Shaw distinguished two levels. The fundamental cause was Arab hostility rooted in disappointed political aspirations and fear for their economic future. The immediate causes included the incidents at the Wall from September 1928 to 16 August 1929, the Jewish demonstration of 15 August, an inflammatory press, and the enlargement of the Jewish Agency in 1929 [cite:rs_rd3_shaw_palquest_d], whose making is told in [scene:us_s03|the enlarged Jewish Agency]. What London did with Shaw's findings, and with the land inquiry that followed, is the subject of [scene:pf_s01|the Passfield White Paper and its reversal].

The ownership question at the Wall itself went to an international body. A commission of three members, none of them British, sat in Jerusalem from 19 June to 19 July 1930 under the approval of the League Council: Eliel Löfgren of Sweden, Charles Barde of Geneva and J. van Kempen of the Netherlands. It reported in December 1930 [cite:rs_rd3_unispal_wall_1930]. It found that the Wall and the pavement before it are Muslim property, and that the Wall is "sacred to both Parties". Jews were to have free access for their devotions, but could bring only the appurtenances permitted under the Turkish regime, and screens separating men and women were barred [cite:rs_rd3_unispal_wall_1930]. The commission thus ruled on the very object, a screen, that had opened the dispute in September 1928. It confirmed Muslim ownership and Jewish access together, and held Jewish worship there to the arrangements of the Ottoman years.

The three main readings of August 1929 rest on different evidence, and each has a strong form. In the Palestinian account, preserved in the Jerusalem Story lexicon under the name "al-Buraq Uprising", the trigger was a provocation: Betar-led demonstrators raised the Zionist flag at a site under Muslim authority, and the response grew from a real fear that the holy places would be taken over [cite:rs_rd3_jerusalemstory_buraq]. The march of 15 August appears in each of the accounts cited here, and Shaw named it among the immediate causes, so this reading draws support from the inquiry's findings as well as from Palestinian memory. In the Jewish account, the cause was a Muslim campaign over the Wall led by the Mufti, and incitement that ended in massacres of unarmed communities [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_prayer_pogrom] [cite:rs_rd3_jewishcurrents_safed]. Its evidence is equally concrete: the Mufti's documented 1928 campaign, the inflammatory material his activists distributed, and the fact that the dead of Hebron, eight American yeshiva students among them, were killed in another town, a day after the outbreak in Jerusalem. The British inquiry stood between the two. It found no premeditation, a share of responsibility on the Mufti, and the 15 August demonstration among the immediate causes, while naming an Arab attack on Jews as the form the outbreak took [cite:rs_rd3_shaw_palquest_d].

Behind the question of the Mufti's role in the riots lies a larger one about what the riots did for him. Historians, among them Oren Kessler in a 2024 account, describe 1929 as the event that made al-Husseini's political reputation among Palestinians, the platform on which his leadership of the 1936–39 revolt was later built [cite:wiki_amin_al_husseini]. That reading places the start of his rise seven years before the revolt. It does not make 1936 less important to his career. It says what came before it and made it possible.

Several things the record does not settle. The first is the Mufti's direct part. That his activists distributed inflammatory material before the riots is documented. Whether he organized the violence itself, or capitalized on tensions that moved beyond his control, is a question historians still debate; Shaw's "share in the responsibility" was a judgment, not a finding of organization [cite:wiki_amin_al_husseini] [cite:rs_rd3_shaw_palquest_d]. The second is the count. The Jewish dead of the week are given as 133 or 113, the Hebron dead as 67 or, by one day-by-day account, 65, and the Arab dead, most of them killed by the forces of order, may have been under-recorded [cite:rs_rd3_jerusalemstory_buraq] [cite:rs_rd3_hrw_hebron] [cite:rs_rd3_ebsco_wwriots]. The third is the rescue: the 435 sheltered in Hebron rest on one archival list as reported by one organization.

sections.h: Palestinian Politics, 1928–1935: From Congress to Parties
sections.html:
The riots of August 1929 came a year after the Palestinian national movement had briefly reunited. A familiar claim holds that the Palestinians had no leaders, no national organization and no political demands before 1948. By 1928 they had already held seven national congresses, and their central demand to Britain was an elected government. From 1919, Muslims and Christians organized together through Muslim–Christian Associations; the congresses chose an Arab Executive under Musa Kazim al-Husseini, called for "a national government responsible to a representative assembly", and rejected the Balfour Declaration and mass Jewish immigration [cite:wiki_palestine_arab_congress] [cite:jerusalemstory_arab_executive]. That earlier history, from the first congress of 1919 to the delegations of 1921–22, is told in [scene:pp_s01|the Palestinian national movement]. What follows begins with the last of those congresses and ends with the party system that stood on the eve of 1936. It is a story of choices made by Palestinians, among themselves and against one another, under a mandatory power that never recognized their Executive [cite:palquest_musa_kazim] [cite:wiki_musa_kazim].

The Seventh Palestinian Arab Congress met in June 1928. Its importance lay in who attended. Raghib al-Nashashibi's opposition bloc took part, and Nashashibi himself joined the Arab Executive that emerged from it [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_nashashibi]. Rivalry between the factions aligned with the Husseini family and those aligned with the Nashashibis had divided Palestinian politics since the British dismissed Musa Kazim al-Husseini as mayor of Jerusalem in 1920 and appointed Raghib al-Nashashibi in his place [cite:palquest_musa_kazim] [cite:wiki_musa_kazim]. The 1928 congress briefly brought the two camps into one front [cite:wiki_palestine_arab_congress]. Nashashibi held the mayoralty throughout: re-elected in 1927, he served until 1934, when Hussein Fakhri al-Khalidi was elected [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_nashashibi].

Two months after the violence of August 1929, Palestinian organization widened. On 26 October 1929 the first Palestine Arab Women's Congress met in Jerusalem, with about 300 delegates. Salma al-Husseini led it; Wahida al-Khalidi and Amina al-Husseini organized it. The congress called for repeal of the Balfour Declaration and an end to Jewish immigration, and it elected a fourteen-member executive [cite:rs_rd3_jerusalemstory_womens]. Its demands matched those of the national congresses. What was new was that women had built their own national body to press them.

The Executive's next move was diplomatic. In 1930, while London weighed the findings of its inquiries into 1929, an Arab Executive delegation went to London. Nashashibi traveled with it in March 1930, and Jamal al-Husseini sat on the delegation that negotiated there in April and May [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_nashashibi] [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_jamal]. The sources used here do not record what the delegation obtained. The policy London published that autumn, and its withdrawal in February 1931, are told in the section on the Passfield White Paper.

In December 1931 the rivalry took international form. The General Islamic Congress opened in Jerusalem on 7 December 1931 with 130 delegates from 22 countries, according to an account in Middle East Eye, and Hajj Amin al-Husseini, the Mufti, was among its main organizers. It resolved to defend the holy places, to boycott Zionist goods, to found an Islamic university in Jerusalem and to form a company to buy Palestinian land [cite:rs_rd3_mee_congress_1931]. The same account records Britain's response: High Commissioner Wauchope questioned the Mufti about the delegates' political speeches; Britain deported Abd al-Rahman Azzam and refused entry to the former caliph Abdulmecid II; and the university project stalled for lack of funds in 1935 [cite:rs_rd3_mee_congress_1931]. The Mufti's congress did not speak for all Palestinians. In the same month Nashashibi held a rival conference in Jerusalem to counter it [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_nashashibi].

Land was a recurring concern. In 1932 the Executive launched a "Piaster Project", a fund to keep land in Arab hands [cite:wiki_palestine_arab_congress]. Like the Islamic Congress's land company, it answered the purchases described in [scene:rd3_land|land and labour, 1922–1933].

The sharpest challenge to the Executive came from inside the national movement. In August 1932 eleven founders, among them Rashid al-Haj Ibrahim, Awni Abd al-Hadi and Muhammad Izzat Darwaza, officially announced the Istiqlal (Independence) Party. It called for full Arab independence and Arab unity, and named British imperialism as the main enemy [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_hajibrahim] [cite:rs_rd3_wiki_istiqlal]. That was a change of target. The congresses had petitioned Britain; Istiqlal treated Britain itself as the adversary, and it attacked the established leadership for inaction in 1932–33 [cite:fhfpal_musa_kazim]. Its reach was limited. According to a reference account drawing on Porath, Khalidi, Kedourie and others, the party never built a large membership; its influence peaked among young educated Palestinians in early 1933 and then fell, partly through Husseini hostility and partly for lack of funds [cite:rs_rd3_wiki_istiqlal]. Its founders remained active: until June 1933 Awni Abd al-Hadi was representing the tenants of Wadi al-Hawarith in court, and Istiqlal joined the protests when the eviction order came [cite:wiki_wadi_al_hawarith].

Open confrontation with the government came in October 1933, called not by Istiqlal but by the Arab Executive. Following its call for protest demonstrations, disturbances broke out in Jerusalem on 13 October, in Jaffa, Haifa and Nablus on 27–28 October, and in Jerusalem again on 28–29 October. The Murison Commission, which investigated them, found that they were "aimed against the Government and not against the Jews" [cite:rs_rd3_murison_palquest]. Its count was exact.
