One policeman and 26 members of the public were killed; 56 police and 187 members of the public were injured. All the public deaths were by gunfire, 15 of them at Jaffa, where police fired 102 rifle and 43 revolver rounds [cite:rs_rd3_murison_palquest]. Musa Kazim al-Husseini, the Executive's president, was injured by British forces at the Jaffa protest [cite:wiki_musa_kazim] [cite:fhfpal_musa_kazim].

The commission reported on 4 January 1934 and found that the police had acted with restraint [cite:rs_rd3_murison_palquest]. The two readings of October 1933 rest on the same report. In Murison's own judgment, the police acted "with restraint and forbearance" and no officer departed from regulations. The protesters' case draws on its other findings: the demonstrations were political protest against government policy, called openly by the national leadership, and every one of the 26 civilian dead was killed by police gunfire, while one policeman died [cite:rs_rd3_murison_palquest]. Its own figures show who bore the cost of that force. A reader can hold both findings at once; the report does not resolve them into one verdict, and neither does this book.

Musa Kazim al-Husseini died in March 1934, and the Arab Executive dissolved that year [cite:wiki_musa_kazim] [cite:palquest_musa_kazim]. Over fifteen years the congresses and their Executive had sent petitions and delegations asking for an elected government; Britain recognized the Zionist Organization's Jewish Agency but never recognized the Palestinians' own Executive [cite:palquest_musa_kazim]. Its end left the field to parties built around the old rivalries.

Nashashibi moved first. Having lost the mayoralty of Jerusalem to Hussein Fakhri al-Khalidi in 1934, he founded the National Defense Party in early December 1934. Its program rejected the Balfour Declaration, Jewish immigration and land sales, and called for parliamentary government; Nashashibi was close to Emir Abdullah [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_nashashibi]. The Husseini camp answered within four months. The Palestine Arab Party was officially established on 27 March 1935, and Jamal al-Husseini, close to the Mufti, was unanimously chosen as its leader [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_jamal]. By the end of 1935, five Arab parties stood where one Executive had been. Late that year they formed a united front, which the American consul general Leland Morris described in April 1936 as a response to a "national emergency" [cite:rs_rd3_frus1936_d512]. How that front met the High Commissioner's offer of a legislative council, and how it held, is the subject of [scene:rd3_council_1935|the legislative council of 1935–36].

The structure that emerged had two poles and a third force. The Husseini pole ran through the Mufti, who held religious office and had organized the Islamic Congress, and through the Palestine Arab Party under Jamal al-Husseini, who was close to him. The Nashashibi pole ran through the National Defense Party, which held to the same rejection of the Balfour Declaration but looked toward parliamentary government and stood close to Emir Abdullah. Istiqlal, small and short of money, named British imperialism as the main enemy. The united front of late 1935 joined them without dissolving them.

Who could act in this structure, and through what, is part of the story. The Palestinian leaders had no recognized channel to government. They had congresses, delegations, the press, demonstrations, and from 1934 parties; the mandatory power had police, deportation and the power to refuse entry. The Islamic Congress shows both sides of that balance. It could gather 130 delegates and pass resolutions on land, boycott and a university; the High Commissioner could question its organizer and Britain could expel a delegate, and the university project stalled in 1935 for lack of funds [cite:rs_rd3_mee_congress_1931].

Several questions remain open. The sources do not say what the 1930 London delegation won or lost in its negotiations. The figures for the Islamic Congress and for Istiqlal's decline come from secondary accounts and are attributed as such. The sources do not name the two smaller parties of the 1935 front, or show how far the front reconciled the Husseini and Nashashibi camps rather than suspending their rivalry. And the Murison report leaves open the question at the center of October 1933: whether a police force that fired 145 rounds at Jaffa and killed 15 people there acted with restraint, as the commission found, or whether the toll itself is the better measure.

sections.h: How Weimar Fell, 1929–1933
sections.html:
The German emigration that reached Palestine from 1933, and the Transfer Agreement that moved part of its capital there, began with the collapse of a democracy in Berlin. That collapse is often told as the work of an unstoppable wave of popular fanaticism. The documented record supports a narrower and more specific account: an economic catastrophe, a real but already declining surge of support for the Nazi Party, a decision taken by a small number of conservative politicians who believed they could control Hitler, and then a fire, an emergency decree, and a legislature that voted away its own authority. Each step can be dated, and at several of them people with power chose.

The first step was financial. The Weimar Republic's recovery in the mid-1920s had been built in large part on a steady flow of American loans. The Wall Street Crash of October 1929 led to the recall of those loans and plunged Germany back into economic catastrophe and mass unemployment [cite:ushmm_nazi_rise_to_power] [cite:history_weimar_republic]. The money ran in one direction and then reversed: American lenders supplied the capital that carried the stabilization, and when they withdrew it, the cost came due in Germany as mass unemployment, borne by a republic that had depended on that capital. The timing of Nazi support matches that sequence. According to the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum's Holocaust Encyclopedia, genuine popular support for Hitler and his party began to accumulate from late 1929 onward, not before, while the economy still functioned [cite:ushmm_nazi_rise_to_power].

That connection has limits, and the record marks them. Economic hardship does not by itself explain Nazi support. Millions of Germans lived through the same conditions and did not become Nazis, and the more immediate causes of what followed were political decisions, not economic forces acting alone.

The second step is the one most often left out. The Nazi Party's electoral high point came in July 1932. By November 1932, three months before Hitler became Chancellor, its vote share had fallen to roughly 33 percent [cite:historycollection_weimar_collapse]. Hitler did not come to power at the crest of a rising wave. He came to power after the wave had begun to fall. That decline is evidence for the view that the Republic might have survived this particular crisis given more time. It is not proof. Historians treat survival as a real possibility; no one can show it would have happened.

The third step was a decision. Franz von Papen, an aristocrat and former chancellor, brokered the arrangement that made Hitler Chancellor. According to the accounts cited here, Papen assured his associates that he had Hitler's measure and could control him from within the cabinet, using him, in the phrase historians use, as a "battering ram" against the political left [cite:historycollection_weimar_collapse] [cite:britannica_third_reich]. Hitler was appointed Chancellor on 30 January 1933 [cite:history_weimar_republic]. This was not a popular revolution. A small circle of men who held real institutional power chose to hand him the office, on the calculation that they would remain in control. The record shows a catastrophic misjudgment about whether he could be controlled. It does not show that Papen or his circle intended, or foresaw, what came after.

The fourth step supplied the emergency. In February 1933 the Reichstag building burned, and the regime used the fire to push through the Reichstag Fire Decree, which suspended civil liberties and made possible the mass arrest of political opponents [cite:history_weimar_republic]. Who set the fire remains a question historians dispute. Its political use does not depend on the answer: whatever its origin, the fire provided the pretext for the decree, and the decree cleared the way for the next step weeks later.

The fifth step ended the Republic in law. In March 1933 Hitler introduced the Enabling Act, which allowed him to pass laws without the approval of Parliament or the President. To secure its passage he forcibly prevented the Communist members of Parliament from voting [cite:history_weimar_republic] [cite:britannica_third_reich]. With its enactment the Weimar Republic's twelve-year democratic experiment ended, not by a street coup but by a legislature voting away its own constitutional authority [cite:history_weimar_republic]. The mechanism is precise. The instrument was a statute passed through the legislature's own procedure; the members who could have opposed it were, in the Communists' case, physically kept from the vote, and the remaining members voted under the climate of intimidation that followed the February decree. The record does not show that every member who voted for the act did so freely.

Two readings of these years meet in the evidence. One emphasizes the depth of the economic collapse and the real popular support the Nazi Party won from late 1929; on that reading the Republic was gravely weakened from below, and the support was genuine. The other emphasizes the decline of November 1932 and the deal that followed; on that reading the decisive act was taken from above, by men who were not swept along by a mass movement but believed they could use one. The record supports both parts, in sequence. Popular support was real and was falling; the appointment was an elite choice; the dismantling of the constitution was carried out through law, under coercion. What it does not support is the familiar picture of a democracy overrun by a fanaticism no one could have stopped.

The record leaves several things open. It does not settle who set the Reichstag fire. It cannot show that the Republic would have survived had Hitler not been appointed when he was; the decline of late 1932 makes that possible, not certain. And it does not show what Papen and his allies expected beyond their belief that they could control the man they empowered. The regime installed by these steps is the one that appears, within months, as a party to [scene:hv_s01|the Transfer Agreement of 1933], and two years later as the author of [scene:hol_s02|the Nuremberg Laws of 1935].

sections.h: Inquiry and Reversal: The Passfield White Paper and the MacDonald Letter, 1930–1931
sections.html:
While the Weimar Republic was failing, London was reconsidering Palestine. British policy there is often described as moving in one steady direction from the Balfour Declaration to the White Paper of 1939. Between March 1930 and February 1931 it moved twice. After the violence of August 1929, two official inquiries concluded that Jewish immigration and land purchase were feeding Arab fears and creating a landless Arab class. In October 1930 London published a policy built on those findings. Four months later the Prime Minister, in a letter to the leader of the Zionist movement, explained it in terms that removed its restrictions. It is the clearest case before 1939 of a British decision on Palestine reversed within months under political pressure, and the immigration figures of the following years show what the reversal allowed.

The first inquiry was the Shaw Commission, sent to investigate the 1929 violence. It reported in March 1930. It found the fundamental cause in Arab hostility rooted in disappointed political aspirations and fear for their economic future, a fear of displacement through Jewish immigration and land purchase, and it recommended that Britain clarify its policy on both [cite:w_shaw] [cite:rs_rd3_shaw_palquest_d]. Its findings on the Mufti and on the riots themselves are told in [scene:s07a4|the Wall and August 1929]. On land it found that the protective ordinances had failed and that a landless class was forming, "a potential danger to the country" [cite:rs_rd3_shaw_palquest_e].

The second inquiry went deeper. Sir John Hope Simpson surveyed land and agriculture across the country; his report was published in October 1930 [cite:rs_rd3_hope_simpson_unispal]. He found that a large share of rural Arab families had too little land to live on, that evictions after land sales were producing a landless class, and that without development there was no margin for further Jewish agricultural settlement [cite:w_hopesimpson]. In 104 surveyed villages, 29.4 percent of families held no land, and he put the land available for new settlement at "100,000 dunams at the outside" [cite:rs_rd3_hope_simpson_unispal]. His full figures, and the Jewish Agency's challenge to them, are set out in [scene:rd3_land|land and labour, 1922–1933].

On the basis of these two reports, the Colonial Secretary, Lord Passfield, issued a White Paper in October 1930. It made immigration depend on Arab as well as Jewish unemployment, and it tightened control of land transfers [cite:w_passfield]. It was the first serious attempt to slow the machinery of settlement the Mandate had set running. The mechanism lay in two levers the Mandatory already held: the rate at which immigration certificates were issued, and the approval of land transfers. The White Paper proposed to tie the first to the condition of the whole labor market, Arab included, and to hold the second more tightly.

The response was immediate. Chaim Weizmann resigned as president of the Jewish Agency in protest. Senior Conservative and Liberal politicians attacked the policy in Parliament and the press as a breach of the Mandate, and the press campaign was intense. In a closely watched by-election at Whitechapel, a constituency with a large Jewish electorate, Labour's majority shrank [cite:w_passfield]. The pressure fell on a minority Labour government [cite:w_passfield]. Nothing in the record requires a hidden hand to explain the outcome. A government without a majority faced an opposition, a press campaign and an electoral warning, all in the open, and gave way.

On 13 February 1931 Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald sent Weizmann a letter, which was read into the record of the House of Commons [cite:w_passfield]. Its text shows exactly how the reversal was done. The letter did not repeal the White Paper. It presented itself as the "authoritative interpretation" of it, and then interpreted it point by point. On immigration, it stated that the government did not contemplate "any stoppage or prohibition of Jewish immigration", and tied any limits to the principle of absorptive capacity, described as "purely economic considerations". On land, it said the 1930 policy did not bar further Jewish land purchase and referred only to "temporary control of land disposition and transfers"; the duty to settle landless Arabs applied to those displaced by land passing into Jewish hands. On labor, it accepted the Jewish Agency's right to affirm the preferential employment of Jewish labor, while saying that the Mandatory must take account of any resulting displacement of Arab labor or rise in unemployment [cite:rs_rd3_macdonald_unispal]. And it restated the Mandate itself: "an undertaking to the Jewish people and not only to the Jewish population of Palestine", a double undertaking to which equal weight was to be given [cite:rs_rd3_macdonald_unispal].

The two sides read the letter in opposite ways, and each reading has a solid basis in the documents. The Zionist reading, which leading opposition politicians had also put in Parliament before the letter was written, was that the White Paper had breached the Mandate, and that the letter corrected the breach [cite:w_passfield]. The letter's own language supports that reading on its terms. If the Mandate was an undertaking to the Jewish people as a whole, not only to the Jews already in Palestine, then a policy that measured immigration by the local labor market alone weighed only one side of a double obligation. The Arab reading was summed up in the name Arab leaders gave the document: the "Black Letter" [cite:w_passfield]. Its evidence is the sequence itself. A policy founded on two official inquiries was withdrawn within four months, through a letter to the head of one party to the dispute, after a campaign waged in Parliament, the press and a by-election.

The letter's effect on Arab trust is documented by Arab officials of the Mandate government itself. On 30 June 1936, 137 Arab senior government officials told the High Commissioner that the Arabs had lost faith in official pledges. They cited the 1931 letter, issued as an interpretation of the 1930 White Paper, as a cause, and recommended that immigration be stopped [cite:rs_rd3_officials_memo_1936]. Five years after it was written, men who served the Mandate administration still cited the letter when they explained their loss of faith in British commitments.

Immigration then rose steeply. Recorded Jewish immigration, as compiled by the United States State Department from British returns, was 4,075 in 1931, 9,553 in 1932, 30,327 in 1933, 42,359 in 1934 and 61,854 in 1935 [cite:rs_rd3_frus1939_d828]. A second series, printed from the historian Yehoshua Porath, gives higher figures for most of these years; both are set out in [scene:rd3_aliyot|immigration, 1923–1936]. The 1935 figure was the highest of the Mandate years. The letter did not by itself produce that rise. From 1933 the Nazi takeover in Germany drove Jewish emigration on a new scale. What the letter did was keep in place the rules under which that emigration could enter Palestine. The Arab Revolt began the following year.

Several questions remain open. The sources do not show which pressure weighed most with MacDonald: the parliamentary attack, the press, the Whitechapel result, or Weizmann's resignation. They do not separate the letter's effect on immigration from the effect of events in Germany; the two arrived together, and any attempt to apportion the rise between them goes beyond the evidence. Nor can they say what the White Paper would have achieved had it stood, since it was never applied as written.

sections.h: Land and Labour, 1922–1933
sections.html:
The findings London adopted and then explained away in 1930–31 were findings about land. Two opposite simplifications surround the land of Mandate Palestine. One holds that the British government sold the country's land to Zionist buyers with little scrutiny or resistance. The other holds that Jewish land purchase was small and sporadic before 1948. The record of the 1920s and early 1930s answers both. The land was not, in the main, sold by Britain. It was bought, privately and lawfully, from landowners, most of them absentees, by Zionist institutions that held it permanently and leased it under terms, in the Jewish National Fund's draft lease, that required Jewish labor. The Mandate tried to protect the tenants who lost their land and failed, and its own inquiries of 1930 measured the result. Resistance was real and documented, in courts and in protest, though it rarely stopped a sale once begun [cite:wiki_sursock_purchases] [cite:israeled_jnf_cultivators_ordinance] [cite:wiki_wadi_al_hawarith].

The legal ground for all of it was older than the Mandate. Under Ottoman law, tenant farmers who had worked land for generations usually held no registered title; when the registered owner sold, the tenant had no ownership claim to assert, so a lawful sale and a lawful eviction could be the same transaction [cite:badil_land_ownership_palestine] [cite:israelfactcheck_ottoman_land_laws]. How that law worked, how the Ottoman restrictions on Jewish purchase were met and circumvented, and how the purchasing institutions were built before 1914 are told in [scene:s04j|the land purchase mechanism].

The largest single seller was a family, not a government. The Sursocks of Beirut, a wealthy Greek Orthodox Christian family, had acquired great tracts of the Jezreel Valley under Ottoman rule; the Ottoman government itself sold them Marj ibn Amir in 1872. Between 1901 and 1925, and mainly in the 1920s, the family sold roughly 60,000 to 75,000 dunams to Zionist purchasing organizations, for a fraction of the land's later value [cite:wiki_sursock_purchases] [cite:sursockhouse_rothschild_purchases]. The main sales fell between 1920 and 1925. The Sursock purchases alone account for about 22 percent of all the land Jews acquired in Palestine up to 1948, and 58 percent of all the land bought from absentee landlords [cite:wiki_sursock_purchases].

The buyers were three institutions with distinct roles. The Jewish National Fund held purchased land as the inalienable property of the Jewish people. The Palestine Land Development Company did the actual purchasing, led by Yehoshua Hankin, who had worked with the Sursock family since 1891, personally negotiated the Sursock deal and most of the major Jezreel Valley acquisitions, and became head of the company in 1932. The Palestine Jewish Colonization Association, PICA, founded in 1924 by Edmond de Rothschild, became through parallel acquisitions the largest single Jewish landowner in Palestine [cite:wiki_yehoshua_hankin]. By the early Mandate years land sold by absentee owners to Jewish buyers went for roughly six Palestine pounds a dunam. Purchasing agents such as Hankin sometimes bought first, at their own financial risk, and were reimbursed by the Jewish Agency or the Fund afterward [cite:emory_zionist_land_acquisition] [cite:palquest_wzo_funding]. The banks and campaigns that supplied the capital are described in the section on the Mandate economy.

What a purchase cost the people living on the land is documented for one group of sales. In the largest single group of Sursock-related purchases, 1,746 Arab farming families, 8,730 people, were evicted. Under the tenure system they were owed no compensation, but they were paid about $17 a person as a goodwill settlement. Across all the Sursock-linked purchases, an estimated 20 to 25 villages were depopulated [cite:wiki_sursock_purchases] [cite:wiki_yehoshua_hankin]. The sources do not date this group of evictions within the sale period, and the figure of $17 describes that group only, not every transaction. Selling land to Jewish buyers was seen by some Arabs as a serious betrayal. In at least one documented case, negotiations stalled for years because the selling landowners did not want to be seen as responsible for the evacuation [cite:wiki_sursock_purchases] [cite:wiki_yehoshua_hankin].

The Jewish National Fund turned each purchase into a permanent holding. Its land was leased long-term rather than sold, so that no later transaction could reverse an acquisition; its founding resolution called the land "the eternal possession of the Jewish people" [cite:jnf_wiki]. The Fund's own history, from its founding in 1901, is told in [scene:s04d|the Jewish National Fund]. Its holdings in these years show the scale. It held 22,363 dunams in 1920. By 1935 it held about 89,500 acres, some 362 square kilometres, across 108 communities [cite:jnf_wiki] [cite:wiki_isaac_leib_goldberg].

The chart of the Fund's holdings shows how the 1920s and early 1930s changed its course. From a first gift of 200 dunams in 1903, it took seventeen years to reach 22,363 dunams in 1920. In the fifteen years that followed it grew to about 362,000 dunams by 1935, more than sixteen times the 1920 figure, and the curve kept rising, to 516,000 dunams in 1940 and about 936,000 by 1947–48 [cite:jnf_wiki] [cite:wiki_isaac_leib_goldberg]. Because Fund land was never resold, the line could only climb. The 1935 point is the 89,500 acres of the sources expressed in dunams, and should be read as an approximation.

The Mandate's role was that of regulator, not seller, and as regulator it failed. Between 1920 and 1940 Britain enacted five separate laws meant to protect tenant cultivators from eviction after a sale. A documented analysis of the period concludes that they "failed to provide the protection that Palestinian Arabs demanded, often due to loopholes, which allowed individuals and agencies to circumvent the legislation" [cite:israeled_jnf_cultivators_ordinance] [cite:badil_land_ownership_palestine]. The Shaw Commission said the same in 1930 about the laws then in force: the Land Transfer Ordinances of 1920 and 1921 had failed, the Protection of Cultivators Ordinance of 1929 did not stop evictions, and the evictions were creating a landless class, "a potential danger to the country" [cite:rs_rd3_shaw_palquest_e]. Later in the decade British policy moved the other way: in 1938 the Mandate authorities allowed Zionist officials to copy land-registration and tax records of Arab ownership in order to facilitate further purchases [cite:israeled_jnf_cultivators_ordinance] [cite:badil_land_ownership_palestine]. Britain's record on land was inconsistent rather than a single policy, and its restrictions on immigration in 1939 cut in the opposite direction.

The case that tested the system came at the end of the 1920s. In 1929 the Jewish National Fund bought 30,800 dunams at Wadi al-Hawarith at auction from absentee landlords; the historian Weldon Matthews counts it as the third-largest single acquisition the Fund made in the whole Mandate period. The Bedouin Palestinian tenants who lived there refused to leave, and the Fund began legal proceedings to evict them. Awni Abd al-Hadi, a leading Palestinian national figure, represented the residents through a court battle that lasted several years. The final eviction order was issued on 15 June 1933. The response was organized and crossed party lines: the Istiqlal Party, the Palestine Communist Party and the Congress of Youth called strikes and issued public declarations of protest [cite:wiki_wadi_al_hawarith]. The case was decided in the Mandate's own courts, under its own law. It shows that resistance reached formal legal representation and cross-party protest when the stakes were high enough. It does not show that every sale met such opposition; many went through with less.

The fullest measurement of all this came from Sir John Hope Simpson. His report, Palestine: Report on Immigration, Land Settlement and Development (Cmd. 3686), carries a covering letter dated 22 August 1930 and was published in October 1930 [cite:rs_rd3_hope_simpson_unispal]. It is the most detailed British land study of the Mandate period [cite:w_hopesimpson]. He adopted the Director of Surveys' estimate of 8,044,000 metric dunams of cultivable land, including 1,500,000 in the Beersheba region, and found that only 40 percent of the hill country was cultivable, not the 66.6 percent that had been assumed. He put Jewish-held land in June 1930 at about 1,250,000 Turkish dunams. Deducting about 900,000 metric dunams of Jewish holdings, he left 5,644,000 metric dunams for non-Jewish cultivators [cite:rs_rd3_hope_simpson_unispal]. The two Jewish figures are in different units, Turkish and metric dunams, and the report as summarized here does not reconcile them further.

His village figures carried the human finding. In 104 surveyed villages, 6,940 of 23,573 families, 29.4 percent, held no land at all. His own enquiry into 688 Arab families displaced by land sales found that only 379 were cultivating land again; the other 309 had joined the landless. He estimated the land available for new settlement at "100,000 dunams at the outside" [cite:rs_rd3_hope_simpson_unispal]. Without development, he concluded, there was no margin for further Jewish agricultural settlement [cite:w_hopesimpson].

Hope Simpson also examined labor, and here he quoted the movement's own documents. The Jewish National Fund's draft lease required the lessee to cultivate "only with Jewish labour", on penalty of ten Palestinian pounds for each breach and repossession of the land after three breaches. The Jewish Agency's constitution of 1920 committed it to colonization "based on Jewish labour". And fewer than one in three of the immigrants who had arrived since 1921 had settled on the land [cite:rs_rd3_hope_simpson_unispal]. Read against the purchase chain, the clause meant that, on the draft lease's terms, a tenant evicted from land the Fund bought could not be hired back to work it. Shaw had added two further findings: the allocation of labor-schedule immigration certificates by political creed was indefensible, and Jewish immigration within the country's absorptive capacity had brought material benefits [cite:rs_rd3_shaw_palquest_e]. The labor movement's own doctrine of "Hebrew labour" is described in the section on the Histadrut.

The Jewish Agency contested Hope Simpson's numbers. In 1931 it published a memorandum, The Statistical Bases of Sir John Hope Simpson's Report, to challenge the report's figures [cite:rs_rd3_cojs_ja_1931]. The two positions stand side by side. Hope Simpson held that without development there was no margin for settlement, that at most 100,000 dunams were available, and that a landless class was forming [cite:rs_rd3_hope_simpson_unispal]. The Agency held that his statistical foundation was unsound [cite:rs_rd3_cojs_ja_1931]. The research for this book has not verified the memorandum's specific arguments, so they are not summarized here. On the Agency's side, the strongest evidence in the record used here comes from a British inquiry: Shaw's finding that Jewish immigration within the country's absorptive capacity had brought material benefits. What London did with these findings is told in [scene:pf_s01|the Passfield White Paper and its reversal].

Much remains unmeasured. The total number of Arab families displaced by land sales in these years is not established; Hope Simpson's 688 families were those his own enquiry traced, and the 1,746 Sursock-linked families are one group of sales. Whether there was room for more settlement in 1930 is a question on which Hope Simpson and the Jewish Agency disagreed, and the Agency's arguments have not been examined here. The full Jewish holding in 1930 is given in two units that the summarized report does not reconcile.

sections.h: The Armed Line: The Haganah, the Irgun and the Jaffa Barrels, 1920–1935
sections.html:
Alongside land and labor, the Yishuv was building a force of its own. A familiar picture of the Mandate years shows one Jewish defense force, the Haganah, acting under a single political direction until it became the army of the new state in 1948. The record for these years shows something less tidy. By the end of 1931 there were already two Jewish armed organizations in Palestine, the Haganah and the Irgun, and by 1940 there would be three. They were divided by documented disputes over strategy and politics, they went through periods of open hostility toward one another, and even at the declaration of statehood they had reached only a partial, negotiated coordination.

The starting point was modest. When the Histadrut, the Jewish labor federation, was founded in December 1920, it took responsibility for defense, and the Haganah was placed under its direct control. Through the 1920s the Haganah had only "a few hundred" volunteer members [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah]. It was a volunteer body of the labor movement, not an army. In 1924 its senior commanders drew up a "Constitution of the Haganah," a first attempt to give the organization written rules. Nor was the labor camp a single body. In 1926 former members of Ha-Shomer formed a separate underground of their own inside the Gedud ha-Avodah [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah]. Even before the Revisionist split that is the usual subject of this story, the Yishuv's armed structure was divided.

The violence of August 1929 changed the Haganah's position. In that month its volunteers helped defend the Jewish communities of Jerusalem, Tel Aviv and Haifa. The massacres of that August happened where the Haganah was absent or weak: in Hebron, in Safed and at Motza [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah]. The lesson the movement drew was organizational. The Encyclopaedia Judaica's account describes the result as a shift toward wider organization and toward public control of the force [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah].

That shift took formal shape in 1931. A national command of six members was set up, with parity between the labor movement and everyone else: three members came from the Histadrut, Eliyahu Golomb, Dov Hos and Meir Rutberg, and three were non-labor members [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah]. The mechanism matters. A defense force that had answered to one party's federation now answered to a body in which labor held half the seats and the non-labor parties held the other half. The commander who opposed public control was removed [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah].

Not everyone accepted the arrangement. A group led by Avraham Tehomi, who had been the Haganah's Jerusalem district commander from 1929 to 1931, seceded. Together with Revisionist groups it formed the Irgun Zvai Leumi, also known as Etzel [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah] [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_tehomi]. Tehomi is the same man whose 1985 account of the 1924 killing of Jacob de Haan is weighed in [scene:dh_s01|the de Haan section]. He did not stay with the organization he founded: he returned to the Haganah in 1937 [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah] [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_tehomi].

The Irgun's founders were officers aligned with Ze'ev Jabotinsky's Revisionist movement, and the point of principle on which they broke was havlagah, the Haganah's policy of restraint in the face of Arab attacks, which they rejected [cite:wiki_irgun]. Through the 1930s and 1940s the Irgun conducted an armed campaign against British rule and against Arab civilian targets. From 1943 it was commanded by Menachem Begin, who later became Israel's sixth Prime Minister [cite:wiki_irgun]. That is a direct, documented personal line from the command of this organization to the country's highest office. The source establishes the founding rationale and the line of command; it does not, on its own, give a full operational history of the Irgun, and this section does not attempt one.

The two positions can be stated in their own terms, as far as the sources record them. The Haganah's leadership held to restraint and, after 1931, to a command shared equally between labor and non-labor members, removing the commander who opposed that public control. The Irgun's founders rejected restraint in the face of Arab attacks and left the Haganah. One reading, which the sources suggest but do not state, is that both answers came out of the same experience of 1929, which had shown how few defenders there were and what happened where there were none.

Between 1931 and 1935 the Haganah built itself into something more permanent. It had urban branches in Jerusalem, Tel Aviv and Haifa, each with memberships "in the hundreds," it ran annual officers' courses, and it had workshops producing hand grenades [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah]. It was still small. It was also now an organization that trained its own officers and made some of its own weapons.

The clearest single episode of these years came at the port of Jaffa in 1935. Rifles and ammunition had been shipped from Belgium hidden in barrels of cement. British authorities seized 537 barrels at Jaffa, and the discovery caused significant unrest among Palestinian Arabs [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah] [cite:rs_rd3_wiki_cement]. One account, drawing on the Palestine Post and the Peel report among other sources, gives the contents as 25 Lewis machine guns, 800 rifles and 400,000 rounds, found in 359 of the drums, and says they were consigned to a merchant in Tel Aviv who was never identified. The same account dates a protest general strike to 26 October 1935 [cite:rs_rd3_wiki_cement]. Those details rest on that one account and are given here as its report.

The sources do not agree on when the shipment was found. The account just cited, relying on Palestine Post reports and the Peel report, dates the discovery to 16 October 1935 [cite:rs_rd3_wiki_cement]. The Encyclopaedia Judaica's entry on the Haganah dates it to 18 November 1935 [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah]. This book has not resolved the difference. The earlier date sits before the reported strike of 26 October; the later one would fall after it. Neither source, as gathered here, names who in the Yishuv ordered the shipment.

One claim about these years does not hold up as stated. A compiled account of Zionist intelligence before 1948, drawn on elsewhere in this library, says that the first Jewish intelligence organization in Palestine was established under the Haganah in 1929. The same account also dates the founding of the Shai, the Sherut Yediot or Information Service, the Haganah's intelligence and counter-espionage arm, to 1940 [cite:shai_wiki]. The two statements may describe different bodies, an informal service in 1929 and a formal one in 1940, but the account does not say so, and this book has not been able to confirm a founding date for any Haganah intelligence body in 1929. The claim is reported here as unconfirmed. The Shai's wartime and American story belongs to a later period and is not told here.

Where the line led is told in later chapters, but its shape follows from what was built in these years. In 1940 the Irgun split in turn. Avraham Stern led a faction out to form Lehi, Lohamei Herut Israel, "Fighters for the Freedom of Israel," often called the Stern Gang, rejecting the Irgun's decision to suspend operations against the British during the Second World War [cite:wiki_lehi_stern_gang]. Stern's group is documented as having explored contact with Fascist Italy and, most controversially, Nazi Germany, in search of any power willing to oppose British rule in Palestine. The episode was widely condemned at the time, including within the broader Zionist movement. The record shows exploratory contact, not a completed cooperation or alliance [cite:wiki_lehi_stern_gang]. That story is told in [scene:lh_s01|Lehi].

In 1944 and 1945, in what became known as the "Hunting Season," the Haganah, under Jewish Agency direction, moved against members of the Irgun and Lehi through surveillance, exposure to the British authorities and detentions, in an attempt to suppress their independent operations and keep political control unified [cite:wiki_hunting_season]. The source documents the pattern rather than every operation. And at independence, when the Haganah became the core of the Israel Defense Forces and the Irgun and Lehi were formally absorbed, the merger was contested. In June 1948 the Altalena affair, an armed confrontation between the new army and Irgun forces over a weapons shipment, left sixteen Irgun members and three soldiers dead; the ship was shelled and burned off Tel Aviv on Ben-Gurion's direct order. Begin's refusal to let the clash become a civil war, in his words "there will be no civil war with the enemy at our gates," is documented as decisive in preventing a wider fight [cite:wiki_altalena_affair]. Most of the roughly 940 passengers aboard were inducted into the army without incident, so the flashpoint was not the whole of the integration [cite:wiki_altalena_affair]. According to a 2026 report in the Jerusalem Post, the wreck was found intact on the Mediterranean seafloor that year, 78 years later [cite:jpost_altalena_wreck_2026]. That ending is told in [scene:mil_s01|1948].

The reason to tell this line in a chapter about building institutions is a matter of consistency. This library gives full weight to the internal divisions on the political side: the Bund, Reform Judaism's early ambivalence, Neturei Karta. A history that tracked those divisions carefully but treated the armed side as a single force would be holding the two to different standards [cite:jvl_altalena_affair]. The record of 1920 to 1935 shows the armed side divided almost from the start: between the labor federation and the old Ha-Shomer men in 1926, between labor and non-labor in the command of 1931, and between restraint and its rejection in the secession of the same year.

Some things the record gathered here does not settle. It gives no membership figures for the Irgun in its first years and no count of the Haganah beyond "a few hundred" and "in the hundreds." It does not name the three non-labor members of the 1931 command or the commander who was removed. It does not establish who arranged the Belgian shipment, or the date it was found. And it does not support the claim of a Haganah intelligence service founded in 1929.

sections.h: The American Palestine Committee, 1932
sections.html:
In 1932, while the Zionist movement in Palestine was building its labor federation, its banks and its defense force, one of its executives in the United States began building something of a different kind: a committee of prominent Americans who were mostly not Jewish. Emanuel Neumann, a member of the Zionist Executive, founded the American Palestine Committee that year to organize prominent, mainly non-Jewish Americans in support of a Jewish homeland [cite:aja_neumann_bio]. The committee's existence and its founder are documented in the records of the American Jewish Archives [cite:aja_neumann_bio].

The committee matters for what it shows about method. A common account of the 1940s holds that the wave of Christian and elite American support for a Jewish state arose on its own. The record shows that the most visible bodies expressing that support were founded and later revived by one Zionist official, working from inside the movement's political office. The support was real; so was the organization behind it. The two facts are not in tension, and this section keeps both.

The sources gathered here say little about the committee's first decade. They record its founding in 1932 and its purpose, and they do not record its membership, its activities or its funding in the 1930s. What they do record is what happened when Neumann returned to it. In January 1941 he joined the Emergency Committee for Zionist Affairs as head of public relations and political action, and from that post he revived the American Palestine Committee, with Senator Robert Wagner as its chairman [cite:aja_neumann_bio]. The mechanism is plain in the titles. The person charged with the Zionist emergency body's public relations and political action was the same person who rebuilt the committee through which prominent non-Jewish Americans would speak.

In December 1942 Neumann organized a second, parallel body for clergy, the Christian Council on Palestine [cite:aja_neumann_bio]. Its founding minutes describe it as an "autonomous committee working in cooperation with the American Palestine Committee" [cite:aja_ccp_minutes_1942]. By the end of the war the American Palestine Committee claimed some 6,500 members, among them senators, congressmen, cabinet members and governors, and by one description mayors; the Christian Council claimed about 3,000 clergy [cite:wiki_american_palestine_committee] [cite:counterpunch_origins_lobby]. These are the committees' own membership claims, not independent counts. In 1946 the two merged into the American Christian Palestine Committee, which disbanded after 1948 [cite:wiki_american_palestine_committee]. How these committees fitted into the wider American campaign of the 1940s is told in [scene:s07f|the American Zionist Emergency Council].

The dispute is over a single word. The Christian Council's founding minutes call it "autonomous" [cite:aja_ccp_minutes_1942]. The historian Peter Grose described the committees' operations as "hardly autonomous" [cite:counterpunch_origins_lobby]. Reporting that draws on Grose's work states that Zionist funds, reaching up to $150,000 by 1946, sustained them [cite:counterpunch_origins_lobby]. That figure is reported, not drawn from a primary financial record, and it should be read that way: this book has not seen the accounts it describes.

The strongest case for "autonomous" is that the committees' members were real people who lent their own names. Nothing in the record gathered here suggests that any of them signed on against their convictions. The strongest case for "hardly autonomous" is structural: both committees were founded by the same Zionist official, the larger one was revived from the Emergency Committee's political office, and, according to reporting on Grose's work, the money that kept them running came from Zionist funds. A body can be sincere in its membership and organized from outside in its operations. The distinction this book draws is between real names lent and organized direction, and the record shows both.

The same arrangement, organized support presented as independent, appears again in later decades, and this library documents it for the predecessors of AIPAC in its own place. The scale should be kept in proportion. The reported $150,000 appears as a bar, labelled $0.15 million, on the chart of documented dollar flows embedded in [scene:hv_s01|the Transfer Agreement section], where it sits beside sums up to several hundred times larger. One reading is that its significance lay not in its size but in what it bought: a public voice that appeared to come from outside the movement.

Several questions remain open on the evidence gathered here. The record does not say what the committee did between 1932 and 1941, whether it was active or dormant, or who paid for it in those years. It does not give a year-by-year account of the reported $150,000 or name its paying body. And it does not show how much direction Neumann's office gave the committees day to day, which is the real substance of Grose's phrase.

sections.h: The Jews of the Arab World, 1929–1936: Baghdad and Constantine
sections.html:
While American Zionists organized at a distance, Jewish communities elsewhere in the Arab world were living through crises of their own. Two places show how differently the early 1930s could run for Jewish communities outside Palestine, and how much turned on the decisions of states and of named individuals. In Iraq, a Jewish community that had taken part in building the new state's institutions found itself, after independence, under a series of restrictions. In French Algeria, Jews of one city were killed in a riot whose causes a recent historian argues lay partly in the politics of the colonial state. Neither case is evidence about Arabs or Muslims as a whole, and neither should be read that way. Each has its own dates, its own actors and its own documentation, and the documentation for the two is not of equal strength.

Iraq first. Under the British Mandate there, according to Sephardi Voices UK, Jews held government posts, Hebrew could be taught, and several Zionist organizations were permitted to operate until 1929 [cite:rs_rd3_sephardivoices_iraq]. Iraq became independent in 1932. In the years that followed, the same source reports, prominent Jews helped build the Iraqi civil service, and several sat in the first independent parliament [cite:rs_rd3_sephardivoices_iraq]. The Mandate-era history of Iraq, and how its independence came about, is told in [scene:irq_e02|Iraq under the Mandate].

From 1934 the picture changed. According to Sephardi Voices UK, Iraqi Jews from that year had to pay a deposit of £50 to travel abroad. In 1935 the teaching of Hebrew was barred, and state secondary schools set quotas on the number of Jewish pupils. In 1936 Jews were dismissed from the civil service [cite:rs_rd3_sephardivoices_iraq]. These measures, if accurately reported, amounted to discrimination by the state against its Jewish citizens in movement, education and employment, within four years of a period in which Jews had helped staff that same state. They rest, however, on a single source, and this book has not found a second, independent account of them. The 1936 dismissals in particular are stated in that source in sweeping terms, and the source does not say how many people were affected or whether every Jewish official was removed. They are given here as that source reports them.

The same source records an episode from 1933 that connects Iraq to the events in Germany described in [scene:hol_s01|Weimar's collapse]. During the first premiership of Rashid Ali al-Gaylani, in 1933, the German chargé d'affaires, Fritz Grobba, was allowed to publish Mein Kampf in Iraqi newspapers [cite:rs_rd3_sephardivoices_iraq]. That was antisemitic propaganda, placed in the Iraqi press by a German diplomat with the permission of an Iraqi government. It is again attested here by one source. What these years led to in Baghdad, the Farhud of 1941, belongs to a later chapter.

Algeria second. In Constantine, in French Algeria, in August 1934, over a few days of violence, 25 Jews and 3 Muslims were killed [cite:rs_rd3_cole_constantine]. Those figures come from the historian Joshua Cole, whose book Lethal Provocation: The Constantine Murders and the Politics of French Algeria (Cornell University Press, 2019) is the study used here.

Cole's argument is about the state, not about the crowd alone. He argues that the French colonial state had an interest in "provoking and nurturing" tension between Jews and Muslims, because that tension helped it resist demands to extend citizenship rights to Algerian Muslims [cite:rs_rd3_cole_constantine]. Cole also identifies Mohamed El Maadi, a veteran with ties to the extreme right, as a key participant in the violence [cite:rs_rd3_cole_constantine]. His account therefore names both a structure, the colonial state's interest, and a specific person with extreme-right ties, rather than attributing the killings to Muslims in general.

That is a historian's argument and should be weighed as one. The source gathered here presents Cole's case through an interview about his book, and it does not set out a rival interpretation; this book has not gathered one. What can be said is that Cole's reading rests on the colonial context of citizenship and on a named participant, and that the killings themselves, 25 Jews and 3 Muslims, are not in question in the sources used here.

Set side by side, the two cases make one point plainly. Antisemitism in these years reached Jewish communities in the Arab world through more than one channel: in Iraq, through state measures and through Nazi propaganda placed by a German diplomat; in Algeria, according to Cole, through violence that a European colonial state had reasons to tolerate or encourage, with a veteran tied to the extreme right among its key participants. Neither source used here ties these events to Palestine.

The gaps are considerable. The Iraqi measures of 1934 to 1936 rest on a single source, and their scale is not recorded: how many travellers paid the deposit, how many pupils the quotas excluded, how many officials lost their posts. The record gathered here says nothing about the Jews of Syria, Lebanon, Egypt, Yemen or Morocco in these years. For Constantine it gives the toll and Cole's argument, but not the course of the riot day by day, or what the French authorities did afterwards.

sections.h: The Transfer Agreement, 1933–1939
sections.html:
In Baghdad a German diplomat placed Nazi propaganda in the press. With the Zionist movement the same regime made a commercial deal. On 25 August 1933 Zionist bodies signed an agreement with the government of Nazi Germany. It let German Jews who were emigrating to Palestine take part of their assets with them, not as money but as German goods. Over the following six years it helped roughly 60,000 people reach Palestine. It also undercut the worldwide boycott of Nazi Germany that had begun in 1933, and it divided the Jewish world more sharply than any other financial arrangement of the pre-state period. It was called the Haavara, Hebrew for "transfer."

A common assumption holds that the Zionist movement and Nazi Germany were simply adversaries from 1933 onward. The documents show something harder to summarize. The two were adversaries, and they also made a commercial agreement, each for its own reasons. Two popular versions of the story each keep only half of that record. One calls Haavara a straightforward rescue; the other calls it collaboration. The documents support both halves at once: a mechanism that moved some 60,000 people out of Nazi reach, and a commercial accommodation that the Nazi state wanted for reasons of its own, chosen by the Zionist movement's own Congress over the objections of some of its own leaders [cite:jvl_haavara].

The agreement had three parties: the Zionist Federation of Germany; the Anglo-Palestine Bank, acting for the Jewish Agency; and the Reich Economics Ministry [cite:wiki_haavara_agreement] [cite:jvl_haavara]. Its mechanism was straightforward in outline. An emigrating German Jew deposited assets in an account in Germany. Those funds were used to buy German export goods, which were shipped to Palestine. When the goods were sold there, the emigrant was repaid in Palestine from the proceeds [cite:wiki_haavara_agreement] [cite:jvl_haavara].

The design explains why each party signed. For the emigrant, it was a way to move part of a lifetime's assets out of Germany. For the Zionist bodies, it brought immigrants and goods to Palestine. For the Nazi state, according to the record, it served two aims. The regime wanted Germany Judenrein, emptied of Jews, and it wanted to break the anti-Nazi boycott of 1933, which had mass Jewish support and which German officials regarded as an economic threat [cite:wiki_haavara_agreement]. Haavara did both. Jews left, and German goods found a market abroad at the very moment a boycott was trying to close markets to them. The rise of that regime and the destruction of the Weimar Republic are told in [scene:hol_s01|Weimar's collapse].

The scale was large for its time. The agreement was a major factor in the emigration of approximately 60,000 German Jews to Palestine between 1933 and 1939 [cite:wiki_haavara_agreement]. By the end of 1937, goods worth 77.8 million Reichsmarks had moved; by the outbreak of war, about 105 million [cite:wiki_haavara_agreement] [cite:jvl_haavara]. The Jewish Virtual Library records the total transfer as £8.1 million in Palestine pounds, roughly $40.4 million at the time, and states that this included £2.6 million provided by the Reichsbank [cite:jvl_haavara]. The war ended the program. How these German arrivals fit into the immigration of the 1930s as a whole, including the peak year of 1935, is set out in [scene:rd3_aliyot|the immigration section].

The Center for Israel Education ties the German trip that Chaim Arlosoroff, head of the Jewish Agency's political department, made shortly before his murder in June 1933 to the Haavara agreement [cite:rs_rd3_cie_arlosoroff]; that claim is weighed in [scene:rd3_arlosoroff|the Arlosoroff section].

A chart of US-dollar flows in the record from 1921 to 1949 shows Haavara at about $40 million for 1933–39, one of the largest bars on it, converted from the 105 million Reichsmarks. The chart's own note warns that its figures are nominal dollars of the year reported, not adjusted for inflation, and that Haavara has been converted at the period estimate [cite:jvl_haavara]. The bars record separate events, in different years and currencies, and should not be added together as one budget [cite:wiki_haavara_agreement]. The smallest bars matter too: the reported $0.15 million that sustained the American Christian committees founded by Emanuel Neumann, discussed in the section on the American Palestine Committee, appears near the foot of the same chart [cite:counterpunch_origins_lobby].

The opposition was real and came from inside the movement as well as outside it. The Revisionist leader Ze'ev Jabotinsky, Rabbi Stephen Wise of the American Jewish Congress, and Abba Hillel Silver all opposed the agreement, on the ground that it sabotaged the boycott [cite:wiki_haavara_agreement] [cite:jvl_haavara]. Their case at its strongest was that the boycott had mass Jewish support and was regarded by German officials themselves as an economic threat, so that a Zionist agreement moving German goods abroad weakened pressure the regime actually felt. The defenders' case at its strongest was the one the numbers make: people were leaving Germany, they could take something with them only by this route, and tens of thousands reached Palestine through it.

The question went to the movement's highest body. The Nineteenth Zionist Congress, meeting at Lucerne in August 1935, voted by a large majority to continue the agreement and placed Haavara under the supervision of the Jewish Agency [cite:wiki_haavara_agreement] [cite:jvl_haavara]. The opponents failed to persuade it. The decision was taken knowingly, two years into the agreement's operation and a month before Germany enacted the Nuremberg Laws. The historian Edwin Black wrote that the agreement "tore the Jewish world apart" [cite:wiki_haavara_agreement]. Haavara also served as the model for a smaller arrangement with Czechoslovakia on the eve of the war [cite:jvl_haavara].

The Haavara transfer appears as one stream among many on the map of how the pre-state build was financed, between the American donors of the 1920s and the fundraising and arms purchases of 1948.

What the record gathered here does not settle is considerable. It does not say how much of each emigrant's assets were lost in the transfer, or on what terms the goods were priced, so the cost to the emigrants themselves cannot be stated. It does not measure how much damage Haavara did to the boycott, only that it undercut it. And it cannot answer the counterfactual on which the moral argument turns: how many of the 60,000 would have reached safety without it.

sections.h: A Murder on the Beach and a Peace That Failed, 1933–1935
sections.html:
The Haavara agreement was signed inside a movement already at war with itself. On the night of 16 June 1933, Chaim Arlosoroff was walking on the beach at Tel Aviv with his wife, Sima, when he was shot. He died early the next morning, 17 June [cite:rs_rd3_cie_arlosoroff] [cite:rs_rd3_jabotinsky_inst]. Arlosoroff was the head of the Jewish Agency's political department. His killing opened two years of open conflict between that leadership and the Revisionist movement led by Ze'ev Jabotinsky, a conflict that ran through a murder trial, a Zionist Congress, an attempt at reconciliation and a vote of the labor federation's members, and ended with the Revisionists leaving the Zionist Organization altogether.

Arlosoroff had come back from Germany about two days before he was shot. The Center for Israel Education links that trip to the Haavara transfer agreement with Nazi Germany, which was formally signed on 25 August 1933, some ten weeks after his death [cite:rs_rd3_cie_arlosoroff]. That link is reported by one source and is given here as its account; the agreement itself is examined in [scene:hv_s01|the Transfer Agreement section].

Three Revisionists were charged. Abba Ahimeir was accused of plotting the killing, and Avraham Stavsky and Zvi Rosenblatt of carrying it out as the gunmen. Sima Arlosoroff identified Stavsky and Rosenblatt [cite:rs_rd3_cie_arlosoroff]. The case did not hold. Only Stavsky was convicted, and in 1934 he was cleared on appeal for lack of corroborating evidence. No one else was ever charged with the murder [cite:rs_rd3_cie_arlosoroff] [cite:rs_rd3_jabotinsky_inst].

The trial was fought in politics as much as in court. Jabotinsky, who believed the accused innocent, campaigned on their behalf for more than a year [cite:rs_rd3_jabotinsky_inst]. The labor movement's leaders accused Revisionist extremists of the killing. At the Eighteenth Zionist Congress, which met in Prague from 21 August to 3 September 1933, the Revisionists were accused of the murder in the movement's own parliament [cite:rs_rd3_jabotinsky_inst]. The Revisionists, for their part, charged that the accusation against them was a "blood libel" [cite:rs_rd3_jta_1985_panel].

The two camps' accounts can be set side by side, as far as the sources record them. Labour's account was that Revisionist extremists, the three accused, had killed Arlosoroff, and it could point to his widow's identification of two of the men. The Revisionists' account was that the accused were innocent and that the accusation was a defamation of their movement; the acquittal on appeal, for want of corroborating evidence, supported them. The sources gathered here record the accusation, the identification, the acquittal and Jabotinsky's campaign. They do not record the speeches or articles on either side.

Half a century later the state took the question up again. In March 1982 the government of Menachem Begin appointed a three-member commission chaired by David Bechor, a former Supreme Court justice. It reported in June 1985. It cleared Ahimeir, Stavsky and Rosenblatt. It could not determine who had killed Arlosoroff, or whether the killing was a political act at all. And it cleared the labor movement of the Revisionist charge that the accusation had been a "blood libel" [cite:rs_rd3_jta_1985_panel]. Each side was thus partly vindicated: the Revisionists in the innocence of the accused, labor in being cleared of the charge of a "blood libel." The murder itself remains unsolved.

The conflict did not wait for the courts. In 1934 Ben-Gurion and Jabotinsky, the leaders of the two camps, signed three agreements in London [cite:rs_rd3_ej_revisionists_j] [cite:rs_rd3_jabotinsky_inst]. One of them was a labor agreement. The sources gathered here do not give the exact dates on which the agreements were signed or set out their full terms. The labor agreement was put to the members of the Histadrut, the labor federation, who rejected it in a referendum [cite:rs_rd3_ej_revisionists_j] [cite:rs_rd3_jabotinsky_inst].

The referendum was held on 25 March 1935. The Jewish Telegraphic Agency's report the next day gave early returns: about 12,000 votes against the agreement and about 9,000 for it. In Tel Aviv the count was 3,983 against and 3,296 for; in Haifa, 3,785 against and 1,555 for [cite:rs_rd3_jta_1935_referendum]. The newspaper Haaretz called the result "a grave mishap for the entire Zionist movement" [cite:rs_rd3_jta_1935_referendum]. The final totals were not in that report, and this book has not found them; the figures above are partial tallies only. Even so, they show a difference between the two cities. In Tel Aviv the vote was close; in Haifa it was more than two to one against.

With the agreement dead, the break followed. Later in 1935 the Zionist General Council adopted a "discipline clause" barring independent political action, the Revisionists voted to secede, and in September 1935 Jabotinsky's New Zionist Organization held its constituent assembly in Vienna [cite:rs_rd3_ej_revisionists]. That story, and the growth of the Revisionist movement that preceded it, is told in [scene:s07a3|the Revisionist line].

The episode mattered beyond the fate of one man. On the reading offered here, the murder, and the accusation that followed it, hardened a division between the labor leadership and the Revisionists that the London agreements tried and failed to close. The secession that followed left the Zionist movement, by the end of 1935, with two rival organizations and two rival armed lines.

The record leaves the central question open. No court and no commission has established who killed Arlosoroff or why. The Bechor commission, half a century later, could not say whether the killing was political. The link between his German trip and Haavara rests on one source. The exact dates and full terms of the London agreements, and the final count of the 1935 referendum, are not in the sources gathered here.

sections.h: The Nuremberg Laws, 1935: Persecution Written into Statute
sections.html:
A month after the Lucerne Congress upheld Haavara, the regime it had dealt with turned its persecution into statute. On 15 September 1935 the Reichstag met in special session at Nuremberg, where the Nazi Party was holding its annual rally. It passed two laws, and it passed them unanimously [cite:ushmm_nuremberg_laws]. The parliament that voted had already surrendered its own authority two and a half years earlier, when the Enabling Act of March 1933 allowed Hitler to make law without the approval of the Reichstag or the President, a measure carried after Communist deputies had been forcibly kept from voting [cite:history_weimar_republic]. The two statutes it approved that day did not burn a synagogue or open a camp. They did something that came first and made the rest administrable: they wrote antisemitism into the law of the German state, defining Jews as a separate category of person by descent and removing them from the body of citizens.

A familiar way of telling this history begins with violence: the mob, the broken windows, the deportations, with laws following later to tidy up what force had already done. The order in the documents runs the other way. By the autumn of 1935 Germany had a complete legal framework that defined who was a Jew, stripped Jews of citizenship and made marriage between Jews and other Germans a crime. That framework stood three years before the mass violence of Kristallnacht, told in [scene:hol_s03|the next stage]. Exclusion was legislated first and then enforced through escalating violence. Law came before the pogrom, not after it.

The first of the two statutes, the Reich Citizenship Law, turned on a single definition. A citizen of the Reich was a person "of German or related blood" who proved through conduct a willingness to serve the German people and Reich [cite:ushmm_nuremberg_laws] [cite:yadvashem_nuremberg_blood_law]. German Jews were reduced from citizens to "subjects" of the state, without full political rights [cite:ushmm_nuremberg_laws]. One sentence of law, defining citizenship by blood rather than by birthplace, residence or belief, removed an entire population from political membership in the state. No shot was fired to do it.

The second statute, the Law for the Protection of German Blood and Honor, passed the same day, reached into private life. It banned marriage between Jews and "subjects of the state of German or related blood," and it declared such marriages void even when they had been concluded abroad for the specific purpose of evading the law. It made "extramarital intercourse" between Jews and non-Jewish Germans a crime. It barred Jews from employing non-Jewish German women under the age of 45 in their households. Violations were punishable by imprisonment [cite:yadvashem_nuremberg_blood_law]. The regime had its own name for the new offense: Rassenschande, "race defilement" [cite:wiki_rassenschande]. The word carried the ideology of the statute in a single term. It presented ordinary love, marriage and domestic employment between Jews and other Germans as a contamination that the state was entitled to punish.

Both laws depended on knowing who was a Jew, and here the regime made its most consequential choice. It did not define a Jew by religion. Under the Nuremberg Race Laws a person with three or four Jewish grandparents was a Jew, whatever that person believed or practised [cite:ushmm_nuremberg_race_laws]. Germans who had not practised Judaism in decades fell within the definition. So did people who had formally converted to Christianity. Belief, conversion and long non-observance offered no exit, because the test was not what a person did or believed but who that person's grandparents had been. The definition was racial in the plainest sense, and it is the clearest evidence that the target of the laws was not a faith but a people the state had decided to classify by blood.

The bureaucracy then extended the classification downward. On 14 November 1935 the First Supplementary Decree to the Reich Citizenship Law created the category of Mischling, "mixed blood," for people with one or two Jewish grandparents, and attached its own separate legal restrictions to it [cite:ushmm_nuremberg_race_laws]. The decree distinguished degrees of Jewish ancestry, each carrying its own legal consequences. Charts were produced so that officials, and ordinary citizens, could work out a person's racial status under the law [cite:facinghistory_nuremberg_laws]. A person's legal standing became the answer to a genealogical sum. The arithmetic was the mechanism: once ancestry could be counted, a clerk could place any German in a category, and the category decided whom that person could marry, whom he or she could employ, and whether he or she was a citizen at all.

The structure of power behind this is simple to state. The decision was made inside the Nazi state and ratified unanimously by a parliament that had already given up its law-making authority. The instrument was statute, followed by decree. The people classified had no means of acting against it: they had lost the standing of citizens by the very law that classified them. The burden fell on German Jews, including converts and the non-observant whom the ancestry test caught, and, through the Mischling decree, on people with one or two Jewish grandparents.

What the 1935 laws meant for Palestine can be stated only as far as the sources go, and they do not go far. Jewish immigration to Palestine reached its highest recorded level of the Mandate years in 1935. The figures compiled by the US State Department from British returns give 61,854 Jewish immigrants that year, against 42,359 in 1934 and 29,727 in 1936 [cite:rs_rd3_frus1939_d828]; a second series, printed by the Jewish Virtual Library after Yehoshua Porath, gives 66,472 for 1935 [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_porath_table]. The difference between the two series, and the composition of the 1935 arrivals, are set out in [scene:rd3_aliyot|the immigration section]. The research does not break the year's arrivals down by country of origin or by month, so it cannot show how many German Jews came, or whether any of the rise followed September rather than preceding it. The surge had begun in 1933, two years before Nuremberg, when the same series records 30,327 arrivals [cite:rs_rd3_frus1939_d828]; and the British labor schedule, which governed one channel of entry, was cut from 8,000 places for April–September 1935 to 3,250 for October 1935–March 1936 [cite:rs_rd3_frus1936_d531]. The most that can be said is that the laws were passed in the year of the peak, while the transfer agreement through which German Jews had been moving to Palestine since 1933 remained in force [cite:wiki_haavara_agreement], as told in [scene:hv_s01|the Haavara Agreement]. The sources here do not measure the effect of the laws themselves on emigration.

The text of the two statutes and of the November decree is documented, and it is unambiguous; on what the laws said, the sources present no dispute. What they leave unsettled is the record of enforcement. The documentation here establishes the provisions and the penalties, not a count of prosecutions for Rassenschande, which varied in intensity across regions and years; it establishes that the Mischling system existed and how it worked, not the full detail of the distinctions it drew between its categories. Nor do the sources say how many people the classification touched in 1935. By the end of 1935 a modern state had defined a part of its own population by ancestry, removed it from citizenship and criminalized its private life, all by unanimous statute and orderly decree, years before the violence that the next stage records.

sections.h: Shaykh 'Izz al-Din al-Qassam: From Jabla to Ya'bad, 1882–1935
sections.html:
Two months after Nuremberg, in Palestine, a Haifa preacher took a small band to the hills. On 20 November 1935, in the hills near Ya'bad, close to Jenin, a British police force fought a small armed band for six hours. When it was over the band's leader, a preacher from Haifa in his fifties, was dead [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_qassam]. Shaykh 'Izz al-Din al-Qassam had spent fifteen years in Palestine as a teacher, imam and official of the Muslim religious courts, and the last several of them, by the accounts that survive, organizing in secret for armed struggle. His life in the field lasted eight days. His death drew the largest funeral Haifa had held, and the argument over what to call him has not ended.

He was not born in Palestine. Al-Qassam was born in 1882 in Jabla, on the Syrian coast south of Latakia, and studied at al-Azhar in Cairo [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_qassam]. He joined the revolt of 1919–20 against the French there, and the French sentenced him to death [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_qassam]. He reached Haifa in late 1920, or in December 1920 in another account, taught at the Burj school, and became imam and preacher at the Istiqlal Mosque [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_qassam] [cite:rs_rd3_majalla_qassam]. The preacher who settled in Haifa already carried a death sentence from one European mandatory power for fighting it.

Through the 1920s his career ran through the ordinary institutions of Muslim public life under the Mandate. In July 1928 he was elected president of the Haifa branch of the Young Men's Muslim Association, and in 1930 the Haifa Shari'a court appointed him a ma'dhun, an official post conferred by the religious court [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_qassam]. These were positions of standing, held in the open. They gave him a pulpit and an association of young men.

Alongside that public life, according to the accounts of his movement, he built a clandestine one. Those accounts describe cells of no more than five men, organized into units for preaching, for intelligence and for military training, and guerrilla attacks on Jewish settlements beginning in 1931 that soon paused after leaks reached the British [cite:rs_rd3_globalsecurity_qassam]. This part of the record rests on reporting rather than on documents, and it is thin. The research behind this book holds no verified list of those attacks, no verified count of their victims and no verified account of their dates and places; figures for them that circulate elsewhere rest on a single unconfirmed source and are not used here. What is reported is the structure: a small, compartmented organization that kept religious teaching, intelligence and arms in separate hands, and that chose Jewish settlements as well as the British as targets.

The decision to go to the hills came in the autumn of 1935, and, by one account, the Mufti did not support it. Al-Qassam wrote to Rashid al-Haj Ibrahim of his plan to take to the hills [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_hajibrahim_h]. Al-Haj Ibrahim was one of the eleven founders of the Istiqlal party, which had named British imperialism as the main enemy [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_hajibrahim]. According to Al Majalla, the Mufti of Jerusalem, Hajj Amin al-Husseini, declined to back a revolt, saying the time was not right [cite:rs_rd3_majalla_qassam]. That account is reported, from one outlet; the research does not hold the Mufti's own words. If it is accurate, al-Qassam went to the hills without the backing of the Mufti, whose place among the rival leaderships and parties of these years is described in [scene:rd3_arab_politics|Palestinian politics, 1928–1935].

The autumn was tense. In October or November 1935 (the sources disagree on the date) the British seized 537 barrels at Jaffa port that had been shipped from Belgium with rifles and ammunition hidden in cement, and the discovery caused significant unrest among Palestinian Arabs; one account dates a protest general strike to 26 October 1935 [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah] [cite:rs_rd3_wiki_cement]. That shipment and the armed bodies of the Yishuv belong to [scene:s07e2|the armed line]. The sources used here do not say whether the seizure bore on al-Qassam's decision, and this book does not assume it did.

On 12 November 1935 al-Qassam declared jihad in Haifa and left for the forests of Ya'bad, near Jenin, with about eleven companions [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_qassam]. Eight days later, on 20 November, he was killed in a six-hour fight with a larger British police force near Ya'bad [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_qassam]. The nearest thing to a contemporary official account in the research is an American one. Leland Morris, the US Consul General, reporting to Washington in April 1936, wrote that al-Qassam's bands had caused the death of one British constable, and that four of his men died and five were captured [cite:rs_rd3_frus1936_d512_h].

How large his following was, and how many died with him, are disputed. Al Majalla, drawing on British archives, puts his fighters at between 50 and 200 and calls a claim of 800 "grossly exaggerated"; it says he died with two colleagues [cite:rs_rd3_majalla_qassam]. The Interactive Encyclopedia of the Palestine Question says al-Qassam and four of his men were killed, and the US consul's despatch likewise reports four of his men killed and five captured [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_qassam] [cite:rs_rd3_frus1936_d512_h]. The consul's figure is the only one here written at the time by an outside official; it agrees with the Palestinian encyclopedia and not with Al Majalla on the dead. None of the sources reconciles the counts.

The response to his death showed a reach that his small band had not. Haifa declared a general strike on 21 November 1935 and held the largest funeral procession the city had seen; he was buried at Balad al-Shaykh [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_qassam]. It came at a moment of unusual Palestinian unity. By late 1935 the five Arab parties had formed a united front, which the same American consul described as a response to a "national emergency" [cite:rs_rd3_frus1936_d512]. The established leaders had not followed al-Qassam into the hills; a crowd of Haifa's people followed his coffin.

What to call him is the oldest dispute about him, and both readings rest on documented ground. Palestinian accounts present al-Qassam as a leader of resistance to British occupation whose death helped ignite the revolt of 1936–39 [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_qassam] [cite:rs_rd3_globalsecurity_qassam]. In that reading he was a man who had already fought one European mandatory power in Syria and chose arms against a second; the fight in which he died was a fight with British police. The other reading starts from the targets. His group's attacks were directed at Jewish settlers as well as at the British, and he called for confronting Jewish settlers "as enemies and not as immigrants or guests" [cite:rs_rd3_globalsecurity_qassam]. In that reading, a movement that attacked civilian settlements was not only an anti-colonial insurgency, whatever its leader's death later came to symbolize. The two descriptions are not mutually exclusive. The documented record supports both halves: an armed campaign against the Mandate power, and attacks on Jewish settlements, with civilians among the targets. This book does not choose between the labels; it sets out what each rests on.

His name outlived him. In 1991 Hamas named its military wing the 'Izz al-Din al-Qassam Brigades, according to Al Majalla [cite:rs_rd3_majalla_qassam]. It belongs to a different era from the one in which he lived.

Much about al-Qassam remains unsettled by the sources available here. The size of his organization rests on estimates that run from 50 fighters to a claimed 800. How many died with him on 20 November is given as two or four. The attacks of 1931 onward are reported in outline but not documented case by case, so their number and their victims cannot be stated.
