The Mufti's refusal rests on a single reported account. Within months the country would be in the general strike and revolt told in [scene:s07a5|the Arab Revolt].

sections.h: The Last Offer Before the Revolt: Wauchope's Council, 1935–1936
sections.html:
Five weeks after al-Qassam's death, Britain made the last political offer of the stage. On 23 December 1935 the High Commissioner for Palestine, Sir Arthur Wauchope, called in the leaders of the Jewish community and laid before them a plan for a legislative council. It would have 28 members: 14 Arabs, 7 Jews and 7 Britons. The government, he told them, was "determined to establish the assembly" [cite:rs_rd3_jta_1935_council]. It was not the first such offer: an earlier one, made in 1922, is told in [scene:rd2_council|the council of 1922–1923]. Thirteen years later the question behind it was still open. Who would have a voice in governing Palestine, in what proportion, and over which questions?

The demand for an elected body had come, from the beginning, from the Arab side. From 1919 the Palestine Arab congresses had asked Britain for a national government responsible to a representative assembly chosen by the country's inhabitants [cite:wiki_palestine_arab_congress]. As recently as December 1934 Raghib al-Nashashibi's new National Defense Party had called for parliamentary government [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_nashashibi]. The Zionist Congress, meeting at Lucerne in 1935, had taken the opposite view, resolving against any council that would fix the Jews as a minority [cite:rs_rd3_jta_1935_council]. Wauchope's offer therefore tested both sides at once, and the way each answered it is the best single view of where Palestinian and Zionist politics stood at the end of 1935.

The terms mattered as much as the numbers. As reported at the time, the basis of representation was to be fixed for five years; one of the elected Arab members was to be a Bedouin; the High Commissioner could nominate members to fill the seats of any community that boycotted the elections; and the council could not deal with the labor immigration schedule [cite:rs_rd3_jta_1935_council]. That last exclusion went to the center of the conflict. The schedule, allotted in half-year periods, had just been cut from 8,000 places for April–September 1935 to 3,250 for the half-year that followed [cite:rs_rd3_frus1936_d531]. It was also only one channel of entry: in the peak year of 1935 fewer than one immigrant in four came under it, as the immigration section shows [cite:rs_rd3_frus1936_d531]. A council barred from the labor schedule would have had no hand on the immigration of workers, a question the Arab congresses had raised since 1919, when they rejected mass Jewish immigration [cite:wiki_palestine_arab_congress]; and the High Commissioner's power to fill a boycotting community's seats meant that refusing to take part would not stop the council from sitting.

The Zionist answer was reported the next day. Chaim Weizmann rejected the plan as contrary to the Mandate, citing the resolution of the Zionist Congress at Lucerne that such a council would fix the Jews as a minority. Yitzhak Ben-Zvi, speaking for the Vaad Leumi, concurred, and so did A. L. Maleh for the Sephardi community [cite:rs_rd3_jta_1935_council]. The case behind the rejection is best put in its own terms. The Zionist reading of the Mandate held that Britain's obligation ran not only to the Jews already in Palestine but to the Jewish people as a whole; the British government itself had put it that way in 1931, calling the Mandate "an undertaking to the Jewish people and not only to the Jewish population of Palestine" [cite:rs_rd3_macdonald_unispal]. On that reading, a legislature apportioned by the population of the moment and frozen for five years would hand a permanent majority a veto over the growth that the Mandate was meant to permit, at the very time that growth was fastest. The Jewish Agency's own figures, prepared for its case to the Peel Commission and so to be read as advocacy, put the Jewish population at 84,000, or 13 percent, in 1922 (the census put that year's share at about 11 percent) and 375,000, or 28 percent, in 1935 [cite:rs_rd3_horowitz_1937] [cite:jvl_census_1931]. Seven seats of 28 was a quarter.

Not every Jewish voice gave the same answer. Rabbi Moshe Blau, speaking for Agudath Israel, said only that the time was "not yet ripe" [cite:rs_rd3_jta_1935_council]. Agudath Israel had been founded in 1912 as a movement of Torah-observant Jews that held itself apart from secular Jewish nationalism [cite:unpacked_neturei_karta_history]. Its answer was a postponement, not a rejection on the Zionist ground of minority status.

The Arab answer was slower and less unanimous. Arab leaders withheld their reply and objected to women voting; the Mufti of Jerusalem, Hajj Amin al-Husseini, was reported to be still opposed [cite:rs_rd3_jta_1935_council]. The arithmetic of the offer allows the Arab objection to be reconstructed in outline, though the sources here do not record it in the leaders' own words. By the Jewish Agency's figures for 1935, the non-Jewish population was 975,000 against 375,000 Jews [cite:rs_rd3_horowitz_1937], roughly seven in ten of the inhabitants; the council would have given Arabs half its seats, with British officials holding a quarter and the High Commissioner able to fill boycotted seats, and it would have had no say over immigration under the labor schedule. To a movement that had asked since 1919 for a government responsible to a representative assembly, it offered half the seats of a body with no hand on immigration under the labor schedule. To the Zionist leadership, the same body offered the majority too much. The record held here does not give the detailed arguments of the Arab parties, and it should not be assumed that all of them shared the Mufti's position. Some, as events showed, did not.

The decision did not rest in Jerusalem. On 24 March 1936 the Prime Minister, Stanley Baldwin, announced a debate on the council in the House of Commons, and the Colonial Secretary, J. H. Thomas, said that final action would wait for it. The Jewish Telegraphic Agency reported that day that Jewish organizations were "unitedly opposed" and that some Arab groups were accepting [cite:rs_rd3_jta_1936_commons]. The chain of authority is plain in the record: the High Commissioner proposed, the Colonial Secretary held final action, and a Commons debate could hold it up. The research behind this book does not establish what the Commons debate concluded, and this account does not guess.

The offer's most lasting effect was on Palestinian unity. By late 1935 the five Arab parties had formed a united front, which the American Consul General described as a response to a "national emergency" [cite:rs_rd3_frus1936_d512]. In April 1936 the same consul reported that the council proposals had broken that front, and that "all thought of united Arab action" on the council had been abandoned [cite:rs_rd3_frus1936_d512_m]. On 5 May 1936, according to the Center for Israel Education, the Mufti and other Arab leaders declined to attend a conference in London on the proposal [cite:rs_rd3_cie_mufti_council]. By then events in Palestine had overtaken the council entirely; what followed belongs to [scene:s07a5|the Arab Revolt].

A common way of telling this period holds that one side or the other simply refused every chance at shared government. The record of 1935–36 is more specific. The offer was put to Jewish leaders in a fixed form; the Zionist leadership rejected it in principle; Agudath Israel deferred; the Arab leadership hesitated and divided, and the Mufti was reported opposed; and the decision was in any case held in London. Several things remain unsettled by the sources available here: what the Commons debate decided, what reasons the Arab parties that accepted gave, how the women's-suffrage objection weighed against the others, and whether the council would ever have sat had the country not moved into revolt.

The council's failure is a fitting place to close this stage, because it showed the structure that fourteen years of building had produced. At the top stood the British state. The Mandate had been in force, by the League Council's own minutes, since 29 September 1923, a date that Professor John Quigley argues had no legal force, so that Britain held Palestine without title [cite:rs_rd3_unispal_mandate_force] [cite:rs_rd3_quigley_2026]. Under it the High Commissioner proposed policy, allotted the labor schedule in half-year periods, and answered to the Colonial Secretary and, through him, to Parliament.

Beside the Mandate government, the Jewish community had built the institutions of a state in all but sovereignty. The Jewish Agency, enlarged in 1929 to give half the seats on its Council to non-Zionists, with Keren Hayesod as its main financial instrument [cite:israeled_weizmann_vol14], was chaired from 1935 by David Ben-Gurion [cite:wiki_histadrut]. The Histadrut, founded in 1920 and restricted to Jews, ran its own construction company, bank and health fund [cite:wiki_histadrut]. The Haganah, placed under the Histadrut's direct control in December 1920, had since 1931 been led by a six-member national command with parity between three Histadrut members and three non-labor members; its urban branches had memberships "in the hundreds," and it ran workshops producing hand grenades [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah]. Outside this structure, and against it, stood the Revisionists. Their New Zionist Organization had met in Vienna in September 1935, said to have been "elected by 713,000 voters," with Ze'ev Jabotinsky as president [cite:rs_rd3_ej_revisionists], and the Irgun had existed since 1931, formed by Avraham Tehomi's group with Revisionist groups after their secession from the Haganah [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah]. The Jewish population, by the Agency's count, had grown from 84,000 to 375,000 in thirteen years [cite:rs_rd3_horowitz_1937]; Tel Aviv alone had about 120,000 people in 1935 [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_telaviv].

The Palestinian Arab side had no comparable apparatus and no recognized representative body. The Arab Executive, never recognized by Britain, had dissolved in 1934, the year Musa Kazim al-Husseini died [cite:palquest_musa_kazim]. In its place stood parties built around rival families and rival programs: Nashashibi's National Defense Party, founded in December 1934 and close to Emir Abdullah [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_nashashibi]; the Palestine Arab Party, established on 27 March 1935 under Jamal al-Husseini, close to the Mufti [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_jamal]; and the Istiqlal, announced in August 1932, which named British imperialism as the main enemy but never built a large membership [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_hajibrahim] [cite:rs_rd3_wiki_istiqlal]. In late 1935 the five parties stood briefly together, and outside all of them a Haifa preacher had taken a band to the hills and died there, as told in [scene:rd3_qassam|the section on al-Qassam].

The year-by-year ledger below sets these years side by side, and most of its rows can be read against the sections of this stage. The Revisionist line runs through it from Betar in 1923 [cite:wiki_betar] to the Paris founding of 1925 [cite:rs_rd3_ej_revisionists]; the Hebrew University opened on 1 April 1925 [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_hebrew_univ]; the 1929 row pairs the violence of August with the enlarged Jewish Agency [cite:israeled_weizmann_vol14]; the 1930 and 1931 rows record the Shaw and Hope Simpson inquiries, the Passfield White Paper and MacDonald's letter of February 1931, which Arab leaders called the "Black Letter" and which withdrew the White Paper's restrictions within four months [cite:w_passfield] [cite:rs_rd3_macdonald_unispal]; and 1933 carries the Haavara Agreement with about 105 million Reichsmarks of goods moved by the outbreak of war [cite:wiki_haavara_agreement]. The 1934 row marks the dissolution of the Arab Executive [cite:palquest_musa_kazim]. The 1935 row gathers the stage's ending in a single line: the peak of immigration, recorded as 61,854 in the State Department series and 66,472 in the Porath series [cite:rs_rd3_frus1939_d828] [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_porath_table], the Nuremberg Laws [cite:ushmm_nuremberg_laws], and al-Qassam's death [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_qassam]. The "what it built" column is the ledger's own summary rather than a finding of this book, and one entry, for 1926, rests on a figure that the research behind this book has not sourced and that is not relied on here.

Read as a whole, the architecture at the end of 1935 was lopsided in a specific, documented way. One community had a funded agency, a labor federation with its own economy, an armed organization under shared command and a rival one outside it, and, by its own agency's count, a population that had more than quadrupled since 1922. The other had a national movement of long standing, a demand for representative government it had pressed since 1919, five parties that could unite only briefly, and no institution that Britain recognized as speaking for it. Britain held the decisions, and had just offered one that neither side would take on its terms. That was the structure that entered 1936.

chapters.label: Stage Four
chapters.title: Pivot to America
chapters.intro:
In the spring of 1936 the Mandate for Palestine was in its second decade, and the forces that would contest it were already organized. Hajj Amin al-Husseini had been Mufti of Jerusalem since 1921, and the Palestinian parties led by his family and by the Nashashibis were rivals. [cite:wiki_amin_al_husseini] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_wiki_ahc] On the Zionist side the Haganah existed without British recognition, Ze'ev Jabotinsky's Revisionists had claimed both banks of the Jordan since 1925, and the Irgun had formed in 1931. [cite:wiki_special_night_squads] [cite:jabotinsky_revisionist_1925] In November 1935 British forces killed Izz al-Din al-Qassam. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_ebsco_strickert] Five months later, on 15 April 1936, two Jews were killed near Tulkarm by most accounts, and within ten days a general strike had been called from Nablus and local committees across the country had united as the Arab Higher Committee. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_origins_yehudai] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_mee_strike] In the United States there was not yet a law requiring anyone working for a foreign cause to register, and the leaders of American Zionism were citizens acting as citizens. [cite:doj_fara]

This stage asks how the center of the Palestine question moved, in less than a decade, from a British administration putting down a rural revolt to the committee rooms of the United States Congress and the platforms of both American parties. It asks with equal weight what each party to the question did as the doors closed on Europe's Jews: what Britain decided and why it abandoned what it had proposed, what the Palestinian Arab leadership chose and what those choices cost, what the Zionist movement demanded and by what means, and what the American president said in public, in private and in writing. The answer is not a single turn but a sequence of them, each documented, and several still argued over.

The cast is wide. In London stood the royal commission known after its chairman as the Peel Commission, a technical commission under Sir John Woodhead, Malcolm MacDonald defending the enforcement of the White Paper of 1939, and its critics in the Commons, Leo Amery, Winston Churchill and Herbert Morrison; in July 1945 Clement Attlee formed a Labour government. [cite:rs_rd4_pw_unccp_1949] [cite:rs_rd4_wp_jvl_debate] [cite:rs_rd4_lab_frus_yale] In Palestine and in exile were al-Husseini, Raghib and Fakhri Nashashibi and the peace bands Britain paid, Jamal al-Husseini's delegation in London, and the neighbouring Arab rulers who mediated the strike's end in 1936 and sent delegations of their own to London in 1939. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_hughes_peacebands_full] [cite:rs_rd4_pw_wiki_london1939] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_hcc] The Zionist movement spoke through Chaim Weizmann and David Ben-Gurion, and in America through Abba Hillel Silver and Stephen Wise, while Hillel Kook, calling himself Peter Bergson, ran an insurgent campaign of his own and Lehi offered to fight on Germany's side. [cite:biltmore_medoff] [cite:azec_case] [cite:w_kook] [cite:academickids_lehi] In Washington Franklin Roosevelt, his State and War Departments, and Senators Robert Wagner and Robert Taft each held a lever; aboard the USS Quincy, King Ibn Saud held another. [cite:djn_1944_hearings] [cite:brookings_quincy_75years] Behind all of them stood the Nazi state, which turned to open violence in November 1938 and to the coordinated murder of Europe's Jews. [cite:ushmm_kristallnacht] [cite:ushmm_wannsee_conference]

The sections follow that sequence. They open with [scene:s07a5|the Arab Revolt] from its first killings to its suppression and its disputed death toll, and with the Peel Commission's partition plan, its proposal to move some 225,000 Arabs, and the three answers it drew. Woodhead and the London conference show how partition was dropped. Évian, where 32 countries declined to take more refugees and Palestine was kept off the agenda, and Kristallnacht four months later frame [scene:rd4_white_paper|the White Paper of May 1939] and the fight over whether it broke the Mandate. [cite:wiki_evian] The war years follow: British training of Jewish fighters, the clandestine fleet and the ships the limit turned away, Lehi and Lord Moyne, al-Husseini's road through Iraq to Berlin, the Vatican's wartime record, and the Holocaust from Wannsee to the counting of six million. The American turn runs through the Biltmore Program, the Bergson campaigns, the watchers in Washington, the Emergency Council's letter machine and the resolutions of 1944–45. The stage closes with Roosevelt's two registers, his concealed illness and the choice of Truman, the meeting at Great Bitter Lake, and Labour's arrival in office.
chapters.outro:
By the end of 1945 the Mandate's structure still stood, but the weight resting on it had moved. Britain still held the Mandate and still governed by the White Paper of 1939. The argument over what should replace it was now being made as loudly in Washington as in Jerusalem or London.

The legal layer had been altered without being resolved. Cmd 6019 of 17 May 1939 ruled out a Jewish state, promised an independent Palestine state within ten years, allowed some 75,000 Jewish immigrants over five years, and made any further immigration depend on Arab acquiescence; Parliament approved it on 23 May. [cite:rs_rd4_wp_cojs_text] [cite:rs_rd4_wp_frus_d841] Whether Britain had the right to adopt it was put to the League and never decided. The Permanent Mandates Commission held unanimously that the policy departed from the interpretation it had always placed on the Mandate, and found by four votes to three that it could not say the policy conformed; the war came before the League Council could act. [cite:rs_rd4_wp_jvl_league] [cite:rs_rd4_wp_wiki_pmc] The Jewish Agency's strongest case was that an Arab veto on immigration could not be squared with the Mandate's duty to "facilitate Jewish immigration." [cite:rs_rd4_wp_bjpa_jacase] The strongest case for it was the Commission minority's, that existing circumstances could justify the policy provided the League Council did not object, together with Britain's own stated objective of an independent state within ten years. [cite:rs_rd4_wp_jewishlink] The record leaves the question where the war left it.

The administrative layer was coercive. To end the revolt Britain sent about 20,000 troops, demolished houses, imposed collective fines on whole neighborhoods, detained and deported, and hanged between 108 and 122 Palestinian Arabs and two Jews. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_origins_yehudai] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_shindler_hughes] The White Paper then placed the remaining levers with the High Commissioner: when 25,000 refugees could enter, general powers over land transfers, and a rule deducting every unauthorized arrival from the quota, which became the ground for suspending the whole six-month quota in July 1939. [cite:rs_rd4_wp_cojs_text] [cite:rs_rd4_wp_frus_d841] At sea the same rule was enforced against particular ships, and the Patria and the Struma together cost more than 1,000 lives. [cite:wiki_patria_disaster] [cite:wiki_struma_disaster] The wartime High Commissioners and Colonial Secretaries are not named in the sources for this stage.

The institutional and financial layer belonged largely to the Yishuv. On the figures in this library's funding ledger, the Jewish Agency's 1939 budget of £720,000 carried £80,000 for defense, and the Kofer HaYishuv levy of 1938 funded the Haganah. Britain trained parts of that force when it needed it, at Ein Harod in 1938, in the Palmach in 1941 and in the Jewish Brigade Group of 1944–45, and jailed members who trained outside its control. [cite:wiki_special_night_squads] [cite:archiveshub_wingate] [cite:wiki_zvi_brenner] The Mossad LeAliyah Bet was created as a branch of the Haganah in 1938, and the Haganah founded the Shai, its intelligence arm, in 1940. [cite:ushmm_aliyah_bet] [cite:shai_wiki] In October 1942 the Zionist General Council made the Biltmore demand for a Jewish Commonwealth binding policy. [cite:biltmore_enc] The movement's fringe stood outside this discipline: Lehi offered in 1941 to fight on Germany's side and killed Lord Moyne in 1944, and the Zionist Executive called its members "traitors." [cite:academickids_lehi] [cite:daat_moyne] In America, by the same ledger's reckoning from Marc Lee Raphael's history, the United Jewish Appeal raised more than $124 million between 1939 and 1945, split among European relief, the Palestine program and resettlement in the United States in shares the record here does not give; the Emergency Council's own files document a method, not a budget.

The Palestinian Arab side ended the stage with the heaviest losses and the weakest institutions. The Arab Higher Committee of April 1936 had joined rival parties under one leadership; by the autumn of 1937 it was outlawed, its members arrested or deported to the Seychelles, its president in exile. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_wiki_ahc] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_jvl_andrews] Walid Khalidi's count of 5,032 Arab dead, against official British figures that are lower and higher estimates that reach 8,000, measures the revolt's cost; the sources used here put Jewish deaths at about 400 to 415 and British deaths at about 100 to 200. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_shindler_hughes] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_unpacked] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_origins_yehudai] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_jvl_riots] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_ebsco_strickert] The rivalry between the Mufti's followers and the Nashashibi peace bands produced hundreds of killings of Palestinians by Palestinians. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_origins_yehudai] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_hughes_peacebands_full] The leadership rejected Peel outright and rejected the White Paper, though a US consul reported "very obvious relief" among Arabs at its terms. [cite:wiki_peel_commission] [cite:rs_rd4_wp_frus_d826] Its strongest case was a majority's claim to an independent government and to a halt to immigration it had never consented to. The strongest case against its choices is the record of rebel violence against other Palestinians and of al-Husseini's own road to Berlin, which remains one man's documented choice, not the record of a people. [cite:wiki_amin_al_husseini]

The regional layer widened in every direction. Arab rulers mediated the end of the 1936 strike; Egypt, Iraq and Saudi Arabia sat at St James's Palace; Iraq's pro-Axis coup collapsed in 1941 into the Farhud, the pogrom whose death toll the sources give as 150 to 180 or higher. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_hcc] [cite:rs_rd4_pw_wiki_london1939] [cite:ushmm_farhud] [cite:wiki_farhud] By 1945 the Saudi king, whose kingdom was already tied to the United States through ARAMCO, held a written presidential undertaking on Palestine. [cite:loc_aramco_oil_pamphlet] [cite:fdr_letter_ibnsaud]

The American layer was the stage's new construction, raised under a 1938 law that for the first time required agents of foreign principals to register. [cite:doj_fara] The Emergency Council, founded in August 1943, ran letter and telegram campaigns from 342 Madison Avenue; the Bergson committees bought pages and filled Madison Square Garden; both parties wrote Palestine into their platforms in 1944, "the first time in American history." [cite:azec_powerbase] [cite:aja_azec_local_1944] [cite:w_wwnd] [cite:aja_azec_appraisal_1944] Against them stood the War and State Departments, which twice asked Congress to wait, and a president who approved silence on Palestine for the war while assuring Arab leaders in writing that he would consult them. [cite:djn_1944_marshall] [cite:brandeis_center_fdr_zionism] [cite:state_dept_oct1945_release] Congress's resolution of December 1945 spoke not of a Jewish commonwealth but of equal rights "regardless of race or creed." [cite:frus1945_concres]

What was settled, then, was narrower than either side's hopes: Britain's partition plan was dead, its White Paper stood, and the Palestinian leadership that might have negotiated its terms was scattered. What was contested ran through the whole stage: whether the White Paper broke the Mandate, whether the Zionist Congress accepted Peel, what Ben-Gurion's letter to his son meant, how many died in the revolt, whether Roosevelt's two voices were statecraft or duplicity. What the record leaves open is the question the stage handed on. A Labour government pledged against the White Paper took office in July 1945, and the State Department forecast that it would modify the immigration limits and not act on its conference's call for Arabs to "move out." [cite:rs_rd4_lab_frus_yale] Roosevelt had died on 12 April 1945, and his promise of consultation passed to a successor who had not been told how ill he was. [cite:arabnews_fdr_ibnsaud] [cite:globalsecurity_fdr_veiled_decline] How those two inheritances would meet the survivors of the Holocaust is the subject of the next stage.

sections.h: The Arab Revolt, 1936–1939
sections.html:
The revolt that opened this period had a prelude. In November 1935 British forces killed Izz al-Din al-Qassam, and historians name his death as part of the background to what followed. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_ebsco_strickert] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_shindler_hughes] The broader timing is also documented. The uprising of 1936 followed the sharpest rise in Jewish immigration under the Mandate, and it came in the same decade that produced the Irgun (1931) and, later, Lehi (1940). Each of these movements, Arab and Jewish, formed in reaction to the other side and to British policy. Naming that pattern explains when the armed movements arose. It excuses none of them, and their attacks on civilians are part of the record on every side.

The immediate trigger came on 15 April 1936. Palestinian Arabs killed two Jews near Tulkarm, Jewish retaliation followed, and riots broke out in Jaffa and Tel Aviv. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_origins_yehudai] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_ebsco_strickert] The sources do not agree on the first incident. The Jewish Virtual Library describes it as an attack on a Jewish bus and gives three Jewish dead, not two. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_jvl_riots]

The strike that followed did not begin at the top. On 19 April a newly formed Arab National Committee in Nablus called for a general strike, the withholding of taxes and a boycott of Jewish products. Local national committees across the country then united on 25 April as the Arab Higher Committee. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_mee_strike] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_origins_yehudai] The new committee was led by Hajj Amin al-Husseini, Mufti of Jerusalem. It declared a general strike with three demands: an end to Jewish immigration, an end to land sales to Jews, and an independent national government. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_origins_yehudai] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_jvl_riots] Another account dates al-Husseini's own strike call, as the committee's president, to 16 May 1936. [cite:ushmm_arab_revolt] Read together, the dates suggest that local committees moved first and the national leadership then took up the strike, though the sources do not explain the gap between them.

The committee's membership was its most striking feature. According to the list drawn from the Peel report, it brought together the leaders of rival clans and parties. Amin al-Husseini was president. Raghib al-Nashashibi represented the National Defense Party, Jamal al-Husseini the Palestine Arab Party, Yaqub al-Ghusayn the Youth Congress, Abd al-Latif Salah the National Bloc and Husayn al-Khalidi the Reform Party. Awni Abd al-Hadi of the Istiqlal was general secretary and Ahmed Hilmi Pasha treasurer. The coalition did not last long: Raghib al-Nashashibi left soon after it was formed. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_wiki_ahc]

The familiar description of the revolt as a spontaneous, leaderless outburst with no lasting result does not fit this record. The strike had a dated origin, a named committee with named officers, a written list of demands and a structure of local committees. Yet the opposite simplification fails too. A named leadership establishes an organized origin and an overall direction. It does not mean that every participant in three years of fighting took orders from al-Husseini, and the sources do not make that claim. The revolt's consequences, as this section and the next show, were large.

The general strike lasted about six months. Its end is recorded in a British document. On 12 October 1936 the General Officer Commanding issued a Special Order announcing that the strike and armed rebellion had been "called off unconditionally by the Higher Arab Committee." [cite:rs_rd4_ar_cojs_gocorder] The rulers of neighbouring Arab states had mediated its end. Different sources name them as the rulers of Transjordan, Iraq, Saudi Arabia and Yemen. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_hcc] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_jvl_riots] Historians weigh the causes differently. Some sources stress the rulers' appeal, together with British concessions and the threat of martial law. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_hcc] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_jvl_riots] Others also point to economic pressure, especially the approaching citrus harvest. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_origins_yehudai] The two explanations are compatible, and the evidence does not let us rank them.

The same Special Order gave the British army's own count of the cost of the strike period. It recorded 25 British soldiers killed and 120 wounded, 7 British police killed and 40 wounded, and 9 Palestine police killed and 64 wounded. It put the total cost of the rebellion so far at no fewer than 300 dead and 1,300 wounded. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_cojs_gocorder] This is the figure of one side, issued at the moment that side declared the rebellion over, and it should be read as such.

London's political answer was already in motion. A royal commission had been appointed in August 1936, during the strike, to investigate the causes of the revolt. [cite:rs_rd4_pw_unccp_1949] [cite:wiki_peel_commission] Its report of July 1937 proposed partition, and its reception is told in [scene:s07a6|the Peel Commission].

Peel's proposal was followed by the revolt's second phase. On 26 September 1937, four gunmen described as followers of al-Qassam killed Lewis Andrews, District Commissioner for Galilee, as he left a service at Christ Church in Nazareth. His police bodyguard died of his wounds. Within 24 hours police had detained about 100 Palestinian Arabs. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_jvl_andrews] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_unpacked]

Britain then moved against the political leadership. It outlawed the Arab Higher Committee, around 30 September 1937, stripped al-Husseini of his offices, arrested members of the committee and deported several of them to the Seychelles. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_jvl_andrews] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_unpacked] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_wiki_ahc] The sequence of al-Husseini's flight is told slightly differently in different sources. One account has him taking sanctuary in the Dome of the Rock on 17 July 1937 to avoid arrest, and then losing his positions after the district commissioner's killing in September. [cite:wiki_amin_al_husseini] Other sources place his refuge in the Haram al-Sharif and his escape in the autumn of 1937. They disagree on where he went: Lebanon, according to Unpacked, or Syria, according to the Jewish Virtual Library. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_jvl_andrews] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_unpacked] The account that sends him to Lebanon continues to Iraq, and historians document that he went on directing the revolt from exile. [cite:wiki_amin_al_husseini] By Unpacked's account, he authorized attacks from abroad on Britons, on Jews, and on Palestinians considered collaborators. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_unpacked] The record establishes that he continued to give direction. It does not itemize every order he sent.

With the leadership gone, the revolt moved into the countryside. Rebel bands set up their own administration there and taxed the peasants. The uprising peaked in the autumn of 1938, when rebels held large parts of the country, and was suppressed by the summer of 1939. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_origins_yehudai] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_ebsco_strickert]

Britain sent about 20,000 troops. Its measures included house demolitions, executions, the outlawing of the Arab Higher Committee, arrests and expulsions of activists, indefinite detention, collective fines on whole neighborhoods, and the disarming of Palestinians. Matthew Hughes's 2019 study of the campaign groups these methods into eight categories. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_origins_yehudai] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_shindler_hughes] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_ebsco_strickert] The instruments mattered because of where they fell. Collective fines landed on neighborhoods, not only on fighters, and indefinite detention held activists without a fixed term.

Executions give one measure of the campaign. Between 108 and 122 Palestinian Arabs were hanged in the 1930s. The reviewer of Hughes's study compares this with the 1,090 Kenyans hanged during the Mau Mau emergency of the 1950s. Two Jews were hanged. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_shindler_hughes]

The revolt was also a civil conflict. Raghib al-Nashashibi, a former mayor of Jerusalem, favoured compromise with the British; the Mufti opposed it. Their rivalry produced hundreds of killings of Palestinians by Palestinians. The Nashashibi-aligned "peace bands" were raised with British and Jewish military and financial help to fight the rebels. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_origins_yehudai] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_hughes_peacebands]

Hughes's study of the peace bands supplies the detail. By March 1938 Fakhri Nashashibi was organizing them from Lebanon. Fakhri 'Abd al-Hadi, a former rebel commander, returned to Palestine on 21 September 1938 with backing from the British consul in Damascus, Gilbert MacKereth. The money is documented. Britain paid band members £P6 a month. The insurgents paid their own men between 30 shillings and £P4. Both men were later killed: Husseini-backed gunmen killed Fakhri Nashashibi in Iraq in 1941, and 'Abd al-Hadi was murdered in 1943. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_hughes_peacebands_full] The 1941 killing belongs to al-Husseini's exile, which continued into an alliance with Nazi Germany from 1941: he met Hitler and recruited for the Waffen-SS, a record set out in [scene:rd4_mufti_war|the Mufti's war]. [cite:wiki_amin_al_husseini] It is his own documented record. The overwhelming majority of Palestinian Arabs had no part in it and no say over it.

The money ran both ways. The rebel bands taxed the villages they held. Britain paid the bands that fought them. And the general strike itself pushed the Yishuv toward a more self-reliant economy. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_origins_yehudai] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_hughes_peacebands_full]

Jewish attacks on Arab civilians are part of the same record. In November 1937 the Irgun abandoned the policy of restraint and killed ten Arab civilians on the day later called "Black Sunday." After an attack on an Arab bus in April 1938, the British hanged Shlomo Ben-Yosef in June 1938. He was one of the two Jews hanged during the revolt. By Unpacked's count, at least 250 Palestinian Arabs had died at Irgun hands by the summer of 1939. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_unpacked] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_shindler_hughes] The Irgun was formed in 1931, and its turn to reprisal belongs to the pattern the opening of this section described. Like the rebels' attacks on Jewish civilians, it is named here for what it was.

How many people died is the most contested question about the revolt. The figures come from different sources, count different things, and should be set out side by side.

For Arab deaths, the most detailed figure comes from Walid Khalidi's analysis of British statistics. He counts 3,832 Palestinian Arabs killed by the British and 1,200 killed in internal strife, 5,032 in all, with 14,760 wounded. Official British figures are lower and divided differently. They give over 2,000 Arabs killed in combat, 108 hanged and 961 killed by "gang and terrorist activities." Reference works round the total to about 5,000. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_shindler_hughes] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_hcc] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_origins_yehudai] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_ebsco_strickert] The Jewish Virtual Library estimates roughly 5,000 dead, 15,000 wounded and 5,600 imprisoned. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_jvl_riots] Middle East Eye gives about 5,000 killed, 15,000–20,000 wounded and 5,600 imprisoned. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_mee_strike] At the high end, Unpacked (Noam Weissman, 2024), drawing on Oren Kessler, gives 5,000–8,000 Palestinian Arab dead and says about 20 percent of Palestinian Arab men were jailed at some point. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_unpacked] The summary published by the Palestinian church committee states that over 10 percent of Palestinian Arab men aged 20 to 60 were killed, wounded, imprisoned or exiled. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_hcc]

For Jewish and British deaths, the scholarly and reference figures cluster closely, and they are the record: roughly 400 to 415 Jews and 100 to 200 British. Ori Yehudai gives about 415 Jews and 100 British. The Jewish Virtual Library gives 415 Jewish deaths for 1936–39. Fred Strickert gives nearly 400 Jews and 200 Britons. Hughes's reviewer writes of "hundreds" of Jews. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_origins_yehudai] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_jvl_riots] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_ebsco_strickert] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_shindler_hughes] Much higher Jewish and British figures, attributed to the US Holocaust Memorial Museum, also circulate. They could not be verified, they conflict with every other source, and they are not used here.

The revolt also moved people. According to the review of Hughes's study, about 40,000 Christian Arabs and others left for Syria and Lebanon during the revolt. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_shindler_hughes]

How to characterize the revolt is itself in dispute, and each reading rests on real evidence. In the Palestinian national reading, as Middle East Eye puts it, the revolt was "the most sustained armed resistance" against the Mandate, a national uprising crushed by brutal British repression. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_mee_strike] The demolitions, collective fines, hangings and detentions described above are its evidence. A critical reading, given by Unpacked, stresses that the rebels also turned on Palestinians, extorting and killing those they deemed disloyal, with leaders encouraging it. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_unpacked] Its evidence is the intra-Palestinian killing and al-Husseini's reported authorization of attacks on supposed collaborators.

Hughes's scholarship takes both seriously. He concludes that the peace bands "never won the war for the British." Collaboration, he finds, was driven more by survival, personal gain and feuds than by political conviction, and "Palestinian collaboration in the 1930s was too partial to damn the Arab revolt." [cite:rs_rd4_ar_hughes_peacebands_full] On that reading the internal violence was real and the uprising was still a national one. Neither fact cancels the other.

On the outcome, historians agree. The revolt failed militarily. The Palestinian leadership was left weak, divided and in exile. Military cooperation between Britain and the Zionist movement deepened, a story taken up in [scene:br_s01|Wingate's Night Squads and the Palmach]. And the general strike pushed the Yishuv toward a more self-reliant economy. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_origins_yehudai] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_shindler_hughes] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_hcc] The ledger of these years shows the sequence at a glance: the revolt in 1936, Peel's partition and transfer proposal in 1937 with the Arab Higher Committee objecting, and in 1939 the White Paper's limit on immigration, which the Zionist movement opposed.

Much remains unsettled. The death toll is the clearest gap: the Arab figures range from British official counts to 8,000, and the sourced Jewish and British figures run from about 400 to 415 and from 100 to 200, beside much higher figures that could not be verified. The sources do not settle the exact date of al-Husseini's flight or its first destination, or how much of the second phase he actually directed from abroad. Nor do they give firm totals for detentions or demolitions. The leadership that had called the strike in 1936 ended the revolt divided and in exile, just as London turned from partition to a policy of its own.

sections.h: The Peel Commission: Partition's First Draft
sections.html:
Britain's political answer to the revolt was a royal commission. The Palestine Royal Commission, known after its chairman as the Peel Commission, had six members. It was appointed in August 1936, while the general strike was still under way. [cite:rs_rd4_pw_unccp_1949] Its task was to investigate the causes of the uprising. [cite:wiki_peel_commission]

Its report, published in July 1937, went much further than an inquiry into causes. It proposed ending the Mandate. In its place there would be an independent Arab state, formed by joining part of Palestine to Transjordan, and an independent Jewish state in another part of the country. Jerusalem and some other places would stay under British mandate, in a British-administered corridor that included the city. [cite:rs_rd4_pw_unccp_1949] [cite:rs_rd4_pw_origins_yehudai] [cite:wiki_peel_commission] It was the first official proposal to partition the territory. The Jewish state would be small. The sources give its size differently: 17 percent of the country according to Ori Yehudai, about 20 percent according to Fred Strickert. [cite:rs_rd4_pw_origins_yehudai] [cite:rs_rd4_pw_ebsco_strickert] The sources consulted here do not explain the difference, and this book gives both figures.

The report did not stop at borders. Beside its partition map it recommended an "exchange of population," compulsory in the last resort. That recommendation, the first time population transfer appeared in an official British document, is the subject of the next section, [scene:pl_s01|Peel's "exchange of population"].

A common belief holds that partition was the United Nations' original idea in 1947, reached through a neutral international process. The record shows otherwise. A British royal commission proposed partition a decade earlier, and both sides had already responded to it, in different ways, before the United Nations took up the question. The UN committee's 1947 map bore a documented resemblance to this earlier partition thinking, which is examined in [scene:s07i|UNSCOP and the 1947 plan]. [cite:peel_report_1937] The resemblance is one of concept and structure. The two maps were not identical line for line, and the claim here is only that the idea came first from London.

Three responses mattered, and they were not alike.

The first came from the Twentieth Zionist Congress, which met in 1937. The movement was deeply divided over the plan, and the Congress produced a carefully balanced position. It rejected the proposed boundaries. It accepted partition in principle, or at least did not reject it, and it authorized continued negotiation with Britain. [cite:rs_rd4_pw_jvl_riots] [cite:jvp_us_admin_partition_timeline] Historians do not settle on a single verb for this. Some write that the Congress "accepted" the principle of partition; others that it "did not reject it outright." [cite:jvp_us_admin_partition_timeline] The difference matters for anyone who later summarizes 1937 in a sentence. A United Nations working paper of 1949 put it more starkly than either: it summarized the outcome as rejection of the plan by both Jews and Arabs. [cite:rs_rd4_pw_unccp_1949] The strongest form of the "acceptance" reading is that the movement's leadership accepted the idea of a Jewish state in part of the country and wanted to bargain over its size. The strongest form of the "rejection" reading is that the Congress refused the plan actually on the table, since the boundaries were the plan. Both readings fit the resolution, which was built to allow both. This book does not choose between them.

The second response was the Arab Higher Committee's, and it was unambiguous. The committee, led by al-Husseini, rejected the plan outright, with no conditional language. [cite:wiki_peel_commission] His role in the violence of 1929 is examined in an earlier chapter. The committee's rejection was its own formal institutional position. It does not show that every person in the Arab population held identical views on partition, and the sources do not measure what others thought.

The third response came from the Revisionist movement. Ze'ev (Vladimir) Jabotinsky had founded the Union of Revisionist Zionists, Hatzohar, in 1925. Its core territorial claim was that the Jewish state must cover both banks of the Jordan River: what later became Israel, the West Bank and Gaza, and the whole of Transjordan. [cite:jabotinsky_revisionist_1925] In 1929–1930 Jabotinsky put the argument in geographical terms:

"What does the word Palestine mean? Palestine is a territory whose chief geographical feature is this: that the River Jordan does not delineate its frontier, but flows through its center."

The movement's anthem made the same claim in verse: "Two Banks has the Jordan — This is ours and, that is as well." [cite:jabotinsky_revisionist_1925] The claim was territorial and historical rather than primarily religious; Jabotinsky was not himself religious. He argued that Britain's 1922 separation of Transjordan from the Palestine Mandate had been an arbitrary partition, one that denied Jews the land needed to absorb millions of future immigrants. [cite:jabotinsky_revisionist_1925] Testifying before the Peel Commission, he argued forcefully against any partition and for Jewish rights to the whole of Mandate Palestine, Transjordan included. [cite:wiki_jabotinsky] This was a consistent position, given on the record to the commission itself. It was not the mainstream Zionist position of 1937, which, as the Congress's resolution shows, was far more ambiguous. The later history of this claim, through Herut and Likud, is traced in [scene:gia_src_s02|the versions of "Greater Israel"].

The plan's effect on the ground was immediate. According to Unpacked and the Jewish Virtual Library, Peel's partition proposal prompted rebel groups to restart the revolt in the autumn of 1937. [cite:rs_rd4_pw_unpacked] [cite:rs_rd4_pw_jvl_riots] The second phase of the uprising, told in the previous section, began in the autumn of that year.

The 1937 rejection is often used as evidence for a later slogan: that the Arabs "rejected every offer." What the record shows is narrower. Arab leaders did reject the 1937 Peel plan, and later the 1947 partition plan. But the slogan compresses a record that runs in two directions. Israel's 1949 refugee offer at Lausanne was made only within a full peace and was later withdrawn. The 2000 Camp David offer is disputed by participants, and some on the American side say it was never written down. Offers in this history were conditional, and both sides refused at different points. Peel, in particular, was refused by both: outright by the Arab Higher Committee, and in its actual boundaries by the Zionist Congress. The slogan is short, and the history behind it is longer and less flattering to whichever side repeats it.

Some questions the record here does not settle. The precise share of the country allotted to the Jewish state differs between sources, and the boundaries of the plan are not set out in the material drawn on for this section. The documents do not say how the Congress's delegates divided, beyond the description of the movement as deeply divided. Nor do they settle whether "acceptance in principle" was a real commitment or a bargaining position. Within sixteen months, London would abandon the plan altogether.

sections.h: Peel's "Exchange of Population": Transfer Enters the Record
sections.html:
The Peel report of July 1937 is remembered for its partition map. Beside the map it made a second recommendation. It proposed an "exchange of population" between the two states it would create. [cite:wiki_peel_commission]

The model was explicit: the exchange of populations between Greece and Turkey in 1923. Approximately 225,000 Arabs would be moved out of the territory allotted to the Jewish state, and about 1,250 Jews out of the Arab state. The report stated that in the last resort the exchange should be compulsory. [cite:wiki_peel_commission] It was the first official British document to put population transfer in writing. The sources round the figures differently. Ori Yehudai gives about 200,000 Arabs and about 1,000 Jews. Middle East Eye gives about 225,000 Palestinians against 1,250 Jews, matching the figures above. [cite:rs_rd4_pw_origins_yehudai] [cite:rs_rd4_pw_mee_strike] Either way, the scale was lopsided. The movement the report envisaged was overwhelmingly of Arabs out of the proposed Jewish state.

A widely held view is that the idea of removing the Arab population from a future Jewish state was invented by Israeli extremists after 1948. The documents do not support that chronology. Compulsory transfer entered the official record in a British royal commission report in 1937. It was then discussed, and not rejected, at the top of the Zionist movement more than a decade before the displacement of 1948. That leaves open what any individual leader privately intended. The concept itself was on the table well before the Nakba.

The mechanism matters. The recommendation was Britain's, made by a royal commission of the Mandatory power. The Arab response was a plain rejection. The Zionist response is the disputed part of the record.

The most quoted evidence is a private letter. In October 1937 David Ben-Gurion wrote to his son Amos. The letter welcomes partition as a stage toward a larger state and discusses the Arab population. [cite:wiki_peel_commission] His diary and letters of the period discuss compulsory transfer as a possibility. One sentence in the Amos letter has become the center of a dispute over its wording. It has been quoted as support for expelling Arabs. In a different reading of the handwritten Hebrew, it says the opposite. [cite:wiki_peel_commission] Historians have not only disagreed about the sentence; some have changed their own positions on it, Benny Morris among them. [cite:wiki_peel_commission]

Each side of this dispute has a serious case. Those who read the sentence as support for expulsion can point to its context: a letter welcoming partition as a stage, written in the same months in which Ben-Gurion's diary and letters weighed compulsory transfer as a possibility. Those who read it the other way rest on the handwritten original itself, arguing that the text does not say what the familiar quotation makes it say. This book does not resolve the sentence. The original wording is not reproduced in the sources available here, and without it no reader can judge between the readings. The dispute should be presented as a dispute.

What is not disputed is that the movement's formal response left the transfer proposal standing. The Twentieth Zionist Congress met in Zurich in August 1937. By this account it accepted partition in principle as a basis for negotiation, a verb other sources soften, as [scene:s07a6|the previous section] shows. On the transfer clause the record is plain: the Congress did not reject it. [cite:wiki_peel_commission] Transfer was therefore a live subject at the highest level of the movement eleven years before 1948. The Arab Higher Committee rejected the Peel report outright, the transfer recommendation with the rest. [cite:wiki_peel_commission]

The word did not leave British politics either. In December 1944 the Labour Party's conference adopted a resolution on Palestine that again spoke of Arabs moving out as Jews moved in. That resolution, and what was expected of Labour once in office, is told in [scene:rd4_labour|Labour and the end of the war].

The record leaves several things unsettled. The exact wording, and so the meaning, of Ben-Gurion's sentence to Amos remains disputed between historians. The sources here do not show how the Congress debated the transfer clause, only that it did not reject it. And the figures themselves differ slightly by source: about 225,000 and 1,250 in the report as cited here, about 200,000 and 1,000 in Yehudai.

sections.h: Partition Dropped: Woodhead and St James's Palace, 1938–1939
sections.html:
The Peel plan did not survive its first two years. Its publication in July 1937 had been followed by the restart of the revolt that autumn and by refusals from both sides, told in [scene:s07a6|the Peel Commission]; a United Nations paper later summed up the outcome as rejection by both. [cite:rs_rd4_pw_unpacked] [cite:rs_rd4_pw_jvl_riots] [cite:rs_rd4_pw_unccp_1949] London's next step was not to impose the plan but to test whether it could be carried out at all.

For that purpose Britain sent a technical commission under Sir John Woodhead. It had four members: Woodhead, Sir Alison Russell, Percival Waterfield and Thomas Reid. It investigated in Palestine from April to early August 1938. [cite:rs_rd4_pw_unccp_1949] [cite:rs_rd4_pw_wiki_woodhead] Those were the months in which the revolt was building toward its peak, told in [scene:s07a5|the Arab Revolt]. The difference from Peel was one of mandate. Peel had been asked to investigate the causes of the revolt. Woodhead's commission, formally the Palestine Partition Commission, was asked a narrower practical question: whether partition could be made to work.

Its report, dated 9 November 1938, set out three boundary plans, labelled A, B and C. The commission preferred Plan C. It proposed that the two states remain in a customs union with the Mandatory government, and it questioned whether partition was economically and politically viable at all. [cite:rs_rd4_pw_ecf_woodhead] [cite:rs_rd4_pw_wiki_woodhead] Its conclusion was that no practical partition plan could be devised, because both Jews and Arabs refused partition. The British government accepted its conclusion that partition was politically, administratively and financially impossible. [cite:rs_rd4_pw_unccp_1949] [cite:rs_rd4_pw_wiki_woodhead]

The political ground is the one the commission spelled out: both communities refused partition. The economic doubt can be read in the commission's own proposal: a customs union with the Mandatory government would have kept the two states tied together after separation. The sources consulted here record these grounds, the three plans and the preference for Plan C. They do not give the population each plan would have placed in each state, and this book does not supply those figures.

Having dropped partition, Britain tried negotiation. It invited the Palestinian Arabs, the neighbouring Arab states and the Jewish Agency to a conference in London in early 1939, known as the St James's Palace conference. [cite:rs_rd4_pw_wiki_london1939] [cite:rs_rd4_pw_cojs_text] The exact dates on which it opened and closed rest on a single reference source and are not given here.

The delegations are documented by name, though from a reference source rather than the conference records. The Palestinian delegation was led by Jamal al-Husseini, a founding member of the Arab Higher Committee in 1936, and included Awni Abd al-Hadi, Musa al-Alami and others, with George Antonius as a secretary. Raghib al-Nashashibi joined two days after the opening. Egypt sent a delegation, as did Iraq, under its Prime Minister Nuri al-Said, and Saudi Arabia, under Prince Faisal. The Jewish Agency's delegation was led by Chaim Weizmann, with Ben-Gurion dominant in its decisions. It included non-Zionists and Rabbi Stephen Wise. [cite:rs_rd4_pw_wiki_london1939] Two features of these lists stand out. The Arab side came as a regional coalition, with three states represented alongside the Palestinians, which suggests that Palestine had become a question for the surrounding governments as well. And the Palestinian delegation brought Husseini and Nashashibi figures together in one delegation, after the split described in the revolt section.

The conference never met as one. The Arab Higher Committee's delegation refused to sit with the Zionist delegation, so the British held separate meetings with each side. [cite:rs_rd4_pw_wiki_london1939] [cite:rs_rd4_pw_cojs_text] Britain was the only party that sat with both.

One strand of the talks went back to the First World War. An Anglo-Arab committee under the Lord Chancellor, Lord Maugham, examined the Hussein–McMahon correspondence of 1915–16. It found that the Arab case had been given too little weight. But the two sides on the committee could not agree on the central point: whether Palestine had been included in the British pledge of Arab independence. [cite:rs_rd4_pw_wiki_london1939] The finding carried weight because of who chaired it, Britain's own Lord Chancellor. It did not settle the question on which the Arab case rested.

The conference failed, and the British government said so in its own words. In the White Paper that followed, it recorded that after talks lasting several weeks, "Neither the Arab nor the Jewish delegation felt able to accept these proposals, and the conferences failed to reach an agreement." [cite:rs_rd4_pw_cojs_text] Britain then issued its own policy. That policy, the White Paper of May 1939, is the subject of [scene:rd4_white_paper|the White Paper].

How to read this sequence is a matter of emphasis more than of fact. One reading stresses British retreat: having proposed partition, London dropped it within sixteen months, once the revolt reached its height and both communities had refused the plan. Another stresses that the refusals were real and mutual, as Woodhead's own conclusion and the 1949 United Nations paper both record. The documents support both. Britain's stated reason for abandoning partition was the refusal of both peoples, and the timing places that decision at the peak of the Arab revolt.

Some questions this record does not answer. The sources here do not name the British ministers who ran the London talks, nor give the conference's exact dates or the populations of the Woodhead plans. They do not record what the separate meetings with the Arab states' delegations discussed. They also do not show whether any version of partition was ever put to the conference.

sections.h: "No One Wants Them": Évian, Bermuda and the Closing Doors
sections.html:
In the summer of 1938, while Woodhead's commission was in Palestine testing whether partition could work, the question of where Europe's Jews could go was put to the world. A common belief about the years before the Holocaust is that the world did what it could for Europe's Jewish refugees. Two conferences, five years apart, show how little that was. The first met in the summer of 1938, about Jewish refugees fleeing the Nazis. The second met in the spring of 1943, with the extermination under way. Both ended the same way. And at both, opening Palestine was kept off the table.

President Roosevelt called the first meeting after Germany annexed Austria. Delegates of 32 countries met at Évian from 6 to 15 July 1938. [cite:wiki_evian] They spoke with sympathy, and almost all of them declined to take more refugees. Britain's delegate, Lord Winterton, said that the United Kingdom "is not a country of immigration." France said it had reached saturation. Brazil asked for certificates of Christian baptism. Canada wanted only experienced farmers. The United States offered only to fill its existing German–Austrian quota, which had gone unfilled in earlier years. [cite:wiki_evian] [cite:newhumanitarian_evian] [cite:facinghistory_evian] The American offer opened no new places. It promised to use places that the law already allowed and that had not been used.

One country made a large offer: the Dominican Republic, under the dictator Rafael Trujillo. The offer came from a regime whose soldiers had massacred thousands of Haitians the year before, in 1937. [cite:wiki_evian] The record here gives no figure for how many refugees the Dominican Republic proposed to take or how many it eventually received, and it does not set out Trujillo's reasons. It records only that the most generous answer at Évian came from a government that had just carried out a massacre.

Palestine was not discussed. At Britain's insistence, any mention of Palestine as a destination was excluded from the agenda. [cite:holocaust_au_evian] [cite:wiki_evian] Golda Meir attended as the Jewish observer from Palestine. She was not permitted to take part. [cite:holocaust_au_evian] The mechanism is plain in the record. Britain held the Mandate and therefore controlled entry to Palestine. The sources here do not give Britain's stated reasons for the exclusion. What they show is the result: the conference was free to discuss any door except the one the Zionist movement was trying to open, and the power that held that door kept it shut.

The conference's failure was noticed in Germany. The Nazi party's newspaper summed it up in three words: "No one wants them." [cite:wiki_evian] Chaim Weizmann gave the Jewish side of the same conclusion. He told the Manchester Guardian that the world was now divided into two kinds of places for Jews: places where they could not live, and places they could not enter. [cite:wiki_evian] The two remarks came from opposite ends of the question and reached the same conclusion. Four months later came the pogrom of November 1938 ([scene:hol_s03|Kristallnacht]).

Five years later the Western powers met again, under far worse conditions. In April 1943, with the extermination of Europe's Jews under way, the United States and Britain held a conference on refugees in Bermuda. A program proposing that Britain open Palestine to refugees was put forward and was not considered. The conference produced little and was widely judged ineffective. [cite:usf_bermuda_evian] Palestine had been kept off the agenda at Évian in peacetime. At Bermuda, in the middle of the killing, it stayed off.

Some things are left open by the record gathered here. It does not list the positions of the other 26 countries at Évian. It does not give the Dominican offer in numbers or say how much of it was carried out. It does not say why Britain insisted on excluding Palestine, or who proposed opening Palestine at Bermuda and on what terms.

The two conferences matter to the story of 1948 in two ways, and both belong in the account. The first is the argument they handed the Zionist movement. When nearly every country refused, the argument that Jews needed a place of their own gained force. Much of what came after in this chapter can be read against that background, among it the clandestine ships ([scene:ab_s01|Aliyah Bet]) and the American campaign for a Jewish commonwealth.

The second is where the decision lay. Britain, which kept Palestine off the agenda at Évian and off the table at Bermuda, held the one door the movement was pushing against. Ten months after Évian, Britain set that policy out in [scene:rd4_white_paper|the White Paper of May 1939], and the clandestine ships of the following years sailed against its limits.

sections.h: Britain Trained the Army That Would Fight It
sections.html:
In the same summer of 1938 that the powers met at Évian, Britain was arming and training Jewish fighters in Palestine. The Jewish fighting force of 1948 is often remembered as self-made, built in defiance of Britain. Defiance is part of the record, and from 1945 it became the larger part. But the documents show something the familiar account leaves out. Between 1938 and 1945, much of that force's training, its fighting method and its future officers came through British channels. Britain opened those channels when it needed Jewish fighters, first against the Arab Revolt and then against the Axis, and closed them, sometimes with arrests, when the need passed. Three episodes show the pattern: Wingate's Special Night Squads in 1938, the Palmach in 1941 and the Jewish Brigade Group in 1944–45. Running beside them was a second story, of the money the Jewish community in Palestine raised to pay for its own defense.

The first channel opened in 1938, at the height of the Arab Revolt ([scene:s07a5|the revolt of 1936–1939]). Captain Orde Wingate was a British intelligence officer and a devout Christian restorationist who embraced the prophetic vision of a Jewish return to the land. He proposed a joint unit of British soldiers and Jewish supernumerary police drawn from the Haganah, the Jewish defense organization that Britain never officially recognized. The Jewish Agency eventually agreed. The Special Night Squads operated from Kibbutz Ein Harod from June to October 1938. About 75 Haganah volunteers served in them. Among them were Moshe Dayan and Yigal Allon, both future generals, and Pinchas Kopel, who later founded the Border Police. [cite:nli_wingate_hebrew] [cite:wiki_special_night_squads] [cite:israeled_wingate]

What Wingate taught was a method: small units moving at night and raiding into Arab villages. Critics argue that the method outlasted him. The Israeli writer Uri Avnery traced a line of retaliation-raid doctrine from Wingate through the Palmach to the Israel Defense Forces. [cite:avnery_dayan_wingate] That is a critic's reading, not a settled finding, and the record gathered here does not test it against the army's own doctrine. It does show two things plainly. The men Wingate trained went on to command. And the squads were a British instrument against the Arab Revolt, staffed partly by Haganah volunteers, whose targets were Arab villages.

The same administration that sponsored the squads also prosecuted Haganah members caught training with arms. Dayan, one of Wingate's trainees, was imprisoned in 1939. [cite:archiveshub_wingate] [cite:avnery_dayan_wingate] One reading fits the two facts into a single policy: training under British command served British aims, and training outside it led to arrest.

The second channel opened under the pressure of the world war. Facing a possible Axis breakthrough in North Africa, Britain cooperated with the Haganah in forming the Palmach in May 1941. After El Alamein, when the danger receded, so did British support. [cite:wiki_haganah_mirror] The pattern was the same as in 1938: cooperation while the threat was acute, distance once it passed.

The third channel came after long negotiation: the British Army announced a Jewish Brigade Group, formed in 1944. It fought the Germans in northern Italy in March 1945. [cite:wiki_zvi_brenner] [cite:wiki_haganah_mirror] The record here says nothing more about the Brigade: not its strength, its casualties or the negotiations that produced it. Nor does it say how many Jews and Arabs from Palestine volunteered for the British forces during the war. Those numbers are not given here, and this book does not supply them from elsewhere.

British training was one input. The other was money raised inside the Jewish community. By 1939 the Jewish Agency's budget carried an £80,000 line for "security service (defense)" within a total of £720,000, about one-ninth of the whole. In 1938, the year of the Night Squads, the community created the Kofer HaYishuv, a levy on cigarettes, restaurant bills and luxuries, to fund the Haganah. These are the first two steps of a funding chain that later ran through American donors and charity channels, a story told in full in [scene:gf_s02|the account of the pre-state army's budgets].

The two streams fit together. The Agency's budget and the levy paid for an organization that Britain did not recognize. Britain trained parts of it when British interests required, and it jailed members caught training with arms. The result by 1947 was a force the Mandate had never legalized: about 10,000 mobilized men and 40,000 reservists, under officers many of whom had learned their trade in British service. [cite:wiki_haganah_mirror] From 1945 those cadres would turn against Britain itself.

How much the British contribution mattered, compared with what the Haganah built for itself, is a question of weight that the record here does not settle. It documents the channels, the dates and the men, but not a measure of how far the 1948 army's effectiveness came from Ein Harod, the Palmach or Italy rather than from its own training. The money record has a matching gap. No audited total of the Haganah's budget is publicly available. The levy and the 1939 budget line are documented individually, and no full account of the army's funding before 1948 can yet be added up from them.

sections.h: Aliyah Bet: The Clandestine Fleet
sections.html:
The Haganah that Britain trained and jailed by turns had a second task besides defense: bringing people in. Postwar Jewish immigration to Palestine is often pictured as a flight of desperate refugees acting on their own. The passengers were desperate, and many of them were refugees in the strictest sense. But the ships that carried them were not spontaneous. From 1938 to 1948 they were organized and routed by a network built for the purpose, run from within the institutions of the Jewish community in Palestine. Both things are true, and the history of Aliyah Bet only makes sense when they are held together.

Aliyah Bet means "immigration B." It was the name for the clandestine immigration of Jews to Palestine against the limits Britain set on legal entry. In 1938, the year of Évian, the Jewish leadership created the Mossad LeAliyah Bet as a branch of the Haganah to coordinate it. [cite:ushmm_aliyah_bet] [cite:wiki_aliyah_bet] It did not hold a monopoly. Revisionist groups ran their own voyages separately. [cite:ushmm_aliyah_bet] It was founded in the same year that 32 countries met at [scene:ev_s01|Évian] and almost all declined to take more Jewish refugees, while Britain kept Palestine off the agenda.

How the operation worked can be read from its parts. The Mossad LeAliyah Bet was an arm of the Haganah, the defense organization of the Jewish community, not an independent charity. It organized ships from Europe's ports, against a British limit on entry that the Royal Navy enforced at sea. The record gathered here does not break the voyages down year by year, and it does not detail the wartime sailings beyond their outcome. Two of the wartime ships, the Patria in 1940 and the Struma in 1942, ended in mass death and are told in [scene:s07b2|the ships the White Paper turned away].

After the war the operation changed in scale. With Britain's quota at about 18,000 a year, the clandestine route became the main one. [cite:ushmm_aliyah_bet] The Brihah ("flight") network, run with Mossad emissaries, partisans and youth movements, moved nearly 200,000 survivors out of displaced-persons camps in Germany, Austria and Italy to ports in Italy, France, Yugoslavia and Greece. Zionist youth movements inside the camps supplied the passengers. [cite:hsb_aliyah_bet_exodus] [cite:ushmm_cyprus_camps] Ships, including a fleet bought and crewed largely by American volunteers, made about 142 voyages in all. More than 90 percent of them were intercepted by the Royal Navy. [cite:ushmm_aliyah_bet] [cite:wiki_aliyah_bet]

Interception did not end the journey, and Britain needed somewhere to put the people it stopped. From August 1946 it interned intercepted immigrants in camps on Cyprus. By 1948 it held about 52,000 people there. The last camp closed in February 1949. [cite:ushmm_cyprus_camps] [cite:ushmm_aliyah_bet] Cyprus was meant to deter. In July 1947 the Exodus 1947, carrying about 4,500 people, was boarded in international waters, and its passengers were sent back not to Cyprus but to camps in Germany. The US Holocaust Memorial Museum reads that decision as an admission that the Cyprus deterrent had failed. [cite:ushmm_cyprus_camps] [cite:ushmm_aliyah_bet] What the Exodus did to international opinion, and whether it moved the United Nations vote, belongs to the next stage and is set out, with both sides of the argument, in the account of the ships linked above.

By 1948 well over 100,000 people had come to Palestine this way, including more than 70,000 Holocaust survivors. [cite:ushmm_aliyah_bet] [cite:jvl_aliyah_bet] Set against the whole of Jewish immigration under the Mandate, that is a large share. Britain's own records count 376,415 Jewish immigrants between 1920 and 1946. A separate estimate puts total Mandate-era immigration, legal and illegal together, at about 480,000. [cite:jvl_aliyah_bet] The two figures measure different things. The British count stops in 1946 and records the entries Britain registered. The larger estimate runs to the end of the Mandate and includes people who entered without Britain's leave. The gap between them is consistent with a clandestine movement of the size given above, but the record here does not reconcile the figures line by line, and the reader should not treat the difference as an exact count of illegal entries.

The same panel shows how the population as a whole was changing. In Britain's 1922 census, 757,182 people were counted in Palestine. By the United Nations committee's estimate in late 1946, the population was about 1.85 million.

The question of what Aliyah Bet was has two answers, and both have evidence behind them. One is the passengers' story. They were survivors with nowhere else to go after the doors closed at Évian. The other is the organizers' story. The movement that carried them was an organized state-in-waiting, with its own intelligence service, logistics, fleet and recruitment, and every intercepted ship became a public argument against the Mandate. An account that keeps only the first misses the organization. An account that keeps only the second misses the people. The record supports both, and neither cancels the other. The youth movements that supplied the passengers in the camps and the Haganah branch that organized the ships were part of the same operation as the people on board.

Some questions remain open on this record. It does not say how the fleet was paid for, beyond noting that American volunteers bought and crewed much of it. It does not break down how many voyages or passengers fall before 1945 and how many after, or how many of the people who took the route were stopped and how many reached Palestine directly. It does not give the Revisionist voyages separately. Those remain for further research.

sections.h: How Did They Get Here? Citizens, Ships and a Law of 1938
sections.html:
The clandestine ships ran from Europe to Palestine; the movement's political turn in these years ran across the Atlantic, to the United States, and a practical question comes with it. Who were the people running the American side of the movement, how did leaders from Palestine and Europe reach them, and under what law did any of it operate? A common assumption is that foreign agents entered the country in secret and worked outside the law. The record points the other way on almost every count.

The leaders of American Zionism were Americans. Louis Brandeis, Rabbi Stephen Wise and Rabbi Abba Hillel Silver were United States citizens, and their advocacy was the legal political activity of citizens. Some of the movement's figures from Palestine had American lives of their own. Golda Meir, then Golda Meyerson, grew up in Milwaukee and emigrated in 1921. She later became Israel's prime minister. [cite:w_golda] David Ben-Gurion, expelled from Ottoman Palestine, lived in New York from 1915 to 1918. There he recruited volunteers for the Jewish Legion, and there he married. [cite:w_bengurion]

Travel was by sea. Visiting leaders such as Chaim Weizmann crossed the Atlantic by ocean liner, as most travelers did. Regular transatlantic passenger flights began only in 1939, with Pan Am's flying boats. [cite:w_boeing314]

The legal frame changed in 1938. Before that year no American law required people working for foreign principals to register at all. Congress passed the Foreign Agents Registration Act in 1938. [cite:doj_fara] The gap before it is real and documented. Anyone who acted for a foreign principal before 1938 could not have been breaking a registration law, because none existed.

Whether the law applied, and to whom, became a real question only later. The Bergson group was watched by the FBI, and that story is told in [scene:fa_s01|who Washington watched]. The first test of the act against the movement's main American apparatus came in 1962, with a Justice Department order to the American Zionist Council ([scene:s11a|the FARA order]). Both came after the law existed; before 1938 there was none to apply.

This short account leaves some things open. The record here does not say how often the visiting leaders crossed or who paid for their travel.

sections.h: Kristallnacht: The Turn to Open Violence
sections.html:
Four months after the Évian conference ended with almost no country willing to take more Jewish refugees ([scene:ev_s01|Évian and Bermuda]), the German state turned to open violence. Over the night of 9–10 November 1938, synagogues burned and Jewish shops were smashed across Germany, Austria and the Sudetenland. More than 30,000 Jewish men were sent to concentration camps. The event marked the turn in Nazi policy from mainly legal persecution toward open, state-organized mass violence.

The familiar account holds that Kristallnacht was spontaneous popular outrage, a crowd reacting to the assassination of a diplomat. The record supports half of it. The killing that served as the pretext was real. The response was neither spontaneous nor simply popular.

The chain began with a deportation. Germany forcibly expelled Polish Jews living in the country to the Polish border town of Zbąszyń, where thousands of them were held in harsh conditions. Among them were the parents of Herschel Grynszpan, a 17-year-old German-born Polish Jew living in Paris. On 7 November 1938, after learning what had happened to his family, Grynszpan shot the German diplomat Ernst vom Rath at the German embassy in Paris. Vom Rath died of his wounds two days later, on 9 November. [cite:ushmm_kristallnacht] [cite:yadvashem_november_pogrom] Grynszpan's motive was personal and is documented: his own parents had just been deported and held at the border. Stating it does not justify or excuse the killing of a man. It records why the shots were fired, which is a different matter from what the German state then did with them.

What the state did was organize. Historians identify the propaganda minister, Josef Goebbels, as seeing in vom Rath's death the moment to unleash violence he had long advocated, and as using it to call for exactly that. [cite:wiki_kristallnacht] The pogrom that followed was coordinated across Germany, Austria and the Sudetenland within a 48-hour window. A crowd that rises on its own does not typically coordinate itself within hours across three countries and regions and strike more than a thousand synagogues at once.
