[cite:whitepaper1939] In effect it would have frozen the Jewish population of Palestine as a permanent minority. Zionist leaders read it as a direct abandonment of the promise of 1917, and it arrived at the moment when Europe's Jews had the most urgent need to leave. [cite:whitepaper1939] The White Paper's full terms and the debate it caused in London and Geneva are set out in [scene:rd4_white_paper|the White Paper of 1939]. What matters here is the line the sources draw from it: Biltmore was triggered directly by the White Paper, which Zionist leaders took as Britain reneging on Balfour entirely. [cite:whitepaper1939]

The war shaped what came next. A regular Zionist Congress could not be convened in wartime, yet the pressure to act was mounting fast. The White Paper had closed most of the door to Palestine just as the Holocaust was accelerating, and reports of the scale of Nazi atrocities were reaching American Jewish leaders through 1941 and early 1942. [cite:biltmore_wiki] The conference at the Biltmore Hotel was called to fill the gap a cancelled Congress had left, and it was treated as the functional equivalent of one. [cite:biltmore_wiki]

The conference sat from 6 to 11 May 1942. About 600 delegates came from 18 countries. [cite:biltmore_wiki] Among them were Chaim Weizmann, president of the World Zionist Organization, and David Ben-Gurion, who led the Jewish Agency's leadership in Palestine. [cite:biltmore_wiki] Their presence in one room mattered, because they disagreed in public about strategy. Weizmann favored continued diplomatic engagement with Britain, the approach that had defined the movement for 25 years. Ben-Gurion, speaking for the Jewish population of Palestine directly, argued that explicit, uncompromising statehood was the only path that could work. [cite:biltmore_medoff] Biltmore is documented as the moment Ben-Gurion's approach prevailed. It was a real internal contest, not a unanimous or inevitable consensus. [cite:biltmore_medoff] That outcome should not be stretched further than the record allows: it does not show that Weizmann's diplomacy was abandoned altogether, or that he opposed the final resolution. It shows that the strategic tension between the two men was settled, for the moment, in Ben-Gurion's direction.

The resolution's key sentence urged that Palestine be established as a Jewish Commonwealth, integrated into the structure of the postwar democratic world. It also demanded that the Jewish Agency, not the British Mandatory administration, be vested with control over immigration. [cite:biltmore_wiki] Both parts answered the White Paper directly. Britain had made future immigration depend on Arab consent; Biltmore asked that it depend on a Jewish body instead.

The word "commonwealth" could be read as a softer goal than statehood. The historian Rafael Medoff's research on the conference addresses the point directly. "Commonwealth" was not meant to suggest anything less than a sovereign state. The delegates had in mind a status like that of Australia or Canada: fully sovereign in practice. [cite:biltmore_medoff] That reading describes the intended weight of the term. It does not mean that all 600 delegates held an identical understanding of it, and the sources do not claim they did. But measured against Balfour's undefined "national home," the change was an escalation, and it was meant as one. [cite:biltmore_medoff]

A conference resolution binds only the people who vote for it. Biltmore became something more because of what happened five months later. In October 1942 the Zionist General Council formally adopted the program as official policy. [cite:biltmore_enc] That step converted it from the position of the delegates who happened to attend into the platform of the whole organized Zionist movement, and it remained the movement's operative goal until late 1946. [cite:biltmore_enc] The ratification was the mechanism that turned one meeting's words into years of political work. The record here documents the top-level decision; it does not trace how each national Zionist body adopted the program in turn. [cite:biltmore_enc]

In America that work ran through the American Zionist Emergency Council, which took the Biltmore position into Congress and the party conventions. By 1944, two years after the hotel conference, according to Silver's own biographical record, Abba Hillel Silver had lobbied for a Palestine resolution and both major American parties had put Palestine into their platforms. [cite:azec_case] One reading is that this speed shows how much organizing capacity already existed. The resolutions and the platforms are told in [scene:us_s05|Palestine in Congress and the party platforms].

The program did not command universal agreement, and the same sources that document Biltmore document opposition to its maximalism. It came from two directions: from those who preferred to continue the diplomatic course, and from those who wanted an explicitly binational state instead of a Jewish one. [cite:biltmore_wiki] The binationalist critique is set out in [scene:s00b3|the binationalist dissent]. Other Jewish dissent from the program, including the American Council for Judaism and the American Jewish Conference of 1943, has not yet been researched for this chapter, and this book leaves it undescribed here rather than describe it without sources. The fair summary is the one the record supports: Biltmore marks the moment the demand for a state became explicit and dominant in the Zionist movement. It is not evidence that every Zionist voice agreed.

Two readings of Biltmore follow from the same facts. In one, it was a response to emergency: a movement that had worked within British promises for a generation watched Britain close the door in 1939, learned of mass murder in Europe, and concluded that only sovereignty, with control of its own immigration, could guarantee a refuge. In the other, it was a claim to sovereignty over the whole of Mandatory Palestine and its Arab population, made by reversing the very condition, Arab consent, that the White Paper had set on further immigration. The documents support the facts both readings rest on: the White Paper as trigger, the demand for all of Mandatory Palestine, the Jewish Agency's control of immigration. They do not settle which reading should govern.

What the record here leaves open is also specific. It does not give the vote at Biltmore or the size of any dissent inside the hall. It does not record how the program's claim to all of Mandatory Palestine was squared, by those who voted for it, with the Arab population living there. And it does not trace the program's reception among Palestine's Arab leaders. What is not in doubt is the change itself: in May 1942, in New York, the movement's stated goal changed from a national home to a state, and in October 1942 that change became binding policy.

sections.h: Six Million: How the Number Is Known
sections.html:
The coordination organized at [scene:hol_s04|Wannsee] produced the murder of millions. The number most often given for the Jewish dead is six million, and a common objection holds that it is a round figure that cannot be checked, one that historians simply accept. The record shows the reverse. The Holocaust is, in the words of the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, the best-documented case of genocide in history [cite:ushmm_evidence_documentation]. Its scale has been established by several independent methods, using different kinds of evidence: demographic reconstruction, captured German administrative records, and a name-by-name documentation project that has so far identified about 4.8 million victims individually and is still continuing [cite:wiki_destruction_european_jews] [cite:wiki_book_of_names] [cite:ushmm_evidence_documentation].

Independent methods. The historian Raul Hilberg built a detailed demographic breakdown of the Jewish dead and arrived at an estimate of 5.1 million [cite:wiki_destruction_european_jews]. The historian Lucy Dawidowicz, working separately in 1975 from birth and death records across the cities of prewar Europe, arrived at 5,933,900 [cite:wiki_destruction_european_jews]. The two used different source material and different methods. Their totals are not identical, and they are not meant to be: they differ by several hundred thousand. But they fall in the same general range, and that convergence between independent methods is itself a form of verification [cite:wiki_destruction_european_jews].

A third line of evidence works in a completely different way. Yad Vashem's Book of Names project records victims one by one, through survivor testimony and archival research. It has so far documented about 4.8 million named victims [cite:wiki_book_of_names]. That number is not a rival estimate of the total. It is a running count of people individually identified, and it grows as research continues. A demographic estimate answers the question of how many people are missing from the population; a list of names answers the question of who they were. Both point to the same scale.

None of this claims precision to the individual person. The Holocaust Memorial Museum's own position is that research continues to refine the estimates as more records come to light [cite:ushmm_evidence_documentation]. That is ordinary historical method. It is a different thing in kind from uncertainty about whether the genocide happened.

Auschwitz: the largest single site. Nazi Germany and its allies established more than 44,000 camps and other sites of incarceration between 1933 and 1945 [cite:ushmm_evidence_documentation]. One of them accounts for a disproportionate share of the dead. Auschwitz operated from May 1940 to January 1945. At least 1.3 million people were deported there, and at least 1.1 million of them were murdered there, the largest death toll at any single site of the Holocaust [cite:wiki_auschwitz_camp] [cite:ushmm_evidence_documentation]. Those figures are documented through camp records, survivor testimony and postwar investigation [cite:wiki_auschwitz_camp]. They apply to Auschwitz specifically. Other sites left different kinds of surviving records, and the Auschwitz figures are not a template applied across the other 44,000.

Liberation, 27 January 1945. As the Red Army approached in January 1945, the SS forced most of the remaining prisoners at Auschwitz onto death marches toward camps inside Germany and Austria. Soviet troops liberated the camp on 27 January 1945 [cite:wiki_auschwitz_liberation]. Since 2005 the date has been commemorated as International Holocaust Remembrance Day [cite:wiki_auschwitz_liberation]. Documented accounts describe the Soviet soldiers, battle-hardened men already accustomed to the deaths of war, as shocked by what they found [cite:wiki_auschwitz_liberation]. The death marches are a separately documented part of this history, with a large death toll of their own that the sources gathered here do not itemize.

Why the precision matters. The care taken over these methods is not pedantry. The Holocaust Memorial Museum documents Holocaust denial directly, and it names its core false claims: that six million deaths never occurred, that Nazi Germany had no official policy of extermination, and that the gas chambers of Auschwitz-Birkenau never existed [cite:ushmm_evidence_documentation]. Against each of these the record converges: captured German administrative records, demographic reconstruction, and individually verified named victims all lead to the same conclusion [cite:ushmm_evidence_documentation]. Wannsee's own document, the Protocol, answers the second claim on its own: an extermination policy that was ordered in July 1941 and coordinated across the ministries in January 1942 was an official one. Legitimate research continues to refine particular figures and details. That work is different in kind from denying the documented core of the genocide, and the two should not be confused.

The arc as a whole. This section closes a sequence that this library traces across five sections. It runs from a democracy's collapse through specific and avoidable decisions by its elites; to a legal architecture of exclusion built before any mass violence; to the open, state-coordinated pogrom of [scene:hol_s03|Kristallnacht] in November 1938; to the formal bureaucratic coordination, at Wannsee, of an extermination decision already taken; and finally to a verified, independently documented scale of six million Jewish dead, established by converging methods and not accepted on faith.

One part of this story is not yet in this volume, and the gap is significant. How the Jewish community of Palestine learned of the killing, when, and what it did in response has not yet been researched for this volume, and nothing about it is asserted here. The sources gathered here also do not reproduce the country-by-country tables behind Hilberg's or Dawidowicz's totals, and they do not give the number of victims of the death marches. Six million is not a figure taken on faith. It is the range to which independent counts, made by different people from different evidence, converge, and about 4.8 million of the dead are now known by name.

sections.h: The Perpetrators' Own Paper
sections.html:
The estimates set out in [scene:hol_s05|How the Number Is Known] were reached by historians after the war. The evidence beneath them is older. Much of it was written by the people who carried out the killing, in the routine forms of a modern state: situation reports, running tallies, minutes, telegrams, statistical summaries, a bound photograph album and the notes for a speech. These records were not composed for posterity. They were written to inform superiors, to coordinate ministries and to account for work done. They were captured by the Allies in 1945, entered into evidence at Nuremberg, and in some cases surfaced only decades later. This section takes the principal documents one at a time: what each is, who wrote it, when, what it says in its own figures and words, where the original is held, and how it came to light. Where the sources consulted here disagree on a date, a figure or a discovery, both versions are given.

The documents did not work alone. The killing depended on infrastructure that left its own paper trail. According to the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, the European rail network played a crucial role in the Final Solution: the Transport Ministry organized the train schedules, and millions of people were transported by rail to killing centers between autumn 1941 and autumn 1944 [cite:rs_rd4_ushmm_railways]. The reports below record the far end of that process.

The Einsatzgruppen reports, 1941–1942. The earliest large body of evidence comes from the Einsatzgruppen. Their reports survive in a series called the Operational Situation Reports USSR, the Ereignismeldungen. A set of 195 of them, covering June 1941 to 1 May 1942, was circulated across branches of the German government, the Wehrmacht among them [cite:rs_rd4_hdot_ezg_auth]. On 3 September 1945 the 6889th Berlin Document Group found the set on the fourth floor of Gestapo headquarters in Berlin [cite:rs_rd4_hdot_ezg_auth].

The reports count. At the Einsatzgruppen trial, the prosecution read from Operational Situation Report No. 128, which stated that "approximately 80,000 persons were liquidated until now by the Kommandos," and from Report No. 106, which stated that approximately 35,000 Jews of Kiev were killed on 29–30 September 1941. Another report gave the figure for Sonderkommando 4a at Kiev as 33,771 [cite:rs_rd4_harvard_nmt9_transcript]. The two Kiev numbers come from different reports, and the trial record preserves both.

The Jäger Report is a local tally of the same kind. It was signed at Kovno on 1 December 1941 by SS-Standartenführer Karl Jäger, commander of Einsatzkommando 3. It states that there are no more Jews in Lithuania apart from working Jews and their families. Yad Vashem holds it under the reference YVA O-18/245 [cite:rs_rd4_yv_jaeger]. According to the English translation published by the University of South Florida's Florida Center for Instructional Technology, and to Holocaust Denial on Trial, the report's running tally ends with the line "Total 137,346," covering 21 June to 1 December 1941 across 113 operations in 71 locations, and the original is held in the Central Lithuanian Archives in Vilnius [cite:rs_rd4_fcit_jaeger] [cite:rs_rd4_hdot_ezg_auth].

These reports were the basis of the prosecution in the ninth of the Subsequent Nuremberg Proceedings, the Einsatzgruppen Case. Twenty-four defendants were indicted, led by Otto Ohlendorf; 22 were tried. The trial ran from 29 September 1947 to 12 February 1948, and the prosecutor, Benjamin Ferencz, relied on the wartime SS reports rather than on witnesses [cite:rs_rd4_ushmm_case9] [cite:rs_rd4_harvard_nmt9_intro]. On 10 April 1948 the tribunal sentenced 14 defendants to death, 2 to life imprisonment and 5 to terms of 10 to 20 years. Only four of the death sentences were carried out, those of Ohlendorf, Naumann, Blobel and Braune, on 7 June 1951 [cite:rs_rd4_ushmm_case9] [cite:rs_rd4_harvard_nmt9_intro]. The sources give two figures for the number of victims attributed to the defendants. The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum gives the indictment's figure as between 723,661 and one million [cite:rs_rd4_ushmm_case9]. Harvard Law School's Nuremberg Trials Project gives the prosecution's estimate as more than one million [cite:rs_rd4_harvard_nmt9_intro].

The Wannsee Protocol, January 1942. The meeting of 20 January 1942 is told in [scene:hol_s04|Wannsee]: fifteen officials, about ninety minutes, Reinhard Heydrich in the chair, nearly six months after Hermann Göring's documented order of 31 July 1941 [cite:yadvashem_wannsee_final_solution] [cite:ushmm_wannsee_conference]. What matters here is the document itself. The minutes were compiled and heavily edited by Adolf Eichmann from notes taken at the meeting; they are not a word-for-word transcript [cite:rs_rd4_ushmm_wannsee_protocol]. Thirty copies were made. The stamp on the surviving copy reads "30 copies" and "16th copy," and copy no. 16 belonged to Undersecretary Martin Luther of the German Foreign Office [cite:rs_rd4_wannsee_text_ee] [cite:rs_rd4_jhi_wannsee] [cite:rs_rd4_ushmm_wannsee_protocol]. The protocol's country table totals "over 11,000,000" Jews. Among its entries it lists the General Government at 2,284,000, Bialystok at 400,000, the USSR at 5,000,000 and England at 330,000, and it lists Estonia as "free of Jews" [cite:rs_rd4_wannsee_text_ee]. As Heydrich presented it, the figure took in Jewish populations in countries not yet under Axis control [cite:ushmm_wannsee_conference]. The surviving protocol, item R 100857, is reproduced courtesy of the Political Archive of the German Foreign Office, the Politisches Archiv des Auswärtigen Amts [cite:rs_rd4_cts_wannsee].

Only one of the thirty copies has been found, according to the House of the Wannsee Conference [cite:rs_rd4_ghwk_files_seized]. How and when it was found is told three ways. The House of the Wannsee Conference states that American soldiers discovered it in a file together with 300 other pieces of evidence, among Foreign Office files seized from external storage; it illustrates the seizure with a photograph of United States troops at Schloss Meisdorf on 19 April 1945 [cite:rs_rd4_ghwk_files_seized]. The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum gives a later and more specific account: the copy came to light among the Foreign Office files in late 1946, when Kenneth Duke, a member of the American microfilming staff, found it and alerted Dr. Robert Kempner in March 1947 [cite:rs_rd4_ushmm_wannsee_protocol]. The Jewish Historical Institute in Warsaw credits Kempner, the prosecutor, with finding it in 1947 [cite:rs_rd4_jhi_wannsee]. The accounts name different finders, and the sources consulted here do not reconcile them. The Holocaust Memorial Museum states that the protocol was first submitted as evidence in 1947, in the Ministries Trial, Case 11 of the Subsequent Nuremberg Proceedings [cite:rs_rd4_ushmm_wannsee_protocol] [cite:rs_rd4_ghwk_files_seized]. It was cited again at Eichmann's trial in Jerusalem in 1961 [cite:ushmm_wannsee_protocol].

The Höfle telegram, January 1943. The second document is a radio message. It was sent by SS-Sturmbannführer Höfle of the staff of the SS and police leader in Lublin, the adjutant to Globocnik, and it was intercepted on 11 January 1943. It reported arrivals at four camps as of 31 December 1942, under single-letter codes: L (Majdanek) 24,733; B (Belzec) 434,508; S (Sobibor) 101,370; and T (Treblinka) 713,555. The total was 1,274,166 [cite:rs_rd4_tna_hoefle_blog] [cite:rs_rd4_sobibor_hoefle] [cite:rs_rd4_hdot_numbers]. The decrypt text held by The National Archives in Britain shows the Treblinka figure as 71,355. The archive notes that this figure is missing a digit; with 713,555, the four camp figures sum to the stated total of 1,274,166 [cite:rs_rd4_tna_hoefle_blog] [cite:rs_rd4_sobibor_hoefle]. According to Sobibor.org and Holocaust Denial on Trial, the telegram also gave figures for the last two weeks of 1942: L 12,761, B 0, S 515 and T 10,335, a total of 23,611 [cite:rs_rd4_sobibor_hoefle] [cite:rs_rd4_hdot_numbers].

The message was one of many German police messages decoded at Bletchley Park. The decrypt is held at The National Archives, Kew, among the GC&CS records, under catalogue reference HW 16/23, dated January 1943 [cite:rs_rd4_tna_hoefle_blog] [cite:rs_rd4_tna_hw16_23]. The sources differ on two points. The National Archives and Holocaust Denial on Trial state that the decrypt was discovered in 2000 among newly declassified records. Sobibor.org dates the discovery to 2001, citing its publication that year by the historians P. Witte and S. Tyas in Holocaust and Genocide Studies, volume 14-3, pages 468–486 [cite:rs_rd4_tna_hoefle_blog] [cite:rs_rd4_hdot_numbers] [cite:rs_rd4_sobibor_hoefle]. The difference may be one of discovery against publication; the sources do not settle it. They also differ on the addressee. The decrypt at Kew is addressed to SS-Obersturmbannführer Heim, Commander of the Security Police in Cracow [cite:rs_rd4_tna_hoefle_blog]. Holocaust Denial on Trial says the figures were sent to Eichmann in Berlin, which would imply a parallel message [cite:rs_rd4_hdot_numbers]. No such second message is described in the sources consulted here.

The Korherr Report, 1943. The same figure appears again in a report that Heinrich Himmler commissioned from the SS statistician Richard Korherr under the title "The Final Solution of the European Jewish Question." According to the Holocaust Memorial Museum, Korherr finished it in January 1943 and gave it to Dr. Rudolf Brandt in March, and a summary was later passed to Hitler [cite:rs_rd4_ushmm_korherr_nachlass] [cite:rs_rd4_hdot_numbers]. Yad Vashem's translation, dated 23 March 1943, gives total evacuations "including Theresienstadt and Special Treatment" of 1,873,549, or 1,786,356 without Theresienstadt [cite:rs_rd4_yv_korherr_text]. Holocaust Denial on Trial reports that the Korherr Report repeats Höfle's exact figure of 1,274,166 for the four camps of Operation Reinhard, and that its figures for the Jews of France (41,911) and Belgium (16,886) closely match the transport lists (41,941 and 16,861) [cite:rs_rd4_hdot_numbers]. On that account, a radio intercept held in British archives and a statistical report written for Himmler give the same number.

The report also shows how the regime managed its own vocabulary. Himmler ordered that the term Sonderbehandlung, "special treatment," of the Jews not be used. Korherr was told to substitute wording meaning "processed through the camps in the Government-General," durchgeschleust. One instance of "Special Treatment" nevertheless remained in the final version [cite:rs_rd4_ushmm_korherr_nachlass] [cite:rs_rd4_hdot_numbers]. The Holocaust Memorial Museum has acquired Korherr's personal papers, Accession 2021.201.1, in 6,142 digital images. They contain two copies of the report [cite:rs_rd4_ushmm_korherr_nachlass].

The Stroop Report, May 1943. The suppression of the Warsaw Ghetto uprising, from 19 April to 16 May 1943, was recorded in an album prepared by SS Major General Jürgen Stroop. Three albums were made, for Himmler, for Krüger and for Stroop himself [cite:rs_rd4_ushmm_stroop_photo] [cite:rs_rd4_barch_stroop]. Copies are held today at the United States National Archives, at the Bundesarchiv in Germany and at Poland's Institute of National Remembrance. The copy used at Nuremberg is in the United States National Archives. The Bundesarchiv states that its own copy was held shortly after the war by SHAEF and reached the Bundesarchiv only in 2005, from the British Foreign Office Research Department's "German Collection" [cite:rs_rd4_barch_stroop]. In the English translation published by the Holocaust History Project, Stroop's teletype of 16 May 1943 reports: "Total number of Jews dealt with 56,065, including both Jews caught and Jews whose extermination can be proved" [cite:rs_rd4_stroop_teletype]. The Holocaust Memorial Museum summarizes the total differently in two places: as "some 56,000" killed or captured, and as "more than 55,000" captured, of whom at least 7,000 were killed [cite:rs_rd4_ushmm_stroop_photo] [cite:rs_rd4_ushmm_denial_nuremberg]. The sources consulted here do not reconcile the teletype's figure with the two summaries.

Himmler at Posen, October 1943. On 4 October 1943 Himmler addressed SS generals at Posen. The United States National Archives holds his handwritten notes for the speech. They use the euphemism Judenevakuierung, "evacuation of the Jews," and the archive states that in sound recordings of the speech Himmler defined "evacuation" as "extermination" [cite:rs_rd4_nara_himmler_notes]. In the speech, Nuremberg document 1919-PS, he spoke of "the extermination (Ausrottung) of the Jewish people" as a page of glory that was never to be written. A transcript runs to 116 pages [cite:rs_rd4_nww2m_posen] [cite:rs_rd4_ghdi_posen] [cite:rs_rd4_ushmm_evidence]. On the National Archives' account, the recordings show what "evacuation" meant in the speech of the man who had ordered that "special treatment" not be used in Korherr's report.

Capture and authentication, 1945. The documents reached the courtroom through a deliberate process of seizure, selection and certification. On 22 November 1945, before the International Military Tribunal, Colonel Robert Storey testified that "literally hundreds of tons of enemy documents and records were screened and examined," and that more than 2,500 documents had been selected and filed at the Nuremberg courthouse, with the originals kept in safes in the Document Room [cite:rs_rd4_avalon_storey]. Each American document received a trial identification number in one of five letter series that indicated how it had been acquired, among them L, R, C and EC; documents such as 2903-PS carry the PS suffix. On 19 November 1945 Major Coogan signed an affidavit, document 001-A-PS, entered as Exhibit USA-1, certifying the photostats as true copies of the originals [cite:rs_rd4_avalon_storey] [cite:rs_rd4_harvard_coogan]. The Holocaust Memorial Museum states that the Allies presented roughly 3,000 tons of documents and records at Nuremberg, drawn from millions of Nazi documents seized in 1945, and that a 1958 National Archives catalog of the captured records ran to 62 volumes [cite:rs_rd4_ushmm_denial_nuremberg].

The records were preserved in copies before the originals went home. The Nuremberg records are in the United States National Archives as Record Group 238. The captured-document series were microfilmed, among them NG (publication T1139, 70 rolls), NI (T301, 164 rolls) and NOKW (T1119, 47 rolls), and the Tribunal's proceedings were published in 42 volumes [cite:rs_rd4_nara_imt_records]. In the early 1950s the Department of the Army, working with the American Historical Association, microfilmed captured records before the originals were returned; by March 1968 the Army had returned 35 shipments to Germany [cite:rs_rd4_nara_return].

The documentary record was matched by a visual one. On 12 April 1945 General Eisenhower visited the camp at Ohrdruf with Generals Patton and Bradley. That day he cabled General George C. Marshall: "The things I saw beggar description." On 19 April he asked Marshall to bring members of Congress and editors to the camps, so that the evidence could not be dismissed as propaganda [cite:rs_rd4_ushmm_ohrdruf]. On 29 November 1945, introduced by the American prosecutor Thomas Dodd, the prosecution at the International Military Tribunal showed an hour-long film, The Nazi Concentration Camps, compiled from footage shot as Allied troops liberated the camps, with clips credited to George Stevens [cite:rs_rd4_ushmm_film] [cite:rs_rd4_ushmm_film_article].

Höss's affidavits and the Auschwitz figure. Not every number in the trial record has stood. The commandant of Auschwitz, Rudolf Höss, signed affidavit 3868-PS at Nuremberg on 5 April 1946. In it he estimated that "at least 2,500,000 victims were executed and exterminated" at Auschwitz by gassing and burning, and that "at least another half million succumbed to starvation and disease making a total dead of about 3,000,000" [cite:rs_rd4_harvard_hoess_3868] [cite:rs_rd4_avalon_hoess]. Testifying before the Tribunal on 15 April 1946, he confirmed the affidavit's contents as true and agreed that Eichmann had told him more than 2 million Jews had been destroyed at Auschwitz. He stated that he had commanded Auschwitz from May 1940 until December 1943 [cite:rs_rd4_avalon_hoess]. In a further affidavit, dated 14 May 1946, he gave 2 million Jews gassed and 500,000 killed by other means [cite:rs_rd4_ushmm_hoess_affidavit].

The Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum states that Höss's figures were "highly overinflated," as Höss himself later said while in Polish custody. The Museum likewise treats as overinflated the Soviet figure of 4 million. The research of Franciszek Piper, published in 1990, gave 1.1 million as the most probable number of victims, and the Museum's present figures are that about 1.3 million people were deported to Auschwitz, of whom about 1.1 million were murdered [cite:rs_rd4_auschwitz_victims]. Höss's total of about 3,000,000 is nearly three times the Museum's figure of about 1.1 million.

Jerusalem, 1961. Adolf Eichmann had edited the Wannsee minutes. His trial of Adolf Eichmann, criminal case 40/61 of the Jerusalem District Court, opened on 11 April 1961. Some 1,600 documents were selected as evidence, most of them bearing Eichmann's signature, and a list of 108 survivor witnesses was prepared [cite:rs_rd4_yv_eichmann_trial]. The sources differ on the date of the verdict. The Holocaust Memorial Museum gives the guilty finding as 11–12 December 1961 and the death sentence as 15 December [cite:rs_rd4_ushmm_eichmann_guilty]. Yad Vashem states that the trial ended on 15 December 1961 with the reading of the verdict, and elsewhere gives 13 December for the guilty finding [cite:rs_rd4_yv_eichmann_trial]. The sources agree that he was sentenced to death on 15 December 1961 and hanged at Ramla prison on 1 June 1962 [cite:rs_rd4_ushmm_eichmann_guilty] [cite:rs_rd4_yv_eichmann_trial].

The Arolsen Archives. The Arolsen Archives hold records concerning the victims rather than the perpetrators. The Allies founded the International Tracing Service in 1948; it is now the Arolsen Archives. It holds information on about 17.5 million people and is part of UNESCO's Memory of the World [cite:rs_rd4_arolsen_profile]. According to a report of the Congressional Research Service, the eleven-nation International Commission agreed in May 2006 to amend the 1955 Bonn Accords, and the archives, then described as some 50 million documents, opened to the public on 28 November 2007 [cite:rs_rd4_crs_its].

What the documents do not show. The perpetrators' records count in their own categories. The Höfle telegram records arrivals at camps, not deaths. The Korherr Report counts "evacuations," and its author was ordered to replace "special treatment" with a phrase about being processed through camps. Himmler's notes say "evacuation," and only the recordings of his speech supply the meaning. The Wannsee Protocol is an edited summary, not a transcript: it records the substance Eichmann chose to set down and, as the account of the meeting stresses, no recorded objection, which is not the same as proof that no one in the room had doubts [cite:rs_rd4_ushmm_wannsee_protocol] [cite:ushmm_wannsee_protocol]. The Einsatzgruppen reports give different figures for the same massacre at Kiev, and the sources give the victims attributed to the Case 9 defendants as between 723,661 and one million (the indictment, per the Holocaust Memorial Museum) or more than one million (the prosecution's estimate, per Harvard's Nuremberg Trials Project).

Much of the record is also simply missing. Of thirty copies of the Wannsee Protocol, one has been found. The Höfle decrypt surfaced among newly declassified British records only in 2000 or 2001, and the Bundesarchiv's copy of the Stroop Report reached it only in 2005. The sources consulted here do not document what other records were destroyed, by whom, or when; that question lies outside the research for this section and is left open. Nor does any single document hold the whole number. The documents described here cover particular units, particular camps, particular periods and particular cities. The total of six million is built, as [scene:hol_s05|How the Number Is Known] shows, by joining them to demographic reconstruction and to the naming of victims one by one. According to Holocaust Denial on Trial, a radio intercept found at Kew in 2000 or 2001 and a statistical report written for Himmler in 1943 give the same figure, 1,274,166. Neither was written for the courts. Himmler had ordered that the term "special treatment" not be used in the second.

sections.h: The American Zionist Emergency Council, 1943–1945
sections.html:
In August 1943, five years before there was a state to lobby for, the leading American Zionist organizations placed their political work under a single body: the American Zionist Emergency Council (AZEC). A familiar account holds that American political support for Israel grew up after 1948, a natural response to the founding of a new democracy. The council's own papers point to an earlier and more deliberate origin. By the time independence was declared, a functioning domestic political organization had already been built, staffed and run for five years. It worked in the open and within the law. Its purpose was to turn the movement's goals into congressional votes and party platforms.

Before 1943 the major American Zionist organizations had operated under separate leaderships and sometimes pursued competing priorities. The council pooled their resources for one purpose, domestic political influence, and ran them as one coordinated operation [cite:azec_powerbase]. Rabbi Abba Hillel Silver and Rabbi Stephen Wise were its first co-chairs [cite:azec_case]. Its importance outlasted its own years: through a documented line of succession, the council became the direct institutional predecessor of AIPAC [cite:azec_powerbase]. That later history belongs to other volumes of this library. What matters here is that the organization existed, and worked, during the war.

It came into being a little more than a year after the Biltmore conference of May 1942 had committed the movement to a "Jewish Commonwealth" in Palestine, and as another, rival campaign was already filling American newspapers with full-page advertisements: the Bergson group's committees, whose story is told in [scene:bg_s01|the Bergson group's campaign]. The council was the mainstream's answer, and its method was different. Where the Bergson committees bought space and staged pageants, the council built a standing national network that could be pointed at Congress on a given week.

Silver's break with quiet diplomacy. The two co-chairs did not share a view of how the work should be done. Silver argued for energetic public-opinion pressure and firm political mobilization. Earlier Zionist leaders had preferred a more cautious diplomatic approach, and Silver's course was an explicit and named departure from it, not a continuation of established practice [cite:azec_case]. Not everyone in the council or the wider movement agreed with the shift. The same period saw a comparable contest over method between Chaim Weizmann and David Ben-Gurion, told in the section on [scene:s07b|the Biltmore Program]. Inside the council the disagreement was serious enough that Silver resigned as co-chairman during a controversy in 1944–45 over how hard the organization should confront the American government; his own archived papers document the episode. He was later reinstated and led the council through 1949 [cite:azec_powerbase]. The internal conflict is part of the record, not a footnote to it.

The method, from the council's own files. The fullest account of how the council worked comes from its internal correspondence, preserved among the Abba Hillel Silver Papers at the American Jewish Archives. These are the organizers' own memos, and they describe a national method run from a New York headquarters at 342 Madison Avenue. Instructions went out to "Chairmen of Local Emergency Committees" in cities across the country [cite:aja_azec_local_1944].

The first test came quickly. When Senators Robert Wagner and Robert Taft introduced their Palestine resolution in January 1944, a memo told the local chairmen that they would be sent sample letters, so that within a concentrated period letters from all over the country would "pour into Washington." The same instructions told local committees to interview their senators and representatives in person and to place letters to the editor in their local newspapers [cite:aja_azec_local_1944] [cite:aja_azec_local_1945]. The sequence below follows those instructions step by step.

Telegram campaigns were aimed at particular members by name. Among them was Representative Sol Bloom, chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee [cite:aja_azec_local_1944]. The council also published a book, America and Palestine, and sent it to every member of Congress. It printed the pro-Zionist statements of nearly 400 members of the 78th Congress, so that each legislator could see in print the public commitments his own colleagues had already made [cite:aja_azec_silver_resignation]. One reading is that the book turned scattered statements into a visible majority and reminded each member that his own words were on record.

The same machinery carried on after the war ended in Europe. In 1945, with Harry Truman now president, local councils mobilized thousands of telegrams to the White House. In Detroit alone, 150 Zionist and community leaders organized the appeal [cite:aja_azec_local_1945]. The council did not reserve its pressure for opponents. In 1948, after Bloom remarked that Truman was "on the right track" during the administration's retreat toward a trusteeship for Palestine, an AZEC staff memo called the remark "horrible" and urged that people in Bloom's district take it up with him [cite:aja_bloom_1948]. That episode lies beyond this chapter, but it shows the method fully formed: an ally who drifted was handled through his own constituents.

One further claim comes from a critic's history rather than from the council's papers, and it should be read as such. According to that account, mail addressed to Senator Wagner in his capacity as chairman of the American Palestine Committee was opened and kept at Zionist headquarters, and Wagner was sent a copy [cite:hnn_clark_truman]. The council's own files, as cited here, do not confirm or refute it. It remains a reported claim from a single critical source.

What the campaign achieved, and when. The results came fast. Silver's biographical record credits his lobbying in 1944 with securing a Palestine resolution in Congress, and in the same year both major parties wrote Palestine into their platforms [cite:azec_case]. The congressional record, set out in the next section, is more exact about what "passage" meant. The House Foreign Affairs Committee approved the resolution on 30 November 1944; the full Congress deferred it that December, and a version was adopted only in December 1945 [cite:aja_azec_dec1944] [cite:frus1945_concres]. Both accounts agree on the substance: within roughly a year of its founding, the council had moved Palestine into the language of both parties and through a congressional committee, four years before there was a state. How those votes and platforms came about is told in [scene:us_s05|Palestine in Congress and the party platforms].

The money behind the movement. The council's files document a method, not a budget. They show organization: memos, sample letters, a book mailed to Congress, telegrams. They do not show money changing hands with legislators, and that is the finding the record supports. The money in the American movement during these years flowed through a different channel: philanthropic giving through the United Jewish Appeal.

The scale of that giving is set out in the library's funding ledger, drawing on Marc Lee Raphael's history of the United Jewish Appeal. In its first year, 1939, the appeal raised $14 million, about $324 million in 2025 dollars. Across the war years, 1939 to 1945, it raised more than $124 million, about $2.4 billion today. The ledger converts each sum using the federal consumer price index, and it carries one caution that matters for any reading of these figures. The campaign split its money three ways: relief for Jews in Europe, the Palestine program, and the resettlement of refugees in the United States. Counting the whole sum as "funding Israel" would overstate what went to Palestine. The ledger's precise split is documented for 1948, when about half of the year's $150 million went to the Palestine arm, about 43% to relief in Europe and the rest to resettlement in the United States; for the war years the record here gives the three destinations but not the shares.

The second panel places the wartime giving on the longer curve. The war years averaged roughly $0.35 billion a year in today's dollars. After 1945 the totals rose steeply, to about $1.65 billion in 1946 and about $2.0 billion in 1948. The rise belongs to the next stage of the story. What the wartime figures show is a giving network that existed alongside, not inside, the political campaign the council ran. The appeal's money went to relief, the Palestine program and resettlement; the council's work in Congress ran on letters, visits and telegrams.

Organized and sincere. The council's papers settle one question and leave another open. They settle that American political support for a Jewish commonwealth did not simply arise of its own accord. It was organized, timed and aimed, from a headquarters with a mailing list, against named members on named dates. They do not show that the sympathy behind the letters was manufactured. The letters were sincere, and the sympathy was real; the council's achievement was to organize both. That method, not money, is what the movement's own files document most fully. Both statements hold together, and neither cancels the other.

The map of the two American machines, the Bergson committees and the council, appears with the account of the Bergson group earlier in this chapter. The map below places the council in the longer structure, the half-century from the Basel Congress to the State of Israel, where it stands as the "US political machine" between the Jewish Agency and the United Nations.

What the record does not settle. The council's files prove a sustained, organized campaign. They do not prove that the council alone set American policy toward Palestine. Truman's eventual decision to recognize Israel in 1948 had several causes, among them domestic electoral calculation and the competing objections of the State Department, and the council's five years of pressure were one factor among them, not the sole or sufficient explanation [cite:azec_powerbase]. Nor does the record here measure how many letters were drafted from the council's samples and how many were written unprompted, or how far any member's vote moved because of them. The papers show what the organizers did; they cannot show what each legislator would have done without them.

sections.h: Palestine in Congress and the Party Platforms, 1944–1945
sections.html:
It is often assumed that Congress and the two American parties took up Palestine only after the war, and then on its merits. The record of 1944 tells a different story. In that election year a resolution for a Jewish commonwealth went before both houses, the Army and the War Department asked Congress to shelve it, both parties wrote Palestine into their platforms, for the first time by the council's own appraisal, and the War Department dropped its objection days before the November vote. The State Department then held the resolution back again. A changed version passed only in December 1945. The story turns as much on the timing of these moves as on their content, and much of it can be read in the American Zionist Emergency Council's own records.

The longer frame. Congress had spoken on Palestine before. After President Wilson endorsed the Balfour Declaration in 1918, Congress passed the Lodge–Fish resolution unanimously in 1922, an episode told in an earlier chapter of this library. Over the following three decades its pattern held. Congress passed or pushed resolutions of support. It never voted to create a Jewish state or to recognize one: partition and recognition, when they came, were acts of the executive [cite:w_celler] [cite:w_sol_bloom]. Congress shaped the climate; the executive made the decisions. The resolutions of 1944–45 belong to that pattern.

The resolutions of January 1944. Early in 1944 two matching resolutions were introduced, each with one Democratic and one Republican sponsor. In the House they were Representatives James Wright, a Democrat of Pennsylvania, and Ranulf Compton, a Republican of Connecticut. In the Senate they were Robert Wagner, a Democrat of New York, and Robert Taft, a Republican of Ohio. Both called for unrestricted Jewish immigration to Palestine and for a "free and democratic Jewish commonwealth" [cite:djn_1944_hearings] [cite:aja_azec_dec1944]. Both demands ran against the British policy of the day, set out in [scene:rd4_white_paper|the White Paper of 1939]. The council's local committees began their first nationwide letter campaign the same month, as the previous section describes [cite:aja_azec_local_1944].

The House Foreign Affairs Committee held hearings. Not every Jewish witness supported the resolution. Among the opponents was Rabbi Morris Lazaron, who told the committee that Zionism was an internal Jewish matter and not a question for Congress [cite:djn_1944_hearings]. His testimony is a reminder that American Jewish opinion in 1944 was not unanimous, and that some of the resistance came from inside the community the council claimed to speak for.

The generals ask for delay. In March 1944 the Army Chief of Staff, General George Marshall, and the Secretary of War, Henry Stimson, asked Congress to postpone action for military reasons. The committee deferred [cite:djn_1944_marshall]. The council's records describe the same step: Stimson opposed the Wagner–Taft resolution on military grounds, and it was put aside [cite:aja_azec_dec1944] [cite:aja_azec_1944_record]. The War Department's case was about the conduct of a war still being fought. The sources here do not set out its full reasoning. The State Department, for its part, had its own plan, approved by Roosevelt, to suppress public discussion of the Palestine question for the duration of the war; that plan and Roosevelt's two registers on Palestine are examined in [scene:s07c2|Roosevelt's wartime position].

"The first time in American history." Blocked in Congress, the issue moved to the parties. That summer both party conventions adopted Palestine planks. The council's own appraisal of the year called it "the first time in American history that Palestine was included in the party platforms" [cite:aja_azec_appraisal_1944]. For an organization founded only the previous August, this was a striking result. It meant that in a presidential election year Palestine had become a matter on which both parties had taken a public position, and on which their candidates could be held to account.

The objection withdrawn, days before the election. In October Stimson wrote to Senator Taft. According to the record of that letter, he told Taft that political considerations now outweighed military ones [cite:aja_silver_1944]. Days before the November election, the War Department had in effect withdrawn its objection [cite:aja_azec_dec1944] [cite:aja_azec_1944_record]. On 30 November, after the election, the House Foreign Affairs Committee approved the resolution [cite:aja_azec_dec1944]. Then, in December 1944, action was deferred again. The council's records attribute the deferral to the insistence of the State Department; another account describes it as a deferral at the administration's request [cite:aja_azec_dec1944] [cite:aja_silver_1944]. The setback prompted an internal crisis at the council [cite:aja_azec_1944_record]. Silver resigned as co-chairman during a 1944–45 controversy over how hard to press the government, as the previous section notes; the record here does not say whether that controversy and this crisis were one and the same.

December 1945: a different text. The resolution came back after the war, with Truman in the White House. On 17 and 19 December 1945 both houses adopted a concurrent resolution [cite:frus1945_concres]. It had the support of the American Palestine Committee and the Christian Council on Palestine [cite:wiki_american_palestine_committee]. Its wording had changed, and the State Department noticed. A department memorandum observed that the resolution called not for a "Jewish commonwealth" but for a "democratic commonwealth in which all men, regardless of race or creed, shall have equal rights" [cite:frus1945_concres]. The phrase that had defined the 1944 text was gone.

Who carried it. The champions in Congress were named members of both parties. Wagner and Taft led in the Senate. In the House, Representative Emanuel Celler of Brooklyn and Sol Bloom, chairman of the Foreign Affairs Committee, were among the leading supporters [cite:w_celler] [cite:w_sol_bloom]. Bloom was also, as the council's own files show, a target of its telegram campaigns: the council pressed its allies as well as its opponents [cite:aja_azec_local_1944].

How the structure worked. The episode shows who held which lever. Members of Congress could introduce and approve resolutions, and the party conventions could adopt planks; both were open to organized constituent pressure, which is where the council concentrated its work. The War Department and the State Department could not vote, but they could ask committees to wait, and in 1944 they did so twice. The force of a resolution or a plank, as the council's own use of them shows, lay in putting members and parties on record. By 1944 Palestine had become a party-platform and election-timing issue, with the military and diplomatic bureaucracies on the other side. It is the same alignment the record shows again in Truman's decisions of 1947–48.

Reading the timing. The sequence invites two readings, and the record supports parts of each. One reads the year as the work of electoral politics: a resolution shelved on military grounds in March was cleared by the Secretary of War in a letter to a Republican senator days before a presidential election, after both parties had written the issue into their platforms. Stimson's own reported words, that political considerations now outweighed military ones, give this reading its strongest support [cite:aja_silver_1944]. The other reading takes the military objection at face value. The resolution came while the war was still being fought; Marshall and Stimson asked only for postponement, not rejection; and after the election the executive branch, through the State Department, again asked Congress to wait, which an administration acting only on electoral motives had no reason to do. The second deferral fits that reading better than the first.

What the record does not settle. The sources here do not show who asked Stimson to write to Taft, or what he weighed beyond the one sentence the record preserves. They do not give the vote counts of December 1945, or explain who changed the resolution's wording from "Jewish commonwealth" to "equal rights," and why. They do not say whether the 1945 text kept the 1944 call for unrestricted immigration. And they do not measure how far the council's letters, telegrams and visits moved any member's position, as against the views members already held. What they do show is that by the end of 1944, four years before statehood, Palestine had been placed inside American electoral politics by an organized campaign, and that the War and State Departments were already its main opponents inside the government.

sections.h: Roosevelt's Hidden Decline and the Choice of Truman, 1944
sections.html:
On 28 March 1944, seven months before the presidential election, a Navy cardiologist examined Franklin Roosevelt and found serious heart disease. The familiar account of the 1944 campaign treats the president's health as a private matter and the doubts raised about it as partisan exaggeration by his opponents. The medical record shows otherwise. The diagnosis was kept secret. Roosevelt's official physician told the public the opposite of what the cardiologist had found. A second doctor's written judgment that the president would probably not survive another term was locked in a vault for more than sixty years. And the man chosen that year as Roosevelt's running mate, who would inherit the presidency and with it the American decisions on Palestine, was kept as uninformed as the voters.

The story belongs in a history of Palestine for one reason. The American commitments of these years, Roosevelt's private assurances to Arab leaders and the public promises of the 1944 platforms, would be carried out or broken by his successor. Who that successor would be was settled in 1944, by a party convention working without the medical facts.

The diagnosis. The examination took place at Bethesda. The cardiologist, Dr. Howard Bruenn, found acute congestive heart failure, an enlarged heart, hypertension and hypertensive heart disease. Bruenn was sworn to secrecy. He did not volunteer a prognosis even to Roosevelt himself, who, by the available account, asked no questions [cite:wiki_dying_president_ferrell]. One historian later wrote that the findings were guarded "on a level with the Manhattan Project." The comparison is striking, but it rests on a documented examination with specific findings, kept from public knowledge by design. What the record does not show is Roosevelt's own state of mind: that he asked no questions is documented; what he privately understood or suspected is not.

The public statement. Roosevelt's official physician since 1933 was Ross McIntire, an ear, nose and throat specialist with no training in cardiology. McIntire assured the press and the nation that the president was "in excellent condition for a man of his age" and that his health was "excellent in all respects" [cite:boston_globe_lahey_memo]. These were not vague reassurances or a difference of medical interpretation. They were specific, quoted public statements, and they contradicted the cardiologist's findings of the same period. The record documents the contradiction. It does not establish McIntire's motive, or exactly how much of Bruenn's findings he knew at the moment he spoke.

The Lahey memorandum. A second physician was consulted separately. Frank Lahey, a Boston surgeon, set down his conclusion in a written memo dated 10 July 1944: Roosevelt was unlikely to survive a full fourth term. The memo was placed in a Boston law firm's vault. It was not found and made public until decades after Roosevelt's death, more than sixty years after it was written [cite:boston_globe_lahey_memo]. The record establishes the memo's content, its date and its eventual disclosure. It does not establish who knew of it in the intervening decades.

Why the vice-presidency mattered. The 1944 Democratic convention replaced the sitting vice-president, Henry Wallace, with Senator Harry Truman of Missouri [cite:wiki_1944_dnc] [cite:wiki_choosing_truman]. The reasons for Wallace's removal, and the question of whether Palestine had anything to do with it, are examined in [scene:s07c4|Henry Wallace and Zionism]. Set beside what Roosevelt's doctors knew, the choice of a running mate was in practice, though not in public understanding, the choice of the next president, and the voters who ratified it in November did not know that. The record draws a line here that should be kept. It does not show that every party leader involved in replacing Wallace knew the specifics of Bruenn's or Lahey's findings. Historical accounts document a general awareness among them that the president's health was declining and that this had political consequences, not knowledge of the diagnosis itself.

Why Truman. The documented reasons for choosing Truman were political. As chairman of the wartime Truman Committee, which investigated profiteering by defense contractors, he had earned real credibility and was ranked by 1944 among the most respected officials in Washington. He was acceptable to the labor unions and had supported the New Deal. But he had also opposed Roosevelt's earlier bid for a third term, which made him tolerable to the conservative Southern Democrats who distrusted Wallace's leftward tilt. Contemporary observers mocked the choice as "the Missouri Compromise," because Truman was no faction's first choice, only a candidate enough factions could accept [cite:trumanlibrary_missouri_compromise] [cite:wiki_1944_dem_vp_selection] [cite:legalclarity_truman_1944_vp].

One complication in his background was real, and it was political. Truman's career had been launched by Tom Pendergast, the corrupt political boss of Kansas City, and party leaders had to work to establish that Truman was not "a Pendergast lackey" [cite:trumanlibrary_missouri_compromise] [cite:legalclarity_truman_1944_vp]. The connection was discussed and had to be answered. A different theory is sometimes offered: that Truman was chosen because his personal finances or tax affairs left him open to pressure. No documented evidence connects his selection to his finances or to any tax matter [cite:trumanlibrary_missouri_compromise] [cite:wiki_1944_dem_vp_selection]. On the record, Truman won the nomination by being broadly tolerable, not because anyone held something over him.

Truman kept in the dark. Several historical accounts describe the new vice-president as kept "entirely in the dark" about how ill Roosevelt was [cite:globalsecurity_fdr_veiled_decline]. The man about to inherit the presidency, and with it the American side of every decision on Palestine that this library follows through 1948, had no more medical information than the public. That claim has a limit. Public speculation about Roosevelt's appearance and vigor was itself widespread and documented, and the accounts do not say Truman had no sense at all that the president was failing. What they say is that he lacked the specific findings Bruenn and Lahey had made.

Roosevelt died on 12 April 1945, two months after his meeting with King Ibn Saud aboard the USS Quincy and a week after his written assurance to the king [cite:arabnews_fdr_ibnsaud]. That meeting and the letter that followed it are told in [scene:s07ca|the Great Bitter Lake meeting]. Their fate passed to a president who had not been told how soon he might have to keep, or break, them.

What the record does not settle. The documents establish the diagnosis, the public statements that contradicted it, the hidden memo and Truman's exclusion from the medical facts. They do not establish what Roosevelt himself believed about his prognosis, what McIntire knew when he spoke, or which party leaders, if any, knew the specific findings when they chose Truman. Nor can they say how the election, or the vice-presidential choice, would have gone had the voters known. Whether the course of American policy on Palestine would have differed under a healthier Roosevelt is a question this record cannot answer, and this book does not speculate on it.

sections.h: Henry Wallace and Zionism
sections.html:
In 1944 the Democratic Party replaced Vice President Henry Wallace on its ticket with Senator Harry Truman, the man who would become president within a year and who, in 1948, would recognize the state of Israel. Seen backwards from 1948, the swap invites a suspicion: that Wallace's views on Palestine had something to do with his removal. A version of the story circulates in which Zionist-aligned donors and organizations preferred Truman after Wallace said something unfavorable about Palestine or about Jews. The documented record answers the question directly, and at each point it runs the other way.

Start with Wallace himself. His interest in Zionism began in the 1930s, while he was serving as Roosevelt's Secretary of Agriculture, and it came through a working relationship rather than a political one. The soil scientist Walter Clay Lowdermilk had examined agricultural conditions in British Mandatory Palestine, and Wallace absorbed his enthusiasm. Wallace later recalled of Lowdermilk: "I don't think he has any Jewish blood, but he was the most complete Zionist convert anyone could ask for." Through that influence Wallace came to see the Jewish settlers in Palestine as frontiersmen on the American pattern. [cite:aish_wallace_zionist] [cite:algemeiner_wallace_zionist] The point that matters for 1944 is the date. Wallace's sympathy was a personal conviction that he described in his own later recollection, and it predated the convention fight by roughly a decade. That fixes where the conviction came from. It does not prove that every later public statement he made on Palestine was free of political calculation, and the sources do not claim that it was.

Then the removal. Historical accounts state plainly that Roosevelt grew wary of Wallace's left-wing, pro-Soviet political tilt, and that this broader concern, not any statement about Palestine, Jews or Zionism, drove the push to replace him. [cite:wiki_1944_dnc] [cite:aish_wallace_zionist] Nor was the decision quiet or uncontested. Wallace kept real support to the end. Labor organizations, including the CIO and the UAW, campaigned for him at the convention itself, and a Gallup poll taken on the day of the convention showed 65% of delegates still favoring Wallace over Truman. [cite:wiki_1944_dnc] That figure describes a contested, actively fought political battle over the general ideological direction of the party, with the man who lost it still the delegates' preference on the day. That is hard to square with the picture of a quiet substitution arranged to please one constituency.

Why the choice of running mate carried so much weight in 1944 is told in [scene:s07c3|Roosevelt's hidden decline]: the president's doctors knew how ill he was, the voters did not, and the vice-presidential slot was in practice a choice of the next president. The same section sets out the documented reasons Truman was chosen in Wallace's place. What concerns this section is narrower. The sources identify the general pattern historians treat as the main driver of Wallace's removal, and that pattern has no documented connection to Palestine or Zionism. They do not claim an exhaustive account of every reason every delegate or party official opposed him, and a minor factor cannot be ruled out from them. What they do show is that the Palestine explanation has no documentary basis, while the ideological one does.

Wallace did not leave the story in 1944. Four years later, running for president as the candidate of the Progressive Party, he returned to the Palestine question from the side opposite to the one the common assumption gives him. The events belong to the period after this chapter, and only their outline is needed here. His campaign literature included a booklet, Meet Henry Wallace, written by James Waterman Wise, the son of Rabbi Stephen Wise, the Zionist leader whose wartime dealings with Roosevelt run through this chapter. The booklet carried a half-page photograph of Wallace "helping the Jewish settlers in Galilee harvest their fields." At rallies Wallace accused Truman of "playing politics with the lives of the people of Israel," aiming directly at Truman's arms embargo on the newly declared state. That attack was the center of his appeal to Jewish voters. [cite:aish_wallace_zionist] It was not the center of his campaign as a whole, which was built mainly on opposition to Cold War policy and support for continued engagement with the Soviet Union. Israel was one real, deliberate element of a broader platform, not its foundation.

The appeal had a measurable effect. New York newspapers reported widespread talk of Jewish voters leaving Truman for Wallace out of dissatisfaction with Truman's Palestine record, and the result was documented as the lowest share of the New York Jewish vote for any Democratic presidential candidate in modern history, except Jimmy Carter's. [cite:aish_wallace_zionist] [cite:algemeiner_wallace_zionist] The sources credit Truman's Palestine record as a contributing factor in that decline, not its only cause. Other parts of Wallace's campaign, and general dissatisfaction with Truman, likely contributed as well.

Put together, the record reverses the assumption twice. In 1944 Wallace was removed for reasons that had nothing documented to do with Palestine, and he was himself a long-standing sympathizer of the Zionist project. In 1948 he became one of Truman's most direct critics from the pro-Israel side, and that criticism cost Truman votes in New York. If the episode points to any electoral incentive, it points the opposite way from the one usually assumed: in the 1948 record it is being seen as insufficiently pro-Israel, not too closely tied to the cause, that carried a cost. That is an inference from one election in one state, and it should be held at that scope. [cite:aish_wallace_zionist]

Several things the record here does not settle. The sources give the New York result only as a ranking, not as a percentage, so the size of the shift cannot be stated from them. They do not separate how much of it came from the Palestine issue and how much from Wallace's wider campaign. And while they find no Palestine dimension to the 1944 decision, they do not record what, if anything, Wallace said in public about Palestine during his vice presidency. The belief that Wallace was pushed aside over Zionism has no documentary support, and the documents that exist point in the other direction.

sections.h: Roosevelt and Ibn Saud at Great Bitter Lake
sections.html:
On 14 February 1945, on his way home from the Yalta Conference, Franklin Roosevelt received King Abdulaziz Ibn Saud of Saudi Arabia aboard the USS Quincy in the Great Bitter Lake on the Suez Canal. [cite:brookings_quincy_75years] [cite:wiki_uss_quincy_ca71] The meeting was not a courtesy stop fitted into a crowded itinerary. Roosevelt arranged it himself, two months before his death and visibly declining. Ibn Saud, the founding monarch of Saudi Arabia, who reigned from 1932 to 1953, rarely left Arabia and had deep reservations about the journey, yet he traveled by ship specifically for the encounter. [cite:wiki_abdulaziz_saudi] Both men went to real, documented lengths to sit in the same room, and the principal subject between them was the future of Palestine.

Why an American president would make that effort has a plain answer in the record. By 1945 the Arabian American Oil Company, ARAMCO, had already established the core of the American–Saudi oil relationship. [cite:loc_aramco_oil_pamphlet] The meeting reflected an existing, high-stakes strategic partnership that the United States government understood clearly, and the Palestine question was becoming entangled with it. The sources establish that the relationship existed and mattered; they do not set out the full scope of ARAMCO's operations or the specific terms of the oil relationship at this date, and nothing here should be read as a claim about them.

The meeting ran for roughly five hours by one account and five and a half by another, longer than most of Roosevelt's wartime sessions with other heads of state. [cite:brookings_quincy_75years] [cite:quincy_meeting_1945] Roosevelt, a habitual chain-smoker, did not smoke throughout it, out of respect for the king's preference. [cite:quincy_meeting_1945] Its official record is a memorandum of conversation drafted by William Eddy, the United States Minister to Saudi Arabia, and Yusuf Yassin, the Saudi Deputy Foreign Minister. Both leaders signed it, and the State Department later published it in its own documentary series, Foreign Relations of the United States. [cite:quincy_meeting_1945] The memorandum is a summary agreed by both sides, not a transcript. No complete stenographic record of the conversation survives, so specific exchanges quoted from the meeting beyond what the memorandum and the later correspondence document should be treated with caution.

The substance was contested, not ceremonial. Roosevelt argued the case for Jewish settlement in Palestine: one account describes him arguing for a Jewish state, the memorandum-based account for a Jewish national home. [cite:wiki_abdulaziz_saudi] [cite:quincy_meeting_1945] By multiple accounts, Ibn Saud pressed back directly and forcefully, describing continued large-scale Jewish immigration as an existential threat to Arab interests in the region. When Roosevelt raised the question of Jewish immigration, the king answered that Jews displaced by Nazi persecution should be given land in Germany, "in the country of their enemies," as he reportedly put it, rather than in Palestine at the expense of its existing Arab population. [cite:ibn_saud_bavaria_quote] In another rendering of the same exchange he proposed that the Jews be given a state in Bavaria. [cite:wiki_abdulaziz_saudi] [cite:brookings_quincy_75years] The exchange is well attested, but it is one moment in a five-hour conversation and does not capture the whole of the king's position.

What Roosevelt gave the king was a specific assurance. The United States government, he said, would make no decision altering the basic situation in Palestine without full, prior consultation with both Arabs and Jews, and would take no action hostile to the Arab people. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] He came away pleased. He later called the meeting "so outstanding a success," and told his daughter Anna that he had "learned more about the whole problem of Palestine and the Middle East by talking with Ibn Saud for five minutes than I could have learned in an exchange of two or three dozen letters." [cite:brookings_quincy_75years]

The king did not leave it at a spoken promise. About three weeks after the meeting he wrote formally to Roosevelt, asking him to oppose continued Jewish settlement in Palestine. [cite:ibn_saud_bavaria_quote] Roosevelt answered on 5 April 1945, one week before his death. In that letter he affirmed that he would "take no action, in my capacity as Chief of the Executive Branch of this Government, which might prove hostile to the Arab people." [cite:fdr_letter_ibnsaud] The letter reaffirmed in writing the commitment made aboard the Quincy, which closes any gap between an informal verbal impression and a deliberate written undertaking by the president himself. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] One account describes Roosevelt as taking the king's concerns seriously enough to respond in writing more than once in the weeks after the meeting; the letter of 5 April is the one whose words the sources quote. The wording also limits the promise: it is given in Roosevelt's own capacity as head of the executive branch. Whether such a letter was an isolated gesture or part of a pattern is taken up in [scene:s07c2|Roosevelt's actual position on Zionism], which shows that the State Department, when it confirmed the letter in October 1945, described it as one of several such letters to Arab leaders.

Roosevelt died on 12 April 1945. On 14 May 1948 his successor, Harry Truman, recognized the state of Israel eleven minutes after its declaration, without the prior consultation with Arab leaders that Roosevelt had promised. [cite:arabnews_fdr_ibnsaud] One account traces the recognition decision through Clark Clifford's domestic electoral calculation rather than through consultation with Arab heads of state; that process belongs to the next stage of this history and is told there. The change between the two presidents is documented. What the documents do not show is Truman's own state of mind about Roosevelt's specific commitment: whether he was personally aware of it, considered himself bound by it, or set out to break it. That he knew of it is a reasonable inference from the continuity of the presidency, but it is an inference, not a finding.

The meeting answers two common assumptions. The first is that American support for a Jewish state ran consistently and without a break from Roosevelt to Truman. The record shows a president who, two months before his death, gave the Arab head of state most affected a direct assurance, spoken and then written, that the United States would not act on Palestine without consulting the Arabs, and a successor who acted without that consultation three years later. The second is that Saudi opposition to a Jewish state in Palestine is a modern political position with no deep roots. The king's objection is on the record in February 1945, in a memorandum both leaders signed and in his own letter three weeks later, more than three years before the state existed. [cite:quincy_meeting_1945] [cite:ibn_saud_bavaria_quote]

How to read the gap between promise and outcome is where accounts part. One reading calls it a promise made and not kept: a deliberate commitment by a sitting president, in his own words, to the affected head of state, followed by an action that ignored it. A second, more cautious reading, taken by the account built on the memorandum, records the 1945 letter and the 1948 recognition as standing in direct and unresolved tension, and declines to adjudicate between them. [cite:fdr_letter_ibnsaud] The second reading has the stronger documentary footing on one point: the promise was Roosevelt's, made "in my capacity as Chief of the Executive Branch," and nothing in these sources shows that it bound his successor. The first has the stronger footing on another: the commitment was specific, written and repeated, and the later decision was taken without the consultation it described.

What the record cannot settle is what Roosevelt himself would have done. He died before the partition vote or the recognition decision came before him, and no evidence exists of how he would have weighed his promise to Ibn Saud against the domestic pressures his successor faced. Nor does any complete transcript allow the meeting's exchanges to be reconstructed word for word. This history documents the promise and the later departure from it, and stops there.

sections.h: Labour and Palestine, 1939–1945
sections.html:
In July 1945 Clement Attlee became Prime Minister at the head of a Labour government. [cite:rs_rd4_lab_frus_yale] On Palestine, Labour came to office with a record, going back six years, of opposing the policy it now inherited, and with a conference resolution on Palestine adopted seven months earlier. Whether that record would become policy was a question American diplomats were already weighing by the end of the month.

The record began in May 1939. In the House of Commons debate of 22–23 May on the White Paper, whose terms and reception are set out in [scene:rd4_white_paper|the White Paper of 1939], Attlee voted against the policy, and so did Hugh Dalton. Herbert Morrison told the House that the government should not adopt a policy "as to which grave doubt exists as to its consistency with the Balfour Declaration and the Mandate." [cite:rs_rd4_lab_frus_yale] [cite:rs_rd4_lab_jvl_debate] Labour members argued in 1939 that the White Paper's limits on immigration and on land transfers were "contrary to the terms of the Mandate." [cite:rs_rd4_lab_frus_yale] This was a legal argument as well as a political one: the objection was not only that the policy was unwise but that Britain, as the mandatory power, had no right under the Mandate to adopt it. Of the three men named here, one was Prime Minister by July 1945.

In December 1944, with the war not yet over, the party's annual conference adopted a resolution on Palestine. It held that there was no case for a Jewish national home "unless we are prepared to let Jews, if they wish, enter this tiny land in such numbers as to become a majority." It went on: "Let the Arabs be encouraged to move out, as the Jews move in." And it proposed re-examining "the possibility of extending the present Palestinian boundaries." [cite:rs_rd4_lab_frus_yale] Each clause cut against the White Paper. The White Paper had capped Jewish immigration and made further entry after five years depend on Arab acquiescence; the resolution called for immigration on a scale to produce a Jewish majority. The White Paper had promised an independent Palestine state within ten years; the resolution spoke of moving the existing population and redrawing the frontier.

The phrase about Arabs moving out did not appear from nowhere. Seven years earlier, in July 1937, the Peel Commission's report had recommended an "exchange of population" on the model of the 1923 Greek–Turkish exchange, compulsory in the last resort, the first official British document to put transfer in writing; that proposal and the Zionist movement's response to it are told in [scene:pl_s01|Peel's "exchange of population"]. [cite:wiki_peel_commission] The Labour resolution differed in its language: it spoke of Arabs being "encouraged" to move, not compelled, and it was a party conference's statement, not a royal commission's recommendation to the government. [cite:rs_rd4_lab_frus_yale] But it shows that the idea of moving Palestine's Arab population, first put on paper by a British commission in 1937, was still being written into the program of a major British party in 1944, now as a call from a party whose leaders, by the State Department's account, had consistently supported the Balfour Declaration.

The sources here record the resolution's words as quoted in an American diplomatic memorandum. They do not include its full text from Labour's own records, the debate that preceded it, who moved it, or how Zionist, Arab or British officials responded to it at the time. What the resolution meant to those who voted for it, and how seriously its authors intended the passage on the Arab population, therefore cannot be settled from this record.

What the new government was likely to do was assessed in Washington by the end of July.
