Liberia's own ambassador complained that the American delegation had threatened aid cuts to several countries in the same period. [cite:militaryhistory_partition_plan] Firestone had no stake in Palestine. The point of the case is the transmission mechanism: a great power's commercial hold over a small client could be turned into that client's vote on a question a hemisphere away. The economic relationship is well documented; the precise way the leverage was exercised is less fully documented than the relationship itself. The corporate pressure and the diplomatic pressure the ambassador described were two separate channels converging on one small state, not one orchestrated scheme.

The Philippines, a recent American possession bound to Washington by aid and security ties, came under American pressure through those economic ties. [cite:militaryhistory_partition_plan] According to the account this book draws on, the Philippine delegation reversed a speech critical of partition and voted yes after American intervention. General Carlos Romulo, the Philippines' own representative, later wrote of being recalled and overruled by his own president: "This particular chapter in history had been exceedingly unpleasant to me." [cite:sagepub_price_resisting_partition] Haiti changed its position after direct communication from the American executive. [cite:militaryhistory_partition_plan] Reports at the time and since describe private approaches to these delegations in the crucial days by influential Americans inside and outside the government; those reports do not name the individuals in the material available here. The evidence is not equal across the three cases. The Liberian link is documented by a serious historian; the exact mechanism behind the Haitian and Philippine shifts is less fully documented, and should be held at that lower confidence.

One delegation said publicly what others did privately. Cuba's delegate announced that Cuba would vote against partition "in spite of the pressure that has been brought to bear upon us." [cite:sagepub_price_resisting_partition] The statement confirms that the same campaign reached states that resisted it as well as those that gave way. Cuba appears in the final list of those voting against. [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_181]

The other great power needed no persuading. The Soviet Union voted yes, and its motive, as the sources describe it, was not sympathy for Zionism, which Soviet doctrine regarded as bourgeois nationalism. Partition would end British rule in Palestine and weaken Britain's position in the Middle East; many of the Jewish community's leaders were socialists who had grown up in the Russian Empire; and a new state looked, in 1947, like a way to reduce a rival empire and gain influence. [cite:un_unispal_186560] The same logic would bring arms to the new state through Czechoslovakia in 1948. Soviet-Israeli relations cooled within a few years, which fits a vote driven by strategy rather than lasting alignment. (The Soviet record is told in [scene:so_s01|the Soviet layer].) Washington and Moscow, already rivals, pushed the same way for opposite reasons. That is convergence, not consensus.

On 29 November 1947 the Assembly adopted the plan by 33 votes to 13, with 10 abstentions. [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_181] The thirteen against were Afghanistan, Cuba, Egypt, Greece, India, Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Syria, Turkey and Yemen. The ten abstaining were Argentina, Chile, China, Colombia, El Salvador, Ethiopia, Honduras, Mexico, the United Kingdom and Yugoslavia. Those in favor included Australia, Canada, France, Poland, Sweden, the Soviet Union, the United States and Uruguay. [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_181] One name in the list carries its own story. Britain, the Mandatory power that would have to hand over the country, abstained.

The resolution was more than a line on a map. It set a timetable. The Mandate was to end "as soon as possible but in any case not later than 1 August 1948." An area with a seaport in the Jewish state was to be evacuated "not later than 1 February 1948." Provisional councils of government were to be in place by 1 April 1948, and the two states were to come into existence two months after the evacuation and "not later than 1 October 1948." A Palestine Commission of five states, Bolivia, Czechoslovakia, Denmark, Panama and the Philippines, was to carry it out. [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_181] The plan, in short, depended on an orderly handover by a power that had abstained, carried out by a commission of five states, against fixed dates.

The two cases presented to the Assembly deserve to be heard in their strongest form. The Jewish Agency's argument, as the UN Yearbook records it, set the plan against the map of the region. The Arab states held about 17,000,000 Arabs in roughly 1,290,000 square miles. Palestine, after the separation of Transjordan, was about 10,000 square miles. On that reckoning the plan gave the Jewish National Home less than one-eighth of the territory originally set aside for it. [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_181] The Agency accepted the plan, though it disliked the borders and the separation of Jerusalem. The Jewish Virtual Library, a pro-Israel reference source, states that the Jews of Palestine were dissatisfied on both counts but "welcomed the compromise." It also reports, citing the writers Avneri and Horowitz, that Arab League Secretary-General Azzam Pasha told David Horowitz and Abba Eban on 16 September 1947: "The Arab world is not in a compromising mood." [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_myths_partition] That exchange is reported second-hand and should be read as such.

The Arab delegations argued on law as well as justice. Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Iraq, Syria and Yemen denounced the plan as contrary to the Charter, illegal and immoral, said they regarded it as a recommendation, and declared that they would not feel bound by it. [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_181] The historian Muhsin Yusuf, of Birzeit University, sets out the reasons for rejection as he reads them: fear of later expulsion and of land confiscation; the injustice of granting statehood to a largely immigrant minority while the majority was denied self-determination; and a view of Zionism as a European imperial project. He recalls that the Arab case to the Anglo-American Committee in 1946 had promised that Jews "will be full citizens" of a Palestinian state. [cite:rs_rd5_yusuf_2002]

Behind both arguments lay the same contested facts: how many people lived where, and who owned the land. The Arab majority of Mandate Palestine had no vote in the General Assembly and no direct representation in the decision that partitioned the territory. [cite:britannica_res181] Arab member states voted against; the people most affected were an object of the resolution, not a participant in it. The 1947 British Mandatory census, as summarized in the sources used here, counted about 1.3 million Arabs and 630,000 Jews in Palestine, which is the reason the familiar claim that the land was largely empty before 1948 does not survive contact with the record. On the overall shares, the sources agree in outline: Jews were roughly a third of the population (one account gives about 30%), Arabs roughly two-thirds (about 70%). [cite:britannica_res181]

The sources do not agree on the precise allocation, and the disagreement matters, because each figure is used to argue a different case. One account in the sources used here gives the Jewish state 55% of the territory and the Arab state 45%, with Jerusalem as an international zone. [cite:britannica_res181] Another, and Yusuf, give the Jewish state 56%; Yusuf gives the Arab state 43%, the other account 44%. [cite:rs_rd5_yusuf_2002] On population inside the proposed Jewish state, the gap is wider. Yusuf counts about 498,000 Jews and about 494,000 Arabs, a near-even split; the Arab state about 725,000 Arabs and 11,000 Jews; and the Jerusalem district about 105,000 Arabs and 100,000 Jews. [cite:rs_rd5_yusuf_2002] The Jewish Virtual Library, citing the historian Howard Sachar, gives the Jewish state about 5,500 square miles with 538,000 Jews and 397,000 Arabs, and the Arab state 4,500 square miles with 804,000 Arabs and 10,000 Jews; citing Aharon Cohen, it adds that about 60% of the Jewish state was Negev desert. [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_myths_partition] Yusuf's figure supports the argument that the Jewish state would have had barely a Jewish majority; Sachar's supports the argument that it would have had a clear one, on land much of which was desert.

Ownership is a separate question from allocation. One account in the sources used here says the Jewish population legally owned under a tenth of the land. [cite:britannica_res181] The summary of the pre-1948 record puts Jewish ownership at approximately 7% of the country's land in 1947. Yusuf gives about 6% of Palestine overall, and about 10% of the land inside the proposed Jewish state. [cite:rs_rd5_yusuf_2002] These figures are close enough to agree on the essential point: the plan assigned a majority of the territory to a community that owned a small fraction of it. They differ enough that any single number should be quoted with its source.

The dashboard panel above sets the two ratios side by side: about 7% of the land in Jewish ownership in 1947, and 56% of the territory allotted to the Jewish state by the plan. [cite:rs_rd5_yusuf_2002] The overview panel below places the same two figures among the other numbers of the pre-state build-out; its land figures are the ones discussed here, and its other figures are taken up where they belong in this library.

The map that follows shows where the vote sits in the larger structure. Resolution 181 stands at the point where two lines meet, the special committee's recommendation of partition and the votes lobbied by the American Zionist political machine, and from it runs the line marked "legal basis claimed" to the state proclaimed in May 1948. This section has added a second American line, as it appears in the record of the three days: an executive pressing for votes, over the objection of its own professionals.

What, then, did the vote decide? It recorded a two-thirds majority for partition, and it created a timetable and a commission. It also left decisive questions open. Those voting against, and several of those abstaining, regarded the resolution as a recommendation; Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Iraq, Syria and Yemen said so in terms. [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_181] Within days the country was at war with itself, and the question of who accepted the plan and who fought over it became a separate story, told in [scene:s09b|the two escalations]. The territorial and demographic shares would soon be overtaken: the war of 1948 produced roughly 700,000 Palestinian Arab refugees, a figure documented by Israeli, Palestinian and international historians, including Israeli scholars working in declassified military archives from the 1980s, and Israel's lines in 1949 lay far beyond those of the plan.

Several things remain unsettled. The record establishes the three-day window, the three changed votes and the leverage on Liberia; it does not establish the full mechanism behind the Haitian and Philippine changes, or which American officials made which approaches. The population of the proposed Jewish state is given differently by serious sources, from a near-even split to a clear Jewish majority, and the land shares vary by a point or two depending on the account. And Forrestal's death, ruled a suicide, remains questioned at the margins without any documented link to his politics. What the record does settle is the shape of the decision: not a serene consensus and not a secret plot, but a contested vote, carried over the line by great-power pressure on small states during a three-day scramble, about a people who were not in the room.

sections.h: Who Spoke for the Palestinian Arabs, 1945–1948
sections.html:
In the years when the Jewish Agency was building a diplomatic case, an arms network and a government in waiting, the Arab side of Palestine's politics was being reorganized from outside the country. On one reading of the record, set out below, the central fact of the period is institutional: the decisions that shaped the Palestinian Arab response to partition were taken, for the most part, not in Jerusalem or Jaffa but in the council chambers of the Arab League, in Cairo, Bludan, Aley and Alexandria. The Palestinian leadership had a voice in those rooms, and a record of its own choices. What it lacked, the sessions below show, was a government of its own and the League's backing for one.

The League's line was set early and held for more than two years. From its founding in March 1945 until Britain's decision to withdraw in the autumn of 1947, the Arab League consistently supported, in the historian Avi Shlaim's words, a "unitary and independent Palestinian state." [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_jps_1990] It was the position the Arab case to the Anglo-American Committee had set out in 1946, when it promised that Jews "will be full citizens" of a Palestinian state. [cite:rs_rd5_yusuf_2002]

The League also rebuilt the Palestinians' own leadership body. The Arab Higher Committee had first been formed in 1936, by the Palestinian parties themselves. After a nine-year hiatus it was re-established in 1946, and this time, Shlaim notes, not by the Palestinian parties but "by a decision of the Arab League." [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_jps_1990] The difference in origin would define the committee's position for the rest of the period: it spoke for the Palestinian Arabs, but it held its mandate from the League.

Its chairman was Hajj Amin al-Husayni, the Mufti of Jerusalem. Al-Husayni had spent the Second World War allied with the Axis powers, a record told in [scene:s07a5|the Arab Revolt and Berlin]. After the war he was refused asylum in Switzerland and held by France, which declined a British proposal to deport him to the Seychelles. In May 1946 he escaped from his residence near Paris to Cairo, where King Faruq of Egypt gave him asylum, and the Arab League made him chairman of the new Arab Higher Committee. [cite:rs_rd5_dipc_husayni] The man who led the Palestinian Arabs through 1947 and 1948 therefore did so from exile in Egypt, under the protection of an Arab king, at the head of a body the League had created.

The League's own decisions on Palestine can be followed session by session. The list compiled by the Jewish Virtual Library from League records gives the following. [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_arableague] In December 1945 the Council set up a committee to enforce a boycott of Zionist goods (Resolution 16) and provided for up to three Palestinian representatives to sit on the Council (Resolution 17). In March 1946 it approved a company with £E1 million to buy Arab land in Palestine. In June 1946, at Bludan, it made the boycott part of the "creed of the Arab nations," called for land sales to Zionists to be made a crime (Resolution 72), and created a Higher Arab Executive for Palestine (Resolutions 80 and 82). In December 1946 it rejected partition (Resolution 142). In October 1947, at Aley, it adopted a resolution titled "Defending Palestine" (the League's own Resolution 181, not to be confused with the UN resolution of the same number a month later), calling for military preparations along the Arab borders. [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_arableague]

The money in these decisions tells its own story. The League's chosen instruments in 1945 and 1946 were economic: a boycott of Zionist goods, a land fund of £E1 million to keep Arab land from being sold, and a call to criminalize sales to Zionists. They were aimed at the mechanism by which the Jewish community had been acquiring land. [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_arableague] When, in February 1948, the Arab Higher Committee asked the League for a loan to meet its administrative costs, the League refused. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_jps_1990]

The year 1947 brought the decisive tests. The Arab Higher Committee chose to boycott the United Nations special committee that visited Palestine that summer, a decision told in [scene:s07i|the UNSCOP section]. The UN partition vote of 29 November then moved the question from argument to war. Two League sessions in the months that followed show how far the League was prepared to go, and how far it was not. For the Cairo session of December 1947, the list records no public announcement, and a decision against formal military intervention unless the United States and Britain intervened militarily. In February 1948 the Council approved political, military and economic measures, including the withholding of petroleum concessions and sanctions on states aiding the Zionists. [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_arableague] The League would arm volunteers and threaten oil concessions; it would not, as of December 1947, commit its member states' armies.

The Mufti wanted something the League would not give. At the Council sessions in Aley in October 1947 and Cairo in December 1947, Shlaim writes, al-Husayni "pleaded passionately for the establishment of a shadow government" under the Arab Higher Committee. In February 1948 the League rejected his demand for a government-in-exile, and refused the loan for the committee's administrative costs. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_jps_1990] In the months when the Jewish Agency was preparing the institutions of a state, the Palestinian leadership was refused both a government and the money to run its own committee.

The fighting forces reflected the same division: the League's own Arab Liberation Army under Fawzi al-Qawuqji and the Husayni family's Army of the Holy War acted without cooperating, as the account of the civil war below shows. [cite:rs_rd5_lodz_2019] And one League member had plans of its own. The Dictionary of the Israeli-Palestinian Conflict describes the League as divided: King Abdullah of Transjordan "opposed every move toward Palestinian independence" and refused to deal with al-Husayni. [cite:rs_rd5_dipc_husayni] Abdullah's separate course, and his contacts with the Jewish Agency, are told in [scene:rd5_abdullah|Abdullah between the Agency, Britain and the League].

The League changed course only after the state of Israel had been proclaimed and the Arab armies had entered the war. The story runs past this chapter's end, but its first steps belong here. On 8 July 1948 the League's Political Committee agreed on a "temporary civil administration" for Palestine, responsible to the League. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_jps_1990] On 20 September 1948, at Alexandria, the Political Committee announced an All-Palestine Government with its seat in Gaza, headed by Ahmad Hilmi Abdul Baqi. On 22 September the Arab Higher Committee proclaimed Palestine independent, and on 30 September a Palestinian National Council met in Gaza under the Mufti's chairmanship. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_jps_1990] Egypt recognized the new government first, in mid-October 1948, followed by Iraq, and then Syria, Lebanon and Saudi Arabia. Britain refused. Abdullah opposed it and said it would not operate in the areas held by his Arab Legion. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_jps_1990]

Abdullah answered with an assembly of his own. On 1 December 1948, according to Shlaim, a congress of about 3,000 delegates at Jericho proclaimed the union of Palestine and Transjordan and acknowledged Abdullah as king. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_jps_1990] Abdullah afterwards stripped al-Husayni of the title of Mufti of Jerusalem. [cite:rs_rd5_dipc_husayni] [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_jps_1990] By the end of 1948, then, two rival claims to speak for the Palestinian Arabs existed: a government in Gaza recognized by five Arab states and chaired in council by the Mufti, and a congress at Jericho that had placed the Arab parts of Palestine under the Transjordanian crown.

Historians weigh this record differently, and the difference is a question about Palestinian agency itself. Shlaim reads it as a story of control: the League reconstituted the Arab Higher Committee, refused it a government-in-exile until September 1948, and armed the Arab Liberation Army under its own command. On this reading the Palestinian leadership's instruments were in other hands, and decisions about Palestine were made by states with their own interests. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_jps_1990] The Dictionary of the Israeli-Palestinian Conflict gives more weight to Palestinian choices, and is harder on them. The Mufti and the Arab Higher Committee pursued their own line, boycotting the UN special committee, pressing for a shadow government and forming the Army of the Holy War; but the 1946 committee was ineffective, its paramilitary forces were uncoordinated, and the League around it was divided. [cite:rs_rd5_dipc_husayni] The two readings are not exclusive. One explains what the Palestinian leadership could not do; the other records what it chose to do, and how weakly it was able to do it.

The record leaves several questions open. The League's session list comes from a compilation of League records rather than from the full minutes, and for the Cairo session of December 1947 it records a decision without any public announcement; what was said in that room is not in the material here. The date and attendance of the Jericho Congress rest on Shlaim's account alone. And the counterfactual that hangs over the period, whether a Palestinian government formed in early 1948, when the Mufti asked for one, would have changed the course of the war, is one the documents cannot answer. What they do establish is the sequence: a League committed to a single Palestinian state, a Palestinian leadership reconstituted by the League and refused a loan, a refusal of government in February 1948, and a government granted in September 1948, four months after the Mandate had ended.

sections.h: Acceptance, Rejection and the Two Escalations
sections.html:
One sentence has long served as the summary of what followed the partition vote: Israel accepted, the Arabs rejected and started the war. In its fuller form the familiar account holds that the Arab side rejected a peaceful UN compromise and at once launched a war against a state that had only accepted it. That sentence joins two separate questions. The first is who accepted and who rejected Resolution 181. The second is how the fighting began, and between whom. The record gives each its own answer, and the answers are not the same shape.

On the first question the familiar account is accurate, and it should be said plainly before anything else. The Jewish Agency accepted Resolution 181, reluctantly, with real misgivings about the plan's narrow borders. The Arab Higher Committee and the Arab League rejected the plan in its entirety. Jamal Husseini, speaking for the Arab Higher Committee, told the United Nations that the partition line would be "nothing but a line of fire and blood." [cite:wiki_un_partition_plan] [cite:palquest_un_partition_1947] On the narrow matter of who said yes and who said no, the documented record is one-sided. The arguments each side made, and the contested figures behind them, are set out in [scene:s09|the section on the vote].

The second question is where the single sentence starts to mislead. Violence escalated sharply from 1 December 1947, immediately after the vote. [cite:explaininghistory_un_partition] What followed for the next five and a half months was not yet a war between states. It was a civil war inside Mandate Palestine, between the Jewish and Arab communities and their paramilitary forces, fought while Britain still formally governed the country. The neighbouring Arab states' armies did not cross a border until 15 May 1948.

The forces on the Arab side were of two kinds, and they did not work together. The Arab Liberation Army was created by the Arab League and led by Fawzi al-Qawuqji. Its forces were volunteers, in the historian Magdalena Pogońska-Pol's description "few in number, and poorly armed." [cite:rs_rd5_lodz_2019] The Army of the Holy War (Jaysh al-Jihad al-Muqaddas) was made up of Palestinian volunteers and was subordinate to the Husayni family. The two acted without cooperating, and, Pogońska-Pol concludes, neither stopped the Jewish forces. [cite:rs_rd5_lodz_2019] The Army of the Holy War's commander was Abd al-Qadir al-Husayni. He re-entered Palestine across the Egyptian border in December 1947 and, after the Arab Higher Committee proclaimed a jihad, re-formed and commanded the force. His explosives unit blew up the Jewish Agency building in Jerusalem; the source does not give the date. [cite:rs_rd5_palquest_abdelqader]

The American government's own historians describe the fighting of these months in terms that favor the familiar account. The State Department's Office of the Historian describes irregular Palestinian Arab bands, attached to Arab Liberation Army units, attacking Jewish cities, settlements and forces, with the Haganah, the Irgun and Lehi fighting back. [cite:rs_rd5_oh_war] That is the strongest documentary support for the reading that the Arab side began the fighting and the Jewish side responded.

Other documented attacks run the other way. In early January 1948 a car bomb at the former Ottoman government house in Jaffa killed 26 people; the material available here gives the toll but does not name who planted the bomb. On 15 February 1948 Haganah and Palmach forces attacked the village of Qisarya near Haifa. [cite:explaininghistory_un_partition] [cite:aljazeera_remix_partition_transcript] The sources this book draws on place Qisarya within a documented pattern of Jewish paramilitary attacks on Palestinian towns and villages in the war's first months, well before the massacre at Deir Yassin, which is told in [scene:ma_s01|Deir Yassin, the Hadassah convoy and Tantura]. [cite:explaininghistory_un_partition] That is the strongest documentary support for the reading that a two-sided war began at once.

The decisive struggle of the spring was over the road to Jerusalem. At the end of March 1948 Abd al-Qadir al-Husayni went to Damascus to seek arms from the Arab League's Military Committee. Jewish forces took al-Qastal, the village overlooking the Jerusalem–Jaffa road. He was killed on 8 April 1948 leading the counter-attack. [cite:rs_rd5_palquest_abdelqader] Read one way, the episode compresses the Palestinian predicament of these months: a local commander who had to travel to the League's Military Committee in Damascus to ask for weapons, and who died on the road he was trying to hold.

Before the Mandate ended, a state army had already entered the fighting in one place. The Arab Legion of Transjordan attacked the Gush Etzion bloc of Jewish settlements; its defenders surrendered, and some were massacred. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_seminar_cw] The source, the historian Avi Shlaim's seminar notes, does not give the date or the number killed, and this book does not supply them.

The second escalation came on 15 May 1948, the day after Israel's declaration of independence, when the armies of neighbouring Arab states invaded. The war they entered ended in 1949 with Israel's territory extending far beyond the lines of the UN plan. [cite:explaininghistory_un_partition] The invasion is real, documented and significant; its course, the Arab League's own stated reasons for it and the forces on each side are told in [scene:rd5_invasion|the Arab states' war]. Its place in the sequence is the point here. It followed five and a half months of civil war already under way. It did not start the fighting.

Set against the record, both popular stories lose something. The reading that "the Arabs rejected and attacked" is supported on the vote, which was a clean Arab rejection backed by a public threat of "fire and blood," and it has support on the fighting: the Office of the Historian describes Arab bands attacking and Jewish forces fighting back, Abd al-Qadir's men bombed the Jewish Agency building, and the Arab Legion attacked Gush Etzion before the Mandate ended. What it cannot carry is the claim that the war began on 15 May with an unprovoked attack on a purely defensive new state. By then the country had been at war for five and a half months, with documented Jewish paramilitary attacks on Arab villages and towns among the events of those months.

The reading that "a two-sided war began at once" is supported by the dates: violence from 1 December, attacks documented in both directions, Qisarya in February, the Jerusalem road in April. What it cannot carry is any suggestion that the rejection was incidental, or that Arab forces were merely reactive. The Arab Higher Committee had promised resistance in advance, and the Army of the Holy War and the Arab Liberation Army were organized to fight. Treating the sequence as a single, uninterrupted chain from the vote to the invasion, in either direction, skips over the civil-war phase that the record documents: a one-sided vote, then a two-sided civil war, then a state-level invasion.

Some things this record does not settle. It does not establish who fired first in the opening days of December, and the sources here do not attempt to. It does not give a count of the dead in the civil-war months, on either side. It leaves the perpetrator of the Jaffa car bomb unnamed in the material available, and leaves the date of the Jewish Agency bombing and the date and toll of Gush Etzion unstated. Nor does it deliver a verdict on responsibility: it does not argue that the Arab League's rejection was justified, or that the later invasion was unprovoked. It establishes the shape of the sequence, and leaves the moral weighing of each side's decisions within it to the reader.

sections.h: After the Vote: Jews of the Arab World, 1947–1948
sections.html:
The war of 1948 is usually told as a war inside Palestine, and its refugees as one people's loss. The record of the same months shows a second set of events running in parallel, outside Palestine. From the day after the partition vote, Jewish communities in Syria, Egypt, Lebanon, Aden, Bahrain, Iraq and Libya came under attack from mobs, under arrest and sequestration by governments, and in Iraq under a law that made Zionism a crime. In Yemen, by the end of 1948, the ruler permitted the Jews to leave. These were not acts of "the Arabs" in general. Each was carried out by a named government, a mob in a named city, or a named organization, and this section ties each one to its author. Together they began the decline of these communities, a story that runs well past 1948 and is set beside the Palestinian displacement in [scene:s00e3|two displacements].

The riots of 30 November to 5 December 1947. On 30 November 1947, the day after the General Assembly voted for partition, anti-Jewish riots broke out in Damascus, Aleppo, Cairo, Beirut and Aden, according to the Center for Israel Education. In Cairo, the same account reports, leaders of al-Azhar declared a holy war against the Zionists. [cite:rs_rd5_cie_arabcities] The worst damage that the sources record in Syria was in Aleppo. A mob broke into the Great Synagogue, destroyed Torah scrolls and damaged the Aleppo Codex; most of the Codex was saved and smuggled to Jerusalem in 1958. Across the city, according to the same account, 150 Jewish homes, 50 shops, five schools and 18 synagogues were destroyed. [cite:rs_rd5_cie_arabcities] On 5 December 1947, in Bahrain, Jewish homes and shops were looted, the synagogue was destroyed and one Jewish woman was killed. [cite:rs_rd5_cie_arabcities]

The deadliest of these riots took place in Aden, then a British colony. The Center for Israel Education lists Aden among the cities where violence broke out after the vote; the accounts of Aden itself date the riots there from 2 December 1947. The toll is disputed. The Center for Israel Education gives 82 Jews killed and 76 wounded. [cite:rs_rd5_cie_arabcities] The Jewish Virtual Library, which credits Wikipedia for its entry, gives between 76 and 82 Jews killed, and also 38 others killed: 33 Arabs, four Indian Muslims and one Somali. It records that 106 of the 170 Jewish-owned shops in Crater were looted. [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_aden] A study of 1951 gives 76 killed and 78 wounded. [cite:rs_rd5_anderson_1951] The sources agree on the order of magnitude, between 76 and 82 Jewish dead, and differ on the exact count. The sources here do not say how the 38 others died.

What the 1951 study is. Much of what is known about the official measures of 1948 comes from one document, and the reader should know what it is. It is "The Situation of Jews in Moslem Countries," by H. Dewey Anderson, chapter XIV of The Arab Refugee Problem, a set of proposals submitted to the United Nations General Assembly in December 1951. It is available today through the Center for Israel Education, which presents it as a UN report. [cite:rs_rd5_anderson_1951] It is a contemporary compilation by a named author, written three years after the events and placed inside a work about the Arab refugees. It is not a resolution or a finding of the General Assembly. Its dates and figures are specific, and they are used below as Anderson's, attributed to him, because the sources gathered for this book do not test them against the governments' own records.

Egypt: arrests, sequestration and bombings. When the Arab armies entered Palestine in May 1948, the Egyptian government turned against the Jews of its own cities. According to Anderson, more than 1,000 Jews were arrested in Cairo on 15 May 1948. Proclamation No. 26, issued on 29 May, sequestered the property of internees; of the 68 sequestration orders issued up to 30 September, 67 involved Jews. Proclamation No. 30, of 6 June, allowed Jews to be searched without a warrant. [cite:rs_rd5_anderson_1951] These were acts of state, published as proclamations, and the ratio of 67 to 68 shows on whom they fell.

Violence followed in Cairo's Jewish quarters. On 20 June 1948 a bombing struck the Karaite quarter. Anderson records 12 houses destroyed and 20 people killed; Wikipedia, citing the historian Beinin, gives 22 killed and 41 wounded. [cite:rs_rd5_anderson_1951] [cite:rs_rd5_wiki_cairo1948] The Cicurel department store was bombed on 19 July, and a bombing on 22 September killed 19 people. [cite:rs_rd5_anderson_1951] [cite:rs_rd5_wiki_cairo1948] In November 1948 the government arrested 32 leaders of the Muslim Brotherhood and banned the organization, and in a trial in 1950 members of the Brotherhood were charged with the bombings of June to November. [cite:rs_rd5_wiki_cairo1948] The sources gathered here record the charge; they do not record the verdict.

Iraq: a law, a hanging and an armistice never signed. Iraq took part in the war from the start. It joined the invasion on 15 May 1948, the day after Israel declared independence, and when the fighting ended it was the only Arab state that had fought which refused to sign an armistice with Israel, leaving a formal state of war that, in the Israeli government's account, has never ended. [cite:govil_aliyah] The invasion itself is told in the section on the Arab states' war. At home, according to accounts of the Iraqi Jewish community, the measures escalated after the partition vote from mob violence to the confiscation of property and prosecutions those accounts call trumped-up. [cite:yated_ezra_nechemia]

The central instrument was a law of July 1948, and the sources describe its penalty differently. Anderson writes that it made Zionist activity punishable by death or by at least seven years' imprisonment. [cite:rs_rd5_anderson_1951] An account in Yated Ne'eman dates the law to 19 July 1948 and gives the penalty as up to seven years in prison. It adds that every Jew was presumed to be a Zionist under the law, so that it worked as a blanket criminalization of the community, and that the testimony of two Muslim witnesses was enough to convict, with little means of appeal. [cite:yated_ezra_nechemia] The two accounts agree on the month and on the law's target; they disagree on the maximum and minimum sentence, and this book cannot settle which is right from the sources it holds.

Further orders followed. On 28 August 1948 Jews were barred from banking and from dealing in foreign currency, and on 19 October they were ordered discharged from government departments, according to Anderson. [cite:rs_rd5_anderson_1951] Between those two dates came the case that the community's own accounts treat as the turning point. On 23 September 1948 Shafiq Ades, a prominent and well-connected Jewish businessman, was publicly hanged in Basra on charges of selling weapons to Israel and to the Iraqi Communist Party. His body was left hanging for hours. [cite:yated_ezra_nechemia] [cite:govil_aliyah] [cite:rs_rd5_anderson_1951] The case is widely cited as the event that convinced much of the community that no one, however powerful, was safe. [cite:yated_ezra_nechemia] That is a judgment about how Iraqi Jews read the hanging, recorded by those who wrote their history; the sources do not describe the proceedings against him, and the charges cannot be tested from them.

Syria, Libya and Yemen. Anderson records that on 15 May 1948, the same day as the Cairo arrests, 250 Jews were imprisoned in Aleppo; that a "second wave of violence" struck the Jews of Tripoli, in Libya, on 14 June 1948; and that in December 1948 the ruler of Yemen permitted the country's Jews to leave. In what became known as "Magic Carpet," 45,009 were evacuated. [cite:rs_rd5_anderson_1951] The airlift itself belongs to the years after this chapter and is told in [scene:ye_s01|the Yemeni airlift].

What 1948 began. The events of 1947–48 were a beginning, not the whole of the story. Over the following decades the large Jewish communities of Iraq, Yemen, Libya, Egypt, Syria and North Africa shrank dramatically. Estimates of the total who left the Arab countries and Iran between 1948 and the 1970s commonly fall between 800,000 and 900,000 people, and the causes varied by country: emigration, pressure, expulsion and state persecution in different proportions. [cite:w_jewish_exodus_arab] Morocco shows the variety. Its Jewish community, rooted there for some two thousand years, numbered in the hundreds of thousands in the 1940s and largely emigrated after 1948, mostly to Israel; between 1961 and 1964 about 97,000 left in Operation Yachin, with payments to the Moroccan government that historians record. [cite:w_yachin] The later exodus from Iraq is told in [scene:irq_e05|the Iraqi exodus].

How to read this record. The war of 1948 is often described simply as a war between Israel and its neighbors, and Iraq's part in it as one army among several. The record of these months adds two things that description leaves out. Iraq's war had a domestic side, a law and a public hanging aimed at its own Jewish citizens, and it ended without the armistice every other Arab combatant signed. [cite:govil_aliyah] [cite:yated_ezra_nechemia] And the same pattern, in different degrees, appears in Egypt, Syria, Aden, Bahrain and Libya: riots on the day after the vote, the destruction of synagogues, killings, and proclamations and laws aimed at Jews by the governments of Egypt and Iraq. That was antisemitic violence and discrimination, and it should be called so. The record does not support treating it as the conduct of an entire people or faith. It names mobs in particular cities, particular governments issuing particular orders, the leaders of a particular institution, al-Azhar, declaring holy war, and, in Cairo, a particular organization whose members were charged in court.

What the record does not settle. The exact death tolls in Aden and in the Cairo bombings remain in dispute, as the figures above show. The penalty in Iraq's July 1948 law is given differently by the two sources. Much of the official record of 1948 reaches this book through a single compilation, Anderson's, made in 1951 for a debate about refugees, and the governments' own archives are not among the sources used here. The outcome of the 1950 trial in Cairo is not recorded in them. Nor do they give the number of Jews who left the Arab countries in 1948 itself, as distinct from the totals for the decades that followed. What is established is the pattern of the first thirteen months: violence by mobs, arrests and sequestration by governments, and a law in Iraq that put a whole community under suspicion.

sections.h: Golda Meyerson's Tour: The Money of Early 1948
sections.html:
In the first weeks of the civil war, the Jewish Agency's most pressing shortage was money. A common account holds that the new state was built and defended chiefly on its own resources. The man who led it said otherwise. When David Ben-Gurion looked back on the winter of 1948, he credited a single fundraising campaign in the United States, and the woman who ran it, with making the state possible. The campaign lasted about two months. It was run by Golda Meyerson, later Golda Meir, and it depended on an American fundraising network that had been built over a quarter of a century and that, through one man, reached directly into the arms network of the same years.

A failed trip, and a substitute. After the partition vote of November 1947, the Jewish Agency needed money quickly. Its treasurer, Eliezer Kaplan, traveled to the United States to raise $7 million and failed. Ben-Gurion proposed going himself; the Agency's executive sent Meyerson instead. [cite:jta_golda_1948] [cite:reformjudaism_golda] She was then acting head of the Jewish Agency's political department, and she left for America in January 1948. [cite:jta_golda_1948]

The organizer. Her opening came through Henry Montor, executive vice-chairman of the United Jewish Appeal. Montor pressed the Council of Jewish Federations to give her a speaking slot at its assembly in Chicago, and it did. [cite:jta_golda_1948] He was not a newcomer to the cause's covert side. Three years earlier, in 1945, Montor had gathered seventeen wealthy businessmen to meet Ben-Gurion at Rudolf Sonneborn's apartment, the meeting that founded the arms-buying network described in [scene:s07d|the Sonneborn meeting]. [cite:jta_golda_1948] The same organizer thus stood behind both the network that bought weapons and the public appeal that paid for them.

The money. The figures come from reporting, and they are given here as reported. The early response, according to reports, came to about $25 million in the first month. Chicago's Jewish federation took out a $5 million loan and handed the proceeds to her. [cite:reformjudaism_golda] [cite:jewishpress_golda_25m] She went on to some twenty cities, and when she returned on 19 March 1948 she was reported to have raised $50 million. [cite:reformjudaism_golda] [cite:jwa_golda_50m] By one comparison, that was several times Saudi Arabia's oil revenue for 1947. [cite:jwa_golda_50m] The money went largely to weapons, including the arms bought from Czechoslovakia. [cite:reformjudaism_golda] [cite:jwa_golda_50m]

Ben-Gurion's response is on record in his own words. He wrote in his diary that her success was "the only ray of light," and he said that history would record that "there was a Jewish woman who got the money which made the state possible." [cite:jta_golda_1948] [cite:yu_golda_archives] Her return date gives the diary entry its context. She came home on 19 March 1948, the same day the United States told the Security Council that partition could not be carried out by peaceful means, a retreat told in [scene:rd5_trusteeship|Washington's retreat]. The American government was stepping back from partition in the week that private American money arrived to pay for its defense.

The machinery behind the speech. The tour was a personal campaign, but it ran on structure. Ben-Gurion's tribute, in the record's own summary, credits American donors' money raised through a federation-and-appeal network that had been built since the 1920s and that, through Montor, overlapped directly with the arms network. [cite:jta_golda_1948] [cite:yu_golda_archives] Meyerson did not have to build an audience. The federations already existed in the cities she visited, and the Chicago assembly brought their leaders into one room. Kaplan had failed to raise $7 million; Meyerson, speaking through that apparatus, was reported to have raised about seven times as much in about two months.

The library's funding ledgers set the tour inside the larger flow of American money that year. The first chart below ranks the dollar sums in the record. The reported $50 million is the second-largest sum shown, behind only the $100 million Export-Import Bank loan of 1949, and well ahead of the $14.5 million paid for Czechoslovak arms in 1948.

The tour also overlapped with the United Jewish Appeal's regular campaign, so its sum cannot simply be added to the appeal's. The ledger, compiled from the JTA archive's year-end report on the 1948 campaign, records a record $150 million for the United Jewish Appeal that year, about $2.0 billion in today's dollars. Of that, $74.7 million went to the United Palestine Appeal, the share for Palestine and then Israel; $64.9 million to the Joint Distribution Committee for relief in Europe; and $10.4 million to resettlement in the United States. The Palestine share was just under half. The ledger notes that Keren Hayesod's own history lists defense among the things its money financed before statehood, and that in 1948 Meyerson's campaign money went largely to weapons.

In constant dollars the 1948 campaign stands at the top of a steep rise. The ledger converts the appeal's totals to 2025 dollars: about $0.32 billion in its first year, 1939; an average of about $0.35 billion a year during the war; then about $1.65 billion in 1946, about $1.59 billion in 1947 and about $2.0 billion in 1948. The peak year was the year of the war.

What the record supports, and what it does not. The documents support three things firmly. Kaplan's attempt failed; Meyerson's succeeded on a scale far beyond his target; and the money paid largely for arms, including the Czechoslovak arms told in [scene:cz_s01|the Czechoslovak pipeline]. They also support the point Ben-Gurion made himself: the claim that the state was built chiefly on its own resources does not survive his own account of where its money came from in the months before independence. What they do not support is any reading of the money as American government money. It came from private donors through private institutions, and in the same weeks the American government was retreating from partition.

The gaps are real. The $25 million and $50 million figures are reported totals, not audited accounts, and the sources do not say how much of the $50 million was new money and how much came through the United Jewish Appeal's own campaign. They do not break down what the money bought item by item, or how much of it reached Czechoslovakia. The comparison with Saudi oil revenue is given without its underlying figure. Ben-Gurion's verdict is a judgment, by the person best placed to make it, and not a measurement; other parts of this chapter show that weapons, diplomacy and the state's own forces each have a claim on the outcome of 1948.

sections.h: The Arms Network in Operation, 1945–1948
sections.html:
Money was only half the problem: weapons still had to be found, bought and moved. The network founded at Rudolf Sonneborn's apartment in 1945, described in [scene:s07d|the Sonneborn meeting], was not a fund or a statement of intent. For three years it bought real weapons, aircraft and machinery in the United States and moved them, through a set of named front operations and transit countries, to the Haganah in Palestine. Two claims about it are common, and the record contradicts both. One is that American law enforcement knew nothing of an organized effort to arm the Haganah before 1948. The other is that the new state's founding war was armed only by its own government. The documents show federal agencies watching parts of the operation while it ran, and a large share of the material reaching Palestine from private American buyers through third countries.

The routes. The network's first problem was the law. Both the United States and Britain maintained embargoes on arms for Palestine, and the network's purchases were designed to defeat them. Academic research on the operation documents purchases of trucks, radios, aircraft parts and weapons components, funnelled through countries that were neutral in the conflict: Czechoslovakia, Panama, Mexico, Canada and France. [cite:mexico_arms] Mexico was one of the named and documented transit points, not an incidental stop. [cite:mexico_arms] The method was simple to describe and hard to police. Goods left the United States for a country that was not at war, and were re-shipped from there to Haganah operatives. The research documents the strategy and the countries; it does not give a shipment-by-shipment ledger of what went by which route. [cite:mexico_arms]

The scale. By late January 1948 the operation had already moved thousands of tons of disguised military material. Over its whole life it sent some 800 disguised shipments, roughly 2,400 tons, and most of them reached their destination before the war ended. [cite:mexico_arms_1948] The volume matters for the second common claim. The weapons that the new state carried into 1948 were bought in part by American citizens, with American donations, and moved through other countries' ports; the Czechoslovak supply that began in January 1948 is the other half of that story, told in [scene:cz_s01|the Czechoslovak pipeline].

Al Schwimmer's airline. The most elaborate single operation was in the air. Al Schwimmer, a veteran of the US Army's Air Transport Command, bought roughly 30 surplus American warplanes and moved them toward Palestine via Panama, Brazil and Casablanca, evading the FBI and the State Department for months. [cite:schwimmer_wiki] The two accounts of his operation name its cover differently. One describes a fictitious Panamanian airline, Lineas Aereas de Panama, created to carry the aircraft. [cite:schwimmer_wiki] The other describes a near-bankrupt charter airline, Service Airways Inc., used as commercial cover to fly aircraft and parts out of the United States. [cite:sdjw_schwimmer] The accounts do not say whether both companies were used at different stages, and this book does not resolve the point.

The crate on the New Jersey dock. By the end of January 1948, a crate marked "used industrial machinery" broke apart while it was being loaded onto a freighter in New Jersey, spilling explosives onto the dock. It was one of 76 identical crates bound for Palestine. [cite:schwimmer_sdjw] The two accounts weigh the incident differently. In one, the accidental spill, not investigative work, gave US authorities their first concrete evidence that the network existed. [cite:schwimmer_sdjw] In the other, the FBI, the Customs Service and other federal authorities had already been uncovering parts of the network while it operated, and the spill accelerated their work into open prosecution. [cite:mexico_arms_1948] The two can be read together: the first account itself claims only that the crate supplied the first concrete evidence, not that the authorities had no suspicion before it.

What the government knew. The fuller record supports the second account. Later scholarship and reporting from the era of declassification confirm that the FBI, the Customs Service and the intelligence units descended from the wartime OSS each uncovered parts of the smuggling operation while it was running, not after the fact. A National Security Council memorandum of the period referred to the operation directly. [cite:ampalestine_haganah] Enforcement was real but partial. Some participants were charged and most were not, and the network's core organizers were never prosecuted. [cite:ampalestine_haganah] Most of the material, as noted, arrived. [cite:mexico_arms_1948] The pattern is not one of a government blind to the network. It is one of agencies that saw parts of it and a government that prosecuted a few of the people at its edges.

A separate investigation. One thing the FBI was doing in the same months is easily confused with this case, and the record keeps them apart. Records obtained decades later under the Freedom of Information Act by the Cato Institute show that the FBI maintained an investigative focus on the Zionist Organization of America, founded in 1897, in 1947–48. [cite:cato_fbi_wiretap] Its reason was not the arms network. The Bureau believed, incorrectly on the evidence of what it overheard, that the organization had been infiltrated or influenced by Communists. The activity it monitored was constitutionally protected and showed no violation of federal law by the organization. [cite:cato_fbi_wiretap] Between September 1947 and May 1948 the FBI also wiretapped Sol Rotenberg, a Jewish political activist tied to the International Workers Order, on the theory that the Order was a Communist Party front. [cite:cato_fbi_wiretap] These were two distinct concerns running at the same time: a Neutrality Act investigation of the arms network, and a counter-subversion inquiry into suspected Communist influence. Reading the wiretaps as part of the arms case, or the arms case as an outgrowth of the wiretaps, merges two files the record keeps separate.

The trial and the pardons. Nine men involved in the network were tried in a federal courthouse in Los Angeles in 1950. [cite:schwimmer_wiki] Schwimmer was convicted under the Neutrality Act and lost his American citizenship. [cite:schwimmer_wiki] One account adds that he was fined $10,000. [cite:sdjw_schwimmer] He later moved to Israel and led its aircraft industry; one account says he founded Israel Aerospace Industries, the other that he became head of Israel Aircraft Industries. [cite:schwimmer_wiki] [cite:sdjw_schwimmer] Charlie Winters was charged with conspiracy to export military aircraft in violation of the Neutrality Act, pleaded guilty and served 18 months in prison. [cite:schwimmer_wiki] [cite:sdjw_winters] One account describes him as the only participant in the network with a documented felony conviction for this activity. [cite:sdjw_winters]

The sources disagree on several details of the legal record, and the disagreements are set out below rather than resolved. Each account is internally specific; neither is obviously the stronger, and the primary court and pardon records are not among the sources used here.

On every version, both men were eventually pardoned by an American president, decades after the trial. [cite:schwimmer_wiki] [cite:sdjw_schwimmer] [cite:sdjw_winters] A man convicted of breaking the Neutrality Act went on to lead the new state's aircraft industry, and the United States later formally forgave both him and Winters. The arc runs from a federal prohibition, through a selective prosecution, to official absolution.

What the record does not settle. The documents establish the routes, the scale of some 800 shipments and roughly 2,400 tons, the Los Angeles trial and the pardons. They do not provide a full ledger of what moved by which route, or a total cost; the library's funding ledger records Schwimmer's roughly 30 aircraft without a price. They name only two of the nine men tried in 1950 and do not give the charges and sentences of the other seven. They do not explain why the network's core organizers were never prosecuted while the agencies knew of its activity, and they disagree on the details shown above. The question of who decided to prosecute so few, and why, remains open.

sections.h: "Czechoslovak Arms Saved the State": The Pipeline of 1948
sections.html:
The American network was one source of the Haganah's arms. The other was a government. A familiar belief holds that the United States armed Israel from its founding. In 1948 it did the opposite. Washington kept its arms embargo in place, and the government that sold the Jewish side the fighters and rifles it used in the war was communist Czechoslovakia, acting with Soviet consent. Some of the money that paid for them was raised in the United States, but the weapons came from the East. The American military relationship with Israel that later defined its arms supply did not exist in 1948. [cite:jpost_czech_arms_saved_israel] [cite:wiki_czech_arms_israel]

The first contract. The pipeline opened before the state did. On 14 January 1948 the Jewish Agency signed its first arms contract with Czechoslovakia, coordinated through "Secretariat D" of the state engineering-works holding. [cite:wiki_czech_arms_israel] [cite:wiki_operation_balak] Two dates frame it. It came four months before independence, at a time when the purchaser was not a state but the Agency that represented the Jewish community of Palestine. And it came three months before the United Nations Security Council imposed its own arms embargo on 17 April 1948, in Resolution 46. [cite:wiki_czech_arms_israel] [cite:wiki_operation_balak] A third date sits awkwardly between them. Czechoslovakia became communist in the coup of February 1948, a month after the first contract, and sold with Stalin's consent. [cite:jpost_czech_arms_saved_israel] [cite:wiki_czech_arms_israel] The sources record Soviet consent for the sales; they do not explain how Moscow's position related to a contract signed before the coup.

Operation Balak. The most striking deliveries came by air. From May to August 1948 a secret airlift, Operation Balak, ran from the Žatec airfield west of Prague, code-named "Zebra," to Ekron. It carried arms, ammunition and personnel, and it carried fighters: the Avia S-199, a Czech-built derivative of the German Messerschmitt Bf 109, dismantled and crated inside C-46 and C-54 transport aircraft. About 25 were delivered, and they formed 101 Squadron. [cite:wiki_operation_balak] [cite:machal_avia_s199] The airlift did not stay secret for long. A defector exposed the Zebra base, the United States pressed the United Nations to have it closed, and operations moved to Nikšić in Yugoslavia. [cite:wiki_operation_balak] [cite:machal_avia_s199] The episode shows Washington's posture plainly: it did not supply arms, and it acted to shut down the supply that was reaching the new state.

The rifles. More came by sea. The deliveries included some 35,000 German-pattern Karabiner 98k rifles and heavy weapons, many of them originally produced for the Wehrmacht. [cite:jpost_czech_arms_saved_israel] [cite:wiki_czech_arms_israel] Many of the rifles of the new state's first war were German-pattern army rifles sold by a Soviet-bloc government.

The other side's suppliers. Czechoslovakia was not the only outside power arming a party to the war. Britain, according to the same sources, supplied aircraft and training to the Arab air forces, while the United States maintained its embargo. [cite:jpost_czech_arms_saved_israel] [cite:wiki_czech_arms_israel] And the Soviet bloc's choice was not lasting. Within months, the record notes, it began shipping the same kind of weapons toward the Arab side. [cite:jpost_czech_arms_saved_israel] The Soviet diplomacy behind the bloc's position in 1947–48 is told in [scene:so_s01|the Soviet layer]; what the arms record shows is a convergence of interest for a period, not an alliance.

The price. In a 1952 report, the Czechoslovak Foreign Minister, Viliam Široký, put the receipts from the sales at almost $14.5 million. [cite:jpost_czech_arms_saved_israel] [cite:wiki_czech_arms_israel] That is the seller's own figure, given four years later, and it is the one the record can cite to a named official. The library's funding ledger shows how uncertain the true cost is. It gives a range for the Czechoslovak arms from $14.5 million to about $90 million, about $0.19 billion to $1.2 billion in today's dollars, and notes that estimates vary up to six-fold. It sets this beside the reported $50 million from Golda Meyerson's American tour, spent mostly on arms, $3 million in letters of credit from Nicaragua's Somoza for arms buying, and Al Schwimmer's roughly 30 aircraft, whose cost the record does not total. Its conclusion is that no audited grand total for the war's arms has been published.

The two ends of the Czechoslovak range each have a case. The low figure has a documentary source in the seller's foreign minister, and it measures receipts. The higher estimates in the ledger are not attributed in the sources used here to a named document, and this book cannot say what they include that Široký's figure leaves out. What is clear is the link between the two halves of the year's money. The reported $50 million that Golda Meyerson brought back from the United States financed weapons purchases, including those from Czechoslovakia, as told in [scene:us_s07|Golda Meyerson's tour]. [cite:reformjudaism_golda] [cite:jwa_golda_50m] American private money paid, in part, for Soviet-bloc arms.

The library's summary of the money behind the state sets these sums side by side: the reported $50 million from the 1948 tour; about $14.5 million paid for Czechoslovak arms, with Stalin's approval; and a $100 million US Export-Import Bank loan earmarked for Israel after recognition. Only the last came from the American government, and it was a loan for building the state, not weapons.

When American arms came. The aid ledger's timeline fixes the American side. From 1948 to 1961 US aid to Israel consisted of economic aid and loans only; Washington avoided selling arms for fear of alienating the Arab oil states. The first American military aid came in 1962, and then as loans. The larger military relationship that followed, from the first congressional earmark in 1971 to the airlift of 1973 and beyond, belongs to later volumes of this library.

Ben-Gurion's verdict. Ben-Gurion left no doubt about how he weighed the shipments. In 1968 he said: "Czechoslovak arms saved the State of Israel, really and absolutely." [cite:jpost_czech_arms_saved_israel] It is the judgment of the man who led the war, given twenty years later. It sits beside his tribute to Meyerson's fundraising as "the money which made the state possible," and the two are not in conflict: the money, in part, paid for the arms.

What the record does not settle. The sources establish the first contract's date, the airlift's route and months, the number of fighters and rifles, and Široký's figure. They do not settle the true price, which ranges six-fold in the estimates, or itemize what was bought for it. They do not show how the January contract, signed before the communist coup, related to the Soviet consent recorded afterwards. They name the defector who exposed the Zebra base only as a defector. And Ben-Gurion's verdict, however weighty, is an assessment rather than a measurement of how much the Czechoslovak weapons, as against other factors, decided the war; the balance of forces is examined in [scene:s10b|the military balance of 1948].

sections.h: Plan Dalet: The Document and the Argument
sections.html:
On 10 March 1948 the general staff of the Haganah issued the operational plan that would govern its conduct in the weeks before and after the British withdrawal. In Hebrew it was Tochnit Dalet; in English it is usually called Plan D or Plan Dalet. [cite:wiki_plan_dalet] A long-standing popular account holds that Palestinians left their homes in 1948 of their own accord, at the urging of Arab leaders, before Jewish forces did anything to them. That account has to reckon with this document. Its text is a primary source and is not in dispute. What historians dispute, working from the same archives, is what the plan was for.

The plan did not come from nowhere. It was the fourth in a series. Walid Khalidi, the Palestinian historian whose 1961 essay set out the argument that it was a master plan, dates the earlier Plan B to September 1945 and Plan C, or Gimmel, to May 1946. Plan C, he writes, was put into practice from 1 December 1947, the first day of the fighting that followed the United Nations vote. Plan D was, in his words, "finalized on 10 March 1948," and its operational objectives were put into practice from 1 April 1948. [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_1988] The dates matter. Plan D was issued nine days before the United States told the Security Council that partition could not be carried out peacefully ([scene:rd5_trusteeship|Washington's retreat]), and its operations began three weeks later.

Khalidi first made his case in a 1961 essay titled "Plan Dalet: Master Plan for the Conquest of Palestine." When the Journal of Palestine Studies republished it in its Autumn 1988 issue (volume 18, number 1), it printed the text of Plan D, dated 10 March 1948, as an appendix. [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_1988] The quotations below are from that translation.

The plan opens with its purpose: "The objective of this plan is to gain control of the areas of the Hebrew state and defend its borders." Its scope reached past those borders, to "areas of Jewish settlement and concentration which are located outside the borders." [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_1988] The plan's provisions on villages are the passage at the center of the argument. They applied to villages inside and near the territory to be held. Brigades were to encircle and search them, and to garrison or demolish them according to their strategic position. [cite:wiki_plan_dalet] Section 4(b) sets out the alternative to holding a village:

Destruction of villages (setting fire to, blowing up, and planting mines in the debris)

Where resistance was met, the same section provides, "the population must be expelled outside the borders of the state." [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_1988] In practical terms, the text gave brigade commanders two courses for a village in or near their area: hold it if it submitted, or, if it resisted, destroy it and expel its people. [cite:wiki_plan_dalet]

The chain of command was simple. The plan was issued from the top, by the general staff. It was carried out by brigades. And it left the judgment at the point of contact, whether a village had resisted, to the commanders on the spot. That last feature is the hinge on which the scholarly argument turns. A reader who sees the text as a design for removing a population reads the discretion as a formality. A reader who sees it as a military plan reads the same discretion as the reason outcomes differed from place to place.

Khalidi also listed the operations that, in his account, carried the plan out between 1 April and 14 May 1948. The names, dates and objectives below are as he gives them. They are his translations and his characterizations, not an Israeli official list. [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_1988]

The list covers the weeks in which the mixed towns fell: Haifa, Jaffa, Safed and others, with the depopulation of several hundred villages. [cite:wiki_plan_dalet] What happened in Tiberias and Haifa, and the separate argument over why Haifa's Arab population left, are told in [scene:rd5_cities|the fall of the mixed towns]. One discrepancy belongs here. In this list Khalidi assigns Haifa to Misparayim and the Jaffa villages to Chametz. In his separate study of Haifa he writes that the operation planned as Misparayim was renamed Chametz. [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_haifa] The two accounts by the same historian do not line up, and the material gathered for this book does not resolve which name the Haifa operation finally carried.

Khalidi's own text contains a correction that is easy to miss. He wrote that "Up to 1 March not one single Arab village had been vacated by its inhabitants." A footnote amends the sentence: at least ten villages had been captured by 1 March 1948. [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_1988] The correction cuts in a specific direction. It weakens the cleanest form of his chronology, in which nothing happened to villages before Plan D. It does not support the older account of a voluntary departure, since the villages in question were captured, not abandoned on instructions.

On what the plan meant, three positions stand side by side.

The first treats Plan Dalet as a master plan. Khalidi's 1961 essay and Ilan Pappé's 2006 book The Ethnic Cleansing of Palestine read it as the blueprint for deliberately removing the Arab population from the territory of the Jewish state. [cite:wiki_plan_dalet] In his 1988 restatement Khalidi argued that Plan D created "the military fait accompli upon which the state of Israel was to be based," and that the exodus was its product. He called the claim that Arab leaders had ordered an evacuation "a piece of mythmaking," citing the radio monitoring records of the BBC and of FBIS. And he faulted Benny Morris for treating the exodus in "an historical vacuum." [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_1988] Pappé went further on the question of terms, arguing that the plan meets the United Nations definition of ethnic cleansing. [cite:pappe_ethnic_cleansing] The strongest form of this case rests on the document's own words: destruction and expulsion were written into an order issued before the Arab states invaded, and the operations Khalidi lists began within three weeks of it.

The second reading is Benny Morris's. His archival work documented the expulsions of 1948 in detail. He reads Plan Dalet as a military plan to secure territory and lines of communication before the Arab states' invasion. Its village provisions, in his account, gave local commanders discretion, which they exercised in some places and not others. Expulsions were decided at brigade level rather than ordered from the center, and the outcome was produced by war and by those local decisions, not by a single master plan. [cite:wiki_plan_dalet] The strongest form of this case rests on the same text read differently: the plan states a military objective, makes expulsion conditional on resistance, and, in Morris's reading, the record of 1948 shows villages treated in different ways under the same orders.

Between these stand other historians, and a third position that this book takes as its own working rule. The text of Plan Dalet is settled, and so is the depopulation that followed. Whether the text caused the depopulation by design, or supplied the frame within which local commanders brought it about, is a genuine dispute among serious historians working from the same archives. [cite:wiki_plan_dalet]

The disagreement is narrower than it first appears, and it does not run where the popular account would place it. None of the three positions supports the claim that Palestinians left before any Jewish forces acted. Khalidi's own footnote records villages captured before March. Morris, whose reading is the less sweeping, is also the historian whose research documented the expulsions. What remains in dispute is design and cause, not whether expulsions took place. How large a part Arab leaders' orders played is a separate question, and an estimate from an Israeli army intelligence report of June 1948 is taken up in [scene:rd5_refugees|the refugee section]. [cite:rs_rd5_lockman_ref]

Several things the record gathered here does not settle. It does not show what written instructions reached each brigade, or how each commander read the village clauses on the day. The operation list rests on Khalidi's translations and characterizations, and his two accounts of the Haifa operation's name do not agree. And the central question, whether the plan was written to produce the exodus or produced it through the choices of men in the field, remains open among historians who have read the same files. This book records the document and the readings, and leaves the reader to set them against the events that follow.

sections.h: Washington Retreats: The Trusteeship Proposal of March 1948
sections.html:
On 18 March 1948 Harry Truman received Chaim Weizmann at the White House. He had refused to see the Zionist leader officially, and the meeting happened only because Eddie Jacobson, his former partner in a Kansas City clothing store, asked him to. [cite:forward_state_dept_truman_israel] The meeting is widely credited with securing Truman's commitment to recognition. [scene:s08|The president and his advisers] tells how it came about. The next day, 19 March, the American ambassador to the United Nations stood up in the Security Council and announced that the United States was stepping back from partition.

Warren Austin told the Council that the partition plan "cannot now be implemented by peaceful means." In its place, he said, "a temporary trusteeship for Palestine should be established under the Trusteeship Council." He asked the Council to request a special session of the General Assembly, under Article 20 of the Charter, and to instruct the United Nations Palestine Commission to "suspend its efforts to implement the proposed partition plan." [cite:rs_rd5_avalon_austin]

A common shorthand holds that the United States backed the Jewish state steadily from the partition vote to recognition. The record of these four months shows something else: a government that voted for partition in November, proposed to suspend it in March, and recognized the new state in May, with its own delegation at the United Nations still arguing for trusteeship when the recognition was announced. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition]

The scale of the retreat is clearest set against what the United States had voted for. On 29 November 1947 it was among the 33 states that adopted the partition resolution, whose timetable ended the Mandate by 1 August 1948, required provisional councils of government by 1 April and two states by 1 October, and gave the work to a five-state Palestine Commission ([scene:s09|Resolution 181]). [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_181] Austin's statement asked that commission to stop, less than two weeks before the date set for the provisional councils.

Trusteeship was not a new idea, and it had not belonged to one side. In 1944 the American Jewish Committee had proposed an international trusteeship instead of a Jewish commonwealth. [cite:djn_1944_hearings] In April 1946 the Anglo-American Committee of Inquiry recommended continuing the Mandate toward a United Nations trusteeship, and declared that Palestine should be neither a Jewish nor an Arab state. [cite:avalon_aac] In May 1948 Hannah Arendt would argue in print for a binational federation under United Nations trusteeship, and Judah Magnes would meet Truman to press the same case. [cite:rs_rd5_manne_2026] What was new in March 1948 was that the government that had led the vote for partition now offered trusteeship as its replacement.

The reasons the State Department gave for caution were on record well before Austin spoke. Loy Henderson, director of Near Eastern Affairs, Under Secretary Robert Lovett and Secretary of State George Marshall opposed early recognition of a Jewish state, arguing that it would damage American relations with the Arab world and endanger the oil supply. [cite:forward_state_dept_told_truman] Austin's own stated ground was narrower and practical: partition could not be carried out without force. [cite:rs_rd5_avalon_austin] By then fighting between Palestine's Jewish and Arab communities had gone on since 1 December 1947 [cite:explaininghistory_un_partition], and nine days before Austin spoke the Haganah had issued Plan Dalet, its plan for the period of the British withdrawal ([scene:pd_s01|Plan Dalet]).

The two events of 18 and 19 March collided because they came from two different parts of one government. The meeting with Weizmann ran through a personal channel, an old friend reaching a tired president, while the professional foreign service was strongly advising the other way. [cite:forward_state_dept_truman_israel] [cite:forward_state_dept_told_truman] The statement at the Security Council came from the diplomatic machinery that Henderson, Lovett and Marshall directed. The material gathered for this book does not show whether Truman knew that Austin would speak on 19 March, what he had told Weizmann in detail, or who drafted the statement and cleared its timing. Those questions are left open here rather than answered by inference.

The reactions were immediate. The Secretary-General, Trygve Lie, saw the new American position as "a rebuff to the United Nations." According to his memoir, as footnoted in the State Department's documentary history, he suggested that he and Austin should both resign; Austin declined. [cite:rs_rd5_frus_austin_1948] An American memorandum recorded that the Arab representatives "were pleased with this latest turn of events, but they did not gloat." [cite:rs_rd5_frus_austin_1948]

For the Jewish Agency, Abba Hillel Silver answered in the Council the same day. He called the proposal "a shocking reversal" of the American position and warned that it was likely "to lead to increased violence in Palestine." [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_trusteeship] On 20 March David Ben-Gurion went further, and his answer amounted to a refusal:

We shall not agree to any kind of trusteeship, whether permanent or temporary, even for the shortest time

He called the reversal "a surrender to the terrorism of the Arab gangs" and said it would not "prevent the establishment of the Jewish State." [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_trusteeship] The two characterizations of what had moved Washington could hardly be further apart. Austin spoke of the impossibility of a peaceful partition. Ben-Gurion spoke of surrender to force. Each was stating his own government's or movement's case, and neither statement settles the motives of the officials who drafted the policy.

The Soviet Union took the opposite course from Washington. When the United States moved toward trusteeship, Andrei Gromyko told the Security Council that the rapid creation of two states was the only way to reduce bloodshed, and Moscow stood behind partition. [cite:yated_stalin_israel] [cite:washinst_who_saved_israel] The Soviet calculation is taken up in the section on Moscow's course; here it matters that in March 1948 the two powers that had voted together in November were on opposite sides of the question.

Austin's proposal did not stop the Jewish Agency from preparing for statehood, as Ben-Gurion had said it would not. On the same day Austin spoke, Golda Meyerson returned from her American fundraising tour with a reported $50 million, spent largely on weapons. [cite:jwa_golda_50m] Plan Dalet's operations began on 1 April. [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_1988] Eight weeks later the United States extended de facto recognition to Israel eleven minutes after its proclamation, while the American delegation at the United Nations was still working for trusteeship. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition]

The record assembled here leaves gaps. It holds Austin's statement and the first reactions to it, but not the proceedings of the special session he requested or what became of the trusteeship draft there. It does not document the internal deliberations that produced the statement, and it cannot say how far Truman's private meeting with Weizmann and his ambassador's public retreat were known to each other at the time. What it does establish is that in the spring of 1948 the United States held two positions at once, and that both were visible to everyone watching.

sections.h: Deir Yassin, the Hadassah Convoy and Tantura: The Massacres of 1948 and How the Record Changed
sections.html:
Two opposite claims about 1948 circulate widely. One holds that no massacres took place. The other holds that only one side suffered them. The record supports neither. In the spring of 1948 Jewish forces killed Arab villagers, and Arab forces killed Jews, sometimes within days of each other and sometimes in answer to each other. What has changed over the decades is not whether these events happened but how much is known about them, and much of that knowledge came from Israeli archives, an Israeli student and Israeli veterans.
