Count Folke Bernadotte had been appointed United Nations mediator on 21 May 1948; he had supervised the first truce and proposed a settlement giving the Galilee to Israel, the Negev to the Arabs and Jerusalem to the United Nations, which both sides rejected. [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_truce1] On 17 September 1948 members of Lehi assassinated him in Jerusalem. The government declared Lehi a terrorist organization and arrested its members. [cite:wiki_bernadotte_assassination] The word matters: the government of the new state applied it, in its own name, to a Jewish underground.

The arrests did not last. In February 1949 the Lehi members were released under a general amnesty. [cite:wiki_bernadotte_assassination] The record gathered here does not say why the amnesty was granted, how many were held, or whether anyone was tried for the killing.

Absorbed, then promoted. The pattern that emerges is not one of suppression alone. Within four months of its founding the state had established a monopoly of armed force, by order, by shelling and by dissolution. [cite:wiki_altalena_affair] [cite:wiki_bernadotte_assassination] Within thirty-five years it had placed the leaders of both absorbed undergrounds in the prime minister's office. Menachem Begin, whose ship the army had shelled, became prime minister in 1977. [cite:wiki_altalena_affair] Yitzhak Shamir, one of Lehi's three leaders, became prime minister in 1983. [cite:wiki_bernadotte_assassination] The line of armed undergrounds that runs through the years before 1948 ends not in their disappearance but in succession to the state's highest office. Begin's new party drew a public protest in a letter signed by Albert Einstein and Hannah Arendt in December 1948, discussed in [scene:rf_s01|the section on the dissenters].

Two readings of this sequence are possible, and the record supports parts of each. One stresses the state's resolve: a provisional government, at war, fired on its own citizens rather than tolerate a private army, and named a Jewish underground's assassination of a UN mediator for what it was. The other stresses how quickly the line was redrawn: the arrests ended in an amnesty within five months of the killing, and the men who had led the Irgun and Lehi later became prime ministers. Both are true of the same events.

What the record does not settle. The sources gathered for this book give the dead of the Altalena but not the fate of its cargo. They name Lehi's members as the assassins of Bernadotte but not the individuals who planned or carried out the killing, and they record the amnesty without its terms or its reasons. They do not say how the Haganah's own structure was carried into the new army. These gaps are real, and this section does not fill them.

sections.h: The Refugees of 1948
sections.html:
The war of 1948 produced two outcomes that have shaped everything since: a Jewish state, and a Palestinian Arab population largely displaced from the territory that state came to hold. Palestinians call the second the Nakba, Arabic for "catastrophe." [cite:npr_hamashistory] Three questions about it have been argued over ever since, and they are best kept apart. How many people became refugees? Why did they leave? And why did they not return? The record answers the first within a range, the second only in part, and the third more clearly than is often supposed.

How many. The displacement began before the Arab armies entered. In its cablegram of 15 May 1948 the Arab League told the United Nations that "approximately over a quarter of a million of the Arab population have been compelled to leave their homes." [cite:rs_rd5_un_s745] That was the League's figure, given on the day of the invasion; an IDF intelligence estimate of June, discussed below, gave a higher one for 1 June.

One figure for the whole war comes from the United Nations itself. In a report dated at Lausanne on 19 August 1949 (document A/AC.25/Com.Tech/9), the Technical Committee of the UN Conciliation Commission for Palestine adopted an estimate made by P. J. Loftus of the UN Statistical Office: about 711,000 refugees from the territory under Israeli control, a figure the committee described as "as accurate as circumstances permit." [cite:rs_rd5_unccp_1949] The same report explained why the number of people drawing relief was larger than the number of refugees: duplicate ration cards, people displaced from other areas, and destitute people who were not refugees at all. [cite:rs_rd5_unccp_1949] The warning matters, because UNRWA's later figure drew on relief rolls.

Rex Brynen's Palestinian Refugee ResearchNet at McGill University set out the range in 1996. It gives the Conciliation Commission's figure as 726,000; UNRWA's 1950 figure as 957,000; the Israeli government's past figure as "as low as 520,000"; and Palestinian researchers' upper estimate as 850,000. [cite:rs_rd5_prrn_1996] The two figures attributed to the Conciliation Commission, 711,000 in its own technical report and 726,000 in Brynen's summary, do not match, and this book gives both. Another account in this book's sources gives a round figure of approximately 700,000. [cite:npr_hamashistory]

The panel above sets that figure, about 700,000 with the UN estimate of about 711,000, beside the land and immigration numbers of the Mandate years. The range around it is wide, and each figure carries its method.

Where they went. According to Brynen, about a third of the refugees went to the West Bank, a third to Gaza, and the rest to Jordan, Syria, Lebanon and beyond. [cite:rs_rd5_prrn_1996] Gaza was then under Egyptian administration and the West Bank under Jordanian. [cite:npr_hamashistory] Lebanon received an estimated 100,000–110,000, the large majority from northern Palestine, including the Acre area, in a country of about 1.3 million people. The International Committee of the Red Cross, and from 1950 UNRWA, ran the camps that resulted. [cite:lebanon_refugee_policy] The receiving states treated them differently. Jordan later gave citizenship to most Palestinians who had come after 1948, under its 1954 nationality law; Lebanon restricted their work and, much later, their right to own property; and the Arab League instructed its members not to grant citizenship, in its words "to avoid dissolution of their identity and protect their right of return." That divergence, and the arguments on both sides of it, are told in [scene:sq_s20|the section on the host countries]. [cite:jns_arab_citizenship] [cite:fmr_lebanon] The displacement became, in the words of one account, the foundational political fact around which every later Palestinian political movement organized. [cite:npr_hamashistory]

Why they left. This is the most disputed of the three questions, and the evidence has to be read with care for who produced it. A central document is an intelligence report of the Israel Defense Forces from June 1948, known through the work of the Israeli historian Benny Morris and summarized by Zachary Lockman. It estimated that by 1 June 1948 about 240,000 Arabs had fled the areas of the Jewish state and about 150,000 had fled other areas. It attributed about 70% of the flight to direct Jewish military operations, 2% to psychological warfare and 2% to expulsion orders, a figure Morris considers an underestimate, and no more than 5% to evacuation orders from Arab leaders. [cite:rs_rd5_lockman_ref] Those numbers were compiled by the army that was doing the fighting, and its own share of responsibility is the largest it records.

The claim that Palestinians left on the orders of their own leaders, broadcast by Arab radio, corresponds to that last category, and the IDF's own estimate put it at 5% or less. The investigation of the radio claim itself is told in the section on independence and the Nakba.

From June 1948 the pattern changed. Morris concludes, according to Lockman, that deliberate expulsions helped create about 300,000 further refugees, but that there was no explicit, general Israeli decision to expel. [cite:rs_rd5_lockman_ref] The expulsion from Lydda and Ramla in July, after Ben-Gurion's reported words "Expel them" and Yitzhak Rabin's signed order, is the best-known case; its tolls are disputed and are set out in the section on the Arab states' war. [cite:rs_rd5_palquest_lydda] [cite:rs_rd5_lockman_war]

Historians divide on what this evidence adds up to. Morris, as Avi Shlaim summarizes him, "rejected both the 'Arab order' and the 'Jewish robber-state' explanations" and treated the refugee problem as "a by-product of the war." Shlaim holds that the evidence "suggests a far higher degree of Israeli responsibility." [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_hnn_ref] Walid Khalidi's reading goes further: that the flight was produced by design, under Plan Dalet, the plan discussed earlier in this chapter. [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_1988] The strongest form of Morris's case is that the flight came in waves with different causes, that most of it followed fighting rather than orders, and that no general order to expel has been found. The strongest form of the opposing case is that the army's own estimate assigns the great majority of the flight to its operations, that deliberate expulsions grew from June, and that a policy need not be written as a general order to be carried out.

Why they did not return. On this point the record is plainer. "As early as June 1948," Lockman writes, "the cabinet had reached a consensus against allowing the refugees to return to their homes." [cite:rs_rd5_lockman_ref] The decision came while the war was still being fought, and before the expulsions from Lydda and Ramla in July. Lockman also writes that a report by Yosef Weitz in October 1948 falsely blamed Arab leaders for organizing the flight. [cite:rs_rd5_lockman_ref] That is Lockman's judgment of Weitz's report; the point it carries is that the "Arab leaders' orders" explanation was being put forward in an Israeli report within months. One offer to settle part of the question came from an Arab government: in 1949 Syria's new military ruler, Husni al-Za'im, offered to resettle 250,000–300,000 refugees in Syria as part of a peace treaty, an offer Ben-Gurion declined and which ended with Za'im's overthrow and execution that August. [cite:tf_zaim] [cite:majalla_zaim] [cite:ecf_zaim] The United Nations' response, and the negotiations that followed, belong to the next stage: see [scene:rr_s01|Resolution 194] and [scene:lau_s01|Lausanne].

The villages. How many Arab villages were emptied depends on what is counted. Morris, in 1987, counted 369. Walid Khalidi's All That Remains (1992) counted 418, excluding towns and 151 places found on other lists. Aref al-Aref counted 399; Nijm and Muammer 443; Saleh 472; and the Palestine Land Society 531 localities, counting tribal lands and towns. [cite:rs_rd5_plands_villages] The source attributes the spread to method: what counts as a village, whether towns and tribal lands are included, and which lists are merged.

What the record does not settle. No single count of the refugees commands agreement; the sources range from 520,000 to 957,000, and even the Conciliation Commission's figure is reported two ways. The share of the flight caused by deliberate expulsion, as against fighting, fear and the collapse of Palestinian society, is estimated from an army report that its own principal interpreter considers incomplete on expulsions. Whether the flight was the product of a plan or of the war is the central argument among historians, and it is not resolved here. The number of Arabs who remained inside Israel in 1948–49 has not been established in the sources gathered for this book. What is not in dispute is the outcome: by the summer of 1949 several hundred thousand Palestinian Arabs were outside the territory Israel held, and its cabinet had reached a consensus, a year earlier, against their return.

chapters.label: Stage Six
chapters.title: Consolidate and Account
chapters.intro:
On 20 May 1948, six days after Israel declared its independence, the United Nations appointed Count Folke Bernadotte, head of the Swedish Red Cross, as its mediator in Palestine. [cite:rs_rd6_britannica_bernadotte] [cite:rs_rd6_un_bernadotte_bio] The war he was sent to stop was still being fought. Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Lebanon and Iraq had invaded after the Mandate ended, and Jordan's Arab Legion held the Old City of Jerusalem and the West Bank. [cite:wikipedia_1948_war] [cite:wiki_jordan_annexation] The new state had been recognized by the United States eleven minutes after its declaration, over the warnings of the State Department and the CIA; de jure recognition would wait until January 1949. [cite:jvl_truman_marshall_dejure] Inside the lines Israel held, its statisticians would count 716,700 Jews and 156,000 non-Jews at the end of the year. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_population] Beyond them, by December, some 700,000 Palestinians were refugees, a number disputed from the start. [cite:rs_rd6_morris_appendix]

This stage asks what became of all that once the shooting stopped. The war had produced facts: positions held, villages emptied, houses occupied, a state with an army and no borders. In the years that followed, each fact was either written into law and treaty or left in suspense, and the choice was rarely made by one party alone. The stage follows both processes, consolidation and accounting. It asks who fixed the lines, who took title to the land, who was admitted as a citizen and who was not, who paid, and what the new international order did, and could not do, for the people the war had displaced. It also closes the account on the years before the state: who funded the build, through which channels, and what the record can and cannot show about money and American politicians.

The cast is the widest in the volume. Israel's government under David Ben-Gurion and Moshe Sharett, and its first parliament, made most of the decisions that turned wartime facts into statute. The United Nations acted through Bernadotte, through Ralph Bunche, who negotiated the armistices after Bernadotte's murder, and through a Conciliation Commission of France, Turkey and the United States. [cite:rs_rd6_nobel_bunche] [cite:rs_rd6_refworld_194] In Washington Harry Truman moved between his Secretary of State, George Marshall, his political aide Clark Clifford and the donors of an election year. Among the Arab states, King Abdullah of Jordan, Egypt's government and a Syrian officer, Husni al-Za'im, each pursued a different settlement. Palestinian leaders acted on both sides of an inter-Arab rivalry, in a government proclaimed in Gaza under Ahmad Hilmi, with a National Council under Hajj Amin al-Husayni, and in a congress at Jericho that proclaimed union with Abdullah's kingdom. [cite:rs_rd6_shlaim_apg_1990] The Jews of Iraq, Yemen, Libya, Egypt and Morocco, West Germany's Konrad Adenauer, the Holy See and an American lobby in the course of renaming itself complete it.

The sections begin with the mediator's two plans and with Truman's decisions from the summer of 1948 to May 1950, including the one decision that a historian ties to a campaign contribution. They then follow how return was barred and the border hardened, who came to govern Arab Palestine, and the regime imposed on the Arabs who stayed inside Israel, before tracing the laws that turned flight into state ownership of land. One week in December 1948 produced the Universal Declaration and Resolution 194; the armistices of 1949 drew lines that, by their own text, were not borders; Lausanne failed over which should come first, peace or return. Israel's constitution was deferred, Syria's offer of peace was declined, and Israel entered the United Nations while the question of Jerusalem stayed open. The refugees' host states, the exodus of the Jews of the Arab world, the mass immigration and the Yemenite children, and the laws defining who belonged follow. The stage then closes the books: the organization that became AIPAC, how the state was paid for, how the flight was explained, how the case was put to Americans, who paid for the pre-state build, and the whole sequence from a bank to a state.
chapters.outro:
This volume began with a loan. In 1694, 1,268 subscribers lent the English Crown £1.2 million through a newly chartered company that became the Bank of England, and a Crown at war against France found a new lender in private subscribers. [cite:rs_rd0_boe_museum] It ends two and a half centuries later with a state drawing on outside money in its own name: a loan from the Export-Import Bank of the United States, bonds sold to buyers abroad, and reparations from West Germany. Between the two lie the structures this volume has traced, laid by many hands over many decades and never by one design. By the early 1950s they stood in six layers, and each held something the others did not.

The legal layer was the longest in the making. The Ottoman Land Code of 1858 required titles to be registered individually, and under the Mandate those registered titles were the instruments that could be sold. [cite:wiki_ottoman_land_code_1858] Balfour's letter of 1917 had no legal force until the Mandate of 1922 wrote it into an instrument of the League of Nations, recognized a "Jewish agency" in Article 4, and bound Britain in Article 2 to the national home, to self-governing institutions and to safeguarding the civil and religious rights of all inhabitants. [cite:rs_md_avalon] The General Assembly's partition resolution passed on 29 November 1947 by 33 votes to 13. [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_181] After 1948 the new state supplied its own law: the Absentees' Property Law of 14 March 1950, the Law of Return of 5 July 1950, the Nationality Law in force from 14 July 1952, and the Land Acquisition Law of 1953. [cite:un_absentees_property_law_text] [cite:rs_rd6_mjl_lawofreturn] [cite:rs_rd6_refworld_nationality] [cite:rs_rd6_badil_landregime] Its membership of the United Nations, granted by Resolution 273 on 11 May 1949, was settled. [cite:rs_rd6_unga273_text] Its borders were not. The Egyptian and Jordanian armistices of 1949 reserved the final settlement, and the Egyptian text said the line was "not to be construed in any sense as a political or territorial boundary." [cite:rs_rd6_arm_egypt_text] Nor did the state give itself a constitution: the Harari Resolution of 13 June 1950 promised one made up of chapters, each a separate basic law. [cite:rs_rd6_dickerman_2007] What was contested was the force of the older texts. Israel held that the Arab invasion had nullified partition and that Resolution 194 tied return to peace; the Arab states at Lausanne demanded the 1947 lines and return first. [cite:un_ccp_fourth_report] [cite:unispal_194_survey]

The administrative layer showed the most continuity. The Mandate's High Commissioner had governed from 1923 with no elected chamber beside him. [cite:rs_lc_albright] The Defense (Emergency) Regulations that Britain issued in 1945 passed into Israeli law in 1948, and under them a military government ruled most Arab citizens of Israel until 1 December 1966. [cite:rs_rd6_korn_adalah] The strongest case for it, made at the time and endorsed by the Rattner Commission in 1956, was that a state with armistices but no peace needed such controls; the strongest case against, made by Alina Korn, is that its purpose was to control movement and keep Arabs from confiscated land, and it rests on conviction figures: about 95 percent of Arab citizens' convictions under the regulations were for administrative offenses, such as lacking a permit. [cite:rs_rd6_korn_adalah] The record documents both purposes and does not weigh them.

The institutional and financial layer was built first by the movement and then by the state. The Jewish Colonial Trust of 1899, the Jewish National Fund of 1901 and Keren Hayesod, which raised $20.1 million worldwide in 1921–29, made fundraising permanent; by 1948 the United Jewish Appeal raised $150 million from more than a million American contributors, of which $74.7 million went to Palestine and $64.9 million to relief in Europe. [cite:jta_kh_decade] [cite:jta_uja_1948] After 1948 a Custodian, a Development Authority and the Fund itself received the land of those classed as absentees; BADIL puts the transfers at nearly 2.4 million dunams, a figure the scholarly sources here do not confirm. [cite:rs_rd6_fischbach_2003] [cite:rs_rd6_badil_landregime] The money became a state's money: $100.0 million of American aid in 1949, all of it economic, more than $52 million in Israel Bonds in their first year, and German reparations that made up 12–14 percent of Israel's imports for a decade. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_usaid_table] [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_bonds] [cite:rs_rd6_nli_reparations] The Knesset voted to negotiate with Germany by 61 to 50, while opponents led by Menachem Begin called the payments "blood money." [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_reparations] [cite:rs_rd6_nli_reparations] What the record leaves open is a total: no audited sum exists for the pre-state build or the Haganah's budget.

The Palestinian Arab layer was a national movement that never acquired a state's instruments. The Arab Executive under Musa Kazim al-Husseini was never recognized by Britain, and its boycott of 1923 defeated the Legislative Council but won no recognition. [cite:palquest_musa_kazim] [cite:rs_lc_cojs_boycott] In 1948 Palestinian leaders proclaimed a government in Gaza that Avi Shlaim calls "a phantom deliberately created by the Arab states," while the Jericho Congress proclaimed the union of Palestine and Transjordan under Abdullah as king. [cite:rs_rd6_shlaim_apg_1990] The refugees were counted from 520,000 to a million, depending on who counted. [cite:rs_rd6_morris_appendix] They were given relief through UNRWA, left outside the 1951 Refugee Convention by its Article 1D, and promised in paragraph 11 of Resolution 194 that those wishing to return "should be permitted to do so." [cite:unrwa_who] [cite:w_refconv] [cite:unispal_194_survey] Their strongest case is that return is a right, reaffirmed by the Assembly every year since 1949; Israel's is that the resolution made return conditional on peace, and that the Arab states first rejected it. [cite:wiki_res_194] [cite:unwatch_194] Arab citizens, among the 156,000 non-Jews counted inside Israel at the end of 1948 by Israeli figures, voted from the first election in 1949, most of them while living under military rule. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_population] [cite:rs_rd6_idi_nazareth] [cite:rs_rd6_korn_adalah] Whether the expulsions of 1948 were planned remains disputed; the claim that the refugees left on a general Arab order is no longer defended by mainstream scholarship. [cite:w_morris_birth]

The regional layer was redrawn twice. Britain made conflicting wartime promises in 1915–16, to Sharif Hussein and to France, and at Cairo in 1921 gave Iraq to his son Faisal and Transjordan to his son Abdullah. [cite:w_mcmahon] [cite:w_sykes_picot] [cite:w_cairo1921] In 1948–50 one of them, Abdullah, annexed the West Bank, and the annexation was condemned within the Arab League. [cite:rs_rd6_loc_jordan] Iraq and Saudi Arabia signed no armistice, and the League's boycott carried the conflict into trade. [cite:rs_rd6_mfa_armistice_map] Syria's military ruler, Husni al-Za'im, offered a peace treaty and the resettlement of 250,000–300,000 refugees, and Ben-Gurion declined. [cite:tf_zaim] [cite:majalla_zaim] The war also ended Jewish life in much of the Arab world: Iraq made Zionism a crime in July 1948, and by the end of 1952, by a State Archives count, Israel had received 377,251 immigrants from Muslim countries. [cite:yated_ezra_nechemia] [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_immigrants_4852] Philip Mendes explains that exodus by push and pull together, against the partisan accounts on either side. [cite:rs_rd6_mendes_2010]

The American layer had the deepest roots and the newest weight. In 1839 Lord Shaftesbury, a British evangelical, pressed for a Jewish return to Palestine, and in 1891 an American evangelist petitioned President Harrison for the same. [cite:wiki_christian_zionism] Congress endorsed the Balfour Declaration in 1922, both party platforms adopted the movement's aims in 1944, and the American Zionist Emergency Council worked Congress district by district. [cite:wiki_lodge_fish] [cite:aja_azec_appraisal_1944] [cite:aja_azec_local_1944] Truman recognized the state against his strategists' advice. In the election summer he stopped pressing Israel on territory and refugees, in part, by John Judis's account, because his campaign needed $100,000 from Abraham Feinberg and Ed Kaufmann; then he threatened a "revision" of policy in May 1949 that he never enforced. [cite:mondoweiss_judis_truman] [cite:jvl_truman_note_may1949] The claim that donors bought policy has that one documented case and no other; the claim that money played no role is contradicted by it. Whether money reached members of Congress before 1948 cannot be known, because the law did not require the records until 1971. [cite:wiki_fcpa_1925]

What, then, did the road from 1694 settle? It settled that a Jewish state existed, with an army, a parliament, a land regime and a law of immigration, and that it rested on institutions built over half a century before it was declared. It did not settle where the state ended, what was owed to the people displaced in its founding, or who would govern the rest of the land. The Holocaust gave the build its urgency; it did not create the apparatus. And the war of 1948, not any plan, decided where the lines ran. Those lines were, by their own text, still not borders. Every volume that follows begins from that fact.

sections.h: The Mediator: Count Bernadotte's Two Plans, May–September 1948
sections.html:
The first outsider to try to turn the war's facts into a settlement was the United Nations' mediator. For four months, from late May to mid-September 1948, one man carried the organization's attempt to stop the fighting and to sketch a settlement. He produced two sets of proposals, very different from each other. Neither was accepted. He was killed the day after the second was dated. Yet his last report outlived him, and two of its proposals reappeared in the General Assembly's Resolution 194 three months later.

The man and the appointment. Folke Bernadotte came to the post with a reputation made in the last months of the Second World War. As head of the Swedish Red Cross he is credited with saving some 20,000 inmates of German concentration camps. [cite:rs_rd6_britannica_bernadotte] He was appointed United Nations mediator in Palestine on 20 May 1948. [cite:rs_rd6_britannica_bernadotte] [cite:rs_rd6_un_bernadotte_bio]

The sources differ, in a small way, on who appointed him. The UN's own press release of 17 September 1948 records that he was chosen by the five permanent members of the Security Council, sitting as a committee of the General Assembly under a General Assembly resolution of 14 May 1948. [cite:rs_rd6_un_bernadotte_bio] Encyclopaedia Britannica says more simply that the Security Council named him. [cite:rs_rd6_britannica_bernadotte] The difference is not trivial for a reader trying to understand where his authority came from. On the UN's account his mandate flowed from a General Assembly resolution, with the five permanent members acting as its committee. On the shorter account it came from the Council. The UN's own contemporary record is the more detailed of the two, but this book records both.

The two truces. His first task was to stop the shooting. The first truce he negotiated took effect on 11 June 1948 and lasted until 9 July. [cite:rs_rd6_un_bernadotte_bio] On 15 July the Security Council ordered a second truce, which was to last "until a peaceful adjustment of the future situation of Palestine is reached." [cite:rs_rd6_un_bernadotte_bio] The difference in wording mattered. The first truce was a pause with an end date, negotiated by the mediator. The second was ordered by the Council and had no end date at all: it was meant to hold until there was a settlement. It was inside that open-ended truce that Bernadotte wrote his final report.

The Rhodes suggestions of 28 June 1948. During the first truce, on 28 June 1948, Bernadotte presented the parties with a set of written suggestions at Rhodes. The American government's published diplomatic record preserves their text. [cite:rs_rd6_frus_bernadotte_june] They did not start from the partition plan. They proposed that Palestine, including Transjordan, might form a union of "one Arab and one Jewish" member. Within that union, the Negev, in whole or in part, would go to Arab territory, and Western Galilee, in whole or in part, to Jewish territory. The City of Jerusalem would be included in Arab territory, with municipal autonomy for its Jewish community. Each member would control immigration within its own borders. [cite:rs_rd6_frus_bernadotte_june]

Two shared facilities would serve the whole union: a free port at Haifa, including the refineries and terminals, and a free airport at Lydda. And the suggestions proposed recognition of the right of people displaced by the conflict "to return to their homes without restriction and to regain possession of their property." [cite:rs_rd6_frus_bernadotte_june] That phrase is the first appearance in this chapter of the language of return. It was unconditional. It set no date, required no prior peace, and offered no alternative of compensation.

According to the mediator's own later report, both parties "flatly rejected" the June suggestions. [cite:rs_rd6_palquest_progress] The sources gathered here record the rejection but not the parties' own statements of their reasons. What the text itself shows is what each side was being asked to accept. The Jewish side was asked to accept a union rather than an independent state with its own frontiers, and to see Jerusalem, with its Jewish community, placed in Arab territory with only municipal autonomy. The Arab side was asked to accept a Jewish member of a joint union, with its own control of immigration. That is a reading of the text, not a record of either side's stated objections. Whatever reasons each gave, the mediator's second plan started from different premises.

The Progress Report of 16 September 1948. The report Bernadotte completed in September, dated 16 September 1948, began from a premise the June suggestions had avoided: "A Jewish State called Israel exists in Palestine." [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_progress_report] [cite:rs_rd6_palquest_progress] The union with Transjordan was gone. In its place the report drew a territorial settlement between a recognized Jewish state and the Arab territory around it.

On territory it reversed part of the June scheme and kept part. The Negev should be Arab territory and Galilee should be Jewish territory. Ramleh and Lydda should be in Arab territory. The precise frontiers would be set by a UN technical boundaries commission. Jerusalem would no longer be placed in Arab territory; it would be under "effective United Nations control." Haifa would be a free port and Lydda a free airport, as in June. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_progress_report] [cite:rs_rd6_palquest_progress]

On the refugees, the report urged that Arab refugees be allowed to return to Jewish-controlled areas "at the earliest possible date," with adequate compensation for those choosing not to return. It proposed a Palestine conciliation commission to carry the settlement forward. And on the Arab territory, it saw "compelling reasons for merging the Arab territory of Palestine with the territory of Transjordan." [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_progress_report] [cite:rs_rd6_palquest_progress] The idea of joining Arab Palestine to Transjordan survived from June, but now as a merger of the Arab part alone, not a union that took in the Jewish state as well.

Set side by side, the two plans show how far the mediator moved in eleven weeks. The June suggestions treated Palestine and Transjordan as one framework to be divided into two members. The September report accepted Israel as a state, gave it Galilee, assigned the Negev, Ramleh and Lydda to Arab territory, removed Jerusalem from either side's control, and turned the right of return "without restriction" into return "at the earliest possible date," paired for the first time with compensation as the alternative.

The assassination. Bernadotte was killed in Jerusalem on 17 September 1948, the day after the report was dated, by members of the Stern Gang (Lehi). A French air force colonel serving as a UN observer, André-Pierre Sérot, was killed with him. [cite:rs_rd6_britannica_bernadotte] [cite:rs_rd6_un_bernadotte_bio] The UN noted that the completed report reached Paris almost simultaneously with the news of his death. [cite:rs_rd6_un_bernadotte_bio] The government's response to the killing, including the dissolution of Lehi and the amnesty that followed, belongs to [scene:mil_s01|the absorption of the undergrounds into one army].

What the report left behind. A plan that both parties rejected in June and that its author did not live to defend in September might have died with him. It did not, for two reasons. The first was Washington. Four days after the killing, on 21 September 1948, Secretary of State George Marshall endorsed the plan, including its award of the Negev to the Arab side, and the endorsement became an issue in an American presidential campaign; how President Truman then backed away from it is told in [scene:tr_s02|Truman's decisions after the election money]. The second was the General Assembly. Two of the report's central proposals, a conciliation commission and the return of refugees with compensation for those who chose not to return, reappeared in the Assembly's Resolution 194 of December 1948, whose full text and competing readings are set out in [scene:rr_s01|Resolution 194]. Britannica also credits Bernadotte's work with laying the groundwork for the UN Truce Supervision Organization and for UNRWA, the relief agency for Palestinian refugees. [cite:rs_rd6_britannica_bernadotte]

What the record does not settle. The documents here establish what Bernadotte proposed, when, and that both sides rejected his first plan. They do not record, in the parties' own words, why each rejected it, nor how either side responded formally to the September report before events overtook it. Nor do they settle the narrower question of which UN body appointed him; the UN's contemporary account and Britannica's summary differ, and both are recorded above. What is beyond doubt is the direction of travel between June and September. A mediator who had begun by trying to fold the new state into a union with Transjordan ended by taking its existence as the starting point, and by proposing the refugees' return, with compensation as its alternative, in terms the General Assembly took up in Resolution 194.

sections.h: Truman After Recognition: A Retreat, a Pledge, and a Threat Not Kept, 1948–1950
sections.html:
Bernadotte's September plan was one of several moments at which Washington had to decide how far to back the new state. American recognition in May 1948 had not settled that question. It opened a two-year sequence in which Harry Truman's decisions moved sometimes toward Israel's position and sometimes against it. Two accounts of that sequence circulate, and they are mirror images. One holds that once the donors had paid, Truman did whatever Israel wanted. The other holds that money had nothing to do with it, and that his policy followed from conviction and from the interests of the United States. Each has a strong form. The first can point to a named donor, a named sum and a historian's account of a decision that changed. The second can point to a president who signed legislation he called discriminatory against Jewish refugees and later threatened Israel in writing. The way to weigh them is to put the decisions in the order they were made, with their dates.

The decision that came first. Recognition itself had been made against the advice of the government's own specialists. Declassified CIA and State Department documents from 1947 and 1948 record consistent warnings against recognizing Israel on strategic grounds. The CIA's assessments noted the Zionist arms-procurement networks operating across Europe and the United States, predicted that recognition would immediately produce armed conflict with the Arab states, and warned of damage to American access to oil. One CIA report held that an arms embargo would lead to peaceful coexistence, the opposite of what followed. The State Department under George Marshall opposed recognition on strategic grounds as well. Truman overruled both. He recognized Israel at 6:11 pm on 14 May 1948, eleven minutes after its declaration of independence, a recognition so fast that his own State Department was caught unprepared. It has been called the fastest diplomatic recognition in American history.

The familiar explanation is that Truman acted from moral conviction about Jewish statehood after the Holocaust, and that the CIA's concerns were one input among many. The documents support a narrower statement: the strategic advice was clear and was set aside, and the decision was political rather than strategic. One reading, made with the advantage of hindsight, holds that this set a pattern in which political decisions overrode intelligence assessments, and that the intelligence relationship which followed began on terms Israel could shape. That is an interpretation of later history, not a finding about 1948, and the later relationship, from the start of James Jesus Angleton's tenure as the CIA's counterintelligence chief in 1954 to the Khrushchev speech of 1956, is told in [scene:cia_s02|the CIA and Israel after 1948].

25 June 1948: the Displaced Persons Act. The first decision of the summer concerned Jewish refugees in Europe rather than the new state itself. On 25 June 1948 Truman signed the Displaced Persons Act "with very great reluctance," saying that it "discriminates in callous fashion against displaced persons of the Jewish faith." [cite:truman_institute_dpact] He did not leave the matter there. He pressed Congress for two years, until the act was amended in 1950. [cite:wjc_dpact] [cite:truman_institute_dpact] The episode does not fit a president acting on donors' instructions, nor one indifferent to Jewish refugees: he signed a law he condemned and then spent two years trying to change it.

Summer 1948: what Truman wanted and did not press. Through the summer, Truman privately wanted Israel to stop taking territory beyond the partition lines, and he was disturbed by its refugee policy. He backed away from pressing either point. The historian John Judis documents that his nearly broke whistle-stop campaign needed $100,000 from two donors, Abraham Feinberg and Ed Kaufmann, at that moment, and that this need was part of the reason he stopped pushing. [cite:mondoweiss_judis_truman] The donors, the sum and the way Judis frames it are the subject of [scene:s07f2|the section on Abraham Feinberg]. The point for this sequence is its date: the retreat came in the summer and autumn of an election year, when the campaign was short of money.

21–28 September 1948: the Bernadotte plan. On 16 September the UN mediator, Count Folke Bernadotte, completed a report that would have given the Negev to the Arab side; the next day he was murdered in Jerusalem. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_progress_report] [cite:rs_rd6_britannica_bernadotte] On 21 September 1948 Secretary of State Marshall endorsed the plan. On 28 September the White House aide Clark Clifford was upset that Marshall had approved it without the President's endorsement, and the camp of Truman's opponent, Thomas Dewey, sought to exploit the episode. [cite:jvl_clifford_bernadotte] [cite:djn_marshall_bernadotte_1948] Truman backed away from the plan. The American government was not of one mind: the Secretary of State had endorsed what the President's aide opposed.

24 October 1948: the pledge. Ten days before the election, and two days after a statement by Dewey, Truman went further. He quoted the Democratic platform, which pledged full recognition of Israel and revision of the arms embargo "to accord to the State of Israel the right of self-defense," and he directed government agencies to expedite Israel's applications for loans. [cite:ucsb_truman_oct24_1948] The timing, in the campaign's last fortnight and on the heels of his opponent, is the documented point.

29 November 1948: the Negev. After winning, on 29 November, Truman reassured Weizmann that Israel would keep the Negev. Two months earlier his Secretary of State had endorsed a plan that would have taken it away.

January 1949: recognition and a loan. Two of the October pledges were then delivered. An Export-Import Bank loan of $100 million was earmarked for Israel, and on 31 January 1949 the United States granted de jure recognition, full legal recognition of the state. [cite:jvl_truman_marshall_dejure] [cite:docsteach_dejure_1949] [cite:djn_1977_truman_note]

The loan's size is best seen against the other dollar sums in this story. The library's money dashboard sets the documented dollar flows of 1921–1949 side by side, in nominal dollars of the year reported. The $100 million loan is the largest bar on it. The $100,000 that Feinberg and Kaufmann raised for the campaign train is the smallest, one-thousandth of the loan. [cite:jvl_truman_marshall_dejure] [cite:mondoweiss_judis_truman]

The contrast cuts both ways. Those who argue that donors bought policy point to the sequence: the campaign took the smaller sum in 1948, and the state received a government loan a thousand times larger in 1949. Those who argue that money played no role point to the scale: a government loan of $100 million was a decision of the United States made through the Export-Import Bank after an election had been won, not a return on a campaign contribution. The documents do not show a link between the two sums. What they show is that the $100,000 was raised at the moment a policy was in play, and that the loan followed a public pledge made in the campaign's last days.

28 May 1949: the threat. Then the pressure returned. On 28 May 1949, while the Lausanne talks were under way, Truman had a secret note delivered to David Ben-Gurion. It said the United States was "seriously disturbed" by Israel's position on territory and refugees. It said Israel should offer territorial compensation for the land it held beyond the partition lines. And it warned that if Israel continued to reject the UN resolution of December 1948, "a revision of its attitude toward Israel has become unavoidable." [cite:jvl_truman_note_may1949] [cite:djn_1977_truman_note] The note took up exactly the two questions, territory and refugees, on which Truman had stopped pressing in the summer of 1948. With the election behind him, he raised them again, in writing.

June 1949: rejection, and no revision. Israel rejected the demands in June. The threatened revision was not carried through. [cite:jvl_truman_note_may1949] [cite:djn_1977_truman_note] The documents gathered here do not explain why Washington did not follow its warning with action. What came at Lausanne after the note is told in [scene:lau_s01|the Lausanne conference].

May 1950: the Tripartite Declaration. In May 1950 the United States joined Britain and France in the Tripartite Declaration on the region. The record gathered here does not set out its terms.

What the dated record supports. Laid out in order, the decisions have a clear shape. Two moves favorable to Israel in 1948, the retreat from the Bernadotte plan and the October pledges, came when money and votes were most needed. After the election Truman both delivered and pushed back: he delivered recognition and the loan, and then, six months later, threatened a revision of policy over the very issues he had set aside. He did not enforce the threat. That record fits neither simple account. It is not the record of a president who did whatever Israel's supporters asked, since in May 1949 he sent a note threatening a revision of policy over territory and refugees. Nor is it the record of a president untouched by his campaign's finances, since a historian names financial need as part of the reason he stopped pressing a point he cared about, at the moment he stopped. The favorable shift clustered around the election; then the pressure returned, and faded.

Several things remain unsettled. The documents establish timing, not motive: they show when Truman moved, not how much weight he gave to money, votes, conviction or advice at each step. Judis's account attributes the summer retreat to financial need "in part," and no source here measures that part. No document here links the campaign contribution to the 1949 loan. And the record gathered for this book does not say why the threatened revision of May 1949 was never carried out, which is perhaps the most consequential question of the sequence, since it was the moment at which Washington had stated its terms and then let them go.

sections.h: Abraham Feinberg: One Donor, One Decision, 1945–1958
sections.html:
The one decision in that sequence that a historian ties to money runs through Abraham Feinberg, a name absent from most popular accounts of 1948. It belongs in them, for a specific reason. He is the person through whom the documented record comes closest to showing a campaign contribution changing a particular decision of the American president. That claim needs to be stated at exactly its documented size, no larger and no smaller, and the rest of his career helps show why.

The man. Abraham "Abe" Feinberg was born in 1908 and died in 1998. He was born and raised in the Bronx and built his fortune in the hosiery business. From 1945 he played a significant role behind the scenes in the relationship between the United States and Israel, a role that lasted until 1968. Across those years he served as a confidant and a key financier to three presidents: Truman, Kennedy and Johnson. [cite:emory_feinberg_thesis] [cite:nationalinterest_feinberg_bomb] He was also one of the original seventeen members of the Sonneborn Institute, the arms-procurement network founded in 1945, whose place in the wider American structure is mapped in [scene:nw_s02|the network of the American build-up]. [cite:emory_feinberg_thesis]

That second fact matters for what follows. Feinberg was not a donor who appears once in the record and then disappears. He links two structures that are often told separately: the private arms-procurement network that operated on American soil from 1945, and the presidential campaign of 1948.

The $100,000. In mid-1948 Truman's campaign was broke, and Thomas Dewey was widely expected to make him a one-term president. Truman needed $100,000, a large sum in 1948, to pay for a whistle-stop tour by train through the Midwest. Feinberg and the jewelry magnate Ed Kaufmann led the fundraising that produced that amount, at that moment. [cite:mondoweiss_judis_truman] [cite:prnewswire_feinberg_fbi]

Feinberg later described his own method plainly. "My path to power," he said, "was cooperation in terms of what they needed — campaign money." [cite:mondoweiss_judis_truman] [cite:prnewswire_feinberg_fbi] The words are his, on the record, not an outside reading of his motives. They describe an exchange in general terms: he supplied what politicians needed, and that was, in his words, his path to power. They do not, by themselves, say what any president gave him.

The decision. The link between the money and a decision comes from the historian John Judis. In mid-1948, by Judis's account, Truman wanted Israel to stop seizing territory by military force beyond the UN partition lines, and he was personally "disgusted" by Israel's refugee policy. He is reported to have said that Jews had turned their own narrative on its head by denying Palestinians the right of return. Judis documents that Truman folded on these impulses in part because he needed the $100,000 from Feinberg and Kaufmann for the whistle-stop tour at that moment. [cite:mondoweiss_judis_truman] The dated sequence of what Truman did and did not do on territory and refugees, from the Bernadotte plan to the threat he sent Ben-Gurion in May 1949, is set out in [scene:tr_s02|Truman's decisions after recognition].

The familiar account holds that Truman's support for Israel was a matter of personal conviction and of a broad political calculation about Jewish voters, with no instance in which financial dependence changed a specific decision. Judis's account is such an instance. It names a donor, a sum, a moment in a campaign, and an objection the President stopped pressing. That is a different and more precise kind of claim than the general statement that money influenced politics.

It is also a limited one, and the limits are in Judis's own words. He says Truman folded "in part" because of the financial need. Money was one cause among others, not the only one. The account is one historian's reading of one decision. It does not show that Feinberg's money bought American policy toward Israel in general, and it does not show what Truman thought he was giving in return. When Truman later threatened Israel over the same two questions, territory and refugees, the money of 1948 did not prevent him. Some accounts go further and place the recognition of Israel, eleven minutes after its declaration of independence, inside the same financial relationship. The sources gathered here cite no document linking the money to recognition itself; they tie the $100,000 to the summer retreat and to nothing else.

Why the smallest sum matters most. On the chart of dollar flows in the previous section, the $100,000 is the smallest bar, one-thousandth of the $100 million Export-Import Bank loan of 1949. [cite:mondoweiss_judis_truman] Yet it is the only sum in that record that a historian ties to a specific policy decision, because, by Judis's account, it was raised at the moment a decision was being made. Its importance comes from its timing, not its size.

The FARA order of 1952. The federal government did eventually reach Feinberg, not for arms but for publishing. In 1952 he was formally ordered to register as an agent of a foreign principal under the Foreign Agents Registration Act. The order concerned Israel Speaks, a bimonthly publication he ran on behalf of Israeli interests, the successor to an earlier publication aligned with the Haganah. [cite:feinberg_fbi_file] [cite:israellobby_feinberg_fbi] Feinberg briefly considered selling the publication to the Jerusalem Post. Instead he shut it down entirely rather than register. [cite:feinberg_fbi_file] The outcome was compliance by closure: there was no prosecution and no fight in court.

The order corrects a claim sometimes made about the Sonneborn network, that none of its figures was ever required to register as a foreign agent and that the network enjoyed complete legal immunity. At least one was ordered to register. [cite:feinberg_fbi_file] It was the first documented order of its kind against a figure from that network, seven years after the network's founding.

The same FBI file, released decades later, shows more. It documents Feinberg's continuing meetings with Sonneborn, and it shows that the Israeli government tasked him with intervening in the criminal prosecutions of members of the arms-smuggling network who had been caught. [cite:feinberg_fbi_file] It is the clearest documented link in the whole chronology between the smuggling network of 1945–48 and a named figure to whom the foreign-agent law was applied.

"Call Abe," 1958. Feinberg's role did not end with the 1948 campaign. According to Avner Cohen's history Israel and the Bomb, David Ben-Gurion secretly named Feinberg his chief coordinator for raising private American funds for Israel's clandestine nuclear weapons program, beginning in 1958. Ben-Gurion is said to have told his staff simply to "call Abe." [cite:nationalinterest_feinberg_bomb] [cite:israellobby_feinberg_fbi] On that account, the man who helped fund a whistle-stop tour in 1948 became, a decade later, the coordinator of private American funds for a clandestine nuclear program. The account is Cohen's. It establishes Feinberg's role and the instruction; it does not give the program's finances or the sums he raised, and that story belongs to a later volume.

What the record shows, and what it does not. Feinberg's career runs from the arms network of 1945 through a presidential campaign, a foreign-agent order and, by 1958, a nuclear fundraising role. Over those years he is documented as a channel: for money into a campaign, for a publication on Israel's behalf, for Israel's government into an American prosecution, and for private funds into a secret program. The one point at which the record ties his money to a specific American decision is the summer of 1948, and it does so through one historian's account, qualified by the words "in part." The record does not show how much weight Truman gave that need against votes, conviction or advice. It does not show any later president changing a decision because of Feinberg's money. And it does not document the size of his later fundraising. Those limits are part of the finding. The case is real, named and specific, and it is one case.

sections.h: Barring Return and Hardening the Line, 1948–1956
sections.html:
Truman's discomfort in the summer of 1948 had two objects, territory and refugees. On the second, the question most often asked about the Palestinian refugees of 1948 is why they did not go home when the fighting stopped. The answer has two parts, and both were in place before the armistices of 1949 were signed. The first was a decision taken by Israel's government in the middle of the war, and the facts that grew up around it. The second was a frontier regime that, in the years after the war, treated those who tried to cross back as intruders. This section follows both, from June 1948 to the eve of the 1956 war.

The decision of 16 June 1948. The decision is known through the research of the historian Benny Morris. As Arthur Hertzberg summarized Morris's research in 1988, Israel's cabinet decided on 16 June 1948 that "there could be no return during the war," leaving the question to be reconsidered later. [cite:rs_rd6_nyrb_hertzberg_1988] The decision was framed as temporary. It barred return for the duration of the fighting and deferred a final answer.

The date matters. It fell during the first truce, twelve days before the UN mediator, Count Bernadotte, proposed at Rhodes that displaced people be allowed "to return to their homes without restriction and to regain possession of their property." [cite:rs_rd6_frus_bernadotte_june] Israel's government had decided against return during the war before the international proposal for return was put on the table.

The facts on the ground. A deferred decision did not leave the question open in practice. Hertzberg, summarizing Morris, wrote that from the summer of 1948 abandoned houses and property were quickly occupied by Jews, and that by the time of the 1949 armistices Israel was both unwilling and unable to allow substantial return. [cite:rs_rd6_nyrb_hertzberg_1988] "Unable" is the important word. Once houses and property had been taken over, a return would have meant undoing that occupation. The legal machinery that converted this occupation into state ownership, from the Custodian of Abandoned Property to the Absentees' Property Law of 1950, is set out in [scene:ap_s01|the section on absentee property].

Who decided the flight itself. Morris's research also bore on the older and more charged question of how the refugees came to leave. According to Hertzberg's account, Morris found no formal decision to expel taken by the highest leaders, while the authority of commanders in the field shaped what happened. [cite:rs_rd6_nyrb_hertzberg_1988] Both halves of that finding are used in argument, often one without the other. Those who reject the charge of a planned expulsion cite the absence of a top-level order. Those who see the outcome as intended point to what commanders did with the authority they held. Morris's own finding contains both: no order from the top, and a war in which those on the ground had wide latitude. Whatever had caused the flight, the June 1948 decision barred return while the war lasted.

The "infiltration" years. Once the armistice lines of 1949 were drawn, people crossed them. Israel called them infiltrators. Who they were and why they came is the central dispute of this period, and the word itself carries one answer to it.

The most detailed study is Morris's Israel's Border Wars. As Avi Shlaim reported in his review of it in 1994, Morris estimated that "90 per cent or more" of the infiltrations of 1949–56 were driven by economic and social concerns rather than political aims: people returning to their homes, their fields, their property or their relatives. [cite:rs_rd6_lrb_shlaim_1994] Morris estimated that between 2,700 and 5,000 infiltrators were killed in 1949–56, "the great majority of them unarmed." [cite:rs_rd6_lrb_shlaim_1994] Israel's army, border guard and police adopted a policy of shooting suspects on sight. [cite:rs_rd6_lrb_shlaim_1994]

The figures need to be read as what they are. The range of 2,700 to 5,000 is an estimate, and a wide one. The 90 percent is Morris's judgment of motive across thousands of crossings, not a count. Both come to this book through Shlaim's review, not from Morris's text directly. And the word "infiltration" covered very different acts: a farmer going back for a harvest, a family visiting relatives across the line, and, increasingly in the mid-1950s, an armed raid. Seen from one side of the line, these were refugees going home to what was theirs. Seen from the other, they were illegal entries into a sovereign state.

Retaliation and Qibya. Israel answered cross-border attacks with retaliation across the line. One instance came in October 1953 at Qibya. Unit 101, under Ariel Sharon, blew up 45 houses and killed 69 Jordanian villagers, "the majority of them women and children." The raid provoked international protest. [cite:rs_rd6_lrb_shlaim_1994]

Israel's leadership was divided over this policy. Morris divided them into "activists," led by David Ben-Gurion and including Dayan and Lavon, and "moderates," led by Moshe Sharett. [cite:rs_rd6_lrb_shlaim_1994] The division ran through the same government. Shlaim, reviewing the book, faulted Morris for underplaying Sharett's secret contacts with Nasser. [cite:rs_rd6_lrb_shlaim_1994]

The fedayeen. The Israeli case rests above all on what the border became by 1955. The Jewish Virtual Library, presenting the Israeli account, records that on 31 August 1955 Nasser announced that Egypt would dispatch "her heroes" to Israel's borders. It describes the fedayeen as fighters trained and equipped by Egyptian intelligence to carry out attacks inside Israel, in breach of the armistice agreements' ban on paramilitary hostilities. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_fedayeen] On this account, whatever most crossings had been in 1949, by 1955 a hostile state was organizing armed attacks across the line, which Israel answered with retaliation. The armistice agreements whose terms the fedayeen breached are described in [scene:rd6_armistices|the section on the 1949 armistices].

Two readings of the same border. The dispute over what infiltration was is not a dispute about whether people crossed. Both readings accept that they did, in large numbers, and that many died. It is a dispute about proportion and about cause.

The first reading, Morris's, holds that the crossings were overwhelmingly economic and social, the movement of refugees toward homes, crops and relatives, and that most of those killed were unarmed. Its strongest evidence is the 90 percent estimate and the death toll. [cite:rs_rd6_lrb_shlaim_1994]

The second reading, presented by the Jewish Virtual Library, holds that the border was a security threat that, by 1955, included fedayeen organized by a hostile government's intelligence service, which Israel answered with retaliation. Its strongest evidence is Nasser's own public announcement and the fact that the attacks breached signed agreements. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_fedayeen]

The two readings describe different parts of the same record and, to a large degree, different years. Morris's estimate covers the whole period of 1949–56; the fedayeen belong chiefly to its last two years. Neither cancels the other. A border can be crossed mostly by unarmed people seeking their property and also be the route of organized armed attacks, and a state can face real attacks while its forces kill thousands of people, most of them unarmed.

What came next, and what the record leaves open. The years of the border wars ended in a larger war. On 29 October 1956, the eve of the Sinai war, a Border Police unit enforcing a curfew killed 49 Arab citizens of Israel returning home to Kafr Qasim, a village about a kilometre from the Green Line. [cite:wiki_kafr_qasim_massacre] That killing, and the trial that followed it, are told with [scene:rd6_military_government|the military government over the Arabs who stayed].

Several things this section cannot settle. The cabinet decision of 16 June 1948 is known here through Hertzberg's summary of Morris, not from the cabinet record itself, and it is described as deferring the question, not closing it; the sources here do not say when, or whether, the government formally reconsidered it. The number of infiltrators killed is an estimate with a range of nearly two to one. And the number of Israelis, civilian and military, killed in cross-border attacks between 1949 and 1956 is not established in the sources gathered for this book. Without that figure the human cost of the border can be counted on one side only, and the reader should know that the count is incomplete, not that the other side's losses were small.

sections.h: Who Would Govern Arab Palestine, 1948–1951
sections.html:
Most of the refugees barred from return were in territory held by Arab armies. By the late summer of 1948 the question of who would govern the parts of Palestine that Israel did not hold had become a contest among Arab governments as much as a matter for Palestinians themselves. Three answers were offered within a few months of one another: an Arab League administration, a Palestinian government proclaimed in Gaza, and union with the Hashemite kingdom across the Jordan. By April 1950 the third had prevailed on the West Bank, Egypt held the Gaza Strip under military administration, and the Gaza government had become, in one historian's word, a phantom. This section follows that contest from September 1948 to the assassination of King Abdullah in July 1951.

A common account holds that Jordan went to war in 1948 purely to destroy the new Jewish state alongside its Arab allies, with no territorial interest of its own. The record of these three years does not bear that out. Jordan's army took and kept territory, and its parliament annexed it. Egypt took and governed another strip of land for nineteen years. Their rivalry over what would become of Arab Palestine was itself one of the forces that shaped the outcome.

The armies came first. Egypt joined Jordan, Syria, Lebanon and Iraq in invading the newly declared State of Israel in May 1948, after the end of the British Mandate. [cite:wikipedia_1948_war] Jordan's Arab Legion, trained and commanded by British officers, took the Old City of Jerusalem and the West Bank. [cite:wiki_jordan_annexation] It was Jordan's most consequential and successful action of the war, and the territory it held afterward would stay under Jordanian administration for the next nineteen years. Egypt's forces ended the war holding the Gaza Strip. Where the armies stood when the fighting stopped decided, in practice, which Arab government would have the power to act in each part of the country.

The Arab League tried to set the terms first. On 8 July 1948 it created a temporary civil administration for Palestine, and in September it agreed to an Arab government seated in Gaza, announced on 20 September. [cite:rs_rd6_shlaim_apg_1990] Two days later, on 22 September, a communiqué of the Arab Higher Committee declared Palestine independent under the All-Palestine Government, headed by Ahmad Hilmi Abdul Baqi. [cite:rs_rd6_shlaim_apg_1990] On 30 September a Palestinian National Council met in Gaza under the presidency of Hajj Amin al-Husayni. It adopted a provisional constitution and declared independence over the whole of Palestine. [cite:rs_rd6_shlaim_apg_1990]

These were acts of Palestinian political leaders, taken in their own name, and they claimed the whole country, not a partition share of it. Five Arab states recognized it. Egypt recognized the new government first, then Iraq, then Syria, Lebanon and Saudi Arabia in the middle of October. King Abdullah of Transjordan refused. [cite:rs_rd6_shlaim_apg_1990]

His refusal was not a passing objection. On the same day the National Council met in Gaza, 30 September 1948, a rival congress in Amman pledged loyalty to Abdullah. On 1 December 1948 the Jericho Congress went further: it proclaimed the union of Palestine and Transjordan and acknowledged Abdullah as king. [cite:rs_rd6_shlaim_apg_1990] The contest thus ran through rival assemblies: one proclaimed independence in Gaza; others, in Amman and Jericho, pledged loyalty to Abdullah and proclaimed union with his kingdom.

Why did the Arab states back a government in Gaza at all? The historian Avi Shlaim, in a study of the All-Palestine Government published in 1990, argues that Egypt sponsored it as a "focal point of opposition to Abdullah," to frustrate the king's plan to join Arab Palestine to Transjordan. His verdict is severe: the government was "a phantom deliberately created by the Arab states, with Egypt at their head." [cite:rs_rd6_shlaim_apg_1990] The events bear out how little ground it had to stand on. After Israel's October 1948 offensive its ministers were moved to Cairo. Gamal Abdel Nasser closed its offices in 1959. [cite:rs_rd6_shlaim_apg_1990]

Shlaim's judgment and the Palestinian initiative are both part of the record, and they do not cancel each other. The declaration of 22 September and the Council of 30 September were real political acts by Palestinian leaders who claimed a state in the whole of their country. Read together, the record suggests that what they lacked was the means to make that claim good: an army, a territory under their own control, and patrons whose interest lay in their success rather than in blocking a rival. The government in Gaza depended on Egypt's sponsorship, and its fate followed Egypt's purposes.

Egypt's own position in Gaza took a form that set it apart from Jordan's. From 1948 to 1967 Egypt administered the Gaza Strip as a military protectorate. It governed the territory directly but never annexed it as Egyptian territory, and Egyptian officials kept to that distinction throughout. The record shows the fact of non-annexation more clearly than the reasons for it. Some accounts stress the Arab League's political consensus against formal annexation; others stress Egyptian strategic caution. The sources used here do not settle which weighed more. After the revolution of 1952, Nasser's rise made Egypt the leading voice of pan-Arabism through the 1950s, and in 1956 his nationalization of the Suez Canal brought an invasion by Israel, Britain and France that was reversed under American and Soviet pressure. [cite:wikipedia_suez_crisis] That war belongs to a later volume. The common belief that Egypt never had any administrative role in Gaza is mistaken: for nineteen years it was the governing power there, a history that still shapes Egypt's relationship with the territory's border.

On the West Bank, Abdullah moved step by step. He took the title of king in December 1948, and in April 1949 he ordered the country renamed the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan. [cite:rs_rd6_loc_jordan] The scale of what he was absorbing was large. About 500,000 Palestinian Arabs had taken refuge in Transjordan or the West Bank. The West Bank itself had about 500,000 indigenous residents. Transjordan's prewar population had been about 340,000. [cite:rs_rd6_loc_jordan] By these estimates the Palestinians brought under the crown, residents and refugees together, outnumbered the kingdom's original subjects by roughly three to one. Elections were held on both banks in April 1950, and after them Abdullah formally annexed the West Bank. [cite:rs_rd6_loc_jordan] The ceasefire lines on which this rested were fixed in the Jordanian–Israeli armistice of April 1949, which is told in [scene:rd6_armistices|the Rhodes armistice agreements].

On 24 April 1950 Jordan's parliament passed the resolution of union. The sources render its central phrase in two slightly different translations. One gives it as support for "complete unity between the two sides of the Jordan and their union into one State," grounded in what the resolution called the "national, physical and geographical unity" of both banks. [cite:wiki_jordan_annexation] Martin Kramer, writing in 2020, quotes it as "complete unity between the two banks of the Jordan, the eastern and western, and their union in one single state." [cite:rs_rd6_kramer_annexation] The meaning is the same in both.

The language is worth reading slowly. The idea that the two banks of the Jordan belong together as one political unit had appeared earlier in this history in Ze'ev Jabotinsky's Revisionist Zionist program, which claimed both banks for a Jewish state. In 1950 the Hashemite Kingdom used the same territorial reasoning in the opposite direction, to bring the West Bank under the crown in Amman. The parallel is one of structure. The sources do not show that either movement borrowed the idea from the other or was answering it.

The next day, 25 April 1950, the British cabinet agreed to recognize the union of Arab Palestine and Jordan together with the State of Israel. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_cab128] The decision paired two recognitions: Britain accepted Jordan's annexation and Israel in the same act.

How many other states recognized the annexation is disputed, and the sources consulted for this book do not settle it. The Library of Congress country study of Jordan says it was recognized only by Britain and Pakistan. [cite:rs_rd6_loc_jordan] Kramer notes that Israelis customarily say either that only Britain recognized it or that Britain and Pakistan did. [cite:rs_rd6_kramer_annexation] Another account, used elsewhere in this library, names three states, Britain, Iraq and Pakistan, and adds that even Britain's recognition excluded Jerusalem. [cite:sixdaywar_jerusalem] All agree that the list was very short and that Britain was on it.

The strongest contemporary regional opposition to the annexation came not primarily from Israel or the Western powers but from Jordan's partners in the Arab League. The Library of Congress study records that the annexation was condemned within the League as advancing Hashemite dynastic ambitions. [cite:rs_rd6_loc_jordan] Weeks after the vote, the League's Political Committee met in Cairo, with Jordan absent, and ruled that the annexation violated the League's own earlier resolution, which had declared that annexation of Arab Palestine by any single Arab state would be treated as a breach of the Charter and subject to sanctions. The committee went so far as to consider expelling Jordan from the League. [cite:sixdaywar_jerusalem] Later scholarship links this rejection partly to competing Arab state ambitions over Palestine's future, a thread the sources here do not fully unpack. The same rivalry that produced the Gaza government in September 1948 shaped the reaction to Jordan's union in 1950.

Jordan's rule over the Old City had another side, which the record documents plainly. During the nineteen years of Jordanian administration, Jewish access to the Western Wall and the other Jewish religious sites of the Old City was denied, contrary to the terms of the 1949 armistice agreement, [cite:rs_rd6_bpb_jerusalem] and dozens of historic synagogues were damaged or destroyed. These facts are corroborated across independent historical accounts.

The contest ended in violence. On 20 July 1951 Abdullah was assassinated as he entered al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem for Friday prayers, with his grandson Hussein at his side. The assassin was a Palestinian, reportedly hired by relatives of Hajj Amin al-Husayni, [cite:rs_rd6_loc_jordan] the man who had presided over the National Council in Gaza less than three years before. The account of who hired him is reported, not established in the sources used here.

By the summer of 1951 the shape that would last until 1967 was in place. Jordan held and had annexed the West Bank and East Jerusalem. Egypt administered Gaza without annexing it. The All-Palestine Government survived only as offices in Cairo. The refugees who had crossed into both territories, and how the host governments treated them, are the subject of [scene:dsp_s01|where the refugees went].

Several questions remain open in the record used here. It does not establish how much support each side commanded among Palestinians in 1948–1950, whether the Gaza government or the Jericho union. The April 1950 elections are recorded, but the sources give no figures on how they were conducted. The reasons Egypt chose administration over annexation in Gaza are disputed. The list of states that recognized Jordan's annexation is given three ways, and the assassin's sponsors are named only on the strength of report. What the record does settle is that no independent Arab government came to rule any part of Palestine in these years, and, on Shlaim's reading, the rivalry between Egypt and Jordan, as well as the war with Israel, had much to do with it.

sections.h: The Arabs Who Stayed, and the Military Government
sections.html:
On the other side of the lines, not every Palestinian Arab inside the territory Israel held in 1949 had left. According to Israel's Central Bureau of Statistics, as compiled by the Jewish Virtual Library, the state's population at the end of 1948 was 716,700 Jews and 156,000 non-Jews. By 1950 it was 1,203,000 Jews and 167,100 non-Jews. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_population] For the next eighteen years most of the Arabs who remained lived under a separate regime that applied to them as one category of citizens.

It is often said that the Arab citizens of Israel have enjoyed equal civil rights since 1948. Part of that is true. They voted from the first election. Yet from the war's last months until December 1966, most of them needed a permit from a military officer to leave their own town or village, lived under curfews, and could be barred from whole districts by a commander's order. Both facts belong in the account.

The vote came first in the public record. In the first Knesset election, in 1949, the Democratic List of Nazareth, an Arab party described as a satellite list of Mapai, won 7,387 votes, 1.7 percent of the total, and 2 seats. [cite:rs_rd6_idi_nazareth] Arab citizens could vote and stand for parliament. The terms on which former Palestinian citizens became Israeli nationals, including the residence test of the 1952 Nationality Law, are told in [scene:rd6_law_of_return|the Law of Return and the Nationality Law].

The military government had begun before that election. The sources date its start differently. The account of the period followed elsewhere in this library dates it from 1949. [cite:wiki_kafr_qasim_massacre] The historian Alina Korn dates its official establishment to October 1948, with five military governors, and notes that when the fighting ended the regime was "neither cancelled nor was it legally regularized." [cite:rs_rd6_korn_adalah] The difference may reflect the formal creation of the governorates in wartime as against the regime's settled form after the armistices. Either way, it outlived the war by seventeen years.

Its legal tools were mostly British. The Defense (Emergency) Regulations of 1945, issued by the Mandate government, were absorbed into Israeli law by Article 11 of the Law and Administration Ordinance of 1948. The most important of them was Regulation 125, which allowed the military commander to declare "any area or location a closed area." To these were added the Emergency Regulations (Security Zones) of 1949. [cite:rs_rd6_korn_adalah] The mechanism was simple. A commander closed an area. Its residents needed a permit to travel outside their localities, and lacking one was an offense.

The power to act sat with the commander. The Arab citizen could apply for a permit but could not compel one. According to Korn, the travel-permit requirement had no legal foundation at all for its first 18 months, until January 1950. [cite:rs_rd6_korn_adalah] Permits were not easily come by. In 1958, Korn reports, only one in three Arabs in the areas under military government held a travel permit. [cite:rs_rd6_korn_adalah]

The courts carried the regime's weight. Korn reports that between 1948 and 1967 about a third of all convictions of Arab citizens were for violations of the Defense Regulations, and that about 95 percent of these were administrative offenses, such as lacking a permit. In 1955, 2,714 of the 2,888 people convicted under the regulations were Arab. [cite:rs_rd6_korn_adalah] The regulations were written in general terms and could in law be applied to anyone. In practice, more than nine in ten of those convicted under them that year were Arab citizens.

What was the regime for? The government justified it on grounds of security. Israel had signed armistices with its neighbors, not peace treaties. The Rattner Commission, which reviewed the regime in February 1956, concluded that it should not end until "true peace" existed. [cite:rs_rd6_korn_adalah] On that view, the controls were needed for as long as there was no peace.

Korn argues that the regime's main purposes were different: to control the movement of Arab residents and to prevent their access to land that had been confiscated. [cite:rs_rd6_korn_adalah] Her own figures, cited above, show that about 95 percent of convictions under the regulations were for administrative offenses such as lacking a permit. The two instruments worked together. Military rule restricted the movement of internally displaced citizens and, combined with the absentee property law, kept them from returning to reclaim their homes. [cite:wiki_present_absentee] That law is told in [scene:ap_s01|the Absentees' Property Law]. Both readings rest on documented material: the security rationale on the government's own statements and the Rattner Commission's finding, the control reading on the conviction figures and the regime's link to the land. The sources used here do not show which consideration weighed more with those who kept the regime in force year after year.

The regime's worst single event came on 29 October 1956, the eve of the Sinai War. Brigadier Issachar Shadmi moved up a dusk curfew on villages near the Jordanian border, without adequate notice to the villagers. When Major Shmuel Malinki asked how to treat villagers returning from work who did not know of it, Shadmi's reply, according to the court record, was that anyone who left his house would be shot. Two of the three units given the order disregarded it. [cite:wiki_kafr_qasim_massacre] The Border Police unit at Kafr Qasim, about a kilometre from the Green Line, did not. It killed 49 villagers returning home after a curfew they had not been told of: 19 men, 6 women and 23 children, the count including an unborn child.
