[cite:rs_cw2_jps_qibya] The unit was short-lived as a separate formation, but its purpose was written into its founding: it existed to answer attacks from across the line with attacks across the line.

It was in action within weeks. Khalidi and Caplan record that Sharon led an attack on the al-Burj refugee camp in Gaza in late August 1953 in which, according to the historian Benny Morris, twenty people were killed, among them seven women and five children, and twenty-two were wounded. [cite:rs_cw2_jps_qibya] The camp lay in the Strip that Egypt administered, and its inhabitants were refugees.

Yehud, 12–13 October 1953. The raid on Qibya followed a killing inside Israel. On the night of 12–13 October 1953 a grenade was thrown into a house at Yehud (the Jewish Virtual Library spells the place Tiryat Yehuda), killing Suzanne Kinyas and her two children. [cite:rs_cw2_jvl_qibya] The Jordanian–Israeli Mixed Armistice Commission, the body set up under the 1949 armistice to rule on violations, called that attack "intolerable aggression." Israel's representative at the United Nations, Eban, later reminded the Security Council of the Commission's words. [cite:rs_cw2_jvl_qibya] [cite:rs_cw2_spv632] The finding matters to Israel's case. The killing of a mother and two children at Yehud was not an Israeli claim alone; the armistice machinery itself, on which Jordan sat, had condemned it.

The decision. The response was planned in the army. According to Khalidi and Caplan, the planning options included "total destruction of the village and maximum harm to the villagers." Moshe Dayan authorized Sharon to choose among them, and the decision was to retaliate "in the firmest possible manner." [cite:rs_cw2_jps_qibya] The Jewish Virtual Library quotes Sharon's diary: "Qibya was to be an example for everyone." [cite:rs_cw2_jvl_qibya] The target was a village across the armistice line, on the Jordanian side.

The night of 14–15 October. The force crossed on the night of 14–15 October 1953. How many houses it destroyed and how many people it killed is given differently by different sources, and the difference should be stated rather than smoothed. Khalidi and Caplan give forty-five houses blown up and sixty-nine villagers killed, all of them civilians, about three-quarters of them women and children; this is also the figure Volume II used. Glubb, the commander of Jordan's Arab Legion, counted sixty-six dead. The Jewish Virtual Library gives fifty homes and 69 civilians. [cite:rs_cw2_jps_qibya] [cite:rs_cw2_jvl_qibya] The sources therefore agree on the order of magnitude, on the fact that the dead were civilians, and, in two of three counts, on sixty-nine; they differ by five on the houses and by three on the dead.

Sharon later gave his own account. In his autobiography, Warrior, he wrote that he had not known the houses were occupied ("I couldn't believe my ears"), suggesting that families had stayed inside expecting only limited damage. [cite:rs_cw2_jvl_qibya] That account, written long afterwards, sits beside the planning option that Khalidi and Caplan record, and the reader can weigh the two. Neither source establishes what the men who set the charges knew of the houses' occupants that night.

What the Foreign Minister knew. The man who would have to defend the raid abroad had not been consulted on its scale. Moshe Sharett, Israel's foreign minister, wrote in his diary on 16 October 1953 that had he feared "such a slaughter" he "would have raised hell," and that "Horror gripped me" when he heard Jordanian radio describe the destruction. [cite:rs_cw2_jps_qibya] The diary matters because it records what ministers discussed in private while the government said something else in public. The contest between Sharett and Ben-Gurion over retaliation, of which Qibya was an early instance, is the subject of [scene:cw2_sharett_ben_gurion|the leadership split].

Washington, 18 October. On 18 October 1953 the State Department expressed "the deepest sympathy for the families of those who lost their lives in and near Qibya." It described an attack "by Israeli forces," said that those responsible "should be brought to account," and announced that it had joined Britain and France in asking the Security Council to consider the frontier, with a direct report from General Vagn Bennike, the Chief of Staff of the UN Truce Supervision Organization. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_qibya_pr] The statement attributed the raid to Israel's forces a day before Israel's Prime Minister denied it. Washington was at that moment also withholding economic aid from Israel over a separate dispute on the Syrian front; Dulles insisted, two days later, that the deferral followed Bennike's ruling on the canal works and not "the more recent incidents," a distinction told in [scene:cw2_banat_yaacov|the Banat Yaacov suspension].

Ben-Gurion's broadcast, 19 October. On the evening of 19 October 1953 Ben-Gurion went on the radio. He denied "the absurd and fantastic allegation that 600 men of the Israel defense forces took part," and said that "not a single Army unit was absent from its base" that night. He attributed the raid to Israeli border settlers whose patience had been exhausted by the killings at Yehud. He regretted that innocent people had been killed, and said that "all the responsibility rests with the government of Transjordan." [cite:rs_cw2_jta_bg_qibya] [cite:rs_cw2_jvl_qibya] The Jewish Telegraphic Agency reported the speech on 21 October under the heading that Ben-Gurion blamed the Qibya provocation on the Arab states' war policy. [cite:rs_cw2_jta_bg_qibya]

Sharett's diary shows that the settlers' story was a choice made in the cabinet, not a misunderstanding. Ben-Gurion insisted that the army not admit responsibility and that the government say border residents "had taken the law into their own hands." Sharett noted that it would not be believed. When the UN observer's account contradicted it, Ben-Gurion wrote in a marginal note that the observer's version was a "fantastic lie." [cite:rs_cw2_jps_qibya] The public denial and the private record are therefore two different kinds of evidence. The broadcast is documented as what Israel's government said; the diary is documented as what its ministers knew. On the question of who carried out the raid, every source here other than the broadcast, including Sharett's private record and Sharon's own later account, places it with Israel's armed forces. [cite:rs_cw2_un_res101] [cite:rs_cw2_frus_qibya_pr] [cite:rs_cw2_jps_qibya] [cite:rs_cw2_jvl_qibya]

Israel's case at the Council. At the United Nations, Israel's argument turned on what had preceded the raid. At the Council's 632nd meeting on 29 October 1953, Eban set the raid against the attacks that had preceded it and reminded the members that the Mixed Armistice Commission had itself called the Yehud killings "intolerable aggression." [cite:rs_cw2_spv632] The strongest form of that case, in its own terms, was this: Israeli civilians were being killed by men crossing from Jordanian-held territory; the armistice machinery could condemn such attacks but not stop them; and a government that answered only with complaints would be inviting more. Israel also asked for a conference with Jordan under Article XII of the armistice agreement. [cite:rs_cw2_un_res101]

Resolution 101, 24 November 1953. The Council answered on 24 November 1953, at its 642nd meeting. Resolution 101 found that the "retaliatory action at Qibya by Israeli armed forces" violated the cease-fire and was inconsistent with the armistice agreement and the United Nations Charter. It expressed "the strongest censure" of that action and called on Israel to prevent such actions in future. [cite:rs_cw2_avalon_res101] [cite:rs_cw2_un_res101] The resolution had a second part, often forgotten. It noted that there was "substantial evidence" of unauthorized crossings of the demarcation line, and it asked Jordan to strengthen its measures against them. It asked the Chief of Staff to report within three months, taking account of Israel's request for an Article XII conference. [cite:rs_cw2_avalon_res101] [cite:rs_cw2_un_res101] It was adopted by 9 votes to none, with Lebanon and the Soviet Union abstaining. [cite:rs_cw2_un_res101]

The two parts of the resolution belong together. The Council did not accept Israel's denial; it named "Israeli armed forces" and censured them in the strongest language it had. Nor did it accept that the border's violence ran in one direction; it found substantial evidence of crossings from the Jordanian side and called on Jordan to act. On this reading, what it would not accept was that the second justified the first.

From unit to doctrine. Censure did not end the policy; it changed its form. In January 1954, according to the Ministry of Defense archive, Unit 101 was folded into paratrooper battalion 890 under Sharon's command. He later commanded Paratroopers Brigade 202, under which cross-border operations continued. [cite:rs_cw2_mod_sharon] A specialist unit had become the core of a regular formation. The raids that followed, at Nahhalin, Gaza, Khan Yunis, Lake Tiberias and Qalqilya, are told in their places later in this chapter.

The word "retaliation." Each party used the same word for its own purpose. Israel's defence establishment wrote it into the unit's charter: Unit 101 existed for "reprisal operations in enemy territory," a phrase that presented each raid as an answer to a prior attack. [cite:rs_cw2_mod_sharon] The Security Council used the word too, but as a charge: "retaliatory action ... by Israeli armed forces" was the thing it found to violate the cease-fire. [cite:rs_cw2_avalon_res101] In the Council's usage, calling an act retaliation identified who had done it and denied that it was lawful; in the army's usage it explained why it had been done. Ben-Gurion's broadcast avoided the word's official sense altogether, presenting the raid as the spontaneous reprisal of settlers rather than a state's act. [cite:rs_cw2_jta_bg_qibya] And the planning record shows that, in this case, the response was not measured against the act it answered: three people had been killed at Yehud; the options considered for Qibya included "maximum harm to the villagers." [cite:rs_cw2_jps_qibya] Whether a policy of this kind deterred attacks or multiplied them was the question that divided Israel's own leaders for the next three years.

The record leaves some things open. The exact wording of the operational order is not in these sources, beyond the planning options Khalidi and Caplan report; nor is the identity of the Yehud attackers, or the village they came from, if they came from one. The counts of houses and dead differ slightly among the sources and cannot be reconciled from them. And Sharon's later statement that he did not know the houses were occupied can be neither confirmed nor refuted from these documents. What is not open is who carried out the raid. The United Nations, the United States government, Israel's own Foreign Minister writing privately, and Sharon himself all place it with the army, against the account that Israel's Prime Minister gave the public on 19 October 1953.

sections.h: Banat Yaacov, 1953: The First Time Washington Held Back Aid
sections.html:
In the autumn of 1953, in the same weeks as Qibya, the United States withheld economic aid from Israel until Israel complied with a request from the United Nations. The dispute was not about a raid but about a canal, dug in a strip of land on the Syrian front whose ownership the 1949 armistice had left unresolved. It lasted eight weeks. It ended with the works suspended, the money released and the underlying quarrel handed to an American envoy. As a case study in how leverage worked in this period, it is unusually complete: the condition, the pressure and the compliance are all on the documentary record.

The zones and the quarrel over them. The armistice with Syria, signed in July 1949, left small demilitarized zones along the frontier whose status was disputed: strips without agreed sovereignty. Volume II tells how those zones were created, and Stage One tells the first Security Council crisis over them, the Huleh drainage of 1951, in [scene:cw1_huleh|the Huleh dispute]. By 1953 Israel's position was explicit. In a meeting recorded by the State Department in 1953–54, Moshe Dayan told American officials that Israel claimed sovereignty over Jewish-owned lands in the zones, that "someone must keep the area alive," and that Israel did not want Syria to have direct access to the Jordan River. [cite:frus_dayan_dmz]

The conduct on both sides of that line is on the record, and neither side's account alone describes it. Syria fired on Israeli farmers and fishermen from the heights above the zones. Israel sent armoured tractors to cultivate disputed land, and carried out reprisal raids. A common account holds that the clashes on this front before 1967 were caused entirely by Syrian shelling from the Golan. The record shows a running contest in which shelling and cultivation drove each other. Dayan himself, in an interview given in 1976 and published in 1997, said that at least 80 per cent of the clashes had been provoked by Israel; that statement, and the dispute over it, are taken up in [scene:rd6_syria_1949|Syria in 1949]. [cite:w_dayan] The later struggle over the Jordan's headwaters, from 1964 to 1967, belongs to Stage Six.

The works, September 1953. On 2 September 1953 Israel began works at Banat Yaacov, inside the Israel–Syria demilitarized zone. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_eban_dulles_sep53] [cite:rs_cw2_frus_res100] Israel's case was that this was a development project. Abba Eban later told Secretary of State John Foster Dulles that it was "an electric power project," that it had been begun with the knowledge of Colonel Tillotson of the UN Truce Supervision Organization, and that no water would actually be diverted until sometime in 1954. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_eban_dulles_sep53]

The officer charged with supervising the armistice asked Israel to stop. On 23 September 1953 General Vagn Bennike, the UNTSO Chief of Staff, asked Israel to "cease its operations in the demilitarized zone" until an agreement was reached. Sharett, Israel's foreign minister, replied on 24 September with reservations. Syria complained to the United Nations on 12 October. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_eban_dulles_sep53]

The lever. Israel had not stopped, and Washington now attached a price to that. In a conversation of about 25 September 1953 with Eban and Shiloah, Dulles said he would "withhold release of MSA funds until the issue of the Jordan waters had been further clarified." MSA funds were economic aid under the Mutual Security programme. Dulles was acting on the advice of Assistant Secretary Henry Byroade. Eban asked him to keep American aid and the water dispute separate. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_eban_dulles_sep53] Dulles did not.

The suspension became public in October. At his press conference of 20 October 1953, two days after the State Department's statement on Qibya, Dulles said no allocation had yet gone to Israel, because "as long as the State of Israel was acting in defiance of that decision" it was questionable whether to make one. He was careful to separate the two crises: the deferral, he said, followed Bennike's decision, not "the more recent incidents." Asked how much was involved, he put the total "in the neighborhood of $100,000,000," after an aide had suggested $50–60 million. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_presser_20oct53] A week later, on 27 October, he added that no new economic-assistance allocations had been made from the fiscal-year fund "either to Israel or any Arab state," and declined to discuss the deferment while the Security Council was seized of the matter. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_presser_27oct53] Qibya and the deferment were thus running side by side in Washington, and Dulles insisted they were separate; the raid is told in the preceding section.

The Council and the suspension. The matter was resolved at the United Nations, not in Washington. On 27 October 1953, at its 631st meeting and on a French draft, the Security Council unanimously adopted Resolution 100. It deemed it desirable that the works begun on 2 September be suspended while the Council examined the question. It noted Eban's undertaking to suspend them "without prejudice" to the merits of the dispute, and it relied on the Chief of Staff to confirm compliance. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_res100] The phrase "without prejudice" was what made the undertaking possible: Israel stopped digging without conceding that it had been wrong to dig. Bennike later reported that the works had stopped at midnight on 28 October. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_res100]

The money followed at once. In Press Release No. 604, issued the day after the resolution, Dulles announced that "the impediment to the present grant of economic aid to Israel has been removed." He recommended about $26 million for the first six months of the fiscal year, the amount tentatively earmarked for Israel under the Mutual Security Act of 1953. He also gave the reason for the suspension in a single sentence: granting aid while Israel ignored the UN request "would tend to undermine the authority" of UNTSO. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_pr604] The Council's consideration of the wider Banat Yaacov question continued for three months more, from its 629th to its 656th meeting, between 27 October 1953 and 22 January 1954. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_res100]

The mechanism. The armistice gave the UN Chief of Staff authority to rule on what could be done in the zones, but no power to enforce his ruling; Bennike could ask, and Israel could reply with reservations. Syria could complain to the Council and did, but had no lever of its own. What turned a UN officer's request into a decision Israel had to meet was an American funding instrument. Dulles did not claim to be judging the water dispute; he said he was upholding UNTSO's authority, and he made the release of money conditional on Israel's compliance with it. The Council then supplied a face-saving form, suspension "without prejudice," and the money moved within a day of the works stopping. The cost fell on Israel, whose grant aid was held for about five weeks; the gain, by Dulles's own account, was to the authority of the armistice machinery.

How much was at stake. The amounts given in the record differ, and the differences are not contradictions so much as different measures. About $26 million was the sum Dulles released in Press Release 604, the tranche earmarked for the first half of the fiscal year. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_pr604] The "neighborhood of $100,000,000" that Dulles recalled at his 20 October press conference, and the $50–60 million his aide suggested, referred to the year's programme as a whole, and neither was offered as a precise statement. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_presser_20oct53] The figure that can be stated with confidence as the money actually held and then released is the $26 million.

The library's dashboard on aid and arms gathers the later occasions on which Washington attached a condition to its support for Israel. Its explanatory panel and its table are shown below.

The table begins in 1987. The episode of 1953 is an earlier documented case of the same pattern, and a clearer one than most: the condition was stated in private on about 25 September and made public on 20 October; Israel gave its undertaking at the Council on 27 October, the release was announced the day after the resolution, and the works stopped at midnight on 28 October. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_eban_dulles_sep53] [cite:rs_cw2_frus_presser_20oct53] [cite:rs_cw2_frus_res100] [cite:rs_cw2_frus_pr604] It does not show that every condition would be met, or that the lever worked on the larger question of who controlled the river. It shows that, on the narrow question of whether Israel would dig in the zone against a UN request while American money was pending, it did.

The Syrian front is one link in a longer chain, which the library's map of the Golan line traces from 1949 to the present.

What came next. The suspension settled nothing about the water itself. On 16 October 1953, while the aid was still being withheld, President Eisenhower named Eric Johnston as his personal representative to discuss the regional development of the Jordan's waters. [cite:rs_cw2_ucsb_johnston] That effort, Washington's diplomatic answer to Banat Yaacov, is told in [scene:cw2_johnston|the Johnston mission].

The record leaves several things unsettled. The sources do not give the outcome of the Council's three months of debate after Resolution 100, or say whether and when Israel resumed any works at Banat Yaacov. They do not give Syria's own statements in its 12 October complaint, so Syria's case is known here mainly through what the UN officer did with it. Dayan's remark to American officials is dated only to 1953–54. And while Dulles's stated reason was the authority of UNTSO, the documents do not show how far other considerations, including the Qibya raid he insisted was separate, weighed in his mind when the money was held.

sections.h: The Johnston Mission, 1953–1955: Dividing the Jordan
sections.html:
The suspension of aid over Banat Yaacov stopped a canal. It did not answer the question the canal had raised: who would use the water of the Jordan, and on what terms. Washington's answer was an envoy. For two years, from October 1953 to October 1955, Eric Johnston travelled between Israel and its Arab neighbours with a plan to divide the river among the four states that shared it. The engineers on both sides accepted his figures. The governments did not sign them. And yet the figures outlived the failure: they were never ratified, but they were broadly observed, and the United States later tied its money to them.

The mandate, 16 October 1953. On 16 October 1953, immediately after the Qibya raid and while American aid to Israel was being withheld over the canal works, President Eisenhower announced that he was sending Johnston "as my personal representative with the rank of Ambassador" to discuss "the mutual development of the water resources of the Jordan River Valley on a regional basis." The statement gave the reason in terms of people rather than water: "some hundreds of thousands of Arab refugees" lacked adequate support, and a plan for the valley could give "a substantial proportion" of them an economic base on the land. [cite:rs_cw2_ucsb_johnston] From the first day, then, the mission was two things at once: a water-sharing scheme and a refugee-resettlement scheme, presented as a single development project.

A State Department telegram of the same month explained why Washington was moving now. An engineering study made by the Tennessee Valley Authority for UNRWA, the UN agency for Palestine refugees, had "just been completed." Its findings "cannot be carried out without political agreement on the part of the riparian states." The best prospects for settling refugees lay in the East and West Ghor. And "Israel's unilateral action in commencing diversion of water in the Demilitarized Zone below Lake Huleh" had raised tension. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_johnston_tel] The same telegram noted a condition that would weigh on Israel: the plan would require it to relinquish "exclusive territorial control over the outlets to Lake Tiberias." [cite:rs_cw2_frus_johnston_tel] The engineering required a political concession from every party, Israel included. How the canal works came to a halt is told in [scene:cw2_banat_yaacov|the Banat Yaacov suspension].

Four plans. Johnston did not bring a finished agreement; he brought a starting point, and each side answered it with its own. The starting point was the Main plan, drawn up by Charles T. Main for the TVA on UNRWA's commission. Its authors stated that it did not "consider political factors or attempt to set this system into the national boundaries now prevailing." [cite:rs_cw2_aquapedia_jordan] Israel answered with the Cotton plan, which brought a second river, the Litani, into the system and raised Israel's share accordingly. The Arab League's Technical Committee, under Egyptian leadership, answered in 1954 with an Arab plan that excluded the Litani and rejected storage in the Sea of Galilee. [cite:rs_cw2_aquapedia_jordan] The final compromise, the Unified or Johnston plan, came out of the negotiations among these three.

The competing allocations, as tabulated by the water-diplomacy analysts Aaron Wolf, Joshua Newton and Matthew Pritchard in the AquaPedia case study, are set out below in millions of cubic metres a year. [cite:rs_cw2_aquapedia_jordan]

The table shows how far apart the opening positions were and where the compromise landed. Israel's own plan asked for more than three times what the Main plan had given it, 400 million cubic metres of it from the Litani. The Arab plan gave Israel less than half the Main figure. The Unified plan returned Israel almost exactly to the Main plan's number, took the Arab plan's figures for Syria and Lebanon unchanged, and gave Jordan somewhat less than the Main plan but more than either of the other two. Two small inconsistencies in the sources should be noted. AquaPedia gives Israel's share under the Main plan as 394 in one place and 393 in another. And it gives Israel 400 under the Unified plan while also noting that Israel's actual share, as the residue of the river after the others had taken theirs, was estimated at about 409 on average. [cite:rs_cw2_aquapedia_jordan]

That residue was the heart of the design. The State Department's later summary of the Unified plan gives fixed allocations to the Arab states and a residual right to Israel: Jordan 720 million cubic metres (377 from the Yarmuk, 100 from the Jordan and 243 from the side wadis); Syria 132 (20 from the Banias, 22 from the Jordan and 90 from the Yarmuk); Lebanon 35, from the Hasbani; and Israel 25 from the Yarmuk, with the remaining waters of the Jordan available to it. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_unified_plan] The arrangement gave the three Arab states certainty and Israel the variable remainder, which in an average year came to more than its nominal figure.

Technical agreement, 1955. By the summer of 1955 the engineers had done their part. Johnston signed a memorandum of understanding with Israel on 5 July 1955, and one with the Arab riparian states' Technical Committee on 11 October 1955. He was told that the plan was technically acceptable to Israel, Jordan, Syria and Lebanon. The United States offered to pay two-thirds of the costs of development. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_unified_plan] [cite:rs_cw2_aquapedia_jordan] The October memorandum was signed by the Arab riparian states' own technical body.

Political refusal, October 1955. The decision did not rest with the engineers. The Arab League's political organs did not endorse the plan. According to the State Department, the League's Political Committee returned it to the Technical Committee for "further consideration." AquaPedia dates the League Council's decision not to accept it to October 1955, citing "the political implications of accepting." [cite:rs_cw2_frus_unified_plan] [cite:rs_cw2_aquapedia_jordan] The Jewish Virtual Library says the mission was abandoned in late 1955. [cite:rs_cw2_jvl_johnston]

Why it failed. The sources offer two kinds of explanation, and they are not mutually exclusive. The first is political. A shared water regime, formally agreed, would have meant a final arrangement with Israel, and accepting it implied recognition of a state the Arab governments did not recognize. AquaPedia's analysts record that Iraq and Saudi Arabia urged Lebanon, Syria and Jordan not to accept; the State Department's summary, in returning the plan for "further consideration," points the same way. [cite:rs_cw2_aquapedia_jordan] [cite:rs_cw2_frus_unified_plan] The second is substantive. The same analysts summarize the Arab objections as suspicion that the plan was designed to Israel's benefit, and fear that water carried to irrigate the Negev would enable more immigration and further expansion. [cite:rs_cw2_aquapedia_jordan] On that reading the refusal was not only about recognition but about what Israel would do with the water.

Both cases have evidence behind them. The political reading is supported by the sequence: the engineers agreed and the politicians declined, and Iraq and Saudi Arabia pressed the riparian states to refuse. The substantive reading is supported by the design itself, in which Israel received the residue of the river, an amount that in an average year exceeded its nominal figure, and by the fact that Israel's own Cotton plan had sought far more. Against any simple picture of Arab obstruction stands one further fact the analysts record: Nasser had been an active advocate of the plan. [cite:rs_cw2_aquapedia_jordan] Egypt had led the Arab League committee that produced the Arab plan, and its leader had argued for agreement. One reading is that the decision turned on politics among the Arab states as well as on the merits of the water; the sources here do not settle it.

Israel's side of the failure is less fully documented in these sources. Israel signed its memorandum in July 1955. The record does not show how its government regarded the plan's requirement that it give up exclusive control of the lake's outlets, or whether it would have ratified a final agreement on those terms had the Arab states accepted. What it shows is that Israel's own opening claim was the largest of the four, and that the compromise brought it back to roughly the engineers' original figure.

What survived. Although never ratified, the allocations were generally adhered to, and the United States tied later funding for water projects in the basin to them. [cite:rs_cw2_aquapedia_jordan] The Jewish Virtual Library says that about 200,000 refugees could have been settled on irrigated land in Jordan under the plan. [cite:rs_cw2_jvl_johnston] That figure is the Jewish Virtual Library's, not a planning document's, and the sources here do not say how it was reached. The water dispute on the Syrian front, which the plan was meant to defuse, went on regardless, and from 1964 turned into a struggle over the river's headwaters, told in [scene:sy_s02|the demilitarized zones and the water war]. Water also reappeared in the larger Anglo-American settlement proposals of 1955, told in [scene:cw2_alpha|the search for a settlement].

The record leaves several questions open. The date of the Arab League's final decision rests on AquaPedia alone; the State Department's summary gives none. The reasons for the refusal come to us chiefly through Western analysts' summaries of Arab positions, not through the Arab governments' own statements, which are not among these sources. The refugees in whose name the mission was launched do not appear in the record as a party: neither their own views of resettlement in the Ghor nor the relation of the plan to the right of return is addressed in these documents. And whether a plan that the engineers of four states accepted could have been carried through by their governments in any political climate of 1955 is a question the record does not answer.

sections.h: After the Coup: Iran's Oil Settled, 1953–1954
sections.html:
Two days before Eisenhower named Johnston, Washington had chosen a second envoy for a second quarrel, over Iran's oil. The overthrow of Iran's government in August 1953 is told in [scene:s11|the coup of August 1953]. What followed it is less often told, and it is where the coup's economic consequences were written down. A familiar account treats the coup as a purely Cold War intervention, anti-communist in purpose, whose only lasting effect was to restore the Shah. The documents of the following fourteen months show something more concrete: a negotiated settlement of the oil dispute, under the new prime minister, General Fazlollah Zahedi, that brought American companies into Iranian oil, kept a large British share, and bound Iran to pay compensation to the company whose holdings it had nationalized. [cite:ourhistory_operation_ajax_shadow]

Washington moved within weeks. On 14 October 1953 Herbert Hoover Jr. was appointed as the Secretary of State's consultant on the Anglo-Iranian oil dispute, and he visited Iran from 17 October to 4 November 1953. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_iran_hoover] The appointment put the United States directly into a quarrel that had until then been between Iran and Britain, and between Iran and one British company, the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company.

Iran's government put its own proposal on the table while Hoover was in the country. On 1 November 1953 Foreign Minister Entezam proposed an international consortium that would buy oil from the National Iranian Oil Company, a consortium in which the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company could take part but without majority control. On 5 December 1953 a British–Iranian communiqué promised a solution that would take account of "the national aspirations of the Persian people" regarding their resources. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_iran_hoover] Read together, the two documents differ in kind. Entezam's design kept Iran's own national company as the seller and the foreign companies as buyers; the communiqué gave the principle of national aspiration a place in the formal record.

The settlement that emerged eight months later was built differently. The agreement in principle with the consortium was signed on 5 August 1954. The Anglo-Iranian Oil Company took a 40 per cent holding and Royal Dutch Shell 14 per cent, the rest going to American and French companies, with two operating companies incorporated in the Netherlands. [cite:rs_cw2_fo_consortium] [cite:rs_cw2_frus_iran_ratify] The State Department's press release of 7 December 1954 named the American participants. Five companies, Gulf, Socony-Vacuum, Standard Oil (New Jersey), Standard Oil of California and the Texas Company, each held 8 per cent, and each could transfer up to one-eighth of its share to other American firms within six months. [cite:rs_cw2_dsb_consortium] The French share is not stated in these documents. By arithmetic from these figures (40 per cent, plus 14, plus five times 8), 6 per cent remained for the French participant; the Foreign Office statement itself says only "American and French companies". [cite:rs_cw2_fo_consortium] [cite:rs_cw2_dsb_consortium]

The same day, 5 August 1954, the Iranian and British delegations issued a joint statement on compensation. Iran agreed to pay the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company a net £25 million, over ten years, interest-free, beginning on 1 January 1957. [cite:rs_cw2_compensation54] The terms were then carried through Iran's own institutions. Iran's Senate passed the oil bill on 28 October 1954 by 41 votes to 4, with 3 abstentions; the Shah signed it on 29 October, and the agreements took effect that day. Hoover called the outcome a "significant victory". [cite:rs_cw2_frus_iran_ratify] [cite:rs_cw2_dsb_consortium]

The mechanism is clearest when the settlement is followed as a flow of money and rights. The oil lay under Iranian soil and had been nationalized. Under the settlement it was worked through a consortium of foreign companies operating through two companies incorporated in the Netherlands, in which the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company, Royal Dutch Shell, American and French companies held fixed shares. The Anglo-Iranian Oil Company, which had lost its position by nationalization, came back with the largest single share and a promise of £25 million. Five American companies entered with 8 per cent each. Iran paid the compensation, on a ten-year schedule that would begin in 1957.

Who gained can be read from the record. The British company kept a continued stake, now shared. The American companies gained access to Iranian oil, which one account describes as the first time American companies had held such access. [cite:ourhistory_operation_ajax_shadow] [cite:rs_cw2_dsb_consortium] Iran, for its part, obtained a settlement of the dispute, a formal acknowledgment of its "national aspirations" in the December communiqué, and a ratification by its own Senate; it gave up £25 million and the design Entezam had proposed. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_iran_hoover] [cite:rs_cw2_compensation54]

How far the settlement "ended Iranian national control" of the industry is the point most worth arguing. That is how one account of the consortium characterizes it: the agreement, negotiated under Zahedi, ended Iranian national control of its oil industry and created an international consortium of American and European companies alongside the British. [cite:ourhistory_operation_ajax_shadow] Set beside the primary documents, the characterization has real support and a real limit. In its favour, Iran's own proposal of November 1953 had foreign companies buying from the National Iranian Oil Company, with Anglo-Iranian denied majority control; what was signed in 1954 instead created foreign-held operating companies, incorporated abroad, in which Anglo-Iranian held the largest share. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_iran_hoover] [cite:rs_cw2_fo_consortium] Against an unqualified reading, the settlement was negotiated with Iran's government, ratified by Iran's Senate and signed by the Shah, and the December communiqué wrote Iran's "national aspirations" into the record. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_iran_hoover] [cite:rs_cw2_frus_iran_ratify] Whether a government installed after the coup could have negotiated otherwise is a question the account of the coup leaves to the reader; the documents of 1954 do not answer it.

The record leaves several things open. It does not set out the precise division of rights between the National Iranian Oil Company and the two operating companies after October 1954, so how much formal ownership Iran retained, as distinct from control of production, cannot be stated from these documents. It does not name the French participant. And it does not show how the £25 million figure was arrived at, or what claims the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company had pressed before agreeing to it.

One account carries the story forward to 1957, when the Shah established the security service SAVAK under General Teymur Bakhtiar with American help, and it states that Israel's Mossad had a co-founding role. [cite:globalsecurity_savak_cia_training] That claim belongs to a later period and is tested in [scene:cw4_iran|Iran and Israel after 1957]. The historian David Menashri, as cited in this volume's first stage, dates the first Israeli intelligence contact with SAVAK to September 1957, when Bakhtiar offered Israel's ambassador an exchange of intelligence, so a founding role is not stated here as established.

sections.h: Two Schools in One Cabinet: Sharett, Ben-Gurion and the Retaliation Policy, 1953–1956
sections.html:
In Israel, meanwhile, policy on the borders was not made by one mind. Between July 1953 and June 1956 the state's founding prime minister withdrew, returned and pushed out his successor, and the argument between them, over whether to answer attacks across the armistice lines with force or to hold back and negotiate, ran through the cabinet for three years. A common picture treats Israel's retaliation raids of the period as the settled policy of a united government. The record shows a contest, fought in cabinet votes, in a diary kept by the man who led the losing side, and in Washington's terms for a security guarantee.

The sequence began with David Ben-Gurion's withdrawal. Speaking to the Knesset in 1965, he recalled that the government granted him a long leave on 7 July 1953. On 18 October 1953 he submitted a three-year security plan, which the government ratified. He resigned with the government on 7 December 1953 and retired to Sde Boker on 13 December. [cite:rs_cw2_mod_bg_portfolio] The dates matter for what came next: the security plan was laid down by Ben-Gurion before he left, days after the Qibya raid of 14–15 October, told in [scene:cw2_unit101_qibya|Unit 101 and Qibya].

Moshe Sharett, until then foreign minister, became prime minister. The Prime Minister's Office lists the Fifth Government, under Sharett, as serving from 26 January 1954 to 29 June 1955. Its listing of the Sixth Government, also Sharett's, gives an end date of 3 November 1955 and a start date that appears garbled, so the exact day the second Sharett cabinet took office cannot be read from that source. [cite:rs_cw2_pmo_govts] The Defence Ministry was held by Pinhas Lavon. Ben-Gurion's own account is that he "returned to the Ministry of Defense with the Knesset approval on February 21, 1955", replacing Lavon in Sharett's cabinet after fourteen months of semiretirement. [cite:rs_cw2_mod_bg_portfolio] [cite:rs_cw2_israeled_bg_return] Lavon's fall followed the failed operation in Egypt told in [scene:lv_s01|the Lavon affair]. From February 1955, then, Sharett was prime minister and Ben-Gurion was his defence minister.

The historians who have read this period most closely describe two schools. Avi Shlaim calls Sharett the leader of the "negotiation" school and Ben-Gurion of the "retaliation" school, and puts the difference between Sharett and Dayan sharply: Sharett "sought to avoid escalation in order to prevent war", while Dayan "needed escalation to bring about war". [cite:rs_cw2_shlaim_east_west] Neil Caplan, who has edited selections from Sharett's diaries, writes that Sharett was "deeply troubled by the growing popularity of the competing 'activist' strategy of stiff reprisals" advocated by Ben-Gurion, Dayan and others. Caplan stresses something easily missed: Sharett led cabinet majorities for restraint, and he blocked proposals to capture the Gaza Strip or the Straits of Tiran. [cite:rs_cw2_caplan_asia] The moderate was not simply overruled. For much of his premiership he won the votes.

The diary is the main witness to the argument, and how it reached print shapes how it can be used. Sharett's diary was first published in a self-censored form; his son Yaakov Sharett later incorporated the remaining entries into the multi-volume Yoman Ishi (Personal Diary). [cite:rs_cw2_caplan_asia] The best-known English excerpts come from a 1980 study by Livia Rokach, published by the Association of Arab-American University Graduates with a preface by Michael Adams. In Rokach's translations the diary records Dayan, on 31 January 1954, answering "of course" when asked whether his course meant war with Egypt; Lavon, on 25 January 1955, proposing to occupy the Gaza Strip and the Syrian demilitarized zone; and Dayan, on 26 May 1955, calling retaliation actions "our vital lymph". [cite:rs_cw2_rokach] After the Israeli raid on Gaza of 28 February 1955, Sharett wrote on 1 March: "It is the same old story: hit and run and try to fool the world." [cite:rs_cw2_rokach]

These are dated entries, and the words are Sharett's record of what he heard and thought. The argument built on them is a different thing. Rokach read the diaries as documenting a deliberate strategy of provocation, retaliation, expansion and subversion driven by Ben-Gurion's activists, with Sharett as a largely powerless moderate. Her study is an argued reading of selected entries, published by an Arab-American academic association, not a neutral edition. [cite:rs_cw2_rokach] Caplan and Shlaim, reading the same diaries, describe a real internal contest instead: Sharett's restraint often prevailed in cabinet, and the activist course won only as the United States refused Israel arms and France offered them. [cite:rs_cw2_caplan_asia] [cite:rs_cw2_shlaim_east_west] The two readings agree on the existence of the activists and on Sharett's opposition to them. They differ on whether the activists' course was a plan pursued from the start or a policy that prevailed as circumstances changed, and on how much power Sharett actually had.

The activists' case deserves to be stated in its own terms. Israeli civilians were being killed across the armistice lines; in March 1954, eleven Israeli citizens were killed on a bus at the Scorpion Pass, and Israel's draft condemning Jordan failed in the armistice commission, whose chairman found the evidence "far from being conclusive". [cite:rs_cw2_un_s3196] [cite:rs_cw2_un_s3252] To Dayan, in the entry already quoted, such actions were "our vital lymph". [cite:rs_cw2_rokach] And the one alternative that might have replaced retaliation, an American guarantee, came with a condition Israel's leaders would not accept. In February 1955, Shlaim records, Dulles offered a mutual defence pact on condition that Israel neither expand its borders by force nor carry out military retaliation. Ben-Gurion and Sharett accepted the first condition but not the second. [cite:rs_cw2_shlaim_east_west] The refusal matters because Sharett joined it: even the leader of the negotiation school would not give up the option of retaliation in exchange for a guarantee.

Sharett's case was equally concrete. In Shlaim's account he sought to avoid escalation precisely in order to prevent war, which the activists' course risked. [cite:rs_cw2_shlaim_east_west] His diary entry after Gaza objected not only to the raid but to the pattern around it, of striking and then trying to mislead the world about what had been done. [cite:rs_cw2_rokach] His cabinet majorities were the means by which he held the activists back, and his blocking of plans to take Gaza or Tiran shows what those majorities prevented. [cite:rs_cw2_caplan_asia]

The politics shifted with the election of the Third Knesset on 26 July 1955. There were 1,057,795 eligible voters, and turnout was 82.8 per cent. [cite:rs_cw2_idi_1955] Mapai won 40 seats with 274,735 votes; Herut 15; the General Zionists 13; the National Religious Front 11; Ahdut HaAvoda 10; Mapam 9; the Religious Torah Front 6; Maki 6; the Progressives 5; the Democratic List for Israeli Arabs 2; Progress and Work 2; and Agriculture and Development 1. [cite:rs_cw2_idi_1955] After about three months of negotiation Ben-Gurion formed a government of Mapai, the National Religious Front (soon the National Religious Party), Ahdut HaAvoda, Mapam and the Progressives, with 75 seats, or 80 counting the Arab lists affiliated with Mapai. The Prime Minister's Office dates this Seventh Government from 3 November 1955. [cite:rs_cw2_idi_1955] [cite:rs_cw2_pmo_govts_1955] Ben-Gurion was prime minister again; Sharett stayed on as foreign minister.

The partnership lasted seven months. Sharett resigned as foreign minister on 18 June 1956, and Golda Meir succeeded him. In a letter of 28 July 1956 Ben-Gurion wrote that Sharett's continuing at the Foreign Ministry "was not for the good of the country" and that foreign policy must serve security needs. [cite:rs_cw2_kaller_bg] [cite:rs_cw2_caplan_asia] The letter survives in a dealer's catalogue description and transcription, which is how it is known here. Shlaim's judgment, quoted by Caplan, is that "Ben-Gurion failed to topple Nasser but he succeeded in toppling Sharett." Shlaim also writes that Ben-Gurion authorized secret talks in France and forced Sharett's resignation about a week later, "clearing the way for war". [cite:rs_cw2_caplan_asia] [cite:rs_cw2_shlaim_east_west] Where those talks led is told in [scene:cw3_sevres|the Sèvres Protocol].

Several questions remain open on this record. The garbled start date of Sharett's second government in the official listing leaves the transition of mid-1955 imprecise. [cite:rs_cw2_pmo_govts] The sources here do not give the contents of Ben-Gurion's three-year security plan of October 1953, so how far it prefigured the retaliation policy of 1955–56 cannot be judged from them. The diary is known in English largely through selections, Rokach's and Caplan's, each made for its own purpose; a reader without the Hebrew Yoman Ishi sees the entries those editors chose. And the central dispute, whether the activists pursued war as a plan or arrived at it as American arms were refused and French arms offered, is not settled by the entries quoted here: they show what Dayan and Lavon said to Sharett and what Sharett thought of it, not what the cabinet as a whole intended.

sections.h: "Under God": Which God? The Pledge and the Motto, 1954–1956
sections.html:
Between February 1954 and July 1956 the United States wrote God into two of its national formulas: the words "under God" into the Pledge of Allegiance, and "In God we trust" into law as the national motto. The words added were few, and the question they leave open is a large one. The 1954 law added the single word "God", unqualified. No Trinity, no Christ and no named faith appears in the Pledge, and none appeared in the Knights of Columbus resolutions of 1952–53 that began the campaign or in the joint resolution Eisenhower signed on 14 June 1954. [cite:rs_cw2_kofc_pledge] [cite:rs_cw2_osg_newdow] So a reader is entitled to ask which God the nation declared itself to be under.

The question is sharper than it looks, because in one strand of American Christian argument the answer is not taken for granted. Whether Muslims and Christians worship the same God was a serious enough question at Wheaton College, an evangelical school, that in December 2015 the college placed a professor on leave for writing that they do, as told below. [cite:rs_cw2_rns_hawkins] The historian Mark Silk writes that after the Cold War the term "Judeo-Christian", which framed the 1954 debate, became "an emblem of evangelical hostility to Muslims". [cite:rs_cw2_silk_judeochristian] Inside that argument two different tests can be distinguished. One holds that "Allah", the God Muslims pray to, is a different god from the God of the Bible. The other holds that a God understood without the Trinity, without Father, Son and Holy Spirit, is not the true God. Yet the Pledge names no Trinity and no Christ at all.

The second test has a consequence that is seldom stated. Judaism rejects the Trinity as firmly as Islam does. Dale Tuggy's survey in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy records that Jewish and Muslim thinkers alike have argued that "the trinitarian doctrine is incompatible with God's unity", and that Muslims charge trinitarians with "associating" another with God. [cite:rs_cw2_sep_trinity_judaic_islamic] On the test "no Trinity, no true God", Judaism's understanding of God fails exactly as Islam's does. In Christian theology, by contrast, the God of Israel is the Father, the first person of the Trinity. [cite:rs_cw2_sep_trinity_judaic_islamic] The objection Jewish thinkers raise against the Trinity is the same objection Muslim thinkers raise. Yet the working category of 1950s America, "Judeo-Christian", took in one of these two non-Trinitarian traditions and left the other out. How that came about is the history this section tells. First, the three traditions themselves.

Three Siblings, Shifting Pairs

When arguments over which God are conducted between two of the three Abrahamic traditions at a time, the third drops out of view. Put the three side by side and the pairs shift with the question asked.

On God's oneness, Judaism and Islam stand together against the Trinity. The Shema, "Hear, O Israel: The LORD is our God; the LORD is one" (Deuteronomy 6:4), is the nearest thing Judaism has to a creed, and Maimonides' second principle states: "This God is One, not two or more than two, but One whose unity is different from all other unities." [cite:rs_cw2_shema_principles] Sura 112 of the Quran, al-Ikhlas, often treated as a summary of Islam's belief in God's oneness (tawhid), reads in one English translation: "Say: He is Allah, the One and Only… He begetteth not, nor is He begotten; and there is none like unto Him." [cite:rs_cw2_ikhlas] And in the Gospel of Mark, Jesus himself names the Shema as the first commandment: "The first of all the commandments is, Hear, O Israel; The Lord our God is one Lord" (Mark 12:29). [cite:rs_cw2_mark1229]

On Jesus, the pairing changes. Islam regards Jesus (Isa) as a prophet and the Messiah (al-Masih) and affirms his virgin birth to Mary; sura 19 is named for her (Maryam). Mainstream Islam rejects his divinity and his place in a Trinity. Judaism accepts neither his messiahship nor his divinity. [cite:rs_cw2_jesus_islam] [cite:rs_cw2_sep_trinity_judaic_islamic] On this question Islam stands nearer to Christianity than Judaism does.

History ran in shifting pairs too. Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), born in Córdoba, wrote the Guide of the Perplexed in Judaeo-Arabic and served as a court physician in Cairo, to Saladin's vizier and to Saladin's son al-Afdal. [cite:rs_cw2_maimonides_bio] When Spain expelled its Jews in 1492, the Ottoman sultan Bayezid II, by one account, sent ships in August 1492 to carry refugees to his empire and ordered his governors to receive them. The same account, an opinion piece, notes that Bayezid valued the refugees' economic potential; the line often attributed to him, that Ferdinand "impoverished his own country and enriched mine", is reported there without a source. [cite:rs_cw2_972_bayezid]

The pairing "Judeo-Christian", which leaves the third sibling out, is not ancient. Silk dates it as a political term to the interfaith anti-fascism of the 1930s and to its spread as a Cold War watchword in the 1950s. [cite:rs_cw2_silk_judeochristian] That is the period of the Pledge.

The question of which God is not one that outsiders have imposed on American Christianity; it divides Christians themselves, and their institutions have answered it in opposite ways. On 10 December 2015 Larycia Hawkins, a professor at Wheaton College, wrote that Muslims and Christians "worship the same God" and wore a hijab in solidarity. On 15 December the college placed her on leave, citing the statement's "theological implications". [cite:rs_cw2_rns_hawkins] The Catholic Church's official teaching takes the other side. Lumen Gentium 16 (1964) says that Muslims, "professing to hold the faith of Abraham, along with us adore the one and merciful God", and the declaration Nostra Aetate (1965) speaks of them with esteem as worshippers of the one God. [cite:rs_cw2_dialog_samegod] On this point the Catholic Church's teaching since 1964 and the position implied by Wheaton's action in 2015 point in opposite directions.

Part of the dispute is a matter of words rather than of theology. "Allah" is the standard Arabic word for God. Arab Christians use it; Arabic translations of both the Hebrew Bible and the Gospels use it; Arabic-speaking Jewish communities used it; and it is related to the Hebrew El and Eloah and the Aramaic Alaha. [cite:rs_cw2_allah_word] To refuse the word is therefore not, in the linguistic sense, to refuse a different deity: an Arabic-speaking Christian reading either Testament in Arabic meets the same word. Whether Muslim and Christian conceptions of God refer to the same being is a theological question, and the institutions above answer it differently. Whether "Allah" names a separate god is a question about Arabic, and the record answers it.

The history of the 1954 change begins with the Catholic fraternal order that started the campaign, told in [scene:cw1_pledge|"Under God", 1951–53]. According to an account published by The Catholic Company, the Knights of Columbus adopted "under God" for their own meetings in 1951, urged a national change at their 1952 Supreme Council, and wrote to every member of Congress in 1953; seventeen resolutions followed in the House. The American Legion credited the Knights with the amendment on 6 October 1954. [cite:rs_cw2_kofc_pledge]

The next push came from a Presbyterian pulpit with the President in the pew. On 7 February 1954 the Rev. George Docherty preached at New York Avenue Presbyterian Church in Washington, with Eisenhower in attendance, that "there was something missing in this Pledge" and that "an atheistic American is a contradiction in terms". [cite:rs_cw2_liberty_docherty] The sermon was framed by the Cold War. The historian Isaac Kramnick quotes Docherty saying he "could hear little Muscovites repeat a similar pledge to their hammer and sickle flag" and that "it is a theological war". [cite:rs_cw2_ffrf_kramnick] Its religious frame was explicitly Christian. As quoted in later reporting, Docherty said, "If you deny the Christian ethic, you fall short of the American ideal of life," and one account quotes him on "the words of Jesus of Nazareth, the living Word of God for the world" as having shaped the nation. [cite:rs_cw2_ds_eisenhower_flagday] [cite:rs_cw2_bng_docherty70]

Members of Congress introduced bills after the sermon, and the change passed both houses in under four months. Eisenhower signed it on Flag Day, 14 June 1954. [cite:rs_cw2_liberty_docherty] [cite:rs_cw2_ffrf_kramnick] His signing statement said that "the millions of our school children will daily proclaim" the nation's dedication to God, that "we are reaffirming the transcendence of religious faith in America's heritage and future", and spoke of "those spiritual weapons which forever will be our country's most powerful resource". [cite:rs_cw2_ucsb_pledge] The phrase "spiritual weapons" presented religion as an asset in the contest with Communism.

The committee reports that carried the bill said the same thing in the language of law, and they took care over establishment. The House report, H.R. Rep. No. 1693 of 1954, stated that the change "is not an act establishing a religion", grounding it instead in "a fundamental belief in God" and in the claim that "the human person is important because he was created by God", set against Communism. The Senate report, S. Rep. No. 1287, called "the spiritual bankruptcy of the Communists" one of "our strongest weapons". As quoted in the federal government's 2003 brief in the Newdow case, neither report names a particular faith. [cite:rs_cw2_osg_newdow]

The motto followed in two separate laws, which are easily confused. The first was a currency act: H.R. 619, approved 11 July 1955, numbered 140 among the public laws of the 84th Congress (chapter 303), provided that all United States currency bear "In God We Trust". [cite:rs_cw2_unt_pl140] The inscription first appeared on paper money in 1957, on the one-dollar silver certificate. [cite:rs_cw2_sconres96] [cite:rs_cw2_hrpt112_47] The second was the motto itself. The House Judiciary Committee's report on H.J. Res. 396, dated 28 March 1956, said it would be "of great spiritual and psychological value to our country to have a clearly designated national motto". [cite:rs_cw2_sconres96] Eisenhower signed the resolution on 30 July 1956. The Statutes at Large print it as Public Law 851, chapter 795, 70 Stat. 732: "the national motto of the United States is hereby declared to be 'In God we trust.'" [cite:rs_cw2_stat70_732] It stands today as 36 U.S.C. §302, the subject of House Report 112-47 of 2011, on reaffirming it as the national motto, and of S. Con. Res. 96, marking its fiftieth anniversary. [cite:rs_cw2_hrpt112_47] [cite:rs_cw2_sconres96]

One widely read account gets the numbering wrong. HISTORY.com attributes the 1956 motto law to Public Law 84-140 and says it also put the motto on paper money. [cite:rs_cw2_history_motto] The statute record settles the point: No. 140 was the currency act of 11 July 1955, and the motto was Public Law 851 of 30 July 1956. HISTORY.com conflated the two laws. [cite:rs_cw2_unt_pl140] [cite:rs_cw2_stat70_732]

On motive the documentary record is consistent. Eisenhower's statement, Kramnick's reading of the sermon and the committee reports all frame the changes as religious revival set against Communism. None of these sources documents any link between the 1954 and 1956 changes and Israel, or any Jewish or Zionist organization. Any reading that connects them to Israel would be interpretation without a documentary basis in these sources. [cite:rs_cw2_ucsb_pledge] [cite:rs_cw2_ffrf_kramnick] [cite:rs_cw2_sconres96] The campaign's documented authors were a Catholic order, a Presbyterian minister, the members of Congress who filed the bills and the President who signed them.

That still leaves the question this section opened with. The record supports two readings of which God was meant, and each has real evidence behind it. The first is that the God of the Pledge was deliberately none in particular. The House report denied that the change established a religion. [cite:rs_cw2_osg_newdow] Eisenhower, as president-elect, had said on 22 December 1952 that "our form of government has no sense unless it is founded in a deeply felt religious faith, and I don't care what it is". The historian Patrick Henry, writing in 1981, recorded slight variations in the line across three reports and read it as meant to include other faiths; Will Herberg and others read it as a generic, thinned religion. [cite:rs_cw2_wiki_dontcare] Half a century later Justice O'Connor, concurring in Elk Grove v. Newdow (2004), described the Pledge as acknowledging religion "in a general way: a simple reference to a generic 'God'", noted that it "does not refer to a nation 'under Jesus' or 'under Vishnu'", and wrote that an acknowledgment could not count as ceremonial deism "if it explicitly favored one particular religious belief system over another". She also acknowledged that some legislators in 1954 may have intended a religious message. [cite:rs_cw2_newdow_oconnor] Even Docherty, on one account, meant the phrase broadly: The Daily Signal, writing in 2026, paraphrases him as saying it would encompass people of all faiths, naming Jews and Muslims. No verbatim quotation of that passage has been found, and the archive link to the sermon manuscript is dead, so the inclusion of Muslims is reported, not confirmed. [cite:rs_cw2_ds_eisenhower_flagday]

The second reading is that in practice the God meant was the Christian God, or the "Judeo-Christian" God of the Bible. The campaign was led by a Catholic order and carried by a Presbyterian sermon that spoke of "the Christian ethic" and of Jesus. [cite:rs_cw2_kofc_pledge] [cite:rs_cw2_bng_docherty70] [cite:rs_cw2_ds_eisenhower_flagday] Baptist News Global, marking the seventieth anniversary in 2024, read the change in that light. [cite:rs_cw2_bng_docherty70] Eisenhower's own 1952 line came, in one report, with a qualifier: "Of course, it is the Judeo-Christian concept, but it must be a religion with all men being created equal." [cite:rs_cw2_wiki_dontcare]

That qualifier names the working category of 1954. Silk dates "Judeo-Christian" as a political term to 1930s interfaith anti-fascism, in particular the National Conference of Christians and Jews, and traces its spread as a Cold War watchword in the 1950s; he quotes Eisenhower's 1952 use. Its proponents meant it to bring Jews into a shared religious foundation. Some Jewish writers objected: Trude Weiss-Rosmarin called it "a totalitarian aberration". After the Cold War, Silk writes, the term became "an emblem of evangelical hostility to Muslims". [cite:rs_cw2_silk_judeochristian] Coined to widen the circle against fascism and then Communism, the term was resisted by some Jewish writers and later served to narrow the circle against Muslims. In 1954 it was one frame through which the unnamed God of the Pledge could be understood, and the President himself used it.

Reading the Architecture: Which God?

What follows is interpretation, not a documented finding. It is this book's own reading of a pattern, set out with the evidence for it and against it so that the reader can weigh it. The reading runs as follows. In 1954, six years after the founding of Israel in 1948, the United States declared itself a nation under a God it did not name. A former president of that country had, the year before, called himself Cyrus, the Persian king of the biblical return. And the same country now gives Israel $3.8 billion a year, under a 2016 agreement covering fiscal 2019–2028. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_usaid_table] On this reading, the unnamed God of the Pledge is the God of Israel.

Three things support it. The first is the frame of the time. The category through which the President himself understood the nation's faith was "the Judeo-Christian concept", a term built, as Silk shows, to join Jews and Christians in one religious foundation, and one that excluded the third Abrahamic tradition. [cite:rs_cw2_wiki_dontcare] [cite:rs_cw2_silk_judeochristian] In Christian theology the God of Israel is the Father, so a Christian hearing "God" could hear the God of Israel without contradiction. [cite:rs_cw2_sep_trinity_judaic_islamic] The second is Truman. In November 1953, at the Jewish Theological Seminary in New York, Eddie Jacobson introduced the former president as "the man who helped create the state of Israel"; Truman replied, "What do you mean 'helped to create'? I am Cyrus," casting himself as the king of the return. [cite:rs_cw2_judis_truman_cyrus] The third is the older Christian Zionist line in American Protestantism, associated with the Scofield Reference Bible and told in Volume II, in [scene:s05|the Scofield Reference Bible].

Several things cut against it, and they are also documented. The motive recorded in the documents was religious revival set against Communism: Docherty's "theological war", Eisenhower's "spiritual weapons", the Senate report's "spiritual bankruptcy of the Communists". No source here links either change to Israel or to any Jewish or Zionist body. [cite:rs_cw2_ffrf_kramnick] [cite:rs_cw2_ucsb_pledge] [cite:rs_cw2_osg_newdow] The campaign was started by a Catholic order whose Church did not then recognize Israel at all: the Holy See signed its Fundamental Agreement with Israel on 30 December 1993 and established full diplomatic relations by a protocol signed on 14 June 1994, effective 15 June. [cite:rs_cw2_holysee_israel_protocol] [cite:rs_cw2_kofc_pledge] The money of the time does not match the money of today. US assistance to Israel in the years of the change was $73.6 million in 1953, $74.7 million in 1954, $52.7 million in 1955 and $50.8 million in 1956; the $3.8 billion a year dates from the 2016 Memorandum of Understanding, for fiscal 2019–2028. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_usaid_table] The Truman line is weaker evidence than it looks: Judis cites it as the basis of Truman's pro-Israel reputation precisely in order to argue that the record of 1947–49 shows a president "filled with doubt and regret", and Judis's own article misdates Cyrus's conquest of Babylon to 593 BCE, where the standard date is 539 BCE. [cite:rs_cw2_judis_truman_cyrus] Truman, besides, had left office before the Pledge was changed; the president who signed "under God" was Eisenhower, and in early 1957 Eisenhower pressed Israel to withdraw from the Sinai over its government's resistance, a confrontation told in [scene:cw3_withdrawal|the withdrawal fight of 1957]. Finally, the documented voices of 1954 that spoke to the question at all spoke either of a God left open to every faith or of a Christian God; none in this record spoke of the God of Israel as such.

The reading is therefore an inference from coincidence in time and from later outcomes, not from any document of 1954 that states it. The evidence for a generic God and the evidence for a Christian God are both in the record; the evidence for an Israel-directed God is a pattern of dates and later sums. This book does not resolve the question, and the reader may weigh it differently.

Some things the record here does not settle. Docherty's full sermon text has not been recovered from a working archive, so whether he named Muslims among those the phrase would include remains unconfirmed. [cite:rs_cw2_ds_eisenhower_flagday] The sources do not show what individual members of Congress who filed the seventeen House resolutions understood by "God", beyond the committee reports' language, and O'Connor herself allowed that some may have meant a religious message. [cite:rs_cw2_newdow_oconnor] And the question that opened this section, whether a God named without the Trinity is the God of Christians, is not one that law or history can answer: Wheaton College's action of 2015 and the Catholic Church's teaching in Lumen Gentium point different ways on it, and the Pledge's own text, by saying only "God", declined to answer it at all.

sections.h: The Year After Qibya: Scorpion Pass, Nahhalin, Byroade and the Bat Galim, 1954
sections.html:
The censure of Israel over Qibya in November 1953, told in [scene:cw2_unit101_qibya|Unit 101 and Qibya], did not end the killing across the armistice lines, and it did not settle how the lines would be policed. The months from March 1954 to January 1955 tested the armistice system on three fronts at once. On the Jordanian line, a massacre of Israeli bus passengers and an attack on a Jordanian village eleven days apart led Israel to walk out of the joint commission meant to investigate both. In Washington, a senior State Department official told Israelis in public what he thought of their state's policies and premises, and drew a formal protest. At Suez, Egypt seized an Israeli ship and held its crew for three months. In each case the record preserves both sides' accounts, and in two of the three the United Nations' own officers declined to say who was responsible.

On 17 March 1954 an Israeli bus on the road from Eilat to Beersheba was attacked at the Scorpion Pass, Ma'ale Akrabim. Israel's letter to the Security Council described "the murder of eleven Israeli citizens". [cite:rs_cw2_un_s3196] The United Nations observer who reached the scene counted four bodies outside the bus and seven inside. Israel's draft resolution named the dead as nine men and two women among the passengers, and two more passengers, a young woman and a nine-year-old boy, were seriously wounded. [cite:rs_cw2_un_s3196] [cite:rs_cw2_un_s3252] The UN count and Israel's count agree: eleven dead.

What divided the parties was responsibility. Israel brought a draft resolution to the Jordan–Israel Mixed Armistice Commission condemning Jordan for the attack. The vote divided along national lines: two for, Israel's delegates; two against, Jordan's; and the chairman abstaining. The draft failed. The chairman explained that "the evidence brought out is far from being conclusive", and said that people from outside Jordan could also have been responsible. [cite:rs_cw2_un_s3252] Israel's case was that infiltrators from Jordan had killed eleven civilians on an Israeli road, and that the body charged with keeping the armistice would not even name the state from whose territory, in Israel's view, they had come. The chairman's case was that the evidence did not show who the killers were or where they had come from. Both positions are in the UN's own report, and the record does not resolve between them.

Israel's response was to leave. After the vote its delegation stated that it was "not in a position, under the present circumstances, to continue its participation". From 23 March 1954 Israel cut all connection with the Commission and stopped attending the local commanders' meetings that handled day-to-day incidents along the line. [cite:rs_cw2_un_s3252] The walk-out removed one party from the body in which both sides' complaints were heard together, five days before the next attack.

On the night of 28–29 March 1954 Nahhalin, a Jordanian village, was attacked. Jordan's complaint gave nine killed, eight men and one woman, and fourteen injured. The Commission's resolution gave a slightly different breakdown: five National Guards and one woman killed in the village, and three Arab Legion soldiers killed when their truck hit a mine on the way to it, with fourteen villagers and five soldiers wounded. [cite:rs_cw2_un_s3251] The two counts reach the same total of nine dead by different routes: Jordan counted eight men and a woman, the Commission six in the village and three soldiers on the road. UN observers found footprints leading from the village to the demarcation line, with similar tracks on the Israeli side, and unexploded devices, some marked with Hebrew letters. Seven house doors and the doors of the mosque had been blown open. [cite:rs_cw2_un_s3251]

The Commission met in emergency session on 30 March 1954. Israel, which had walked out a week earlier, did not attend. Jordan's resolution was adopted with Jordan and the chairman voting in favour; it condemned Israel "in the strongest terms" and called on it to punish those responsible. [cite:rs_cw2_un_s3251] The contrast with the Scorpion Pass vote is the mechanism at its plainest. With the parties' delegations voting against each other, the chairman's vote decided the outcome. At Scorpion Pass he found the evidence inconclusive and abstained, and no one was condemned. At Nahhalin he found physical evidence leading to the Israeli side and voted with Jordan. Israel's absence meant that its own account of Nahhalin was not heard in that forum, and the sources do not record what that account was.

Israel took its case to a forum it was still attending. On 5 April 1954 it asked the Security Council to take up its complaints against Jordan, including Jordan's refusal to attend a conference under Article XII of the Armistice Agreement. [cite:rs_cw2_un_s3196] The UNTSO chief of staff's reports on both incidents followed in June 1954. [cite:rs_cw2_un_s3252] [cite:rs_cw2_un_s3251]

While the Council took up the Jordanian file, the argument moved to American platforms. Assistant Secretary of State Henry Byroade spoke to the Dayton World Affairs Council in April 1954. The date is recorded two ways: the State Department's own memorandum, in Eban's account, places it on 9 April; Rafael Medoff, writing in 2014, places it on 19 April. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_byroade] [cite:rs_cw2_medoff_byroade] On 1 May 1954 he spoke again, in Philadelphia, to the American Council for Judaism. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_byroade] [cite:rs_cw2_medoff_byroade] As Medoff quotes him, Byroade urged Israelis to "look upon yourselves as a Middle Eastern state, rather than as a headquarters… of a world-wide grouping of people of a particular religious faith", to "drop the attitude of the conqueror", and to halt "retaliatory killings". In Philadelphia he named Israel's calls for "greatly expanded immigration" as feeding Arab fears of expansion. [cite:rs_cw2_medoff_byroade] Byroade's reasoning, as he gave it, was regional: Israel's integration into its neighbourhood, an end to reprisals, and the removal of what he saw as a source of Arab fear.

The Israeli reply came at the top. In May 1954 Abba Eban told Dulles, in a meeting recorded by Parker T. Hart with Shiloah also present, that the Dayton reference to Israel's ties with Jews elsewhere "wounded the feelings of millions outside Israel and hundreds of thousands within that country", and that raising immigration had been "entirely unnecessary". The Department had issued a corrective, Press Release 231 of 5 May, but Eban said it had not undone the impression. He also acknowledged that Israeli papers had run headlines such as "U.S. Threatens Israel", which he called distortions. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_byroade] Israel's government protested formally against "unjustified interference in matters which are purely Israel's own concern". The Zionist leader Emanuel Neumann denounced what he called "Byroadeism". According to Medoff, the administration stood by Byroade. [cite:rs_cw2_medoff_byroade]

The exchange shows two governments arguing over where the line between foreign policy and a state's self-definition lay. For Byroade, immigration and Israel's relation to Jews abroad were matters of regional security, because they shaped Arab perceptions. For Eban and the Israeli government, they were Israel's own concern and, in Eban's words, touched the feelings of millions outside the country. The quarrel was between named officials stating their reasons, and the record keeps it there. The Anglo-American search for a settlement that followed is told in [scene:cw2_alpha|Operation Alpha].

The third front opened at Suez in the autumn. On 28 September 1954 Egyptian authorities seized the Israeli-flagged Bat Galim at the southern end of the Suez Canal; the ship was bound for Haifa. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_batgalim] [cite:rs_cw2_jta_batgalim] Egypt complained to the armistice machinery on 6 October that the crew had attacked two Egyptian fishing boats with automatic fire in the Gulf of Suez, killing two fishermen. [cite:rs_cw2_un_s3323] On 19 November 1954 the Egyptian–Israeli Mixed Armistice Commission rejected Egypt's draft and adopted Israel's, which found the complaint "unfounded"; the chairman said "conclusive evidence has not been produced" of an attack. Six days later, on 25 November, the Commission's Special Committee ruled that the word "unfounded" should not be used, and that the decision was "not intended as a judgment on the facts". [cite:rs_cw2_un_s3323] The UN thus declined to find that the fishermen's deaths had happened as Egypt alleged, and also declined to find that they had not.

The crew paid for the deadlock. The ten crewmen, the captain and nine sailors, were held for 94 days and released on 1 January 1955, sent across the Gaza Strip on foot. The captain said they had been beaten. Egypt offered to release the ship only if it sailed south, away from the Canal. [cite:rs_cw2_jta_batgalim] [cite:rs_cw2_frus_batgalim] That condition shows what was at stake: whether an Israeli vessel could use the Canal at all, a question the Security Council had addressed in its resolution of 1 September 1951, told in [scene:cw1_suez_blockade|the 1951 resolution]. When the Council discussed the case in January 1955, the United States, Britain, France and Brazil said Egypt's action violated that resolution, and on 13 January the Council's President stated that members agreed it had "continuing validity and effect". [cite:rs_cw2_frus_batgalim] The sources record no new resolution: the Council reaffirmed the old one. Nor do they record the ship's release.

The record leaves the central questions of responsibility open, as the UN's own officers did. Who killed the passengers at the Scorpion Pass is not established; the chairman's words, "far from being conclusive", remain the last official word in these sources, and Israel's position that the killers came from Jordan remains its position. [cite:rs_cw2_un_s3252] Who carried out the Nahhalin attack is not stated in Israel's own voice anywhere in these sources; the Commission's finding rests on physical evidence, and Israel was not present to answer it. [cite:rs_cw2_un_s3251] Whether the Bat Galim's crew fired on Egyptian fishermen is likewise unresolved: Egypt charged that they did, the Commission found no conclusive evidence, and then withdrew the word that would have cleared them. [cite:rs_cw2_un_s3323] And the exact date of Byroade's Dayton speech differs between the State Department record and Medoff, by ten days.

sections.h: Operation Susannah and the Lavon Affair, 1954–1955
sections.html:
In the summer of 1954 Egypt and Britain were negotiating the evacuation of British forces from the Suez Canal area, a negotiation whose terms are followed in [scene:cw2_free_officers|the section on Egypt's revolution]. In the same months, Israel's military intelligence service, Aman, set in motion a covert operation inside Egypt meant to damage Egypt's relations with the West while that negotiation went on. Israel's own Defense Ministry archive, which calls the episode "the 'Unfortunate' or the Lavon affair," describes it as "a failed Israeli covert operation." [cite:rs_cw2_mod_lavon] The operation came to be known as Operation Susannah. Its exposure cost two of its operatives their lives on a Cairo gallows, sent others to prison for years, forced a defence minister from office, and opened a quarrel over a single question, who gave the order, that Israeli politics did not put to rest for nearly a decade.
