[cite:rs_cw2_adst_aswan] [cite:rs_cw2_frus_dulles_hussein] When the offer was withdrawn, by the oral histories' account, Egypt turned to the Soviet Union; Wilkins later described the dam as a "$600 million project under the Russians." [cite:rs_cw2_adst_aswan] That figure and Dulles's $1.3 billion are not reconciled in the sources used here, and they may not measure the same thing. The Canal Company passed from its British and French owners to Egypt, with full compensation offered to them. [cite:rs_cw2_state_suez]

Egypt's case, as far as the record used here gives it, rested on sovereignty and on need: the 1954 accord with Britain had recognized the Canal as "an integral part of Egypt", and the dam was, in its ambassador's words, the only answer to the country's population problem. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_suez_base] [cite:rs_cw2_frus_dulles_hussein] The British and French case, and what both governments did about it, belong to the next stage.

What remains open is the weight of each reason. The memoranda of 19 July record what Eisenhower and Dulles said to each other and to Egypt's ambassador; the oral histories record what officials remembered later; neither tells us which consideration was decisive, or whether the threatened congressional ban would have passed. The record used here also gives no primary text of the December 1955 offer itself. On the evening of 26 July 1956 the Canal Company had been nationalized by Egypt, the dam had no Western financier, and the crisis that followed is told in Stage Three, with Egypt's side of it in [scene:egi_src_s02|Egypt and Suez].

sections.h: The Architecture on 26 July 1956
sections.html:
When Nasser announced the nationalization of the Suez Canal Company on 26 July 1956, the structure that the next stage's crisis would test had been built in the three years before. It was not built by one government or to one design. It was assembled from separate decisions taken in Jerusalem, Cairo, Washington, London, Paris, Moscow and Prague, and at the United Nations, each for its own reasons, and each contested by someone inside the same government. This section sets out how those threads stood on that day: who held power, through what instrument, for what stated interest, and who opposed it from within.

The first thread was retaliation as Israeli policy. It had an institutional birth date. In August 1953 Ariel Sharon was appointed to establish and command Unit 101, created, in the words of Israel's Ministry of Defense archive, "to carry out reprisal operations in enemy territory"; in January 1954 the unit was folded into paratrooper battalion 890, and the cross-border operations continued under the paratroopers. [cite:rs_cw2_mod_sharon] The operations that followed form a line through the stage: Qibya in October 1953, the Gaza raid of 28 February 1955, Khan Yunis at the end of August 1955, Lake Tiberias in December 1955, Qalqilya in October 1956. [cite:rs_cw2_jps_qibya] [cite:rs_cw2_mod_black_arrow] [cite:rs_cw2_un_a3157] [cite:rs_cw2_unyb1956] Israel presented the raids as answers to attacks across the line that it named and documented, from the killing of a mother and her two children at Yehud in October 1953 to the bus at the Scorpion Pass in March 1954 and the four civilians killed near Kfar Menahem in August 1955; on the Scorpion Pass, the UN chairman of the armistice commission found the evidence "far from being conclusive" as to who was responsible. [cite:rs_cw2_jvl_qibya] [cite:rs_cw2_un_s3196] [cite:rs_cw2_un_s3427] [cite:rs_cw2_un_s3252] Three of the raids drew the Security Council's censure: Resolution 101 on Qibya, adopted 9–0 with Lebanon and the Soviet Union abstaining; Resolution 106 on Gaza, unanimous; Resolution 111 on the lake, unanimous, warning of "further measures under the Charter". [cite:rs_cw2_un_res101] [cite:rs_cw2_un_res106] [cite:rs_cw2_un_res111] The Council could censure, and could send its Secretary-General, who came back in May 1956 with cease-fire assurances that every government made conditional on the others' conduct. [cite:rs_cw2_unyb1956] Neither censure nor the mission stopped the raids or the attacks across the line.

The policy had its opponents inside Israel's own cabinet. Avi Shlaim describes two schools, Sharett's "negotiation" school and Ben-Gurion's "retaliation" school: Sharett "sought to avoid escalation in order to prevent war", while Dayan "needed escalation to bring about war". [cite:rs_cw2_shlaim_east_west] Neil Caplan records that Sharett led cabinet majorities for restraint and blocked proposals to capture Gaza or the Straits of Tiran. [cite:rs_cw2_caplan_asia] The contest had a price in Washington, too. Dulles offered a mutual defence pact in February 1955 on two conditions, that Israel not expand its borders by force and not carry out military retaliation; Ben-Gurion and Sharett accepted the first and refused the second. [cite:rs_cw2_shlaim_east_west] Sharett's case, in Shlaim's account, was that avoiding escalation was the way to prevent war. By 26 July 1956, on one reading, the argument had been settled by office, not by persuasion. Ben-Gurion had returned as defence minister on 21 February 1955 and as prime minister on 3 November 1955; Sharett had resigned as foreign minister on 18 June 1956, and two days after the nationalization, according to a dealer's description of the letter, Ben-Gurion wrote to him that his continuing at the Foreign Ministry "was not for the good of the country". [cite:rs_cw2_mod_bg_portfolio] [cite:rs_cw2_pmo_govts] [cite:rs_cw2_kaller_bg] Shlaim's judgment, quoted by Caplan, is that "Ben-Gurion failed to topple Nasser but he succeeded in toppling Sharett." [cite:rs_cw2_caplan_asia]

The second thread was Washington's attempt to manage the conflict with the instruments it had, and the limits of each. The first was money. In September 1953, on Assistant Secretary Byroade's advice, Dulles withheld Mutual Security funds while, as he put it, Israel was "acting in defiance" of the UN Chief of Staff's decision on the works at Banat Yaacov; the works stopped at midnight on 28 October, and Press Release 604 recommended about $26 million, saying that aid granted while Israel ignored the UN "would tend to undermine the authority" of its truce organization. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_eban_dulles_sep53] [cite:rs_cw2_frus_presser_20oct53] [cite:rs_cw2_frus_res100] [cite:rs_cw2_frus_pr604] It was a lever that worked, on a narrow question, because a UN officer's ruling gave it a fixed point. The second instrument was development. Eric Johnston's water plan was declared technically acceptable to Israel, Jordan, Syria and Lebanon, with the United States offering two-thirds of the costs, and was then not endorsed by the Arab League's political organs, whose Council decided against it in October 1955 by AquaPedia's dating. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_unified_plan] [cite:rs_cw2_aquapedia_jordan] The third was diplomacy. Operation Alpha, begun with Britain on 20 December 1954, put forward a Negev land link, the resettlement of 75,000 refugees in Israel and non-belligerence; Dulles's address of 26 August 1955 offered a loan for compensation and a treaty guarantee of agreed borders; Robert Anderson carried it to Ben-Gurion, Sharett and Nasser from January to March 1956, and, according to the Jewish Virtual Library, both sides rejected it. [cite:rs_cw2_jvl_alpha] [cite:rs_cw2_ecf_alpha] [cite:rs_cw2_jvl_dulles55] The fourth was arms, and here Washington chose refusal: Israel's requests after the Czech deal were postponed on 13 December 1955 and finally rejected in April 1956. [cite:rs_cw2_shlaim_arms] The fifth was the Aswan offer, withdrawn on 19 July 1956. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_aswan_ike]

Several of these instruments had opponents within the American government as well as outside it. The decision on Aswan is the clearest case. The memoranda of 19 July give a policy judgment about Egypt; Robert Bowie and Fraser Wilkins later named a hostile Congress, with cotton growers, supporters of Israel and the China lobby among its constituencies, as the real constraint; Parker Hart called Dulles's decision "impulsive". [cite:rs_cw2_frus_aswan_ike] [cite:rs_cw2_adst_aswan] State and Congress pulled in different directions; within State, officers disagreed with their Secretary. Washington's public line was itself contested: Byroade's speeches of April and May 1954 were protested by Israel's government and denounced by Emanuel Neumann as "Byroadeism", and the administration stood by him. [cite:rs_cw2_medoff_byroade] Washington and London did not always speak together either. When Eden proposed on 9 November 1955 that Israel and the Arab states "must make some compromise between these two positions", Dulles replied from Geneva that the "US is in no sense committed". [cite:rs_cw2_frus_eden_uk]

The third thread was the entry of the Soviet bloc. It came through Egypt, by sale, and it came at Egypt's request. On 15 June 1954 Nasser told the Soviet ambassador that Britain had stopped arms shipments and that Egypt could not meet "a hundredth of its army's needs". [cite:rs_cw2_wilson_solod] On 27 September 1955 he announced that Czechoslovakia would supply tanks, MiG-15s and bombers, in a deal the Jewish Virtual Library values at "more than $83 million"; Egypt paid in cotton and rice, with a million Egyptian pounds already sent to Prague "on account". [cite:rs_cw2_jvl_czech] [cite:rs_cw2_frus_tel632] Assistant Secretary George Allen explained that American arms talks with Egypt had stalled on Washington's requirement of a military mission. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_allen_czech] Whether Israel's Gaza raid drove Nasser to Moscow, as Shlaim and Allen held, or the Baghdad Pact did, as Eban argued, is disputed; the Soviet record of June 1954 shows the request predated both. [cite:rs_cw2_shlaim_gaza] [cite:rs_cw2_frus_eban_allen] [cite:rs_cw2_solod_gaza]

The fourth thread answered the third. With Washington refusing, Israel turned to France. Shimon Peres went directly to the French defence establishment, and Shlaim reads the two Western motives against each other: "France offered arms in the hope of inducing Israel to go to war against Egypt," while "America allowed its allies to supply arms to Israel on condition that Israel did not go to war." [cite:rs_cw2_shlaim_arms] That is his interpretation. The State Department's own count, in September 1956, was that Israel was believed to hold 24 Mystères and possibly 48, with France proposing to sell 24 more. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_mystere]

The fifth thread was the region choosing sides. Iraq and Turkey signed the Baghdad Pact on 24 February 1955; Britain adhered on 5 April, Pakistan on 23 September and Iran on 23 October 1955. [cite:rs_cw2_avalon_baghdad] The United States stayed out, for reasons a State Department position paper of November 1956 listed: renewed Israeli demands for a security guarantee, Senate ratification, Hashemite–Saudi–Egyptian rivalries and Soviet reaction. It paid its share of the budget, $76,350, and sat on the committees all the same. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_baghdad_us] At Bandung in April 1955, twenty-nine Asian and African states met without Israel, which was not invited despite Burma's U Nu, and declared "support for the rights of the Arab people of Palestine"; Nasser emerged there, in Zachary Karabell's phrase, as an international leader. [cite:rs_cw2_enc_bandung] [cite:rs_cw2_jta_bandung] Jordan showed what the choice cost a government caught between the two: its prime minister's move toward the Pact in December 1955 brought three days of riots and his fall, and in March 1956 King Hussein dismissed Glubb, whose "open endorsement" of the Pact's supporters was among the reasons the Amman report listed. [cite:rs_cw2_loc_jordan] [cite:rs_cw2_wilson_glubb]

The sixth thread was Egypt's own consolidation, which had its own opponents and its own violence. The Free Officers' coup of 23 July 1952 produced a contest in 1954 that Nasser won over Naguib; the Suez base agreement of 19 October 1954 provided for British troops to leave the Canal Zone; the Manshiya shooting a week later led to the Muslim Brotherhood's banning and more than a thousand arrests; Naguib was removed in November 1954; and on 23 June 1956 Nasser, the only candidate, was elected president with 99.95 per cent, as HISTORY.com reports. [cite:rs_cw2_ebsco_farouk] [cite:rs_cw2_frus_suez_base] [cite:rs_cw2_origins_mb] [cite:rs_cw2_frus_naguib] [cite:rs_cw2_history_nasser] Israel's covert attempt to damage Egypt's ties with the West during the base talks, Operation Susannah in July 1954, ended with two Egyptian Jews hanged in Cairo on 31 January 1955 and a dispute over who ordered it, followed by Lavon's resignation in February 1955. [cite:rs_cw2_mod_lavon] [cite:rs_cw2_jr_hanged]

Two further threads ran beneath the diplomacy. The first was intelligence. From 1954 James Angleton headed the CIA's new Counterintelligence Staff and controlled its Israel account, which the CIA's own historian calls "an administrative anomaly" and a foundation of his influence; he saw Israel "as a bastion against the Soviet Union". [cite:rs_cw2_robarge] The text of Khrushchev's secret speech reached Washington through that channel in the spring of 1956, by the account Shammai Siskind gives. [cite:rs_cw2_meq_siskind] No formal written liaison agreement for these years is documented in the sources used. [cite:rs_cw2_robarge] [cite:rs_cw2_meq_siskind] The second was oil. After the coup of 1953, Iran's oil was settled in a consortium signed on 5 August 1954: the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company 40 per cent, Royal Dutch Shell 14 per cent, five American companies 8 per cent each, and by arithmetic 6 per cent for the French participant, with operating companies incorporated in the Netherlands and £25 million in compensation to the Anglo-Iranian company from 1957. [cite:rs_cw2_fo_consortium] [cite:rs_cw2_dsb_consortium] [cite:rs_cw2_compensation54]

The last thread was American and domestic. On 14 June 1954 Eisenhower signed the bill adding "under God" to the Pledge of Allegiance, speaking of "those spiritual weapons which forever will be our country's most powerful resource"; in July 1955 Congress required "In God We Trust" on all currency; and on 30 July 1956, four days after the nationalization, he signed the joint resolution making it the national motto. [cite:rs_cw2_ucsb_pledge] [cite:rs_cw2_unt_pl140] [cite:rs_cw2_stat70_732] The documented motive was religious revival set against Communism. None of the sources used here links either change to Israel or to any Zionist organization, and this book draws no such link as a finding. [cite:rs_cw2_ffrf_kramnick] [cite:rs_cw2_sconres96]

Set side by side, the threads show who acted, for what stated reason, and who resisted inside the same house.

The pattern these threads make is convergence, not design. Britain negotiated over its Canal base and joined Iraq in the Pact; Egypt sought the British out, arms on its own terms and a dam on its own terms; Israel's activists sought deterrence and arms, and its moderates sought to avoid escalation; Washington weighed its steps against Moscow's reaction, as its own papers show, and found no instrument that bound both sides at once. France's interests, by Shlaim's reading, ran toward a war with Egypt. [cite:rs_cw2_shlaim_arms] No single government controlled the outcome, and none of the sources used here shows one doing so.

What the record leaves open is the weight of each thread. It does not settle whether the Gaza raid or the Baghdad Pact turned Nasser to Prague, since he had asked Moscow before either; whether Aswan was withdrawn for Egypt's conduct or for Congress's mood; or whether Sharett's restraint could have held had Washington sold Israel arms in December 1955. [cite:rs_cw2_solod_gaza] [cite:rs_cw2_adst_aswan] [cite:rs_cw2_shlaim_arms] Those questions run forward into [scene:cw2_aswan|the end of the dam offer] and the crisis of the autumn, told in the next stage.

chapters.label: Stage Three
chapters.title: Strike and Withdraw
chapters.intro:
On 26 July 1956 Nasser nationalized the Suez Canal Company, a joint British and French enterprise that had run the Canal since 1869, and offered "full economic compensation" for it. He acted after the United States and Britain had refused Egypt economic aid, and Eden judged in private that "the Egyptian has his thumb on our windpipe." [cite:rs_cw3_origins_hahn] [cite:rs_cw3_milestones_suez] Israel's grievances with Egypt were older: a Canal still closed to its shipping five years after the Security Council had called on Egypt to lift the restrictions, the Straits of Tiran closed since September 1955, Czechoslovak arms, and a military treaty binding Egypt to Syria and, later, Jordan. [cite:rs_cw1_frus1951_res95] [cite:rs_cw3_jafi_fedayeen] [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_bg_7nov] Within three months the two quarrels had become one war.

This stage asks how a war planned in secret by three governments was fought, stopped and undone within about five months, and what that reversal left in place. It asks with equal weight what the war did to the people who had no say in it: Arab citizens of Israel under curfew, refugees in Gaza under a new occupation, and the Jews of Egypt.

The cast spans four capitals and the United Nations. In Jerusalem, Ben-Gurion was prime minister, with Moshe Dayan commanding the campaign, Shimon Peres dealing with France, Abba Eban carrying Israel's case in Washington and, by March 1957, Golda Meir speaking for Israel at the United Nations as foreign minister. [cite:rs_cw3_shlaim_sevres] [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_bg_mar57] In Paris stood Mollet, Pineau, Bourgès-Maunoury and General Challe; in London, Eden and Selwyn Lloyd. [cite:rs_cw3_shlaim_sevres] In Cairo, Nasser. In Washington, Eisenhower and Dulles, with Treasury Secretary Humphrey holding the purse and a Congress whose leaders would not follow the President all the way. [cite:rs_cw3_boughton_fd] [cite:rs_cw3_frus17_d120] Moscow spoke through Bulganin's notes. [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_bulganin1] At the United Nations, Hammarskjöld, Canada's Lester Pearson and the Director of UNRWA each left a record that shaped the outcome or the account of it. [cite:rs_cw3_frus16_d467] [cite:rs_cw3_unrwa_a3212] And in a village called Kafr Qasim, a brigade commander, Issachar Shadmi, a Border Police major, Shmuel Malinki, and a lieutenant, Gabriel Dahan, stood in a chain of command whose last link was a platoon at the village entrance. [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_kq]

The sections follow events in order. They begin with [scene:cw3_road_to_war|the road to war] and Israel's case for it in its own words, then the conference at Sèvres, where Britain, France and Israel wrote down who would attack whom, and when. The first evening of the war brings the killings at Kafr Qasim, inside Israel. The fighting itself follows, in Sinai and at Port Said, with every casualty figure and its source. Washington then turns on its allies at the United Nations and with money and oil; Khan Yunis and Rafah record what happened in Gaza in the first days of occupation; Moscow's notes arrive in the week of Hungary; and Israel moves in about thirty-six hours from talk of a "Third Kingdom" to agreeing to withdraw. Egypt's measures against its Jews, Israel's four months of rule in Gaza and the withdrawal fight of early 1957 come next. Two sections then follow Kafr Qasim through its trial and its long memory, beyond the period of this stage, and the last, [scene:cw3_aftermath|the architecture in spring 1957], takes stock of the order that replaced the one the war broke.
chapters.outro:
By March 1957 every army that had crossed into Egypt the previous autumn had left it, and almost nothing else stood where it had stood in July 1956. The stage's own closing section sets out the regional order of that spring and the Eisenhower Doctrine that framed it, in [scene:cw3_aftermath|the architecture in spring 1957]. What follows takes the structure layer by layer, and asks what each layer had settled.

The legal layer was rebuilt in the General Assembly. With Britain and France vetoing the American and Soviet drafts on 30 October, the Security Council used Uniting for Peace to pass the question on, and the Assembly then spoke in numbers no invader could match: 64 to 5 for the cease-fire of 2 November, 74 to 2 on 2 February 1957 to "deplore" Israel's non-compliance. [cite:rs_cw3_unu_ufp] [cite:rs_cw3_unispal_sc119] [cite:rs_cw3_unproj_997] [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_1124] Israel returned behind armistice lines that Ben-Gurion had said on 7 November had "no more validity," calling the armistice agreement itself "dead and buried." [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_bg_7nov] Its claim to the Straits of Tiran rested on a different kind of instrument: an American aide-mémoire calling the Gulf "international waters" and declaring the United States "prepared to exercise the right of free and innocent passage," and Israel's own stated "assumptions" read into the Assembly's record on 1 March. [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_aidememoire] [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_bg_mar57] Neither was a treaty. Inside Israel the war produced a doctrine of law. The Kafr Qasim court, sitting from March 1957, would rule in October 1958 that an order over which "a black flag flies" must be refused. [cite:rs_cw3_orbach_2013] [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_kq] In Egypt the war produced a law of a different kind: Nationality Law No. 391 of 22 November 1956, which barred undefined "Zionists" from nationality. [cite:rs_cw3_jjac_egypt]

The administrative layer shows how each state governed people it treated as a wartime risk. Israel's Arab citizens in the Triangle were placed under a curfew announced, at Kafr Qasim, thirty minutes before it began, and news of the killings there was censored, with the press blackout lifted only after about two months. [cite:rs_cw3_robinson_2003] [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_kq] For four months Israel also ruled Gaza's "some 300,000" people through a military government, reinstated councils and local police under the Israel Police. [cite:rs_cw3_morris_gaza] Egypt detained about 1,000 Jews and put Jewish property under administrators by military proclamation. [cite:rs_cw3_jta_2006_egypt] [cite:rs_cw3_jjac_egypt]

The institutional and financial layer is where the war was decided after the shooting stopped. UNEF, created by the Assembly in early November, reached Egypt on 15 November and stood by March on the Gaza line and at Sharm el-Sheikh, on Egyptian soil and so only as long as Egypt allowed. [cite:rs_cw3_origins_hahn] [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_bg_mar57] Britain's reserves fell below the $2 billion floor; Humphrey made support conditional on "conforming to rather than defying the United Nations"; and the $561 million IMF drawing came only once withdrawal was agreed, while the oil plan was held back, in Eisenhower's words, "until the invading powers accepted immediate withdrawal." [cite:rs_cw3_boughton_fd] [cite:rs_cw3_frus16_d612] Against Israel the levers were named but never pulled: Dulles listed German reparations, Israel Bonds and US aid on 20 February, and the leaders of Congress declined to follow. [cite:rs_cw3_frus17_d120]

The Palestinian Arab side appears in this stage mostly in the record of what was done to it, though not only: at Kafr Qasim the villagers prevented the accused from being brought to the state's reconciliation ceremony. [cite:rs_cw3_palquest_kq] The UNRWA Director received lists naming 275 people at Khan Yunis and 111 at Rafah, and could verify neither; the sources record no Israeli investigation. [cite:rs_cw3_unrwa_a3212] At Kafr Qasim the dead number forty-nine by the village's own count, forty-seven or forty-eight in other sources, and in November 1957 the state offered IL5,000 per victim and a sulha that, in Robinson's account, villagers were pressured to attend. [cite:rs_cw3_djn_comp] [cite:rs_cw3_robinson_2003] One difference between the two is documented: the killings inside Israel went to a court, and for those in Gaza no proceeding appears in the record.

The regional layer turned on Cairo. Nasser kept the Canal and, in Hahn's words, gained prestige as "a leader who had defied European empires and survived a military invasion by Israel." [cite:rs_cw3_origins_hahn] Eden resigned in January 1957. [cite:rs_cw3_milestones_suez] Between 23,000 and 25,000 Jews left Egypt after a minister's proclamation that "all Jews are Zionists and enemies of the state." [cite:rs_cw3_jta_2006_egypt] [cite:rs_cw3_fathom_julius] Israel came away with a French alliance and a reactor of twice the promised capacity, delivered in September 1957. [cite:rs_cw3_shlaim_sevres] The American layer is the plainest change of all: Washington, which had not been told of Sèvres, asked the Security Council, as Moscow did, for Israel's withdrawal, carried the Assembly against its allies, held back their money and oil, and by March had written its own commitment to the region into law. [cite:rs_cw3_unu_ufp] [cite:rs_cw3_origins_hahn] [cite:rs_cw3_pl85_7]

On this reading of the record, what was settled was who could end a war in the Middle East: not the powers that started this one, but Washington acting through the United Nations and its own Treasury. What was contested was the war's nature. Israel's strongest case was Ben-Gurion's of 17 November, that a return to the armistice meant "a return to murder, blockade, and boycott," backed by 1,300 Israelis killed or wounded across eight years by the Jewish Agency's count. [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_bulganin] [cite:rs_cw3_jafi_fedayeen] The strongest case against it rests on documents too: a secret protocol fixing the attack as a pretext for Britain and France, an annexation point Ben-Gurion sought at Sèvres, and Gaza listed, on the Katif Center's account, among the war's aims. [cite:rs_cw3_shlaim_sevres] [cite:rs_cw3_katif_gaza] The record leaves open how many died at Khan Yunis, Rafah and Port Said; whether Egypt was beaten in Sinai or withdrew; whether Israel meant to keep Gaza; and what Plan Mole, still redacted, provided for. Ben-Gurion's own warning, that the next war might be long and fought without "helping forces from abroad," returns in [scene:s12|1967]. [cite:rs_cw3_jpost_dec56]

sections.h: From Nationalization to War, July–October 1956
sections.html:
Stage Two ended on 26 July 1956, with the Suez Canal Company in Egyptian hands, a story told in [scene:cw2_aswan|the end of the dam offer]. The hinge can be stated in a sentence. Nasser nationalized the Company after the United States and Britain refused to provide economic aid to Egypt; Eden's private judgment, as the historian Peter Hahn quotes it, was that "the Egyptian has his thumb on our windpipe." [cite:rs_cw3_origins_hahn] The Company was a joint British and French enterprise that had run the Canal since its construction in 1869, and Nasser offered "full economic compensation for the Company." [cite:rs_cw3_milestones_suez] Three months later Egypt was at war with Israel, Britain and France at once. This section follows the road between those two points as the diplomatic record lays it out, and sets out the case Israel's government made for war in its own words, beside the case its critics make.

Diplomacy, and hints of force. The first response of the maritime powers was conference diplomacy. The State Department's own documentary series, Foreign Relations of the United States, groups the weeks of August and September 1956 under the London conferences and the scheme that grew from them, the Suez Canal Users' Association. [cite:rs_cw3_frus16_ch3] On 9 September 1956 Dulles proposed that association of "18 of the world's leading maritime nations." The State Department's Office of the Historian records that the plan failed to win full support from any of the contending powers, and that through August, September and October Britain "repeatedly hinted that it might resort to force." [cite:rs_cw3_milestones_suez] Conference diplomacy produced a plan; it did not produce agreement, and the British hints of force continued alongside it.

The parallel crises. The Canal was not the only crisis in the region that autumn, and the documentary record shows how the others ran alongside it. The same volume of Foreign Relations organizes the weeks from 19 September to 4 October under the heading "Increasing Violence Along the Israel–Jordan Border," together with the Macmillan visit; and the weeks from 5 to 29 October under four headings at once: the Security Council debate on the Canal, "the Iraqi Proposal to Move Troops Into Jordan," Anglo-American differences over the users' association, and "Israeli Mobilization." [cite:rs_cw3_frus16_ch3] The headings are the editors' arrangement of the documents, not a narrative, and the sources used here do not give the contents of those files. What they show is the shape of the problem as Washington saw it in October: a Canal dispute among the maritime powers, a violent Israeli–Jordanian frontier, a proposal to move Iraqi troops into Jordan, and an Israeli mobilization, all in the same weeks.

Ben-Gurion's statement of 15 October. Two weeks before the war, at the 169th session of the Third Knesset, Ben-Gurion gave the government's account of Israel's position. He told the house that the Hebrew year 5716 had been "a turning point in our security situation." He said that Egypt "still sits in the Gaza Strip," and that between 1954 and 1955 Egypt had caused Israel 242 casualties. He presented the government's posture as defensive preparation, not a first strike. [cite:rs_cw3_knesset_15oct56] The statement matters in two ways. It is the clearest public record of how Israel's government framed the threat on the eve of war; and, read beside the conference that opened at Sèvres a week later, it can be read as a measure of how far the public posture stood from the plan about to be written down there. That conference is the subject of [scene:cw3_sevres|the next section].

Israel's case, in its own terms. The fullest statement of why Israel went to war came afterwards, in Ben-Gurion's speech to the Knesset of 7 November 1956. He named four reasons. The first was the renewal of the fedayeen raids. The second was "the maritime blockade of Israel and the organization of an economic blockade against Israel throughout the world." The third was the Czechoslovak arms, "enormous quantities of heavy arms." The fourth was a "tripartite military alliance" of Egypt, Jordan and Syria, with their forces "placed under Egyptian command." [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_bg_7nov] The Jewish Agency's historical account supplies the numbers on which that case rests. It states that between 1948 and 1956 "a total of 1,300 Israeli citizens were killed or wounded" in cross-border attacks; it records Egypt's announcement in September 1955 that the Straits of Tiran were closed to all vessels; and it records the Egypt–Syria military treaty of October 1955, which Jordan later joined. [cite:rs_cw3_jafi_fedayeen] These are the Agency's figures, not an independent tally, and the 1,300 counts killed and wounded together across eight years; but they are the figures Israel's argument used.

The maritime blockade Ben-Gurion named had a history at the United Nations. On 1 September 1951 the Security Council, in Resolution 95, had called on Egypt to end its restrictions on "the passage of international commercial shipping and goods" through the Canal, by eight votes to none, a ruling Egypt contested and the story of which is told in [scene:cw1_suez_blockade|the Canal closed to Israel]. [cite:rs_cw1_frus1951_res95] [cite:rs_cw1_spv558] Five years later the restriction still stood, and the Tiran closure of September 1955 had added a second one at the Gulf of Aqaba. [cite:rs_cw3_jafi_fedayeen]

Stated at full strength, the argument ran like this. For two years raids had been organized from Gaza, which Egypt administered. Egypt barred Israeli-bound shipping from the Canal in defiance of a Security Council ruling, and from September 1955 closed the Straits of Tiran to all vessels. Egypt was receiving from Czechoslovakia what Ben-Gurion called "enormous quantities of heavy arms," in October 1955 it had concluded a military treaty with Syria, which Jordan later joined, and by Ben-Gurion's account their forces were placed under Egyptian command. A government that waited for those forces to be ready would be choosing the time of its enemy's attack. Ben-Gurion described the campaign afterwards as "an action in self-defence in accordance with Article 51 of the Charter of the United Nations." [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_bg_mar57] [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_bg_7nov]

The critical case. Against this stands a second reading, and it rests on documents too. The first is the Sèvres protocol itself: the timing and form of Israel's attack were fixed in a secret agreement with Britain and France whose purpose, on their side, was a pretext to occupy the Canal Zone. Avi Shlaim, who reconstructed the conference, reads Ben-Gurion's aims there as reaching beyond defence to territory, and calls the protocol "a monument to French opportunism, Eden's duplicity, and Ben-Gurion's paranoia," a verdict that is his interpretation. [cite:rs_cw3_shlaim_sevres] The second concerns Gaza. According to the Gush Katif Heritage Center's history of the Strip, which cites Hagai Huberman, Ben-Gurion, then defence minister, proposed on 29 March 1955 that Israel reconquer the Gaza Strip, and the government rejected the proposal; and at the cabinet meeting of October 1956 that approved the operation, he listed among the war's aims "[control of] the Gaza Strip." [cite:rs_cw3_katif_gaza] If that account is right, the Strip that Ben-Gurion described to the Knesset on 15 October as the place where Egypt "still sits" was also, in the cabinet room, an objective.

The two cases are not as opposed as they first appear, and neither disposes of the other. The raids, the blockade, the arms and the joint command were real grievances, documented in Israel's own records and, for the Canal, in a Security Council resolution. That Israel had reasons to fear Egypt does not settle why it attacked when it did and in the form it did; the Sèvres record answers that second question, and it answers it with the interests of London and Paris as much as with Israel's. Both can be true together: a government with genuine security grievances chose to act through a secret alliance that served other purposes, and its own aims, by the critical account, included ground it had already sought to take.

What the record leaves open. The sources used here establish what Ben-Gurion told the Knesset and what the Gush Katif Heritage Center reports of the cabinet, but they do not include the cabinet minutes themselves, so the October 1956 war-aims list is known here only through a single attributed account. The Jewish Agency's 1,300 and Ben-Gurion's 242 count different periods and are not broken down into dead and wounded in these sources; no independent tally was found to check them against. The contents of the American files on the Israel–Jordan border and on Iraq's proposal to move troops into Jordan are named in the record's headings but were not consulted. And how much weight each of Israel's four stated reasons carried in the decision, against the opportunity France offered, is a question the documents in this section do not settle. They do show that in October 1956, while Israel's government spoke publicly of defence, Washington's files were already headed "Israeli Mobilization," and the terms of the war were about to be written down at Sèvres.

sections.h: The Protocol of Sèvres, 14–25 October 1956
sections.html:
Eden denied for the rest of his life that there had been any collusion with Israel. [cite:rs_cw3_shlaim_sevres] The document that proves otherwise was signed on the evening of 24 October 1956 in a villa at Sèvres by representatives of Britain, France and Israel, and the British prime minister ordered every copy destroyed. One survived in Ben-Gurion's waistcoat pocket. What follows is drawn from Avi Shlaim's reconstruction of the conference, published in International Affairs in 1997, which draws on the participants' own accounts, among them Pineau's record and Peres's writing, and from the accounts of how the Israeli copy came to light. [cite:rs_cw3_shlaim_sevres]

Chequers, 14 October. The plan reached Eden from Paris. On 14 October 1956, at Chequers, General Maurice Challe, accompanied by France's acting foreign minister Albert Gazier, put to him what became known as the "Challe scenario": Israel would attack Egypt in Sinai, and Britain and France would then have a pretext to occupy the Canal Zone. Shlaim quotes Nutting that Eden "could scarcely contain his glee," and gives Eden's reply: "So that lets us off the hook." [cite:rs_cw3_shlaim_sevres] Since the nationalization, as [scene:cw3_road_to_war|the previous section] showed, Britain had hinted at force without finding a ground for it that the other powers would accept. The scenario offered one. Britain and France would not appear as the attackers of Egypt; they would appear as the powers separating two combatants and protecting the Canal.

The villa, 22–24 October. The conference opened at 4 p.m. on Monday 22 October 1956. Britain was represented by Selwyn Lloyd, who came incognito, with Donald Logan. Israel sent Ben-Gurion, Moshe Dayan and Shimon Peres, with Mordechai Bar-On as secretary. The French side was the largest: Mollet, Christian Pineau, Bourgès-Maunoury, Challe, Mangin and Abel Thomas. The British were absent on 23 October. Patrick Dean and Logan arrived at 4:30 p.m. on 24 October, and the protocol was signed that evening. [cite:rs_cw3_shlaim_sevres]

The composition of the delegations tells part of the story. France sent six men and Israel four, Ben-Gurion among them. Britain sent Lloyd under cover on the first day, stayed away on the second, and on the third sent Dean and Logan to sign. On this record, the government that would later deny the meeting kept its own presence at it slight and hidden.

Ben-Gurion's fears. Ben-Gurion came to Sèvres with two fears, and the protocol was shaped by both. The first was of Egyptian bombing. He feared that "Tel Aviv could be wiped out" unless the Royal Air Force first destroyed Egypt's air force. The second was of British betrayal. Shlaim records that it was Ben-Gurion who took the initiative in proposing that the agreement be written down, as "a guarantee against betrayal by Perfidious Albion." [cite:rs_cw3_shlaim_sevres] The phrase marks how little he trusted the partner whose bombers he needed. An Israeli attack that Britain then failed to follow would have left Israel alone at war with Egypt, and condemned by the powers that had invited it.

A "real act of war." A credible pretext needed more than a skirmish: if Britain was to intervene as protector of the Canal, the Israeli attack had to appear to threaten it. Dayan's revised plan answered that need. It called for "a real act of war": a paratroop drop on the Mitla Pass, about thirty miles from the Canal, with a mechanized brigade thrusting westward, so that Britain would have a credible pretext to intervene about 36 hours later. [cite:rs_cw3_shlaim_sevres] The design was political as much as military. A drop deep in Sinai, close to the Canal, would look like a threat to it; and the interval of a day and a half was, on this logic, meant to let the ultimatum follow without seeming prearranged.

The fantastic plan, and the eighth point. Ben-Gurion's ambitions at Sèvres went beyond the operation. On 22 October he laid out a reorganization of the region that he himself called "fantastic": Jordan divided, Israel extended to the Litani, the Canal internationalized, and Nasser removed. At his request an Israeli eighth point was added to the draft, seeking "permanent annexation of the entire area east of the El Arish-Abu Ageila, Nakhl-Sharm el-Sheikh" line. Pineau recorded it. Britain and France never backed it, and it is not in the signed text. On 24 October Ben-Gurion put Israel's central interest in one sentence: "The Straits of Tiran are the State of Israel's Suez Canal." [cite:rs_cw3_shlaim_sevres] The distinction between what Ben-Gurion proposed and what was signed is the heart of the argument over his motives, and both halves of it belong in the account. He sought territory; his partners declined to underwrite it; and what he secured in writing was the Straits.

The seven articles. The protocol itself is short. Paraphrased from Shlaim, its seven articles set out a timetable and a division of roles.

Read as a mechanism, the articles turn on the second. The "appeal" to both sides on 30 October was written before either side had fired, and its terms were fixed in advance. Israel, whose forces would be in Sinai, would be asked to stand ten miles from the Canal; Egypt, on its own soil, would be asked to withdraw from its own waterway and accept Anglo-French occupation of key positions, within twelve hours. Read this way, a demand drafted to be refused was the trigger for Article 3. Article 4 gave Israel its own aim, Tiran and the western shore of the Gulf, on terms of studied neutrality from its partners. Article 5 kept Jordan out of the war on both sides: Israel would not attack it, and Britain would not come to its aid if Jordan attacked Israel. Article 6 kept the whole secret.

Signed, then hidden. The protocol was signed by Patrick Dean, ad referendum, that is, subject to his government's approval; by Christian Pineau; and by David Ben-Gurion. Eden, by Shlaim's account, "was clearly surprised and very put out" that it had been committed to paper at all, and ordered all copies "rounded up and delivered to No. 10 for destruction." The British copy was destroyed. On 25 October Dean and Logan tried to persuade the French and the Israelis to destroy theirs, and failed. [cite:rs_cw3_shlaim_sevres] Ben-Gurion's copy, "thrust deep into the pocket of his waistcoat," went into the Ben-Gurion Archives. It became public when photocopying was permitted for a BBC documentary in 1996. A contemporary account of the BBC's search reports that the British copy had been "burned almost as soon as it was signed," and that the French said theirs had been "misplaced." [cite:rs_cw3_shlaim_sevres] [cite:rs_cw3_jj_sevres] A photocopy of the three French pages was found by Pineau's widow in 2002, according to the Wikipedia account, which is used here for reference only. [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_sevres]

The reactor. Sèvres carried a second agreement that appears nowhere in the protocol. Peres wrote that during a break before the signing on 24 October he "finalized with these two leaders," Mollet and Bourgès-Maunoury, "an agreement for the building of a nuclear reactor at Dimona." An earlier reactor agreement dated from 21 September 1956. By Shlaim's account Pineau opposed and Mollet was undecided; in September 1957 France delivered a reactor of twice the capacity previously promised. [cite:rs_cw3_shlaim_sevres] The war plan and the reactor agreement were concluded at the same meeting, partly by the same men, and the larger reactor followed the war. How the reactor was built and how Washington discovered it belong to Stage Four and to [scene:s11b|Dimona].

Washington outside. The protocol's sixth article bound its signatories to strict secrecy, and the secrecy held against Washington. Peter Hahn writes that American officials did not anticipate the collusion before hostilities began. [cite:rs_cw3_origins_hahn] The United States would meet the war not as a party to the plan but from outside it; its response is told later in this stage.

The dispute over motives. On what Sèvres was, the record is now settled: it was a written agreement to stage a war. On why each party joined it, historians differ, and the strongest form of each case deserves a hearing. Shlaim's reading is that France was the matchmaker, Eden duplicitous, and Ben-Gurion's demand for a written guarantee the product of a mistrust of Britain verging on paranoia; Israel's wider aims, the "fantastic" plan and the annexation point, show to him something more than self-defence. His verdict is plainly an interpretation: "The Protocol of Sèvres was thus a monument to French opportunism, Eden's duplicity, and Ben-Gurion's paranoia." [cite:rs_cw3_shlaim_sevres]

Israel's own account frames its part differently. Ben-Gurion described the campaign afterwards as self-defence under Article 51 of the United Nations Charter, against Egypt's raids and blockade, and France was the one arms supplier willing to help. [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_bg_mar57] On that view, a small state facing a rearming enemy took the only alliance on offer, and the written protocol was ordinary prudence toward a partner with every reason to deny it later, as Eden in fact did. The historian Michael Oren argues that the war partly completed what the 1949 armistices had left open. [cite:rs_cw3_oren_hnn] Ben-Gurion's fear of betrayal, on this reading, was not paranoia but foresight: the British copy was destroyed, reportedly almost as soon as it was signed.

The two readings can be weighed against the same evidence. Ben-Gurion's eighth point and his talk of the Litani support Shlaim's view that his aims at Sèvres reached past defence; his own description of the plan as "fantastic," and the fact that he signed without it, show a leader who knew the difference between what he wanted and what he could get. The signed text gave Israel's aim at Tiran its partners' neutrality, and no more. Whether that was the limit of Israel's purpose or only the limit of its partners' consent is the question on which the two readings divide.

What the record leaves open. The protocol's articles are known here through Shlaim's paraphrase; the sources used for this section do not reproduce the text itself. The French copy's history between 1956 and 2002 rests on a single reference account. What was said on 23 October, when the British were absent, is not recorded in these sources. Nor do they show how far the British cabinet as a whole knew of the signed document, or what exactly Mollet and Bourgès-Maunoury committed to on the reactor during the break on 24 October beyond Peres's own words. What is not open is that three governments agreed in writing, five days before the war, on who would attack whom, when, and on what pretext, and that one of them spent the rest of its prime minister's life denying it.

sections.h: Kafr Qasim, 29 October 1956
sections.html:
On the afternoon that Israel's army crossed into Sinai, a curfew was imposed on a row of Arab villages inside Israel, close to the line with Jordan. By half past six that evening, at the western entrance to one of them, Kafr Qasim, a Border Police platoon had shot dead dozens of the village's own people as they came home from work. They were Israeli citizens. The regime under which they lived, the military government that ruled most of Israel's Arab citizens from 1949 to December 1966 through permits, curfews and closed areas, is told in Volume II in [scene:rd6_military_government|the Arabs who stayed, and the military government], and is not retold here. [cite:wiki_kafr_qasim_massacre] [cite:conversation_kafr_qasim_60] This section follows one evening of it: how an order was given, how it travelled down a chain of command, what it produced at one village and not at others, and how the state kept the result from its own public for weeks.

The familiar account holds that the Arab citizens of Israel have enjoyed equal civil rights since 1948. They did vote from the first election, and Volume II gives that fact its due. What happened at Kafr Qasim shows the other half of their position in 1956. A curfew could be laid on their villages by a military commander, at half an hour's notice, under a regime that applied to them and not to their Jewish neighbours, and those who enforced it were armed.

The villages and the curfew. The villages concerned lay in what was called the "Little Triangle," a strip of land near the Jordanian line that Jordan had ceded to Israel under the 1949 armistice. Palestinian citizens of Israel then numbered about 160,000, and most of them lived under the military government. [cite:rs_cw3_palquest_kq] [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_kq] Eight months earlier, in February 1956, the Rattner Commission had concluded that the regime should not end until "true peace" existed; the government's case for it was security, while the historian Alina Korn has argued that its main purposes were controlling Arab residents' movement and keeping them from confiscated land. [cite:rs_rd6_korn_adalah] On 29 October 1956, the first day of the war, the Triangle villages were placed under a wartime curfew running from 5 p.m. to 6 a.m. [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_kq] [cite:rs_cw3_palquest_kq]

The timing was the heart of what followed. According to the Jewish Virtual Library's account, the order reached the Border Police at 3:30 p.m., before most villagers could be told of it, and it stated that "any Arab on the streets was to be shot." [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_kfar_kassem] At Kafr Qasim, according to PalQuest, the Institute for Palestine Studies' encyclopedia, and Wikipedia's account of the trial record, a sergeant told the village's mukhtar, its headman, at 4:30 p.m. that the curfew would begin at 5 p.m. [cite:rs_cw3_palquest_kq] [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_kq] The historian Shira Robinson describes a curfew announced only thirty minutes before it began. [cite:rs_cw3_robinson_2003] On these accounts, villagers already out at work had no way of knowing that the hour at which they would be outside their homes had become a crime.

The chain of command. The man who changed the curfew hours was Issachar Shadmi, the brigade commander. The sources differ on his rank: Wikipedia's account of the trial record gives him as a colonel, other summaries as a brigadier, and this chapter therefore calls him by his post. [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_kq] [cite:wiki_kafr_qasim_massacre] Below him was Major Shmuel Malinki, commanding the Border Police unit, and below Malinki the platoon at Kafr Qasim, under Lieutenant Gabriel Dahan. [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_kq]

What passed between Shadmi and Malinki is the most important single question about the evening, and the two men gave different answers. Malinki testified that he asked how villagers returning from work, unaware of the curfew, were to be treated, and that Shadmi told him: "I don't want sentimentality and I don't want arrests." Malinki then relayed the order to his men in these words: "Anyone leaving his home shall be shot; there shall be no arrests." [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_kq] The summary of the court record that underlies this library's account gives Shadmi's reply as being that anyone who left his house would be shot. [cite:wiki_kafr_qasim_massacre] Shadmi, for his part, denied that the question of villagers returning from work had come up at all. [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_kq] These are testimonies, given by men whose own liability turned on them, and they are given here as such, from Wikipedia's summary of the trial record rather than from the transcript itself.

The fields. When the sergeant gave the mukhtar his half-hour's warning, the mukhtar raised the obvious difficulty: some 400 villagers were still out in the fields. He was told that they would be taken care of. [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_kq] [cite:rs_cw3_palquest_kq]

Five to half past six. Between 5 and 6:30 p.m., in nine separate shooting incidents at the western entrance to the village, Dahan's platoon shot workers as they returned, on foot, on bicycles and in trucks. [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_kq] [cite:rs_cw3_palquest_kq] The village lay about a kilometre from the Green Line. [cite:wiki_kafr_qasim_massacre] The people killed were coming home after a curfew they had not been told of. [cite:wiki_kafr_qasim_massacre] [cite:conversation_kafr_qasim_60]

The villages where no one was shot. Kafr Qasim was not the only village under the order. The same curfew lay on the other villages under Shadmi's command, and in them no villagers were shot, because the local commanders did not carry out the order as Malinki's unit at Kafr Qasim did. [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_kq] Of the three units given the order, two disregarded it. [cite:wiki_kafr_qasim_massacre] That fact cuts in two directions, and both belong in the account. It shows that the order could be read, by officers on the same evening and under the same pressures, as one not to be obeyed literally; that bears on the standard of manifest illegality the court would later set out. And it shows that the outcome at Kafr Qasim depended on choices made at the bottom of the chain as well as at the top.

How many died. The number of dead is given differently in different sources, and the differences are small but should not be hidden. Forty-seven is the figure in the Jewish Virtual Library, the Encyclopaedia Judaica, Jonathan Cook's 2008 article and a JTA report of 2016. Forty-eight is the figure in a JTA dispatch from Jerusalem in November 1957, which spoke of "the murder of 48 Arabs," in Shira Robinson's scholarship ("the border-patrol killing of 48 Palestinian citizens") and in the Times of Israel in 2021, which counted an unborn child as a forty-ninth. Forty-nine is the figure in Kafr Qasim's own commemoration, in a JTA report of 1999, in Ynet in 2014, in the Jewish Virtual Library's page of Knesset highlights, and in President Herzog's words in 2021. Middle East Eye gives "fifty." [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_kfar_kassem] [cite:rs_cw3_ej_kafr_qasim] [cite:rs_cw3_cook_2008] [cite:rs_cw3_stljl_60th] [cite:rs_cw3_djn_comp] [cite:rs_cw3_robinson_2003] [cite:rs_cw3_toi_herzog] [cite:rs_cw3_jta_1999] [cite:rs_cw3_ynet_rivlin] [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_knesset3] [cite:rs_cw3_mee_kq]

The gap between the counts lies mainly in one death. Among the dead was a pregnant woman, and whether her unborn child is counted separately makes the difference between forty-eight and forty-nine; the remaining variation comes largely from the way sources round. [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_kq] The breakdown most often given is 19 men, 6 women and 23 children, the children aged between 8 and 17; those figures sum to forty-eight, and the count of forty-nine adds the unborn child. [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_kq] [cite:wiki_kafr_qasim_massacre] Ynet adds that 13 people were wounded. [cite:rs_cw3_ynet_rivlin] The count is therefore disputed, though narrowly. Forty-nine is the village's own figure and the one most later Israeli reporting uses; the Encyclopaedia Judaica and the Jewish Virtual Library give forty-seven, and the 1957 JTA dispatch and Robinson's scholarship forty-eight. Where the chapter refers back to the dead, it gives the range.

The silence. The killings happened on the first evening of a war. According to the Jewish Virtual Library, news of the killings was censored and the public learned of them only weeks later. [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_kfar_kassem] PalQuest records that the government and the army used "a variety of tactics" to conceal what had happened, and that journalists, activists and Communist members of the Knesset nevertheless reached the village through the checkpoints. [cite:rs_cw3_palquest_kq]

The sequence of the following weeks, as Wikipedia's account gives it, ran as follows. An internal inquiry began on 1 November. About two weeks after the killings, two Communist Knesset members, Tawfik Toubi and Meir Vilner, entered the village. Ben-Gurion first referred to the incident in public on 12 November. It then took about two months of lobbying before the blackout on the press was lifted. [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_kq] Jonathan Cook reports a remark of Ben-Gurion's from that time: "those who gave the order will get a strict verdict. I don't think the soldiers are guilty." [cite:rs_cw3_cook_2008] The court's outcome ran the other way: the soldiers and their officers were convicted, while Shadmi, tried separately, was fined a token sum, ten prutot by most accounts, as the next section shows.

Was it ordered from above? This is the question every reader asks, and the record of the evening itself answers it only in part. It establishes that the curfew and its timing came from the brigade commander, Shadmi; that Malinki testified Shadmi told him he wanted no sentimentality and no arrests; that Malinki passed down an order to shoot anyone leaving home; and that Shadmi denied the question of returning workers was ever raised. [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_kq] It establishes that two of the three units given the order did not shoot. [cite:wiki_kafr_qasim_massacre] On that record the order to shoot came at least from Malinki, the officer above the platoon, and the words that framed it are attributed to the brigade commander by Malinki's testimony, which Shadmi denied. Whether anything higher stood behind it, in particular a contingency plan for the Triangle's population in wartime known as Plan Mole, became a separate argument decades later, when trial records were released in 2022; that argument, and what the released records do and do not show, is set out in [scene:cw3_kafr_qasim_memory|the sulha, Plan Mole and the memory of Kafr Qasim].

Why it mattered. One argument about Kafr Qasim, made in this library's own summary of the period, holds that before Israel governed a single Palestinian in the West Bank or Gaza it had already run, for eighteen years, a separate regime for Palestinian citizens inside its own borders, with the absentee laws keeping them from their property and a massacre whose commander, as the next section shows, paid a token fine; on this reading the 1967 occupation inherited a model rather than inventing one. [cite:wiki_kafr_qasim_massacre] [cite:conversation_kafr_qasim_60] That is an interpretation of the record, not a finding within it, and Volume II's account of the military government sets out the security case on which the government defended the regime. What the evening of 29 October itself shows is narrower and firmer: a curfew imposed on citizens with half an hour's warning, an order that at least one officer relayed as an order to shoot, and a Border Police platoon that carried it out against people walking, cycling and riding home from work.

The record leaves several things open. The trial transcript itself has not been read for this section; the testimony of Malinki and Shadmi is given from a reference summary of it. Shadmi's rank differs between the sources. The precise wording of the order that reached the Border Police at 3:30 p.m. is known only through the Jewish Virtual Library's paraphrase and Malinki's version of it. And why the platoon at Kafr Qasim fired where the units in neighbouring villages did not is not explained by any source used here, beyond the fact that their commanders chose differently. The court that tried the men, the sentences it gave and what became of them are told in [scene:cw3_kafr_qasim_trial|the Kafr Qasim trial].

sections.h: Kadesh and Musketeer: The War, 29 October–22 December 1956
sections.html:
The war ran on two timetables. Israel's campaign in Sinai, which it called Operation Kadesh, lasted about a hundred hours. The Anglo-French operation, Musketeer, began two days after Israel's, put troops ashore only after Israel's fighting was nearly over, and ended with a cease-fire less than two days after its first troops landed; the last of its soldiers left Egypt on 22 December. The secret timetable that bound them, the Sèvres protocol, is told in the previous section. This section follows what the armies actually did, then counts the dead, as far as the sources allow.

Egypt's own long history with Gaza, which it had administered since 1948 as a military protectorate without ever annexing it, is told in Volume II, in [scene:rd6_arab_palestine|who would govern Arab Palestine]. That history is the background to one of the war's first objectives. More broadly, Suez belongs to a decade the region's political record marks as one of overturned governments and foreign intervention: Husni al-Za'im's coup in Syria on 30 March 1949, the first of three that year; the Free Officers' overthrow of King Farouk in July 1952; the removal of Iran's prime minister by the CIA and MI6 in August 1953; the invasion of Egypt in 1956; and the fall of Iraq's monarchy on 14 July 1958, which belongs to Stage Four. [cite:w_1949_syria_coup] [cite:w_1952_egypt] [cite:w_1953_coup] [cite:w_suez] [cite:w_1958_iraq] The familiar claim that the region's wars and dictatorships grew only from local culture and religion does not survive that list. In three of its five events, outside powers were involved: American officials had contacts with Za'im before his coup, the degree of their direction being debated; the CIA and MI6 organized the Iranian coup; and in 1956 two European powers invaded Egypt alongside Israel. [cite:w_1949_syria_coup] [cite:w_1953_coup] [cite:w_suez]

Kadesh: Sinai in a hundred hours. The Israel Defense Forces date the start of Operation Kadesh to 17:00 on 29 October 1956, with the first paratroop landing in Israel's military history, near the eastern approaches of the Mitla Pass. [cite:rs_cw3_idf_sinai] The historian Michael Oren writes that the landing came "at dawn"; the IDF's own time is used here. [cite:rs_cw3_oren_hnn] The drop was the "real act of war" Dayan had designed at Sèvres: deep in Sinai, close enough to the Canal to give Britain and France their pretext. [cite:rs_cw3_shlaim_sevres] The campaign was commanded by Lieutenant General Moshe Dayan, and the IDF gives its length as 100 hours. [cite:rs_cw3_idf_sinai] The IDF and Defense Establishment Archives put it the same way: the peninsula was occupied "within 100 hours," between the war's start on 29 October and 5 November 1956. [cite:rs_cw3_idf_archive]

The fighting was not uniform. According to the US Library of Congress's country study of Egypt, Egyptian forces resisted at Abu Uwayqilah, which Israeli sources call Abu Ageila, and at the Mitla Pass. After the Anglo-French bombing of the air bases, Nasser pulled his troops out of Sinai to protect the Canal. [cite:rs_cw3_loc_egypt] Israel occupied the Gaza Strip on 2 November and Sharm el-Sheikh on 5 November 1956; these dates come from a year chronology and from Benny Morris's account of the occupation of Gaza, which has it beginning on 2–3 November. [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_1956israel] [cite:rs_cw3_morris_gaza] Article 4 of the Sèvres protocol had provided for Israel to occupy the western shore of the Gulf of Aqaba and the islands of Tiran and Sanafir, and Ben-Gurion had called the Straits of Tiran "the State of Israel's Suez Canal." [cite:rs_cw3_shlaim_sevres] What the occupation of Gaza meant for its people, including the killings at Khan Yunis on 3 November, is told in [scene:cw3_gaza_killings|Khan Yunis and Rafah].

The balance of forces is given differently by different sources. Lance Janda, in a reference work, puts the forces at 45,000 Israelis against 30,000 Egyptians; Ben-Gurion told the Knesset that Egypt had "over 30,000 men" in Sinai. [cite:rs_cw3_janda_ebsco] [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_bg_7nov]

Musketeer: from the air to Port Said. General Sir Charles Keightley's despatch on Operation Musketeer, published in the London Gazette on 12 September 1957, is the British commander's own account of the operation. By his record, Royal Air Force Valiant and Canberra bombers began attacking Egyptian airfields at 16:15 GMT on 31 October. The Sèvres protocol had set the Anglo-French attack for early that day, if Egypt refused the ultimatum; the bombing began in the late afternoon. By the end of 2 November the Egyptian Air Force was, in Keightley's word, "all but" neutralized. [cite:rs_cw3_keightley] [cite:rs_cw3_shlaim_sevres] The landings came three days later. At 08:20 GMT on 5 November about 600 men of 3 Parachute Battalion Group jumped onto Gamil airfield, and about 460 French paratroopers dropped at Port Fuad. The seaborne assault followed at 04:50 GMT on 6 November, when Royal Marine commandos landed; 45 Commando was carried in by 22 helicopters. [cite:rs_cw3_keightley]

The ground operation was stopped almost as soon as it began. The cease-fire was ordered from London at 17:00 GMT on 6 November and took effect at 23:59 GMT that night. The force ashore nonetheless kept growing for weeks after the fighting stopped: it peaked on 1 December at 13,500 British and 8,500 French troops, some 22,000 men. The last of them were aboard ship by 17:10 GMT on 22 December 1956. [cite:rs_cw3_keightley] Why London stopped, and how Washington's votes, money and oil brought it to stop, is told in [scene:cw3_un_ceasefire|Washington against its allies].

Counting the dead. No single figure for any party's losses can be given without its source, and for Egypt no official figure was found at all. The numbers below are set out with their sources and their ranges.

For Israel, the counts cluster but do not agree. The IDF gives 171 soldiers killed in battle; the Jewish Agency gives 172 IDF soldiers. [cite:rs_cw3_idf_sinai] [cite:rs_cw3_jafi_fedayeen] Ben-Gurion's first public figure, on 7 November 1956, was "about 150 killed," an early count; by 5 March 1957 he gave "170 killed and 1 prisoner." [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_bg_7nov] [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_bg_mar57] Janda's reference work gives 189 killed and 899 wounded. [cite:rs_cw3_janda_ebsco] The official later figures run from 170 to 172; the full range across these sources is about 150 to 189.

Egypt's losses rest entirely on foreign estimates. The Library of Congress study, citing foreign military observers, gives about 1,650 ground forces killed, about 4,900 wounded and more than 6,000 captured or missing. [cite:rs_cw3_loc_egypt] Janda estimates 1,030 killed and 4,000 wounded. [cite:rs_cw3_janda_ebsco] Keightley called Egyptian losses "much more difficult to assess," and naval-history.net, which reproduces the despatch with notes, estimates them at "well in excess of 1,000 military killed." [cite:rs_cw3_keightley] Egypt's military dead therefore lie somewhere between about 1,030 and about 1,650 on these estimates. On 27 December 1956, 5,580 Egyptian prisoners of war were exchanged for four Israelis held by Egypt. [cite:rs_cw3_sahistory_pows]

The dead of Port Said and Port Fuad are the least certain of all. According to Christopher Weeks's summary, the British estimated that 650 Egyptians died in Port Said during the invasion and occupation, and 100 more in Port Fuad; his summary leaves unclear what share were civilians. Keightley's despatch records "some 60 of the enemy" killed at Port Fuad. Egypt's letter to the United Nations of 5 November 1956 (A/3292) alleged attacks on civilians but gave no figures. [cite:rs_cw3_weeks_portsaid] [cite:rs_cw3_keightley] The civilian toll at Port Said is not settled by these sources.

For Britain and France the figures are official but changed with time. Keightley's despatch gives 16 British killed and 96 wounded, and 10 French killed and 33 wounded. On 12 December 1956 the Defence Ministry told the House of Commons that the latest figure was 21 British killed and 112 wounded; the later figure includes deaths during the occupation, among them an officer killed in an ambush in December. [cite:rs_cw3_keightley] [cite:rs_cw3_hansard_12dec56]

Beaten, or withdrawn? The two sides have told the Sinai campaign differently from the start. Israel's account is that the IDF "crushed" the Egyptian army and took the peninsula in 100 hours, an account Morris's history of the occupation shares. [cite:rs_cw3_idf_sinai] [cite:rs_cw3_morris_gaza] Nasser's account is that Egypt had not been defeated by the Israelis but had withdrawn from Sinai to defend the Canal against the Anglo-French attack. [cite:rs_cw3_loc_egypt] Each version has evidence on its side. The speed of the Israeli advance, the 5,580 prisoners against four, and the loss of Gaza and Sharm el-Sheikh support the first. [cite:rs_cw3_sahistory_pows] The Library of Congress study supports part of the second: it records real resistance at Abu Ageila and the Mitla Pass, and it dates Nasser's pull-back to after the Anglo-French bombing of his air bases, which is to say after the war had become a war on two fronts. [cite:rs_cw3_loc_egypt] The two claims are about different things. One measures what the Israeli army achieved in Sinai; the other explains why the Egyptian army was not there to stop it. The sources used here do not show how the Sinai fighting would have gone had Egypt faced Israel alone.

The wider outcome was clearer. The invasion achieved its immediate military objectives, and it was reversed under pressure from both the United States and the Soviet Union, a pressure that ran, unusually for the Cold War, against Washington's own allies. [cite:wikipedia_suez_crisis] [cite:w_suez] That reversal is the subject of the sections that follow in this stage.

"A war deluxe." Ben-Gurion drew his own lesson within weeks, and it was a warning. At a debriefing of the senior command on 27 December 1956, the day the prisoners were exchanged, he told the officers: "this was a war deluxe." "You cannot learn from it how to fight the next war," he said, and there was "no basis to assume that in the next war, we will have helping forces from abroad." [cite:rs_cw3_idf_archive] [cite:rs_cw3_jpost_dec56] The Sinai campaign had been fought with Egypt's air bases under Anglo-French bombing and its army pulling back to the Canal. His words suggest the point he was making: that Israel's soldiers should not mistake those conditions for their own strength.

What the record leaves open. No Egyptian official count of the dead was found, so every Egyptian figure here is a foreign estimate, and the estimates differ by more than six hundred. The civilian dead of Port Said are known only through a British estimate, at second hand, that does not separate civilians from soldiers, and Egypt's own complaint to the United Nations gave no number. The two figures for Port Fuad, 100 and "some 60," cannot be reconciled from these sources. The Israeli figures differ by up to 39 between the earliest count and the highest. The hour of the Mitla drop is given as 17:00 by the IDF and as dawn by Oren. And the question of whether Egypt was beaten in Sinai or chose to leave it rests on what Egypt's army would have done without the Anglo-French attack, which the documents used here cannot show.

sections.h: Washington Against Its Allies: The United Nations, the Cease-Fire and the Money, October–December 1956
sections.html:
The familiar account of Suez says that the United States stopped the war by standing on principle at the United Nations. That account is true as far as it goes. The primary record shows something more layered: an American government that had not been told of the plan its allies had made with Israel, that moved the question out of a deadlocked Security Council and into the General Assembly, that carried the Assembly against Britain and France, and that then, when votes alone did not finish the matter, held back money and oil until the invaders agreed to leave. This section follows that sequence from the first vetoes of 30 October 1956 to the last British and French troops leaving Port Said on 22 December. The secret arrangement that set the war in motion is told in [scene:cw3_sevres|the Sèvres Protocol]; Peter Hahn writes that American officials did not anticipate the collusion before hostilities began. [cite:rs_cw3_shlaim_sevres] [cite:rs_cw3_origins_hahn]

The Office of the Historian of the State Department summarizes Washington's course in two sentences. The United States voted for the UN resolutions condemning the invasion and "approving the creation of a U.N. peacekeeping force," and it "pressured Britain and France to accept a United Nations ceasefire on November 6." [cite:rs_cw3_milestones_suez] The State Department's own documentary series, Foreign Relations of the United States (FRUS), lays out the same weeks in the order its editors found them in the files: deadlock in the Security Council, the convening of the first emergency special session of the General Assembly, the Anglo-French bombardment and the creation of the UN Emergency Force (30 October–5 November); then the assault on the Canal Zone, "the threat of Soviet intervention" and acceptance of a cease-fire (5–6 November); then "the European oil supply problem and the activation of the Middle East Emergency Committee's plan" and the Anglo-French decision to withdraw (7 November–4 December). [cite:rs_cw3_frus16_ch3] The order matters. Diplomacy at the UN came first; the oil and IMF measures documented below came after the guns had stopped, and were used to turn a cease-fire into a withdrawal, though Hahn counts financial pressure among the reasons the cease-fire itself was accepted.

The Council deadlocked, 30–31 October. Israel's campaign in Sinai had begun at 17:00 on 29 October. [cite:rs_cw3_idf_sinai] The next day, at the Security Council's 749th and 750th meetings, two draft resolutions were put to the vote, one American (S/3710) and one Soviet (S/3713/Rev.1). Each called for Israel to withdraw. Britain and France vetoed both. [cite:rs_cw3_unu_ufp] The United States and the Soviet Union had both asked the Council for an Israeli withdrawal, and two of Washington's allies had stopped it.

The way around the veto was a procedure known as Uniting for Peace, under which an emergency session of the General Assembly could be called when the Council could not act. On 31 October, at its 751st meeting, the Council adopted Resolution 119 (S/3721), citing the "lack of unanimity" of its permanent members at the two meetings of the day before and "Considering that a grave situation has been created by action undertaken against Egypt." It called the first emergency special session of the Assembly under that procedure. [cite:rs_cw3_unispal_sc119] [cite:rs_cw3_unu_ufp] The vote was 7 to 2, with France and the United Kingdom against and Australia and Belgium abstaining. [cite:rs_cw3_unispal_sc119] The British and French votes against it did not stop it; the resolution was adopted. The mechanism shifted the forum from a body in which two of the invaders held a veto to one in which, as the following days showed, they could only be outvoted.

Resolution 997, 2 November. The emergency session convened at 5 p.m. on 1 November 1956. After some five hours of debate it adopted Resolution 997 (ES-I), drafted by the United States (A/3256), at about 4:20 a.m. on 2 November. [cite:rs_cw3_frus16_d467] The text was a cease-fire resolution. It urged an immediate cease-fire and a halt to moving forces and arms into the area; it urged the parties to the 1949 armistice agreements to withdraw behind the armistice lines, to stop raids across them and to observe the agreements; it recommended that members send no military goods to the area; it urged that the Suez Canal be reopened once the cease-fire took effect; it asked the Secretary-General to report on compliance; and it kept the Assembly in emergency session. [cite:rs_cw3_palquest_997] [cite:rs_cw3_frus16_d467]

Sixty-four states voted for it. Five voted against: Australia, France, Israel, New Zealand and the United Kingdom. Six abstained: Belgium, Canada, Laos, the Netherlands, Portugal and South Africa. [cite:rs_cw3_unproj_997] The Canadian abstention was the most consequential of them, and it was not a vote for the invaders. Canada's Lester Pearson abstained because the text took no United Nations step toward a settlement. He wanted the Secretary-General authorized to arrange a UN force, and Dulles said that the United States would welcome a Canadian proposal. [cite:rs_cw3_frus16_d467] In the documents used here, the idea of a UN force, rather than a bare demand that the armies stop, first appears at that point.

The UN Emergency Force, 4–7 November. Three more resolutions followed within two days. Resolution 998 (ES-I) of 4 November passed by 57 votes to none, with 19 abstentions, among them Britain, France, Israel, Egypt, the Soviet Union and its allies. Resolution 999, adopted the same day, passed by 59 to 5 with 12 abstentions; the five against were the same five who had opposed 997. Resolution 1000 of 5 November passed by 57 to 0 with 19 abstentions. [cite:rs_cw3_unproj_998] [cite:rs_cw3_unproj_999] [cite:rs_cw3_unproj_1000] These were the resolutions that created and organized the UN Emergency Force, UNEF. Their operative texts were not among the documents fetched for this book, so their provisions are not described here beyond that. [cite:rs_cw3_unproj_998]

On 7 November, at the Assembly's 567th plenary meeting (document A/3354), Resolutions 1001 and 1002 (ES-I) were adopted. [cite:rs_cw3_undl_1001] [cite:rs_cw3_undl_1002] The language of 1002 shows what had not yet happened, a day after the guns fell silent. It "Calls once again upon Israel immediately to withdraw all its forces behind the armistice lines" established by the agreement of 24 February 1949, and "once again upon the United Kingdom and France immediately to withdraw all their forces from Egyptian territory." [cite:rs_cw3_unispal_1002] The Jewish Virtual Library gives its vote as 65 to 1 with 10 abstentions; that figure rests on that source alone. [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_1002] The text of 1001 was not fetched.

The table answers one question that the familiar account blurs: how broad the line against the invasion was. Read one way, it was an American achievement. Resolution 997 was the American draft, and the United States carried the Assembly against its own allies. [cite:rs_cw3_frus16_d467] [cite:rs_cw3_milestones_suez] Read another way, the consensus was broad but not universal, and not simply Washington's. On the roll calls recorded here, only the three invading states, Australia and New Zealand voted no. Canada and several other Western states abstained on 997 because they wanted a UN force rather than a bare cease-fire, and the Soviet bloc abstained on the resolutions that created that force. [cite:rs_cw3_unproj_997] [cite:rs_cw3_unproj_998] [cite:rs_cw3_unproj_1000] Both readings fit the record. The United States wrote the first text; the proposal for a UN force came, in this record, from Canada's Pearson, with Dulles's welcome, and Hahn credits Eisenhower with organizing the force.

The cease-fire, 6 November. British paratroopers jumped onto Gamil airfield and French paratroopers onto Port Fuad on 5 November, and Royal Marine commandos landed on 6 November. [cite:rs_cw3_keightley] An East German newspaper, the Berliner Zeitung, reported from Cairo that day that British paratroopers had taken the Port Said airfield, called the invasion fleet "the largest fleet to operate in the Mediterranean since the Allied landing in Sicily," and relayed Egyptian claims of civilian casualties without verifying them. [cite:rs_cw3_ghdi_berliner] The same day, under what Hahn calls American "political and financial pressure," the belligerents accepted the cease-fire. [cite:rs_cw3_origins_hahn] General Sir Charles Keightley's despatch records that it was ordered from London at 17:00 GMT on 6 November and took effect at 23:59 GMT that night; Hahn gives 7 November as the day it took effect. [cite:rs_cw3_keightley] [cite:rs_cw3_origins_hahn] The Soviet notes of 5 November, which FRUS files under the same days, are the subject of [scene:cw3_soviet_hungary|Moscow's notes and Budapest]. [cite:rs_cw3_frus16_ch3]

The day after the cease-fire the telephone lines between Washington and London were busy. On 7 November Eisenhower and Eden spoke at 8:43, 9:55 and 10:27 a.m.; Eisenhower sent Eden and Guy Mollet messages about the Gruenther mission; and on 8 November at 3:15 p.m. the President spoke with Treasury Secretary Humphrey. [cite:rs_cw3_frus16_ch3subch1] The FRUS list gives the times and the participants; the call to the Treasury can be read as the first sign in it that the next phase would be fought with money.

Pressure on Israel ran on a separate track the same day.
