On 7 November Hammarskjöld told Ambassador Lodge that General Burns had reported that Israel intended, and might already have begun, to force the observers of the UN Truce Supervision Organization out of Gaza. Hammarskjöld warned that persistent Israeli defiance could provoke so strong a reaction in the UN that Israel might be expelled. [cite:rs_cw3_frus16_d534] Israel's reply to that pressure came within a day, and is told in the next sections.

Sterling. The financial lever worked on Britain, and its mechanism is documented by James Boughton, writing for the International Monetary Fund. The Bank of England defended the pound's parity of $2.80 with Britain's reserves, and treated $2 billion as the floor for that defence. The Anglo-French offensive, Boughton writes, "greatly accelerated the drain on U.K. reserves," and a "massive loss of reserves" in November pushed them below that floor. [cite:rs_cw3_boughton_fd] Below that floor the parity was in danger, and the help Britain needed would have to come with American agreement.

Humphrey's position, as Boughton records it, was that the United States would support Britain when Britain was "conforming to rather than defying the United Nations." Harold Macmillan tried to meet Humphrey in late November and failed. [cite:rs_cw3_boughton_fd] The condition was the same one the Assembly had voted: leave Egypt. On 3 December, once the withdrawal had been agreed, Humphrey proposed an immediate drawing of $561 million plus a stand-by credit of about $739 million, $1.3 billion in all, equal to 100 per cent of Britain's quota at the Fund. On 4 December Macmillan announced the November losses and "an immediate approach" to the IMF. The Fund's Executive Board approved the package with one abstention, Egypt's, and Britain drew the $561 million at once. [cite:rs_cw3_boughton_fd] In a working paper on the same events, Boughton adds that all four combatants, Britain, France, Israel and Egypt, obtained IMF financing, which was "highly unusual for the time." [cite:rs_cw3_boughton_wp]

Oil. The second lever was fuel. By mid-November, Britain and France said, Europe's oil supplies had fallen "25 to 30 percent below their normal needs." Until the end of November, according to a FRUS editorial note, the United States refused to put "the plan of action prepared by the Middle East Emergency Committee" into effect, offering the oil "if those two countries complied with the United Nations resolutions" and withdrew. [cite:rs_cw3_frus10_d234] At a conference with the President on 25 November, Eisenhower explained the delay in his own words: "we have held up this measure until the invading powers accepted immediate withdrawal of their troops." Hoover urged that the emergency committee be started "very soon," and the President wanted it announced as a measure to prevent "widespread suffering in Europe." [cite:rs_cw3_frus16_d612] The record thus shows the oil held back as leverage and then released with a humanitarian explanation, by the President's own direction.

The force arrives, the invaders leave. UNEF's first troops arrived in Egypt on 15 November. [cite:rs_cw3_origins_hahn] The Anglo-French force ashore did not shrink at once; it peaked on 1 December at 13,500 British and 8,500 French troops. [cite:rs_cw3_keightley] Britain and France completed their withdrawal from Port Said on 22 December 1956; Keightley's despatch records the last troops aboard at 17:10 GMT. [cite:rs_cw3_keightley] [cite:rs_cw3_origins_hahn] Israel's forces remained in Sinai and Gaza, and the Assembly's demand on Israel, repeated in Resolutions 1123 and 1124 of January and February 1957, became the subject of [scene:cw3_withdrawal|the withdrawal fight of 1957]. [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_1124]

The quarrel among the Western allies did not last. The Office of the Historian links the American public criticism of Britain and France to Eden's resignation in January 1957, and records that by March 1957 relations between Washington and London had recovered under Harold Macmillan. [cite:rs_cw3_milestones_suez] The wider settlement of 1957 is told in the closing section of this stage.

Principle or money? Historians and the official record give two answers to why Eisenhower turned on his allies, and they are not exclusive. The first is the one the Office of the Historian and Hahn emphasize. Washington had not been told of the collusion; it feared that the Soviets "would intervene to assist Nasser"; and in the same week it was making a "strident condemnation of the Soviet intervention in Hungary"; on this reading, a government condemning one intervention that week was poorly placed to excuse another. [cite:rs_cw3_milestones_suez] [cite:rs_cw3_origins_hahn] On that reading the cease-fire was an act of policy and principle, carried through the UN.

The second answer puts the levers at the centre. FRUS places the oil supply problem and the Treasury at the heart of the November decisions, and Hahn himself describes the pressure as "political and financial." [cite:rs_cw3_frus16_ch3] [cite:rs_cw3_frus16_ch3subch1] [cite:rs_cw3_origins_hahn] Boughton and the 25 November memorandum show the mechanism directly: British financing was tied to compliance with the UN, and oil was held back until withdrawal was accepted. [cite:rs_cw3_boughton_fd] [cite:rs_cw3_frus16_d612] The strongest form of this case is that resolutions had been passed since 2 November without moving a single soldier out of Egypt, and that the withdrawal came only when Britain could not defend its currency without American consent.

There is a strong reply to the second case, and it comes from the same documents. The UN votes, the Soviet threats and the British cabinet's own decision of 6 November to accept the cease-fire all came first. The IMF package was proposed on 3 December, after the cease-fire and after the decision to withdraw, not before them. [cite:rs_cw3_boughton_fd] [cite:rs_cw3_origins_hahn] On this reading money did not stop the war; it fixed the terms of the exit and made sure the withdrawal, once promised, was completed. The record supports that sequence. It does not show which consideration weighed most with Eden's cabinet on 6 November.

Several things remain open. The operative texts of Resolutions 998, 999, 1000 and 1001 were not fetched for this book, so the terms on which UNEF was created are known here only from the votes. The vote on Resolution 1002 rests on a single source, and that source does not name the state that voted against it. The content of the Eisenhower–Eden telephone calls of 7 November and of the Gruenther messages is not described in the document list that records them. And the weight each lever carried in London, the votes, the Soviet notes, the reserves or the oil, is a matter of inference: the documents show that all four were in play in the same weeks, and that Washington used the last two deliberately, but not which of them decided the outcome.

sections.h: Khan Yunis and Rafah, November 1956
sections.html:
Israeli forces entered the Gaza Strip on 2 November 1956, in the first days of the Sinai campaign. The Strip had been under Egyptian administration since 1948, a nineteen-year arrangement told in [scene:egi_src_s02|Egypt and Gaza, 1948–67]; about three-quarters of its people, by Morris's account, were refugees from the war of that year. [cite:rs_cw3_morris_gaza] Within ten days of the Israeli entry, two incidents took place in its southern towns that remain among the most disputed events of the war: at Khan Yunis on 3 November and at Rafah on 12 November. What happened in each is known chiefly through one document, the special report that the Director of UNRWA, the United Nations agency for the Palestine refugees, submitted to the General Assembly covering the period from 1 November to mid-December 1956. [cite:rs_cw3_unrwa_a3212] Almost every later figure is measured against it, and its own author was careful to say how much it could not establish.

The document. The report was published as United Nations document A/3212/Add.1, in the official records of the General Assembly's eleventh session (Supplement 14A, 1957). [cite:rs_cw3_unrwa_a3212] It is not the record of an inquiry. It is the account of an agency that was serving the refugees of Gaza when the Strip changed hands, and that received, in the weeks that followed, lists of names of the dead. Its value lies in the fact that it records both what the Israeli authorities told the Director and what the refugees told him, and that it says plainly where the two diverged.

Khan Yunis, 3 November. The report's paragraph 23 opens with the plain fact: "The town of Khan Yunis and the Agency's camp adjacent thereto were occupied by Israel troops on the morning of 3 November." [cite:rs_cw3_unrwa_a3212] The Director then gives the two accounts he received. The Israeli authorities "state that there was resistance to their occupation and that the Palestinian refugees formed part of the resistance." The refugees state "that all resistance had ceased at the time" and that "many unarmed civilians were killed as the Israel troops went through the town and camp." The Director did not choose between them. He noted only that there was "some conflict in the accounts given as to the causes of the casualties." [cite:rs_cw3_unrwa_a3212]

On the number, he was equally careful. He had received lists "numbering 275 Individuals, of whom 140 were refugees and 135 local residents of Khan Yunis." In the same paragraph he wrote: "The exact number of dead and wounded is not known." [cite:rs_cw3_unrwa_a3212] The distinction matters for everything that follows. The figure of 275 is the length of the lists the agency received, broken down by whether the person named was a refugee or a resident of the town. It is not a count that the agency itself verified, and the report does not present it as one.

Rafah, 12 November. The second incident took place nine days later and in different circumstances. According to paragraphs 24 to 27 of the report, the Rafah killings "occurred during a screening operation conducted by the Israel forces." Israel said the refugees were "hostile" and that there was "some resistance"; the refugees denied it. [cite:rs_cw3_unrwa_a3212] Here the Director went further than at Khan Yunis and gave his own finding. Loudspeaker announcements "were not heard by some of the refugee population," and "some Israel soldiers apparently panicked and opened fire on this running crowd." The lists for Rafah numbered "111, of whom 103 were refugees, seven local residents, and one an Egyptian." [cite:rs_cw3_unrwa_a3212]

The Director's finding at Rafah is the closest the report comes to a judgement of cause, and it is worth reading precisely. It rejects neither account in full. It does not accept the Israeli claim of resistance as the explanation, and it does not adopt the language of deliberate killing. It describes a failure of communication followed by fire from soldiers who, in the word he chose, "apparently" panicked. The word suggests an inference from what he was told rather than something his staff had witnessed.

The smaller incidents. The two towns were not the only places where people died. In paragraph 29 the Director recorded a further list of "sixty-six individuals, of whom forty-eight were refugees," killed in smaller incidents between 1 and 21 November: some in the fighting, some for breaking the curfew, some by accident. He described Khan Yunis and Rafah as "the only major ones of their kind." [cite:rs_cw3_unrwa_a3212] The historian Benny Morris adds that dozens more people, mostly captured fedayeen or Egyptian prisoners of war, were killed in the weeks after the conquest. [cite:rs_cw3_morris_gaza]

What the Director could not do. The report is explicit about its limits, and those limits are themselves part of the record. The United Nations Truce Supervision Organization, whose officers would normally have investigated incidents of this kind, could not do so, because their movement in Gaza "had been restricted by the Israel authorities" (paragraph 21). "It has not been possible to verify individually listed death[s]," the Director wrote, and "it is most unlikely that lists of casualties can ever be made complete," because many burials "were made without identification" (paragraph 30). [cite:rs_cw3_unrwa_a3212] Pressure on the observers was reported at the time. On 7 November the Secretary-General, Hammarskjöld, told the American ambassador, Lodge, that General Burns had reported that Israel intended, and might already have begun, to force the Truce Supervision observers out of Gaza. [cite:rs_cw3_frus16_d534] The body that might have produced an independent count was therefore kept from the place where the count was needed.

The other figures. Every later number for Khan Yunis and Rafah comes from a source with its own standpoint, and each needs to be read as what it is.

Israel's figure for Rafah was 48 dead, which Morris confirms as the Israeli count, against UNRWA's list of 111. [cite:rs_cw3_morris_gaza] For Khan Yunis no separate Israeli total appears in the sources used here. Israel's position, as TIME reported it in its coverage of Joe Sacco's Footnotes in Gaza, is that "Israel denies that either event was a massacre," disputes the figures, and says its soldiers killed smaller numbers while suppressing riots and resistance. [cite:rs_cw3_time_sacco]

Palestinian sources give higher totals. For Khan Yunis they give 415 killed and 57 missing; for Rafah, 197 killed and 23 disappeared. [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_khanyunis] [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_rafah] Abdel Aziz al-Rantisi, as cited by Filiu, gave 525 Gazans killed. [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_khanyunis] These figures reach this book through encyclopedia articles that attribute them to their named sources; they are reported here as the claims of those sources, not as independent tallies.

Sacco reconstructed both events from the testimony of survivors. Residents told him that about 100 men were shot at the caravanserai in Khan Yunis. [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_khanyunis] TIME notes that Sacco himself describes such testimony as subject to "the frailty of memory." [cite:rs_cw3_time_sacco] The journalist Amira Hass, writing in 2010, reported the United Nations estimates as 275 at Khan Yunis and more than 100 at Rafah, noted that no photographs of the killings appear to exist, and treated one witness, who was six years old in 1956, with explicit caution. [cite:rs_cw3_hass_internazionale]

A British newspaper report pointed lower. For Rafah, The Times of London reported "some 60" dead. [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_rafah]

Morris, an Israeli historian, has given the events two different numerical treatments. In work of 1994 and 2011 he put the dead at "about two hundred" across both towns. [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_khanyunis] In 2024 he wrote that at Khan Yunis "some 275 civilians and POWs were murdered" according to the Palestinians and UNRWA, and that at Rafah Israel said 48 were killed and UNRWA 111. [cite:rs_cw3_morris_gaza] His later formula attributes the 275 to UNRWA, but the Director's report itself, as quoted above, speaks of lists of 275 "Individuals" whose exact number of dead and wounded "is not known"; it does not describe them as murdered. Morris accepts the word massacre for both events. [cite:rs_cw3_morris_gaza] [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_khanyunis]

Read together, the figures fall into a pattern. The UNRWA lists, made close to the events by an agency on the spot, sit in the middle. Israel's count for Rafah is under half of UNRWA's. The Palestinian counts run above it by roughly half at Khan Yunis and by three-quarters at Rafah. The lowest figure is The Times's "some 60" for Rafah; the highest is al-Rantisi's 525. The spread is wide, but no source puts the dead of either town in single figures, and every source that counts both towns together puts their combined dead in the hundreds.

Israel's context. The Israeli case, stated at full strength, does not begin in November 1956. Gaza was the base from which the fedayeen, the armed infiltrators who crossed into Israel in 1954–56, had operated; Morris writes that their raids were run by Egyptian military intelligence, and he sets the November killings against that background. [cite:rs_cw3_morris_gaza] Ben-Gurion had told the Knesset on 15 October 1956 that Egypt had caused Israel 242 casualties in 1954–55 [cite:rs_cw3_knesset_15oct56]; the Jewish Agency counts 1,300 Israelis killed or wounded across 1948–56. [cite:rs_cw3_jafi_fedayeen] The soldiers who entered Khan Yunis did so in a war, in a town where, by Israel's account, some of the refugees took part in the resistance. These facts, told more fully in [scene:cw3_road_to_war|the road to war], are the context Israel's account invokes. They do not settle the question the UNRWA report leaves open: whether, at Khan Yunis, the killing took place during resistance or after it had ended, and whether the people killed were fighters or unarmed. Context explains the circumstances of an act. It cannot establish what the act was.

The dispute. The two cases can be put in their strongest forms. The first holds that these were massacres of civilians. The refugees told the United Nations at the time that resistance had ended before the killing at Khan Yunis; the Palestinian counts run from 275 to 415, with more missing, there and to 197 at Rafah; and Sacco's witnesses describe men lined up and shot. [cite:rs_cw3_unrwa_a3212] [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_khanyunis] [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_rafah] [cite:rs_cw3_time_sacco] The second is Israel's: its troops met armed resistance at Khan Yunis and a riot at Rafah, it put the Rafah dead at 48, and it denies that either was a massacre. [cite:rs_cw3_morris_gaza] [cite:rs_cw3_time_sacco] Between the two stand two sources that are neither Palestinian advocates nor Israeli officials. The United Nations Director could verify neither version and judged that at Rafah some soldiers had panicked. [cite:rs_cw3_unrwa_a3212] Morris, an Israeli historian who also documents the fedayeen campaign, uses the word massacre for both. [cite:rs_cw3_morris_gaza]

Was anyone held to account? None of the sources drawn on for this section records an Israeli investigation of either incident, or any prosecution. The contrast with another killing of the same week is direct. At Kafr Qasim, inside Israel, on 29 October 1956, Border Police shot dead villagers who were Israeli citizens; that case went to a military court, as the next sections of this chapter tell. No equivalent proceeding for Khan Yunis or Rafah appears in the record used here. The Truce Supervision officers who might have investigated were kept out, and the agency that did report could not verify its own lists. [cite:rs_cw3_unrwa_a3212] Israel's later occupation of the Strip, of which these were the first weeks, is told in [scene:cw3_gaza_occupation|Gaza under Israeli rule].

What the record leaves open. The number of dead at Khan Yunis is not established and, by the Director's own judgement, never will be completely, since many were buried without identification. Whether resistance had ended there when the killing took place is disputed between the only two accounts given at the time, and the sources used here contain no independent witness to settle it. At Rafah, the Director's finding of panic is the only account of cause from outside the two parties, and he hedged it with the word "apparently." The range between Israel's 48 and the Palestinian 197 for Rafah, and between The Times's "some 60" and al-Rantisi's 525, cannot be closed from these documents. What is not open is that a United Nations agency, working in Gaza in November 1956, received lists naming 275 people at Khan Yunis and 111 at Rafah, and recorded the refugees' statement that many of the dead were unarmed civilians.

sections.h: Moscow's Notes and Budapest, November 1956
sections.html:
Two invasions ran through the same November week. In Egypt, Britain, France and Israel were fighting a war that the United States was trying to stop at the United Nations. In Hungary, the Soviet Union had intervened, and the United States was condemning it. The Office of the Historian of the State Department sets the two side by side: the same week that Washington pressed its allies to halt, it made a "strident condemnation of the Soviet intervention in Hungary." [cite:rs_cw3_milestones_suez] That overlap is the setting in which Moscow sent its notes to the invaders of Egypt, and in which American officials weighed them.

The sources fetched for this book are thin on Hungary itself. They establish the American condemnation, and Peter Hahn's account adds two observations: that unrest in Hungary had distracted American officials in the weeks before the Suez war, and that, in their view, the turmoil left Soviet leaders "prone to impulsive behavior." [cite:rs_cw3_origins_hahn] The dates and course of the Hungarian rising and of the Soviet intervention are not in those sources, and this section does not supply them from elsewhere. What the record does show is how Hungary was used in the argument over the Middle East, by Washington and by Moscow.

The threat, 5–6 November. The editors of the State Department's documentary series, Foreign Relations of the United States, gave the documents of 5 and 6 November a title that puts the Soviet threat at the centre: "Anglo-French Assault On the Canal Zone; the Threat of Soviet Intervention; Acceptance of a Cease-Fire." [cite:rs_cw3_frus16_ch3] According to Hahn, Soviet leaders threatened to "intervene in the fighting" and to retaliate against London and Paris with weapons of mass destruction, and intelligence reports of Soviet forces concentrating in Syria alarmed American officials. [cite:rs_cw3_origins_hahn] The Office of the Historian records American concern about "the possibility that the Soviets would intervene to assist Nasser." [cite:rs_cw3_milestones_suez] Whether the forces in Syria existed on the scale reported is not established by these sources; what is established is that the reports alarmed American officials.

Nikolai Bulganin, the Soviet premier, wrote to each of the three invading governments on 5 November. The letters were not identical.

To Ben-Gurion he wrote that the Israeli government "is playing with the fate of peace, with the fate of its own people, in a criminal and irresponsible manner." Its policy, the letter went on, "will place a question [mark] upon the very existence of Israel as a State." The Soviet government had decided to advise its ambassador "to leave Israel and immediately go to Moscow." [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_bulganin1] The passages quoted here name no weapon. Their threat is to Israel's existence as a state, and the concrete step they announce is the recall of the ambassador.

To Guy Mollet, in Paris, Bulganin wrote that the Soviet Union was prepared to employ "all modern forms of destructive weaponry" to halt the intervention in Egypt. That phrase comes from the summary prepared by the Centre virtuel de la connaissance sur l'Europe (CVCE) of the letter as printed in the French diplomatic documents (Documents diplomatiques français 1956, volume III, pages 212–213); the full text was not fetched. [cite:rs_cw3_cvce_mollet] The letter to Eden, in London, was not fetched either, so its wording is known here only through what the Jewish Telegraphic Agency later reported of all three. [cite:rs_cw3_djn_23nov56]

That report, carried in the Detroit Jewish News on 23 November 1956, gave the demands common to the letters to Eden, Mollet and Ben-Gurion: immediate withdrawal, reparations to Egypt, and an objection to stationing the UN force anywhere but on both sides of the armistice lines. [cite:rs_cw3_djn_23nov56] The last point bore on Israel directly. Ben-Gurion had told the Knesset on 7 November that Israel would not agree to a foreign force in its territory or in any area it held; Moscow's position was that if a UN force stood anywhere, it should stand on Israel's side of the line as well. [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_bg_7nov]

Ben-Gurion's first answer, 8 November. Ben-Gurion replied on 8 November. He expressed "surprise and sorrow at the threat against Israel's existence and well-being contained in your Note," and said that Israel's course "is not and will not be decided by any foreign factor." [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_bulganin1] The reply was dated the same day on which Ben-Gurion told Eisenhower that Israel would withdraw from Sinai once satisfactory arrangements were made for the UN force, a retreat told in [scene:cw3_third_kingdom|the Third Kingdom and the retreat]. The two letters of 8 November therefore went in different directions: to Moscow, a refusal to be decided by any foreign power; to Washington, a conditional agreement to leave.

The American side drew the connection explicitly. On 8 November Assistant Secretary of State Rountree told Eban, for Israel, that Israel's withdrawal mattered for "Western-Soviet relations and the relationship between the United States and Israel," and that failing to comply "would endanger world peace." [cite:rs_cw3_frus16_d557] In Washington's framing the Soviet threat was a reason for Israel to leave quickly, not a pressure to be defied.

The second exchange, 15–17 November. Bulganin wrote again on 15 November, referring back to "my letter to you of 5 November" and demanding Israeli withdrawal, compensation to Egypt and the return of property. [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_bulganin] Ben-Gurion's reply of 17 November is the fullest statement of Israel's case that the exchange produced. "It was, therefore, the elementary duty of our Government to take defensive measures," he wrote. "Any return to the Armistice Agreement means a return to murder, blockade, and boycott, directed against Israel." And he wrote: "We have not destroyed a single Egyptian town, nor have we caused harm to any civilian centre." [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_bulganin] That last sentence was written after the killings at Khan Yunis on 3 November and Rafah on 12 November, which the Director of UNRWA recorded in a special report and which are told in this chapter's section on Khan Yunis and Rafah; the reader can set the claim beside that record. [cite:rs_cw3_unrwa_a3212]

The strongest form of Israel's case in these letters is the one Ben-Gurion made: the armistice regime of 1949 had not given Israel security from raids, from the closure of its shipping lanes or from economic boycott, and a demand to return to it was a demand to return to those conditions. The Soviet case, in its own terms, was that the invaders should withdraw, compensate Egypt and return its property.

Hungary as an argument, 16 November. Washington used Hungary in its own diplomacy with the Arab world. On 16 November Eisenhower wrote to King Saud of Saudi Arabia. He cited "the ruthless suppression of the people of Hungary in their quest for freedom" as "indicative of the fate of any who become dominated by the Soviet Union," and asked the King to encourage Egypt to cooperate on "the fundamental problems which gave rise to the current crisis." [cite:rs_cw3_kingsaud_ike] Saud's own message, to which Eisenhower was replying, had spoken of "Israeli-French-U.K. aggression against Egypt." [cite:rs_cw3_kingsaud_ike] The exchange can be read as Washington's attempt to have the King see the Soviet Union as the danger to the region, while the King's own message named the invasion of Egypt as the aggression.

What ended the war? Two answers are given, and both have evidence. The first holds that the Soviet threat did it. Moscow's warnings, tinged with the language of nuclear weapons, and the reports from Syria made the war look like a path to escalation between the great powers; the cease-fire was accepted on 6 November, the day after the notes; and Israeli accounts give the Bulganin letter weight in the decision to withdraw. [cite:rs_cw3_origins_hahn] [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_bulganin] The strongest version of this case rests on timing and on the State Department's own filing, which places "the Threat of Soviet Intervention" between the assault on the Canal and the acceptance of the cease-fire. [cite:rs_cw3_frus16_ch3]

The second answer holds that American pressure did it. The Office of the Historian and Hahn credit the cease-fire to American "political and financial pressure" and to the votes at the UN, which had begun on 2 November, three days before the notes. [cite:rs_cw3_milestones_suez] [cite:rs_cw3_origins_hahn] On this reading Washington treated the Soviet threat as a reason to end the war quickly, as Rountree told Eban, rather than as the cause of its end; and the financial and oil levers described in [scene:cw3_un_ceasefire|Washington against its allies] did the work of turning the cease-fire into a withdrawal. [cite:rs_cw3_frus16_d557] Both readings agree on what happened and in what order. They differ on weight, and the documents fetched here do not show what any of the three invading cabinets said in private about the Soviet notes when they decided.

The intelligence side of the Soviet–Israeli–American triangle in 1956, the Angleton years at the CIA, is told elsewhere in this library, in [scene:cia_s03|the Khrushchev speech] and Stage Two.

The gaps are specific. Bulganin's letter to Eden was not fetched, and the letter to Mollet is known only through a summary, so the exact form of the threat to London and Paris rests on Hahn's description and the CVCE's paraphrase. The Soviet troop concentrations in Syria are known here only as intelligence reports that alarmed American officials, not as a verified deployment. The course of events in Hungary is outside what these sources record. And whether Moscow ever intended to act on its threats is not something any document fetched for this book shows.

sections.h: The Third Kingdom and the Retreat, 6–8 November 1956
sections.html:
A common memory of the Sinai campaign holds that Israel won the war and was then forced out of its gains over the following months, in the long diplomatic fight of early 1957. That fight happened, and it is told in [scene:cw3_withdrawal|the withdrawal fight of 1957]. But the decision in principle to withdraw was taken much faster, within about a day and a half of Israel's moment of greatest triumph. Between a victory letter read to the troops at Sharm el-Sheikh and a government statement accepting the UN's resolution, Israel's public position moved from the language of ancient kingdoms to the promise that it had "never planned to annex the Sinai desert." The documents of 6, 7 and 8 November 1956 record that turn hour by hour.

The victory. The IDF Archives state that Israeli forces occupied the Sinai peninsula "within 100 hours," and that it was in Israeli hands by 5 November 1956; Sharm el-Sheikh was taken that day. [cite:rs_cw3_idf_archive] [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_1956israel] At Sèvres on 24 October Ben-Gurion had said that "The Straits of Tiran are the State of Israel's Suez Canal." [cite:rs_cw3_shlaim_sevres]

At a ceremony at Sharm el-Sheikh the day after the fighting ended, about 6 November, Moshe Dayan, who commanded the campaign, read the troops a letter from Ben-Gurion. According to an account in the Israeli news site Walla, which quotes the Hebrew in 2023, the letter linked the conquest to biblical history and said that Yotvat (Tiran), described in the letter as a former independent Hebrew state, "will return to be part of the Third Kingdom of Israel." [cite:rs_cw3_walla_third_kingdom] The phrase placed Tiran inside the kingdom it named. The letter's archival text and its exact date were not fetched for this book; the quotation rests on Walla's report.

A second witness remembered the same moment from the other side of Israeli politics. Uri Avnery, a journalist at the time and a political opponent of Ben-Gurion, recalled in his book Israel Without Zionists Ben-Gurion's "victory announcement ... proclaiming the 'Third Kingdom of Israel'" and then, within about a day, "his speech announcing, in a broken voice, that he had acceded to President Eisenhower's request and agreed to the retreat." [cite:rs_cw3_avnery] That is a recollection, written later, by a man who opposed the government. It agrees with Walla on the phrase and with the documents below on the speed of the reversal; its description of Ben-Gurion's voice is Avnery's alone.

The Knesset, 7 November. On 7 November Ben-Gurion reviewed the campaign before the Knesset. His reasons for the war, the fedayeen raids, the blockade, the Czechoslovak arms and the joint command of Egypt, Jordan and Syria, are set out in this chapter's opening section. [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_bg_7nov] On the future, the speech took positions that left almost no room for retreat. "The armistice agreement with Egypt is dead and buried and cannot be restored to life," he said. The armistice lines had "no more validity." And: "On no account will Israel agree to the stationing of a foreign force, no matter how it is called, in its territory" or in any area Israel held. At the same time he offered Egypt direct peace negotiations without preconditions. [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_bg_7nov] [cite:rs_cw3_frus16_d534]

The speech was given on a day of mounting pressure elsewhere. The Soviet notes of 5 November had already arrived; his reply of 8 November is told in [scene:cw3_soviet_hungary|Moscow's notes and Budapest]. [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_bulganin1] The same day Hammarskjöld warned Ambassador Lodge that persistent Israeli defiance could prompt so strong a UN reaction that Israel might be expelled. [cite:rs_cw3_frus16_d534] And in the evening, in Washington, the President wrote.

Eisenhower's message, 7 November. The message Eisenhower addressed to Ben-Gurion on 7 November was sent at 6:52 p.m. Washington time; a copy had been handed to Reuven Shiloah at 6:15. It urged Ben-Gurion to "comply with the resolutions of the United Nations General Assembly," and it warned that an Israeli refusal to withdraw "could not but bring about the condemnation of Israel as a violator" and could "impair the friendly cooperation between our two countries." [cite:rs_cw3_frus16_d550] [cite:rs_cw3_app_ike_7nov] As of 2 a.m., the FRUS record notes, it had not yet reached him. [cite:rs_cw3_frus16_d550] It was released publicly on 8 November. [cite:rs_cw3_app_ike_7nov] One reading of the phrase "friendly cooperation between our two countries" is that the President was telling the Prime Minister that the relationship itself was in question.

The reply and the statement, 8 November. Ben-Gurion's reply of 8 November conceded the central point while keeping a condition. Israel would "willingly withdraw our forces," he wrote, upon the "conclusion of satisfactory arrangements with the United Nations" for the international force. "We have never planned to annex the Sinai desert." And he asked that Egypt abandon "its policy of boycott and blockade" and enter direct peace negotiations. [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_ike_bg] [cite:rs_cw3_app_ike_7nov] The day before, he had said Israel would accept no foreign force on ground it held; now the arrangements for that force were the condition of Israel's leaving.

The government's statement of the same day put the decision more plainly: "It was finally agreed to accept the United Nations Resolution and withdraw Israel's forces." It listed the war's three aims: to destroy the forces that threatened Israel, to liberate Israeli territory held by an invader, and to secure free navigation in the Gulf of Eilat and the Suez Canal. It acknowledged that only the first had been fully achieved. And it quoted the Prime Minister: "There is no power in the world which can nullify our victory." [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_cabinet_8nov] The statement did not mention Tiran as part of any kingdom. Its second aim, "Israeli territory held by an invader," it did not further define in the text fetched here.

The manner of leaving. In Washington on the morning of 8 November, at 10:45, Eban met Assistant Secretary of State Rountree. He told him that the manner of Israel's withdrawal mattered as much as the act itself. The State Department, for its part, opposed a visit by Ben-Gurion to Washington that would bypass the UN, and approved a meeting only "after compliance." [cite:rs_cw3_frus16_d557] Rountree also tied the withdrawal to relations with Moscow, a point taken up in the account of the Soviet notes. Israel was asking for a negotiated exit with something to show for it; Washington was offering a meeting only after Israel had done what the UN asked. That gap, between withdrawal on terms and withdrawal first, is what the next four months were fought over.

Begin's position, 16 November. Not everyone in the Knesset accepted the turn. On 16 November Menachem Begin praised the government's refusal to leave Sinai until Egypt made peace, and concluded, in the summary published by the Menachem Begin Heritage Center of a report in the Jewish Herald, that parts of the Land of Israel still needed to be liberated. [cite:rs_cw3_begin_center] The source is a summary, not Begin's words, and it describes the government's position as a refusal at a moment when the government had already agreed in principle to withdraw on conditions. The difference shows how the 8 November decision could be read at home: as a promise to leave, or as a refusal to leave until conditions were met.

What "Third Kingdom" meant. Two readings of the episode are offered, and each has documentary support. The first takes the language at face value: Ben-Gurion's letter tied Tiran and Sinai to the biblical kingdoms, and his Knesset tone the next day was that of a leader claiming lasting gains; on this reading the rhetoric expressed a territorial and messianic claim that was then abandoned under pressure. [cite:rs_cw3_walla_third_kingdom] [cite:rs_cw3_avnery] The record of Sèvres gives this reading weight: an Israeli eighth point sought "permanent annexation" of the area east of a line from El Arish through Abu Ageila and Nakhl to Sharm el-Sheikh, and Britain and France never backed it. [cite:rs_cw3_shlaim_sevres]

The second reading treats the letter as rhetoric for soldiers on the day of victory, not policy. On 8 November Ben-Gurion wrote to the President that Israel had "never planned to annex the Sinai desert," and the cabinet accepted withdrawal within a day; the war aims it listed were security and navigation, not territory in Sinai. [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_ike_bg] [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_cabinet_8nov] The strongest form of this case is that a government planning annexation would not have agreed to leave in principle within thirty-six hours of conquest. The strongest reply is that the agreement was made under the pressure of a Soviet threat, an American warning and a UN demand arriving together, and that a letter to the American President is the last place one would expect an annexationist aim to be stated. The documents fetched here do not settle which reading is right; they establish that both the letter and the disavowal were written, a day or two apart, by the same man.

The memory. The episode outlived 1956. The scholar Uri Bar-Joseph, reviewing work by the historian Avi Raz in 2013, summarizes it as "brutal pressures" by the Eisenhower administration that led Ben-Gurion to announce a full withdrawal 24 hours after a Knesset speech implying that Israel was not ready for one. That memory, Bar-Joseph writes, weighed on Israel's cabinet in June 1967. [cite:rs_cw3_barjoseph_hdiplo] How it did so belongs to [scene:s12|the crisis of May–June 1967].

Several things remain open. The text and date of the "Third Kingdom" letter are known only from Walla's 2023 report and Avnery's recollection; no archival copy was fetched. What passed in Israel's cabinet between the Knesset speech of 7 November and the decision of 8 November is not in these documents, and so the relative weight of Eisenhower's message, the Soviet note and the UN's warning cannot be measured from them; Eisenhower's message, by FRUS's own note, had not yet reached Ben-Gurion in the early hours of 8 November. And the conditions Ben-Gurion attached to withdrawal on 8 November, the "satisfactory arrangements" for the UN force, were not defined in the letter; what they turned out to mean is the story of the withdrawal fight.

sections.h: The Jews of Egypt, 1956–1958
sections.html:
Volume II followed Egypt's Jewish community from about 75,000 people in 1948 through the bombings of that year, in [scene:rd6_exodus|the Jews of the Arab world], and left the decisive rupture to this volume. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_egypt] This section tells that rupture. In the months after Israel, Britain and France invaded Egypt in October and November 1956, the Egyptian government detained Jews in their hundreds, issued a nationality law that excluded "Zionists" without defining the word, published a proclamation declaring that "all Jews are Zionists and enemies of the state," and placed Jewish property under state administration. Within about two years, between 23,000 and 25,000 Jews had left. These were the acts of a government, its ministries and its military authorities; they are documented as such here, and the record of them does not license any statement about Egyptians or Muslims as a people.

The sources. The documentation for these events comes from three kinds of source, and the reader should know which is which. The first is reporting by the Jewish Telegraphic Agency: an article by Brenda Gazzar published on 21 December 2006, reported from Ramat Gan, which draws on historians. [cite:rs_cw3_jta_2006_egypt] The second is advocacy: an essay by Lyn Julius in the journal Fathom in autumn 2017 (Julius directs the advocacy group Harif), and an undated report by the advocacy organization Justice for Jews from Arab Countries (JJAC), which credits the Historical Society of Jews from Egypt. [cite:rs_cw3_fathom_julius] [cite:rs_cw3_jjac_egypt] The third, used in Volume II, is the Jewish Virtual Library's summary of contemporary wire reports by the Associated Press and the New York World-Telegram. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_egypt] The legal details below, the numbers of laws and articles and the published sequestration lists, come from the advocacy sources. The texts of the nationality law and of the military proclamation themselves were not fetched. The overall numbers of those detained and of those who left are corroborated by the JTA and by the contemporary reports.

Arrest and expulsion, November 1956. The arrests began with the war. According to the JTA, citing historians, about 1,000 Jews in Egypt, many of them Egyptian citizens, were detained or imprisoned during the Suez crisis. [cite:rs_cw3_jta_2006_egypt] The contemporary reports cited by the Jewish Virtual Library give the same order: about 1,000 detained. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_egypt] Julius gives a sequence. A first wave of about 500 Jews was given 24 hours to leave; about 900 more were arrested by 7 November 1956; and detainees were held at the Abbasiya school, where there were 500, half of them stateless, and at Les Barrages prison, where there were 300. [cite:rs_cw3_fathom_julius] The JTA's account of the expulsions distinguishes two groups: Egypt expelled British and French nationals, among whom were many Jews, and it also expelled about 500 Jews who held no British or French passport. [cite:rs_cw3_jta_2006_egypt] The first group was expelled as nationals of states then at war with Egypt; the second held no such nationality, and the JTA counts them separately, as Jews.

The nationality law, 22 November. On 22 November 1956 Egypt enacted Nationality Law No. 391 of 1956. According to the JJAC report, the law barred "Zionists" from Egyptian nationality, without ever defining the term, and allowed the Interior Ministry to declare a person's nationality forfeited (Article 18). [cite:rs_cw3_jjac_egypt] The mechanism lay in the missing definition. A law that withholds nationality from a political category it does not define leaves the ministry free to decide who falls inside it.

The proclamation, 23 November. The next day supplied a definition of its own. On 23 November 1956 a proclamation by Egypt's Minister of Religious Affairs, read in mosques, declared that "all Jews are Zionists and enemies of the state," and promised their expulsion. [cite:rs_cw3_fathom_julius] [cite:rs_cw3_jjac_egypt] The contemporary Associated Press and New York World-Telegram reports cited by the Jewish Virtual Library record the same proclamation and the same words. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_egypt] This is antisemitism in its plainest form, and it was a state act: a government minister declared every Jew, by virtue of being a Jew, an enemy of the state. Read beside the law of the previous day, it erased the line between a political allegiance and a people.

Sequestration. Property followed persons. Under Military Proclamation No. 4, according to the JJAC report, orders issued between 1 and 20 November 1956 placed the property of hundreds of Jews under Egyptian administrators; the published lists named 486 persons and firms, of which at least 95 per cent were Jewish. [cite:rs_cw3_jjac_egypt] The JTA and Julius both give about 500 Jewish companies sequestered between November 1956 and March 1957. Julius adds that about 800 more enterprises were blacklisted, and that the custodians charged a fee of 10 per cent. [cite:rs_cw3_jta_2006_egypt] [cite:rs_cw3_fathom_julius] Those who left could not take their property with them. According to Julius, departing Jews received exit visas stamped "ONE WAY-NO RETURN," signed declarations "donating" their property to the state, and were allowed one suitcase and a small sum of money. [cite:rs_cw3_fathom_julius]

Departure. Between 23,000 and 25,000 Jews left Egypt from November 1956, by expulsion or under heavy pressure. The JTA gives that range for the period through 1957; Julius gives it through 1958. [cite:rs_cw3_jta_2006_egypt] [cite:rs_cw3_fathom_julius] The contemporary reports cited by the Jewish Virtual Library describe almost 25,000 as expelled and their property confiscated. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_egypt] More than 6,000 left by ship with the Red Cross by 1957, and by that year, according to the JJAC report, the community numbered about 15,000. [cite:rs_cw3_jjac_egypt] Roughly half of Egypt's Jews, Julius writes, eventually went to Israel. [cite:rs_cw3_fathom_julius] The Jewish Agency's own historical account describes the emigration of many Egyptian Jews to Israel as "an indirect outcome of the war." [cite:rs_cw3_jafi_fedayeen]

The limits. Julius, whose account is among the strongest statements of the case that this was persecution, records its limits herself. Jews of Egyptian nationality were at first spared; some expulsion orders were rescinded; Greeks, Armenians and Italians were not targeted in 1956; and the wider nationalizations of the 1960s also hit non-Jewish families. [cite:rs_cw3_fathom_julius] Her first point sits in some tension with the JTA's report that many of the roughly 1,000 detained were Egyptian citizens. [cite:rs_cw3_jta_2006_egypt] The two may describe different measures, detention on one hand and expulsion on the other, but the sources fetched here do not reconcile them. Her third point cuts in a particular direction: if communities of foreign origin in general had been the target, Greeks, Armenians and Italians would have been treated alike in 1956, and by her account they were not.

Why it happened: the dispute. Two explanations are offered, and the evidence for each should be stated at its strongest.

The first is that this was state persecution of Jews as Jews. Its evidence is the documents' own words and numbers: a minister's proclamation that "all Jews are Zionists and enemies of the state"; a nationality law aimed at an undefined category of "Zionists"; sequestration lists at least 95 per cent Jewish; and, on Julius's account, the sparing of Greeks, Armenians and Italians in the same months. Julius and the JJAC report make this case, and Julius reports Krämer's view that Jews alone were targeted because of the conflict with Israel. [cite:rs_cw3_fathom_julius] [cite:rs_cw3_jjac_egypt] The strongest form of the argument is that the measures did not stop at enemy nationals: they reached stateless Jews and Egyptian-citizen Jews, and the proclamation addressed every Jew.

The second explanation places the events in the context of war and decolonization. Egypt had been invaded by Britain, France and Israel; it expelled British and French nationals as enemy nationals, and many of the Jews who left were among them. Julius reports that Joel Beinin holds this view and blames Zionism for what befell the community, and she notes that British and French nationals were expelled too. [cite:rs_cw3_fathom_julius] Those who take this view also point to Operation Susannah: in July 1954 Israeli military intelligence activated a cell of Egyptian Jews, recruited for the purpose, to plant incendiary bombs in Egypt, an affair told in [scene:lv_s01|Operation Susannah and the Lavon affair]. On this reading, Israel's war and that earlier operation sharpened measures that were, at root, war measures. Philip Mendes, whose work Volume II used, offers a wider caution: many Egyptian Jews appear to have left for economic reasons rather than because of specific persecution, and the departure of Jews from Arab countries as a whole is best explained as "a complex combination of push and pull factors." [cite:rs_rd6_mendes_2010] Mendes describes the two partisan versions of the larger story, one attributing the exodus almost solely to Arab violence and the other to "a malicious Zionist conspiracy," and rejects both. [cite:rs_rd6_mendes_2010]

The two explanations are not wholly exclusive. On this book's reading, the record supports the second as far as British and French nationals are concerned: they were expelled as nationals of enemy states. It does not support it as an account of the proclamation of 23 November, which named no state, no nationality and no act, only Jews. Whatever Israel's conduct in 1954 or 1956, a government's declaration that all Jews are enemies of the state is a statement about Jews, and the documents record it as made.

Egypt's expulsions are often set against the Palestinian displacement of 1948 as two halves of a single exchange of populations. Whether that framing holds is examined in [scene:s00e3|the two displacements], which finds the two processes different in mechanism, duration and documentation.

The gaps here are substantial and should be stated. The texts of Nationality Law No. 391 and of Military Proclamation No. 4 were not fetched, so their provisions are known only through an advocacy report and an advocacy author; the overall numbers of those detained and of those who left are corroborated by other reporting, but the laws' exact wording is not established here. The number of British and French nationals expelled in 1956, and how many of them were Jews, is not given by any source fetched. The relation between the 1,000 detained (JTA) and the 900 arrested by 7 November (Julius) is not explained. And the views of Krämer and Beinin are known here only as Julius reports them; their own writings were not consulted.

sections.h: Gaza Under Israeli Rule, November 1956–March 1957
sections.html:
For four months in the winter of 1956–57, Israel governed the Gaza Strip. It was the first time the Strip had come under Israeli rule, and the episode had three features: a military government over a population most of whom were refugees from 1948, an argument inside Israel about whether the territory should be held, and an outside power that decided the matter. The killings at Khan Yunis and Rafah in the first days of the occupation are told in [scene:cw3_gaza_killings|Khan Yunis and Rafah]. This section follows what came after them: how Israel ran the Strip, what it planned for it, and why it left on 8 March 1957.

The people. According to the historian Benny Morris, Israel's military government ruled "some 300,000 Palestinian Arabs," about three-quarters of them refugees of 1948. [cite:rs_cw3_morris_gaza] They were not Egyptian citizens. Egypt, which had administered the Strip since 1948, had never given its inhabitants Egyptian citizenship, as Morris notes; that administration is told in Volume II. [cite:rs_cw3_morris_gaza] The point bears on Ben-Gurion's later argument, told below, that the Strip "was never Egyptian."

Curfew and screening. The UNRWA Director's special report, covering 1 November to mid-December 1956, gives the closest contemporary picture of daily life under the new authority. A curfew was imposed at the outset, and from 5 November it was lifted for six daytime hours. By late November there was "generally free movement of persons throughout the Strip outside curfew hours." Screening of the population continued "apparently in an orderly fashion," with detainees taken to interrogation centres. The refugees, the Director wrote, lived "under considerable tension." [cite:rs_cw3_unrwa_a3212] The report's word "apparently" can be read as a marker of distance: the agency appears to have been describing what it could observe, not what it had verified inside the interrogation centres.

The agency's own position was precarious. The Director warned that "unless immediate measures were taken to put an end to such happenings" it could not continue its work, and staff for whom there was no work were put on leave without pay after 1 January 1957 (paragraphs 17 and 28). [cite:rs_cw3_unrwa_a3212] The organization that fed and taught the refugee majority was telling the General Assembly that the conditions of the first weeks threatened its ability to operate at all.

How the Strip was governed. Morris describes an administration that rebuilt local institutions under Israeli supervision rather than replacing them. Municipal councils were reinstated; Khan Yunis's was restored on 3 December 1956. Schools reopened, with 30 of 200 textbooks removed as Egyptian propaganda. By late December four police stations staffed by local men were operating under the supervision of the Israel Police. [cite:rs_cw3_morris_gaza] The arrangement put Gazans in the front offices of town hall, classroom and police station, while authority over each ran to Israeli officers above them.

Two further measures in Morris's account show the military government reshaping the Strip as well as administering it. Bedouin living in the coastal dunes were ordered to move south-west of Rafah; the source for the order is a report of 16 December 1956 by the United Nations envoy, Colonel K. R. Nelson. And monuments to Colonel Mustafa Hafiz, who had run the fedayeen, were destroyed. [cite:rs_cw3_morris_gaza] One reading of the second act follows from Israel's case for the war. Hafiz's raids from the Strip had been at the centre of Israel's case for the war, as told in [scene:cw3_road_to_war|the road to war]; on that reading, removing his monuments was a statement about whose memory the Strip would now keep.

The plan to keep it. Ben-Gurion, Morris writes, hoped to keep the Strip. On 19 December 1956 he told the Knesset that Israel would never let Egypt resume control of the Strip. On 23 January 1957 he argued, "This Strip was never Egyptian." [cite:rs_cw3_morris_gaza] The argument appears to rest on the legal status described above: Egypt had administered Gaza but never made its people citizens, so its return to Egypt was not, in his framing, a restoration of anything Egypt had held by right.

The decisions of the government and the Knesset in January went in the same direction. The Gush Katif Heritage Center, citing Hagai Huberman (2019), records that a Nahal outpost was set up at Rafiah on 3 January 1957; that the government resolved on 13 January 1957 that "Israel will hold the Gaza Strip," opposing a United Nations force for its security; and that the Knesset approved the decision not to withdraw from Gaza on 23 January 1957. [cite:rs_cw3_katif_gaza] Morris describes a government "Blueprint for Gaza," dated 31 January 1957, which called Gaza and the nearby Jewish settlements "a topographical and economic unit." [cite:rs_cw3_morris_gaza]

A second account of January. Not every source describes January 1957 in the same terms. According to Eli Ashkenazi, writing for Walla News in 2023, Israel agreed in January 1957 to pull its army out of Gaza while leaving its police and administrative forces in place, and then withdrew in stages. [cite:rs_cw3_walla_third_kingdom] That account and the Katif Center's do not have to contradict each other, since a decision to "hold" the Strip could be carried out by civil administration rather than by troops; but they place different emphasis on the same weeks, one on keeping the territory and the other on pulling the army back. The sources used here do not show how the two were reconciled inside the cabinet. On 15 February the American embassy reported that the prospect Ben-Gurion most adamantly opposed was the return of Egyptian authority to Gaza "under any guise"; about 22 February he said Israel was prepared to withdraw its military forces from Gaza. [cite:rs_cw3_frus17_d100] [cite:rs_cw3_frus17_d132] That exchange belongs to the story of the withdrawal fight told in the next section.

The dispute: annexation or security? Whether Israel meant to keep Gaza is answered differently depending on which documents are given weight. The case for retention rests on a run of records: Ben-Gurion's December and January statements in the Knesset, the cabinet resolution of 13 January, the Knesset vote of 23 January, the Blueprint, and the Nahal outpost all point the same way. [cite:rs_cw3_morris_gaza] [cite:rs_cw3_katif_gaza] To these the Katif Center adds that Ben-Gurion had proposed retaking the Strip as early as March 1955 and that the cabinet listed control of it among the war's aims in October 1956, both told in [scene:cw3_road_to_war|the road to war].

The case for security is Israel's stated one, and it is not a thin case. Israel argued that only it could stop the fedayeen raids from the Strip, and it set as its condition for leaving a United Nations, not an Egyptian, administration. [cite:rs_cw3_walla_third_kingdom] [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_bg_mar57] On this reading, the January resolutions were bargaining positions meant to prevent Egypt's return rather than declarations of annexation, and the outcome Israel finally accepted, a United Nations force in Gaza, was the security arrangement it had set as its condition. In his address to the Knesset of 5 March 1957, Ben-Gurion counted United Nations forces in Gaza among the campaign's gains. [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_bg_mar57]

The two readings are not mutually exclusive. A government can want both security and territory, and the documents show both aims stated by the same men in the same months. What the sources used here do not contain is a single document in which the cabinet chose between them; the decision was in the end made for it in Washington and New York.

The end. Israel left Gaza completely on 8 March 1957. [cite:rs_cw3_walla_third_kingdom] Morris gives the same date and the reason: the withdrawal came "under international (mainly US) pressure," after four months of military rule. [cite:rs_cw3_morris_gaza] The diplomacy that produced it, from the General Assembly's resolutions to Eisenhower's address of 20 February and the American statement on the Straits of Tiran, is told in the section that follows.

What the record leaves open. The sources drawn on here give the institutions of the occupation but few numbers for its operation: how many people were detained in the screening, how many Bedouin were moved, and how many Israeli personnel administered the Strip are not given. The text of the Blueprint for Gaza is known only through Morris's summary, and the January decisions are known through the Katif Center's account rather than from the cabinet's own minutes. Whether the government's January position was a plan to annex or a lever to prevent Egypt's return is disputed, and the documents support parts of both answers. What the people of Gaza themselves thought of the councils and police stations set up under Israeli supervision is not recorded in these sources beyond the UNRWA Director's description of a refugee population living "under considerable tension."

sections.h: The Withdrawal Fight, January–March 1957
sections.html:
Britain and France completed their withdrawal from Port Said on 22 December 1956. [cite:rs_cw3_keightley] Israel had not left Sinai or the Gaza Strip. The General Assembly had called on it to withdraw behind the armistice lines in November, and on 7 November had called "once again" for it to do so, a sequence told in [scene:cw3_un_ceasefire|Washington against its allies]. [cite:rs_cw3_unispal_1002] Israel's government had announced on 8 November that it accepted the United Nations resolution and would withdraw; but its own statement that day listed three war aims, destroying the forces that threatened Israel, liberating Israeli territory held by an invader, and securing free navigation in the Gulf of Eilat and the Canal, and said that only the first had been fully achieved. [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_cabinet_8nov] The withdrawal fight of January to March 1957 was about the other two. Israel sought to leave only on terms: no return of Egypt to Gaza, and an assured passage through the Straits of Tiran. The United States held that a state which had invaded could not set terms for leaving. How that difference was resolved, and what Israel actually received, can now be read from the primary record on both sides.

The Assembly loses patience. On 19 January 1957 the General Assembly adopted Resolution 1123. On 2 February it adopted Resolution 1124 by 74 votes to 2, with 2 abstentions. The second resolution "Deplores the non-compliance of Israel to complete its withdrawal behind the armistice demarcation line" and called on Israel to complete it "without further delay." [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_1124] The vote was nearly unanimous, and the word "deplores" moved the Assembly from requesting compliance to recording its absence. Behind the vote lay the question of what would follow if Israel still did not comply. Many members, as Secretary of State Dulles would write to Senator Lyndon Johnson that month, favoured economic sanctions. [cite:rs_cw3_frus17_d127]

The aide-mémoire of 11 February. Washington's answer to Israel's demand for terms came in a written statement handed to Ambassador Eban on 11 February 1957 and released on 17 February. Its two parts dealt with the two places Israel was holding. On Gaza it said Israeli withdrawal "should be prompt and unconditional," and that the United Nations Emergency Force (UNEF) should "move into this area and be on the boundary between Israel and the Gaza Strip." On the Gulf of Aqaba it said that "the gulf comprehends international waters," in which no nation had the right to prevent "free and innocent passage," and that the United States "is prepared to exercise the right of free and innocent passage and to join with others" to secure it. [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_aidememoire] [cite:rs_cw3_israeled_ike]

The document gave Israel nothing on Gaza beyond a United Nations force on the boundary. On Tiran it gave a statement of American policy and a declared readiness to act on it, not a treaty or a guarantee. That distinction, between a policy and a guarantee, would govern everything that followed.

Eban saw value in it at once. Meeting Robert Murphy the same day, with Reuven Shiloah present, he said that if nothing else Israel had "focused American thinking on the Gulf of Aqaba problem," and that "a good deal of the momentum in favor of sanctions would evaporate" once the American position was known. [cite:rs_cw3_frus17_d79] One reading of his remark is tactical: the paper did not meet Israel's terms, but it moved the United States onto Israel's ground on the one issue Israel had called vital, and it might take the pressure for sanctions off the table.

Ben-Gurion holds out. In Jerusalem the Prime Minister played for time. On 15 February the American embassy reported that Ben-Gurion was "pleased with intent of United States suggestions if not their particulars" on Tiran, but feared that UNEF might leave Sharm el-Sheikh before a settlement, in which case Israel would have "no other recourse than to fight or submit." On Gaza, the embassy reported, the "Prospect which he most adamantly opposes is return of Egyptian authority there under any guise." And it added a line of plain observation: "He frankly hoping for time." [cite:rs_cw3_frus17_d100]

Three or four days later, around 18–19 February, Ben-Gurion appealed to Dulles "personally to obtain postponement of UN discussions." "Withdrawal under present circumstances will spell disaster for us," he wrote, and for the United Nations to proceed "is to adopt double standard of morality." He recalled Eban for consultation. [cite:rs_cw3_frus17_d111] The phrase "double standard of morality" was the core of Israel's case, and it deserves to be stated in its strongest form: in Israel's view, as Ben-Gurion's other messages that month show, withdrawal without an assured passage through Tiran, and with Egyptian authority able to return to Gaza, would leave Israel facing the conditions it had gone to war over. [cite:rs_cw3_frus17_d100] [cite:rs_cw3_frus17_d132]

The sanctions meeting, 20 February. On the evening of 20 February, from 8:30 to 10:55, Eisenhower and Dulles met the bipartisan leadership of Congress at the White House. The record shows how far the administration was prepared to go and how far Congress was prepared to follow. Eisenhower said sanctions "might take various forms." Dulles listed "German reparation payments to Israel, world-wide sale of Israeli government bonds, and US aid" as areas for consideration. [cite:rs_cw3_frus17_d120] Each was a channel through which money reached Israel.

The congressional leaders did not rally to the idea. Knowland proposed a resolution under which failure to comply within 30 days "would properly subject the offender to economic, moral and diplomatic sanctions." Senator Johnson "asked if sanctions were the best move." Fulbright wanted nothing that looked like "a commitment to go to war." Rayburn wanted no "part of a Congressional resolution." [cite:rs_cw3_frus17_d120] Johnson had written to Dulles on 11 February; the Secretary's reply, delivered on 22 February, said that "There is strong sentiment among many members of the United Nations for economic sanctions," that the President would be "reluctant" to see sanctions become the only remedy, and that Israel had received "important assurances" but "apparently has felt that those assurances were not sufficient." [cite:rs_cw3_frus17_d127]

The address of 20 February. The same evening Eisenhower took the case to the public in a radio and television address. Its central passage was a question: "Should a nation which attacks and occupies foreign territory in the face of United Nations disapproval be allowed to impose conditions on its own withdrawal?" Israel, he said, "insists on firm guarantees as a condition to withdrawing its forces of invasion," and "the United Nations has no choice but to exert pressure upon Israel to comply with the withdrawal resolutions." [cite:rs_cw3_app_20feb57]

The address was not only a warning. Eisenhower also told the country that UNEF "should be placed on the Egyptian-Israeli Armistice lines," that the Gaza Strip should no longer be "a source of armed infiltration and reprisals," and that "no nation has the right to prevent free and innocent passage in the Gulf." He reminded his listeners that the United States had given Israel "on February 11 a statement of United States policy." [cite:rs_cw3_app_20feb57] Ben-Gurion later quoted another line of the speech as part of what Israel had obtained: "we should not assume that if Israel withdraws, Egypt will prevent Israeli shipping." [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_bg_mar57] The address refused Israel's conditions while stating publicly, in the President's voice, the substance of two of them. It did not mention American aid to Israel. [cite:rs_cw3_app_20feb57]

The money at stake. The levers Dulles named on 20 February show what the United States could have reached in 1957, and what it could not. There was no American military aid to Israel to suspend. In the aid relationship as this library traces it, the years 1948 to 1961 were a period of economic aid and loans only, with Washington avoiding arms sales for fear of alienating the Arab oil states; the first American military aid, as loans, came in 1962.

That is why Dulles's list ran to German reparations and the sale of Israel Bonds as well as American aid: two of the three were not American government money at all: one was paid by West Germany, and the other was the world-wide sale of Israel's own government bonds. [cite:rs_cw3_frus17_d120] The library's table of cases in which Washington clearly attached conditions to aid begins much later. Its first entry is 1987, when Israel's cabinet cancelled the Lavi fighter, a programme carrying about $1.8 billion in American aid, under American pressure; its next American-money case is the $10 billion in loan guarantees held for 120 days over settlements in 1991–92.

The episode of February 1957 is not in that table; no sanction was imposed. But it is a documented occasion on which an American President and Secretary of State discussed, with the leaders of Congress, using money that reached Israel to force a change in its policy, and the record of the evening shows Congress declining to go along.

The dispute: was there a sanctions threat? Two readings of the record are possible, and each has its documents. On the first, the United States threatened sanctions in substance: the President said publicly that the United Nations had "no choice but to exert pressure," and the Secretary of State named reparations, bonds and US aid as possible levers to the congressional leadership. [cite:rs_cw3_app_20feb57] [cite:rs_cw3_frus17_d120] On the second, there was no formal threat: no American sanction was imposed, Dulles told Johnson the President was "reluctant" to reach for sanctions, leaders of both parties resisted, and the deal of 1 March came through assurances, not penalties. [cite:rs_cw3_frus17_d127] [cite:rs_cw3_frus17_d120] [cite:rs_cw3_frus17_d169] The two readings agree on what was said and done. They differ on whether pressure that was named, discussed and broadcast but never applied counts as a threat. Ben-Gurion's message of about 22 February, below, shows the Israeli government treating it as one.

The turn, 22 February to 1 March. About 22 February, two days after the address, Ben-Gurion told the American embassy that Israel was prepared to withdraw its military forces from Gaza, and would not occupy Sharm el-Sheikh "after Israel's free passage through Tiran Straits had been assured." Eban would make a "further effort to reach understanding with USG." Against sanctions, he said, "we shall resist it with every ounce of our moral strength." [cite:rs_cw3_frus17_d132] The concession on the army in Gaza and the defiance on sanctions came in the same message.

A week later the shape of the settlement was clear in Washington. At 5:36 p.m. on 28 February Dulles told the British, Canadian and French envoys that Israel would announce, in effect, "its unconditional withdrawal in the areas now occupied." It would get nothing beyond the prior United Nations resolutions, while stating "assumptions" already contained in United Nations texts and its own "expectations." The American position on Aqaba, he said, was unchanged from the aide-mémoire of 11 February. [cite:rs_cw3_frus17_d169]

On 1 March the Israeli government authorized the Foreign Minister, Golda Meir, to announce at the United Nations that "Israel will withdraw from the Gaza Strip and Sharm el-Sheikh." The announcement rested on stated assumptions, among them "That the take-over from the military and civilian control of Israel will be exclusively by the UNEF." It also declared that interference with Israeli ships "will be regarded by Israel as an attack entitling it" to act in self-defence. [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_bg_mar57] [cite:rs_cw3_katif_gaza] The assumptions were Israel's own statements, recorded in the Assembly; nothing in the sources used here shows any other government signing them. The self-defence clause, by contrast, was a warning addressed to Egypt and to the future.

A further document stands behind the decision, and it is one this book has not been able to read directly. In his address to the Knesset on 5 March, Ben-Gurion said that a letter from Eisenhower dated 2 March preceded the cabinet's approval of the withdrawal from Gaza, which he dates to 2 March. [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_bg_mar57] The letter itself was not fetched for this book and is known here only through Ben-Gurion's account. His dating also sits awkwardly with the record of 1 March, when the government had already authorized Meir to announce the withdrawal; the sources do not explain whether the cabinet of 2 March confirmed, completed or formally approved what had been announced the day before.

What Israel said it had won. Ben-Gurion's address of 5 March set out the government's account. The American memorandum of 11 February, he said, "declares that the United States is ready to make use of freedom of passage in the Straits," and it had welcomed a United Nations force at Sharm el-Sheikh. Free passage through Tiran was "vital to Israel, and is also of great importance to other countries," and UN forces now stood at Sharm el-Sheikh and in Gaza. [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_bg_mar57] Israel completed its withdrawal from Gaza on 8 March 1957 and from Sinai the same month. [cite:rs_cw3_morris_gaza] [cite:rs_cw3_walla_third_kingdom] UNEF remained in Egypt, in Peter Hahn's words, "as a buffer against Egyptian-Israeli hostilities," until Nasser ordered it out in May 1967. [cite:rs_cw3_origins_hahn]

The dispute: guarantees or none? Whether Israel left with guarantees is the question on which the whole episode turns, and the two answers rest on the same documents read differently. Ben-Gurion's case was that Israel left with assurances: the American memorandum on the Straits, Eisenhower's public words of 20 February, his letter of 2 March, and a United Nations force at Sharm el-Sheikh gave Israel what he called the gains of the campaign. [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_bg_mar57] The opposing case, put by the historian Uri Bar-Joseph, is that Israel left "without formal security gains" under "brutal" American pressure; on this reading the assurances were unilateral statements and assumptions, and UNEF could be withdrawn at Egypt's request, as it was in 1967. [cite:rs_cw3_barjoseph_hdiplo] [cite:rs_cw3_origins_hahn] Dulles's own words on 28 February, "unconditional withdrawal," with Israel getting nothing beyond the prior resolutions, support the second reading as a description of the form of the deal. [cite:rs_cw3_frus17_d169] The aide-mémoire's stated readiness to "exercise the right of free and innocent passage" supports the first as a description of its substance. [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_aidememoire]

The arrangement was tested ten years later, when Nasser ordered UNEF out in May 1967; that crisis is told in [scene:s12|the June 1967 war] and, for the question of who fired first, in [scene:iaa_s04|1967]. Bar-Joseph notes that the memory of the 1957 pressure weighed on Israel's cabinet in June 1967. [cite:rs_cw3_barjoseph_hdiplo]

What the record leaves open. Eisenhower's letter of 2 March, which Ben-Gurion said preceded the cabinet's decision, has not been read for this book, and its contents are known only through Ben-Gurion's account. The text of Resolution 1123 of 19 January was not fetched, and is known here only by its date. Whether Eisenhower would in the end have supported sanctions in the General Assembly had Israel refused is not settled by the documents: he named the possibility in public, his Secretary of State listed the levers in private, and he told Congress, through Dulles, that he was reluctant. And whether Israel's 1 March assumptions bound anyone but Israel was, in 1957, a question of interpretation; the sources here show Israel stating them and no other government formally accepting them. What is not open is the outcome. Israel withdrew from Gaza and Sinai without the formal guarantees it had demanded, with a public American statement of policy on the Straits, and with a United Nations force on Egyptian soil that remained only so long as Egypt allowed it.

sections.h: The Kafr Qasim Trial and the Black Flag, 1957–1960
sections.html:
The killing at Kafr Qasim on 29 October 1956, told in [scene:mg_s01|the previous section], took forty-seven, forty-eight or forty-nine lives, depending on the source and on whether an unborn child is counted. It was kept from the Israeli public for weeks. When it could no longer be kept, the state put the men who had done the shooting on trial before its own military court. The trial produced two results that have been argued over ever since. It convicted eight members of the Border Police of killing Israeli citizens, and its presiding judge wrote a test for unlawful orders that the Israeli army still teaches. Yet within about a year of the verdict, on most accounts, every one of the men was out of prison, and the brigade commander who had set the curfew was tried separately, on charges the sources describe differently, and fined a sum so small that it became a byword. Both results are documented, and neither cancels the other.

The court and the charge. The case was heard by a military court presided over by Judge Benjamin Halevy, as case MD/57/3, the Military Advocate against Major Shmuel Malinki and 10 others. [cite:rs_cw3_orbach_2013] [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_kq] The Jewish Virtual Library gives eleven Border Police officers and men as charged; Ynet, writing in 2014, says thirteen were tried. [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_kfar_kassem] [cite:rs_cw3_ynet_rivlin] The case title, Malinki "and 10 others," matches the figure of eleven. [cite:rs_cw3_orbach_2013] The historian Danny Orbach, who worked from the court's protocol, footnotes sessions running from March 1957 to January 1958. [cite:rs_cw3_orbach_2013] The trial therefore ran for the better part of a year.

The verdict, 16 October 1958. The court gave its judgment on 16 October 1958, almost two years after the killing. The Jewish Telegraphic Agency reported it from Tel Aviv on 24 October. Eight of the accused were convicted. Major Shmuel Malinki, who had relayed the order to his men, was sentenced to 17 years. Lieutenant Gabriel Dahan, whose platoon had fired at the village entrance, and Lance Corporal Shalom Offer received 15 years each. Corporals Gavriel Ulliel and Edmond Nachmani and Privates Makhluf Karoush, Eliyahu Avraham and Albert Pahims received seven years each. The officers were stripped of their rank. [cite:rs_cw3_djn_verdict] [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_kq]

The judgment set out why. As the JTA dispatch quoted it, the court held that an officer "should display courage not only in the face of the enemy." It stated its "clear and unreserved belief" that it is forbidden for a soldier in any army to "kill without due process of law." And it found that Malinki had extended an illegal order "by including women and children." [cite:rs_cw3_djn_verdict] The last finding matters for the question of where responsibility lay. On the court's reading the order Malinki received was already illegal, and he made it worse in passing it down.

The black flag. The passage for which the trial is remembered is Halevy's test of when a soldier must refuse an order. As Leora Bilsky quotes it, "Illegality that pierces the eye and revolts the heart" overrides the duty to obey.
