[cite:rs_cw3_wiki_kq] [cite:rs_cw3_orbach_2013] [cite:rs_cw3_cook_2008] The image the ruling gave the doctrine is a flag: a "manifestly illegal" order is one over which "a black flag flies," and soldiers must refuse it. That standard is still taught in the Israeli army. [cite:wiki_kafr_qasim_massacre] [cite:conversation_kafr_qasim_60] The doctrine answered, in law, the defence that every defendant at Kafr Qasim could make: that he had done what he was told. The court accepted that the men had received orders and held that these were orders no soldier could lawfully carry out.

Orbach's reading of how the doctrine was made is worth setting beside the usual account, which credits it to the bench. In his study of the trial he argues that the black-flag doctrine emerged from the clash between the trial's attorneys, its defendants and its judges, not from the judges alone, and that the trial as a whole reshaped relations between Israel's army and its civilian state, and the civic standing of the country's Arab minority. [cite:rs_cw3_orbach_2013] On his account the doctrine was the product of an adversarial process.

The reactions. The JTA dispatch of October 1958 recorded how different parts of Israeli society, and its neighbours, took the verdict. The defendants' families campaigned for pardons. The Chief of Staff, Chaim Laskov, told the chief military prosecutor to study whether further trials were needed, including of Shadmi. The opposition party Herut said the verdict had "left confusion in the minds of soldiers." In Kafr Qasim, the village elders called it "courageous" and "just." Across the line, the Jordanian newspaper Falastin praised the court's "firmness," but alleged that Shadmi had been smuggled out of the country. [cite:rs_cw3_djn_verdict] The elders' judgment deserves notice. The people with the most reason to doubt the court said, in October 1958, that it had done justice; what followed in the next year would test that view.

Shadmi's trial. Issachar Shadmi, the brigade commander who had changed the curfew hours, and whom Malinki had testified told him he wanted no sentimentality and no arrests, was not tried with the men below him. He was tried separately, by a special court-martial. Orbach notes that the prosecutor, Brigadier General Moshe David, did not hold Shadmi responsible for the killings and charged him only with procedural offences. [cite:rs_cw3_orbach_2013] In February 1959, as Wikipedia's account has it, Shadmi was acquitted of murder and convicted of extending the curfew without authority. [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_kq] The two accounts sit uneasily together, since one says no killing charge was brought and the other records an acquittal of murder; the sources used here do not resolve the point.

"Shadmi's penny." The penalty was a fine, and the sources describe it in several ways. Wikipedia, Yuval Ben-Ami in +972 Magazine and Tom Segev (as quoted on the site Hyehudi) all give 10 prutot. [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_kq] [cite:rs_cw3_972_benami] [cite:rs_cw3_hyehudi_leibowitz] The pruta was the thousandth part of the Israeli lira, so 10 prutot was one hundredth of a lira, which is how this library's summary of the period states it. [cite:wiki_kafr_qasim_massacre] [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_kq] The Jewish Virtual Library also gives 10 prutot but describes the sum as "1/1000 of an old Israeli pound," which contradicts its own figure, since 10 prutot was a hundredth. PalQuest gives "a single pruta (a thousandth of the Israeli pound)." Jonathan Cook calls it "a penny." [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_kfar_kassem] [cite:rs_cw3_palquest_kq] [cite:rs_cw3_cook_2008] The figure most sources share is ten prutot, one hundredth of a lira, and that is the figure this chapter uses; the others are recorded in the table below. Whatever the exact coin, the point on which every source agrees is that it was a token. Palestinian citizens of Israel remember it as "Shadmi's penny." [cite:conversation_kafr_qasim_60] [cite:wiki_kafr_qasim_massacre]

The reductions. The long sentences of October 1958 did not last. On 3 April 1959 the appeal court cut Malinki's sentence to 14 years and Dahan's to 10. The Chief of Staff then reduced them further, to 10 and 8. President Ben-Zvi pardoned or reduced the sentences of the others. With a one-third remission, according to Wikipedia, all of them were out of prison by about November 1959. [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_kq] The Jewish Virtual Library states that "no one served more than three and a half years"; PalQuest, that "by 1960, all soldiers had been released." [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_kfar_kassem] [cite:rs_cw3_palquest_kq] The three accounts are compatible in substance and differ in emphasis and date: within a year or a little more of a judgment that set seventeen years as the heaviest sentence, no one convicted of the killings remained in prison.

Afterwards. The two officers went on to official posts. According to Wikipedia's account, Malinki was put in charge of security at the Negev Nuclear Research Center, and Dahan was placed in charge of "Arab affairs" in Ramla in 1960. [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_kq] PalQuest describes the same pattern as the government having "compensated" the killers with official posts, including posts over Arab citizens in Lydda. [cite:rs_cw3_palquest_kq] The officer who had led the platoon that fired on the returning workers of Kafr Qasim was, four years later, responsible for Arab affairs in an Israeli town.

A protest from within. Not every Israeli voice in the debate that followed came from the defendants' side. Yeshayahu Leibowitz responded in Haaretz, in a passage Tom Segev quotes in The Seventh Million, with a sarcastic call for "a mass petition" to revise the Nuremberg judgments, since the men convicted there had also acted on orders. [cite:rs_cw3_hyehudi_leibowitz] One reading of the comparison is that it was meant to show where the argument for leniency led: if obedience excused the men of Kafr Qasim, it excused everyone who had ever pleaded it.

Accountability, or its absence? The trial supports two readings, and each rests on documents. The first holds it a landmark. An Israeli military court convicted Israeli soldiers of killing Arab citizens of Israel, in a judgment that said plainly no soldier in any army may "kill without due process of law," and in doing so it created the doctrine of the manifestly unlawful order, which has outlived every sentence it imposed. [cite:rs_cw3_djn_verdict] [cite:rs_cw3_orbach_2013] The elders of Kafr Qasim called the verdict just in 1958, and two later Israeli presidents, Rivlin and Herzog, are counted on this side of the argument. Orbach's argument that the trial reshaped civil–military relations gives this reading its strongest scholarly form.

The second reading looks at what happened to the people rather than to the doctrine. The commander who set the curfew and, on his subordinate's testimony, framed the order was charged, on Orbach's account, only with procedural offences, and fined a token sum. Every sentence was cut until no one convicted served more than three and a half years. And the two convicted officers were given posts in security and in Arab affairs. [cite:rs_cw3_palquest_kq] [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_kq] [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_kfar_kassem] PalQuest calls the outcome "a mockery of justice." [cite:rs_cw3_palquest_kq] On this view the doctrine was real, and so was the state's unwillingness to let it cost anyone very much.

The two readings are not, in the end, opposed claims about the facts; they agree on the facts and differ on which of them defines the trial. The record leaves some things unsettled. The number tried is given as eleven or thirteen. Whether Shadmi faced a murder charge at all is stated differently by Orbach and by Wikipedia's account. The exact coin of his fine varies by source. Who decided to try Shadmi apart from his subordinates, and on narrower charges, is not documented in the sources used here beyond the prosecutor's name, and Laskov's instruction to consider further trials is not followed, in these sources, by any record of a further trial. What the villagers were paid, the reconciliation ceremony the state organized in 1957, and the long argument over whether the killing was linked to a plan for the Triangle's population are told in [scene:cw3_kafr_qasim_memory|the sulha, Plan Mole and the memory of Kafr Qasim].

sections.h: After Kafr Qasim: Compensation, the Sulha, Plan Mole and the Long Memory
sections.html:
This section runs well past the period of this chapter, and deliberately so. What the state paid for the killings at Kafr Qasim, and the reconciliation ceremony it staged in November 1957, belong to the months covered here. But the argument over what the killing meant, and in particular whether it was linked to a plan to drive the Arab population of the Triangle across the border into Jordan, was carried on for more than six decades, and it turned in 2022 on trial records that stayed closed until that year. That argument is followed here to its documented end, and nothing beyond the record of compensation, commemoration, the released records and the state's later words is told. The killing itself is in [scene:mg_s01|Kafr Qasim, 29 October 1956], and the trial in [scene:cw3_kafr_qasim_trial|the Kafr Qasim trial].

The price of a life. In November 1957, a year after the killing and while the trial was still being heard, a special commission recommended what the state should pay. According to a JTA dispatch from Jerusalem, published on 15 November 1957, it proposed IL5,000 to the heirs of each man and woman killed, other sums for dependants and for the wounded, and an additional IL1,000 for the heirs of a pregnant woman. Ben-Gurion pledged to honour the recommendation. [cite:rs_cw3_djn_comp] In the commission's terms, the unborn child whom the village counts as its forty-ninth victim appears as an extra thousand pounds. The same dispatch spoke of "the murder of 48 Arabs." [cite:rs_cw3_djn_comp]

The Encyclopaedia Judaica gives the total: a public board under Pinhas Rashish, the mayor of Petah Tikva, decided to pay IL500,000 in all. [cite:rs_cw3_ej_kafr_qasim] What reached individual survivors could be much less. Jonathan Cook reports that one of them, Saleh Khalil Issa, received 700 lira, less than a year's wage. [cite:rs_cw3_cook_2008] The sources do not say how the half-million was divided among the families, the dependants and the wounded, so Issa's figure cannot be placed within it; it is a single survivor's sum, reported half a century later.

The sulha, 20 November 1957. Five days after the compensation dispatch, the state staged a ceremony of reconciliation in the village. It was called a sulha. According to the historian Shira Robinson, more than 400 guests attended on 20 November 1957, among them cabinet ministers, Mapai legislators, officials of the military government and Histadrut leaders; the event was publicized in the state-sponsored Arabic and Hebrew press. [cite:rs_cw3_robinson_2003]

The ceremony is remembered very differently from the way it was presented. Robinson calls it a "charade" that villagers were pressured to attend. Slyomovics and Khleif, as cited in Wikipedia's account, describe it as "forced upon the villagers." [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_kq] [cite:rs_cw3_robinson_2003] The villagers were not without means of refusal: PalQuest records that they prevented the accused men from being brought to it. [cite:rs_cw3_palquest_kq] The setting itself carried the argument: the ceremony of reconciliation was organized by the state whose police had done the killing, while their officers were still on trial. The state's own aim in using the form, beyond what Robinson's description of the guests and the press coverage shows, is not documented in the sources used here.

Monument and museum. The village's memory was set in stone in 1976, when the first monument was raised. Its inscription called the killings a "painful tragedy" and did not name who had carried them out. [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_kq] [cite:rs_cw3_palquest_kq] Thirty years later, on 29 October 2006, a museum opened in Kafr Qasim, and the education minister, Yuli Tamir, ordered schools to commemorate the event. [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_kq] [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_kfar_kassem] At the sixtieth anniversary in 2016, about 4,000 people marched, and Ayman Odeh called on the government to recognize "the terrible massacre in Kfar Kassem and the historical crimes." [cite:rs_cw3_stljl_60th] Palestinian citizens of Israel had by then long remembered Shadmi's token fine as "Shadmi's penny." [cite:conversation_kafr_qasim_60]

Plan Mole: the claim before the records. The question argued longest about Kafr Qasim is whether the curfew and the killing had a purpose beyond enforcing a curfew. Long before any records were opened, the historian Tom Segev wrote that the sealing-off of the Triangle villages was part of "a contingency plan to expel the inhabitants to Jordan under cover of the war." Cook quoted the line in 2008. [cite:rs_cw3_cook_2008] The plan's name, in the accounts that followed, was Plan Mole, in Hebrew Hafarperet. [cite:rs_cw3_peoplesdispatch] [cite:rs_cw3_mee_kq]

The fight for the records, 2017–2022. The full transcripts of the trial stayed closed for decades. The historian Adam Raz, of the Akevot Institute, applied for their release in about 2017. On 15 December 2021 the Military Prosecution dropped most of its objection. The Military Court of Appeals decided the matter on 31 March 2022, under a gag order; the order was eased on 17 May and lifted on 31 May 2022. The transcripts were published at the end of July 2022. [cite:rs_cw3_akevot_records] [cite:rs_cw3_akevot_mole] [cite:rs_cw3_newarab_kq] [cite:rs_cw3_peoplesdispatch]

What the transcripts contain. The newly released pages contain the testimony of the Border Police commander Chaim Levy. According to Haaretz's reporting of 29 July 2022, as summarized by Peoples Dispatch and Middle East Eye, Levy testified that Shadmi had said "it's desirable that there be some fatalities," and that "the killing of a few people as an intimidation measure can encourage movement eastward." The transcripts also refer to a plan to move the Triangle's Arab population to Jordan in time of war. [cite:rs_cw3_peoplesdispatch] [cite:rs_cw3_mee_kq] This is testimony attributed to Shadmi by another officer, reported through press summaries of a newspaper's reading of the records; Shadmi's own denial at trial, that the question of returning workers had come up at all, stands on the record beside it. [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_kq]

What they do not contain. The text of Plan Mole itself, and related military documents, remained redacted after the 2022 release, according to PalQuest. The New Arab reported that "information on an Israeli plan to deport" Palestinian citizens to Jordan was withheld. [cite:rs_cw3_palquest_kq] [cite:rs_cw3_newarab_kq] What the plan ordered, and whether the killing at Kafr Qasim was meant to set it in motion, therefore rests on testimony about it, not on its own text. [cite:rs_cw3_palquest_kq] [cite:rs_cw3_newarab_kq]

The dispute. Two readings of the released record can be made, and both should be given in their strongest form. The first holds that the killing was part of, or at least linked to, a plan to expel. Its evidence is Levy's testimony that Shadmi called fatalities "desirable" as a way to "encourage movement eastward," the transcripts' references to a wartime plan to move the Triangle's population to Jordan, Segev's earlier statement of "a contingency plan to expel the inhabitants to Jordan under cover of the war," and PalQuest's account of Plan Mole as intended to terrorize and to deport. [cite:rs_cw3_peoplesdispatch] [cite:rs_cw3_cook_2008] [cite:rs_cw3_palquest_kq] On this reading a curfew announced with thirty minutes' warning, on the first evening of a war, in villages a kilometre from the border, was not an administrative blunder.

The second holds that the released record does not show this. The plan's own text is still redacted, so what it provided for is not known. Shadmi denied at trial that the question of returning workers had come up at all. Two of the three units given the order did not shoot, which is hard to square with a plan whose execution depended on killings. And the 1958 court tried the killing as an unlawful order carried out by named officers, not as an act of state policy. [cite:rs_cw3_newarab_kq] [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_kq] [cite:rs_cw3_djn_verdict] On this reading the documents establish testimony about intent, and the existence of a contingency plan, but not an executed policy of expulsion. The two readings agree that a plan was referred to and that a senior officer was said, in testimony, to have spoken of deaths as useful. They divide on whether that testimony describes what happened at Kafr Qasim, and the redacted pages are where the answer would be.

The state's words. Israel's presidents came to Kafr Qasim slowly, and the change in their language can be measured. In December 2007 President Peres said, in Ynet's rendering, "A most difficult incident happened here, which we deeply regret." [cite:rs_cw3_ynet_rivlin] On 26 October 2014 President Rivlin became the first sitting president to attend the village's ceremony, and said: "It was an atrocious massacre. A severe crime was perpetrated here." [cite:rs_cw3_ynet_rivlin] On 29 October 2021 President Herzog went further: "on behalf of myself and the State of Israel, I ask for forgiveness." [cite:rs_cw3_toi_herzog] [cite:rs_cw3_stljl_60th] In fourteen years the head of state's vocabulary moved from an "incident" regretted, to a "massacre" and a "crime," to a request for forgiveness in the state's name.

The legislature did not follow. The Knesset voted down a Joint List bill for the state's formal recognition of the massacre, by 93 votes to 12. Wikipedia, citing Haaretz, dates the vote to 26 October 2021; the Times of Israel places it on the day before Herzog's visit. [cite:rs_cw3_wiki_kq] [cite:rs_cw3_toi_herzog] So in the same week of October 2021 the president asked forgiveness in the name of the state, and the parliament declined to recognize, in law, what he had asked forgiveness for. Kafr Qasim's dead, counted among the documented lives lost to the conflict, appear in this library's [scene:pm_s02|ledger of lives and displacement].

Several things remain unsettled. The text of Plan Mole has not been published, and until it is, whether the killing was meant to trigger it cannot be decided from documents. The testimony about Shadmi's words reaches this book through press summaries of Haaretz's reporting rather than the transcript itself. How the IL500,000 was distributed is not recorded in the sources used here. The date of the Knesset vote differs slightly between the two accounts of it. And no source used here records a formal state act of recognition: as of the latest record here, October 2021, recognition had come from the presidency in words, and been refused by the Knesset in a vote.

sections.h: The Architecture in Spring 1957
sections.html:
On 9 March 1957, the day after the last Israeli troops left the Gaza Strip, President Eisenhower signed into law a joint resolution of Congress on the Middle East. [cite:rs_cw3_pl85_7] [cite:rs_cw3_morris_gaza] The two events, a day apart, mark the end of the Suez–Sinai war and the shape of what replaced the order it had broken. Britain and France had gone to war in October 1956 over the Canal; by the spring their forces were gone, the British Prime Minister had fallen, and the United States had written into its own law an offer of money and, if necessary, armed force to the states of the region. Israel had gone to war, by its own account, to destroy the forces that threatened it and to open the Straits of Tiran; it had withdrawn from everything it took, with a United Nations force in its place and an American statement of policy on the Straits. Egypt had lost Sinai and Gaza for four months and kept the Canal. This section takes stock of that architecture: who now held power in the region, through what instruments, and who was left outside them.

Eden falls, and the alliance is repaired. Eden resigned in January 1957. The State Department's Office of the Historian links his fall to the public criticism the United States directed at its allies during the crisis. [cite:rs_cw3_milestones_suez] [cite:rs_cw3_origins_hahn] The rupture did not last. By March 1957, under Harold Macmillan, relations between Washington and London had recovered. [cite:rs_cw3_milestones_suez] The speed of the repair is itself part of the record. The United States had used the General Assembly and its financial weight against Britain in November, as told earlier in this chapter; four months later the alliance was intact. On one reading its terms had changed: in the Middle East, the senior partner was now in Washington.

The Eisenhower Doctrine: the request. The instrument of that change was the Doctrine that bears Eisenhower's name. On 1 January 1957 the President met congressional leaders at the White House for four hours; on 5 January he asked Congress for authority to give military and economic aid to Middle Eastern states and to use force to protect them. [cite:rs_cw3_lawfare_waxman] The request came while Israel was still in Sinai and Gaza, and the debate in Congress ran in parallel with the withdrawal fight told in the previous section.

The House of Representatives passed the measure, House Joint Resolution 117, on 30 January 1957 by 355 votes to 61. The Senate passed it, as amended, on 5 March 1957 by 72 to 19. [cite:rs_cw3_voteview_h3] [cite:rs_cw3_voteview_s10] The margins were wide in both chambers, but the Senate took five weeks longer than the House and changed the text. One exchange that Waxman records shows the hesitation. Senator Richard Russell warned against any appearance that only "a small war" might follow; Eisenhower replied that "should Russia move it could not possibly be a small war." [cite:rs_cw3_lawfare_waxman]

What the law said. Public Law 85-7, 71 Statutes at Large 5, approved 9 March 1957, is short, and each of its six sections defined a piece of the new structure. [cite:rs_cw3_pl85_7]

Section 1 authorized the President "to cooperate with and assist any nation or group of nations in the general area of the Middle East" in developing economic strength to maintain their independence. [cite:rs_cw3_pl85_7] [cite:rs_cw3_cornell_22usc1961]

Section 2 was the heart of it. The United States "is prepared to use armed forces" if the President deemed it necessary to assist any nation that requested help "against armed aggression from any country controlled by international communism," acting "consonant with the treaty obligations of the United States and with the Constitution." [cite:rs_cw3_pl85_7] The clause named one threat only. On a plain reading of its wording it did not reach a war between Israel and an Arab state, or between Arab states, unless one of them could be described as controlled by international communism.

Section 3 provided the money, and its terms are precise. The President could use up to $200,000,000 "from any appropriation now available" under the Mutual Security Act of 1954, for the rest of fiscal year 1957, and only fifteen days after reporting to the congressional committees. The resolution itself authorized no new appropriation. [cite:rs_cw3_pl85_7] [cite:rs_cw3_cornell_22usc1961] The Doctrine did not add to the foreign-aid budget; it gave the President authority to redirect money Congress had already voted, under congressional notice.

Section 4 declared support for the United Nations Emergency Force, the body now stationed between Egypt and Israel. Section 5 required the President to report to Congress each January and July. Section 6 let the resolution expire on a presidential finding or a concurrent resolution of Congress. [cite:rs_cw3_pl85_7] [cite:rs_cw3_cornell_22usc1961]

Where the money went. According to the historian Peter Hahn, the United States under the Doctrine "immediately dispensed tens of millions of dollars in aid" to Turkey, Iran, Pakistan, Iraq, Saudi Arabia, Lebanon and Libya. [cite:rs_cw3_origins_hahn] Israel is not on his list; the Doctrine's first beneficiaries were other states of the region, several of them Arab. How the money was divided among the recipients is not established in the sources used for this book; the allocations of the Richards mission remain an open question. The force clause was tested the next year. In 1958 Eisenhower sent about 14,000 troops to Lebanon, but, as Matthew Waxman notes, without citing the resolution. [cite:rs_cw3_lawfare_waxman] That episode belongs to Stage Four.

The dispute: communism or succession? What the Doctrine was for is read in two ways. By its text, it was about communism: the force clause applies only to aggression "from any country controlled by international communism." [cite:rs_cw3_pl85_7] The Office of the Historian frames it differently, as a response to American concern about European power in the region after Suez, one that "gave the administration increased power to aid countries in the region"; and Hahn records the aid flowing at once to regional allies. [cite:rs_cw3_milestones_suez] [cite:rs_cw3_origins_hahn] On this second reading, the Doctrine was the means by which the United States took up the role in the Middle East that Britain and France had lost at Suez, with anti-communism as its legal basis rather than its whole purpose. On this book's reading the two are compatible: the law's stated enemy was Moscow, and its practical effect was to put Washington where London and Paris had stood.

Nasser. Whether Egypt's army was beaten in Sinai or withdrew to defend the Canal is disputed, as the account of the war itself shows; politically, Nasser emerged stronger. In Hahn's words, Nasser gained prestige among Arab peoples as "a leader who had defied European empires and survived a military invasion by Israel." [cite:rs_cw3_origins_hahn] He kept the Canal, whose nationalization had begun the crisis. He now hosted on Egyptian soil a United Nations force, which remained until he ordered it out in May 1967; his later wars are told in [scene:egi_src_s03|Egypt's wars, 1967–73].

The war's cost also fell on Egypt's Jews. The Jewish Agency's history records that many Egyptian Jews emigrated to Israel as "an indirect outcome of the war." [cite:rs_cw3_jafi_fedayeen] That phrase leaves out what the documents show of arrests, expulsions and the proclamation of 23 November 1956, told in full in [scene:cw3_egypt_jews|the Jews of Egypt].

Israel's gains. For Israel the balance sheet was mixed, and both columns are documented. On the gains side, Ben-Gurion told the Knesset on 5 March 1957 that free passage through the Straits of Tiran had been secured, "vital to Israel, and is also of great importance to other countries," and that UN forces stood at Sharm el-Sheikh and in Gaza. [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_bg_mar57] The Israel Defense Forces describe the campaign as "an impressive military success" because it halted the attacks from the Egyptian border. [cite:rs_cw3_idf_sinai] UNEF remained on Egyptian soil as "a buffer against Egyptian-Israeli hostilities" until May 1967. [cite:rs_cw3_origins_hahn]

The French alliance outlasted the war. The reactor agreement Peres finalized at Sèvres, told with the conference itself, bore fruit in September 1957, when France delivered a reactor of twice the capacity first promised. [cite:rs_cw3_shlaim_sevres] That story belongs to Stage Four. So does a second consequence: between 1956 and 1958, meetings in Europe, Ankara and Tehran produced the "Trident" intelligence alliance of Israel, Iran and Turkey, driven in part by the Sinai campaign and concern over Nasser's Egypt, and told in [scene:ira_s00c|the periphery alliance]. [cite:foreignaffairs_trident_legacy]

Israel's costs. On the other side of the ledger, Israel had withdrawn from all it had taken without a peace treaty or a recognized border change; the assurances it relied on were an American statement of policy and its own stated assumptions in the General Assembly, and whether these amounted to guarantees is disputed, as the previous section showed. It had been condemned by an Assembly in which only Britain, France, Australia and New Zealand had voted with it on the cease-fire, and it had been publicly pressed by an American President. [cite:rs_cw3_unproj_997] [cite:rs_cw3_app_20feb57] And it had been seen to fight alongside Britain and France, the two powers whose regional role, in Hahn's account, the war ended. [cite:rs_cw3_origins_hahn] Inside Israel, the war's first day had also been the day of the killings at Kafr Qasim, whose trial opened in March 1957. On 29 October 1957, the first anniversary of both, a grenade thrown into the Knesset chamber wounded Ben-Gurion and several ministers. [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_knesset3]

The dispute: who won? The question has two well-argued answers. The first is that Israel won, militarily and strategically. Michael Oren, offering an interpretation, argues that Israel emerged "economically, diplomatically, and militarily stronger," and that the war partly fulfilled goals the 1949 armistices had left open: Tiran opened, the fedayeen stopped, the French alliance and its reactor secured. [cite:rs_cw3_oren_hnn] The IDF's own verdict, as above, rests on the end of the raids from the Egyptian border. [cite:rs_cw3_idf_sinai]

The second answer is that Nasser won, politically. He kept the Canal and gained standing across the Arab world; Britain and France lost their regional role; and Israel was tied to the colonial powers and forced out without a treaty. [cite:rs_cw3_origins_hahn] Oren himself reports this case from his opponents: Avi Shlaim and other New Historians argued that Israel paid a heavy political price for aligning with colonial powers, and Fromkin called the victory Pyrrhic. [cite:rs_cw3_oren_hnn] Those last two judgements reach this book through Oren's summary of them, not from their own texts.

The two answers are measuring different things. Oren and the IDF count what changed on Israel's borders and in its alliances in the decade that followed; Hahn, Shlaim and Fromkin count what changed in the region's politics and in Israel's standing within them. On the documents used here, both sets of changes happened. On this book's reading, Britain and France were the clear losers in either accounting, and the United States, which had fought no battle, emerged with the largest new role.

Ben-Gurion's own verdict. The man who had led Israel into the war gave the army a sober one. Addressing the army's senior command on 27 December 1956, in the debriefing in which he called the campaign "a war deluxe," a phrase discussed in the account of the war itself, he warned that the next war "could be a prolonged one" and that Israel might then be "the defenders" rather than the attackers. [cite:rs_cw3_jpost_dec56] There was, he said, "no basis to assume that in the next war, we will have helping forces from abroad." [cite:rs_cw3_idf_archive] [cite:rs_cw3_jpost_dec56]

What the record leaves open. How the Doctrine's money was divided among the states Hahn names, and what the Richards mission allocated to each, is not established in the sources used for this book. Whether the Doctrine was chiefly about communism or chiefly about succeeding Britain and France is a matter of interpretation; its text supports the first, its context and its first payments the second. And who won the war depends, as shown, on what is being counted. What the documents used here do show is the structure that stood in spring 1957: British and French forces out of Egypt and Eden out of office; the United States committed by statute, with up to $200 million of existing funds and an offer of force against communist aggression; Egypt in possession of the Canal and host to a United Nations force it could dismiss; and Israel back behind the armistice lines, with Tiran open on the strength of an American statement of policy, a French reactor on the way, and no treaty.

chapters.label: Stage Four
chapters.title: Arm
chapters.intro:
In March 1957 Israel left Sinai and Gaza, forced out by American and Soviet pressure after the war told in [scene:cw3_withdrawal|the withdrawal]. It came out of that war with less than it wanted and more than it showed. It stood outside every regional alignment, since Western defence in the region had been organized around the Baghdad Pact without it. It had no American weapons of consequence: the largest American arms sale to Israel had carried a ceiling of $1 million. [cite:rs_cw4_kramer_hawks] It had no written guarantee from Washington, only the Eisenhower Doctrine's promise of support against a Communist attack, never put on paper. [cite:rs_cw4_frus58_d36] What it did have, unannounced, was a French commitment made in the autumn of 1956 to supply a research reactor, and a request on the table in Paris for a plant to extract plutonium. [cite:rs_cw4_goldschmidt] [cite:rs_cw4_fas_israel]

This stage asks how Israel armed itself in the five years after Suez, and from whom: a reactor able to produce plutonium from France, money and arms from a West Germany that would not exchange ambassadors with it, secret partners beyond the Arab states, and, in August 1962, the first major American weapon. It asks with equal weight what each supplier wanted in return, who inside each government resisted, and what Israel told the governments that found out. The answer is not one decision but a set of channels, most of them secret, each run by a few officials and each contested inside its own government.

The cast is wide. In Israel, Ben-Gurion led the government until he resigned in protest in January 1961, a resignation that forced an early election; Shimon Peres ran the French and German channels; Isser Harel's Mossad ran the intelligence partnerships, the capture of Adolf Eichmann and the negotiation over Morocco's Jews; Golda Meir and Abba Eban carried the diplomacy. In France a small circle of ministers and atomic officials made the reactor agreement over the hesitation of the head of their own atomic agency, and Charles de Gaulle tried to take back part of it. In Bonn, Franz Josef Strauss and Konrad Adenauer made a partnership kept off the books. In Washington, Eisenhower and Dulles declined to arm Israel or guarantee it in writing; Eisenhower's administration discovered Dimona late and handed the question to Kennedy, who accepted a visit in place of inspection and in 1962 offered the Hawk. [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] [cite:rs_cw4_barjoseph] Around Israel stood Nasser's United Arab Republic, Adnan Menderes's Turkey, the Shah's Iran and a new king in Morocco. Palestinians appear in the governments' papers chiefly as refugees; in these same years Fatah took shape abroad and Al-Ard inside Israel. [cite:rs_cw4_palquest_fatah] [cite:rs_cw4_jiryis_pij]

The sections that follow begin with [scene:cw4_french_deal|the French reactor], from Atoms for Peace in 1955 to de Gaulle's compromise of 1960. The regional story comes next: the periphery doctrine and its secret intelligence pact with Turkey and Iran, the upheavals of 1958 in Lebanon and Iraq, and the ten days in August when Israel closed its airspace to Western flights. Two sections turn inward and outward from Israel's own society, to the protest of North African immigrants at Wadi Salib in 1959 and to Palestinian politics in exile and under military rule. The armistice lines with Syria and the Sinai surprise of 1960 follow, then Bonn's quiet partnership and the politics of the Eichmann case, and Iran's oil, intelligence ties and de facto recognition. The core of the stage is the reactor's discovery: how Washington found it, what each government said in the disclosure month of December 1960, and Kennedy's first visit and his meeting with Ben-Gurion at the Waldorf-Astoria. The Lavon affair's second round, which brought down the government, the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, and the agreement that opened Morocco's gates complete the picture, and the stage closes with [scene:cw4_hawk|the Hawk decision], when American refusal became an offer.
chapters.outro:
By the end of 1962 Israel was armed through channels that had not existed in March 1957, and almost none of them rested on a public commitment. Each was run by a few officials, each was disputed inside the government that ran it, and each left a record thinner than the thing it built.

The legal layer was the thinnest. The French agreement of 1957 is known in outline, not in text: a 24-megawatt reactor with systems built for three times that power, a reprocessing plant covered by protocols that were never written down, and a signature that, in Peres's and Goldschmidt's accounts, was backdated by a day because the Bourgès-Maunoury government had fallen, though the signing date is given several ways. [cite:rs_cw4_fas_israel] [cite:rs_cw4_goldschmidt] [cite:rs_cw4_peres_memoir] De Gaulle's compromise of 1960 set it on new terms, Israel's pledge of no weapons and no reprocessing against France's agreement not to insist on inspection. [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_nuclear] Ben-Gurion then refused inspection by the International Atomic Energy Agency "until all reactors are treated as equals." [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] The pact with Turkey was a secret agreement between prime ministers; Iran's recognition of Israel was de facto, and spoken of in public only in 1960; Bonn withheld diplomatic relations. [cite:rs_cw4_schonmann_2024] [cite:rs_cw4_frus58v12_d273] [cite:rs_cw4_kas_borchard] What did take public legal form was American: the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 and the Agency for International Development, created inside the State Department by Executive Order 10973. [cite:rs_cw4_eo10973] At the United Nations, Resolution 138 asked Israel for "appropriate reparation" for Eichmann's seizure, and Resolution 171 called its raid of March 1962 "a flagrant violation." [cite:rs_cw4_unsc138] [cite:rs_cw4_unsc171]

The administrative layer shows who could act. Israel's armament ran through the Prime Minister: Peres for France and Germany, Manes Pratt at Dimona, the Mossad, under Harel and directly under Ben-Gurion, for the Trident, SAVAK's training, Eichmann and Morocco. [cite:rs_cw4_alpher_brookings] [cite:rs_cw4_isa_eichmann] [cite:rs_cw4_wiki_yachin] The cabinet was not bypassed. It adopted the periphery on 20 July 1958 and divided six to five over Hausner's Lavon opinion and over immunity for Eichmann's defence witnesses. [cite:rs_cw4_schonmann_2024] [cite:rs_cw4_djn_1960_10] [cite:rs_cw4_isa_eichmann] Nor could the Prime Minister always carry it. In the Lavon quarrel, at bottom a fight over which forum could find the facts, a committee of ministers cleared Lavon, Ben-Gurion resigned in protest on 31 January 1961, and the election that followed cost Mapai five seats. [cite:rs_cw4_cie_bg_resigns] [cite:rs_cw4_idi_1961] Inside Israel the same years produced Wadi Salib, where the Etzioni commission, as its report is summarized, found no deliberate discrimination by state institutions but discrimination at lower levels of implementation. [cite:rs_cw4_hamichlol_wadisalib]

The institutional and financial layer is where the record is most divided. West Germany's "Aktion Geschäftsfreund" sent 629.4 million marks to 1965, booked through a Frankfurt development bank as aid to unnamed developing countries, alongside military financing put at 340 million marks by German records and 500 million by one historian. [cite:rs_cw4_barjoseph] American aid ran in the tens of millions a year, $93.4 million in 1962, of which $13.2 million was military and all of that loans. [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_aid_table] Iran sold the crude that made the Eilat pipeline work. [cite:rs_cw4_frus58v12_d273] Morocco was paid, by reported terms, $500,000 down and then a sum for each emigrant. [cite:rs_cw4_aish_egoz] Who paid for Dimona is the open question at the center of this layer. Eisenhower said "we do not know where they have obtained the funds"; the estimates ran from the embassy's $17.8 million in foreign exchange to $100–200 million; Peres put a known half at about $40 million, from donors in one version and from the government in another; and the case that German money filled the gap is a probability on indirect evidence for Bar-Joseph, who concedes it cannot be asserted unequivocally, and unproven on the documents. [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] [cite:rs_cw4_natinterest]

The Palestinian layer was a politics without a channel to any of these decisions. Fatah's founders in Kuwait, whose movement became public in Beirut in October 1959, chose to act independently of the Arab governments; Al-Ard, inside Israel and under military government, chose the licensing law, the companies registry and the courts, and was refused a newspaper licence. [cite:rs_cw4_palquest_fatah] [cite:rs_cw4_jiryis_pij] In the documents where the refugees' future was discussed, at the Waldorf in May 1961 and in Feldman's talks of August 1962, they did not speak: Ben-Gurion called them the Arab states' "best weapon at hand," Kennedy cited America's 70 percent of UNRWA's costs, and the Johnson plan did not win Israel's consent in August 1962. [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_memcon] [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_feldman_aug19]

The regional layer turned in 1958. The United Arab Republic, the fall of Iraq's monarchy and the American landing in Lebanon remade the region, and the loss of Iraq brought Turkey toward Israel. The Trident that followed was, in Alpher's assessment, lopsided, and Israel valued it chiefly as proof that it was not isolated. [cite:rs_cw4_liel_bmlv] [cite:rs_cw4_apn_review] [cite:foreignaffairs_trident_legacy] Egypt broke with Iran after the Shah spoke of recognition in July 1960, for reasons the sources weigh differently. [cite:rs_cw4_iranica_akhavi] On the armistice lines, the Mixed Armistice Commission condemned Israel's attack on Tawafiq and the Security Council called its attack of March 1962 a flagrant violation, while Egypt's move into Sinai in February 1960 showed how little warning Israel might have. [cite:rs_cw4_unyb1960] [cite:rs_cw4_unsc171] [cite:rs_cw4_wiki_rotem]

The American layer moved furthest. In August 1958 Washington refused Israel arms and a written guarantee and Dulles approved "extreme caution" in encouraging Ben-Gurion's periphery plan. [cite:rs_cw4_schonmann_2017] By December 1960 it had judged that weapons were "at least one major purpose" at Dimona. [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] By 1962 it had accepted Israeli assurances and two visits on Israeli terms, and had offered the Hawk, which it told the world was "purely defensive" while renewing to Nasser its assurances about the reactor. [cite:rs_cw4_frus61_d53] [cite:rs_cw4_frus62_d87] [cite:rs_cw4_kramer_hawks]

What was settled, then, was the existence of the channels and Israel's place at their center. What was contested was what they were for. Israel's strongest case was Ben-Gurion's: a small state forced out of Sinai, refused American arms and a written guarantee, facing a neighbour he expected to do "what Hitler did," would not leave its survival to another government's word. [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_memcon] The strongest case of its critics was put by its own allies: Eisenhower's advisers found the plant "not for peaceful uses," cabled about a "lack of candor," and Kennedy warned that the United Arab Republic would follow Israel into the field; inside Israel, according to Aronson, Leibowitz and Livne's committee was the only public voice of dissent. [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_memcon] [cite:rs_cw4_aronson_ch6] What the record leaves open lies at the reactor's heart: whether a separation plant existed in 1961 that two visitors were kept from seeing, who paid for Dimona, and what Ben-Gurion meant by "for the time being." Those questions passed to Kennedy's confrontation of 1963, told in [scene:s11b|the 1963 letters].

sections.h: The French Reactor, 1955–1960
sections.html:
The war of October and November 1956, told in [scene:cw3_war|the Suez war], ended for Israel in a forced withdrawal from Sinai and Gaza. It also left behind something that outlasted the withdrawal: an agreement with France that gave Israel a reactor able to produce plutonium. The story of how that agreement was reached, signed, built and then nearly undone runs from 1955 to the end of 1960. It is a story told almost entirely from French recollections, Israeli memoirs and the work of a small number of American and Israeli scholars. That limits what can be stated with certainty, and the limits are part of the record.

Two tracks: the open one. Israel's nuclear program began on two tracks at once, one public and one secret. On 12 July 1955 Israel signed a general "Atoms for Peace" agreement with the United States, the second country to do so. In the same year, according to William Burr and Avner Cohen's documentary collection for the National Security Archive, Ben-Gurion launched a secret feasibility initiative and delegated it to Shimon Peres. [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] The public track produced a small American research reactor. On 20 March 1957 Israel signed a contract with the American firm AMF for a 1-megawatt pool reactor at Nahal Soreq. Construction began in January 1958, the final contract was signed on 19 March 1958, and the reactor reached criticality in a public ceremony in June 1960. [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] Soreq was everything that the second track was not: small, American, announced and celebrated.

Israel did try the American route for something larger first. In July–September 1956 Ernst David Bergmann asked the United States for a reactor and heavy water. The Atomic Energy Commission was willing, but only under stricter safeguards, and Israel dropped the probe. [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] The episode matters for what followed. A reactor from Washington would have come with conditions on how it was used and who could see it. Israel looked elsewhere.

The request in Paris, September 1956. It looked to France. The fullest account of the first request comes from Bertrand Goldschmidt, of France's atomic energy commission, the Commissariat à l'énergie atomique (CEA), in an interview that Avner Cohen recorded in Paris on 15 June 1993. It is a recollection given almost four decades after the event, and Cohen himself notes that Goldschmidt often said he did not remember. [cite:rs_cw4_goldschmidt] With that caution, Goldschmidt recalled attending the meeting in September 1956 at which Peres asked for French help. The request had two parts. The first, a reactor, was "relatively easy to agree upon." The second, a plant to extract plutonium from the reactor's spent fuel (a reprocessing plant), was "quite difficult." [cite:rs_cw4_goldschmidt]

The difficulty lay inside the CEA. According to Goldschmidt, the high commissioner, Francis Perrin, hesitated for weeks over the reprocessing plant until Pierre Guillaumat urged Goldschmidt to persuade him. Perrin later accused Goldschmidt of "extorting" his signature. [cite:rs_cw4_goldschmidt] The two halves of the request were not equivalent. A research reactor could be presented as science. A separation plant was the step that turned a reactor's output into material for a weapon, and the man at the head of France's atomic agency did not want to sign for it. That he was brought round, by his own colleague's account, at Guillaumat's urging, suggests that the decision was made by a small circle within the French state and against reluctance inside it.

France agreed in the autumn of 1956. According to the Federation of American Scientists and the Jewish Virtual Library, it agreed at that stage to supply an 18-megawatt (thermal) research reactor. [cite:rs_cw4_fas_israel] [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_nuclear] The Nuclear Weapon Archive, a privately compiled reference last revised in 1997, calls the Suez Crisis "the genesis of Israel's nuclear weapons production program" and dates a secret meeting of Golda Meir, Peres and the French ministers Pineau and Maurice Bourgès-Maunoury to 7 November 1956. [cite:rs_cw4_nwa_isrhist] The Archive is a reported source and gives no document for the meeting, so its date rests on its own authority. Its framing, that the war and the nuclear agreement were bound together, is consistent with the timing in the other sources: the request came in September, the war in October, and the agreement was developed over the following year. What those sources do not establish is what was said in any one meeting.

The agreements of 1957. What France offered grew between 1956 and 1957. The Federation of American Scientists and the Jewish Virtual Library both state that a revised agreement, which they date to 3 October 1957, provided for a 24-megawatt reactor, not 18, and that its cooling and waste systems were designed for three times that power. The chemical reprocessing plant, the "quite difficult" half of Peres's request, was covered in protocols that were not written down. [cite:rs_cw4_fas_israel] [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_nuclear] Those three features, a reactor larger than first offered, systems built for far more than its rated power, and a separation plant agreed only in unwritten form, are the core of what the documentary record can say about the deal.

A fuller version comes from a single reported source. Rebecca M. Miller, writing in The National Interest, describes the 1957 package as three confidential contracts: one for a 24-megawatt heavy-water reactor, a loan of 385 tonnes of natural uranium, joint nuclear-weapons research and production, and backing for a plutonium extraction plant. [cite:rs_cw4_natinterest] That account goes further than the others in one respect that matters, since it names weapons research as a term of the agreement. It is attributed here to its author and has not been confirmed from the other sources gathered for this section, which speak of a reactor and a reprocessing plant but not of a weapons clause.

The signature and its date. When the 1957 agreement was signed is itself disputed, and the dispute is revealing rather than trivial. The Federation of American Scientists and the Jewish Virtual Library give 3 October 1957. Burr and Cohen's briefing book gives 3 October or 30 October 1957. [cite:rs_cw4_fas_israel] [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_nuclear] [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] A second set of sources tells a different story, in which the date on the document is not the date it was signed. According to the Center for Israel Education, Prime Minister Maurice Bourgès-Maunoury dated his approval 30 September but signed on 1 October, the day his government fell. [cite:rs_cw4_cie_backdate] Goldschmidt, in his 1993 interview, said the document was backdated by one day because Bourgès-Maunoury had lost a no-confidence vote, and that his successor, Félix Gaillard, was "totally unaware" of it on taking office. [cite:rs_cw4_goldschmidt]

Peres told the same story from the Israeli side. In his memoir he recalled watching Bourgès-Maunoury, after his government had fallen, sign the letter authorizing the reactor sale and date it the previous day. "I asked no questions," he wrote, and he called it "the most generous display of friendship I had ever known." [cite:rs_cw4_peres_memoir] The two accounts are therefore of different kinds. One gives a calendar date taken from the agreement's face, and the sources that hold it differ among themselves by four weeks. The other is the testimony of two men who said they were present, one French and one Israeli, and who agree that the date on the paper was earlier than the day it was signed, placing the signature inside the life of a government that had already fallen. If accurate, the second account suggests that the commitment was made by a prime minister whose government had lost a no-confidence vote, and, by Goldschmidt's account, that his successor took office unaware of it. The sources gathered here cannot settle which date is right, and this section gives none as certain.

Building in secret. The reactor was built at Dimona, outside the inspection system of the International Atomic Energy Agency, under Colonel Manes Pratt. At the peak of construction about 1,500 Israelis and some French workers were employed. The largest components, such as the reactor tank, passed through French customs described as parts of a desalination plant bound for Latin America. [cite:rs_cw4_fas_israel] [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_nuclear] When the ground was broken is reported differently: the Nuclear Weapon Archive dates it to early 1958, while the American scientists who visited the site in 1961 were told that ground was broken in 1959. [cite:rs_cw4_nwa_isrhist] Neither date is confirmed by a primary document in the sources gathered here.

A heavy-water reactor needs heavy water, and here the record reaches beyond France. On 25 February 1959 Israel and Norway signed an agreement under which Norway, through the seller NORATOM, sold Israel 20 tons of heavy water, shipped via the United Kingdom. Richard Kerry, the American political officer in Oslo, warned that disclosure could embarrass Norway. [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] The Federation of American Scientists separately reports that the French Air Force secretly flew up to four tons of heavy water to Israel. [cite:rs_cw4_fas_israel] The two reports are not alternatives. Both may be true, and they describe two different channels, one commercial and documented in American records, the other military and reported by a single scholarly source.

The mechanism, then, ran through a few hands. In Israel, Ben-Gurion authorized the program and delegated it to Peres; Bergmann had made the failed American approach; Pratt built the site. In France, the decision was made at the level of ministers and the leadership of the CEA, and by the account of a man who was there it was pushed through over the reluctance of the agency's own head. The customs declaration and the absence of inspection kept it from outside view. Who paid for the construction is not stated in the sources for this section; the question of where Dimona's money came from was raised by American officials in December 1960 and is taken up later in this chapter.

De Gaulle's review, 1960. Under Charles de Gaulle the agreement came under review. In May 1960, according to the Federation of American Scientists and the Jewish Virtual Library, France pressed Israel to disclose the project and accept international inspection, threatening to withhold the reactor's fuel. De Gaulle offered to sell Israel fighter aircraft in exchange for halting work on the reprocessing plant. The Jewish Virtual Library adds that de Gaulle feared a scandal at a time when France's position was already strained by the Algerian war. [cite:rs_cw4_fas_israel] [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_nuclear]

The historian Shlomo Aronson puts the matter more sharply. He writes that de Gaulle "secretly advised Israel that he had decided to abrogate the 1957 accord," at the moment in May 1960 when Pinhas Lavon was reviving the affair that bore his name, and that this crisis was concealed and became widely known only years later. [cite:rs_cw4_aronson_ch6] The timing meant that Ben-Gurion faced the threatened loss of the French reactor and the reopening of the Lavon affair in the same weeks; the political half of that story is told later in this chapter, in the section on the Lavon affair reopened.

The compromise. The crisis was resolved by a compromise. France would supply the uranium and components already ordered and would not insist on inspections. Israel, for its part, would state that it had no intention of making atomic weapons, would not reprocess plutonium, would reveal the reactor, and would finish it without French help. [cite:rs_cw4_fas_israel] [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_nuclear] The Nuclear Weapon Archive dates the agreement to November 1960. [cite:rs_cw4_nwa_isrhist]

What the compromise changed is disputed. On one reading, held by the Federation of American Scientists and the Nuclear Weapon Archive, it was a real change: Israel pledged no weapons and no reprocessing, agreed to reveal the reactor, and work on the plutonium plant halted. [cite:rs_cw4_fas_israel] [cite:rs_cw4_nwa_isrhist] On the other, the Jewish Virtual Library says that little changed in practice. [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_nuclear] The second reading draws support from later work by Cohen and Burr, who document a concealed underground separation plant at Dimona; that evidence belongs to the American visits of the Kennedy years and is weighed in the sections that follow. The strongest form of the first case is that France did withdraw its help on the separation plant, which by Goldschmidt's account had always been the hard part, and that Israel made formal commitments it had not made before. The strongest form of the second is that the reactor, its oversized systems and the uranium already ordered all remained, that France gave up any claim to inspect, and that Israel was left to finish the work alone and unwatched.

The case for and the one voice against. Israel's leaders did not explain the program in public in these years, so its rationale has to be read from what was done rather than from what was said. The section on the Trident, later in this chapter, gives a former Israeli intelligence officer's account of Ben-Gurion's grand strategies, among which a nuclear deterrent stood beside a great-power ally and alliances beyond the Arab states. The strongest Israeli case, in those terms, is that a small state that had just been forced out of Sinai by both superpowers, and that had been refused a reactor without American conditions, sought a means of security that did not depend on anyone else's guarantee. The strongest case against was made at the time by Israelis themselves. According to Aronson, the only public voice of internal controversy over Dimona was the Public Committee for Nuclear Disarmament in the Middle East, led by Yeshayahu Leibowitz and Eliezer Livne. [cite:rs_cw4_aronson_ch6] The sources gathered here record the committee's existence and its leaders but not its arguments in its own words, and this section does not supply them.

What the record does not settle. Several things remain open. The exact date on which the 1957 agreement was signed cannot be fixed from these sources; the candidates are 30 September (as dated), 1 October (as signed, by the backdating accounts), 3 October and 30 October. The terms of the agreement are known in outline but not from its text: the reprocessing protocols were unwritten by design, and the fuller three-contract version with its weapons clause rests on one reported source. When construction at Dimona began is reported as early 1958 and as 1959. What the 1960 compromise actually changed at the site is disputed between sources that say the separation plant was halted and sources that say little changed. And the date of de Gaulle's message, as Aronson describes it, is given only as May 1960.

The familiar account is that Israel's nuclear program was a single secret decision, hidden from everyone. The record is more divided: a French president who, within three years, tried to take back the most sensitive part of what his predecessors had given, and an Israeli government left to finish the work alone. How the United States learned of the reactor is told in [scene:cw4_dimona_discovery|how Washington found Dimona]. Kennedy's escalating confrontation with Israel's government over Dimona belongs to 1963 and is told in [scene:s11b|the 1963 letters].

sections.h: The Periphery and the Trident, 1957–1958
sections.html:
The French reactor answered one of Israel's weaknesses after Suez. Another was diplomatic: in 1957 Israel stood outside every regional alignment. Western regional defence had been organized without it, in the alliance told in [scene:cw2_baghdad_bandung|the Baghdad Pact and Bandung], and the Sinai war had then ended with American and Soviet pressure forcing Israel's withdrawal. The answer that Ben-Gurion's government worked out between early 1957 and the autumn of 1958 was to look past its Arab neighbours to the states beyond them: Turkey, Iran and Ethiopia, and in some versions Sudan. Israeli officials came to call this the periphery. Its most concrete product was a secret intelligence pact with Turkey and Iran, the Trident.

The word. "Periphery" was Israel's own policy language, and it describes the region as seen from Jerusalem: an inner ring of hostile Arab states and an outer ring of non-Arab states that might be friendly. The historian Noa Schonmann, who has worked through the Israeli archival record, notes that Israeli documents used another phrase for it, the "Outer Circle." [cite:rs_cw4_schonmann_2024] Both terms carry a point of view. Turkey, Iran and Ethiopia were not peripheral to themselves. Each was a state with its own government and its own reasons for dealing with Israel, and, on Alpher's account below, each kept the relationship at the level it chose. This section uses the word because it was the policy's name, not as a description of the countries it named.

The roots, 1957. The first approach in the record came from Ethiopia, not from Israel. According to Schonmann, Emperor Haile Selassie initiated contact in February 1957 through Israel's defence ministry delegation in Paris. [cite:rs_cw4_schonmann_2024] Ben-Gurion's thinking about Turkey can be followed in his private writing. On 15 September 1957 he wrote to his daughter that the Middle East had only two stable states, Turkey and Israel; on 16 October 1957 he recorded in his diary that Israel and Turkey were the only stable, free and democratic countries in the region. Both are cited by the scholar Alon Liel. [cite:rs_cw4_liel_bmlv] Schonmann writes that the foundations of the policy were in place by the Syrian crisis of August 1957. [cite:rs_cw4_schonmann_2024]

The first meeting with Turkey's leadership took place in Paris. On 15 December 1957 Israel's ambassador to Italy, Eliyahu Sasson, met the Turkish Prime Minister, Adnan Menderes, and proposed linking the Mossad with Turkey's intelligence service. [cite:rs_cw4_schonmann_2024] The proposal was for intelligence cooperation, not a public alliance, and that shape held for the whole of what followed.

The next meeting showed where the two governments' interests parted. At a follow-up in early April 1958, Menderes proposed a coup in Syria. Ben-Gurion rejected it. [cite:rs_cw4_schonmann_2024] The Turkish Prime Minister brought to the relationship an aim of his own, the overthrow of the government of a neighbouring state, and the Israeli Prime Minister declined to join it. Whatever the periphery became, it was not, in its first year, an agreement in which one side simply adopted the other's plans.

July 1958: from contacts to policy. The turn came with the revolution in Baghdad on 14 July 1958, told in the next section, which killed Iraq's king and its prime minister. Liel writes that the Baghdad Pact thereby lost its main pillar, and that Turkey sought closer ties with Israel. [cite:rs_cw4_liel_bmlv] For Ankara, the Arab state on which its regional alliance had rested had fallen to a government it could not count on. For Jerusalem, the same event made an approach that had been tentative look necessary.

Ben-Gurion moved within a week. Schonmann writes that he presented the plan to his government on 20 July 1958, when it was adopted as state policy. Her sources are the Israel State Archives' minutes of the government meetings of 20 and 28 July 1958 and of the Knesset Foreign Affairs and Security Committee of 16 July and 19 August 1958. [cite:rs_cw4_schonmann_2024] The archival trail matters, because it shows that the periphery was not the private project of one man or one service. It went before the cabinet twice and the Knesset's security committee twice in five weeks.

The letter to Eisenhower, 24 July 1958. Four days after the cabinet decision, Ben-Gurion wrote to President Eisenhower seeking American support for a pact of Turkey, Iran, Ethiopia and Sudan with Israel. The letter's central image survives in two renderings. Schonmann translates it as "a strong dam against the Nasserist–Soviet torrent"; Liel's German version reads, in English, "a strong dam against Nasser's wild Sovietism." [cite:rs_cw4_schonmann_2017] [cite:rs_cw4_liel_bmlv] The two are close in sense and both present Nasser's Egypt and Soviet influence as a single flood. They differ in emphasis: one speaks of a "Nasserist–Soviet" current, the other of Nasser's own "Sovietism." The original Hebrew or English text is not among the sources gathered here, and this section does not choose between the translations. Eisenhower replied on 25 July, promising a fuller answer from Secretary of State Dulles. [cite:rs_cw4_schonmann_2017]

What did Ben-Gurion want from Washington? Schonmann's answer is that the plan aimed at "political friendship" with non-Arab states rather than military aid, and at creating "a phantom of a pact" that would persuade Washington of Israel's regional value. [cite:rs_cw4_schonmann_2024] The phrase is hers, and it is an interpretation, but it fits the shape of the letter: a pact presented to the United States as a barrier against Nasser and Moscow, which would make Israel worth supporting. Isser Harel, the head of the Mossad, put the same idea in other words, describing Israel as possibly "the long arm" of the United States in Asia and Africa. [cite:rs_cw4_schonmann_2024] Yossi Alpher, a former Israeli intelligence officer and the author of Periphery: Israel's Search for Middle East Allies (2015), summarizes Ben-Gurion's pitch to Washington as "you've got NATO, we have Trident." [cite:rs_cw4_alpher_brookings]

The agreement with Turkey, August 1958. According to Schonmann, a secret, formal political agreement between the Israeli and Turkish prime ministers was signed in August 1958. [cite:rs_cw4_schonmann_2024] Beyond that, the sources diverge on two points: where it was made, and what it did to the level of relations.

On the first, Liel and the journalist Amotz Asa-El both describe a secret visit by Ben-Gurion to Ankara. [cite:rs_cw4_liel_bmlv] [cite:rs_cw4_asael_aijac] Schonmann, in the work cited here, does not state where the agreement was signed. The Ankara visit therefore rests on two later accounts, one in Liel's study and one in the Australia/Israel Review, and is not confirmed by the archival scholarship.

On the second, the disagreement is direct. Asa-El says the two leaders agreed to upgrade relations to full embassies. [cite:rs_cw4_asael_aijac] Liel writes that relations reached ambassadorial level only in January 1992. [cite:rs_cw4_liel_bmlv] A Turkish research site, STRASAM, citing Israel's published foreign-policy documents, lists the points agreed: closer political, military, economic and cultural ties, cooperation between the two General Staffs, and the return of envoys to their posts. [cite:rs_cw4_strasam] The two positions can be read together. If the text provided for envoys to return, it restored representation without necessarily raising it, which would square with Liel's 1992 date; Asa-El's "full embassies" may describe an intention rather than an act. That reconciliation is offered here as a possibility, not a finding. The documents cited by STRASAM are the nearest thing to the text in these sources, and they speak of envoys, not ambassadors.

The Turkish side of this story is often summarized by a claim the record does not support: that Turkey has always been hostile to Israel. Turkey and Israel had established diplomatic relations in March 1949, the first Muslim-majority state to do so, a story that belongs to Volume II; and in 1958 Turkey entered a secret intelligence pact with Israel and Iran. [cite:w_isr_tur] The partnership of the 1990s, with its military agreements, lies well beyond this chapter. For the period here, the plain fact is that the Turkish government chose a secret alignment with Israel at the moment its own alliance system broke.

The Trident, autumn 1958. The intelligence pact followed. Schonmann writes that after October 1958 the Trident brought the heads of the Israeli, Turkish and Iranian secret services together in semi-annual conferences, with Ethiopia joining later. [cite:rs_cw4_schonmann_2024] Alpher dates the first trilateral meeting to late September or early October 1958, and says Israel informed the Americans as soon as it was concluded. [cite:rs_cw4_alpher_relay] Another account traces the alliance's formation through meetings in Europe, Ankara and Tehran between 1956 and 1958, and names its drivers as Israel's 1956 Sinai campaign, concern over Nasser's Egypt, the Iraqi coup of 1958 and shared fears of Soviet influence. [cite:foreignaffairs_trident_legacy] [cite:wiki_alliance_periphery] The Iranian side of the relationship, which had begun with oil and with contacts between the Mossad and Iran's security service, is told in the section on Iran and Israel later in this chapter.

How it worked. The Trident was an arrangement among intelligence services, not among governments in public, and its machinery reflected that. According to Alpher, its "primary purpose" was intelligence on Syria, Iraq and Soviet penetration of the region, and on the Israeli side it was run by the Mossad directly under the prime minister. [cite:rs_cw4_alpher_brookings] Alpher says that Turkish scholars told him "no more than 20 people in Turkey" knew of it. [cite:rs_cw4_alpher_brookings] Israel's presence in Tehran was formally a trade delegation, and, in his words, Turkey, Iran and Ethiopia all "kept it at low level to keep their Arab friends happy." [cite:rs_cw4_alpher_brookings]

That last phrase, on Alpher's account, is the key to the partners' side of the bargain: each had relations with Arab states that it valued, and kept its tie to Israel low to protect them. The structure that resulted was secret and asymmetric. Alpher's assessment, as a review of his book summarizes it, is that the Trident was lopsided, with Iran and Turkey exploiting Israeli intelligence. [cite:rs_cw4_apn_review] Another account puts the same point from Israel's standpoint: Israel provided substantially more intelligence and expertise than it received, and valued the arrangement chiefly as proof, aimed at the Americans, the Soviets and the Arab states, that it was not regionally isolated. [cite:foreignaffairs_trident_legacy] These are the judgments of a participant and of one later account, and they are labelled as such. They agree with Schonmann's archival reading in one respect: the value of the periphery to Israel lay as much in what it showed Washington as in what it delivered.

The money. The sources say little about who paid, with one exception. Alpher says that CIA money built a Trident headquarters near Tel Aviv, which the Mossad turned "into a training facility very quickly." [cite:rs_cw4_alpher_brookings] That is a participant's account and is not confirmed from American records in the sources gathered here. If accurate, it means that Washington, whatever its diplomats said about the pact, paid for part of its infrastructure.

Washington's answer. How the United States received the periphery is disputed, and the two accounts come from different kinds of evidence. Alpher, the participant, says Dulles gave a "lukewarm blessing." [cite:rs_cw4_alpher_brookings] Schonmann, working from the American archives, finds something cooler. The State Department's Policy Planning Staff wrote on 11 August 1958 that "the cornerstone of the suggested entente is not firm," and on 18 August Dulles approved "extreme caution in giving Ben-Gurion further encouragement or support." [cite:rs_cw4_schonmann_2017] Just before them came the overflight crisis of 1–10 August, told in [scene:cw4_overflights|the overflight crisis], after which Israel's own ambassador spoke of the need to remove American "doubts about Israel's steadfastness." [cite:rs_cw4_frus58_d36]

The strongest form of each case can be stated. On Alpher's side: Israel told Washington of the Trident as soon as it was concluded, the CIA by his account helped pay for its headquarters, and nothing in the record shows the United States trying to stop it. On Schonmann's: the internal American papers of August 1958 show the planners doubting the pact's foundation and the Secretary of State ordering restraint in encouraging it. Both may be true at once. A government can decline to back a policy in its diplomacy while its intelligence service quietly funds the part it finds useful. The sources do not show whether that is what happened, only that the diplomatic record and the participant's memory point in different directions.

A later American telegram, reporting Ben-Gurion's account of a secret talk with Iran's General Teymur Bakhtiar, records the policy in the form Washington understood it: Israeli policy aimed in part to strengthen relations with Turkey, Iran, Ethiopia and Sudan, and possibly later Iraq. [cite:rs_cw4_frus58v12_d273] The telegram's own date is uncertain, a question taken up in the section on Iran, but its list matches Ben-Gurion's letter of 24 July closely.

What it was for. Alpher places the periphery among Ben-Gurion's grand strategies: "periphery doctrine is one, a nuclear deterrent is another, a great power, or super power ally, is a third," the fourth being mass immigration. [cite:rs_cw4_alpher_brookings] Set beside the French reactor of the same years, told in the opening section of this chapter, the list explains the policy's logic as its makers saw it. A state surrounded by hostile neighbours and never granted a written guarantee by the United States sought allies beyond the ring, a deterrent of its own, and a great-power patron, and used the first to win the third. That is the strongest Israeli case for the periphery, and it does not depend on any claim about the peoples of the partner states: it was a policy toward their governments, which had their own reasons for accepting it. Alpher's own verdict was mixed. He judged the periphery "on balance ... a strategic success," while calling the partners "fair-weather friends, to a large extent." [cite:rs_cw4_alpher_brookings]

The common account holds that Iran's only relationship with Israel before 1979 was commercial, oil and arms, with no state-level intelligence alliance, and that Turkey was always hostile. The record of 1957–1958 shows both to be wrong. Turkey's Prime Minister signed a secret political agreement with Israel's, and both countries' intelligence chiefs, with Iran's, met twice a year from the autumn of 1958. The Shah's public part in the oil embargo of 1973, while the cooperation continued, and his acknowledgment of the ties in 1975 belong to later volumes and are told in [scene:ira_s00c|the Trident and the embargo].

What the record does not settle. The exact place of the August 1958 agreement is not settled: Ankara rests on Liel and Asa-El and is not stated by Schonmann. Whether that agreement raised relations to embassy level is disputed, and the agreed text as summarized speaks only of envoys returning. Who first conceived the doctrine is not established in these sources. The original wording of the "dam" sentence is known only in two translations. The CIA's funding of the Trident's headquarters rests on Alpher's account alone. And how much the pact actually delivered, beyond the conferences and the proof of Israel's regional value, cannot be measured from the record gathered here; the judgment that it was lopsided comes from the Israeli side and has not been tested against Turkish or Iranian sources.

sections.h: 1958: The Year the Region Turned
sections.html:
Ben-Gurion turned to the periphery in a year when the region seemed to come apart around Israel. Stage Three closed with the Eisenhower Doctrine, told in [scene:cw3_aftermath|the aftermath of Suez], as the frame of American policy in the region. In 1958 that frame was tested. Between February and October 1958 two Arab states merged, a rival union was formed and destroyed, a monarchy fell, and American Marines landed on a Mediterranean beach while British paratroopers flew into Amman. Israel took no part in any of these events, but each of them changed its position, and by the end of July its government had made its own choice about where it stood. Two explanations of the year have been argued over ever since: that the crisis was driven from Cairo, and that it grew from each country's own politics.

Two unions, February 1958. In February 1958 Egypt and Syria joined to form the United Arab Republic, with Nasser as its ruler. A rival union of two monarchies, the Arab Union of Jordan and Iraq, was formed in answer. It lasted from February to August 1958. [cite:rs_cw4_kramer_docs] [cite:rs_cw4_riedel_1958] [cite:rs_cw4_cannon_ebsco] The two unions drew the region's line in its plainest form that year: on one side the republic that Nasser led from Cairo and Damascus, on the other two kingdoms, one of which, Iraq, was the main pillar of the Baghdad Pact. [cite:rs_cw4_liel_bmlv]

Lebanon, from May. The first crisis came in Lebanon. Unrest began in May 1958 when President Camille Chamoun appeared to be seeking a second term. The American intelligence community's own assessment, Special National Intelligence Estimate 36.4–58 of 5 June 1958, put the cause plainly: "the present conflict was touched off by indications that Christian President Chamoun intended to amend the constitution." [cite:rs_cw4_kramer_docs] The historian Bruce Riedel describes what followed as a rebellion by Lebanon's Muslim population and some Christians against a term that his article calls unconstitutional. [cite:rs_cw4_riedel_1958] The magazine New Lines adds that Chamoun's forces killed several Nasserite protesters, and that a small civil war followed between pro-Chamoun Christian militias and Sunni and Shiite fighters inspired by Nasser. [cite:rs_cw4_boswall_newlines]

Chamoun had another explanation. He blamed Nasser, charging that arms were being smuggled into Lebanon from the United Arab Republic. The United Nations tested the charge. In June 1958 the Security Council sent the UN Observation Group in Lebanon, known as UNOGIL, nearly 600 strong and staffing 49 observer posts. [cite:rs_cw4_cannon_ebsco] According to Riedel, the UN inspectors did not support Chamoun's allegations. [cite:rs_cw4_riedel_1958]

The two readings of Lebanon's crisis should be set side by side, because both were held at the time by people with standing to hold them. The first is domestic: a president's bid for a second term, which Riedel's article calls unconstitutional, and a rebellion against it. This reading is supported by the American estimate of 5 June, which named Chamoun's intention to amend the constitution as the spark, and by Riedel and New Lines. [cite:rs_cw4_kramer_docs] [cite:rs_cw4_riedel_1958] [cite:rs_cw4_boswall_newlines] The second is regional: Nasser's new republic, with Syria now under its rule, arming the opposition to a pro-Western government. Its strongest evidence is that the fighters opposing Chamoun were, by New Lines's account, inspired by Nasser, and that Chamoun made the charge. Its weakness is that the observers the UN sent to find the smuggling did not support it, by Riedel's account. [cite:rs_cw4_riedel_1958] The sources here do not say that no arms crossed. They say that the evidence put to the United Nations did not establish the charge, and that Washington's own estimators located the cause in Beirut.

The same estimate looked ahead to an American intervention. It judged that Israel "would probably avoid direct involvement," and CIA Director Allen Dulles said that "Israel will probably stay out" if the United States intervened. It expected the Soviet reaction to be "confined to vigorous diplomatic and propaganda action" unless American forces fought on the territory of the United Arab Republic.
