[cite:rs_cw4_kramer_docs] Israel did stay out of the fighting, and Moscow's answer, when it came to Israel on 1 August, was a diplomatic note. [cite:rs_cw4_schonmann_2017]

Baghdad, 14 July. What changed the summer was not Lebanon but Iraq. On 14 July 1958 an army coup in Baghdad, which surprised American and British intelligence, killed King Faisal II, the crown prince and the prime minister, Nuri al-Sa'id. [cite:rs_cw4_riedel_1958] [cite:rs_cw4_kramer_docs] The White House record of that day shows how uncertain Washington's knowledge was: Dulles reported that "the Crown Prince has been killed, and perhaps Nuri also." [cite:rs_cw4_kramer_docs] Iraq's monarchy was overthrown. [cite:w_1958_iraq] The consequences reached well beyond Iraq. Liel writes that the Baghdad Pact thereby lost its main pillar, and that Turkey sought closer ties with Israel, a turn told in [scene:cw4_periphery|the periphery and the Trident]. [cite:rs_cw4_liel_bmlv] The Arab Union of Jordan and Iraq ended the same summer. [cite:rs_cw4_cannon_ebsco]

Eisenhower convened the National Security Council the same day. In his memoirs he wrote: "we feared the worst…the complete elimination of Western influence in the Middle East." [cite:rs_cw4_riedel_1958] [cite:rs_cw4_kramer_docs] The sentence suggests that it was not Lebanon's presidency alone that Eisenhower feared for, but the whole Western position in the region.

Blue Bat and Amman. On 15 July United States Marines landed near Beirut, in Operation Blue Bat. About 1,700 came ashore in the first contingent at Khalde, backed by three carrier groups. [cite:rs_cw4_riedel_1958] [cite:rs_cw4_kramer_docs] Britain moved in parallel. On 14 July Prime Minister Macmillan referred to a planned British contingent of "about 3,700," and British paratroopers flew to Amman to support King Hussein. [cite:rs_cw4_kramer_docs] [cite:rs_cw4_boswall_newlines] The route those British flights took, over Israel, would produce a crisis of its own in August.

How large the American force became is reported differently. Riedel gives a peak of "almost 15,000" Marines and soldiers; Byron Cannon gives about 14,000; New Lines says the force never exceeded 14,000. [cite:rs_cw4_riedel_1958] [cite:rs_cw4_cannon_ebsco] [cite:rs_cw4_boswall_newlines] The difference is about a thousand men and the sources do not resolve it. The other figures come from one source or another. One American died from sniper fire; Cannon adds three accidental deaths. The intervention cost about $200 million, according to New Lines. All American forces had left by 25 October 1958. [cite:rs_cw4_riedel_1958] [cite:rs_cw4_cannon_ebsco] [cite:rs_cw4_boswall_newlines]

How Lebanon's crisis ended. The landing did not decide Lebanon's politics; a Lebanese compromise did. General Fuad Chehab, the commander of the Lebanese army, was chosen in 1958 as the compromise successor to Chamoun; Cannon dates the choice to October, and New Lines says that Nasser favoured the outcome. [cite:rs_cw4_cannon_ebsco] [cite:rs_cw4_boswall_newlines] Riedel records an act of improvisation on the ground: the American ambassador, he writes, disobeyed instructions to broker the Lebanese army's escort of the Marines. [cite:rs_cw4_riedel_1958] The force landed during Chamoun's presidency thus left behind his successor, an outcome that, by New Lines's account, the man Chamoun had blamed for the crisis favoured. That outcome can be read as support for the domestic reading: the crisis was settled by a Lebanese compromise that Nasser favoured, not by the removal of his influence.

The American dissent. Not everyone in Washington accepted the case for intervention. According to Riedel, Senators John F. Kennedy and J. William Fulbright opposed it, and Kennedy argued that Nasser was not a Soviet puppet. [cite:rs_cw4_riedel_1958] Their objection, on one reading, went to the premise. The Eisenhower Doctrine, as Secretary Dulles described it to Israel's envoys that August, promised support to Israel if it were attacked by a Communist power; if Nasser was an Arab nationalist acting for his own ends rather than Moscow's, then the doctrine's logic did not reach him, and sending troops against his influence was a different kind of act from the one the doctrine described. [cite:rs_cw4_frus58_d35]

Israel's position, July 1958. Israel stayed out, as the American estimators had predicted. But it did not stay silent. Its government's view of the summer was set out to Dulles in London on 27 July 1958 by its envoys, Abba Eban and Reuven Shiloah. They told him that Israel had no expansionist ideas, that it would not seek to take the West Bank if that could be avoided, but that it wished to avoid hostile forces on its border. Ben-Gurion believed, they said, that Jordan "could be preserved only if anti-Nasser forces in the area cooperated among themselves." [cite:rs_cw4_frus58_d31] The two statements fit together. Read together, they put Israel's interest in a Jordan that survived rather than one absorbed by the United Arab Republic, and its proposed means in cooperation among the forces opposed to Nasser, which matches the periphery pact that Ben-Gurion had put to Eisenhower three days earlier. The qualification "if that could be avoided" is also part of the record; the envoys did not rule out every circumstance.

Dulles, for his part, read the moment as a check to Nasser. He judged that Nasser's anger at the landings reflected the fact that they had checked his success. [cite:rs_cw4_frus58_d31] What Israel received from Washington that week was an assurance in general terms. Eisenhower's letter to Ben-Gurion of 25 July 1958 said that Israel could "be confident of United States interest in the integrity and independence of Israel." [cite:rs_cw4_frus58_d31] It was an expression of interest, not a guarantee. Within days Israel's government would close its airspace to the British and American flights to Jordan, and in the argument that followed, its complaint that it had never been given a written guarantee came into the open. That story is told in [scene:cw4_overflights|the overflight crisis].

What 1958 changed. A familiar account holds that the region's autocracies and wars grew only from its own culture and religion. The record of 1958 does not support that, and it does not support the opposite simplification either. Lebanon's crisis began, by the reckoning of Washington's own estimators, with a president's attempt to extend his term; Iraq's monarchy was ended by its own army; the United Arab Republic was a union of two governments. These were political events with political causes. At the same time, the United States landed an army in Lebanon at a cost of about $200 million, Britain flew troops into Jordan, and Eisenhower, by his own account, acted in fear of "the complete elimination of Western influence in the Middle East." The year's events were made by local actors and foreign powers together, and neither account alone explains them.

The record leaves several questions open. How many American troops were in Lebanon at the peak is given as about 14,000 and as almost 15,000. Whether arms crossed from Syria into Lebanon in any quantity is not settled by these sources; what is settled is that the UN observers did not support Chamoun's charge. The planning of the Baghdad coup, and why it surprised both American and British intelligence, is not described in the sources gathered here. And the meaning of the American ambassador's disobedience in Beirut, as Riedel reports it, is given in a single sentence that the sources do not expand. For Israel, the summer's lasting result was clear enough: the fall of the Iraqi monarchy brought Turkey towards it, and the Anglo-American response brought Israel's airspace into the Cold War.

sections.h: Ten Days in August: The Overflight Crisis of 1958
sections.html:
The British paratroopers who flew to Amman in July 1958, and the American airlift to Jordan, flew over Israel to get there. For about three weeks Israel allowed it. Then, on 2 August, it ordered the flights stopped. Eight days later they resumed, and the American Secretary of State declared the matter closed. In between, the Secretary of State rebuked Israel's ambassador to his face, and Israel set down in writing what it wanted from the United States and had not been given. Why Ben-Gurion stopped the flights is still argued.

Before the crisis. The flights followed from the events told in [scene:cw4_1958|the year the region turned]: the coup in Baghdad on 14 July and the British decision to send paratroopers to support King Hussein in Amman. According to a report of the Jewish Telegraphic Agency published on 8 August 1958, Israel had first permitted the British paratroop overflights about three weeks earlier, hoping for firmer Western action against Nasser. [cite:rs_cw4_djn_1958] The decision was a choice, not a formality. It put Israel's territory in the service of a British operation in an Arab state, at a moment when Israel's government was also asking Washington to back a pact against Nasser, as told in [scene:cw4_periphery|the periphery and the Trident].

1 August: two letters on one day. On 1 August 1958 the Soviet Union sent Israel a note calling it "an immediate associate" in aggressive acts against Arab countries. Ben-Gurion wrote in his diary that the note was "paved with threats to the 'national interests' of Israel." [cite:rs_cw4_schonmann_2017] On the same day, in Washington, Dulles dated his reply to Ben-Gurion's periphery letter of 24 July. It said that "we are prepared to do what we can to be of assistance," and that "we believe that Israel should be in a position to deter an attempt at aggression by indigenous forces." [cite:rs_cw4_schonmann_2017] The second sentence may have mattered more to Israel: it was an American statement, in writing, that Israel should be able to deter attack by its neighbours. But the letter reached the American embassy only on 2 August and was delivered to the Israelis on 4 August. [cite:rs_cw4_schonmann_2017] When it gave its stop order, Israel's government had the Soviet note in hand and not the American letter.

2 August: the stop order. On 2 August Israel's Assistant Director General, Comay, told the American ambassador, Lawson, that overflights "by US planes must stop immediately," with "no flights even tonight." Ben-Gurion made the same demand of the British. [cite:rs_cw4_frus58_d34] Lawson's telegram home gave his reading of the cause. Ben-Gurion, he judged, "does not feel he has firm basis to resist strong Cabinet and potential public opposition to overflights." Comay called the Soviet note "firm and threatening." [cite:rs_cw4_frus58_d34] The ambassador's report thus pointed to two pressures at once: a Soviet note that the Israeli official himself described as threatening, and a cabinet and public that Ben-Gurion could not, in Lawson's view, carry with him.

3 August: the rebuke. The next day Dulles received Israel's ambassador, Abba Eban, and Minister Yaacov Herzog at his residence. The American record of the conversation, titled "Israeli Decision to Request U.S. to Cease Overflights of Israel," shows him angry. He called it "particularly shocking that Israel would do this without any consultation with the US." He reminded them that "the Eisenhower Doctrine made clear" that the United States would support Israel if it were attacked by a Communist power, and he asked whether Israel felt "so menaced by the USSR that it would do whatever the Soviet Union requested." [cite:rs_cw4_frus58_d35] Schonmann, drawing on the same archives, quotes him calling the step "a show of fear for the Russians to behold." [cite:rs_cw4_schonmann_2017]

Eban's answer that day did not dwell on Moscow. He explained that the British request "involved the sending of additional troops into Jordan," which were "an added convenience but not crucial." [cite:rs_cw4_frus58_d35] The argument was that Israel had not abandoned the West at a moment of need: the troops already in Amman were there, and what Israel had refused was more of them.

5 August: the letter and the list. Two days later the Israelis came back with a letter. On 5 August Eban, Herzog and Shimon Peres gave the Acting Secretary of State, Herter, Ben-Gurion's letter consenting to the resumption of American airlift flights. Eban told Herter that Israel's doubts had not stemmed from the Soviet note, which Israel did not plan to answer hastily. He proposed technical talks with Colonel Harkabi to end the airlift as soon as American needs allowed, and suggested the Aqaba route as an alternative. And he said that the most urgent issue was "the elimination of U.S. doubts about Israel's steadfastness." [cite:rs_cw4_frus58_d36]

Ben-Gurion's letter went further than consent. It complained that "we have not been successful in receiving arms assistance from the United States" and that "we have never been granted a guarantee of our integrity," and it noted that the American assurance of help under the Eisenhower Doctrine had never been put in writing. It proposed closer ties among the countries of the periphery. Peres then set out Israel's arms needs. [cite:rs_cw4_frus58_d36] The letter turned a crisis over flights into a statement of grievance. Israel had lent its airspace to two Western powers; in return it had a verbal assurance, a presidential expression of "interest" in its integrity, and a letter from Dulles that had arrived after the crisis began. It had no arms from the United States and no written guarantee.

The last row of that comparison was never said to the Israelis. It comes from internal American papers of 11 and 18 August, found by Schonmann and weighed in [scene:cw4_periphery|the periphery and the Trident]. [cite:rs_cw4_schonmann_2017] Together with Eisenhower's letter of 25 July, which offered Israel confidence in "United States interest in the integrity and independence of Israel," they show the distance between what Israel asked for that summer and what Washington was prepared to give. [cite:rs_cw4_frus58_d31]

6–10 August: the resumption. The American airlift resumed on 6 August. On 10 August Dulles wrote that "we can consider the situation which arose out of the interruption of our flights a closed matter," and Israel renewed the overflights. Ben-Gurion wrote that he had gained "a free hand" in drafting the reply to Moscow. [cite:rs_cw4_schonmann_2017] The phrase suggests what he thought he had won: not the arms or the guarantee he had asked for, but room to answer the Soviet Union in his own way without American objection.

The press account at the time was blunter. The Jewish Telegraphic Agency reported that Israel "apparently yielded to pressure from the United States." It also reported that, according to Israeli sources, the ban had been prompted not by the Soviet note but "by British attempts to set Israel up as a bogey in the present crisis." The same paper reported a new Soviet map that placed Jerusalem and central Palestine in Jordan. [cite:rs_cw4_djn_1958]

Why did Ben-Gurion stop the flights? Two explanations were given at the time, and both have evidence behind them.

The first is that Israel gave way to the Soviet note and to pressure at home. This was Dulles's reading on 3 August, when he asked whether Israel would do "whatever the Soviet Union requested," and it is close to Lawson's of 2 August, which placed the cause in strong cabinet and potential public opposition that Ben-Gurion did not feel able to resist. [cite:rs_cw4_frus58_d35] [cite:rs_cw4_frus58_d34] Its strongest evidence is the timing: the stop order came the day after the Soviet note arrived, and the Israeli official who delivered it described that note to the American ambassador as "firm and threatening." [cite:rs_cw4_frus58_d34] Ben-Gurion's own diary entry, that the note was "paved with threats," shows that he took it seriously. [cite:rs_cw4_schonmann_2017]

The second is that the Soviet note was not the cause, and that the decision turned on domestic and British politics. This was Eban's account to Dulles and to Herter, and it was the account Israeli sources gave the Jewish Telegraphic Agency. [cite:rs_cw4_frus58_d35] [cite:rs_cw4_frus58_d36] [cite:rs_cw4_djn_1958] Its strongest evidence is what Israel actually refused and when it relented. It refused additional British troops, which Eban called "not crucial," and it resumed the American flights within four days, before it had answered Moscow at all. The Israeli sources' charge that Britain was setting Israel up "as a bogey" points to a fear that Israel would be made to carry the cost of an operation that was not its own. [cite:rs_cw4_djn_1958] On this reading, the stop order was a protest against being used without being supported, and Ben-Gurion's letter of 5 August, with its list of what Israel had not received, is the evidence of what the protest was about.

The two readings are not wholly exclusive. Lawson's telegram itself joined the Soviet note to the cabinet's opposition, and a cabinet's opposition to overflights may have rested on fear of Moscow, on resentment of London, or on both. What the sources show is that the explanation given changed between 2 and 5 August: on the first day an Israeli official stressed the Soviet threat, and three days later Israel's ambassador said the Soviet note had not been the reason.

An accidental crisis? Schonmann offers a third way of reading the episode, which she calls "the accidental crisis in American–Israeli relations." Her point turns on dates. Dulles's letter, with its promise of help and its statement that Israel should be able to deter attack, and the Soviet note were dated the same day, 1 August; and the Israeli stop order was given on 2 August, before the American letter was delivered on the 4th. [cite:rs_cw4_schonmann_2017] Had the letter arrived first, the implication runs, Ben-Gurion might have weighed the Soviet threat against an American assurance in hand. This is her interpretation, and it is labelled as such here. It explains the timing well. It explains less well why Ben-Gurion's letter of 5 August, written after the Dulles letter had been delivered, still complained that Israel had no arms and no written guarantee; Dulles's letter, generous as it was in tone, gave neither.

What it showed. Whatever its cause, the crisis exposed the terms of the relationship. Israel's airspace mattered to Britain and to the United States in July 1958, and Israel used that fact, for four days, to make its case. The Secretary of State's response was to question Israel's nerve. The case Israel made, arms and a written guarantee and support for its periphery, was not met that summer; within days of the crisis's end the American planners were advising caution on the periphery, and the arms question returned in the Hawk decision of 1962, told at the end of this chapter.

The record leaves several things unsettled. Ben-Gurion's own explanation of the stop order is not among the sources gathered here beyond his diary's description of the Soviet note and his later line about a "free hand." The cabinet discussion that Lawson referred to is reported only through the ambassador's reading of it. Whether British flights resumed on the same terms as the American ones is not stated. And Israel's reply to the Soviet note, which Ben-Gurion felt free to draft as he wished, is not described in these sources.

sections.h: Wadi Salib, 1959: "Is Our Blood Cheap?"
sections.html:
The crises of 1958 turned on Israel's place among states. The crisis of 1959 turned on the place of its own citizens. The mass immigration of 1948–52, and the transit camps that received hundreds of thousands of newcomers, are told in Volume II, in [scene:rd6_ingathering|the mass immigration]. By the summer of 1959 most of those immigrants had been in the country for years, and the question was no longer how to house them in the first months but what kind of place they had been given in the state. In July of that year the question was put in the street, in one neighbourhood of Haifa, by a union of immigrants from North Africa. Its causes were argued over at the time and have been argued over since, in two accounts: the one the protesters wrote and the one the state's commission of inquiry gave.

A neighbourhood twice settled. Wadi Salib had a history before 1959 that shaped its geography. Before 1948 it was a mainly Muslim quarter of Haifa, home to families such as that of the former mayor 'Abd al-Rahman al-Hajj. In the war of 1948 its Palestinian residents were uprooted and became refugees, and Jewish migrants, most of them from North Africa, were settled in the houses they had left. [cite:rs_cw4_naor_ijmes] [cite:rs_cw4_cie_wadisalib] The neighbourhood that protested in 1959 was therefore one built on an earlier displacement: the people who lived there had arrived as the state's newest citizens in the houses of people who had become refugees. The scholarship used here does not record whether the 1959 protesters or the authorities spoke of that history at the time.

The shooting, 8 July 1959. On the night of 8 July 1959 police shot and wounded Akiva Yaakov Elkrif, a resident of the neighbourhood who had been born in Morocco. [cite:rs_cw4_naor_ijmes] [cite:rs_cw4_cie_wadisalib] How the shooting came about is disputed, and the protest began from it. The Center for Israel Education says that the police were trying to arrest Elkrif for being drunk and disorderly. It also says that witnesses disagree on whether he provoked them. [cite:rs_cw4_cie_wadisalib] The neighbourhood's own reading was that the shooting was unjustified, and the union that organized the protest put that reading into the title of its broadsheet. [cite:rs_cw4_naor_ijmes] None of the sources used here settles which version is correct; they establish that a man was shot and wounded by police, and that what he did before the shot was fired is contested.

The procession, 9 July. The next day the protest acquired a leader and an organization. David Ben-Harush, a resident born in Casablanca, had founded the Union of Migrants from North Africa early in 1959. On 9 July he led a procession from the Rambam Synagogue to police headquarters. The union's broadsheet that day was titled "Is Our Blood Cheap?" According to Moshe Naor's study of the protest, published in the International Journal of Middle East Studies in 2024, the protesters damaged cafés, a bank, and buildings belonging to Mapai and to the Histadrut. [cite:rs_cw4_naor_ijmes] The choice of targets is part of the record: the crowd turned on Mapai and the Histadrut, not only on the police.

The spread, July 1959. On 10 July rumours spread that Elkrif had died. In the clashes that followed, 13 police and 2 demonstrators were hurt, and 34 people were arrested. During July protests spread beyond Haifa, to Beersheba, Acre, Tiberias and Migdal HaEmek. After the union's leaders were arrested, the protest in Wadi Salib resumed from 31 July. Ben-Harush was jailed and tried. [cite:rs_cw4_cie_wadisalib] [cite:rs_cw4_wiki_wadisalib] [cite:rs_cw4_naor_ijmes] These figures rest on the Center for Israel Education and an encyclopedia summary as well as on Naor, and they are given here as those sources report them. The sources used here do not record the outcome of Ben-Harush's trial or his sentence.

The commission, 19 July–17 August. The government answered with an inquiry. On 19 July 1959 it set up a commission under Judge Moshe Etzioni. The commission heard 46 witnesses in public sessions and reported on 17 August 1959. [cite:rs_cw4_naor_ijmes] Its members, according to a Hebrew encyclopedia's summary of the report, included Rabbi Yitzhak Abuhatzira and the sociologist S. N. Eisenstadt. [cite:rs_cw4_hamichlol_wadisalib] One finding is quoted directly in Naor's study: "in most instances, half of [the protestors] were children, women, and adolescents." [cite:rs_cw4_naor_ijmes] The title of Naor's article, "The Children of Wadi Salib and the 1959 Moroccan Jewish Protest in Haifa," carries the same emphasis.

The protesters' account. The protesters left their own record, in the union's broadsheets. Naor's reading of them is that they framed the protest around poverty, jobs, housing and education. [cite:rs_cw4_naor_ijmes] The first broadsheet's question, "Is Our Blood Cheap?", can be read as joining the shooting to that wider claim: that a life from this neighbourhood was held cheap, as its people felt they were treated in work, housing and schooling. In the protesters' reading, and in the reading of many researchers since, Wadi Salib was a protest against the marginalization of Jews from North Africa by an establishment led by Jews of European origin. That is how the Center for Israel Education summarizes it, and it is the reading Romanenko surveys in the research literature. [cite:rs_cw4_naor_ijmes] [cite:rs_cw4_cie_wadisalib] [cite:rs_cw4_romanenko]

The state's account. The state's account came from three directions. The first was the city. Haifa's mayor, Abba Khoushi, said that the riots were mainly led by women and children. [cite:rs_cw4_naor_ijmes] The second was Mapai. A Mapai broadsheet in August claimed that the protest had support from Herut, the opposition party. [cite:rs_cw4_naor_ijmes] That was a political explanation, not a social one: it located the cause in a rival party rather than in the neighbourhood's conditions, and it was made in the same year as a general election. The third and most formal was the commission. According to a summary of sections 9–14 of its report, the Etzioni commission found no deliberate discrimination by state institutions. It found a "sincere will" at the level of policy to attend to the Mizrahi communities, and discrimination at the lower levels where policy was carried out. Etzioni wrote, in that summary's rendering, "here we all sinned." [cite:rs_cw4_hamichlol_wadisalib] The finding was therefore not an acquittal. It placed the failure in implementation rather than intention, at the lower levels where policy was carried out rather than the level where it was made, and its chairman described the failure as a shared one.

The two accounts are not as far apart as their tone. The commission did not deny that discrimination happened; it denied that it was deliberate policy. The protesters' broadsheets, as Naor summarizes them, spoke of poverty, jobs, housing and education: of results, in their streets and schools, rather than of a written policy of exclusion. Where they divided most sharply was on responsibility: whether failures at the lower levels of the state, repeated across a whole population of immigrants, could be separated from the policy that set those levels to work. The Mapai broadsheet's charge about Herut was of a different kind from either, and neither the commission's summary nor Naor's study records evidence for or against it.

The scholarship. Two recent studies take the argument further, and they agree on more than they disagree. Naor argues that poverty, housing and school dropout were central causes. [cite:rs_cw4_naor_ijmes] R. E. Romanenko, writing in 2025, argues that the causes lay less in deliberate discrimination than in an absorption policy that neglected the economic integration of Mizrahi immigrants, and that this neglect produced a sense of grievance and of discrimination as the immigrants perceived it. [cite:rs_cw4_romanenko] Romanenko's position sits close to the commission's on the question of intent, and close to the protesters' on the question of outcome: the immigrants were left behind, whether or not anyone had designed it. Naor's emphasis on children and school dropout gives the protest a concrete social base that neither the mayor's remark nor the party's broadsheet allowed it.

The election and the laws. The protest entered politics directly. Ben-Harush ran for the Knesset in the 1959 election from prison, on the list of the Union of North African Immigrants, and the list did not pass the threshold. [cite:rs_cw4_wiki_wadisalib] [cite:rs_cw4_hamichlol_wadisalib] (Naor names his organization the Union of Migrants from North Africa; the encyclopedias name the electoral list the Union of North African Immigrants. The sources do not say whether these are translations of one name.) Its effect on policy was slower and less visible than its effect in the street. Naor argues that the protests led to government measures, among them the Youth Law (Care and Supervision) of 1960 and the Child Benefit Law. [cite:rs_cw4_naor_ijmes] Both answered, on paper at least, the conditions that his study places at the centre of the protest: children out of school and families without enough to live on.

Wadi Salib stands at one end of a longer history of how the young state received the Jews of the Arab world, a history that includes [scene:s00e2|the exodus and what followed it] and the families' accounts of infants taken from the immigrant camps, told in [scene:mz_s02|the Yemenite children affair]. It should be described for what the documents show it was: a protest by a named union, in a named neighbourhood, after a named man was shot, answered by a named mayor, a named party and a named commission. It was not the voice of a whole community, and the commission's finding was not the voice of a whole state.

What the record leaves open. Several questions cannot be answered from the sources used for this section. The exact wording of the Etzioni report on discrimination is known here only through a secondary summary of its sections 9–14, not from the report itself, so the phrases "sincere will" and "here we all sinned" are given as that summary renders them. How many votes Ben-Harush's list won, and what sentence he received, are not recorded in these sources. Whether Elkrif provoked the police on 8 July is still disputed by the witnesses whom the Center for Israel Education cites. And the Mapai claim that Herut supported the protest is documented only as a claim.

sections.h: Palestinian Politics, 1957–1962: Fatah Abroad, Al-Ard at Home
sections.html:
The houses of Wadi Salib had belonged to Palestinians who became refugees in 1948, and the refugees' own politics did not stop in 1948 either. The diplomacy of these years was conducted almost entirely between governments: Israel's, the United States', France's, West Germany's, and those of the Arab states. In the American and Israeli records of these years, Palestinians appear mainly as refugees, a question to be settled between governments, rather than as political actors. That was not because they had stopped acting. Between 1957 and 1962 two movements took shape that would matter for decades, one among Palestinians abroad and one among the Palestinian Arabs who had remained inside Israel and become its citizens. Neither was large at the time. Both were defined by a choice to act as Palestinians in their own name: abroad, independently of the Arab governments; inside Israel, as a Palestinian national movement among the state's Arab citizens.

The ground both stood on was the war of 1948. About 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled from their homes in that war, the event Palestinians call the Nakba, or "catastrophe." The refugees settled in Gaza, then under Egyptian administration, in the West Bank, then under Jordanian administration, and in Lebanon, Syria and Jordan. That displacement was the political fact around which every later Palestinian movement organized. [cite:npr_hamashistory] A decade later, Palestinians were scattered across those places and beyond them.

Fatah in Kuwait. One of those places was Kuwait. According to the Interactive Encyclopedia of the Palestine Question, published by the Institute for Palestine Studies, Fatah's core group was "most likely founded in Kuwait in autumn 1957." Its founders were five or six Palestinian expatriates, most of them from Gaza, among them Yasir Arafat and Khalil al-Wazir; Salah Khalaf and Kamal Adwan joined soon after. [cite:rs_cw4_palquest_fatah] The date is disputed. The Encyclopedia of the Modern Middle East and North Africa reports that some of the founders themselves date the movement to 1959, when the Kuwait group took over a magazine. [cite:rs_cw4_emmena_fatah] The two dates may describe different things: the first the gathering of a small group, the second the moment it acquired a public voice. The sources used here do not resolve which the founders meant, and both positions are given.

The magazine was Filastinuna – nida' al-hayat, published in Beirut. In its first issue, in October 1959, the movement's name first became public. The name was a reversed acronym of Harakat al-tahrir al-watani al-Filastini, the Palestinian National Liberation Movement. [cite:rs_cw4_palquest_fatah] [cite:rs_cw4_emmena_fatah]

"Palestine first." What made the group distinct was not its size but its argument. Fatah took the prevailing slogan of the day, which made Arab unity the road to Palestine, and reversed it, holding that "the liberation of Palestine is the road to Arab unity." It sought to act independently of Arab governments and parties, and it asked its activists to give up their party affiliations. Its principles were armed struggle, "Palestine first," and non-interference in the internal affairs of Arab states. [cite:rs_cw4_palquest_fatah] [cite:rs_cw4_emmena_fatah] The last of these principles can be read as the practical condition of the second: a movement that wished to operate from Arab capitals without being captured by them had to promise not to meddle in their politics. Fatah was, in the later summary of NPR's history of the period, explicitly secular and nationalist, and it sought Palestinian statehood through a combination of armed struggle and political negotiation. [cite:npr_hamashistory]

In the years covered here Fatah was a magazine and a network, not an armed force. Its armed operations, and the Arab League's creation of the Palestine Liberation Organization in 1964 under Ahmad Shuqayri, which partly pre-empted Fatah, belong to Stage Six. Fatah's military wing began operations at the end of 1964, and Fatah became the dominant faction in the PLO by 1969. [cite:rs_cw4_emmena_fatah] [cite:npr_hamashistory] The later rivalry between the PLO and the Islamist movement that became Hamas is told in [scene:hma_src_s02|Palestinian political origins].

Al-Ard inside Israel. Inside Israel the setting was entirely different. Most of the Arab citizens of the state lived under the military government whose structure Volume II describes and whose Border Police unit killed 49 villagers at Kafr Qasim in 1956, as told in [scene:mg_s01|eighteen years of military rule]. That regime remained in force throughout this period. It was under it that Al-Ard was founded in 1959, as the first Palestinian national movement among Israel's Arab citizens after 1948. Its leaders included Sabri Jiryis, Habib Qahwaji, Saleh Baransi and Mansour Kardosh. [cite:rs_cw4_jiryis_pij] [cite:rs_cw4_konrad_972] According to Edo Konrad, writing in +972 Magazine, it emerged from the remains of the Popular Front, a grouping of nationalists and communists. [cite:rs_cw4_konrad_972]

Al-Ard's demands were stated in its own documents. It called for equal rights for Arab citizens and for recognition of the refugees' right to return. Its bylaws argued: "If the Jews have a right to an independent state, the people of Palestine also have a right to an independent state." [cite:rs_cw4_jiryis_pij] That sentence can be read as the movement's own answer to the charge later brought against it: it argued from a Jewish right to statehood to the same right for Palestinians.

A newspaper one issue at a time. The state's response came first through licensing. Al-Ard was refused a licence for a newspaper. It found a way around the refusal in a rule surviving from the Mandate that allowed one issue of an unlicensed publication a year. Al-Ard published issue after issue under changing titles, each of which kept the words "al-Ard." After the thirteenth issue its leaders were convicted of publishing without a licence. [cite:rs_cw4_jiryis_pij] [cite:rs_cw4_konrad_972] The tactic tells something about both sides: the movement's leaders chose a legal device rather than an underground press, and the authorities answered with prosecution under the licensing law rather than with a charge about the content of what was printed.

The movement then tried to set up a printing company. The registrar refused to register it, on grounds of "public security and interest." The company was registered in early 1962, after the Supreme Court ruled that the registrar had no power to assess questions of national security. [cite:rs_cw4_jiryis_pij] [cite:rs_cw4_konrad_972] The ruling was a limit on an official's discretion, not a judgment on Al-Ard's aims; it held that a companies registrar was the wrong official to decide whether a company endangered the state.

"Two organizations which resent Israel." The government's view was given by the Prime Minister. Ben-Gurion told the Knesset that there were "two organizations which resent Israel," and named Al-Ard among them. [cite:rs_cw4_jiryis_pij] The sources used here do not give the date of the statement or name the second organization.

The two readings. Al-Ard has been read in two ways, and the court that ruled on it in 1965 divided along the same line. In the first, it was a civil-rights and national movement, suppressed because it voiced dissent. That is the reading of Fida Jiryis, writing in the Palestine-Israel Journal in 2023, and of Konrad in +972 Magazine, whose article argues that dissent has always been off limits to Arab citizens in Israel's democracy. [cite:rs_cw4_jiryis_pij] [cite:rs_cw4_konrad_972] Its strongest evidence is the movement's own record: it used the courts and the licensing law, registered a company, and wrote into its bylaws a recognition of Jewish statehood alongside a claim to Palestinian statehood. In the second reading, Al-Ard was a movement aimed at the destruction of the state. That was the view of the Haifa district commissioner, of the security services, and, in 1965, of the majority of the Supreme Court. [cite:rs_cw4_jiryis_pij] [cite:rs_cw4_konrad_972] Its strongest statement is the court majority's, through Justice Agranat: that the list aimed at "the elimination of the State of Israel." The sources used here give the conclusion of those officials and judges more fully than the evidence they relied on.

The end, 1964–1965. The movement's end falls after this stage and is told here in brief. Al-Ard was outlawed in 1964. Jiryis attributes the order to Prime Minister Eshkol; +972 Magazine attributes it to the Defence Minister. Eshkol held both posts, so the two accounts may describe the same act. In October 1965 the Supreme Court upheld, by two votes to one, the disqualification of Al-Ard's Socialist List. Justice Agranat held that the list aimed at "the elimination of the State of Israel." Justice Cohn dissented, finding no "real or clear or present danger." [cite:rs_cw4_jiryis_pij] [cite:rs_cw4_konrad_972] The court's division reproduces the two readings above, inside a single bench.

The two movements of these years made the same move in different settings. Fatah, abroad, refused to wait on the Arab states; Al-Ard, inside Israel, organized as a Palestinian national movement among the state's Arab citizens. One chose armed struggle as a principle from the start. The other chose the licensing law, the companies registry and the courts. They were answered differently: Fatah was partly pre-empted by the Arab League's creation of the PLO; Al-Ard was prosecuted, outlawed and, finally, kept off the ballot by the Supreme Court.

What the record leaves open. The founding date of Fatah remains disputed between autumn 1957 and 1959, and the sources do not settle it. The Arab Nationalist Movement, the other main current of Palestinian political organization in these years, is not documented in the sources used for this section, so its part in the story cannot be told here. The exact date of the Supreme Court's ruling on Al-Ard's printing company is not given; only its result, in early 1962, is. The date of Ben-Gurion's Knesset statement and the identity of the second organization he named are not recorded here. And the evidence on which the Haifa district commissioner and the security services based their view of Al-Ard is reported only in its conclusions, through the movement's sympathetic historians and the court's majority opinion.

sections.h: The Armistice Lines, 1960–1962: Tawafiq, Rotem and Lake Tiberias
sections.html:
Along the armistice lines, Arab and Israeli governments met not in politics but in fire. Between 1960 and 1962 the lines that reached the United Nations were chiefly the Syrian ones, where the armistice of 1949 had left demilitarized zones and a lake whose status Israel and Syria did not see alike. The long history of those zones, and the water war of 1964–67 that grew out of them, is told in [scene:sy_s02|the demilitarized zones and the water war]. Two flare-ups there, in 1960 and 1962, came before the United Nations, and between them came a crisis in the Sinai. For the Syrian episodes the record consists chiefly of what the UN and the United States government wrote down, and in each Israel and its neighbour gave differing accounts.

The cultivation line, January 1960. The dispute began with ploughing. The Yearbook of the United Nations for 1960 records that Israeli cultivation in the southern demilitarized zone, north of Lake Tiberias, had spread eastward since the founding of Kibbutz Beit Katzir, cutting Arab farmers off from the lake. On 20 January 1960 the UN Chief of Staff, acting as chairman of the Mixed Armistice Commission, proposed a practical line. Israel ignored the proposal without expressly rejecting it. [cite:rs_cw4_unyb1960] The UN's account matters for what followed: eleven days before the raid, the UN's own officer had addressed the expansion of cultivation as the problem and offered a line that one side did not take up.

Tawafiq, 31 January–1 February 1960. On the night of 31 January–1 February 1960 Israeli forces shelled Arab positions and occupied Tawafiq, a village about 1,300 metres east of Beit Katzir, and withdrew the same day. The Israel–Syria Mixed Armistice Commission condemned Israel for an attack that caused the village's "almost total destruction." [cite:rs_cw4_unyb1960] Israel's case, as the Yearbook records it, was that Syrian positions at Tawafiq had been harassing Beit Katzir since December 1959, and that Israel had cleared forces "illegally entrenched there." [cite:rs_cw4_unyb1960] The United Arab Republic, of which Syria was then a part, said that Israeli forces had advanced on Arab farmers. [cite:rs_cw4_unyb1960]

The two cases can be stated at their full strength from the same UN record. Israel's was that a kibbutz inside the zone was under fire from positions that had no right to be there, and that clearing them was defence. The UAR's was that Israeli forces had advanced on Arab farmers; and the UN record adds that Israeli cultivation had spread east, cutting Arab farmers off from the lake, that the UN had offered a line less than two weeks earlier which Israel had left unanswered, and that the armistice commission condemned an attack that almost destroyed the village. Neither account, as the Yearbook records them, denies the other's facts outright. They differ on which came first and on whether the response matched what provoked it.

A later account adds detail that the Yearbook does not give. Wikipedia's article on the episode, citing the historians Bar-Joseph and Gluska, says that the raid was called Operation Hargol, that it was carried out by the Golani Brigade, and that it followed Syrian shelling which killed an Israeli policeman on 31 January. It gives the dead as 9 Syrians and 3 Israelis. [cite:rs_cw4_wiki_rotem] Those figures are reported, not established from a primary source used here, and the UN Yearbook excerpt gives no casualty count to set beside them.

Radio Cairo, 3 February. The raid was answered first on the air. On 3 February 1960 Radio Cairo declared: "Our forces, reinforced after the unification of Egypt and Syria, have taught the Israelis a lesson." It added: "In the south, our heroes are stationed on the border, awaiting the signal." [cite:rs_cw4_cojs_radio_cairo] The broadcast joined the Syrian front to the Egyptian one, as the union of the two countries now allowed Cairo to do, and it pointed south.

The Rotem crisis, February–March 1960. What followed in the south was, in the title of Uri Bar-Joseph's 1995 study, "Egypt's Sinai surprise of 1960," and Israel was "caught unaware." [cite:rs_cw4_barjoseph_1995] The fullest account available here is Wikipedia's, which rests on Bar-Joseph's work, and it is given as reported. Between about 17 and 24 February 1960 Egypt moved its 2nd Infantry and 4th Armoured Divisions into Sinai under radio silence. An Israeli reconnaissance flight confirmed the move on 23 February. Rabin is quoted as saying: "We've been caught with our pants down." On 25 February the General Staff issued the orders called "Rotem." Ben-Gurion refused a full call-up and authorized 7,000 reservists. Egypt's withdrawal began on 9 March. [cite:rs_cw4_wiki_rotem] [cite:rs_cw4_barjoseph_1995]

The episode was short, but its mechanism is precise. Two divisions moved into Sinai over about a week before Israel's reconnaissance confirmed them. Ben-Gurion chose a limited call-up of 7,000 reservists over a full one, and Egypt began to withdraw on 9 March. Historians, as Wikipedia summarizes their view, describe Rotem as a "trial run" for May–June 1967, when Nasser again moved forces into Sinai, that time in public. [cite:rs_cw4_wiki_rotem] [cite:rs_cw4_barjoseph_1995] The phrase is an interpretation, made with hindsight. It holds that the 1960 episode taught both sides something that shaped 1967; the sources used here do not record what either side's planners in 1967 said they had learned from 1960.

Lake Tiberias, March 1962. Two years later the lake itself was the issue. Exchanges of fire between Syria and Israel began on 8 March 1962. On the night of 16–17 March, according to Syria's complaint to the Security Council, Israel made a raid in force from the demilitarized zone. [cite:rs_cw4_frus62_d251] [cite:rs_cw4_unsc171] Israel's counter-claim was that Syrians had fired on its fishermen and on police boats on Lake Tiberias. Israel also asserted sovereignty over the whole lake. The State Department's legal adviser judged that this claim was not finally established, though Israel held exclusive control of the lake. [cite:rs_cw4_frus62_d251]

Israel's case, at its strongest, was the one it had made at Tawafiq: its citizens, here fishermen and the police who protected them, were under fire from Syrian positions on the shore, on a lake that Israel controlled and regarded as its own. Syria's case was that the attack of 16–17 March was a raid in force out of a zone that was meant to be demilitarized. The American legal opinion did not choose between the narratives, but it did weigh in on one premise of Israel's: control of the lake was a fact, sovereignty over all of it was a claim.

Resolution 171, 9 April 1962. The Security Council answered on 9 April 1962. Resolution 171 deplored the hostile exchanges between Syria and Israel that had begun on 8 March 1962. It reaffirmed the Council's resolution 111 of 1956, and it determined that "the Israel attack of 16-17 March 1962 constitutes a flagrant violation of that resolution." It called on both parties to observe the demilitarized zone. It passed by 10 votes to none, with France abstaining. [cite:rs_cw4_unsc171] It had two parts: one that spread responsibility for the exchanges across both sides, and one that singled out Israel's attack of 16–17 March.

How the draft lost its "balance." The State Department's internal account of the drafting, sent by Battle to Bundy in April 1962, shows how the text came to take that shape. The draft that the United States and Britain prepared had been balanced, in the Department's word, by a paragraph on Syrian actions of 8 March. But the US mission concluded that the facts did not support blaming Syria alone for them, and the text became, in the Department's phrase, "less 'balanced' if more objective." A Syrian draft, which the Department called "completely one-sided," was not pressed to a vote. [cite:rs_cw4_frus62_d251] The document records an American government deciding on the evidence that a paragraph meant to share blame with Syria could not be sustained, and saying so internally in plain terms. It also records the Department's dismissal of Syria's own text as "completely one-sided."

The mechanism. Set side by side, the two Syrian episodes show the same structure. In the demilitarized zones neither side had sovereignty that the other accepted, and the armistice machinery, in this record, proposed lines and condemned attacks but did not enforce either. Israel acted on the ground, by cultivation, and answered fire with raids in force; Syria's positions fired on the kibbutz and, Israel said, on its boats. The Mixed Armistice Commission in 1960 condemned the Israeli raid, and the Security Council in 1962, while deploring exchanges on both sides, singled out the Israeli attack as a flagrant violation. Israel, for its part, ignored the cultivation line and asserted sovereignty over the whole lake. The Sinai crisis between them showed, in Bar-Joseph's title, an Israel "caught unaware."

What the record leaves open. Several things cannot be settled from the sources used for this section. The Rotem crisis is documented here only through Wikipedia's account of Bar-Joseph's work and the bibliographic record of his 1995 study, not through a primary document or the study's text; its details, including Rabin's remark and the figure of 7,000 reservists, are therefore reported, not verified. (Wikipedia cites Bar-Joseph's work as 1996; the study itself is dated 1995.) The casualties at Tawafiq rest on that same secondary account. The casualties of the March 1962 fighting on Lake Tiberias are not recorded in any source used here. And who fired first on 8 March 1962 is not resolved: Israel said Syria did, and the US mission concluded only that the facts did not support blaming Syria alone.

sections.h: Bonn's Quiet Partnership, 1957–1962: Strauss, Adenauer and "Aktion Geschäftsfreund"
sections.html:
Egypt's divisions began to leave Sinai on 9 March 1960. The next day Ben-Gurion had an appointment with Eisenhower, and four days later he met Konrad Adenauer in New York. In the five years after the Sinai war, Israel built a relationship with a state that would not exchange ambassadors with it, and whose head of government many Israelis bitterly opposed meeting at all: the Federal Republic of Germany. The reparations agreement of 1952, told in [scene:rd6_financing|financing the new state], had opened a channel for money between the two governments. What followed between 1957 and 1962 was different in kind. It ran largely through the two defence establishments, it was kept secret by both sides, and part of it was booked in Bonn's accounts as something it was not. Whether any of that money paid for Israel's nuclear reactor at Dimona is still argued, and the evidence on both sides is set out below.

A common account treats Germany's support for Israel as the work of a lobby, on the model of the organizations that grew up in Washington and London. The record of these years points elsewhere. In Germany the relationship was made by a handful of officials at the top of two governments, acting on state policy and in secret, rather than through an organized lobby.

Bonn, 3 July 1957. The channel opened between two defence officials. According to the historian Uri Bar-Joseph, Shimon Peres met West Germany's Defence Minister, Franz Josef Strauss, in Bonn on 3 July 1957. Israel asked for two submarines. Strauss, in Bar-Joseph's account, was ready to "build bridges" and was interested in what the Israeli army had learned in the Sinai war. [cite:rs_cw4_barjoseph] The submarines were not built in Germany. Bar-Joseph writes that they were bought in Britain with German money, for less than the cost of a single French Vautour aircraft. Trade ran the other way as well: Germany bought about $30 million worth of Israeli-made combat materiel. [cite:rs_cw4_barjoseph]

The contact did not lapse. The historian Michael Brenner notes that by 1960 Strauss and Peres, by then Israel's deputy defence minister, had been in touch for years, and that they spoke at the time of the meeting between their heads of government in March 1960. [cite:rs_cw4_ja_brenner]

The road to New York, February–March 1960. In March 1960 Ben-Gurion was to see two heads of government in the United States, the American President and the West German Chancellor. The American half of the arrangement survives in the State Department's record. On 1 February 1960 Israel's ambassador, Harman, asked Secretary of State Herter for a private meeting between Ben-Gurion and President Eisenhower. He suggested an honorary degree from Brandeis University as the occasion, so that Ben-Gurion could come "quietly." Herter told him an official invitation was out of the question. A handwritten note on the memorandum records the President's approval of an appointment at 11 a.m. on 10 March 1960. [cite:rs_cw4_frus58_d119] The record shows how the appointment was arranged; it does not include what Ben-Gurion and Eisenhower said to each other on 10 March.

The Waldorf-Astoria, 14 March 1960. Four days later Ben-Gurion, then 73, met Chancellor Konrad Adenauer, 84, in the presidential suite on the 35th floor of the Waldorf-Astoria hotel in New York. No official transcript of the meeting exists. [cite:rs_cw4_kas_borchard] [cite:rs_cw4_ja_brenner] [cite:rs_cw4_barjoseph] What is known of its content comes from the participants' later statements and from what each government did afterwards. Michael Borchard, historian of the Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung, writes that Ben-Gurion proposed economic aid of $500 million as a loan for Israel's further development, and brought a wish list that included guided missiles and submarines. Adenauer agreed to help without naming a sum. [cite:rs_cw4_kas_borchard] Bar-Joseph gives the request in a different form, as $40–50 million a year for ten years, which comes to the same order of magnitude. [cite:rs_cw4_barjoseph]

Afterwards Ben-Gurion said: "Das Deutschland von heute ist nicht das Deutschland von gestern" ("The Germany of today is not the Germany of yesterday"). He said it against bitter opposition from many Israelis. [cite:rs_cw4_kas_borchard] [cite:rs_cw4_ja_brenner] The sentence was a political claim, and the Germany Ben-Gurion described was not free of yesterday's men. Hans Globke, Adenauer's chief adviser, was one of several figures around the Chancellor with a Nazi-era past: Brenner writes that he had written commentaries on the Nuremberg Laws, while the Israel State Archives say he helped draft them. The minister Theodor Oberländer resigned a few months after the Waldorf meeting when his own past became public. [cite:rs_cw4_ja_brenner] [cite:rs_cw4_isa_eichmann] Ben-Gurion's sentence did not deny those facts. It can be read as a wager that the state Adenauer led could be judged by what it now did, and that Israel needed what that state could give.

"Aktion Geschäftsfreund." What it gave was a loan, disguised. According to Bar-Joseph, the arrangement agreed after the Waldorf meeting was code-named "Aktion Geschäftsfreund" ("Operation Business Friend"). It provided about $50 million a year for ten years, at 3.6% interest. The money did not go to Israel under Israel's name. It was routed through a government-owned development bank in Frankfurt and booked as transfers under agreements with unnamed developing countries. The first payment came in December 1961. [cite:rs_cw4_barjoseph] The sources do not record Bonn's own reasons for the disguise. The context suggests one: West Germany was withholding diplomatic relations from Israel for fear that Arab states would recognize East Germany in return, and an open loan on this scale would have been hard to reconcile with that policy. [cite:rs_cw4_kas_borchard]

The German documents that Bar-Joseph cites give the transfers year by year: 82 million marks in 1961, 97.6 million in 1962, 150 million in 1963, 149.8 million in 1964 and 150 million in 1965, a total of 629.4 million marks to 1965. The Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung gives a close figure on a slightly different basis: almost 630 million DM up to 1966, not counting weapons. [cite:rs_cw4_barjoseph] [cite:rs_cw4_kas_borchard] The two series agree on the size of the economic loan. Neither, by itself, says what Israel did with it.

The weapons. Alongside the economic loan ran a separate stream of military aid and arms financing, and here the sources disagree on the sum. German documents, under the heading "Frank/Kol," put military-related aid and arms financing from 1962 to early 1965 at 340 million marks. The historian Roni Stauber, writing in 2022, puts it at 500 million marks. Bar-Joseph reports both figures. [cite:rs_cw4_barjoseph] The difference of 160 million marks is not explained in the material available here; it may reflect what each counted as military aid, but the sources do not say, and neither figure can be preferred on the evidence fetched for this book.

Did German money pay for Dimona? The strongest case on each side deserves to be stated in full.

The case that it did is circumstantial, and its proponents say so. Bar-Joseph argues that West Germany was the "major funder" of Dimona through the Negev loan. [cite:rs_cw4_barjoseph] The points that support him are in the record set out above: a loan of about $50 million a year, agreed at a meeting with no transcript, booked in Bonn's accounts under other countries' names, and arranged while the Peres–Strauss defence channel was open. The title of Bar-Joseph's article speaks of "historical clues." The German newspaper Die Welt, as reported by The National Interest, went further and judged the German funding of the program "with near certainty." It cited a claim by Strauss that Ben-Gurion and Adenauer had discussed Israel's nuclear program when they met in Paris in 1961. [cite:rs_cw4_natinterest] Bar-Joseph adds a thread from the Eichmann trial, Peres's recollection that Ben-Gurion linked the trial to the Dimona reactor, which is weighed with Strauss's warnings about Globke in [scene:cw4_eichmann|the Eichmann section]. [cite:rs_cw4_barjoseph]

The case that it is unproven rests on what is missing. Bar-Joseph himself concedes that the Israeli documentation on how the loan was used is missing, and that it is "impossible to assert unequivocally" that Bonn underwrote the reactor. [cite:rs_cw4_barjoseph] No transcript of the Waldorf meeting exists, so no record shows the reactor being discussed there. [cite:rs_cw4_kas_borchard] Germany has been silent on the question, and Peres denied that German money funded Dimona. [cite:rs_cw4_natinterest] The Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung describes the money as development aid. [cite:rs_cw4_kas_borchard] Strauss's claim about Paris in 1961, on which Die Welt relied, is the claim of one participant, reported second-hand.

Peres's own accounts of who did pay complicate the picture further, because they do not agree with each other. Bar-Joseph reports Peres saying that about half the cost of the reactor and its complex, about $40 million, came from donations by wealthy Jews. The National Interest reports Peres saying that $40 million of Israeli government funds went to Dimona and that this was only half the cost. [cite:rs_cw4_barjoseph] [cite:rs_cw4_natinterest] Both versions put a known payment at about $40 million and both say it covered only half. They disagree on whether that half came from private donors or from the state, and neither says where the other half came from. That unexplained half is the space into which the German hypothesis fits; it is also, on the evidence, only a space.

A state policy, not a lobby. The contrast with Britain in the same years is instructive. In 1957, the year Peres met Strauss in Bonn, Labour Friends of Israel was founded, a group that describes itself as a Westminster lobby promoting the State of Israel. [cite:wiki_israel_lobby_uk] With the later Conservative Friends of Israel, founded in 1974, it is one of the cross-party parliamentary groups through which support for Israel has been organized in British politics. [cite:wikipedia_cfi_uk] The British pattern ran through parliamentarians and party organizations, in public. The German pattern of 1957–1962 had nothing comparable. It was made by a defence minister, a chancellor and his staff, and a development bank, acting on a decision of state and in secret. German support for Israel has been described since as driven primarily by explicit government policy tied to historical responsibility, rather than by an organized lobby of the British or American kind; how later German leaders named that doctrine, as Germany's Staatsräson, is told in [scene:wr2_s01|Germany's reason of state].

The cost of secrecy. The arrangement depended on Bonn's refusal to recognize Israel. West Germany put off Israel's requests for diplomatic relations until 1965 for fear that Arab states would recognize East Germany in return. The secrecy did not last. The arms deliveries became public in 1964, military aid was temporarily halted, and the two states established diplomatic relations on 12 May 1965. [cite:rs_cw4_kas_borchard] [cite:rs_cw4_ja_balke] That end belongs to a later stage of this volume. In the years covered here, Israel received German money and German-financed arms from a government that would not exchange ambassadors with it, and Bonn obtained a relationship it could value without having to defend in public.

Some things the record leaves open. What Ben-Gurion and Adenauer said at the Waldorf-Astoria is known only from later accounts. What Israel did with the 629.4 million marks it received to 1965 is not shown by any Israeli document available here, and so the question whether German money paid for any part of Dimona cannot be settled on present evidence: it is a strong inference for one historian and a newspaper, and an unproven claim on the documents. The size of Germany's military aid in 1962–1965 is given as 340 million marks by German records and 500 million by one historian, without a reconciliation. Peres is reported in two incompatible versions on who paid for half the reactor.

sections.h: Eichmann, 1960–1962: The Capture, the Security Council and the Trial as Politics
sections.html:
Less than two months after Ben-Gurion met Adenauer, Israel seized the man whose trial would test that partnership. The trial of Adolf Eichmann is remembered for its evidence: the documents bearing his signature, the survivors who testified, the record of the destruction of European Jewry set out in a Jerusalem courtroom. That evidence is told, with its numbers and its documents, in [scene:rd4_documents|the documents of the Holocaust]. Between May 1960 and June 1962 the case was also an act of state: an abduction from a sovereign country, a dispute before the United Nations Security Council, a set of decisions in Israel's cabinet about how a trial should be run and what it should and should not say, and West German concern over whose officials would be named. How Israel's government handled each of those questions shaped what the trial became.

The familiar account holds that a group of private volunteers found Eichmann and brought him to Israel, and that the world accepted the result. The government's own archive tells it differently. Israel's official position in 1960 was indeed that volunteers had acted. The Israel State Archives now publish the record showing that the Prime Minister authorized the operation and that the state's intelligence service carried it out, and they note that Israel's version was not accepted at the time.

Buenos Aires, 11–20 May 1960. According to History Today, Eichmann was living in Argentina as "Ricardo Klement." On 11 May 1960 a small team of Mossad agents seized him outside his house at 14 Garibaldi Street in Buenos Aires. On 20 May he was flown out on an El Al aircraft, by way of Dakar. [cite:rs_cw4_historytoday_eichmann] The Israel State Archives record the decision behind the operation: Ben-Gurion authorized the head of the Mossad, Isser Harel, to carry out the abduction despite the diplomatic risk. After the aircraft reached Israel, the Mossad handed Eichmann to the Israel Police. Eichmann gave his captors a letter saying that he was ready to stand trial in Israel. [cite:rs_cw4_isa_eichmann] The letter was given while he was held by the people who had seized him, and as evidence of consent it carries that limitation.

The announcement, 23 May 1960. Ben-Gurion told his cabinet first. Asked at the meeting that day how it had been done, he answered: "That is why we have a security service." He refused to name the country. The same day he told a hastily summoned session of the Knesset that the security services had found Eichmann and that he would be tried in Israel. [cite:rs_cw4_kramer_mosaic] [cite:rs_cw4_isa_eichmann] The phrasing to the Knesset placed the state's services at the center of the capture. The account the government gave abroad two weeks later did not.

The note to Argentina. Israel's ambassador presented a note to the Argentine government, reported on 8 June 1960 in the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung. It said that Eichmann had been taken by Israeli "volunteers" and had "traveled to Israel of his own accord," that the Israeli government had not known he was in Argentina, and it expressed regret if Argentine law or Argentine sovereignty had been violated. [cite:rs_cw4_ghdi_faz] Golda Meir defended the act in a speech in Milwaukee: "I am not claiming that this is a normal situation ... But we are also not dealing with a normal case." [cite:rs_cw4_ghdi_faz] Her sentence conceded the irregularity and argued that the case was exceptional. The note, by contrast, conceded no part for the state in the act.

Argentina goes to the Council. Argentina recalled its ambassador from Tel Aviv and took the matter to the Security Council. It demanded that the Council censure Israel and that Eichmann be returned. [cite:rs_cw4_isa_eichmann] [cite:rs_cw4_wiki_res138] Israel's reply, in its letter S/4342 of 21 June 1960 and in Meir's statement of 22 June, rested on three points: private volunteers had acted, the matter lay outside the Council's competence, and it should be settled between the two governments. [cite:rs_cw4_wiki_res138] The Israel State Archives note simply that Israel's version was not accepted. [cite:rs_cw4_isa_eichmann] Whether Argentina also expelled Israel's ambassador in this period has not been verified in the sources used for this book; only the recall of Argentina's own ambassador is documented here.

Resolution 138, 23 June 1960. The Council acted at its 868th meeting, on 23 June 1960. The resolution's operative language is precise. It declared that acts such as this one, "which affect the sovereignty of a Member State," may, if repeated, endanger international peace and security. It requested the Government of Israel "to make appropriate reparation in accordance with the Charter of the United Nations and the rules of international law." And it expressed the hope that friendly relations between the two countries would be advanced. [cite:rs_cw4_unsc138] It was adopted by 8 votes to none. Poland and the Soviet Union abstained; Argentina, a party to the dispute, did not vote. [cite:rs_cw4_unsc138]

What "appropriate reparation" meant was left open. Argentina's delegate, Mario Amadeo, declined to say whether it meant Eichmann's return. [cite:rs_cw4_wiki_res138] On one reading, the ambiguity let the resolution pass without either government having to accept a defeat: Argentina had a finding that its sovereignty had been affected, and Israel had not been ordered to give up its prisoner.

Whether the Council condemned Israel is itself disputed, and the disagreement turns on what counts as condemnation. The Israel State Archives describe the resolution as condemning Israel, and in substance the case is strong: the Council found that an act affecting a member state's sovereignty had occurred, addressed its request for reparation to Israel alone, and acted despite Israel's argument that the matter lay outside its competence. [cite:rs_cw4_isa_eichmann] The case on the other side rests on the text. Resolution 138 condemns no state by name, speaks of such acts in general terms and of their possible future danger if repeated, and asks for a reparation that the complaining party itself would not define. Argentina had asked for censure and Eichmann's return; the text secured neither in so many words. [cite:rs_cw4_unsc138] [cite:rs_cw4_wiki_res138] Both readings are fair to the document; they differ on whether a request for reparation is a condemnation in all but name.

The joint statement, 3 August 1960. The dispute ended where Israel had said it belonged, between the two governments, but on terms that included what Israel's note had avoided. A joint Israeli–Argentine statement of 3 August 1960, drafted with Shabtai Rosenne and containing Israel's apology, acknowledged the violation of Argentine sovereignty and declared the dispute closed. [cite:rs_cw4_wiki_res138] [cite:rs_cw4_isa_eichmann] Eichmann stayed in Israel.

Preparing the case. Inside Israel the work of building a prosecution began at once. The police set up a special unit, Bureau 06, under Avraham Selinger, to interrogate Eichmann and gather evidence; the work took about nine months. The Attorney-General, Gideon Hausner, led the prosecution. [cite:rs_cw4_isa_eichmann] On 29 May 1960, less than a week after the announcement, Ben-Gurion set out what the trial was for. It should encompass the whole story of the Holocaust, he said, and it "must be conducted according to all accepted procedures." The archives summarize his principles in four parts: the trial was to be held at all costs; its educational value was to be stressed; Israel was to gain political benefit from it while limiting the risk to its relations with West Germany; and it was to be fair. [cite:rs_cw4_isa_eichmann] Those four aims did not always point the same way, and much of the trial's politics, as the archives record it, can be read as a trading of one against another.

The German question. The third principle touched the most sensitive question. West German officials hoped that Israel would not use the trial against Germany. Their concern had a name. Hans Globke, Adenauer's chief adviser, had, in the archives' words, helped draft the Nuremberg Laws; East Germany's lawyer, Friedrich Kaul, used him in propaganda against Bonn. Adenauer defended Globke. Ben-Gurion asked Hausner to say "Nazi Germany" rather than "Germany." [cite:rs_cw4_isa_eichmann] The sources describe Globke's past in slightly different terms: the archives say he helped draft the Nuremberg Laws, while the historian Michael Brenner writes that he wrote commentaries on them. [cite:rs_cw4_ja_brenner]

There was more at stake than words. In the same months, as told in [scene:cw4_europe|Bonn's quiet partnership], West Germany was arranging a secret loan of about $50 million a year to Israel and financing arms. According to the historian Uri Bar-Joseph, Franz Josef Strauss, the West German defence minister, stressed to Israeli officials during the trial that naming senior Bonn officials, especially Globke, would put that arrangement at risk. Bar-Joseph also quotes Shimon Peres as saying that Ben-Gurion linked the Eichmann trial to the Dimona reactor. [cite:rs_cw4_barjoseph] These are a historian's reporting and a participant's recollection, not a document of the time, and they should be read as such. They are consistent with Ben-Gurion's own written principle of limiting the risk to relations with Bonn, and with his instruction to Hausner. What they do not show is that any specific evidence was withheld from the court.

Fairness, decided by vote. The fourth principle was tested in the cabinet. The government voted 6–5 to let two Germans with Nazi pasts testify for the defence with immunity from prosecution. It agreed to pay $20,000 toward the cost of the defence. And it passed a special law allowing a foreign lawyer, Robert Servatius, to appear for Eichmann. [cite:rs_cw4_isa_eichmann] The narrow vote shows how contested the question was: almost half the cabinet would have refused immunity to defence witnesses with Nazi pasts. Concern about how the trial would be seen abroad was recorded as well: in a document on American opinion, Michael Arnon warned against a "show trial." [cite:rs_cw4_isa_eichmann]

Trial, sentence, appeal. The trial opened on 11 April 1961 before a panel headed by Judge Moshe Landau. Sentence of death was passed on 15 December 1961. The Supreme Court rejected the appeal on 29 May 1962. [cite:rs_cw4_isa_eichmann] What the court heard, and the dates on which the sources differ for the verdict itself, are told in [scene:rd4_documents|the documents of the Holocaust].

Clemency. The last decisions were political as well as legal. The archives record that the letters reaching the authorities showed near-complete public support for the death sentence. A group around Martin Buber and Hugo Bergman dissented: they asked President Ben-Zvi to annul the sentence. Inside the cabinet, the Finance Minister, Levi Eshkol, proposed commuting it to life imprisonment; the government rejected his proposal. Ben-Zvi denied clemency, and Eichmann was executed on the night of 31 May–1 June 1962. [cite:rs_cw4_isa_eichmann] Buber and Bergman's appeal was a minority position against the near-complete support recorded in the letters, but it was not isolated: a minister in the government that decided the question had proposed sparing Eichmann's life as well.

What the trial changed. Ben-Gurion's second principle, the trial's educational purpose, is the one the archives judge to have been achieved. They record that the trial shifted Israeli attitudes toward the Holocaust. [cite:rs_cw4_isa_eichmann] The archives' publication does not set out in detail what the earlier attitudes were or how the change was measured, and this book does not supply them. The effect abroad is recorded in a survey: the archives' survey recorded a sharp rise in arrests, trials and extraditions of Nazi criminals in the year after the capture. [cite:rs_cw4_isa_eichmann] An abduction that the Security Council had found to affect a state's sovereignty was followed by an increase in the ordinary legal pursuit of the same class of criminal. The survey as summarized does not break the rise down by country.

The case for Israel's conduct, in its strongest form, is the one Meir gave in Milwaukee: the act was irregular, but the case was not a normal one, and the crimes in question justified an exception. The case against it, as Argentina put it to the Council, is that the act violated Argentine sovereignty; and Israel's account to Argentina of who had acted differs from what its own archive now shows. The Council's resolution and the joint statement of 3 August accepted parts of both: Israel apologized and acknowledged the violation, and Eichmann was tried in Jerusalem.

Several things remain open. Whether Argentina expelled Israel's ambassador, as well as recalling its own, has not been confirmed. Whether West German pressure, or the arrangement with Bonn, affected what the prosecution said about officials of the Federal Republic rests on later recollection and a historian's reconstruction rather than on a document of the time. How Israeli attitudes toward the Holocaust changed, beyond the archives' general statement, is not detailed in the sources used here. And the most famous argument about the trial, Hannah Arendt's and her critics', lies outside the sources of this volume, so it is noted here and not summarized.

sections.h: Iran and Israel, 1957–1960: Oil, Intelligence and a Recognition Never Announced
sections.html:
The Eichmann case put Israel before the Security Council. Its relationship with Iran was built to stay out of view of any such forum. Iran's relations with Israel before 1953, and the coup of August 1953 that restored the Shah's power, are told earlier in this volume, in [scene:s11|the coup of 1953]. By the late 1950s the relationship had become something neither government described in public. Iran sold Israel oil; its new intelligence service asked Israel's for training; Israeli agricultural experts worked in Iranian ministries; and Israel's mission in Tehran called itself a trade delegation. In July 1960 the Shah said in public, briefly, what all this implied, and Egypt broke off relations with Iran. Two questions about it are still answered differently: when Iran recognized Israel, and why Egypt broke with Iran.

The record of these years shows two governments that dealt with each other closely and deliberately, for interests each could name, while keeping the extent of their dealings out of view. What divided them in public was not hostility but the cost of being seen together.

Oil first, 1956. The first thread was commercial. According to the historian Noa Schonmann, oil trade between Iran and Israel began quietly in late 1956, at Iran's initiative. [cite:rs_cw4_schonmann_2024] A US embassy telegram printed in the State Department's documentary series, Foreign Relations of the United States, records that Israel depended on Iran for the oil for its Eilat pipeline, under a contract recently signed with the Rothschild group. [cite:rs_cw4_frus58v12_d273] Iran was the supplier on which the pipeline depended.

The intelligence services, 1957–1958. The second thread ran between the intelligence services. Iran's internal security service, SAVAK, was founded in 1957, with American and Israeli help, as told in [scene:ira_s00b|the 1954 consortium and SAVAK's founding]. Schonmann writes that in 1957 SAVAK's director, General Teymur Bakhtiar, met an Israeli representative in Paris, and that the Shah wanted the Mossad to train Iranian agents in surveillance and listening techniques. By November 1957 high-level visits and exchanges of liaison officers had followed. In late February 1958 the head of the Mossad, Isser Harel, visited Tehran. [cite:rs_cw4_schonmann_2024] In Schonmann's account it was the Shah who wanted the training.

One further step is reported but less firmly documented. According to Paul Iddon, writing in The New Arab, the Shah in 1958 secretly arranged with Israel to set up an anti-Nasser broadcasting station at Ahvaz, in the province of Khuzestan. [cite:rs_cw4_newarab_iddon] That claim rests on a single later account and has not been corroborated in the other sources used here. If it is accurate, it shows the two governments acting together against a common rival, Nasser, and not only exchanging oil and training. These ties ran alongside, and fed into, the wider Israeli effort of 1957–1958 to build alliances on the region's edges, told in [scene:cw4_periphery|the periphery doctrine].

A trade delegation. The form of Israel's presence in Iran mattered as much as its substance. Yossi Alpher, a former Israeli intelligence officer, has said that Israel's presence in Tehran was formally a trade delegation, and that it was kept at a low level so as not to offend Iran's Arab partners.
