[cite:rs_cw4_alpher_brookings] That is a participant's later account rather than a document of the time, but it fits the rest of the record: the relationship was real, and both governments kept its official face small.

Bakhtiar's complaint. What Iran wanted from these ties is visible in a conversation Ben-Gurion reported to the American embassy. The telegram printed in Foreign Relations records his account of a secret talk, around 27 July, with Bakhtiar, whom Ben-Gurion called the "No. 2 man Iran who had ear of Shah." Bakhtiar told him that Iran felt "let down" by the United States, because Turkey and Pakistan received far more American arms, and asked whether Iran "should … turn to Russia." Ben-Gurion replied that Iran had no alternative to close alliance with the West. [cite:rs_cw4_frus58v12_d273] The exchange shows an Israeli prime minister arguing the West's case to the head of an Iranian service, and doing so in a conversation he then reported to Washington.

The same telegram notes that several Israeli cultural and agricultural experts had visited Iran at Iran's request, and that one Israeli was serving as a consultant to Iran's Ministry of Agriculture. [cite:rs_cw4_frus58v12_d273] The relationship was not confined to oil and intelligence. It extended into Iran's civil administration, again at Iran's invitation.

The date of this telegram is uncertain, and the uncertainty matters. Its file number reads as August 1959. But the editors' note attached to it describes the Shah's statement of July 1960, discussed below. The talk with Bakhtiar "around 27 July" may therefore belong to 1959 or to 1960, and the sources used for this book do not settle which. [cite:rs_cw4_frus58v12_d273] If it was 1960, Bakhtiar's complaint came in the same week as the Shah's public statement on Israel; if 1959, a year earlier.

The Shah's statement, July 1960. In July 1960 the Shah was asked at a press conference whether Iran would recognize Israel. According to Shahrough Akhavi, writing in the Encyclopaedia Iranica, he said that Iran "had recognized Israel years ago." [cite:rs_cw4_iranica_akhavi] The FRUS editors give the fuller version: on 24 July the Shah announced that Iran's de facto recognition of Israel had existed since 1949, although Iran's envoy had been recalled from Tel Aviv in 1951, and that de jure recognition had never been in question. [cite:rs_cw4_frus58v12_d273] The distinction between the two terms carried the weight of the statement. De facto recognition acknowledges that a government exists and deals with it; de jure recognition is the formal, legal act. The editors' phrase that de jure recognition "had never been in question" can be read as meaning that formal recognition was not on offer; their summary does not say more, and the Shah's own words beyond it are not in the sources used here.

The sources disagree on when that de facto recognition began. The Shah, as the FRUS editors summarize his statement, put it in 1949. The New Arab gives 1950, and Akhavi records that the Shah denied any change in Iran's dealings with Israel "since 1950." [cite:rs_cw4_frus58v12_d273] [cite:rs_cw4_newarab_iddon] [cite:rs_cw4_iranica_akhavi] The difference may lie in what each source counts as the act of recognition, but none of them explains it, and the year cannot be fixed from these sources alone.

The break with Egypt. According to Akhavi, Nasser attacked the Shah's "pro-Zionist" policies and broke diplomatic relations with Iran. [cite:rs_cw4_iranica_akhavi] The New Arab reports that Nasser denounced the Shah for "selling himself cheaply to imperialism and Zionism," and that Iran's Foreign Minister, Abbas Aram, answered by calling Nasser a "feeble-minded pharaoh of Egypt." [cite:rs_cw4_newarab_iddon] A religious voice was added to the political one: Akhavi records a telegram to the Shah from Shaltut, saying that the recognition had hurt Egyptian sentiment and the feelings of the 'ulama of al-Azhar. [cite:rs_cw4_iranica_akhavi] The FRUS editors describe the rupture from the other end: after Arab and especially Nasser's criticism, Iran declared the representative of the United Arab Republic in Tehran persona non grata. [cite:rs_cw4_frus58v12_d273] The two accounts are not incompatible, since each government took a step against the other, but the sources do not establish which came first.

Why Egypt broke with Iran. The obvious answer is the one Nasser gave: the Shah's statement on Israel. The FRUS editors and The New Arab both connect the rupture to it directly, and the sequence of statement, denunciation and break supports them. [cite:rs_cw4_frus58v12_d273] [cite:rs_cw4_newarab_iddon] Akhavi offers a different reading. He suggests that the break may have owed more to Iran's growing ties with the Arab states of the Gulf than to Israel. [cite:rs_cw4_iranica_akhavi] On that view, Israel was the occasion rather than the cause: the Shah's remark gave Nasser a ground for a rupture whose stakes lay in Iran's relations with the Gulf states. Akhavi presents it as a suggestion, not a demonstration, and the sources used here do not contain the evidence that would decide between the two readings.

The interests on each side can be stated plainly from these sources. Iran sold oil to a buyer that needed it, sought the intelligence training its ruler wanted, brought in agricultural expertise, and, if the Ahvaz report is accurate, gained a partner against Nasser, while keeping relations formally at a level its Arab partners could accept. Israel gained the crude that made the Eilat pipeline work, a working relationship with Iran's government and its security service, and a listener in Tehran whom Ben-Gurion could urge to stay with the West. Each government was acting for its own reasons, and the record shows neither acting as the other's instrument.

The record leaves several points open. The year of the Bakhtiar conversation, 1959 or 1960, cannot be fixed from the telegram as printed. The year of Iran's de facto recognition is given as 1949 and as 1950. The Ahvaz broadcasting station rests on one report. Whether Israel or the Gulf weighed more in Nasser's decision is a matter of interpretation on which the sources divide. And the content of the oil contract with the Rothschild group, its volumes and its price, is not given in the material used here. Iran's Jewish community, which forms part of this relationship's background, is discussed elsewhere in this library.

sections.h: How Washington Found Dimona, 1958–1960
sections.html:
In the same summer of 1960 in which the Shah spoke of Israel in public, the first solid report of what Israel was building in the Negev reached the American embassy in Tel Aviv. By the autumn of 1960 a French-built reactor complex had been rising in the Negev near Beersheba for more than two years. How Israel obtained it, through agreements with France signed in 1957 and a construction site run in secret, is told in [scene:cw4_french_deal|the French agreement]. What follows is the other side of the same years: what the government of the United States knew about the site, when it knew it, and why it took until December 1960 for the knowledge to reach the President's table as a formal judgment. It is an intelligence story, and the documents that tell it were written partly by the officials who missed the signs and partly by those who were later asked to explain why.

The first questions, 1958. Washington did ask. On 7 March 1958 a State Department instruction, A-128, asked the embassy in Tel Aviv for information on Israel's atomic energy program. On 15 April 1958 the embassy's second secretary, Lewis Townsend, met Ernst David Bergmann, the scientist who had approached the Atomic Energy Commission for a reactor in 1956. Bergmann told him that a claim about uranium made by a man named Benard was untrue. The embassy reported the conversation in Despatch 652 the next day, 16 April 1958. [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] The exchange was routine in form: an instruction went out, a diplomat asked a question, an official gave an answer, and a despatch came back. Nothing in it obliged anyone in Washington to look further.

What else was said in April 1958 mattered more, though no one saw it at the time. Bergmann had also mentioned an "experimental reactor." That remark was read in Washington as a reference to Soreq, the small research reactor that the American firm AMF had contracted in March 1957 to build for Israel under the Atoms for Peace program. [cite:rs_cw4_nsa_reveal] [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510]

What the post-mortem found. The clearest account of the failure is the government's own. An intelligence post-mortem was delivered to President Kennedy's office on 31 January 1961. It found that information on the site had been available to some parts of the intelligence community as early as April 1958, and that site information which reached intelligence channels in mid-1959 "was discounted." It blamed reports that had been lost and dots that were "not properly connected," among them Bergmann's April 1958 "experimental reactor" remark, which analysts had wrongly tied to Soreq. [cite:rs_cw4_nsa_reveal] [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] The post-mortem is a confession of a particular kind. It does not say the government was deceived about facts it had looked for; it says pieces of the record were in the government's possession and were set aside or misfiled.

What the U-2 saw. One question the documents do not settle is the role of aerial photography. Three positions are on record about what photographs taken by the U-2 reconnaissance aircraft showed. The Federation of American Scientists and the Jewish Virtual Library say that U-2 overflights captured Dimona's construction in 1958, but that the site was not identified as nuclear until 1960. [cite:rs_cw4_fas_israel] [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_nuclear] The Nuclear Weapon Archive goes further, saying that US intelligence identified a probable reactor complex before the end of 1958. [cite:rs_cw4_nwa_isrhist] William Burr and Avner Cohen, who edited a published collection of the declassified documents, say it is unclear whether U-2 photographs were especially telling, and that the photographs of the site taken in late 1960 came from military attachés. [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] The first two positions imply that Washington had seen the site in 1958 and failed to understand it; the third implies that the images that counted came later. The 1961 post-mortem, as Burr and Cohen present it, points the same way as they do: information existed from April 1958 but was discounted or lost, so that the government as a whole did not know until the middle of 1960. [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] [cite:rs_cw4_nsa_reveal] None of the sources used for this chapter reproduces a 1958 U-2 photograph of Dimona or a 1958 analytical report identifying it.

A businessman's report, July 1960. On Burr and Cohen's reading of the record, the United States first learned of Dimona in midsummer 1960, and from an American corporate official in Tel Aviv rather than from any intelligence service. [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] [cite:rs_cw4_cns_2015] In late July 1960 an employee of AMF, D. Anderson, reported a conversation with Daniel Kimhi of Naptha Petroleum. According to Anderson, Kimhi said that French personnel were building "a 60 megawatt atomic power reactor" near Beersheba. The embassy passed the report to Washington in Tel Aviv Despatch 75, dated 2 August 1960, the earliest reference to Dimona among the US documents declassified so far. [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] [cite:rs_cw4_cns_2015] AMF was the firm that had contracted to build Soreq, the open American project; its employee heard about the French one in conversation. [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510]

A "textile plant." American officials also saw the site for themselves, and were told what it was not. During a helicopter ride over the area, Addy Cohen, an official of Israel's Finance Ministry, described it as a "textile plant." The briefing book that published the documents dates this episode to September 1960 in some places and, in one document, to February 1960. [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] The difference matters. If the ride took place in February, an American official had looked at the site and been given a cover story months before Anderson's report; if in September, the cover story was offered after the embassy had already been alerted. The documents as published do not resolve which date is right. Addy Cohen reappears in December, telling American diplomats a very different story.

Paris and London, November 1960. In November the question moved from the embassy to the capitals. On 22 November 1960 an official of France's Atomic Energy Commission, the CEA, told John Rouleau of the US Atomic Energy Commission that France was not collaborating with Israel on a power reactor. [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] [cite:rs_cw4_nsa_reveal] The denial was carefully bounded. What France had agreed to supply, according to the sources on the 1957 agreements, was a research reactor, not a power reactor, together with a reprocessing plant covered by unwritten protocols. [cite:rs_cw4_fas_israel] [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_nuclear] Three days later, on 25 November, Secretary of State Herter told the British ambassador, Harold Caccia, that Israel might be building a plutonium-producing reactor with French aid. [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] [cite:rs_cw4_nsa_reveal] By then the suspicion had reached the level of the Secretary of State and had been shared with Washington's closest ally.

Gomberg's debriefing, 1 December 1960. The technical judgment that turned suspicion into alarm came from an academic. Henry Gomberg, a professor of nuclear engineering at the University of Michigan, had visited Israel, and he was debriefed in Washington on 1 December 1960. He judged the Beersheba site a "large classified project" with a reactor "far beyond any kind of a training reactor," one that would be "capable of producing weapons grade plutonium." He estimated its power at about 250 megawatts thermal and noted its resemblance to France's G-1 reactor at Marcoule. [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] [cite:rs_cw4_nsa_reveal]

The estimates of the reactor's size are themselves part of the story. Anderson's source spoke of 60 megawatts; Gomberg put it at about 250 megawatts thermal. The agreement with France, according to the sources on the 1957 deal, was for a 24-megawatt reactor whose cooling and waste systems were designed for three times that power. [cite:rs_cw4_fas_israel] [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_nuclear] No American observer had yet been inside, and each figure was an outsider's estimate.

The intelligence machinery responds, 2–8 December. Within a week the formal machinery produced two documents. On 2 December 1960 the Joint Atomic Energy Intelligence Committee issued a report titled "Israeli Plutonium Production." It referred to a "plutonium separation plant." [cite:rs_cw4_cns_2024] [cite:rs_cw4_cohen_burr_2025] When the National Security Archive released the report in December 2024, its editors called it the first and only known US intelligence report to state that Dimona would include a reprocessing plant; later US intelligence treated that question as unsettled until the late 1960s. [cite:rs_cw4_cns_2024] [cite:rs_cw4_cohen_burr_2025] The point is not small. A separation, or reprocessing, plant is the facility that extracts plutonium; it was the part of the French package that, by the French official Bertrand Goldschmidt's later recollection, had been "quite difficult" to agree. [cite:rs_cw4_goldschmidt]

On 8 December 1960 came Special National Intelligence Estimate 100-8-60. It judged that "plutonium production for weapons is at least one major purpose" of the project, and that Israel "will produce some weapons grade plutonium in 1963-64 and possibly as early as 1962." The same day, CIA Director Allen Dulles briefed the 470th meeting of the National Security Council, showing photographs taken by the US Army attaché, and Herter put the cost of the project at $40–80 million. [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] [cite:rs_cw4_cohen_burr_2025] The Federation of American Scientists also dates to 8 December 1960 a CIA report on Dimona's implications for the spread of nuclear weapons. [cite:rs_cw4_fas_israel]

How the machinery worked, and where it failed. The chain in the figure shows who could act on a report. An embassy officer could ask questions and send despatches, but could not compel an answer from the Israeli government or a site visit. The State Department could instruct the embassy and raise the matter with the French and British. The formal judgments in December came from the Joint Atomic Energy Intelligence Committee and from a special national intelligence estimate, and it was in that form that the matter reached the National Security Council, where the President and his senior advisers could decide what to do. Information had to travel the whole length of that chain to become policy. The post-mortem's finding is that, in 1958 and 1959, it did not: a remark was filed under the wrong reactor, and a report in mid-1959 was discounted before it reached the people who could weigh it. [cite:rs_cw4_nsa_reveal] [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] When the chain did work, in the last week of November and the first week of December 1960, it moved fast: from Herter's word to Caccia on 25 November to an estimate and a National Security Council briefing on 8 December took less than two weeks.

Failure or success? Burr and Cohen, the editors of that collection, give a hard judgment on the American side. They call the delay "a major blunder, what is called in our times an intelligence failure," and compare it to the failures that preceded India's nuclear tests of 1974 and 1998. Seen from the other side, they call it "a tremendous counterintelligence success for Israel." [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] [cite:rs_cw4_cns_2015] Their argument has a counterfactual edge: earlier pressure from Washington on France, which supplied the reactor, and on Norway, which sold the heavy water, might in their view have stopped the project. [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] These are their judgments, not findings of the documents. The case for them rests on the post-mortem's own admission that information was available from April 1958. The case against the stronger version rests on the uncertainty about what the U-2 photographs showed and when, and on the fact that the one embassy report of 1958 described here records a direct denial from Bergmann. Whether Washington failed to see what was in front of it, or was successfully kept from seeing it, is a question of emphasis on which the record supports both readings in part.

Several things remain open. The documents published so far do not show what the mid-1959 information was, who discounted it, or why. They do not settle whether any U-2 photograph taken in 1958 was recognized at the time as showing a reactor. The date of the "textile plant" helicopter ride is given two ways in the same collection. And the 2 December 1960 report's reference to a separation plant raises a question that the sources here do not answer: why a finding made in the government's first formal report was treated by later American intelligence as unsettled for most of the decade. What is settled is the sequence. By 8 December 1960 the United States government had concluded, in a national estimate, that weapons were at least one major purpose of the Negev reactor, and the day before it had summoned Israel's ambassador for an explanation. [cite:rs_cw4_nsa_reveal] What followed is told in [scene:cw4_dimona_december|the disclosure month].

sections.h: The Disclosure: December 1960–January 1961
sections.html:
In the first week of December 1960 the United States government reached a formal conclusion about the reactor in the Negev: a national intelligence estimate of 8 December judged that "plutonium production for weapons is at least one major purpose." [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] How that judgment was reached is told in [scene:cw4_dimona_discovery|how Washington found Dimona]. The six weeks that followed, from 7 December 1960 to 19 January 1961, when Eisenhower's outgoing administration reported to Congress, turned a secret into a public fact. Washington confronted Israel and France, the story reached American television, and Ben-Gurion stood up in the Knesset to describe a project his government had built without announcing it. What each government said in those weeks, and what the officials on the other side believed, is the record from which every later argument about Dimona begins.

Where this begins. The program at Dimona was built with French technical assistance in the late 1950s and early 1960s, and Israel's government has never confirmed or denied that it possesses nuclear weapons, a policy usually called "nuclear ambiguity" and maintained since the 1960s. [cite:israel_nuclear_fas] The weeks described here are where that policy's public life starts. Its later history, including the estimates of an arsenal that the Federation of American Scientists puts at about 90 warheads and that the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists and the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute have put at between 80 and 400 at various times, the Symington Amendment of 1976, which requires an end to US aid to countries that deliver or receive nuclear enrichment technology outside international safeguards, and the photographs that the Dimona technician Mordecai Vanunu gave to the London Sunday Times in 1986, belongs to later volumes. [cite:israel_nuclear_fas] [cite:symington_amendment] [cite:vanunu_wiki] One claim from that later history must be marked here because it is sometimes attached to these origins. Another part of this library states that the arsenal was built partly with weapons-grade uranium stolen from NUMEC, a nuclear-fuel plant in Apollo, Pennsylvania, and that the CIA and FBI concluded Israel had taken it. That claim is contested, not established. [cite:nsarchive_numec] The FBI investigated NUMEC's missing uranium from 1965 to 1980, and the CIA concluded that environmental sampling near Dimona in 1968 had detected uranium enriched to the same unusual specification as NUMEC's missing material; but no one was ever charged, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission said in 2009 that it had no documents proving a diversion had occurred and could not conclude that one had not, and the question remains officially unresolved. [cite:nsarchive_numec] [cite:apolloaffair_summary] The case begins after this chapter's period and is told in [scene:fis_s07a|NUMEC]; so does the wider pattern of Israeli intelligence activity in the United States that another part of this library dates from the 1960s.

The summons, 7–9 December. On 7 December 1960 the State Department summoned the Israeli ambassador for an explanation. At a luncheon of the Operations Coordinating Board the same day, Livingston Merchant said that the Department would be "the sole spokesman" on the matter. [cite:rs_cw4_nsa_reveal] [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] The aim was one voice, under the Secretary of State. On 9 December Secretary of State Herter showed Ambassador Avraham Harman photographs of the site, and he called in the French chargé d'affaires. [cite:rs_cw4_nsa_reveal] [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510]

What France said, 16 December. France answered at a higher level. At the NATO meeting in Paris on 16 December 1960, Foreign Minister Maurice Couve de Murville acknowledged that the Negev reactor was a "replica of [the] Marcoule plant," the French site whose G-1 reactor Henry Gomberg had compared it to a fortnight earlier. He said France would supply raw materials and would receive the plutonium. Asked how the project was being paid for, he said he "assumed the money came from US." [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] That last remark landed on a sensitive question in Washington, because the United States was giving Israel aid, and it would be raised at the White House three days later. The question of who did pay, including the disputed claim of West German money, is examined earlier in this chapter, in the section on Bonn's quiet partnership.

Television, 18 December. On 18 December 1960, on NBC's Meet the Press, John McCone, the chairman of the Atomic Energy Commission, said that Israel had not "revealed" the reactor to the United States. [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] The State Department had wanted to be the sole spokesman; within eleven days, another agency's head had spoken on national television.

The President's meeting, 19 December. The next day Eisenhower met his advisers. His words were about money. "We do not know where they have obtained the funds," he said, and the United States had an interest in knowing "because of the aid we are giving them." He cited evidence that the project would cost $100–200 million. The Secretary of Defense, Thomas Gates, said, "our information is that the plant is not for peaceful uses." McCone said, "there is a chemical separation plant there." CIA Director Allen Dulles said that Israel was trying to confuse Dimona, "a large production installation," with the small Soreq reactor. Eisenhower agreed that Israel should allow inspection of the kind the International Atomic Energy Agency carried out. [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] [cite:rs_cw4_nsa_reveal] The meeting shows where the weight of opinion lay among the President's senior advisers: the Pentagon, the Atomic Energy Commission and the CIA all doubted the peaceful account, and McCone, in this meeting, named the separation plant that the intelligence report of 2 December had described.

Harman's account, 20 December. On 20 December Harman gave Herter Israel's version. Israel, he said, was "building an additional research reactor of 24 megawatts capacity in the Negev," and "a reactor of this size is not of industrial importance." It had been begun a year earlier and would take three to four years to complete. Asked what would be done with the plutonium, he said he could not answer. He cited a French Foreign Office announcement of 19 December giving assurances that the reactor was for peaceful use. [cite:rs_cw4_frus58_d180] The figure of 24 megawatts was the one written into the 1957 agreement with France, according to the sources on that agreement; those sources add that its cooling and waste systems were designed for three times that power. [cite:rs_cw4_fas_israel] [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_nuclear] Harman's statement that the work had begun a year earlier sits awkwardly beside the Nuclear Weapon Archive's dating of groundbreaking to early 1958. [cite:rs_cw4_nwa_isrhist]

Ben-Gurion in the Knesset. Ben-Gurion then made the reactor public in Israel. He told the Knesset it was "exclusively for peaceful purposes," in the words Burr and Cohen quoted in 2015, and that it was "a research reactor ... which will serve the needs of industry, agriculture, health, and science," in the words Cohen and Burr quoted in 2025. [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] [cite:rs_cw4_cohen_burr_2025] The Federation of American Scientists and the Jewish Virtual Library summarize the statement as describing a nuclear research center built for "peaceful purposes." [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_nuclear] [cite:rs_cw4_fas_israel] The date of the speech is itself given two ways. The Nuclear Weapon Archive and one passage of the 2015 briefing book date it 21 December 1960; Cohen and Burr in 2025, and another passage of the same 2015 briefing book, date it 22 December. [cite:rs_cw4_nwa_isrhist] [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] [cite:rs_cw4_cohen_burr_2025] The sources used for this chapter do not include the Knesset record that would settle it.

"Misbehaving a little." In private, an Israeli official said something different. On 21–22 December 1960 Addy Cohen of the Finance Ministry, the same official who had once called the site a "textile plant," told American diplomats that Israel had "been misbehaving a little" and that the reactor could be used "for weapons purposes." The embassy reported it in Tel Aviv Telegram 574 of 23 December. [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] The telegram records a remark to diplomats, not a statement of policy. But it was made on the same days as the Knesset speech, and it conceded to Americans the possibility the speech denied.

Ben-Gurion and Reid, 24 December. Ben-Gurion objected to the publicity. Meeting the American ambassador, Ogden Reid, on 24 December 1960, he asked: "Why in [the] States is everything being told [to] everybody?" [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] Cohen and Burr also quote him telling Reid in this period that "we are not a satellite of America ... and will never be a satellite." [cite:rs_cw4_cohen_burr_2025] The second remark states the Israeli position at its strongest: a sovereign state's defence program was not subject to another government's approval, however close the two were. The first was a complaint about publicity; it came six days after McCone's television appearance, though the record quoted here does not say which disclosure he had in mind.

Washington is not satisfied. The American reply was blunt. A State Department telegram to Tel Aviv at the end of December 1960 said that "Neither Dept nor other interested Washington agencies consider Ben Gurion's statements thus far satisfactory." It stated that "USG policy is unequivocally opposed to proliferation of nuclear weapons capabilities," and it added that Washington would "not welcome new round of alarmist publicity." [cite:rs_cw4_frus58_d181] Another telegram, of 31 December, cited a "clearly apparent lack of candor." Merchant recorded Allen Dulles's complaint that Israel had "by no means come clean with us." [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] The two halves of the late-December telegram pull in different directions, and that was the administration's position: it wanted a full account from Israel, and it did not want the public argument to grow.

The money. Eisenhower's question about funds was never answered in these weeks, but the estimates show how far apart the guesses were. On 28 December 1960 the embassy in Tel Aviv estimated Dimona's cost at $17.8 million in foreign exchange and 29.2 million Israeli pounds. [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] Herter had put it at $40–80 million on 8 December; Eisenhower cited $100–200 million on 19 December. [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] The embassy divided its estimate into a foreign-exchange share and a share in Israeli pounds; the documents used here give no rate for combining the two, and none says which estimate was closest. The question of cost mattered politically because of the aid: if a project of $100 million or more was being financed while Israel received American assistance, Eisenhower's advisers wanted to know from where. Reid, on the same day as the embassy estimate, suggested bringing in the International Atomic Energy Agency or internationally known scientists to examine the site. [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510]

No inspection, 4 January 1961. Ben-Gurion answered the call for inspection on 4 January 1961. Israel, he said, "has no plans for producing nuclear weapons," and it would not accept inspection by the International Atomic Energy Agency "until all reactors are treated as equals." [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] [cite:rs_cw4_nsa_reveal] The condition was framed as a principle of equal treatment among states; in practice it meant no international inspection.

The handover, 19 January 1961. On 19 January 1961 the outgoing administration sent a summary to Congress's Joint Committee on Atomic Energy. It recorded Israel's statement that all plutonium produced at Dimona "will be returned to France." [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] [cite:rs_cw4_nsa_reveal] That assurance fitted what Couve de Murville had said in Paris a month earlier, that France would receive the plutonium. It answered the question Harman had said on 20 December he could not answer. Burr and Cohen write that Eisenhower's administration, with weeks left in office, kept the matter under State Department control until Kennedy took office, and that Kennedy then "chose the toughest path of struggle and confrontation," while Johnson later "planted the seeds of compromise." [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] That arc is their interpretation of the whole decade, and its 1963 climax is told in [scene:s11b|Kennedy's letters of 1963].

Was the December account true? Two positions stand on the record. Israel's account, given by Harman to Herter, by Ben-Gurion to the Knesset and on 4 January, and in the assurance passed to Congress on 19 January, was of a 24-megawatt research reactor for peaceful purposes whose plutonium would go back to France. [cite:rs_cw4_frus58_d180] [cite:rs_cw4_nsa_reveal] The strongest case for taking it at face value in December 1960 is that it matched what France said, that no outsider had yet been inside the plant, and that the Prime Minister repeated it publicly. Against it stand the judgments of American officials at the time: Gates, McCone and Dulles at the White House on 19 December, and the cables on "lack of candor"; and, decades later, Cohen and Burr's conclusion that the account was false, resting chiefly on the separation plant that Israel concealed. [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] [cite:rs_cw4_cohen_burr_2025] Addy Cohen's private remark of 21–22 December sits between the two: an Israeli official conceding that the reactor could be used for weapons, on the days his Prime Minister was telling the Knesset it was for peace.

The record leaves open several things. It does not establish who paid for the reactor, or which of the December cost estimates was nearest the truth. It gives two dates for Ben-Gurion's Knesset statement and does not settle them. It shows what American officials believed about a separation plant in December 1960, but not, from the documents of that month, what they could prove. And Ben-Gurion's statement that Israel had "no plans" for nuclear weapons, made on 4 January 1961, was a statement about intentions that no inspection was then permitted to test. The incoming administration inherited all of these questions. How it set about answering them is the subject of the next section.

sections.h: The Lavon Affair Reopened, 1960–1961: A Question That Brought Down a Government
sections.html:
On 25 December 1960, while Washington was still pressing Ben-Gurion over Dimona, a committee of his own ministers reported on a question from 1954, and his government began to come apart. Stage Two told the operation itself: how Israeli military intelligence activated a cell of Egyptian Jews in July 1954 to plant incendiary devices at American libraries, British-owned cinemas and a post office in Egypt, how the cell was caught, who was executed and imprisoned, and how Defence Minister Pinhas Lavon resigned in 1955 without anyone establishing who had given the order. That account is in [scene:lv_s01|Operation Susannah and the Lavon affair, 1954–1955]. This section takes up the second round. Six years after the operation, the dispute it left behind returned to Israeli politics with a new charge, that the case against Lavon had been built on forged documents and false testimony. Within four months the quarrel had produced a ministerial inquiry that cleared him, a Prime Minister who refused to accept the result, and a resignation that ended the government; an early general election followed in August 1961.

The familiar summary of the affair says that the reopened scandal "contributed to Ben-Gurion's resignation in 1963." [cite:wiki_lavon_affair] That compresses two separate events. The record shows that the affair produced its own resignation first: David Ben-Gurion resigned as prime minister on 31 January 1961 in protest at the cabinet's exoneration of Lavon, and that resignation forced an election in August 1961. [cite:rs_cw4_cie_bg_resigns] [cite:rs_cw4_brit_lavon] His later resignation of 1963 belongs to Stage Five, where its date and circumstances are examined in [scene:cw5_bengurion_resigns|Ben-Gurion's resignation of June 1963]. Both resignations belong to the same long quarrel. They should not be merged into one.

The question underneath both rounds was never whether Israel had carried out the operation. Israel later honoured the surviving operatives publicly, in 2005, as Stage Two records. [cite:wiki_lavon_affair] The argument of 1960 and 1961 was about something narrower and, for the governing party, more dangerous: which Israeli official had given the order, and whether the evidence that had forced a minister out in 1955 was genuine.

The charge, October 1960. By 1960 Lavon had a new office. He was secretary-general of the Histadrut. In October 1960, according to reports of the Jewish Telegraphic Agency carried in The Detroit Jewish News, he charged that forged documents and perjured testimony had been used to force his resignation as defence minister in 1955. [cite:rs_cw4_djn_1960_10] A committee under Supreme Court Justice Haim Cohn examined it. The JTA reported that the Cohn committee recommended further investigation. [cite:rs_cw4_djn_1960_10] Michael Oren, writing later, goes further: he states that Cohn found evidence of perjury. [cite:rs_cw4_oren_lavon] The two descriptions are compatible, a finding of possible perjury being a reason to investigate further, but they are not the same statement, and the sources used here do not include the committee's own text.

What to do with the Cohn report became a cabinet matter. The Attorney-General, Gideon Hausner, wrote an opinion on it, and the cabinet voted six to five to publish that opinion. Ben-Gurion abstained. [cite:rs_cw4_djn_1960_10] The vote's margin shows how far the government was already divided, and the abstention marks the Prime Minister's position from the start: he did not want the matter settled by ministers.

Who could decide. The mechanism of the affair in 1960 was a contest over forum, not only over facts. Three bodies claimed or were offered the right to establish what had happened in 1954. The Knesset's Foreign Affairs and Security Committee took testimony; Shimon Peres, then Deputy Defence Minister, appeared before it for two and a half hours. [cite:rs_cw4_djn_1960_10] The cabinet could appoint ministers to examine the evidence. And Ben-Gurion insisted on a third course: a new judicial commission, not the Knesset committee, should establish the facts. [cite:rs_cw4_djn_1960_10]

The JTA's report of 28 October 1960 described what the affair was doing to the governing party. It split Mapai between its veterans and its "young guard." [cite:rs_cw4_djn_1960_10]

A compromise was available. Oren writes that Moshe Sharett and Levi Eshkol proposed a way to clear Lavon without implicating other members of Mapai, and that Ben-Gurion rejected it. [cite:rs_cw4_oren_lavon] The compromise would have closed the case politically. Ben-Gurion's refusal kept it open, consistent with his demand that the facts be found by a judicial body.

The Committee of Seven, December 1960. The cabinet chose the ministerial course. A committee of seven ministers, chaired by the Justice Minister, Pinhas Rosen, examined the case and reported on 25 December 1960. It cleared Lavon of responsibility. [cite:rs_cw4_djn_1961_01] [cite:rs_cw4_nli_lavon] The National Library of Israel, in its collection on Israeli elections, summarizes the committee's conclusion: Lavon had not given the order and had not been aware of the operation. It adds that Colonel Binyamin Gibli was forced to leave the army. [cite:rs_cw4_nli_lavon] Gibli had been the military intelligence chief in 1954, and his account had been that Lavon gave the order. [cite:wiki_lavon_affair]

The committee's finding thus reversed the burden that Lavon had carried since 1955. In 1955 he had resigned, with the order unresolved. Now a body of the government had found for Lavon and against Gibli's account, and Gibli's military career ended.

"Half-truths." Ben-Gurion rejected the report. According to the JTA, reporting in late January 1961, he called the committee's report "half-truths, bias and miscarriage of justice." [cite:rs_cw4_djn_1961_01] He then threatened to resign. Eshkol dissuaded him, and Ben-Gurion wrote accepting the report as "the last word." [cite:rs_cw4_djn_1961_01] The retreat was brief.

The fight moved to the Histadrut, where Lavon held office. Three Mapai members of the Histadrut's central committee resigned, citing loss of confidence in Lavon. Lavon refused to step down. "If the party decides it has no confidence in me," he said, "that is a different matter." [cite:rs_cw4_djn_1961_01] The sentence placed the decision exactly where the party's leadership did not want it: Lavon would leave only if Mapai, as a party, voted against a man its own government had just exonerated.

The resignation of 31 January 1961. Ben-Gurion resigned as prime minister on 31 January 1961, in protest at the cabinet's exoneration of Lavon. [cite:rs_cw4_cie_bg_resigns] [cite:rs_cw4_oren_lavon] Britannica records that he said he would not return to office while Lavon remained secretary-general of the Histadrut, and that Mapai's central committee then voted to remove Lavon from that post. [cite:rs_cw4_brit_lavon] The order of events is the substance of the episode. A ministerial committee cleared a minister; the Prime Minister resigned over the clearance; the party then removed the cleared man from his office in the labour movement, and the Prime Minister's condition for returning was met.

The two cases can be stated at full strength. Lavon's case was that a committee of the government had examined the evidence and found that he had not given the order and had not known of the operation, and that the account against him had come from an officer who was then forced out of the army. [cite:rs_cw4_nli_lavon] [cite:rs_cw4_djn_1961_01] Ben-Gurion's case was that the facts had to be established by a judicial commission, not by the Knesset committee or by ministers, and that the committee's verdict was, in his words, "half-truths, bias and miscarriage of justice." [cite:rs_cw4_djn_1960_10] [cite:rs_cw4_djn_1961_01] Each case was about the forum as much as the facts. Neither was tested before a court.

The election of 15 August 1961. The resignation brought the country to the polls early. The election to the Fifth Knesset was held on 15 August 1961, about 21 months after the previous one; the Israel Democracy Institute attributes the early date to the Lavon affair. [cite:rs_cw4_idi_1961] Turnout was 81.6% of 1,271,285 eligible voters. Mapai won 42 seats, five fewer than before. Herut and the Liberals won 17 each, the National Religious Party 12, Mapam 9 and Ahdut HaAvoda 8. [cite:rs_cw4_idi_1961]

Mapai remained by far the largest party, but five seats had gone, and forming a government took four months of coalition talks. [cite:rs_cw4_idi_1961] The Israel Democracy Institute's judgment of the affair is broad: it touched nearly every public institution, and it may have marked the start of Mapai's decline. [cite:rs_cw4_idi_1961] The second half of that judgment is offered as a possibility, and it is reported here in the same terms. What the figures show directly is a governing party that kept power but paid for the quarrel in seats and in months.

When the charge came: a conflict in the sources. One reference work dates the affair's second round differently. Britannica places Lavon's accusation against the officers in September 1961. [cite:rs_cw4_brit_lavon] That date cannot be reconciled with the contemporary record. The JTA reported the charge, the Cohn committee and the cabinet's six-to-five vote in October 1960, and the Center for Israel Education likewise has the affair resurfacing in 1960. [cite:rs_cw4_djn_1960_10] [cite:rs_cw4_cie_bg_resigns] A September 1961 accusation would also fall after the committee that answered it, after the resignation that protested that answer, and after the election that the resignation caused. This section follows the contemporary reports and notes the conflict rather than silently correcting it.

Was Lavon cleared? The answer depends on what counts as clearing. In one sense he plainly was: a committee of seven ministers found on 25 December 1960 that he had not given the order and had not known of the operation. [cite:rs_cw4_djn_1961_01] [cite:rs_cw4_nli_lavon] In another sense he was not. The Prime Minister called the finding "half-truths, bias and miscarriage of justice" and demanded a judicial inquiry; none was held in the record used here, and the origin of the order was never settled by a court. [cite:rs_cw4_djn_1961_01] [cite:rs_cw4_djn_1960_10] The summary that this library carries from the start, that the question of the order's origin "remained formally unresolved," still stands at the end of this round. [cite:wiki_lavon_affair] The only formal finding was a ministerial one, and the man who rejected it was the Prime Minister.

The cost of the second round, like the first, fell unevenly. In 1954 and 1955 the operatives in Egypt had paid with their lives and liberty, two executed, one dead by his own hand in prison and others sentenced to long terms, while the dispute among those who planned the operation played out in Israeli politics. [cite:wiki_lavon_affair] In 1960 and 1961 the cost was political and fell on the men in Israel: Gibli lost his army career after the Committee of Seven reported, Lavon lost the Histadrut after a party vote, and Ben-Gurion gave up the premiership and went to an election that cost his party five seats. [cite:rs_cw4_nli_lavon] [cite:rs_cw4_brit_lavon] [cite:rs_cw4_idi_1961]

What the record does not settle. Several points remain open on the sources used here. The exact date and vote by which Mapai's central committee removed Lavon from the Histadrut are not established; Britannica records the decision but the sources used for this section do not give its date or tally, and a date of February 1961 has not been verified. [cite:rs_cw4_brit_lavon] The text of the Cohn committee's report and of Hausner's opinion is not among them, so whether Cohn "found evidence of perjury," as Oren writes, or recommended further investigation, as the JTA reported, cannot be checked against the documents themselves. [cite:rs_cw4_oren_lavon] [cite:rs_cw4_djn_1960_10] And the question that began the affair, which official gave the order in July 1954, was answered by a committee of ministers in December 1960 and by no court, then or afterwards, in the record used here.

sections.h: Kennedy's First Months and the First Visit to Dimona, 1961
sections.html:
Eleven days before Ben-Gurion resigned, John F. Kennedy took office, on 20 January 1961, with the Dimona question already open on his desk. The outgoing administration had told Congress on 19 January that Israel promised to return all of the reactor's plutonium to France, and Ben-Gurion had refused international inspection, as told in [scene:cw4_dimona_december|the disclosure month]. [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] Between Kennedy's inauguration and the end of May 1961 the new administration settled on a course: it accepted Israel's assurances provisionally, asked for an American visit to the site in place of international inspection, waited four months for it, and received a report that the reactor was what Israel said it was. Whether that report was right is one of the sharpest disputes in the history of the program.

Rusk's memorandum, 30 January 1961. Ten days into the new administration, Secretary of State Dean Rusk sent Kennedy a memorandum titled "Israel's Atomic Energy Activities." Ben-Gurion, Rusk wrote, had given "categoric assurances supported by appropriate public statements" that "Israel does not have plans for developing nuclear weaponry." The Israeli and French assurances "appear to be satisfactory." But the Department regarded the matter as "not a single episode but a continuing subject," requiring "a continuing watch." [cite:rs_cw4_frus61_d5] [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_rusk] The United States, Rusk added, was encouraging Israel to permit "a qualified scientist from the United States or other friendly power to visit the Dimona installation." He recalled that in 1955, under Atoms for Peace, the United States had undertaken to help Israel's atomic energy program. [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_rusk] [cite:rs_cw4_frus61_d5]

The memorandum set the terms of the whole year. Its first half accepted Israel's word; its second half asked to see for itself. The reference to 1955 can be read as a reminder that American help to Israel's atomic program under Atoms for Peace was a matter of record, giving Washington a standing to ask.

"On a secret basis," 31 January. The next day Kennedy met Ogden Reid, who had been ambassador in Israel through the disclosure in December. Reid told him an inspection could be arranged "if it is done on a secret basis," and that "we can accept at face value Ben Gurion's assurances that the reactor is to be devoted to peaceful purposes." [cite:rs_cw4_nsa_first] Reid's advice combined trust with a condition: a visit, kept secret. The condition echoed the December episode, when Ben-Gurion had asked Reid, "Why in [the] States is everything being told [to] everybody?" [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510]

Waiting, January to April. The invitation did not come quickly. On 28 March 1961 Assistant Secretary of State G. Lewis Jones told Ambassador Avraham Harman that the United States had been "faithfully waiting since early January" for the invitation Israel had promised. Harman suggested that nothing be done before Passover. [cite:rs_cw4_nsa_first] On 12 April, according to the National Security Archive, Harman proposed a meeting between Kennedy and Ben-Gurion; the archive's editors read the Dimona visit as its tacit condition. [cite:rs_cw4_nsa_first] The linkage, if that is what it was, made sense from both sides. Israel sought a meeting with the new President; Washington sought a visit to the reactor; on the archive's reading, neither was offered without the other.

The invitation and its terms, April 1961. In April Harman delivered "an invitation for an American to visit the Dimona reactor site during the week of May 15." He asked that the visit be kept secret, because publicity "could have a most undesirable effect," and he described it as the discharge of Ben-Gurion's specific promise. [cite:rs_cw4_frus61_d31] Two American officials raised a difficulty. Philip Farley warned that labelling the visit secret "might be counter-productive," and Jones noted "a good deal of Congressional interest." [cite:rs_cw4_frus61_d31] Secrecy protected Israel from publicity; Jones's note about Congress shows why it was awkward for Washington, which had a domestic audience waiting for an answer.

Signals before the visit. Two Israeli signals in these weeks point in different directions. On 16 May, according to the National Security Archive, the Israeli diplomat Mordechai Gazit hinted to Farley that Israel might be interested in a nuclear option for deterrence. The archive's editors read the remark as a possible "trial balloon." [cite:rs_cw4_nsa_first] It was a hint, recorded by the American side, and its meaning is an inference by the editors. And Foreign Minister Golda Meir reportedly objected to the visit itself, "concerned about the implications of misleading the American scientists." [cite:rs_cw4_nsa_first] That report, if accurate, is the more striking. It does not come from a document Meir wrote, and it should be read as reported; but it describes an Israeli minister worried before the visit that the visitors would be misled.

The visit, May 1961. The two visitors were scientists of the Atomic Energy Commission, Ulysses M. Staebler and Jesse W. Croach. Even the dates of their visit are given three ways. The editors of the State Department's documentary series, Foreign Relations of the United States, say that the visit, accepted on 28 April for 15 May, was moved to 18 May. [cite:rs_cw4_frus61_d31] The National Security Archive says that the two men arrived on 17 May and visited Dimona on 20 May, escorted by Ephraim Katzir and Manes Pratt, the officer who had directed the reactor's construction. [cite:rs_cw4_nsa_first] The Wilson Center's archive summary says they toured Israel's nuclear sites from 17 to 22 May 1961. [cite:rs_cw4_wda_123836] The three accounts can be partly reconciled, since a tour of several sites from 17 to 22 May would contain a day at Dimona, but the sources used here do not settle whether that day was 18 or 20 May.

What the scientists reported. Staebler and Croach briefed the State Department on 25 May. They said they had been received "with cordiality" and that "nothing was concealed from them." The complex occupied a square 750 metres on each side. The reactor might cost about $15 million, with about $20 million more for supporting plant. The Israelis told them that ground had been broken in 1959 and that the reactor would "not be completed before 1964." [cite:rs_cw4_frus61_d53] Their conclusions were measured. "There is no present evidence that the Israelis have weapon production in mind." The reactor would eventually produce small quantities of plutonium suitable for weapons, as other reactors of its size did. Israel's secrecy was "regrettable, but perhaps understandable." And there was "strong evidence of close French scientific collaboration and support." [cite:rs_cw4_frus61_d53] The report that Executive Secretary Battle sent to Bundy at the White House on 26 May said the reactor was "of the scope and peaceful character previously described to the United States." [cite:rs_cw4_frus61_d53] [cite:rs_cw4_nsa_first] [cite:rs_cw4_wda_123836]

The figures can be set against those of December. The scientists' estimate, about $35 million for reactor and plant together, was above the embassy's foreign-exchange figure of $17.8 million and below Herter's $40–80 million and the $100–200 million Eisenhower had cited. [cite:rs_cw4_frus61_d53] [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] The date Israel gave them for the groundbreaking, 1959, also differs from the Nuclear Weapon Archive's early 1958. [cite:rs_cw4_nwa_isrhist] And the report said nothing of the "plutonium separation plant" that the Joint Atomic Energy Intelligence Committee had described on 2 December 1960, or of the "chemical separation plant" McCone had named at the White House. [cite:rs_cw4_cns_2024] [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510]

Did they see what was there? The dispute over this visit has two positions, and each deserves its full weight. The first is the scientists' own. Staebler and Croach were technical officers of the Atomic Energy Commission, sent to look at a reactor; they reported that nothing was concealed from them and that there was "no present evidence" of weapons intent. [cite:rs_cw4_frus61_d53] [cite:rs_cw4_wda_123836] Their wording was careful. "No present evidence" is a statement about what they saw, not a guarantee about the future, and they noted that the reactor would in time produce plutonium suitable for weapons. Read narrowly, their report may have been accurate about the reactor building they were shown.

The second position is Avner Cohen and William Burr's. Writing in 2025, they argue that the account Pratt gave the visitors, that Dimona would give "experience in the construction of a nuclear facility which would prepare (Israel) for nuclear power in the long run," was false. They write that Dimona's personnel spent weeks preparing before American teams arrived, and that Israel concealed the underground separation plant. They attribute the finding of deception to a State Department intelligence memorandum of 1967 and to later reporting. [cite:rs_cw4_cohen_burr_2025] Meir's reported concern about "misleading the American scientists" fits their case, as does the 2 December 1960 report of a separation plant that the visitors did not mention. [cite:rs_cw4_nsa_first] [cite:rs_cw4_cns_2024] The strength of this position is that it rests on later American government findings and on the Israeli side's own reported worries; its limit, in the sources used here, is that the 1967 memorandum itself is known through Cohen and Burr's account of it, not reproduced.

The two positions are not strictly opposed. The scientists could have reported truthfully what they were shown, and what they were shown could have been arranged so that the decisive facility was not among it. That is in substance what Cohen and Burr argue. Whether it was so in May 1961 specifically, as distinct from the later visits of the 1960s, depends on evidence that the documents of 1961 do not contain.

The record leaves several questions open. It does not show what Kennedy himself made of the report in the days after 26 May. It does not settle the date of the visit, or the year of the groundbreaking. It records Gazit's hint and Meir's objection only as the American side and later historians report them. And it does not show, from documents of 1961, whether the separation plant then existed in a form that two visitors could have been kept from seeing. What it does show is that by the end of May 1961 the Kennedy administration had its visit and a reassuring report, and that both were in hand when Kennedy met Ben-Gurion in New York four days later, as told in [scene:cw4_waldorf_1961|the Waldorf meeting]. The confrontation over regular inspections came two years later, in [scene:s11b|Kennedy and Dimona, 1963].

sections.h: Kennedy and Ben-Gurion at the Waldorf-Astoria, 30 May 1961
sections.html:
Four days after the White House received its scientists' report on Dimona, Kennedy met Ben-Gurion for the first time. The meeting had been sought by Israel through the spring, and in the National Security Archive editors' reading the visit to the reactor was its tacit condition, as told in [scene:cw4_kennedy_dimona|Kennedy's first months]. [cite:rs_cw4_nsa_first] It took place in New York, not at the White House, and it was fitted into Kennedy's journey to Vienna for his summit with Khrushchev. Three records of it survive, and they do not say quite the same thing about the subject that mattered most.

Who was in the room. The two men met in the President's suite at the Waldorf-Astoria on 30 May 1961, from 4:45 to 6:15 in the afternoon. With them were Israel's ambassador, Avraham Harman; Myer Feldman; and Assistant Secretary of State Phillips Talbot. [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_memcon] [cite:rs_cw4_nsa_doc9b] The meeting covered three subjects: the reactor, weapons, and the Palestinian refugees.

Dimona. In the official American memorandum of the conversation, Kennedy described Dimona as "a large reactor, with plutonium producing capability." Ben-Gurion replied that Israel's "main—and for the time being, only—purpose is this," by which he meant economic development, including "the economic desalinization of sea water." He added that "in three or four years we might have need for a plant to process plutonium." [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_memcon] Kennedy said that two American scientists "had given him a good report of it," and he asked whether neutral scientists could observe it as well. Ben-Gurion asked, "who are really neutrals these days?" Kennedy suggested "the Scandinavians and the Swiss," and Ben-Gurion said he had no objection. [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_memcon]

The exchange is short, and almost every phrase in it carries weight. "For the time being" left the future open in the Prime Minister's own words. A plant to process plutonium, in three or four years, was the facility that the Joint Atomic Energy Intelligence Committee had reported on 2 December 1960 and that the May visitors had not mentioned; here Ben-Gurion named it as a possible future need rather than an existing structure. [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_memcon] [cite:rs_cw4_cns_2024] And the answer to Kennedy's request for neutral observers was an agreement in principle with no date attached.

Three records of one exchange. The official memorandum is not the only version. The National Security Archive has published a draft of the same memorandum, written before it was edited, and it differs from the official versions. According to the archive, the draft includes Ben-Gurion's tacit acknowledgment of a weapons potential and a statement suggesting that Israel kept its freedom of action on eventual reprocessing. [cite:rs_cw4_nsa_doc9b] The Israeli minutes of the meeting record Ben-Gurion as saying that "for the time being, the only purposes" were "for peace," and then: "we will see what happens in the Middle East." [cite:rs_cw4_nsa_doc9b]

Two readings follow from the three texts. On the first, which the official memorandum and the Israeli minutes both support, Ben-Gurion gave Kennedy a peaceful purpose qualified only by "for the time being," and a possible reprocessing plant years off. On the second, which rests on the unedited draft as the National Security Archive presents it, he went further: he tacitly acknowledged that the reactor gave Israel a weapons potential and reserved Israel's freedom to reprocess. [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_memcon] [cite:rs_cw4_nsa_doc9b] The Israeli minutes' "we will see what happens in the Middle East" can be read as closer to the draft than to the edited text, since it made Israel's purpose conditional on the region. What the record does not show is who edited the American draft, or why the passages were changed.

Weapons in the region. The conversation then turned to Egypt and to weapons. Ben-Gurion said that "in ten or fifteen years the Egyptians presumably could achieve it themselves," and that "If they should defeat us they would do to the Jews what Hitler did." Kennedy answered that "the UAR would not permit Israel to go ahead in this field without getting into it itself." [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_memcon] The two statements frame the dilemma from both sides. Ben-Gurion's was the case for Israel's security put at its starkest, in terms of Hitler's destruction of the Jews, against a neighbour whose capacity he expected to grow. Kennedy's was the case against proliferation: an Israeli nuclear program would not stay Israel's alone, because the United Arab Republic would follow.

The Hawk. Israel had asked for missiles. Kennedy replied that "while the Hawk is a defensive weapon it is also a missile," that "we are reluctant to introduce missiles into the Middle East," and that "we do not want to see Israel at a disadvantage." [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_memcon] In May 1961 that was a refusal with a promise inside it. How the refusal became an offer fifteen months later is told in [scene:cw4_hawk|the Hawk decision].

The refugees. On the Palestinian refugees of 1948, Ben-Gurion said the Arab states "regard the refugees as the best weapon at hand" and "don't care what happens to people." Kennedy referred to the United States paying 70% of UNRWA's costs. [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_memcon] Each man spoke from his own position. Ben-Gurion's charge put responsibility for the refugees' condition on the Arab governments; it is his statement, and the memorandum records no reply to it from any Arab government, nor any voice of the refugees themselves. Kennedy's figure put on the table what the refugees cost the United States, and so why Washington had an interest in a settlement. Neither statement settles who was responsible for the refugees' plight, a question this library examines in its account of 1948 and after.

How much weight did Dimona carry? The National Security Archive's editors judge that the reactor took "no more than ten to fifteen minutes" of a meeting of about an hour and a half, and that Kennedy "exerted no new pressure." They quote a biographer: "Ben Gurion felt relieved. The reactor was saved, at least for the time being." On their reading, the confrontation over Dimona was postponed for two years. [cite:rs_cw4_nsa_first] This is the editors' assessment. The documents support its core: Kennedy cited his scientists' "good report," asked for neutral observers, and accepted Ben-Gurion's agreement in principle without terms or dates. [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_memcon]

Briefing the Arab states. Washington also had to explain the meeting to Arab governments. Talbot briefed the representatives of ten Arab states afterwards; the memorandum of the briefing was drafted on 7 June 1961. He told them that Ben-Gurion's assurance that the program was "for peaceful purposes only" was firm, and that Kennedy had expressed concern about proliferation and satisfaction with the assurances. The Sudanese ambassador asked about "Israel's second reactor." The Iraqi ambassador asked about American arms aid to Israel; according to the memorandum, Talbot said that question was not pursued at the meeting. [cite:rs_cw4_frus61_d59] On the refugees, the Department's public statement said the United States "will fully support moves made by the Commission," meaning the Palestine Conciliation Commission, and Ben-Gurion's reported comment on the Commission's effort was "It's worth a try." [cite:rs_cw4_frus61_d59]

Set beside the record of 30 May, the briefing was a simplification. Talbot told the Arab representatives of a firm assurance "for peaceful purposes only"; the official memorandum had Ben-Gurion speaking of a purpose that was peaceful "for the time being," and a reprocessing plant possibly to come. [cite:rs_cw4_frus61_d59] [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_memcon] The briefing memorandum, as summarized in the sources used here, also leaves unclear whether "the meeting" at which the Iraqi question was not pursued was the Waldorf meeting or the briefing itself; the Waldorf memorandum does record Kennedy discussing the Hawk. [cite:rs_cw4_frus61_d59] [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_memcon]

The second visit, September 1962. On 17 June 1961 a circular telegram reported the results of the May inspection to American posts abroad. [cite:rs_cw4_frus62_d87] The next visit came more than a year later and on Israel's timing. On 26 September 1962 Israeli officials took two visiting scientists of the Atomic Energy Commission to Dimona without warning, for a tour of 40 minutes. A State Department circular drafted on 24 October 1962 reported "no evidence of preparation for nuclear weapons production" and "Work on reactor progressing normally." [cite:rs_cw4_frus62_d87] The same circular instructed the embassy in Cairo, in connection with the Cuban crisis, to renew to Nasser the assurances about Dimona given in June 1961. [cite:rs_cw4_frus62_d87] The assurance Washington had passed to Arab governments after the Waldorf meeting was thus being renewed to Egypt during the Cuban crisis, on the strength of an unannounced 40-minute tour.

How many visits? The two visits of 1961 and 1962 were the start of a series whose size is itself counted differently. Cohen and Burr give eight American visits between 1961 and 1969, seven of them after Kennedy forced regular visits in 1963. The Federation of American Scientists gives seven during the 1960s and says they were tightly controlled by Israel. [cite:rs_cw4_cohen_burr_2025] [cite:rs_cw4_fas_israel] The sources used here do not reconcile the difference of one.

The gaps in the record are specific. It does not show who edited the draft memorandum of the Waldorf meeting, or why. It does not record any follow-up on the Scandinavian and Swiss observers to whom Ben-Gurion agreed in principle. It does not say whether the 40-minute tour of September 1962 included the place where the December 1960 intelligence report had located a separation plant. And the Arab briefing records the Sudanese ambassador's question about a "second reactor" but, in the sources used here, not the answer. By the end of 1962 the arrangement that began at the Waldorf was in place: Israeli assurances, occasional American visits on Israeli terms, and American assurances passed on to Arab capitals. It held until Kennedy tried to change its terms in 1963, as told in [scene:s11b|Kennedy and Dimona, 1963].

sections.h: The Foreign Assistance Act of 1961: The Legal Frame of American Aid
sections.html:
When Kennedy spoke at the Waldorf of missiles and of UNRWA's costs, the American aid he could offer still ran under a patchwork of laws that Congress replaced in 1961. Volume II followed American money to Israel through the loans and grants of the state's first years, and Stage One of this volume took up the shift of 1951–53 in [scene:iaa_s01|the early aid relationship]. By the end of the 1950s the flow was steady but small, and the law that governed it was a patchwork of programs and agencies. In 1961 Congress replaced that patchwork with a single statute, the Foreign Assistance Act, and the new administration created a single agency to run it. The Act still governs American foreign aid. That continuity has produced a lasting confusion about what the Act of 1961 contained, and this section begins by separating what was enacted in 1961 from what was added to it later.

The statute and the agency. The Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 is Public Law 87–195, printed at 75 Stat. 424. [cite:rs_cw4_usc_2378_1] [cite:rs_cw4_eo10973] It did more than authorize spending. It required that a new agency replace two existing ones, the International Cooperation Administration and the Development Loan Fund, within 60 days of the Act's enactment. [cite:rs_cw4_eo10973] [cite:rs_cw4_frus61v9_d117] The editors of the State Department's documentary series, Foreign Relations of the United States, note the change in an editorial note on the agency's founding. [cite:rs_cw4_frus61v9_d117]

The President acted by executive order. Executive Order 10973, dated 3 November 1961, directed the Secretary of State to "establish an agency in the Department of State to be known as the Agency for International Development." [cite:rs_cw4_eo10973] [cite:rs_cw4_ebsco_aid] The placement matters to the mechanism. The new agency sat inside the State Department, so the delivery of economic assistance was tied administratively to the conduct of foreign policy rather than standing apart from it. Congress, for its part, kept the power of the purse: for fiscal year 1962 it appropriated $4.515 billion in foreign assistance. [cite:rs_cw4_ebsco_aid]

The structure that resulted had three parts, each with its own power. Congress wrote the statute and appropriated the money year by year. The President, through the executive order, decided how the work was organized and placed it under the Secretary of State. The new agency administered the programs. A recipient government, Israel included, held none of these powers: in the documents of 1961 the decision to give, and on what terms, lay with Congress and the executive.

One basic fact is missing from the record assembled for this book: the day on which President Kennedy signed the Act. It was not found in the pages consulted, and this section does not supply it. What is documented is the sequence that followed: the 60-day deadline written into the Act, and the executive order of 3 November that met it by creating the agency. [cite:rs_cw4_eo10973] [cite:rs_cw4_frus61v9_d117]

What Israel received. Within this frame, American aid to Israel in the late 1950s and early 1960s was modest, and its military share was small. The series compiled by the Congressional Research Service, reproduced by the Jewish Virtual Library, gives the totals in millions of dollars: 50.8 in 1956; 40.9 in 1957; 85.4 in 1958; 53.3 in 1959, of which 0.4 was military; 56.2 in 1960, of which 0.5 was military; 77.9 in 1961; 93.4 in 1962, of which 13.2 was military and 45.4 economic; and 87.9 in 1963, of which 13.3 was military. [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_aid_table] The same series records that American military aid to Israel from 1959 to 1973 took the form of loans. [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_aid_table]

Three things stand out in these figures. The first is scale. For fiscal year 1962 Congress voted $4.515 billion for foreign assistance worldwide; Israel's total from the United States for 1962 was $93.4 million. [cite:rs_cw4_ebsco_aid] [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_aid_table] The second is the military line. It is not empty before 1962: the series shows $0.4 million in 1959 and $0.5 million in 1960, both as loans. It is very small, however, until 1962, when it reaches $13.2 million. [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_aid_table] The jump falls in the year of the decision to sell Israel the Hawk air-defence missile, though the series does not say what the 1962 loans paid for. That decision, and the argument over whether American military aid to Israel "began" in 1959 or in 1962, are the subject of [scene:cw4_hawk|the Hawk decision]. The third is that the totals for 1962 are not fully broken down in the figures used here. Military aid of 13.2 and economic aid of 45.4 together account for $58.6 million of the $93.4 million total; the series as reproduced does not say what category the remainder belongs to. [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_aid_table]

Section 620I: a 1996 provision with a 1961 number. The Foreign Assistance Act is best known today in connection with Israel for one section. Section 620I, codified at 22 U.S.C. 2378-1, provides: "No assistance shall be furnished under this chapter or the Arms Export Control Act to any country when it is made known to the President that the government of such country prohibits or otherwise restricts, directly or indirectly, the transport or delivery of United States humanitarian assistance." [cite:rs_cw4_usc_2378_1] Because the section carries the Act's numbering, it is routinely described as "Section 620I of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961," and the account of it elsewhere in this library implies a 1961 date. [cite:aljazeera_620i_explainer] [cite:jstreet_enforce_law]

That dating is wrong, and the correction can be made from the statute itself. Section 620I was not part of the Act as passed in 1961. The source credit in the United States Code shows that it was added by Public Law 104–208 (division A, title I, section 101(c), title V, section 559), enacted on 30 September 1996. [cite:rs_cw4_usc_2378_1] The number places the provision inside the 1961 Act; the text was enacted thirty-five years later. The condition it sets, on a recipient's treatment of American humanitarian deliveries, was not part of the law that Kennedy's administration administered in 1961 and 1962.

The provision's origin lies not in the Middle East but in the Caucasus. Brian Finucane, writing in Just Security in March 2024, traces it to Turkey's closure of its land border with Armenia in the 1990s. A Humanitarian Aid Corridor Act was introduced in 1994 by Representative Richard Lehman; Senator Bob Dole offered a version in 1995; the measure finally became law as an amendment to an appropriations act. [cite:rs_cw4_finucane_js] According to Finucane, President Clinton found that the law was triggered in Turkey's case but waived it on national-interest grounds, and the provision then lay dormant until Senator Todd Young invoked it in 2017 over Yemen. [cite:rs_cw4_finucane_js]

The two datings can each be traced to their source, and the disagreement is not really one of evidence. The 1961 dating follows the section number and common usage; the 1996 dating follows the statute's own enactment history, which the Code records and Finucane explains. [cite:rs_cw4_usc_2378_1] [cite:rs_cw4_finucane_js] This book uses the second. The point is not pedantic. A reader told that the law has stood since 1961 may conclude that it was designed with Israel in mind, or that it went unused against every recipient for six decades. The record shows a provision written in 1996 about Turkey and Armenia, waived in its first test, and revived in 2017 over Yemen.

Its application to Israel belongs to a much later period. On 13 October 2024 Secretary of State Blinken and Secretary of Defense Austin sent Israel a letter citing Section 620I and NSM-20, a memorandum issued in February 2024, that set 15 measures to be met within 30 days, including a minimum of 350 aid trucks a day; humanitarian groups counted an average of about 42 a day over that period, Israel's own figure for October was 57.7, and the administration said afterwards that Israel had taken some steps and that support would proceed. Israel denies blocking aid. [cite:aljazeera_ultimatum_outcome] [cite:jstreet_enforce_law] Earlier, in May 2024, a State–Defense report to Congress had concluded that Israel was not blocking humanitarian assistance; ProPublica reported that two US agencies, including USAID, had found the opposite and that Blinken rejected their findings, and a senior State Department official resigned in protest. [cite:foreignpolicy_620i_scorecard] [cite:motherjones_620i_letter] According to the account in this library, current as of October 2026, NSM-20 was later rescinded. That episode, the Leahy laws that sit beside Section 620I and the general point that each such law turns on a formal executive finding are told in full in [scene:law_s01|the laws already on the books].

What the record does not settle. On the material used here, the date on which Kennedy signed the Foreign Assistance Act is not established. The CRS figures for Israel are given by year without saying, in the version reproduced, whether the years are fiscal or calendar, and the 1962 total is only partly broken down. [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_aid_table]

sections.h: Morocco's Jews, 1956–1962: The Ban, the Egoz and the Start of Operation Yachin
sections.html:
In the same months of 1961 that Washington rebuilt its aid machinery, Israel's emissaries were negotiating a payment of a different kind, with the Moroccan monarchy. Morocco's Jewish community was one of the oldest and largest in the Arab world, present for some two thousand years and numbering in the hundreds of thousands in the 1940s. Most of it emigrated after 1948, mostly to Israel. [cite:w_yachin] The years before 1961 are told in [scene:oa_s03|Volume II's account of Morocco], and the wider departures of Jews from Arab and Muslim countries in [scene:s00e2|the history of the Jews of the Arab world]. This section takes up the years between Moroccan independence in 1956 and the end of 1962, when emigration to Israel moved from a forbidden, clandestine traffic to a secret agreement between Israeli negotiators and the Moroccan monarchy, with money changing hands.

It is sometimes said that relations between Morocco and Israel began with the agreements of 2020. The record of 1961 shows something different: emissaries of Israel's government negotiating directly with a Moroccan prince and a Moroccan minister, and an agreement, kept secret, under which tens of thousands of Moroccan Jews left for Israel with their government's quiet consent. [cite:w_yachin] [cite:rs_cw4_wiki_yachin] That was not diplomatic recognition, and it was not public. It was a working relationship, conducted through secret negotiators and a front organization.

The ban. After Morocco became independent in 1956, emigration to Israel was officially banned. [cite:rs_cw4_aish_egoz] [cite:rs_cw4_pnr_yakhin] The sources disagree on when the prohibition became formal. Aish and the website Point of No Return place the ban from independence in 1956; the Wikipedia article on Operation Yachin, which draws on works by the historian Michael Laskier and by Bialer, Abecassis and Szulc, dates the formal prohibition to 1959, under pressure from the Arab League. [cite:rs_cw4_aish_egoz] [cite:rs_cw4_pnr_yakhin] [cite:rs_cw4_wiki_yachin] The two dates may describe different things, an obstruction in practice from 1956 and a formal ban from 1959, but the sources used here do not say so, and the difference is left as they give it.

King Mohammed V's own position, as the sources report it, was that he preferred Moroccan Jews to stay, and he barred foreign action to encourage them to emigrate. [cite:rs_cw4_wiki_yachin] [cite:rs_cw4_pnr_yakhin] That was the position of a newly independent state toward a part of its own citizenry, and it can be read in more than one way: as a sovereign's refusal to let a foreign state recruit his subjects, as an accommodation with Arab League policy, or as an obstacle to people who wished to leave. The sources support each element without settling their weight.
