People left anyway. Between 1956 and 1961 about 30,000 Jews left Morocco clandestinely; another count gives 29,400. [cite:rs_cw4_aish_egoz] [cite:rs_cw4_wiki_yachin] [cite:rs_cw4_pnr_yakhin] Most went through the Mossad's underground. [cite:rs_cw4_aish_egoz] [cite:rs_cw4_pnr_yakhin]

The Egoz, 10 January 1961. The cost of that underground was paid at sea. The Egoz, formerly the Pisces, was a converted British naval vessel. According to Aish and Point of No Return, it had made 12 trips carrying more than 300 Jews from northern Morocco to Gibraltar. On 10 January 1961 it sank about ten miles off the coast. [cite:rs_cw4_aish_egoz] [cite:rs_cw4_pnr_yakhin] Those two sources give 44 dead, among them the Mossad's envoy on board, Chaim Tzfarti. Twenty-two bodies were never recovered, sixteen of them children's. Three crew members escaped in the only lifeboat. [cite:rs_cw4_aish_egoz] [cite:rs_cw4_pnr_yakhin] One passage of the Wikipedia article, describing the "Pisces tragedy," gives 46 dead instead. [cite:rs_cw4_wiki_yachin] The sources used here do not explain the difference of two.

On one reading, the sinking showed what the ban had produced: families travelling at night on a small vessel, under an intelligence service's direction, because the legal road was closed.

A new king and a negotiation. Hassan II acceded to the throne on 26 February 1961, and the formal ban ended around this time. [cite:rs_cw4_wiki_yachin] [cite:rs_cw4_pnr_yakhin] Negotiations followed. According to the reported accounts, Isser Harel assigned Alex Gatmon to open them in early May 1961. Morocco's negotiators were Prince Moulay Ali and the Labour Minister, Abdelkader Benjelloun. HIAS served as the front organization. A compromise was reached by the end of July 1961. [cite:rs_cw4_wiki_yachin] [cite:rs_cw4_pnr_yakhin]

The mechanism had three parties, each with a defined role. On Israel's side, Harel and Gatmon negotiated, and the Mossad had already run the clandestine route. The Moroccan monarchy, through a prince and a minister, granted permission. HIAS gave the arrangement a public face that was neither Israeli nor Moroccan. None of the three was the emigrants themselves, whose departure was the object of the agreement.

The money. The agreement is reported to have provided for a down payment of $500,000, then $100 for each emigrant up to the first 50,000, and $250 for each emigrant after that. [cite:rs_cw4_aish_egoz] [cite:rs_cw4_pnr_yakhin] [cite:rs_cw4_wiki_yachin] According to Szulc, HIAS financed about $50 million of the operation's costs. [cite:rs_cw4_wiki_yachin] Historians, as summarized in the account carried elsewhere in this library, record that Israel, together with American Jewish organizations, made payments to the Moroccan government to allow the departures. [cite:w_yachin]

The flow of money can be stated plainly, within the limits of the sources. It came from Israel and from HIAS. It moved through a secret agreement, not a published treaty. It went to the Moroccan state, in a lump sum and then per person, so that the payment grew with every departure. What Morocco's government gained was money and, as the sources give Hassan II's motives, the chance to appear favourable to the West. [cite:rs_cw4_wiki_yachin] [cite:rs_cw4_aish_egoz] What Israel gained was immigrants. What the community bore is the subject of the dispute below.

The operation begins. Operation Yachin began at the end of November 1961. [cite:rs_cw4_wiki_yachin] [cite:rs_cw4_pnr_yakhin] Emigrants left by air and by sea from Casablanca and Tangier and travelled via France and Italy. [cite:rs_cw4_wiki_yachin] [cite:rs_cw4_pnr_yakhin] This chapter ends in 1962, while the operation was still running. It continued until the spring of 1964, and its total therefore reaches beyond this period: estimates of departures range from 90,000 to 97,000, and Abecassis gives 97,005 for 1961–64. [cite:rs_cw4_wiki_yachin] [cite:rs_cw4_pnr_yakhin] The account of Morocco carried elsewhere in this library gives about 97,000. [cite:w_yachin] The result for the community is plain in its numbers: Morocco's Jewish population, 162,420 at the start of 1961, had fallen to about 53,000 by 1967. [cite:rs_cw4_wiki_yachin] [cite:rs_cw4_pnr_yakhin] Israelis of Moroccan descent became one of the largest communities in Israel. [cite:w_yachin]

Rescue or paid transfer? The same events are read in two ways, and each reading has evidence behind it. The first treats Yachin as a rescue. In this account, carried by Point of No Return, Moroccan Jews faced a ban on leaving and a hostile climate, and the agreement opened a closed door. [cite:rs_cw4_pnr_yakhin] Laskier's scholarship supports part of this case: he notes propaganda in the nationalist press and arrests, and Wikipedia's summary reports his judgment that the threat to the community was "not entirely unsubstantiated." [cite:rs_cw4_wiki_yachin] The Egoz, on this reading, shows what the alternative to an agreement was.

The second reading treats Yachin as a negotiated, paid emigration that emptied one of the oldest Jewish communities in the Arab world. Simon Levy, a Moroccan Jew of the left, described the departures as a trauma. The historian Susan Gilson Miller called them a "monumental national tragedy." [cite:rs_cw4_wiki_yachin] In this view the community's end was arranged between two states, each acting for its own reasons, with payment per head, and the loss was Morocco's as well as the community's.

The readings do not exclude each other. The ban and the hostile press are documented; so are the payments and the collapse of the community's numbers. What divides them is the weight given to each, and the question of choice: how far the departures were what the emigrants wanted, and how far they were produced by pressure at home and by an agreement made over their heads. The sources used here do not record the emigrants' own reasons in their own words, and no generalization about Moroccans, or about Moroccan Jews, can be drawn from the positions of the officials and writers named above. Each spoke for himself or herself, or for a government.

What the record does not settle. The agreement's terms rest on secondary and advocacy sources, and on Wikipedia's citations of Laskier, Bialer and Szulc; no primary text of the agreement, and no scholarly text of its terms, was among the sources used for this section. The payment figures, $500,000 down, $100 and $250 per emigrant, should therefore be read as reported, not as established from the document. [cite:rs_cw4_wiki_yachin] [cite:rs_cw4_aish_egoz] [cite:rs_cw4_pnr_yakhin] The date of the formal ban, 1956 or 1959, remains in conflict, as does the Egoz's death toll, 44 or 46. The total of the operation is an estimate with a range, 90,000 to 97,000. And how the payments were made, to whom in the Moroccan state, and how they were recorded is not documented in these sources.

sections.h: The Hawk Decision, 1960–1962: From Refusal to Offer
sections.html:
Israel could pay Morocco to open a door. It could not buy American weapons of any consequence: for most of the period covered by this chapter, Washington gave money, not arms. American aid ran in the tens of millions of dollars a year, with only small military loans, as the section on the 1961 aid law shows. In August 1962 that changed. President Kennedy decided that Israel could buy the Hawk, an American surface-to-air missile, an anti-aircraft weapon. [cite:rs_cw4_cie_hawk] [cite:wiki_israel_us_military_relations] The decision took more than two years to reach, was argued over inside the administration at every step, and was tied, in the memorandum that carried it to the President, to an American plan to settle the Palestinian refugee question.

What kind of weapon. One account carried elsewhere in this library describes the 1962 sale as "the first US sale of offensive weaponry to the Israeli military." [cite:wiki_israel_us_military_relations] That description is wrong on the record and should be corrected at the outset. The Hawk was an air-defence missile. Kennedy himself, in May 1961, called it "a defensive weapon." [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_memcon] The State Department's circular of 7 September 1962 instructed American posts to present it as purely defensive, a response to the Soviet build-up. [cite:rs_cw4_kramer_hawks] What made the Hawk a threshold was not that it was offensive. It was that it was a missile, and that it was the first major American weapons sale to Israel. Kennedy's own sentence of 1961 holds both halves: "while the Hawk is a defensive weapon it is also a missile." [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_memcon] The later account's framing, in which the Hawk opens a line of offensive sales continued under Johnson, is examined in [scene:s11d|what Johnson actually did].

The refusals of 1960. Israel had been asking for some time. According to the Center for Israel Education, negotiations for the Hawk had begun in 1958. [cite:rs_cw4_cie_hawk] In 1960 the answer was no. The Pentagon said that Hawks were unavailable, and Livingston Merchant recommended against a sale that would cost "close to $40 millions" for six batteries. [cite:rs_cw4_kramer_hawks] The figure set the problem. A White House staff note of 8 May 1961 put the cost higher, at "$50 million," and observed that "our largest previous sale to Israel had a ceiling of $1 million." [cite:rs_cw4_kramer_hawks] Israel was asking for a purchase forty or fifty times larger than anything the United States had sold it before.

Kennedy at the Waldorf, May 1961. Ben-Gurion put the request to the new President in person, at the Waldorf-Astoria in New York on 30 May 1961, a meeting whose nuclear and refugee exchanges are told in [scene:cw4_waldorf_1961|the Waldorf meeting]. On missiles, the official memorandum records Kennedy's answer in three parts. The Hawk was "a defensive weapon" but "also a missile"; "we are reluctant to introduce missiles into the Middle East"; and "we do not want to see Israel at a disadvantage." [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_memcon] The first two clauses explained the refusal. The third can be read as leaving the door open: if the balance shifted against Israel, the reluctance could yield.

Deferral, June 1962. A year later the State Department still advised waiting. A paper of 7 June 1962 recommended deferral, judging that "Israel is in little actual danger of an Arab assault now." [cite:rs_cw4_kramer_hawks] The judgment was a military one: on its reasoning, if Israel was not in danger, there was no reason to bring American missiles into the region.

Rusk's review, 7 August 1962. Within two months the department's position had changed. Rusk's review of 7 August 1962 recommended offering the Hawk "after consultation with the British and discussion with the UAR." His grounds were intelligence that the United Arab Republic, Egypt, was obtaining comparable missiles from the Soviet Union, and the judgment that the Hawk would "reduce considerably" Israel's vulnerability to surprise air attack. [cite:rs_cw4_kramer_hawks] The argument had turned from Israel's danger in general to a specific Soviet supply. On that reasoning, if Egypt was getting Soviet missiles, the United States would no longer be the first to bring missiles into the region.

Feldman's memorandum, 10 August 1962. Three days later Myer Feldman, who had sat in on the Waldorf meeting, sent Kennedy a memorandum that tied the missiles to something else. [cite:rs_cw4_frus62_d18] [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_feldman_aug10] At issue was a plan for the Arab refugees, known as the Johnson plan. Feldman wrote that "The only chance the plan has for success" lay in telling Ben-Gurion that the United States would guarantee Israel's security and provide Hawks. He urged that the missiles be available "no later than mid-1964," since an offer for 1966 "would be worse than no offer at all." [cite:rs_cw4_frus62_d18] [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_feldman_aug10]

Feldman did not expect the plan to be welcomed by anyone. On the Israeli side he anticipated objection to the plan's lack of any numerical limit on refugees who might return, and to its burden on a state that had, he noted, absorbed some 500,000 Jewish refugees from Arab countries and about 50,000 Arab refugees. On the Arab side he anticipated insistence on full return. He called Ben-Gurion "the most violent opposition." And he estimated the plan's cost to the United States at "about $30 million a year—if we are lucky." [cite:rs_cw4_frus62_d18] [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_feldman_aug10] In Feldman's design the Hawk was the price of Ben-Gurion's consent: a security guarantee and a missile to make acceptable a refugee plan that Israel's Prime Minister was expected to fight.

The meeting of 19 August 1962. Feldman carried the message himself. His telegram, sent under the name "Barnes," reports a meeting of three and a half hours on 19 August 1962 with Ben-Gurion, the Foreign Minister Golda Meir and Teddy Kollek. Feldman told them that the President had decided Israel could have the Hawk, with the terms to be settled later. [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_feldman_aug19] [cite:rs_cw4_kramer_hawks] Ben-Gurion's reply put the arms question in his own terms: he "would gladly agree to no missiles at all if Nasser would agree to arms limitations and controls." [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_feldman_aug19] [cite:rs_cw4_kramer_hawks]

On the refugee plan the Israelis gave little. Ben-Gurion said that no area would accept anything except repatriation. Meir said Israel would accept it only if Nasser resettled designated refugees in the UAR and refrained from propaganda urging repatriation. Feldman answered with the American estimate that "not more than one refugee in ten would seek repatriation." [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_feldman_aug19] [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_rusk_aug21] The refugees themselves, whose return or resettlement was the subject of the conversation, do not speak in these documents. Their position appears only as Feldman's expectation of an Arab insistence on full return and as Ben-Gurion's account of what they would accept. [cite:rs_cw4_frus62_d18] [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_feldman_aug19]

"A statement in principle," 21 August 1962. Two days later Rusk explained the decision to the American embassy in Cairo. His telegram described the offer as "a statement in principle in the absence of arms limitation" and "not an undertaking for delivery at specific time of specific number of missiles." It noted that Israel might prefer Britain's Bloodhound missile instead. [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_rusk_aug21] The language was careful. It presented the Hawk as conditional on the absence of an arms agreement, which matched Ben-Gurion's own offer to forgo missiles if Nasser accepted controls, and it committed Washington to no date and no number.

Approval and presentation. The sale was approved on American credit in late August 1962. [cite:rs_cw4_kramer_hawks] A State Department circular of 7 September instructed American posts to present the Hawk as purely defensive, a response to the Soviet build-up. [cite:rs_cw4_kramer_hawks] The first missiles were delivered in early 1965. [cite:rs_cw4_kramer_hawks] Israel was believed, according to the Center for Israel Education, to have become the first nation outside NATO to obtain the Hawk. [cite:rs_cw4_cie_hawk] Robert Komer, in his oral history of 1969, later said that "the Hawks marked the watershed." [cite:rs_cw4_kramer_hawks]

The money. The sale was a sale, not a gift, and it was made on credit. [cite:rs_cw4_kramer_hawks] The Congressional Research Service series shows the military line in these years, though it does not say what the loans paid for. American military aid to Israel, all of it in the form of loans from 1959 onward, was $0.4 million in 1959 and $0.5 million in 1960, and $13.2 million in 1962; in 1963 it was $13.3 million. [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_aid_table] [cite:rs_cw4_cie_hawk] The estimates of the Hawk's cost, close to $40 million in 1960 and $50 million in 1961, were far larger than any single year's military line in that series. [cite:rs_cw4_kramer_hawks] [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_aid_table] The sale's final price and its credit terms are not in the sources used here, so the chain from the cost estimates to the yearly loan figures cannot be traced.

The timeline of the aid relationship shown above summarizes these years in two rows: "1948–1961: economic aid and loans only," and "1962: first US military aid, as loans." The CRS figures refine both. The first row is right in substance but not to the letter, since the series shows small military loans of $0.4 million in 1959 and $0.5 million in 1960. The second row is right if "first military aid" means the first of any size: $13.2 million in 1962, the year of the Hawk decision. [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_aid_table] The difference between the two readings is the third of the disputes below.

Three disputes. The first is whether Nasser was told. Feldman, in his oral history of 1967, said that "Nasser was not told about it." [cite:rs_cw4_kramer_hawks] The documents of August 1962 point the other way, or at least to an intention: Rusk's review of 7 August recommended the offer "after consultation with the British and discussion with the UAR," and the telegram of 21 August went to the embassy in Cairo, explaining the decision as a statement in principle. [cite:rs_cw4_kramer_hawks] [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_rusk_aug21] A telegram of instruction to an embassy shows what Washington planned to say; it does not by itself show what Nasser was told, or when. Feldman's recollection, five years later, is a participant's memory; the telegrams are contemporary but record intention. The sources used here do not settle which is right.

The second dispute is why Kennedy sold the Hawk at all. The documents of August 1962 give two reasons. One is the military balance: Soviet missiles and aircraft were reaching the UAR, and the Hawk would reduce Israel's exposure to surprise air attack. The other is the refugee plan: Feldman's memorandum makes the Hawk the inducement for Israeli acceptance of the Johnson plan. [cite:rs_cw4_kramer_hawks] [cite:rs_cw4_frus62_d18] Against these, Ari Lance Buchman's 2013 honors thesis at Emory University argues that the decision was driven mainly by domestic politics, to win the backing of pro-Israel opinion, and that it cost Kennedy his attempt at a rapprochement with Nasser; his title calls it "a missed opportunity." [cite:rs_cw4_buchman_emory] The strongest form of the first case is that every contemporary document gives security and the refugee plan as the grounds, and that the decision followed a specific intelligence finding about Soviet supply. The strongest form of the second, as the documents themselves allow it to be put, is that the decision reversed the department's judgment of June that Israel was in little actual danger, and that the refugee plan Feldman tied to the Hawk did not win Israel's consent at the meeting of 19 August, yet the offer stood. [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_feldman_aug19] [cite:rs_cw4_frus62_d18] [cite:rs_cw4_kramer_hawks] Buchman's argument is known here from his thesis's abstract only, and the evidence he relies on for the domestic motive is not among the sources fetched.

The third dispute is when American military aid to Israel began. On the CRS series, it began in 1959, with a military loan of $0.4 million. [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_aid_table] On the account of Komer and of the documents compiled by Martin Kramer, it began in 1962, with the Hawk, the first major sale: "the Hawks marked the watershed." [cite:rs_cw4_kramer_hawks] Both are accurate on their own terms. One counts the first dollar; the other counts the first weapon system that changed the relationship.

What came next. The decision opened a new phase in the relationship, and its terms were worked out in the months that followed, including the talks of December 1962, told in Stage Five in [scene:cw5_palm_beach|the terms of the relationship, 1962–63]. In the same months the administration was pressing Israel over Dimona; the two tracks, arming Israel conventionally while seeking to restrain its nuclear program, ran side by side from here on. [cite:wiki_israel_us_military_relations] [cite:state_frus1964_68v18]

What the record does not settle. On the sources used here, the sale's final price and credit terms are not established. Arab and Soviet reactions to the decision are not documented in them, beyond the August instructions to the Cairo embassy. Whether Nasser was told, and when, remains in conflict between Feldman's later memory and the contemporary telegrams. The domestic-politics reading rests on a thesis known here only by its abstract. And the Johnson plan, to which Feldman tied the missiles, is described in these documents only through the objections each side was expected to raise and the estimate that "not more than one refugee in ten would seek repatriation"; the plan's own text is not among them. [cite:rs_cw4_jvl_feldman_aug19]

chapters.label: Stage Five
chapters.title: Confront
chapters.intro:
By the autumn of 1962 the Kennedy administration had committed itself to two things in the Middle East at once. It had offered Israel the Hawk anti-aircraft missile, the first American military aid to Israel, extended as loans, and in late September it had sent American scientists on a brief second visit to the reactor at Dimona, which the State Department reported to its posts as finding "no evidence" of preparation for weapons. [cite:rs_cw5_frus18_d87] It had also, since the spring of 1961, been courting Gamal Abdel Nasser. Kennedy had written to six Arab heads of state offering help on the refugee question "on the basis of the principle of repatriation or compensation," and American food aid to Egypt under PL-480 had reached $180.3 million in fiscal 1962. [cite:rs_cw5_jvl_jfk_arab_letter] [cite:rs_cw5_frus17_d249] On 8 October 1962 a multi-year food agreement with the United Arab Republic was signed, with Kennedy asking for "minimum publicity." [cite:rs_cw5_frus18_d70] Neither line of policy had yet been tested against the other, and the question of what the United States would require of Israel in return for its support had not been asked in writing.

This stage follows the months in which it was asked. Between November 1962 and November 1963 Washington confronted Israel's government over Dimona and confronted the American body that received the Jewish Agency's money over the Foreign Agents Registration Act, while it tried to hold Cairo and Riyadh on opposite sides of a war in Yemen. The question the stage answers is what those confrontations settled, and what they left in place, by the time the President was killed in Dallas on 22 November 1963. That date ends the stage as a fact of timing. The record reached for this book connects it to neither dispute as a cause.

The actors are named states, offices and organizations. In Washington stood the President; his brother Robert F. Kennedy, whose Justice Department issued the order of 21 November 1962 to the American Zionist Council; Robert Komer of the National Security Council staff; the intelligence analysts who wrote NIE 30-63 and Sherman Kent's memorandum of March 1963; Ambassador Barbour in Tel Aviv; and Senator J. William Fulbright, whose Foreign Relations Committee examined the agents of foreign principals in thirteen parts. [cite:israellobby_org_fara_doj_order] [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] [cite:rs_cw5_ol_hearings] In Israel stood David Ben-Gurion, Shimon Peres and Golda Meir; Isser Harel, head of the Mossad until his forced resignation in 1963; and Levi Eshkol, who succeeded Ben-Gurion in 1963. [cite:rs_cw5_enc_harel] [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_bengurion] Among American organizations stood the American Zionist Council, the Jewish Agency's American Section, already a registered agent, Isaiah L. Kenen's committee, and the American Council for Judaism, which, according to Grant F. Smith, welcomed the order. [cite:rs_cw5_djn_19630628] [cite:rs_cw5_smith_podcast] In the region stood Nasser, Crown Prince Faisal of Saudi Arabia, the Ba'athist officers who seized Baghdad and Damascus in February and March 1963, and Ahmad Shukairy, chosen in 1963 as Palestine's representative at the Arab League, who spoke at the United Nations in November. [cite:rs_cw5_riedel_yemen] [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_ramadan] [cite:rs_cw5_palquest_shuqayri]

The sections open with [scene:cw5_nasser_outreach|Kennedy's wager on Cairo] and the war in Yemen that tested it. They then take up the order to the American Zionist Council and the question of which body was which, the terms Kennedy set with Meir at Palm Beach, and the estimates that turned Washington's view of Dimona from reassurance to alarm. The Senate inquiry is set out as a whole before its part on the Jewish Agency. Between them come the German scientists in Egypt and the fall of Harel, the two Ba'athist coups and the short-lived Cairo union, and [scene:s11b|the battle of the letters] between Kennedy and Ben-Gurion, which ended with a letter that was never delivered and a resignation. Eshkol's answer, the dissent of the American Council for Judaism and Shukairy's speech at the United Nations follow, and the stage closes with [scene:s11c|22 November 1963], told as a question of timing.
chapters.outro:
By the end of 1963 the two confrontations of Kennedy's last year had produced something less than either side had asked for and more than either had conceded at the start. Neither ended in a ruling, a treaty or a prosecution. Each ended in an arrangement that rested on consent, on silence or on a reading of the record that the other party did not share.

The legal layer is the thinnest. The Foreign Agents Registration Act of 1938 was a disclosure law, not a prohibition, and the order of 21 November 1962 that the American Zionist Council register under it was never enforced to completion. [cite:israellobby_org_fara_doj_order] By nearly every account the Council never registered; a single 2016 version of a Wikipedia article says otherwise, and no primary document reached supports it. [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_azc_2016] The Senate inquiry that surrounded the order ran under Senate Resolution 26 to 31 January 1964, with expenses capped at $48,600 and a duty to recommend changes to the law; the sources reached do not show its report. [cite:rs_cw5_sres26] The Attorney General's report for 1964 counted 480 registrants and no prosecutions, and a proposal, not yet law, to make registrants keep separate books. [cite:rs_cw5_doj_fara_1964] On the side of the alliance, nothing was written into law either. Kennedy's promise at Palm Beach of support "in case of an invasion" stayed a spoken assurance, and through the summer of 1963 he remained "unwilling to make 'explicit' guarantees." [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters]

The administrative layer held the real outcome on Dimona. The instrument was correspondence: Kennedy's warning that American "commitment to and support of Israel could be seriously jeopardized," Eshkol's reply of 19 August agreeing to regular visits in principle, Kennedy's "basic agreement" of 26 August, and the memorandum of 16 September that named the "plutonium separation plant." [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] The State Department could ask; it could not compel. Israel's prime minister and cabinet gave or withheld consent to the timing and frequency of the visits, and the six-month interval was declined while Kennedy was alive. Inside Washington, the estimates of January to May 1963 had turned "no evidence" into a forecast of capability, a device by late 1965 or more likely 1966, without claiming knowledge of a decision. [cite:rs_cw5_frus18_d87] [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] Inside Israel the structure changed hands: Isser Harel was forced to resign after clashing with Ben-Gurion and Peres over the campaign against the German scientists, and Ben-Gurion resigned on 16 June for "personal reasons" he never explained publicly. [cite:rs_cw5_enc_harel] [cite:rs_cw5_israelhayom_2013] [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_bengurion]

The institutional and financial layer is where the dispute is sharpest and least settled. The Jewish Agency's payments to the Council stand at $5,100,001.02 for 1955 to 1962 in the Senate record and at $1.5 million in Barda, unreconciled. [cite:jta_fulbright_jewish_agency_hearing] [cite:rs_cw5_barda_2026] The strongest case on one side, Smith's, is that a registered foreign agent's money reached American lobbying through an unregistered body. The strongest case on the other, Barda's and Neumann's, is that the documented payments, $38,000 for subscriptions, bought copies of a newsletter, ended in 1962, and, by Neumann's account, left the committee's chairman saying there was "no wrong doing." [cite:rs_cw5_smith_podcast] [cite:rs_cw5_djn_19630816] What emerged was AIPAC's defence that it is funded by American donors, not by the Israeli government. [cite:factually_aipac_fara] Money moved in the other direction too: PL-480 aid to Egypt of $180.3 million in fiscal 1962, and, on Kenen's account, a Hawk loan of about $25 million over ten years and American aid to Israel that he put at about $85 million in 1963, a figure from a transcription not yet checked against the original. [cite:rs_cw5_frus17_d249] [cite:rs_cw5_kenen_uja_1963]

On the Palestinian Arab side, the year produced a voice more than an institution. Ahmad Shukairy, chosen by the Arab League in 1963 as Palestine's representative, told a UN committee on 14 November that 1,120,170 refugees lived on about six cents a day, demanded the return of their property and called its seizure "genocide," his charge. [cite:rs_cw5_palquest_shuqayri] [cite:rs_cw5_un_spc407] The United States answered that he had made many misstatements and would say no more. [cite:rs_cw5_un_spc407] The sources reached do not show what came of Kennedy's 1961 offer of help "on the basis of the principle of repatriation or compensation." [cite:rs_cw5_jvl_jfk_arab_letter] The organization Shukairy would lead was created only in 1964.

The regional layer was in motion. Egypt and Saudi Arabia had accepted disengagement terms for Yemen and shared the cost of UN observers, yet by Riedel's account each had told the UN mediator by April that it would not do its part, and Egypt's force had grown to about 30,000 by March 1963. [cite:rs_cw5_unyom] [cite:rs_cw5_riedel_yemen] The union proclaimed in Cairo on 17 April for "the liberation of Palestine" had collapsed by 22 July, and Iraq's Ba'athist government fell in November; whether the United States helped bring about Iraq's February coup is still argued among named scholars. [cite:rs_cw5_countrystudy_syria] [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_ramadan] [cite:rs_cw5_gibson_majalla] By the end of the year pressure and diplomacy had driven the German scientists out of Egypt; according to Bergman, West Germany offered them jobs and nearly all accepted. [cite:rs_cw5_jvl_damocles]

The American layer held both policies at once. Washington fed Cairo, armed Israel on credit, and, in the editors' reading, pressed Israel over Dimona out of a view of proliferation as "a major challenge to American power." [cite:rs_cw5_frus18_d70] [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] Kennedy was killed in Dallas on 22 November 1963. That is a fact of timing. Johnson kept insisting on the visits; the foreign-agents order was never enforced to completion, and no source cites a document recording a decision to stop. [cite:rs_cw5_frus6468_summary] [cite:rs_cw5_smith_ipa_2022] No official inquiry or historian reached for this book connects the death to either dispute as a cause. [cite:wiki_warren_commission] Claims that AIPAC was involved in the assassination circulate, Barda reports, and he finds "no evidence whatsoever" for them; this book reports them as claimed and unsupported. [cite:rs_cw5_barda_2026]

What was settled, then, was narrow: a federal order existed and went unenforced, and Israel accepted American visits in principle, without the six-month interval Kennedy had asked for. What was contested was what each meant: whether the Agency's money was a subsidy or a sale, and whether "basic agreement" was verification or its form. What the record leaves open is how much of the money reached lobbying, who decided the order would lapse, and what Israel had decided about Dimona. Those questions pass to [scene:cw6_johnson_eshkol|Johnson and Eshkol].

sections.h: Kennedy and Nasser, 1961–1962: The Wager on Cairo
sections.html:
The confrontations of 1962 and 1963 between Washington and Israel, over the reactor at Dimona and over an American lobby's money, took place inside a larger American policy aimed at Cairo. From the spring of 1961 John F. Kennedy tried to draw Gamal Abdel Nasser, president of the United Arab Republic, away from dependence on the Soviet bloc, with letters, with a visit that was weighed in Washington, and above all with American wheat. Much else in this stage, the war in Yemen, the Arab unity talks of 1963, the American reading of Israel's fears, can be read against that wager. This section tells how Washington made it and argued for it, from the documents the State Department has since published.

Six letters, 11 May 1961. On 11 May 1961 Kennedy sent letters to six Arab heads of state: Nasser; Chehab of Lebanon; Hussein of Jordan; Qassim of Iraq; Saud of Saudi Arabia; and Imam Ahmed of Yemen. [cite:rs_cw5_jvl_jfk_arab_letter] The text, a State Department telegram reproduced by the Jewish Virtual Library, named the "unresolved Arab-Israel controversy" as an underlying tension in the region and conceded at once that "No easy solution presents itself." [cite:rs_cw5_jvl_jfk_arab_letter] What it offered was specific. The United States, the letter said, was "willing to help resolve the tragic Palestine refugee problem on the basis of the principle of repatriation or compensation," a position it anchored in American "support for General Assembly recommendations concerning the refugees." It promised that Washington would use its influence to make the Palestine Conciliation Commission "intensify its efforts." [cite:rs_cw5_jvl_jfk_arab_letter]

A common picture of American policy in the region runs in a straight line toward Israel, as though the relationship deepened by a kind of gravity from one administration to the next. This initiative points another way. It went to six Arab rulers, not to Israel; it spoke of repatriation as well as compensation; and it tied the United States, in writing, to the General Assembly's refugee recommendations. The letter did not say how repatriation would be carried out, or how Israel's government would be brought to accept it. It was an opening, written to be received as one.

"Anxious to get closer to this fellow." The push inside the administration came within weeks. In June 1961 the UAR's ambassador suggested to Senator Fulbright that American food aid under PL-480 be put on a multi-year basis. [cite:rs_cw5_frus17_d64] On 8 June Walt Rostow told Under Secretary Ball that "the President is anxious to get closer to this fellow." Bundy forwarded a proposal for a visit by Nasser. The State Department's historians, summarizing the file in an editorial note, record the condition attached to it: the visit made sense if it could proceed without "disruptive Zionist action." [cite:rs_cw5_frus17_d64] The phrase is the officials' own, as the note gives it, and it suggests that the domestic politics of an approach to Cairo were weighed from the start. It does not show who in the United States was expected to object, or how; the note says no more.

Nasser's answer, 22 August 1961. Nasser replied on 22 August 1961. A State Department memorandum, prepared by Veliotes for Battle and sent to Bundy in September, judged that the reply made "the usual remarks about Israel" but did "not close the door to further initiatives with respect to the Palestine question." [cite:rs_cw5_frus17_d103] It is a measured reading: it registered the disagreement and set it aside. The Egyptian side of the letter is known in this book only through excerpts published in 2018 by the news site Egyptian Streets. According to those excerpts, Nasser wrote that "the problem is – no doubt – that of Palestine"; he attacked the Balfour Declaration as a promise made by Britain over land it did not own; and he urged that "the time has come when the United States should open her eyes." [cite:rs_cw5_egyptianstreets_letters] The same article cites Mohamed Hassanein Heikal for a count of 91 letters between the two men from 1961 to 1963. [cite:rs_cw5_egyptianstreets_letters] The full texts were not reached for this book, and the count is Heikal's.

Set side by side, the two readings of the same letter are instructive. Nasser, on the excerpts, placed Palestine at the centre and called on the United States to change its view. The State Department filed those passages under "the usual remarks" and fastened on what was not said: that the door was not closed. Both readings could be true at once; on this book's reading, the policy that followed rested on the second.

The offer, December 1961. In about early December 1961 Rusk instructed the embassy in Cairo to tell Nasser that the United States was "prepared in principle" to work out a multi-year PL-480 arrangement, possibly worth "several hundred million dollars," tied to the UAR's development plans. [cite:rs_cw5_frus17_d148] The telegram noted, in the same breath, that a multi-year request from Israel was also pending. [cite:rs_cw5_frus17_d148] Aid to Cairo was thus weighed alongside Israel's own claim on the same programme; the documents fetched here do not say how the Israeli request was answered.

How the wheat worked. The mechanism was laid out for the President in April 1962. A memorandum from Hamilton, the Administrator of the Agency for International Development, transmitted on 17 April 1962, gave the size of the programmes for Egypt by fiscal year. PL-480 programmes had been $81.4 million in fiscal 1960, $102.8 million in fiscal 1961 and $180.3 million in fiscal 1962, of which wheat accounted for $76.6 million. AID expected fiscal 1963 needs of about $140 million. [cite:rs_cw5_frus17_d249] The argument for these sums was strategic. AID argued that the aid freed Egypt's foreign exchange, so that the UAR would "become less dependent upon assistance from the Soviet Bloc." [cite:rs_cw5_frus17_d249]

The figures show a programme that more than doubled in two fiscal years, before any multi-year agreement had been signed. Who held the power in this chain is plain from the documents: the President decided, the State Department and AID proposed and carried out, and the UAR asked, first through its ambassador to a senator. What the documents fetched here do not show is the rest of the ledger: who in Egypt or the United States gained or bore the cost, or whether the foreign exchange saved was in fact spent away from Soviet suppliers. AID's rationale is an argument made to win approval, not a measured result.

Komer's case, October 1962. By the autumn of 1962 the region had shifted under the policy. In late September an army-led rebellion in Yemen overthrew the new imam and proclaimed a republic, which the UAR recognized at once; that war is the subject of [scene:cw5_yemen|the next section]. The multi-year agreement was ready for signature at the moment Egypt was committing itself in Yemen. Robert W. Komer urged Kennedy in early October 1962 to sign it anyway. [cite:rs_cw5_frus18_d70] His memorandum set out his reasons. The agreement had been promised in May. The UAR had cooperated over "the Hawk offer," the American offer of Hawk missiles to Israel, which, Komer wrote, had "jolted UAR"; how that offer was decided belongs to [scene:cw4_hawk|the Hawk decision] in the previous stage. The UAR had also cooperated over the Johnson Plan, which Komer names but which the documents fetched for this book do not describe. And the Nasser policy as a whole, Komer argued, mattered more than the Yemen policy. He was candid about the cost: "nothing we do will be right." [cite:rs_cw5_frus18_d70]

Komer's memorandum is the clearest single statement in these papers of how Washington understood its own position. In the same months it was offering missiles to Israel and food to Egypt, and Komer, at least, expected the UAR to resent what Israel received. The Hawk offer had been made despite its effect in Cairo; the wheat agreement would be signed despite Egypt's role in Yemen. Read this way, the policy did not choose between the two countries. It tried to keep both within reach.

Signed quietly, 8 October 1962. Kennedy approved on 5 October 1962, asking for "every effort to insure minimum publicity." [cite:rs_cw5_frus18_d70] On 8 October 1962 Kaissouni, for the UAR, and Talbot, for the United States, signed the agreement. [cite:rs_cw5_frus18_d70] The request for minimum publicity is documented; its reason is not stated in the record fetched here, and this book does not supply one.

The correspondence continued. The two men kept writing through the crises that followed. Kennedy's last letter to Nasser, in August 1963, as excerpted by Egyptian Streets, hoped that "mutual understanding will keep those differences within intransgressible bounds." [cite:rs_cw5_egyptianstreets_letters] The sentence can be read as a summary of the policy: it did not expect agreement, only limits.

What the record leaves open. Several things are not settled by the documents reached for this book. The total value of the agreement signed on 8 October 1962 is not given in them; Rusk's "several hundred million dollars" was a possibility named ten months earlier, not the signed figure, and AID's projection of about $140 million was for a single year. The Nasser visit proposed in June 1961 is documented as a proposal, and the sources do not show it taking place. Nasser's letters are known here only in excerpt, through a news site, and Heikal's count of 91 letters has not been checked against an archive. The Johnson Plan that Komer cites is named but not described. And whether the wheat did what AID promised, loosening Cairo's dependence on the Soviet bloc, is a question the April 1962 memorandum could only predict. What the documents do settle is the direction of American policy across these months: toward Cairo, by the President's deliberate choice, argued in the language of the Cold War, and carried forward even as Egypt went to war in Yemen.

sections.h: Yemen, 1962–1963: The War That Tested the Wager
sections.html:
Kennedy's approach to Nasser, told in [scene:cw5_nasser_outreach|the previous section], had barely been sealed with wheat when a revolution in Yemen put it to its hardest test. From the autumn of 1962 Egypt and Saudi Arabia backed opposite sides of a civil war in Yemen. Washington was tied to both: to Cairo by the policy it had just signed, to Riyadh by its commitment to Saudi security. Israel, on one scholar's account, entered the war too, covertly and on the royalist side. This section follows the war from September 1962 to November 1963, as far as it touched those four capitals.

The revolution, September 1962. Imam Ahmed, one of the six Arab rulers to whom Kennedy had written in May 1961, died on 19 September 1962. Muhammad al-Badr succeeded him. A week later an army-led rebellion overthrew al-Badr and proclaimed the Yemen Arab Republic. [cite:rs_cw5_unyom] [cite:rs_cw5_riedel_yemen] Recognition from the new republic's patrons came within days, though the sources date it slightly differently. The United Nations' own history records that the UAR recognized the new government on 29 September and the Soviet Union the next day, 30 September. Bruce Riedel, in a 2021 essay for the Brookings Institution, dates Soviet recognition to 1 October, and dates the first Soviet airlift flight to Sanaa to 30 September. [cite:rs_cw5_unyom] [cite:rs_cw5_riedel_yemen] The difference is a single day, but it changes the order of events: read against Riedel's date for the first airlift flight, the UN's dates put Soviet recognition on the same day as that flight; on Riedel's own dates, the airlift preceded recognition. The sources reached here do not settle which is right.

Washington's first reading. The CIA saw quickly what kind of war this would be. A brief of 2 October 1962, quoted by Riedel, warned that "a civil war is shaping up with direct backing from the UAR for one faction and from Saudi Arabia for the other." [cite:rs_cw5_riedel_yemen] Three days later, on 5 October, Crown Prince Faisal of Saudi Arabia met Kennedy. Kennedy declined to intervene in Yemen, but he reaffirmed American support for Saudi security, increased the Navy's port visits to the kingdom and expanded training for the Saudi air force. [cite:rs_cw5_riedel_yemen] The meeting fell on the same day that Kennedy approved the multi-year food agreement with the UAR, after Komer had argued that the Nasser policy mattered more than the Yemen policy. [cite:rs_cw5_frus18_d70] Washington was reassuring Riyadh and feeding Cairo in the same week, while the two were arming opposite sides.

The scale of Egypt's commitment. Egypt's role grew fast. The CIA estimated 4,000 Egyptian troops in Yemen on 31 October 1962. Riedel gives about 30,000 by March 1963, and about 70,000 by 1966. [cite:rs_cw5_riedel_yemen] Within five months, on these figures, the deployment had grown more than sevenfold. The later figure belongs to the next stage, but it shows where the commitment that began in the autumn of 1962 would lead.

Recognition, 18–19 December 1962. Kennedy's answer to the war was to try to end it by diplomacy, and his instrument was recognition. The State Department proposed a statement that both the new republic and the UAR would make. On 18 December 1962 the Yemen Arab Republic issued a communiqué embodying the American text, and on 19 December the UAR issued a nearly identical one. The United States recognized the Yemen Arab Republic on 19 December 1962, saying that the two statements provided a basis for ending the conflict. [cite:rs_cw5_frus18_d116] [cite:rs_cw5_oh_yemen] The mechanism was a bargain in sequence: public commitments first from Sanaa and Cairo, American recognition on the same day as the second. According to Riedel, Kennedy did so despite pressure from Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Britain, and the UN General Assembly recognized the republic the next day. [cite:rs_cw5_riedel_yemen]

On this book's reading, the decision fits the policy Washington had argued all year. To recognize the republic was to accept the outcome Nasser was fighting for, in exchange for public statements that pointed toward disengagement. Among those who objected, on Riedel's account, was the kingdom whose security Kennedy had reaffirmed to Faisal ten weeks earlier. The administration acted as though it could hold both lines at once; the sources reached here do not record its reasoning.

Bunker's mission, March–April 1963. The statements did not end the fighting. In the spring came mediation, through Ellsworth Bunker. Bunker arrived in Riyadh on 6 March 1963. According to Riedel, Faisal reluctantly agreed to end Saudi support for the royalists if Egypt withdrew, and Nasser promised to withdraw "gradually" if Saudi aid stopped. [cite:rs_cw5_riedel_yemen] The terms were reported by the UN Secretary-General on 29 April 1963. Saudi Arabia would end its aid to the royalists; Egypt would withdraw its forces in phases; and a demilitarized zone would run 20 kilometres deep on each side of the Saudi–Yemeni border. [cite:rs_cw5_unyom]

The observers, June–July 1963. On 11 June 1963 the Security Council, by resolution 179, authorized an observer mission to watch the disengagement. The United Nations Yemen Observation Mission began on 4 July 1963. Egypt and Saudi Arabia shared its costs, estimated at under $1 million. [cite:rs_cw5_unyom] The arrangement shows who paid: the two outside patrons of the war, not the United States or the UN's general budget, bore the cost of verifying their own withdrawal.

Did the disengagement work? The record supports two readings, and each rests on its own evidence. On paper it did. The UN's history records that Saudi Arabia, the UAR and the Yemen Arab Republic accepted identical terms in April 1963, and that the observer mission deployed in July as agreed. [cite:rs_cw5_unyom] That is the strongest case for the policy: the war's two foreign sponsors had accepted identical terms, under international supervision, within seven months of the revolution. In practice it did not. Riedel reports that by April 1963, the month the terms were reported, Egypt told the UN mediator it would not withdraw, and Saudi Arabia that it would not stop aiding the royalists. [cite:rs_cw5_riedel_yemen] The mission itself, which began in July 1963, ended on 4 September 1964, and on Riedel's figures Egyptian forces in Yemen went on growing to about 70,000 by 1966. [cite:rs_cw5_unyom] [cite:rs_cw5_riedel_yemen] The two readings are not contradictory. One describes what the parties signed; the other, on Riedel's account, what they told the mediator and what they then did.

Hard Surface, July–November 1963. Kennedy's other instrument was force, shown rather than used. Under Operation Hard Surface the United States sent F-100 fighters to Saudi Arabia from July 1963, the first American combat deployment to the Arabian Peninsula, according to Riedel; it ended in November 1963. [cite:rs_cw5_riedel_yemen] The deployment ran alongside the observer mission. While UN observers watched the border to verify a withdrawal, American aircraft stood in the kingdom, a visible form of the commitment to Saudi security that Kennedy had reaffirmed to Faisal in October 1962. That was the shape of the policy by the end of 1963: diplomacy with Cairo, protection for Riyadh, and no intervention in Yemen itself.

Israel's part, on Riedel's account. Israel appears in this war in one source reached for this book. Riedel writes that Israel joined the covert campaign on the royalist side: the Mossad ran an operation called Rotev, and the Israeli Air Force dropped weapons to the royalists, flying over Saudi Arabia with Saudi approval. [cite:rs_cw5_riedel_yemen] His essay gives no dates for these operations, so this book cannot say whether they fell within 1962–63 or later, and no second source reached here confirms them. The claim is Riedel's, and it is recorded as his. If it is accurate, it would mean that Israel and Saudi Arabia were acting on the same side of an Arab civil war against Egypt, while the United States was trying to end that war on terms Egypt had accepted.

What the record leaves open, and what came after. Several points are not settled by the sources reached here. The date of Soviet recognition differs by a day between the United Nations and Riedel. The troop figures after October 1962 are Riedel's, not documents quoted in full. Israel's covert role rests on Riedel alone, without dates. And the question whether the disengagement failed because neither patron meant to honour it, or because events overtook it, is not answered by the documents here: the record shows what each side signed and, on Riedel's account, what each told the mediator, not what their governments privately intended. The war outlasted the observers and outlasted Kennedy. Its course from 1964, the growth of Egypt's force and what that commitment meant for Egypt's position by the spring of 1967, belongs to [scene:cw6_yemen|Stage Six]. The Yemen Arab Republic broke relations with the United States on 7 June 1967. [cite:rs_cw5_oh_yemen]

sections.h: The Order of 21 November 1962: The Justice Department and the American Zionist Council
sections.html:
Volume II traced the line from the wartime American Zionist Emergency Council, founded in 1943, to the American Zionist Council and to Isaiah L. Kenen's lobbying committee, and it recorded the bare fact of the Justice Department's foreign-agent order of 21 November 1962, in [scene:s07g|From AZEC to AIPAC]. This section does not retell that lineage. It takes up the order itself: what the law it invoked required, what money it rested on, how the Council fought it, which organization was which on the day it was issued, and what the record does and does not show about how the episode ended.

The claim to be tested is a common one. It holds that AIPAC has always been a purely domestic American lobby, independent of the Israeli government, and that the foreign-agent question is a modern invention of its critics. The record does not support the second half of that claim. In 1962 the Justice Department of the United States, under an Attorney General who was the President's brother, formally ordered the umbrella body over the lobbying committee to register as the agent of a foreign principal. [cite:israellobby_org_fara_doj_order] [cite:acjna_fara] But the record also does not support the opposite claim, that the order proved the lobby was a foreign agent. It was an order, not a judgment. It was contested by the Council, according to the main account of the episode, it was never tested in a court, and the organization it named and the organization known today as AIPAC were, by most of the evidence, not the same body.

What the law required. The Foreign Agents Registration Act was passed in 1938. It required any person or organization acting "at the order, request, or under the direction or control" of a foreign principal to register publicly and to disclose the relationship, its funding and its activities. [cite:israellobby_org_fara_doj_order] It was a disclosure law, not a prohibition. Registration did not make an organization illegal; it made its relationship with a foreign principal a matter of public record. According to Kobby Barda's summary of the Act as it then stood, an agent had to register within ten days of becoming one, and failure carried penalties of up to five years in prison, fines, or both; Barda puts the ceiling at up to ten years where the principal was a foreign government. [cite:rs_cw5_barda_2026] In practice, violations were usually treated as civil or administrative matters to be resolved by registering, not by prosecution. [cite:israellobby_org_fara_doj_order] The law was not new to this circle of organizations. The same question had been put a decade earlier in Feinberg's case, as Volume II recounts, and Isaiah Kenen himself had earlier been a registered foreign-agent lobbyist and an employee of Israel's information office at the United Nations, a status that ended when he moved to the American committee. [cite:wrmea_aipac] The Jewish Agency's own American Section, moreover, was already a registrant under the Act in 1963, as the agent of the World Zionist Organization and the Jewish Agency in Jerusalem. [cite:rs_cw5_djn_19630628] The question in 1962 was therefore not whether the Agency was a foreign agent; it had registered as one. The question was whether an American body that received the Agency's money had become one too.

The order. On 21 November 1962 the Internal Security Section of the Justice Department ordered the American Zionist Council to register as an agent of a foreign principal under the Act. [cite:israellobby_org_fara_doj_order] Grant F. Smith of IRmep, an advocate of the lobby's registration whose work is the main account of the episode reached for this book, frames it as an order to register as an Israeli foreign agent. [cite:rs_cw5_smith_podcast] The issuing authority was Robert F. Kennedy's department; he served as Attorney General throughout his brother's presidency, from 1961 to 1963, and the Internal Security Section acted under his authority. [cite:israellobby_org_fara_doj_order] The order did not come from nowhere. The Eisenhower administration had pressed the Council on the same question through the 1950s. [cite:mercury_aipac_fara] What changed in November 1962 was form: informal pressure became a written order with a date and a sum attached. [cite:israellobby_org_fara_doj_order] In the Senate, J. William Fulbright was pressing the same question through the Foreign Relations Committee in the same period. [cite:wrmea_aipac]

No surviving document reached for this book records either Kennedy brother explaining why the department acted on this matter at this time. The sources document the institutional actions, the order, the hearings and a later FBI offer, but not the private reasoning behind them, and this book does not supply one. [cite:israellobby_org_fara_doj_order]

The money. The order's basis was money from the Jewish Agency for Israel. The department alleged that the Council had received more than $5 million from the Agency over the preceding eight years, and one account describes the allegation as funding by the Israeli government through the Agency's New York office. [cite:azc_fara_doj] [cite:acjna_fara] Smith states that the money was routed to the Council for lobbying and propaganda. [cite:rs_cw5_smith_podcast] [cite:rs_cw5_smith_antiwar_2013] A more exact figure appears in the record of the Senate inquiry that followed: $5,100,001.02, paid by the Jewish Agency to the American Zionist Council between 1 January 1955 and 31 December 1962, which Fulbright entered into the Foreign Relations Committee's record in 1963. [cite:jta_fulbright_jewish_agency_hearing] The two figures are close but not the same thing. The order spoke of "more than $5 million" over eight years; the Senate figure runs to the last day of 1962, more than five weeks after the order was signed, so it cannot be the sum the order itself recited. The order's own text is not among the sources reached for this volume.

A third figure stands against both. Barda, writing in Modern Judaism in 2026, gives $1.5 million for the same years, presenting it as a claim raised in the matter without stating its source and without mentioning the $5.1 million figure. [cite:rs_cw5_barda_2026] The two totals have not been reconciled, and this book does not choose between them. What the Agency's money actually bought, and how the two sides at the Senate hearing described it, is the subject of [scene:cw5_jewish_agency_hearing|the Jewish Agency before the committee].

How to characterize the payer was itself disputed. Fulbright treated the Agency's payments to the Council as functionally equivalent to direct funding of an American lobby by the Israeli government; the Agency's counsel rejected that on the record, in an exchange told with the hearing. [cite:jta_fulbright_jewish_agency_hearing] The Agency, at work since 1929, served as a bridge between Israel and Jewish communities abroad, including on fundraising and immigration. Both characterizations are documented, and the dispute was never settled in court, because the matter never reached one. [cite:jta_fulbright_jewish_agency_hearing]

The Council's fight. What followed the order is known chiefly through Smith's account, and it should be read as his. According to Smith, the Council fought the order. It retained Simon H. Rifkind, whom Smith describes as a friend of President Kennedy. Rifkind argued that registration would "choke the very life" out of the Zionist movement, and said that the Council would stop routing Jewish Agency money into the United States for lobbying and propaganda. [cite:rs_cw5_smith_podcast] Said Arikat, writing in Al-Quds in May 2026 and citing period Justice Department correspondence without naming the documents, adds that the Council sought a 120-day delay and mobilized lawyers, public-relations firms and sympathetic members of Congress. [cite:rs_cw5_arikat_2026]

The order was argued among American Jewish organizations as well as between the Council and the government. Smith reports that the American Council for Judaism, whose dissent from Zionism is told later in this stage, welcomed the order, and that the New York Times sought inside information on it. [cite:rs_cw5_smith_podcast] Inside the government, too, the pressure did not run one way. Smith reports that Justice Department lawyer Nathan Lenvin told the Council's representatives that the Fulbright hearings showed the Council had not been distributing "educational" material but receiving large Agency transfers for publicity and lobbying. He also reports a Wall Street Journal story that Justice officials were weighing the risk of offending Jewish opinion, a story that, in his account, prompted letters to Congress and to Robert Kennedy urging enforcement. [cite:rs_cw5_smith_podcast] And Smith reports that in October 1963, as evidence of foreign control accumulated, the FBI offered to help enforce the order. [cite:rs_cw5_smith_podcast] [cite:israellobby_org_fara_doj_order]

Meanwhile, according to the accounts this library drew on earlier, the Council temporarily stopped distributing certain publications funded from abroad, the Near East Report among them, to meet the department's interim demands, while its core domestic work continued with little interruption. [cite:israellobby_org_fara_doj_order] Kenen's own affidavit to the Senate committee put the end of the Council's purchases of that newsletter in 1962. [cite:rs_cw5_barda_2026]

Did the Council register? Almost every account says it did not. Smith and Arikat both write that the order was never enforced to completion and the Council never registered; the earlier accounts this library drew on say the same. [cite:rs_cw5_smith_podcast] [cite:rs_cw5_arikat_2026] [cite:acjna_fara] One source says otherwise. A version of the Wikipedia article on the Council, as it stood on 7 March 2016, said that President Kennedy and the Attorney General "forced the AZC to register as a foreign agent". [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_azc_2016] No primary document reached for this volume supports that statement, and it conflicts with every other source. It is recorded here so the reader who meets it knows it is the outlier. The Justice Department's own report on the Act for 1964 does not mention the American Zionist Council at all. [cite:rs_cw5_doj_fara_1964]

Which body was which. The most consequential confusion in this story concerns names. Three bodies were involved in 1962, and the sources do not agree on how the third of them stood.

The first was the American Zionist Council itself. Founded in 1949 as a tax-exempt umbrella body representing nine nationwide Zionist organizations, it was led by figures including Louis Lipsky. [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_azc] [cite:israellobby_org_fara_doj_order] It is the body the order named. It did not end in 1963: according to Powerbase, it was renamed the American Zionist Federation in May 1970 and the American Zionist Movement in 1993. [cite:rs_cw5_powerbase_azc] Smith's statement that the Council fought the order before it eventually shut down should be read against that continuity. [cite:rs_cw5_smith_podcast]

The second was the Jewish Agency's American Section, the registered foreign agent that paid the money.

The third was Kenen's lobbying committee, and here the accounts divide. The account this library first drew on holds that AIPAC began in 1951 as a subcommittee-level body under the Council's umbrella, that it was still inside the Council when the order was issued, and that in early 1963, in direct response to the order, the Council's lobbying function was separated into an independent American Israel Public Affairs Committee, presented as funded solely by private American donations and so not a foreign agent. [cite:israellobby_org_fara_doj_order] A second account in the library puts it more sharply: the Council's functions moved, weeks after the order, into a newly incorporated AIPAC, legally distinguishable from the Council. [cite:factually_aipac_fara] The 2016 Wikipedia snapshot says AIPAC incorporated separately six weeks after the order, and Smith writes that the lobbying division "split off" six weeks after it. [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_azc_2016] [cite:rs_cw5_smith_antiwar_2013]

The other account dates the committee much earlier and treats it as separate long before 1962. The current Wikipedia article, citing Nancy Jo Nelson in the Journal of Palestine Studies (1980), dates Kenen's unincorporated American Zionist Committee for Public Affairs (AZCPA) to 1951, records that Kenen was the Council's Washington representative from 1951 to 1953, and says the Council divested itself of the committee in 1954 because its leaders did not want tax-exempt funds used for lobbying. [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_azc] Barda, working from the Council's own records, dates the decision to create the new lobbying arm to March 1954, after Council elections on 28 February 1954, with a letter to its executive committee dated 15 March 1954. [cite:rs_cw5_barda_2026] Kenen himself, speaking off the record to a United Jewish Appeal audience in New York on 13 September 1963, described his American Zionist Committee for Public Affairs as founded in 1953 and later renamed the American Israel Public Affairs Committee. [cite:rs_cw5_kenen_uja_1963] The renaming is dated to 1959 by Wikipedia, citing Doug Rossinow in Modern American History (2018), and to 1958 by Barda. [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_azc] [cite:rs_cw5_barda_2026] On either date, AIPAC bore its name three or four years before the order. And by Kenen's affidavit to the Senate committee, he had stopped his own work for the Council in July 1960. [cite:rs_cw5_barda_2026]

One reading reconciles them: each account dates something real. On that reading, the earlier dates mark the creation of a lobbying committee distinct from the tax-exempt Council and the adoption of its present name; Kenen, by September 1963, spoke of AIPAC as a going concern with a past. [cite:rs_cw5_kenen_uja_1963] The 1963 date, where the sources give it, marks a further separation of whatever lobbying function the Council still held, in the weeks after the order. The two can both be true only if the Council retained some lobbying role after 1954, and the sources reached here do not establish what that role was. What they do not support is the version in which AIPAC was invented in 1963 to escape the order: the name and the committee existed before it. Nor do they support the version in which the order had nothing to do with the lobby: the Council it named had paid for Kenen's newsletter, and had employed Kenen, within the eight years the order covered. [cite:rs_cw5_barda_2026] On the account that dates a restructuring to early 1963, the record shows a documented organizational change, on a documented timeline, in response to a documented federal order: order, then restructuring, in that order, within months. It does not show whether the change was purely cosmetic or purely substantive. That depends on whether the post-1963 funding arrangement was a genuine and complete break from foreign money or chiefly a legal repositioning, an open question that the public record reached here does not settle. [cite:israellobby_org_fara_doj_order]

How it ended. The documented sequence has an order but no recorded conclusion. Smith states that the Justice Department kept the order secret until 2008 and has never tried to enforce it since; he calls the effort "serious, but fizzled out". [cite:rs_cw5_smith_ipa_2022] The sources divide on why. Smith says the effort "gradually falls apart" after November 1963, and Arikat describes a loss of momentum under President Johnson; neither cites a document recording a decision to stop. [cite:rs_cw5_smith_podcast] [cite:rs_cw5_arikat_2026] Barda argues the opposite case: the lobby had separated from the Agency's money, whose purchases ended in 1962, and operated lawfully as a domestic lobby, so there was nothing left to enforce. [cite:rs_cw5_barda_2026] Some writers go further and tie the end of the effort to President Kennedy's death; Philip Giraldi, writing in 2017, says only that the Council "was pressured" by the Justice Department in 1962 and 1963 and that "Kennedy's death stopped that effort". [cite:rs_cw5_giraldi_2017] [cite:crustnews_aipac_history] That is a statement of sequence, not evidence of cause, and it is examined, with the other claims of a link, in [scene:s11c|22 November 1963].

Two later attempts to compel registration, a petition in 1988 and a bill in 2024, belong to later chapters. Neither succeeded. [cite:crustnews_aipac_history]

The record leaves several things open. The text and signatory of the 21 November 1962 order are not in the sources reached for this volume, so the order's own wording of its sum and its grounds cannot be quoted. The size of the Agency's payments stands at three figures, more than $5 million in the order, $5,100,001.02 in the Senate record and $1.5 million in Barda, and they have not been reconciled. Almost everything known about the Council's fight, Rifkind's argument, Lenvin's warning, the Wall Street Journal report and the FBI's offer, rests on Smith's account, the work of an advocate for registration, and has not been independently confirmed from the documents themselves. No document shows why enforcement stopped, or that anyone decided it should. What the record does establish is narrow and solid: a federal order, on a stated date, naming a specific organization, on the ground of a specific stream of money from a body already registered as a foreign agent. That is more than the claim that the question was invented by modern critics allows, and less than the claim that the order proved what it alleged.

sections.h: Palm Beach, December 1962: The Terms of the Relationship
sections.html:
Stage Four ended with two decisions of the summer and autumn of 1962: Kennedy's offer of the Hawk anti-aircraft missile to Israel, and a second, brief American visit to the reactor at Dimona in late September, both told in [scene:cw4_hawk|the Hawk decision]. This section takes up what those two decisions left behind. By the turn of 1962–63 Washington had begun to arm Israel, had looked at Dimona twice and found nothing it was prepared to call alarming, and had not yet decided what the relationship between the two states actually was. The best record of how Kennedy himself described it in that winter comes from a private conversation with Israel's foreign minister at Palm Beach, two days after Christmas.

"No evidence": the circular of October 1962. A month after the September visit, the State Department told its own diplomats what that visit had found. A circular airgram, CA-4726, titled "Israel's Dimona Reactor" and drafted on 24 October 1962, informed American posts that a recent visit by American scientists had again found Israel's statements of peaceful intent consistent with what they had seen, and that there was "no evidence" of preparation for the production of weapons. [cite:rs_cw5_frus18_d87] Two details of the circular say as much about the politics of the reactor as its finding does. The embassy in Tel Aviv was excluded from the distribution, and no publicity was planned. [cite:rs_cw5_frus18_d87] The reassurance went to American posts; it was not meant to become a public American certificate of the reactor's innocence, and the American embassy in the country whose reactor it described was left off the list.

The visit on which the circular rested was not one its own later editors admired. William Burr and Avner Cohen, who edited the declassified record of the following year's correspondence for the National Security Archive, call the improvised second visit of late September 1962 a "fiasco." [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] That is the editors' judgment; it is not the judgment the State Department recorded in October 1962. The two readings sit some distance apart, and the distance is itself part of the story of 1963. The circular represented what Washington was prepared to say in the autumn of 1962. Within three months, as the next section shows, its own intelligence community was saying something rather different.

Palm Beach, 27 December 1962. Golda Meir, Israel's foreign minister, met Kennedy at Palm Beach on 27 December 1962. The record of the meeting, reproduced by the National Security Archive, shows Kennedy acknowledging a United States "special relationship" with Israel. It also records, for the first time explicitly, an American commitment to support Israel "in case of an invasion." [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] Both phrases are recorded as Kennedy's own, and the second is described as the first explicit commitment of its kind.

He attached a limit in the same conversation. The relationship, Kennedy said, could not be allowed to damage American ties with the other states of the region. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] The two halves belong together. The phrase "special relationship" is often quoted on its own, as if it described an alliance; in the record of the meeting it arrived with a condition that described a balance. Kennedy was at that moment pursuing the opening to Nasser's government in Cairo described at the start of this stage, and the Palm Beach formula was compatible with it. On this reading, Israel was to have a promise of support against invasion; the Arab states were not to have reason to conclude that the United States had chosen a side.

On the reactor, the record of Palm Beach is short. Kennedy spoke of nonproliferation only vaguely, and Meir "reassured the President" that there would not be "any difficulty" over Dimona. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] Nothing in the record shows Kennedy asking for a further visit, a schedule of visits, or any assurance more specific than the one Meir volunteered. That restraint did not last. Three months later the State Department was instructing its ambassador in Tel Aviv to seek "semi-annual" visits to the site, the opening of the exchange told in [scene:s11b|the battle of the letters]. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters]

The money and the missiles. The commitments of Palm Beach had a material counterpart in the Hawk. The terms of the sale are not given in the declassified documents collected for this stage. One contemporary account gives figures. Isaiah L. Kenen, the founding director of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, told an off-the-record session of the United Jewish Appeal's Third Annual Young Leadership Conference in New York on 13 September 1963 that the Hawk missiles were financed by a loan of about $25 million, repayable over ten years. [cite:wrmea_aipac] [cite:rs_cw5_kenen_uja_1963] The interest rate in the surviving text of his address is illegible. [cite:rs_cw5_kenen_uja_1963]

In the same address Kenen put American aid to Israel at about $85 million in 1963, up from about $60 million a year earlier in the decade. [cite:rs_cw5_kenen_uja_1963] These figures should be read for what they are. They are Kenen's, given in a speech, not a government accounting. They survive as an optical-character-recognition text of a document held in the Herbert A. Friedman Collection at the American Jewish Archives, and they have not yet been checked against the scanned page; they are given here as approximate, as he gave them, and not as exact amounts. [cite:rs_cw5_kenen_uja_1963] What they show with more confidence is the direction he described to his audience: more American money in 1963 than in the years just before, and a missile sale paid for on credit rather than given.

The aid panel below sets that year in the longer sequence. It marks 1948 to 1961 as a period of economic aid and loans only, and 1962 as the year of the first American military aid to Israel, extended as loans. Kenen's description of a ten-year loan for the Hawk is consistent with that row: on his account, the missiles were bought on credit, not granted. How far that dating holds is examined in Stage Four; the panel records it as given.

A promise, not a guarantee. The Palm Beach language was a spoken assurance recorded in a memorandum of conversation. It was not a treaty, a joint declaration or a public commitment, and through the summer of 1963 Kennedy remained "unwilling to make 'explicit' guarantees." [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] On the record reached here, the commitment of December 1962 was the outer edge of what Kennedy was prepared to say, not the first step toward something more formal. How Ben-Gurion pressed on that edge in the spring, and how Kennedy held it, belongs to the battle of the letters.

Two policies at once. The documents of these months show the same administration moving in two directions, and neither cancels the other. The United States was selling Israel a missile system on credit, raising its aid on Kenen's figures, and, in the President's own words, acknowledging a special relationship and a commitment against invasion. The same government had already begun, in its intelligence agencies, to treat Dimona as a potential weapons programme, and within months would press Israel hard on the reactor. Kennedy armed Israel and pressed it on Dimona in the same year; the record does not support a reading of 1962–63 that keeps only one of the two.

The longer argument over what the alliance that began in these years has given the United States, and at what cost, is set out at its strongest in [scene:wa_s07|the case for the alliance], which carries that argument forward from the Hawk sale to the present. That argument belongs to later decades. In the winter of 1962–63, the relationship had a name, a missile loan and a spoken promise, and its two governments had not yet tested how much weight any of them would bear.

The record leaves several things open. The text of the Hawk loan agreement, its interest rate and its final value are not in the sources collected for this stage; the only figures are Kenen's, given in a speech and surviving in an unchecked transcription. The Palm Beach memorandum records Kennedy's words but not what, if anything, he intended "in case of an invasion" to require in practice, and no later document in this stage tests it. Nor does the record explain why the State Department kept its October circular from the embassy in Tel Aviv, beyond the fact that it did.

sections.h: From Reassurance to Alarm: The Estimates of January–May 1963
sections.html:
In October 1962 the State Department told its posts abroad that American scientists had found "no evidence" at Dimona of preparation for weapons production. [cite:rs_cw5_frus18_d87] By the end of May 1963 the President of the United States was telling the French foreign minister, on the French record of the conversation, that both their countries would be blamed for an Israeli bomb. The documents of these months record no new American visit to the reactor; they record a change in how Washington read it. Over five months a sequence of estimates, memoranda and one presidential directive moved Washington's view of Dimona from a question settled by inspection to a capability with a forecast date. This section follows those documents in the order they were written, because the order is the argument.

NIE 30-63, 23 January 1963. A National Intelligence Estimate is the coordinated judgment of the American intelligence community, prepared for the President and his senior advisers; it is the government's formal assessment, not one agency's speculation. [cite:wilsoncenter_kennedy_dimona_61_62] National Intelligence Estimate 30-63, dated 23 January 1963, judged that at maximum capacity Dimona "could produce sufficient plutonium for one or two weapons a year." [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] The sentence is conditional at both ends. It speaks of full power, which the reactor had not reached, and of what it "could" produce, not of what Israel intended to do with it. The estimate addressed capability; it did not claim that weapons had been built or that Israel's government had decided to build them. [cite:wilsoncenter_kennedy_dimona_61_62] It was nonetheless the first formal judgment of this period to put a number on what the reactor could yield.

Airgram A-517, 13 February 1963. Three weeks later the embassy in Tel Aviv gave a different reading. On 13 February 1963 the embassy's airgram A-517, written by the science attaché Robert Webber, judged that Israel was "not making a serious effort" to build weapons at that time.
