He also recorded the Israeli assurances of "peaceful purposes," which, he wrote, the United States was "inclined to believe." [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] The memorandum thus records three things at once: what had been gained, what had not, and the degree of trust on which the remainder rested.

The visit that came after the reactor. The visit before activation did not take place. According to the Israelis, the reactor went critical on 26 December 1963. The Hebrew-language website of the Israel Atomic Energy Commission gives July 1963 for the start of operations. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] The two dates cannot be reconciled from the sources reached here, and they may not measure the same event: one names criticality, the other the start of operations. What both show is that the visit Eshkol had promised for before criticality did not happen before it, on either date. The first visit under the new arrangement took place on 18 January 1964. The editors write that it "may have been delayed because of Kennedy's assassination." [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] They offer that as a possibility and draw no other connection; what the record shows about the weeks around 22 November is set out in [scene:s11c|22 November 1963].

What the first team found. The January 1964 team's report, written by Harry S. Traynor and dated 30 January 1964, found no suspicion of weapons work. It called Dimona "an ambitious project for a country of Israel's capabilities," put its cost in the range of $60 million, and recorded that the team had been told of 20 tons of uranium concentrate from a foreign source that was not named. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] The team added a caution: "even such an intrusive technique would not prove that the facility was being used only for peaceful purposes." [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] The inspectors themselves said in their first report that what they were doing could find evidence of weapons work but could not establish its absence.

The money in the report raises questions the report does not answer. Who paid the $60 million, through what budget and from what sources, is not in the material reached for this section. Nor is the origin of the 20 tons of uranium concentrate, whose foreign source the report does not name. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters]

What became of the arrangement. Visits followed every year from 1964. The sources do not agree on how many. The National Security Archive's 2019 briefing book speaks of "a series of six annual U.S. inspections" from 1964 to 1969, ended under Nixon. Cohen and Burr, writing in 2025, say seven visits "took place after Kennedy forced Israel to accept regular visits in 1963." [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] [cite:rs_cw5_majalla] The State Department's own historians record that under Kennedy Israel agreed to periodic visits by American scientists, that the Johnson administration kept insisting on them, and that the visitors found no evidence of a weapons program while suspicions continued. [cite:rs_cw5_frus6468_summary] Cohen and Burr, drawing on the later record, write that Israel completed a "super-secret underground separation plant" in 1965 and began producing weapons-grade plutonium in 1966; that the American scientists "never found direct evidence" of weapons work; and that the CIA's assessments were never shared with the inspection teams. [cite:rs_cw5_majalla] [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_findings] The visits under Johnson, and how much they could see, are the subject of [scene:s11d|Johnson's inspections].

Did Kennedy get what he asked? Two answers can be given from the same documents, and each has real support. The first is that, in principle, he did. Kennedy's own letter of 26 August described "basic agreement on regular visits," and visits followed every year from 1964. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] On this reading, an American president obtained from a new Israeli prime minister, against the resistance of some of his cabinet, a standing arrangement under which American scientists entered Dimona year after year.

The second answer is that, in substance, he did not. Eshkol never accepted visits twice a year with full access; the visit promised for before criticality did not take place before it; and the visitors never found direct evidence of the weapons work that, by Cohen and Burr's account, followed, including an underground separation plant completed in 1965. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] [cite:rs_cw5_majalla] [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_findings] On this reading the agreement gave Washington the form of verification without its function: annual visits on terms the host controlled, by teams who, as their first report warned, could not prove a negative, and who were not given what American intelligence suspected. The difference between the two readings is largely the difference between the principle, which Eshkol conceded, and the interval and access, which he did not. Kennedy's word "basic" covered the gap between them.

The mechanism. The structure of the arrangement explains why both readings are possible. Washington's instrument was a letter, carrying a warning without a named sanction, from a government that refused Israel an explicit guarantee. Israel's instrument was consent: the prime minister and his cabinet decided whether, when and how often the visits happened, and the hosts controlled the site the visitors toured. The State Department could ask; it could not compel. The inspectors could look; they could not look at what they were not taken to. Within those limits, the outcome of 1963 can be read as a negotiated compromise in which each side kept the point it cared about most. Israel kept control of the timing and frequency of access, and the United States kept the right to come back.

The record leaves several things open. The cabinet debate that Barbour described is known only from his report; which ministers resisted, and why, is not in the documents reproduced here. The date on which the reactor began to operate is given two ways, and the sources reached do not resolve them. Whether the delay of the first visit to January 1964 had anything to do with the events of November is offered by the editors only as a possibility. The number of later visits is given as six and as seven. And how the reactor and its uranium were paid for and supplied is not answered in this material. What is not open is the shape of the agreement itself: Eshkol conceded regular visits in principle, declined the six-month interval, and the visit he promised for before criticality came after it.

sections.h: Dissent Among American Jews: The American Council for Judaism and "Peoplehood"
sections.html:
The Justice Department's order of November 1962 and the Senate inquiry of 1963 are often told as a contest between the American government and a pro-Israel lobby. The record of these years shows a third party to the argument, and it was not outside the Jewish community. The American Council for Judaism, an organization of American Jews opposed to Zionism, welcomed the order, argued in public over what the relationship between American Jews and the State of Israel meant in law, and drew answers from the American Zionist Council and from the head of the Jewish Agency's American Section. The questions raised by the foreign-agents inquiry were also being argued among American Jewish organizations themselves, by name and on paper.

Origins, 1942. The Council was founded in 1942 by 36 Reform rabbis led by Louis Wolsey. They acted in protest at a resolution of the Central Conference of American Rabbis supporting a Jewish army in Palestine. Within a year the leadership had passed to the layman Lessing J. Rosenwald and to Rabbi Elmer Berger. [cite:rs_cw5_jvl_acj]

Before and after 1948. The Council's position was more specific than a general hostility to Jewish settlement in Palestine. Before 1948 it accepted the recommendation to admit 100,000 Jews to Palestine, while opposing the creation of a Jewish state. After the state was founded, its aim shifted: it sought to limit Israel's influence on the Jews of the Diaspora. It also built an institutional alternative. By the end of 1955 it had set up ten schools teaching classical Reform Judaism. [cite:rs_cw5_jvl_acj]

In an unsigned article of 1997, the Council gave its own account of its work in these years. It says it sponsored speakers who were concerned that Judaism was being subsumed by Israeli nationalism, and that Senator J. William Fulbright, chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, whose committee conducted the 1963 inquiry, appeared on one of its platforms. The article gives no date for that appearance. [cite:rs_cw5_acj_1997] These are the Council's statements about itself, written more than three decades later, and the sources reached here do not confirm them independently.

The order of 1962. When the Justice Department ordered the American Zionist Council to register under the Foreign Agents Registration Act in November 1962, the American Council for Judaism welcomed it, according to Grant F. Smith of IRmep, an advocate of registration. [cite:rs_cw5_smith_podcast] The order itself, and the American Zionist Council's resistance to it, are told in [scene:s11a|the FARA order]. The welcome was consistent with the Council's long-standing aim of limiting Israel's influence on the Jews of the Diaspora. The sources reached do not quote a statement the Council issued in November 1962, so its stated reasons at the time are not on the record here.

Of the Senate committee's examination of the Jewish Agency in the summer of 1963, the Council's 1997 account gives the same reading as Smith: that the evidence showed Agency money funding American lobbying and public relations. That account adds claims about closed sessions and White House intervention that the contemporary reports found do not confirm. Those claims, and the opposing reading of the Agency's chairman, are set out in [scene:cw5_jewish_agency_hearing|the Jewish Agency before the committee]. [cite:rs_cw5_acj_1997]

The "peoplehood" exchange, spring 1964. The sharpest public argument came the following spring. On 14 March 1964 the Council wrote to the State Department about the legal status of "Jewish peoplehood." The Department replied on 20 April 1964, and the Council publicized the reply. The American Zionist Council answered that "the concept of Jewish people-hood is purely a spiritual and cultural one." [cite:rs_cw5_djn_19640515] The Jewish Telegraphic Agency's dispatch, printed in the Detroit Jewish News on 15 May 1964, is the source for the exchange; the summary reached here does not quote the State Department letter's own wording, and this book does not supply it.

The American Zionist Council's sentence is the one document of the exchange quoted in full here, and its timing gives it weight. It came from the organization whose relationship to the Jewish Agency the Senate had just examined, and which the Justice Department had ordered to register as an agent of a foreign principal. In it, that organization placed the bond of Jewish "people-hood" in the spiritual and cultural sphere, with the word "purely." [cite:rs_cw5_djn_19640515] The sources reached do not record how either side characterized the outcome. As a matter of reading only, the sentence can be taken two ways: as the Zionist Council's answer to the suggestion that its work made American Jews part of a foreign political body, or as the agreement on a narrow definition that the Council for Judaism had been seeking. Both readings rest on the same sentence.

The Jewish Agency answers. The argument reached the State Department again through the Jewish Agency itself. Rose L. Halprin, chairman of the Jewish Agency's American Section, corresponded with Phillips Talbot, the Assistant Secretary of State, in May and June 1964 about the Council's statements. In October 1964 she sought advice on how to rebut an article by W. T. Mallison Jr. on Jewish peoplehood and on the Council's views. [cite:rs_cw5_cornell_konvitz] The record of this correspondence survives in a file headed "Jewish Agency, 1963–1970" in the papers of Milton R. Konvitz at Cornell University; the description reached here is the archive's finding aid, not the letters themselves. [cite:rs_cw5_cornell_konvitz] It shows that the Jewish Agency's American Section treated the Council's arguments as serious enough to take up with an Assistant Secretary of State and to seek a rebuttal.

What the dissent shows. The Council's place in this story is a corrective to two simpler accounts. One treats the foreign-agents inquiry as an attack on American Jews from outside; the record shows that an organization of American Jews, founded by Reform rabbis and led by Rosenwald and Rabbi Elmer Berger, supported the order and argued the case for separating religion from the Israeli state. The other treats the Council's position as the hidden view of American Jews generally; the sources reached here make no such claim. Both the Council and the bodies that answered it, the American Zionist Council and the Jewish Agency's American Section, were named organizations with named leaders, and the argument between them is documented as an argument between organizations, not as the opinion of a community.

Several things remain unsettled by the sources reached. The State Department's letter of 20 April 1964 is known here only through the Council's publicity and the JTA's report of it, and its exact terms are not quoted. Talbot's replies to Halprin, and whatever rebuttal of Mallison was finally written, are described only in an archival finding aid. The date of Fulbright's appearance on a Council platform, and the Council's own claims about the 1963 hearing, rest on its unsigned 1997 account. The size of the Council's membership in these years is not given in this material. What is documented is the argument itself: in 1962–64 the legal meaning of the tie between American Jews and Israel was contested between American Jewish organizations, in letters to the State Department, by name.

After the June 1967 war the Council declined: several prominent lay supporters left it, Elmer Berger was ousted as executive vice president in 1968, and the Council's journal Issues ceased publication in November 1969. [cite:rs_cw5_jvl_acj]

sections.h: A Palestinian Answer at the UN: Ahmad Shukairy, 14 November 1963
sections.html:
Most of the documents of 1963 that this stage has followed were written in Washington, Jerusalem and Cairo, by governments. On 14 November 1963 a Palestinian spoke in a United Nations committee room, and his words survive in the official summary record. Ahmad Shukairy's statement to the Special Political Committee is one of the few places in this year's record where the refugees' case was put in a Palestinian's own terms, and it is set down here in those terms, with his figures and his characterizations marked as his.

Who he was. Shukairy came to the committee with a long diplomatic career behind him. He had been appointed an assistant secretary-general of the Arab League on 2 March 1951. From the autumn of 1957 until 1962 he served Saudi Arabia as its minister of state for United Nations affairs and its permanent representative to the UN. [cite:rs_cw5_palquest_shuqayri] [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_shukeiri] In 1963 Ahmad Hilmi Abd al-Baqi, who had represented Palestine at the Arab League, died. The Arab Higher Committee nominated Shukairy to succeed him, and the Council of the Arab League chose him as Palestine's representative at the League. The sources give the year of that choice, not the date. [cite:rs_cw5_palquest_shuqayri] [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_shukeiri] He had spent five years speaking at the UN for a sovereign state; by November 1963 he held the Arab League's choice as Palestine's representative at the League.

The meeting. On 14 November 1963 the Special Political Committee of the eighteenth General Assembly took up the annual report of the Commissioner-General of the United Nations Relief and Works Agency, UNRWA. Shukairy spoke at the committee's 407th meeting as spokesman for the group named in document A/SPC/89. [cite:rs_cw5_un_spc407] The record is a summary record, not a verbatim transcript, and the words quoted below are the summary's.

The refugees' condition. Shukairy credited the Commissioner-General, Davis, and his predecessors with giving "a true picture of the distressing condition" of the refugees. He said they lived on about six cents a day, and he told the committee that UNRWA's objectives had not been met. [cite:rs_cw5_un_spc407] He put the refugee population at 1,120,170 as of June 1963. That is his figure, given in his statement; the summary does not record its source, and it is reported here as he gave it. [cite:rs_cw5_un_spc407]

Property, and the word he used. He argued that Arab property should be returned to its owners. To make the case that the refugees had gained little from what they had lost, he cited figures published by the Jewish Agency in May 1951 on the revenue from Arab property, and argued that little of it had reached the refugees. He called the seizures "genocide." [cite:rs_cw5_un_spc407] The word is his charge, made in a political forum; the summary record reports it as his, and this book does so too. The underlying claim he was making, that property belonging to the refugees was producing revenue in which they did not share, rested in his telling on the Jewish Agency's own figures; the summary reached here does not reproduce those figures, and they cannot be checked from it.

His use of the Fulbright inquiry. Shukairy also turned to Washington. He cited the Senate Foreign Relations Committee's inquiry of August 1963 as showing that the American Zionist Council had received funds from Israel to "combat Arab propaganda," and he urged member states to outlaw such campaigns. [cite:rs_cw5_un_spc407] The record does not verify that characterization. The part of the Senate hearings he was referring to concerned the activities of the Jewish Agency for Israel and related lobbying organizations, one of thirteen parts of a wider inquiry into the agents of foreign principals in the United States. [cite:rs_cw5_ol_hearings] What those hearings established about the Agency's payments to the Council, and how large they were, was in dispute then and is in dispute now; the evidence is set out in [scene:cw5_jewish_agency_hearing|the Jewish Agency before the committee].

His reading had a direct counterpart from the other side, given three months earlier. In August 1963 Dr Emanuel Neumann, chairman of the Jewish Agency–American Section, told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency that Senator Fulbright had praised the Agency's achievements and said repeatedly that there was "no wrong doing," and that the only question left open was technical: whether the Agency's periodic reports were detailed enough. Neumann called the outcome a vindication: "a prolonged and meticulous examination has turned up absolutely nothing damaging to the status of the Jewish Agency." [cite:rs_cw5_djn_19630816] Each man was describing the same hearings, and each was a party to the question. Neither account is confirmed by the hearing record in the sources reached for this section.

The American reply. The United States representative, recorded as Mr Cook, answered briefly. He said that Shukairy had made many misstatements and had been abusive, that "personal insult did no service to the Palestine refugees," and that he would not respond further. [cite:rs_cw5_un_spc407] The summary does not say which statements he considered misstatements, or what he took to be insulting. His refusal to engage point by point left Shukairy's figures and charges unanswered on the record of that meeting, and it also left the American government's own objections unspecified. Whether Israel's delegation answered at the same meeting is not in the material reached here.

Why the meeting matters. The exchange shows the structure within which a Palestinian claim could be made in 1963. The refugees' case reached the General Assembly through a committee reviewing a relief agency's report; it was made by a man speaking as spokesman for a group named in a committee document, whose Palestinian role came from the Arab League's choice, not from a Palestinian state or an elected body; and the United States answered it, on the record of that meeting, with a brief dismissal. Shukairy, for his part, drew the American controversy over the foreign-agents law into the UN, and used a domestic Senate inquiry as evidence for a charge against Israel before an international audience. The two readings of that inquiry, his and Neumann's, show how quickly a hearing whose published record was still being compiled in late 1963 had become an argument abroad. [cite:rs_cw5_sres26]

Within weeks his role changed. The Cairo summit of January 1964 authorized him to prepare the First Palestine National Congress, which met in Jerusalem from 28 May to 2 June 1964, created the Palestine Liberation Organization, and elected him chairman of its Executive Committee. [cite:rs_cw5_palquest_shuqayri] That story belongs to the next stage, in [scene:cw6_summits_plo|the summits and the PLO].

The record leaves several things open. The day on which the Arab League chose him as Palestine's representative in 1963 is not established. The source of his figure of 1,120,170 refugees, and the content of the Jewish Agency's 1951 figures that he cited, are not given in the summary record. The summary record condenses his speech; it is not his own text. And his reading of the Fulbright inquiry, like Neumann's opposite one, is a party's characterization; neither is settled by the documents reached for this section.

sections.h: 22 November 1963: A Question of Timing
sections.html:
On 22 November 1963 President Kennedy was killed in Dallas. At that moment two disputes between his administration and Israel's institutions were unresolved: the Justice Department's order that the American Zionist Council register as a foreign agent, and the arrangement for American scientists to visit the reactor at Dimona. Two simple accounts of what followed are in circulation. One holds that nothing in American policy toward Israel changed, and that Johnson carried on exactly as Kennedy had set things. The other holds that both disputes collapsed on the day Kennedy died. The record supports neither in that simple form. This section sets out where each dispute stood that week, what the documents show happened to each afterwards, and what the record says, and does not say, about any connection between them and the President's death. The date enters this history as a fact of timing. Nothing in the documents reached for this book makes it more than that.

The foreign-agents order, November 1963. A year after the Justice Department's order of November 1962, the American Zionist Council had not registered, by the account of nearly every source; a single 2016 version of a Wikipedia article says otherwise, and that dispute is set out in [scene:s11a|the FARA order]. [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_azc_2016] The last active step toward enforcement, as Grant F. Smith of IRmep, an advocate of registration, reports it, came in October 1963, when the FBI offered to help enforce the order as evidence of foreign control accumulated. [cite:rs_cw5_smith_podcast] [cite:antiwar_where_did_aipac_come_from] The Senate inquiry that had examined the Jewish Agency's payments to the Council in the summer was still formally open: its mandate ran to 31 January 1964, when its report was due, and its published record was still being compiled in late 1963, with a sworn letter dated 21 October 1963 printed in its final part. [cite:rs_cw5_sres26] Smith also reports that, before November, a Wall Street Journal story described Justice Department officials weighing the risk of offending Jewish opinion, which prompted letters to Congress and to Robert F. Kennedy urging enforcement. [cite:rs_cw5_smith_podcast] On his account, then, the order stood that week with an offer of help from the FBI behind it and hesitation inside the department that issued it.

Dimona, November 1963. The inspection question had been settled in principle three months earlier, in the exchange told in Eshkol's answer. Levi Eshkol's reply of 19 August 1963 accepted regular visits in principle but not the twice-yearly interval Kennedy had asked for; Kennedy's reply of 26 August assumed "basic agreement on regular visits"; and a memorandum of 16 September recorded Israel's agreement to a "thorough" visit, including the "plutonium separation plant," before the reactor's activation. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] In the week of 22 November that visit had not yet been held. Its terms, and the point Eshkol had declined, had been fixed while Kennedy was alive.

The assassination. President John F. Kennedy was assassinated in Dallas, Texas, on 22 November 1963. Two official bodies inquired into the killing and its causes: the Warren Commission, whose investigation of 1964 concluded that Lee Harvey Oswald acted alone, and the House Select Committee on Assassinations in 1979. Neither identified Israeli nuclear policy, Dimona or the dispute with the American Zionist Council as a factor in the assassination. [cite:wiki_warren_commission]

Dimona after November. The visit promised for before criticality did not take place before it. By the Israeli account the reactor went critical on 26 December 1963; the Hebrew website of the Israel Atomic Energy Commission gives July 1963 for the start of operations. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] The first visit under the 1963 arrangement was held on 18 January 1964. William Burr and Avner Cohen, the editors of the declassified Kennedy–Ben-Gurion–Eshkol letters, write that it "may have been delayed because of Kennedy's assassination." [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] That is the only connection the editors draw between the assassination and Dimona, and they put it as a possibility about a delay of weeks, not as a finding about policy. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters]

The demand itself continued. Cohen and Burr write that Johnson, like Kennedy, pressed for inspections to verify Eshkol's pledge that Dimona was for peaceful purposes. [cite:rs_cw5_cns_duplicity] The State Department's own historians record that the Johnson administration kept insisting on the visits begun under Kennedy, and that the visitors found no evidence of a weapons program while suspicions continued. [cite:rs_cw5_frus6468_summary] How hard Johnson pressed is a matter of reading. The journalist Seymour Hersh, in The Samson Option (1991), describes Johnson as personally opposed to Israel acquiring nuclear weapons, holding that "a nuclear Israel was unacceptable," but pursuing the point with markedly less sustained pressure than Kennedy had applied through 1963. The National Security Archive's 2020 release of records from 1964–65 presents visits that satisfied Washington enough to keep the wider relationship in place without the unrestricted access Kennedy's letters had demanded. [cite:nsarchive_duplicity_1964_65] The visits continued every year through the decade; the sources count them as six and as seven. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] [cite:rs_cw5_majalla] By January 1965 the outside consultant Henry Kissinger was privately telling American diplomats of his near-certainty that Israel had begun weapons development. [cite:nsarchive_duplicity_1964_65] What those visits saw and missed belongs to the years after this stage, and is told in [scene:s11d|Johnson's inspections].

The foreign-agents order after November. Smith writes that after 22 November 1963 the effort to enforce the order against the American Zionist Council "gradually falls apart." He cites no document recording a decision to drop it. [cite:rs_cw5_smith_podcast] The final outcome is not in doubt, whatever its cause: the Council was never ultimately compelled to register under the Act. Where the sources date a restructuring of its lobbying function to early 1963, that restructuring stood, unchallenged to completion by any further federal enforcement action. [cite:antiwar_where_did_aipac_come_from] On the account Volume II drew on, the registration pressure dissolved after the assassination, which is a correlation of timing and not proof of cause or of anyone's intent, and it did not resume under later administrations at comparable intensity until decades later. [cite:crustnews_aipac_history] Smith states elsewhere that the Justice Department kept the order secret until 2008 and has never tried to enforce it since, and he calls the effort "serious, but fizzled out." [cite:rs_cw5_smith_ipa_2022] Kobby Barda, writing in Modern Judaism in 2026, explains the same outcome differently. He argues that the matter had become moot: the lobby had separated from the Jewish Agency's money, the Agency's subscription purchases having ended in 1962, and operated lawfully as a domestic lobby, so there was nothing left to enforce. [cite:rs_cw5_barda_2026] The two explanations differ on why enforcement stopped. They agree on what the record lacks: neither cites a Johnson administration document recording a decision.

Two different kinds of claim. Claims that join these disputes to 22 November 1963 are of two kinds, and they need to be kept apart, because the evidence for each is different.

The first kind is a claim about consequences: that Kennedy's death changed what happened to the two disputes afterwards. The editors' remark about the January visit is one such claim, made cautiously. Smith's "gradually falls apart" places a change after the date. Philip Giraldi, writing in The American Conservative in 2017, says that the Council "was pressured" by Kennedy's Justice Department in 1962 and 1963, and that "Kennedy's death stopped that effort." [cite:rs_cw5_giraldi_2017] Said Arikat, in a news analysis for Al-Quds of 30 May 2026, writes that after the assassination the pressure "steadily lost momentum" under Johnson and was "never meaningfully revived." [cite:rs_cw5_arikat_2026] Giraldi's and Arikat's statements assert a sequence. Neither cites a document of a decision, or a source attributing the change to the assassination. [cite:rs_cw5_giraldi_2017] [cite:rs_cw5_arikat_2026] These are claims about the effect of a change of president on policy, and claims of that kind can in principle be tested against the record. On the record reached here, the Dimona demand continued under Johnson, and the end of the foreign-agents effort is described, by Smith and Barda alike, without any document of a decision.

The second kind is a claim about causes: that the disputes over Dimona or the foreign-agents order had some part in the killing itself. Such claims exist. Barda writes that recent conspiracy claims allege that AIPAC was involved in the assassination. He calls the theory "baseless," and says that a review of the released files found "no evidence whatsoever" linking AIPAC to it. [cite:rs_cw5_barda_2026] His only named source for the spread of these claims is a report of the Combat Antisemitism Movement, dated 6 March 2025, on JFK conspiracy theorists and bot activity; he names no individual who makes them. [cite:rs_cw5_barda_2026] Barda places the 1963 Fulbright hearing "in the shadow of" these claims, and identifies Smith as the leading researcher on the foreign-agents question; he does not attribute any assassination claim to Smith. [cite:rs_cw5_barda_2026] Neither does this book attribute one to Smith, Giraldi or Arikat: the passages of theirs reached here make statements about what happened to policy after 22 November, not about why Kennedy was killed.

No source reached for this book presents evidence for a claim of the second kind. The two official inquiries named above did not identify either dispute as a factor. [cite:wiki_warren_commission] The editors of the Dimona documents connect the assassination to Dimona only through the possible delay of a single visit. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] Avner Cohen, whose work is considered the standard academic reference on Israel's nuclear history, and Seymour Hersh both document the Kennedy–Israel nuclear dispute in detail without asserting or implying a connection to the assassination. Claims that the killing was connected to Dimona or to the lobby are therefore reported here as what they are: claimed, and unsupported by any evidence in the record. Barda's evidence that they spread comes from a report by the Combat Antisemitism Movement; this book reports them only as claims, and extends them to no people and no community.

Testing the timing claim. The method in the panel above asks two questions of any claim, and a third about what has been left out. Applied to the claim of consequence, it gives a divided answer. Is the fact true? The dated facts are. Kennedy died on 22 November 1963; the last enforcement step Smith reports came in October; the first Dimona visit came in January 1964; the order was not enforced to completion. Does it prove the conclusion? No. A sequence of dates does not by itself show that one event produced another, and for the foreign-agents order the record holds no document of a decision to stop, while Barda offers a different explanation that does not depend on the date at all. What is left out? For Dimona, the fact that the terms Kennedy was unable to obtain, a visit every six months, had already been declined in August, while he was alive, and the fact that Johnson went on demanding visits. For the foreign-agents order, Smith's own report of hesitation inside the Justice Department before November. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] [cite:rs_cw5_cns_duplicity] [cite:rs_cw5_smith_podcast]

Applied to the claim of cause, the method stops at the second question. The first fact, the coincidence of dates, is true. Nothing in the record carries it to the conclusion, and the official inquiries and the historians of the period give no support to it. [cite:wiki_warren_commission] [cite:rs_cw5_barda_2026]

What changed under Johnson. Set against the two simple accounts this section began with, the record shows something between them. Policy did not continue "exactly" as before: the foreign-agents order was never enforced to completion, and Hersh describes less sustained pressure on Dimona, and the 2020 release describes visits without the unrestricted access Kennedy had asked for. Nor did both disputes collapse on one day. The Dimona demand continued, the visits began in January 1964 and went on for the rest of the decade, and the end of the foreign-agents effort came without a recorded date or decision. How Johnson inherited and handled Kennedy's two lines of policy toward Israel and Egypt is the opening subject of the next stage, in [scene:cw6_johnson_eshkol|Johnson and Eshkol].

The record leaves open, on the foreign-agents order, who in the Justice Department decided, or allowed, that it would not be enforced, and when; no document of that decision is cited by Smith or by Barda, or was found in this book's research. On Dimona, whether the January visit was in fact delayed by the assassination is put by the editors only as a possibility, and the date the reactor began operating is itself given two ways. The details of the two official inquiries are taken here from a single reference summary and have not been re-verified for this book. What the record does show is plain. There is no document, official finding or historical study among the sources reached that connects Kennedy's death to Dimona or to the foreign-agents dispute as a cause. The record is silent on any such link, and this book says so in those words. It shows two real, independently documented policy disputes and one real, independently investigated assassination, close together in time. It does not show, and no credible investigation or historian has shown, that these threads are causally connected. Setting documented facts side by side is not the same as claiming that they caused each other, and this book states that distinction directly rather than leaving it to inference.

chapters.label: Stage Six
chapters.title: Escalate
chapters.intro:
Stage Five ended in Dallas on 22 November 1963. Lyndon Johnson inherited a Middle East policy that had been built to avoid choices. [cite:wiki_warren_commission] Israel had received its first American military aid in 1962, as loans, and the Hawk missile, but no American tanks; its embassy was already pressing for them, on the strength of Eshkol's letter of 4 November. [cite:merip_us_aid_israel_1990] [cite:wiki_israel_us_military_relations] [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d7] Eshkol had agreed in August to regular American visits to Dimona in principle, without committing to the twice-yearly visits Washington wanted. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] Washington fed Egypt under a multi-year food agreement signed in October 1962. [cite:rs_cw5_frus18_d70] About 30,000 Egyptian troops, by Bruce Riedel's account, were fighting in Yemen by March 1963, against royalists whom Saudi Arabia supplied. [cite:rs_cw5_riedel_yemen] [cite:rs_cw6_fp_yemen] The Ba'th had held power in Damascus since the coup of 8 March 1963. [cite:rs_cw6_locsyria] Ahmad al-Shuqairi had been chosen by the Arab League Council as Palestine's representative at the League, but the PLO did not yet exist. [cite:rs_cw5_palquest_shuqayri] Israel's project to draw water from the Jordan was under way by the end of the year. [cite:rs_cw6_palquest_chron] Inside Israel, military government still ruled Arab citizens in the areas it covered, though personal travel permits had been cancelled on 21 October. [cite:rs_cw6_akevot_gl17005] On the Egyptian side of the southern line stood the United Nations Emergency Force, and only there, because Israel had refused it on its side of the line. [cite:rs_cw6_a6730] The State Department's historians give Johnson's method a name: keeping the Arab-Israeli dispute "in the icebox." [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_sum_a]

This stage asks how that order gave way, in three and a half years, to the crisis of May 1967, and through whose decisions. The answer the documents give is not one escalation but several, running side by side and feeding one another: an arms race that turned the United States from a refuser of tanks into Israel's direct supplier; a quarrel over the Jordan's waters; a Palestinian armed campaign sponsored by one Arab government and launched from the territory of two others; Israeli reprisals; a radical government in Damascus and a defence pact that tied it to Cairo; and, in May 1967, a Soviet warning of an Israeli concentration against Syria that the United Nations' observers could not find. The stage asks with equal weight what each government believed it was doing, and what the record cannot show of their intentions.

The cast is wide. In Washington stood Johnson and his advisers Bundy, Komer and Rostow, Secretary of State Rusk, Secretary of Defense McNamara, and Ambassador Barbour in Tel Aviv. In Israel stood Levi Eshkol, Abba Eban, the chief of staff Yitzhak Rabin, and, outside the government until June 1967, Ben-Gurion's new list, Rafi, with Moshe Dayan and Shimon Peres. [cite:rs_cw6_idi_rafi] In Cairo stood Nasser, his chief of staff Muhammad Fawzi and his foreign minister Riad; in Amman, King Hussein; in Damascus, after February 1966, Salah Jadid, Nureddin Atassi and Hafiz al-Assad. [cite:rs_cw6_locsyria] Shuqairi's Palestine Liberation Organization and Fatah's military wing, al-Asifa, acted on their own account. Bonn acted through Ludwig Erhard, East Berlin through Walter Ulbricht, Moscow through Kosygin, and the United Nations through U Thant and his commanders in the field. Israel's Supreme Court, the Atomic Energy Commission in Washington and the Bank of Israel each left their own record.

The sections follow that story roughly as it unfolded. They open with [scene:cw6_johnson_eshkol|Johnson and Eshkol], and with the Arab summits of 1964 and the founding of the PLO. The Jews of Egypt and Morocco after Suez, the water war, and the al-Ard movement and the Yeredor case follow. Bonn's secret tanks lead to recognition, and Fatah's campaign begins as Washington makes its first direct tank sale. The shortage of uranium at a plant in Pennsylvania, Syria's radical turn, and the Skyhawks and Dimona visits of 1966 come next. The raid on Samu and the end of military government close 1966, and a section on Israel's politics and recession shows the country that entered the crisis. Egypt's war in Yemen, the air battle of 7 April 1967 and [scene:cw6_may_crisis|the crisis of May] bring the stage to [scene:cw6_tiran_june4|its last thirteen days], ending with Israel's cabinet decision of 4 June 1967.
chapters.outro:
This volume began with lines that were, by their own text, not borders, and it ends on the eve of a war fought across them. The Egyptian armistice of 1949 had said its line was "not to be construed in any sense as a political or territorial boundary." [cite:rs_rd6_arm_egypt_text] What changed in the eighteen years between was everything built around the lines: who armed whom, who could restrain whom, and who was bound to fight if a neighbour was struck. By the eve of the war that structure stood in six layers, laid by many governments.

The legal layer grew dense and stayed weak. The Security Council asked Jordan in 1953 to stop the crossings, but its censures fell mainly on Israel's raids: Qibya in 1953, the raid at the lake of December 1955, when in January 1956 it held that Syrian interference "in no way justifies the Israel action," and Samu in 1966, when Resolution 228 declared that "actions of military reprisal cannot be tolerated" by 14 votes to none, with the United States in favour. [cite:rs_cw2_avalon_res101] [cite:rs_cw2_un_res101] [cite:rs_cw2_un_res111] [cite:rs_cw6_res228] [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d349] None of these was enforced. The one instrument that changed facts on the ground after Suez was UNEF, and it stood only on Egyptian soil because Israel would not host it; U Thant held that it rested on the host's consent, and on 18 May 1967 Egypt withdrew that consent. [cite:rs_cw6_a6730] [cite:rs_cw6_s7906] The American aide-mémoire of 1957 had called the Gulf of Aqaba "international waters"; in May 1967 Israel claimed a right of innocent passage and the UAR claimed territorial waters, and no court ruled between them. [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_aidememoire] [cite:rs_cw6_s7906_t] Inside Israel the Supreme Court gave the state a doctrine of its own in 1965: "defensive democracy," which barred an Arab list over Justice Cohn's dissent that the law said a list "shall be confirmed." [cite:rs_cw6_yeredor]

The administrative layer shows power held close. Military government ruled most Arab citizens of Israel from 1949 until 1 December 1966. [cite:wiki_kafr_qasim_massacre] Its governorships ended by a civilian decision over the army's objection, but the Emergency Regulations stayed in force, enforced by a reinforced police and Shin Bet, and the adviser who planned the change called it mainly "psychological." [cite:rs_cw6_akevot_gl17005] Whether that ended military rule is still argued; the Institute for Palestine Studies dates full abolition to late 1968. [cite:rs_cw6_palquest_mg_e] In Damascus, power passed by coup in 1963 and 1966 to a party faction whose leader, Jadid, led through his party post while others held the state's offices. [cite:rs_cw6_locsyria] [cite:rs_cw6_gs_syria] In Jerusalem, a cabinet deadlocked from 23 to 27 May was widened on 1 June with Dayan and Begin, and on 4 June authorized military action. [cite:rs_cw6_isa_cabinet_t] [cite:rs_cw6_mfa_4june]

The institutional and financial layer moved furthest. American aid to Israel was economic through the 1950s, $73.6 million in 1953 and $50.8 million in 1956; the first military aid came in 1962, as loans, when the Hawk sale dwarfed a previous ceiling of $1 million. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_usaid_table] [cite:merip_us_aid_israel_1990] [cite:rs_cw4_kramer_hawks] Within four years Washington had financed German tanks with $24 million of kits on credit, sold 210 tanks for about $42 million and 48 Skyhawks for about $50 million, and sold Jordan 36 F-104s for cash. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d99] [cite:rs_cw6_komer_jul1965_t] [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d273] Bonn turned its undelivered tanks into 140 million DM, and its reparations, by a press report that does not reconcile with the 3 billion DM agreed, ran out in 1965–66. [cite:rs_cw6_serr_bpb] [cite:rs_cw6_jta_reparations_1965] [cite:rs_cw6_bpb_lux] Egypt's food aid shrank to a $70 million credit. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_sum_a] Beneath the arms lay the reactor that Washington judged in 1960 to have weapons as "at least one major purpose," visited by nine American teams between 1961 and 1969, none of which knew of its reprocessing plant. At Apollo, 93.8 kg of uranium went unexplained; the AEC found no evidence of theft, there is no sign it looked for any, and the editors of the primary record judge the evidence of diversion "strong but not incontrovertible." [cite:rs_cw4_ebb510] [cite:rs_cw6_jvl_burr_cohen] [cite:rs_cw6_nsa_numec] At home, Israel entered 1967 in recession, with unemployment at 10.3 percent at the end of 1966. [cite:rs_cw6_boi_1966_ch9]

The Palestinian Arab layer changed most in kind. In the 1950s Palestinians appeared chiefly as the subject of other governments' plans; by 1967 they had organizations of their own. The PLO, founded in Jerusalem in 1964 by appointed delegates under Hussein's sponsorship, adopted a Charter that called Israel's establishment "illegal and false." [cite:rs_cw6_palquest_chron] [cite:rs_cw6_charter_1964] Fatah's campaign from 1965, backed by Syria and funded, in the CIA's account, chiefly by wealthy Palestinians in Kuwait and Saudi Arabia, produced 61 incidents that Israel attributed to it by December 1966, launched from Jordan and Lebanon without their governments' approval. [cite:rs_cw6_cia_dec1966] Palestinian citizens of Israel who tried to organize outside the parties saw al-Ard banned and its list barred. [cite:rs_cw6_yeredor] The Institute for Palestine Studies records that Palestinians mark Fatah's first operation as the start of their contemporary revolution. [cite:rs_cw6_ipsp_fatah] Israel answered the raids with reprisals on West Bank targets, harsher and more frequent from May 1965, according to GlobalSecurity's account. [cite:rs_cw6_gs_jordan_f] Who created the PLO, and whose was the first operation, the record leaves open.

The regional layer was rebuilt around pacts. The Czech arms deal of 1955 brought Soviet-bloc weapons to Egypt; at Sèvres in 1956 Britain, France and Israel agreed in writing on a war; and from 1958 Israel built secret ties with Turkey and Iran, the "Outer Circle" that Schonmann says was meant to create "a phantom of a pact" and persuade Washington of Israel's regional value. [cite:rs_cw2_jvl_czech] [cite:rs_cw3_shlaim_sevres] [cite:rs_cw4_schonmann_2024] Then came the Egypt–Syria pact of November 1966 and the Egypt–Jordan pact of 30 May 1967, which, on one reading, made a clash on the Syrian or Jordanian line Cairo's affair as well. [cite:rs_cw6_locegypt] [cite:rs_cw6_gs_jordan_t] Egypt entered the crisis with part of its army still in Yemen. [cite:rs_cw6_fp_yemen] The Jews of Egypt had largely left after Suez, and more than 97,000 had left Morocco by 1964. [cite:rs_cw6_uw_egypt1956] [cite:rs_cw6_julius_fathom] [cite:rs_cw6_cie_yachin]

The American layer turned from rationing arms to supplying them. Washington, which had refused Israel arms in 1956, by 1966 was writing nuclear pledges into arms sales: "will not be the first to introduce nuclear weapons," in one wording, and "unless others do" in another. [cite:rs_cw2_shlaim_arms] [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d185] [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d273] It also restrained: Johnson warned after Samu that another such raid would suspend shipments, and on 26 May told Eban that Israel "will not be alone unless it decides to go it alone." [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_sum_samu] [cite:rs_cw6_frus19_d77] No document consulted records a trade of ambiguity for arms, or a green light.

What, then, did the Cold War years settle? They settled that Israel would be armed by the United States, which armed Jordan too, while Egypt had drawn on the Soviet bloc since 1955. [cite:rs_cw2_jvl_czech] They did not settle the lines, the refugees, the waters or the Strait. What was contested on 4 June was whether Israel faced an imminent attack: its ministers believed it did, Nasser had spoken, in the Israeli Foreign Ministry's translation, of destroying Israel, and American intelligence judged Egypt's deployment defensive. [cite:rs_cw6_tal_t] [cite:rs_cw6_nasser_26may] [cite:rs_cw6_frus19_d77] What the record leaves open is what Moscow and Cairo intended. Those intentions, and the lines of 1949 themselves, were tested in the war that followed. It is the subject of Volume IV, Six Days, Two Fronts, which opens with [scene:s12|the Six-Day War].

sections.h: Johnson and Eshkol: Two Capitals in the Icebox, November 1963–1966
sections.html:
Kennedy's death on [scene:s11c|22 November 1963] left the pressure he had put on Israel over its reactor at Dimona, and the policy around it, to Johnson. What Johnson did with that inheritance in his first eight months comes down to three questions: how he answered Israel's first request for American tanks, how he received the first Israeli prime minister to make an official visit to Washington, and how, in the same weeks, he worked to keep Nasser's Egypt from treating Dimona as a reason for war. The documents show a president who did not choose between the two capitals. He tried to hold both.

The policy Johnson inherited. The State Department's historians, summarizing the documents they published for 1964–1968, describe Johnson's approach as a continuation of Kennedy's: good relations with both Nasser's United Arab Republic and Israel at once. Central to it, in their words, was keeping the Arab-Israeli dispute "in the icebox." [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_sum_a] The phrase describes a method rather than a goal. Washington did not try to settle the conflict; it tried to keep each side's demands from forcing a choice that would cost it the other. Kennedy's two pressure tracks, the inspection of Dimona that he had demanded in [scene:s11b|the letters of 1963] and the registration order against the American Zionist Council, passed to a president who wanted both handled without a public break.

Israel's request: tanks first. The first test came from Israel's embassy. In a meeting recorded for the file by Komer, Ambassador Harman, Minister Gazit and the military attaché, Colonel Ram Ron, put Israel's needs to Bundy and to Komer himself. Komer's record refers back to Eshkol's letter of 4 November 1963 and to a meeting of 14 November 1963; the Israelis were pressing a request already in train before Kennedy's death. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d7] They asked for three things: surface-to-surface missiles, modern tanks, and some answer to the growing naval strength of the United Arab Republic. Tanks were the immediate priority. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d7]

The tank request was specific. Israel wanted to replace about 300 Shermans with 200 M48A3s and 100 M60s, and then to obtain about 200 more M60s over two to three years. To show what the burden already was, the memo recorded that defence took about 40% of Israel's regular budget and 11% of its gross national product. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d7] Those two figures carried the Israeli argument: a state already spending at that rate was asking for help it said it could not finance alone.

Bundy's answer. Bundy's reply, as Komer recorded it, went to each request in turn and gave little. On missiles he was dismissive of the threat Israel cited: "in practical military terms Nasser's missiles were useless." He then turned the question back on Israel. Missiles added to Israel's "existing nuclear potential," he warned, could open a new dimension in the arms race. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d7] In a memo of record, a senior White House official spoke to Israeli diplomats of their country's nuclear potential as a thing that already existed, and tied it to the missile request. Bundy also warned that 1964 would be a hard year because of the pro-Israeli stance the United States planned to take on the Jordan waters. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d7] One reading is that Washington's support on water was offered as a reason it could not do more on arms; the memo records the warning, not that reasoning.

Early 1964: no, but through Europe. An interagency review in early 1964 settled the tank question for the time being. The United States declined to sell tanks directly, the editors write, because of its policy of not becoming a major arms supplier to the region. It agreed instead to help Israel obtain tanks from Europe. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_sum_a] The decision had two halves, and both mattered. The refusal kept the formal policy intact; the help through Europe meant that Israel would get the armour by another route, with Washington's knowledge and assistance. How that route ran through West Germany, and what happened when it became public, is told in [scene:cw6_germany|Bonn's secret tanks].

Dimona and Nasser, March–June 1964. While the tank question was being settled, Johnson pressed Eshkol on a different point, and here Eshkol held out for three months. The episode is documented by William Burr and Avner Cohen in a National Security Archive collection of 2020. Washington wanted to tell Nasser, in effect, that Dimona was not what he feared. Eshkol refused to allow it on 3 March and again on 23 March 1964. [cite:rs_cw6_jvl_dimona_nasser] On 19 March Johnson wrote to him that the danger was "a desperate pre-emptive attack." [cite:rs_cw6_jvl_dimona_nasser] Eshkol refused again in a reply of 21 April. [cite:rs_cw6_jvl_dimona_nasser] The phrase implies Johnson's reasoning: a reassured Nasser was less likely to strike. Eshkol's reasons for refusing are not set out in the summary of the record consulted here, beyond his question on 1 June, below.

The visit, 1–2 June 1964. Eshkol arrived in Washington at the start of June. Welcoming him at the White House on 1 June 1964, Johnson called it "the first official visit by a Prime Minister of Israel," and pledged that the United States would continue to help, "particularly in the field of desalinization of water." [cite:rs_cw6_ucsb_welcome] The public emphasis was water, not arms. In private the talks covered both. According to the American memorandum of conversation, Johnson told Eshkol that the United States "could not provide tanks directly" but would help Israel get them elsewhere. Eshkol asked: "please do not push us into the Centurions." Johnson said that the United States was "violently against nuclear proliferation." And on the issue Bundy had flagged months earlier he was unequivocal: "We back Israel fully on the Jordan water." [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d65]

Komer's account to Under Secretary Ball, by telephone, gives the President's private line more bluntly. On tanks, Johnson had told Eshkol "we could not give them but we would help all we could." He had raised Dimona. He hoped Israel would "bite the bullet on the IAEA," the International Atomic Energy Agency, the international body whose controls Washington wanted applied to Israel's reactors. And he asked Israel not to "force us to say publicly that we are behind you." [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d66] That last request is the icebox policy in a sentence. Washington would support Israel; it did not want to be made to say so in a way that cost it Cairo.

On Dimona and Nasser, the first day of talks brought one more refusal. On 1 June Eshkol asked, "Why tell Nasser?" On 2 June, after a private meeting, he conceded, according to Komer's memo of 3 June as Burr and Cohen give it. [cite:rs_cw6_jvl_dimona_nasser] The same day the two governments issued their joint statement. It restated American support for "the territorial integrity and political independence of all countries in the Near East," voiced concern at "the diversion of vitally important resources from development to armaments," and agreed on joint studies of desalting. [cite:rs_cw6_joint_stmt_1964] Read against the private record, one reading gives each clause its own weight: the first was the old American formula, offered to all states in the region and not to Israel alone; the second was a polite reproach to everyone buying weapons, Israel included; the third was the visible reward.

What Komer counted. Komer reported to the President that the visit was "a distinct plus." He listed what Israel had agreed to. It would let the United States reassure Nasser on Dimona. It would accept observers from the IAEA in a joint desalting study. It accepted IAEA controls, in principle, on any large desalting reactor. And it would seek an IAEA agreement on its small reactor within nine months. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d68] Each concession was real and each was limited. None of them put Dimona, the reactor that mattered, under international safeguards; the IAEA was to enter by way of the desalting study, any large desalting reactor, and the small reactor. On this reading, Komer's four points show what Washington could obtain in exchange for warmth and water: access at the edges of the programme, not at its centre.

The Egyptian track. The other capital was being worked at the same time, and the documents make the balance visible. Johnson wrote to Nasser, and the letter produced a pledge in July 1964 that the United Arab Republic would not develop nuclear weapons. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_sum_a] Washington then tried to go further. In September 1964 McCloy went to Cairo on missiles, the subject Bundy had told the Israelis did not matter militarily but which Israel cited as a reason for its own requests. The mission failed: Nasser told him that only a solution of the Palestine problem would end the arms race. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_sum_a] The two governments had each given Johnson something on nuclear weapons in the summer of 1964, and neither would give him anything on the arms race itself.

Relations with Cairo then ran downhill. The State Department editors trace the decline through disputes over Yemen, the Congo and Vietnam. Aid connected with the Congo ended in April 1965; the last funds under P.L. 480, the American food-aid programme, were released in June 1965; and in June 1966 Rusk advised against renewing the P.L. 480 agreement, the United States extending $70 million in food credit instead. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_sum_a] The shrinking of food aid from a programme to a credit line marks how far the Egyptian half of the icebox policy had worn by 1966, while the Israeli half, as the following sections show, moved from refusing tanks to selling them.

Did the visit change arms policy? The record supports two readings, and they turn on different time frames. On the first, the visit changed nothing on arms. The memorandum of conversation and Komer's account to Ball both record the same answer the interagency review had already reached: the United States "could not provide tanks directly" and would only help Israel obtain them from Europe. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d65] [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d66] On this view, what Eshkol took home was water, desalting and warm words; the policy against becoming a major arms supplier held. On the second reading, the visit opened the road to the change it formally refused. The volume's editors note that the European route, German tanks fitted with American modernization kits, depended on secrecy, and that within a year Washington was selling tanks to Israel directly. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_sum_a] The first reading is the better account of what was decided in June 1964; the second is the better account of what that decision led to once the secret could not be kept. The documents consulted here do not show that anyone in Washington planned the second outcome in June 1964.

What the record does not settle. Several things remain open. The memoranda record that Eshkol conceded on Nasser after a private meeting on 2 June, but not what was said in it, or what, if anything, he was offered. The editors' summary records that Johnson's letter to Nasser produced the July pledge, but it does not, in the text consulted here, say what the letter told Nasser about Dimona. Komer's four concessions are documented as promises; whether Israel sought the IAEA agreement on its small reactor within the nine months is not in these sources. And the larger question the icebox policy posed, whether holding both capitals was possible at all, was not answered in 1964. It was answered over the next three years, as tanks, aircraft, water and raids each forced the choice that Johnson had hoped to postpone.

sections.h: The Summits and the PLO: The Arab Side of 1964
sections.html:
The previous section followed Washington's year from the American side. The Arab states had their own year in 1964, and it began with water: Israel's project to divert the Jordan, and what the Arab governments would do about it. Out of that decision came three things that shaped the rest of this stage: a pattern of summit meetings among Arab heads of state, a joint military command, and a new Palestinian body with its own charter. This section tells that year, and the two after it, from the documents the Arab governments and the Palestinian congress themselves produced, set beside what American intelligence made of them.

The invitation, 23 December 1963. On 23 December 1963 Nasser invited the Arab heads of state to Cairo to discuss how to confront Israel's project to divert the Jordan. According to the chronology of the Institute for Palestine Studies, Israel had begun that project by the end of 1963. [cite:rs_cw6_palquest_chron] The occasion matters to the story. The first Arab summit was not called to found a Palestinian organization; it was called about water, and the Palestinian question entered its agenda through the larger matter of how the Arab states would face Israel together.

Cairo, 13–17 January 1964. The kings and heads of state met at the headquarters of the Arab League in Cairo from 13 to 17 January 1964. Their final communiqué condemned Israel's plan to "divert the course of the River Jordan" as a threat to the riparian rights of the Arab states. It agreed that the governments would suspend the media campaigns they had been waging against one another, a truce among Arab governments that is easy to overlook. And it set the next meeting for August 1964, in Alexandria. [cite:rs_cw6_ecf_communique] What the summit chose to do about the diversion, and why, is told in [scene:cw6_water|the water war].

The communiqué also spoke of the Palestinians. It referred to "organizing the Palestinian people" so that they could take part in liberating their country, and it affirmed "the sacred right of the Palestine Arab people to self determination." [cite:rs_cw6_ecf_communique] It did not, in so many words, name a Palestinian entity. [cite:rs_cw6_ecf_communique] [cite:rs_cw6_jvl_summit_1964] [cite:rs_cw6_palquest_chron] The wording was a mandate, not yet an institution, and the man the summit entrusted with organizing the Palestinian people was Ahmad al-Shuqairi. [cite:rs_cw6_palquest_chron]

The Unified Arab Command. An Arab summit also created a Unified Arab Command. The State Department's editors record its effect from the American side: King Hussein of Jordan's request for American arms in 1964 came under pressure from the Command. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_sum_plo] A country-history account published by GlobalSecurity.org, an unattributed text, says the Cairo summit of January 1964 created the Command under an Egyptian commander. [cite:rs_cw6_gs_jordan_a] One reading of the mechanism: a joint command was a new channel through which the Arab states, and on the GlobalSecurity account Egypt in particular, could press a neighbour of Israel on how it armed itself, and the editors' note shows it bearing on Hussein's own request for American arms; that request reappears in [scene:cw6_tanks|the first American tank sale].

Jerusalem, 28 May–2 June 1964. Shuqairi's mandate became an organization within five months. The first Palestinian National Congress met in Jerusalem on 28 May 1964, under the sponsorship of King Hussein, with nearly 400 delegates, all of them appointed. On 2 June it announced the Palestine Liberation Organization, approved a National Charter and a Basic Law, and elected Shuqairi as president. [cite:rs_cw6_palquest_chron] Each of those details points in a different direction. The meeting was Palestinian in membership; its delegates were appointed, not elected; and it met under the Jordanian king's sponsorship. The organization it founded was the creation of all three facts at once.

The Charter in its own words. The Charter of 1964 is the clearest statement of what the new organization claimed, and its key articles are best read as written. Article 2 defines the territory: "Palestine with its boundaries at the time of the British Mandate is a regional indivisible unit." [cite:rs_cw6_charter_1964] Article 17 calls the partition of 1947 and the establishment of Israel "illegal and false." Article 18 calls the Balfour Declaration and the Mandate "fraud." [cite:rs_cw6_charter_1964] Article 7 addresses Jews: Jews of Palestinian origin "are considered Palestinians if they are willing to live peacefully and loyally in Palestine." [cite:rs_cw6_charter_1964]

Taken together, these articles denied Israel's legitimacy outright. The Charter did not dispute Israel's borders or its policies; it declared the state's founding illegal and its legal foundations fraudulent, and it defined the whole territory of the Mandate as one indivisible Palestinian unit. Article 7 counted Jews of Palestinian origin as Palestinians only on a condition: that they be willing to live peacefully and loyally in Palestine. That is what the document says, and it should be stated plainly. It is equally a statement of what one organization's founding text said in 1964, adopted by a congress of appointed delegates; it is not evidence about the views of Palestinians or Arabs as peoples, and the sources here do not treat it as such.

Article 24 and the dispute over it. One clause of the Charter has had a long second life. Article 24 states that the organization "does not exercise any regional sovereignty over the West Bank in the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan," and it names the Gaza Strip and the Himmah area in the same clause. [cite:rs_cw6_charter_1964] Critics of the PLO cite this article to argue that Palestinians did not claim the West Bank and Gaza before 1967. [cite:rs_cw6_rabbani_charter] [cite:rs_cw6_charter_1964] The analyst Mouin Rabbani, writing in 2025, reads the same text the other way. Article 2, he argues, already defines Palestine as the whole territory of the Mandate, and Article 24 only defers to the administration Jordan, Egypt and Syria were then exercising over those areas. He adds the context of authorship: the 1964 Charter was drafted by delegates chosen by Arab governments; the Charter of 1968, drafted mainly by the guerrilla movements, dropped the clause. [cite:rs_cw6_rabbani_charter]

Both readings rest on the text, and the text supports each in part. Article 24 does disclaim sovereignty over the West Bank and names Gaza and Himmah; Article 2 does define Palestine as the whole Mandate territory. Whether the first article limited the claim or merely postponed its exercise is the question the two sides answer differently, and the Charter alone does not settle it.

Alexandria, September 1964. The second summit met not in August, as Cairo had planned, but at Alexandria from 5 to 11 September 1964. According to the Institute for Palestine Studies, it recognized the PLO over the opposition of Syria and Saudi Arabia. [cite:rs_cw6_palquest_chron] The Washington Institute's survey of the summits dates the formal approval of the PLO to 11 September 1964. [cite:rs_cw6_winep_summits] The objections matter as much as the approval. The new organization did not enter Arab politics with every Arab government behind it; it was recognized by a summit in which two governments opposed it.

Casablanca, 1965. The third summit, at Casablanca, ended on 18 September 1965. The Washington Institute's survey records that it took no notable decisions. [cite:rs_cw6_winep_summits] After two years of summitry the institutions the meetings had created, the joint command and the PLO, existed; the unity on which they depended had not deepened.

Who created the PLO? The question has two documented answers, and each is supported by a different kind of source. The first answer is that the Arab League and Nasser created it. A memorandum of the CIA's Office of Current Intelligence dated 2 December 1966 says the PLO was formed in 1964 with the sanction of the Arab League, and that Nasser had considerable influence over it. Its radio station, the "Voice of Palestine," broadcast from Cairo. [cite:rs_cw6_cia_dec1966_plo] On this account the PLO was an instrument of the states, and above all of Egypt: the summit gave the mandate, Cairo gave the voice. The second answer is that a Palestinian congress created it. The Institute for Palestine Studies stresses that a Palestinian national congress, meeting in Jerusalem, founded the organization and elected its own leadership, though with appointed delegates and under Jordanian sponsorship. [cite:rs_cw6_palquest_chron] On this account the states made the occasion, but Palestinians made the organization. The two answers are not exclusive. The documents show a League mandate, a Jordanian host, Egyptian influence and a Palestinian congress, and the weight a reader gives each depends on whether the question is who made the PLO possible or who constituted it.

The army. The CIA's memorandum of December 1966 also describes the organization's attempt to build an army. The PLO, it says, tried to form a Palestine Liberation Army around the Palestinian units already serving in the Egyptian, Syrian and Iraqi armies. [cite:rs_cw6_cia_dec1966_plo] The detail suggests how far the organization depended on host states two years after its founding: its army was to be assembled from units that belonged to other governments' forces.

Hussein's break, July 1966. The organization's Jordanian sponsor turned against it within two years. In July 1966, according to the GlobalSecurity account, Hussein withdrew official endorsement and support from the PLO after friction over its taxing Palestinians and distributing arms in the West Bank and in the refugee camps. The PLO and the Syrian government then turned against him. [cite:rs_cw6_gs_jordan_a] This account rests on a single unattributed country-history text and is reported here as that source's account. If it is accurate, the break set Article 24 against practice: an organization that disclaimed sovereignty over the West Bank was taxing and arming there, and the government that ruled the West Bank withdrew its support.

What the record does not settle. The sources consulted here leave several questions open. They do not say how the nearly 400 delegates to the Jerusalem congress were chosen, or by whom, beyond that they were appointed. They give the Unified Arab Command's founding to the January summit only on the authority of one unattributed account, and they do not describe its forces or its record. They date Hussein's break and its causes from that same single source, without a Jordanian or PLO document. And the two great disputes, over Article 24 and over who created the PLO, cannot be closed from the texts, because each side reads the same documents for a different question. Meanwhile the guerrilla movements that would draft the Charter of 1968 were beginning a campaign of their own, told in [scene:cw6_fatah|Fatah's raids].

sections.h: The Jews of Egypt and Morocco, 1956–1964
sections.html:
The summits of 1964 were one part of the Arab world's story in these years. Another was the departure of its Jewish communities. Volume II told that departure up to the Suez war in [scene:rd6_exodus|the exodus of 1948–56]; this section picks up the story in the weeks after Suez and follows it to 1964, in the two countries for which the record has been researched, Egypt and Morocco. The two cases are very different. In Egypt a community already much reduced was largely emptied in about two years, under measures taken by the Egyptian government after the Suez attack of 1956. In Morocco a far larger community left over three years under a negotiated arrangement between the Moroccan king and Israel's prime minister, with money paid per person. Both belong to the history of this stage, because both changed where the Jews of these countries lived by the eve of June 1967.

Egypt before Suez. Israel's Foreign Ministry estimated that there were 75,000 to 80,000 Jews in Egypt in 1948. About 40,000 of them remained after Israel's independence. [cite:rs_cw6_uw_egypt1956] These figures come from a summary by the Stroum Center for Jewish Studies at the University of Washington, which draws on the historian Joel Beinin's study The Dispersion of Egyptian Jewry. On these figures, the community that faced the Suez war was about half the size it had been in 1948.

Arrests and expulsions, 1956. Beinin's account, as the Stroum Center summarizes it, records what followed the attack on Egypt. About 1,000 Jews were arrested in Cairo in 1956, roughly half of them Egyptian citizens. About 13,000 British and French citizens, many of them Jews, were expelled after the Suez attack. Another 500 Jews who held neither British nor French nationality were also expelled. And about 450 Jewish-owned businesses were confiscated. [cite:rs_cw6_uw_egypt1956] The distinction between the categories is the mechanism. The expulsion of British and French nationals was an act against the citizens of two states at war with Egypt, and it took many Jews with it because many Jews in Egypt held those nationalities. The arrest of Jews who were Egyptian citizens, the expulsion of 500 Jews who held neither nationality, and the confiscation of Jewish-owned businesses were, on Beinin's account, measures that reached people because they were Jews. Read that way they were antisemitic in the plain sense of the word, and they were the acts of the Egyptian government of the day.

The order of 15 November 1956. A factsheet issued by the American Jewish Committee in March 1957, cited by the Stroum Center, describes the procedure. Jews were told on 15 November 1956 to report to the Interior Ministry and to leave within days. Those who left signed a "voluntary" renunciation of their claims, their property and their citizenship. By 10 February 1957, 8,500 had left by ship for Europe. [cite:rs_cw6_uw_egypt1956] The quotation marks around "voluntary" are in the source; the form recorded consent, and the circumstances in which it was signed are the reason the word is in quotation marks.

The Stroum Center also cites figures from JIMENA: about 25,000 departures in 1956, and about 15,000 Jews left in 1957. [cite:rs_cw6_uw_egypt1956] The second figure is given in the summary in that form, and it can be read either as departures in 1957 or as the number still in Egypt that year; the source does not say which.

Lyn Julius, writing in 2017 in Fathom, an advocacy publication, gives a similar total over a longer period: 23,000 to 25,000 departures between November 1956 and the end of 1958. She records at least 500 Jewish firms sequestered between November 1956 and March 1957, and exit visas stamped "ONE WAY-NO RETURN," and she writes that the community fell to a few thousand during the 1960s. [cite:rs_cw6_julius_fathom] Her figures run close to the JIMENA figures on departures and slightly above Beinin's on businesses (at least 500 sequestered against about 450 confiscated), though the two counts may not measure the same thing, since sequestration and confiscation are different legal acts.

Expelled or emigrated? Whether Egypt's Jews were expelled after Suez is disputed, and the dispute is about more than words. On one side, Beinin documents what he calls a "systematic expulsion": the arrests, the expulsions of British, French and stateless Jews, and the forced renunciations. [cite:rs_cw6_uw_egypt1956] Julius goes further in her framing, presenting the exodus as antisemitic persecution. [cite:rs_cw6_julius_fathom] The strongest form of this case rests on the order of 15 November and the renunciation forms: people told to leave within days, who signed away property and citizenship to do so, did not choose to emigrate in any ordinary sense.

On the other side, the writer Eyal Sagui Bizawe, in a 2017 article in Haaretz quoted by the Stroum Center, argues that "most of Egypt's Jews were not expelled," and objects to the way the Israeli school curriculum frames their departure. Many already held European nationality, on this account, and chose Europe. [cite:rs_cw6_uw_egypt1956] The strongest form of this case rests on the numbers and the destinations: many of those who left already held European nationality and went to Europe, and a single word, "expelled," flattens a set of different situations into one story. The two positions agree on the measures; they differ on whether those measures describe what happened to most of the community or to part of it. The sources consulted here do not give a breakdown, by nationality, of everyone who left, and without it the question cannot be settled by counting.

Morocco: Operation Yachin. The second case was an organized emigration. According to the Center for Israel Education, an educational organization whose timeline is the source for this account, Operation Yachin began on 28 November 1961 under an understanding between King Hassan II and Ben-Gurion. By 1964 more than 97,000 Jews had left Morocco, travelling via France or Italy; some settled in France, Canada or the United States rather than Israel. [cite:rs_cw6_cie_yachin]

The arrangement had a price. The same account says Israel agreed to pay $500,000, plus $100 for each emigrant for the first 50,000 and $250 for each one after that, and that HIAS contributed $50 million to the operation's costs. [cite:rs_cw6_cie_yachin] The terms describe the mechanism: emigration organized under an understanding between two heads of government, paid for by Israel per head, at a rate that rose once the first 50,000 had gone, with HIAS contributing $50 million. The account does not say, in the text consulted here, to whom in Morocco the payments were made, and it is a single educational source; these figures are reported as its figures, not as a documented ledger.

What the record does not settle. This section rests on three sources: a university summary of Beinin's scholarship and of the documents and figures it cites, an essay in an advocacy publication, and an educational timeline. Beyond the questions already noted, they leave several things open. They do not say how many of Egypt's Jews went to Israel and how many to Europe or elsewhere. They do not give a Moroccan or Israeli government record of the Yachin payments, or say who received them. Nor do they say what led the Moroccan government to agree to an arrangement of this kind, or what the conditions of Morocco's Jews were before it. And the story of the Jews of Iraq, Syria, Libya and Yemen between 1956 and 1967 has not been researched for this book; its absence here is a gap in the research, not a sign that nothing happened in those countries.

sections.h: The Water War, 1964–1966
sections.html:
It was water that had brought the Arab heads of state to Cairo in January 1964.
