Stage Two left the Syrian frontier with its disputed demilitarized zones and the American attempt, through the Johnston Plan, to divide the Jordan's waters by agreement; this section picks up [scene:sy_s02|that thread] in 1964, when Israel began drawing water from the Jordan basin on its own and the Arab states answered by trying to divert the river's headwaters before they reached it. Each scheme was an engineering project; each was also a claim about who had a right to the river; and the fight over them ran straight into the raids and air battles that led toward 1967.

The plan that was never ratified. The background is the mediation of the American envoy Eric Johnston from 1953 to 1955. The parties negotiated, and by 1955 the negotiators had reached a technical plan for sharing the Jordan system. Israel accepted it. The Arab League declined to ratify it, according to the scholar Ines Dombrowsky, because a treaty with Israel would have meant recognizing Israel. [cite:rs_cw6_dombrowsky_bpb] On one reading, the plan's fate shaped what followed. The engineers had agreed on numbers, but there was no signed agreement that either side was bound by, and each could later claim to be acting within the plan or to be free of it.

The Carrier. Israel built on the plan's numbers without the treaty. Aaron Wolf, in his study of the hydropolitics of the Jordan for the United Nations University, writes that Israel's National Water Carrier was supported "within the Johnston allocations," and that by 1964 enough of it was complete for diversions from the Jordan basin to the coastal plain and the Negev to be imminent. [cite:rs_cw6_wolf_unu] The Carrier entered operation in 1964. It drew from Lake Tiberias, which meant lifting the water from 212 metres below sea level. [cite:rs_cw6_dombrowsky_bpb] [cite:rs_cw6_wolf_unu] Wolf gives Israel's withdrawal as 320 million cubic metres a year from 1964. [cite:rs_cw6_wolf_unu]

The exact date of the opening is less certain than the year. The Center for Israel Education, an educational organization, dates the Carrier's start to 10 June 1964 and gives its two trunk lines a capacity of 1.7 million cubic metres a day. [cite:rs_cw6_cie_carrier] That date rests on a secondary timeline; no primary record of the opening was consulted for this book, and the date should be read as that source's. What the scholarly sources agree on is the year and the scale.

The phrase "within the Johnston allocations" is Israel's case in brief. The Johnston Plan had been negotiated under American sponsorship, Israel had accepted it, and the quantity Israel drew could be presented as no more than the share the plan had assigned. To the Arab states, the same project was an Israeli diversion of a shared river, carried out without any agreement they had signed; the Cairo summit's communiqué had condemned it as a threat to Arab riparian rights. The two cases did not meet, because one rested on a plan and the other on the refusal to ratify it.

Washington's position. The United States took a side on the water, and said so in private. Before the Carrier opened, Bundy warned Israeli diplomats that 1964 would be a difficult year because of the pro-Israeli stance Washington planned to take on the Jordan waters. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d7_w] In June 1964 Johnson told Eshkol: "We back Israel fully on the Jordan water." [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d65_w] Support for the Carrier did not extend to force in its defence. The State Department's editors record that Washington asked Israel to pursue peaceful means on the Jordan waters rather than preemptive action. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_sum_w] The American position, then, had two halves: Israel's withdrawal was legitimate, and Israel should not strike first to protect it.

The Arab choice, 1964. At the Cairo summit of January 1964, according to Wolf, the Arab states weighed three options: complaint to the United Nations, diversion of the Jordan's upper tributaries, or war. A military assessment found the Arab states unprepared to defend diversion works. [cite:rs_cw6_wolf_unu] The finding mattered: it meant that any diversion would be built within reach of Israeli forces by states that did not expect to be able to protect it. The September 1964 summit chose diversion nonetheless. It agreed to finance works in Lebanon and Syria and to help Jordan build a dam on the Yarmuk. [cite:rs_cw6_wolf_unu] The sources consulted here do not give the sums or say which governments paid what.

The diversion scheme. Work began in 1965. The plan would have diverted two of the Jordan's sources before they reached Israel: the Hasbani into the Litani, inside Lebanon, and the Banias into the Yarmuk, where the water would be impounded by a dam at Mukheiba. Together the works could divert up to 125 million cubic metres a year. [cite:rs_cw6_wolf_unu] Lebanon stopped its part of the work in July 1965. [cite:rs_cw6_wolf_unu] That left the Syrian works on the Banias as the part of the scheme still being built.

The strikes of 1965. Israel attacked the diversion works in Syria in March, May and August 1965. [cite:rs_cw6_wolf_unu] How it did so is disputed between the two scholarly sources consulted here. Wolf writes that Israel used long-range tank fire, not artillery or aircraft, and that it chose this method partly because of American warnings against preemptive action. [cite:rs_cw6_wolf_unu] Dombrowsky writes that Israel "bombed" the construction site several times shortly after work began. [cite:rs_cw6_dombrowsky_bpb] The difference is not a quibble. Wolf's account describes a calibrated use of force, shaped by Washington's request and kept below the threshold of air attack; Dombrowsky's word, if taken literally, describes air power. Wolf gives the months and the weapon and ties the choice to the American request for restraint; Dombrowsky gives no further detail. Neither source gives casualty figures or an order of battle, and the sources here cannot settle the point beyond that.

Dombrowsky records that the Banias diversion project was finally abandoned in 1966. [cite:rs_cw6_dombrowsky_bpb] The sources consulted here do not set out the decision to abandon it, but the outcome matched what the Arab states' own military assessment of January 1964 had foreseen: works that could not be defended were not completed. [cite:rs_cw6_wolf_unu] [cite:rs_cw6_dombrowsky_bpb] The broader account of the Syrian frontier drawn on here, which describes the strikes as hitting the works in "1965–67," gives a longer span than either scholarly source, which place the attacks in 1965 and the abandonment in 1966.

The first Palestinian attack on the Carrier. The Carrier was also a target for the new Palestinian armed groups. Wolf calls an attempt to sabotage it on 31 December 1964 "the PLO's first action." [cite:rs_cw6_wolf_unu] The Institute for Palestine Studies and Benny Morris, as cited by the Center for Online Judaic Studies, give the first operation to Fatah instead, on 1 January 1965 or the night of 2 January. [cite:rs_cw6_ipsp_fatah_w] [cite:rs_cw6_cojs_morris_w] The three versions are set side by side in [scene:cw6_fatah|Fatah's armed campaign]. Whoever carried it out, the first Palestinian armed operation of this period was aimed at the water.

From water to the border war. The water war did not end when the diversion was given up; it changed form. Wolf records border air battles in July 1966 and April 1967 as part of what he calls a "prolonged chain reaction of border violence." [cite:rs_cw6_wolf_unu] The Syrian frontier, where the zones had been disputed since 1949, became the place where the engineering conflict turned into a military one.

On the Syrian line the water war joined an older quarrel over the demilitarized zones that the armistice of 1949 had left without agreed sovereignty, the stage that the map of the Golan line in [scene:cw6_syria|Syria's radical turn] labels "DMZ & water war" and "both sides." [cite:frus_dayan_dmz] [cite:w_dayan] The familiar account holds that the clashes on this frontier were caused entirely by Syrian shelling from the Golan. The documented conduct of both sides does not support so simple a version, and the water war is part of the reason: the Carrier, the diversion and the strikes on the diversion were each a deliberate act by a government, and each was answered.

One later statement sharpens the dispute without settling it. In an interview given in 1976 and published in 1997, Moshe Dayan said that at least 80 percent of the clashes had been provoked by Israel, which sent tractors into the zones until the Syrians fired. [cite:w_dayan] It is his own account, given long after the events, and it has been contested by others. It concerns the zones in general rather than the water works in particular, and it is evidence of how one senior participant later judged Israeli conduct, not a count of incidents. The dispute over who bore more responsibility for the Syrian frontier continues.

What the record does not settle. On the sources consulted here, several points remain open: the exact date the Carrier opened, which rests on one secondary timeline; whether Israel's strikes on the diversion works were made by tank fire alone or also from the air; the date of the first sabotage attempt against the Carrier and which organization made it; and the sums the Arab summit committed to the diversion, and who paid them. Nor do they record what the water war cost in lives on either side.

sections.h: Al-Ard and the Yeredor Case: Organizing Under Military Government, 1959–1965
sections.html:
While Israel and its neighbours fought over the Jordan's water, Palestinian citizens inside Israel were testing what political room the state would allow them. The regime of military government over Israel's Arab citizens is described in Volume II in [scene:rd6_military_government|military government], and its end in 1966 in [scene:cw6_military_rule_end|the next stage of that story]. This section concerns something the regime's structure does not show on its own: what happened when Palestinian citizens of Israel tried to organize politically outside the existing parties, between 1959 and 1965. The answer came in three stages, from the administration, from the Minister of Defence, and finally from the Supreme Court.

A vote lost by one, 1963. The political setting is shown by a vote in the Knesset in 1963. An opposition motion to end military rule failed by a single vote. Two Arab members linked to Mapai, Jabr Muadi and Thiab Ubaid, voted with the government. [cite:rs_cw6_palquest_mg] The episode is recorded in the Institute for Palestine Studies encyclopedia. One reading is that it shows the two channels through which Arab citizens could act in parliament at the time. One ran through members linked to Mapai and voting with the government, whose votes could decide a question as close as this one. The other ran outside it, and that was the channel al-Ard tried to open.

From the Popular Front to al-Ard. According to the journalist Edo Konrad, writing for +972 Magazine in 2015, al-Ard grew out of a "Popular Front" formed by nationalists and communists in 1959. Konrad names Fouzi El-Asmar as one of its founders. [cite:rs_cw6_konrad_972] Konrad's essay is a work of advocacy journalism, and it is the source here for most of what is known about the group's early life; its account of events is reported as his, and its interpretation is marked as such below.

On his account, the authorities closed successive versions of al-Ard's newspaper, and they refused to register the group as an economic company. Its members were placed under surveillance, and some were jailed or banished to the Negev. [cite:rs_cw6_konrad_972] The pattern he describes is one of administrative obstruction rather than a single prohibition: each attempt to publish or to incorporate was met by a refusal, and the group's members were subject to the powers of a state that still governed its Arab citizens under military government.

The courts and the ban, 1964. The decisive legal step came in 1964. In the case of Sabri Jiryis v. District Commissioner of Haifa, HCJ 253/64, the Supreme Court held that al-Ard sought to deny Israel's existence. The Minister of Defence declared it an unlawful association the same year. [cite:rs_cw6_yeredor] [cite:rs_cw6_konrad_972] The two steps were distinct: the court made a finding about al-Ard's aims; the ban was an act of the executive, made by the Minister responsible for defence, not by a court. From 1964 al-Ard as such could not lawfully exist.

The Socialists' List, 29 September 1965. Its members then tried to stand for parliament. For the elections to the Sixth Knesset, an Arab list of ten candidates, called the Socialists' List, was submitted to the Central Elections Committee. On 29 September 1965 the Committee refused to confirm it. Its grounds were that most of the candidates were members of al-Ard and that "its initiators deny the integrity of the State of Israel and its very existence." [cite:rs_cw6_yeredor] The list's supporters appealed to the Supreme Court. The case is known by the name of its appellant: Yeredor v. Chairman of the Central Elections Committee for the Sixth Knesset, EA 1/65.

The majority: "defensive democracy." The Court dismissed the appeal by a majority. President Agranat and Justice Sussman formed the majority; according to Justice Sussman's opinion, the decision was given on 12 October 1965. They held that the Knesset could not be used as an instrument to pursue the destruction of the state. Sussman described the approach as a "defensive democracy." [cite:rs_cw6_yeredor] The strongest form of the majority's case is this. A democracy is not obliged to lend its own parliament to those who seek to abolish the state the parliament serves; the Court had already found, in the Jiryis case, that al-Ard sought to deny Israel's existence; and a list made up mostly of members of a body already declared unlawful was, on that finding, an attempt to carry an unlawful association's aims into the legislature. The majority held that such a list could be barred even without an express statute: a state may defend itself against its own destruction even where the law has not spelled the power out.

The dissent: Justice Cohn. Justice Haim Cohn dissented, and his reasoning was textual. Section 23 of the Knesset Elections Law said that a duly submitted list "shall be confirmed." No statute empowered the Committee to reject one. And there was, in his view, no "real, clear and present danger" that might justify going beyond the statute. He wrote that the right to vote and to be elected "is one of the fundamental rights of the citizen." [cite:rs_cw6_yeredor] The strongest form of the dissent is that the case was not about al-Ard's views at all, but about who may take a citizen's right to stand for election away: on Cohn's reading, only the legislature could do so, by statute, and a committee that did so without one acted beyond its power, whatever it thought of the candidates.

Defence of the state, or suppression of organizing? The two opinions frame a dispute that has outlasted the case. On one side stands the majority's reasoning: a list whose initiators deny the state's existence may be barred even without an express statute, because a democracy may defend itself. [cite:rs_cw6_yeredor] Its supporters can point to the Court's own prior finding in the Jiryis case, and to the limit built into the principle as the majority stated it: it reached a list whose initiators denied the state's existence and sought its destruction.

On the other side stand Justice Cohn's dissent and, in a different register, Konrad's essay. Cohn's objection was legal: the rejection had no statutory basis. [cite:rs_cw6_yeredor] Konrad's is an interpretation of the whole period, made in advocacy journalism fifty years later: that the state treated secular Palestinian organizing as a threat regardless of its ideology. [cite:rs_cw6_konrad_972] The strongest form of this side's case joins the two. The obstruction of al-Ard, on Konrad's account, took the form of closed newspapers and a refused registration as well as the ban; the 1965 decision barred ten candidates on the ground that most of them belonged to a banned body and that the list's initiators denied the state's existence; and the right being withdrawn was, in a dissenting justice's words, among the citizen's fundamental rights. Konrad's broader claim, that ideology did not matter to the state's response, is his interpretation and is not established by the judgment itself, which rested expressly on al-Ard's denial of Israel's existence.

The two cases rest on different questions. The majority asked whether al-Ard's aims could be carried into the Knesset; the dissent asked whether the Committee had the power to stop them. An answer to the first does not answer the second, which is why the judgment has remained both an authority for "defensive democracy" and a reference point for its critics.

What the record does not settle. The sources consulted here leave much of al-Ard's own history open. They do not give the text of its programme or of the newspapers that were closed, so the reader cannot check the Court's characterization of its aims against its own words. They do not give the number of members surveilled, jailed or banished, or the dates of those measures, beyond Konrad's general account. They do not name the ten candidates of the Socialists' List, or say what became of them after October 1965. And they do not record how Arab citizens voted in the election from which the list was barred.

sections.h: Bonn's Secret Tanks and the Road to Recognition, 1964–1965
sections.html:
Al-Ard's members were contending with their own state; Israel's government, in the same years, was looking abroad for arms, and not only to Washington. West Germany's material link to Israel began with the reparations agreement signed at Luxembourg in 1952, told in [scene:rd6_financing|financing the new state], and it grew a second, secret strand from 1957, when Shimon Peres and Franz Josef Strauss first met at Strauss's home in Rott am Inn, as Stage Four recounts. This section follows that secret strand to the point where it broke into the open. Between October 1964 and August 1965 a covert tank transfer, arranged among Bonn, Washington and Jerusalem, was exposed, cancelled and converted into cash, and the crisis it set off ended in full diplomatic relations between the Federal Republic and Israel.

The secret channel. According to Marcel Serr, writing in 2015 in Aus Politik und Zeitgeschichte, the journal of Germany's Federal Agency for Civic Education, Peres and Strauss first met secretly in the winter of 1957, and in August 1962 Chancellor Adenauer approved a secret Israeli wish list worth 240 million DM that included tanks. [cite:rs_cw6_serr_bpb] The arrangement had no public footing. Bonn had no embassy in Israel. What gave the channel its larger significance in 1964 was Washington. Early that year, after an interagency review, the Johnson administration had declined to sell tanks to Israel directly, citing its policy of not becoming a major arms supplier to the region, but had agreed to help Israel obtain them from Europe. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_sum_a] Germany was the European source that was found, and that decision is the background of [scene:cw6_johnson_eshkol|Eshkol's visit to Washington in June 1964].

What Rusk told Johnson, October 1964. The shape of the deal is set out in a memorandum the Secretary of State, Rusk, wrote for President Johnson in October 1964 under the title "FY-1965 Help to Israel," sent with a covering note from three White House aides, Feldman, Bundy and Komer. Rusk told the President that Israel would receive 150 M48A1 tanks from West Germany "as is," together with about 250 British Centurions. The covering memo described the German part as "150 German M–48s, with an option on 82 more." [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d99]

The United States did not stand aside. Under the arrangement Washington sold Israel kits to modernize the German M48s, worth about $24 million, on Military Assistance Program credit: ten years at 3.5 percent interest, with 10 percent down. "In the interests of secrecy," the tanks were to be fitted in Italy with diesel engines and larger guns. Washington also speeded deliveries of replacement American tanks to West Germany so that the German ones could be released. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d99] On one reading, the arrangement was built to keep the United States from appearing as a supplier of tanks to Israel, while American credit, American kits and American replacement tanks made the transfer possible.

The secrecy was also written into the paperwork as a condition. A letter exchange of 15 November 1964 provided that if the transaction became public before the United States judged secrecy unnecessary, the United States "might exercise its right of cancellation." [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d99] Washington had kept the right to walk away if the arrangement came to light.

The leak and the Hallstein trap. The secrecy did not hold. According to the German Federal Archives, the deliveries became public in October 1964; Serr dates the first Egyptian press reports to the autumn of that year. [cite:rs_cw6_barch_triangle] [cite:rs_cw6_serr_bpb] The exposure put Bonn in a bind of its own making, and the mechanism that made it a bind was the Hallstein Doctrine. In force since 1955, it held that recognition of the German Democratic Republic by a third state was an unfriendly act to which Bonn could respond by breaking relations. [cite:rs_cw6_kas_relations] [cite:rs_cw6_barch_triangle] The doctrine was West Germany's main instrument for keeping East Germany isolated. In effect, it also gave every government that Bonn wished to keep from recognizing East Berlin a lever over Bonn: the threat to do exactly that.

Nasser used the lever. In January 1965 he announced that Walter Ulbricht, East Germany's head of state, would visit Egypt. Serr records that after the announcement Chancellor Erhard's government said it would stop arms deliveries to areas of tension, Israel included. [cite:rs_cw6_serr_bpb] The sequence suggests that Bonn gave up the tanks in the hope of keeping Cairo from a step toward East Germany.

It did not keep it. Ulbricht arrived in Egypt on 24 February 1965 and was received with military honours, though without formal recognition of the GDR. Bonn then cut its economic aid to Egypt. [cite:rs_cw6_kas_relations] [cite:rs_cw6_serr_bpb] The sources differ by a day on when he left: Serr gives 1 March 1965, while the Konrad Adenauer Foundation and the Federal Archives give 2 March. [cite:rs_cw6_serr_bpb] [cite:rs_cw6_kas_relations] [cite:rs_cw6_barch_triangle] The difference does not affect the sequence. What matters is that Nasser had stopped short of formal recognition of the GDR, and Bonn had lost its tank deliveries and its standing in Cairo all the same.

Erhard's decision, 7 March 1965. Erhard's answer was to turn the crisis around. On 7 March 1965 the Chancellor announced immediate negotiations with Israel on diplomatic relations. According to the Konrad Adenauer Foundation, he used his authority to set policy guidelines and did so without first informing the cabinet or his Foreign Minister, Schröder. His own emissary to Israel, Kurt Birrenbach, learned of the decision from the Israelis in Tel Aviv. [cite:rs_cw6_kas_relations] The decision was a Chancellor's, taken over the heads of the ministers who would have to carry it out, and it reversed a policy that had kept Bonn and Jerusalem without formal ties for more than a decade while money and arms moved between them.

From tanks to cash. The undelivered arms did not simply vanish from the books. Serr writes that they were converted into a payment of 140 million DM, which allowed Israel to buy weapons elsewhere. [cite:rs_cw6_serr_bpb] Only 40 of the German tanks had been delivered by then. The gap was filled by Washington. In July 1965 the United States agreed to sell Israel 110 M48A2C tanks to replace the rest, together with kits to convert the 40 that had arrived. [cite:rs_cw6_komer_jul1965] That sale, which the Jewish Virtual Library, citing the Israel State Archives, presents as the first US agreement to sell Israel tanks directly, is told in [scene:cw6_tanks|the first direct tank sale]. [cite:rs_cw6_jvl_mou_1965] The secrecy clause of November 1964 had been designed to keep Washington's role hidden. When the secret broke, the outcome was the reverse: the United States became the direct supplier it had tried not to be, though still in secret.

Recognition, 12 May 1965. Diplomatic relations were established on 12 May 1965. The first West German ambassador, Rolf Pauls, presented his credentials to President Shazar on 19 August 1965. [cite:rs_cw6_kas_relations] [cite:rs_cw6_barch_triangle] The arrival of a German ambassador in Israel was the formal close of the arrangement in which reparations and weapons had moved without an embassy on either side.

The Arab response is recorded differently in the two sources consulted for it, and the difference is one of both number and kind. Serr writes that thirteen Arab states withdrew their ambassadors from Bonn immediately after relations were established. [cite:rs_cw6_serr_bpb] GlobalSecurity's history of Jordan says that in May 1965 Jordan joined nine other Arab states in breaking relations with West Germany, which makes ten. [cite:rs_cw6_gs_jordan_g] Withdrawing an ambassador and breaking relations are not the same act, and it is possible that both accounts are accurate for different groups of states; neither source consulted here lists the states by name, so the two figures cannot be reconciled from them. The direction of the response is not in doubt: the Hallstein Doctrine had been built to let Bonn punish governments that recognized East Germany, and in 1965 it was Arab governments that withdrew from Bonn because Bonn had recognized Israel.

Two readings of the turn. The documents support two ways of reading what happened, and they are not exclusive. From Bonn's side, the record is of a government losing control of a covert policy: a secret deal leaked, a doctrine designed to isolate East Germany was turned against Bonn, and the Chancellor recovered the initiative only by acting over his cabinet. [cite:rs_cw6_kas_relations] [cite:rs_cw6_serr_bpb] From Israel's side, the same months turned a covert supply relationship, which could be halted when it became embarrassing (and was), into open relations with a state that was still paying it reparations, together with 140 million DM to buy arms elsewhere and a direct American tank sale. [cite:rs_cw6_serr_bpb] [cite:rs_cw6_komer_jul1965] Egypt, for its part, showed that Bonn's arms to Israel could be made to cost Bonn; but Ulbricht's reception stopped short of the formal recognition that would have triggered the Hallstein Doctrine against Cairo. [cite:rs_cw6_kas_relations]

The reparations running out. Recognition came as the 1952 agreement was ending. Under the Luxembourg Agreement, as the Federal Agency for Civic Education summarizes it, West Germany committed 3 billion DM to Israel, 450 million DM to the Claims Conference and a special fund of 50 million DM, paid partly in German goods such as ships, locomotives and factory machinery. [cite:rs_cw6_bpb_lux] In March 1965, in the middle of the crisis, the Jewish Telegraphic Agency reported from Bonn that 1965–66 was the agreement's last year. Israel was to receive 300 million marks ($74 million) of goods that year, which would bring the goods it had received to 2.4 billion marks ($600 million). [cite:rs_cw6_jta_reparations_1965] That report does not reconcile with the 3 billion DM headline: it leaves 600 million DM unaccounted for, and the dispatch does not say how the difference was settled or whether it reflects a different way of counting. No German or Israeli government record of the final settlement was consulted for this book, so the question stays open here.

What the record does not settle. Several things remain unresolved in the sources used here. The October 1964 plan spoke of about 250 British Centurions alongside the German tanks, and of an option on 82 more M48s; the documents consulted do not say what became of either. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d99] The two accounts of the Arab response give different numbers for different acts and do not name the states. The end of the reparations is known only from a press report whose total does not match the agreement's. And the reasoning behind Erhard's decision of 7 March is recorded here only in its form, as an exercise of the Chancellor's guideline authority without prior consultation, not in his own explanation of why he chose recognition rather than further retreat. [cite:rs_cw6_kas_relations]

sections.h: Fatah Takes Up Arms, January 1965–Spring 1967
sections.html:
In the first days of 1965, as Bonn's secret tank deal was coming apart, a Palestinian organization, Fatah, began an armed campaign against Israel through its military wing, al-Asifa. [cite:rs_cw6_palquest_chron_f] Over the next two and a half years its raids, and Israel's answers to them, became one of the threads that drew the region toward the crisis of May 1967. The campaign was low in intensity and large in consequence. It drew Syria in as a sponsor, put Jordan and Lebanon in the position of hosts to raids they had not approved, and gave the United Nations Secretary-General one of his named causes of the tension on the eve of war. This section follows it from its first operation to the spring of 1967.

The first operation, in three versions. The opening act of the campaign is dated and described differently by the three sources consulted for it, and the differences are of substance, not only of date. They are set out here side by side, without a choice among them.

The encyclopedia of the Institute for Palestine Studies dates the first operation to dawn on 1 January 1965, against an Israeli water network, and records that Ahmad Muhammad Musa, known as "Salama," was killed. It notes that Palestinians mark that date as the start of their contemporary revolution. [cite:rs_cw6_ipsp_fatah] The historian Benny Morris, as summarized by the Center for Online Judaic Studies, dates the raid to the night of 2 January 1965: a squad planted a charge by the National Water Carrier in the Galilee; the charge was found and defused; on its way back the squad was intercepted by a Jordanian patrol, its leader was shot dead and the others were arrested. [cite:rs_cw6_cojs_morris] The water scholar Aaron Wolf records a failed attempt to sabotage the Carrier on 31 December 1964 and calls it "the PLO's first action." [cite:rs_cw6_wolf_unu_f]

Some of the differences may be differences of framing. A charge planted on the night of 31 December could be dated to the morning of 1 January by one source and to the following night by another, and a raid can fail in its object and still be the start of a movement. But two points cannot be reconciled from these sources. One is how the leader died: the Palestinian encyclopedia records a death without, in the claim consulted here, naming who killed him, while Morris says he was shot after a Jordanian patrol intercepted the squad. The other is whose operation it was: Wolf names the PLO, which a CIA memorandum describes as formed in 1964 with Arab League sanction, while the other two name Fatah. [cite:rs_cw6_cia_dec1966_plo] The stakes of the first point are political as well as factual. If the first casualty of the Palestinian armed struggle fell to a Jordanian patrol, the episode shows from its first night that the Arab governments on whose territory the raids began did not control them. That theme recurs in the documents that follow.

The target is the one point on which all three agree. The first operation was aimed at Israel's water system, at the moment when Israel's National Water Carrier was entering operation and the Arab states had decided to divert the Jordan's headwaters, as told in [scene:cw6_water|the water war]. [cite:rs_cw6_ipsp_fatah] [cite:rs_cw6_cojs_morris] [cite:rs_cw6_wolf_unu_f]

Syria as sponsor. The campaign grew with a state behind it. The State Department historians record that Fatah incidents along Israel's borders, supported by Syria, increased from mid-1965, and that American officials opposed Israeli reprisals and urged action through the United Nations. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_sum_f] A CIA memorandum of 2 December 1966 set out what the support consisted of: Damascus gave Fatah a base, training and a propaganda outlet. [cite:rs_cw6_cia_dec1966] The same agency called Syria in that memorandum "the most bellicose Arab state," a judgment that belongs to the story of Syria's radical turn, told later in this stage. [cite:rs_cw6_cia_dec1966_s]

The money. According to the same CIA memorandum, Fatah's money came mainly from wealthy Palestinians in Kuwait and Saudi Arabia. [cite:rs_cw6_cia_dec1966] The memorandum describes private funding, not funding by the Kuwaiti or Saudi governments, and the distinction matters for the mechanism. Syria supplied the territory, the training and the voice; private Palestinian money from the Gulf paid for the organization. The cost of the raids fell on the Israelis who were their targets and, through Israel's reprisals, on targets in the West Bank. What the money bought in arms, and in what sums, the memorandum does not say.

Raids from territory whose governments had not agreed. The most consequential feature of the campaign was its geography. The CIA memorandum says that infiltrations were launched from Jordanian and Lebanese territory "without the approval of either the Jordanian or the Lebanese government." [cite:rs_cw6_cia_dec1966] The territory named is not Syria's: the governments whose borders were crossed were not the sponsors. GlobalSecurity's history of Jordan describes the same structure from Amman's side: Fatah and the PLO raided Israel without clearance from the Unified Arab Command or from Jordan, which had tried to avoid incidents that invited reprisals. In that account, Israel's reprisals on West Bank targets grew harsher and more frequent from May 1965. [cite:rs_cw6_gs_jordan_f] That is a reported account, not a primary document, but it agrees with the CIA's on the central fact.

The mechanism created a chain in which no single government held all the links. Fatah chose the targets. Syria supplied the base and training. Jordan and Lebanon had the borders across which raids came but had not approved them. Israel answered with reprisals, and from May 1965, in GlobalSecurity's account, increasingly on the West Bank under Jordan. And Washington, which opposed the reprisals, could urge but not prevent. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_sum_f] The objection to the reprisals was put most sharply in Washington after the raid on Samu in November 1966, when Johnson's adviser Rostow called it "aimed at the wrong target." [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d333] That episode, in which a mine killed three Israeli soldiers and Israel struck the Jordanian-held village of Samu, is told in [scene:cw6_samu|Samu and Resolution 228]; the sources there differ on whether the mine was Fatah's (the Israeli army's archive) or, as the CIA reported Israel's attribution, the Palestine Liberation Front's. [cite:rs_cw6_idf_archive_samu] [cite:rs_cw6_cia_dec1966_samu]

Lebanon. The Lebanese border had its own story. "The Lebanese-Israeli border was quiet until around 1965 when the Fatah movement started launching low-intensity attacks on Israeli positions," writes Hilal Khashan, professor of political science at the American University of Beirut. [cite:lebanon_1948_war] The Lebanese army tried to counter these operations, but Lebanese opinion divided along sectarian lines: broad sympathy in Muslim and pan-Arabist communities, and reluctance among Maronite Christian parties that did not want Lebanon drawn into a conflict they felt did not concern it directly. [cite:lebanon_1948_war] It is sometimes said that armed conflict on the Israel–Lebanon border began only after Israel's conquests of 1967. Khashan's account dates it two years earlier, and shows the Lebanese state already caught between the raids launched from its soil and the division they opened within it.

The count by December 1966. By the end of 1966 the campaign had a number attached to it. The CIA memorandum of 2 December 1966 says Israel attributed 61 sabotage incidents to Fatah since it emerged in January 1965. [cite:rs_cw6_cia_dec1966] The figure is Israel's attribution as the CIA reported it, not an independent count, and the memorandum as consulted does not itemize the incidents, their targets or their casualties.

Toward the crisis. In Wolf's account, the water dispute and the raids fed what he calls a "prolonged chain reaction of border violence," with border air battles in July 1966 and April 1967. [cite:rs_cw6_wolf_unu] Israel's leaders placed the responsibility on Damascus: the Chief of Staff, Rabin, said its "authorities are behind the terrorists," according to Tal. [cite:rs_cw6_tal_jvl] Whether Israeli pressure or Syrian-sponsored raids did more to drive the Syrian front is a dispute taken up with the April air battle.

In May 1967, reporting to the Security Council on the situation in the Near East, U Thant named "El Fatah activities, consisting of terrorism and sabotage" as a major factor in the tension. [cite:rs_cw6_thant_s7896] It was a contemporary judgment from outside the parties.

The word "terrorism." The sources do not all use the same word, and the choice of word carries a judgment. U Thant's report characterized the activities themselves as "terrorism and sabotage." [cite:rs_cw6_thant_s7896] The CIA memorandum, in the claims consulted here, counts "sabotage incidents" and "infiltrations." [cite:rs_cw6_cia_dec1966] Rabin, as Tal reports him, spoke of "the terrorists" and laid them at Syria's door. [cite:rs_cw6_tal_jvl] Khashan writes of "low-intensity attacks on Israeli positions." [cite:lebanon_1948_war] The Institute for Palestine Studies describes the first operation as the start of a revolution. [cite:rs_cw6_ipsp_fatah] These are not interchangeable descriptions. U Thant was not a party to the conflict, and his word is the one in the UN's own record; but the sources consulted here describe the targets of the first raids as water installations and military positions, and they do not itemize the later incidents in a way that would show which were aimed at civilians and which at soldiers or infrastructure. A reader can see from the documents who used which word and in what setting. The record assembled here does not supply the incident-by-incident detail on which a fuller judgment of the campaign's character would rest.

The war of June 1967, its consequences for the Palestinians and for Lebanon, and Fatah's later place within the PLO, the broader body founded in 1964, belong to [scene:s12|the June war] and the volume that follows. [cite:lebanon_1948_war]

What the record does not settle. The documents used here do not settle the date, the outcome or the authorship of the first operation, and the three accounts are given as they stand. They do not itemize the 61 incidents Israel attributed to Fatah, so their targets and casualties cannot be counted from them. They name the sources of Fatah's money in general terms but give no sums. They establish that Syria provided a base, training and propaganda, but not what orders, if any, passed from Damascus to Fatah's operations.

sections.h: From Bonn to Washington: The First Direct Tank Sale, February–July 1965
sections.html:
While Fatah's first raids were drawing Israeli reprisals, Washington was changing its own policy on arms. In the first half of 1965 the United States did what it had refused to do a year earlier: it agreed to sell tanks to Israel directly. The decision came in two steps, a secret memorandum of understanding transmitted from the American embassy in Israel on 10 March 1965 and a closing deal reported to President Johnson on 29 July. Neither step began with Israel. It began with Jordan, and with the collapse of [scene:cw6_germany|the German route].

What Israel had asked for. Israel's request had been on the table since late 1963: 200 M48A3s and 100 M60s to replace about 300 Shermans, with surface-to-surface missiles and an answer to the naval strength of the United Arab Republic besides. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d7] Washington's answer, repeated by Johnson to Eshkol in June 1964 as told in [scene:cw6_johnson_eshkol|Johnson and Eshkol], was that it "could not provide tanks directly" but would help Israel get them in Europe. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_sum_a] [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d65] In mid-1964, then, American tanks for Israel were to come, if at all, by way of Germany, refitted in Italy with American kits and kept secret.

That route failed in stages. After the deliveries became public in the autumn of 1964 and Nasser invited East Germany's head of state to Cairo, Bonn halted its arms deliveries to Israel; only 40 of the German tanks had arrived. [cite:rs_cw6_serr_bpb] [cite:rs_cw6_komer_jul1965]

The Jordan problem. At the same moment Washington faced a request from Amman. The State Department's historians record that King Hussein's 1964 request for American arms came under pressure from the Unified Arab Command, which an Arab summit had created. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_sum_plo] In February 1965 the administration concluded that a tank sale to Jordan was necessary, because Hussein warned that he would otherwise be pressed to accept Soviet aircraft; at the same time it tried to talk him out of supersonic jets. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_sum_t] The reasoning was the Cold War's: if Jordan did not get Western tanks it might get Soviet planes. But a sale to an Arab neighbour with no matching sale to Israel was what Eshkol objected to. According to the editors, his strongly negative reaction convinced policymakers that a direct sale to Israel would be needed. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_sum_t] On the editors' account, the decision to arm Jordan led to the decision to arm Israel directly.

The Harriman–Komer mission and the conditions Israel refused. During the mission of Harriman and Komer, Washington tried to attach conditions to future arms: nuclear inspections, a pledge on the waters of the Jordan River, and referral to the United Nations. According to the editors, Israel resisted them, and Johnson then offered a package. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_sum_t] On one reading, the three conditions went to the three things Washington most wanted from Israel in these years: access to Dimona, restraint in the water conflict with its neighbours, and the use of the UN rather than force. None of them appears among the clauses of the text that followed.

The memorandum of 10 March 1965. The agreement that resulted was transmitted to Washington by the American ambassador, Barbour, on 10 March 1965. Read clause by clause, it did six things. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d185]

First, the United States reaffirmed its concern for Israel's security and integrity. Second, Israel reaffirmed that it "will not be the first to introduce nuclear weapons into the Arab-Israel area." Third, the United States undertook to sell Israel "at least the same number and quality of tanks that it sells to Jordan." Fourth, it undertook to complete the deliveries of the German M48s. Fifth, it undertook to help Israel obtain "a certain number of combat aircraft, if not from Western sources, then from the United States." Sixth, both governments agreed to full secrecy. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d185]

The State Department editors summarize the aircraft clause as covering up to 24 combat aircraft, and they date Israel's nuclear reaffirmation to 11 March 1965, a day after the telegram. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_sum_t] The Jewish Virtual Library, citing the Israel State Archives, presents the memorandum as the first American agreement to sell tanks to Israel directly, and says it implied that Israel would not oppose American arms sales to Jordan. [cite:rs_cw6_jvl_mou_1965] That last reading is an inference from the text, not a clause in it, and it is reported here as the Library gives it.

The structure of the memorandum is its meaning. The tank clause tied Israel's supply to Jordan's: whatever Washington sold Amman, it would match for Israel in number and quality. The aircraft clause kept Europe as the first supplier and the United States as the fallback. The nuclear clause gave Washington a written Israeli pledge, but not the inspections it had asked for. And the secrecy clause continued the logic of the German deal. The United States had not wanted to be seen as Israel's arms supplier; now it would be one, but not yet in public.

Komer closes the deal, 29 July 1965. On 29 July 1965 Komer reported to Johnson under the heading "U.S. Closes Deal on Tanks for Israel, Moves On to Planes." The United States would sell Israel 110 M48A2C tanks to replace the German ones that had not been delivered, and 100 M48A1 tanks to match those sold to Jordan, for around $42 million spread over two years or more, together with conversion kits to fit 105 mm guns on the 40 tanks Bonn had already delivered. [cite:rs_cw6_komer_jul1965_t] Both halves of the March memorandum's tank clauses were now filled: the German shortfall and the Jordanian match.

The planes were another matter. Komer added that Rusk was "strong against any US sale" of the 24 aircraft, "so we'll stall for a while and try to shift them to Europe." [cite:rs_cw6_komer_jul1965_t] The Secretary of State and the White House staff were not of one mind. The aircraft question was settled only in February 1966, with the Skyhawk sale told in the next part of this stage.

Where 1965 sits in the longer record. The chart below sets this deal against the longer arc of American support.

From 1948 to the early 1960s, American assistance to Israel was economic aid and loans only; Washington avoided selling arms for fear of alienating Arab oil-producing states. The first American military aid came in 1962, and it came as loans rather than grants. [cite:merip_us_aid_israel_1990] The same year saw the sale of Hawk anti-aircraft missiles, told in Stage Four and Stage Five. [cite:wiki_israel_us_military_relations] The financing terms of that era recur in this section: the German tank kits of 1964 were sold on credit of ten years at 3.5 percent with 10 percent down, and in February 1966 McNamara would describe the same terms, 10 percent down, 3.5 percent interest and ten years, as the Hawk terms. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d99] [cite:rs_cw6_hoopes_t]

What 1965 changed was the kind of weapon and the channel. A defensive missile system had been sold in 1962; in 1965 the United States agreed to sell tanks, and to do so directly rather than through a European intermediary. It also wrote into the agreement a rule linking Israel's supply to an Arab state's: "at least the same number and quality of tanks that it sells to Jordan." [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d185] The money involved was modest beside later decades, around $42 million for 210 tanks over two years or more, and Komer's report does not say on what credit terms it was to be paid. [cite:rs_cw6_komer_jul1965_t] The familiar idea that American arms for Israel began with the war of 1967 does not survive these documents; nor does the opposite idea, that Washington simply supplied what Israel asked. The tanks came because Jordan was being armed, on terms Israel negotiated against conditions it refused, and the planes Israel wanted were held back for another half year, with the Secretary of State opposed to any American sale.

The nuclear words. The memorandum's nuclear clause is the most quoted line in it, and the American record of 1965–66 does not repeat it consistently. Within a year McNamara was asking Israel to reaffirm a pledge "not to be the first power in the Middle East to manufacture nuclear weapons," and Komer was reporting a pledge not to go nuclear "unless others do." [cite:rs_cw6_hoopes_t] [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d273_t] To introduce, to manufacture and to go nuclear conditionally are three different undertakings on their face; the three wordings are compared in [scene:s11d|the Skyhawk sale of 1966]. What the record does show is that the first of these written assurances was obtained in the same weeks in which Israel refused Washington's condition of nuclear inspections during the Harriman–Komer talks. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_sum_t]

What the record does not settle. Several things are not settled by the documents used here. The delivery dates of the tanks sold in July 1965 are not in them; Komer's report gives the deal, not the schedule. [cite:rs_cw6_komer_jul1965_t] Nor do they say how many tanks Jordan actually received or what Jordan paid, beyond the fact that Israel's 100 M48A1s were meant to match them. And the reading that the memorandum bound Israel not to oppose arms for Jordan rests on one account citing the Israel State Archives, not on a clause in the American text. [cite:rs_cw6_jvl_mou_1965]

sections.h: NUMEC: The Uranium Shortage at Apollo, 1957–1967
sections.html:
In early 1965, while Washington was arguing with Israel over inspections at Dimona, a routine count at a nuclear-fuel plant in Apollo, Pennsylvania, found that a significant quantity of government-owned highly enriched uranium could not be accounted for. The plant belonged to the Nuclear Materials and Equipment Corporation, NUMEC. The question of where that uranium went has never been officially answered. It has been asked, in one form or another, since 1965, and its most serious form, whether some of it reached Israel's weapons program, has been argued for decades without a charge, a trial or a finding. This section tells what the documents show for the first decade, from the company's founding in 1957 to a government audit of June 1967, drawing chiefly on the primary records published by the National Security Archive in 2016 in a briefing book edited by Roger J. Mattson, Avner Cohen and William Burr. [cite:rs_cw6_nsa_numec] What happened from 1968 onward is told only in outline here, as it falls outside this volume's period.

The question is best approached from what the editors themselves concluded. They call the evidence of diversion "strong but not incontrovertible." The Atomic Energy Commission said it found no evidence of theft; there is no sign that the AEC or the FBI looked for such evidence when the loss was found; and many CIA records remain redacted. [cite:rs_cw6_nsa_numec] Each of those three facts limits the others. The absence of a finding of theft has to be read beside the absence of a search for one, and both beside the records that are still closed. The account that follows keeps them together.

Founding, 1957. NUMEC was formed in 1957, with investors from Apollo Industries and with Zalman Shapiro as a founder and later its president. Nuclear Regulatory Commission records say that processing of highly enriched uranium at Apollo began in 1957, and that fuel manufacture began in 1959. [cite:rs_cw6_nsa_numec] The company processed government-owned enriched uranium into fuel for naval and commercial reactors. [cite:apolloaffair_summary] The uranium was not NUMEC's. It belonged to the United States government and was leased to the company, which meant that the government, through the AEC, was both the owner of the material and the regulator responsible for counting it. [cite:rs_cw6_nsa_numec]

The shortage, 1965. In early 1965 a routine AEC inventory found a significant shortage of government-owned highly enriched uranium leased to NUMEC. On 10 August 1965 Shapiro told the AEC's commissioners that NUMEC had already paid the AEC "up to $1 million for material losses" in earlier years. [cite:rs_cw6_nsa_numec] The admission suggests how losses had been handled until then: as a commercial matter, settled by payment to the owner. It also shows that the 1965 shortage was not the first.

The AEC's accounting experts then ran a plant-wide inventory in November 1965. An AEC survey report of 6 April 1966 put the cumulative inventory difference at 178 kg of U-235, of which 93.8 kg was unexplained. [cite:rs_cw6_nsa_numec]

"Not now warranted," February 1966. Between the November inventory and the April report, the AEC's chairman made a decision of lasting consequence. On 14 February 1966 Glenn Seaborg told the Joint Committee on Atomic Energy that "an inquiry by the FBI is not now warranted." [cite:rs_cw6_nsa_numec] The mechanism matters here. The material was the government's, and the AEC both owned it and counted it. One account describes AEC leadership as having discouraged bringing in the FBI at all, keeping the matter deliberately "in-house." [cite:foreignpolicy_numec] Seaborg's words to the Joint Committee are the documented form of that choice.

The FBI's question, June 1966. The FBI did come to Shapiro in 1966, but on another matter. On 15 June 1966 its Pittsburgh office interviewed him about whether he should register under the Foreign Agents Registration Act. He described ISORAD, a joint venture of NUMEC and the Israeli Atomic Energy Commission. He was not asked about the missing material. [cite:rs_cw6_nsa_numec] The interview records, from Shapiro's own account, a formal business tie between his company and Israel's atomic energy authority; it records nothing about the uranium, because the question was not put.

A later summary account states that the FBI investigated NUMEC from 1965 to 1980. [cite:apolloaffair_summary] The primary documents for 1965–67 do not show an FBI inquiry into the loss in those years: the AEC chairman told Congress in February 1966 that none was warranted, and the FBI's one documented contact, in June 1966, concerned foreign-agent registration. [cite:rs_cw6_nsa_numec] The two statements can be reconciled only if the 1965 start date is counted from the discovery of the loss rather than from an investigation of it. On the documents published by the editors, a request for an investigation of Shapiro's relationship with the Israeli government came from the CIA in 1968, as told below. [cite:rs_cw6_nsa_numec]

The GAO's figure, June 1967. A report by the General Accounting Office dated 20 June 1967 said that NUMEC's records showed cumulative losses of U-235 through 31 December 1966 of about 260 kg, about 1.2 percent of receipts. [cite:rs_cw6_nsa_numec] It is the last of the figures that falls inside this volume, and it was dated ten days after the war of June 1967 ended.

How much was missing. No single number answers that question, because the sources measure different things at different dates. Each figure has to be kept with its unit, its date and its source. The AEC's April 1966 report gave a cumulative inventory difference of 178 kg of U-235, of which 93.8 kg was unexplained; the editors' introduction speaks of about 200 kg. [cite:rs_cw6_nsa_numec] The GAO in June 1967 gave cumulative losses through the end of 1966 of about 260 kg. [cite:rs_cw6_nsa_numec] A later summary account gives documented inventory losses of 269 kg before 1968 and 76 kg after, and describes them as the largest at any American commercial nuclear facility. [cite:apolloaffair_summary] And the figure most often quoted, 206 pounds, is about 93 kg, close to the AEC's unexplained 93.8 kg rather than to its total. [cite:nsarchive_numec] [cite:rs_cw6_nsa_numec]

The distinction between these figures is the heart of the matter. A loss recorded in a plant's books, an inventory difference and an unexplained remainder are three different quantities. Part of an inventory difference can be explained, as the AEC's own split between 178 kg and 93.8 kg shows; a figure of losses is not a figure of material taken. The question whether any of it was diverted turns on the unexplained part, and on what happened to it. The documents of 1965–67 establish the quantities; they do not establish the cause.

Shapiro. The scrutiny of the case has always centred on NUMEC's president. In the documents of these years, his tie to Israel is a declared, formal one: ISORAD, the joint venture with the Israeli Atomic Energy Commission that he described to the FBI. [cite:rs_cw6_nsa_numec] Later records go further. According to FBI reports declassified between the mid-1980s and 2009, Shapiro had contacts with Israeli "Science Attaché" officials and with individuals from Shin Bet and Mossad believed to be tied to LAKAM, the scientific-intelligence unit that would later run Pollard. [cite:nsarchive_numec] Those reports belong to the later investigations, and they record contacts, not a transfer of material. Shapiro was never charged. In 2009 his lawyer asked the Nuclear Regulatory Commission to clear him formally; the Commission refused, stating that it had no documents proving that diversion had occurred but could not conclude that it had not. He died in 2016. [cite:apolloaffair_summary]

Dimona in the same years. The NUMEC shortage was found in the same months in which American scientists were trying, with limited success, to see inside Israel's reactor at Dimona, a story told in [scene:s11d|Johnson's two tracks]. The two questions ran in parallel, in different agencies, and nothing in the documents of 1965–67 connects them. At Dimona, Eshkol insisted on 4 January 1965 that the American visitors come as "invited guests," not "inspectors." [cite:rs_cw6_jvl_burr_cohen] The team of 1966 found no evidence of weapons work but could not account for 80 to 100 tons of uranium concentrate bought from Argentina. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d289] And Dimona's reprocessing plant, William Burr and Avner Cohen write, was hidden from all nine AEC teams that visited between 1961 and 1969. [cite:rs_cw6_jvl_burr_cohen]

The two cases should not be merged. The Argentine material was uranium concentrate, a different material from the highly enriched uranium missing at Apollo, and the 1966 team's inability to account for it is a separate finding. One reading finds a shared pattern in the American response in these years: in both, the government agencies responsible accepted limits on what they checked. At Dimona those limits were set by Israel; at Apollo, on the documents, the decision not to bring in the FBI was the AEC's own. [cite:rs_cw6_jvl_burr_cohen] [cite:rs_cw6_nsa_numec]

After 1967, in outline. The case changed in 1968, beyond this volume's period, and is told in the volumes that cover those years. Three later documents frame it. On 2 April 1968 the CIA's Director, Richard Helms, asked Attorney General Clark for a "discreet intelligence investigation" of Shapiro's relationship with the Israeli government, which Hoover approved on 6 May; on 10 September 1968 four Israelis, among them Avraham Hermoni and Rafi Eitan, visited the Apollo plant. [cite:rs_cw6_nsa_numec] Eitan was later exposed as LAKAM's chief in the Pollard affair of 1985. [cite:nsarchive_numec] The briefing book reports a CIA conclusion that environmental sampling near Dimona in 1968 had detected uranium enriched to the same unusual specification as NUMEC's missing material, and that Helms raised it with Johnson personally, in an exchange still classified. [cite:nsarchive_numec] And a GAO study of 1978, declassified in May 2010, concluded that a concerted, timely effort by the AEC, the CIA and the FBI could plausibly have resolved the diversion question, "if they desired to do so": a finding about the effort, not about the uranium. [cite:apolloaffair_summary]

The claim and the record. It is often assumed that if American uranium had gone to Israel's weapons program, it would have been prosecuted as the serious national-security crime it would have been. The documents of 1965–67 show why that assumption cannot settle the question in either direction. No one was prosecuted, but no one, on the record, was looking for a crime in those years: the AEC declined an FBI inquiry, and the FBI's interview concerned registration, not uranium. [cite:rs_cw6_nsa_numec] The absence of a prosecution therefore tells us little about what happened to the material. Equally, the absence of a finding of theft does not establish that there was none: the AEC said it found no evidence of theft, but there is no sign that it looked for such evidence. [cite:rs_cw6_nsa_numec]

What the record does not settle. Where the unexplained uranium went is not established by any document consulted for this book. The editors, who assembled the fullest primary record, judge the evidence of diversion "strong but not incontrovertible." [cite:rs_cw6_nsa_numec] Against it stand the AEC's statement that it found no evidence of theft and the fact that no one was ever charged. [cite:rs_cw6_nsa_numec] [cite:apolloaffair_summary] The quantity in question differs by source and by measure, from 93.8 kg unexplained in April 1966 to about 260 kg of recorded losses in June 1967. Many CIA records remain redacted. And the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's own position, as stated in 2009, is that it can neither show that diversion occurred nor conclude that it did not. [cite:apolloaffair_summary] Whether diversion took place remains, on the record, a contested question.

sections.h: Syria's Radical Turn, 1963–1966
sections.html:
While Washington's agencies were counting uranium at Apollo and negotiating visits to Dimona, the government Israel would face across its northern border in 1967 was taking shape. Between March 1963 and November 1966 Damascus passed through two coups, a failed countercoup and a purge of the founders of its own ruling party, and emerged with a government that an American intelligence assessment called "the most bellicose Arab state," bound by treaty to Egypt and sheltering the Palestinian guerrilla organization to which, by the same assessment, Israel attributed 61 sabotage incidents since January 1965. [cite:rs_cw6_cia_dec1966_s] [cite:rs_cw6_cia_dec1966] [cite:rs_cw6_locegypt] This section follows that turn and the mechanism that tied it to the Israeli frontier. It stops short of the air battle of 7 April 1967, which belongs to the spring of the following year.

The Ba'th takes power, 1963. The Ba'th party came to power in Syria in the coup of 8 March 1963. From July 1963 the dominant figure was Amin al-Hafiz. The party was not united. Between May 1964 and February 1966, according to the Library of Congress's country study, power struggles between its centrist and leftist wings brought two Alawi generals, Salah Jadid and Hafiz al-Assad, to decisive power. [cite:rs_cw6_locsyria]

The same years saw Syria act against the line taken by Cairo on Palestinian matters. At the Arab summit at Alexandria in September 1964, the League recognized the new Palestine Liberation Organization over Syrian and Saudi opposition, according to the Institute for Palestine Studies' chronology. [cite:rs_cw6_palquest_chron] The PLO was, in the CIA's later description, an organization over which Nasser had considerable influence. [cite:rs_cw6_cia_dec1966_plo] Damascus would find its own Palestinian instrument elsewhere.

The coup of 23 February 1966. On 23 February 1966 Jadid, Assad and Nureddin Atassi carried out a coup that put the more radical wing of the Ba'th in power. [cite:rs_cw6_locsyria] GlobalSecurity calls it "the bloodiest of the many coups d'etat since 1949." That is that source's characterization; the consulted sources give no casualty figure against which to test it. Amin al-Hafiz was wounded and arrested, and Aflaq and Bitar were expelled from the party. [cite:rs_cw6_gs_syria] The coup was therefore not only a change of government but a break within the Ba'th itself: the faction that won expelled leading figures of its own party.

The new order took shape within days. Assad's appointment as defence minister was announced after the coup. On 1 March 1966 a government was formed with Atassi as president and Yusuf Zuayyin as prime minister, while Jadid led through his post in the party. [cite:rs_cw6_gs_syria] The arrangement put the formal offices in one set of hands and the real authority, through the party, in another; and it put the army, the institution that would face Israel, under Assad. It did not end the contest for power. A countercoup by the Druze officer Salim Hatum failed on 8 September 1966. [cite:rs_cw6_gs_syria] The GlobalSecurity account, on which the details of March and September rest, is a reported source and not a scholarly study; the Library of Congress confirms the coup of 23 February and its leaders, but not the later details. [cite:rs_cw6_locsyria] [cite:rs_cw6_gs_syria]

The mechanism: base, training, propaganda. What tied Syria's internal upheaval to the Israeli border was its sponsorship of Fatah. The CIA's memorandum of 2 December 1966 sets out the instruments in three words: Damascus gave Fatah a base, training and a propaganda outlet. [cite:rs_cw6_cia_dec1966_s] The FRUS editors record that Fatah's incidents along Israel's borders, supported by Syria, increased from mid-1965. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_sum_f] The money, according to the same CIA memorandum, did not come mainly from Syria: Fatah's funds came chiefly from wealthy Palestinians in Kuwait and Saudi Arabia. [cite:rs_cw6_cia_dec1966] Nor did its raids leave mainly from Syrian soil. The CIA wrote that infiltrations were launched from Jordanian and Lebanese territory "without the approval of either the Jordanian or the Lebanese government." [cite:rs_cw6_cia_dec1966]

That arrangement is the key to the period's logic. A government in Damascus could sponsor an armed campaign whose operations crossed into Israel from its neighbours' territory, and whose consequences, in Israeli reprisal, would fall first on those neighbours. Less than three weeks before the CIA wrote, Israel's raid at Samu had struck Jordan, not Syria, and an American official had called it "the wrong target." [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d333] Fatah's own campaign, and the dispute over its first operation, is told in [scene:cw6_fatah|Fatah's campaign].

Syria was also, in these years, the site of the Arab plan to divert the Jordan's headwaters. The September 1964 summit chose diversion and financed works in Lebanon and Syria, and Israeli forces attacked the works in Syria in March, May and August 1965. [cite:rs_cw6_wolf_unu] That contest is told in [scene:cw6_water|the water war]. It meant that by 1966 the Syrian front carried two quarrels at once: one over water and the zones along the line, and one over the guerrillas Damascus supported.

The pact with Egypt, November 1966. In November 1966 Egypt and Syria signed a five-year defence pact. [cite:rs_cw6_locegypt] The sources consulted for this section give its date and term but not its text. Its importance lay in what it linked. Before November 1966 a clash on the Syrian line was a matter between Israel and Damascus; afterwards it engaged Cairo's commitments as well. It was signed in the weeks before the CIA described Syria as the most bellicose Arab state. [cite:rs_cw6_cia_dec1966_s] Syria's relations with its other neighbour also worsened that year: after Hussein withdrew Jordan's official endorsement of the PLO in July 1966, the PLO and the Syrian government turned against him, according to GlobalSecurity's account. [cite:rs_cw6_gs_jordan_a]

The Soviet dimension. Accounts of this period often place the Soviet Union behind the Damascus government. The sources consulted for this chapter do not document Soviet arms, advisers or political backing for Syria between 1963 and 1966, and this section does not assert any. The first dated Soviet act in this record that concerns Syria comes in May 1967, when Moscow told Egypt that Israel was massing forces to attack Syria, information that, Elbahtimy writes, "proved to be false"; that warning opens the crisis told later in this chapter. [cite:rs_cw6_elbahtimy] Whatever Soviet support Damascus enjoyed before that point is not established here.

The line on the map. The frontier where these forces met is drawn in the map below, which traces the Golan line from 1949 to the present. Its first two stages fall before June 1967. The map opens in 1949 with the armistice, which left small demilitarized zones along the line without agreed sovereignty. Its second stage, "DMZ & water war, 1949–67," is labelled "both sides," and the label is the record's. In a meeting with American officials in 1953–54, recorded by the State Department, Moshe Dayan said Israel claimed sovereignty over Jewish-owned land in the zones, that "someone must keep the area alive," and that Israel did not want Syria to have direct access to the Jordan River. [cite:frus_dayan_dmz] Syria fired on Israeli farmers and fishermen from the heights; Israel sent armoured tractors to cultivate disputed land and carried out reprisal raids. [cite:frus_dayan_dmz] [cite:w_dayan] From 1964 the dispute over the zones was joined by the dispute over water. The map's arrow from the second stage to June 1967 is labelled "escalation"; this section has followed the Syrian politics that drove it from the Damascus side, and the water war told elsewhere in this chapter follows it on the ground, including Dayan's own later account, given in 1976 and contested, that most of the clashes were provoked by Israel.

Who drove the Syrian front? On this question the sources divide. The Library of Congress's Egypt study and the historian Henry Laurens put Israeli threats against the government in Damascus at the centre; the CIA, in December 1966, put Syria's sponsorship of Fatah there. [cite:rs_cw6_locegypt] [cite:rs_cw6_laurens] [cite:rs_cw6_cia_dec1966_s] The two readings, and the documents on each side, are set out with the spring of 1967, when the dispute came to a head.

What the record does not settle. The consulted sources leave much of Syria's own decision-making unseen. They do not contain Syrian government documents explaining why the Jadid regime backed Fatah, or how far the officers in Damascus controlled the raids they sponsored. They give no casualty figure for the coup of 23 February 1966 to support or test GlobalSecurity's description of it as the bloodiest since 1949. They do not give the text of the November 1966 pact with Egypt, or its exact day. And they do not document Soviet backing for Damascus before May 1967. The border with that government in the spring of 1967 is the subject of [scene:cw6_april_1967|the 7 April air battle].

sections.h: Skyhawks and Dimona, 1966: Two Tracks Side by Side
sections.html:
In February 1966, the month Damascus changed hands, Washington took its next decision on arms for Israel. By then the Johnson administration was running two policies toward Israel at once, and the record of that year shows them more clearly than any before it. On one track Washington was becoming Israel's supplier of weapons: tanks in 1965, and in February 1966 the first American combat aircraft. On the other it was trying, through visits of American scientists to the reactor at Dimona, to satisfy itself that Israel was not building a nuclear weapon. The two tracks met in the same documents. The conditions attached to the aircraft sale included a nuclear pledge and an inspection clause, and Rusk told Eban in the same year that the nuclear question was a "matter of fundamental significance" to the relationship. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d298] This section follows both tracks through 1966, and corrects several details in the way the story is often told.

When the arms relationship began. A common account holds that American arms sales to Israel began only after 1967, as a reward for the victory of the Six-Day War. The dates do not support it. The Kennedy administration approved the sale of Hawk missiles to Israel in 1962, while it was pressing Israel hard over Dimona: arming Israel conventionally while working to stop it going nuclear. [cite:wiki_israel_us_military_relations] [cite:state_frus1964_68v18] That earlier decision belongs to Stage Four and Stage Five and is weighed with the case for the alliance in [scene:wa_s07|the strongest case for the alliance]. One description of it needs correcting here, because it is often repeated. The Hawk is a surface-to-air missile, an air-defence system for shooting down aircraft; it was not offensive weaponry, and calling it "the first US sale of offensive weaponry" misdescribes it. What the record establishes is the date, five years before the war. The terms of that sale mattered later, because in February 1966 McNamara offered aircraft on "the Hawk terms." [cite:rs_cw6_hoopes_feb1966] No source consulted for this section explains, in a single statement of strategy, why the same administration pursued nuclear restraint and conventional supply together; the decisions are documented more fully than any unified rationale connecting them. [cite:state_frus1964_68v18]

Six decisions, 1964–1966. Between Kennedy's death and the spring of 1966 the American position moved, step by step, from refusing to sell tanks to selling aircraft: no direct sale but help in Europe in early 1964, German M48s with American kits in October, tanks for Jordan in February 1965, the memorandum of 10 March, and the direct tank deal of 29 July, when Rusk was still "strong against any US sale" of the 24 planes the memorandum had held out. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_sum_a] [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d99] [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_sum_t] [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d185] [cite:rs_cw6_komer_jul1965_t] That sequence is told in full in [scene:cw6_tanks|the first direct tank sale].

This also corrects a second common detail, that "M-48 Patton tanks" were "delivered in 1965." [cite:wiki_israel_us_military_relations] The record is more particular. Forty German M48s had reached Israel when the German route was closed; the American direct sale of 210 M48s was agreed in July 1965 for delivery over two years or more, and the delivery dates themselves are not in the sources consulted for this chapter. [cite:rs_cw6_komer_jul1965_t] The M48s came first through Germany and then by direct American sale.

The White House meeting of 12 February 1966. The aircraft promised in March 1965 were decided eleven months later. On 12 February 1966 Johnson met Rusk, McNamara, Vance, Bell, Hare and Komer on "Israel/Jordan matters." The proposal before them was to sell Israel 48 aircraft centred on the A-4E Skyhawk attack aircraft, and to offer Jordan "36 F–104s or F–5s." Israel had also asked for the A-6, and McNamara ruled it out: it cost about four times as much as the A-4E, it was short because of Vietnam, and Israel would have had only a one-squadron force of it. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d270] Johnson told McNamara to tell the Israelis the decision was final. He proposed trading the numbers of aircraft and the sums of aid for Israeli help in keeping Congress quiet about both sales, Israel's and Jordan's, and said Congress was pressing him; he had already spoken to twelve congressmen, and to Eban. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d270] On one reading, the memorandum shows a president who treated domestic politics as part of the arms decision and expected Israel's government to help manage it.

McNamara and Eban. The same day McNamara put the offer to Israel's foreign minister, Abba Eban. According to the memorandum of conversation drafted by Townsend Hoopes, he offered 24 A-4Es with an option on 24 more, at about $26 million for the first 24, on the Hawk terms: 10% down, 3.5% interest and ten years to pay. [cite:rs_cw6_hoopes_feb1966] The offer carried five conditions. Israel was to go on relying mainly on Europe for its aircraft; to reaffirm its undertaking "not to be the first power in the Middle East to manufacture nuclear weapons"; to accept periodic inspection of Dimona; not to use American aircraft as nuclear carriers; and to keep the deal entirely secret until Washington decided how to make it public. [cite:rs_cw6_hoopes_feb1966] Three of the five conditions concerned nuclear weapons. In this document the two tracks were not parallel; they were written into one transaction.

The deal Komer reported. Late in February Komer told Johnson that Israel had accepted. The United States would sell "48 A4Es (about $50 million)." Israel would quietly support the sale of 36 second-hand F-104s to Jordan, for cash, at 12 a year from 1968; it would reaffirm its pledge not to go nuclear "unless others do"; and it would stop pressing for more aircraft for several years. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d273] The Jordanian half of the bargain had its own clock. Hussein had asked for a quick answer, saying that otherwise he would have to accept MiGs when Arab leaders met on 14 March 1966. Johnson approved going ahead. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d273] The money moved in two directions at once: on credit to Israel, for cash from Jordan, with each sale made to keep the other side from buying elsewhere, and Soviet aircraft as the alternative Washington was trying to forestall in Amman.

One printed summary of these events is wrong and should not be followed. The State Department historians' summary of the volume says that "agreements were reached for the sale of 48 F–4s to Israel and 36 F–104s to Jordan." [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_sum_s] The documents printed in the same volume, the record of the 12 February meeting and Komer's report, and the McNamara–Eban memorandum, all name the A-4E Skyhawk, 48 aircraft. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d270] [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d273] [cite:rs_cw6_hoopes_feb1966] The summary's "F–4" appears to be an error. The F-4 Phantom was a later decision, approved in 1968, after the war. [cite:jvl_1968_phantom_sale]

The aircraft did not arrive before the war. The first four Skyhawks were unloaded at Haifa port on 29 December 1967, according to the Israeli Air Force as reported by Ynet. [cite:rs_cw6_ynet_skyhawk] Other accounts give their delivery simply as 1968. [cite:wiki_israel_us_military_relations] Either way the point about chronology stands: the sale was decided in February 1966, sixteen months before the June war, though the aircraft flew for Israel only after it.

The inspection track: what "inspection" meant. The Dimona visits that sat beside these sales had begun under Kennedy, and the record of the Johnson years shows what they could and could not see. On 5 December 1963 Israel invited American representatives to visit between 10 and 15 January 1964. In mid-January three American scientists spent one day, about eleven hours, at Dimona, and reported that "all significant facilities at this site were inspected." They judged it "an ambitious project" with a research purpose, and estimated that without outside help Israel could not produce a first device until two or three years after deciding to. [cite:rs_cw6_jvl_burr_cohen]

The next visit was negotiated over terms. In October 1964 Eshkol asked to postpone it until after Israel's elections, then set 30 January 1965. On 4 January 1965 he rejected the American conditions of at least two full days, full access and independent measurements, insisting that the team come as "invited guests," not "inspectors." [cite:rs_cw6_jvl_burr_cohen] The distinction was the whole question. An inspector has rights; a guest sees what the host shows. The January 1965 team, Ulysses Staebler of the Atomic Energy Commission, Floyd Culler of Oak Ridge and Clyde McClelland of ACDA, reported on 5 February 1965 that "nothing [at the site] suggests an early development of weapons program," and recommended visits "at intervals not to exceed one year." [cite:rs_cw6_jvl_burr_cohen]

Not every American official believed the reports. In January 1965 Henry Kissinger met Israeli officials and scientists, and on 1 February told the American embassy that he had "a strong belief that Israel is already embarked on a nuclear program," naming Shimon Peres as "the strongest champion" of nuclear weapons as an absolute deterrent.
