[cite:rs_cw6_jvl_burr_cohen] [cite:rs_cw6_cns_duplicity] The embassy's science attaché, Robert Webber, rejected the theory that Dimona was a bluff on 9 April 1965, and on 18 November 1965 said the reactor made "no sense except as the basis for a weapons project." Burr and Cohen call him a rare exception among Johnson's officials. [cite:rs_cw6_jvl_burr_cohen] [cite:rs_cw6_cns_duplicity]

The visit of 1966. A three-man American team visited Israel's atomic sites from 31 March 1966. Its report, forwarded to McNamara by the Director of the Defense Intelligence Agency on 4 May, found "no evidence that Israel is producing or intends to produce nuclear weapons material." Dimona was running at much reduced power, and there was no chemical separation plant there. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d289] The same report recorded what the team could not settle. It could not account for 80 to 100 tons of uranium concentrate that Israel had bought from Argentina; it could not determine whether a small separation plant existed elsewhere; and it judged that a concealed one could escape detection. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d289] The two American documents disagree on the visit's length. The State Department telegram of 11 June 1966 dates it 31 March–1 April 1966; the DIA memorandum of 4 May dates it 31 March–4 April. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d298] [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d289] The sources consulted do not resolve the difference, which matters because the length of a visit was exactly what Eshkol and Washington had argued about.

The demand of 11 June 1966. Washington then asked for more. On 11 June 1966 the State Department instructed its embassy to ask for visits every six months, with full access to facilities and records. Its reasoning was arithmetical. A reactor of Dimona's size, run to produce weapons-grade plutonium, could discharge a fuel load about every six months; run for peaceful purposes, about every two years. A visit once a year could therefore miss a weapons cycle entirely. Rusk had told Eban that the issue was a "matter of fundamental significance" to the relationship. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d298] The FRUS editors record that Johnson's wider effort to secure inspection of all Israeli nuclear facilities by the International Atomic Energy Agency failed, and that Rusk warned in 1966 that Israel would "lose U.S. support" if it went nuclear. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_sum_d]

What the pledge said. The comparison shows why the wording has been argued over. In the memorandum of 10 March 1965 Israel reaffirmed that it "will not be the first to introduce nuclear weapons into the Arab-Israel area"; the FRUS editors date that reaffirmation to 11 March 1965. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d185] [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_sum_t] Eleven months later McNamara's condition spoke of not being the first power in the Middle East "to manufacture" nuclear weapons, and Komer reported a pledge not to go nuclear "unless others do." [cite:rs_cw6_hoopes_t] [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d273_t] To "introduce" is not the same act as to "manufacture," and a pledge conditional on others is not the same as an unconditional one. The records do not show whether the American officials who used the different phrases meant them as the same undertaking, or whether the Israelis who accepted each of them understood them alike.

What every team missed. The most important fact about the visits was established only decades later. William Burr and Avner Cohen, publishing declassified records through the National Security Archive in November 2020, write that Dimona's underground reprocessing plant was hidden from every American team, and that none of the nine Atomic Energy Commission teams that visited between 1961 and 1969 knew of it. [cite:rs_cw6_jvl_burr_cohen] [cite:nsarchive_duplicity_1964_65] The National Security Archive's summary adds that CIA reporting was never shared with the inspection teams; that by late 1966 CIA reports claimed a fully assembled bomb was weeks away, a view the State Department did not accept; and that Eshkol refused a nuclear test in order to preserve his understandings with the United States. [cite:rs_cw6_nsa_israel_findings] The same summary reports Cohen's finding that Israel had improvised two nuclear devices and placed them on operational alert in late May 1967; that rests on one scholar's research and is reported here as his finding. [cite:rs_cw6_nsa_israel_findings]

This corrects a third detail in the common account. It is often said that there were six American visits to Dimona between 1964 and 1969, increasingly staged, with staged control rooms shown to the visitors, and the 2020 release is cited for it. [cite:nsarchive_duplicity_1964_65] The sources consulted for this chapter do not contain either the count of six or the staged control rooms. Burr and Cohen give nine AEC teams across 1961–1969, not six across 1964–1969, and what they document is concealment, a plant kept hidden and access limited by the host, rather than staging. [cite:rs_cw6_jvl_burr_cohen] The difference is not trivial. A staged visit implies a performance mounted for the visitors; a concealed plant and an "invited guests" visit imply something the record does support: a host who set the terms of what was seen, and visitors who accepted them.

Were the visits a real check? Two readings of the evidence stand. On the first, the visits did what they were designed to do: the teams of 1964, 1965 and 1966 each reported no evidence of a weapons programme, and the DIA wrote in May 1966 that no convincing intelligence contradicted them. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d289] [cite:rs_cw6_jvl_burr_cohen] On this view, Washington had no documentary basis at the time for acting on suspicion against the findings of its own scientists. On the second, the visits were too constrained to check anything: Burr and Cohen document Israeli limits on time and access and the concealment of the reprocessing plant from every team, and Kissinger and Webber judged at the time that a weapons programme was under way. [cite:rs_cw6_jvl_burr_cohen] [cite:rs_cw6_cns_duplicity] The title Burr and Cohen gave their collection, "Duplicity and Self-Deception," names both halves of their reading: concealment by the host, and an American government that did not share its own intelligence with its own inspectors. [cite:rs_cw6_jvl_burr_cohen] [cite:rs_cw6_nsa_israel_findings]

A trade, or two policies? By the late 1960s the shape of the relationship was set in a way that lasted: the United States did not force genuine nuclear transparency, and the conventional military and diplomatic relationship deepened. [cite:state_frus1964_68v18] It is tempting to describe this as a bargain, nuclear ambiguity tolerated in exchange for arms. The documents of 1966 come close to it: McNamara's offer made a nuclear pledge and Dimona inspection conditions of the Skyhawk sale. [cite:rs_cw6_hoopes_feb1966] But the conditions ran the other way from the bargain the phrase implies. Washington offered aircraft in return for nuclear restraint and inspection, not in return for silence about a bomb, and it pressed for more inspection, not less, four months later. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d298] No document consulted for this book states an explicit policy of tolerating nuclear ambiguity in exchange for the arms relationship. The pattern is observable in the outcomes across the period; it is not proved as a stated trade by any single record. [cite:state_frus1964_68v18] The later consequences, including the American legal mechanisms that were never applied to Israel's arsenal, are told in [scene:cia_s16|the Dimona surveillance loop].

What the record does not settle. Several things remain unsettled by these sources. The dates of the 1966 visit differ between two American documents of the same spring. The delivery dates of the American M48s are not in the record consulted here. The relation between the three wordings of Israel's nuclear pledge, introduce, manufacture, or go nuclear "unless others do," is not explained by any document in which an official sets them side by side. Whether the 80 to 100 tons of Argentine concentrate were ever accounted for is not stated. And the claim that by May 1967 Israel had two improvised devices on alert rests on one scholar's research.

sections.h: Samu, November 1966: The Raid, the Report and Resolution 228
sections.html:
Nine months after the Skyhawk decision, the arms relationship met its first test on the ground. On the morning of 13 November 1966 Israeli forces crossed the armistice line into the Jordanian-ruled West Bank and destroyed much of the village of As Samu. The raid struck a government that, by Washington's reckoning, had kept up a good system of tacit cooperation with Israel on the border. In the days that followed it produced an urgent American review of how to help Jordan, a warning from the American president to Israel, riots against King Hussein's government in the West Bank, and, twelve days after the raid, a Security Council censure for which the United States voted. The best record of what happened on the ground is the report of the United Nations Truce Supervision Organization, and this section begins there, noting at each point which details the observers saw for themselves and which rest on the word of Jordanian witnesses.

The mine, 11 or 12 November. The raid answered a killing. The archives of the Israel Defense Forces describe the operation, which they call Operation Magressa, as a response to a mine attack near the West Bank border two days earlier, in which three Israeli soldiers on patrol were killed, and they attribute the mine to Fatah. [cite:rs_cw6_idf_archive_samu] An American document of the time gives a different attribution and a slightly different date: the CIA memorandum of 2 December 1966 says Israel attributed the mining of the road on 12 November to the Palestine Liberation Front. [cite:rs_cw6_cia_dec1966_samu] Walt Rostow's memorandum to Johnson of 15 November also counts three Israelis killed. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d333] The sources therefore agree that three Israeli soldiers died, and the Israeli archive places the attack near the West Bank border; they differ on whether the group was Fatah or the Palestine Liberation Front, and on whether the mine was laid on the 11th or the 12th. The campaign of raids of which this mine was part, and the 61 sabotage incidents Israel attributed to Fatah by December 1966, are told in [scene:cw6_fatah|Fatah's campaign]. [cite:rs_cw6_cia_dec1966]

The morning of 13 November. The report of UNTSO's Chief of Staff, Lieutenant-General Odd Bull, to the Secretary-General, circulated as document S/7593, reconstructs the morning by the clock. According to Jordanian witnesses quoted in the report, Israeli tanks crossed the line at about 05:45. UNTSO asked for a ceasefire by 08:55 and received no Israeli reply. The chairman of the Mixed Armistice Commission then called a ceasefire for 09:45, which both sides accepted. United Nations observers reached the scene at 10:35. [cite:rs_cw6_untso_s7593] The sequence matters for what follows: the observers arrived nearly five hours after the crossing, when the fighting was over, and what they could verify was the damage, not the conduct of the operation.

The report's description of the force is accordingly second-hand. Jordanian witnesses described about 80 M-48 Patton tanks, two columns of more than 40 half-tracks, 155 mm and 105 mm guns, and Mirage aircraft; UNTSO recorded these details as their testimony and did not independently verify them. [cite:rs_cw6_untso_s7593] In Washington Rostow described a "3000-man raid with tanks and planes." [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d333] The two descriptions agree on armour and aircraft; neither is a count by a neutral observer.

What the observers found. The physical findings are UNTSO's own. As Samu was a village of about 5,000 people in 1,200 houses. The observers found 125 houses completely demolished, along with the village clinic, a six-classroom school and a workshop; one mosque and 28 houses were damaged. At Khirbet Jimba 15 stone huts had been destroyed, and the police post at Rujm el Madfa'a was almost totally destroyed. [cite:rs_cw6_untso_s7593] The CIA's figure five days later, about 150 buildings destroyed, is of the same order. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d338]

The dead. The number killed is less certain, and UNTSO's own report does not settle it. Its totals give 3 civilians and 15 soldiers killed, and 97 civilians and 37 soldiers wounded; yet the same report notes death certificates for 14 military personnel and 5 civilians. [cite:rs_cw6_untso_s7593] The two counts within one document differ by one soldier and two civilians, and the sources consulted do not explain the discrepancy. Israel declined to produce its own casualties as witnesses before the observers. [cite:rs_cw6_untso_s7593] The CIA, writing on 18 November, gave a much higher figure: about 50 killed, half of them soldiers. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d338] That estimate is more than twice either of UNTSO's, and the CIA document as consulted does not give its basis. UNTSO's counts put soldiers at most of the dead; the CIA puts them at about half.

Israel's case. The Israeli rationale, in its strongest form, ran as follows. Israeli soldiers had been killed by a mine near the West Bank border, and the West Bank was territory Jordan ruled. [cite:rs_cw6_idf_archive_samu] By December 1966 Israel attributed 61 sabotage incidents to Fatah since its emergence in January 1965. [cite:rs_cw6_cia_dec1966] On this reasoning, a government whose patrols were being killed from across the line was entitled to strike the territory from which the attackers came. The IDF archive presents the operation as exactly that: a response to the mine attack launched from the West Bank. [cite:rs_cw6_idf_archive_samu]

Washington's objection. The American government did not accept the case, and its reasons are on paper. On 15 November Rostow told Johnson that the raid "was out of all proportion to the provocation and was aimed at the wrong target." It had, he wrote, "wrecked a good system of tacit cooperation between Hussein and the Israelis," and he suggested slowing military deliveries to Israel "inconspicuously." [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d333] The phrase "the wrong target" carried the whole objection. The government that sponsored Fatah, in the CIA's account, was Syria's; the government that had kept its border with Israel quiet was Jordan's, and it was Jordan that had been struck. [cite:rs_cw6_cia_dec1966] The same day Assistant Secretary of State Sisco told Israel's ambassador, Harman, that Washington was "dismayed by Israeli attack," feared that "this is not the end but the beginning," and expected a "strong resolution" at the United Nations. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d335] Syria's sponsorship of Fatah is the subject of [scene:cw6_syria|Syria's radical turn].

The danger to Hussein. The CIA spelled out what the raid meant for Jordan. Its special memorandum of 18 November judged that the raid had "shattered the modus vivendi" on the border, that Jordan's army was "clearly humiliated," and that a coup or assassination attempt against Hussein "cannot be ruled out." [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d338] The Jordanian objection, put in its strongest form and in the terms of these American documents, was that the king had kept a system of tacit cooperation with Israel on the border, that the raiders were not his, and that the blow had fallen on his army and his throne rather than on their sponsors. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d333] Unrest followed. According to GlobalSecurity's account, rioting against the Jordanian government followed in the West Bank on a scale beyond any earlier unrest, and Hussein used the army to restore order. [cite:rs_cw6_gs_jordan_samu]

Johnson's letters. On 23 November Johnson wrote to Hussein. "Words of sympathy are small comfort when lives have been needlessly destroyed," the letter began, and the president ordered an urgent review of how the United States could help. [cite:rs_cw6_lbj_hussein] To Israel he sent a warning. The FRUS editors record that Johnson told Israel that another such raid would lead to the suspension of American military shipments. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_sum_samu] Coming nine months after the Skyhawk sale told in [scene:s11d|the two tracks of 1966], the warning put the new supply relationship itself on the table.

Resolution 228, 25 November 1966. The Security Council voted twelve days after the raid. Resolution 228 censured Israel for "a large-scale and carefully planned military action" in breach of the United Nations Charter and of the Israel–Jordan armistice, and warned that "actions of military reprisal cannot be tolerated." It was adopted by 14 votes to none, with New Zealand abstaining; the United States voted in favour. [cite:rs_cw6_res228] [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d349] Read against Israel's case, the resolution's two key phrases can be taken as an answer to it: "carefully planned" rejected any reading of the raid as a spontaneous or local response; "military reprisal" named the policy and declared it unacceptable whatever the provocation.

The money that followed. The raid's last consequence was a bill, and Jordan presented it. Jordan's army commander, General Khammash, asked Washington for what Rostow called "a stupendous $200 million." Rostow planned to "whittle" it down, and the FRUS editors record that a military aid package for Jordan was agreed in December 1966. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d355] [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_sum_samu] The sum of that package is not given in the sources consulted. The chain, as these American documents present it, runs: an Israeli raid humiliated Jordan's army; the United States, fearing for Hussein's throne, paid to rearm it; and the cost of the raid to Washington was counted partly in aid to the country that had been struck.

What the record does not settle. Several questions the sources do not answer. Who laid the mine, Fatah or the Palestine Liberation Front, is given differently by the Israeli archive and the CIA, and its date by a day. The size and composition of the raiding force rest on Jordanian testimony and on Rostow's round figure, not on a neutral count. The number of Jordanian dead differs within UNTSO's own report and the CIA's estimate is more than twice either figure, and none of the sources consulted reconciles them. The size of December's aid package to Jordan, and the date and scale of the West Bank riots beyond GlobalSecurity's account, are not in the record here. Nor do these documents show why Israel's government chose Jordan rather than Syria as the target; the American objection that it was "the wrong target" is a judgment by its critics, not an account of its reasoning.

sections.h: The End of Military Government, 1963–1966
sections.html:
Six days after the Security Council censured the raid on Samu, Israel ended a regime of its own making inside its borders. For most of Israel's first two decades the majority of its Arab citizens lived under a military administration that required permits to leave their localities, imposed curfews and designated closed areas; it was abolished in 1966. [cite:wiki_kafr_qasim_massacre] [cite:conversation_kafr_qasim_60] How that regime was built and run from 1949 is told in Volume II, in [scene:rd6_military_government|the military government], and its worst single event, at Kafr Qasim on 29 October 1956, in Stage Three. This section takes up only its ending: how it was eased from 1963, how it was dismantled in 1966, and what remained in place when the military governors left.

The common claim that Arab citizens of Israel have enjoyed equal civil rights since 1948 does not survive the dates. A separate administrative regime applied to one category of citizens until December 1966. [cite:wiki_kafr_qasim_massacre] But the ending itself is also less simple than a single date suggests, and the file kept by the Prime Minister's Adviser on Arab Affairs, now in the Israel State Archives and published by the Akevot Institute, shows why. [cite:rs_cw6_akevot_gl17005]

The legal basis, 1963. The regime rested not on a statute of the Knesset but on the Defence (Emergency) Regulations of 1945. In March 1963 the Military Advocate General, Meir Shamgar, circulated a secret thirteen-page manual on those regulations, printed in 30 copies. [cite:rs_cw6_akevot_gl17005] The manual is a reminder that, whatever changed in the years that followed, the legal instrument on which control rested was being codified for internal use at the very moment the easing began.

The easing, October–November 1963. The first large change came in the autumn of 1963. On 21 October 1963 Eshkol cancelled the general requirement that Arab citizens carry personal travel permits. A directive of 3 November 1963 by the Chief of Staff, Zvi Tzur, then created a general permit for most residents of the Triangle and Wadi 'Ara, excluding the Negev and six border villages; cut the military zones in the Galilee from 17 to nine; and kept eleven "abandoned villages" closed. [cite:rs_cw6_akevot_gl17005]

The link between closure and land is explicit in the file. At a meeting chaired by the Adviser on Arab Affairs, Shmuel Toledano, on 18 November 1965, nine villages were reviewed for opening; those with unresolved "land issues" stayed closed. [cite:rs_cw6_akevot_gl17005] The review was conducted under the civilian adviser, and the test the file records for keeping a village closed was an unresolved question of land.

The decision, January 1966. On 12 January 1966 the Prime Minister told the Knesset that the government planned to abolish the military government within a year. The army did not agree: the Chief of Staff had argued for keeping it in eased form. [cite:rs_cw6_akevot_gl17005] The decision was therefore a civilian one, taken over military objection. Arab citizens' own political organizing in these years, and the state's response to it, are the subject of [scene:cw6_al_ard|al-Ard and the courts].

The directives of 27 February 1966. How the regime would be replaced was settled at a meeting on 27 February 1966 chaired by the Prime Minister's adviser Isser Harel. Its directives drew the essential line: the apparatus of military government would be dismantled, but the Defence Regulations would stay in force. Enforcement would pass to the Israel Police and, in some cases, to the Shin Bet. The Shin Bet was to be reinforced; new police stations were to be built; a police reserve unit was to be formed for "mixed communities"; and a demolition unit was to be created for "illegal construction." [cite:rs_cw6_akevot_gl17005] The powers were not abolished. They were transferred, and the bodies that received them were strengthened to hold them.

The announcement and the date. The public account of the change reached the press at midyear. The Jewish Telegraphic Agency reported on 30 June 1966 that the military governorships would end on 1 December 1966 for about 150,000 Arab citizens, mainly along the Jordanian border and around Nazareth, and that a special police headquarters for the Arab minority had already been set up. [cite:rs_cw6_jta_jun1966] Eshkol gave the Knesset formal notice of abolition on 8 November 1966. Because the regime rested on military regulations rather than on a law, no legislation was needed to end it, according to the Economic Cooperation Foundation's account. [cite:rs_cw6_ecf_abolition] On 1 December 1966 the governorships ended.

What remained. After abolition the police, under the Chief of Staff's supervision, were tasked with enforcing the Emergency Regulations, according to the Institute for Palestine Studies' encyclopedia. [cite:rs_cw6_palquest_mg_e] The regulations that stayed in force included the power to declare closed areas (Regulation 125), restriction orders (Regulation 109), police supervision (Regulation 110), administrative detention (Regulation 111, replaced in 1979) and deportation (Regulation 112). [cite:rs_cw6_palquest_mg_e] [cite:rs_cw6_akevot_gl17005] After December 1966 these powers could be exercised by the police under the same legal text.

The men who planned the change described it in their own words. Toledano called it mainly "psychological." A 1963 document on the regime's aims, in the same file, put it more fully: "the main change is external-psychological that gives a feeling of equality." [cite:rs_cw6_akevot_gl17005] The phrase is the adviser's office describing its own policy, and it is central to one side of the dispute over what the abolition meant.

Did 1 December 1966 end military rule? Two readings of the record stand, and each rests on documents. On the first, the answer is yes, formally and in substance: the military governorships were abolished and their powers passed to civilian bodies, for some 150,000 citizens who had lived under them. [cite:rs_cw6_jta_jun1966] [cite:rs_cw6_ecf_abolition] The general requirement to carry personal travel permits had been cancelled in 1963. On this reading that change, at least, was more than a matter of perception. [cite:rs_cw6_akevot_gl17005]

On the second reading, what ended was the military apparatus, not the regime of control. The state's own archive file shows the Emergency Regulations kept in force and their enforcement transferred to the police and the Shin Bet, which were reinforced for the purpose; Toledano himself called the change a mainly "psychological" one. [cite:rs_cw6_akevot_gl17005] The Institute for Palestine Studies' encyclopedia places the full legal abolition of military rule later, in late 1968. [cite:rs_cw6_palquest_mg_e] The two readings are not wholly in conflict. Both accept that the governorships ended on 1 December 1966; they differ on whether the governorships were the thing that mattered.

One interpretive reading carries the argument further. It holds that before Israel governed a single Palestinian in the West Bank or Gaza, it had already run an eighteen-year separate regime for Palestinian citizens inside its own borders, and that the occupation which began in 1967 inherited a model rather than inventing one. That is a reading of the sequence, not a documented finding; the sources consulted here document the regime and its transfer of powers, not any decision to carry the model across the line in 1967.

What the record does not settle. The documents consulted for this section do not show how often the retained regulations were used against Arab citizens after December 1966, or whether their use rose or fell once the police took them over. They do not say which villages among the eleven closed in 1963 and the nine reviewed in 1965 were opened, or when. The date of full legal abolition, late 1968 in the Institute for Palestine Studies' account, is not confirmed by an Israeli government source in this chapter. And the Chief of Staff's arguments for keeping the regime in eased form are recorded only as a position, not in his own words.

sections.h: Israel at Home, 1965–1967: Rafi, the Sixth Knesset and the Recession
sections.html:
The government that ended military rule in December 1966, and that faced the crisis of May 1967, was not the one Ben-Gurion had led. It was a coalition built after a party split and an election, and it governed an economy that had stopped growing. Both facts shaped the country that entered the last weeks before the war, and neither is visible in the familiar account that moves straight from the arms and border stories of these years to the crisis itself. This section sets out the political arithmetic and the economic record as Israel's own institutions documented them.

Ben-Gurion's break. In 1965 David Ben-Gurion and a group of his associates left Mapai and founded a new list, Rafi. According to the Israel Democracy Institute's party profile, three disputes drove the break: Ben-Gurion's push to reopen the Lavon affair, his opposition to Mapai's joint list with Ahdut HaAvoda, and his doubts about the leadership of his successor as prime minister, Levi Eshkol. Moshe Dayan, Shimon Peres and Yitzhak Navon were among Rafi's members. [cite:rs_cw6_idi_rafi] The Lavon affair itself is told in the earlier stages of this volume. What matters here is that Ben-Gurion now stood outside the party that governed, and that Dayan and Peres went with him.

The election of 2 November 1965. The Sixth Knesset was elected on 2 November 1965. Of 1,499,988 eligible voters, 83.0 percent voted. [cite:rs_cw6_idi_1965] The results show a field reorganized into blocs. Mapai and Ahdut HaAvoda ran together as the Alignment and won 45 seats with 36.7 percent of the vote. On the right, Herut and the Liberals had merged as Gahal, which won 26 seats with 21.3 percent. The National Religious Party took 11 seats, Rafi 10, Mapam 8, the Independent Liberals 5, Agudat Yisrael 4 and Rakah 3. [cite:rs_cw6_idi_1965]

Neither of the new blocs did as well as its parts had done separately. Measured against its components' previous totals, the Alignment came back five seats fewer and Gahal eight fewer. Rafi's 10 seats, the institute records, disappointed Ben-Gurion. [cite:rs_cw6_idi_1965] Rafi's exact vote is given two ways by the same institute, and the discrepancy should be stated rather than smoothed. Its party profile gives 95,328 votes, or 7.9 percent. [cite:rs_cw6_idi_rafi] Its election table prints 42,654 votes beside the same 7.9 percent and the same 10 seats, a figure that cannot be reconciled with that share. [cite:rs_cw6_idi_1965] This book uses the party profile's figure, and flags the table.

Eshkol's coalition. Forming a government took more than two months of negotiation. The coalition Eshkol assembled brought together the Alignment, the National Religious Party, Mapam, the Independent Liberals and Poalei Agudat Yisrael, with the Arab lists affiliated with the Alignment: 75 members in all. [cite:rs_cw6_idi_1965] Both Rafi and Gahal stayed outside it. That arrangement held until the eve of the June 1967 war, when Eshkol brought both into a national unity government. [cite:rs_cw6_idi_1965] [cite:rs_cw6_idi_rafi] The mechanism matters for what followed. In the spring of 1967 the parties that were not in government included Ben-Gurion's own list, with Dayan in it, and the main opposition on the right. When the crisis came, the pressure to widen the cabinet had a ready address: the two lists the 1965 coalition had left out.

The recession. The second fact about Israel in 1966 is economic, and the best source for it is the Bank of Israel's own annual report for that year. Real gross national product grew by 0.6 percent in 1966, against 8.2 percent in 1965. Real GNP per head fell by 2.0 percent. Gross investment fell by 18.4 percent, and investment in construction by about 20 percent. [cite:rs_cw6_boi_1966_ch2] An economy that had grown by more than eight percent in one year had, in the next, all but stopped.

The Bank attributed the turn mainly to falling demand after the boom of 1961–64. "The recessionary forces operating in 1966," it wrote, "largely emanated from the construction sector." It listed the causes: overinvestment in housing; steep wage increases, with wages per employee up 19 percent in 1966; lower immigration and lower transfers from abroad; and government restraint. [cite:rs_cw6_boi_1966_ch2] In the Bank's account these were not separate shocks: the construction boom, the fall in immigration and the fall in transfers from abroad all appear on the same list of causes.

Policy, late. The Bank's account of government policy is critical, and it is the government's own central bank that makes the criticism. At the end of 1964 the government decided to moderate economic activity, but in 1965 it raised demand instead. The curbs came in 1966, a year in which no new development projects were started. Late in 1966 the government reversed course, turning to capital spending, deficit financing and easier credit. The Bank judged that the reversal came too late. [cite:rs_cw6_boi_1966_ch2] On one reading of this record the slowdown was partly the planned result of policy, and the planners, by the Bank's own reckoning, had first delayed the brake and then held it on past the point where it was needed.

Who bore the cost. The cost fell on workers who lost their jobs. The Bank's chapter on population, labour force and employment gives unemployment, by the manpower surveys, at an average of 3.6 percent in 1965, or 33,200 people. In 1966 the average was 7.4 percent, or 70,200 people, and in the last quarter of 1966 it reached 10.3 percent, or 99,100 people. [cite:rs_cw6_boi_1966_ch9] Registered job seekers rose from 5,463 in December 1965 to 19,376 in December 1966, more than three and a half times as many. [cite:rs_cw6_boi_1966_ch9]

Immigration and emigration. The same chapter records a change in what was driving the population's growth. Net immigration accounted for 49 percent of population growth in 1964, 31 percent in 1965 and 12 percent in 1966. [cite:rs_cw6_boi_1966_ch9] Emigration rose. The Bank's preliminary figures for 1966 showed more people leaving than in 1964 or 1965, though not many more than the 10,900 who had left in 1963. [cite:rs_cw6_boi_1966_ch9] A year in which net immigration supplied about an eighth of the population's growth, against nearly half two years earlier, marked a turn in its own right.

What the record does not settle. The documents consulted for this book stop with the Bank's 1966 report. They do not give the unemployment figures for the first months of 1967, so the peak of the recession, and whether the late-1966 reversal had begun to work by May, cannot be stated from them. Nor does any source here connect the recession to the decisions of May and June 1967. Meir Amit would tell the American defence secretary on 1 June that the mobilization was straining the economy, but that is a statement about the reserves called up in the crisis, not about the recession that preceded it. How that government widened on 1 June 1967, and who joined it, is told in [scene:cw6_tiran_june4|the last section of this stage].

sections.h: Egypt in Yemen, 1962–1967
sections.html:
Israel entered 1967 in recession; Egypt entered it at war. When its army moved into Sinai in May 1967, part of it was somewhere else. Since the autumn of 1962 Egyptian troops had been fighting in Yemen, in a civil war that had begun as a short commitment and had not ended. The familiar story of the May crisis sets Egypt's forces against Israel's as if the two armies faced each other at full strength. The record of the Yemen war complicates that picture. It does not explain the crisis, and no source cited here claims that it does, but it is part of the condition of the army Nasser sent forward.

A short mission. Egypt entered Yemen's civil war in September 1962, after a coup overthrew the country's monarchy. According to the historians Eugene Rogan and Tewfik Aclimandos, Anwar Sadat was among the aides who assured Nasser that a short, small-scale mission would be enough. [cite:rs_cw6_rogan_aclimandos] The first deployment, according to Foreign Policy, was a single company of commandos. [cite:rs_cw6_fp_yemen]

It did not stay small. Nasser himself later said that the force had grown to "70,000 troops." [cite:rs_cw6_fp_yemen] Bruce Riedel, writing for the Brookings Institution, gives the expeditionary force's peak at the same figure, 70,000. [cite:rs_cw6_riedel_cia] The war was also a contest between states. Saudi Arabia supplied the royalists loyal to the deposed Imam, al-Badr, while Egypt carried the war beyond Yemen's borders, striking Saudi territory and the Aden Protectorate from the air. [cite:rs_cw6_fp_yemen] Two Arab governments were thus on opposite sides of a war in the peninsula through the same years as the Arab summits of 1964 and 1965.

The attempt at Jeddah. In 1965 Nasser went to Jeddah to make peace with King Faisal of Saudi Arabia. The agreement did not hold. According to Foreign Policy, the Yemeni factions rejected a settlement that had been made over their heads. [cite:rs_cw6_fp_yemen] The two outside powers could agree with each other; they could not deliver the parties actually fighting. Egypt's army remained committed.

What it cost. The cost to Egypt is given in two figures that are often set against each other as if they disagreed. They measure different things. Riedel gives Egypt's losses by 1967 as 25,000 casualties, a figure that counts the wounded as well as the dead. [cite:rs_cw6_riedel_cia] Foreign Policy gives at least 10,000 Egyptian dead over the five years of the war. [cite:rs_cw6_fp_yemen] The two need not conflict; neither can be checked against the other from these sources, because neither breaks its total down.

Still there in May 1967. Egyptian forces were still in Yemen when Nasser moved his army into Sinai in May 1967. [cite:rs_cw6_fp_yemen] How many were there at that moment is not established by any source consulted for this book. The peak of 70,000 is a figure for the war's height, not for May 1967, and it should not be read as the number missing from Sinai. Their withdrawal, settled at the Khartoum summit, belongs to the aftermath of [scene:s12|the Six-Day War]. [cite:rs_cw6_fp_yemen]

The historians' judgment. Rogan and Aclimandos, in their chapter of the Cambridge volume on the origins and consequences of 1967 edited by Wm Roger Louis and Avi Shlaim, call Yemen "an unwinnable war, Nasser's Vietnam." They conclude that the campaign "fatally impaired" Egypt's performance in June 1967. [cite:rs_cw6_rogan_aclimandos] Their claim is carefully bounded. They do not argue that Yemen alone caused Egypt's defeat; they argue that it weakened the army that had to fight. [cite:rs_cw6_rogan_aclimandos] The chapter as consulted here is its published abstract, so the evidence on which the judgment rests in detail cannot be set out from it.

Washington's reading of the balance. The United States government had its own assessment of what Egypt's army could do, and it was made in the crisis itself. On 22 May 1967 Nasser announced the closure of the Strait of Tiran, told in [scene:cw6_tiran_june4|the last section of this stage]. The next day, 23 May, the CIA's Office of Current Intelligence produced an assessment that Johnson had requested. It judged, according to Riedel, that Israel could defend itself against any combination of Arab enemies and could launch a major offensive. A joint paper by the CIA and the Defense Intelligence Agency at the end of May went further: Israel, it judged, would take Sinai in "several days." [cite:rs_cw6_riedel_cia] The same analysis called Arab unity "fiction," and found no serious military coordination among the Arab states. [cite:rs_cw6_riedel_cia]

Riedel's summary, as consulted here, does not tie these judgments to Yemen, and it would go beyond the sources to say that the war in the peninsula was what the analysts had in mind. On one reading, though, the two records point the same way. Egypt's army had spent five years in a war its own leaders had expected to be short, at a cost Riedel puts at 25,000 casualties, against forces backed by another Arab government; and Washington's analysts, looking at the balance in late May, saw neither Arab military superiority nor Arab military coordination.

What the record does not settle. Three things remain unsettled here. The number of Egyptian troops in Yemen in May 1967 is not verified. The breakdown of the casualty figures is not given. And the degree to which Yemen, rather than other causes, impaired Egypt's army in June is a judgment, made by Rogan and Aclimandos with an explicit limit on it, not a measured finding.

sections.h: The Syrian Front, Spring 1967
sections.html:
Egypt's army was still in Yemen when the Syrian front, to which Cairo was now bound by treaty, flared. By the spring of 1967 Israel's border with Syria was the site of repeated clashes. The government in Damascus was the product of the coup of February 1966, told in [scene:cw6_syria|Syria's radical turn], and in November 1966 it had signed a five-year defence pact with Egypt. [cite:rs_cw6_locegypt] The pact is the hinge of this section. On one reading, before it, a clash on the Syrian line was Syria's affair. After it, a clash on the Syrian line was a test of whether Egypt would honour its commitment, and of whether Nasser would act when his new ally was struck.

The Syria that Israel faced. The American government's own view of Damascus was severe. In December 1966 the CIA called Syria "the most bellicose Arab state," and reported that it gave Fatah a base, training and a propaganda outlet. [cite:rs_cw6_cia_dec1966_s] Fatah's raids into Israel, launched in the CIA's account from Jordanian and Lebanese territory, are the subject of [scene:cw6_fatah|Fatah's campaign]. On the Israeli side the raids were the grievance; on the Syrian side, Israel's answers to them were.

7 April 1967. On 7 April 1967 fighting on the Syrian border became a land and air engagement, as GlobalSecurity describes it. [cite:rs_cw6_gs_jordan_s] In the air, Israeli aircraft shot down six Syrian fighters, according to Fanack. [cite:rs_cw6_fanack] The sources consulted for this book do not give the incident that began the fighting that day, the losses on the ground, or Israel's own losses, and they are not supplied here.

The historian Henry Laurens reads the day's significance in Cairo rather than in Damascus. The shooting down of six Syrian MiGs, he writes, exposed Nasser's inaction to his Arab critics. [cite:rs_cw6_laurens] Five months after signing a defence pact with Syria, Egypt had watched Syria's air force lose six aircraft and had done nothing. In Laurens's account, that inaction was noticed by Nasser's Arab critics, and became a political cost as well as a military fact. Laurens's reading is an interpretation of Nasser's position, not a record of his deliberations; but if it is right, it helps explain why the next alarm from the Syrian front would find Cairo under pressure to be seen to act.

Israel's warnings. In the same spring, Israel's leaders spoke in terms that went beyond the raids themselves. The historian David Tal records that the chief of staff, Rabin, said that the Damascus "authorities are behind the terrorists," which Tal reads as hinting at a change of regime. [cite:rs_cw6_tal_jvl] Tal also records that Prime Minister Eshkol warned that "the last 14 incidents might lead us to take measures no less harsh than those taken on April 7th." [cite:rs_cw6_tal_jvl] Eshkol's words place his warning after 7 April; Tal, as consulted here, does not give the exact date of either statement. The Library of Congress study of Egypt summarizes the period more broadly: in 1967, it says, Israeli leaders repeatedly threatened to invade Syria and overthrow its government if the raids across the Syrian border did not stop. [cite:rs_cw6_locegypt]

The word "terrorists" in that sentence is Rabin's, as Tal records it, and this book quotes it as his. The CIA's December 1966 memorandum is the source for who backed the raiders. How the sources of the period used the term, and what they meant by it, is examined in the section on Fatah's campaign.

Who was escalating. The question of who drove the Syrian front toward war is disputed, and the two readings rest on different documents. The first emphasizes Israeli pressure. The Library of Congress study puts Israel's repeated threats against Syria at the centre of its account of 1967, and Laurens describes Rabin's "show of force" against Syria. [cite:rs_cw6_locegypt] [cite:rs_cw6_laurens] On this reading, Israeli threats to strike at the government in Damascus, and an air battle that showed Israel could do so, were what turned a border dispute into a crisis involving Egypt.

The second reading emphasizes Syria's sponsorship of the raids. The CIA, in December 1966, described Syria as the most bellicose of the Arab states and the patron of Fatah: base, training, propaganda. [cite:rs_cw6_cia_dec1966_s] On this reading, Israel's warnings were a response to a campaign of attacks across its border that a government was sponsoring, and Eshkol's reference to fourteen incidents was a count of what Israel was being asked to absorb. Both readings have documentary support, and the two are not exclusive. The CIA described Syrian conduct in 1966; the Library of Congress and Laurens describe Israeli statements chiefly in 1967; each can be true at once. What it does not show is which, in the minds of the decision-makers in Damascus, Jerusalem and Cairo, weighed more.

What the record does not settle. Several things the reader would want are missing from the sources. The incident that set off the fighting of 7 April is not described; nor are the fourteen incidents Eshkol counted, nor the casualties on either side. The dates of Rabin's and Eshkol's statements are not given. And there is no Egyptian document here recording how Cairo judged its obligations under the November 1966 pact after the air battle. On 13 May 1967 a Soviet warning reached Cairo that Israel was about to attack Syria. That warning, and what followed it, is the subject of [scene:cw6_may_crisis|the May crisis].

sections.h: The Crisis Opens, 13–19 May 1967
sections.html:
The Soviet warning with which the spring's Syrian story ends opened the crisis on Israel's southern front. In six days in May 1967 the position there was transformed. On 13 May the Soviet Union warned Egypt that Israel was about to attack Syria. By 19 May the United Nations Emergency Force, which had stood on the Egyptian side of the line, was leaving, and Egyptian troops were moving into Sinai. The familiar account tends to tell this week as a single movement, with one cause and one intention behind it. The documents tell it as a chain of separate decisions, taken in Moscow, Cairo, New York and Jerusalem, each by people who could see only part of the chain. Why the chain began, and what Nasser meant by the steps he took, are among the most disputed questions of the period. This section sets out what each document says, and where the historians who have read them part company.

The Soviet warning, 13 May. On 13 May 1967 the Soviet Union told Egypt that Israel was massing forces to attack Syria. According to the historian Hassan Elbahtimy, writing for the Wilson Center's Cold War International History Project, the warning spoke of about 11 brigades and came through at least three channels: to Anwar Sadat during a stop in Moscow, and in Cairo through Egyptian intelligence and through the Foreign Ministry. Elbahtimy writes that the information "proved to be false." [cite:rs_cw6_elbahtimy] The Library of Congress study of Egypt gives the warning differently: Israel, it says, was reported to have mobilized two brigades on the frontier, after which Nasser sent troops toward the border, and Syria followed. [cite:rs_cw6_locegypt_m] The two accounts differ by a factor of more than five on the size of the force the Soviets reported, and the sources here do not explain the difference. They agree on what matters most for what followed: a Soviet report of an Israeli concentration against Syria reached Cairo on 13 May.

Fawzi on the Syrian border, 14 May. The next day General Muhammad Fawzi, Egypt's chief of staff, went to the Syrian border. His visit is recorded in a transcript of an interview he gave on 28 February 1997, held by the Liddell Hart Centre at King's College London, which covers the visit and the Soviet reports. [cite:rs_cw6_fawzi_kcl] The archive's catalogue description, which is all that was consulted for this book, does not state what Fawzi concluded about whether Israeli troops were massed there. [cite:rs_cw6_fawzi_kcl] That gap is important, and it should not be filled by assumption. What Egypt's chief of staff saw on the Syrian front on 14 May, and what he reported to Nasser, is not established here.

Into Sinai. Egyptian forces began to move into Sinai. The historians Tal and Laurens both read the deployment of 14 May as deterrence: a signal, meant to dissuade Israel from striking Syria, by moving force where Israel could see it. [cite:rs_cw6_tal_m] [cite:rs_cw6_laurens_m] In Jerusalem the movement was read in much the same way at first. Israel's cabinet heard on 17 May that Egyptian forces were moving into Sinai, and, according to the Israel State Archives' summary of its meetings, it worked on the assumption that the move was mainly for show, not for war. [cite:rs_cw6_isa_cabinet] On the same day, Laurens writes, two Egyptian reconnaissance aircraft flew over Dimona, whose reactor is the subject of earlier sections of this stage, without being detected. [cite:rs_cw6_laurens_m]

The letter to Rikhye, 16 May. The next step was taken at 22:00 Gaza time on 16 May. Brigadier Eiz-El-Din Mokhtar handed the commander of the United Nations Emergency Force, Major-General Indar Jit Rikhye, a letter from General Fawzi. [cite:rs_cw6_frus19_d6] [cite:rs_cw6_a6730] The letter said that the troops of the United Arab Republic, as Egypt then called itself, were concentrated in Sinai to act if Israel attacked any Arab country, and it asked UNEF to withdraw from its observation posts along the border. Fawzi's text read:

I request that you issue your orders to withdraw all these troops immediately.

[cite:rs_cw6_frus19_d6] [cite:rs_cw6_a6730]

U Thant, the Secretary-General, answered the same evening. Any such request, he replied, had to come to him directly from the government of the UAR, not from its army to a field commander. On receiving it he would "order the withdrawal of all UNEF troops from Gaza and Sinai," and would inform the General Assembly at the same time. [cite:rs_cw6_frus19_d6] Fawzi had asked for the force to leave the border posts. U Thant's reply spoke not of the posts but of all UNEF troops, in Gaza and in Sinai.

Riad's request, 18 May. The formal request came from Egypt's foreign minister, Riad. It reached U Thant at noon New York time on 18 May. The UAR, it said, "has decided to terminate the presence of the United Nations Emergency Force." [cite:rs_cw6_a6730] [cite:rs_cw6_s7906] U Thant consulted UNEF's Advisory Committee. The committee did not ask for a session of the General Assembly. He replied to Egypt that evening. [cite:rs_cw6_a6730] [cite:rs_cw6_s7906]

The force and its foundation. What was leaving was a force of 3,378 men on 15 May 1967, drawn from seven countries: Brazil, Canada, Denmark, India, Norway, Sweden and Yugoslavia. It had been stationed only on the Egyptian side of the line, because Israel had refused to have it on its own side. [cite:rs_cw6_a6730] That fact shaped the legal argument that followed. A force that stood on one country's territory alone depended on that one country's consent.

U Thant set out his reasoning in his reports to the General Assembly and the Security Council. UNEF, he argued, rested on the consent of the host country. A peacekeeping force could not function without that country's "continuing consent and co-operation," and the movements of UAR troops had in any case already made the force unworkable on the ground. [cite:rs_cw6_s7906] [cite:rs_cw6_a6730] He also addressed a private note that Hammarskjöld had written in 1957 about the terms of UNEF's presence. That note, U Thant wrote, "cannot affect in any way the basis for the presence of UNEF." [cite:rs_cw6_s7906] [cite:rs_cw6_a6730] The documents consulted for this book give U Thant's ruling on the note, not the note's own text, and this book does not characterize it beyond his words.

The mechanism is clear from these documents. The power to end UNEF's presence lay with Egypt, as host. The Secretary-General judged that he had no power to keep a force on territory whose government had withdrawn its consent, and his reply to Fawzi spoke of withdrawing the whole force. The Advisory Committee could have asked for the General Assembly to meet; it did not. Israel, which had refused the force on its own side of the line, had no part in the decision. Whether U Thant could or should have delayed, consulted more widely, or offered a partial withdrawal is a question the record frames but does not answer, and his own reports are the case for the decision he made.

The dates. The dates of the withdrawal request are given differently in the secondary literature, and the differences are worth stating because they change how the sequence reads. The United Nations record, and the State Department's editorial note on it, date Fawzi's letter to 16 May and the formal UAR request to 18 May. [cite:rs_cw6_a6730] [cite:rs_cw6_frus19_d6] The Library of Congress study gives 16 May; GlobalSecurity gives 18 May; Fanack gives 19 May. [cite:rs_cw6_locegypt_m] [cite:rs_cw6_gs_jordan_m] [cite:rs_cw6_fanack_m] The UN record is the primary source, and it shows that the two dates belong to two different documents, a military letter and a governmental request. Accounts that give one date have chosen one of the two, or, in Fanack's case, a date that matches neither.

U Thant's report of 19 May. On 19 May U Thant reported to the Security Council. Two of his findings bear directly on the warning that had begun the week. The observers of the UN Truce Supervision Organization, he wrote, had "confirmed the absence of troop concentrations" on both sides of the Syrian line. [cite:rs_cw6_s7896] [cite:rs_cw6_s7906] The concentration the Soviet warning described was not there for the UN's observers to see. He also wrote that statements attributed to senior Israeli officials had been "so threatening as to be particularly inflammatory," and that the situation was "more menacing" than at any time since the autumn of 1956. [cite:rs_cw6_s7896] [cite:rs_cw6_s7906] The report thus cut in two directions at once. It found no troop concentrations on the Syrian line of the kind the warning described, and it found statements attributed to senior Israeli officials particularly inflammatory. It did not say which of the two had weighed more in Cairo.

Kosygin and Eshkol. The question of the Soviet warning was carried into the next fortnight in a direct exchange between the two governments. On 26 May Kosygin wrote to Eshkol, urging him to "resort to all measures to prevent a military conflict." Eshkol replied on 1 June that "there were no Israeli concentrations at the Syrian border," and that he had invited the Soviet ambassador to visit the frontier and see for himself. [cite:rs_cw6_kosygin_eshkol] Israel's denial and the UN observers' finding therefore point the same way.

Why did Moscow send the warning? If the warning was false, the obvious question is why it was sent, and on this the historians divide three ways. The first position is that of Ginor and Remez, as Elbahtimy summarizes their work: they portray the Soviet Union as manipulating events toward war. [cite:rs_cw6_elbahtimy] The second is Elbahtimy's own. Working from Egyptian minutes and testimony, he finds Moscow acting as a force for restraint once the crisis was under way, and taken aback by how events developed; but he allows that the false report may still have set off the chain of decisions that led to the closure of the Strait of Tiran. [cite:rs_cw6_elbahtimy] The third is David Tal's: the warning was false, and its motive remains unexplained. [cite:rs_cw6_tal_m]

Each position can point to something in the record. On the manipulation thesis, the documented fact is that the Soviet Union passed to an ally, through three channels at once, a military report that the UN's observers did not confirm. Elbahtimy's restraint thesis rests on the Egyptian record of what Soviet officials actually said once the crisis had begun. Tal's agnosticism rests on the absence, in the sources he used, of any document that states the motive. The documents consulted for this book do not decide among them, and this book does not. Elbahtimy and Tal both treat the warning as false, a point the UN observers' report of 19 May and Eshkol's letter of 1 June both support; how Ginor and Remez treat its accuracy is not stated in Elbahtimy's summary.

What did Nasser intend? The second dispute concerns Egypt. One reading, shared by Tal, Laurens and the Library of Congress study, is that Nasser's move into Sinai and his request to remove UNEF were deterrence on Syria's behalf: a show of force to dissuade an Israeli attack on his ally, which escalated in part because UNEF left faster than he expected. [cite:rs_cw6_tal_m] [cite:rs_cw6_laurens_m] [cite:rs_cw6_locegypt_m] On this reading the steps were meant to be seen, not to be used, and Nasser's later steps were, in Tal's words as summarized here, partly forced by how fast UNEF left.

The other reading begins from Egypt's own words. Fawzi's letter of 16 May did not describe a defensive posture alone; it said that Egyptian troops were concentrated in Sinai to act against Israel if Israel attacked any Arab country. [cite:rs_cw6_frus19_d6] And Nasser's own public statements in the days after 19 May went considerably further, as the next section shows. On this reading the request to remove the only international force between the two armies was a step whose consequences Egypt's leaders could foresee, whatever they intended by it. Both readings use Fawzi's letter; they differ on whether its conditional, "if Israel attacked," is the operative part.

What the record does not settle. Four things remain open after the documents of this week have been read. Why the Soviet Union sent a report that the UN's observers did not confirm is not established by any document consulted here. What General Fawzi concluded on the Syrian border on 14 May is recorded in an interview transcript whose contents this book has not seen. Whether Nasser, in asking for UNEF's withdrawal from the border posts, expected or wanted the whole force to leave is a matter of inference from his later conduct, not of record. And why the Soviet warning spoke of 11 brigades in one account and two in another is not explained. Three days later Nasser announced the closure of the Strait of Tiran, the subject of [scene:cw6_tiran_june4|the stage's last section].

sections.h: From Tiran to the Cabinet Decision, 22 May–4 June 1967
sections.html:
By 19 May 1967 the United Nations force had been asked to leave Sinai and Egyptian troops were moving in, as told in [scene:cw6_may_crisis|the crisis's first week]. What followed over the next thirteen days was a contest of speeches, letters and meetings among five governments, which ended on 4 June with a decision by Israel's government. This section tells those thirteen days from the documents, and stops there. Three questions about them are still argued: whether Israel faced an imminent attack, whether the United States gave Israel a "green light," and whether the Strait of Tiran was in fact closed. A fourth, smaller question, how Israel's ministers voted on 4 June, turns out to be unsettled too.

Nasser's speech, 22 May. On 22 May Nasser spoke to the Egyptian armed forces. He claimed the Gulf of Aqaba for Egypt:

The Aqaba Gulf constitutes our Egyptian territorial waters. Under no circumstances will we allow the Israeli flag to pass through the Aqaba Gulf.

[cite:rs_cw6_nasser_22may] In the same speech he said that Israel had decided "to carry out an aggression against Syria as of May 17," the claim of the Soviet warning that the UN observers had found no troop concentrations to support, and he said: "we are ready for war." [cite:rs_cw6_nasser_22may]

U Thant in Cairo, and Israel's casus belli. U Thant learned of the restrictions at Tiran while on his way to Cairo, where he stayed from the afternoon of 23 May until 25 May. [cite:rs_cw6_s7906_t] His report of 26 May records the two positions in the language of law. Israel held that closing the Strait to Israeli ships, or restricting cargoes bound for Israel, would be a casus belli, a cause for war, and it claimed a right of innocent passage. The UAR claimed the waters as its own territorial waters. [cite:rs_cw6_s7906_t] Each government thus presented the same strait under a different legal rule, and each rule, if accepted, settled the question in its favour.

Was Tiran closed? The point seems obvious, but the sources do not agree on it. Nasser announced the closure on 22 May, and Israel treated it as a casus belli, as the UN record shows. [cite:rs_cw6_nasser_22may] [cite:rs_cw6_s7906_t] The Library of Congress study of Egypt, however, says that he never carried out the threat. [cite:rs_cw6_locegypt_t] The sources consulted here do not record a ship stopped at the Strait between 22 May and 4 June, nor do they record one passing through. What is documented is the announcement and the response to it; whether the blockade was enforced in practice is not settled by these documents. For Israel's cabinet, the announcement was the act that mattered.

The cabinet, 23–27 May. Israel's government met repeatedly and could not agree. According to the Israel State Archives' summary of its cabinet meetings, on 23 May the cabinet defined the blockade as aggression but reached no consensus on a military response, and gave diplomacy time. On 26 May it could not agree whether to act. An all-night session on 27 May weighed the appeals for restraint that had come from foreign leaders without agreeing on a plan. [cite:rs_cw6_isa_cabinet_t] Five days after the announcement, the government that had declared closure of the Strait a cause for war had not decided to go to war over it.

The military advice reaching the government was not uniform either. Fanack records that the chief of staff, Rabin, called the blockade a "to be or not to be" issue, and that the head of military intelligence, Aharon Yariv, warned Eshkol that Egyptian forces in Sinai had moved to an offensive posture. [cite:rs_cw6_fanack_t] Tal records that on 22 May, the day of the speech, Rabin saw no sign that Nasser intended war. [cite:rs_cw6_tal_t] The two statements are not necessarily in conflict; they may describe a judgment that changed as the Egyptian deployment grew. But the sources do not date Rabin's "to be or not to be," so the change cannot be traced day by day from them.

Eban and Johnson, 26 May. On 26 May Eban met Johnson. According to the American record of the conversation, Johnson told him: "our best judgment is that no military attack on Israel is imminent." McNamara cited three intelligence groups that had judged the Egyptian deployments defensive. [cite:rs_cw6_frus19_d77] Johnson called the closure of the Strait illegal. And he put the American position in a sentence that would be repeated:

Israel will not be alone unless it decides to go it alone.

[cite:rs_cw6_frus19_d77] He stressed "Constitutional processes," and the need for the support of Congress before the United States could act. [cite:rs_cw6_frus19_d77] The President was telling Israel two things at once: that the United States regarded the closure as illegal and that Israel would not be alone unless it went alone, and that the United States would not act without the support of Congress.

Nasser to the trade unionists, 26 May. On the same day, Nasser spoke to Arab trade unionists in terms that went beyond the Strait. According to the Israel Ministry of Foreign Affairs' translation, he said: "The battle will be a general one and our basic objective will be to destroy Israel." He said too that Egypt could have told UNEF to leave "within half an hour." [cite:rs_cw6_nasser_26may] The Library of Congress study adds a qualification from the other direction: Nasser publicly denied that Egypt would strike first, while Amer and the defence minister, Shams Badran, reportedly urged him to. [cite:rs_cw6_locegypt_t] The statement of 26 May is a head of state's declared aim of destroying a neighbouring state, and it is quoted here exactly. It is also a public speech, made in the same weeks in which, by the Library of Congress study's account, the same man was publicly denying an intention to strike first, and the record does not establish which of the two governed Egypt's planning.

Kosygin and Badran in Moscow, 26 May. Badran was in Moscow that day. According to the Egyptian minutes, Kosygin told him: "Politically, you prevailed. Militarily you prevailed." [cite:rs_cw6_elbahtimy_t] Elbahtimy reads the Egyptian record of these talks as Moscow urging restraint: Egypt had won its point, and should stop there. [cite:rs_cw6_elbahtimy_t] On the same day Kosygin wrote to Eshkol urging him to prevent a conflict, as told in the previous section.

Jordan joins, 30 May. On 30 May Hussein signed a military alliance with Egypt that placed the Jordanian army under the field command of an Egyptian general officer. [cite:rs_cw6_gs_jordan_t] [cite:rs_cw6_tal_t] For the Israeli argument that the country was being encircled, the pact of 30 May was a new fact: Egypt in Sinai, Syria bound to Egypt by the pact of November 1966, and now Jordan.

Dayan and Begin, 1 June. On 1 June Moshe Dayan became defence minister. That day Dayan and Menachem Begin attended a cabinet meeting for the first time, before they had been sworn in. [cite:rs_cw6_isa_cabinet_t] [cite:rs_cw6_fanack_t] Laurens describes the result as a unity government. [cite:rs_cw6_laurens_t] Dayan was a member of Rafi, Ben-Gurion's list. Rafi and Gahal had both been left outside the coalition Eshkol formed after the 1965 election, as told in the section on Israel at home, and on the eve of the war he brought both into a national unity government. [cite:rs_cw6_idi_1965] [cite:rs_cw6_idi_rafi] The government that would decide on war was therefore wider than the one that had deadlocked in May.

Amit and McNamara, 1 June. On the same day Meir Amit saw McNamara. The American memorandum for the record says that Amit told him Israel's mobilization of about 100,000 people was straining the economy and that "time is very much against Israel." He called the Soviet claim of a planned Israeli attack on Syria a "sheer fabrication." He estimated about 4,000 casualties in a campaign in Sinai. McNamara promised to convey his views to the President. [cite:rs_cw6_frus19_d124]

Twenty-five years later Amit gave a fuller account. In 1992 he said that he had told McNamara he would personally recommend action, and that McNamara had replied, "the president knows that you are here." The contemporary American record notes no such exchange. [cite:rs_cw6_frus19_d124] The two are different kinds of evidence: a memorandum written at the time by the American side, and a recollection given a quarter of a century later by the Israeli participant. Neither can be checked against a third record from the sources here.

Johnson's letter, 3 June. On 3 June Johnson wrote to Eshkol. The United States, he said, was pursuing a declaration by the maritime powers on passage through Tiran. He repeated, in slightly different words from 26 May, that "Israel will not be alone unless it decides to go alone," and he urged Israel "not to make itself responsible for the initiation of hostilities." [cite:rs_cw6_lbj_3june] The same day, Laurens notes, Rusk sent a telegram describing an "apocalypse psychology" on both sides. [cite:rs_cw6_laurens_t]

The decision of 4 June. On 4 June the ministerial defence committee met with the rest of the government. The IDF and Defense Establishment Archives give the decision as one "to take military action to free Israel from the suffocating aggression grip tightening around it." [cite:rs_cw6_mod_going_to_war] The decision as the Ministry of Foreign Affairs published it is worded differently: it authorized "the Prime Minister and the Minister of Defence to take steps necessary for the protection of Israel." [cite:rs_cw6_mfa_4june] The historian Yaakov Lozowick, who read the Security Cabinet transcripts after their release (935 pages, covering 36 meetings from January to July 1967), writes that on 4 June the cabinet "directed the IDF to break the Arab choke ring" and left the details to Eshkol and Dayan. [cite:rs_cw6_lozowick]

On the vote, the records diverge. The IDF archives state that the decision was taken "by a majority of 18." [cite:rs_cw6_mod_going_to_war] Lozowick, reading the transcripts, gives no vote count and records no formal dissent; the two Mapam ministers, Barzilai and Bentov, still wanted a final message sent to the great powers first. [cite:rs_cw6_lozowick] The archive's phrase is not explained in the sources here, and the transcripts as Lozowick reads them record no division. The count remains open.

Did Israel face an imminent attack? This is the first and largest of the disputes about these thirteen days. The case that it did rests on documents of its own. Israeli ministers feared that they would be struck first; Tal quotes the fear in the words "If we will not be the first to strike, Nasser will eliminate us." [cite:rs_cw6_tal_t] The head of military intelligence warned that the Egyptian forces in Sinai had shifted to an offensive posture. [cite:rs_cw6_fanack_t] And Nasser had said in public, on 26 May, that Egypt's basic objective in the coming battle was to destroy Israel. [cite:rs_cw6_nasser_26may] Add the Egypt–Jordan pact, the departure of UNEF, and a mobilization that, by Amit's account, was straining the economy, and the strongest form of the Israeli case is that waiting was itself a risk the state could not take.

The case that it did not rests on other documents. American intelligence told Eban on 26 May that no attack was imminent, and that three intelligence groups judged the Egyptian deployments defensive. [cite:rs_cw6_frus19_d77] Rabin, on 22 May, saw no sign that Nasser intended war. [cite:rs_cw6_tal_t] Laurens and Tal read Nasser's conduct as deterrence and brinkmanship, not a plan to attack. [cite:rs_cw6_laurens_t] [cite:rs_cw6_tal_t] On this view the danger was real but not imminent. Laurens's own conclusion, drawing on Rusk's "apocalypse psychology," is that the war came from miscalculation on both sides, not from a deliberate trap laid by either. [cite:rs_cw6_laurens_t] The documents support both readings in part. They show that Israel's government believed itself in danger, and that the American government, on its own intelligence, did not believe an Egyptian attack was imminent. Which judgment was correct is not something the record of 22 May to 4 June can settle.

Did Washington give a "green light"? The written American record is cautionary throughout. Johnson's words of 26 May and his letter of 3 June both told Israel not to begin hostilities and tied American action to Congress and, by 3 June, to a declaration by the maritime powers. [cite:rs_cw6_frus19_d77] [cite:rs_cw6_lbj_3june] Against that stand Amit's 1992 account of his meeting with McNamara, and the historians cited by Elbahtimy, who speak of an "amber" light given during Amit's visit of 1 June. [cite:rs_cw6_frus19_d124] [cite:rs_cw6_elbahtimy_t] The contemporary memorandum of that meeting records McNamara promising only to convey Amit's views. [cite:rs_cw6_frus19_d124] The documents show what Washington wrote; what Israel's leaders understood from what was said but not written down is the question the "amber light" reading addresses, and the record here does not answer it.

What the record does not settle. Several points remain open. Whether the Strait of Tiran was closed in practice, as opposed to by announcement, is disputed between Nasser's own words and the Library of Congress study. How many ministers voted for the decision of 4 June is given as "a majority of 18" in one archive and not at all in the transcripts as Lozowick reads them. What McNamara said to Amit beyond what the American memorandum records rests on a single later recollection. Whether Egypt's leaders meant to attack is contested between their public words, which spoke of destroying Israel, and the assessments of American intelligence, which found their deployment defensive.

That is where this volume ends. What followed is told in [scene:s12|the Six-Day War]; the question of who fired first, and how it was reported, in [scene:iaa_s04|who fired first].

books.title: The Divine 3+1
books.subtitle: The 3 Parents of Israel
books.intro:
This volume asks a question that circulates widely and is rarely tested: whether three cities that do not run like ordinary cities, the City of London, Vatican City and Washington, DC, together brought a fourth sovereign, the State of Israel, into being. Its title states the claim as its author holds it. Its method is to test that claim city by city, against the documents, and to report what survives.

Each city is assigned the function it is said to have performed: London finance, Rome theology, Washington force. Each is examined first as an institution, how it is governed and how it differs from every other powerful city, and then as an actor, through what its institutions supplied to the Zionist movement and the state and what they withheld. Each part ends with the same test and a dated verdict. A fifth part examines the child itself, the government of Israel, and a sixth sets the three verdicts side by side.

The volume builds on the earlier books of this library and on the newer research gathered since. Where it repeats an earlier finding it links to it; where newer sources correct one, it says so. It does not assume that the three cities acted together, and it does not assume that they did not. It reports what the documents show, names what they leave open, and keeps the reader able to check every claim against its source.

chapters.label: Part One
chapters.title: Not Ordinary Cities
chapters.span: Sovereignty, status and what a parent is
chapters.intro: Before any of the three cities can be tested as a parent of Israel, the reader needs to know what each of them is. The popular story calls all three "sovereign city-states" and moves on. The record does not allow that shortcut. One of the three is a sovereign state, one is a privileged local authority, and one is a federal district with less self-government than an ordinary American city. Part One sets out the tests by which lawyers and political scientists decide what counts as sovereignty, applies them to the three cities and to Israel, compares the cities side by side on the points that bear on power, and then defines the test that each of the following parts will apply: what a "parent" is, which function each city is said to have performed, and what kind of document would prove or disprove it.
chapters.outro:
Part One has fixed the terms. Of the three cities, only Vatican City is a sovereign state, and only since 1929; its foreign relations belong to the Holy See, a church authority recognized by 184 states. [cite:dv1_wiki_vatican] [cite:dv1_dfat_holysee] The City of London is a local authority with privileges that Parliament preserves and could remove, down to its own police force. [cite:dv1_wiki_city] [cite:dv1_police_act_1996] The District of Columbia is governed in the last resort by Congress, which reviews its laws and approves its budget. [cite:dv1_conan_dc] [cite:dv1_crs_dc_homerule] Israel, the fourth, is a state under the Montevideo test in its own right, and under that convention its existence does not depend on any other state's recognition. [cite:dv1_montevideo]

What is settled, then, is that the power the three names stand for lies mostly outside the three cities themselves: in the London market and the British state, in the Holy See, and in the federal government of the United States. What is contested is whether each of those powers acted as a parent, and in which years. What the record leaves open, so far, is whether any of them coordinated with the others. Each part that follows applies the same five-step test, beginning with [scene:dv2_square_mile|the Square Mile].

sections.h: What a Sovereign Is, and Why the Word Misleads
sections.html:
The claim this volume examines is usually told with one word doing most of the work. The City of London, Vatican City and Washington, DC are said to be three "sovereign" cities, standing apart from the countries around them, and Israel is said to be a fourth sovereign they brought into being. Before the record of any of the four can be weighed, the word has to be pinned down, because it means several different things, and the popular story moves between them without saying so. A city can be independent of the country around it in law, in practice, in money or in name, and these are not the same. This section sets out the two standard ways of testing sovereignty and applies them to each of the four places, so that the rest of the volume can say precisely which kind of independence each one has.

The legal test. The most widely cited legal definition of a state comes from the Montevideo Convention on the Rights and Duties of States, signed on 26 December 1933 by the states of the Americas. Its first article says that a state, as a person of international law, should possess four things: a permanent population, a defined territory, a government, and the capacity to enter into relations with other states. [cite:dv1_montevideo] Two further articles matter for this volume. Article 3 says that the political existence of a state is independent of recognition by other states, and Article 8 says that no state has the right to intervene in the internal or external affairs of another. [cite:dv1_montevideo] The convention was a regional treaty, and its definition has been criticized and refined since, but its four criteria remain the usual starting point when lawyers ask whether a place is a state.

The political test. The second way of testing comes from political science, and it is more skeptical. In Sovereignty: Organized Hypocrisy (1999) the political scientist Stephen Krasner argued that states have never been as sovereign as the textbooks suppose. Rulers, in his account, mainly want to stay in power, and differences of power and interest explain how states behave better than international norms do. He called the result "organized hypocrisy": norms of sovereignty that are long-standing, widely professed and frequently violated. [cite:dv1_princeton_krasner] Krasner also separated the word into four meanings. Domestic sovereignty is exclusive legal authority within a territory. Interdependence sovereignty is the capacity to control what flows across a border, such as money, goods and people. International legal sovereignty is recognition by other states as a juridically independent entity. Westphalian sovereignty is the exclusion of outside powers from a country's own structures of authority. [cite:dv1_holsti_review] A place can have one of these and lack the others.

Krasner's four meanings are the right tool for this volume because each of the three cities is famous for one kind of independence and lacks the rest, and because the fourth sovereign, Israel, has been argued over in precisely his terms: recognized in law by most states, dependent on outside support in ways critics call a loss of independence. The four tests below are applied in that spirit, as questions rather than verdicts.

The City of London fails the legal test outright. It has a small permanent population, a defined territory and a government, but it has no capacity to enter into relations with other states, and its law is made for it by the Parliament of the United Kingdom. [cite:dv1_wiki_city] Its independence is of a different and older kind. Its privileges were granted by royal charter and confirmed by custom, and later Acts of Parliament preserved them by express exception, as [scene:bc_s01|the library's first study of the City] and [scene:dv2_square_mile|Part Two of this volume] show. In Krasner's terms it holds a fragment of domestic authority within its square mile and none of the other three.

Vatican City passes every test, but only from 1929.
