The Lateran Treaty, signed on 11 February 1929 and in force from 7 June that year, created a sovereign enclave inside Rome, and it is today an elective absolute monarchy in which the pope holds executive, legislative and judicial power. [cite:dv1_wiki_vatican] Its foreign relations are conducted not by the city but by the Holy See, the pope's authority over the Catholic Church, which is a separate legal person and has full diplomatic relations with 184 states, the European Union and the Order of Malta. [cite:dv1_dfat_holysee] That distinction, between a city of a few hundred residents and a church authority with a worldwide reach, is the most important one in this volume's part on Rome.

The District of Columbia is the reverse of a sovereign city. The Constitution gives Congress power "to exercise exclusive Legislation in all Cases whatsoever" over the federal district, and Congress holds over it the combined powers of a local and a national legislature. [cite:dv1_conan_dc] The district's independence is from any one of the states, which is why it was created, not from the federal government, which governs it. The power associated with Washington in this volume does not belong to the district at all. It belongs to the federal government that sits there.

Israel, the fourth, meets the legal test as a matter of record. It declared its independence on 14 May 1948, was recognized by the United States within minutes and by the Soviet Union within days, and was admitted to the United Nations on 11 May 1949. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] [cite:wiki_soviet_arab_israeli] [cite:rs_cw1_iranica_israel] Under Article 3 of the Montevideo Convention its existence as a state does not depend on any other state's recognition, a principle that cuts both ways in this volume: it means that Israel's statehood is not in law a gift from its "parents," and it also means that the parents' recognition, money and protection have to be weighed as political facts rather than legal ones. [cite:dv1_montevideo]

The result of these tests is the frame for everything that follows. Only two of the four places are sovereign states, Vatican City and Israel. The other two are cities whose names stand for something larger: the City of London for the financial market and the British state around it, and Washington for the government of the United States. The volume therefore asks, in each part, not what a "sovereign city" did, but what the institutions behind each name did, and it tests each claim against the documents. [scene:bc_s06|The library's earlier examination of the three-enclaves claim] found no documented coordination among the three. This volume does not assume the opposite. It asks a narrower question, city by city: what each one supplied to the making of the fourth.

Two limits on this section should be stated. The Montevideo definition is a treaty among American states and is widely used rather than universally binding, and the meaning of sovereignty is disputed among scholars in ways this section does not try to settle. Krasner's account is one influential argument among several, presented here through his publisher's summary and a scholarly review rather than a full reading of the book. Neither limit changes the plain legal facts on which the comparison rests.

sections.h: Three Cities Side by Side
sections.html:
The three cities in this volume are usually described together, as if they were the same kind of place. Set side by side, they turn out to have almost nothing in common except an unusual relationship with the country around them. One is a medieval corporation with fewer residents than a small town and one of the largest financial markets in the world inside its boundary. One is the smallest state on earth, the seat of the Catholic Church's central government. One is a federal district of nearly seven hundred thousand people, governed in the last resort by a legislature its residents do not vote for. This section compares them on the points that matter for the question of power: what each one is in law, how large it is, who governs it, who polices it, who votes, and who speaks for it abroad.

The City of London. The City covers 1.12 square miles and had 8,583 residents at the 2021 census. It is surrounded by Greater London but remains separate from the London boroughs, and as a ceremonial county it is unique in one small way: its Commission of Lieutenancy is headed by the Lord Mayor rather than by a Lord-Lieutenant appointed by the Crown. [cite:dv1_wiki_city] Inside its boundary lie the Inner Temple and the Middle Temple, two of the few surviving "liberties," enclaves treated as independent and outside any parish. [cite:dv1_wiki_city] The City elects its own council and its own Lord Mayor, and it is one of very few places in Britain where businesses as well as residents vote; Part Two sets out how that franchise works and how large it is. [cite:dv2_wiki_corporation]

The City also has its own police force, separate from London's Metropolitan Police. The Police Act 1996 lists "the City of London police area" as one of the police areas of England and Wales and provides that the Common Council "is to continue to be the police authority" for it. The Common Council must issue a policing plan before each financial year, and the Commissioner of Police for the City of London must report to it. [cite:dv1_police_act_1996] This is the clearest single example of how the City differs from an ordinary London borough. It is also a reminder of where the difference comes from: the force exists and answers to the Common Council because an Act of Parliament says so, and Parliament can change the arrangement. [cite:dv1_police_act_1996]

Vatican City. Vatican City is the smallest state in the world, and even its size is recorded two ways. Some references give 49 hectares (0.49 square kilometers) and others 44 hectares (109 acres); the difference has been traced to an atlas of 1930 that listed 44 hectares and was corrected to 49 in 1945 and 1946. [cite:dv1_wiki_vatican] Both figures are in circulation, and this volume records both. In 2024 the city had 882 residents of any citizenship, and a further 372 Vatican citizens, mostly diplomats and cardinals, lived elsewhere. [cite:dv1_wiki_vatican]

The city is an elective absolute monarchy. The pope holds all executive, legislative and judicial power, and is chosen for life by the cardinals in conclave; the present pope, Leo XIV, was elected on 8 May 2025. [cite:dv1_wiki_vatican] Its security is kept by two bodies. The Corps of Gendarmerie, founded by Pope Pius VII in 1816, numbered 122 sworn members in 2022 and handles policing, border and traffic control and criminal investigation under the Governorate of the Vatican City State; it also hosts Interpol's national bureau for the city. [cite:dv1_wiki_gendarmerie] The Pontifical Swiss Guard, which dates its founding to 22 January 1506, was enlarged from 110 to 135 members in 2019, and recruits only unmarried Catholic Swiss men who have completed Swiss military training. [cite:dv1_wiki_swissguard] Between them the two bodies number about 257 people, set against 882 residents; the two are not the same population, but the comparison gives a rough sense of scale.

The city's foreign relations are not its own. They are conducted by the Holy See, the authority the pope holds over the Catholic Church, which is a separate subject of international law from the territory over which it has direct sovereignty. [cite:dv1_dfat_holysee] The Holy See has full diplomatic relations with 184 states, as well as the European Union and the Order of Malta. It has been a permanent observer state at the United Nations since 6 April 1964 and has chosen not to seek membership, while belonging in its own right to several of the UN's specialized agencies, among them the World Intellectual Property Organization, the International Telecommunication Union and the Universal Postal Union. [cite:dv1_dfat_holysee] [cite:dv1_wiki_holysee_un] When this volume says "Rome" or "the Vatican" acted toward Palestine or Israel, it nearly always means the Holy See, not the city, and nearly always means acts that predate the city's existence or reach far beyond it.

The District of Columbia. The district had an estimated 693,645 residents on 1 July 2025, on 61.13 square miles of land. [cite:dv1_census_dc] Its legal basis is a single clause of the Constitution, which gives Congress power "to exercise exclusive Legislation in all Cases whatsoever" over a district "not exceeding ten Miles square" ceded by particular states to become the seat of government. [cite:dv1_conan_dc] Over that district Congress holds the powers of both a local and a national legislature. It is not required to give the district an elected government, and it is not forbidden to delegate its powers to one. [cite:dv1_conan_dc]

The district's own government has risen and fallen with Congress's choices. An elected mayor governed from 1820; elected government ended after financial scandals in 1874; a commission appointed by the President ruled from 1878, and an appointed mayor-commissioner and council from 1967. [cite:dv1_conan_dc] The present arrangement rests on the Home Rule Act, approved on 24 December 1973, which provided for an elected mayor and council. [cite:dv1_crs_dc_homerule] It came with conditions that no state government faces. Most of the council's laws take effect only after lying before Congress for thirty days in session, and laws on crime and criminal procedure for sixty. All of the district's spending must pass through the federal appropriations process. [cite:dv1_crs_dc_homerule] Congress has used its formal veto sparingly, nullifying district laws through disapproval resolutions four times, in respect of acts of 1979, 1981 and 1990 and, most recently, the Revised Criminal Code Act, disapproved by a resolution signed on 20 March 2023, and has more often shaped the district's affairs through riders attached to appropriations bills. [cite:dv1_crs_dc_homerule] [cite:dv1_crs_in12122] That count is as of the Congressional Research Service's April 2023 update. District residents vote for President under the Twenty-third Amendment and elect a delegate to Congress who cannot vote on the floor; an amendment to give them full representation failed to win ratification. [cite:dv1_conan_dc]

What the comparison shows. The three cities are unusual in three opposite directions. The City of London has more self-government than its size would suggest, kept by privilege and statute rather than by sovereignty. Vatican City has full sovereignty over almost no territory, and its significance lies in the church authority it houses rather than the ground it covers. The District of Columbia has less self-government than any comparable American city, because it was designed to belong to the federal government rather than to any state. The popular story that groups them as three sovereign city-states treats these three different kinds of strangeness as one. They are not one, and the power that each name stands for, the London market and the British state, the Holy See, and the government of the United States, has to be traced separately. That is the plan of the three parts that follow.

A few points in the comparison rest on reference summaries rather than primary documents, and they are marked as such in the research file: the Vatican's area and residents, the size of its two security bodies, and the City's liberties. [cite:dv1_wiki_vatican] [cite:dv1_wiki_gendarmerie] [cite:dv1_wiki_swissguard] [cite:dv1_wiki_city] The district's figures come from the Census Bureau and the Congressional Research Service, and the City's police arrangements from the text of the statute. [cite:dv1_census_dc] [cite:dv1_crs_dc_homerule] [cite:dv1_police_act_1996] The sources used here do not describe the District's police force or its chain of command, and the table says only what they support.

sections.h: Three Functions, One Test
sections.html:
A volume that calls three cities the parents of a state owes the reader a definition of the word. Without one, any contact between a city's institutions and the Zionist movement or the State of Israel can be counted as parenthood, and the claim becomes impossible to test because nothing could count against it. This section sets out the definition the volume uses, the three functions it assigns to the three cities, the kinds of document that would count as evidence for each, and the single test that each city's part ends with. It also states, in its strongest form, the hypothesis about Rome that gives this volume its sharpest question.

What a parent is here. In this volume a parent is a power that supplied something the Jewish national home, and later the State of Israel, could not have had without it, at a time when no one else was supplying it. Three parts of that definition do the work. The thing supplied must be specific and documented: a letter, a law, a loan, a vote, a shipment. It must have been needed: something the movement or the state could not readily have found elsewhere. And it must be dated, because the same power can be indispensable in one decade and obstructive in the next, as Part Two shows for London. [scene:dv2_parent_test|London's test] is the model for the others.

Three functions. Each of the three cities is assigned one function, because each stands, in the popular telling, for one kind of power.

London stands for finance: money, credit, and the legal and institutional forms through which money moves. Evidence for this function would be companies chartered there, loans raised there, currency issued or reserves held there, and the acts of the government seated there that gave the movement a legal frame in which its money could work.

Rome stands for theology: the religious ideas that gave a political project legitimacy in the eyes of Christians, and the institutional decisions of the Catholic Church about the Jewish people, the Holy Land and the state. Evidence for this function would be papal and curial acts, the Holy See's diplomatic record, doctrinal statements, and the documented reception of those statements by governments and believers. Because Christian Zionism, the movement that gave Zionism its broadest Christian support, grew mainly out of Protestant theology, the part on Rome has to ask whose theology did the parenting, not only what the Vatican said. [cite:wiki_christian_zionism]

Washington stands for force: arms, money for arms, diplomatic protection and recognition. Evidence for this function would be the acts of the United States government: recognition, votes and vetoes at the United Nations, aid agreements, appropriations, and arms transfers, each dated and sourced.

The fourth step matters most. The test is built to look as hard for what a city withheld as for what it gave. That is not a gesture of balance. It is the only way to tell a parent from a power that happened to share some interests with the movement for a time. A city whose institutions supplied something indispensable and never opposed the project would be a parent in the fullest sense. A city that supplied something and later fought the project, as London did after 1939, is a parent of a more limited kind. And a city whose documented acts were mainly opposition would not be a parent at all, unless the opposition can be shown to have been a cover.

The front hypothesis. That last possibility is the subject of this volume's hardest chapter. The publicly documented record of the Holy See toward Zionism, as the earlier volumes of this library show, is largely one of refusal. In January 1904, according to Herzl's diary, Pius X told him that he could not support Zionism, because the Jews had not recognized Christ; in April 1949 Pius XII asked the world's Catholics to press for an international status for Jerusalem; and the Holy See did not recognize the State of Israel until it signed the Fundamental Agreement on 30 December 1993. [cite:dv1_ej_piusx] [cite:dv1_rnc_1949] [cite:jcpa_vatican_israel_recognition] The hypothesis this volume tests is that this refusal was a public facade: that the Holy See was connected to the project from the start, and kept its support out of view so that no one would question it. It is a serious hypothesis about how power behaves, and it is stated here in its strongest form so that it can be tested fairly.

A hypothesis of this kind makes predictions, and that is what allows it to be tested. If the refusal was a front, the private record should contradict the public one: there should be documents in which papal diplomats encouraged what they publicly opposed, money or favors moving from the Holy See to the movement, or a pattern in which public opposition never cost the movement anything it needed. If the refusal was genuine, the private record should match the public one, and the opposition should have been costly: it should have spent the Holy See's own influence, provoked complaint from Zionist leaders, and left traces in the archives of governments the Holy See lobbied. The archives of Pius XII's pontificate, opened to researchers in 2020, are the most important new source on this question, [cite:wiki_pius_xii_holocaust] and Part Three draws on what has been published from them.

One piece of evidence often cited for the hypothesis needs to be placed correctly from the start. The documented loans between the papacy and the Rothschild houses in the nineteenth century ran from the bankers to the Pope, not the other way, beginning with the loan agreed in 1831 with the Papal States. [cite:wiki_rothschild_loans_holy_see] They show a financial relationship between a Jewish banking family and the papal government half a century before political Zionism existed. Whether that relationship bears on the Holy See's later conduct toward Zionism is one of the questions Part Three takes up; [scene:bc_s03|the library's account of the papal loans] sets out what is known about them and how thin the sourcing is.

What the test does not assume. The test is applied to each city on its own evidence. It does not assume that the three cities coordinated, and it does not assume that they did not. If documents show coordination, the composite part of this volume will report them. [scene:bc_s06|The library's earlier examination of the three-enclaves claim] found none, and the parts that follow begin from that finding without treating it as final. What the volume will not do is infer coordination from parallel interests. Three governments can each support the same outcome for reasons of their own, and the record of such convergence is a finding in its own right, not evidence of a single hand.

Some claims about the three cities are kept out of this volume unless new documents support them, because the earlier book from which it grows examined them and found no record. They include the claim that the Orsini family descends from the biblical Nimrod, the claim that an Act of Congress of 1871 turned the United States into a corporation, the reading of the District of Columbia's flag as an emblem of the three cities, the claim that the Rockefeller and Rothschild fortunes are one, and the claim that a single coordinated group directs all three cities. Each is named so that the reader knows it was considered and why it is absent.

The test is the same in every part, and so is its last question. For London the answer is already in: a financial and imperial parent, through the British state and the London market rather than the City Corporation, decisive between 1917 and 1939 and then withdrawing. Rome and Washington are tested in the same way, and the fourth sovereign, the child, is examined in its own right before the volume sets the three verdicts side by side.

chapters.label: Part Two
chapters.title: London: The Financial Parent
chapters.intro:
London is the first of the three cities this volume examines, and the one whose part in the making of Israel is easiest to document. The difficulty is not finding London in the record. It is deciding which London is meant. The word covers at least four different things: a medieval corporation that governs one square mile, a financial market that has outgrown that square mile many times over, the private banking houses that did business inside it, and the British state that sat a mile and a half to the west, in Whitehall and Westminster. Each of the four did something different, and the familiar claim that "the City of London" created Israel runs them together.

This part takes them apart. It begins with the Corporation itself: its charters, its government, its unusual electorate and its officer in Parliament, so that the reader knows exactly what kind of body it is and what kind of power it holds. It then turns to the money: the Bank of England, the chartered companies of empire, and the scale of London's markets today. The Rothschild house appears where the documents place it, inside the City's institutions and on the floor of its gold market. Then come the financial companies of the Zionist movement, which were registered in London, and the plumbing of Mandate Palestine, whose currency was managed and whose reserves were held there. Only after all of that does the part reach the British state's decisions, from Palmerston to Balfour to the White Paper of 1939 and the grudging recognition of 1949.

The question the part answers is the one in this volume's title. In what sense, if any, was London a parent of the State of Israel, and through which of its institutions? The answer, set out in the closing parent test, is that London was a parent in a specific and documented way, and that the familiar version of the claim points at the wrong building.
chapters.outro:
Part Two set out to find London in the making of Israel, and found four Londons, each with its own record.

The Corporation of the City of London is a real and unusual body. It holds its rights by charter and by prescription older than Parliament's reforms, it was left untouched in 1835, it gives businesses a vote, and it keeps an officer, the Remembrancer, who watches Parliament from the under-gallery on its behalf. [cite:dv2_lma_william] [cite:dv2_col_mayoralty] [cite:dv2_wiki_remembrancer] Its power is the power of a privileged local authority and a voice for the finance industry. It is not sovereign, and in the decisions that produced a Jewish national home and then a state it does not appear. [cite:wb_jc_rothschild2017]

The London market is a different and much larger thing: the state's bank since 1694, the home of chartered companies that once ruled a subcontinent, and today the largest center of currency trading in the world, ringed by offshore jurisdictions whose rules an advocacy group and the British tax authority describe very differently. [cite:rs_rd0_boe_museum] [cite:dv2_wiki_eic] [cite:dv2_boe_triennial_2025] [cite:dv2_ferret_cthi_2024] Its power is to lend, clear, price and give legal form, and the Zionist movement used it: a bank incorporated there in 1899, a land fund in 1907, a fundraising arm founded there in 1920. [cite:jct_wiki] [cite:dv2_wiki_jnf] [cite:keren_hayesod_wiki]

The Rothschild house stood inside the City's institutions, won its seat in Parliament for the City in 1858 after a long fight against a Christian oath, chaired the gold fix for eighty-five years, and received the Balfour letter as the movement's address in London. [cite:dv2_wiki_lionel] [cite:dv2_ra_goldfix] [cite:wb_bl_addms41178] And the British state, in Whitehall, issued the promise, held the Mandate, managed the country's money through a London board, and then, from 1939, restricted, abstained, cut the money off and recognized the new state late. [cite:rs_a22_frus] [cite:dv2_unccp_assets] [cite:rs_rd4_wp_cojs_text] [cite:rs_rd5_langham_exit]

What is settled, then, is that London was a parent, and which London it was: the British government and the legal and financial machinery of the London market, decisively between 1917 and 1939. What is contested, or simply unrecorded in the sources used here, is the founders' reason for choosing English incorporation, the fate of the blocked balances, and how much of the movement's money passed through London rather than New York. What the record rules out is the story of a sovereign Square Mile directing the whole. The next part turns to the second parent, a city that is a sovereign state, and to the harder question this volume has promised to test: whether the Holy See's public refusal to support a Jewish state was the whole of its record, or a front for something else.

sections.h: A Corporation Older Than the Kingdom It Sits In
sections.html:
The oldest document in the City of London's keeping is a strip of vellum about six inches long and an inch and a half wide. It was written in 1067, a few months after William of Normandy was crowned in Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day 1066, and it was written in Old English rather than in the conqueror's own Norman French. It is addressed to "William the bishop and Godfrey the portreeve and all the burgesses within London both French and English." [cite:dv2_lma_william] It has been in the City's archive continuously ever since, and it is the place to begin, because it shows something that the rest of the City's history repeats. The charter granted nothing new. It confirmed what the citizens already had: that they were "law-worthy, as you were in the days of King Edward," that every child would be his father's heir, and that the king would not suffer any person to do them wrong. [cite:dv2_lma_william] The new king was not creating London's liberties. He was promising not to take them away.

That pattern, a power that already existed being recognized and preserved by each new authority, is the core of what makes the City unusual. It also explains why the City is so often misdescribed. A body whose privileges were confirmed by a conqueror, and later by kings and Parliaments, can look from a distance like a body that stands above them. The documents show the opposite relationship, and they show it repeatedly.

The mayoralty came next. The first recorded Mayor of London was Henry Fitz-Ailwyn, in 1189. [cite:dv2_col_mayoralty] Before him, the Crown appointed the sheriffs who answered for the City; until 1199 they were royal appointments, and after the creation of the mayoralty they became subordinate to the Mayor. [cite:dv2_gresham_travers_2013] In 1215 the City gained the right that defined its later independence. King John granted it a charter, early in May of that year, allowing the citizens to elect their own Mayor. The legal historian Anthony Arlidge notes that John asked for no payment for it. [cite:dv2_col_mayoralty] [cite:dv2_gresham_arlidge_2015]

The timing mattered. John was then at war with his own barons, and he was trying to keep the capital on his side. He failed. The rebels reached London's walls on 17 May 1215, and the gates were opened to them. The chronicler Roger of Wendover wrote that the rich citizens favored the rebels while the poor were afraid to speak against them. [cite:dv2_gresham_arlidge_2015] On 15 June 1215, at Runnymede near Windsor, the king sealed Magna Carta; under the peace the barons were to hand London back by 15 August, and they refused. [cite:dv2_wiki_magna_carta] The charter's thirteenth clause guaranteed the City of London its ancient liberties and free customs. [cite:dv2_gresham_arlidge_2015] When the charter was reissued and confirmed in 1297, in the version now held by the United States National Archives, the provision appeared as clause 9: "The city of London is to have all its ancient liberties and customs." [cite:dv2_nara_mc1297] Who the Mayor was that summer is recorded two ways. Arlidge identifies the Mayor who had sided with the rebels as probably Serlo the mercer, while the standard list of the twenty-five barons charged with enforcing the charter includes "William Hardell, Mayor of the City of London." [cite:dv2_gresham_arlidge_2015] [cite:dv2_wiki_magna_carta] The sources used here do not reconcile the two. Either way, the City's chief officer stood with the barons against the king.

The office acquired its grander title slowly. "Dominus major" appears in thirteenth-century Latin, "Lord Mair" in English in 1414, and the prefix "Right Honourable" was in use by the sixteenth century. Some seven hundred men and two women have held it, almost always for a single year. [cite:dv2_col_mayoralty] The current holder, Dame Susan Langley, is the 697th. [cite:dv2_wci_lordmayor]

Behind the mayoralty stood the elected bodies. Aldermen consulted the citizens of their wards from the thirteenth century. Regular meetings of a common council began in 1376, and the council has been elected since 1384. [cite:dv2_gresham_travers_2013] By the time England had a Parliament in anything like its modern form, the City already had a government with elected members, its own officers and its own courts.

What the City does not have is a founding document. No charter survives that first created the Corporation, and the law treats it as incorporated "by prescription": it exists because it has always existed, and its legal existence has been continuous for centuries. [cite:dv2_wiki_corporation] One consequence is unusual in British public law. The Corporation can alter its own constitution by an Act of its own Common Council. [cite:dv2_wiki_corporation] Another followed in 1835. That year Parliament passed the Municipal Corporations Act, which swept away and rebuilt the old closed corporations of England's towns. The City was left out. It was not reformed then. [cite:dv2_wiki_corporation]

The result is a local authority whose shape is medieval. The City covers 1.12 square miles, and at the 2021 census 8,583 people lived there. [cite:dv1_wiki_city] It is surrounded on every side by Greater London, but it is not one of Greater London's boroughs, and it remains separate from them. It is a ceremonial county in its own right, and where every other county has a Lord-Lieutenant representing the Crown, the City has a Commission of Lieutenancy headed by the Lord Mayor. [cite:dv1_wiki_city] Inside its boundaries sit two smaller anomalies, the Inner Temple and the Middle Temple. They are among the few surviving "liberties," treated as independent enclaves outside any parish, and the Corporation is not given general authority over them, although many of its statutory functions reach into them. [cite:dv1_wiki_city] [cite:dv2_wiki_corporation] An enclave within an enclave is about as far as English local government goes in the direction of a separate jurisdiction.

It is not far enough to make a state. The popular claim, examined in an earlier volume of this library, holds that the City is a sovereign city-state beyond the reach of Parliament and the Crown. [scene:bc_s01|The Square Mile] sets out why the documents do not support it, and [scene:bc_s06|Three enclaves, one trope] shows how the claim travels. The short version is visible in the City's own statute book. When the City wanted to reform its own elections in 2002, it had to go to Parliament, and the preamble of the Act that resulted records, in the standard wording of a private Act, that its objects "cannot be attained without the authority of Parliament." [cite:dv2_wiki_remembrancer] A sovereign does not ask another legislature for permission to change its franchise. The Corporation does, and has done so for centuries. Its liberties survive because Parliament keeps choosing to preserve them, usually by writing an express exception for the City into each new Act. [cite:wiki_city_of_london_corporation]

The four standard tests of statehood, set out in the Montevideo Convention of 1933, are a permanent population, a defined territory, a government, and the capacity to enter into relations with other states. [cite:dv1_montevideo] The City has the first three in miniature. It does not have the fourth. It sends no ambassadors and receives none, signs no treaties, and holds no seat in any international body. What it has instead is something the Convention does not measure: a privileged and formal position inside the government of a state that does all of those things. That position, and the people who fill it, are the subject of the next two sections.

The record leaves some things unsettled. The sources used here give the 1067 charter's date and contents but not the circumstances of its drafting, and they date King John's charter only to "early May" 1215, without resolving the exact day. The claim that the City is older than Parliament is true in the sense set out above, that the City had elected councils before Parliament took its modern form; it should not be stretched into a claim that the City preceded English law or the Crown, which it did not.

sections.h: How the Square Mile Governs Itself
sections.html:
Most of the City of London's government looks, at first sight, like any British local council. It collects business rates, manages social housing, cleans the streets and carries out the functions of a London borough under the same statutes. [cite:dv2_wiki_corporation] [cite:dv2_col_keyfacts] The differences lie in who sits on its councils, how they get there, and what else the Corporation does with the wealth and standing it has accumulated over eight centuries. This section takes those in turn: the offices, the electorate, and the reach.

The offices. At the top is the Lord Mayor, who serves a one-year term and chairs both of the City's governing courts. Nobody can become Lord Mayor without first having been elected an Alderman and then having served as one of the City's two Sheriffs. [cite:dv2_gresham_travers_2013] The City is divided into 25 wards. Each ward elects one Alderman for a six-year term, and together they form the Court of Aldermen. The ward residents and business voters also elect the 100 members of the Court of Common Council, the main legislative and executive body, which sits with the Aldermen and holds powers similar to those of a London borough council. Common Council elections take place every four years, and they have traditionally not been fought on party lines. [cite:dv2_gresham_travers_2013]

The two Sheriffs and the Lord Mayor are not chosen by the ward electorate at all. They are chosen by the liverymen of the City's livery companies, the descendants of its medieval craft and trade guilds. The liverymen elect the Sheriffs each Midsummer Day, and each September they meet in Common Hall to choose the next Lord Mayor from among the eligible Aldermen, usually by acclamation, though a contested vote is possible. Travers counted 108 livery companies when he described the system in 2013. [cite:dv2_gresham_travers_2013] [cite:dv2_wci_lordmayor] The Corporation's most visible office, in other words, is filled through a franchise that has no counterpart anywhere else in British public life: membership of a guild.

The Lord Mayor's year is spent to a large extent representing the City at home and abroad. Day-to-day political leadership is usually associated instead with the chairman of the Policy and Resources Committee, who is often described as the Corporation's de facto political leader and who represents the City among the leaders of London's councils. According to the sources consulted for this book, Chris Hayward has held the post since 5 May 2022, succeeding Catherine McGuinness. [cite:dv2_wiki_corporation]

The electorate. The feature of the City's government that most surprises outsiders is who gets to vote for it. In every other British local election, the right to vote follows residence. Businesses voted in local elections elsewhere too until 1969, when that franchise was abolished everywhere except here. [cite:dv2_wiki_corporation] In the City it was not only kept but widened. The City of London (Ward Elections) Act 2002 "greatly increased the business franchise," and a reform taking effect in 2003 redrew the wards to give the residential areas more representation while extending the business vote at the same time. [cite:dv2_wiki_corporation] [cite:dv2_gresham_travers_2013]

The rule is set by the size of the workforce. A business based in the City may appoint one of its employees as a voter for every five staff, up to ten voters, and one further voter for every fifty staff beyond that. Residents each have one vote. [cite:dv2_wiki_2025_election] The appointed voters have to meet conditions of service in the City, and the qualifying date is 1 September of the election year. [cite:dv2_gresham_travers_2013] [cite:dv2_wiki_corporation]

The effect on the balance of the electorate is large, and the figures available come from sources of different kinds. A reference summary puts the business vote at about 24,000 in 2009, far above the number of resident voters. [cite:dv2_wiki_corporation] For 2013, the Green Party, which campaigns to abolish the business vote, put it at some 32,000 against about 9,000 resident votes; those are a campaigner's figures. [cite:greenparty_remembrancer_2013] The Corporation itself counts about 8,600 residents and 614,500 people working in the City, one in every 52 workers in the United Kingdom. [cite:dv2_col_keyfacts] The sources used for this book do not give the split between resident and business voters for the most recent election, and the reader should treat the 2009 and 2013 numbers as indications of scale rather than current counts.

That most recent election was held on 20 March 2025, for all 100 seats of the Court of Common Council. Forty-five of the hundred councillors were returned without a contest, in 14 of the 25 wards. Independents won 83 seats, Labour 7 and the local group Temple and Farringdon Together 10. Turnout, where there was a contest, ranged from 11 percent in Farringdon Without to 49 percent in Portsoken and Vintry. [cite:dv2_wiki_2025_election] Nearly half the governing council, in other words, was chosen without any vote being cast.

The reach. A body with that electorate also holds wealth and functions well beyond those of a council of 8,600 residents. One of its main funds, City's Cash, a private endowment built up over centuries, was long criticized for being kept out of public view, until the Corporation began publishing fuller accounts of it in 2012. In December 2012, after criticism of its lack of financial transparency, it disclosed that City's Cash held more than £1.3 billion; by March 2016 net assets were put at £2.3 billion. [cite:dv2_wiki_corporation] The Corporation reports property assets of about £3 billion across some 250 properties and spends about £130 million a year on heritage and culture. [cite:dv2_col_keyfacts]

Much of that reach lies outside the Square Mile. The Corporation manages about 11,000 acres of natural habitat in London and the Home Counties, including Hampstead Heath, Epping Forest and Burnham Beeches. [cite:dv2_col_keyfacts] [cite:dv2_wiki_corporation] It runs London's wholesale markets, which it says support 10,250 jobs and move a million tonnes of produce a year, and its Port Health Authority patrols 94 miles of the tidal Thames. [cite:dv2_col_keyfacts] It controls three independent schools and owns the Guildhall School of Music and Drama. [cite:dv2_wiki_corporation]

It also has its own police force. The Common Council is the police authority for the City, whose force is separate from London's Metropolitan Police. [cite:dv2_wiki_corporation] That small force has a national role far larger than its patch. Under an agreement with the Home Office, and with Home Office funding, the City of London Police is the National Lead Force for fraud: it sets the national strategy for policing fraud, coordinates fraud reporting across the country through Action Fraud, triages and allocates fraud cases nationally, and investigates the most significant and complex frauds. [cite:dv2_gov_nlf] It is also the National Police Chiefs' Council lead for economic, cyber and business crime. [cite:dv2_col_keyfacts] The force that polices the country's financial district also leads the country's response to financial crime.

The Corporation does not hide what it is for. Its own description of its purpose includes supporting the financial services industry and representing its interests. [cite:dv2_wiki_corporation] Each Lord Mayor serves as an international ambassador for the United Kingdom's financial and professional services, travelling abroad to represent the City. [cite:dv2_wci_lordmayor] Its critics read the same facts more darkly. The journalist George Monbiot argued that the Corporation's power helps to explain why the regulation of banks was scarcely better after the 2008 crash than before it. [cite:dv2_wiki_corporation] That is an argument, not a finding, and the sources used here do not measure the Corporation's effect on any particular piece of regulation.

What the record does establish is the shape of the arrangement. A local authority whose electorate is weighted toward the firms in its streets, which elects its figurehead through the guilds, which holds a large private endowment, which polices the nation's fraud, and which describes itself as an advocate for finance, sits at the center of one of the world's largest financial markets. None of that makes it a state. All of it makes it a very unusual kind of council, and it has one more feature that no other council in the country has: a permanent officer assigned to Parliament.

sections.h: The Remembrancer: The City's Officer in Parliament
sections.html:
On 6 February 1571 the Corporation of the City of London created a new office and gave it an old-fashioned name. The Remembrancer was to keep the City's important business "in remembrance." The first holder was Thomas Norton, and his original task was bookkeeping: bringing the Corporation's journals and records up to date. [cite:dv2_wiki_remembrancer] [cite:dv2_wanderer_remembrancer] Over the following centuries the office became something else. It is now the channel through which the Lord Mayor and the City deal with the Sovereign, the Royal Household and Parliament, and it serves as the City's chief of protocol. [cite:dv2_wiki_remembrancer] It is the most discussed of the City's institutions, because no other local authority in Britain has an officer whose permanent job is to watch Parliament on its behalf.

What the office does in Parliament is a matter of record. The Remembrancer is a parliamentary agent. The office monitors legislation, reports to the Corporation on bills that touch the City's interests, briefs members of Parliament, submits evidence to select committees, and drafts and promotes the Corporation's own private bills. [cite:dv2_wiki_remembrancer] [cite:dv2_wanderer_remembrancer] In 2011, according to reporting in The Guardian, the department had a budget of £6 million and employed six lawyers to scrutinize prospective legislation and give evidence to committees. [cite:dv2_wiki_remembrancer] The most recent holder recorded in the sources used here is Paul Double, the 45th Remembrancer, in post since 2003; in November 2022 he submitted the City of London (Markets) Bill to Parliament, to which the London Borough of Havering objected. [cite:dv2_wanderer_remembrancer]

Where the Remembrancer sits is another matter, and here the popular account and the record part company. A widely repeated claim holds that the Remembrancer has a seat on the floor of the House of Commons, beside or behind the Speaker's chair, the only person who is not a member allowed there. Versions of the claim have appeared in print, including in a textbook published in 2017, and an earlier volume of this library repeated it. [cite:dv2_wiki_remembrancer] [scene:bc_s01|The Square Mile] The House of Commons Commission has stated otherwise. The Remembrancer may watch proceedings from the visitors' under-gallery, near the Serjeant at Arms, by the Speaker's permission and not by right; he has no access beyond the bar of the House, and none to the floor. [cite:dv2_wiki_remembrancer] [cite:dv2_wanderer_remembrancer] Not being a member, he can neither speak in debates nor vote. [cite:dv2_wanderer_remembrancer]

The same correction applies to a second part of the legend. The Remembrancer is notified of private bills that affect the City, as any affected party is. The office is not shown public bills before they are published. [cite:dv2_wiki_remembrancer] In 2013 the Green Party member of Parliament Caroline Lucas wrote to the Speaker, John Bercow, asking him to consider removing the Remembrancer from the floor of the House and to end claimed privileges of seeing draft legislation. [cite:dv2_wiki_remembrancer] Her letter is part of the record; so are the documents, set out below, that bear on the two privileges it described.

The correction does not make the office trivial. An officer with a budget of millions and a team of lawyers, whose only job is to track legislation for one client and to argue that client's case to members and committees, is a lobbyist, and a permanent one. George Monbiot described the Remembrancer in 2011 as "an official lobbyist." [cite:dv2_wiki_remembrancer] The author Nicholas Shaxson has called the office "the world's oldest institutional lobbyist." [cite:greenparty_remembrancer_2013] The difference from other lobbyists is not a privileged seat. It is age, continuity and institutional standing: an office that has been doing this work since 1571, on behalf of a body that is itself part of the state's local government.

The office's own history shows what that work has looked like when the City felt threatened. In 1854 it spent £2,750 on "private opposition" to a government bill. Between 1835 and 1875, by one account, its lobbying helped defeat bills and reports that would have reformed the City on at least twelve occasions. [cite:dv2_wanderer_remembrancer] In 1884 a government-backed bill to reform the government of London ran out of parliamentary time after a campaign largely run by the Remembrancer of the day, Gabriel Goldney, which cost £19,500. Goldney later admitted to a select committee that he had paid a go-between to have men break up meetings. [cite:dv2_wanderer_remembrancer] The office did not always win. In 1863 it failed to stop a bill letting the Metropolitan Board of Works drive Queen Victoria Street through the City's territory. And it has used the same machinery for ends few would object to: in 1878 the Epping Forest Bill it promoted passed Parliament, and the forest it protected is still managed by the Corporation today. [cite:dv2_wanderer_remembrancer] [cite:dv2_col_keyfacts]

What the record does not show should be stated as precisely. The sources used here describe the office's functions, its budget in one year, and several historical campaigns. They do not measure how often, in recent decades, its work has changed the text of a law, and they do not establish any role for the Remembrancer in British policy toward Palestine or Israel. The office's documented concern has been the City's own powers, privileges and property. Its importance to this volume is structural. It shows that the body which governs the country's financial district has, alone among British local authorities, a permanent and long-established channel to the legislature, and it shows that the channel has been used, when the City's privileges were at stake, with persistence and money. Whether that channel shaped any particular decision on finance is a question the documents leave open.

sections.h: The Money Machine: From the Bank of England to the Offshore Network
sections.html:
The Corporation governs one square mile. The financial market that grew up around it is a different thing, much larger and much less tidy, and it is this market, rather than the Corporation's council chambers, that gives "the City" its meaning in most sentences. To understand what London could do for a movement or a state in the twentieth century, and what it can do now, the reader needs a sense of how that market was built and how large it has become. This section follows four stages: the state's bank, the chartered companies of empire, the deregulation of 1986, and the offshore network that now surrounds the market.

The state's bank. The founding of the Bank of England in 1694 is told in full in [scene:rd0_bank1694|an earlier volume]. The essentials bear repeating because so much else rests on them. After Charles II's government stopped repaying its debts to London's goldsmith-bankers in 1672, the Crown could not easily borrow. When William III needed money for war with France, a scheme proposed by the Scottish merchant William Paterson raised £1.2 million from 1,268 subscribers in eleven days. The subscribers lent through a chartered company, the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, which received its Royal Charter on 27 July 1694 and was paid 8 percent interest by the government. [cite:rs_rd0_boe_museum] [cite:rs_rd0_boe_hf1970] [cite:dv2_dmo_boe] The arrangement turned a private loan into a permanent institution through which the state borrowed, and it made the City's lenders partners in the state's wars.

The partnership lasted two and a half centuries before the state took the Bank over. It was nationalised in 1946, a change that the government's own debt office says "made little immediate practical difference": the Bank remained the Treasury's adviser, agent and debt manager. In 1997 it was given its independence as a central bank, and in April 1998 the management of government debt passed to a new Debt Management Office. [cite:dv2_dmo_boe] For most of the period this volume covers, then, the institution at the center of British public finance was a privately owned corporation with a royal charter.

The chartered companies. The City's merchants did not only lend to the state. They also carried the state's flag abroad under charters of their own. On 31 December 1600 Elizabeth I chartered "the Governor and Company of Merchants of London Trading into the East-Indies," the East India Company, whose headquarters, East India House, stood on Leadenhall Street. [cite:dv2_wiki_eic] After the Battle of Plassey in 1757 the Company expanded from trade into rule, and at its height its three presidency armies numbered about 260,000 soldiers. A reference summary repeats a common estimate that the Company handled half of the world's trade in the mid-1700s and early 1800s; that figure is an estimate and should not be read as a measured share. After the rebellion of 1857 the Government of India Act 1858 transferred its territories, administration and armies to the Crown, and the Company was dissolved on 1 June 1874. [cite:dv2_wiki_eic] A private corporation registered in the City had governed a subcontinent for a century.

The City's past also includes men whose fortunes were tied to slavery, and the Corporation has had to decide how to remember them. In January 2021 it voted to remove the statues of William Beckford and Sir John Cass from Guildhall over their links to slavery. In October 2021 it reversed the decision and kept the statues with plaques explaining those links, citing a poll in which 71 percent of respondents wanted them kept and the difficulty of altering a Grade I listed building. [cite:dv2_cityam_statues_2021] The episode is small, but it shows the Corporation acting as the keeper of a long institutional memory, as it has since its first charter.

The deregulation of 1986. By the 1980s London's stock market still worked under rules a Victorian broker would have recognized. That changed on 27 October 1986, the day the City called the Big Bang. The old separation between brokers and jobbers was abolished, overseas firms were allowed to compete in London, and electronic trading was introduced, moving business onto the telephone and the screen. [cite:dv2_moneyweek_bigbang] Foreign banks rushed in, mergers followed, and the market's center of gravity began to move east to Canary Wharf. Some critics argue that the looser rules of that era contributed to the crisis of 2008; the claim is debated, and the sources used here record it as an argument rather than a finding. [cite:dv2_moneyweek_bigbang]

The scale today. The measurable result is a financial center with few equals. Every three years the world's central banks survey trading in currencies and derivatives through the Bank for International Settlements. In April 2025, the most recent survey, average daily foreign-exchange trading in the United Kingdom was $4,745 billion, 37.8 percent of all the currency trading in the world, and the United Kingdom remained the single largest center. It accounted for 49.6 percent of global turnover in over-the-counter interest-rate derivatives, an average of $4,320 billion a day. [cite:dv2_boe_triennial_2025] Three years earlier the shares had been 38.1 percent and 45.5 percent: London's lead in currencies held steady, and its lead in derivatives grew. [cite:dv2_boe_triennial_2022] Within the Square Mile itself, the Corporation counts 614,500 workers, reports that the City holds one in every five financial-services jobs in Great Britain, and puts the City's annual economic output at nearly £85 billion. [cite:dv2_col_keyfacts]

The offshore network. London's market does not end at the coast. Around it sit the Crown Dependencies, Jersey, Guernsey and the Isle of Man, each with its own legislature, and the British Overseas Territories, among them the British Virgin Islands, the Cayman Islands and Bermuda. [cite:metabunk_city_sovereign_debunk] [cite:dv2_ferret_cthi_2024] The independent campaign group Tax Justice Network publishes two indices that measure what it calls tax-haven risk. Its Corporate Tax Haven Index, released on 1 October 2024, ranked the British Virgin Islands, the Cayman Islands and Bermuda first, second and third in the world, attributed about a third of global corporate tax-abuse risk to the United Kingdom and its network, and estimated that countries lose £63 billion a year in corporate tax through that network, or £126 billion including evasion by wealthy individuals. [cite:dv2_ferret_cthi_2024] Its 2020 Financial Secrecy Index moved the United Kingdom from 23rd to 12th place, a change it attributed mainly to the territories and dependencies. [cite:dv2_taxjournal_fsi_2020]

Those figures come from an advocacy organization with a stated position, and they are estimates built on its own methods. The government's tax authority, HMRC, answered the 2024 index by pointing out that Jersey and Guernsey have committed to recording the true owners of companies and to sharing that information on request. [cite:dv2_ferret_cthi_2024] The disagreement is real and should be presented as one. What is not disputed is the structure: a very large financial market in London, linked by law, language and long habit to a ring of smaller jurisdictions with their own rules.

The power this section describes is power of a particular kind. It is not the power to command, which London's market has never had. It is the power to lend, to clear, to price and to hold: to raise money for governments and companies on terms that other centers cannot match, to keep the reserves of currencies that are not its own, and to give legal form to institutions that operate elsewhere. Those were exactly the services a political movement without a state, and later a state without much capital, would need. The sections that follow trace how the Zionist movement and Mandate Palestine used them.

sections.h: Inside the City's Institutions: Emancipation, the Gold Fix and the Mansion House
sections.html:
The Rothschild name carries more weight in the popular story of London's power than any other, and much of that weight is legend. The best-known episode, Nathan Rothschild racing news of Waterloo to the stock exchange, traces back to a pamphlet published in 1846 to stir hostility toward Jews; [scene:bc_s02|the London house's record] sets out what the documents show instead. That record is one of loans to states, a supply of coin to the Bank of England in the panic of 1825, and the £4 million the London house advanced to the British government in 1875 to buy the Khedive of Egypt's Suez Canal shares. [cite:wiki_dairnvaell_satan_pamphlet] [cite:jwatte_rothschild_myths_record] [cite:rs_rd0_hefler_2023] [cite:dv2_wiki_lionel] This section follows a different thread: how a Jewish banking family, and Jewish citizens of the City more broadly, entered the City's own institutions, and how those institutions in turn became a public stage for Jewish causes in the century before Zionism.

The oath. Until the 1830s, the City's offices and Parliament's seats were closed to Jews by a religious test. Office-holders had to swear an oath "upon the true faith of a Christian." The first breach came inside the City. In 1835 David Salomons was elected one of the City's two Sheriffs. He could not take the Christian oath, and Parliament passed the Sheriffs' Declaration Act later that year so that he could serve, making him the first Jewish Sheriff of the City of London. [cite:dv2_wiki_salomons] [cite:dv2_wiki_emancipation] In December 1835 he was elected an Alderman, and the same oath disqualified him. He was elected again in 1847, after the Religious Opinions Relief Act amended the oath, and this time he took his place. The Aldermen chose him as Lord Mayor, and he served from 10 November 1855 to 8 November 1856, the first Jewish Lord Mayor of London. [cite:dv2_wiki_salomons]

Salomons was also a founder of the London and Westminster Bank, and in 1851 he tested the same barrier in Parliament. Elected member for Greenwich, he took his seat without the Christian words of the oath, voted three times, was removed by the Serjeant-at-Arms and was fined £500. [cite:dv2_wiki_salomons] The City's own electorate was making the same point at the same time. In 1847 its voters returned Lionel de Rothschild, head of the London house, as one of the four members of Parliament for the City of London. He could not take his seat. He was returned again and again, and in 1849 he resigned and stood once more at a by-election to strengthen his claim. In 1850 he entered the chamber and was allowed to swear on the Hebrew Bible, but was required to leave when he left out the words "upon the true faith of a Christian." [cite:dv2_wiki_lionel] [cite:dv2_wiki_emancipation]

The Jews Relief Act of 1858 broke the deadlock by allowing each House to decide its own oath. On 26 July 1858 Lionel de Rothschild took the oath with his head covered, said "so help me, Jehovah," and took his seat as the first Jewish member of Parliament, sitting for the City of London. [cite:dv2_wiki_lionel] [cite:dv2_wiki_emancipation] In 1885 his son Nathaniel became Lord Rothschild, the first Jewish peer. [cite:dv2_wiki_emancipation]

This history matters to the question of power for a reason that runs against the legend. The barrier these men faced was a law written to exclude Jews from public life, and its removal came from a political campaign fought in the open, through elections the City's voters kept repeating. The documents show a family and a community gaining ordinary civic rights late and against resistance. They do not show a family that already controlled the institutions it was trying to enter.

The gold fix. The Rothschild house's most visible place in the City's machinery came later, in the market for gold. On 12 September 1919 the first London Gold Fixing was held at N M Rothschild & Sons' offices at New Court. Representatives of the five members of the London gold market, N M Rothschild & Sons, Mocatta & Goldsmid, Pixley & Abell, Samuel Montagu & Co. and Sharps Wilkins, each sat at a desk with a telephone and a small Union Jack flag. By tradition the Rothschild representative sat at the center as chairman. [cite:dv2_ra_goldfix] For eighty-five years the London gold price was fixed in a Rothschild office. In 2004 the firm decided to withdraw from the fixing; its last participation was on 4 May 2004. [cite:dv2_ra_goldfix]

The fixing was a real position of influence, and the family's own archive describes it. It was also a shared one: five firms took part, and the house left the arrangement by its own decision. Read in isolation, "the Rothschilds set the price of gold" sounds like command. Read with the record, it describes the chairmanship of a market committee.

The Mansion House. The City's institutions also gave Jewish causes a public platform, and the Lord Mayor's residence was its usual setting. On 3 July 1840 a meeting summoned by the Lord Mayor at the Mansion House protested the ritual-murder accusation against the Jews of Damascus, in which two of the accused had died under torture, and demanded the release of those still held. The Lord Mayor sent the meeting's resolutions to the foreign ambassadors in London. [cite:dv2_je_mansion_house] [cite:rs_ch01_ej_damascus] The Damascus affair itself, and the mission of Moses Montefiore and Adolphe Crémieux that ended it, are told in [scene:ch01_hatred|the history of the old hatred]. In 1882, after a series of articles by Joseph Jacobs on the persecution of Jews in the Russian Empire, the Lord Mayor convened another Mansion House meeting; the fund it launched raised £108,000 for the persecuted Jews of Russia. On 10 December 1890 a meeting at Guildhall deplored "the renewed sufferings of the Jews in Russia" and sent a memorandum asking the tsar to grant his Jewish subjects equality. The tsar refused to receive it, and it came back through the Foreign Office. About £100,000 was collected, and the committee that managed it became the Russo-Jewish Committee. [cite:dv2_je_mansion_house]

These were humanitarian meetings, not Zionist ones. Political Zionism did not yet exist in 1840 or 1882, and nothing in the record presents the meetings as aimed at a Jewish state. Their significance for this volume is the precedent they set. By the 1880s the City's highest office had become a recognized place from which British public opinion spoke about the treatment of Jews abroad, and the Lord Mayor's name carried that opinion to foreign governments. When the Zionist movement arrived in London a generation later, it found a city whose institutions already had a habit of engagement with Jewish questions, and a banking community, Jewish and Gentile, long accustomed to financing causes overseas.

The gaps should be stated. The sources used here do not name the Lord Mayors who chaired the meetings of 1840 and 1882, and they do not give the date in 1882 on which the Mansion House meeting was held. They describe the gold fixing's form and its Rothschild chairmanship, not how much influence the chairman had over the price on any given day. And they do not connect any of the episodes in this section to the later decisions of the British government on Palestine, which were taken elsewhere, by other people, for reasons set out later in this part.

sections.h: The Movement's Companies Were London Companies
sections.html:
A political movement without a state cannot issue currency, levy taxes or borrow on its own credit. What it can do is form companies, and the Zionist movement did so from its second year. The striking fact about those companies, set out across the earlier volumes of this library and gathered here, is where they were formed. The movement's bank, its land fund and its permanent fundraising arm were each created as English legal entities in London, and two of them kept their London registration for decades. If London was a financial parent of the Jewish state, this is where the relationship is written down most plainly: not in the Corporation's minute books, but in the register of English companies.

The bank. The Second Zionist Congress, meeting in 1898, decided to create a financial institution of its own. On 20 March 1899 the Jewish Colonial Trust was incorporated in London under the English Companies Acts, with an authorized capital of £2,000,000 in shares of £1 each. [cite:jct_wiki] It was a company selling shares, not a charity collecting gifts, and the shares were priced low and could be paid in installments so that working people across Europe could become owners. Theodor Herzl bought the first 1,000 shares himself. [cite:jct_wiki] [cite:jewishencyclopedia_colonial_trust] [cite:bia_jewish_colonial_trust] The Trust fell well short of its target: about 250,000 shares were sold, raising about £250,000, one-eighth of the authorized sum. Control, meanwhile, stayed with a small founding group through a block of founders' shares carrying extra votes. [cite:jct_wiki] [cite:wiki_jewish_colonial_trust] [scene:s04c|The Trust's own history] follows the design and the shortfall in detail.

A bank incorporated in London still had to reach Palestine. On 27 February 1902 the Trust founded the Anglo-Palestine Company, with initial capital of about £50,000, as its operating arm. It opened its first branch in Jaffa in 1903, financed land purchase, agriculture and settlers' credit cooperatives, and by 1914 had branches in Jerusalem, Beirut, Hebron, Haifa, Safed, Tiberias and Gaza. In 1909 it lent to the Ahuzat Bayit association, which used the money to build the first neighborhood of what became Tel Aviv. [cite:apc_wiki] [cite:encyclopedia_jewish_colonial_trust] It became the Anglo-Palestine Bank around 1930 and Bank Leumi in 1950–51, one of the major banks of the State of Israel. [cite:apc_wiki] [cite:jewishencyclopedia_colonial_trust] The parent company in London raised the capital; the subsidiary in Jaffa put it to work.

The land fund. The Jewish National Fund was established at the Fifth Zionist Congress in Basel in 1901, four years after Hermann Schapira had first proposed a national land fund at the First Congress in 1897. Its legal home, too, became London. On 8 April 1907 it was incorporated there as an association limited by guarantee, under the name "Juedischer Nationalfonds (Keren Kajemeth Le Jisroel), Limited." The London company was renamed in October 1921 and again in January 1926, and it was dissolved and reconstituted as an Israeli company only in 1953, five years after the state was founded. [cite:dv2_wiki_jnf] An English company with the Hebrew name Keren Kayemeth Leisrael Limited still appears on the register at Companies House, number 00092825, incorporated on 8 April 1907 and recorded as dormant since 2009. [cite:dv2_powerbase_kkl]

From its beginning the fund leased its land on long terms rather than selling it. By the eve of statehood it had acquired 936,000 dunams, and other Jewish bodies and private buyers about 800,000 more. In 1948 the fund held 54 percent of the land owned by Jews in Palestine, which was a little under 4 percent of all the land of Mandatory Palestine. [cite:dv2_wiki_jnf] Those two proportions, measured against different totals, are easy to confuse, and they are best read together: the fund was the largest Jewish landholder, and Jewish landholding as a whole was a small share of the country. The land system the fund built, and how most of the territory of the new state came instead through the war of 1948, is set out in [scene:s04j|the land-purchase pipeline] and [scene:s07|the Mandate].

The fundraising arm. The third institution was born in London in the same way. In July 1920, at the Zionist conference held in London from the 7th to the 24th, the World Zionist Organization founded Keren Hayesod, the Palestine Foundation Fund, as its permanent fundraising arm. It aimed to raise £25,000,000 in five years, accepted donations from non-Zionists, and asked supporters to pledge a fixed share of their income. It financed immigration, settlement, defense and water works, and invested in the Palestine Electric Company and the Palestine Potash Company. In 1926 it moved its headquarters from London to Jerusalem. [cite:keren_hayesod_wiki] [cite:dv2_wiki_keren_hayesod] [scene:s04i|Keren Hayesod's founding] gives its first campaigns, and [scene:us_s01|the first American campaigns] the fight over who controlled its American money.

Why London? The sources used here do not record the founders' own reasons for choosing English incorporation, and the reader should not supply one. What they do show is how the choice fitted what followed. From 1917 the British government was the power that had promised the movement a national home, and from 1920 it was the power that governed the territory in which the companies worked. [cite:balfour_letter] [cite:mandate_palestine_wiki] By then the movement's bank and land fund were already English companies, and its new fundraising arm was founded at a conference in London. One reading is that an English company was the natural vehicle for a movement that hoped for, and then had, a British patron. That is an inference from the sequence of dates, not a documented motive, and it is offered as one.

The fifth line of the money chain above needs a word of explanation. Under the Ottoman land system, title to much farmland was registered in the names of village heads, merchants and absentee families, while the peasants who worked it went on doing so as tenants. When such land was sold, the record shows tenant cultivators being evicted, with compensation on terms set by the purchaser; the documented evictions of this kind belong mainly to the 1920s. [cite:wiki_ottoman_land_code_1858] That mechanism, and the disputes over its scale, are told in [scene:ot_s01|the Ottoman land code]. It is noted here because a money chain has two ends, and the companies chartered in London financed one of them.

What this section establishes is narrow and solid. The three central financial institutions of the Zionist movement before 1948 were formed in London as English legal entities: a bank in 1899, a land fund in 1907 and a fundraising arm in 1920. One moved to Jerusalem in 1926, and the land fund remained an English company until 1953. None of them was an arm of the City of London Corporation, and none was created by the British government. They were the movement's own companies, built on the legal and financial infrastructure that London offered to anyone who could use it. That use of London's legal machinery is the first documented sense in which London was a parent.

sections.h: Plumbing a Mandate Through London
sections.html:
From 1920 to 1948 Britain governed Palestine, and the earlier volumes of this library tell that government's politics: the High Commissioners, the commissions, the riots and revolts, the White Papers. This section looks at something less often described, the financial plumbing beneath the politics. Where was the country's money issued, where were its reserves kept, which banks carried its payments, and which London companies built its largest pieces of infrastructure? The answer to each question leads back to London, and the last of them leads to a single order of the British Treasury in February 1948 that cut the plumbing off.

The currency. In 1926 the British Colonial Secretary appointed a Palestine Currency Board, and from 1 November 1927 the board issued the Palestine pound, fixed at par with sterling and divided into 1,000 mils. [cite:wiki_palestine_pound] [cite:israelmint_pcb_notes] No body in Palestine, Jewish or Arab, issued the country's money or set its value. [scene:us_s06|An earlier volume] noted that its sources did not say how the board's reserves were held. A working paper prepared by the secretariat of the United Nations Conciliation Commission for Palestine after the Mandate ended supplies the answer. Palestine's currency was backed by British government securities and sterling, held in London by the Currency Board. The board's assets made up more than half of all of Palestine's sterling balances, which the UN Palestine Commission put at more than £50 million. [cite:dv2_unccp_assets] Every Palestine pound in circulation was matched, in other words, by assets lodged in the capital of the governing power.

The board did not operate its own branches in Palestine. According to the Conciliation Commission's note on currency and banking, it worked there "through the agency of Barclay's Bank." [cite:dv2_unccp_banking] Barclays had arrived through a merger. The Anglo-Egyptian Bank, which often acted as banker to British authorities in the Mediterranean, had opened branches in Jerusalem and Jaffa in 1918; in 1925 Barclays merged it with two other overseas banks to form Barclays Bank (Dominion, Colonial and Overseas). [cite:dv2_wiki_anglo_egyptian] A London clearing bank, in short, was the channel through which the Mandate's London-managed currency reached the country.

The banks. Within that system three kinds of bank did business. There were foreign banks, Barclays and the Ottoman Bank among them. There was the Zionist movement's own bank, the Anglo-Palestine Bank, still a subsidiary of the London-incorporated Jewish Colonial Trust, as the previous section showed. And there were Arab banks. The Conciliation Commission named the Arab Bank and the Arab National Bank as "the two big Arab banks" and estimated Arab bank deposits at about £12,500,000 at the end of 1945. [cite:dv2_unccp_banking] The figure is an estimate in a working paper, and the scanned document is partly illegible, but it is a useful corrective to accounts in which the Mandate economy had only one community with money in the bank.

The oil line. One of the major works built across Mandate Palestine was not built by the Mandate government or by the Zionist movement. It was built by the Iraq Petroleum Company, in which Anglo-Iranian and Shell each held 23.75 percent. Between 1932 and 1934 the company laid a pipeline from the oilfields of Kirkuk to the Mediterranean, splitting into two branches, one to Tripoli in Lebanon and one to Haifa. [cite:dv2_wiki_kirkuk_haifa] [cite:rs_rd3_gulbenkian_pipeline] The transit agreements with Palestine and its neighbors had been signed in the first three months of 1931. [cite:rs_rd3_gulbenkian_pipeline] The first oil reached Haifa in October 1934, on the 14th by one account and the 16th by another, and opening ceremonies were held in January 1935. [cite:dv2_wiki_kirkuk_haifa] [cite:rs_rd3_gulbenkian_pipeline] At Haifa, Consolidated Refineries Ltd, owned jointly by Anglo-Iranian and Shell, built a refinery that began production on 29 November 1939. [cite:dv2_wiki_kirkuk_haifa]

The pipeline drew the country's politics into its path. During the Arab revolt of 1936–1939 it was attacked repeatedly, and Captain Orde Wingate's joint British and Jewish Special Night Squads were formed largely to protect it. The Irgun later attacked it too. [cite:dv2_wiki_kirkuk_haifa] An oil company's pipeline, in other words, was a main reason for a British unit that trained Jewish fighters alongside British soldiers. The revolt itself is told in [scene:s07a5|the Arab revolt].

The cut-off. As the Mandate ended, the plumbing was closed from London. On 22 February 1948 a British Treasury order excluded Palestine from the sterling area and blocked its accumulated sterling balances. The blocked sums included the Currency Board's assets and more than £3 million left over from three bond issues made in Palestine since 1944, which were invested in British government securities "pending a general settlement of the question." [cite:dv2_unccp_assets] The Conciliation Commission's later note described Palestine's sterling credits as largely "blocked in London." [cite:dv2_unccp_banking] The question of what became of those balances after 1948, and how they were divided between Israel and the Arab states and individuals with claims on them, is not answered in the sources used here, and it is left open.

Two months later the refinery stopped. On 12 April 1948 the Haifa refinery shut down indefinitely after a strike by its Arab workers. After the war, the Haifa branch of the pipeline was cut off from Iraqi oil and never restored; deliveries resumed on a much smaller scale in October 1949, using crude from Venezuela. [cite:dv2_wiki_kirkuk_haifa] The Mandate's currency outlived its government by three months: the Currency Board's notes stayed in circulation until 18 August 1948, when the new state's own notes took their place. Those first Israeli notes were printed not in London but in New York, by the American Bank Note Company, at the request of the Anglo-Palestine Bank's chairman. [cite:wiki_palestine_pound] [cite:israelmint_aplb_series] [cite:jhom_anglo_palestine_notes]

The detail is a fitting end to the Mandate's financial story. For twenty-one years the country's money had been issued, backed and banked through London. When the state that succeeded the Mandate needed a currency of its own, the bank that supplied it belonged to a trust incorporated in London almost fifty years before, but the notes came from America. The handover from one patron to the next, told in the parts of this volume on Washington, can be read in the printer's imprint.

What the record leaves open has already been noted in passing and should be gathered here. The Conciliation Commission's documents are scanned working papers, partly illegible, and some of their figures cannot be read reliably; this section uses only those that can. The sources do not say what the peg to sterling cost or gained the country's economy, how the blocked balances were finally settled, or how the burden of the February 1948 order was shared among Jewish and Arab depositors. The two dates for the first oil at Haifa, 14 and 16 October 1934, are both recorded, and the difference is not explained.

sections.h: Whitehall, Not the Guildhall: What the British State Did
sections.html:
Everything in this part so far has concerned the City in the narrow sense, the corporation, its market and the companies registered there. The decisions that turned a political movement into a national home, and a national home into a state, were taken somewhere else. They were taken by Foreign Secretaries, Cabinets and Colonial Secretaries, in Whitehall and Westminster, and recorded in Cabinet papers and command papers rather than in the Corporation's records. This section gathers those decisions, each told at length in an earlier volume, so that the reader can see in one place what London, as the capital of a state, actually did. The striking thing about the list is that it runs in both directions.

The first sponsorship, 1839–1840. The British state's interest in a Jewish presence in Palestine began half a century before political Zionism. In 1839 Anthony Ashley-Cooper, Lord Shaftesbury, an evangelical peer and the stepson-in-law of the Foreign Secretary, pressed Lord Palmerston to sponsor Jewish settlement in Palestine under British protection. In 1840 Palmerston instructed his ambassador at Constantinople to urge the Ottoman sultan to encourage Jewish settlement, and the new British consulate in Jerusalem was given a brief to protect Jews. [cite:wiki_christian_zionism] [cite:wiki_shaftesbury] The motive, as [scene:bc_s05|Restoration before Zionism] shows, was both theological and imperial: a protected Jewish presence would be a British foothold in Ottoman Syria. It drew on no Jewish request, and it settled no one.

The promise, 1917. The decisive act came in wartime. On 2 November 1917 the Foreign Secretary, Arthur Balfour, signed a letter declaring that the government viewed "with favour the establishment in Palestine of a national home for the Jewish people," and sent it to Lord Rothschild at 148 Piccadilly, asking him to pass it to the Zionist Federation. [cite:wb_bl_addms41178] [cite:wb_ra_balfour] The letter was drafted with the Zionist leadership, among them Chaim Weizmann, whose wartime work on acetone for British munitions had given him access to the Prime Minister and to Balfour.
