[cite:balfour_letter] The War Cabinet approved it for reasons ministers could name: the Suez Canal and the route to India, the goodwill Weizmann had earned, and a mistaken belief in a unified and powerful "world Jewry" that could be won to the Allied side, a belief that was itself an antisemitic premise. [cite:cohen_palestine_great_powers] The only Jewish member of the Cabinet, Edwin Montagu, opposed the policy in a memorandum of 23 August 1917, calling Zionism "a mischievous political creed." [cite:wb_tna_cab21_58_218] [scene:s06|The Balfour Declaration] and [scene:rd2_addressee|why the letter went to Walter Rothschild] tell the whole story. Two facts in it bear directly on this part. The addressee was chosen because the Zionist leaders "had no address" and he had a fine one; and nothing in the record of the letter gives the City of London Corporation any part in it. [cite:wb_jc_rothschild2017]

When the letter was written, Palestine was still Ottoman. British forces took Beersheba on 31 October 1917 and Jerusalem only on 9 December. [cite:w_sinai_palestine] Britain was promising a country it did not yet hold.

The legal frame, 1920–1923. The promise became international law in stages. At San Remo on 25 April 1920 the Allied powers assigned Britain the Mandate for Palestine. The League of Nations Council approved the Mandate's text in July 1922, and it entered into force on 29 September 1923, a date that has since been challenged. [cite:rs_a22_frus] [cite:rs_md_lon1923] [cite:rs_md_quigley_oj] The Mandate wrote the Balfour Declaration into binding articles, obliged Britain to facilitate Jewish immigration and "close settlement by Jews on the land," and recognized a Jewish public body to work with the administration. [cite:mandate_palestine_wiki] [cite:rs_md_avalon] The first High Commissioner, appointed in 1920, was Sir Herbert Samuel, a British Jew and a committed Zionist. [cite:wiki_herbert_samuel_hc] For a quarter of a century the British state then governed the country: its passports, courts, police, railways, ports and currency. [cite:mandate_palestine_wiki] [scene:s07|The Mandate] and [scene:blg_s01|by what right] set out the text and the legal disputes over it.

The retreat, 1939–1949. The same state then turned against the policy it had launched. On 17 May 1939, in the command paper Cmd 6019, it allowed some 75,000 Jewish immigrants over the next five years and provided that "no further Jewish immigration will be permitted unless the Arabs of Palestine are prepared to acquiesce in it." [cite:rs_rd4_wp_cojs_text] [cite:rs_rd4_wp_frus_d841] Zionist leaders read it as an abandonment of the promise of 1917, and it came at the moment Europe's Jews most needed somewhere to go. [cite:whitepaper1939] [scene:rd4_white_paper|The White Paper of 1939] gives its terms and the fight over whether it broke the Mandate. After the war, the Labour government's Foreign Secretary, Ernest Bevin, failed to find a settlement. In February 1947 the Cabinet referred the question to the United Nations "without British recommendations." [cite:rs_rd5_cojs_bevin_1947] On 26 September 1947 the Colonial Secretary told the UN that Britain "was not prepared to undertake the task of imposing a policy in Palestine by force of arms." [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_creechjones] When the General Assembly voted for partition on 29 November 1947, by 33 votes to 13 with 10 abstentions, Britain was among the abstainers. [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_181] [cite:rs_rd5_langham_exit]

The Mandate expired at midnight on 14 May 1948, hours after the State of Israel was declared in Tel Aviv, with no power ready to carry out the partition plan. [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_declaration] [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_creechjones] Britain gave the State of Israel de facto recognition only on 29 January 1949, eight months after its declaration, and de jure recognition on 27 April 1950; [cite:dv2_fathom_aridan] and the historian Raphael Langham describes Bevin's acceptance as "grudging." [cite:rs_rd5_langham_exit] Washington had recognized the state eleven minutes after it was declared, and Moscow gave full recognition on 17 May. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] [cite:wiki_soviet_arab_israeli] [scene:rd5_britain_exits|How Britain left] follows the last year of the Mandate in full.

London and Israel since. The relationship did not end in 1949, but its character changed. The City appears in the later record as one financial partner among many. In January 2018 the Lord Mayor, Charles Bowman, a senior partner at PwC, led a business mission to Tel Aviv and Jerusalem, met Israel's economy minister to discuss a possible free-trade agreement and the governor of the Bank of Israel to discuss financial links, laid a wreath at Yad Vashem, and also met Palestinian business leaders in the occupied territories. He described the mission as part of building ties with growing markets after Britain's departure from the European Union. [cite:dv2_jn_bowman_2018] [cite:dv2_jc_bowman_2018] That is the Lord Mayor's ordinary ambassadorial role, the same one he plays in dozens of other countries. It is documented, and it is modest.

Set out together, the British state's record supports a clear conclusion and rules out a popular one. It supports the conclusion that London, meaning the British government, was the indispensable sponsor of the Jewish national home between 1917 and 1939: it issued the promise, wrote it into international law, governed the country for a quarter of a century, admitted immigration under its terms, and let the movement's institutions grow under its protection. It rules out the claim that this sponsorship was continuous or unconditional. From 1939 the same government restricted immigration, abstained on partition, refused to enforce it, left without an orderly handover, and recognized the new state late and reluctantly. A parent that launches a child and then tries to hold it back is still a parent. But it is a different kind of parent from the one the familiar story describes, and the next part of this volume shows that the role of principal sponsor passed, in these years, to Washington, though not without conditions of its own: the United States kept an arms embargo on all the belligerents through the war of 1948. [cite:rs_rd5_oh_war_b]

sections.h: The Parent Test: What London Gave, and What It Withheld
sections.html:
This volume calls London the financial parent of Israel. The sections of this part have now set out the record on which that title has to stand or fall, and it is time to weigh it. The test is simple to state. A parent, in the sense this volume uses, is a power that supplied something the new state could not have had without it, at a time when no one else was supplying it. Measured that way, London has a strong claim. But the claim belongs to some of the four Londons named at the start of this part and not to others, and the record also contains a decade in which London worked against the child it had helped to start.

What the record supports. Four contributions are well documented. First, the promise: the British government issued the Balfour Declaration in November 1917, before it held Jerusalem, and addressed it to Lord Rothschild in London. [cite:wb_bl_addms41178] [cite:w_sinai_palestine] Second, the legal frame: the British government took the Mandate, which wrote that promise into international law and bound the governing power to facilitate Jewish immigration and settlement. [cite:rs_a22_frus] [cite:mandate_palestine_wiki] Third, the legal vehicles: the movement's bank, its land fund and its fundraising arm were each formed as English entities in London, in 1899, 1907 and 1920, and the land fund stayed an English company until 1953. [cite:jct_wiki] [cite:dv2_wiki_jnf] [cite:keren_hayesod_wiki] Fourth, the plumbing: for twenty-one years Palestine's currency was issued by a board appointed in London, backed by reserves held in London, and carried in the country by a London bank. [cite:wiki_palestine_pound] [cite:dv2_unccp_assets] [cite:dv2_unccp_banking] The sources used here record no other power supplying any of the four in those years, though the Mandate itself was conferred through the League of Nations.

What the record limits. Four limits are equally documented. First, the Corporation of the City of London, the medieval body that governs the Square Mile, appears in none of the decisive acts. It did not draft or send the Balfour letter, it did not hold the Mandate, it did not incorporate the movement's companies, and it did not manage Palestine's currency. [cite:wb_jc_rothschild2017] Its documented engagement with Jewish causes before 1948 is humanitarian, at the Mansion House in 1840 and 1882 and at Guildhall in 1890, and its documented engagement with Israel since is a Lord Mayor's trade mission of the kind it sends to many countries. [cite:dv2_je_mansion_house] [cite:dv2_jn_bowman_2018] Second, the Rothschild house's documented role is one of address, finance and civic standing, not command; the gold fix it chaired was a five-firm committee, and its later Israeli philanthropy is told in other volumes. [cite:dv2_ra_goldfix] Third, the British state's support was not continuous: from May 1939 it capped immigration, in 1947 it handed the question to the United Nations and abstained on partition, and it recognized Israel only in January 1949. [cite:rs_rd4_wp_cojs_text] [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_181] [cite:rs_rd5_langham_exit] Fourth, London's financial plumbing was cut, not handed over: the Treasury order of 22 February 1948 blocked Palestine's sterling balances, and the new state's first notes were printed in New York. [cite:dv2_unccp_assets] [cite:jhom_anglo_palestine_notes]

The verdict. The record supports calling London the financial and imperial parent of the Jewish state, on two conditions. The London that did the parenting was the British government and the legal and financial infrastructure of the London market, not the Corporation of the City of London. And the parenting was concentrated in the years 1917 to 1939, when it was decisive, and was followed by a decade of restriction and withdrawal. Both conditions matter. The first rules out the popular claim that a sovereign "Crown corporation" in the Square Mile directed the creation of Israel; [scene:bc_s01|the library's first examination of the City] and [scene:bc_s06|its examination of the three-cities claim] found no document for that, and nothing in this part's newer research changes the finding. The second explains why the volume needs two more parents. By 1948 the child London had launched was seeking money, arms and recognition elsewhere, and found the first and third of them in Washington.

One further point belongs here, because it bears on how the three parents relate to each other. Nothing in the sources used for this part shows the British government, the London market or the Corporation coordinating with the Holy See or the United States government on Palestine as a joint undertaking. What the record does show is Britain handing the question to the United Nations without recommendations in 1947 and abstaining, while Washington voted for partition and recognized the state within minutes. [cite:rs_rd5_cojs_bevin_1947] [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] That is the record of two governments acting on different judgments, not of a single design. The parts that follow test the same question for Rome and Washington on their own evidence.

The gaps that remain are named so that later research can close them. The sources used here do not show how the blocked sterling balances were settled after 1948, or what share of the Jewish Colonial Trust's capital was raised in Britain as against Eastern Europe. They do not give the founders' own reasons for incorporating in London. And they do not measure how much of the Zionist movement's spending between 1920 and 1948 passed through London at all, as against the American campaigns told in [scene:us_s01|an earlier volume]. Each of those would sharpen the verdict. None of them, on the evidence so far, would reverse it.

books.title: Follow the Money
books.subtitle: The Pro-Israel Lobby in American Government and Around the World
books.intro:
This volume follows the money. It asks how much American organizations that support Israel have spent to shape American government, through which channels, at which levels, against whom and with what result; and how similar organizations work in other democracies. It is built from public filings: Federal Election Commission reports, lobbying disclosures, foreign-agent registrations, congressional travel records, nonprofit tax returns, and the reporting of named journalists who have read them.

It defines its subject by organizations, not by people. Pro-Israel money here means money moving through committees, lobbies, foundations and registered agents whose stated purpose is to support Israel; it never means money given by any religious or ethnic group, and the book treats no donor's identity as evidence of anything. It keeps money and motive apart: what members received and what was spent against them is documented; why they voted as they did is a separate question, and the book says so wherever it arises. And it reports competing figures side by side, with their dates and definitions, rather than choosing the largest.

Ten parts follow. The first fixes the definitions and the channels. The second describes AIPAC, the organization at the center of the American network. The third counts the money cycle by cycle; the fourth names the largest recipients in each party; the fifth follows the campaigns to unseat members of Congress; the sixth turns to members who refuse the money and to those who left office under attack. The seventh follows the trips, the eighth the state and local level, and the ninth the lobby abroad. The last part sets the whole architecture out on one page, with what it costs.

chapters.label: Part One
chapters.title: What Counts, and How It Moves
chapters.intro: Before any figure in this volume can mean anything, three things have to be fixed: what counts as pro-Israel money, through which legal channels it moves, and how a number drawn from those channels should be read. Part One sets them out. It defines the subject by organizations and filings, never by the religion or origin of any donor; it describes the six channels, from a $5,000 check to an unlimited super PAC campaign; and it gives five questions to ask of every figure, with examples of what goes wrong when they are skipped.
chapters.outro:
Part One fixed the terms. Pro-Israel money, in this volume, is money that moves through American organizations whose stated purpose is to support Israel or the US–Israel relationship; it is American money, because foreign money is barred from American elections, except in the one channel, foreign-agent registration, where the Israeli government's own contracts are disclosed. [cite:fec_foreign_nationals] [cite:dc_parscale_fara] It moves through six channels with very different limits: capped contributions, uncapped earmarking, unlimited super PAC spending, lobbying, charity-paid travel and registered foreign agents. [cite:pm_fec_limits] [cite:pm_sludge_jeffries] [cite:pm_wiki_superpac]

What is settled is the legal structure and the long record: about $108.6 million in pro-Israel contributions from 1990 to 2012, mostly from individuals, and no candidate money from AIPAC itself before its PAC was formed in December 2021. [cite:pm_jvl_pacs] [cite:opensecrets_aipac_2019] What is contested is how to count, since trackers' totals for the same cycle differ widely, and what the money does, since the records show money and votes moving together but not which drives which. [cite:pm_sludge_100m_2026] [cite:guardian_gaza_donors] Part Two turns to the organization at the center of the network, and to how it was built: [scene:pm2_origins|AIPAC's architecture].

sections.h: What Counts as Pro-Israel Money
sections.html:
Every argument about pro-Israel money in American politics begins with a number, and most arguments go wrong at the same place: before the number, in the definition of what was counted. A figure can describe money given to a candidate or money spent attacking one. It can cover one election or a thirty-year career. It can come from a single organization or from a tracker that adds together every group with "Israel" in its mission. Two honest people can quote figures that differ several times over and both be right, because they are counting different things. This part of the volume sets out the definitions the rest of it uses, the legal channels through which the money moves, and the rules for reading any figure that follows. It is the shortest part of the book and the one the others depend on.

A definition by organization, not by identity. In this volume, "pro-Israel money" means money that moves through organizations whose stated purpose is to support Israel or the relationship between the United States and Israel: political action committees, super PACs, lobbying organizations, charitable foundations and the registered agents of the Israeli government. It does not mean money given by Jewish Americans, and nothing in this volume treats a donor's religion, ancestry or ethnicity as evidence of anything. Individual donors appear in this book only where the public record names them as major donors to the vehicles being studied, and they appear for what they gave, not for who they are. The same rule applies in Part Nine to every other country.

American money, a foreign-policy cause. The second definition concerns where the money comes from. Federal law bars foreign nationals, including foreign governments, foreign political parties and foreign corporations, from making contributions or expenditures, directly or indirectly, in any federal, state or local election in the United States; lawful permanent residents are not covered by the ban. [cite:fec_foreign_nationals] The campaign records studied in this volume therefore do not show money from the government of Israel. They show money from American citizens and residents, given through American organizations, in support of a foreign-policy outcome. That is the accurate frame, and it cuts in two directions at once. It rules out the claim, common online, that Israel pays American politicians through their campaign accounts; the records do not show that. It also rules out the opposite claim, that the money is too small or too scattered to matter; the records show sums that, in some years and some races, are among the largest in American politics.

There is one channel in which a foreign government does pay, openly, and it is not a campaign channel. Under the Foreign Agents Registration Act of 1938, a person or firm working in the United States for a foreign principal must register and disclose the work. Israel's government uses that channel. In September 2025 two firms registered as its agents for paid messaging campaigns in the United States, one of them run by a former manager of Donald Trump's presidential campaign. [cite:pc_fara_complaint] [cite:dc_parscale_fara] Those registrations, and what they disclose, are set out in [scene:ip_s02|the simulation's account of Clock Tower X] and in Part Nine. AIPAC, the largest of the American organizations, is not registered under the act. It says it represents Americans and receives no money from any foreign government; its critics argue that its alignment with Israel's policy priorities should bring it within the law. The history of that dispute, from the Justice Department's 1962 order to the American Zionist Council, the body from which Kenen's committee had been separated, to the Senate's inquiry of 1963, is told in [scene:s11a|the order of 21 November 1962] and [scene:cw5_fulbright_inquiry|the Fulbright inquiry].

The long record. Pro-Israel money is not new, and it was not always large. The Center for Responsive Politics, which publishes OpenSecrets, has kept a pro-Israel category for decades. Its figures for 1990 to 2012 show $108.6 million in contributions to federal candidates over twelve election cycles: $71.5 million from individuals, $34.5 million from political action committees and $2.5 million in "soft money" given to parties before that practice was banned. About two-thirds went to Democrats and one-third to Republicans. The cycle totals ranged from $5.6 million in 1996 to $14.0 million in 2008. [cite:pm_jvl_pacs] For most of that period the money moved through several dozen independent PACs and through individual donors, not through AIPAC. As OpenSecrets noted in 2019, AIPAC itself did not contribute to candidates at all. [cite:opensecrets_aipac_2019]

Those figures look modest beside what followed. In December 2021 AIPAC announced that it would form its own PAC and a super PAC, [cite:pm_factcheck_udp_2022] and from the 2022 cycle onward pro-Israel campaign money grew several times over: on a broader measure that includes super PAC spending, AIPAC's two committees alone spent $44 million in 2022 and $95.1 million in 2024, as Part Three shows cycle by cycle. [cite:pm_israelite_2024] The change was not only in size. It was in kind. A super PAC does not give money to candidates; it spends money to elect or defeat them. The largest sums in this volume are of that second kind, and the most consequential of them were spent in primaries against sitting members of Congress.

What this volume does not claim. Three limits apply to everything that follows. First, receiving money is legal and does not by itself show why any member of Congress votes as he or she does. Donors often give to candidates who already agree with them, and the direction of cause between money and position is a question the campaign records alone cannot settle. Second, pro-Israel organizations disagree with one another. J Street, which calls itself "pro-Israel, pro-peace" and campaigns for a two-state solution, is counted as pro-Israel by most trackers, and in 2018 it described itself as the largest pro-Israel PAC in the country; [cite:pm_jstreet_2018] so is the Republican Jewish Coalition; so is AIPAC. Adding them together, as some trackers do, produces a large number that describes no single interest. Third, other interests spend more on some channels. In 2018, before AIPAC entered campaign giving, AIPAC spent about $3.5 million on lobbying and all pro-Israel groups together about $5.0 million, against $94.8 million by the US Chamber of Commerce; by OpenSecrets' count pro-Israel donors ranked thirty-fourth among interest groups giving to members of Congress that year. [cite:pm_tablet_lobbying] Part Three sets the comparison out for the years since.

What the volume does claim is narrower and better documented. It is that a network of American organizations, built over seventy years, now moves money through every legal channel open to it, at every level of American government, in amounts that are public and can be counted; that its largest single sums have been spent in primaries against members of Congress who broke with the network's positions, as Part Five documents race by race; and that similar organizations, smaller and less documented, operate in other democracies. The next section sets out the channels.

sections.h: Six Channels: How the Money Moves
sections.html:
Political money in the United States does not move through one pipe. It moves through several, each created by a different law or court decision, each with its own limits and its own rules of disclosure. The pro-Israel network uses all of them, and much of the confusion in public argument comes from treating money in one channel as if it had moved through another. A $5,000 check from a political action committee and the roughly $14.5 million a super PAC spent against one House member in 2024 [cite:factcheck_udp_2024] are both "pro-Israel money," but they are different acts, regulated differently, and they say different things about the relationship between a donor and a member of Congress. This section describes the six channels in the order a reader will meet them in this volume.

1. Direct contributions. The oldest channel is a contribution from a political action committee to a candidate's campaign. It is tightly limited. For the 2025–2026 cycle a multicandidate PAC may give a candidate $5,000 per election, and an individual may give $3,500 per election; a primary, a general election, a runoff and a special election each count separately. [cite:pm_fec_limits] Both the PAC and the campaign report the money, so it is the most visible channel and, in dollar terms, the smallest. For decades this was where independent pro-Israel PACs operated, while AIPAC itself gave nothing, [cite:opensecrets_aipac_2019] and it is the channel most people picture when they hear that a member "took money" from a lobby.

2. Earmarked contributions. The second channel multiplies the first. Under federal rules, an individual may give money to a candidate through an intermediary, a "conduit," which passes it on and reports where it came from and where it went. [cite:pm_ecfr_1106] Each donation is still capped at the individual limit, and so long as the intermediary does not exercise "direction or control" over the donors' choices, the gifts do not count against its own limit, so there is no ceiling on how many it can pass to the same candidate. [cite:pm_ecfr_1106] AIPAC PAC uses this channel heavily. It runs a website where its members can choose AIPAC-endorsed candidates and give to them; the payments are processed by a company called Democracy Engine, and donors agree that their gifts are "earmarked donations within the meaning of 11 C.F.R. §110.6(b)." [cite:pm_sludge_jeffries] The practical effect is that a PAC limited to $5,000 per election can direct hundreds of thousands of dollars, or more, to a single campaign. Sludge reported in November 2025 that AIPAC PAC had directed more than $1 million in earmarked donations to the House Democratic leader, Hakeem Jeffries, who had told a radio interviewer that AIPAC's PAC could give him "$5,000 or $10,000 per cycle." [cite:pm_sludge_jeffries] Both statements can be true at once; they describe different channels. Earmarked money appears in a candidate's reports as contributions from individuals, so a reader who looks only for checks from AIPAC PAC will miss most of it.

3. Super PAC spending. The third channel is the one that changed the scale of pro-Israel money. A super PAC is a committee that makes only independent expenditures: it may raise and spend unlimited sums to support or oppose candidates, but it may not give money to them or coordinate its spending with them. The form was created in 2010, by the Supreme Court's decision in Citizens United v. FEC and, two months later, by a federal appeals court's decision in SpeechNow.org v. FEC, which held that a committee making no contributions could accept unlimited contributions. [cite:pm_wiki_superpac] AIPAC's super PAC, the United Democracy Project, was formed on 3 January 2022. [cite:pm_wiki_aipac] A super PAC's money appears in a race as television, digital and mail advertising, and in the races studied in Part Five that advertising rarely mentioned Israel. [cite:punchbowl_udp_no_israel] A super PAC may also give money to other super PACs, which then spend it under names of their own. Super PACs report like other committees, but a group formed close to an election may not have to disclose its donors until after voters have voted. [cite:pm_wiki_superpac] The "pop-up" committees this makes possible are documented in the 2026 races in Part Five.

4. Lobbying. The fourth channel is not campaign money at all. It is paid advocacy: staff and hired firms who meet members of Congress, their aides and executive officials to argue for policies. Lobbying organizations report what they spend each quarter. In this channel the pro-Israel organizations are not large. In 2018 AIPAC reported about $3.5 million in lobbying, roughly the 147th largest figure in the country, against $94.8 million for the US Chamber of Commerce. [cite:pm_tablet_lobbying] AIPAC's influence, as writers sympathetic to it have argued, has never rested on its lobbying budget; [cite:pm_tablet_lobbying] it has rested on its network of donors and activists and on the other five channels.

5. Charity-sponsored travel. The fifth channel runs through the House and Senate ethics rules. After the scandal around the lobbyist Jack Abramoff, Congress tightened the rules on privately paid travel in 2007. Registered lobbyists and the organizations that employ them may generally sponsor no more than a one-day trip for a member or staffer, and every privately paid trip must be approved in advance by the chamber's ethics committee and disclosed within fifteen days of return in the House and thirty in the Senate. [cite:pm_citizen_travel] The rules left room for charitable and educational organizations. AIPAC's charitable affiliate, the American Israel Education Foundation, uses that room to pay for week-long trips to Israel. Craig Holman of Public Citizen, who helped draft the 2007 law, told The Intercept that "these trips would be illegal otherwise," and the foundation's donors are redacted from its public tax filings. [cite:intercept_aief_donors] Part Seven follows the trips: who goes, how often, what they cost, and who else runs them.

6. Registered foreign agents. The sixth channel is the only one in which a foreign government's own money appears, and it appears because the law requires it to. The Foreign Agents Registration Act requires anyone working in the United States on behalf of a foreign principal to register with the Justice Department and report the work and the payments. In September 2025 Israel's Foreign Ministry, through a German subsidiary of the advertising group Havas, retained at least two American firms for messaging campaigns, and both registered: Bridges Partners, for a campaign of paid social-media influencers, and Clock Tower X, owned by Brad Parscale, for a larger campaign aimed at young Americans and at how artificial-intelligence chatbots describe Israel. [cite:pc_fara_complaint] [cite:dc_parscale_fara] These are disclosed public-relations contracts, not campaign contributions, and they are described in full in Part Nine.

Two features of the channels matter for everything that follows. The first is that the largest flows are the least personal. Direct contributions, the channel most talked about, are capped and small; the largest sums spent in primaries moved through super PACs that never gave a candidate a dollar. The second is that the channels are open to everyone. Labor unions, industries, ideological groups and other foreign-policy constituencies use the same pipes, and in lobbying many of them spend far more. [cite:pm_tablet_lobbying] What sets the pro-Israel network apart in the record is not a channel no one else can use. It is the combination: pro-Israel money appears in all six, at every level of government, for a single foreign-policy cause, with the American organizations active in the first five and the Israeli government's own contracts, separate from them, in the sixth.

The channels also leave gaps, and they should be named. Earmarked money is reported under individual donors' names, so totals depend on how a tracker attributes it. Super PAC money passed to other committees can be followed only as far as the next committee's filings. Charitable donors to travel foundations are not public. And campaign records say nothing about the most important question a reader will ask, which is whether any of it changed a vote. The next section sets out how to read the numbers with those gaps in mind.

sections.h: How to Read a Number
sections.html:
The figures in this volume come from public filings, but almost none of them can be read without a short set of questions. Which election does the figure cover? Was the money given to a candidate or spent for or against one? Whose definition of "pro-Israel" produced it? On what date was it counted? And what does it show about the member who received it, as opposed to the organization that gave it? This section takes the questions one at a time, with examples from the record, so that the reader can apply them to any figure in the parts that follow, and to the figures quoted elsewhere.

One cycle or a whole career. Federal campaign money is organized in two-year cycles that end with each November election. A figure for "the 2024 cycle" covers money given or spent from January 2023 to December 2024. A career total covers every cycle since a member first ran, sometimes thirty years or more. The two are often confused, and the confusion is not always innocent. The career totals compiled by the tracker Track AIPAC, used in Part Four, place Senator Susan Collins of Maine first among all senators of either party, at about $4.1 million; that sum covers every race she has run, not one election. [cite:trackaipac_congress] A figure for a single cycle would be much smaller. Neither number is wrong, but a sentence that quotes the career figure as if it were one election's money misleads.

Given to, or spent for, or spent against. The second question separates the channels described in the previous section. Money given to a campaign, directly or through earmarking, is money the candidate can spend. Money a super PAC spends for a candidate is not given to that candidate at all; the candidate cannot direct it, and in law must not coordinate with it. Money spent against a candidate is the opposite of support. Trackers that compile "pro-Israel money" by member often add independent spending made on a member's behalf to the money the member received, which is a reasonable way to measure who benefited but not a measure of what the member took. In Track AIPAC's list, the Michigan Democrat Haley Stevens shows a career total of about $36.3 million, of which about $1.4 million was given to her campaigns and about $34.9 million was spent by others on her behalf. [cite:trackaipac_congress] Those are different facts, and this volume reports them separately.

Whose definition. The third question concerns the boundary of the category. OpenSecrets' pro-Israel category, the oldest consistent series, counts contributions from PACs and individuals it classifies as pro-Israel. [cite:pm_jvl_pacs] Track AIPAC counts all pro-Israel PACs, including J Street, adds the large individual donors to those PACs, and adds outside spending; it describes its own definition as broad. [cite:trackaipac_congress] [cite:wiki_trackaipac] Other trackers add still more. One third-party aggregator, Gen Us, has claimed $231.8 million in pro-Israel money for the 2026 cycle against an FEC-based figure of $104.3 million for AIPAC's two committees, a gap explained mostly by what each counted. [cite:pm_sludge_100m_2026] [cite:pm_genus_tracker] This volume uses the narrower, itemized figures wherever they exist, names the tracker whenever it uses a broader one, and does not add figures produced under different definitions.

On what date. Campaign finance is reported in stages, and the same race can produce several "final" figures as late filings arrive. The United Democracy Project's spending against Representative Cori Bush of Missouri in 2024 has been reported at figures from $5.2 million to $8.6 million, depending on the date of the filing and on whether spending for her opponent is included. [cite:factcheck_udp_2024] [cite:rollcall_bush_primary_2024] In the 2026 Kentucky primary against Representative Thomas Massie, FactCheck.org reported in August that the super PAC had spent over $3 million opposing him, while Louisville Public Media's tally of all filings put its spending at $4.1 million. [cite:pm_factcheck_udp_2026] [cite:lpm_massie_gallrein_funding] Where sources differ, this volume gives the range and the date of each figure rather than choosing one.

What the money shows about the member. The last question is the hardest, and the campaign records cannot answer it alone. A member who receives large sums from pro-Israel donors and votes for military aid to Israel may vote that way because of the money, or may receive the money because of the votes, or both, or neither. Donors give to candidates who already agree with them. The Guardian's analysis of members' most recent elections, mostly those of 2022, found that members who received more pro-Israel money were more likely to back military support for Israel, but that party affiliation, not money, best predicted what members said about civilian casualties in Gaza, and that the data could not show that the money changed anyone's position. [cite:guardian_gaza_donors] This volume holds to that limit. It reports what members received, what was spent for and against them, and what they said and did, side by side. It does not claim that a vote was bought unless a document says so, and in the record studied here none does.

The limit runs in the other direction too. The absence of proof that money changed a vote is not proof that it did not. Critics of these campaigns argue that a primary costing $14 million to remove a sitting member, when it succeeds, warns every other member without anything being written down; supporters answer that voters, not money, decided each race. Part Five sets out what those campaigns were, in which races, at what cost and with what result, and the reader can weigh both claims.

chapters.label: Part Two
chapters.title: AIPAC: The Architecture
chapters.intro: At the center of the American network stands one organization. Part Two describes it: how a one-man office opened in 1951 became AIPAC, the episodes that shaped its reputation, the four legal bodies through which it now works, how much each takes in according to its own tax returns, how little it spends on lobbying compared with its reputation, and the decision of December 2021 that turned a lobby without a campaign budget into the largest electoral spender among pro-Israel groups. The earlier history is told in other volumes and linked here rather than retold.
chapters.outro:
Part Two set out the organization at the center of the network. AIPAC grew from Isaiah Kenen's office, opened in 1951 and given its present name in 1959, into a membership organization that reports more than five million members; it is built as four bodies: a 501(c)(4) lobby, a 501(c)(3) foundation that pays for congressional travel, a PAC and a super PAC. [cite:pm_wiki_aipac] [cite:pm_pp_aipac990] [cite:pm_pp_aief990] Its lobbying spending is small, about $3.5 million in 2018 and $3.8 million in 2025; its campaign spending, since December 2021, is large: $44 million in 2022, $95.1 million in 2024, and more than $100 million in the 2026 cycle by August. [cite:pm_tablet_lobbying] [cite:pm_cjn_lobby2025] [cite:pm_israelite_2024] [cite:pm_sludge_100m_2026]

What is settled is the structure and the size. What is contested is the old question of what the structure is: an American advocacy organization exercising ordinary rights, or a body that should be treated in law as acting for a foreign state; and the newer question of what its campaign money does. What the record leaves open is the money behind the foundation and the lobby, whose donors are not public. Part Three counts the campaign money cycle by cycle.

sections.h: From a One-Man Office to the Largest Foreign-Policy Lobby
sections.html:
AIPAC began as one man's office. Its founder, Isaiah L. Kenen, had directed the lobbying of the American Emergency Committee on Zionist Affairs from 1943, served as the Jewish Agency's information director at the United Nations and sat on Israel's first delegation there before he moved to Washington in 1951. [cite:rs_cw1_jta_kenen_obit] Earlier volumes of this library tell that beginning in detail: [scene:cw1_lobby|the lobby in its Cold War frame] follows Kenen's first campaign, for Israel's first American aid grant, and [scene:s07g|the line from AZEC to AIPAC] traces the organizations from which his committee grew. This section does not retell them. It follows the organization from that office to the institution that, by the 2020s, outspent every other committee OpenSecrets classed as pro-Israel, [cite:pm_israelite_2024] and it marks the episodes that shaped how it works and how it is argued about.

A separate committee, and the foreign-agent question. The structure Kenen chose carried a legal argument inside it. His lobbying had secured $65 million and then $73 million in American aid for Israel in 1951 and 1952. In 1953 he formed the American Zionist Committee for Public Affairs, a body separate from the American Zionist Council, partly because of concerns about registration under the Foreign Agents Registration Act; it began work in 1954 and took the name American Israel Public Affairs Committee in 1959, by most accounts, though Kenen's obituary dates the new name to 1954. [cite:pm_wiki_aipac] [cite:rs_cw1_jta_kenen_obit] The concern was not hypothetical. The Council's purchases of Kenen's newsletter had been paid for in part by the Jewish Agency, a body already registered as a foreign agent, [cite:rs_cw5_barda_2026] and in November 1962 the Justice Department ordered the Council to register; the Senate Foreign Relations Committee examined the payments the following year. Those events are told in [scene:s11a|the order of 21 November 1962] and [scene:cw5_jewish_agency_hearing|the Jewish Agency before the Senate]. The separation Kenen designed is the root of the argument that has followed AIPAC ever since: it says it is an American organization, funded by Americans, that receives no money from Israel or any foreign group, and its critics, from Senator J. William Fulbright in the 1970s to the former CIA officer Victor Marchetti in the 1980s, have argued it should register anyway. [cite:pm_wiki_aipac]

From lobby to network. For its first two decades AIPAC was a small Washington office whose best-known product was Kenen's newsletter, the Near East Report. [cite:rs_cw5_barda_2026] The change came under Kenen's successors. Morris Amitay followed him in 1974, and Thomas Dine, who became executive director in 1980, built a national grassroots organization of members and donors around the Washington staff. [cite:pm_wiki_aipac] The model was the one AIPAC used until 2021: a lobby that gave no money to candidates itself, surrounded by members who did. In the same period it lost a major fight: in 1981 the House voted to block President Reagan's sale of AWACS surveillance aircraft to Saudi Arabia, but the Senate narrowly declined to, and the sale went ahead over the lobby's opposition, a fight told in [scene:aw_s01|AWACS, 1981]. Its reputation for electoral power dates from the same years. In 1982 activists connected with AIPAC backed Richard Durbin against Representative Paul Findley of Illinois, and in 1984 they backed Paul Simon against Senator Charles Percy; both incumbents lost. [cite:pm_wiki_aipac] How much the pro-Israel money decided those races, against all the other causes of a close election, is disputed, and Part Five returns to them as the first precedents for the unseating campaigns of the 2020s.

Two scandals. Two episodes from the following decades are still cited whenever AIPAC's influence is discussed, and both are documented. In 1992 AIPAC's president, David Steiner, was recorded without his knowledge in a telephone call with a New York property developer, Haim Katz, who gave the tape to the Washington Times. On the tape Steiner claimed that AIPAC had "a dozen people in the campaign, in the headquarters, in Little Rock" working for Bill Clinton, and spoke of positions such as secretary of state with the words "we're just negotiating." After the transcript was published Steiner said his statements were "simply and totally untrue," apologized, and resigned in November 1992. [cite:pm_wiki_steiner] The episode proved that an AIPAC president had boasted of influence over appointments; it did not prove that he had any, and he denied it.

The second episode involved the law. In 2005 Lawrence Franklin, a Defense Department analyst, pleaded guilty to passing classified information, some of it to two senior AIPAC staff members, Steven Rosen and Keith Weissman. AIPAC dismissed both men in April 2005, and they were indicted under the Espionage Act for receiving and passing on national defense information. In 2009 the government dropped all charges, saying that the judge's rulings had made a conviction unlikely and that it did not want to reveal classified information at trial. [cite:pm_wiki_franklin] [cite:pm_wiki_aipac] Franklin was convicted; the AIPAC staff members were not, and AIPAC itself was never charged.

The argument that never closed. Through all of it, the question Kenen's structure was built to answer stayed open. To AIPAC and its supporters, it is what it says it is: an American membership organization, funded by private donations, that advocates for a policy, the support of an ally, that most American voters and both parties have long endorsed. To its critics, its closeness to the priorities of successive Israeli governments makes it something the law ought to treat differently. The 1962 order, the 1963 hearings, the arguments of Fulbright and Marchetti and the questions raised again in the 2020s are all versions of the same dispute. [cite:pm_wiki_aipac] This volume does not settle it. It describes what AIPAC and its affiliates do with money, which is a matter of public record, and leaves the legal characterization to the reader. The next section sets out the structure through which that money now moves.

sections.h: Four Bodies, One Network: How AIPAC Is Built
sections.html:
AIPAC is not one organization but four, each a different kind of legal entity, each allowed to do things the others may not. Seen from outside, they share a name, a headquarters and a mission. In law they are separate, and the separation is what lets the network work through every channel described in Part One. This section sets out the four, what each is permitted to do, how large each is according to its own filings, and what is known and not known about where their money comes from.

AIPAC itself. The parent body is registered as a 501(c)(4) "social welfare" organization in Washington. That status allows it to lobby without limit, but gifts to it are not tax-deductible. [cite:pm_pp_aipac990] Its annual tax returns, which are public, give a measure of its size that does not depend on anyone's estimate. In the fiscal year that ended in September 2016 it reported revenue of $105.9 million; in 2019, the last year before the pandemic, $133.9 million; in 2020, $96.6 million; in 2022, $73.5 million; and in 2023, $79.4 million. In the fiscal year ending September 2024, the year after the attacks of 7 October 2023, its revenue reached $156.4 million, the highest in the series, and in 2025 it reported $122.5 million, with net assets of $177.6 million. [cite:pm_pp_aipac990] Its chief executive for most of those years, Howard Kohr, was its highest-paid officer, with reported compensation of about $1.49 million in 2025. [cite:pm_pp_aipac990] AIPAC had 376 employees in 2022, and in 2025 it reported more than five million members and seventeen regional offices. [cite:pm_wiki_aipac]

The foundation. The second body is the American Israel Education Foundation, a 501(c)(3) charity, tax-exempt since 1989. [cite:pm_pp_aief990] Because it is a charity, gifts to it are tax-deductible and it may not lobby, but it may pay for educational travel, and under the congressional ethics rules described in Part One it can sponsor trips that AIPAC, as an employer of lobbyists, could not. [cite:intercept_aief_donors] It shares AIPAC's offices, board members and part of its logo, and its donors are redacted from its public tax filings. [cite:intercept_aief_donors] It is large in its own right: revenue of $59.2 million in fiscal 2024 and $61.1 million in 2025, and net assets of $220.3 million, more than AIPAC's own. [cite:pm_pp_aief990] What it spends its money on is described in Part Seven.

The PAC. The third body is AIPAC PAC, created on 15 December 2021. [cite:pm_factcheck_udp_2026] Like every PAC it may give a candidate no more than $5,000 per election, but its main work is the earmarking channel described in Part One: it steers its members' individual donations to the candidates it endorses. [cite:pm_sludge_jeffries] By its own account, more than 10,000 AIPAC members gave over $53 million to candidates through it in the 2024 cycle, which it described as more than any other PAC. [cite:pm_aipac_memo_2024]

The super PAC. The fourth body is the United Democracy Project, formed on 3 January 2022. [cite:pm_wiki_aipac] It makes the independent expenditures, for and against candidates, that account for the largest sums in this volume. Its money comes from AIPAC itself and from individual donors, whose names it must report; in its first cycle AIPAC gave it $8.5 million, the WhatsApp co-founder Jan Koum $2 million, and four other donors $1 million each. [cite:pm_factcheck_udp_2022] Its spokesman has described its purpose as building "the broadest bipartisan pro-Israel coalition in Congress possible." [cite:pm_factcheck_udp_2022]

The meeting. One more element of the structure is not a legal entity but a gathering. For decades AIPAC's annual Policy Conference in Washington was among the largest political events in the capital. Nearly 20,000 delegates attended in 2016, and about 18,000 in March 2019, including 4,000 students; Israel's prime minister addressed the 2019 conference by satellite. [cite:pm_wiki_aipac] [cite:pm_aljaz_pc2019] The last in-person conference was held in 2020; AIPAC replaced the 2021 conference with a virtual event and cancelled the 2022 conference, citing the pandemic. [cite:pm_jstar_pc2022] The conference had been the network's most public face. Its end, as Part Three shows, coincided with the network's shift toward its least public channel, the super PAC.

What the structure shows, and what it hides. The four bodies divide the work along the lines the law draws. The 501(c)(4) lobbies, and its donors do not appear in its public filings. The 501(c)(3) pays for travel with tax-deductible gifts whose givers are redacted. The PAC reports its contributions and itemizes, by name, every earmarked gift over $200 to the Federal Election Commission. The super PAC reports its donors too, but can pass money to other committees whose names say nothing about Israel. The result is a network in which some parts are among the most transparent in American politics and others among the least, and in which the public record is fullest for the money given to candidates and thinnest for the money behind the trips and the lobbying. The next section turns to the lobbying.

sections.h: The Lobbying: A Small Budget and a Large Reputation
sections.html:
AIPAC calls itself a lobby, and lobbying is what its name describes. Yet in the one channel built to measure lobbying, the quarterly disclosures every lobbying organization must file with Congress, its spending has always been modest. That gap, between a small lobbying budget and a reputation as one of the most powerful lobbies in Washington, is the best clue to how the network actually works, and it has been pointed out as often by AIPAC's defenders as by its critics.

The disclosed figures. In 2018 AIPAC reported $3,518,028 in lobbying, according to OpenSecrets figures compiled by Tablet magazine, which ranked it about 147th among all lobbying organizations that year. All pro-Israel groups together spent about $5.0 million. The largest lobbying spenders were in another league: the US Chamber of Commerce reported $94.8 million and the National Association of Realtors $72.8 million, and companies such as Boeing, Amazon and Exxon Mobil each spent between three and four and a half times what AIPAC did. [cite:pm_tablet_lobbying] AIPAC's quarterly spending rose after the attacks of 7 October 2023, when it reported more than $800,000 in a single quarter, [cite:pm_cns_2024] and its annual figures for the two years that followed were about $3.3 million in 2024 and almost $3.8 million in 2025. [cite:pm_cjn_lobby2025]

Two cautions apply to the table. First, several of these organizations lobby on many subjects, from social services to civil rights, and their totals are not all Israel-related. Second, lobbying disclosures record what an organization pays its own lobbyists and outside firms to lobby; they do not record the time its members spend calling and meeting their own representatives, which for a membership organization like AIPAC may be a large part of the effort and is not measured anywhere.

What it lobbies for. AIPAC describes its aim, in its own words, as encouraging and persuading "the U.S. government to enact specific policies" that support the relationship with Israel. In its account of the 2023–24 Congress it pointed above all to money: an emergency package of $14.3 billion and what it called the largest funding package in Israel's history, worth $18.1 billion. [cite:pm_aipac_memo_2024] Its long-standing positions include strong support for military aid to Israel and opposition to the 2015 nuclear agreement with Iran, which it supported the United States leaving in 2018. [cite:pm_wiki_aipac] The aid itself, how it is structured and where it is spent, is the subject of other volumes in this library; this one follows the money that moves the other way, from American donors into American politics.

Where the influence comes from. If not from lobbying dollars, from where? Writing in Tablet in 2019, before AIPAC gave a single dollar to a campaign, Armin Rosen argued that its strength lay in a network: AIPAC-connected activists who give to future members of Congress early in their careers, and whose support signals to other pro-Israel donors which candidates are worth backing. [cite:pm_tablet_lobbying] On this account, AIPAC's real asset was never its lobbying budget but its ability to mobilize the donations of its members, which at that time flowed through independent PACs and individual checks. The decision AIPAC took two and a half years later, described in the next section, can be read as a decision to bring that network's money under its own name and control.

The gap between the lobbying figures and the reputation therefore does not show that the reputation is exaggerated, nor that it is deserved. It shows that the reputation does not rest on lobbying. The disclosed lobbying is real but small; the campaign money, which Parts Three to Five count, is large; and the trips, which Part Seven follows, have reached hundreds of congressional offices: the foundation sponsored 868 trips for 463 offices from 2012 to 2023. [cite:cnsmd_aief_explorer] A lobby's power, on this evidence, is better measured by all six channels together than by the one that bears its name.

sections.h: The Turn of December 2021
sections.html:
For seventy years AIPAC kept out of campaign spending. Its members gave; it did not. In December 2021 it reversed that rule. It announced that, ahead of the 2022 elections, it would form a political action committee and a super PAC, [cite:pm_factcheck_udp_2022] and in the four years that followed the two committees became the largest spenders among all the committees OpenSecrets classes as pro-Israel. [cite:pm_israelite_2024] This section follows the decision, the first cycle, the controversy that greeted it, and the scale it reached by 2026. The races themselves, and what the money did in them, are the subject of Part Five.

The first cycle. AIPAC PAC was created on 15 December 2021 and the United Democracy Project on 3 January 2022. [cite:pm_factcheck_udp_2026] [cite:pm_wiki_aipac] The super PAC moved fast. By the end of June 2022 it had raised almost $27.6 million, and by 2 August it had spent nearly $24.3 million in independent expenditures, all of it in Democratic primaries; FactCheck.org found it the largest outside spender in that year's Democratic primaries. [cite:pm_factcheck_udp_2022] Its largest donors were AIPAC itself, at $8.5 million, and a handful of very wealthy individuals: Jan Koum, a co-founder of WhatsApp, gave $2 million, and Jonathon Jacobson, Paul Singer, Bernard Marcus and Haim Saban gave $1 million each. [cite:pm_factcheck_udp_2022] Its spokesman, Patrick Dorton, explained the purpose in two sentences that remain the clearest statement of it: "What we're trying to do is build the broadest bipartisan pro-Israel coalition in Congress possible," and "There was rising concern in the pro-Israel community about candidates for Congress who held radical anti-Israel views." [cite:pm_factcheck_udp_2022]

The endorsement controversy. The PAC's first endorsements drew criticism from an unexpected side. Among the candidates AIPAC PAC endorsed in 2022 were Republican members of Congress who had voted against certifying the 2020 presidential election; by one account 37 of them were among 130 endorsements announced in March, and J Street, in August, put the number of such members AIPAC had supported at 109. [cite:pm_wiki_aipac] [cite:pm_jstreet_sedition] The two figures describe different points in the year and should not be read as one count. Asked whether there was any pro-Israel candidate AIPAC would rule out, its chief executive, Howard Kohr, answered: "I'd have to think about that." J Street's policy director called on AIPAC to set "some moral red lines." [cite:pm_jstreet_sedition] The committees' stated test was support for the US–Israel relationship; the super PAC's website describes its work as helping to elect candidates who support that relationship. [cite:pm_factcheck_udp_2022] The episode showed the logic of the new structure: a single-issue PAC, endorsing on a single issue, across both parties.

2024: the scale. In the 2024 cycle the two committees together spent $95.1 million, according to FEC filings compiled by OpenSecrets, more than double the $44 million of 2022, and more than every other committee OpenSecrets classed as pro-Israel. [cite:pm_israelite_2024] The super PAC alone raised $87.1 million in that cycle and spent about $61.4 million. [cite:pm_factcheck_udp_2026] AIPAC's own account, published the day after the election, said its PAC had endorsed 361 candidates, that 326 had won their general elections, 120 Democrats and 206 Republicans, and that more than 10,000 members had given over $53 million to candidates through it. It credited the super PAC with helping to decide nine races, including the defeats of Representatives Jamaal Bowman of New York and Cori Bush of Missouri. [cite:pm_aipac_memo_2024] The win rate needs a caution: by the memo's own account, the endorsements covered 75 percent of House members and 84 percent of senators in the cycle, so a high rate of victory reflects whom AIPAC endorsed as much as what it spent. [cite:pm_aipac_memo_2024]

2026: more money, different names. By June 2026 the super PAC had raised about $104 million for the 2026 cycle, already more than in the whole of 2024, and had spent about $52.5 million. [cite:pm_factcheck_udp_2026] The change in 2026 was not only in size but in visibility. Politico reported that the super PAC had routed more than 40 percent of its primary spending that year through pop-up and pass-through committees, groups with names unrelated to Israel that received its money and spent it under their own. [cite:pm_factcheck_udp_2026] Counting spending by both committees, the super PAC and the PAC together, Sludge put AIPAC's 2026 election spending at $104.3 million by early August, a figure for money spent, separate from the super PAC's $104 million raised. [cite:pm_sludge_100m_2026] Who received that money, and against whom it was spent, is set out in Parts Three to Five.

The turn of 2021 changed what AIPAC is. Until then it was a lobby surrounded by donors; afterwards it was a lobby with its own electoral machine. Its supporters describe the change as a natural extension of its members' civic rights, and point out that every major interest in American politics, from labor to industry, has PACs and super PACs of its own. Its critics argue that a lobby whose cause is a foreign country's security now decides, with sums no individual member of Congress can match, who among them faces a well-funded primary. Both descriptions rest on the same filings. What those filings show, cycle by cycle, is the subject of the next part.

chapters.label: Part Three
chapters.title: The Money, Cycle by Cycle
chapters.intro: Part Three counts the money. It begins with the long, steady record from 1990 to 2020, when pro-Israel contributions came from individuals and several dozen independent PACs and rarely exceeded $15 million a cycle, and follows the rise after 2021, when AIPAC's own committees multiplied the totals. It names the largest donors where the filings do, keeps general party giving by pro-Israel donors out of the pro-Israel totals, and sets the money beside other interests: smaller than finance, real estate or cryptocurrency, larger than any other foreign-policy cause in the record.
chapters.outro:
Part Three set the totals out. From 1990 to 2020 pro-Israel PACs gave between about $2 million and $9 million a cycle, and in 2018, the fullest pre-2021 cycle, pro-Israel donors and groups spent just over $22 million on contributions and lobbying together, most of it to Democrats. [cite:pm_jvl_pacs2020] [cite:pm_guardian_2019] After 2021 AIPAC's two committees alone spent $44 million in 2022 and $95.1 million in 2024 on OpenSecrets' count, and more than $100 million in the 2026 cycle by August; other pro-Israel committees grew too, the Republican Jewish Coalition's fourfold. [cite:pm_israelite_2024] [cite:pm_sludge_100m_2026]

What is settled is the growth, from tens of millions to more than a hundred million a cycle, and its shift toward Republican candidates in general elections and against progressive Democrats in primaries. What is contested is the right total, which depends on what is counted, and how to treat large partisan donors such as the Adelsons, whom this volume keeps separate. What the record leaves open is the per-cycle list of recipients built from the FEC's own files, which Part Four begins.

sections.h: Thirty Years of Steady Money, 1990–2020
sections.html:
For three decades before AIPAC entered campaign spending, pro-Israel money in American elections followed a steady, modest course. It came from individual donors and from several dozen independent political action committees, most of them small, some of them regional, and it went mostly to Democrats. This section sets out that long record from the oldest consistent series, kept by the Center for Responsive Politics, and looks closely at the one cycle, 2018, for which a full analysis was published. It is the baseline against which the changes of the 2020s have to be measured.

The PAC series. OpenSecrets' series of contributions from pro-Israel PACs to federal candidates begins in 1990. It shows about $4.0 million in that cycle, a range of between about $2.1 million and $4.3 million a cycle through the 1990s and 2000s, and then a slow rise: $5.1 million in 2012, $5.9 million in 2014, $7.5 million in 2016, and $8.7 million in both 2018 and 2020. In thirty years the PACs gave $71.3 million. [cite:pm_jvl_pacs2020] PAC money was always the smaller part. From 1990 to 2012, when the Center also published totals for individual donors, individuals gave about twice as much as the PACs, $71.5 million against $34.5 million, figures from an earlier release of the Center's data that do not match the PAC table above. [cite:pm_jvl_pacs]

Who gave. Over the thirty years the largest pro-Israel PAC was not AIPAC, which gave nothing, nor a hawkish group. It was J Street's PAC, which describes itself as "pro-Israel, pro-peace" and supports a two-state solution, with $14.5 million in contributions; it gave about $4 million in 2018 alone. Next came NORPAC, a long-established committee based in New Jersey, with $8.1 million, then National PAC with $4.5 million, the Republican Jewish Coalition with $3.4 million and the National Action Committee with $2.9 million. [cite:pm_jvl_pacs2020] [cite:pm_jstreet_2018] The largest giver in the long series was thus the most dovish of the groups, a fact that sits awkwardly with both the defenders and the critics of "the lobby" as a single bloc.

The 2018 cycle in full. The Guardian's analysis of OpenSecrets data for 2018 gives the fullest picture of a single pre-2021 cycle. Pro-Israel donors and groups spent more than $22 million that cycle on lobbying and campaign contributions together. About $5 million went to lobbying, the most since tracking began in 1998, AIPAC accounting for about $3.5 million of it. Just under $15 million went to candidates' campaigns, the most since 1990, reaching 269 members of the House and 57 senators, with Democrats receiving about twice as much as Republicans. [cite:pm_guardian_2019] The largest recipients were Senators Bob Menendez of New Jersey ($548,507), Ted Cruz of Texas ($352,894), Sherrod Brown of Ohio ($230,342) and Tammy Baldwin of Wisconsin ($229,896), and the Texas Senate candidate Beto O'Rourke ($226,690). [cite:pm_guardian_2019]

The scale, in proportion. In 2018 pro-Israel donors ranked thirty-fourth among interest groups giving to members of Congress. [cite:pm_tablet_lobbying] The securities and investment industry spent $389 million in the same cycle and the real-estate industry $186 million. [cite:pm_guardian_2019] By that measure pro-Israel campaign money was a middling interest, large for a foreign-policy cause and small beside the great economic interests. Its distinctive feature was not size. It was organization: a single-issue constituency, active in both parties, whose donors, as Part Two describes, gave early to promising candidates and signalled to one another whom to back. [cite:pm_tablet_lobbying]

The long series has two limits that matter for what follows. It counts contributions only: before 2010 there were no super PACs, and before 2022 pro-Israel independent spending was comparatively small. And it depends on OpenSecrets' classification of which PACs and donors are pro-Israel, a judgment other trackers make differently. The next section turns to the cycles after 2021, when both limits stopped holding.

sections.h: The Money After 2021
sections.html:
From the 2022 cycle the record of pro-Israel money changes in two ways at once. The amounts rise steeply, and the measures multiply, because money now flows through channels the old series did not count. This section sets out the figures for 2020 to 2026 channel by channel, with the source and date of each, and explains why figures that look as if they describe the same thing do not.

Contributions to candidates. The Washington Report on Middle East Affairs, an advocacy publication critical of the lobby that tabulates FEC data, counted pro-Israel PAC contributions to House and Senate candidates of $12.7 million in the 2020 cycle, $17.2 million in 2022 and $44.7 million in 2024. [cite:pm_wrmea_2024] Those figures are larger than OpenSecrets' PAC-only series, which put 2020 at $8.7 million, [cite:pm_jvl_pacs2020] most likely because they count earmarked money and a wider set of committees, though the publication does not set out its method; the two series should not be joined into one line. WRMEA's count rose about three and a half times between 2020 and 2024; AIPAC's PAC alone reported more in earmarked contributions in 2024, $55.2 million on Sludge's count, than WRMEA counted for all pro-Israel PACs, so the series measure different things. By AIPAC's own account its PAC passed more than $53 million from over 10,000 members to candidates in the 2024 cycle, [cite:pm_aipac_memo_2024] and Sludge's count of the final filings found more than $55.2 million donated to federal candidates by the PAC. [cite:pm_sludge_final2024] In the 2026 cycle the PAC had given $45.9 million by the end of July, almost all of it earmarked, with particular attention to members of the House and Senate defense and appropriations committees. [cite:pm_sludge_pac2026]

AIPAC's two committees together. Adding the super PAC's spending to the PAC's gives the measure most often quoted. On OpenSecrets' count the two committees spent $44 million in 2022 and $95.1 million in 2024. [cite:pm_israelite_2024] Sludge, counting all disbursements in the final 2024 filings, including the super PAC's operating costs and its transfers to six other committees, put the 2024 total at nearly $126.9 million. [cite:pm_sludge_final2024] For 2026, Sludge counted $104.3 million by early August, and the super PAC alone had raised about $104 million by June. [cite:pm_sludge_100m_2026] [cite:pm_factcheck_udp_2026] The differences are of scope and date, not of fact: whether transfers and overheads are counted, and when the filings were read.

The other committees. AIPAC was not the only pro-Israel group whose spending grew. OpenSecrets' figures for 2022 and 2024 show the Republican Jewish Coalition and its super PAC rising from $4.5 million to $19.7 million, J Street from $8.6 million to $14.6 million, and NORPAC from $1.6 million to $2.7 million; Democratic Majority for Israel was the only major pro-Israel group to spend less, $4.8 million against $7.7 million. [cite:pm_israelite_2024]

The shift in kind. The figures show two changes beyond size. The first is in direction. In 2018 the money as a whole favored Democrats about two to one. [cite:pm_tablet_lobbying] [cite:pm_guardian_2019] By AIPAC's account, 206 of the 326 general-election winners it backed in 2024 were Republicans, [cite:pm_aipac_memo_2024] while its super PAC's largest sums were spent against Democrats in Democratic primaries. The second is in method. Until 2021 almost all pro-Israel money was given to candidates; in 2022 the largest sums were spent around them, and in 2024 contributions and outside spending were of similar size, the outside spending in advertising that, as Part Five shows, rarely mentioned Israel, and from 2026 increasingly through committees with unrelated names. [cite:punchbowl_udp_no_israel] [cite:pm_factcheck_udp_2026]

What is not yet counted. Two gaps remain. Per-cycle lists of the largest recipients in each party, built from the FEC's own files rather than a tracker's compilation, are being assembled for Part Four; until they are complete, that part uses the career totals compiled by Track AIPAC and the 2018 figures above, and says so. And the 2026 figures stop at the dates given. The general election of November 2026 and the final reports that follow it will change every 2026 number in this section.

sections.h: Who Pays, and How It Compares
sections.html:
Two questions follow from the totals. Where does the money come from? And how large is it beside the other interests that spend in American elections? This section answers both from the disclosures. It names donors only where the public record names them as the largest givers to the committees studied here, and it keeps separate a kind of giving that is often added to pro-Israel totals but does not belong in them.

The super PAC's donors. A super PAC must report its donors, and the reports show that AIPAC's super PAC depends on a small number of very large gifts. In its first cycle AIPAC itself gave it $8.5 million, Jan Koum, a co-founder of WhatsApp, $2 million, and Jonathon Jacobson, Paul Singer, Bernard Marcus and Haim Saban $1 million each. [cite:pm_factcheck_udp_2022] In 2024 the largest donors were Koum ($5 million), Jacobson (nearly $4.6 million), Marcus ($3 million) and David Zalik ($2 million). [cite:factcheck_udp_2024] In 2026 FactCheck.org named Singer, Blair Frank, Marc Rowan and Saban among its top donors. [cite:pm_factcheck_udp_2026] The PAC is different: its money comes in earmarked contributions from more than 10,000 members, each capped at the individual limit. [cite:pm_aipac_memo_2024] The network's two committees therefore rest on two different bases, a broad membership for the money given to candidates and a narrow group of very wealthy donors for the money spent against them.

A kind of giving kept separate. Some of the largest donors associated with the cause of Israel in American politics give most of their money not to pro-Israel committees but to general party committees. Sheldon and Miriam Adelson are the leading example. New York magazine's tally of their lifetime political giving is about $273 million for Sheldon Adelson, who died in 2021, and $284 million for Miriam Adelson; in 2018 they spent $123 million on the midterm elections, nearly all of it benefiting Republicans, and in 2024 Miriam Adelson gave about $100 million to a super PAC supporting Donald Trump. [cite:wiki_miriam_adelson] [cite:pm_sludge_2019] [cite:wiki_preserve_america] Their stated priorities included moving the American embassy to Jerusalem, which Trump did in his first term. [cite:aj_adelson_knesset] That giving is real and large, but it went to committees whose purpose was to elect Republicans, not to support Israel, and adding it to "pro-Israel money" would mix two different things. This volume reports it here, names it as what it is, and leaves it out of the pro-Israel totals. The same rule applies to Haim Saban's gifts to Democratic committees, $3.3 million in 2018. [cite:pm_sludge_2019] The single exception in the totals is Miriam Adelson's $5 million to the Republican Jewish Coalition's super PAC in 2024, which was a pro-Israel committee's money and is counted. [cite:pm_israelite_2024]

The scale in proportion. Against other single-issue spenders, pro-Israel money is large but not the largest. The cryptocurrency industry's super PAC, Fairshake, and its affiliates spent more than $133 million in 2024, more than AIPAC's two committees by most counts, and had raised more than $193 million for 2026 by January of that year. [cite:pm_wiki_fairshake] Against the great economic interests it is smaller still: in 2018 the securities industry spent $389 million on federal elections and real estate $186 million. [cite:pm_guardian_2019] Against other foreign-policy causes, on the other hand, it has no near rival in the record used here. In 2018 the US-Cuba Democracy PAC, one of the best known of them, gave about $171,000. [cite:pm_guardian_2019]

One more channel, counted elsewhere. The Guardian's 2018 analysis added a figure from a different law. Agents registered under the Foreign Agents Registration Act on behalf of Israeli principals reported about $46.3 million in 2017 and 2018, the third-largest country total after Japan and South Korea; about $2.1 million of it was for political activity and $44.2 million for tourism promotion and other commercial work. [cite:pm_guardian_2019] That money is the Israeli state's and Israeli companies' own, spent openly through registered agents, and it is the subject of Part Nine.

The comparisons point in two directions, and both should be kept. Measured against all the money in American politics, pro-Israel spending is a middle-sized interest, smaller than finance or real estate and, in recent cycles, than cryptocurrency. Measured against other causes concerned with a foreign country, it is in a class of its own. What makes it unusual is less its size than its use: spent through every channel, in both parties, and, at its largest, against sitting members of Congress.

chapters.label: Part Four
chapters.title: The Recipients
chapters.intro: Part Four names the recipients. It sets out the career totals of the Congress sitting in 2026, by chamber and party, from the compilation of FEC data by the advocacy group Track AIPAC, with the cautions that compilation requires; then the cycle-by-cycle record since 2016, from the one published ranked list for 2018 and from lists being built directly from the FEC's own files. It keeps money given to a member apart from money spent on a member's behalf, and it does not treat any total as an explanation of a vote.
chapters.outro:
Part Four named the recipients. In the Congress of 2026, on Track AIPAC's career totals, the largest sums belong to members for whom outside groups spent heavily in primaries, Haley Stevens, George Latimer and Wesley Bell above all; among senators Susan Collins and Adam Schiff lead; the leaders of both parties in the House are on the lists; and a small group of progressive Democrats and one Republican, Thomas Massie, stand at zero. [cite:trackaipac_congress] In 2018, the last cycle before AIPAC's own committees, the largest recipients were senators of both parties, led by Bob Menendez and Ted Cruz. [cite:pm_guardian_2019]

What is settled is who received what, on each tracker's definition. What is contested is what the totals mean, since careers, states and seats shape them as much as positions do. What the record leaves open is the full set of single-cycle rankings since 2016, which are being built from the FEC's files. Part Five, which comes next in the volume's order, follows the money that was spent against members rather than given to them.

sections.h: The Current Congress: Who Has Received the Most
sections.html:
The question most readers ask first is the simplest: which members of Congress have received the most pro-Israel money? The most complete answer available for the Congress sitting in 2026 comes from Track AIPAC, an advocacy group critical of the lobby that compiles Federal Election Commission data for every member. Its figures, read as of 5 July 2026, are used in this section with three cautions stated at the start. They are career totals, covering every race a member has run, not a single election. They count all pro-Israel PACs, including the dovish J Street, and the large individual donors to those PACs. And they add outside spending made on a member's behalf, which is money the member did not receive. [cite:trackaipac_congress] [cite:wiki_trackaipac] Each figure below gives the direct and outside parts separately where they matter.

The Senate. Among Senate Democrats the largest total is Adam Schiff's, about $5.6 million, almost all of it, about $5.0 million, spent by outside groups on his behalf in his 2024 Senate race. Jacky Rosen of Nevada follows with about $2.3 million, mostly given directly, then Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock of Georgia and Cory Booker of New Jersey, each with between $850,000 and $960,000. The top twenty-five Senate Democrats together account for about $22.1 million. Four members of the Democratic caucus, Bernie Sanders, Chris Van Hollen, Jeff Merkley and Peter Welch, are listed at nothing. [cite:trackaipac_congress] Among Senate Republicans, Susan Collins of Maine leads every senator of either party with about $4.1 million, nearly all of it, $3.6 million, given directly over a long career. Ted Cruz of Texas follows with about $1.4 million, then Tom Cotton, John Cornyn and Mitch McConnell, each near $1 million. The top twenty-five Republicans total about $18.9 million; at the other end, Rand Paul of Kentucky is listed at $2,000. [cite:trackaipac_congress]

The House. The House lists show the difference between money given and money spent more sharply than any other figures in this volume. The top three House Democrats, Haley Stevens of Michigan with about $36.3 million, George Latimer of New York with about $19.2 million and Wesley Bell of Missouri with about $18.1 million, owe almost all of their totals to outside spending in contested primaries: about $34.9 million, $16.2 million and $13.7 million respectively.
