[cite:trackaipac_congress] Latimer and Bell are the challengers who defeated Jamaal Bowman and Cori Bush in 2024, and most of Stevens's total was spent in her 2026 Senate primary, with some in her 2022 primary against Andy Levin, told in Part Five. The top twenty-five House Democrats total about $128.8 million. The House Democratic leader, Hakeem Jeffries, is listed at about $1.5 million, all of it direct. Seven Democrats, among them Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Rashida Tlaib, Ilhan Omar and Summer Lee, are listed at nothing. [cite:trackaipac_congress]

House Republicans' totals are an order of magnitude smaller and mostly given directly. Mark Messmer of Indiana leads with about $2.9 million, $2.5 million of it outside spending in his 2024 primary, followed by Don Bacon of Nebraska, Juan Ciscomani of Arizona, Mike Lawler of New York and Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana, each with between $1.1 million and $1.3 million given directly. The top twenty-five total about $21.8 million. Thomas Massie of Kentucky is listed at nothing. [cite:trackaipac_congress]

What the lists show, and what they do not. Read with their cautions, the lists show three things. The money reaches the leadership of both parties, the Speaker and the Democratic leader among them. The largest totals belong not to the members who have taken the most money but to those for whom the most was spent, in primaries against candidates the lobby opposed. And the members at zero are a small and identifiable group: a handful of progressive Democrats and one libertarian Republican. What the lists do not show is why any member votes as he or she does. A member's total reflects the length of a career, the cost of a state's races and the competitiveness of a seat as much as any position on Israel, and the records cannot say whether the money followed the votes or the votes the money. [cite:guardian_gaza_donors] The next section turns from careers to single cycles, which are the better measure of what each election cost.

sections.h: Cycle by Cycle, 2016–2026
sections.html:
Career totals favor long careers and expensive states. A fairer measure of what each election cost is the money a member received in a single two-year cycle. This section sets out what the record used here documents cycle by cycle since 2016, separately for each party and chamber, and it states plainly where the record is still being assembled.

How the cycle lists are being built. OpenSecrets publishes per-cycle lists of the largest recipients of pro-Israel money, but its definitions are its own and its pages could not be read for this volume. To avoid relying on any single tracker's classification, the lists for each cycle from 2016 to 2026 are being built directly from the Federal Election Commission's bulk files of committee-to-candidate transactions. The method takes every contribution, earmarked pass-through and independent expenditure made by a defined list of pro-Israel committees, and totals them by candidate, cycle, chamber and party, keeping money given to a candidate separate from money spent for or against one. The list of committees is published with the results so that any reader can check what was counted. Until those lists are complete, this section reports the one cycle for which a published analysis gives a ranked list, 2018, and the current Congress's career totals given in the previous section.

2018. In the 2018 cycle pro-Israel donors and groups gave just under $15 million to candidates for Congress, reaching 269 members of the House and 57 senators, with Democrats receiving about twice as much as Republicans. [cite:pm_guardian_2019] The largest recipients were all senators or Senate candidates.

Several of those names recur across cycles. Ted Cruz, second in 2018, is second among Senate Republicans in the career totals of 2026, with about $1.4 million, and is the senator who has described himself as Israel's "strongest defender." [cite:trackaipac_congress] [cite:cruz_senate_ami] The 2018 list also shows how the money was distributed before AIPAC's own committees: the largest single giver that cycle was J Street's PAC, and the top recipients were mainly Democrats. [cite:pm_tablet_lobbying] [cite:pm_guardian_2019]

2022 and 2024. For the two cycles after AIPAC entered campaign spending, the record used here documents the largest recipients by a different measure: the money spent for or against candidates in primaries, set out race by race in Part Five. The Guardian's analysis of members' most recent elections, mostly those of 2022, found that the six largest recipients of pro-Israel donor money were all centrist Democrats who had beaten progressive opponents, together receiving about $25 million, some 42 percent of all pro-Israel donor money reaching sitting members. [cite:pm_guardian_2024] In 2024, by AIPAC's own account, its PAC passed money to candidates in both parties, 206 of its 326 winning general-election candidates being Republicans; its largest single earmarked total that the record names was more than $3.1 million to Wesley Bell. [cite:pm_aipac_memo_2024] [cite:pm_sludge_2024]

The cycles still to be filled. Ranked lists by party and chamber for 2016, 2020, 2022, 2024 and 2026, built from the FEC files, will be added here when the run described above is complete and its committee list has been reviewed. Until then, a reader who wants a single cycle's ranking can find it, under OpenSecrets' own definitions, on its pro-Israel recipients pages, and should read it with the five questions of Part One.

chapters.label: Part Five
chapters.title: The Unseating Campaigns
chapters.intro: The largest sums in this volume were not given to anyone. They were spent, by super PACs, in primaries, to elect some candidates and defeat others, most often sitting members of Congress or candidates who had broken with the lobby's positions. Part Five follows those campaigns: the older defeats often cited as precedents, then the super PAC's three cycles, 2022, 2024 and 2026, race by race, with the amounts, the outcomes and the other forces in each race. It reports wins and losses alike, and it keeps the question of what the money decided separate from the record of what was spent.
chapters.outro:
Part Five followed the money into the primaries. Before 2010 the record is thin: four defeats between 1982 and 2002 in which pro-Israel donors backed the challenger, without figures that can be checked. [cite:pm_wiki_aipac] [cite:pm_jweekly_mckinney] From 2022 it is exact. The super PAC spent nearly $24.3 million in its first cycle's Democratic primaries, winning most and losing in Pennsylvania and Michigan's 13th; [cite:pm_factcheck_udp_2022] in 2024 it spent almost $9.9 million against Jamaal Bowman and more than $5.2 million against Cori Bush, and both lost; [cite:factcheck_udp_2024] in 2026 it helped defeat Thomas Massie alongside the president, and lost in Michigan, California and Illinois despite record sums. [cite:lpm_massie_gallrein_funding] [cite:pm_sludge_100m_2026] [cite:pm_kqed_wahab] [cite:pm_prospect_illinois]

What is settled is the spending and the results. What is contested is the effect: whether the money decided races that had other causes, and whether, as critics argue, its main work is done in the races it never has to enter, by members who choose not to risk one. What the record leaves open is the full 2026 cycle, which was still running when this was written. Part Six turns to those members: the ones who refuse the money, and the ones who left office under attack.

sections.h: Before the Super PAC: Four Defeats, 1982–2002
sections.html:
The campaigns this part follows, from 2022 to 2026, are large, recent and fully documented in federal filings. They have a prehistory, and it is often cited, sometimes as proof that the pattern is old and sometimes as proof that it is a myth. Four defeats of sitting members of Congress, in 1982, 1984 and 2002, are the usual examples. This section sets out what the sources used here document about each, which is less than the stories told about them, and why the evidence is thinner than for the races that follow.

Findley and Percy. In 1982 Representative Paul Findley of Illinois, a Republican, lost his seat to the Democrat Richard Durbin. In 1984 Senator Charles Percy of Illinois, a Republican, lost to the Democrat Paul Simon. In both races activists associated with AIPAC backed the challenger. [cite:pm_wiki_aipac] The races entered the lobby's reputation as proof that crossing it could end a career. Like any close election they had other causes, which the sources used here do not weigh, and those sources do not quantify the pro-Israel money in either race, and this volume does not supply a figure.

Hilliard and McKinney. The two defeats of 2002 are closer to the modern pattern, and better reported. In June of that year Representative Earl Hilliard of Alabama, a member of the Congressional Black Caucus who had been critical of Israeli policy, lost a primary runoff; Black Caucus leaders publicly questioned the role pro-Israel money had played in his defeat. [cite:pm_jweekly_mckinney] In August Representative Cynthia McKinney of Georgia, a five-term incumbent whom that newspaper's headline called "anti-Israel," lost her primary to Denise Majette, a former state judge, by 58 percent to 42. Majette had strong support from pro-Israel contributors outside Georgia; the contemporary account in J., the Jewish weekly of Northern California, quoted a political scientist, Gilbert Kahn, saying that the money gave Majette the "nest egg" she needed to put herself before voters. [cite:pm_jweekly_mckinney]

The same account recorded the other causes. Republicans crossed over to vote in the Democratic primary, urged by Georgia party leaders, and McKinney herself blamed them: Republican voters, she said, "wanted to beat me more than the Democrats wanted to keep me." The regional director of the Anti-Defamation League attributed her defeat to her statements after the attacks of 11 September 2001, which, she said, voters saw as "fringe positions." McKinney also had substantial outside support of her own. [cite:pm_jweekly_mckinney] Both sides, in other words, had money in the race, and the contemporary record does not let a reader isolate the effect of either.

Why the old cases are weaker evidence. All four races share a feature that sets them apart from what came later. The money in them moved as individual contributions and through independent PACs, given to the challenger; it did not move through a super PAC spending in its own name, because no such thing existed before 2010. That makes the money harder to count and easier to dispute. In the races of 2022 to 2026, by contrast, a single committee connected to AIPAC reported every dollar it spent for and against named candidates. The modern record therefore answers a question the older one cannot: not whether pro-Israel donors preferred one candidate, which they often did, but how much an organization spent, on what, and against whom. The rest of this part follows that record, race by race.

sections.h: 2022: The First Cycle
sections.html:
The United Democracy Project spent its first money in the Democratic primaries of 2022, and it spent almost all of it there. By early August it had made nearly $24.3 million in independent expenditures, every dollar of it for or against candidates in Democratic contests, which made it the largest outside spender in that year's Democratic primaries. [cite:pm_factcheck_udp_2022] The pattern of that first cycle set the template for the next two: large sums, concentrated in a handful of safe Democratic districts where the primary decided the seat, for candidates described as mainstream or moderate and against candidates on the party's left.

The races. In Maryland's 4th District the super PAC spent about $4.26 million against Donna Edwards and $1.7 million for Glenn Ivey, who won. In North Carolina it spent $2.13 million for Valerie Foushee in the 4th District and $2.1 million for Don Davis in the 1st, with $335,000 against his opponent Erica Smith; both won. In Texas's 28th District it spent $423,000 for Representative Henry Cuellar and $1.43 million against his progressive challenger Jessica Cisneros, and Cuellar won the runoff. [cite:pm_factcheck_udp_2022] Those were victories by the committee's own measure.

Not every race went its way. In Pennsylvania's 12th District it spent $2 million against Summer Lee, a state legislator, and $660,000 for her opponent Steve Irwin; Lee won the primary and the seat. In Michigan's 13th District it spent $2.74 million for Adam Hollier and $1.43 million against Shri Thanedar, and Thanedar won. [cite:pm_factcheck_udp_2022] The committee's first cycle established, from the start, that money could be outspent by voters.

Andy Levin. The most discussed race of the year was in Michigan's 11th District, where redistricting set two sitting Democrats, Haley Stevens and Andy Levin, against each other. The super PAC spent $3.88 million for Stevens and $342,000 against Levin, and Stevens won. [cite:pm_factcheck_udp_2022] The Guardian reported that pro-Israel groups had poured millions into the race. [cite:guardian_levin_2022] The defeat of a sitting Democrat with a long record of support for Israel and for a two-state solution made plain, in a way the other races did not, that the committee's line ran between candidates the committee judged reliable on its positions and those it did not.

The concentration. The Guardian's later analysis of the money reaching sitting members showed how concentrated the 2022 effort had been. The six largest recipients of pro-Israel donor spending in that cycle, all centrist Democrats who had beaten progressive opponents, accounted for about $25 million, some 42 percent of all pro-Israel donor money reaching current members; nearly $5.4 million had been spent backing Haley Stevens alone and about $2.8 million backing Don Davis. [cite:pm_guardian_2024] Democratic Majority for Israel, a separate pro-Israel PAC, claimed that its endorsed candidates won more than 80 percent of their races that year, a claim the Guardian did not verify. [cite:pm_guardian_2024]

One race in 2022 showed another feature of the method. In Minnesota's 5th District, Representative Ilhan Omar faced a primary challenger, Don Samuels. The super PAC did not advertise in its own name; it gave $350,000 to a separate committee backing Samuels, and the transfer became public only after the vote, which Omar won by about 2,500 votes. [cite:jewishinsider_udp_omar_2022] Money routed through other committees, which became a large share of the super PAC's spending by 2026, began here, in a single race and a single transfer.

The first cycle's results were mixed in the ledger and clear in their effect on the argument. Supporters of the super PAC pointed to its record of victories in open seats and its defeat of candidates they regarded as hostile to Israel. Critics pointed to the sums, to the defeat of a Jewish Democrat over policy, and to advertising that, in many of these races, said little or nothing about Israel at all, attacking candidates instead on other issues. [cite:punchbowl_udp_no_israel] Both camps agreed that the money had changed the conduct of Democratic primaries. The next cycle tested how far it could go against sitting members.

sections.h: 2024: Bowman and Bush
sections.html:
The war in Gaza that followed the attacks of 7 October 2023 turned the next primary season into the most expensive test yet of the super PAC's method. AIPAC's PAC more than doubled its weekly fundraising after the attacks, [cite:pm_cns_2024] and by August 2024 the super PAC had raised about $68.4 million and spent about $56 million, and its largest donors were again a small number of very wealthy individuals: Jan Koum gave $5 million, Jonathon Jacobson nearly $4.6 million, Bernard Marcus $3 million and David Zalik $2 million. [cite:factcheck_udp_2024] It concentrated its money, as in 2022, in Democratic primaries, but this time its two largest targets were sitting members of Congress, both progressive critics of Israel's conduct of the war: Bowman had co-sponsored a resolution calling for a ceasefire in Gaza, and Bush had opposed sending offensive weapons to Israel. [cite:wiki_bowman_primary_2024] [cite:rollcall_bush_primary_2024]

Jamaal Bowman, New York's 16th District. The super PAC spent almost $9.9 million opposing Representative Jamaal Bowman and nearly $4.8 million supporting his challenger, George Latimer. Latimer won on 25 June with more than 58 percent of the vote to Bowman's 41. [cite:factcheck_udp_2024] The advertising tracker AdImpact counted $14.9 million in super PAC advertising in the race, 59 percent of all the money spent on it. [cite:pm_adimpact_2024] The New York Times wrote that the spending "eclipsed what any interest group has ever spent on a single House race." [cite:factcheck_udp_2024] After the result AIPAC said the super PAC "will continue to support leaders who promote our partnership with Israel." [cite:factcheck_udp_2024]

Cori Bush, Missouri's 1st District. In St. Louis the super PAC spent more than $5.2 million against Representative Cori Bush and $3.3 million for her challenger, Wesley Bell, according to FactCheck.org's count of filings through September; later tallies that include all spending in the race put the super PAC's total at about $8.6 million. [cite:factcheck_udp_2024] [cite:rollcall_bush_primary_2024] Bell won on 6 August. AIPAC's PAC had also steered more than $3.1 million in earmarked contributions to Bell's own campaign by the end of July. [cite:pm_sludge_2024]

The other races. The super PAC spent about $4.6 million against Dave Min, a candidate for an open seat in California's 47th District; Min nonetheless finished in the top two and advanced to the general election. [cite:factcheck_udp_2024] It spent about $3.7 million for Sarah Elfreth in an open Maryland seat, who won. [cite:pm_adimpact_2024] And for the first time it spent in Republican primaries, about $3 million against four Republican candidates, two of whom lost: John Hostettler, in Indiana's 8th District, against whom it spent $1.8 million while the Republican Jewish Coalition's super PAC spent $1.2 million for his opponent Mark Messmer; and Representative Bob Good of Virginia. [cite:factcheck_udp_2024] [cite:pm_adimpact_2024] Across the cycle, the super PAC spent about $12.4 million supporting some Democrats and more than $20 million opposing others. [cite:factcheck_udp_2024]

A race it chose to skip. In Minnesota, Representative Ilhan Omar faced the same challenger she had beaten in 2022. Her opponents spent only about $110,000 against her, after AIPAC reportedly judged the challenger too weak to win, against the $23.2 million spent to defeat Bowman and Bush the same year. [cite:abc538_squad_spending] [cite:washex_omar_2024] The comparison is a reminder that the money followed a judgment about which seats could be taken, not only about which members the network most opposed.

What the advertising said. In these races the super PAC's advertising generally did not mention Israel. It attacked Bowman and Bush on their records and their reliability as Democrats, and in Bowman's case on his statements. [cite:punchbowl_udp_no_israel] [cite:factcheck_udp_2024] Its supporters regard that as ordinary campaigning: an independent committee may choose whatever message it thinks will persuade voters. Its critics argue that it allowed a foreign-policy lobby to remove members of Congress without voters knowing that foreign policy was the reason. Both descriptions are consistent with the filings.

The results of 2024 were the high point of the method's reputation. AIPAC's own summary credited the super PAC with helping to decide nine races, Bowman's and Bush's among them. [cite:pm_aipac_memo_2024] What the filings cannot show is how many votes the money moved. Both races had other dynamics, and the sources used here do not separate the effect of the spending from them. They show that record sums, in Bowman's race the largest any interest group had spent on a House primary, were spent to defeat two sitting members who had criticized Israel's conduct of the war, and that both were defeated.

sections.h: Thomas Massie: The Republican Primary
sections.html:
Until 2026 the super PAC's largest campaigns had all been fought inside the Democratic Party. In May of that year it took part in the most expensive House primary in American history, and the target was a Republican. Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky's 4th District had taken no money from pro-Israel PACs, had voted against foreign-aid packages including aid to Israel, and had criticized the lobby's influence openly. [cite:trackaipac_congress] [cite:mee_massie_aipac] He lost his primary on 19 May 2026 to Ed Gallrein, by 54.9 percent to 45.1. [cite:lpm_massie_gallrein_funding] This section sets out the money, the other force in the race, and the words of both sides, because the race is cited as proof of two different things, and the record supports parts of each.

The money. Louisville Public Media's tally of all filings put the race's total cost at about $37 million, with about $32.6 million of that in advertising according to the tracker AdImpact, a record for any House primary. [cite:lpm_massie_gallrein_funding] [cite:mee_massie_aipac] Pro-Israel committees provided a large share. By Louisville Public Media's count AIPAC's super PAC spent $4.1 million against Massie and the Republican Jewish Coalition's super PAC, the RJC Victory Fund, $3.9 million, about $8 million in all; FactCheck.org, counting at a different date, put the AIPAC super PAC's spending at over $3 million against Massie and nearly $500,000 for Gallrein, and Politico counted more than $9 million from pro-Israel groups. [cite:lpm_massie_gallrein_funding] [cite:pm_factcheck_udp_2026] By AdImpact's measure pro-Israel groups bought about half of the advertising that benefited Gallrein. [cite:mee_massie_aipac]

The other force. The pro-Israel committees were not alone, and on most accounts they were not the decisive force. President Trump recruited Gallrein and endorsed him in October 2025 against Massie, who had crossed him on several fronts: on the release of the Justice Department's files on Jeffrey Epstein, on the American strikes on Iran, and on the 2025 tax-and-spending law. [cite:pbs_massie_takeaways] [cite:wapo_massie_loses] A super PAC aligned with the president, MAGA KY, spent about $7.4 million. [cite:lpm_massie_gallrein_funding] The Associated Press judged Trump's opposition the key factor in the result, and PBS described the outcome as leaving "no doubt" about the president's power over his party. [cite:pbs_massie_takeaways] On these accounts, Massie faced a serious challenge with or without the pro-Israel spending.

What each side said. Both sides described the race in terms of Israel. Before the vote Massie said that a "foreign lobby has fully funded" the effort against him "to the extent that they've never done in any Republican race ever before." [cite:mee_massie_aipac] The super PAC's spokesman called him "the most anti-Israel Republican in the House," and after the result AIPAC congratulated Gallrein on "defeating anti-Israel incumbent Thomas Massie." [cite:pm_factcheck_udp_2026] [cite:mee_massie_aipac] The pro-Israel committees, in other words, claimed the result as theirs, and the president's allies claimed it as his. Both claims rest on real spending; neither can be measured against the other from the filings.

What the race shows. Three things can be said from the record. First, the pro-Israel committees spent more against Massie than in any previous Republican race, and their spending was a large share of the record total. Second, their spending converged with the opposition of the most powerful figure in Republican politics, and the sources used here attribute the result chiefly to him. Third, the convergence was itself the pattern: a member who opposed both the president and the lobby's priorities faced both at once. Comparing Massie with a colleague makes the point concrete. Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, also a Republican, has described himself as Israel's "strongest defender" in the Senate, has received about $1.4 million from pro-Israel PACs and donors over his career, and has faced no comparable campaign. [cite:cruz_senate_ami] [cite:trackaipac_congress] The records differ chiefly in position. [scene:cm_s09|The simulation's comparison of Cruz, Omar and Massie] sets the three records side by side.

The race is cited in two directions: as proof that opposing the lobby is fatal even for a Republican, and as proof that the lobby had become, for the first time, an open issue in a Republican primary. That argument, and the members of both parties who have chosen to refuse the money, are the subject of Part Six.

sections.h: 2026: More Money, Different Names, Mixed Results
sections.html:
The 2026 cycle brought the largest sums yet and the most losses. By June the super PAC had raised about $104 million for the cycle, more than in the whole of 2024. [cite:pm_factcheck_udp_2026] It also changed how it spent. Politico reported that more than 40 percent of its primary spending in 2026 went through pop-up and pass-through committees, groups with names unconnected to Israel that received its money and spent it under their own. [cite:pm_factcheck_udp_2026] And for the first time it faced an organized opponent: a super PAC formed specifically to counter it. This section follows the year's main races in the order they were held, then sets the whole cycle out in a single ledger. Because the cycle was still running when this volume was written, every figure carries the date of the filing it comes from.

New Jersey, February. The year began with a result that cut both ways. In a special Democratic primary for New Jersey's 11th District, the super PAC spent more than $2.3 million against Tom Malinowski, with advertisements saying he had "voted with Trump and the Republicans to fund ICE." Malinowski lost by 889 votes in an eleven-candidate field to Analilia Mejia, who has said she believes Israel committed genocide in Gaza. [cite:pm_njmonitor_malinowski] The super PAC had helped defeat a candidate it opposed and, in doing so, helped elect one far more critical of Israel. AIPAC's spokesperson answered the result with a promise: "Our six million members will be very active this election cycle." [cite:pm_njmonitor_malinowski]

Illinois, March. On 17 March four open House seats in and around Chicago held their primaries. AIPAC-linked committees spent more than $21 million across the four, most of it through newly formed committees with names such as Affordable Chicago Now and Elect Chicago Women rather than in AIPAC's own name; in the 7th District the super PAC spent about $5 million directly for Melissa Conyears-Ervin. [cite:pm_prospect_illinois] [cite:pm_factcheck_udp_2026] Its candidates won two of the four seats, Donna Miller in the 2nd and Melissa Bean in the 8th, and lost two: Conyears-Ervin in the 7th and Laura Fine in the 9th, where Daniel Biss won. [cite:pm_prospect_illinois] In all, about $92 million of outside money was spent on the four House races and the state's Senate primary. [cite:pm_prospect_illinois]

Kentucky, May. The defeat of Thomas Massie, told in the previous section, was the super PAC's largest success of the spring, achieved alongside the president. [cite:lpm_massie_gallrein_funding] [cite:pbs_massie_takeaways]

Maryland, June. In Maryland's 5th District the super PAC spent over $1 million for Adrian Boafo, who won the primary on 23 June. [cite:pm_factcheck_udp_2026]

Michigan, August. The largest single campaign in the super PAC's history was fought in the Democratic primary for an open Senate seat in Michigan. It spent more than $30.6 million supporting Representative Haley Stevens and opposing Abdul El-Sayed. [cite:pm_sludge_100m_2026] El-Sayed won on 4 August. AIPAC responded that its members "remain determined to ensure that voters reject Dr. El-Sayed and his radical anti-Israel agenda in November." [cite:pm_itt_elsayed] The race was the clearest single test of whether money on this scale could carry a statewide Democratic primary, and it could not.

California, August. Two weeks later, in a special election runoff for California's 14th District, the super PAC spent $2.4 million for Melissa Hernandez and gave more than $1.5 million to another committee, BOLD America, which spent over $2 million helping her. Aisha Wahab, a progressive state senator, won by 53 percent to 47. [cite:pm_kqed_wahab] [cite:pm_aljaz_wahab]

The opposition. The cycle also produced the first super PAC organized against AIPAC's. American Priorities filed with the Federal Election Commission on 12 February 2026, pledged more than $10 million, and raised $3.85 million in its first quarter. It spent about $1 million for Nida Allam in North Carolina's 4th District, where she lost to Valerie Foushee by less than a percentage point; about $2 million for Adam Hamawy in New Jersey's 12th, who won; more than $400,000 for Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania's 3rd, who won; and $2 million for three New York candidates in June, two of whom, according to the reference summary used here, defeated AIPAC-endorsed incumbents, Representatives Dan Goldman and Adriano Espaillat. [cite:pm_wiki_ampri] Its sums were a small fraction of the super PAC's, and in Illinois it chose not to spend at all.

The ledger, read plainly. In the nine races in the table the super PAC's side won five and lost four; measured by money, its largest bet of the cycle, more than $30 million in Michigan, was a loss. That is a much weaker record than AIPAC's claims for 2024, and it is consistent with the claim, made by the super PAC's opponents, that by 2026 the money had itself become an issue in Democratic primaries. It does not show that the spending had no effect: several of the results were close, and the filings cannot show what the margins would have been without it. Nor is the cycle over. The general elections of November 2026, the primaries not covered here and the final filings will change the record, and the conclusion of this volume returns to it with the latest figures available.

chapters.label: Part Six
chapters.title: Refusing the Money, and Leaving Under Fire
chapters.intro: Part Six turns from the money to the members. A small group in Congress takes no pro-Israel money at all, and in 2025 a few members who had taken it began to refuse it. Some of those who refused and criticized the lobby faced its largest campaigns or formal rebuke; one, Marjorie Taylor Greene, left Congress after being attacked by its leading organizations and abandoned by the president. This part sets out who refuses the money, what happened to them, and the full sequence of Greene's break and resignation, with her own reasons and her critics' accusations side by side.
chapters.outro:
Part Six followed the members. A handful take no pro-Israel money: four senators in the Democratic caucus, several progressive House Democrats and, until 2026, Thomas Massie; in 2025 three Democrats who had taken AIPAC money said they would stop. [cite:trackaipac_congress] [cite:pm_gazette_reject] Those who broke with the network faced either its money, in primaries, or its public condemnation, and in two Republican cases the opposition of the president as well. [cite:factcheck_udp_2024] [cite:pbs_massie_takeaways] Marjorie Taylor Greene, attacked by AIPAC as "the newest member of the anti-Israel Squad" and by others as antisemitic, resigned after the president withdrew his support, and gave his treatment of her as her reason. [cite:pm_aljaz_aipac_mtg] [cite:pm_npr_mtg_resign]

What is settled is the sequence of events and the words on each side. What is contested is the meaning of the accusations of antisemitism in each case, and the weight of the network against the weight of the president in the Republican cases. What the record leaves open is the effect the network's record has on members who were never targeted. Part Seven turns to the trips.

sections.h: The Members at Zero
sections.html:
Every list in Part Four ends with a short group of names beside which the figure is nothing. In the Congress of 2026, on Track AIPAC's count of career pro-Israel money, four senators in the Democratic caucus stand at zero: Bernie Sanders, Chris Van Hollen, Jeff Merkley and Peter Welch. In the House, seven Democrats do, among them Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Rashida Tlaib, Ilhan Omar, Summer Lee, Pramila Jayapal, Greg Casar and Ayanna Pressley, and one Republican, Thomas Massie. [cite:trackaipac_congress] This section asks what is documented about the members who refuse the money: who they are, whether their number is growing, and what has happened to them.

A small group, growing slowly. For most of the period this volume covers, refusing pro-Israel money was unusual and largely confined to members already known as critics of Israeli policy. That began to change in 2025. During the August recess of that year three House Democrats who had taken AIPAC money said they would take no more: Deborah Ross of North Carolina, who had received $41,900 in the 2022 cycle and $97,876 in 2024; Valerie Foushee of North Carolina, who had received more than $800,000 in direct and bundled AIPAC giving and about $2 million in super PAC support in her first race; and Morgan McGarvey of Kentucky. [cite:pm_intercept_ross] [cite:pm_gazette_reject] They acted, the reporting found, after constituents raised the issue at town-hall meetings, in a year when Gallup found that only 8 percent of Democrats approved of Israel's military action in Gaza, down from 36 percent in November 2023. [cite:pm_gazette_reject] Three members is a small share of the 120 Democrats elected in 2024 with AIPAC's endorsement, and others said they would keep taking the money. [cite:pm_gazette_reject] The 2026 primaries, described in Part Five, showed the money itself becoming an issue in Democratic campaigns.

What happened to the members at zero. The record of the members who criticized the lobby includes both the largest spending against sitting members and formal rebukes. Two progressive members of the House in 2024, Jamaal Bowman and Cori Bush, were defeated in primaries in which AIPAC's super PAC spent record sums against them, in Bowman's case more than any interest group had spent on a single House race, as Part Five sets out. [cite:factcheck_udp_2024] The Republican at zero, Thomas Massie, lost in 2026 in the most expensive House primary on record, with the president also against him. [cite:lpm_massie_gallrein_funding] The case of Ilhan Omar shows the institutional side.

Ilhan Omar. In February 2019, asked who was paying members of Congress to support Israel, Omar replied on Twitter "AIPAC!" and "It's all about the Benjamins." Leaders of both parties said the words invoked the antisemitic trope of Jewish money, and she apologized. Days later she spoke of "the political influence in this country that says it is OK for people to push for allegiance to a foreign country"; the Anti-Defamation League's chief executive urged the Speaker to hold a vote, and the House passed a resolution, broadened to condemn many forms of bigotry, by 407 to 23, with Omar voting in favor. [cite:axios_omar_removal] [cite:nbc_omar_vote_2019] In February 2023 the House voted 218 to 211, on party lines, to remove her from the Foreign Affairs Committee, citing six of her statements, the "Benjamins" tweet among them; the Democratic leader, Hakeem Jeffries, called it "political revenge." [cite:cbs_omar_removal] In her primaries, a challenger raised nearly $500,000 from pro-Israel donors in 2020; in 2022 AIPAC's super PAC gave $350,000 to a separate committee backing her opponent, a transfer disclosed only after the vote she won by about 2,500 votes; in 2024 her opponents spent only about $110,000, AIPAC having reportedly judged the challenger too weak. [cite:strib_omar_2024] [cite:jewishinsider_udp_omar_2022] [cite:washex_omar_2024]

The comparison above is the one the simulation draws in [scene:cm_s07|the asymmetry test], and it has two readings, both documented. On one, a member's public commitment to the defense of a foreign state drew no institutional response, while a member's criticism of the pressure to make such commitments drew a congressional vote. On the other, the response to Omar was a response to language that invoked a long-standing antisemitic trope about Jews and money, for which she herself apologized, and not to her criticism of policy. [cite:nbc_omar_resolution] Both readings rest on the same sequence of events. The next section turns to the one member in the record who left Congress altogether.

sections.h: Marjorie Taylor Greene: The Break, the Attacks and the Resignation
sections.html:
Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia was, until 2025, a longtime ally of President Trump in the House. [cite:pm_reuters_trump_mtg] Within a few months of that year she broke with the pro-Israel network, was attacked by it in terms rarely used against a Republican, broke with the president, lost his endorsement, and announced her resignation from Congress. Because her departure is often described as the clearest case of a member driven out by pro-Israel pressure, and as often as the departure of a member who had made antisemitic statements, this section sets out the documented sequence in order, with each side's words, and keeps the two forces in the story, the pro-Israel network and the president, side by side.

The break. In late July 2025 Greene wrote that the attack of 7 October 2023 was horrific and the hostages must be returned, but that "so is the genocide, humanitarian crisis, and starvation happening in Gaza." Reuters later described her as the first Republican member of Congress to call the crisis in Gaza a genocide. [cite:pm_aljaz_aipac_mtg] [cite:pm_reuters_trump_mtg] In the same month she offered an amendment to the 2026 defense appropriations bill to strip $500 million a year in cooperative missile-defense funding for Israel, the money for the Iron Dome, Arrow and David's Sling systems. She called it "money we don't have" and said Israel was "very capable of defending themselves." The House rejected the amendment by 422 votes to 6; the six in favor were Greene, Thomas Massie, Ilhan Omar, Al Green, Summer Lee and Rashida Tlaib. [cite:pm_ji_mtg_amendment] She had taken no money from AIPAC; a later review by a conservative news service found no public record of any direct AIPAC donation to her. [cite:pm_dcnf_mtg_aipac]

The attacks. AIPAC answered on 7 August 2025. It called her accusation of genocide "disgusting" and said: "Let's call this what it is: Marjorie Taylor Greene is the newest member of the anti-Israel Squad." Greene replied: "Bring. It. On.," adding, "I can't be bought and I'm not backing down!!" [cite:pm_aljaz_aipac_mtg] The criticism that followed went beyond her positions on Israel to her character. Jewish Insider, a publication covering Jewish and Israel-related politics, published an account of what it called her amplification of antisemitic rhetoric. It cited, among other things, an earlier claim of hers that space-based weapons connected with the Rothschild family had caused California wildfires; a post saying "I'll never take 30 shekels," which it read as invoking Judas and Israel's currency; and posts suggesting that a foreign government or "powerful people" might target her. It quoted AIPAC's spokesman calling her statements "rancid anti-Israel and unhinged raving," and reported that the Republican Jewish Coalition had endorsed challengers to defeat her in her primary. [cite:pm_ji_mtg_rhetoric] The same account recorded her own demands: that AIPAC and other pro-Israel groups register as foreign agents, and her description of the Anti-Defamation League as a "dangerous hate group." [cite:pm_ji_mtg_rhetoric]

The president. The decisive break came from another direction. Greene had also broken with the White House on tariffs, on inflation and health-care costs and on foreign policy, and she had signed the petition to force a House vote on releasing the Justice Department's files on Jeffrey Epstein. On 14 November 2025 President Trump withdrew his endorsement on Truth Social, saying that all he saw her do was "complain, complain, complain," and that he would back the "right candidate" against her in a primary. She said he had "attacked me and lied about me," and linked the attack to her push for the Epstein files. [cite:pm_reuters_trump_mtg]

The resignation, in her words. A week later, on 21 November, Greene announced that she would resign from Congress on 5 January 2026. Her stated reasons were about the president. Her disagreements with him, she wrote, "should not result in me being called a traitor and threatened by the President of the United States"; she would not "endure a hurtful and hateful primary against me by the President we all fought for"; and, in the sentence most quoted, "I refuse to be a 'battered wife,' hoping it all goes away and gets better." [cite:pm_npr_mtg_resign] NPR's account described the Epstein files as the final straw and noted her opposition to the strikes on Iran and to support for Israel's war in Gaza. [cite:pm_npr_mtg_resign] Her letter did not name Israel; it spoke of "foreign interests" and of her opposition to foreign wars and foreign aid. [cite:pm_ji_mtg_resign] When the president later called her a "traitor," she answered by posting an image showing $0.00 in AIPAC money beside her name and more than $230 million beside his, Track AIPAC's figure for pro-Israel spending benefiting him since 2020, with the words "I AM AMERICA FIRST." [cite:pm_dcnf_mtg_aipac]

The reaction. The pro-Israel network's response to her resignation was open satisfaction. The Republican Jewish Coalition posted a clip of the president waving, captioned "And we say bye bye." Representative Randy Fine of Florida wrote: "One antisemite down. One to go." [cite:pm_ji_mtg_resign]

What the record shows. The documents support three statements and rule out a fourth. First, Greene broke with the pro-Israel network over Gaza and military aid in the summer of 2025 and was attacked by its leading organizations in the strongest terms, including by AIPAC by name and by the Republican Jewish Coalition through its support for primary challengers. Second, the attacks included accusations of antisemitism that cited specific statements of hers, some made years earlier; whether those statements were antisemitic, as her critics say, or whether the accusation was used to discredit her criticism of Israel, as her defenders say, is a judgment the reader can make from the statements themselves. Third, the event that preceded her resignation, and the one she gave as its reason, was the president's withdrawal of support and his promise to back a challenger. What the record does not support is the claim that pro-Israel pressure alone drove her from office. By her own account the decisive pressure came from the president. Her critics, for their part, pointed to her own statements. The two forces converged, as they did against Thomas Massie in the same months, and the record does not let a reader weigh one against the other.

sections.h: Two Kinds of Pressure, and What Is Not Documented
sections.html:
A question often asked is whether Marjorie Taylor Greene was the only member to leave government under attack from pro-Israel voices. The record used here answers it in two parts. On resignations, in the record used here, Greene is the only member of Congress whose departure from office followed a public campaign against her by the pro-Israel network, and even in her case the president's opposition came first in her own account. On defeats, the answer is no: several members lost their seats after the largest campaigns the network has run. This section sets the cases side by side and states what they do and do not show.

Two kinds of pressure. The cases show two different instruments. The first is money: super PAC spending in a primary, the subject of Part Five, which was spent against Bowman and Bush, both defeated in 2024, and against Massie, defeated in 2026. The second is reputation: public statements by the network's organizations and allies that a member is "anti-Israel" or antisemitic, which in Omar's case were followed by formal action in the House and in Greene's preceded her resignation. The two instruments are often used together, and the second has a feature the first does not. An accusation of antisemitism can be made against any critic, and it can also be true. The record shows both: statements by Omar and by Greene that critics described as invoking antisemitic tropes, which in Omar's case she apologized for; and members such as Andy Levin, who is Jewish, and Thomas Massie, against whom no such accusation appears in the record used here, opposed for their positions. A reader assessing any single accusation has to look at the words it cites.

Convergence, not a single hand. In the two Republican cases, the pro-Israel network's opposition converged with the president's. Massie and Greene had both crossed Trump on the Epstein files and on the strikes on Iran, and both had opposed military aid to Israel. [cite:pbs_massie_takeaways] [cite:pm_reuters_trump_mtg] The record shows the two forces acting against the same members in the same months. It does not show that one directed the other. Greene herself implied that pro-Israel interests stood behind the president's turn against her, posting the figure for pro-Israel spending that had benefited him. [cite:pm_dcnf_mtg_aipac] That is her reading. The documents show the spending and the timing; they do not show coordination, and this volume does not supply it.

What is not documented. Three things should be stated plainly. The record used here contains no other member who resigned under comparable attack; if there are such cases, they are not in the sources this volume has reached, and later research may find them. The record does not show what members who were never targeted decided because they saw what happened to those who were; that effect, which critics regard as the network's most important, leaves no filing. And the record does not show that any member who took the money voted differently because of it. What it does show is a consistent pattern in who was opposed: members of both parties, of different ideologies, whose common feature was a break with the network's positions on Israel.

chapters.label: Part Seven
chapters.title: The Trips
chapters.intro: Part Seven follows the trips. In Congress, AIPAC's charitable foundation has paid for most of the members' travel to Israel since 2012, under an exception to the 2007 ethics law that allows charities to sponsor trips lobbies cannot; about half of the House serving in 2024 had taken one. Below Congress, community groups, police-exchange programs and, in 2025, the Israeli government itself have paid for state legislators, mayors and police chiefs to travel, with far less of it on record. This part sets out the rules, the numbers, the costs, the itineraries and the gaps.
chapters.outro:
Part Seven followed the trips. More than a quarter of the House's privately sponsored foreign trips since 2012 went to Israel, three-quarters of them paid for by AIPAC's foundation, at a cost of at least $10 million; about half of the House serving in 2024 had traveled with AIPAC. [cite:cnsmd_trips_study] The trips are allowed because the 2007 ethics law exempted charities, an exception AIPAC sought. [cite:intercept_aief_donors] Below Congress, about 250 state legislators traveled in 2025 at the Israeli government's expense, and police officials have traveled on exchange programs since the early 2000s. [cite:pm_idcap_50states] [cite:jta_adl_police]

What is settled is who paid and who went. What is contested is what the trips are: education about an ally, or a curated introduction by the same network that funds campaigns. What the record leaves open is the full extent of travel below Congress, which no federal body records, and the identity of most of the foundation's donors. Part Eight turns to the state and local level.

sections.h: The Congressional Trips
sections.html:
Of all the channels described in Part One, the trips are the one that reaches the most members of Congress, and the one most members have used. Since 2012 about half of the House members serving in 2024 had traveled to Israel on a trip paid for by AIPAC's charitable foundation. [cite:cnsmd_trips_study] This section sets out how the trips are allowed, how many there have been, what they cost, who goes and what they see, from a study of congressional travel records by the Howard Center for Investigative Journalism, published by Capital News Service, and from reporting on the foundation's own filings.

How the trips are allowed. After the lobbying scandals around Jack Abramoff, the Honest Leadership and Open Government Act of 2007 restricted travel paid for by lobbyists and the organizations that employ them. AIPAC, which employs lobbyists, could no longer sponsor week-long trips itself. The law left an exception for charitable organizations, and according to The Intercept AIPAC campaigned for it; it has since paid for the trips through the American Israel Education Foundation, a 501(c)(3) charity it founded, which shares its offices, board members and part of its logo. Craig Holman of Public Citizen, who helped draft the 2007 law, put it plainly: "These trips would be illegal otherwise." [cite:intercept_aief_donors] AIPAC's own account is that it uses the foundation to work within the law; critics call the arrangement the "AIPAC loophole." [cite:cnsmd_trips_study]

The scale. House members and their staff reported about 4,100 privately sponsored foreign trips from 2012 to 2023. More than a quarter of them went to Israel, more than to the whole of the Western Hemisphere and Africa combined, and about three-quarters of the Israel trips were paid for by AIPAC's foundation. [cite:cnsmd_trips_study] The Howard Center's database lists 868 trips sponsored by the foundation for 463 congressional offices; the offices that traveled most were those of Steny Hoyer, the long-serving Democratic leader, with 22 trips, Kevin McCarthy, the former Republican speaker, with 19, and Hakeem Jeffries, the current Democratic leader, with 10. [cite:cnsmd_aief_explorer] The Senate's travel reports, more than 2,600 in the same period, could not readily be analyzed by sponsor or destination, so the Senate's share is not known. [cite:cnsmd_trips_study]

The cost. The trips are not cheap, and they are not the largest of the foundation's expenses. By LegiStorm's count, AIPAC-related travel cost at least $10 million from 2012 to 2023. [cite:cnsmd_trips_study] In 2019, the busiest recent year, donors financed 129 trips at a total cost of $2.32 million, taking 64 Democrats and 65 Republicans on fourteen separate departures; from 2019 to late 2023 the foundation spent $6.1 million on 309 trips, 144 for Republicans and 165 for Democrats. [cite:intercept_aief_donors] A single trip can cost more than $10,000 a person, and members may bring senior staff, spouses or children. [cite:intercept_aief_donors] The foundation spent $68,000 on two trips for Representative Glenn Ivey of Maryland, including luxury accommodation. [cite:cnsmd_trips_study] Set against the foundation's annual revenue of about $60 million, the trips are a modest share of what it spends. [cite:pm_pp_aief990]

What they see. The itinerary of a June 2024 trip, reconstructed by the Howard Center, gives a picture of the program. The delegation spent four days in Israel and stayed at the Kempinski hotel in Tel Aviv. It met Prime Minister Netanyahu, the defense minister, Yoav Gallant, and the National Unity leader Benny Gantz, heard briefings on the attacks of 7 October, visited the site of the Nova music festival and met families of hostages. It did not visit Gaza or the West Bank, and its members met fewer Palestinians than travelers on J Street's trips. [cite:cnsmd_trips_study] The foundation describes its trips as education about the US–Israel relationship that includes meetings with Israeli leaders across the political spectrum. [cite:cnsmd_trips_study] J Street, the second-largest sponsor, runs smaller trips that include Palestinian communities; the foundation's volume was nearly seven times J Street's. [cite:cnsmd_trips_study]

Who pays. The foundation's donors are redacted from the copies of its tax returns made public. One unredacted filing, for 2019, obtained by reporters, named eight donors, among them the Koret Foundation, the Charles and Lynn Schusterman Family Foundation and the Paul E. Singer Foundation. [cite:intercept_aief_donors] Because gifts to a charity are tax-deductible, critics of the arrangement argue that the public shares the cost of the trips through the donors' deductions; its defenders answer that the same is true of every charity.

What the trips do. The trips are the orientation layer of the network: the place where members meet Israel's leaders, see the country's security problems on the ground, and form relationships with the organization that later endorses them and steers its members' donations to them. The record shows the sequence; it does not show what any member took away. Supporters regard the trips as legitimate education about an ally. Critics regard them as a one-sided introduction, paid for by the same network that funds members' campaigns. Both descriptions fit the itinerary. The trips resumed about five months after 7 October 2023, and between March and early September 2024 eight of them took 71 House members and staff to Israel. [cite:cnsmd_trips_study]

sections.h: Below Congress: Statehouses, City Halls and Police Chiefs
sections.html:
The congressional trips are recorded because federal ethics rules require it. Below Congress, the trips are at least as numerous and much less visible, because no federal body records the travel of state legislators, mayors or police chiefs. What is known comes from state disclosure filings where they exist, from the sponsors' own announcements and from local reporting. This section sets out what that record shows, including a program in which the Israeli government itself paid for American state legislators' travel.

"50 States, One Israel." In September 2025 about 250 state legislators from across the United States attended a conference in Israel called "50 States, One Israel." It was financed by Israel's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, through its consulates, which invited the legislators and paid their expenses. [cite:pm_idcap_50states] [cite:lincolnchron_gomberg] The participants met Israeli leaders, among them President Isaac Herzog, met families of victims of the 7 October attacks and visited communities attacked that day. [cite:pm_idcap_50states] One of the Idaho participants, Representative Bruce Skaug, said the Israeli consulate in San Francisco had invited him and paid all his expenses, and that he believed he had been invited because he supported Israel and had co-sponsored Idaho's 2021 law against boycotts of Israel. [cite:pm_idcap_50states] Not every participant came away in agreement: Idaho's House minority leader, Ilana Rubel, used a state dinner to raise civilian casualties in Gaza directly with President Herzog. [cite:pm_idcap_50states] The program differs from everything else in this part in one respect. Every other trip described here was paid for by an American organization; this one was paid for by a foreign government, openly, for officials who make the state laws and manage the state funds described in Part Eight.

Community sponsors. Most state and local trips are paid for by American organizations, often local Jewish community bodies. In 2024 the Jewish Community Relations Council and the Jewish Federation of Los Angeles paid nearly $82,000 to send seven California legislators to Israel. [cite:calmatters_israel_trips] The Combat Antisemitism Movement led delegations of mayors and of fifteen state legislators the same year. [cite:inn_cam_mayors] In Massachusetts, a bill introduced in 2026 sought to restrict lobby-funded travel by state officials after trips that its advocates say have taken scores of officials to Israel. [cite:masspeace_travel_bill] These sponsors are community organizations, not the national lobby, and their trips are reported, where they are reported at all, only under state rules that vary widely.

Police. A separate set of programs has taken American police officials to Israel since the early 2000s. Three intermediaries ran them: the Anti-Defamation League's National Counter-Terrorism Seminar, the Law Enforcement Exchange Program of the Jewish Institute for National Security of America, founded in 2002, and the Georgia International Law Enforcement Exchange at the University of Georgia, which reports more than 1,100 participants across 290 programs. More than 1,000 American officials, among them police chiefs from Los Angeles, Atlanta and St. Louis County and federal agents, have taken part. [cite:jta_adl_police] [cite:jvl_police] The sponsors describe the trips as briefings and meetings on counterterrorism, not field training. [cite:reason_police] Critics, led by the Jewish Voice for Peace campaign "Deadly Exchange" from 2017, argue that they spread militarized and surveillance-heavy policing; in 2018 Durham, North Carolina became the first American city to bar such exchanges. [cite:wiki_deadlyex] The ADL paused its trips in 2019. [cite:jta_adl_police] No public evidence connects any particular use of force by American police to these programs, and this volume makes no such claim.

What no one records. The gap in the record is structural. Congress requires its members to disclose every privately paid trip; no federal body records the travel of state and local officials, and the states' own rules vary. The people who make decisions about state pension funds, state contracts and state laws on boycotts, the subjects of Part Eight, can therefore travel at a foreign government's or an advocacy group's expense with no record a reader in another state could find. The simulation's account of [scene:cm_s11|the trips below Congress] collects what has been reported. A complete count does not exist.

chapters.label: Part Eight
chapters.title: State and Local
chapters.span: Anti-boycott laws, bonds, police and statehouses
chapters.intro: Part Eight goes below Congress. In the states, pro-Israel advocacy has produced two results that federal politics did not: laws against boycotts of Israel, passed or ordered by thirty-eight states in less than a decade, and public treasuries that bought more than $1.7 billion of Israeli government bonds in the nine months after 7 October 2023. This part sets out how each came about, what each requires or risks, and the disputes over both, in the courts and in public.
chapters.outro:
Part Eight followed pro-Israel advocacy into the states. Thirty-eight states adopted laws or executive orders against boycotts of Israel between 2015 and 2024, from a model act drafted in 2015 and with the lobbying of AIPAC, the Israel Action Network and local federations; the courts divided, and the Supreme Court declined in 2023 to review the law the Eighth Circuit had upheld. [cite:pm_wiki_antibds] [cite:pm_aclu_waldrip] State and local treasuries bought more than $1.7 billion of Israeli bonds after 7 October 2023, from a seller that courted their officials with trips and awards. [cite:pm_icij_bonds]

What is settled is the law and the purchases. What is contested is whether the laws penalize protected political expression and whether the bond purchases served the funds' beneficiaries or a cause. What the record leaves open is how many officials who wrote the laws or bought the bonds had traveled at a sponsor's expense, since no federal body records their travel. Part Nine turns to other countries.

sections.h: Thirty-Eight States: The Laws Against Boycotting Israel
sections.html:
The most durable result of pro-Israel advocacy below the federal level is not a sum of money but a body of law. Between 2015 and 2024, thirty-eight American states passed laws or issued executive orders discouraging boycotts of Israel. [cite:pm_wiki_antibds] The laws answer the boycott, divestment and sanctions movement, known as BDS, which campaigns for economic pressure on Israel over its treatment of Palestinians. [cite:pm_wiki_antibds] This section sets out where the laws came from, what they require, how the courts have treated them, and why the federal versions failed.

Origin. Illinois became the first state to explicitly penalize boycotts of Israel when its governor signed SB 1761 on 23 July 2015; South Carolina had a law of its own the same year. Later in 2015 the Israel Allies Foundation drafted a model act combining the two, and the laws spread quickly. AIPAC, the Israel Action Network and local Jewish federations lobbied for them, and a lobbyist for the Israeli-American Council drafted or pushed bills in several states. [cite:pm_wiki_antibds] By 2024 the count stood at thirty-eight. [cite:pm_wiki_antibds]

What the laws require. The laws take two forms. Contract laws require businesses and individuals who contract with the state to certify that they are not boycotting Israel; some exempt small contractors or contracts below a dollar threshold. Investment laws require state pension and investment funds to avoid or sell holdings in companies that boycott Israel, and several states, Arizona, Florida, Illinois, Indiana and Colorado among them, keep published lists of companies they have found to be boycotting. [cite:pm_wiki_antibds] Arkansas's law, for example, applies not only to Israel but to "Israeli-controlled territories," which brings boycotts limited to the occupied territories within its reach. [cite:pm_aclu_waldrip]

The courts. The laws raised a First Amendment question, whether a consumer boycott is protected political expression, and the courts have not answered it the same way. In Kansas a federal court enjoined the state's law as likely unconstitutional, and the legislature narrowed it in 2018. In Arizona a court enjoined the law in 2018, and it too was amended, ending the case. In Texas a federal court ruled in April 2019 that the state's law was an unconstitutional restriction on speech based on viewpoint. [cite:pm_wiki_antibds] The case that went furthest came from Arkansas. In 2018 the Arkansas Times, a weekly newspaper that said it was not boycotting Israel, refused on principle to sign the certification required to renew an advertising contract with a state college. A three-judge panel of the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals held the law unconstitutional, but the full court, rehearing the case, upheld it in June 2022, reasoning that purchasing decisions in a boycott are not expressive enough to be protected, even though speech supporting a boycott is. On 21 February 2023 the Supreme Court declined to hear the newspaper's appeal. [cite:pm_aclu_waldrip] [cite:pm_wiki_antibds] The law stands, and so do most of the others.

The federal attempts. Congress tried and failed to pass a federal version. The Israel Anti-Boycott Act of 2017 died in Congress. The Combating BDS Act passed the Senate in January 2019 but was never taken up by the House. The House did pass, in July 2019, a non-binding resolution condemning the boycott movement, by 398 votes to 17. [cite:pm_wiki_antibds] The anti-boycott law is therefore almost entirely a state-level achievement, which is why the state legislators who write and vote for such laws are of particular interest to the sponsors of the trips described in Part Seven. One of them, an Idaho legislator, said he believed he was invited to Israel at the Israeli government's expense in 2025 because he had co-sponsored his state's law. [cite:pm_idcap_50states]

The laws' supporters argue that states, like any purchaser, may decide whom they do business with, and the Eighth Circuit accepted that the Arkansas law served commercial purposes. [cite:pm_wiki_antibds] Their opponents, including the American Civil Liberties Union, argue that the laws single out one side of a political debate for penalty and that the right to boycott, recognized for civil-rights boycotts, should not depend on its target. [cite:pm_aclu_waldrip] For this volume the relevant fact is the scale of the achievement: in less than a decade, a policy goal pursued by pro-Israel organizations became the law of three-quarters of the states, without a federal statute.

sections.h: Public Money: State and City Treasuries in Israel Bonds
sections.html:
The money in most of this volume flows from private donors into American politics. One flow runs the other way, from American public treasuries to the government of Israel, and it is decided not by Congress but by state treasurers, county officials and pension boards. It takes the form of Israeli government bonds, sold in the United States by a private corporation acting for Israel's Ministry of Finance. This section sets out how the sales work, how much state and local governments bought after 7 October 2023, who bought most, and the disputes the purchases have raised. It relies on an investigation by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists published in July 2024.

The seller. Israel Bonds, formally the Development Corporation for Israel, was launched in New York in 1951. It is registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission as the underwriter of Israeli government bonds sold in the United States and acts as a private seller for Israel's Finance Ministry. In more than seven decades it has raised $52 billion. It began by selling to individual buyers abroad, and over time expanded to banks, institutional investors and state and municipal governments; its sales have historically risen in times of crisis. [cite:pm_icij_bonds] The ICIJ found that it courted public officials with exclusive trips to Israel that included meetings with senior officials and military tours, with galas and leadership awards, and with conferences at which it paid speakers' expenses. [cite:pm_icij_bonds]

The surge after 7 October. In the nine months after the attacks, American states and municipalities bought more than $1.7 billion of Israeli bonds. [cite:pm_icij_bonds] The purchases were fast and public. Pennsylvania's treasurer agreed to a purchase within an hour of being told of the opportunity on 10 October 2023, and later doubled it. Ohio's treasurer announced $20 million more on 11 October; he had bought $357.5 million since 2019. Palm Beach County, Florida, announced an additional $160 million in October, raised the share of its portfolio it could hold in Israeli bonds from 10 to 15 percent in March 2024, and by April held about $700 million of a $4.67 billion portfolio, calling itself the world's largest investor in Israel Bonds. The State of Florida held more than $250 million. [cite:pm_icij_bonds]

The disputes. The purchases raised three kinds of objection. The first is financial: credit agencies downgraded Israeli government debt during the war, and a former chief investment officer of Pennsylvania had warned in 2021 about Israel's political instability and the bonds' lack of an open market, advice that was not followed. Israel Bonds answers that Israel has never missed a payment of interest or principal in its history. [cite:pm_icij_bonds] The second is ethical: the ICIJ documented trips and hospitality offered to the officials who decide the purchases, and a law professor, Richard Painter, said the mixing of personal and official business "seem[s] to go well beyond" what is acceptable; Israel Bonds says its marketing is "legitimate, appropriate, and common practice." [cite:pm_icij_bonds] The third is legal and political: in May 2024 three Palm Beach County residents sued a county official, alleging that the investments were made for "social, ideological, and political reasons" in breach of fiduciary duty, and the advocacy group DAWN asked the Justice Department whether Israel Bonds should be registered as a foreign agent, which Israel Bonds denies. [cite:pm_icij_bonds]

The bonds belong in a volume about pro-Israel money for a reason that is easy to miss. They are not political contributions, and buying them is legal. But apart from the military aid appropriated by Congress, which other volumes of this library describe, they are a major channel through which American public money goes to the government of Israel, and it is decided by state and local officials, the same officials whom Israel Bonds courts with trips and awards. The record does not show that any purchase was made because of a trip or an award. It shows that the seller offered both, and that the purchases rose sharply when Israel was at war.

chapters.label: Part Nine
chapters.title: The Lobby Abroad
chapters.span: UK, Canada, Europe, Australia, Latin America, Africa, Asia
chapters.intro: Part Nine leaves the United States. It begins with the one actor present in every country studied, the government of Israel, whose budget for public diplomacy rose to about $730 million for 2026. It then follows the national organizations and parliamentary networks that advocate for Israel in Britain, Europe, Canada, Australia, Latin America, Africa and Asia, giving amounts where they are known and naming the gaps where they are not. It ends by testing a common explanation of all this activity: that it exists to keep arms and aid flowing to Israel and to protect its standing at the United Nations.
chapters.outro:
Part Nine followed the money abroad. Israel's own spending on public diplomacy grew from about $150 million in 2025 to a budgeted $730 million for 2026, and the Quincy Institute estimates more than $1 billion since October 2023. [cite:pm_jta_730m] [cite:pm_quincy_eighth] In Britain, about 180 MPs in the 2019–24 Parliament received pro-Israel funding worth more than £1 million; in Canada, CIJA lobbied or hosted 58 percent of the MPs running in 2025 before the country barred lobby-sponsored travel; in Europe, ELNET has drawn at least $11 million from American funders since 2022; and the Israel Allies caucus network reached 50 countries. [cite:pm_declassified_quarter] [cite:pm_maple_cija] [cite:pm_intercept_elnet] [cite:pm_ih_iaf50]

What is settled is the scale where disclosure exists, the fact that most of the private money, at home and abroad, is American, and the rise of the Israeli government's own budget above any single American organization's. What is contested is how much any of it achieves: ELNET credits itself with a German arms purchase, Israel's own diplomats doubt that messaging can outweigh policy, and the British debate turned on whether to examine the influence at all. What the record leaves open is almost everything in countries without disclosure rules. The hypothesis that the effort serves arms and aid fits the United States and Germany; the hypothesis that it protects Israel's place at the United Nations fits only when restated as a contest for votes and observer seats. Part Ten draws the whole architecture together.

sections.h: The State's Own Channel: What Israel Spends Abroad
sections.html:
Everything in Parts Two to Eight concerns American organizations spending American money. This part turns abroad, and it begins with the one actor whose money appears in every country studied: the government of Israel itself. Unlike the American organizations, it may not give or spend in American elections. [cite:fec_foreign_nationals] What it may do, in the United States and elsewhere, is pay for public diplomacy, as every government does: advertising, hosted delegations, cultural programs and, in the United States, the work of agents who register their contracts under the Foreign Agents Registration Act. Since the war that began in October 2023 that spending has grown faster than any other figure in this volume.

The budget. Israel's budget for 2026 sets aside about $730 million for public diplomacy, known in Hebrew as hasbara, more than four times the roughly $150 million of 2025, which was itself about twenty times what Israel had spent before the war. The foreign minister, Gideon Sa'ar, argued that the money should be thought of "like investing in jets, bombs and missile interceptors." [cite:pm_jta_730m] The Quincy Institute, a Washington research group that favors restraint in American foreign policy, estimates that Israel has likely spent more than $1 billion on public diplomacy since 7 October 2023, more than $100 million of it through contracts registered under the Foreign Agents Registration Act. [cite:pm_quincy_eighth]

What it buys. In 2025 the spending included a $50 million advertising campaign on Google, YouTube, X and Outbrain; about $40 million to host some 400 foreign delegations of lawmakers, pastors, influencers and university presidents; a $4.1 million campaign aimed at evangelical churches; and the paid influencer network known as the Esther Project. [cite:pm_jta_730m] The Quincy Institute counted 300 delegations sponsored by the Foreign Ministry in 2025, with 6,000 participants from 70 countries. [cite:pm_quincy_eighth] The trip for 250 American state legislators described in Part Seven was one of them. [cite:pm_idcap_50states]

The registered contracts. In the United States the largest contracts are public because the contractors registered. In September 2025 two firms registered as agents of Israel's government, both working under contracts with the advertising group Havas: Bridges Partners, which ran the Esther Project, a campaign of up to $900,000 to pay 14 to 18 American social-media influencers, none of whom has been named or has registered; and Clock Tower X, owned by Brad Parscale, Donald Trump's campaign manager in 2020, for a campaign aimed at young Americans and at how artificial-intelligence chatbots describe Israel. [cite:pc_fara_complaint] [cite:dc_parscale_fara] The size of the Clock Tower X contract is reported differently by different sources: a contract of record of $6 million, later raised to $9 million, with $15 million received according to a May 2026 supplemental filing and about $13 million disbursed in six months, and $46.5 million over a year in the Quincy Institute's account. [cite:dc_parscale_fara] [cite:intercept_parscale] [cite:pm_quincy_eighth] The Quincy paper also lists smaller registered contracts, among them $3.2 million for a firm aimed at evangelical Christians. [cite:pm_quincy_eighth] The simulation's accounts of [scene:ip_s01|the Esther Project] and [scene:ip_s02|Clock Tower X] give the filings in detail.

Does it work? Israeli and American specialists quoted by the Jewish Telegraphic Agency doubted that it would. Nicholas Cull of the University of Southern California, Shibley Telhami of the University of Maryland and Ilan Manor of Ben-Gurion University argued, in different words, that messaging cannot overcome objections to policy; Israel's consul general in Los Angeles defended the spending and called for more of it on American film and television. [cite:pm_jta_730m] The question for this volume is narrower. The state's spending is the one part of the pro-Israel effort abroad whose size is known with any precision, because the United States requires its agents to report. In most other countries, as the following sections show, there is no equivalent requirement, and the record is thinner.

sections.h: Britain: The Friends of Israel and the Petition
sections.html:
Britain has no organization like AIPAC's super PAC, and none of the sources used here records outside spending against a sitting MP at a British election. Pro-Israel influence in Westminster runs instead through donations to MPs and sponsored trips, both of which MPs declare in their Register of Members' Financial Interests, the record on which the count below is based. The main vehicles are the parliamentary Friends of Israel groups attached to the parties. This section sets out what the declarations show, according to the one systematic count of them, and the parliamentary argument the count helped provoke in 2026.

The count. In June 2024 the investigative outlet Declassified UK published an analysis of MPs' declarations in the 2019–24 Parliament. It found that about 180 of the 650 MPs had received funding from pro-Israel groups, individuals or Israeli state institutions, worth more than £1 million in all, including more than 240 paid trips to Israel costing more than £500,000. By party the count was 130 Conservatives, 41 Labour, 3 Liberal Democrats and 3 from the Democratic Unionist Party. Conservative Friends of Israel had funded 118 sitting Conservative MPs on 160 trips costing more than £330,000; Labour Friends of Israel had funded trips for 32 Labour MPs costing more than £64,000; more than 40 MPs had received funding from Israeli state institutions. [cite:pm_declassified_quarter]

The party leadership. The count also traced funding to the leadership of the Labour Party, which took office in July 2024. Sir Trevor Chinn, a businessman, gave £50,000 to Keir Starmer's campaign for the party leadership in 2020 and went on to finance eight members of his front bench; seven members of Starmer's cabinet had accepted trips to Israel funded by Labour Friends of Israel. [cite:pm_declassified_quarter] [cite:pm_aljaz_ukdebate] The declarations show the gifts. As with the American recipients in Part Four, they do not show that any position was taken because of them.

The petition and the debate. In early 2026 a parliamentary e-petition calling for a public inquiry into pro-Israel and Israeli state-linked influence on British politics gathered 118,306 signatures, more than enough to be considered for a debate. [cite:pm_aljaz_ukdebate] The government said in April that existing rules already provided transparency and that it did not support an inquiry, adding that the Prime Minister had asked the Ethics and Integrity Commission to review lobbying, disclosure and access to government. [cite:pm_aljaz_ukdebate] [cite:pm_jn_petition] The Jewish Leadership Council said the petition offered "no credible evidence" for its claims and drew on tropes widely recognized as antisemitic, and asked for it to be taken down; the request was refused. [cite:pm_jn_petition] MPs debated it in Westminster Hall on 22 June 2026. The Conservative MP who opened the debate for the Petitions Committee, John Lamont, said he did not support the petition: it singled out one country when many lobby in Britain, it echoed old claims of Jewish control of politics, and the clearest documented cases of foreign interference involved Russia and China. He also said Israel's government could be criticized and that rules on lobbying and donations should apply to every country alike. As with every debate on a petition, there was no vote. [cite:pm_wb_ukdebate]

Both sides of the argument rest on a fact the other accepts. The money and the trips are on the public register, which is how Declassified UK could count them, and which is the government's reason for saying no inquiry is needed. The difference from the United States lies elsewhere. The British record shows nothing like the primary spending of Part Five; what it shows, on a large scale, is funding that reached more than a quarter of the House of Commons in a single Parliament, much of it in the form of the instrument described in Part Seven, the paid trip.

sections.h: Europe, Canada, Australia and the Caucus Network
sections.html:
