Outside Britain and the United States, the record of pro-Israel advocacy is patchier, because few countries require lobbyists to disclose what they spend. What can be documented falls into two patterns. In wealthy democracies allied with the United States, national organizations modeled more or less closely on AIPAC lobby parliaments and take their members to Israel. In much of Latin America, Africa and Asia, the main vehicle is different: a network of parliamentary caucuses organized around Christian support for Israel. This section takes the two patterns in turn and gives the amounts where they are known.

Europe: ELNET. The European Leadership Network, known as ELNET, was founded in October 2007 and is registered in Belgium, France, Germany, Poland, Britain, Italy and Israel; it describes itself as "the most influential pro-Israel advocacy organisation in Europe." One of its co-founders, Raanan Eliaz, had worked as a consultant for AIPAC. [cite:pm_wiki_elnet] [cite:pm_intercept_elnet] Much of its money comes from the United States. According to The Intercept, its American fundraising arm, Friends of ELNET, began in 2012 with nearly $1 million from the advocacy group StandWithUs, raised more than $9.1 million in 2023, and has received at least $11 million from more than 100 American foundations and charities since 2022. ELNET says it has taken about 300 European policymakers on trips to Israel, and it has credited its own work for Germany's approval of a $3.5 billion purchase of Israel's Arrow 3 missile-defense system. [cite:pm_intercept_elnet] [cite:pm_wiki_elnet] That claim is ELNET's own. The decision was the German government's, and the record does not allow the lobby's share in it to be measured.

Canada: CIJA. Canada's lobbying registry makes public the contacts of the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs, a Canadian advocacy body. Analyzing the registry, the Canadian outlet The Maple found that CIJA had lobbied, or sponsored trips to Israel for, 156 of the 269 sitting MPs running in the 2025 election, 58 percent; it had lobbied them 579 times since 2008 and spent C$678,277 on their trips since 2007. In May 2023 Canada's Commissioner of Lobbying wrote that sponsored travel "could reasonably be seen to create a sense of obligation," and the Lobbyists' Code was changed that month to bar lobby groups from sponsoring travel for officials they lobby. [cite:pm_maple_cija] Canada is the one country in this volume that closed the channel described in Part Seven.

Australia: AIJAC. The Australia/Israel and Jewish Affairs Council runs the Rambam program, which takes federal politicians, journalists and others to Israel; a delegation in 2012, for example, included six Coalition MPs and senators. [cite:pm_aijac_rambam] The sources reached for this volume give no total for the program's cost or the number of Australian politicians who have taken part.

The caucus network. The Israel Allies Foundation, the body that drafted the model anti-boycott law described in Part Eight, also runs the widest international network in this volume. It grew from the Knesset Christian Allies Caucus, formed in 2004, and the Congressional Israel Allies Caucus, formed in 2006, and in December 2020, when Honduras formed a caucus, it counted 50 countries and about 1,200 parliamentarians. [cite:pm_wiki_iaf] [cite:pm_ih_iaf50] Its affiliates have included caucuses in the Philippines, South Korea and Japan in Asia, South Africa, Malawi and Cameroon in Africa, Brazil and Honduras in Latin America, and the European Parliament. [cite:pm_wiki_iaf] [cite:pm_ih_iaf50] It calls its method "faith-based diplomacy," and its president, Josh Reinstein, has called the network "the greatest tool that Israel has in its diplomatic arsenal." [cite:pm_ih_iaf50] Its own budget is small: about $1.4 million of revenue in 2018, from American donors including the Moskowitz family foundations, and from Concert, an Israeli nonprofit that receives matching funds from Israel's government, an arrangement the Forward said raised a question under the Foreign Agents Registration Act. [cite:pm_wiki_iaf] Its stated goals include anti-boycott laws and the moving of embassies to Jerusalem, and it linked the new caucuses in Honduras and Guatemala to those countries' embassy decisions. [cite:pm_wiki_iaf] [cite:pm_ih_iaf50]

Two things stand out from the table. The first is the scale of American money abroad: ELNET's European work is substantially funded from the United States, and the Israel Allies network was built from an American base. The second is how little is known. Among the sources used here, only those for Britain, Canada and the United States count lawmakers' or lobbyists' dealings from public registers; for most of the countries in the caucus network, the record consists of the network's own announcements.

sections.h: Testing a Hypothesis: Arms, Aid and Standing at the United Nations
sections.html:
A common explanation of pro-Israel advocacy abroad, and one this volume was asked to test, is that it serves two practical ends: keeping military aid and arms flowing to Israel, and protecting Israel's standing at the United Nations. The explanation can be checked against the record assembled in this part. The result is mixed. One half of it fits the evidence in the two countries that matter most; the other half needs to be restated before it fits at all; and in much of the world the benefits run in a different direction from the one the hypothesis assumes.

Arms and aid. Israel buys most of its imported weapons from two countries. According to estimates by the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute for 2019 to 2023, the United States supplied 69 percent of Israel's arms imports and Germany about 30 percent; American military aid alone exceeds $3 billion a year. [cite:pm_wapo_suppliers] The two countries with the best-documented pro-Israel advocacy among Israel's suppliers, the United States with AIPAC and Germany, where ELNET is registered, are therefore the two on which Israel's arms supply depends. That fits the hypothesis. But elsewhere the arms trade runs the other way. Israel was the world's ninth-largest arms exporter in the same period, and its largest customers were India, which took 37 percent of its exports, and the Philippines, which took 12 percent; Israel supplied 28 percent of the Philippines' arms imports and 11 percent of Morocco's. [cite:pm_globes_exports] Germany's purchase of Arrow 3, which ELNET counts among its successes, was also a sale by Israel, not aid to it. [cite:pm_intercept_elnet] In those countries the interest that advocacy may serve is commercial and strategic, and the buyer, not Israel, is the one receiving arms.

Standing at the United Nations. Israel's membership of the United Nations is not in question. It was admitted by General Assembly Resolution 273 on 11 May 1949, and no mechanism of the advocacy described here concerns it. [cite:rs_rd6_unga273_text] What advocacy abroad has sought is something narrower: votes. Netanyahu told Israel's envoys to Africa that his first interest there was to "dramatically change the situation regarding African votes at the UN," and to change their voting patterns. [cite:pm_alg_netanyahu_un] Status in regional bodies has been contested in the same way. The chair of the African Union Commission granted Israel observer status in 2021; South Africa protested, and after an Israeli diplomat was removed from the union's summit in February 2023 the status was suspended pending review by a committee, with Israel blaming "extremist states like Algeria and South Africa." [cite:pm_aljaz_au] Restated as a hypothesis about votes and observer seats rather than recognition, this half fits the record: it is a stated goal of Israeli diplomacy and of the caucus network, whose aims include embassy moves to Jerusalem. [cite:pm_wiki_iaf]

What the other countries gain. The hypothesis also leaves out why governments abroad respond. The best-documented case is Guatemala, which moved its embassy to Jerusalem in 2018. Israel had been Guatemala's largest supplier of weapons, training and surveillance technology in the 1980s, after the United States cut off military aid in 1977, and analysts tied the embassy decision to that history, to the president's evangelical political base, and to Guatemala's dependence on American aid and goodwill. [cite:pm_pitt_guatemala] In that account the aid at stake is American aid to Guatemala, and the road to it runs through Washington, where the United States had opened its own embassy in Jerusalem on 14 May 2018. [cite:wiki_unsc478] A Central American government aligning with Israel was aligning with the United States as well. The caucus network's appeal to Christian voters, "faith-based diplomacy" in its own phrase, points to the same mixture of motives: religious conviction among parliamentarians and their voters, as well as interest. [cite:pm_ih_iaf50]

The amounts complete the picture. Against the American military aid of more than $3 billion a year, the international advocacy described in this part is small: an Israeli budget for public diplomacy of about $730 million in 2026, the largest single item; at least $11 million from American funders to ELNET since 2022; a little over £1 million to British MPs in a five-year Parliament; less than C$700,000 on Canadian MPs' trips over about eighteen years; and a caucus network run on about $1.4 million a year. [cite:pm_jta_730m] [cite:pm_intercept_elnet] [cite:pm_declassified_quarter] [cite:pm_maple_cija] [cite:pm_wiki_iaf] By the measure of money, the private side of the effort is overwhelmingly American; since 2023, however, the Israeli government's own budget has been the largest single sum. Abroad it is cheaper, harder to see and, on the evidence here, aimed less at keeping Israel's place in the world than at turning that place into votes, purchases and embassies.

chapters.label: Part Ten
chapters.title: The Whole Architecture, and What It Costs
chapters.intro: Part Ten draws the volume together. It sets out the whole architecture on one page, from the donors at the top to the members, legislatures and treasuries at the bottom, at home and abroad; it gathers the totals from the earlier parts into a single table, with their sources and their definitions; and it asks what the architecture costs, and who pays, before closing with what the record settles and what it leaves open.
chapters.outro:
Part Ten drew the volume together. Pro-Israel money in American government runs through a small number of organizations, AIPAC's four bodies at the center, whose campaign money grew from about $15 million a cycle in pro-Israel contributions in 2018 to between $95 million and $127 million for AIPAC's two committees alone in 2024; it reaches members of Congress through contributions, primaries and trips, the states through laws and bond purchases, and other countries through parallel organizations and the Israeli government's own budget. [cite:pm_sludge_100m_2026] [cite:cnsmd_trips_study] [cite:pm_wiki_antibds] [cite:pm_icij_bonds] [cite:pm_jta_730m]

What is settled is the structure and the scale, from filings the organizations made themselves. What is contested is what the money does, and how to count it. What the record leaves open is the donors who are not disclosed, the officials whose travel is not recorded, and the effect of the network on members it never had to oppose.

sections.h: The Architecture on One Page
sections.html:
The nine parts before this one each followed a single channel. Put together, they describe one architecture with a clear shape. At the top are donors, most of them American individuals and foundations, whose money is pooled by a small number of organizations. In the middle are those organizations, AIPAC's four bodies above all, and the channels the law allows each of them: lobbying, campaign contributions, earmarking, independent spending, charity-paid travel. At the bottom are the places the money reaches: members of Congress and candidates, state legislatures and treasuries, and, through parallel organizations and the Israeli government's own spending, parliaments abroad. The figure below sets the architecture out by level, with the largest documented sum at each point.

The totals. The table gathers the volume's principal figures in one place. Each comes from a different source, measures something different and covers a different period, so the figures cannot be added together into a single total, and this volume does not attempt one. They show the order of magnitude of each channel and how it has changed.

Three changes. Read across the parts, the architecture has changed in three ways in the period this volume covers. The first is scale: campaign money tied to the network rose from about $15 million a cycle in pro-Israel contributions in 2018 to between $95 million and $127 million for AIPAC's two committees alone in 2024, depending on the count. [cite:pm_jvl_pacs2020] [cite:pm_sludge_100m_2026] The second is method: a network that for seven decades lobbied and steered donations without spending in its own name now spends directly in primaries, often in advertising that does not mention Israel and, increasingly in 2026, through committees whose names do not show who funds them. [cite:punchbowl_udp_no_israel] [cite:pm_factcheck_udp_2026] The third is reach: the Israeli government, once a background presence, became a direct spender on American opinion and American officials, through registered agents and through trips it paid for itself. [cite:pm_quincy_eighth] [cite:pm_idcap_50states] The simulation's account of [scene:cm_s00|pro-Israel money in Congress] follows the same architecture scene by scene.

sections.h: What It Costs, and Who Pays
sections.html:
The question of what the architecture costs has two answers, and the volume has kept them apart. The first is the money spent by the network itself, which its donors pay and which the filings record. The second is the costs that fall on others: the public, the taxpayers of states and cities, and the people whose rights or votes the architecture touches. This section sets out both, then closes the volume with what the record settles, what it leaves contested and what it leaves open.

The network's own money. The money AIPAC and its allies spend is private, legal and disclosed in the channels the law requires, and it is paid for by the donors who give it. Measured against the sums at stake, it is not large. Over $100 million in a cycle is a large sum in primaries, where a single race can be decided by a few million dollars; it is small next to the more than $3 billion a year in American military aid that the network supports. [cite:pm_sludge_100m_2026] [cite:pm_wapo_suppliers] The comparison does not show that the spending buys the aid. The aid predates AIPAC's committees by decades. It shows the proportion: the price of the political effort is a small fraction of the policy it defends.

The costs that fall on others. Three of the volume's channels place costs on people who did not choose to pay them. The trips are paid for by a charity, so its donors deduct their gifts, and critics argue that the public bears part of the cost of the travel through the tax deduction; defenders answer that the same is true of every charity. [cite:intercept_aief_donors] The anti-boycott laws in many of the thirty-eight states require contractors to certify their position on one country, a requirement the Arkansas Times refused; the courts have divided, and the Arkansas law stands. [cite:pm_wiki_antibds] [cite:pm_aclu_waldrip] And the bond purchases place the savings of public funds in a single foreign government's debt, a choice that a former Pennsylvania investment chief warned against and that some Palm Beach County residents have challenged in court. [cite:pm_icij_bonds] These are not costs in the sense of money taken; they are costs in the sense of choices made for the public by officials whom the network courts.

The cost to the political process. The last cost is the one the record measures least well. Critics of the network argue that its principal effect is not the races it enters but those it never has to enter: members who decline to criticize Israel because they have seen what happened to Bowman, Bush and Massie. [cite:factcheck_udp_2024] [cite:pbs_massie_takeaways] Defenders answer that members who support Israel do so because they and their voters believe in the alliance, and that the network's money follows positions rather than creating them. The filings cannot settle this argument, because the effect critics describe would leave no filing. What the filings do show is that the network's spending has helped defeat members of both parties, that it has lost several of its largest campaigns, and that it has spent most heavily in primaries. [cite:pm_factcheck_udp_2022] [cite:pm_sludge_100m_2026]

What is settled. The structure and the scale. The network is built from organizations with documented legal forms; its spending is disclosed, and since 2021 it has grown from millions to more than a hundred million dollars a cycle. The recipients, the targets and the trips are on the record, in the United States and in Britain and Canada. The Israeli government's own spending on influence has grown fastest of all since 2023.

What is contested. What the money does. Whether it changes votes or follows them; whether its primary spending decided races that had other causes; whether accusations of antisemitism against its critics are accurate in each case or used as a weapon; whether the trips educate or recruit; whether the anti-boycott laws protect states or penalize speech; and how to count, since the trackers' totals for the same cycle differ widely.

What is open. The donors behind AIPAC's lobby and foundation, which are not public; the travel of state and local officials, which no federal body records; the per-cycle recipient lists built from the Federal Election Commission's own files, which are still being compiled for this library; the full results of the 2026 cycle, which was still running when this was written; and, outside the few countries with disclosure laws, almost everything about the lobby abroad.

The architecture is not hidden. Most of the figures in this volume come from filings that the organizations made under laws that require them to, or from journalists and researchers who have read those filings. What the filings do not show is intent, and the volume has not supplied it. A reader who wants to know whether this architecture is an alliance's ordinary advocacy or something more has the same documents to read as its defenders and its critics, and now has them in one place.

books.title: Gaza, Documented
books.subtitle: Palestine Under the Architecture, 1917–2026
books.intro:
This volume follows one strip of land, about 360 square kilometres, through a century of the architecture this library documents. It asks what happened in Gaza, to whom, by whose decision and at whose cost, and it answers from the record: censuses and armistice texts, UN resolutions and agency reports, court orders and findings, the work of historians and the testimony of the people who lived it.

It begins before the State of Israel, with a town on the old coast road between Egypt and Syria, and follows it through the war of 1948, which made the strip and filled it with refugees; nineteen years of Egyptian rule; the occupation from 1967; the uprisings, the Oslo years, the settlements and the withdrawal of 2005; the blockade from 2007 and the wars that followed it; the attack of 7 October 2023; and the war since, its dead, the famine findings and the cases in the international courts. Four parts then step back: one follows the money, from the economy of occupation to aid and reconstruction; one asks who decides Gaza's fate; one sets out the plans American and Israeli leaders have made for its future, and who is making them; and one asks how all of this reached, or did not reach, American audiences. The last part sets out what is settled, what is contested and what is still open.

The volume holds to the standard of the library. Every load-bearing claim carries its source. Where sources disagree, especially on the number of the dead, the figures are set side by side with their method and their date rather than reduced to the largest or the smallest. It describes the acts of governments, armies and armed groups, not the character of peoples, and it treats the suffering on every side as a fact to be recorded, not a point to be scored.

chapters.label: Part One
chapters.title: Gaza Before the State, and the Refugees
chapters.intro: Part One goes back before the strip existed. It finds Gaza as a town and a district of Mandate Palestine, follows the war of 1948 in the south as the Egyptian army advanced and was driven back, and shows how the line where the fighting stopped became the edge of a new and never quite defined territory. It ends with the people who filled that territory: the refugees, who by the end of the war outnumbered Gaza's own residents by more than two to one.
chapters.outro:
Part One found the strip's origins in the record. Gaza was a town of about 34,000 and the centre of a district of 137,000 under the British Mandate, overwhelmingly Arab, with a Jewish community that had ended in 1929 and one Jewish outpost founded in 1946. [cite:gz_wiki_subdistrict] [cite:gz_nli_jews] [cite:gz_wiki_kfardarom] The war of 1948 left Israel with most of the district and Egypt with a remnant of about 361 to 365 square kilometres, enclosed by an armistice line that both sides said was not a border. [cite:gz_palquest_refugees] [cite:gz_golan_2024] [cite:gz_wiki_history] Into it came more than 200,000 refugees, joining about 80,000 residents, and the international relief created to keep them from starvation became permanent when the return promised in Resolution 194 did not happen. [cite:gz_palquest_refugees] [cite:gz_un_res302] [cite:rs_rd6_refworld_194]

What is settled is how the strip was made and who filled it. What is contested is the size of the 1948 exodus as a whole, and the meaning of the right of return. What the record leaves open, from 1949 on, is the strip's status: governed by Egypt, annexed by no state, and home to people who were citizens of no state. Part Two follows the nineteen years of Egyptian rule and the occupation that began in 1967.

sections.h: A Town on the Coast Road
sections.html:
Before there was a Gaza Strip there was Gaza, a town and the district named after it, and the strip that bears its name today is the small part of that district the Egyptian army still held when the war of 1948 ended. To understand what was lost and what remained, this section sets out the town and its district as they stood under the Ottoman Empire and the British Mandate: their place on the map, their people, and the small Jewish presence the record shows among them.

An Ottoman district on a frontier. From the sixteenth century Gaza was part of the Ottoman Empire. [cite:gz_wiki_history] When the Ottomans reorganized southern Palestine in 1872 they made Jerusalem an independent district, a mutasarrifate, and Gaza became one of its districts, alongside Jaffa and Hebron. [cite:rs_rd1_jerusalemstory] Gaza's position on the coast road between Egypt and Syria made it a frontier town, and in 1906 the Ottoman and British empires fixed the boundary between Ottoman territory and British-controlled Egypt. [cite:gz_wiki_history] The treaty of 1979 confirmed that line between Egypt and former Mandate Palestine as Egypt's permanent border. [cite:gz_treaty1979]

The battles of 1917. The First World War brought the front to Gaza's edge. The British Egyptian Expeditionary Force attacked the Ottoman defences there in March and again in April 1917 and was defeated both times. It broke through further east at Beersheba at the end of October, fought the Third Battle of Gaza on the night of 1 to 2 November, and occupied the town on the morning of 7 November, after the Ottoman garrison had withdrawn in the night. Gaza had had about 40,000 inhabitants before the war; the British bombardment that preceded its capture severely damaged or destroyed most of its housing. [cite:gz_wiki_gaza3] Five days earlier, in London, the British government had issued the Balfour Declaration, as [scene:dv2_parent_test|the volume on the three parents] sets out. From 1920 to 1948 Britain governed Gaza as part of Mandatory Palestine. [cite:gz_wiki_history]

The people of the district. The Mandate government's last official population estimates, the Village Statistics of 1945, shows the Gaza subdistrict with 137,180 people: 133,040 Muslims, 2,890 Jews and 1,250 Christians. The town of Gaza itself had 34,250 inhabitants, of whom 33,160 were Muslims, 1,010 Christians and 80 Jews. [cite:gz_wiki_subdistrict] The subdistrict stretched well north and east of the present strip; it included the town of al-Majdal, beside the site of ancient Ashkelon, [cite:gz_oup_morris_majdal] and dozens of villages on the coastal plain whose fate in 1948 is told in the next section. [cite:gz_wiki_subdistrict]

Gaza's Jews. A small Jewish community had lived in Gaza at many points in its history. In its last period it was renewed in the second half of the nineteenth century, mostly by Sephardi traders, and had close to a hundred members before the First World War, when the Ottomans expelled most Jews of foreign nationality and the community effectively lapsed. Jews returned slowly after the British conquest; in 1926 the community's secretary counted 51. In the riots of 1929, Gaza's Jews barricaded themselves in a hotel near the police station and were then taken, with the help of some local Arabs and the British police, to the railway station and by train to Lod. The National Library of Israel calls it "the end of the Jewish community in Gaza." [cite:gz_nli_jews] The 1945 estimates nonetheless list 80 Jews in the town; the sources consulted do not say who they were. [cite:gz_wiki_subdistrict]

Kfar Darom. One Jewish settlement stood inside what became the strip. On 6 October 1946 a group of new immigrants set out from Be'erot Yitzhak to found Kfar Darom, south of Gaza town, on land that had been a Jewish-owned orchard since 1930 and had been destroyed during the Arab revolt of 1936 to 1939. [cite:gz_wiki_kfardarom] It was part of the Jewish Agency's plan of eleven new outposts in the Negev. [cite:gz_wiki_history] Its history is short and returns twice in this volume: it was besieged and abandoned in 1948, and rebuilt as an Israeli settlement after 1967, only to be evacuated again in 2005. [cite:gz_wiki_kfardarom]

The picture this record gives is of a district with an overwhelmingly Arab population, a historic town at its centre, and a small Jewish presence, a few dozen people in the town and one outpost inside the later strip. Within two years almost all of that would change: most of the district would be inside Israel, most of its villages would be empty, and the remaining sliver around Gaza town would hold more than three times as many people as before.

sections.h: 1948: How the Strip Was Made
sections.html:
No one planned the Gaza Strip. The UN partition plans of 1947 assigned the southern coastal plain to a prospective Arab state, and the war that followed decided what was left of it. [cite:gz_golan_2024] The strip is the ground the Egyptian army still held when the fighting stopped. Its boundary with Israel was fixed in the armistice of 1949, which adopted a line set out in a UN memorandum of November 1948 and required Israeli forces to pull back from Beit Hanun; the historian Arnon Golan argues that the line was finally delineated only by a local agreement in 1950. [cite:gz_armistice_text] [cite:gz_golan_2024] This section follows the war in the south from the first attacks to the armistice, and sets out what that line was, and was not, in law.

The first months. Fighting in the south began before the British left. By April 1948 Arab forces had surrounded Kfar Darom, and on 10 April a battalion of Muslim Brotherhood volunteers from Egypt attacked it and was beaten back with heavy losses. When the Mandate ended and Egypt's regular army crossed the frontier on 15 May, the outpost was among its first targets; the attack was repelled, with Egyptian losses given in Israeli accounts as 70 killed and 50 wounded. [cite:gz_wiki_kfardarom] Egypt was one of the Arab states whose forces entered Palestine that day, with Syria, Iraq and Lebanon, while Transjordan's forces intervened in areas assigned to the Arab state or to Jerusalem. [cite:rs_rd5_oh_war_b] Kfar Darom held out until the night of 8 July, when the Israeli command approved its evacuation; Egyptian troops entered it the next day and found it empty. [cite:gz_wiki_kfardarom]

A Palestinian government in Gaza. In September 1948, with the Egyptian army holding the southern coast, the Arab League agreed to an Arab government for all of Palestine with its seat in Gaza. It was announced on 20 September; on 22 September the Arab Higher Committee declared Palestine independent under the All-Palestine Government headed by Ahmad Hilmi Abdul Baqi, and a Palestinian National Council meeting in Gaza on 30 September adopted a provisional constitution. Egypt recognized the government first, followed by Iraq, Syria, Lebanon and Saudi Arabia, among others; King Abdullah of Transjordan refused. [cite:rs_rd6_shlaim_apg_1990] The historian Avi Shlaim argues that Egypt sponsored it chiefly to block Abdullah's plan to join Arab Palestine to his kingdom, and calls it "a phantom deliberately created by the Arab states, with Egypt at their head"; after Israel's October offensive its ministers were moved to Cairo. [cite:rs_rd6_shlaim_apg_1990] The library's account of [scene:rd6_arab_palestine|what became of Arab Palestine in 1948] follows the rival claims in full.

Operation Yoav. The decisive fighting came in the autumn. On 15 October 1948, during the second truce, which had no fixed end, Israeli forces launched Operation Yoav, designed to break the Egyptian line that cut the Negev off from the north. According to the Institute for Palestine Studies' encyclopedia, drawing on Benny Morris, Israeli troops provoked Egyptian fire on a supply convoy to open the offensive, and artillery and aircraft were used to "soften up" villages before they were occupied. By the time the operation ended on 4 November, Israeli forces had broken the Egyptian line and occupied most of the villages of the Gaza district. [cite:gz_palquest_yoav] Egyptian troops remained besieged at al-Faluja until the armistice. [cite:rs_rd6_arm_egypt_text] Al-Majdal, a town of about 10,000 residents before the war, was bombed in October and captured on 4 November; about 1,000 of its Arabs remained. [cite:gz_stein_majdal] In the course of the war, tens of thousands of Palestinians fled or were expelled into what became the strip. [cite:gz_wiki_history]

The armistice line. Egypt and Israel signed a general armistice at Rhodes on 24 February 1949, one of four agreements Israel concluded with its neighbours that year; Egypt kept the strip, as Jordan kept the West Bank. [cite:rs_rd5_oh_war_b] The agreement separated the two armies along a demarcation line, and both parties declared that the line was a military arrangement and not an international border. [cite:gz_wiki_history] The library's account of [scene:rd6_armistices|the 1949 armistices] sets out their terms. What the line enclosed was the remnant of a district: Israel held all of the Beersheba subdistrict and most of the Gaza subdistrict, and the rest, about 361 square kilometres or 1.3 percent of Mandate Palestine, became the Gaza Strip. [cite:gz_palquest_refugees] Other sources give 365 square kilometres. [cite:gz_golan_2024] A year later, on 22 February 1950, Egyptian and Israeli officers meeting at El Auja agreed a modus vivendi dividing the Gaza–Rafah area into patrol zones, to reduce friction between soldiers and villagers. It stated that it was "of a purely local character" and changed neither side's position on the demarcation line. [cite:gz_un_modus] The historian Arnon Golan, who traced the strip's formation from 1947 to that agreement, describes the result as an "allegedly provisional" entity whose formal status was never determined. [cite:gz_golan_2024]

The record therefore settles how the strip came to be: not by any plan for it, but as the ground one army still held when the war stopped, inside a line both sides insisted was temporary. What it left unsettled, from the first day, was what the strip was: neither part of Egypt nor of Israel, nor the seat of a state that functioned. The next section turns to the people that line enclosed.

sections.h: A Quarter of a People on One Percent of the Land
sections.html:
The armistice line closed around about 80,000 people who had lived in that part of the Gaza district before the war. By the time it was drawn, more than 200,000 others had arrived, from the rest of the district and from as far north as the Lydda area. [cite:gz_palquest_refugees] The strip that the war made was, from its first day, a place of refugees, and it has remained one. This section sets out how many came, where they were housed, who took responsibility for them, and the legal limbo in which they and the strip's original residents were left.

The numbers. The total number of Palestinian refugees from the war of 1948 was disputed from the start, and the dispute is set out in [scene:rd6_exodus|the library's account of the exodus]: Israel's government put it at 520,000 to 530,000, Arab officials spoke of 900,000 or a million, and the British estimated 810,000 in February 1949, of whom they placed 210,000 in Gaza. [cite:rs_rd6_morris_appendix] The Institute for Palestine Studies' encyclopedia puts the refugees who reached the strip at "more than 200,000", against a resident population of 80,000. [cite:gz_palquest_refugees] Taken together, the figures mean that the strip's population roughly tripled in a matter of months, and that refugees outnumbered the original residents by more than two to one. The historian Jean-Pierre Filiu's summary is starker: by the war's end, a quarter of Mandate Palestine's Arab population was in Gaza, on about one percent of its land. [cite:gz_wiki_history]

The camps. The first refugees slept wherever there was a roof or none: in mosques, schools and private homes, in military barracks and on open ground. The American Friends Service Committee, a Quaker relief body, then set up camps on land allocated by the Egyptian administration, named after the nearest towns. The Institute's encyclopedia dates Jabaliya and Nuseirat to 1948; al-Maghazi, Deir al-Balah, Khan Yunis and Rafah to 1949; Shati, the Beach camp, to 1951; and al-Bureij to 1952. [cite:gz_palquest_refugees] All eight were still standing in 2023; Part Seven records what the war since has done to them. On the eve of the war of 2023, AFP reported, citing UNRWA, that more than two-thirds of Gaza's 2.4 million people were registered refugees. [cite:gz_afp_camps]

UNRWA. On 8 December 1949 the UN General Assembly adopted Resolution 302, which established the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East to carry out "direct relief and works programmes" with the host governments. It recognized that continued assistance was necessary "to prevent conditions of starvation and distress", and it was framed as temporary: the agency was also to plan, with the governments of the region, for the time when international relief would end. [cite:gz_un_res302] UNRWA began operating on 1 May 1950 and took over the camps. [cite:gz_palquest_refugees] Its first report listed Gaza as one of its five fields of operation. [cite:rs_cw1_un_yearbook_1951] The relief was meant to be temporary because the refugees were meant to go home or be resettled. A year before, on 11 December 1948, the General Assembly had resolved in paragraph 11 of Resolution 194 that refugees wishing to return to their homes and live at peace with their neighbours should be permitted to do so, with compensation for those who chose not to, and had charged a Conciliation Commission with facilitating "repatriation, resettlement and economic and social rehabilitation." [cite:rs_rd6_refworld_194] Neither return nor resettlement followed. In 1951 the Conciliation Commission recorded that Israel was not prepared to implement paragraph 11 and the Arab governments were not prepared to implement paragraph 5, on negotiating a final settlement, and that neither side showed a willingness to move from its position; [cite:rs_cw1_unccp_a1985] [scene:rd6_return_barred|the library's account of the barred return] sets out the record. The camps became permanent.

Al-Majdal, 1950. The movement of people into the strip did not end with the armistice. About 1,000 Arabs had remained in al-Majdal after its capture in November 1948, and by 1950, with returnees and natural growth, there were about 2,700. In June 1950, according to the historian Benny Morris, the Israeli government began moving them out, at the urging of Moshe Dayan: the transfer began on 14 June, and Ben-Gurion authorized it on 19 June on condition that the residents agreed. Morris attributes the departures mainly to systematic intimidation, although most of those who left signed forms declaring that they went voluntarily. Most went to Gaza; some went to Lod and Ramle inside Israel. Ben-Gurion suspended the operation in October 1950 after objections from the Histadrut, the labour federation; by the end about twenty remained. [cite:gz_oup_morris_majdal] [cite:gz_stein_majdal] Jewish immigrants had begun moving into the town's empty houses in 1949; it is today part of the Israeli city of Ashkelon. [cite:gz_stein_majdal]

A people without a state. The residents and refugees of Gaza were left without a state of their own or anyone else's. Egypt governed the strip through a military governor but never annexed it, and it did not offer its people Egyptian citizenship; until 1961 they travelled, if they travelled at all, on documents of the All-Palestine Government, [cite:gz_palquest_refugees] which by then had no power and had moved to Cairo, where Nasser dissolved it in 1959. Egypt also restricted movement in and out of the strip, which limited the work its population could find. [cite:gz_wiki_history] In 1955 Egypt issued a Basic Law for the strip, which took effect in 1958 and reserved four seats on its Legislative Council for refugees. [cite:gz_palquest_refugees] Part Two takes up those nineteen years of Egyptian rule, and the occupation that followed them.

chapters.label: Part Two
chapters.title: Egyptian Rule and the Occupation
chapters.intro: Part Two covers the thirty-eight years between the armistice and the first uprising. For about eighteen of them Egypt governed the strip without annexing it, and the strip became the front line of a border war; for the rest, Israel occupied it, counted its people, put down an insurgency, drew its workers into the Israeli economy and planted settlements among its refugee camps. The Cold War volume of this library tells the years to 1967 in detail; this part gathers what that volume found about Gaza and carries the story to the eve of December 1987.
chapters.outro:
Part Two followed Gaza through two rulers. Under Egypt, from 1949 to 1967, the strip was a stateless refugee territory and the front line of a border war: Israeli raids and the Egyptian-run fida'i units, the 1955 uprising against a plan to resettle refugees in Sinai, and the Israeli occupation of 1956, with the killings at Khan Yunis and Rafah. [cite:rs_cw2_mod_black_arrow] [cite:rs_cw2_palquest_gaza] [cite:rs_cw3_morris_gaza] Under Israel from 1967, its 356,000 people were counted, governed by the military, and subjected after 1970 to a campaign that demolished some 2,000 homes and displaced nearly 16,000 people; its workers were drawn into the Israeli economy, and settlements were planted on its land from 1970. [cite:gz_jvl_census67] [cite:gz_wiki_insurgency] [cite:gz_carnegie_labor] [cite:gz_wiki_gushkatif]

What is settled is the sequence of rule and the main acts of each ruler. What is contested is the death tolls of 1955 and 1956, set out side by side here, and the judgment on the campaign of 1971: effective pacification, or collective punishment that stored up resentment. What the record leaves open is the strip's status, which the armistice, the Camp David framework and the peace treaty each declined to settle. Part Three follows the uprising, the Oslo years, the settlements and the withdrawal of 2005.

sections.h: Nineteen Years Under Egypt, 1949–1967
sections.html:
The Cold War volume of this library follows the border war between Israel and Egypt in detail, and much of it was fought in and around Gaza. This section gathers what that volume established about the strip under Egyptian rule, with links to the full accounts, so that the story of Gaza can be read in one place. The pattern it shows is of a territory whose people belonged to no state, policed by one army and raided by another, and treated by both as a security problem before anything else.

A frontier of raids. Refugees crossing the armistice line to reach their old fields and homes, and armed infiltrators among them, made the strip's edge violent from the start, and Israel answered with reprisal raids, a policy argued over inside the Israeli government itself. [cite:rs_cw2_caplan_asia] In late August 1953, according to the historians Walid Khalidi and Neil Caplan, a unit led by the 25-year-old Ariel Sharon attacked the al-Burj refugee camp in the strip. [cite:rs_cw2_jps_qibya] On the night of 28 February 1955 Israeli forces crossed into the strip and attacked an Egyptian army camp in what Israel's Defense Ministry archive records as Operation Black Arrow; the archive counts thirty-eight Egyptian soldiers and eight Israelis killed, while Egypt's letter to the Security Council gave 37 soldiers and 2 civilians killed. [cite:rs_cw2_mod_black_arrow] [cite:rs_cw2_un_s3365] The library's [scene:cw2_gaza_raid|account of the Gaza raid] sets out its causes and its consequences.

Gaza against its own rulers. One of those consequences was a revolt in the strip against Egypt itself. On 1 March 1955 a mass demonstration in Gaza chanted against relocation and against "US agents"; Egyptian police fired on it and killed a textile worker, Hosni Belal. The protesters' main demand was the cancellation of a plan to resettle refugees in the Sinai, and the protests were organized jointly by communists and the Muslim Brotherhood. [cite:rs_cw2_palquest_gaza] The plan was real: UNRWA had been working with Egypt on Sinai schemes since 1950, and in June 1953 it had reserved $30 million of its $200 million reintegration fund for a scheme to resettle 60,000 Gaza refugees there. [cite:rs_cw1_newlines_sinai]

The fida'i units. In September 1955 Egypt formed Palestinian fida'i units, Battalion 141, under Lieutenant Colonel Mustafa Hafez, based in Gaza, and their raids into Israel continued until Israeli intelligence assassinated Hafez in July 1956. [cite:rs_cw2_palquest_gaza] In mid-August 1956 mines and attacks near the strip killed four Israeli citizens, and the next day nine Egyptians were killed when their car was ambushed. [cite:rs_cw2_unyb1956] By the eve of the Suez war, Ben-Gurion told the Knesset that Egypt "still sits in the Gaza Strip." [cite:rs_cw3_knesset_15oct56]

Occupation and killings, 1956. Israeli forces entered the strip on 2 November 1956, in the first days of the Sinai campaign, and governed some 300,000 people, about three-quarters of them refugees of 1948. [cite:rs_cw3_morris_gaza] Within ten days, at Khan Yunis on 3 November and at Rafah on 12 November, Israeli troops killed large numbers of men; the counts are disputed and set out in [scene:cw3_gaza_killings|the library's account of Khan Yunis and Rafah]. Benny Morris records that "some 275 civilians and POWs were murdered" at Khan Yunis according to the Palestinians and UNRWA, and that at Rafah Israel said 48 were killed and UNRWA 111. [cite:rs_cw3_morris_gaza] Israel denied that either event was a massacre. [cite:rs_cw3_time_sacco] Ben-Gurion hoped to keep the strip, telling the Knesset in January 1957 that "this Strip was never Egyptian," but under international, mainly American, pressure Israel withdrew completely on 8 March 1957. [cite:rs_cw3_morris_gaza] A UN Emergency Force stayed on the Egyptian side of the line until Nasser ordered it out in May 1967. [cite:rs_cw3_morris_gaza]

The quiet decade. After 1957 the strip was quieter. Egypt issued a Basic Law for it in 1955, in force from 1958, with four seats on its Legislative Council reserved for refugees; it continued to issue identity documents but not citizenship, and to restrict movement in and out. [cite:gz_palquest_refugees] [cite:gz_wiki_history] The Palestine Liberation Organization, founded in 1964, named the Gaza Strip in its charter as territory over which it claimed no regional sovereignty, a clause the library's account of [scene:cw6_summits_plo|the PLO's founding] sets in context. [cite:rs_cw6_charter_1964] In May 1967 Egypt's chief of staff asked the UN force to withdraw from its observation posts on the border; the UN Secretary-General, U Thant, replied that any withdrawal would have to be of all its troops from Gaza and Sinai, and the force's departure became one of the steps toward war. [cite:rs_cw6_frus19_d6]

sections.h: June 1967: Counted, Governed, Pacified
sections.html:
On 6 June 1967, the second day of the Six-Day War, Israeli forces took the Gaza Strip from Egypt. [cite:gz_wiki_occupation] This time they stayed. This section sets out what Israel found there, how it governed, and how it put down the armed and civil resistance of the first four years, including the campaign of 1971 that reshaped the refugee camps and, in the words of the general who led it, kept the strip quiet for fifteen years.

The count. In the summer of 1967 Israel's Central Bureau of Statistics took a census of the newly occupied territories. Its first findings, published on 3 October 1967, counted 356,000 people in the Gaza Strip, 175,000 of them living in refugee camps, and another 33,000 in northern Sinai. [cite:gz_jvl_census67] Its tables, which survive in digitized form, include data about respondents' 1948 refugee status. [cite:gz_levy_census67] After 1948 the strip had held about 80,000 original residents and more than 200,000 refugees; [cite:gz_palquest_refugees] by 1967, after an unknown number had left during and after the June war, about half of those counted still lived in the camps.

The government. In June 1967 Israel set up a military government for the civilian populations of all the territories it had taken: the West Bank, Gaza, Sinai and the Golan Heights. [cite:gz_wiki_occupation] In 1982, after the peace treaty with Egypt, Israel replaced the military government's civilian functions with the Civil Administration. [cite:gz_wiki_occupation]

Resistance, 1967–1971. Gaza did not settle. Armed factions, the leftist Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine the most prominent among them, attacked Israeli forces, and, by one contemporary report, killed mostly Arabs, some of them marked as suspected collaborators, while civilians organized strikes, boycotts of Israeli goods and demonstrations; in May 1968 women blocked roads and marched on the military governor's offices, and in February 1969 a schoolgirls' riot in Gaza spread to the West Bank. In October 1970 the New York Times correspondent James Feron reported that Gaza was the only area taken in 1967 where attacks continued "unabated," with several killings, grenade attacks or acts of sabotage each week, most of the victims Arabs. [cite:gz_wiki_insurgency]

Sharon's campaign. In 1970 the army's Southern Command under General Ariel Sharon expanded a campaign of what it called pacification, and after the killing of two Israeli children of the Aroyo family in January 1971 it intensified it. Its methods were mass arrests, search-and-destroy operations, demolitions, deportations, a fence around the strip, and wide roads cut through the refugee camps so that armoured vehicles could move through them. In the summer of 1971 bulldozers demolished about 2,000 homes and displaced nearly 16,000 people in Rafah camp and other camps; about 2,000 of the displaced were sent to El-Arish in Sinai and hundreds to the West Bank. [cite:gz_wiki_insurgency] Drawing on the economist Sara Roy, one account puts the number of relatives of suspected guerrillas deported to detention camps in Sinai at 12,000, and records that displaced families moved in 1972 to "Canada Camp," on the Egyptian side of the Rafah border, took about twenty years to come back. [cite:gz_mada_sinai] The same account records that early versions of the Allon Plan, the Israeli blueprint for the territories, envisioned moving hundreds of thousands of Gaza's Palestinians to Sinai and the West Bank; the plan was not carried out in that form. [cite:gz_mada_sinai]

The verdicts on it. By the historian Mark Tessler's account, the armed factions were left fragmented and ineffective, and Sharon told Time magazine in 1989 that the strip stayed quiet for fifteen years afterwards. Tessler also records that Israel used collective punishment to deter support for resistance, and quotes an Arab soldier in the Israeli army, Rafik Halabi, who called the main legacy the "festering resentment" of Gaza's people. [cite:gz_wiki_insurgency] Both judgments rest on the same events. The fifteen years of quiet Sharon claimed ended, as Part Three shows, in Jabaliya in December 1987.

sections.h: Workers, Settlers and a Status Left Open, 1967–1987
sections.html:
After the campaign of 1971 the occupation of Gaza settled into a form that lasted until the first uprising. Three things defined it: the strip's workers were drawn into the Israeli economy, Israeli settlements were planted on its land, and the strip's political future was discussed by others and left unresolved. This section takes them in turn.

Labour. From 1967 Israel tied the economy of the occupied territories to its own. Moshe Dayan described the territories as "a source of factors of production, especially unskilled labor." Between 1967 and 1990, between 35 and 40 percent of the employed Palestinian labour force worked in Israel, most of it in low-paid jobs. [cite:gz_carnegie_labor] The figure is for the West Bank and Gaza together. From the early 1990s Israel required those workers to hold permits subject to security clearance. [cite:gz_carnegie_labor]

Settlements. The first plans for Israeli settlement in the strip came within a year of its capture: in 1968 Yigal Allon proposed two military Nahal outposts in central Gaza, and in 1970 a Nahal outpost was built near the site of Kfar Darom, the village abandoned in 1948; it became a civilian settlement in 1989. [cite:gz_wiki_gushkatif] The settlements grew into the bloc known as Gush Katif, which numbered 17 settlements and about 8,600 residents before 2005. [cite:gz_wiki_gushkatif] By 2005 there were 21 settlements in the strip with about 9,000 settlers, among about 1.3 million Palestinians; the historian Jean-Pierre Filiu calculated that each settler had about 400 times the land and 20 times the water allotted to a Palestinian farmer. [cite:gz_wiki_occupation] The settlements are followed to their evacuation in Part Three.

A future discussed by others. When Egypt and Israel made peace, Gaza's fate was set aside. The Camp David framework of 17 September 1978 provided for "transitional arrangements for the West Bank and Gaza for a period not exceeding five years", under which "a self-governing authority" freely elected by the inhabitants would replace the military government and give them "full autonomy", and Israeli forces would withdraw and redeploy to specified security locations. [cite:gz_campdavid] The autonomy was never established. The peace treaty of 26 March 1979 fixed Egypt's border with Israel at the old line between Egypt and Mandate Palestine "without prejudice to the issue of the status of the Gaza Strip." [cite:gz_treaty1979] Egypt recovered Sinai; the strip it had governed for most of two decades stayed under occupation, and its status, which the armistice of 1949 had left open, was left open again. In 1982 Israel transferred the administration of civilian life in the territories from the military government to a new Civil Administration. [cite:gz_wiki_occupation]

By the mid-1980s, the strip's people lived under military rule, with no citizenship, no elected government and no settled status, many of them dependent on work in the country that occupied them, living beside Israeli settlements. In December 1987 the uprising that became known as the intifada began in the Jabaliya camp. [cite:gz_wiki_history] Part Three begins there.

chapters.label: Part Three
chapters.title: Uprising, Oslo, Settlements and Withdrawal
chapters.intro: Part Three covers the eighteen years from the first uprising to the Israeli withdrawal. It begins in the Jabaliya camp in December 1987, where an uprising that spread across the occupied territories began; the same week, a new Islamist movement in the strip named itself Hamas. It follows the Oslo agreements into Gaza, where a Palestinian Authority took over the cities while Israel kept the settlements, the borders and the permits, and it ends with the removal of the settlements in 2005 and the argument, still unresolved in the record, over whether the occupation ended with them.
chapters.outro:
Part Three followed Gaza from uprising to withdrawal. The first intifada began in Jabaliya on 9 December 1987; in its first year 142 Palestinians were killed in the strip, and over six years, by B'Tselem's count, 1,087 Palestinians and 179 Israelis were killed in both territories, while Palestinian militants executed hundreds of suspected collaborators. [cite:gz_wiki_intifada1] Hamas, founded the day after it began, set out in 1988 a charter rejecting any settlement. [cite:gz_wiki_hamas] The Oslo agreements brought a Palestinian Authority to Gaza in 1994 while Israel kept the settlements, the crossings and the permits, and the second intifada followed the lapse of the interim period in 1999. [cite:gz_wiki_gazajericho] [cite:gz_carnegie_labor] [cite:gz_wiki_intifada2] In 2005 Israel removed all 21 settlements and its army, and kept control of the strip's borders, airspace, sea and registry. [cite:gz_wiki_disengagement]

What is settled is the sequence and the numbers as the named organizations counted them. What is contested is whether Israel helped the Islamist movement grow in its early years, what the disengagement was for, and above all whether the occupation ended in 2005. What the record leaves open is the question the next part answers in detail: what control from outside meant for the people inside, once Hamas took power in the strip and Israel and Egypt closed it.

sections.h: December 1987: The Uprising, and Hamas
sections.html:
The fifteen years of quiet that Ariel Sharon claimed for his campaign of 1971 ended in the Jabaliya refugee camp, the largest in the strip. [cite:gz_afp_camps] What began there in December 1987 became the first intifada, an uprising across the West Bank and Gaza that lasted until the Oslo agreements. The same week, Gaza's branch of the Muslim Brotherhood gave itself a new name and a new purpose. This section sets out how the uprising started, what it cost by the competing counts, and how Hamas came into being.

Jabaliya, 8–9 December 1987. On 8 December an Israeli truck crashed into cars carrying Palestinian workers returning from work at the Erez checkpoint, killing four people, three of them from Jabaliya. Rumours spread that the crash was deliberate, in revenge for the stabbing death of an Israeli businessman; Israel denied it. The next day young people in the camp threw stones and, according to the army, petrol bombs at army vehicles, and soldiers opened fire, killing 17-year-old Hatem al-Sesi. [cite:gz_wiki_intifada1] Demonstrations spread from the camp to the rest of the strip and to the West Bank.

The cost. In the uprising's first year 142 Palestinians were killed in the Gaza Strip, 77 of them shot, 37 from the effects of tear gas and 17 from beatings; no Israelis were killed there that year. Tear gas was used heavily in the camps, among them al-Shati, Jabaliya and Bureij, and one calculation counts 60,706 people injured in Gaza by gunfire, beatings or tear gas between 1988 and 1993. [cite:gz_wiki_intifada1] Across both territories, the Israeli human rights organization B'Tselem counts 1,087 Palestinians killed by Israeli forces over the six years, about 240 of them children, with other estimates running to 1,204 or higher, and 179 Israelis killed by Palestinians; official Israeli figures give 200 Israelis. Palestinian militants executed an estimated 771 suspected collaborators by the count of the Associated Press, or 942 by the army's. [cite:gz_wiki_intifada1] Israel arrested tens of thousands, with estimates ranging from 57,000 to 120,000, deported 481 people and demolished between 1,882 and 2,532 homes. Because many of those killed in the first months were civilians and youths, defence minister Yitzhak Rabin adopted a fallback policy known as "might, power and beatings." [cite:gz_wiki_intifada1]

The birth of Hamas. Gaza's Islamist movement predated the uprising. In 1973 the cleric Ahmed Yassin founded the Mujama al-Islamiya, a charitable association linked to the Muslim Brotherhood. Hamas, the Islamic Resistance Movement, dates its founding to 10 December 1987, the day after the uprising began, when the Brotherhood in Gaza took up an activist and nationalist line under that name. [cite:gz_wiki_hamas] Its charter, signed on 18 August 1988, defined it as a wing of the Muslim Brotherhood, called for an Islamic state in all of Palestine and rejected any negotiated settlement, saying the conflict could be resolved only through jihad. [cite:gz_wiki_hamas] In 2017 Hamas published a "Document of General Principles and Policies" that accepted a Palestinian state on the 1967 lines without recognizing Israel; it did not formally repudiate the charter. [cite:gz_wiki_hamas]

A disputed beginning. Whether Israel helped the movement grow is a question the record raises but does not close. The historian Rashid Khalidi and reporting in the Times of Israel are cited for the view that Israel initially and discreetly supported the Islamists as a counterweight to the secular PLO. Israel also acted against the movement: in December 1992 it deported more than 400 suspected Hamas members to southern Lebanon. [cite:gz_wiki_hamas] The later chapters of this volume, and the library's [scene:s20|account of October 7], return to the record of Israeli policy toward Hamas, which is better documented for the years after 2007 than for the 1980s.

sections.h: Oslo in Gaza, 1994–2000
sections.html:
The Oslo agreements came to Gaza first. The Declaration of Principles signed in Washington on 13 September 1993 promised Palestinian self-government for an interim period of up to five years, beginning with an Israeli withdrawal from Gaza and the West Bank town of Jericho, with talks on Jerusalem, refugees, settlements, security and borders deferred. [cite:gz_wiki_oslo1] This section sets out what the agreement for Gaza transferred, what Israel kept, and how the economic arrangements and closures of those years kept the decisions that governed the strip's livelihood outside it.

The Cairo agreement. On 4 May 1994 Yitzhak Rabin, now prime minister, and Yasser Arafat signed the Agreement on the Gaza Strip and the Jericho Area. It created the Palestinian Authority, provided for a Palestinian police force, and required Israeli forces to withdraw from parts of the Gaza Strip and from Jericho within three weeks. Israeli troops remained at the Rafah crossing into Egypt and around the Israeli settlements. The agreement also carried the Paris Protocol, which set the economic relations between the Authority and Israel and integrated the Palestinian economy into Israel's. [cite:gz_wiki_gazajericho] On 1 July 1994 Arafat returned to Gaza City, his first visit in twenty-five years, and on 5 July the Authority was formally inaugurated. In 1995 the agreement was folded into the broader interim agreement known as Oslo II. [cite:gz_wiki_gazajericho]

Closure and permits. The agreements did not change the arrangement that governed the strip's largest source of wages. From the early 1990s Israel had imposed a regime of closures under which Palestinian workers needed permits subject to security clearance, and the Oslo accords left that regime in place. [cite:gz_carnegie_labor] A worker's income now depended on a permit that Israel could suspend at any time, on a security judgement that was Israel's alone. The pattern, of a Palestinian government responsible for the strip's people while the strip's borders, crossings and access to work were controlled from outside, is the one that runs through the rest of this volume.

The interim period was meant to end on 4 May 1999 with a permanent agreement. [cite:gz_wiki_oslo1] It did not. The second intifada began on 28 September 2000, after Ariel Sharon's visit to the Temple Mount, known to Muslims as the Haram al-Sharif, and is usually dated to the truce of February 2005. By 30 April 2008, B'Tselem had counted 4,745 Palestinians killed by Israeli security forces and about 1,053 Israelis killed by Palestinians since September 2000. From Gaza, armed groups fired Qassam rockets and mortars at Israeli towns such as Sderot, and Israeli operations in Rafah destroyed more than 1,500 houses, according to Human Rights Watch. [cite:gz_wiki_intifada2] Before the uprising was over, the Israeli government had decided on a course that no agreement required: to leave Gaza on its own terms.

sections.h: Disengagement, 2003–2005: Leaving, and What Stayed
sections.html:
In 2005 Israel removed every settlement and every soldier from inside the Gaza Strip. It did so unilaterally, without an agreement with the Palestinian Authority. This section sets out how the decision was made, what the withdrawal involved, what Israel kept, and the argument, which the record states but does not settle, over whether the occupation of Gaza ended in September 2005.

The decision. Prime Minister Ariel Sharon, who as a general had led the campaign of 1971 in Gaza, first presented the plan to withdraw from Gaza at the Herzliya Conference on 18 December 2003, and set it out to President George W. Bush in a letter of 14 April 2004. His own party's members rejected it in a referendum on 2 May 2004, 65 percent against; the cabinet approved an amended version by 14 votes to 7 on 6 June; the Knesset gave preliminary approval by 67 to 45 on 26 October, and on 16 February 2005 passed the Disengagement Plan Implementation Law by 59 votes to 40. [cite:gz_wiki_disengagement]

The reasons given, and an adviser's words. What the withdrawal was for was disputed from the start. Sharon said in August 2005 that Israel "cannot hold on to Gaza forever" and that it was acting "out of strength and not weakness"; his deputy Shimon Peres said Israel was disengaging "because of demography"; and the plan was presented as a way to "improve Israel's security and international status" without negotiations. [cite:gz_wiki_disengagement] Sharon's senior adviser, Dov Weisglass, gave a different account in an interview with Haaretz on 6 October 2004: the disengagement, he said, supplied "the amount of formaldehyde" needed so that there would be no political process with the Palestinians, and he described it as freezing the peace process. [cite:gz_wiki_disengagement] The interview, the record notes, "bolstered the position of critics of the plan", who read it as evidence that the withdrawal was meant to freeze the conflict rather than to open a path to a Palestinian state; the government's own stated reasons were the ones above. [cite:gz_wiki_disengagement]

The withdrawal. The 21 settlements in the strip were evacuated between 15 and 22 August 2005, Netzarim last; about 8,000 to 9,000 settlers left, two-thirds of them accepting compensation for leaving voluntarily. Demolition crews razed about 2,800 homes and public buildings. The last Israeli soldier left on 12 September 2005, and Egypt was permitted to station 750 border guards along the Philadelphi corridor on the Egypt–Gaza frontier. The whole operation is estimated to have cost about $2 billion. [cite:gz_wiki_disengagement] [cite:gz_wiki_gushkatif] Kfar Darom, founded in 1946 and abandoned in 1948, whose name was revived by a settlement built nearby in 1970, was evacuated on 18 August. [cite:gz_wiki_kfardarom]

What stayed. The soldiers and settlers left; Israel's control of the strip's borders did not. After September 2005 Israel kept control of Gaza's airspace and territorial waters, of six of its seven land crossings (the seventh, at Rafah, lay on the Egyptian border, though Israel kept effective control over its operation until at least May 2011), and of the population registry that determines who is a resident; it kept the right to re-enter militarily; and the strip remained dependent on Israel for water, electricity and telecommunications. [cite:gz_wiki_disengagement]

The argument is not academic. If Israel remained the occupying power, it remained bound by the law of occupation's duties toward Gaza's population; if it did not, its duties were narrower, and Israel's Supreme Court held in 2008 that they derived from the armed conflict, its control of the crossings and the strip's essential humanitarian needs. [cite:gz_ahmed_hcj] In 2024 the International Court of Justice took a functional view: Israel's obligations under the law of occupation in Gaza remained "commensurate with the degree of its effective control over the Gaza Strip." [cite:gz_oj_icj] [cite:gz_lieber_icj] Part Seven returns to it. What the record settles is the physical fact: from September 2005 there were no Israeli settlers or soldiers inside the strip, and every way in or out of it ran through Israel or, at Rafah, through a crossing whose operation Israel still controlled. [cite:gz_wiki_disengagement]

chapters.label: Part Four
chapters.title: The Blockade, and How It Works
chapters.intro: Part Four describes the system that governed Gaza from 2007 to 2023. It begins with the election of 2006 and the fighting of June 2007 that left Hamas in control of the strip, then sets out, piece by piece, how Israel and Egypt closed it: what was allowed in and out, who could leave, how far fishermen could sail and how close farmers could go to the fence. It ends with what the closure did to the strip's economy, water, electricity and health, as the UN measured it, and with the legal judgments made about it, which disagree.
chapters.outro: Part Four followed Gaza from the withdrawal to the closure. Hamas won the Palestinian legislative elections of January 2006, a soldier, Gilad Shalit, was captured that June, and in June 2007 Hamas took sole control of the strip after fighting Fatah. [cite:gz_wiki_battle2007] [cite:gz_wiki_shalit] In September 2007 Israel's cabinet declared Gaza "hostile territory" and authorized restricting fuel, power, goods and people. [cite:gz_un_hostile2007] The closure that followed limited what entered, almost ended what left, confined fishermen and farmers, and made leaving the strip a matter of permits, while Egypt kept Rafah closed or limited. [cite:gz_wiki_blockade] [cite:gz_un_gaza10] By the UN's measures it left an economy shrinking beside a growing West Bank, an aquifer unfit to drink and 1.2 million people in need of aid. [cite:gz_un_gaza10] [cite:gz_un_gaza2020] The ICRC called it collective punishment; the Palmer panel found the sea blockade a legitimate security measure, without adjudicating legal liability; Israel's Supreme Court allowed its fuel and power cuts while holding Israel to the strip's essential humanitarian needs. [cite:gz_icrc_2010] [cite:gz_palmer] [cite:gz_ahmed_hcj] Part Five turns to the wars fought across it.

sections.h: 2006–2007: An Election, a Capture, a Takeover
sections.html:
Within two years of the withdrawal, Gaza had a different government and a different relationship with the world around it. This section sets out the three events that produced the blockade: an election that Hamas won, a raid that took an Israeli soldier into Gaza, and a short war between Palestinian factions that ended with Hamas alone in control of the strip.

The election. On 25 January 2006 Hamas won the election to the Palestinian Legislative Council, in a vote that international observers judged free and fair, and on 29 March it formed a government. [cite:gz_wiki_battle2007] The response was immediate. Israel withheld the tax revenue it collected on the Palestinian Authority's behalf, the Quartet of the United States, the European Union, Russia and the UN stopped aid to a Hamas-led government. [cite:gz_wiki_blockade] [cite:gz_wiki_battle2007]

The capture. On 25 June 2006 militants from Gaza crossed into Israel through a tunnel near Kerem Shalom, attacked an army post, killed two soldiers and took a third, Gilad Shalit, back into the strip. Hamas held him for more than five years; he was freed on 18 October 2011 in exchange for 1,027 Palestinian prisoners. [cite:gz_wiki_shalit]

The takeover. Fatah and Hamas signed the Mecca Agreement on 8 February 2007 to halt the fighting between them and formed a unity government in March, but in June fighting broke out again. Between 7 and 15 June 2007 Hamas forces took the strip's security headquarters and Fatah's bases; on 14 June President Mahmoud Abbas dissolved the unity government and declared a state of emergency, and by 15 June Hamas controlled the whole strip. Egypt and Israel then largely sealed their crossings with Gaza. [cite:gz_wiki_blockade] The Palestinian Centre for Human Rights counted at least 161 people killed. [cite:gz_wiki_battle2007]

A contested account. What the fighting was is disputed. Fatah and its supporters called it a Hamas coup. In April 2008 the journalist David Rose, writing in Vanity Fair, reported documents suggesting that the United States had worked with the Palestinian Authority and Israel on a plan to oust Hamas by force, which Hamas had pre-empted; David Wurmser, formerly Vice President Dick Cheney's chief Middle East adviser, was quoted saying that what happened was "an attempted coup by Fatah that was pre-empted before it could happen." [cite:gz_wiki_battle2007] The record shows the outcome without settling the intentions: from June 2007 Hamas governed Gaza, and the Palestinian Authority, under a new prime minister appointed by Abbas, governed the parts of the West Bank under its control.

sections.h: How the Closure Worked
sections.html:
The closure of Gaza was not a single act but a system of rules, permits and limits, maintained by Israel on three sides of the strip and by Egypt on the fourth, and adjusted many times over sixteen years. This section sets out its parts in turn: the decision that founded it, and what it did to goods, people, the sea and the land. Israel's stated aims were to prevent the smuggling of weapons into Gaza, to stop the rocket fire from the strip, and to exert economic pressure on Hamas. [cite:gz_wiki_blockade]

The founding decision. On 19 September 2007 Israel's Security Cabinet, meeting under Prime Minister Ehud Olmert, unanimously decided that Hamas was "a terrorist organization that has taken control of the Gaza Strip and turned it into hostile territory." It cited the continuing Qassam rocket fire at Sderot and other communities, and it authorized reducing the supply of fuel and electricity to Gaza, restricting the passage of goods, and restricting the movement of people in and out, to be carried out after legal review "taking into account both the humanitarian aspects relevant to the Gaza Strip and the intention to avoid a humanitarian crisis." [cite:gz_un_hostile2007] Egypt had closed its crossing at Rafah after the takeover. [cite:gz_wiki_blockade]

Goods. For the first three years Israel admitted a restricted list of goods. Items it classed as "dual-use", which included construction materials and computer equipment, were allowed only as part of approved projects run by donors, and Israel banned virtually all exports; Israeli security officials, as reported, described the export ban as "a political decision to separate Gaza from the West Bank." [cite:gz_wiki_blockade] In January 2008 an Israeli government document titled "Food Consumption in the Gaza Strip — The Red Lines", estimated that each Gazan would need 2,279 calories a day to avoid malnutrition. It became public in 2012 after the Israeli human rights group Gisha filed a freedom-of-information petition and Israel's Supreme Court ordered its release; the Defense Ministry said the plan it described was never put into effect. [cite:gz_jta_redlines]

The flotilla, and the easing of 2010. On 31 May 2010 Israeli naval forces boarded a flotilla of ships sailing to break the blockade, and killed nine passengers aboard the Mavi Marmara. [cite:gz_wiki_blockade] [cite:gz_palmer] Facing mounting international calls to ease the blockade, Israel announced in June 2010 that it would allow nearly all civilian goods into Gaza while continuing to block weapons and dual-use items, and Egypt partially reopened Rafah, opening it on a regular but limited basis from May 2011. [cite:gz_wiki_blockade] The UN Secretary-General's panel of inquiry, chaired by Geoffrey Palmer, found in September 2011 that the naval blockade was "a legitimate security measure" whose implementation complied with international law, but that the decision to board with such force was "excessive and unreasonable"; it also found that the soldiers met "significant, organized and violent resistance from a group of passengers", that the flotilla "acted recklessly", and that Israel had given no satisfactory explanation for any of the nine deaths. It recommended that Israel keep easing its restrictions "with a view to lifting its closure." [cite:gz_palmer]

People. Leaving Gaza meant leaving through Israel's Erez crossing with an Israeli permit, or through Rafah when Egypt opened it. Israel considered exit applications from only a small number of labourers, less than five percent of the number considered in 2000. [cite:gz_wiki_blockade] Patients needing treatment outside the strip, whose referrals tripled between 2006 and 2016 to 24,616, saw the share of exit permits approved fall from 90 to 62 percent. [cite:gz_un_gaza10]

Sea and land. The Oslo agreements had envisaged that Gaza's fishermen could fish up to 20 nautical miles from shore; from 2006 the limit Israel enforced varied between 3 and 6 miles, occasionally 9. Along the land fence Israel declared "access-restricted areas" that at times covered up to 35 percent of Gaza's farmland and up to 85 percent of its fishing waters. Between 2007 and 2017, according to the UN, Israeli fire in those areas killed 389 people and injured 2,829. [cite:gz_un_gaza10]

Each part of the system had a security rationale that Israel stated, and each had a cost that the UN and humanitarian organizations measured. The next section sets the measurements out, and the legal judgments that were made about them.

sections.h: What the Closure Did, and What the Law Said
sections.html:
The closure's effects were measured, year after year, by UN agencies, the World Bank and humanitarian organizations working inside the strip. Their figures describe an economy that contracted while its neighbour grew, a water supply that failed, and a population that came to depend on aid. Israel's stated position throughout was that the restrictions answered a real threat, the rocket fire from Gaza and the smuggling of weapons to Hamas, and were meant to put economic pressure on Hamas. [cite:gz_wiki_blockade]

Work and income. According to the UN Country Team, unemployment in Gaza rose from 34.1 percent in early 2006 to 40.6 percent at the end of 2016, and among women from 35.1 to 64.4 percent. Over the same decade GDP per person in Gaza fell by 5.3 percent while in the West Bank it rose by 48.5 percent. [cite:gz_un_gaza10] The World Bank estimated losses to Gaza's GDP from the closure at more than 50 percent, and poverty stood at about 40 percent in 2015. [cite:gz_wiki_blockade] By 2017 food insecurity stood at 47 percent, and about 1.2 million people needed humanitarian aid. [cite:gz_un_gaza10]

Water and power. In 2012 the UN warned, in a report titled "Gaza in 2020: A liveable place?", that the strip's only aquifer could become "unusable as early as 2016, with the damage irreversible by 2020," that 90 percent of its water was already unsafe to drink without treatment, and that the population would reach 2.1 million by 2020. It called the economy, as it stood, "fundamentally unviable." [cite:gz_un_gaza2020] Five years later the UN recorded 96.2 percent of the aquifer's water as unfit for human consumption, a decline both reports attribute to over-extraction, seawater intrusion and contamination. In 2017 power cuts reached up to 20 hours a day after Gaza's power plant shut down in a fuel-tax dispute between the Palestinian Authority and Hamas, and the PA cut its payments for Israeli-supplied electricity. [cite:gz_un_gaza10]

The legal judgments. The closure was judged under international law by several bodies, and they did not agree. The International Committee of the Red Cross said on 14 June 2010 that "the closure therefore constitutes a collective punishment imposed in clear violation of Israel's obligations under international humanitarian law," while acknowledging Israel's right to address its legitimate security concerns. [cite:gz_icrc_2010] The UN Secretary-General's Palmer panel, a year later, found the naval blockade "a legitimate security measure" lawfully implemented, a finding the panel said did not adjudicate legal liability, in a report adopted by its chair and vice-chair after consensus failed; it recommended that the restrictions be eased toward lifting the closure. [cite:gz_palmer] Israel's Supreme Court held in 2008 that Israel no longer had effective control inside Gaza but remained bound to meet the strip's essential humanitarian needs. [cite:gz_ahmed_hcj]

The three judgments looked at different parts of the closure and reached different conclusions; none was a binding ruling on the closure as a whole, and the Palmer panel stated that it was not adjudicating legal liability. The UN's measurements of conditions in Gaza are set out above, and the stated Israeli rationale alongside them. The wars of the following years, the subject of Part Five, were fought over a strip already in this condition.

chapters.label: Part Five
chapters.title: The Wars, 2008–2021
chapters.intro: Part Five covers the four wars fought between Israel and the armed groups in Gaza between 2008 and 2021, and the mass protests at the fence in 2018. Each began with a sequence of events both sides describe differently, and each section sets out that sequence as the record gives it, the aims Israel stated, the dead as each counting body counted them, and the findings of the inquiries that followed. The figures differ by source, sometimes widely, and the differences are given rather than resolved.
chapters.outro: Part Five followed four wars and a season of protest.
