The courts. The ICJ genocide case runs to written pleadings due in 2029; the ICC warrants for Netanyahu and Gallant stand, with Israel's challenge to the court's jurisdiction pending as of late 2025. [cite:gz_icj_timelimits] [cite:gz_toi_icc2025]

Accountability in Israel. No state commission of inquiry into October 7 has been set up. [cite:gz_ynet_inquiry2026]

The volume ends where the record does. Gaza's history since 1948 has been decided mostly by others, from Cairo, Jerusalem and Washington, and by the armed movement that governed it from 2007; its people have lived inside the consequences. What the record documents, it has stated; where it divides, both sides are given; what is still to be decided is named above.

books.title: The West Bank, Documented
books.subtitle: Settlements, Separation and Expansion, 1947–2026
books.intro:
This volume follows the West Bank, the hill country west of the Jordan River, about 5,655 square kilometres, from the partition plan of 1947 to October 2026. It asks what happened to the land and to the people on it: who governed them, how the land passed from Palestinian to Israeli control acre by acre, how movement, law and surveillance were organized around that change, and what the law says about it and why it has not been enforced.

It begins with the plan that assigned this hill country to an Arab state that was never created, and with the war of 1948 that left it in Jordan's hands. It follows nineteen years of Jordanian rule; the occupation of 1967 and the first settlements; the settlement enterprise that grew from them; the map drawn at Oslo, which divided the territory into Areas A, B and C; the barrier, the roads and the checkpoints that divided the Palestinian towns from one another; the two legal systems and the surveillance that govern daily life; the demolitions, the evictions and the settler violence through which communities have been displaced; and the years since October 2023. Four parts then step back: to the law and the reasons it has not been enforced; to the split between Fatah's West Bank and Hamas's Gaza; to the money; and to what is settled, contested and open.

The volume holds to the standard of the library. Every load-bearing claim carries its source. Israel's stated reasons, security above all, are given beside each policy, and where the record divides, both sides are given. It describes the acts of governments, armies, settler organizations and armed groups, not the character of peoples. Its companion is Gaza, Documented, and the two volumes are written to be read together.

chapters.label: Part One
chapters.title: The Hill Country and the Partition
chapters.intro: Part One covers the two years in which the West Bank was made. It begins with the United Nations plan of November 1947, which assigned the hill country of Samaria and Judea to an Arab state, and sets out what each of the planned states was to receive, by land, by population and by kind of land. It follows the war that began the next day and ended with the hill country in Jordanian hands and much of the rest of the planned Arab state inside Israel, and it ends with the armistice line of 1949, the line now called the Green Line.
chapters.outro: Part One followed the making of the West Bank. The 1947 plan gave the proposed Arab state the hill country of Samaria and Judea and gave the Jewish state, about 56 percent of the land, most of the Negev desert, the Jezreel Valley and most of the coastal plain, when Jews owned about 6.6 percent of Palestine. [cite:wb_ej_partition] [cite:rs_rd5_yusuf_2002] [cite:wb_wiki_landpurchase] The war that followed left Israel holding about 78 percent of the Mandate, including towns such as Lydda and Ramle that the plan had assigned to the Arab state, whose people were driven east. [cite:rs_rd6_mfa_armistice_map] [cite:rs_rd5_palquest_lydda] Jordan's Arab Legion held the hills, as its king had told the Zionist leaders he would, and the armistice of April 1949 drew the Green Line around them. [cite:rs_rd5_cie_golda] [cite:rs_rd6_arm_jordan_text] What is settled is the plan's terms and the line. What is contested is the plan's fairness, argued from the same map, and the causes of the exodus. What was left open was the fate of the territory the plan had meant for an Arab state, and Part Two follows Jordan's answer.

sections.h: The Plan of 1947
sections.html:
Two states, six pieces. On 29 November 1947 the UN General Assembly adopted, by 33 votes to 13 with 10 abstentions, a plan to divide Palestine into a Jewish state and an Arab state, joined in an economic union, with Jerusalem under international rule. [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_181] Each state was to consist of three sections linked at two crossing points. The Arab state was to include western Galilee, the hill country of Samaria and Judea, excluding Jerusalem, and the coastal strip from Isdud to the Sinai frontier. The Jewish state was to include eastern Galilee, the Jezreel Valley, most of the coastal plain, and the Negev. [cite:wb_ej_partition] Most of the hill country assigned to the Arab state became the West Bank. [cite:wb_wiki_westbank]

Land and people. The figures most cited for the plan come from two sides of the debate and agree on its shape. The Palestinian historian Muhsin Yusuf gives the Jewish state 56 percent of the land and the Arab state 43 percent. The Jewish state would hold about 498,000 Jews and about 494,000 Arabs, and the Arab state about 725,000 Arabs and 11,000 Jews. [cite:rs_rd5_yusuf_2002] The Jewish Virtual Library, citing the historian Howard Sachar, gives the Jewish state about 5,500 square miles with 538,000 Jews and 397,000 Arabs, and the Arab state 4,500 square miles with 804,000 Arabs and 10,000 Jews. [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_myths_partition] When the plan was adopted, Jewish buyers legally owned about 6.6 percent of Palestine's land. A further 46 percent was state domain, much of it held on hereditary lease or of undetermined ownership. [cite:wb_wiki_landpurchase] By Yusuf's figures, Jews owned about a tenth of the land inside the Jewish state they were allotted. [cite:rs_rd5_yusuf_2002] A Pakistani amendment to cap land ownership at 10 percent per group was voted down, 22 to 8. [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_181]

Desert, and the valleys. The quality of the land is argued from both sides. The Institute for Palestine Studies says the Jewish state received about two-thirds of the coast, including Haifa and Tel Aviv, "and the fertile lowland plains," and the plan gave it the Jezreel Valley and most of the coastal plain. [cite:wb_palquest_partition] [cite:wb_ej_partition] The Jewish Virtual Library answers, citing the scholar Aharon Cohen, that about 60 percent of the Jewish state was Negev desert, "while the Arabs occupied most of the agricultural land." [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_myths_partition] A British inquiry of 1930 had found that only about 40 percent of the hill country could be cultivated. [cite:rs_rd3_hope_simpson_unispal] The two cases read the same map: the Jewish state's share took in most of the Negev and most of the coastal lowland; the Arab state's was chiefly hill country, with western Galilee and the southern coast.

Acceptance and rejection. The Jewish Agency accepted the plan. Jewish leaders were dissatisfied with the territory and with Jerusalem's separation, and the Jewish Virtual Library says they "welcomed the compromise." [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_myths_partition] The Arab Higher Committee and the Arab states rejected it. Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Iraq, Syria and Yemen called it contrary to the UN Charter, illegal and immoral, and said they would not feel bound by it. [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_181] Yusuf sets out the Arab reasons as he reads them: the fear of later expulsion and land confiscation, and the injustice of granting statehood to a largely immigrant minority while the majority was denied self-determination. [cite:rs_rd5_yusuf_2002] The library's volume The Road to 1948 tells the story of the vote and the plan in full. [scene:s09|The partition vote]

sections.h: The War in the Hills
sections.html:
A quiet understanding. Before the fighting began, the ruler whose army would take the hill country had already met the Zionist leadership. In early November 1947, at Naharayim on the Jordan, King Abdullah of Transjordan told Golda Meyerson (later Meir) that he intended to annex the Arab areas of Palestine; she replied that the Zionist leaders would not oppose this if there were no clashes between Jewish and Transjordanian forces. On 10 May 1948 Meyerson crossed to Amman in disguise; Abdullah said he was now "one of five," bound to the other Arab states, and asked, "why don't you wait a few years?", urging her to drop the demand for free immigration. [cite:rs_rd5_cie_golda]

Plan D. Fighting between the communities followed the partition vote. On 10 March 1948 the Haganah finalized Plan D, whose stated objective was "to gain control of the areas of the Hebrew state and defend its borders," including Jewish settlements outside them, and which, for enemy villages used as bases, provided for "destruction of villages," especially those "difficult to control continuously," and, where resistance was met, for the population to be "expelled outside the borders of the state"; "in the absence of resistance," garrison troops were to occupy the village. The Palestinian historian Walid Khalidi argues that it created "the military fait accompli upon which the state of Israel was to be based." [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_1988] Benny Morris concluded that there was no explicit, general Israeli decision to expel. [cite:rs_rd5_lockman_ref] On 9 April, at Deir Yassin, a village outside Jerusalem, fighters of the Irgun, the underground led by Menachem Begin, and of Lehi, with Haganah and Palmach support, killed about 100 to 110 villagers, by the estimates of Benny Morris and a Birzeit University study, and expelled the rest. [cite:wb_wiki_deiryassin] Contemporary accounts put the dead at 254; a letter to the New York Times signed by Albert Einstein, Hannah Arendt and others repeated the figure then current, "240 men, women, and children," and described the village as "not a military objective." [cite:rs_rd5_einstein_nyt]

The Arab Legion. When the Arab armies entered on 15 May, Transjordan's Arab Legion, according to the US State Department's historians, fought only in areas allotted to the Arab state or to the international zone of Jerusalem. [cite:rs_rd5_oh_war_b] It held the hill country and the road to Jerusalem at Latrun, where it repelled three Israeli frontal attacks between 25 May and 9 June, and on 28 May took the Jewish Quarter of Jerusalem's Old City. Iraqi forces held the triangle of Jenin, Nablus and Tulkarm in the north. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_seminar_war] On 13 May, the day before the Mandate ended, the Arab Legion and local villagers overran Kfar Etzion, in the Gush Etzion bloc south of Bethlehem; about 127 defenders died, some of them killed after surrendering, and the bloc's other three settlements surrendered the next day, their people taken to Jordan as prisoners. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_seminar_cw] [cite:wb_wiki_kfaretzion]

Lydda and Ramle. The towns of Lydda and Ramle lay inside the planned Arab state, on the plain below the hills. In July, Operation Dani took them. On 12 July, after Arab Legion armoured cars entered Lydda and a brief firefight followed, Israeli troops opened fire in the town; Benny Morris, citing the Palmach's own history, puts the dead at about 250, and Palestinian accounts give between 80 and 176 killed at the Dahmash mosque and more than 400 in the town. [cite:wb_wiki_lydda] [cite:rs_rd5_palquest_lydda] Yitzhak Rabin, who signed the expulsion order, gave two accounts of how it was decided: in a 1977 interview, that Ben-Gurion, asked by Yigal Allon about the inhabitants, waved his hand and said "Expel them"; in his memoir manuscript, that Ben-Gurion waved his hand without speaking. Allon denied asking, and the historian Yoav Gelber attributes the decision to Allon. Israeli censors removed the episode from Rabin's memoir. [cite:rs_rd5_lockman_war] [cite:wb_wiki_lydda] The towns held 50,000 to 70,000 people. Palestinian sources estimate that about 70,000 were forced out on 13 July and that close to 1,000 died in the towns and on the march east, toward the hills held by the Arab Legion; Morris puts the deaths on the march at "a handful and perhaps dozens." [cite:rs_rd5_palquest_lydda] [cite:wb_wiki_lydda]

The Road to 1948 volume sets out the exodus as a whole, and the dispute over its causes, in detail. [scene:rd5_refugees|The refugees of 1948]

sections.h: The Green Line
sections.html:
Rhodes, 3 April 1949. Israel and Jordan signed their armistice at Rhodes. Its Article II states that no provision would prejudice the rights, claims and positions of either side in a final settlement. [cite:rs_rd6_arm_jordan_text] The 1949 armistice lines left Israel holding about 78 percent of the Mandate's area, as Israel's own Foreign Ministry describes it. The agreements were meant to be interim, until peace treaties replaced them; the line became known as the Green Line. [cite:rs_rd6_mfa_armistice_map]

Wadi Ara. The armistice moved the line eastward in one place. Under Article VI, Jordanian forces replaced the Iraqi army on the northern front, and the Wadi Ara area, villages in the hills of the "Triangle," passed to Israel. The agreement said their people would keep "full rights" of residence, property and freedom. [cite:rs_rd6_arm_jordan_text]

Jerusalem divided. The plan had made Jerusalem and Bethlehem an international zone. The war left Israel holding West Jerusalem and Jordan holding East Jerusalem, including the Old City, the Temple Mount and the Western Wall, and Jews were denied access to their holy places there. [cite:rs_rd6_bpb_jerusalem]

The refugees in the hills. The war's refugees did not stay inside the line that had been drawn around their homes. British officials in February 1949 estimated that 320,000 of them were in the West Bank, more than in any other single place, out of an estimated 810,000 in all; the UN later registered 726,000, and Israel officially put the total at 520,000 to 530,000. [cite:rs_rd6_morris_appendix] The Library of Congress study of Jordan gives the West Bank's own people at about 500,000, and says about 500,000 refugees took refuge in the West Bank or across the river. [cite:rs_rd6_loc_jordan] The hill country that the plan had set aside for an Arab state now held most of what was left of Arab Palestine. Within a year it would be annexed by a neighbouring king.

chapters.label: Part Two
chapters.title: Under Jordan
chapters.intro: Part Two covers the nineteen years in which the West Bank was part of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan. It sets out how Jordan absorbed the territory, the citizenship it gave its people and the recognition it did not receive; what Jordanian rule meant for East Jerusalem and its holy places; and the border war along the Green Line, from the infiltrations and reprisals of the 1950s to the raid on Samu in 1966, which set the West Bank against its own king months before the war that ended his rule there.
chapters.outro: Part Two followed the West Bank under Jordan. Proclaimed in union with Transjordan at Jericho in 1948 and annexed in April 1950, it was recognized as Jordanian by almost no one, and the Arab League treated Jordan as holding it in trust. [cite:rs_rd6_kramer_annexation] [cite:wb_wiki_annex] Its people, residents and refugees alike, became Jordanian citizens with half the seats in parliament, [cite:wb_wiki_annex] [cite:wb_palquest_nationality] while Israelis were barred from the holy places of the Old City. Across the Green Line, Israel's free-fire policy against infiltrators, most of them unarmed, killed thousands, and infiltrators killed Israelis; and reprisal raids on Qibya in 1953 and Samu in 1966 drew UN censure; Samu set the West Bank rioting against Hussein months before he lost it. [cite:rs_rd6_lrb_shlaim_1994] [cite:wb_wiki_fedayeen] [cite:rs_cw2_avalon_res101] [cite:wb_wiki_samu] [cite:rs_cw6_res228] What is settled is the sequence of Jordanian rule. What was left open is whose territory it was, a question Jordan's annexation did not settle and that Israel's occupation, the subject of Part Three, reopened.

sections.h: The Annexation
sections.html:
From Jericho to Amman. In September 1948 Egypt sponsored an All-Palestine Government in Gaza; on 30 September 1948, the day a Palestinian National Council met in Gaza, a rival congress in Amman pledged loyalty to King Abdullah, and on 1 December 1948 a congress of notables at Jericho proclaimed the union of Palestine and Transjordan. [cite:rs_rd6_shlaim_apg_1990] Abdullah renamed his country the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan in April 1949, held elections on both banks of the river in April 1950, and then formally annexed the West Bank. [cite:rs_rd6_loc_jordan] On 24 April 1950 the Jordanian parliament resolved in favour of "complete unity between the two banks of the Jordan, the eastern and western, and their union in one single state." [cite:rs_rd6_kramer_annexation]

Recognition. Almost no one recognized it. Britain recognized the union while excluding Jerusalem, and Iraq recognized it; whether Pakistan did is disputed, and the Library of Congress study names Britain and Pakistan as the only two. [cite:wb_wiki_annex] [cite:rs_rd6_loc_jordan] In May 1950 the Arab League's Political Committee found the annexation illegal, and Saudi Arabia, Lebanon, Syria and Egypt sought Jordan's expulsion; in June the League settled on treating Jordan as holding the territory in "trust" until a final settlement. [cite:wb_wiki_annex]

Citizens of Jordan. Alone among the Arab states that took in large numbers of refugees, Jordan gave them citizenship as a class, along with the West Bank's own people. A 1949 amendment to the nationality law effectively imposed Jordanian citizenship on local Palestinians and refugees alike, [cite:wb_wiki_annex] and the West and East Banks received equal representation in parliament, twenty seats each in 1950. [cite:wb_wiki_jo1950] The Nationality Law of 1954 granted citizenship to "any person who, not being Jewish, possessed Palestinian nationality before 15 May 1948" and lived in the kingdom. [cite:wb_palquest_nationality] The refugees of 1948 living in the kingdom thus became Jordanian citizens, while their claim to return, set out in the UN's Resolution 194, remained. [cite:rs_rd6_refworld_194]

East Jerusalem. Jordan held the Old City. King Hussein, who came to the throne in 1952 after his grandfather Abdullah was assassinated at al-Aqsa in 1951 and his father Talal abdicated, called East Jerusalem in 1953 the "alternative capital" of the kingdom. [cite:wb_wiki_annex] [cite:rs_rd6_loc_jordan] [cite:wb_loc_jordan] Jordan expelled the Jewish residents of East Jerusalem, much of the Old City's Jewish Quarter, including the Hurva Synagogue, was destroyed, and the committee the armistice had set up to arrange access to the holy places never met, so Israelis could not reach the Western Wall. [cite:wb_wiki_annex] [cite:rs_rd6_bpb_jerusalem]

The PLO, born in Jerusalem. It was in Jordanian Jerusalem, on 28 May 1964, under King Hussein's sponsorship, that the first Palestinian National Congress met, and on 2 June it announced the Palestine Liberation Organization. [cite:rs_cw6_palquest_chron] Its charter stated that the organization did "not exercise any regional sovereignty over the West Bank in the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan." [cite:rs_cw6_charter_1964] Two years later, after friction over the PLO's taxing of Palestinians and its distribution of arms in the West Bank and the camps, Hussein withdrew his support. [cite:rs_cw6_gs_jordan_a]

sections.h: The Border War
sections.html:
Infiltration. The Green Line ran between villages and their fields, and across it lay the homes many refugees had fled. Through the early 1950s thousands crossed it. The Israeli historian Benny Morris estimated that 90 percent or more of these crossings in 1949–1956 were made to return to homes, harvest fields, recover property or see relatives, rather than to attack. Israel's army, border police and police adopted a policy of shooting suspects on sight, and between 2,700 and 5,000 infiltrators were killed in those years, by Morris's estimate "the great majority of whom were unarmed." [cite:rs_rd6_lrb_shlaim_1994] Infiltrators also killed Israelis. The historian Martin Gilbert counted 967 Israelis killed in 1951–1955; Morris called that figure "pure nonsense," three to five times higher than contemporary Israeli reports. [cite:wb_wiki_fedayeen]

Qibya, 1953. After a grenade attack on a house in the Israeli town of Yehud in October 1953 killed a woman and her two children, [cite:rs_cw2_jvl_qibya] Israel's Unit 101, commanded by Ariel Sharon, crossed into the West Bank village of Qibya, blew up 45 houses and killed 69 villagers, "the majority women and children." [cite:rs_rd6_lrb_shlaim_1994] Israel's own foreign minister, Moshe Sharett, wrote that had he had any reason to fear "such a slaughter," he "would have raised hell." [cite:rs_cw2_jps_qibya] The UN Security Council expressed "the strongest censure." The resolution also noted "substantial evidence" of crossings of the demarcation line and asked Jordan to strengthen its measures against them. [cite:rs_cw2_avalon_res101] The library's account of [scene:cw2_unit101_qibya|Unit 101 and Qibya] sets out the raid in full.

Fatah, and Samu, 1966. By the mid-1960s the raids came from organized Palestinian groups, chiefly Fatah, which crossed into Israel from Jordanian territory without the approval of the Jordanian government, which tried to avoid incidents that invited reprisals. [cite:rs_cw6_cia_dec1966] [cite:rs_cw6_gs_jordan_f] On 13 November 1966, after a mine, which the Israeli army attributed to Fatah, killed three Israelis on border patrol near the line, Israeli forces with tanks and aircraft entered the West Bank village of Samu, near Hebron. [cite:rs_cw6_idf_archive_samu] [cite:wb_wiki_samu] The UN counted 125 houses destroyed, the Israeli army 40; sixteen Jordanian soldiers and airmen and three civilians were killed, and one Israeli officer. [cite:wb_wiki_samu] President Johnson's adviser Walt Rostow called the raid "out of all proportion to the provocation" and "aimed at the wrong target"; the Security Council, with the United States voting in favour, censured Israel. [cite:rs_cw6_frus18_d333] [cite:rs_cw6_res228]

The raid turned the West Bank against its own government. Riots spread across the territory with demands that Hussein be overthrown, and Jordanian police killed four Palestinians putting them down. [cite:wb_wiki_samu] [cite:rs_cw6_gs_jordan_samu] Six months later, on 30 May 1967, Hussein placed his army under Egyptian command, [cite:rs_cw6_gs_jordan_t] and within a week he had lost the West Bank. [scene:cw6_samu|The Samu raid]

chapters.label: Part Three
chapters.title: 1967: Occupation, and the First Settlements
chapters.intro: Part Three covers the first decade of Israeli rule, from the war of June 1967 to the change of government in 1977. It begins with the war's effects in the West Bank: a second exodus across the Jordan, villages emptied and razed, and a UN resolution whose missing word has been argued over ever since. It follows the annexation of East Jerusalem and its enlarged boundary, and ends with the first settlements, built after the government's own legal adviser warned that they would breach the Fourth Geneva Convention.
chapters.outro: Part Three followed the first decade of occupation. The war of 1967 drove about 300,000 Palestinians from the West Bank and Gaza, many for the second time, and the Latrun villages were razed. [cite:wb_prrn_1967] [cite:wb_wiki_imwas] Within three weeks Israel brought 70 square kilometres of East Jerusalem and the surrounding villages under its law, a step the Security Council declared invalid. [cite:wb_wiki_ejannex] Resolution 242 called for withdrawal "from territories occupied," in words read two ways ever since. [cite:wb_wiki_242] The government's own legal adviser warned that civilian settlement would breach the Fourth Geneva Convention; the government settled Kfar Etzion under military cover, followed the Allon Plan's lines, and accepted the settlers of Hebron. [cite:wb_gorenberg_meron] [cite:wb_wiki_allon] [cite:wb_wiki_hebron] By 1977 about 4,400 settlers lived outside East Jerusalem. [cite:wb_peacenow_pop] What is settled is the sequence. What is contested is whether the Convention applies, which Part Ten takes up. What changed in 1977 is the subject of Part Four.

sections.h: June 1967
sections.html:
The war. In six days in June 1967 Israel took the West Bank, East Jerusalem, the Gaza Strip, the Sinai and the Golan Heights. [cite:wb_wiki_westbank] For the West Bank, the war meant a second exodus. About 300,000 Palestinians fled the West Bank and Gaza, some 200,000 of them across the Jordan River to the East Bank; about 180,000 became refugees for the first time, and the rest were refugees of 1948 uprooted a second time. [cite:wb_prrn_1967]

The Latrun villages. Near Latrun, where the Arab Legion had held the road to Jerusalem in 1948, the army emptied three villages: Imwas, Yalo and Beit Nuba. Some 8,000 people were ordered by loudspeaker to march toward Ramallah, and when residents tried to return their homes had been razed, on the orders of the chief of staff, Yitzhak Rabin. Moshe Dayan wrote that the houses were destroyed "not in battle, but as punishment." Israel said the villagers had taken part in attacks on Jerusalem in 1948 and helped an Egyptian commando raid in the war. In 1973 the Jewish National Fund of Canada raised $5 million to build a recreational park, Canada Park, on the site. [cite:wb_wiki_imwas]

Resolution 242. On 22 November 1967 the UN Security Council adopted, unanimously, the resolution that has framed every peace plan since. It emphasized "the inadmissibility of the acquisition of territory by war," called for the "withdrawal of Israeli armed forces from territories occupied in the recent conflict," affirmed every state's right to live "within secure and recognized boundaries," and called for "a just settlement of the refugee problem." [cite:wb_wiki_242] The English text says "territories," without "the" or "all"; the equally authentic French text says "des territoires occupés," which can be read as "the occupied territories." Its British and American drafters said the omission was deliberate; those who read it as requiring full withdrawal point to the French text and to the preamble's rule against acquiring territory by war. [cite:wb_wiki_242] The two readings, both documented, have been argued over for six decades.

sections.h: East Jerusalem
sections.html:
The laws of June 1967. Within three weeks of the war, Israel annexed East Jerusalem in all but name. On 27 June 1967 the Knesset amended the law to let the government apply Israeli law to any area it designated, and the next day the government applied it to an enlarged city: about 70 square kilometres were added to Jerusalem's boundaries, only about 6 of them the Jordanian municipality of East Jerusalem and about 64 taken from 28 surrounding villages and from parts of Bethlehem and Beit Jala. [cite:wb_wiki_ejannex]

The Mughrabi Quarter. In the Old City, the Mughrabi Quarter in front of the Western Wall was bulldozed to make room for the plaza that stands there now. [cite:wb_wiki_ejannex] After nineteen years in which Jews could not reach the Wall, Israel opened it; the families of the quarter in front of it lost their homes.

The world's response. On 21 May 1968 the Security Council declared Israel's legal and administrative measures in Jerusalem invalid and called for them to be rescinded. When the Knesset passed a Basic Law on Jerusalem in 1980, the Council declared it "null and void" and asked states with embassies in the city to withdraw them. [cite:wb_wiki_ejannex] Israel's position is that the city, united, is its capital, and the UN's is that East Jerusalem is occupied territory. [cite:wb_wiki_ejannex] The enlarged boundary drawn in June 1967 remains the line inside which, as later parts show, Israel builds without calling it settlement.

sections.h: The Warning, and the First Settlements
sections.html:
The Meron opinion. In September 1967 the Prime Minister's Office asked the Foreign Ministry's legal counsel, Theodor Meron, whether Israel could settle civilians in the territories it had taken. His answer was unequivocal: "civilian settlement in the administered territories contravenes the explicit provisions of the Fourth Geneva Convention." The opinion went to the justice minister. Days later the cabinet approved Prime Minister Levi Eshkol's announcement of an "outpost" at Kfar Etzion, south of Bethlehem, presented as a base of the army's Nahal corps, though it had no connection with the military. [cite:wb_gorenberg_meron]

Israel's legal position. Israel adopted a different reading of the law from Meron's. It argued that the West Bank had belonged to no recognized sovereign when it was taken in 1967, since almost no state had recognized Jordan's annexation; that the Fourth Geneva Convention, which covers the occupation of "the territory of a High Contracting Party," therefore did not apply to it as a matter of law; and that Israel would nonetheless observe its "humanitarian and customary provisions." Critics answered that the Convention protects people, not sovereign claims, and applies whenever a population falls under an army's control. [cite:wb_cow_israelview] Part Ten sets the two positions out in full.

The Allon Plan. On 27 July 1967 the minister Yigal Allon proposed that Israel keep most of the Jordan Valley, East Jerusalem and the Etzion area and offer the populated hill country to Jordan. The cabinet never formally adopted the plan, and King Hussein rejected it, but in the first decade of occupation settlement largely followed its lines: a ring of settlements along the Jordan Valley and around Jerusalem, away from the Palestinian towns. [cite:wb_wiki_allon]

Hebron. Hebron had held a Jewish community until 1929, when 67 Jews were killed by Arab rioters. [cite:wb_wiki_hebron] In 1968 a group led by Rabbi Moshe Levinger rented the city's main hotel and refused to leave, with the tacit support of Eshkol and Allon. The government moved them to a nearby army camp, and from it grew the settlement of Kiryat Arba, beside the city; from 1979 settlers moved into the old Hadassah building in the centre of Hebron itself. [cite:wb_wiki_hebron] The pattern, a settlement begun without authorization and then accepted by the government, would be repeated for decades.

The numbers. The first decade's settlement was small. By the count of the Israeli group Peace Now, 1,500 settlers lived in the West Bank outside East Jerusalem in 1972 and 4,400 in 1977. [cite:wb_peacenow_pop] By early 2025 the figure was more than 529,000, with about 246,000 more in East Jerusalem. [cite:wb_wiki_popstats] Part Four follows the change that began in 1977.

chapters.label: Part Four
chapters.title: The Settlement Enterprise
chapters.intro: Part Four covers the sixteen years from the Likud's victory in 1977 to the Oslo agreement of 1993, the years in which settlement in the West Bank became a mass enterprise. It follows the religious movement that drove it and the government that adopted its programme; the legal mechanism devised after the Supreme Court barred the seizure of private land, by which hundreds of thousands of dunams were declared "state land"; and the settler underground that bombed Palestinian mayors and plotted to blow up the Dome of the Rock.
chapters.outro: Part Four followed settlement from a movement into a state enterprise. Gush Emunim, founded in 1974, forced its first settlements on a reluctant government; after 1977 the Likud adopted plans that put settlements among the Palestinian towns of the hill country, and the settler population outside East Jerusalem grew from 4,400 to 116,300 by 1993. [cite:wb_ej_gush] [cite:wb_peacenow_pop] When the Supreme Court barred the seizure of private land at Elon Moreh, the government declared 908,000 dunams "state land" under an Ottoman code, about 16 percent of the territory, which Israel holds it may administer in trust. [cite:wb_dweikat] [cite:wb_wiki_stateland] A settler underground maimed two mayors, killed three students in Hebron and planned to destroy the Dome of the Rock; its members were convicted, and some were pardoned. [cite:wb_wiki_1980bomb] [cite:wb_csm_underground] Part Five turns to Oslo, and the map it drew.

sections.h: The Movement and the Government
sections.html:
Gush Emunim. The "Bloc of the Faithful" was founded at Kfar Etzion at the beginning of 1974, in the aftermath of the 1973 war, and its ideology was rooted in the teaching of Rabbi Zvi Yehuda Kook, for whom settling the whole Land of Israel was a religious duty. Its attempts to settle in the hills of Samaria, the first near Oron and then near Sebastia, were removed by the army seven times; after the eighth, at the old Sebastia railway station at Hanukkah 1975, the government compromised and let the settlers stay in an army camp at Kaddum. [cite:wb_ej_gush] The pattern of the Hebron hotel was repeated: an unauthorized settlement, a standoff, and a compromise that left the settlers in place.

1977. When the Likud under Menachem Begin won the election of 1977, Gush Emunim presented the new government with an "emergency" settlement plan, and its blueprint of October 1978 resembled those drawn up by Matityahu Drobles, joint head of the Jewish Agency's settlement department, and by the agriculture minister, Ariel Sharon. [cite:wb_ej_gush] Where the Allon Plan had kept settlement to the Jordan Valley and the edges of Jerusalem, these plans put settlements in the hill country itself, among the Palestinian towns. [cite:wb_wiki_allon]

The numbers. In sixteen years the settler population outside East Jerusalem grew more than twenty-five-fold, from 4,400 in 1977 to 116,300 in 1993, by the count of the Israeli group Peace Now. [cite:wb_peacenow_pop] The Gaza volume's account of [scene:gz2_economy|the same period] shows how the Camp David framework of 1978 and the peace with Egypt in 1979 left the territories' status unresolved.

sections.h: How the Land Was Taken
sections.html:
Elon Moreh, 1979. In the first years the army requisitioned private Palestinian land for settlements "for military needs." In 1979 the landowners of Rujeib, near Nablus, challenged the seizure of their fields for the settlement of Elon Moreh, and Israel's Supreme Court ruled in their favour. Under Article 52 of the Hague Regulations, it held, private land could be taken only for genuine military needs, and here political and ideological considerations, including pressure from Gush Emunim, had been dominant; a military administration, it added, cannot create facts on the ground meant to outlast military rule. [cite:wb_dweikat]

"State land." The government did not stop settling; it changed the method. After Elon Moreh the authorities turned to a stringent reading of the Ottoman Land Code of 1858, under which land that was not registered and continuously cultivated could be declared the property of the state. Between 1979 and 1992 they declared more than 900,000 dunams of the West Bank state land, about 16 percent of the territory, by the count of the Israeli human rights group B'Tselem. Israel's position, as summarized in the record, is that such land is public land that an occupying power may administer. [cite:wb_wiki_stateland] Once declared, it became the reserve on which most new settlements were built.

The Civil Administration. In 1981 the military government created, by Military Order 947, a Civil Administration to run the territories' day-to-day affairs. It sits under the Defence Ministry's Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories, issues the permits Palestinians need to enter Israel, to travel and to work, and approves the building of housing in settlements. [cite:wb_wiki_civadmin] For the next four decades, the same office would decide both where Palestinians could build and where settlers could.

sections.h: The Underground, and the Uprising
sections.html:
The mayors. On 2 June 1980 car bombs planted by Israeli settlers exploded under the cars of West Bank mayors. Bassam Shakaa of Nablus lost both legs, and Karim Khalaf of Ramallah lost a leg; a bomb meant for the mayor of al-Bireh blinded the Druze police officer who tried to defuse it. [cite:wb_wiki_1980bomb]

The Islamic College, and the Dome. In July 1983 gunmen from the same network attacked the Islamic College in Hebron, killing three students and wounding 33. When the network, known as the Jewish Underground, was broken up in 1984, its members turned out to include men who had planned to blow up the Dome of the Rock, one of Islam's holiest sites. In July 1985 three settlers were convicted of murder for the college attack and twelve more of crimes ranging from weapons possession to manslaughter and conspiracy. [cite:wb_csm_underground]

The pardons. Settlement leaders campaigned for clemency, and after Israel released Palestinian prisoners in an exchange in May 1985, Foreign Minister Yitzhak Shamir and several other politicians called for the members to be freed. [cite:wb_csm_underground] One member, Ira Rappaport, convicted of membership in a terrorist organization and of aggravated assault, was pardoned by President Chaim Herzog and released in 1988. [cite:wb_wiki_1980bomb]

The uprising. In December 1987 the first intifada began in Gaza and spread across the West Bank, with strikes, boycotts, stone-throwing and mass arrests, and it lasted until the Oslo agreements. The Gaza volume sets out its course and its toll in both territories. [scene:gz3_uprising|The first intifada] The years of the intifada led to the talks between Israel and the PLO at Oslo, the subject of Part Five.

chapters.label: Part Five
chapters.title: Oslo's Map: Areas A, B and C
chapters.intro: Part Five covers the Oslo years, from the handshake of 1993 to the outbreak of the second intifada in 2000. It sets out the map drawn by the Interim Agreement of 1995, which divided the West Bank into Areas A, B and C as a temporary arrangement on the way to a final settlement that never came; what life in Area C, the largest of them, came to mean for Palestinians who wanted to build; and two developments of the same years, the closing of central Hebron after the massacre of 1994 and the spread of settlement outposts that the government's own report later found it had helped to fund.
chapters.outro: Part Five followed the Oslo years. The Interim Agreement of 1995 divided the West Bank into Areas A, B and C, leaving about 72 to 74 percent under full Israeli control as a temporary step; the handovers stalled, and by 2013 Area C still covered about 63 percent, while the Palestinian areas formed 165 separate enclaves. [cite:wb_wiki_oslo2areas] In Area C, less than one percent of the land had an approved Palestinian plan, 2 percent of permit requests were granted, and more than 14,000 demolition orders were issued. [cite:wb_ocha_areac] The settler population outside East Jerusalem grew from 116,300 to 198,300 during the peace process. [cite:wb_peacenow_pop] After the Hebron massacre of 1994 it was Palestinians who were barred from the city's main street, and a government report found the state had helped fund 105 unauthorized outposts. [cite:wb_wiki_shuhada] [cite:wb_csm_sasson] Part Six turns to the barrier, the roads and the checkpoints that fixed the islands in place.

sections.h: Three Areas
sections.html:
The Interim Agreement. The second Oslo agreement, signed on 28 September 1995, divided the West Bank into three kinds of territory. In Area A, the main Palestinian towns, the new Palestinian Authority held full civil and security control. In Area B, most of the villages, it held civil control while security was shared with Israel. Area C, defined simply as everything outside A and B, stayed under full Israeli civil and security control. At the start, Area A was about 3 percent of the West Bank, Area B about 23 to 25 percent, and Area C about 72 to 74 percent. [cite:wb_wiki_oslo2areas]

The redeployments that stopped. The arrangement was meant to be temporary. Israel was to hand over further parts of Area C in stages, with the transfers due to be completed by the end of 1999. The Wye River Memorandum of 1998 set out a further 13 percent, which would have reduced Area C to about 61 percent; Israel carried out a withdrawal from 2 percent, and during the second intifada it reoccupied the whole territory. By 2013 the commonly cited figures were about 18 percent for Area A, 22 percent for Area B and 63 percent for Area C (the sources' figures sum to slightly more than 100), and the temporary map had become the lasting one. [cite:wb_wiki_oslo2areas]

Islands. Areas A and B are not two blocks of land. They are 165 separate enclaves with no territorial contiguity between them, each surrounded by Area C. [cite:wb_wiki_oslo2areas] To travel from one Palestinian town to another, Palestinians pass through territory Israel controls, which is where, as Part Six shows, the checkpoints, the barrier and the restricted roads came to stand.

Settlement in the peace years. The Oslo agreements did not freeze settlement. In the year of the first agreement, 1993, 116,300 settlers lived in the West Bank outside East Jerusalem; by 2000, when the talks collapsed, there were 198,300, by Peace Now's count. [cite:wb_peacenow_pop] The Gaza volume sets out the Camp David summit of 2000 and the second intifada that followed it. [scene:gz3_oslo|Oslo, and the second intifada]

sections.h: Building in Area C
sections.html:
The planning system. In Area C, the Israeli Civil Administration is the planning authority for Palestinian villages as well as for settlements. According to the UN's humanitarian office, less than one percent of Area C is covered by a planning scheme for Palestinian communities approved by the Civil Administration, while the outline plans of Israeli settlements cover at least 8.5 percent of it. Palestinian communities have drawn up 123 outline plans and submitted 109; five had been approved, as of 2021. [cite:wb_ocha_areac]

Permits and demolitions. Without an approved plan, a building permit is almost impossible to get. Between 2009 and 2018 the Civil Administration granted 98 of 4,422 Palestinian requests for building permits in Area C, about 2 percent. Families who build without one build under the threat of a demolition order, and between 1988 and 2014 the Civil Administration issued more than 14,000 of them against Palestinian structures in Area C. [cite:wb_ocha_areac] Part Eight follows the demolitions themselves.

Israel's position, set out by its coordinator of activities in the territories in answer to the UN in 2015, is that under the interim agreements construction in Area C requires the approval of the responsible authorities; it disputed the UN's figures as "inconsistent with the situation on the ground," said the Civil Administration was processing thirteen Palestinian master plans, four of them completed, and described a plan to give Bedouin communities land with water, power and sewage. [cite:wb_cogat_2015] The UN's figures, from 2021, and Israel's 2015 statement are the two documented accounts of how the planning law is applied to the two populations that share the area.

sections.h: Hebron, and the Outposts
sections.html:
The massacre. In February 1994, during the first months of the Oslo process, a settler from Kiryat Arba, Baruch Goldstein, opened fire on Muslims at prayer in the Cave of the Patriarchs in Hebron, killing 29. [cite:wb_wiki_hebron] [cite:wb_wiki_shuhada] After the riots that followed, the army did not close the settlement; it closed Shuhada Street, the main market street of the old city, to Palestinians, and shut 304 Palestinian shops and warehouses. [cite:wb_wiki_shuhada]

The divided city. In the Hebron Protocol of 1997 the city was divided into H1, under the Palestinian Authority, and H2, the centre around the settler enclaves, under Israeli control, and Israel agreed to reopen Shuhada Street. [cite:wb_wiki_hebron] [cite:wb_wiki_shuhada] Traffic was allowed back for about a year, but the shops stayed shut, and the street was closed again; it remains closed to Palestinian shops and vehicles, and in parts to Palestinians on foot. In a 2005 plan presented to Israel's High Court, the stated purpose was the protection of the Jewish community. By 2007 the Israeli human rights group B'Tselem found that 42 percent of the Palestinians of the H2 centre, 1,014 families, had left their homes. [cite:wb_wiki_shuhada]

The outposts. Through the Oslo years, and after them, small settlements were set up without government authorization, the "outposts." In March 2005 a government report written by Talia Sasson counted 105 of them, and found that the government itself funded at least part of them: the Housing Ministry supplied hundreds of mobile homes and millions of dollars, other officials connected them to electricity, and military administrators allowed 54 to go up on private Palestinian land. Sharon's spokesman blamed the West Bank's overlapping legal codes; the government said its policy was not to establish new settlements. [cite:wb_csm_sasson]

chapters.label: Part Six
chapters.title: The Wall, the Roads and the Islands
chapters.intro: Part Six describes the physical system that, since 2000, has determined where Palestinians in the West Bank can go: a barrier whose route runs mostly inside the territory, a network of checkpoints, gates and roadblocks that by the end of 2025 numbered more than nine hundred, and roads built across Palestinian land that Palestinians have been barred from using. It sets out Israel's stated reason, security, beside each part of the system, and the judgment of the International Court of Justice on the barrier.
chapters.outro: Part Six followed the system of movement. The barrier begun during the second intifada runs 85 percent inside the West Bank and will cut off 9 percent of it; Israel says its sole purpose is to stop attacks, and the International Court of Justice, by fourteen votes to one, advised in 2004 that it was contrary to international law and that the settlements it protects were established in breach of that law. [cite:wb_ocha_barrier2022] [cite:wb_asil_icj2004] By the end of 2025, 925 checkpoints, gates and roadblocks restricted 3.4 million Palestinians, 43 percent more than the twenty-year average, [cite:wb_ocha_move2026] and roads such as Route 443, built on expropriated land, stayed closed to them as a main route despite a Supreme Court ruling. [cite:wb_btselem_443] Part Seven turns to the law and the surveillance that govern the people inside the islands.

sections.h: The Barrier
sections.html:
The route. Israel began building the barrier during the second intifada. Its constructed and planned length is 713 kilometres, more than twice the length of the Green Line, because it does not follow the line. Eighty-five percent of its route runs inside the West Bank, and when it is complete it will cut off about 9 percent of the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, on its western side. [cite:wb_ocha_barrier2022]

Israel's case. Israel built the barrier, it told the International Court of Justice, for one purpose: to "effectively combat terrorist attacks launched from the West Bank," in an intifada in which about 1,000 Israelis were killed by Palestinians, [cite:gz_wiki_intifada2] and it described the barrier as temporary. [cite:wb_asil_icj2004]

The Seam Zone. Between the barrier and the Green Line lies what Israel calls the Seam Zone. About 11,000 Palestinians who live there need permits or special arrangements simply to live in their homes, and about 150 Palestinian communities elsewhere own farmland inside it. Farmers reach their land through 69 gates in the barrier, most of them opened only during the olive harvest, for limited hours. The army rejected 31 percent of farmers' permit applications in 2014 and 67 percent in 2020, and the number of applications fell by 77 percent between 2014 and 2021. [cite:wb_ocha_barrier2022]

The World Court. On 9 July 2004 the International Court of Justice, by fourteen votes to one, advised that the barrier's construction inside the occupied territory was contrary to international law, that it should be dismantled and reparation made, that the Fourth Geneva Convention applies to the territory, and that the settlements "have been established in breach of international law." The UN General Assembly endorsed the opinion, 150 to 6. The one dissenter, the American judge Thomas Buergenthal, agreed that the segments built to protect settlements violated humanitarian law, but found the Court's treatment of Israel's right of self-defence legally doubtful. [cite:wb_asil_icj2004] The opinion was advisory; the barrier was not removed, and by December 2022, 65 percent of its route had been built. [cite:wb_ocha_barrier2022]

sections.h: Checkpoints, Gates and Roads
sections.html:
925 obstacles. Inside the West Bank, movement is shaped by a second system. At the end of 2025 the UN's humanitarian office counted 925 obstacles that permanently or at times restrict the movement of 3.4 million Palestinians: 89 checkpoints staffed around the clock, 218 partial checkpoints, 232 road gates, 114 stretches of fencing or trenches, 167 earth mounds and 105 roadblocks. That was 43 percent more than the average of the previous twenty years. More than 120 new road gates were installed in 2025 alone, and 159 of the gates are frequently closed, cutting a village off from the main road at a soldier's decision. At least 459 of the obstacles block or slow access from Palestinian towns to main roads, 121 of them on Road 60, the West Bank's main north–south highway. [cite:wb_ocha_move2026]

The roads. Some roads were built across Palestinian land and then closed to Palestinians. Route 443, which links Jerusalem with the Tel Aviv area through the West Bank, was widened in the 1980s on thousands of dunams expropriated from Palestinian villages, with the army telling the court it would serve the local population. After shootings on the road in 2002 Israel barred Palestinians from using it, by car or on foot. In December 2009 the Supreme Court ordered the total ban lifted; the army's new arrangements, two more checkpoints among them, still kept Palestinians from using it as their main route to Ramallah, and more than a hundred shops along it have closed. [cite:wb_btselem_443]

The islands. Put together with the Oslo map, these measures produce the geography the Palestinians of the West Bank live in: 165 separate enclaves of Areas A and B, surrounded by Area C, [cite:wb_wiki_oslo2areas] joined by roads that can be closed at any of 925 points, [cite:wb_ocha_move2026] and cut off from 9 percent of their own land by a barrier. [cite:wb_ocha_barrier2022] Israel's stated reason for the barrier and the controls is security against attack, as it told the International Court of Justice; [cite:wb_asil_icj2004] the UN's counts do not record a reason for each obstacle. What they record is the result: movement between Palestinian towns depends on gates, permits and checkpoints controlled by the Israeli army.

chapters.label: Part Seven
chapters.title: Two Legal Systems, and the Watchers
chapters.intro: Part Seven describes the law under which the Palestinians of the West Bank live, and the systems that watch them. Since 1967 two legal systems have operated side by side in the same territory, one for Israeli citizens and one for Palestinians. This part sets out how they differ, as an Israeli civil-rights group documented and as Israel's own Justice Ministry defended; the military courts and their conviction rate; detention without charge; the detention of children; the facial-recognition systems used at checkpoints; and the conclusion of three human rights organizations, which Israel rejects, that the whole amounts to apartheid.
chapters.outro: Part Seven set out the law and the watchers. Israeli settlers live under Israeli law and courts; their Palestinian neighbours under military orders and military courts, which in 2010 convicted in 99.74 percent of trials, a distinction Israel's Justice Ministry defends on security grounds. [cite:wb_acri_twosys] [cite:wb_972_conviction] Thousands are held without charge, 3,577 in September 2025, [cite:wb_mem_hamoked2025] and UNICEF found that the ill-treatment of detained children "appears to be widespread, systematic and institutionalized." [cite:wb_un_unicef2013] Facial-recognition systems built only on Palestinians' data watch the checkpoints of Hebron. [cite:wb_toi_redwolf] Three human rights organizations, one of them Israeli, concluded that the system amounts to apartheid; Israel called the charge "divorced from reality." [cite:wb_oj_apartheid] [cite:wb_vibes_amnesty] Part Eight turns to the people who lose their homes.

sections.h: Two Systems of Law
sections.html:
One territory, two laws. An Israeli settler and a Palestinian neighbour in the West Bank do not live under the same law. The Israeli settler remains under Israeli law and Israeli courts, and Israel's Supreme Court has held that its Basic Laws protect them there. The Palestinian is governed by military orders issued by army commanders since 1967, layered on the Jordanian law in force before, and is tried in military courts for offences ranging from traffic violations to petty theft. The Association for Civil Rights in Israel, documenting the two systems in 2014, called the result "institutionalized discrimination." Israel's Justice Ministry, responding, did not dispute the facts it described, but defended them on security grounds. [cite:wb_acri_twosys]

The military courts. In 2010, according to an internal army document reported by Haaretz, 99.74 percent of the trials of Palestinians in the military courts ended in conviction: 25 acquittals in 9,542 cases. [cite:wb_972_conviction]

Detention without trial. The army can also hold Palestinians without charge or trial, by administrative detention orders, on intelligence that neither the detainee nor their lawyer is shown. In August 2023, before the war, HaMoked, an Israeli rights group working from Israel Prison Service data, counted 1,201 Palestinians held in this way, the most in the monthly counts rights groups have kept since 2001, though B'Tselem recorded a higher figure in 1989. [cite:wb_tna_hamoked2023] By September 2025 it counted 3,577 administrative detainees, among 11,040 Palestinian prisoners, and 2,662 more held as "unlawful combatants." [cite:wb_mem_hamoked2025]

Children. In 2013 UNICEF reported that about 700 Palestinian children aged 12 to 17 were arrested, interrogated and detained each year by the army, police and security agents, and found that their ill-treatment "appears to be widespread, systematic and institutionalized": arrests at night by heavily armed soldiers, abuse during transfer, interrogation involving physical violence and threats, shackling in court and detention inside Israel, away from their families. It also noted that Israel had raised the age of adulthood in its military courts from 16 to 18. [cite:wb_un_unicef2013]

sections.h: The Watchers, and the Word Apartheid
sections.html:
Blue Wolf. In 2021 the Washington Post reported that the army had been building a database of the Palestinians of Hebron: soldiers photographed residents, children among them, with a phone app called Blue Wolf that matched faces against a large database, and former soldiers said units were rewarded for taking the most photographs. [cite:wb_toi_redwolf]

Red Wolf. In May 2023 Amnesty International reported that since 2022 the army had used a facial-recognition camera system called Red Wolf at checkpoints in Hebron, relying on databases made up exclusively of Palestinians' data. Asked about it, the army said it carries out "necessary security and intelligence operations" and that "naturally, we cannot refer to operational and intelligence capabilities." [cite:wb_toi_redwolf] For the Palestinians of central Hebron, the checkpoint between their home and the rest of their city is now also a camera that knows their face.

The apartheid findings. Taking the two legal systems, the movement restrictions and the land policies together, three human rights organizations reached a conclusion that Israel rejects. In January 2021 the Israeli organization B'Tselem concluded that the regime governing Israel and the occupied territories "has become an apartheid regime." In April 2021 Human Rights Watch found that the crimes against humanity of apartheid and persecution were being committed in the occupied territories. In February 2022 Amnesty International argued that apartheid had been practised against Palestinians across all territory under Israel's control. [cite:wb_oj_apartheid] Israel's foreign minister, Yair Lapid, called Amnesty's findings "divorced from reality," said that "Amnesty quotes lies spread by terrorist organisations," and the foreign ministry asked it to withdraw the report. [cite:wb_vibes_amnesty]

Whether the system is apartheid is a legal judgment, and the record holds the findings and the rejection side by side. What Israel's Justice Ministry did not dispute is the description underneath both: two populations in one territory, under two systems of law. [cite:wb_acri_twosys] Part Ten returns to the International Court of Justice, which addressed the question in 2024.

chapters.label: Part Eight
chapters.title: Displacement, House by House
chapters.intro: Part Eight follows the people who lose their homes. Displacement in the West Bank happens in two ways that the record keeps apart. The first is by the state: demolitions of buildings put up without Israeli permits, eviction cases in the courts, and the declaration of firing zones. The second is by settlers: attacks on herding communities, and the outposts built beside them. This part sets out the counts kept by the United Nations and by Israeli monitoring groups, four named places (Masafer Yatta, Khan al-Ahmar, Sheikh Jarrah and Huwara), what Israel's courts decided and why, how often settler violence ends in a charge, and what Israel's leaders have said about it.
chapters.outro: Part Eight followed the people who lose their homes. In 2025 Israeli authorities demolished 1,657 Palestinian structures, 93 percent for lack of a permit that Israel's planning system seldom grants; Israel's position is that unauthorized building is enforced against under the interim agreements. [cite:wb_ocha_snap2025] [cite:wb_cogat_2015] Israel's Supreme Court upheld the firing zone at Masafer Yatta and approved the demolition of Khan al-Ahmar, and East Jerusalem's courts hear eviction cases under a law that lets only one side reclaim what it lost in 1948. [cite:wb_sabrang_masafer] [cite:wb_toi_khan] [cite:wb_nrc_sj] Settler attacks rose to 1,828 in 2025; herding outposts spread across about 14 percent of the West Bank; 57 communities were emptied in little over a year after October 2023; and 93.6 percent of police files on settler violence closed without a charge, while Israel's leaders described the attackers as a minority. [cite:wb_ocha_snap2025] [cite:wb_pn_badsamaritan] [cite:wb_972_villages] [cite:wb_yeshdin_2025] [cite:wb_toi_netanyahu2025] Part Nine turns to everything that changed after 7 October 2023.

sections.h: Demolished for Lack of a Permit
sections.html:
The count. In 2025 Israeli authorities demolished 1,657 Palestinian structures in the West Bank, according to the UN's humanitarian office. Of these, 1,538, or 93 percent, were demolished because they had been built without an Israeli permit; 87 were punitive demolitions, mostly the family homes of attackers; 32 were destroyed in military operations. [cite:wb_ocha_snap2025] Part Five showed why permits are scarce: in Area C, where Israel controls planning, less than one percent of the land has been planned for Palestinian building, and few applications are approved. [scene:wb5_areac|Area C and the permit regime]

Over the longer run, the UN counted nearly 12,000 people displaced by permit demolitions in Area C between 2009 and 2025, about two-thirds of them from Bedouin and herding communities, and 2025 was the second-worst year in that series. Punitive demolitions since 7 October 2023 displaced 420 more people, 166 of them children. [cite:wb_ocha_upd348] Israel's position, set out in Part Five, is that building in Area C requires approval under the interim agreements, and that unauthorized building is enforced against. [cite:wb_cogat_2015] Most of 2025's record displacement came from a different source, the army's operations in the northern refugee camps, which Part Nine covers. [cite:wb_ocha_snap2025]

Masafer Yatta

In the hills south of Hebron, about 7,400 acres were declared Firing Zone 918, a military training area, in the early 1980s. More than a thousand Palestinians live there, in eight villages, many of them in caves and herding hamlets. After two decades of litigation, Israel's Supreme Court ruled on 4 May 2022 against the residents. It accepted the state's case that they had not proven they lived there permanently before the zone was declared, and it treated the prohibition on forcibly transferring an occupied population as a treaty rule that Israeli courts could not enforce. The Norwegian Refugee Council said the ruling opened the door for the army to uproot entire Palestinian communities, and UN human rights experts urged Israel to stop the forcible transfer of the residents. [cite:wb_sabrang_masafer]

Khan al-Ahmar

Khan al-Ahmar is a hamlet of Bedouin, fewer than 200 in 2021 and about 300 by 2026's count, of the Jahalin tribe beside the main road from Jerusalem to Jericho. Its school was built, with Italian money, from mud and old tyres. In 2018 Israel's Supreme Court approved its demolition. The state's case was that the shacks and tents had been built without permits and stood dangerously close to a highway; the residents answered that Israel almost never grants Palestinians permits in that area. The state offered a site near Abu Dis with water, electricity, sewage and a new school. Successive governments then asked the court for delays; critics said they wanted to avoid an international incident over a village that the European Union and rights groups had taken up, and the pro-settlement group Regavim went to court to force the demolition. [cite:wb_toi_khan] In May 2026 Smotrich ordered preparations to evacuate the village; as of that month the order still needed the cabinet's approval and had not been signed. [cite:wb_newarab_khan2026]

Sheikh Jarrah

In East Jerusalem the eviction cases run through civil courts. A law of 1970 allows Jews to reclaim property in East Jerusalem lost in 1948. The Absentees' Property Law of 1950 prevents Palestinians from reclaiming property they lost inside Israel. In 2021 the Norwegian Refugee Council counted about 970 Palestinians in East Jerusalem at risk of eviction, in 218 households with cases filed against them. [cite:wb_nrc_sj] In Sheikh Jarrah the claim is held by Nahalat Shimon, a company owned by a firm registered in Delaware, which bought it from two Jewish associations that had acquired the land in the late nineteenth century. In March 2022 the Supreme Court let four families stay at least until the land is formally registered; in April 2024 a lower court ordered the Diab family, 23 people, out. [cite:wb_pn_diab] The District Court rejected their appeal in February 2025; in November 2025 the Supreme Court agreed to hear a further appeal and froze the eviction, where the case stood at the end of 2025. [cite:wb_amnesty_diab2025]

The claimants' case, as the courts have heard it, rests on documents of purchase from the nineteenth century; the families and rights groups point to the asymmetry in the table. [cite:wb_pn_diab] [cite:wb_nrc_sj] Both describe the same two laws.

sections.h: Settler Violence
sections.html:
The count. The UN's humanitarian office records settler attacks that cause casualties or damage. It counted 1,449 in 2024 and 1,828 in 2025, about five a day. In 2025 it recorded 240 Palestinians killed in the West Bank, 225 of them by Israeli forces and nine by settlers, and 17 Israelis killed by Palestinians. [cite:wb_ocha_snap2025] Settlers injured 772 Palestinians in 2025 up to early December, in attacks across more than 270 communities. [cite:wb_ocha_upd348]

Huwara, 26 February 2023

On 26 February 2023, a Palestinian gunman shot dead two Israeli brothers, Hillel and Yagel Yaniv, as they drove through Huwara, a town south of Nablus. That night hundreds of settlers entered Huwara and nearby villages and set fire to homes, shops and cars. One Palestinian, Sameh Aqtesh, was killed and about a hundred were injured. The army's regional commander, Major General Yehuda Fox, called it "a pogrom carried out by outlaws." Days later the finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, said Huwara should be "wiped out"; he later said he had spoken in anger. A court ordered the arrested suspects released; the Defence Ministry placed two people in administrative detention. [cite:wb_wiki_huwara]

The Herding Outposts

The newest form of settlement is the herding farm: one family or a few young men, a flock, and a fence, set up on a hill beside Palestinian grazing land. Peace Now and Kerem Navot, two Israeli groups that track settlement, counted more than a hundred such outposts in 2025, and calculated that through grazing, settlers had taken control of at least 786,000 dunams, about 14 percent of the West Bank. The outposts are unauthorized under Israeli law, but the groups traced state money to them: NIS 54 million under a budget line for security needs of settlement points, about NIS 3 million in Agriculture Ministry grazing grants, and roughly 80,000 dunams allocated for grazing by the Settlement Division. [cite:wb_pn_badsamaritan]

Since October 2023. In the first weeks of the Gaza war, the UN counted 828 people from 15 herding communities displaced amid settler violence and new restrictions. In Khirbet Zanuta, south of Hebron, 24 families took down about fifty structures and left on 28 October 2023, after three attacks that month. [cite:wb_ocha_herders2023] By December 2024, Kerem Navot counted 57 communities displaced since October 2023, 50 of them entirely, and at least 41 new outposts and herding farms. Zanuta's families went back in August 2024 under a High Court ruling, and left again within weeks. [cite:wb_972_villages] In 2025 the UN reported that Ein Samiya, a Bedouin community near Ramallah, had been fully displaced. [cite:wb_ocha_upd348]

Who Is Charged

Yesh Din, an Israeli rights group, has followed police files on settler violence since 2005. Of the files it monitored through 2025, 93.6 percent were closed without an indictment, and about 3 percent ended in a full or partial conviction. [cite:wb_yeshdin_2025] Police investigations themselves fell, by Channel 12's count, from 235 in 2023 to 60 in 2025 up to November, under a national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, who oversees the police. [cite:wb_toi_netanyahu2025] Some cases are charged: five settlers were indicted for an attack on a school at al-Muarrajat in 2024. [cite:wb_972_villages]

Israel's answer. In November 2025, after settlers torched factories and a mosque, Prime Minister Netanyahu promised "very forceful action against the riots against IDF soldiers," and said the extremists were a minority who did not represent "the large community of law-abiding, loyal settlers." The army's chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, strongly condemned the attacks, and President Herzog called them "shocking and grave." The army's own count of "nationalistic crime" incidents by Israelis had reached 704 in 2025 by mid-November, more than in all of 2024. [cite:wb_toi_netanyahu2025] The record holds both: leaders who condemn the violence, and figures showing that very little of it ends in court.

chapters.label: Part Nine
chapters.title: Since October 2023
chapters.intro: Part Nine covers the West Bank since 7 October 2023, while the world's attention was on Gaza. Two things happened at once. The violence rose: the UN counted 1,001 Palestinians killed in the West Bank in two years, 43 percent of all those killed there in twenty years, [cite:wb_ohchr_1001] Israelis were killed in attacks, and in 2025 the army emptied three refugee camps in the north, in what researchers describe as the largest displacement there since 1967. [cite:wb_wiki_ironwall] And the settlement project moved faster than at any time since it began, with record approvals, new settlements, the E1 plan and votes in the Knesset to annex. This part sets out both, with the figures of the counting bodies, Israel's stated reasons, and where things stood in October 2026.
chapters.outro: Part Nine covered the West Bank since 7 October 2023. The UN counted 1,001 Palestinians killed there in two years, 213 of them children, and 59 Israelis killed by West Bank Palestinians. [cite:wb_ohchr_1001] Operation Iron Wall emptied three refugee camps of more than 33,000 people, who had not returned by July 2026; the UN said it may amount to forcible transfer, and Israel calls it counter-terrorism. [cite:wb_jurist_ohchr2026] Settlement moved faster than ever: a record 27,941 units advanced in 2025, 102 settlements approved since December 2022, and E1 approved with a minister's promise to "bury the idea of a Palestinian state." [cite:wb_pn_mirabilis] [cite:wb_itv_e1] The Knesset voted for annexation in principle; the US President said it would not happen, after revoking the sanctions on violent settlers. [cite:wb_toi_71_13] [cite:wb_toi_trump_annex] [cite:wb_ofac_20250124] Part Ten turns to the law.

sections.h: The Dead, Since 7 October 2023
sections.html:
In the two years from 7 October 2023 to 17 October 2025, the UN Human Rights Office counted 1,001 Palestinians killed in the West Bank and East Jerusalem, 213 of them children. Israeli forces killed 968 of them; settlers, alone or together with soldiers, killed 33. In the same two years 59 Israelis, 22 of them members of the security forces, were killed in attacks by West Bank Palestinians in the West Bank and in Israel. [cite:wb_ohchr_1001]

The UN office concluded that 449 of those killed by Israeli forces were unarmed and not involved in violence when they were shot, and that Israel announced investigations only rarely. It said the pattern suggested force was being used "as a tool to control and repress." The army described many of those killed in its airstrikes as "terrorists," and in one case acknowledged it had not sufficiently verified who it struck. [cite:wb_ohchr_1001] In 2025 alone, the UN's humanitarian office counted 240 Palestinians and 17 Israelis killed in the West Bank, and 3 more Israelis killed in Israel by Palestinians from the West Bank. [cite:wb_ocha_snap2025]

Iron Wall: the Northern Camps

On 21 January 2025 the army launched Operation Iron Wall in the Jenin refugee camp, and extended it to Tulkarm within the week. The army's stated aim was to degrade the armed groups' infrastructure and remove imminent threats. The Palestinian Authority's own forces had been fighting the armed groups in Jenin camp since December 2024. In February Israeli tanks entered Jenin, the first in the West Bank since 2002, and the defense minister, Israel Katz, said the troops would stay. The army reported 102 militants killed. [cite:wb_wiki_ironwall]

More than 33,000 people were displaced from the three camps in January and February 2025, and as of July 2026 they had not been allowed back. In September 2026 the UN Human Rights Office reported that the displacement may amount to forcible transfer, a crime against humanity, and called it "large-scale, long-term and systematic." Israel describes the operation as counter-terrorism against armed groups and their weapons in the northern West Bank. [cite:wb_jurist_ohchr2026] As of October 2026, according to public trackers, the operation had not been declared over and the army controlled the three camps; UNRWA's estimate of the displaced exceeds 40,000. [cite:wb_wiki_ironwall]

sections.h: The Fastest Years of Settlement
sections.html:
The numbers. Peace Now and Kerem Navot, which track settlement from Israeli government records, counted 27,941 settlement housing units advanced through planning in 2025, more than double the previous annual record. Since December 2022, the cabinet has approved 102 new settlements, 34 of them in a single decision in March 2026. New outposts, built without authorization, rose from 33 in 2023 to 61 in 2024 and 91 in 2025, most of them farms and hilltop outposts of the kind described in Part Eight. [cite:wb_pn_mirabilis]

Who runs it. The coalition agreement of December 2022 created a Settlements Administration in the Defense Ministry under Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister and leader of Religious Zionism, who was given a second ministerial post there. In June 2023 the cabinet moved the approval of settlement planning to him, and powers over civilian affairs in Area C that had been held by the army were moved to a civilian deputy reporting to his administration. In March 2023 the Knesset repealed the part of the 2005 disengagement law that barred Israelis from the northern West Bank. In February 2026 the cabinet transferred some demolition powers in Areas A and B, which Oslo gave to the Palestinian Authority, to Israeli authorities, for sites deemed to harm heritage, the environment or water, and changed the rules on Israelis buying West Bank land. [cite:wb_pn_mirabilis]

E1

E1 is the land between Jerusalem and the settlement of Ma'ale Adumim. Building there would link the two, effectively divide the West Bank in two, and, its critics say, make a Palestinian capital in East Jerusalem effectively impossible. Under international pressure, the plan had been frozen for two decades. In August 2025 Israel's planning council gave final approval to 3,401 homes there. Smotrich, announcing it, said the plan would "permanently bury the idea of a Palestinian state," and that "they will talk about a Palestinian dream, and we will continue to build a Jewish reality." He presented it as Israel's answer to the decisions of Britain, France and Canada to recognize a Palestinian state. [cite:wb_itv_e1] [cite:wb_pn_mirabilis]

The Annexation Votes, and Washington's Answer

On 23 July 2025 the Knesset voted 71 to 13 for a non-binding motion declaring the West Bank "an inseparable part of the Land of Israel" and calling on the government to apply Israeli sovereignty to the settlements, Judea, Samaria and the Jordan Valley. [cite:wb_toi_71_13] On 22 October 2025, during a visit by Vice President JD Vance, a bill to apply sovereignty to all the settlements passed a preliminary reading by 25 votes to 24. Netanyahu's office called it a "deliberate political provocation" by the opposition and said that without his party's support it would go nowhere. Vance called it "a very stupid political stunt." President Trump said, "It won't happen," because "I gave my word to the Arab countries," and that Israel "would lose all of its support from the United States" if it annexed. [cite:wb_toi_trump_annex]

Sanctions, Imposed and Lifted

On 1 February 2024 President Biden signed Executive Order 14115, declaring settler violence a national emergency that "undermine[s] the security of Israel," and creating sanctions on those who attacked civilians, forced them from their homes or seized their property. Four settlers were named first; more followed. [cite:wb_willkie_14115] On 20 January 2025, his first day back in office, President Trump revoked the order. Four days later the Treasury removed everyone it had sanctioned under the order, among them the settlement organization Amana, the Hilltop Youth, and several herding farm outposts; the list also included one Palestinian armed group, the Lions' Den of Nablus. [cite:wb_ofac_20250124]

Where the record stands, as of October 2026: no law of annexation has been passed, and the US President has said none will be; while the administration of the territory, the pace of settlement and the removal of US sanctions have all moved in the direction the annexation motions called for. Part Ten turns to the law that all of this is measured against.

chapters.label: Part Ten
chapters.title: The Law, and Why It Isn't Enforced
chapters.intro: Part Ten turns to the law. It is often said that nobody does anything about the settlements. The record shows something more specific: a rule written in 1949, a series of rulings and resolutions that have applied it to the West Bank, and a set of reasons, each documented, why none of them has been enforced. This part sets out the rule, Israel's legal position and how it has changed, the shifting positions of the United States, the rulings of the UN Security Council, the International Court of Justice, the General Assembly and the International Criminal Court, and, for each, what happened next.
chapters.outro: Part Ten set out the law. The Fourth Geneva Convention forbids an occupying power to transfer its own civilians into occupied territory, and Israel's own legal adviser warned in 1967 that settlement would breach it. [cite:wb_fmep_art49] [cite:wb_gorenberg_meron] Israel's position is that the territory is not occupied in the classic sense and that the settlements are legal. [cite:wb_cow_israelview] [cite:wb_wiki_levy] The Security Council in 2016, the World Court in 2004 and 2024, and the General Assembly in 2024 said otherwise; the ICC opened an investigation in 2021. [cite:wb_wiki_2334] [cite:wb_asil_icj2004] [cite:wb_jurist_icj2024] [cite:wb_ahram_unga2024] [cite:wb_aj_icc_timeline] Each stopped at a documented point: advisory opinions without enforcement, non-binding resolutions, Israel's refusal to comply, and US positions that changed from Hansell to Reagan, from Pompeo to Blinken, and from settler sanctions to sanctions on the Court. [cite:wb_jvl_hansell] [cite:wb_tablet_forty] [cite:wb_axios_blinken] [cite:wb_jurist_iccsuit] Part Eleven turns to the split between the West Bank and Gaza.

sections.h: The Rule
sections.html:
Article 49. The Fourth Geneva Convention, adopted in 1949 after the Second World War, governs how an occupying power treats an occupied population. Its Article 49 forbids "individual or mass forcible transfers" of the occupied population, "regardless of their motive," and its last paragraph adds: "The Occupying Power shall not deport or transfer parts of its own civilian population into the territory it occupies." [cite:wb_fmep_art49] Part Three showed that in September 1967 Israel's own Foreign Ministry legal adviser, Theodor Meron, warned that civilian settlement in the territories would breach this provision. [cite:wb_gorenberg_meron]

Israel's Position

Israel's official position is that the convention does not apply to the West Bank as a matter of law, because the territory was not the recognized sovereign territory of another state when Israel took it in 1967; Jordan's annexation, as Part Two showed, was recognized by almost no one. Israel has pledged to comply with its "humanitarian and customary provisions." [cite:wb_cow_israelview] In 2012 a committee appointed by Prime Minister Netanyahu and chaired by a former Supreme Court justice, Edmund Levy, went further: it concluded that Israel's presence in the West Bank is not an occupation in the classic sense, that the settlements are legal, and that unauthorized outposts should be legalized.
